Chapter 1 – Exposition of the Elements (*Dhātunirdeśa*) from the *Sphuṭārthā* [Abhidharmakośabhāṣya].
Abhidharmakośavyākhyā 1: The First Chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Elements" (Dhātunirdeśa).
Homage to the Destroyer of Māra’s Army.
He of great strength, whose tusks are wisdom and meditative concentration,
having torn asunder the fivefold prison of birth,
has entered the peaceful forest of nirvana.
I bow my head to that Nāga of Teachers,
who performs the work of a Teacher in the world by means of his treatises on the ultimate truth;
whom they call the foremost of the wise, like a second Buddha.
By that one named Vasubandhu, who will become the ultimate kinsman of the world,
this *Abhidharmakośa*— which is a summary of the *Abhidharma*—
has been composed; it is a jewel of a treatise extracted from the ocean of the *Abhidharmabhāṣya*.
This commentary has been composed by me according to its name, *Sphuṭārthā*. Furthermore,

that excellent exposition of the meaning of the words which was well-composed by the commentators Guṇamati, Vasumitra, and others, and in which the meaning was recorded as "this is the intended sense," is also approved by me.

Having exposed those interpretations which have deviated from the established tenets and were composed by them here and there, I have set forth this correct explanation; for those who have exerted themselves in the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā* as well as in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Let this interpretation be examined by them as to whether it is logical or not;
if it is logical, it should be accepted, and if not, it should be rejected or otherwise formulated.
For the intellect of one such as I cannot possibly fail when dealing with a difficult subject.
Having paid homage to him who, having utterly destroyed all darkness, lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra, [I shall compose] this treatise on the true meaning (yathārtha-śāstra).
Explaining the meaning of this verse, "I shall proclaim the treatise, the Abhidharmakośa," the Master says:
desiring to compose the treatise, and for the purpose of making known the greatness of his own Teacher, he begins his salutation to him by first recounting his qualities.
Desiring to compose— that is, desiring to create— the treatise *Abhidharmakośa*, [the author] pays homage to his own teacher,
his personal teacher; for that Blessed One is the teacher of the Master [Vasubandhu], since he has entered into that teaching.

Or rather, by that Teacher, who is dependent upon great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the entire world has been embraced as his own; therefore, for the sake of making known his greatness, even the Teacher is "his own"—that Blessed One is his own Teacher.

Thus, "great-souledness" (*māhātmya*) refers to the perfection of the accomplishment of one's own and others' welfare; it is for the purpose of making that known, that is, for the purpose of bringing about its realization.

The meaning is that he begins the salutation to him by first proclaiming his qualities— that is, by first describing his virtues; although one should say "he began" (*ārabdhavān*) because it is an action in the past, the use of the present tense form is intended to show that the commencement of the salutation continues even now,
or because the commencement of the salutation has not ceased through the succession of disciples.
Even in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*), such usage of words is observed; for instance, in the statement "Now,
the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*),
this word "now" (*atha*) is employed in the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*).
If it is argued that the realization of greatness occurs through the mere description of qualities and not through prostration, we say no; for the latter serves as an indicator of the former.
For greatness is indicated by the act of salutation;
alternatively, greatness is made known precisely by the description of qualities, not by the salutation itself.
However, the commencement of the salutation is for the sake of generating one's own merit.
Alternatively, we explain that the purpose of proclaiming the majesty [of the deity] therein is based on the conduct of the virtuous;

for the virtuous, having performed worship, praise, and salutation to their chosen deity, begin their work in order to demonstrate their adherence to right conduct (*sad-ācāra*). Thus, it is due to the practice of the virtuous that [the majesty] is proclaimed there.
In order to generate reverence for that [Buddha], reverence is generated; furthermore, in order to listen with respect to his teaching, one listens with respect;
and in order to gradually produce the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one listens with respect.

The production of that [treatise] is for the sake of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), and that, in turn, is for the sake of attaining *nirvāṇa*, which is characterized by the cessation of all suffering; thus, the ultimate purpose is established. However, the Teacher has stated only one purpose—to make known his own greatness—because it is the immediate purpose.
But the others have not been mentioned because they can be inferred;

thus, although the word *yaḥ* (who) is a general term, it functions as a specific reference because it is governed by the qualifier "the Blessed Buddha. Regarding this, he says: "With reference to the Blessed Buddha."
Just as among these Brahmins, he who is fair-complexioned and wears white garments is Devaśarman,
so too here,
he who has utterly destroyed all darkness in every way [is the one].
Having paid homage to him who has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra— thus the word "yat" (who) refers specifically to the Blessed Buddha.

For indeed, no one other than the Buddha can possibly exist as distinguished by such qualities; therefore, he explains [the word "Buddha"] by saying "he who," referring to the Blessed Buddha. Thus, the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
He is "Buddha" because of the blossoming of his intellect; the meaning is that he is fully awakened, just as one says "a fully blossomed lotus."

Alternatively, others maintain that the meaning is "awakened" (*prabuddha*) because of the departure from the two-fold sleep of ignorance; thus, "the awakened person" (*prabuddhapuruṣa*) is an instance where the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of both the object and the agent (*karmakartṛ*).
The meaning is that he is called "Buddha" because he has awakened by himself (*svayaṃ budhyate*).
We see no fault even in applying the suffix *kta* in the sense of an object (*karman*),
for the meaning is that he has been awakened to or known by other Buddhas or others, owing to his being endowed with the perfection of all virtues and being completely free from all defects.

The inclusion of the second word "bhagavantam" (the Blessed One) is for the purpose of removing any possibility of disrespect; for in the world, it is observed that names used without an honorific title are regarded with disrespect, as in the case of "Devadatta."
The authors of the *Vinayavibhāṣā*, however, formulate a fourfold alternative (catuṣ-koṭika):
there is one who is a Buddha but not a Blessed One (bhagavān),
namely a Pratyekabuddha, who can be called a Buddha because he is self-enlightened (*svayambhu*).
But it is not because the Blessed One has failed to fulfill the equipment of giving and so forth;
for one who possesses greatness is called "Blessed."

The Blessed One is not a Buddha [in the sense of being fully awakened], because he is a Bodhisattva in his final existence who has fulfilled the perfections such as generosity but has not yet attained complete enlightenment;
and the Blessed One is both [a Bodhisattva and a Buddha].
There is no third alternative, since these modes have been excluded; therefore, the Buddha, the Blessed One, possesses both qualifications.
He is "one by whom darkness has been destroyed" (*hatāndhakāra*), meaning either that the darkness belonging to him has been destroyed, or that by him [darkness] has been destroyed.
In a genitive *bahuvrīhi*, as in "killed by the road" (*mārgeṇa hataḥ*), the agent "road" (*mārga*) must be supplied;
however, in a third-case *bahuvrīhi*, the instrument "by the road" (*mārgeṇa*) must be supplied.
Another says:

The presentation of two analyses is for the purpose of including both meanings of the root *han*, namely "to strike" (*hiṃsā*) and "to go" (*gati*). When the analysis is "its darkness has been struck down" (*hatam asyāndhakāram*), then the root *han* is taken in its sense of "going."
The meaning is that its darkness has departed;
however, when it is a third-case *bahuvrīhi* compound,
then the root *han* is understood in the sense of "killing."
The meaning is that darkness has been destroyed by him;
thus, having first formed a single compound from the two words *uta* and *ari*, he subsequently forms a locative tatpuruṣa compound:
*sarvasmin hatāndhakāraḥ*, which becomes *sarvahatāndhakāraḥ*.
And that being the case, the word *hata* does not undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*) here;
furthermore, it must be considered by what rule this locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*) is formed—
it is a compound according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*.
The word *hatāndhakāra* is listed among the *śauṇḍādi* group;
since the *śauṇḍādi* group is formed by way of its general form (*ākṛtikṛta*), its inclusion therein should be understood as being according to the sequence [of the list],
or else by means of a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) regarding the locative case.

Alternatively, the compound is formed by general rule (*utsarga*): while the term *sub* is in effect, that which ends in a *sub*-suffix is compounded with another *sub*-ending word whenever desired; or else, such a *tatpuruṣa* not otherwise defined should be understood as belonging to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka*. Thus, how is it that "darkness" (*andhakāra*), having become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), is connected with the word "in all" (*sarvasmin*)?
For that destruction of darkness through which the Blessed One is joined with the state of having destroyed darkness must be understood as the basis of all for that destruction of darkness,
just as one is called a "cheat" because of his skill with dice.
Just as that person is a rogue by virtue of being endowed with the quality characterized by roguery, and he is the substratum for that [quality],
so too should it be understood in this case.
Moreover, we observe that a compound is possible here in another way as well:
"destroyed in everything" (*sarvasmin hataṃ sarvahatam*),
or "destroyed in every manner" (*sarveṇa prakāreṇa sarvahataṃ sarvathā sarvahatam*).

"By this [knowledge], darkness has been destroyed in every way and for everyone," or "darkness has been destroyed by him in every way and entirely"— thus, the word *hata* (destroyed) is placed in grammatical apposition with *andhakāra* (darkness), yet it does not undergo the rule of prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*).
"In every way" means through the disappearance of both afflicted and non-afflicted darkness regarding all that is to be known, characterized by the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Brahmin, 'all' refers to everything, namely the twelve sense-bases."
What is meant here by the word "darkness" (*andhakāra*)? Is it the nocturnal gloom?
No;
rather, it should be understood that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is called darkness because it obstructs the perception of reality.
For the word *andhakāra* is well-known in the sense of nocturnal darkness;
it is called "darkness" (*andhakāra*) because it makes people as if blind,
due to its obstruction of the perception of forms such as cloth and so forth that exist in reality.
By virtue of that similarity, ignorance also receives the name "darkness" because it obstructs the vision of the true nature of reality, such as suffering and the other truths;
and that is what this "it" refers to— namely, that ignorance.
"By the attainment of the counteragent" means by the attainment of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
The "adverse element" (*vipakṣa*) is the affliction (*kleśa*); it is called the "counteragent" (*pratipakṣa*) because it is the side (*pakṣa*) that opposes the adverse element.
Alternatively, untainted knowledge (*jñāna anāsrava*) is the counteragent to ignorance (*ajñāna*); [the phrase refers to] by the attainment of that.

The meaning is that [ignorance] is "destroyed"—that is, rendered abandoned through the non-practice of awakening—in every way, everywhere, and with respect to all objects of knowledge, because it possesses the nature of never arising again.
Therefore, [the term] "he" refers to the Blessed One;
however, since Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas are also worthy of honor, the word "Pratyekabuddha" is placed first [in the compound].
"According to one's wish" means with permission,
but not in every respect,
because of the complete disappearance of non-afflicted delusion.

But surely, all contaminated things have been abandoned by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas just as they have been by Buddhas; why then is it said that for them there is the absolute departure of afflicted delusion?
For it has been said:

"I do not declare the making of an end to suffering without having directly known even a single dharma," and likewise, "I do not declare the making of an end to suffering without having fully understood and abandoned even a single dharma."
Therefore, even for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, that respective non-afflicted ignorance is indeed abandoned through the abandonment of desire and attachment, just like the eye and other faculties;
otherwise, there would be no end to suffering for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is indeed true.
For them, even non-afflicted ignorance is indeed abandoned, just like afflicted ignorance;
however, although it is abandoned, it still manifests for them, as is the case with the eyes and other faculties.
For the Buddha, however, once it is abandoned, it does not manifest.
For this very reason, it is further specified as "destroyed because it is of a nature not to arise again";
otherwise, he would have simply said that it is abandoned in every way and with respect to all objects of knowledge.
As for those who explain that the cessation of affliction for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas occurs merely through the removal of afflicted delusion:
That [previous] misinterpretation of theirs, namely that "it is as has been stated," is refuted by the words "for thus it is for them," and so forth;
"for thus" (tathā hi) means "because" (yasmāt).
Alternatively, "thus" (*tathā*) means "not in every respect"; the word "for" (*hi*) indicates the reason;
and "of these" (*eṣām*) refers to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding the qualities unique to a Buddha and so forth,

concerning objects that are extremely remote in space and time, and regarding objects such as form and so forth which, though not having the nature of a Buddha-attribute, are of infinite variety and exist in extremely remote places and times.
The meaning is that non-afflicted ignorance indeed exists and indeed manifests there;
among those qualities of a Buddha, such as the unique [āveṇika] qualities and so forth,
there is ignorance on the part of those other than a Buddha because their intrinsic nature is supremely subtle and profound.
As it has been said:

"Śāriputra, do you know the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, his aggregate of concentration, his aggregate of wisdom, his aggregate of liberation, and his aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation? When thus questioned by the Blessed One, the Elder Śāradvatīputra replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
But as for other material objects that are aggregates of atoms,
if they are situated at an extremely remote distance—
even those which are non-material and unmanifest— [they do not serve as objects].
If even those [beings] are located in extremely remote regions,
there is ignorance regarding them as well, because their location is separated by many world-systems;
for it is heard that the Elder Maudgalyāyana did not know the location of his own mother, who was born in the Mārīcī world-system, an extremely remote region.

Even regarding objects belonging to extremely remote past or future times, ignorance certainly arises because those things have been separated by the destruction and reappearance of many intervening eons.

Indeed, it is heard that the Elder Śāriputra rejected a man seeking ordination because he did not perceive the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*); however, the Blessed One perceived his roots of merit conducive to liberation and spoke [of them].
"For I perceive in him a very subtle seed of liberation, like gold hidden within the crevice of a mineral-bearing rock."
And that man has gone forth as a renunciant; thus,
regarding the objects difficult to comprehend, which consist of infinite distinctions such as the elements, destinies, modes of birth, and rebirths.
Ignorance certainly exists for them;
for thus it has been said:
"The cause of even a single eye on a peacock's feather possesses every possible form."
For that knowledge is the power of an omniscient one; it cannot be known by those who are not omniscient.
Thus, these are the four causes of non-knowledge.
Among these, one, two, three, or four [perfections] should be applied as they occur in various instances;
thus, "the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit" is the detailed explanation.
Practice for the sake of one's own benefit is "the practice for one's own benefit."
The perfection of the practice for one's own benefit (*ātmahitapratipatti-sampat*) means the accomplishment of the fruit of that practice;
this perfection should be understood as having the nature of the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The perfection of the practice for the benefit of others (*parahitapratipatti-sampat*) is to be considered in exactly the same way.
Others explain it as follows: "the practice for one's own benefit," "the accomplishment of one's own benefit," and "the acquisition of one's own benefit"— this is the meaning.
Its perfection is precisely the perfection of the practice for one's own benefit; in the same way, the perfection of the practice for the benefit of others is also to be explained.
Furthermore, having the nature of bringing about the cessation of all suffering, it has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra.
According to this statement,
*saṃsāra* means wandering (*saṃsaraṇa*), the state of coming and going (*ājavaṃjavībhāva*), that is to say, the succession of births and deaths;
or alternatively, *saṃsāra* is the triple world (*traidhātuka*), because sentient beings wander within it.
"Samsāra-paṅka" means the mire of cyclic existence; it is so called because of its similarity to a mire.
Therefore, he says:
"For samsāra is like a mire, because it is a place where the world clings and because it is difficult to cross."
For mud in this world is a place of attachment because its nature is to cause one to sink;
for that very reason it is difficult to cross,
being difficult to cross either due to its instability or because it must be crossed by relying on others.
For cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is also a place of attachment because it is moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*),
and it is difficult to cross; for that very reason, it is difficult to cross because it is agitated by views and doubt, or because it must be crossed by relying upon the Buddha.

Therein, the Blessed One, feeling compassion and taking pity upon the world of sentient beings— which is submerged therein, whether by way of entering into identity with it or by way of being its constituent parts— and which is without protection or refuge, extends his hands through the teaching of the true Dharma;
for the teaching of the true Dharma itself constitutes his hands.
The plural number is used for "their gifts" because of the great number of those to be rescued; by means of them, he has uplifted [beings] according to their respective capacities.
Just as in common worldly usage, even when "according to their capacity" (*yathābhavyam*) is not explicitly stated, it is understood because that is how it is observed;
for example, when it is said, "Having brought the Brahmins, he fed them," those who were capable of being fed and were present there— whether in the village or the city— are understood to be meant.
It is understood that he fed those very [brahmins],
because it is impossible to feed all the brahmins of the world; likewise here too, [he feeds] only those persons who are capable of being uplifted.
Thinking, "He has indeed rescued that very [work]," he therefore explains it as "according to one's capacity," having paid homage to him.

Thus, having prostrated with the head— since the word *namaḥ* (homage) has the act of prostration as its basis, the word *namaskṛtya* (having paid homage) means "having prostrated"— and since in the world prostration is understood to be performed with the head, he says "with the head. Furthermore, the homage of speech and mind, though not explicitly mentioned here, is established by implication, because [physical] action is preceded by the verbal expression of qualities and is preceded by mental action.
Regarding the word "tasmai" (to him), what is the characteristic of this dative case here?
On this point, many commentators are confused;
Ācārya Guṇamati and his disciple Ācārya Vasumitra have said:
The rule that "the dative case is used in connection with the words *namaḥ* and so forth,
because of their connection with *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *alaṃ*, and *vaṣaṭ*" is incorrect.
When used in conjunction with the word *namaḥ*, that fourth case ending occurs [only] when it is independent;
however, this word *namaḥ* is not independent because it has become established [as a subordinate element].
For this very reason, it was explained by this same Master [in his *Vyākhyāyukti*]:

"Having paid homage to the Sage with the head"—thus the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is employed here because it is characterized by its being the object of an action (*karmalakṣaṇā*). Therefore, [the opponent argues] that the dative case (*caturthī*) is not used in connection with the word *namaḥ*. Others maintain that the dative has been used in place of the accusative. However, this is merely their own preference, for there is no grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) for it. By what, then, is this dative case justified? We explain that this dative is characterized by the recipient (*sampradāna*). How is the designation "recipient" established? According to the author of the *Cūrṇi*: "That which one intends to reach through the object (*karman*) is the recipient. Here, the word "object" (*karman*) is described in both ways [as the direct object and as the means].

There are two types of *karman*: technical (*pāribhāṣika*) and worldly (*laukika*). When the technical *karman*—defined as "that which is most desired by the agent"—is relied upon, then that toward whom the agent intends [to direct] what is most desired by him receives the designation *sampradāna*; thus, the expression "he gives a cow to the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya gāṃ prayacchati*) is established. However, when the worldly *karman*—defined as "action" (*kriyā*)—is relied upon, then that toward whom the agent intends [to direct] the action receives the designation *sampradāna*; thus, the expression "for battle" (*yuddhāya*) is established.

Just as in the case of "He girds himself for his master" (*saṃnahyati patye*), where the agent intends battle through the act of girding and the master through the act of lying down—thereby establishing that battles and the like receive the designation *saṃpradāna* (recipient)—so too here, the Teacher intends the scripture through the act of salutation. Therefore, the designation *saṃpradāna* applies to the Teacher; and since the designation *saṃpradāna* exists, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is employed according to the rule "the fourth case is used for the *saṃpradāna*. Having established this, [he says]:
"To him who is the foremost among those who speak after first bowing, who has become the authority in the scripture, and who desires the welfare of the world..."

If, after bowing to the Teacher, the Sugata, the Protector— such as the word forms "tāyine" (PS I ab) and others mentioned in various poetic treatises (*kāvyashāstra*)— are indeed intended [to be included], then they must be designated as the *sampradāna* (recipient).
In the phrase "having bowed to the sage with his head" (*namaskṛtya muniṃ mūrdhnā*), the accusative case does not apply;
this is not a fault, for grammatical relations (*kāraka*) arise from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).

When there is the intention to express the object (*karman*), then the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is used; when there is the intention to express the recipient (*sampradāna*), [then the dative case is used].
Then both [the positions]— that it is the fourth [case] and that it is [a compound]— are established,
as in the case of the *Arthaśāstra*.

The word *śāstṛ* is a derivative (*auṇādika*) term; according to the rule "the suffixes *tṛn* and *tṛc* are added after [roots] such as *śaṃs* and *kṣad* when forming a name (*sañjñā*), provided they do not end in *i*," it becomes *śāstṛ*, ending in the suffix *tṛn* and lacking the augment *iṭ*.
Now, does it not indeed become *śāstṛ* when it is a name?
And this perception is not merely perception;
for perception is of two kinds: specific perception and general perception.

Specific designations (viśeṣasañjñā) are such as "Devadatta" and "Yajñadatta," while general designations (sāmānyasañjñā) are such as "mother" and "father"; for even mother and the others are indeed established as designations in that context.

In the case of *naptṛ*, *neṣṭṛ*, *tvaṣṭṛ*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhrātṛ*, *jāmātṛ*, *mātṛ*, and *pitṛ*, as well as *duhitṛ*, [the rule applies]; thus, for example, this designation "mother" (*mātā*) is used for all mothers,
and "father" (*pitā*) for all fathers.
Thus, for all teachers, there is this designation "Teacher" (śāstṛ);
however, that Teacher is of two kinds:
one who does not correspond to reality and one who corresponds to reality.
And while Pūraṇa and others are not in accordance with reality,
the Tathāgata is in accordance with reality;
therefore, he distinguishes him by saying that he teaches in accordance with reality and without error, thus he is the "Teacher in accordance with reality" (yathārthaśāstṛ).
And this qualification is for the purpose of indicating the means for accomplishing the welfare of others;
for this very reason, he says:
"He reveals the means for accomplishing the welfare of others," and so forth.

"But not by the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) or the granting of boons (*vara*). The word "power" (*prabhāva*) is connected with each [term], namely: "by the power of supernatural faculties" and "by the power of granting boons. The power of supernatural faculties is, for example, Viṣṇu’s manifestation of his universal form (*viśvarūpa*).
The power of granting boons is like the popular saying that Maheśvara grants a boon;
alternatively, it is a three-member dvandva compound:
supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the granting of boons (*varapradāna*), and majesty (*prabhāva*).
"Power" (*prabhāva*) is a specific kind of capacity.
Now, it is true that even Buddhas occasionally display miracles of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) for those to be converted;
this is indeed so.

However, there is the question: "While they may achieve mere conversion through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*), how will they cross over saṃsāra by means of the gradual cultivation of the antidotes to passion and so forth?"
Regarding the word "having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*),
because the rule for the suffix *ktvā* requires another action,
the rule for *ktvā* applies when there are two actions performed by the same agent, with the *ktvā*-ending action occurring at the earlier time.

If it is argued that "I shall expound the treatise" (*śāstraṃ pravakṣyāmi*) refers to a collection of names (*nāmasamūha*) that illuminates specific meanings, and that such a collection is untenable because of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), [we reply as follows:]
There is no cognition that apprehends that [collection], because it is a conceptual construction of an aggregate of forms;
and it is called a "treatise" (śāstra) because it instructs disciples.
The intention of the question "What is the treatise? and "What is its name?
is that the etymological explanation of this work, titled *Abhidharmakośa*, will now be stated.
Let this matter rest for now;
since the understanding of the meaning of a whole is preceded by the understanding of the meanings of its parts, he first asks regarding the meaning of the parts:
"What is this so-called Abhidharma?"
"Abhidharma is pure wisdom along with its attendants"—
in this statement, since wisdom is predominant at the time of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), "wisdom" is mentioned according to its primary function.
"Pure" means untainted (*anāsrava*),
because "taints" (*mala*) is a synonym for "outflows" (*āsrava*);
"with their attendants" means together with their retinues.
Just as a servant, even while moving together with a king, is called a "follower of the king" because he acts in accordance with him,
so too here, although they arise at the same time, the co-existent factors are called "followers."

But what are those mental states and mental factors? They are the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) and the [conditioned] factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.
Is it not the case, however, that the mind is primary among the mental factors?
For these mental factors (caittas) are so called because they are either thoughts (cittīya) or existences belonging to the mind (citta);
therefore, wisdom alone can be the retinue of the mind,
but the mind cannot be the retinue of wisdom, since it is the mind that is the mental factor itself.
This is true;
however, at the time of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), while wisdom (*prajñā*) acts as the sovereign over the entire collection of mental factors (*caitta*),
in certain instances a particular phenomenon assumes predominance.
For example, at the time of full conviction, there is faith and so forth; thus,
the five untainted aggregates (anāsrava-pañcaskandhaka) constitute the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), which is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) within that collection.
That which is feeling among the aggregates is the aggregate of feeling; that which is perception...
That is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);
volition and so forth, as well as birth and so on, are the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha);
and consciousness (vijñāna) here is the [aggregate of] consciousness.
"This is the aggregate of knowledge" refers to the ultimate reality itself as that which pertains to the ultimate.

Alternatively, that which exists in the ultimate sense is "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*); or, that which sports in or moves within the ultimate is "ultimate. The conventional, however, is the transactional (*sāṃvyavahārika*).

And that which is for the sake of attaining that— namely, wisdom together with its attendants— is what is intended here by the term *abhidharma*. This refers to the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as the wisdom acquired through birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), along with their attendants, all of which serve to attain that untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom either directly or indirectly.

That Abhidharma is also conventional; therein, that which arises from the application of hearing is "consisting of hearing" (śrutamayī), that which arises from the application of rational reflection is "consisting of reflection" (cintāmayī),
and that which arises from the application of cultivation is "consisting of cultivation" (bhāvanāmayī).
"Born of acquisition at birth" (*upapattipratilambhajā*) means "pertaining to acquisition at birth" (*upapattipratilambhikā*).
Since it possesses acquisition at birth, the suffix *-ṭhan* is applied according to the rule *ata iniṭhanau*; because of this application of *-ṭhan*, there is no *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel.

The Abhidharma pertaining to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara) consists of four aggregates—namely, that which consists of hearing, reflection, innate acquisition, and cultivation—because of the absence of concomitant matter.

However, the Abhidharma pertaining to the form realm (rūpāvacara) consists of five aggregates, because of the presence of the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyāna-saṃvara). This also applies to the treatise (śāstra).
Thus, regarding that Abhidharma treatise, there is a difference in interpretation as to whether it is "with its attendants" or "without its attendants";
some maintain that it is [without its attendants] because it consists of a collection of non-mental and mental factors.
"With its followers" means that some do not include them because birth and so forth are possible; however, others do include them,
for this Abhidharma consists of a single aggregate (skandha).
Or it consists of two aggregates, and for that [person], there are birth and so forth;
however, others explain that "the treatise" refers to the *Jñānaprasthāna*.
That [Abhidharma], which constitutes its very body, has six feet:

the *Prakaraṇapāda*, the *Vijñānakāya*, the *Dharmaskandha*, the *Prajñaptiśāstra*, the *Dhātukāya*, and the *Saṅgītiparyāya*. Therefore, that treatise (*śāstra*) also, together with its followers, is called "conventional Abhidharma" because it leads, through a succession of stages, to the attainment of ultimate Abhidharma. For the wisdom acquired through birth follows the meaning of that [ultimate Abhidharma] by means of hearing the treatise.

The sequence is as follows: from that which consists of hearing arises that which consists of reflection; from that which consists of reflection arises the contaminated [wisdom] consisting of cultivation; and from that arises the uncontaminated wisdom.
In this context, the word "this" (*tad*) or "that" (*idam*) is used for the purpose of introducing a statement.
"This" refers to the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) and conventional (*sāṅketika*) Abhidharma, defined as that which maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇadhāraṇa*).
"The ultimate dharma" (*paramārthadharma*) means that which is the object (*artha*) of the supreme (*parama*) knowledge; thus it is the ultimate.
The ultimate object is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); because it is the foremost of all phenomena (*dharma*), it is the ultimate truth.
It is both the ultimate truth and a phenomenon, thus "ultimate-truth-phenomenon" (*paramārthadharma*), or else it is the characteristic of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
The specific and general characteristics— such as the earth element having the characteristic of hardness, or [the fact that] it is impermanent, suffering, and so forth—
the *abhidharma* is the teaching (*dharma*) directed toward (*abhimukha*) these for the sake of their acquisition, penetration, or realization;
it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "ku-gati-prādayaḥ."

But surely, when *abhi* is compounded with a word denoting a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the rule "the indeclinable *abhi* and *prati* form an *avyayībhāva* compound when used in the sense of direction toward" would apply;
for when *abhi* is compounded with a characteristic, it results in an *avyayībhāva*.
For example, moths fly into a fire;
the moth's flight is characterized by the fire,
and that fire is its characteristic mark.
But this dharma is not the characteristic of another;
rather,
it is itself the characterized object.

Since even that which is called "Abhidharma" in a conventional sense— the Teacher himself— is oriented toward Nirvana or the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) for the purpose of attaining or illuminating them, how much more so is the ultimate [Abhidharma]? Therefore, by means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, "Abhidharma" is established.
The Abhidharma has been explained;
thus, the meaning of its individual components has been understood through the definitions of their intrinsic natures and classifications.
However, the meaning of the whole has not yet been grasped; therefore, he asks about the meaning of the whole.
But how is this treatise called the *Abhidharmakośa*?
It is so called because that treatise named *Abhidharma*, which was mentioned immediately prior, exists "in its meaning" within this [work]. Thus, it is understood as referring to that [treatise].
"By way of meaning, not by way of the letter": this entry is by way of meaning, not in its entirety;
therefore, the compound *yathāpradhānam* is an *avyayībhāva*.
"Contained within" means entered;
this treatise of mine serves as a treasury for that subject matter,
being like a storehouse.
In this sense, it is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound:
"the treasury of the Abhidharma" (abhidharmakośa),
for it is there that the sword [of the Abhidharma] enters.
Is that his treasury,
or rather is it the Abhidharma, such as the *Jñānaprasthāna* and so forth, which serves as the basis for this treatise of mine?
For from that Abhidharma of the Sage, this treatise of mine has been extracted.
Since "in terms of meaning" (arthataḥ) is the governing term, therefore, in the sense that "this Abhidharma is its treasury" (kośa),
this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The Abhidharmakośa is that which has the Abhidharma as its sheath; for that from which a sword is drawn out is called its sheath.

This indicates that the collective meaning of this treatise as the *Abhidharmakośa* has also been understood; [the question] "For what purpose, then, is the instruction on Abhidharma? What is its utility? means: for what reason? What is the purpose?
For the study of a treatise that possesses a purpose is beneficial,
not that which lacks a purpose;
and by whom was this [treatise] first taught?
By whom was this Abhidharma first taught?
The intention is that the treatise taught by an authoritative person (āpta) ought to have its origin in a worthy source;
thus, the qualification "first" is used.
Because the teaching was established only after the synthesis of the views of the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others,
there is indeed a dispute regarding the initial teaching; for that reason.
The meaning is that the Teacher, the author of the treatise, pays respect— that is, he shows reverence— to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the proximate treatise, in order to speak of it and compose it.

Having thus posed two questions, he says— beginning with the detailed phrase "the discernment of phenomena" (*dharmāṇāṃ pravicaya*)— in order to demonstrate that the Abhidharma treatise possesses a purpose and is based on the instruction of an authoritative teacher;
for without the discernment of phenomena, one cannot [realize] that form and feeling are impermanent, suffering, and so forth.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "there is no other means for the pacification of the afflictions"; thus,
it follows by implication that this very [path] is indeed the means for the pacification of the afflictions.
Just as when it is said that there is no means for sustaining life without food, it follows by implication that food itself is the means for sustaining life;
so too,
if there were no subsiding of the afflictions (*kleśa*), what would there be?
Therefore he says:
"And by means of the afflictions, the world wanders here in the ocean of existence."
By this, he shows the necessity of pacifying the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Existence" (*bhava*) and "saṃsāra" have the same meaning; existence itself is an ocean, hence "the ocean of existence" (*bhavārṇava*).
Existence is like the ocean because of its similarity to a bathing place;

the inclusion of the word "here" is for the purpose of negating an existence distinct from the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha) whose characteristics are directly perceived within this ocean of existence.
In this case, the world revolves because of its state of identity;

for even when expressing a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is seen [to be expressed] by means of identity, as for example: "The grove stands in the *palāśa* trees because of the non-utilization of other trees."
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), however, by indicating that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) has the sense of a cause (*hetu*), the meaning of "cause" is expressed through the causative suffix (*ṇic*);
and since the afflictions (*kleśa*) cause the world to wander,
the phrase "therefore" (*ataḥ*) serves as a restatement of the previously mentioned reason.
Since this is so, the meaning is that the Abhidharma has been indicated;

for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)—which is the means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and no other phenomenon—is the connection for the teaching of the Abhidharma. Therefore, it is said: "for that reason."
That very cause is the "cause of that";
because it is the cause of that, or because it arises from that, it is the "cause of that.
Thus, for the sake of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), the discernment of phenomena has the teaching of the *Abhidharma* as its cause.

The Teacher, the Buddha, taught the Abhidharma so that there might be an investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). For this very reason, it is said that without the instruction of the Abhidharma, a disciple is not capable of investigating phenomena;
thus, the word *udita* is the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) of the root *vad*, with the semivowel *v* changed to its corresponding vowel *u* (samprasāraṇa).
It is not derived from the root *i* preceded by the prefix *ut*, as that would be incompatible with the meaning.
The word "udita" means "taught," and thus they have the same meaning;
the particle "kila" indicates the opinion of another.
The meaning is that this is the opinion of the Ābhidharmikas, but not ours, the Sautrāntikas;
for indeed, the authors of the Abhidharma treatises are heard of [in tradition].
For example: the noble Kātyāyanīputra is the author of the *Jñānaprasthāna*, the Venerable Vasumitra of the *Prakaraṇapāda*,
and the Venerable Devaśarman of the *Vijñānakāya*.
Ārya Śāriputra [is the master] of the *Dharmaskandha*,
Ārya Maudgalyāyana of the *Prajñaptiśāstra*,
and Pūrṇa of the *Dhātukāya*.
Regarding the *Saṅgītiparyāya*, who is Mahākauṣṭhila? What is the meaning of "Sautrāntika"? [They are] those for whom the sūtras are the authority, not the treatises (*śāstra*).
If those Sautrāntikas do not accept the treatises as authoritative, how is it that their own system establishes the three baskets (piṭakas)— namely,
the Sūtra-piṭaka, the Vinaya-piṭaka, and the Abhidharma-piṭaka?
For even in the Sūtras, the Abhidharma Piṭaka is recited in the phrase "a monk who is conversant with the three Piṭakas"; this is not a fault,
for it is specific types of Sūtras, such as the *Arthaviniścaya* and others, in which the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are described that bear the designation "Abhidharma."
To dispel this doubt, they say:
"But that was spoken by the Blessed One in a scattered manner," and so forth, just as [it was done] by the Elder Dharmatrāta in the *Udānavarga*.

The Vaibhāṣikas say: "Just as in that Sūtra [the *Saṃyuktāgama*], statements such as 'Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent' were spoken by the Blessed One in various places, categorized, and compiled together for the sake of those to be trained (*vineya*), so too the Abhidharma—whose essential nature is the instruction on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)—was spoken by the Blessed One in various places according to the needs of those to be trained. Subsequently, the Elder Kātyāyanīputra and others compiled these teachings and established them in works such as the *Jñānaprasthāna*."
The Vaibhāṣikas are those who play with or practice the Vibhāṣā,
or those who know the Vibhāṣā; the suffix *ṭhak* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *uktha*.
"Contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena":
those which are together with contaminants are contaminated;
those in which contaminants do not exist are uncontaminated.
"Both with outflows and without outflows"—this is the summary.
A phenomenon (*dharma*) is so called because it maintains its own specific and general characteristics;
this is the concise explanation of all phenomena.
There are only as many phenomena as there are, namely those with outflows and those without outflows;
there are no phenomena apart from these.
Therefore, it says "of all phenomena."
"Summary exposition" means a concise exposition;
however, the detailed exposition will follow later until the completion of the treatise.
Furthermore, there are other summary expositions as well.
Why has this concise enumeration been stated— such as "conditioned and unconditioned," "material and immaterial," "visible and invisible," and so forth?
When what has been stated is there no further objection?
Alternatively, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the defiled and purified sides, since that is the aim of the treatise;
for by understanding those two sides, one attains the supreme good through abandoning the side of defilement and practicing the side of purification.
"Conditioned things, excluding the Path, are with-outflows" means they are exclusively conditioned, not unconditioned.
Are all conditioned phenomena, such as form and so forth, produced by causes and conditions?
He says: "No."
"Devoid of the path" means devoid of the truth of the path;
since the truth of the path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), there would be an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, he qualifies [the term] in this way.
This is what is meant:
Excluding the truth of the path, all conditioned phenomena are with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
But how, then, are they with-outflows?
If they were with-outflows merely through association with the outflows, then only afflicted minds and mental factors would be with-outflows.
Not others; rather,

because they arise together with the outflows (*āsrava*), the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) would be "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) for a sentient being in whose continuum a defilement (*kleśa*) is currently active, according to the possibility,
but not for one in whom no defilement is active.
Nor are external phenomena [tainted];
rather, those which are the bases of the outflows are tainted.
If only the six internal sense bases were "with outflows" (sāsrava),
then the objects of the outflows would also have to be with outflows; consequently, even the truths of cessation and the path would result in being with outflows.
Furthermore, a higher stage (*ūrdhvā bhūmiḥ*) would be "with outflows" (*sāsravā*) because of the outflows that have the higher stages as their object; therefore, he says:
"Because the outflows pursue them, they are 'with outflows'. The word *tasmāt* ("therefore") must be supplied from the preceding [sentence].
"Follow along" means they obtain nourishment,
or it means they obtain a firm footing;
through the acquisition of nourishment or the acquisition of a firm footing, those [defilements] such as passion continue to proliferate.
Others explain it as follows:
just as one says "this food of mine adheres" (anuśete) meaning it is wholesome and becomes favorable,
so too do passion and the other [afflictions] adhere to those phenomena (dharmas).
The meaning is that it becomes concordant;
for impure (*sāsrava*) phenomena are produced by karma moistened by passion and the like,
and the variety of the world is born of karma.
According to this statement, they are called *anuśayas* because they "lie along" (*anuśerate*), meaning they attain nourishment in accordance with their conditions;
or alternatively, they are called *anuśayas* because the conditions "lie along" (*anuśerate*) within them, acting in conformity with them.
Their persistence (anuśayana) is to be understood either by way of their object (ālambana) or by way of association (samprayoga);
however, the master Guṇamati explains it here [as follows]:
for what reason? Because, although all phenomena serve as objects for the outflows (āsrava), only conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), excluding the Path, are called "with outflows" (sāsrava).

The claim that all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are the objects (*ālambana*) of those with outflows (*sāsrava*) is un-Abhidharmic; for space (*ākāśa*) and cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not objects of the outflows,
and only six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are taught to have the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Furthermore, false view and doubt that have cessation and the path as their objects, the ignorance associated with them, and independent ignorance—
these six are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, and they have the untainted as their domain.
Because of this statement,
we see that this is not well-written;
"kāmam" means "even though" or "granted."

Alternatively, the particle *kāmam* has the sense of admission (*abhyupagama*). The meaning is that it is indeed admitted that outflows (*āsrava*) arise even with the truths of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects; such is the case regarding those two truths, cessation and the path.
We shall explain this in the very exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),
under the section stating: "They do not have the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) or higher realms as their objects, because they are not appropriated and because they are opposed [to them]."
For when an object has been appropriated by the view of self and craving for self,
other latent dispositions are able to adhere to it, just as dust settles upon a moist cloth.
Furthermore, that which is untainted (anāsrava) is not so,
nor is a higher stage;
therefore, they do not increase (anuśerate) with respect to those [objects], as they do not have them as their focal objects (ālambana).

Furthermore, because both nirvāṇa and the path are discordant with them, and because a higher stage is discordant with the afflictions that take it as their object while a lower stage is discordant with those of the stages above, for these reasons as well, the afflictions do not find a foothold within them.

Regarding the objection that "the soles of the feet [are not placed] on a heated stone" implies that the Truth of the Path is untainted (*anāsrava*), and that the threefold unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is established by logical necessity (*arthāpatti*) and thus need not be explicitly stated in the Sūtra— against such an objection, Master Guṇamati first says:
"This must indeed be stated."
What is the reason?
For the path is of two kinds: mundane and supramundane;
therefore, it is stated once more for the sake of distinction.

For this very reason, the inclusion of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) here is well-established; moreover, what is established is understood through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), whereas what is not established is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Others explain that this is stated again— though already established through presumptive reasoning (arthāpatti)— in order to eliminate the suspicion of a third category,
just as there are three types of feelings.
Just as there are pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feelings],
so too might phenomena (dharmas) be conceived as being with-outflows (sāsrava), without-outflows (anāsrava), or both with-and-without-outflows.

Alternatively, if it is neither contaminated (*sāsrava*) nor uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), then by implication, what are those things that have been excluded? Are they exclusively uncontaminated, or rather exclusively both contaminated and uncontaminated?
Or rather, one might doubt whether it is "neither of the two," for there exists the possibility of the conceptual distinction between being substantial and being without outflows; how so?
First, according to the Vaibhāṣika system,

there are two types [of defiled states]: those with latent dispositions (*sānuśaya*) and those without latent dispositions (*an-anuśaya*), based on the statement that "the defiled is [with] latent dispositions because of the presence of the latent tendencies."

Those [factors] such as the eye and so forth, or external objects such as visible forms and so forth, which are unafflicted, are "with outflows" (sāsrava) only through those outflows that are currently active as latent tendencies (anuśaya); they are not "with outflows" through those outflows that are no longer latent, having been abandoned.
Through those non-latent outflows, they are not with outflows.

However, according to the system of the Dārṣṭāntikas, even if [the defilements] have not been abandoned— even if they exist in the mental continua of others— the [faculties] are indeed *sāsrava* (with-outflows). Furthermore, by this same reasoning, the eyes and so forth existing in the continuum of an Arhat, as well as external objects such as forms and so forth,
are *anāsrava* (without-outflows), because they do not serve as a basis for the outflows.
Since those [faculties] are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) because they are not the antidote to the outflows (*āsrava*),
there arises a doubt that the status of being "with outflows" or "without outflows" (*anāsrava*) regarding the eye and so forth is merely figurative (*pāryāyika*).
To eliminate that doubt, this is stated:

"The untainted [factors] are the truth of the path and the threefold unconditioned; thus, without qualification, these are exclusively untainted and not tainted, as has been stated"—this being a restatement. "In that case, on which side do the Arhat’s eye and so forth belong? they say. To this, the Vaibhāṣikas reply:
How are those things established as "with outflows" (sāsrava) when the outflows have been abandoned?
Those things in which the outflows lie latent (anuśerate), have lain latent, or will lie latent— those are "with outflows."
For even when intending to express a meaning pertaining to the three times, usage in the present tense is observed in common worldly parlance, as in: "He who protects the subjects is the king."
Since it is understood that whoever has protected and whoever will protect is likewise a king,
it is therefore explained in this way.
Alternatively, even if they are not "with outflows" (sāsrava) because their outflows have been abandoned,
they are nonetheless certainly with outflows due to the immeasurable outflows that have not been abandoned— even those belonging to the mental continua of others;
for is it not the case that this follows from the concise exposition itself?
It does not follow that there is a third category [of phenomena] consisting of those that are both with-outflows and without-outflows.
In this regard, because the formation of a *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder) compound is possible,

the term "sāsravānāsravāḥ" is a *ekaśeṣa* meaning "those that are both with-outflows and without-outflows," [derived from] "those with-outflows (*sāsravāḥ*) and those without-outflows (*anāsravāḥ*), and those with-outflows and without-outflows (*sāsravānāsravāḥ*)."
"Even for [words] that are not of the same form, a single remainder (ekaśeṣa) is desired,
as in the rule 'guṇo yaṇṅ-lukoḥ'; thus others have said."
This is indeed established by implication;
however, this detailed exposition is stated for the sake of clarification.
For example, everything is already established by the rule itself: "A qualifier [is compounded] with a qualified object in various ways."
Just as the detailed exposition beginning with "pūrvakāla," "eka," "sarva," "jara," "purāṇa," "nava," and "kevala" [are used] with a word in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa),
so too, because this threefold unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is not commonly recognized, he asks: "Which is the threefold unconditioned?"
The mention of "threefold" is for the purpose of determining the exact number;
for there are some who assert that there is only one conditioned phenomenon, namely *nirvāṇa*, such as the Vātsīputrīyas,
while others, such as the Vaiśeṣikas, maintain that there are many conditioned phenomena, such as atoms and so forth.

In order to refute that view, [the author] establishes the limit [of categories] by asking "which two?"— he asks specifically about cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
Space is not [the cause] of space, because it is well-known in the world;
in that context, "space" means non-obstruction, and "therein" (*tatra*) is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*).
Whether as an agent-noun or an object-noun,
that dharma which does not obstruct other dharmas nor is obstructed by others is space, whose intrinsic nature is non-obstruction.
Because its object is not perceptible, it is inferred through the non-occurrence of other properties,
and not as a mere absence of obstruction;
for this very reason, it is explained in such a manner.
Regarding the statement "where there is the movement of form":
if that which neither obstructs nor is obstructed is space (ākāśa).
Conditioned factors such as mind and so forth, though non-obstructive, likewise [occupy space]; they do not reach space, nor do they obstruct others, because of their state of being non-obstructive.
For those possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhimantaḥ*) obstruct the course of others' minds and mental factors by means of the power of their own mind and mental factors;
however, since analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) do not act as obstructions, they do not result in [the same] as space (*ākāśa*).

Because it acts as an obstruction by being the necessary impediment to the attainment of conjunction for those substances whose nature is not to produce conjunction, and because it acts as an impediment to their production;
or else, that which has non-obstruction alone as its defining characteristic and no other characteristic is space (*ākāśa*).
And since those two possess other characteristics, they do not attain the status of space.
Otherwise, space would either fail to be omnipresent or would be impermanent,
because it exists only in the absence of obstruction.
Furthermore, because [space] is absent when that [obstruction] is absent—

for indeed, in the case of walls and such, there is the obstruction of another form— there follows the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of space, since the characteristic of space would be absent therein.
Furthermore, since that [space] comes into being again once walls and such are removed, it would follow that it is impermanent;
yet it does not follow that it is impermanent,
for even there, space certainly exists because it provides room for the walls and such.
For if there were no space there, that very wall or other object would have no room and could not exist; however,
the fact that another form cannot exist there is due to the obstruction of the wall and so forth, not due to the absence of space.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "O Gautama, on what is the earth established?
"The earth, O Brahmin, is established upon the circle of water."
"O Gautama, on what is the circle of water established?
It is established on the wind.
O Gautama, on what is the wind established?"
"It is established in space.
"O Gautama, where is space established?
"You overstep [the bounds], Great Brahmin; you overstep them, Great Brahmin!"
"Space, O Brahmin, is non-abiding and without support," and so forth;

therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that space exists. By specifying it as "that which is dissociation" (*visaṃyoga*), both impermanence (*anityatā*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) are excluded.
For those two cessations do not have the characteristic of dissociation;
dissociation is the state of being dissociated from the afflictions,
or it is that dharma which constitutes the definitive obstruction to the acquisition of conjunction.

That analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) belongs to the Noble Truths beginning with suffering; because of this inclusion of a qualification, "analytical discernment" (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) is understood to be only untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*),
for mundane wisdom does not take the aspects (*ākāra*) of the Truth of Suffering and so forth.
What then?
It is a specific kind of wisdom characterized by aspects such as the peacefulness of the higher stages and the coarseness of the lower stages.

The inclusion of the term "distinction" (*viśe�sa*) is for the purpose of including the wisdom (*prajñā*) of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, cessation attained by means of that specific wisdom is "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*),
formed by eliding the middle term.
There is an extension [of the rule] for compounds such as *śākapārthiva* (the vegetable-loving king),
as in "vegetable-loving kings" (*śākapriyāḥ pārthivāḥ*), where the middle term is elided by specific intention;

if only untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom were understood here, then cessation attained through the mundane path would not be included, and thus the definition would result in being non-pervasive (*avyāpin*).
Is it not the case that the cessation of all contaminated things within the three realms is attained through uncontaminated wisdom? Yet,
that cessation does not exist [as a separate entity].
What is the purpose of mundane wisdom (*laukikī prajñā*)— which is attained through mundane wisdom alone and not through the untainted (*anāsrava*)—
when any cessation (*nirodha*) whatsoever is attained by means of the mundane path?
Furthermore, since that very [cessation] is attained through supramundane [wisdom],
only supramundane wisdom is involved therein, not mundane wisdom;
and analytical cessation exists as a substantial entity because it is taught among the exposition of the four truths, just like the truth of the path— so say the Vaibhāṣikas.
"Separately" (pṛthak-pṛthak) means "diversely" (nānā);
for "as many as are the substances in conjunction" refers to the state of being conjoined, which is conjunction (saṃyoga).
Substances that are for the purpose of conjunction are "conjunction-substances";
or, they are called "conjunctions" because they are conjoined within them;
or, they are "conjunction-substances" because they are both conjunctions and substances.
"Contaminated entities" means as much as has been said:
"For a contaminated entity is like a pillar, the fetters are like a rope, and the person is like an ox," as stated by the Blessed One;
"otherwise" means if [the person] were one and the same.
"The realization of the cessation of all afflictions" means the attainment of the cessation of those afflictions to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation [of the truths] such as the origin;
[otherwise], the cultivation of the remaining antidotes would be useless.

The meaning is that the production of the path of counteraction— which consists of the vision and cultivation that abandon the remaining afflictions, as well as [the truths of] origin and so forth— would be purposeless. As for what was stated, "Cessation is without a counterpart" (asabhāga),
where was this said?
In a sutra,
when asked by her former husband, the householder Viśākha, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā said:
"Noble lady, is cessation homogeneous?"
"Non-participating, Venerable Viśākha," he said;
having perceived that the meaning is "cessation which has no counterpart," he asks,
"What is the meaning of this?"
For if there were multiplicity, another [dharma] would be similar to it; such is the opponent's intention.
[The Sautrāntika replies: "It has no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Thus, "similar cause" and "similar" (*sabhāga*) have the same meaning, due to the elision of the word "cause" (*hetu*).
For we observe people employing parts of words in place of whole words, and parts of sentences in place of whole sentences;
for example, *Satyabhāmā* as *Bhāmā*, *Devadatta* as *Datta*, and "enter the *piṇḍī*" as "enter the *tarpaṇa*.
Indeed, the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is eternal.
What need has that [non-homogeneous cause] for a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)? It is called a non-homogeneous cause (*asabhāgahetu*);
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has no homogeneous part" (*asabhāga*), i.e., that which lacks a homogeneous counterpart.
"Belonging to nothing" means that this analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is not the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) of any other dharma; this is what is intended. What is the reason?

It is accepted that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) exists only among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); in this context, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "that which is homogeneous," and not [a bahuvrīhi] meaning "one for whom no homogeneous [factor] exists."
The meaning is that there is no other cessation similar to this cessation;
[it is] "another cessation" which is an absolute obstacle to arising—
that is, an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas through non-analytical [cessation], an absolute obstacle, an absolute and definitive obstruction.
"Other" refers to cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
For it is "other" than the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) mentioned immediately prior;
here, the negative particle *a-* is used in the sense of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*).
The meaning is that it is not attained through analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyā*); or alternatively, in the sense of a partial negation (*paryudāsa*),
it is that which is other than analytical discernment, namely, the deficiency of conditions (*pratyayavaikalya*).
Cessation not attained through analytical discernment is "cessation not through discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
due to the elision of the middle term.
This is illogical;
for since the deficiency of conditions is itself an absence,
how can that cessation be attained by means of an absence?
There is no fault because it is used figuratively;
or rather, "non-analytical cessation" (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is merely stated as being distinct from "analytical cessation" (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha),
and not as involving the operation of the deficiency of conditions.

The mention of "arising" (*utpāda*) is for the purpose of excluding cessation through impermanence (*anityatā-nirodha*); cessation through impermanence is an absolute obstruction to the persistence of a phenomenon (*dharma-sthiti*), but not to its arising.
The inclusion of the term "absolute" (*atyanta*) is for the purpose of excluding the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).

For these [obstructions] are an impediment to the arising of future minds and mental factors, but not an absolute one, because that state of being an impediment is merely temporary— just as in the case of the eye and mind being occupied with a single form, and so forth.
The word "yathā" (as) indicates an illustration;
for example, one whose eye and mind are both engaged with a single blue form is called "one whose eye and mind are engaged with a single form."

The meaning is that all those other forms of his— other than the blue being perceived, such as other blues, yellows, reds, whites, and so forth, including both color-forms and shape-forms, as well as sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles— pass away; they transcend the present time-path and enter the past time-path.
"Having those as their objects" means that these [minds] have as their objects those things— blue and so forth— just mentioned; thus they are "those having those as their objects."
Which are the five groups of consciousness?
By them...
"For they are not capable," and so forth;
for those five groups of consciousness are not able to grasp even their own past objects as an objective support,
because the five groups of consciousness have only the present as their objective support.
Now, why do [cognitions] not arise by taking another present object, such as a different blue thing, as their support?
It is impossible for this to be so, because all phenomena are necessarily restricted to the fourfold [temporal] set.
Regarding the cause, the fruit, the basis, and the object:
whatever is the object of a particular consciousness, that alone shall be its object, and nothing else.
Because of the deficiency of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), those five groups of consciousness do not arise again;
therefore, it is said that this is their "cessation through non-analytical discernment" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth.
Due to the deficiency of conditions for these five groups of consciousness—specifically the deficiency of the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya)—they do not arise.

For mind and mental factors arise only when four conditions are present: the causal condition (hetu), the immediately preceding condition (samānantara), the object-condition (ālambana), and the dominant condition (adhipati).
If there is a deficiency in even one of these, they do not arise.
Others say it is due to the deficiency of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*);

for at that time, the immediately preceding condition— which is characterized by mind and mental factors— provides scope only for the arising of that single blue-cognition, and not for other cognitions such as another blue object and so forth.
Because multiple consciousnesses cannot arise simultaneously, this is merely an illustration;

in the same way, for all five types of persons—including those who have attained *kṣānti*—there is the attainment of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) regarding future states of rebirth in the miserable realms (*āpāyika*), due to the deficiency of conditions, namely, the manifestation of conditions that are incompatible with their arising. This should be understood as the general principle to be applied.

And with reference specifically to cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), the Blessed One, concerning the person who has entered the stream (*srota-āpanna*), said: "For him, the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts have ceased.
Thus, the non-arising of such future phenomena due to the deficiency of conditions is called cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is not logical for there to be an absolute non-arising of something merely due to a deficiency of conditions,
because when conditions of the same kind as those arise again, its production would necessarily follow;
for what obstacle could there then be to its production?
"Regarding the fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭi) here," and so forth:

here, in the detailed exposition of the characteristics of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), for what purpose is the fourfold response to questions set forth? It is for the sake of analytical clarification (*vyutpatti*).
For example, regarding those contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena that have already passed, are presently occurring, or are destined to arise:
because they are contaminated, only cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is obtained,
since the arising of those that have passed or are present has already been accomplished.
Furthermore, because things subject to arising necessarily come into being,
non-analytical cessation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is not obtained;
for non-analytical cessation is characterized by the absolute prevention of arising.
For example, regarding unconditioned phenomena that are untainted (*anāsrava*) and characterized by non-arising (*anutpatti-dharma*):
because their arising is absolutely obstructed, they possess the nature of non-arising; and for this reason, their cessation through non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is obtained.

For example, when one of the paths of those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) belonging to the six stages— the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the [four] dhyānas— is manifested, the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) of the remaining five is obtained,
but not their analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), because they are untainted (*anāsrava*); for that which is faultless does not require abandonment.

The inclusion of the term "having the nature of non-arising" (*anutpattidharma*) is for the purpose of excluding that which has already arisen, that which is presently arising, and that which is destined to arise;
for even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), by its very nature, possesses the quality of non-arising,
and thus this qualification is added so that [the definition] does not over-apply to it.
For some, the reading is as follows: "of those [dharmas] that are untainted and of a nature not to arise.
For them, how is it that there is no consequence of including unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas?
The reference here concerns those phenomena for which both analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) are possible;
these two cessations are not possible for unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
For non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is the absolute obstruction to arising; yet there is no arising of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding those things whose nature is non-arising (*anutpatti-dharman*), this is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*):
it refers to those other similar phenomena that are distinct from those whose nature is arising (*utpatti-dharman*).
What are those things whose nature is non-arising, and what are their counterparts?
They exist only within the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Those who assert that there is no [cessation] for conditioned phenomena claim that both exist— namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—
as is the case, for example, with those phenomena that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); such is the detailed explanation.
Because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), this analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is attained;
when that occurs, the attainment of these two is intended. However, their attainment does not necessarily occur simultaneously, for in some cases analytical cessation is attained first.
Subsequently, there is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).

For example, when the eye and mind of an Arhat are engaged with a single form, a certain cessation not through deliberation is attained beforehand for the five groups of consciousness that would otherwise have other forms and so forth as their objects.
Subsequently, there is cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*),
such as the simultaneous [cessation] of certain miserable destinies for one who has attained receptivity (*kṣānti*).

For example, when the antidote to the most intense of the intense afflictions arises for one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), both the analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) of those future intense afflictions are obtained simultaneously; in the same way, this should be applied as appropriate to other cases, such as the untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena that are past, present, or destined to arise.
Because it is impossible to obstruct the arising of these [dharmas] such as the past and so forth, non-analytical cessation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is not obtained for them;
and because they are untainted (anāsrava), analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is also not obtained for them.
However, since unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas lack arising, there is no non-analytical cessation for them.
It was stated previously that non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is the absolute obstruction to arising;
and because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) does not exist [for unconditioned phenomena] either.

Thus, since there is little to be said regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), having concluded the questions concerning it, he now introduces the preliminary discussion (*upodghāta*) with the intention of explaining conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding what was said— that conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path, are with-outflows—
what are those conditioned phenomena?
Furthermore, those conditioned phenomena are:
The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is stated for the purpose of indicating another classification; whereas the previous classification was "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "without outflows" (*anāsrava*),
this, however, is a further classification,
as it is separated by the mention of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The repetition of the term "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) is for the purpose of excluding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
the word "those" (te) refers back to what was previously mentioned.
And which are those previously mentioned:
those with outflows that have not been abandoned,
and those whose intrinsic nature is the truth of the path that have been abandoned.
How is it understood that both [categories] are intended when it is said,
"those which are with outflows are the aggregates of clinging"?
Thus, because of the statement that the contaminated is extracted from the uncontaminated,
those five aggregates, beginning with form, whose characteristics will be explained below,
are to be understood as conditioned.
Their mutual inclusion consists in the apprehension of form and so forth, for the purpose of excluding other aggregates such as morality and the rest;

for there are indeed five other aggregates: the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The mention of "aggregates" (*skandha*) is for the purpose of excluding objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;
these two terms, *sametya* and *sambhūya*, are synonyms.
Alternatively, *sametya* means having come together, that is, having met and being mutually dependent upon one another.
By the phrase "having come together" (*sambhūya*), he demonstrates the meaning of the prefix *sam*;
for it does not mean "produced by a single cause," since even when there is the very minimum of causes, there must necessarily be two causes.
For it is said: "Mind and mental factors arise from four [conditions]; the two meditative attainments from three; and others from two."

Regarding the expression "like milk" (*dugdhavat*), because the Sanskrit word ends in a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), he demonstrates the example by means of that very word ending in a *niṣṭhā*:
"like milk" (*dugdhvat*) means milk, that is, *kṣīra*.
It is logical that what has been drawn out from the breasts is "milk," whereas that which will be drawn out [is yet to be so designated].
And that which is not at all being milked, but remains situated within the cow itself,
