does not logically qualify as "milk," yet it is nevertheless called "milk" in common worldly usage.
Likewise here too, those conditioned phenomena that will be produced and are subject to arising in the future, as well as those that will not be produced and are not subject to arising,
are also called "conditioned" because they belong to that same class and possess similarity in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
"Those very [factors] are the time-periods," and so forth;

this is the entirety of the Abhidharma. Since it is said that [the Abhidharma] is the meaning of the Sūtras, the touchstone of the Sūtras, and the commentary on the Sūtras, there is here a mention of the "time-periods" (adhvan) and so on—even though they were already mentioned in the Sūtras—insofar as they are synonyms for the aggregates (skandha) in the form of what has gone, what is going, and what will go.
This path has been explained with reference to the path as it is commonly understood in the world;
for thus it is said in the world:
"this path has gone to the village," "this path is going," and "this path will go."
In the same way, here too, the term "paths" (*adhvan*)— referring to that which has gone as the past, that which goes as the present, and that which will go as the future—
is explained with this meaning by taking into account the etymological rule (*nairukta-vidhāna*) that they are called "paths" because they are "consumed" (*adyante*) by impermanence.

Because they have a beginning and an end and are consumed by impermanence, they are called "paths" (*adhvan*); thus, it is precisely the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) that the Blessed One taught by the term "path.
By the term "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*), those same conditioned phenomena were also taught:
"Monks, there are these three bases of discourse—neither four nor five—relying upon which the noble ones engage in discourse."
What are the three?
The past subject of discourse, the future subject of discourse, and the present subject of discourse; "discourse" means speech, and so forth.
"Discourse" (*kathā*) means a sentence, which is a sound consisting of phonemes;
its "subject matter" (*vastu*) means the referent (*viṣaya*) of the name; furthermore, by the name, the "object" (*artha*) is that which is denoted (*abhidheya*).
For it will be stated later:
"Speech operates upon the name; the name illuminates the object."

If indeed the "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*) is merely a portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), how is it that by the term "basis of discourse" only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are expressed? To this he says:
"But because [the word] 'basis' (*vastu*) is taken in its primary sense, the conditioned is called the basis of discourse.
For otherwise, [as explained in] the detailed exposition...

If a meaningful entity (*sārthaka-vastu*) were not included, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇa* treatise which states that "the bases of discourse (*kathāvastu*) are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
By what reasoning, then, is a meaningful entity grasped?
The subject matter of discourse is twofold: direct and indirect.
That which is called the direct subject matter—
For that object is indirectly the object of the name which constitutes its own objective domain;
therefore, it is established as the object of that [name] as well.

Why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) not stated to be a basis for discourse (*kathāvastu*), given that it is a name belonging to the [three] time periods? Because there is no compatibility of meaning between that which belongs to the time periods and that which does not; or because the word *vastu* (basis) is intended to convey two meanings: "object" (*viṣaya*) or "cause" (*hetu*).
For that which is both the object of discourse and possesses causes and conditions is a "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*); however,
since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a cause or condition for discourse, it is not a basis of discourse.
Alternatively, because past and other conditioned phenomena possess such a vast variety of forms, they are suitable for narration:
"In such and such a way, the Tathāgata Dīpaṅkara existed; in such and such a way, the Tathāgata Maitreya will exist."
Since it is said that "King Kapphiṇa was thus and so," only conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are stated to be the subject matter of discourse, not unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).

If it is argued that "the nirvāṇa of all conditioned things" refers to nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*), then [one must admit] that such [nirvāṇa] exists for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); thus, there is a logical connection between that which is with outflows and the state of being accompanied by essence (*sanissāratva*).
But regarding the truth of the path,

for those who understand the discourse on the Dharma as being like a raft, even dharmas must be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas; thus, it is indeed appropriate that even the truth of the path has an exit,
and so all conditioned phenomena possess an exit.
"Having a real basis" (*savastuka*) means that effects first abide in this [basis] and subsequently arise from it;
thus, "real basis" (*vastu*) means the cause. Since these [dharmas] possess that, they are called "having a real basis."
For in the teaching, the word *vastu* (thing/entity) is seen in five senses:
as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as objective support (*ālambana*), as that which is to be bound (*saṃyojanīya*), as cause (*hetu*), and as appropriation (*parigraha*).
First, regarding intrinsic nature:
When a thing has been acquired and one is possessed of that thing, it is understood that [one is possessed] by way of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) with respect to the object (*ālambana*).
"What are the objects of knowledge?
He replied:
"All phenomena are to be known by means of knowledge; the meaning is that they are to be known according to their actual state and according to their objective support."
Regarding the object that is conducive to fettering:
it is that very object with which one is bound by the fetter of attachment and also by the fetter of aversion.
Regarding the cause,
what are the phenomena that possess a real entity?
They are all conditioned phenomena.

Regarding "possessing," one abandons the possession of fields, houses, shops, and wealth, and thus becomes abstinent from them; here, the word *vastu* should be understood as a term for a cause (*hetu*).
The word "kila" indicates the opinion of another; however, his own view is indicated by this [statement].
Conditioned phenomena possess a basis and possess intrinsic nature,
whereas unconditioned phenomena lack a basis because they exist only as designations;
thus, those very same [phenomena] are called "conditioned."
He shows that those which were previously mentioned as being with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava)—
namely, those which are with-outflows are the aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha)—
are what is to be supplied here by the word "of them" (teṣām).
He examines that which is established as being implied by the meaning: "What is accomplished?"
The aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) and so forth have been taught in the Sūtras; therefore, they are explained here.
It has been stated in detail that the entirety of Abhidharma is the meaning of the Sūtras.
Because they arise from that [clinging], they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*); that is, aggregates produced from clinging (*upādānasambhūta*),
with the middle term elided.

Just as fire produced from grass is "grass-fire" and fire produced from chaff is "chaff-fire," others establish that the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) are formed by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) without eliding the middle term.
And they demonstrate this in the same way that fire [consisting] of grass is called "grass-fire," [referring to] those things reckoned as sentient beings.
Those aggregates of clinging (upādānaskandha) are so called because they have karma moistened by afflictions as their cause;
but how are external entities "aggregates of clinging"?
They too are produced from clinging.

According to the established tenet that "the variety of the world is born of karma," [the self] is subject to that [karma], just as in the case of "the king's man"; for example, a man who is subject to the king is called "the king's man."
Thus, the aggregates are subject to grasping because they proceed toward different objects of perception under its influence;
or rather, grasping arises from them.
This is merely an explanation of the meaning; however, the words should be stated thus:
the aggregates are "appropriation-aggregates" (upādānaskandha) because they are the source or the causes of appropriations, like a tree with flowers and fruit.
Just as a tree is the source or cause for the production of flowers or fruits,
it is likewise called a "flower-tree" or a "fruit-tree."

The aggregates of Arhats are also subject to the grasping belonging to other continua because they produce transformation; since grasping belonging to other continua can also arise from them, it is not contradictory for these to be "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*),
for the "conflicts" (*raṇa*) are indeed the afflictions (*kleśa*), due to their harming oneself and others.
For those things which afflict both oneself and others are *raṇas*; the meaning is that they are battles (*yuddhas*).
And in the same way, the defilements (*kleśas*) are called *raṇas*.

"Because they are accompanied by those [latent tendencies]" (*tadanuśayitatvāt*). The meaning is that they are "accompanied" (*anuśayita*)—that is, attended to—by them. Alternatively, they are "accompanied" (*anuśayita*) because they have been made to possess latent tendencies (*anuśayin*) by them. The state of being so is "the fact of being accompanied by them" (*tadanuśayitatva*); therefore, "because of that fact of being accompanied by them. Alternatively, it is the fact that they possess latent tendencies (*anuśayitatva*) with respect to those [defilements]; for that reason, they are "with conflict" (*saraṇa*), just like "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Whatever explanation was given regarding the state of being "with outflows," that very same one should be stated here as well. (AKBh 1.8cd)

"Because it is contrary to the noble ones, it is suffering. It is contrary to the noble ones by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). "From this, suffering arises; therefore, it is the origin (*samudaya*). They explain that the aggregates (*skandha*) functioning as causes are the origin, while the aggregates functioning as effects are suffering.

"It is called 'the world' (*loka*) because it disintegrates. Regarding this very body, which is a mere fathom in length and has red horses [for its breath], I teach the world and the origin of the world—so says the Sūtra. Furthermore, the Blessed One himself stated: "It is called 'the world' because it disintegrates (*lujyate*) and falls apart (*pralujyate*). The meaning is that it disintegrates, that is, it perishes. Here, the root *luj* is intended, not *lok*. However, by means of etymological rules (*nairukta*), the letter *ga* is replaced by the letter *ka*, and thus it becomes "the world" (*loka*).

"View resides in this. Because of the statement, "O monks, whoever perceives anything as self or as belonging to a self, they perceive these very five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha) as self or as belonging to a self," it follows that the aggregates of clinging are the locus of views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*).
Regarding "existence" (*bhava*): only contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are expressed by the word "existence," because of the statement, "What is existence? It is the five aggregates of clinging.
Furthermore, these terms such as "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and so forth would also apply to the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
For even the truth of the path is suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);
moreover, as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth, it is from this [path] that contaminated things arise and disintegrate.
The meaning is that the view takes that as its object and arises with respect to it;

this is not a fault. For the application of words depends upon conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Those factors (*dharma*) which, by virtue of being the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), are disagreeable to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), painful, and antagonistic, yet are well-known to be productive of that [suffering] and generators of the nourishment of views—[it is with reference to these that the term is used].
In this beginningless saṃsāra, these [phenomena] perish and come into being;
it is among them, and not within the truth of the path, that suffering and the other [truths] have been designated by the Noble Ones.
Therefore, only those phenomena that are with-outflows (sāsrava) are denoted by terms such as "suffering," and not those that are without-outflows (anāsrava).
For when it is said that "a cow (go) is so called because it goes (gacchati)," not every goer is called a cow;
therefore, it is well stated that [the truths are] suffering, origin, and so forth.
(AKBh 1.9)

"Form" refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). "Five" is for the purpose of excluding the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*). "Objects" (*artha*) means sense-fields (*viṣaya*); they are called objects because they are reached (*aryante*) or known. The repetition of "five" is for the purpose of excluding the objects of the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). "The bases of the consciousnesses of those [objects]"—the word "those" (*tat*) refers back to the objects. Consciousnesses regarding those objects, or of those objects, are "the consciousnesses of those"; the bases of those are "the bases of the consciousnesses of those."

"Transparent matter" (*rūpaprasāda*) means that they are both matter (*rūpa*) and transparent (*prasāda*); thus, they are "transparent matters. By this qualification, the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is excluded. For the mind is also the support for its respective consciousness;

however, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "the [five] are co-nascent with them," the mind does not have the nature of matter (*rūpasvabhāva*), and for this reason it is excluded.

If it is argued that the inclusion of the term "form" (*rūpa*) here is for the purpose of excluding faith (*śraddhā*), since there would be no application of faith by means of the qualification "they are the supports of that consciousness," [we reply:
no.
Since the assumption of a *bahuvrīhi* compound would entail that consequence,
the assumption of a *bahuvrīhi* is precluded when "form" (*rūpa*) is mentioned;
for there is no translucent matter (*prasāda*) consisting of form upon which those consciousnesses could be conceived as depending.
Furthermore, the mention of "clarity" (*prasāda*) is for the purpose of making known a specific kind of clarity that is distinct from the objects perceivable by the sense faculties;
for the Vaibhāṣikas assert that the sense faculties are merely specific transformations of the primary elements (*bhūta*).
But in the teaching (pravacana), it is not thus; rather,
the sense-faculties (indriya) are distinct from objects such as form, transparent, beyond the reach of the senses, and inferable from their own cognitions.
The qualification "those for whom the bases such as the eye are seen" and "the supports of their respective consciousnesses" is intended to prevent confusion regarding their mutual characteristics;
for if he had merely said, "the eyes and so forth are translucent matter," [the distinction would not have been clear].
Is it the eye, or the ear and so forth, that is the "eye"?
Because it is specified thus:
"that translucent matter which is the support of visual consciousness."
Therefore, that is called "the eye," and thus there is no confusion of characteristics;
for neither the ear nor any other sense organ is the basis for visual consciousness.
In this same manner, up to the point of the basis of tangible-object consciousness, that translucent matter which is the support is to be called the body-faculty,
as stated by the Blessed One.
The intention is that this explanation follows the Sūtra; how so?
"Internal" (ādhyātmika) means that which is the support of consciousness (vijñāna).
For it will be stated that the word "self" is used metaphorically for the mind;
[the term] *adhyātma* means "with reference to the self," and that which pertains to the internal (*adhyātma*) is precisely *ādhyātmika*.
The meaning of the word "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) is stated as "the cause for that which is to be produced in the self characterized by mind";
that is to say, it refers to the basis of consciousness (*vijñānāśraya*).
Alternatively, the detailed explanation begins with the words "those which... (*yāni*).
Alternatively, by that word "that," the sense-faculties are intended;
for this is well-established in the scriptures as "eye-consciousness," "ear-consciousness," and so forth,
but not as "form-consciousness" or "sound-consciousness."
However, such a thing might occasionally occur in the world;
therefore, this alternative explanation is resorted to,
and so he says:
And by doing so, the treatise (*prakaraṇagrantha*) is also followed in detail:
"How is that which is unestablished here proven by means of that which is itself unestablished?
For the eye itself is indeed unestablished."
If that [support] is not established, then visual consciousness is also not established;
how then can it be proven by that [support] to have it as its basis?
These five specific types of consciousness are indeed already established.
However, for the purpose of characterizing their mutual distinctions, we demonstrate them by distinguishing those [faculties] through the eye and so forth;
what is meant is this:
that translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which is the support of this first, singular, self-cognizable specific consciousness.
That faculty of the eye,
and so on up to that translucent matter which is the basis for this fifth specific consciousness that is self-cognizable, is the body-faculty (kāyendriya).
The proof of the unestablished by means of the unestablished is not valid;
for instance, the claim that "the object of the eye is of two kinds because of the distinction between color and shape" [is unestablished].
Since that [color] is well-known in the world, its specific characteristic is not stated; rather, only its classification is explained:
"color is of four kinds, beginning with blue," namely, blue, red, yellow, and white are the colors.
Others explain that "others" refers to the various types of those [clouds], such as *abhra* and so forth.

Other variations of that [color] arise from specific combinations of the four primary colors, such as blue and so forth; thus, not only clouds and the like, but also the color of a crow’s egg and so on are produced.
This "configuration" (saṃsthāna) is a particularity of shape.
Furthermore, that very same [category] is divided into twenty types by way of internal subdivisions,
namely: blue, yellow, and so forth.
Shape is of eight kinds, from long to irregular;
the remaining twelve kinds are color; thus [the elements] are of twenty types, and space is of one color.
That which is seen from afar, having the appearance of a beryl wall—
round, circular, globular, and wheel-like.

The statement "where there is the perception of forms that are elevated, such as those with a coarse nature, or depressed, such as those with a low-lying nature" is intended to demonstrate the distinction between shadow and darkness.
The meaning is that it has not been elaborated nor analyzed.
This is what is investigated here:
if clouds and so forth are merely distinctions within the fourfold set of colors such as blue and do not exist apart from them.
Just as the colors such as "crow-egg" and so forth are not mentioned here,
so too should clouds and the like not be mentioned;
this has not been considered by the commentators.
However, it can indeed be said that because they resemble illusory forms, those clouds and so forth, although consisting of distinctions such as blue and other colors,
are mentioned separately; for they appear like walls from a distance, yet when one approaches them closely, they are no longer seen.
Let it not occur to anyone that this is nothing at all,
or that there is doubt about it.
These clouds and so forth are mentioned in order to eliminate the doubt regarding that [appearance], as to whether it exists or is merely an illusion.
These indeed exist as having the nature of the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*); "the region of length and so forth" means the region extending from length up to thickness.
Which is that region? He says:
"having the nature of bodily intimation" (*kāyavijñaptisvabhāva*).
For bodily intimation is sometimes long, sometimes short, and sometimes even irregular (*visātā*).
Furthermore, how is that [bodily action] to be understood?
It is that bodily action which is originated by a mind having that [shape] as its object;
however, it should be understood that what lacks the nature of bodily action—such as length and so forth—is excluded.
There remains that which is twofold,
namely that which has been excluded, such as "long" and so forth.
For clouds, smoke, dust, and mist are indeed seen; since there is a discernment of length and so forth among blue and other colors,
there is the apprehension of long and other spatial configurations within the shadows and darknesses of blue, yellow, red, white, and gloom.
Therefore, the intention is that these too are included within the third alternative (koṭi).
But how can a single substance exist in both ways?
How can a single substance consist of both color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna)?
For it is your established tenet that the form of configuration (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*) is a distinct substance from the form of color (*varṇa-rūpa*),
because both are perceived therein, since both color and configuration are apprehended there.
For this [word] *vid* has the meaning of "knowledge" and not the meaning of "existence";

the sense is that this form belongs to the verbal root *vid* meaning "to know," which takes the *luṅ* (class 6) conjugational suffix (*vikaraṇa*), and not to the verbal root *vid* meaning "to exist," which takes the *śyan* (class 4) conjugational suffix.
"In that case, cognition proceeds with both aspects, but there is no single substance possessing two characteristics"— this is the Vaibhāṣika rebuttal;
however, the Master [Vasubandhu] argues that this consequence would then apply even to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*).
For when bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is being apprehended, the apprehension of color does not fail to occur;
this is the intention of the Vaibhāṣikas:
that the apprehension of blue and so forth, or the apprehension of light, occurs independently of shape (*saṃsthāna*).
However, the apprehension of bodily intimation proceeds independently of color,
whereas the apprehension of the remaining bases of form proceeds in dependence upon both color and shape;
thus, this teacher, who follows the Sautrāntika position, does not accept this point.
For this apprehension of shape is not visual;
rather, it is a mental construction,
for shape is indeed nothing other than a particular arrangement of color.
There is no such substance as shape (*saṃsthāna*); for when color is not perceived, there is no perception of shape,
and this will be examined in the section on action (*karman*) in the Abhidharmakośa.
The phrase "designated as sentient and non-sentient" means that it consists of vocal intimation (vāg-vijñapti) as sound and that which is distinct from it;
some read the text as "reckoned as sentient and non-sentient."
And this alone is the intended meaning here;

for if the intended meaning were "arising from the continuum of sentient beings or non-sentient beings," then the subsequent explanation to be stated— namely, that "the sound of vocal intimation is called 'sentient,' while other sounds are called 'non-sentient'"— would be entirely purposeless.
Therefore, the reading "and that which is called sentient and non-sentient" should be clearly recited;
[regarding the phrase] "having as its cause the appropriated great elements," the "appropriated" refers to the present elements that are inseparable from the sense faculties.

"Having the great elements (mahābhūta) as its cause that are appropriated or not appropriated" means that these [sounds] have as their cause the great elements which are either appropriated or not appropriated,
such as the sound of the hand or the voice.
If it is intended that [the sound] arises from the continuum of a sentient being,

then even an externally emanated form in human shape might produce the sound of words with its hands; and that [sound] should be understood as having for its cause the primary elements (mahābhūta) that are not appropriated (anupātta), because it exists apart from the sense faculties (indriya).
And he may even speak human speech according to the will of the creator; for it is said that when one speaks,
all those who have been created speak as well.
When one person remains silent, they all become silent;

and regarding that externally produced sound, it is caused by the unappropriated great elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta-hetuka*), as in the case of the sounds of wind, forest trees, and rivers. This is what is included here.
Just as sound is used for the purpose of illustration, that which is called "sentient" refers to vocal intimation-sound, while that which is "non-sentient" refers to other [sounds]; thus,
it is explained as "sentient" because it pertains to sentient beings.
For it is by means of the sound of vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti-śabda*) that this is recognized as a sentient being;

excluding that sound of vocal intimation, any other sound—even the sound of a hand—is designated as "non-sentient," let alone that which is born from a non-sentient continuum (*asattva-santāna*). Thus it is explained.

Thus, that which has appropriated primary elements as its cause is designated as "sentient" (sattvākhya) or "non-sentient" (asattvākhya). Furthermore, even that which has non-appropriated primary elements as its cause—such as the sound of emanations (nirmita), which is of the nature of vocal intimation (vāg-vijñapti)—is designated as "sentient";
whereas the sound of one's own hands, or the sounds of wind, trees, and so forth, is designated as "non-sentient."
Sound is of four kinds, which become eightfold again through the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant;
however, unlike a single atom of color,
sound does not exist by depending on two sets of the four primary elements.
The meaning is that, because it is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), it is like a color-atom (*varṇaparamāṇu*); thus,
"taste is sixfold."
With reference specifically to the six fundamental types [of taste], it has been stated thus:

due to the particular mutual combinations of the six tastes, an exceedingly great variety of tastes arise; for indeed, in the *Caraka-saṃhitā*, sixty-three tastes are taught through the conjunctions of combinations of one, two, three, four, five, and all six.
"Because of the equality or inequality of fragrance between pleasant and unpleasant odors" means because of the non-intense or intense nature of the fragrance;
in this view, fragrance is held to be of two kinds.
"But the treatise is threefold" means that there is another, a third, which is "equal to the fragrance";
others, however, explain it differently.
"Uniform fragrance" means that it is simply one part of those two [fragrances]; thus the meaning remains the same,
though the terminology differs, as in "coldness" versus "that which produces a desire for warmth."
With reference to its arising, it is said thus:
that dharma which produces heat and desire is the form derived from what is called "cold."

Even if one does not experience that [hunger] in summer, it should nevertheless be understood as cold itself because it belongs to the same class; this is due to the metaphorical designation of the effect by the name of the cause.
Hunger (*jighatsā*) is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*).
The cause of that is the derived matter (upādāyarūpa) called hunger, which is touched by the body-faculty (kāyendriya) within the belly.
Just as the arising of Buddhas is called "bliss" because it is the cause of the bliss of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*) and the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*),
so too should thirst be described in the same way.
The intention here is that when accumulated [substances] are weighed again, it is because they possess the nature of subtle heaviness (*sūkṣmagurutva*).
The inference in this regard is that clothing and so forth belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) possess heaviness.
Because of the relationship between the container and the contained,
like a bowl and a jujube fruit,
there is indeed that which bestows grace.

The word "kila" (it is said) is for the purpose of indicating the Vaibhāṣika position; however, our own view is that concentration alone is the supportive factor here— what is the use of this imagined cold?
"When there is the exclusion of that particular mode" means when there is the mental engagement with the causes for modes such as blue and so forth;
in this way, it applies to auditory consciousness and the others as well.

Regarding this manifold sound that has been described, auditory consciousness is sometimes produced by a single substance when there is a differentiation of its specific type, and sometimes by many substances when there is no such differentiation.
For example, just as for one hearing a collection of musical sounds consisting of various forms of sound such as high and low pitches,
so too should the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses be applied to their respective objects;
however, the tactile consciousness consists of at most five [types].
How is it that sometimes it arises from a single substance? It is when there is a delimitation of its specific type;
sometimes from two, up to five, when there is no such delimitation.
And as for [the claim] that it is due to one quality such as smoothness,
what is the reason for this?
It is because qualities such as roughness depend upon a different set of four primary elements (*bhūta*).
"But is it not the case," and so forth in detail:

just as mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is established as having a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) for its object because it grasps the objects of visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses by synthesizing them together, so too,

since a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) grasps those four— whether many or few— objects of the four visual consciousnesses that have blue, yellow, red, and white as their respective objects by synthesizing them, it follows that this [visual consciousness] would also have a general characteristic for its object.
Considering that the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*) is its object,
the same should be applied to auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses with respect to their own respective objects,
namely, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense-fields.
One's own characteristic is the *svalakṣaṇa*;
the specific characteristic of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is the *āyatanasvalakṣaṇa*,
such as being cognizable by visual consciousness, and so forth.

Alternatively, these five groups of consciousness are held in the teaching to have the sense-spheres (āyatana) as their objects by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), namely the sense-sphere of form and so forth;
it is not the case that they are held to have the substantial own-characteristic (*dravyasvalakṣaṇa*) as their object— this is the point under discussion.

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of substances such as blue and so forth is either their being cognizable by visual consciousness and the like through the aspect of blue and so on, or the aspect of blue itself; since these five groups of consciousness are not asserted to have that [specific characteristic] as their object, there is no fault.
Regarding the phrase "when objects are encountered simultaneously":
it is possible for the body-faculty and the tongue-faculty to encounter their respective objects at the same time,
yet it is not possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously.
Therefore, he asks: "Which consciousness arises first?"— namely,
that whose object is more intense.
If the object of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is more intense, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises first;
if the object of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) is more intense, tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*) arises first;
but when the objects are equally attained, they are simultaneous—this is the meaning.
Why does tongue-consciousness arise first?
Because the mental continuum is inclined toward the desire to eat.
The meaning is that because the physical body is inclined toward the desire for food,
as stated previously that "tongue-consciousness arises first," it follows by implication that "body-consciousness will arise later";
therefore, this is investigated here.
Is that body-momentary-object which was encountered simultaneously with the tongue-momentary-object where that body-consciousness arises,
or is it in another body-consciousness-momentary-object?
He says, "In another [case]";
how is the restriction of the object not violated?
This is not a fault.
That consciousness which has that object as its focal point is ceased through non-analytical cessation,
yet another body-consciousness similar to it arises.
Therefore, it is said that it arises after that, by means of a metaphorical attribution of oneness based on the commonality of its birth;
because it has been separated by the manifold elaborations of various discourses, the section concerning the enumeration of non-manifestation (avijñapti) is as if lost,
and for this reason, he introduces the following.
The five sense objects and the manner of their apprehension have been explained; as for the statement "sometimes visual consciousness arises from a single substance," and so forth,
the genitive case in the word *teṣām* (of them) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
Now, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) must be explained.
Since matter consists of the five sense-faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter itself, it is non-informative matter alone that remains;
therefore, it must be explained as the occasion for the definition of its characteristics.
Some read the commentary as "of one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind";
in this reading, the analysis of the Sūtra is as follows.
One who has no distracted mind is "one without a distracted mind" (*vikṣiptācittaka*);
alternatively, one who has either a distracted mind or no mind at all is "one without a distracted mind. In this case, there is the elision of one instance of the word *citta*.
Some read it thus:
"of the distracted" (*vikṣiptasya*);
in this reading, having first formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the two subsequent words, the analysis (*vigraha*) is subsequently performed as follows.
"Distraught and without mind" means "the distraught person whose mind is distraught.
"Of one whose mind is distraught" means "also of one whose mind is other than that," which is to say, of one whose mind is other than an undistraught mind.
For example, the mind that originates a wholesome unmanifest [action] is wholesome;
one whose mind is other than that— namely, one with an unwholesome or neutral mind—
is intended here as "one whose mind is distracted."
However, for unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*), the motivating mind is unwholesome;
it should be understood that at other times, when one possesses a wholesome or neutral mind, or even a distracted mind, [the non-informative action continues].

The phrase "even for one whose mind is directed elsewhere, or even for one who is without mind" means that by the word "even," it is understood to include one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as one whose mind is undistracted and possessed of mind; thus,
the meaning is that this applies even to a third person distinct from these two types of individuals.
The meaning is that "continuity" (*anubandha*) refers to a "stream" (*pravāha*), which is a phenomenon characterized by a constant flow; here,
the stream-bearer is indicated by means of the stream, because it is to be identified by the stream.
Alternatively, "anubandha" means that which binds along;

it is a term of explanation meaning "stream" (*pravāha*). Having formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound, [it refers to] a phenomenon (*dharma*) for which there is a "flow" (*vāha*)—that is, one that has proceeded (*pravṛtta*) or is excellent (*prakṛṣṭa*). Thus, it is a "stream" (*pravāha*).
That very [stream] is specified;
it is not the case that the stream itself is wholesome or unwholesome.
The restriction "only wholesome and unwholesome" means that there is no neutral [state];
by this, it should be understood that the eyes and so forth are excluded.

Since there is also such a continuous flow of acquisition (*prāpti*), its acquisition likewise flows even for one whose mind is distracted or undistracted, and it is exclusively wholesome or unwholesome; therefore, in order to distinguish it [from that], it is said:
"derived from the great elements" (*mahābhūtāny upādāya*).
The meaning is that it has the great elements as its cause; just as when it is said, "fire exists depending upon fuel," it is understood that fire has fuel as its cause.
"Because of being the cause of birth and so forth" means:
it is the cause of birth because [the elements] give rise to it from them, by way of generating, supporting, maintaining, sustaining, and nourishing.
The cause of reliance (*niśraya-hetu*) is so called because that which has arisen conforms to the primary elements (*bhūta*), like relying on a teacher and others;
the cause of support (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*) is due to its state as a foundation, like a wall for a painting;
and the cause of sustenance (*upastambha-hetu*) is because it is a cause of non-interruption.
What are the great elements upon which [it] depends as its cause of nourishment— given that it is a cause of growth—
and what are the great elements that serve as its basis?
Or rather, they say that the "great elements of reliance" are the "great elements of the basis," for the purpose of making known the designation of that name.

The meaning is that it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*) because, although its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of form and action, it does not inform another like informative action (*vijñapti*).
For what purpose are both qualifiers—"although its intrinsic nature consists of form and action"—used?
[It is to exclude] that entity which has the intrinsic nature of form alone, but not the intrinsic nature of action.
That which does not cause [the object] to be perceived,
such as the eye and so forth,
is also of the nature of activity alone and not of the nature of form.
Even that does not lead to the ultimate,
such as volition;
however, that which possesses the nature of both [is different].
That makes another understand;

for example, communication (vijñapti) communicates to another the mind that has originated it—whether that mind be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, gentle, cruel, or neither. Thus it makes another understand.
"Therefore, [it is] like informative [action]" (*vijñaptivat*) is an application of a dissimilar example (*viparīta-dṛṣṭānta*).
"In brief" (*samāsatas tu*) means that,
for the sake of the student's easy understanding, the Master (*ācārya*) shows that nature of non-informative action (*avijñapti-rūpa*) concisely by means of this statement.
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is wholesome or unwholesome matter produced from informative action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
this should be applied according to the circumstances as follows:
it is wholesome matter produced from bodily and vocal informative action, comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint, or comprised within neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint.
Furthermore, the unwholesome is comprised within non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) or comprised within neither restraint nor non-restraint; however,
that which arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is exclusively wholesome,
and it is of two kinds.

It has the nature of derived matter (upādāyarūpa), being of the nature of the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyānasaṃvara) produced from contaminated concentration (sāsravasamādhi), and of the nature of the untainted restraint (anāsravasaṃvara) produced from untainted concentration (anāsravasamādhi).
It should be understood that [unmanifest form] does not have the nature of mind, mental factors, and so forth;
but would it not follow, then, that even manifest action (vijñapti) would be unmanifest?
For that too is produced from a preceding manifest action that has become its homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Because of the restriction that it is "only wholesome or unwholesome," there is no over-extension to informative action (*vijñapti*),
for informative action can also be neutral (*avyākṛta*).

For this very reason, even though the divine eye and ear arise from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are derived matter born of informative action, they do not entail being non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
In this regard, the master Saṅghabhadra refutes this sūtra on the definition of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), stating:
"It is deficient and devoid of the treatise; a loss of its meaning follows, as there is the addition of the word 'also' (*api*) and the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is left unqualified here."
For "continuity" (*anubandha*) has been explained as a stream (*pravāha*);
and the first moment is not the stream, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, since that [first moment] is not included here by the definition, [the definition] is deficient.

Furthermore, since a stream (*pravāha*) is not a substantial entity (*adravyatva*), it follows that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) would be non-substantial; thus, it would contradict the treatise (*śāstra*).

Moreover, for one who is in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), there is no continuity (*anubandha*) for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind (*acittaka*); consequently, that non-informative matter would not be established, which is a flaw.
If you argue that this fault does not apply because there is a continuity of that [non-informative matter] for one whose mind is not distracted, [we reply:]...

It follows that for a virtuous or non-virtuous representation (vijñapti), there would be the consequence of it having the characteristic of a non-representation (avijñapti); thus, its reality would follow even for one who is without mind (acittaka). Furthermore, the word "also" (api) is redundant because its purpose has already been fulfilled by the preceding phrase;
for by the phrase "even for one whose mind is distracted" (vikṣiptacittaka), all states involving a mind are already included.
What other state, moreover,
could be included by the second word "also" (api), such that the mention of the word "also" would be superfluous? What other state is there?

Since that which would be included by the second *api* (also) is already expressed by the word *api*, the mention of it as "additional" (*adhika*) is redundant; furthermore, with reference to the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), the connection with virtuous non-informative matter (*śubhā-vijñapti-anubandha*) ought to have been specified,
yet it was not specified even in the commentary— thus, what was to be qualified remains unqualified.
Furthermore, this other qualification, "unimpeded matter" (*apratighaṃ rūpam*), remains unspecified;
thus, because it is corrupted by many such defects, this definition is not coherent.
To this, we reply:
As for what was stated— that because the continuum is taught as non-informative (avijñapti), the first moment would not be non-informative—
this person should first be asked:
what is this so-called "continuum"?
If the term "stream" (pravāha) refers to many moments,
then the first moment also would be established as a stream,
because [the definition] holds that a stream consists of many moments beginning from the first moment.
For instance, the designation "flow" (pravāha) applies to the water emerging from a spring or a pond, beginning with the very first particles of water;
thus, there is no lack of pervasiveness in the definition.
Furthermore, when one says "it follows" (anubadhnāti), the word "continuity" (anubandha)—ending in the *ac*-suffix—refers to the substance itself.
At that time, there is not even the slightest suspicion of deficiency;
for this very reason, the fault of deviating from the scriptures is also avoided.
Furthermore, it is called a "stream" (*srotas*) because it is a succession of successions (*anubandhānām anubandha*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault here because it falls under the category of matter (*rūpa*);
however, because it exists as a continuous flow, it is indicated by the term "flow.
Thus, even for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) that is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), there is no failure to include it.

For although that [non-informative action] does not continue through a continuum that is distracted or without mind, it certainly continues through a continuum that is undistracted and possessed of mind;
however, because of the commonality of its genus as non-informative action, that which follows even for one who is distracted or without mind is called "non-informative action" (avijñapti).
As for what was said—
"If it is argued that this fault does not apply because it is a consequence for one whose mind is undistracted"—
if [it refers to] the consequence belonging solely to one whose mind is undistracted;

You say that this [non-informative action] is also non-informative (*avijñapti*), and thus there is no abandonment of the non-informative action associated with meditative absorption (*samāhita*); you further state that informative action (*vijñapti*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—is likewise [non-informative], and thus it follows that it would be non-informative for you.
But that too is not a fault, because of the restriction that it is "only" wholesome or unwholesome.
For since informative action (*vijñapti*) can indeed be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it does not follow that informative action is non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
or else, this undesirable consequence will not arise because of the attainment of excellence (*prakarṣagati*).
For that which is a continuous succession in an intensified manner is precisely the non-informative (avijñapti);
and informative action (vijñapti), unlike the non-informative, does not continue in an intensified manner.
Even with respect to the non-informative [matter], because its cessation is observed,
that which was said—
that the word "also" (*api*) is an excessive statement— is [refuted].
That too is incorrectly stated;
for although the word "api" is read only once here in the sūtra,
in the commentary (vṛtti) its meaning is connected with those two types of persons, and thus it is read twice again.

By means of that single word "api" (also/even) recited in the Sūtra, the Master—by stating that very third type of person, who possesses mind (*sacittaka*), as the basis for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in contrast to the distracted and the contrary—demonstrates that the two types of persons previously mentioned by his own name, namely the distracted and the one without mind, are the basis for non-informative matter by virtue of their common nature; thus he declares that non-informative matter is an entity distinct from informative matter, mind, and mental factors.
For there are only three types of persons: one whose mind is dissimilar to the informative matter, one whose mind is similar to the informative matter, and the one without mind.

In this context, "one whose mind is distracted" refers to one whose mind is of a different nature from that of informative action (*vijñapti*); for such a person, those vocal and bodily informative actions have ceased.
However, in the case of one who is without mind (*acittaka*), even the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have ceased.
In this regard, this non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is a distinct entity from the informative [action] (*vijñapti*) and from the complex of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitasika-kalāpa*),
because it is distinguished from these by way of its continuity;
demonstrating that very point, he says:
Regarding the phrase "even for one whose mind is distracted":
it is not a special case that non-informative action (avijñapti) occurs for one whose mind is undistracted,
for informative action (vijñapti) also occurs for such a person.
However, the distinction is that [the non-informative] continues even for one whose mind is distracted;
for such a person there is no informative action (*vijñapti*),
yet the non-informative (*avijñapti*) persists as a continuous connection, and thus it is distinguished from the informative.
Likewise, it is not a distinguishing feature that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) continues for one whose mind is distracted,
for his mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) also certainly continue.
However, the fact that it continues even for one who is without mind (*acittaka*) is indeed a distinguishing feature.
For in that state, the mind and mental factors have ceased, yet the non-informative [matter] persists; thus it is distinguished from the mind and mental factors.

Therefore, in order to distinguish it as a separate entity, even when one is in a state of undistracted mind, or when one is without mind, or in the third stage [of meditative attainment], it is designated by that single word "also" (*api*).

For this very reason, the Master used the word "also" (*api*) to indicate that [the state occurs] even for one whose mind is not distracted and who possesses a mind (*sacittaka*), because this constitutes the third case;
otherwise, he would have said either "even for one whose mind is not distracted" (*avikṣiptacittakasyāpi*) or "even for one who possesses a mind" (*sacittakasyāpi*).

For example, suppose there are three men in the world: one is wealthy, and the other two possess only a small amount of wealth. Having observed them, when one person says that Viṣṇumitra’s wealth surpasses [that of the others], the second person would likewise speak.

The meaning is as follows: by the word *api* in the phrase "Devadatta and Yajñadatta also have wealth," Viṣṇumitra is also indicated (*lakṣyate*)— even though that *api* has, as it were, entered into a state of duality relative to Devadatta and Yajñadatta— but he is not explicitly released (*avasṛjyate*).
Therefore, the word "api" (also/even) here is indeed redundant;
likewise, it should be understood here as well regarding that which was further stated:
And with reference to that which is without thought (*acittaka*), it must be specified that there is a connection with a pure non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
yet even this is nothing, for this definition, even when specified by this qualification, applies to the entire class of non-informative action.

In your own system as well, regarding the unmanifest (avijñapti) characterized by suchness, the connection with pure unmanifest [form] is not specified with respect to the state of being without thought (acittaka);
for it is held that even when a dissimilar mind has arisen or when there is a cessation of thought,
that which is informative, non-obstructive form is indeed accepted as the unmanifest.
Thus,

it will be explained in the fourth chapter of the Kośa that this unmanifest [form] (*avijñapti*), which arises from manifest [action] (*vijñapti*) and is exclusively wholesome, occurs even for one who is without thought;
and that it is "without resistance" (*apratigha*) without further qualification.
We shall demonstrate that as well later on,
in the section where it is established by restriction that "the ten material elements are with resistance" (*sapratigha*), thereby showing that only these ten elements possess resistance.
Non-informative matter (avijñapti) is recited in the list of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu),
and it will be established that it is non-obstructive (apratigha);
therefore, this definition of non-informative matter belonging to our own school is thus free from fault.
"Let it be just so:
'the elements are the earth-element,' and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "element" (dhātu) is for the purpose of excluding earth and the other elements when they consist merely of color and shape.
They are called *dhātus* because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Thus, they are *dhātus* because they maintain hardness and other such specific characteristics, as well as the derived matter of the eye and so forth.
Furthermore, the eighteen *dhātus* are so called because they maintain their own specific and general characteristics (*svasāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

Alternatively, the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*) is the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*), or, disregarding the sense of "sustaining," in the teaching of the six elements, the meaning of "element" is the sense of being the seed of renewed existence; for they nourish existence. Their "greatness" is due to their being the basis for all other forms of matter (*rūpa*) and because of their grossness.

The meaning is that it is "great" because it serves as the basis for all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). Regarding the phrase "in those whose functions are manifested," it means those in which the functions— such as supporting (*dhṛti*) and so forth— are manifested, that is, made manifest, by those great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air have their functions manifested therein;
because these great elements (mahābhūtas) possess great structural arrangements and great compositions, they extend what is real, and thus they are called "elements" (bhūtas).

"Perfectly established through the functions of support and so forth" is a designation of the functions of support and so forth among earth and the other elements, for the purpose of inferring the remainder;
for, since cohesion, maturation, and expansion are observed in the substance of earth such as a stone, the existence of the remaining elements— water, fire, and air— is inferred.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the existence of earth, fire, and wind is established by the observation of the functions of supporting, heating, and moving in water; and the existence of earth, water, and fire is established by the observation of stability, cohesion, and motion in a flame.
Furthermore, "expansion" (*vyūhana*) means growth; "creeping forth" (*prasarpaṇa*) is the production of bodies and so forth in another location through a continuous series;
and regarding "heat" (*uṣṇatā*), although it is a designation for an essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is expressed with an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).
Heat itself is the nature of heat;
because it arises in another location, like the movement of a lamp-flame,
there is no traveling to another location for momentary things, since they arise precisely where they exist.
Destruction occurs in that very same place;
therefore,
it is said that the movement of the stream of primary elements has the nature of producing [them] in another location.
Because they are momentary,
like a lamp,
the primary elements are also momentary.
Because it is a form (*rūpa*),
like a lamp;
and since a lamp is well-known to be momentary (*kṣaṇika*), this serves as the example.
Since its intrinsic nature is manifested through action,
lightness is distinguished by the action of motion—
that lightness which consists of the nature of motion.

Regarding that wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*), which is lightness and motion: since in the teaching (*pravacana*) that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) which is itself light is spoken of as the earth-element and so forth, as well as "earth" and so forth, he therefore asks.
What, then, is the distinction between these? It is by way of worldly designation (*lokasañjñā*) or by way of worldly convention (*lokasaṃvyavahāra*);
"vātyā" is a collection (*samūha*) of winds (*vāta*).
The suffix *yan* in [the word] *brāhmaṇyādi* is applied in the sense of a collection according to the rule *brāhmaṇādibhyo yan*;
furthermore, because it denotes a feminine gender, the suffix *cāp* is applied.
For it has been stated thus in the *Arthavargīya*: [text follows].
The *Arthavargīya* sūtras are recited in the *Kṣudraka*; therein it is said,
"If he, being full of desire," and so forth.
If the desires of that embodied being— who is full of longing and born of his own will— are not fulfilled, do not come to pass,
then he is tormented as if pierced by an arrow; the meaning is that he is afflicted.

In the sutra passage, "O monks, it is called 'form' (rūpyate) because it is broken (rūpyate) by this [sensation] which is delimited by the sense of affliction," the word *rūpyate* is determined to have the meaning of affliction alone;
for it is logical that one who is pierced by an arrow and one who is possessed by desire are afflicted because they experience suffering.
But how is form (*rūpa*) afflicted?
Therefore he says,
"producing transformation," which means producing change.
And thus, since this meaning holds true here— namely,
that "one is perceived as if pierced by an arrow"— if the meaning "it undergoes modification" is also accepted, the sense becomes even more appropriate.
Resistance (*pratighāta*) is the obstruction of another’s arising in one’s own location;
[if that is so,] then what is the nature of an atom?
The form that is a substantial atom does not qualify as form,
because it lacks the quality of being affected (arūpaṇa).
The intention is that, because there is no material transformation (*arūpaṇa*) when there is partlessness (*niravayavatva*),
this objection is presented against both positions:

namely, that a substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*), due to its partlessness, cannot be subject to material transformation— whether in the form of being struck down (*bādhana*) or in the form of resistance (*pratighāta*).
Indeed, there is no single atom existing as a separate entity; thus,
the apprehension of it as "one" is for the purpose of illustrating the substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*), meaning that it exists separately, not within a composite aggregate.
Is there anything of such a kind that, while existing within an aggregate, is eternal? [No. In the desire realm, that which is without sound consists of eight substances.

From such statements as these, it follows by implication that that which exists within an aggregate (*saṅghāta*) is indeed subject to transformation (*rūpyate*); thus, this is intended to mean that the form of a substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu-rūpa*), when situated within an aggregate, is transformed, obstructed, and struck.
"In that case, the past and the future... and so forth;
because the past and the future lack spatial location (*adeśatva*), they are not transformed (*na rūpyate*), they are not obstructed (*na bādhyate*), nor are they impeded (*na pratihanyate*);
"that too," and so forth.
That too is "material" (rūpita) in the sense of having been affected by past obstruction and resistance,
and it will be "materialized" (rūpayiṣyamāṇa) in the sense of those same two meanings for that which possesses the nature of arising in the future.

And "of that same kind" means belonging to the class of things characterized by the property of arising; thus, even that which has not yet arisen—belonging to the class of things characterized by the property of non-arising—is fuel, just like wood.
Furthermore, that which has already burned and that which will burn hereafter are also of that same kind, and therefore they too are fuel.
Furthermore, regarding fuel of that same kind which, having been intended for the purpose of fuel, perishes in the interim without even reaching the fire:
in that case, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) would not qualify as form (*rūpa*).
Why?
Because it does not go back;
for by virtue of its non-retrogression, it is neither obstructed nor repelled,
since that [mind] also consists of representation and formative transformation— this is the detailed explanation.
Informative action (vijñapti) is that which originates non-informative action (avijñapti);
because that [informative action] is subject to transformation (rūpaṇā), the non-informative action is also transformed,
just as the shadow moves when the tree that produces it moves.
In the same way,
by the phrase "not because of non-modification," a defect in the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) is raised.
For another has indeed asserted that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) conforms to the transformations of its own producer because it is something produced.
"The statement 'like the shadow of a tree' contradicts his own prior admission;
for he has admitted that even when there is a transformation of the informative [action], there is no transformation of the non-informative [action]."

For instance, when one breaks the *añjali* gesture and forms the *kapota* gesture, it is accepted that the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) undergoes a transformation, but not the non-intimation (*avijñapti*). Therefore, the argument that "upon the cessation of the intimation, there would be a cessation of the non-intimation" is not a valid proof; furthermore, by this very point, a contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣa-viparyaya*) is also raised against this proposition.
If it is maintained that this has the nature of a tree's shadow— since it is observed that when the tree ceases, the shadow ceases—
and thus it would be like that, someone objects: "No, because there is no modification," thereby pointing out that what was said is not correct.

It is claimed that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is indeed modified when there is a modification of informative action (*vijñapti*), because when the informative action is weak, medium, or intense, the non-informative action likewise becomes weak, medium, or intense;
however, this is incorrect.
Why is it that the arising of non-informative matter itself occurs in this way— as weak, medium, or intense?
But it is not a modification;
for modification is the production again in another way of a dharma that has already arisen,
and that is what is intended by "formability" (rūpaṇa).
"Because it is based on the primary elements (bhūta)," says another— namely, the elder master Vasubandhu;
he states that the mention of "elements" is for the purpose of demonstrating the basis (*āśraya*).
Therefore, the other [opponent] raises an objection:
"In that case, the same would apply to visual consciousness and the others," and so forth;
for since the bases such as the eye are material (*rūpaṇāt*), it follows that those consciousnesses would also be material.
"This is an uneven comparison," says a certain teacher following the tradition of the elder master Vasubandhu, offering a rebuttal:
"For the non-informative [action]... and so forth.
Just as a shadow exists by clinging to and depending upon a tree, and light likewise exists in relation to a gem,
so too those [causes] are merely the conditions for the arising of those [effects].
The sense is that they are not connected;
to this, the other replies:
"This, first of all, is not the Vaibhāṣika position," and so forth.
This is not the Vaibhāṣika position;
rather, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, shadow consists of color-atoms that exist depending upon their own set of four primary elements, and not upon a tree;
likewise, light consists of color-atoms that exist depending upon their own set of four primary elements, and not upon a jewel.
Because they are separate substances,

and thus lack the relationship of a substratum and its cause, the shadow and the light do not adhere to the jewel and the tree in the same way that the unmanifest (avijñapti) adheres to the great elements; therefore, there is a lack of commonality between the example and the subject of the illustration, even though [the shadow and light] are dependent upon them— this is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, even if it is admitted that there is an indirect dependence upon it— namely,
that the shadow rests upon its own constituent elements (bhūta),
and those elements rest upon the tree.
The light, too, is dependent on its own primary elements (bhūta),
but those primary elements are dependent on the jewel because they conform to it.

Nevertheless, it is uncommon because it is admitted that even when the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the basis for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) have ceased, that [non-informative matter] itself does not cease; thus,
after the first moment, non-informative matter belonging to the desire realm is produced from past primary elements.
Since this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*),
that which was stated— "therefore this is not a valid refutation; for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is like a shadow to a tree," and so forth— is not tenable.
Others, however, offer a rebuttal here; thus, the Master himself, supporting that view, says:
"The basis has undergone a change."
The meaning is that it is twofold:
some things, such as the eye and so forth, are susceptible to transformation because they possess resistance; others, such as the mind, are not susceptible to transformation.
Therefore, because of the reversal [of the reason], the consequence is not the same;
"matter (rūpa) because of being matter" means because of the mattering of its basis.
Regarding this, they raise the objection: "If it is by such a process that the non-informative (avijñapti) arising from informative action (vijñapti) possesses the nature of form (rūpatva),
then how can that which arises from meditative concentration (samādhi) possess the nature of form?"
Because it belongs to that same class, that too is form; what, then, is this "belonging to that same class"?
The meaning is: by having the great elements as its basis.
Because they serve as the causes for the production of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) and so forth, those very things are the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*artha*).

Thus, according to the needs of those to be trained (*vineya*), the Blessed One gave three types of teaching: the teachings on the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).
And those very phenomena that were taught among the aggregates (skandhas) are the same as those taught among the bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu);
however, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena alone are additional here.
And since the entire Abhidharma is an exposition of the Sūtras,
it is therefore said:
"The faculties and their objects are those very same [as mentioned before]," and so forth.

Furthermore, this master, seeking brevity, demonstrates without explicitly stating the characteristics of the aggregates such as sensation that the phenomena whose intrinsic nature is the aggregate of form exist within the bases and elements;

he does so by means of the concise expression "the faculties and their objects," where the repetition of "faculties and their objects" serves as a qualification intended to exclude other faculties and other objects.

In the classification of the bases (*āyatana*), however, according to their respective order, there are ten bases: the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*), up to the body-base (*kāya-āyatana*) and the tangible-base (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*).

In the classification of the elements (*dhātu*), those same ten are the ten elements: the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*), the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*), up to the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*) and the tangible-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*).
Thus has the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) been explained, along with its classification into bases and elements.
Since it has not been stated that the entire aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is established as bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*)—
because non-informative form (*avijñaptirūpa*) will be discussed later—
how can this be said?

The statement "it has been said" is an indication made in the sense of frequency; the meaning is that the establishment of the aggregate of form as bases and elements has for the most part been explained.
Just as there is the designation "a heap of beans" even when only a few pea-particles are present, so too is experience threefold; thus,
*anubhūti* (the act of experiencing) is *anubhava* (experience), which is enjoyment (*upabhoga*).
Of what mind or person is that [state] threefold?

Is it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant? Abiding as it is, it is experienced by this [consciousness] as having the nature of directly realizing its own essence, which is free from joy, distress, and both;
thus it is called "experience" (*anubhava*).
Alternatively, "experience" (*anubhava*) means that which experiences;

others say it is a specific mental factor (*caitasika-viśeṣa*) occurring in states characterized by the increase or decrease of body and mind, or in states free from both, and is the experience of contact (*sparśa*).
Furthermore, the prefix *anu-* signifies a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), meaning it is the mark of contact.
The meaning is that the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) is the experience of the signs of contact;
its nature consists in the grasping of signs.
The sign (*nimitta*) is a specific state of an object, such as blueness;
its apprehension (*udgrahaṇa*) is its discernment (*pariccheda*); that which consists of this [apprehension] has that as its intrinsic nature (*tatsvabhāvā*).
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "suffering and so forth," blood and other such things are included;
this is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

If perception were essentially of the nature of discernment (*pariccheda*), then in its association with [the five sensory consciousnesses], it would grasp at signs (*nimitta*); consequently, all five groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) would be conceptual (*vikalpaka*).
They would not exist;
for perception associated with the five consciousnesses is not sharp,
whereas that associated with the body of mental consciousness is sharp— thus it alone is said to be conceptualizing.
The six groups of perception (*saṃjñākāya*) are like the [six] feelings (*vedanā*);
just as it was explained in detail that there is "feeling born of eye-contact," so too should it be stated in detail that there is "perception born of eye-contact."
"Other than the four" means that,
from among the four aggregates—

namely, the three aggregates beginning with the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) already mentioned, and the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) which has been indicated or will be explained— the formations (saṃskāra) other than these four constitute the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

Since it is stated in the Sūtra that "the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is what? and "it is the six groups of volition (cetanākāya)," [it follows that] the six groups of volition are the aggregate of formations.
They are predominant in formative activity;
for it is said that "karma is the cause of rebirths," meaning they are predominant in the formative activity [of thinking], "May I become thus and thus."

However, desire (*chanda*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and so forth, because they conform to volition (*cetanā*)—that is, by following its mode, cause, and state—should be understood as belonging to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) alone.
This being the case, it is said that a collection of phenomena (*dharmarāśi*) engaged in the act of forming is a "formation" (*saṃskāra*).
Others, however, say:

It has been stated that volition (*cetanā*) is primary in the conditioning of the conditioned; therefore, although the term "volition" is used in the Sūtra to include all conditioned phenomena— both associated and dissociated— it is this very aggregate alone that is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), because of its predominance.
Considering it to be "the aggregate of the conditioned," one conditions the conditioned; thus, by means of a future designation, the five aggregates of the future are called "conditioned.
For otherwise, as the detailed explanation goes...

If, according to the explanation in the Sūtra, volition alone is accepted as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and not the other remaining mental factors such as desire (*chanda*), nor the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) such as acquisition (*prāpti*), then these would not be included within the aggregates because they lack the defining characteristics of the aggregates, such as "being affected by transformation" (*rūpaṇā*) which applies to the aggregate of form and so forth.
Furthermore, because [ignorance] is not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) by taking the sūtra literally,
it would not be included among the aggregates; consequently, it would lack the status of being the truths of suffering and its origin.
Thus, thorough knowledge and abandonment would not occur;

for there is no thorough knowledge of suffering and no abandonment of its origin if one has not directly realized it by means of the worldly path and has not fully understood it by means of the supramundane path.

Alternatively, it is stated in another sutra that [suffering] is not abandoned without having seen through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and without having fully understood through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*):
"I do not say that there is an end to suffering without having fully understood even a single dharma and without having abandoned it."
The meaning is that I speak of the cessation of suffering.
But surely, space and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are not fully understood by the supramundane path;
nevertheless, the end of suffering is still desired [to occur].

There is no fault, because [the statement] refers to the basis of affliction (saṅkleśavastu) with intentional meaning (abhisandhi), and because, according to the Sautrāntika view, it exists as a conceptual designation (prajñaptisat);
for those two are not the actual bases of affliction.

If it is asked why these two— the truths of cessation and the path— are not also objects to be fully known (*parijñeya*) because they are not bases of affliction, [the answer is: although they are not bases of affliction,
their status as objects to be fully known is established because of their connection with the truths of suffering and its origin.
For it is in this way that yogis investigate: "What is the cessation of this suffering which has a cause, and by what means is that cessation attained?"
They also fully comprehend the truths of cessation and the path,
yet they do not fully comprehend space and analytical cessation because these two have no connection with suffering;
however, during the stage of preparatory application, they cultivate through mundane knowledge the realization that all phenomena, in their general form, are without self.
"Designated as the sphere-base and the element of phenomena" means:
both the base (*āyatana*) and the element (*dhātu*) are "base-element";
that which is both a phenomenon (*dharma*) and a base-element is the "phenomena-base-element" (*dharmāyatanadhātu*).

Because they are designated by that name, these— the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations— are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
"Along with the unmanifest and the unconditioned" means together with the unmanifest and the unconditioned [factors] such as space; thus,
in the teaching on the bases (*āyatana*), it is called the "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*).

And in the teaching on the elements (*dhātu-deśanā*), it is stated that there are seven substances, namely: the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*sañjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
"Consciousness is the individual representation"—
this is the meaning of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*); "individual representation" (*prativijñapti*) means that, because the context concerns the aggregates,
the prefix *prati* has the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*).
The meaning is that, depending upon each respective object (*viṣaya*),

there is apprehension (*upalabdhi*), which is the grasping of the mere thing (*vastu-mātra*); however, the mental factors (*caitasika*) such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth consist in the grasping of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
The "six groups of consciousness" (ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ) refers to the six collections of consciousness;
the "six consciousnesses" and also the "mind" (manas) refer to the six elements of consciousness (ṣaḍ vijñānadhātavaḥ), corresponding respectively to that which is eye-consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna).
That which is eye-consciousness-element is thus, up to: that which is mind-consciousness is the mind-consciousness-element.
All these six together should be understood as the mind-element (*manodhātu*);
for that consciousness which has immediately passed away from the six is the mind.
Here, the genitive case in "of the six" (*ṣaṇṇām*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*).
The meaning is that [the result arises] from those very [moments] themselves and not from anything else;

the mention of "immediately following" (anantara) is for the purpose of excluding what is intervened by another cognition, for [the result arises] from that which follows immediately after [its cause] without being intervened by another cognition.
That [immediately preceding moment] is its basis; however, that which is separated is not its basis,
for this [basis] belongs to something else.

Because that [mind] is immediately contiguous, even the mind of entry into meditative attainment— which, due to this very reason, has long since passed away during a state devoid of consciousness— serves as the basis for the mind of emergence,
since it is not interrupted by any other consciousness.
The inclusion of the term "past" is for the purpose of excluding the present;
for in that state, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is present as its support (*āśraya*),
and therefore it is held to be past.
And this very point is stated for the purpose of establishing the sixth basis;
the mention of "consciousness" (vijñāna) is intended to exclude [the bases] that have immediately preceded feeling and the other [skandhas].
