For since the term "that which is mind" (*yan dhi tan manaḥ*) is a designation of a genus (*jāti*), there is no use of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*); however, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), because the intention is to express the meaning of a substance (*dravya-padārtha*), there is the use of distributive repetition:
"whatever consciousness has just ceased, that is the mind-element (*manodhātu*)."
It is as follows: "that very same [thing]" and so forth.

Just as that very same son receives the designation of "father" from another's perspective, and that very same fruit receives the designation of "seed" from another's perspective, so too here, that very same element of visual consciousness and the rest receives the designation of the "mind-element" (manodhātu) because it serves as the basis for another.
There are seventeen elements, or twelve;
for those which are the six consciousness-elements are themselves the mind-element.

Since the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is identical to the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñānadhātavaḥ*), they are mutually inclusive. If the six consciousness-elements are taken, there is no purpose for the mind-element, and thus there would be seventeen elements;
if the mind-element is taken, there is no purpose for the six consciousness-elements, and thus there would be twelve elements.

"For the sake of establishing a sixth basis" means that the establishment of a basis for the five consciousness-elements is not accepted because their own bases, such as the eye and so forth, are already established;
since there is no other basis for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is posited in order to establish its basis.
By way of establishing six groups beginning with the basis (*āśraya*), there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The sixfold basis consists of the eye and so forth, ending with the mind;
the sixfold based consists of eye-consciousness and so forth, ending with mind-consciousness.

According to the Yogācāra perspective, the six objects—beginning with form and ending with phenomena—are distinct from the six consciousnesses; furthermore, they maintain that the mind-element (*manodhātu*) exists as something separate from the six consciousnesses.
Likewise, the Tāmraparṇīyas postulate that the "heart-base" (*hṛdayavastu*) is the physical support for the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
And they explain that this [form] exists even in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
for even in the formless realm, form is intended by them; and the prefix *ā-* in the word *ārūpya* is used in the sense of "slight," as in the case of *āpiṅgala*.
Regarding the "final mind," it means that at the time of nirvana without remainder, the mental faculty (manas) will no longer exist.
The meaning is that the mind-element (manodhātu) will not exist;
for since it does not exist,
it does not arise.
"Nor even by way of mental transformation," and so forth;
this is not so.
Why?
Because even that final moment of consciousness exists as a support by way of its nature as the mind (*manas*),
and because there is a deficiency in other [necessary] factors.

The intention is that because of the deficiency of the causes— namely, karma and afflictions leading to renewed existence— there is no production of a subsequent consciousness; thus, there is no consciousness for the reconnection of rebirth (*punarbhava-pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna*).
This is investigated here:
it has been stated that the eighteen elements (dhātu) exist because of the establishment of the sixfold sets of basis, based, and object.
The sixfold group of the supported (āśrita-ṣaṭka) is first established,
from the visual consciousness-element up to the mental consciousness-element;
is a sixfold group of supports (āśraya-ṣaṭka) established for this sixfold group of the supported in their respective order?

"The eye-element is the support of the eye-consciousness-element, up to the mind-element being the support of the mind-consciousness-element. He replied, "So be it. [The interlocutor asks: "But what then, when the eye is 'partially homogeneous' (tatsabhāga)?"
Of what is that the support?
It is the support of nothing at all.
How then was this said?
The eye-element is the basis of the visual consciousness element, and so forth; thus, the eye is precisely the basis.
However, that which is not a basis for anything is the "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) eye.
Even that [eye] is established as the eye-element precisely because it belongs to that same class;
the same should be stated up to the body-element.
Furthermore, is the mind-element also the support only for the mind-consciousness-element?
"No," he says,
"for that is also accepted as the basis for the visual consciousness element and so forth; for he will say thus:"
"The basis of the last [consciousness] is past; for the five [sensory consciousnesses], it is also simultaneous with them" (AK I 44cd).
Since that [basis] is not the basis for others, the establishment of a sixth basis does not occur.
This also serves as the basis for the sixth [consciousness] where possible; furthermore,
the sixfold objective field is the object of the visual consciousness-element, and so on, up to the mental consciousness-element, whose object is the dharma-element.
This is now investigated:
Is the form-element (rūpadhātu) that which serves as the objective support for the eye-consciousness element, just as all forms are the objective support for it?
In this way, up to the element of body-consciousness, as many tangible objects as there are that serve as its objective support constitute the element of the tangible;
likewise, for the element of mind-consciousness, as many phenomena as there are that serve as its objective support [constitute the element of mental objects].
Regarding the phrase "that is the dharmadhātu," the Elder said:
"The dharmadhātu has the nature of all phenomena; the meaning is that it has the nature of the eighteen elements."
How is the classification of these internal and external elements established?
For it is held that the twelve beginning with the eye are internal, while the six are external.
"For if even those were included within the *dharmadhātu*, confusion would result.
The Elder said:
"Their status as internal or external is merely figurative (*pāryāyika*)."
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept that the eye and so forth are internal because they are the supports of the consciousnesses, yet external because they are objects of mental consciousness.
Because it contradicts the Sūtra;
for it is stated in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣu, the dharmas are an external sense-field (āyatana), not included among the eleven sense-fields, invisible, and non-obstructive."

Therefore, the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) must be accepted as consisting of seven substances, because its nature consists of non-informative matter (avijñapti), feeling (vedanā), perception (sañjñā), formations (saṃskāra), space (ākāśa), cessation through deliberation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha). In that case, however, the explanation of the object (ālambana) of the mental-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) remains incomplete.
Furthermore, it is not accepted that the description of the objects (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness and the others is incomplete;
this is indeed so.

However, because the six [faculties] beginning with the eye are described as the bases (*āśraya*), while visual consciousness and the others are described as the supported (*āśrita*), and because the five [objects] beginning with visible form are described as the objects of the five groups of consciousness, they explain that even though these [five objects] are objects of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they are not included within the *dharmadhātu*.
In brief, however, the "comprehensive inclusion of all" (sarvasaṅgraha) is to be understood;
yet, although there is a comprehensive inclusion of all by means of the sense-bases (āyatana) and so forth as well, it is not [the comprehensive inclusion] in brief.
Rather,
this has been stated in brief, extracted from the three extensive teachings.

The aggregate of form is subsumed by the aggregate of form; it consists of the ten bases and elements whose intrinsic nature is the sense faculties and their objects, as well as a portion of the base of mental phenomena and the element of mental phenomena consisting of non-informative matter.
The aggregate of consciousness is subsumed by the base of the mind.
That very same mind-base (*manāyatana*) is included within the seven consciousness-elements (*cittadhātu*),

and the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*sañjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*) are included within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) include non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), which is thus included twice here.
For example, regarding the sense-faculty of the eye:
the sense-faculty of the eye is devoid of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates such as sensation, the bases such as the ear, the elements, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path;
therefore, this was said.

The eye-faculty is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the eye-base (*cakṣurāyatana*), and the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), as well as within the truths of suffering and its origin, because it has those as its intrinsic nature; it is not included within other aggregates and so forth, because it is devoid of their nature.
Thus, here a "great" [category] is subsumed under [other] "great" [categories], but a "great" [category] is not subsumed under a "small" one.
How so? The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is great because it comprises all forms,
whereas the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is small because it is merely a portion of the aggregate of form.
The visual faculty is subsumed within the aggregate of form,
but the aggregate of form is not subsumed within the visual faculty,
because the aggregate of form exists apart from the visual faculty.
It is just as the footprint of an elephant encompasses the footprint of a bird, but the footprint of a bird does not encompass the footprint of an elephant; so it is in this case.
However, when the equal is mutually included by the equal— just as the eye faculty is included by the eye base,
and the eye base is also included by the eye faculty— this should be understood as the method of the Abhidharma.
Just as [one wins over] assemblies by means of the articles of attraction (*saṅgrahavastu*), there are four articles of attraction:
generosity (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and consistency of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
There are four assemblies— the nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
and by them there is a gathering of those [monks],
but that is only occasional.
Sometimes there is existence, sometimes it is occasional;
sometimes a gift is given to them and pleasant words are spoken,
yet this is not true gathering.
It has been stated that the conventional and the practical are [designations], whereas the inclusion of intrinsic nature is ultimate; thus,
due to the commonality of genus, object, and consciousness, there is the state of being a single element (*ekadhātutā*).
Even though there is a duality of the eye and so forth, this is what is meant by implication:
the establishment of the distinction between the elements (*dhātu*) occurs according to possibility, based on the distinctions of genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
But it is not due to a difference in their bases;
for in that regard, there is a mutual difference in genus, object, and consciousness among the eye-element and the others,
whereas for the form-element and the others, there is only a difference in genus and consciousness.
There is a distinction among the elements of consciousness regarding their origin and objective sphere;
for even in the case of mental consciousness, the dharma-element is its unique objective sphere,
and the same should be applied to auditory and olfactory consciousness as well.
There is a commonality of genus for both because they possess the nature of the auditory faculty;
a commonality of object for both because they have sound as their objective domain;
and a commonality of consciousness for both because they are based upon the same auditory consciousness.

Therefore, the auditory element (*śrotradhātu*) is indeed only one; the same should be applied to the olfactory [element] as well, because there is no difference in its function. If that were so, it would follow that two [elements] do not arise; therefore, he says:
Regarding the statement "for the sake of beauty, there is the arising of pairs":

because [if there were only one], there would be a single locus for the eye and ear, and a single nostril cavity; thus, a great deformity (*vairūpya*) would result. Since there is the occurrence of a single locus for the eye and ear, and a single nostril cavity, a great deformity would ensue.
[Objection: But surely, even though camels, cats, owls, and the like possess pairs of eyes and so forth, they do not possess the beauty of the physical basis (*āśraya*).
In relation to other classes of beings, their beauty as a physical basis does not exist; however,
in relation to their own class, for whoever possesses a pair such as the eyes and so forth, there is beauty of the physical basis within that specific class.
"That which does not exist has no disfigurement"—
this is beyond reproach;
however, Master Saṅghabhadra has explained the meaning of this sūtra as follows.
"For the sake of beauty" means for the sake of sovereignty;
for it is taught that one who is endowed with sovereignty shines in the world.
And these [organs] are the bases of those sense-faculties.
For them, there would be mastery over pure seeing, hearing, smelling,
and so forth; however, just as pure seeing does not occur with only one eye,
so it is not the case for the others either.
In this way, their status as faculties (indriyatva) would be lost;
therefore, this was said for that purpose,
meaning "for the sake of clear perception."
In this case as well, it could be argued thus:
let a single, extensive karma be produced as the basis for a perfectly clear perception; what is the use of a division of bases?
In the *Vibhāṣā*, however, these two positions are recorded for the sake of clarity:
"arising from both" is one view, and "for the sake of manifestation" is another.
Enough of this digression.
But is it not the case that the arising of the two sense-faculties due to the power of karma is stated here to be for the sake of beauty and for the sake of manifestation;
thus, the emergence of the two sense-faculties is said to be solely through the power of karma?
How so?
Thus, based on the support of these differentiated parts, sentient beings’ conceit regarding beauty, practiced since beginningless time, proceeds.

Therefore, it is said that as those two sense organs are being produced by karma preceded by a desire for that [beauty] and preceded by a desire for clear perception, they arise for the sake of beauty and for the sake of manifestation.
The aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana),
and elements (dhātu) have the meanings of "heap," "gate of arrival," and "lineage" respectively; thus,
these are called "those whose meanings are heap, gate of arrival, and lineage."

What are the meanings of the terms "aggregates" (skandha), "bases" (āyatana), and "elements" (dhātu)? Alternatively, what are the meanings of the terms "heap" (rāśi), "gate of arrival" (āyadvāra), and "lineage" (gotra)?
Which are the aggregates, bases, and elements?
They are so called because they are mentioned in the Sūtra.
In the Sūtra it is said that "the meaning of 'aggregate' (skandha) is the meaning of 'heap' (rāśi)"; thus, whatever is the meaning of a heap, that is the meaning of an aggregate.
He shows this by means of the Sūtra: "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth;
[the term] "in a single mass" (*aikadhyam*) refers to this.
"Unified within a single realm" means that it has ceased through impermanence;
the meaning is that it has ceased by way of impermanence, which is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
The inclusion of impermanence (*anityatā*) is for the purpose of excluding other types of cessation;
for cessation is fivefold:

cessation by characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*), cessation by attainment (*sampatti-nirodha*), cessation by birth (*upapatti-nirodha*), cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).

If one were to say that "past form" is simply that which has ceased, then because this would be stated without qualification, it would follow that the cessation of meditative attainments (*samāpatti-nirodha*) and so forth would also be [past],
yet it is not accepted that these possess the nature of the past.

For the cessation of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-nirodha*) is indeed the cessation of future mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) only; the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is also the cessation of these very same [factors], but only those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) also belongs only to those future phenomena that are subject to non-arising;
therefore, this mention of impermanence is for the purpose of grasping the cessation of their characteristics,
[indicating] that the future is unarisen.
That which has not yet attained the state of being present is "present" in the sense of having arisen but not yet ceased;
the inclusion of the term "arisen" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the future.
The inclusion of the term "unceased" is for the purpose of qualifying the past;
for although the future is unceased, it has not arisen,
whereas although the past has arisen, it is not unceased.
The internal is that which belongs to one's own continuum,
such as the eye and so forth; the external is other than that, such as visible form and so forth.
That very same [element] which belongs to another continuum and is reckoned as non-sentient is [external];
or, from the perspective of the sense bases (*āyatana*),
the five internal [bases] beginning with the eye, whether they fall within one's own or another's continuum, are internal.

Because of the statement "twelve are internal," the other [elements]— the five external objects such as visible form and so forth, whether they belong to one's own or another's continuum, those not reckoned as sentient beings, and non-informative matter— are external.
Considering that it has the nature of external sense-bases,
it is coarse and possesses resistance, having the nature of an accumulation of atoms.
Subtle, non-obstructive,
unmanifest form,
or relative [form].
Alternatively, something may be coarse or subtle in relation to something else;
for example, a louse is coarse in relation to a nit,
while a nit is subtle in relation to a louse.
This being so, that which possesses resistance is both gross and subtle,
whereas that which lacks resistance is only subtle because it is not accumulated; thus,
[the claim of its grossness] is unestablished due to its being relative.
That very same minute louse is coarse in comparison to the dust mote in a window beam,
yet that same coarse louse is minute in comparison to a flea; thus, coarseness and minuteness are not fixed, like "this shore" and "the other shore"—
how indeed can this be?
The gross becomes subtle, and the subtle becomes gross;
this is not due to a difference in relative dependence.
The difference in dependence is "dependence-difference" (*apekṣābheda*).

Therefore, it is not unestablished that whatever is coarse in relation to something can never be subtle in relation to that same thing; the meaning is that it is never the case that the very same thing is the object of dependence [in both ways].
"Like father and son" means,
for example, Devadatta's son is Yajñadatta,
and Yajñadatta's son is Viṣṇumitra.
That Yajñadatta is a father in relation to Viṣṇumitra and a son in relation to Devadatta; yet,
despite this relativity, his status as both father and son is not thereby invalidated.
Due to the difference in relativity,
for that same Yajñadatta is not a son when considered in relation to Viṣṇumitra,
nor is he a father when considered in relation to Devadatta.
In the same way,
that which is inferior is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) because it is abandoned by the virtuous;
that which is sublime is unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*) because it is not defiled by the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The past and the future are distant because they have departed from the continuum and because they have not yet been reached; the present is near because it is contiguous with the continuum. This applies likewise up to consciousness.

Whatever feeling there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; far or near—all that, having been gathered together as one, is designated by the term "aggregate of feeling" (*vedanā-skandha*).

In the same way, this should be stated for each up to consciousness (*vijñāna*), until all of it, having been gathered together as one, is designated by the term "aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The pastness and so forth of these [factors] such as feeling are just like that of form;
however, this is the distinction: among feeling and the others, the fourfold group beginning with feeling is coarse and based on the five sense faculties.
Because it is formless, there is no coarseness inherent within it;
it is subtle because its mental basis is also formless,
or [it is subtle] by way of its level (*bhūmi*).
Coarse and subtle [feelings] and so forth:
feeling belonging to the desire realm is coarse,
while that belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is subtle.
The coarse belongs to the level of the first dhyāna,
while the subtle belongs to the level of the second dhyāna; and so on, up to the coarse belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
The [aggregate of] feeling at the stage of the peak of existence is subtle;
as it is with feeling, so it should be stated for all [aggregates] up to consciousness.
The Elder named Bhadanta—
either a certain Sautrāntika of that name or Bhagavadviśeṣa— said:
Regarding the statement "this is the Elder Dharmatrāta," we say here:
if Dharmatrāta is a proponent of the existence of the past and the future, [then he is the one referred to].
The phrase "he" means neither a Sautrāntika nor a Dārṣṭāntika;
for he will state later that the Venerable Dharmatrāta is a proponent of the transformation of entities (bhāvānyatvika).
He reportedly says that when a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (adhvan), there is a change in its state (bhāva) but not a change in its substance (dravya);
and this Venerable One, who adheres to the Sautrāntika view, is recorded in the Vibhāṣā.
"Bhadanta said," and so forth;
likewise, Bhadanta Dharmatrāta is also recorded by his own name in the *Vibhāṣā*,
as in "Bhadanta Dharmatrāta said," and so forth.
By this it is indicated that the Venerable Dharmatrāta was some other elder monk belonging to the Sautrāntika school;
"perceptible by the five sense-faculties" refers to the pentad beginning with form,
while "subtle" refers to another pentad beginning with the eye.
And "non-informative" (avijñapti) is "agreeable" (manāpa);
"agreeable" means that which attains the mind, i.e., that which is pleasing to the mind.
Furthermore, reconnection (*punar-saṃdhikaraṇa*) should be observed here;

because [the word] *pūrvatrāsiddham* is understood in the sense of "slightly" (*īṣadartha*), it means "partially established," and thus there is the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*ekasavarṇadīrghatva*) in the expression *dūram adṛṣyadeśam*.
With reference to the locus of the substratum— that is, the locus of the support and the substratum—
it is "visible" (dṛśya) because it can be seen;
that which has such a visible locus is called the "locus of the visible" (dṛśyadeśa), meaning the locus that serves as the support for the visible.
Or it may have as its locus the substratum of the visible object,
such as a jujube fruit in a bowl, or the eye and so forth.
That which is near is a visible location, whereas the opposite is distant;
it is not said that the distant is invisible.
For even something nearby may not be seen due to its extreme subtlety,
yet it is not considered distant because it occupies a visible location.
But for what purpose is it explained by the Venerable One in this way— that [the past and so forth] are expressed by their own respective terms—
since otherwise there would be the fault of redundancy?
Their being distant or near, however, is due to the power of their basis;

since those [factors] such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth, being formless, do not occupy a spatial location, it should therefore be stated that feelings and so forth are "distant" when their basis is not perceived.
"Having their bases visible nearby" means that coarseness and subtlety are as previously described;
the coarse [consciousness] has the five sense-faculties as its basis.

The subtle mental [bases] are so called because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arising (*āya*), that is, the production, of mind and mental factors; since consciousness arises in dependence upon a dyad, the status of all as bases (*āyatana*) is established.
"In a single basis or continuum" means:
either in the body, which is characterized as a composite whole (*samudāya*),
or in the continuum (*santāna*), which is characterized as the flow of the mind and other mental factors.
What are the sources of one's own birth? This is the subject at hand.
Because it is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
the eye that has arisen previously is the homogeneous cause of the subsequent one; thus, "source" (*ākara*) means "element" (*dhātu*),
just as gold and other substances arise from a source.
These are their sources;
however, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would not be a realm (*dhātu*),
for the unconditioned is neither the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of itself nor of anything else.
In that case, what is the meaning of "sources" (*ākara*) for mind and mental factors? This is the subject under discussion.

Since consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality, all the elements (dhātus) serve as conditions for consciousness along with its associated mental factors; they are necessarily its objective support (ālambana) and its predominant condition (adhipati).
Thus, like a heap or a person, the aggregates (skandhas) exist as conceptual designations (prajñaptisat).
Because it is denotable by the word "heap" (rāśi),
like a heap of grain or like a person (pudgala).

For that person (*pudgala*) exists only as a designation (*prajñaptisat*), because its intrinsic nature is not apprehended independently of the causes for the designation of form and so forth; and since it is like a heap of grain in the sense of "bearing the burden of what is to be done" (*kāryabhārodvahanārtha*), the burden itself is the task, hence it is called the "burden of what is to be done."
That which carries something is called a "bearer" (*udvahana*);

the bearing of the burden of duty is the "bearing of the burden of duty" (*kāryabhārodvahanam*), which is a region of the body; that is what is called a "shoulder" (*skandha*) in common worldly usage.
By this [designation] as well, the burden of the task is carried, because of such statements as "the six sense bases have name-and-form as their condition";
therefore, the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) is a metaphorical expression, like the word "aggregate," or it has the sense of "a portion."
Or rather, the meaning is "for the purpose of non-destruction";
that [interpretation] which goes from "the cutting off of form" up to "the cutting off of consciousness" is contrary to the sūtra.
Both of these— namely, the purpose of bearing the burden of the task and the purpose of excision—
are "extraneous to the sūtra" (utsūtra), having departed from the sūtra;
for the sūtra is [as follows], and he explains that at length.
"Each one individually," and so forth;
to the question "How so? he says: all this, in the form of the past and so on, is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) taken one by one, each individually.
By "collection" (samudaya), the substance that constitutes the collection is expressed;
for the intention [of the Sūtra] is that this is the aggregate of those past and other forms.
It is stated exactly thus in the Sūtra as well.
"What is the earth element?
Hair of the head, hair of the body," and so forth;
each individual substance, such as hair and the rest, is understood to be the earth element.

And this solution can also be stated regarding the positions that [the compound] has the sense of "bearing the burden of the task" (*kāryabhārodvahanārtha*) or "separating the meanings" (*arthapracchedārtha*);
it cannot be said that it is impossible [in those cases],
because of the surplus of wording in the expression "having condensed them into a single unit" (*aikadhyam abhisaṅkṣipya*).
It is not possible to understand each individual [atom] as the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
for if that were the meaning,
he would have simply said "all of that is the aggregate of form."

By the statement "not having condensed the objects into a single unity," the teacher's position is established that the aggregates (*skandhas*) exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*), just like a heap; however,
it should be understood that when the aggregates are described as substantially existent (*dravyasat*), this is because they consist of a collection of such [substantially existent] things.
"Even those that possess form," and so forth.
The mention of "possessing form" is for the purpose of distinguishing them from those that do not possess form;
for the mental base (*manāyatana*), being formless, maintains the status of a cause even when it is not aggregated.
Even the material sense-bases, such as the eye and so forth, become gateways for the arising of mind and mental factors only when they are assembled, not when they are unassembled;
therefore, because they possess the characteristic of being an assembly, like the aggregates (*skandha*), they would be nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).
For the five groups of consciousness have as their basis and object that which is accumulated.
"It is not so, because there is no cause for [the effect] to arise from the causes taken individually or as a complete collection"—
this is not correct.
Why?
Because each one individually is a cause when they are complete and assembled;
for these many atoms of the eye and so forth, while mutually dependent, possess the nature of being causes one by one.
But it is not so for those who are not combined;
just as when pulling a piece of wood, many pullers are individually incapable,
yet when they have come together and depend upon one another, they possess the capacity.

Or, just as individual hairs, when situated separately, are incapable of being the cause for the visual consciousness of one with ophthalmia, but when combined— even if not joined together— they are capable; in the same way,
the atoms of the sense organs such as the eye and the atoms of objects such as visible form are each individually incapable of producing visual and other types of consciousness.
But when combined, they are capable;
for the power of entities should be understood as being such,
or rather, due to their cooperation with the object.
If the state of being a door of arrival belonged to many [atoms], then there would be a "basis of a collection" (*samudāyāyatana*) rather than a "substantial basis" (*dravyāyatana*);
for since the atoms of the sense-faculties and their objects constitute a door of arrival only when aggregated, that would be a basis of a collection and not a distinct, individual basis.
And the status of being distinct bases (*pṛthag-āyatanatva*) is accepted because of the Sūtra stating "there are twelve bases," and the proof for this is established here:
those which are cooperative causes (*sahakāriṇaḥ*).
The atoms of the substance that constitutes the collection of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) do not possess the nature of a collection together with those [other atoms],
because they are the cause of visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*),
just like the atoms of the substance that constitutes the collection of the eye-base and the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*).
Just as the atoms that constitute the aggregate substance of the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) are to be applied,
so too should they be applied up to the atoms that constitute the aggregate substance of the body-base (*kāya-āyatana*); for it is said thus in the *Vibhāṣā*.
By this [statement] as well, he explains that the aggregates are conventionally existent;
however, the distinction is that they are shown there by way of metaphorical designation even though they do not exist as substantial entities.
But a word whose meaning is specific depends upon the designation of the aggregates; thus,
it depends upon the designation "aggregate."
The meaning is that "aggregate" (rāśi) depends upon a designation;
"an atom of one element" refers to a portion of any one of the ten material elements, such as the eye and so forth.

Thus, why is this [term] not established as referring to a portion of any one of these sense-bases (*āyatana*) or of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)? For when a designation is intended, a word that applies to the whole (*pradeśin*) is not restricted to a mere part (*pradeśa*).
Now, what is meant by "does not depend on the designation of the aggregates"? This is the subject under discussion.
He said: "An atom is a single element," and so forth;
it refers to each one of those bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), as well as whichever one among them is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).

For there is indeed a metaphorical designation (upacāra) of the whole in its part; thus, even in a part—that is, in a single atom—there is a metaphorical designation as "form-aggregate" (rūpaskandha) and as "the element of the form-base" (rūpāyatana-dhātu), just as in the case of [the designation of] one or another [particular] form-base element.
In this context, the suffix -vat is used in the sense of "that which belongs to that."

Just as when one part of a cloth is burned, it is said "the cloth is burned," so too the word "cloth," though applied to the whole, is used metaphorically for a portion, namely a single part of the cloth.
In the same way, the word "aggregate" (skandha), which is applied to a collection of forms such as those of the past and so forth, is also used metaphorically for a part, namely an atom; therefore,
only the aggregates are conventionally real (prajñaptisat), whereas the sense-bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu) are not.
When, however, the compound is formed as "the aggregates are form and so forth" (rūpādīnāṃ skandhāḥ),
rather than "form itself is the aggregate" (rūpāṇy eva skandhāḥ), then the intended meaning is that the aggregates exist as substantial entities (dravyasantaḥ).
This is investigated here:

what is the reason that, although there is mutual dependence between the atoms of the sense faculties (*indriya-paramāṇu*) and the atoms of the objects (*viṣaya-paramāṇu*) for the arising of consciousness, these two are not established as having a single sphere (*ekāyatana*)— as is the case with the atoms of the sense faculties alone—
since all the atoms of the visual faculty and so forth serve as common causes for the arising of their respective consciousnesses?
But the atoms of the object are not like that;
for instance, the atoms of the visual faculty serve as causes for the arising of a cognition of a blue object, yet they also serve as causes for the arising of a cognition of yellow and other colors.
Yellow and other [colors] do not [contribute] to the arising of consciousness;
therefore, because the atoms of the visual faculty and the atoms of their objects function unequally and are situated in separate locations.

It should be stated that it is not logical for the atoms of the eye and visible forms to be established as a single sense-base (*ekāyatana*), and likewise, up to the atoms of the body-faculty and tangible objects, it is not logical for them to be established as a single sense-base;
this is because of the threefold nature of delusion, faculties, and inclinations.
The meaning is: "due to the threefold nature of delusion, wisdom, and resolve.
There are three modes, hence "traidham"; some say that the suffix *aṇ* is used here in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), thus forming *tridhaiva traidham*.
Others say that *traidha* means "threefold state," with the suffix *ṇ* added in the sense of a state (*bhāva*);
thus, it refers to the threefold nature of delusion, faculties, and inclinations.
Regarding the phrase "by grasping [them] as a mass," some hold that having grasped the mental factors (*caitta*) as a mass, they grasp those very same factors as a self (*ātman*),
because the grasping of a self proceeds only when there is grasping of a mass.

For them, there is the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*); for in that [teaching], mental factors (*caitta*) are taught as threefold by way of the division into feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*)—which conceives of this [collection] as a single lump and not as specific mental factors—is countered.

Alternatively, some who are deluded think that this physical form is a "self," and that this self is the feeler, the perceiver, and the volitional agent; for them, the teaching on the aggregates is intended.

The grasping at a self— the notion that "this mass is not of the nature of a self, yet these mental factors, namely feeling, perception, and formations, proceed here"— is countered [by the realization that] some are deluded by grasping at a self in the mass [of aggregates], thinking it exists in form alone; this is the subject under discussion.
The teaching regarding them is with effort;
for in that [teaching], form is divided in many ways according to the distinctions of the eye and so forth,
whereas mental factors (*caitta*) are grouped together as a single *dharmāyatana*, and mind (*citta*) is [grouped] as the *manāyatana*.
Some are deluded regarding form and mind; for them, the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is precisely intended to counteract the grasping at a self as a solid mass.
For in that [classification], form is divided in many ways according to the distinctions of the eye and so forth,
and mind is divided according to the distinctions of the eye-consciousness element and so forth;
however, mental factors are not [so divided] because they are taught as being only the dharma-element.
By that [practice], the delusion consisting of the grasping at a solid mass of form and mind is counteracted, as are the faculties; such is the detailed explanation.
There are three types of persons, due to their having sharp, medium, or dull faculties.

Alternatively, there are three types of persons: one who understands through a condensed presentation (*udghaṭita-jña*), one who understands through an elaborate exposition (*vipañcita-jña*), and one for whom the words alone suffice (*padaparama*).
Among these, the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*) is for those of sharp faculties;
for, due to their sharp faculties, they are able to comprehend the distinctions of the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) precisely by means of the analysis of the aggregates.
As it was said: "O monk, that which is not yours—that Dharma—must be abandoned.
He replied, "I do not understand, Blessed One.
[The Blessed One asked: "How, O monk, do you understand the meaning of what has been spoken by me in brief?"
"Venerable sir, form is not my self;
that dharma of mine must be abandoned," and so forth—
this is the teaching on the sense bases for those of middling faculties.
For they, being of middling faculties, are able to comprehend the differentiation of the elements through a moderate, rather than an overly extensive, differentiation of the bases;
however, the teaching on the elements is not for those of dull faculties by means of the concise differentiation of the aggregates.

For, due to their dull faculties, they are unable to comprehend [the Dharma] in its undifferentiated state through the power of their own intelligence; furthermore, since inclination (*ruci*) is also threefold,
the threefold nature of inclination arises from the force of prior habitual practice.
Alternatively, those whose conduct is characterized by tranquility (śamatha) have a preference for the concise;

those whose conduct is characterized by both tranquility and insight (vipaśyanā) have a preference for the intermediate; and those whose conduct is characterized by insight have a preference for the extensive.
"But what is the reason? and so forth. [Objection:
Has not the reason already been stated—that the teaching on the aggregates is for those who are deluded regarding mental factors because they grasp at a composite self? [Response:
True, it has been stated.

Since those mental factors (*caitta*) are already distinguished [within the aggregate of formations], why is it that only feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates from the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and not any others? What is the reason for this?
"Attachment to sensual pleasures," and so forth:
this refers to the clinging to sensual pleasures and to [wrong] views.
Of these two attachments, which are the roots of dispute, feeling and perception are respectively the primary causes.

By mentioning the "principal" [cause], it is implicitly stated that ignorance and the other factors are non-principal causes; for householders cling to sensual pleasures through the power of relishing feeling,
and views arise through the power of distorted perception.
Regarding the question "What do they cling to?",

those who perceive non-dharma as dharma and dharma as non-dharma, and who perceive a self in what is not-self and so forth, cling to such things as the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Who are those who have mostly gone forth?
"For one greedy for sensation," and so forth.
Attached to sensation and distorted by the four perversions, one undergoes a succession of births in saṃsāra due to the causal sequence; thus,

the four reasons for the order of the aggregates will be explained according to their coarseness, their nature as affliction, their function as a vessel and so forth, and their correspondence to the realms.
For form is the coarsest of all because it possesses resistance;
among the formless [aggregates], feeling is coarse by way of its manifest activity,
for thus do they designate it.
The first reason is that because the perception "there is a sensation in my hand" and "there is a sensation in my foot" is more gross than consciousness,
and because formations (saṃskāra) are more gross than consciousness, those that are more gross were mentioned first according to their degree of grossness.
Alternatively, in this beginningless saṃsāra, men and women are mutually enamored of each other’s forms;
and that [enamorment] arises from a craving for the taste of sensation,
which [craving] in turn results from a perversion of perception.
The second [order] is according to the sequence of defilement (*yathāsaṃkleśa*), because the mind is defiled by the afflictions which are the inversion of that [reality].
Or, it is according to the sense of being a vessel and so forth; for the aggregates, beginning with form, are like a vessel, food, condiment, cook, and eater—this is the third [order].
Or, from the perspective of the elements: the desire realm is characterized by the forms of the objects of sensual pleasure;
the meditative absorptions are characterized by feeling;
and the three formless realms are characterized by perception.
The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested solely by formative forces (*saṃskāra*);

these are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and consciousness is established within them. Thus, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed; this is the fourth reason.
And for that very same reason regarding the sequence, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates.

Since these [two] are more gross, being the causes for the sequence of afflictions and serving as food and condiment, and since the two elements are characterized by them, they cannot yet be included within these [three] because the meaning is untenable— that is,
because the meaning of "being subject to transformation" (*rūpaṇa*) and so forth is neither applicable nor possible.
Up to the nature of consciousness itself, it is impossible to include [the self] within these very five aggregates because they do not possess that nature;
nor can a sixth aggregate be posited, for what reason? Because it would be logically inconsistent with the facts.
The meaning is that [the category of unconditioned phenomena] is not possible as having past and so forth as its referents.

Now, one might object: since the unconditioned phenomena are numerous, would it not be appropriate to posit another "aggregate of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*)? Why [then] refer to past and so forth?
And this is incorrect because, since unconditioned phenomena lack proximity to any location, they cannot be condensed;
[the objection] that it is "for the purpose of making known the basis of affliction" and so forth is not valid,
because the basis of affliction is not [unconditioned], as it is free from outflows (*anāsrava*).
There is no entity of purification because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
for the intended meaning is that an entity of obstruction is indeed a cause of obstruction.

Alternatively, when "the aggregate of form" is mentioned, up to "the aggregate of consciousness" is mentioned, it is understood that the aggregate of form, up to the aggregate of consciousness, constitutes both the entity of affliction (*saṃkleśavastu*) and the entity of purification (*vyavadānavastu*).

However, when "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*) is stated, it is not possible for the object of defilement and purification to be understood; thus, for those who hold such a view, this same logical consequence would apply even to the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
For them, just as the cessation of a jar is not itself the jar, so too [the unconditioned cannot be an aggregate].

In that case, since "the cessation of the elements" would not be the elements, and "the cessation of the sense-bases" would not be the sense-bases, the unconditioned would not be established even within the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana); furthermore,
it would be illogical [to claim] that all phenomena are subsumed within the elements and sense-bases.

The word "again" (*punaḥ*) is introduced to show that this refers back to the statement "another way [of explaining] the aggregates has been stated"; thus, he indicates [the following] by saying "all that is most gross."
Form is coarser than all [the aggregates] beginning with feeling, because it possesses such qualities as being visible and possessing resistance,
whereas feeling and the others are formless.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*);
the meaning is that feeling (*vedanā*) is coarse because its activity (*pracāra*) is coarse and its manifestation (*samudācāra*) is coarse.
Compared to the other two—formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—feeling is coarse, whereas perception (*saṃjñā*) is [coarse] compared to the other two.
Because it is well-known through the discernment of signs,

formative activity (*saṃskāra*) is coarser than consciousness (*vijñāna*), since its characteristic is the volitional formation [expressed as] "may I be happy, may I not be suffering"; consciousness, however,
is the most subtle of all, because its characteristic is mere apprehension.
And just as it is appropriate to present the meaning to those to be trained according to what is most gross, such is the sequence of the aggregates.
Furthermore, because of their greed for the relish of feeling,
men and women become mutually enamored of form due to their attachment to the relish of feeling.
"Craving for that" refers to craving for sensation;
it arises from a perversion of perception.

For even pleasant feeling is suffering by way of the suffering of conditioned change (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), because one grasps at it as being permanent and so forth; thus it is said in detail that "the vessel and the food [are both suffering]."
Form is like a vessel because it is the basis for feeling;
feeling is like food because it is to be relished;
and perception is like a seasoning because it seasons feeling by grasping its specific signs.
Or, considering that feeling is pleasing by the power of perception (*saṃjñā*), perception— which functions as the seasoning—
and volition— which functions as the cook— having conditioned the resultant feeling, bring it forth; thus consciousness becomes the enjoyer, because it favors that [feeling].
Or the sequence is according to their purpose, such as for bathing and so forth, or according to the roots; this is the detailed explanation.
The objects of desire themselves are the forms (*rūpa*).
The desire realm is manifested and revealed by these;
the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are manifested by feeling;
and the first dhyāna is manifested by the faculties of mental joy and pleasure.
The second dhyāna is characterized by the faculty of mental joy;
the third is characterized by the faculty of pleasure; and the fourth dhyāna is characterized by the purity of the faculty of equanimity.
The three formless attainments are characterized by perception:
the sphere of infinite space is characterized by the perception of space;
the sphere of infinite consciousness is characterized by the perception of consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness is characterized by the perception of nothingness;
the peak of existence is characterized by mere formations,
for there volition projects a lifespan of eighty thousand eons.
Why is consciousness (vijñāna) mentioned last of all? To this he says: "These are the stations of consciousness," and so forth.
There are four stations of consciousness;
the station of consciousness associated with form is the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The four dhyānas are accompanied by feeling;
the three formless attainments are accompanied by perception;
the peak of existence is accompanied by volitional formations.
Consciousness established within those four stations of consciousness is mentioned last of all because it is dependent upon them;
thus, the sequence of the aggregates is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the field and the seed.
For this very reason, there are exactly five aggregates—neither fewer nor more.
The meaning is that, by way of such reasons as grossness and so forth, they are neither fewer nor more; thus,
because their objects are present, those which have present objects were mentioned first.
Those [cognitions] whose objects are clearly manifest—
and since those with clearly manifest objects are easy to understand— they were explained first;
and those whose objects are present necessarily have their prior occurrences [already established], and thus they too were explained first.
But the mind, having unrestricted objects, is difficult to understand because its objects are manifold and its activity generally occurs subsequently;
how so? He says:

Some have the present as their object, some have the three times or the non-time as their object; by the word "some," it is meant that some have the past as their object, some the future, and some the three times—
as in the case of [the cognition] "all phenomena are without self."
The meaning is that it has as its object something not belonging to any of the [three] time periods—that is, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Thus, the mind has an indefinite object;
and for that reason, it was stated later that it is not easily understood.

For it is observed in the world that what is taught first is easily understood; thus, the "fourfold" refers to the four beginning with the eye, which have as their objects the derivative forms (upādāyarūpa) such as visible form, and so forth.
Therefore—
That was previously stated regarding the body;
however, the object of the body is indefinite:
sometimes it is the primary elements (*bhūta*), and sometimes it is the derivative matter (*bhautika*), provided there is a perception of distinctness.
Sometimes both [occur] if there is apprehension without distinction;
the remainder [is explained] as being "from the other" according to the circumstances, as previously stated regarding the distant and more rapid functioning;
thus, the remainder refers to the eye and so forth.

The meaning is that this should be applied by dividing [the process] according to its occurrence at a distance, more quickly, or most quickly—that is, from two [causes] come two, one from one, and again one from one—relative to what else is possible.
To the question "How so? he says:

The eye and the ear indeed have distant objects; therefore, they were mentioned before the pair consisting of the nose and the tongue. Between these two, the eye and the ear, the activity of the eye extends to a greater distance, because even when one sees a river from afar, one does not hear its sound.
Therefore, it follows that it was mentioned first;
the eye was mentioned before the ear because its activity is more rapid than theirs.
Regarding those two, the nose and the tongue, he explains why the nose was mentioned before the tongue:
because one perceives the odor of food even before it has reached the tongue.
This is investigated here:
how is it that the nose and the tongue grasp objects that have come into contact with them?
The odor residing in edible food is perceived by that sense of smell, but that which does not reside in edible food is not perceived; rather,
another odor arises from the wind, or the odor is perceived as it comes along with subtle particles of the edible food.
Since there is no perception of odor for one who is breathless,
it should not then be said that the odor of food is perceived by the tongue even though it has not reached it.
There is no fault in this, because the statement was made with the intention that the food in the form of a morsel has not yet reached the tongue;
for in this way, the sense of smell functions so rapidly that it perceives a fragrance even when it has merely come into contact with a portion of the food.
However, the tongue does not taste a flavor that has come together with a part of the food;
rather, it tastes only the flavor that has come together with the morsel of food. Thus, it should be understood that [the tongue] does not function more rapidly [than the other senses].
Demonstrating how this is for the sake of distinction, he says:
"So that it may be understood individually," and so forth;

that is, so that it may be known that each one of these [bases] is a source of faults (*doṣa*), because the five [faculties] beginning with the eye are established as the possessors of objects (*viṣayin*) and the five [objects] beginning with form are established as the objects (*viṣaya*).
The totality [of the elements] does not constitute the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*); rather, it is only one.

Furthermore, there would be no mutual distinction [between them] if other names were uttered merely for the sake of specification—such as "the nine sense-bases from the eye-base up to the body-base," and "the sound-base up to the tangible-base."
Why is a different name not also given to the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*)? To this he says:
because it is that which, being distinguished by [the terms] "eye" and so forth, is neither designated by the names "eye" and so forth, nor is it form (*rūpa*).
Thinking, "One will know that visible-object base," no other name for it is stated;
just as when all the cows have been marked, if there is one cow that is not marked, the very absence of a mark on her constitutes her being marked.
In the same way, it is due to its predominance; that is, the predominance of the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is established by three reasons:
because it is characterized by being affected (rūpaṇa) through the contact of hands and so forth.

Because it is defined by its indication of location as "this is here" or "that is there," and because it is commonly recognized in the world as "this very thing is form," one base (āyatana) was taught specifically for the purpose of distinction.
How is it for the purpose of specification?
It is so that it may be understood that each of these twelve possesses the status of an *āyatana* because they are established as subject and object respectively, and not all of them collectively;
and by specifying [them] with "the eye" and so forth, it is indicated that which is not designated as "eye" and so on, namely, *dharma*.
Thinking that this will be understood as the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), no other name is stated for it;

by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of feeling, etc.," there is the inclusion of perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), [all] by way of twenty varieties.
Because it is stated that "form is twofold and twentyfold," and because it is the objective domain of the three [types of] eyes.
The fleshly eye belongs to those such as ourselves;
the divine eye belongs to the gods;
and the noble wisdom-eye belongs to the noble ones, being untainted knowledge that takes the four truths as its object.
Therefore, it is form alone that is the object of the three [types of] eyes,
and not the eye and so forth; for this reason:

That alone is said to be the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), and not the others; for those Sautrāntikas according to whom the word of the Buddha has speech as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it has vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) as its intrinsic nature.
For them, these [objects] are comprised within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
because the sense-field of sound (śabdāyatana) is comprised within the aggregate of form;
whereas for those [others], they have the nature of name (nāma).
For those [teachers] for whom [the Buddha's words] are considered to consist of sound because they are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*),
the Abhidharmikas, however, maintain that the word of the Buddha has the nature of both [sound and name].
For it is said in the *Jñānaprasthāna*:
"What is the word of the Buddha?
It is whatever speech, utterance, discourse, song, etymology, path of speech, vocal sound, vocal action, or vocal intimation of the Tathāgata."
Should the word of the Buddha be said to be wholesome,
or should it be said to be indeterminate?
It should be wholesome.
What might be the indeterminate? It is the speech, up to the vocal intimation, of a Tathāgata who possesses a wholesome mind while speaking words that are wholesome.

"Which [of these] is the indeterminate [state], and what is this dharma called 'Buddha-word' spoken by the Tathāgata who possesses an indeterminate mind? As before, immediately following that, it was stated: "What is this dharma called the Buddha-word?"

Regarding the sequential arrangement, sequential placement, and sequential conjunction of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*), those Abhidharmikas [hold that] these eighty thousand aggregates of dharma (*dharmaskandha*) are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
As for the scriptural statement: "I have personally received from the presence of the Blessed One more than eighty thousand aggregates of dharma."

Regarding the phrase "eighty-four thousand aggregates of dharma" (*caturaśītidharmaskandhasahasrāṇi*), there is a scriptural reading (*sūtrapāṭha*) in another school stating that this is the measure of the treatise (*śāstra*); thus,
one [view] holds that the measure of the treatise is its "measure of the treatise" (*śāstrapramāṇa*).
Some say that this aggregate of dharma (dharmaskandha) is measured by the extent of the treatise; thus, its measure is that of the treatise.
And that [treatise] consists of six thousand [verses];
that treatise known as the *Dharmaskandha* is six thousand units in length according to the standard of the text;
however, those eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* have now disappeared.
"But this one thing remains," they say; [this refers to] the teaching regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth individually.
The phrase "others say" (*apare āhuḥ*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
Each individual discourse on the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is a "dharma-aggregate" (*dharmaskandha*);
these dharma-aggregates are explained as numbering eighty thousand,
and herein the [treatises] on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and other topics will also be explained.

By the inclusion of the phrase "of the knowledge resulting from resolve, the absence of strife, and so forth," the bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*), the paths of action, the meditation on the foul, mindfulness of breathing, and so on are included.

However, the aggregate of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) is described as the antidote to specific temperaments; the word "but" (*tu*) is intended either to refute the previously mentioned position or to serve as a restriction.
"By way of the distinctions of conduct such as passion, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth"— by the word "and so forth," views, doubt, and others are included;
some sentient beings are of passionate temperament.
Some have a temperament of hatred, some have a temperament of desire,
and some have a temperament of pride.
Some have a temperament characterized by views,
some have a temperament characterized by doubt, and some have a temperament characterized by passion and hatred.
Some have conduct characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion;
some have the latent tendency of passion with the application of hatred; and some have the latent tendency of hatred with the application of passion.
Some have artificial passion while suppressing hatred,
and some have artificial hatred while suppressing passion; it was for their sake, as an antidote, that these were spoken by the Blessed One.
"Whatever other aggregates, bases, and elements there may be," and so forth;
whatever aggregates, bases, and elements there are, they too are to be explained and subsumed within these very same aggregates, bases, and elements.

Having reflected upon their respective intrinsic natures as they are established in this treatise, the aggregates (skandhas) should be assigned to the aggregates, the bases (āyatanas) to the bases, and the elements (dhātus) to the elements. Thus,
the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
because the nature of the aggregate of ethical discipline consists in the abstention from bodily and vocal [misconduct].

The remaining [factors] are included within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), because concentration and the others are mental factors; here, "liberation" (vimukti) is intended to mean resolute conviction (adhimokṣa).
And since the knowledge and vision of liberation is nothing other than a specific form of wisdom (*prajñā*),
these eight [factors]— because they have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their intrinsic nature— are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Which are the eight?
The spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red,

and white will be explained as having non-greed (alobha) as their intrinsic nature; for it is said that "non-greed is eightfold," and non-greed is included within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Therefore, their inclusion [is established];
however, since they possess retinues and have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature, why are they not included within the spheres of mind and mental phenomena?

What constitutes the retinue and the concomitants of that non-greed? They are: the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which is the form that accompanies it; the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*); the mental factors associated with it, such as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth, which constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth; and the consciousness within this collection, which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Thus, these possess the nature of the five aggregates.

However, the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) of infinite space and infinite consciousness in the ninth and tenth [categories] will be explained later, as will the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana). Since these have non-attachment (alobha) as their intrinsic nature, they consist of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana);
yet, together with their attendants, since they consist of the nature of the five aggregates, they should be explained as before by way of the spheres of mind and mental objects (manodharmāyatana).
The two totalities (kṛtsna) of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, as well as the four [formless attainments] beginning with the sphere of infinite space—

namely, the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception— are comprised within the two bases of mind and mental objects (manodharmāyatana), because they have the nature of the four aggregates; for there is no aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) therein.
"The five bases of liberation," and so forth;
it is stated in the Sūtra:
"These five are the bases of liberation."
What are the five?
Here, monks, either the Teacher teaches the Dharma, or some other wise person who occupies the position of a teacher among his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Just as his teacher, or any other wise fellow-celibate in the position of a guru, teaches the Dharma to him,
so too does he come to experience the meaning and experience the Dharma within those teachings;
and for one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dharma, joy arises.
In one who is gladdened, joy arises;
in one whose mind is joyful, the body becomes tranquil;
with a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated;
one whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are and sees things as they truly are;
understanding things as they truly are and seeing them as they truly are, one becomes disenchanted.
Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate;
being dispassionate, one is liberated.
This is the first basis for liberation.
Abiding therein, for a monk or a nun, unestablished mindfulness becomes established,
the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated,
and the unabandoned outflows are brought to exhaustion.
Furthermore, he attains the unsurpassed security of Nirvana which he had not yet attained.
Moreover, O monk, it may be that the Teacher does not teach the Dharma, nor does any other wise person standing in the place of a teacher or a fellow practitioner;
rather, one recites aloud in detail the teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered.

To the extent that he recites them aloud in detail— just as they were heard, just as they were taught, and just as they were mastered— to that same extent he becomes one who realizes the meaning within them, as previously described;
this is the second sphere of liberation.

"Abiding therein," as before; furthermore, O monk, it may be that neither does the Teacher teach the Dharma, nor does some other wise person in the position of a teacher or a fellow practitioner of the holy life,
nor does anyone else extensively proclaim to others the teachings as they have been heard, as they have been taught, and as they have been mastered.

To the extent that one extensively elucidates for others the teachings as they were heard, as they were taught, and as they were mastered, to that same extent one comes to experience the meaning within those teachings; as described previously,
this is the third basis of liberation.
"Abiding therein," as before;
furthermore, O monk, it is not that the Teacher— as before—
neither recites [the teachings] himself nor proclaims them to others.
Rather, he reflects upon, weighs, and examines those teachings exactly as they were heard and exactly as they were mastered;
and in whatever way he reflects upon them, up to examining them as they were heard and mastered, in that very way he experiences the meaning within those teachings, as previously described.
This is the fourth base of liberation;
for one established therein, [it is] as before. Furthermore, O monk, it is not indeed [the case that] "the Teacher," and so on, as before.

He neither recites it, nor explains it to others, nor reflects upon it; rather, by means of this, he has properly, thoroughly, and well grasped one of the auspicious signs of concentration— well attended to, well cultivated, well mastered, and well investigated— such as a livid corpse, or a festering corpse, or a bloated corpse, or a fissured corpse, or a mangled corpse, or a scattered corpse, or a skeleton.
To the extent that he has thoroughly penetrated any particular auspicious sign of concentration as previously described,
to that same extent he becomes a penetrator of the meaning within those phenomena, as previously described;
this is the fifth base of liberation.
"Of one who stands therein," as before;
it is a specific kind of wisdom that is the gateway for the arrival of liberation,
and wisdom is subsumed within the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Together with their attendants, they are included within the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects (*śabda-manodharmāyatana*).
Among these, because there is the grasping of sound during teaching, recitation, and the proclamation to others, there is the sphere of sound;
however, as for the spheres of mind and mental objects, since they exist everywhere as the attendants of wisdom (*prajñā*), they are subsumed under all three.
Regarding the two bases,
it is stated in the Sūtra:
"May there be sentient beings who possess form, yet are without perception and without discernment."
For example, there are the gods who are non-percipient beings;
this is the first base.
There are formless beings who, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, dwell having attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
For example, the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is the second sphere. Within these two spheres, the non-percipient beings are comprised by ten bases (*āyatana*).
Because the sense bases of odor and taste are absent there,
at the times of death and rebirth they possess the mind-base (*manāyatana*); thus,
those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are included within the mind-base and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*), as is the subject under discussion.
Because they are formless,
it is stated in the Sūtra that even in the *Bahudhātuka* [Sūtra], there are sixty-two elements (*dhātu*).
The Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"To what extent, Bhadanta, is one wise and skilled in the elements?
The Blessed One replied:
The wise Ānanda knows and sees the eighteen elements as they truly are:
the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; and so on, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
Thus, Ānanda, one knows and sees these eighteen elements as they truly are;
one also knows and sees the six elements as they truly are:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Furthermore, one knows and sees six other elements as they truly are:

the element of sensual desire, the element of ill will, the element of cruelty, the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-cruelty; thus one knows and sees these other six elements as they truly are.
He knows and sees, as they truly are, the four elements: the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of mental joy, and the element of mental grief;
and the element of equanimity, the element of ignorance, the element of feeling, the element of perception, the element of volitional formations, and the element of consciousness.
He knows and sees the three realms— the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm— as they truly are; furthermore,
he also knows and sees another three realms as they truly are.
He knows and sees, as they truly are, the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of cessation— these three other realms—
as well as the past realm, the future realm, and the present realm.
He also knows and sees three other realms as they truly are:
the inferior realm, the middling realm, and the sublime realm;
he also knows and sees these three other realms as they truly are.
One knows and sees, as they truly are, another three elements: the wholesome element, the unwholesome element, and the indeterminate element;
as well as the element of those in training, the element of those beyond training, and the element of neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
He knows and sees both elements as they truly are—
the element with outflows and the element without outflows—
and he also knows and sees two other elements as they truly are.
"One knows and sees these two elements— the conditioned element and the unconditioned element— as they truly are;
to this extent, Ānanda, a wise person becomes skilled in the elements."
Thus, these sentences should be understood as being connected here and should also be recited individually in the middle [of the text];
however, they have not been written by me for fear of prolixity, and it should be known that their inclusion is to be understood according to the appropriate context.
To begin with, there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*); these [unconditioned phenomena] are indeed included within those very eighteen elements,
wherein the six beginning with the earth element are found.
Of those first four, there is inclusion within the element of the tangible;
the space element is included within the element of form because its intrinsic nature is light and darkness;
and the consciousness element is included within the seven mental elements.
Among the six [realms] beginning with the desire realm (kāmadhātu), it is the desire realm—specifically sensual desire (kāmarāga)—that is intended here;
and that is mental (caitasika).
The realms of ill-will (vyāpāda) and so forth are likewise exclusively mental.
The inclusion of these within the *dharmadhātu* means that even the six [elements] beginning with the pleasure element (*sukhadhātu*) are included in that very same [dharmadhātu],
as are the four elements beginning with the feeling element (*vedanādhātu*), three of which are included within the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), it exists within the seven elements of consciousness;
among the three [realms] beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it exists within the eighteen elements of the desire realm,
and within fourteen elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.

The inclusion of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is stated within the mind-element (manodhātu), the mental-object element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu); however,
for the three beginning with the form realm (rūpadhātu), the inclusion is stated in two [elements],
while that of the cessation realm (nirodhadhātu) is in the mental-object element (dharmadhātu).
The three [categories] beginning with the past realm are each subsumed within the eighteen realms:

the three beginning with the wholesome are subsumed within the wholesome and unwholesome realms, as well as within the seven mental realms (the six consciousnesses and the mind-element) among the form, sound, and dharma realms; and the indeterminate realm is subsumed within all eighteen realms.

Regarding the three categories of the learner (śaikṣa), the non-learner (aśaikṣa), and the realm (dhātu) and so forth: two [of these] are included within the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element; the third is included within all eighteen elements; and the first [category] is included within all eighteen elements, both with and without outflows (sāsrava-anāsrava).
The inclusion of the second [category] is within the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element;

the inclusion of the first [category] is within the eighteen elements; and the inclusion of the second [category] is within the phenomena-element, specifically regarding the conditioned and unconditioned elements.
These are the sixty-two elements (dhātu) which are mentioned there in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*;
however, the characteristics of two among them have not been stated.
The characteristics of the earth element and the others have been stated: they are established by their functions of supporting and so forth, and consist of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
But has not the characteristic of the consciousness-element also been stated, by the expression "consciousness is the cognition of each object"?
It has been correctly stated that this is the definition of all consciousnesses; however,
regarding the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*), has it been analyzed here whether "consciousness" is intended to mean only a specific portion of consciousness or rather the whole of it?
And space as an unconditioned phenomenon has the characteristics previously described,
but it is not the space element;
for this [element] must necessarily be distinct from [unconditioned] space.
For it has been stated in another sutra: "O monk, this person consists of six elements.
With this intention, he said that the definition of the two [aggregates] has not been stated;
for this very reason, he says:
In that case, should space itself be understood as the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), and all consciousness as the consciousness-element (*vijñānadhātu*)?
Regarding the phrase "in the mouth, nose, etc.," the word "etc. includes the ears and so forth; and it is said [that these are perceived] by means of light and darkness.
The word *kila* is intended to indicate the opinion of others;
however, one's own view is indicated by the underlying intention that space is merely the absence of obstructive substance (*sapratigha-dravya*),
and that its nature consists of night and day.
This is because darkness existing at night and light characterized by the sun's heat are intended [here], or else this designation is used in its general sense:
"matter (rūpa) is indeed that which resides in a heap (cita)."
