That which, abiding in the intellect and abiding in the aggregate [of the body],

excessively kills and is itself killed, is called *agha*; according to the rules of etymology (*nirukta*), the substitution of the vowel 'a' for the word "excessively" (*atyartha*) and the substitution of 'gha' for the root "to kill" (*han*) have been made.
"Adjacent to that" means that it is established in relation to the vicinity— that is, the proximity— of that wall or other such object.
In this explanation as well, the word "kila" (it is said) is intended to indicate the Vaibhāṣika interpretation;
however, his own position, which is stated later, is expressed [by the words] "and that is agha. (p. 078)

Because another form is not obstructed there, it is "not obstructed" (apratigha); considering that "another form is in this," it is called "neighboring" (sāmantaka) to another form—that is, to that which resides in the collection (cita).
In this case, the compound is a *karmadhāraya*.
It is called "the vicinity of evil" (*aghasāmantaka*) because it is both evil (*agha*) and a vicinity (*sāmantaka*); that is,
consciousness is intended here as the cause of rebirth, being defiled (*sāsrava*).
If it is asked, "What [is the reason]? he says:
because these six elements are accepted as the basis for birth.
"O monk, this person consists of six elements," because of the statement that "the descent of the embryo into the mother's womb occurs in dependence upon six elements";
for these indeed constitute birth, and so forth.
For these [elements] are the basis for birth because they are its progenitor, nourisher, and nurturer;
here, the consciousness-element (vijñānadhātu) is the progenitor, as it is the seed of rebirth.
The primary elements are the nourishers because they serve as its support;
the space element is the developer because it provides room; for this very reason, these are designated as "elements" (dhātu).
They are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they provide the connection for rebirth;
however, untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are not like this,
and thus are not the basis for birth, because they bring about the cessation of birth.
Regarding the statement "this visible thing here is form," what is this so-called "visibility" (nidarśana),
by virtue of which connection with that specific quality that object can be demonstrated as such?

That distinction is called "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*). By means of speech, the visual consciousness of another has arisen; that is the demonstration. That which exists together with it is "with demonstration. Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), only one element here—the form element (*rūpadhātu*)—is "with demonstration."
By the restriction that "only the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is visible," it is implied that the remaining [realms] are invisible;
furthermore, by this, its preeminence as being visible is stated.
Furthermore, there is no consequence of the fault of redundancy because that [point] is established;
and these subdivisions, such as "visibility" (*sanidarśanatā*) and so forth, are for the most part shown exactly as they are stated in the Sūtras.
For it is said in the Sūtra:

"O monk, the eye is an internal sense-sphere (*āyatana*); it is a translucent form derived from the four great elements, material, invisible, and possessing resistance. Up to: O monk, the body is an internal sense-sphere, as before."
"Monk, the internal sense-sphere of the mind is formless, invisible, and non-obstructive; monk,
the external sense-sphere of visible forms,
derived from the four great elements, is material, visible, and obstructive."
For sounds, monk, are an external sense-sphere derived from the four great elements, material, invisible, and offering resistance; and so on,
up to tangible objects, monk, which are an external sense-sphere.
The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements— which is invisible and possesses resistance— these phenomena, O monk, are an external sense base;
they are not included within the eleven sense bases, being invisible, non-resistant, and formless.

And these classifications of the elements themselves are explained up until the completion of the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*, because they consist of the analysis of matter and consciousness; thus it is said: "The ten material [elements] possess resistance."
The inclusion of the term "possessing form" (rūpin) is for the purpose of excluding that which is formless;
"form" (rūpa) is so called because of its transformation (rūpaṇā), and those things which possess this [quality] are "possessors of form" (rūpiṇaḥ).

Regarding the term "place" (*deśa*), it refers to the five sense-bases beginning with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and their five corresponding objective elements; thus, how is the exclusion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) effected?
For that too can indeed be said to be material (*rūpin*).
In that context, because of the restriction "only those possessing form" due to the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*),
those elements which have the nature of form alone are to be understood as being included; thus, [the inclusion of other categories] is excluded.
But the *dharmadhātu* has both material and immaterial natures; thus,
it obstructs the arising of another in its own location, and so forth—
wherein there is a single resistant (*sapratigha*) entity.
In that case, the arising of a second [moment] does not occur,
just as a hand struck against another hand or against a stone is repelled.
It does not arise in the place of the hand or in the place of the stone;
nor does even the stone arise in the place of those two, the hand and the stone.
"It is obstructed in water" means that it functions within its own object, namely water;
the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāya*) is for the purpose of excluding fishermen and others.
"There is neither here nor there" refers to those whose death is certain within the womb;
these are the signs [of such].
The meaning is "these various kinds";
by the inclusion of "titīla" (ants), "jatunya" (spiders), and so forth, there is the inclusion of thieves, humans, tigers, and others.
That in which something has its activity (kāritra) is its object (viṣaya); thus, activity is human effort (puruṣakāra).
The activity of the eye, ear, and so forth, consists in seeing, hearing, and so on, with respect to visible forms, sounds, and so on.

And that [basis] should be understood as characterized by a specific capacity for being the support (*āśrayabhāva*) with respect to one's own mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), which is grasped by the mind and mental factors through the application of a staff and a prop;
whereas that which is the object (*ālambana*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth,
is thus, in this case, the object of the mind and mental factors themselves.
Furthermore, the object of the eye and the other [senses] is not only that of the mind and mental factors;
therefore, because they do not proceed beyond it,
whatever in the world does not proceed beyond a certain point is obstructed therein, such as [a hand] against a piece of wood or a wall.

Likewise, the eye and other [faculties] do not exercise their activity beyond the object; rather, they exercise it only upon the object itself. Therefore, it is said that they "meet resistance" (pratighāta) therein.
Alternatively, "resistance" here refers to a mere encounter (nipāta); such is the detailed explanation.
In this context, "nipāta" means falling upon its own object; the meaning is that its activity (*kāritra*) is its engagement with its own object.

Regarding the passage beginning with "here, by way of obstruction and resistance," the detailed explanation is as follows: among the statement "the ten [realms] are with resistance" (*sapratigha*), it is intended that those ten realms are "with resistance" by way of *āvaraṇapratighāta* (obstructive resistance). This is because, if one were to include both *viṣayapratighāta* (resistance regarding the field) and *ālambanapratighāta* (resistance regarding the object), it would follow that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are also "with resistance. Therefore, there is a fourfold question (*catuṣkoṭika*); "fourfold" (*catuṣkoṇa*) means having four modes (*catuḥprakāra*).

"Subsequent-footed" (paścātpādaka): if one stands up to answer after grasping the latter part of the question, that is "subsequent-footed. If one does so after grasping the former part, that is "prior-footed" (pūrvapādaka).

They are also called "with resistance" (sapratigha) because of the obstruction of objects; for those mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta) are indeed with resistance both through the obstruction of objects and the obstruction of focal points (ālambana).
The five sense-faculties are not "with resistance" (sapratigha) by way of resistance toward an object, because they lack an object;
for it is said in detail: "wherever the mind intends to arise," meaning wherever—in terms of both the physical basis (*āśraya*) and the objective support (*ālambana*)—the mind desires to arise.
Obstruction (*pratighāta*) is non-arising; it can be produced by others through an intervening obstruction.
That very thing is "with obstruction" (*sapratigha*) because of that obstruction characterized by an intervening obstruction, due to its state of being obstructed.
Others say that it is characterized by resistance (*sapratighatva*) because it obstructs the arising of another in its own location;
what, then, is that which has the nature of the five sense-faculties and the five object-domains?

By contrast, that which is non-obstructive is intended as that wherein the arising of the mind cannot be hindered by others. Just as, in the case of the mental element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), others cannot create an internal obstruction to the arising of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
it is therefore established that the nature of the seven mental elements and the mental-object element is non-obstructive.
"The eight are indeterminate" means that these eight are exclusively indeterminate;
they are called "indeterminate" because they are not defined as being either wholesome or unwholesome, being distinct from both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Only those [factors] that are indeterminate (avyākṛta) are intended here, and not the wholesome (kuśala), because they are not designated as either wholesome or unwholesome;
nor are they the unwholesome (akuśala), because they are not designated as either wholesome or indeterminate.
Because wholesome and unwholesome states are designated as such by virtue of their being wholesome or unwholesome,
the application of words depends upon convention and common usage; thus,
the others are of three kinds.
The term "elements" (dhātavaḥ) is understood as the subject;
the restriction is that they are of three kinds only, not manifold nor two-fold.
The detailed explanation is that those associated with non-greed and so forth are wholesome (kuśala).
The seven mental elements associated with non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, shame, and dread of blame are wholesome (*kuśala*).
Those associated with greed, hatred, delusion, lack of shame, and lack of dread of blame are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
They are called "wholesome" because they have departed from what is contemptible, have escaped it, have gone beyond it, and have moved away from it.
Alternatively, wisdom (*prajñā*) is like *kuśa* grass because it is sharp; those who take up or grasp that [wisdom] are "skillful" (*kuśala*),
while those opposite to them are "unskillful" (*akuśala*).

Others, however, maintain that those [factors] which are non-associated with non-greed and so forth, as well as greed and so forth, are the indeterminate *dharmadhātu*; this is the detailed explanation.
That which has been described as having the nature of non-greed and so forth—this is what is meant.
Feeling and the other [mental factors] associated with non-greed and so forth;
the dissociated [factors] such as acquisition (prāpti) and birth (jāti), which are originated by non-greed and so forth.
The unmanifest (avijñapti),

analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), and the other [non-analytical cessation]— thus the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is of four kinds as wholesome; that which has greed and so forth as its intrinsic nature, or is associated with or originated from them, is unwholesome.
The other neutral [phenomenon] is that which is neither produced through association with a nature such as non-greed and so forth,
nor produced through association with a nature such as greed and so forth;
it is space and cessation not through deliberation.
And for these, as far as possible, there are acquisition, birth, and so forth; this is the indeterminate *dharmadhātu*,
while the other two are also indeterminate.

Other than those two elements of form and sound produced by wholesome and unwholesome minds, the other elements of form and sound—produced by neutral minds and comprised within bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*), as well as those not comprised within intimation—are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
It is determined that all [these] belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
thus, it is established that they all indeed belong to the desire realm.
Because they are included merely within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
but not individually in their entirety, he says:
Regarding the statement "there are fourteen in the realm of form," it is because those two— namely odor and taste— are edible food.
For even odor is a subtle edible food; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of its absence there.
Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the tangible element in that realm of form (rūpadhātu), because it would be [regarded as] edible food.
Since it is an established tenet that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the realm of desire consists of three bases (*āyatana*),
it would follow by extension that odor and taste are also [edible food].
The meaning is that those two which do not have the nature of nutriment would exist there;
however, the tangible does exist.

Is it for the purpose of enjoyment by way of being the support for the sense faculties, by way of being a receptacle, and by way of being a covering? Furthermore, others say— as the Venerable Śrīlāta says—
“by way of being accompanied by pliancy.”
The meaning is: "by that which has arisen together with pliancy, accompanied by bodily flexibility.

Here, the Master, disregarding the view of the venerable Śrīlāta and seeing that the Vaibhāṣika position is open to objection, begins his definitive determination with the words, "If that is so," and so forth.
The Vaibhāṣikas have effectively asserted this:
that odor and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) because they serve no purpose.
The Master refutes that position, [arguing] "like the objects of the female and male faculties," for that position is flawed.

Because it is flawed by the contradiction of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyayāpakṣāla*), for the subject intended here is that which possesses existing perceivers of itself— namely, the elements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) called odor and taste— and it follows that such a subject would instead possess non-existing perceivers of itself.
For just as the objects of the female and male faculties, being devoid of purpose, lack a perceiver of their own, so too it follows that the objects known as odor and taste [lack such perceivers];
yet there is clearly an inference [to the contrary].
By which this subversion of the specific property of the subject is manifested:
"The nose and tongue faculties do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), because their objects are useless [there],
just like the male faculty."
A certain follower of the Vaibhāṣika school offers a rebuttal,
stating in detail that there is indeed a purpose:
without those two— the sense-faculties of smell and taste— there would be no physical beauty of the body, nor would there be vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*).
By this sublation by perception (*dṛṣṭabādha*), he turns back the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*);
for in this case, inference is what sublates perception.
To the question "What is that [inference]? it is said:
In the form realm, the nose and tongue faculties exist because they serve a purpose,
just like the eye faculty.
The Master says:
"If this is the purpose," and so forth;
he shows that the reason—that there is beauty of the basis and speech through the basis alone and not through the sense faculty—is unestablished (*asiddha*).
The Vaibhāṣika teacher says:
"Not the base devoid of faculties," and so forth;
[this means that] in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there cannot exist a base of the olfactory or gustatory faculties that is devoid of the faculties themselves.
"Because it is the locus of the faculties,
like the locus of the male faculty"—
by this, he establishes the proven fact that [the body] possesses a purpose.
The Teacher says:
"It is logical that its non-existence [there] is so," and so forth;
it is logical that the basis for the male faculty cannot exist there because it would be purposeless.
The bases of the olfactory and gustatory faculties, however, serve a purpose because they function as the support for the beauty of the body and for speech;
therefore, their existence even without the faculties themselves is logical.
The proof for this is stated as follows:
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), the bases of the olfactory and gustatory faculties exist even though they lack those faculties themselves,
because they serve a purpose, just like the base of the visual faculty.

By this, he establishes that very point regarding the unestablished nature of its having a purpose. Thus, when a certain proponent of the Vaibhāṣika school who asserts that [the sense organs] have a purpose has been refuted, the Vaibhāṣikas— showing that the objection "In that case, it would follow that the olfactory and gustatory faculties also do not exist because they lack a purpose," which was stated at the outset, is merely a fallacious refutation— say:
"Even though it is purposeless," and so forth;
just as for those destined to die in the womb, their birth is purposeless,
for they do not experience the sight of forms and so on.
In this way, the production of the olfactory and gustatory faculties in the realm of form would likewise be purposeless;
therefore, the olfactory and gustatory faculties do not exist in the realm of form because they serve no purpose.
By the example "like the male organ," the teacher demonstrates that the charge of being purposeless is inconclusive; he says:
"Let it be indeed purposeless," and so forth.
The manifestation of the sense faculties would be purposeless,
yet it is not without a cause, because conditioned phenomena possess causes;
and he who is free from craving for objects is necessarily so regarding the sense faculties as well.
By this, the absence of a logical reason is demonstrated;
and thus the proof is stated as follows:
the faculties of smell and taste do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Because it would be without a cause, like a causeless sprout or like the male organ; or else, why would the male organ itself not be produced? Thus the Teacher himself sets forth this dilemma.
What is the intention [behind this objection]?
If the production of the olfactory and gustatory faculties occurs without purpose or even without a cause, why then is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) not also produced?
For this is the position of the Vaibhāṣikas.
The continuum of a sentient being in the form realm possesses the sense-faculties together with the nose,
because it possesses vitality in relation to form,
just like the continuum of a sentient being belonging to the desire realm.
The Teacher, however, by asking "Why would even the male faculty not be produced? demonstrates the reversal of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya*) in that position:
the subject is the continuum of sentient beings in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), which lacks the male faculty;
its reversal is the state of possessing the male faculty.
The Vaibhāṣikas offer this rebuttal: "Because it would cause ugliness.
To the question "How so? they reply:
"The male faculty does not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu)."
Because it causes ugliness, like being one-eyed or having a withered arm,
our proposition is not subverted by that inference.
If the intention is that "what is seen does not invalidate [the argument]" because of the established tenet of the Naiyāyikas,
the Teacher says:
"Why would the testicles and private parts enclosed within a sheath not be beautiful?"
The "secret part" (guhya) refers to the male organ; that which is enclosed in a sheath (kośa) at the base (vasti) is the "sheathed secret part" (vastiguhya), which remains covered by a sheath.
"For those whose private organs are thus sheathed in a sheath, does this not appear beautiful? It certainly does appear beautiful; this is the meaning.
By this, he demonstrates that the [alleged] lack of beauty is unestablished."

And the detailed argument that "arising does not occur by virtue of a purpose" implies, through the force of circumstantial evidence (*arthāpatti*), that the male organ (*puruṣendriya*) must be produced by virtue of a purpose— this is what is asserted by the Vaibhāṣikas when they state that it would otherwise be unseemly (*aśobhākaratva*).
And how is it that this thesis is sublated by inference, because it has the flaw of being the opposite of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*)? It is explained as follows:
The male organ is not produced by the force of a purpose,
because it is produced from its own causes, like one-eyedness or lameness.
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"In that case, it contradicts the Sūtra," and so forth.
This position—that there exists a continuum of sentient beings in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) who lack the sense-faculties of smell and taste—is flawed.
Because it would contradict the previous position;

for the Blessed One stated that beings belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) are "unimpaired" and "possessing unimpaired faculties," since they lack one-eyedness or mutilation and because their eyes and other faculties are not deficient.
The Master says:
"Those which are there," and so forth.

Since those [beings] in the form realm possess the eye and other faculties—though lacking the olfactory faculty and the rest—the phrase "those whose faculties are not deficient" is taken as referring to the meaning of the Sūtra, and thus there is no contradiction.
The Vaibhāṣikas describe it thus:
"They indeed exist," and so forth;
for although the faculties of smell and taste exist there in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), their objects—odor and flavor—do not.
For, through the gateway of one's own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), craving arises in living beings toward the six sense bases, such as the eye and so forth, by way of their own continuum;
and karma, moistened by that [craving],
[continues] in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) along with its causes, including the faculties of smell and taste.
And therefore, because they possess causes, those two indeed exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), just like a sprout and so forth which have causes.
And by this they demonstrate that the proof stated— that the nose and tongue faculties do not exist in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) because they lack a cause— is unestablished; however,
in the case of the male faculty, [it is absent] by way of sexual contact.
What is the manifestation of craving? This is the subject under discussion; and beings belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) are free from passion for sexual contact.
Therefore, in that realm, action is not preceded by craving;
because it is thus without a cause, the male faculty does not exist there, just like a sprout that lacks a cause. Thus it is established that in the form realm there are only fourteen elements.
"Those pertaining to the formless realm," and so forth:

by the restriction that only the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) pertain to the formless realm, it is implied that other elements do not exist there;
for those who are free from passion for form are reborn there.

Therefore, the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is form— the five beginning with the eye and the five beginning with visible form— do not exist, nor do the five consciousness-elements that have them as their bases and objects; thus,
those [bases] beginning with the eye and those [objects] beginning with visible form are, respectively, the bases and the objects of those [consciousnesses].
Since these [three] have those as their bases and objects—

meaning that because the bases, such as the eye, and the objects, such as visible form, are absent, those [bases and objects] also do not exist there— it follows that these three elements, whether with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*), are likewise non-existent there.
Since it has been established that "only these three are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava)," for what purpose is this stated: "but the remaining ones are with-outflows"?
Is it not the case that by the restriction "only these three are with-outflows" (sāsrava),
it is established that the remaining [dharmas] are with-outflows? It is not so established.
In order to dispel the doubt as to how the remaining [factors] could be exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava) or exclusively without-outflows (anāsrava), this is stated:
The remaining [elements] are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*).

As for the statement "the five consciousness-elements are indeed with vitarka and vicāra," the word "indeed" (*hi*) is used for the purpose of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), meaning they are exclusively with vitarka and vicāra.
"The last three are of three kinds" means that the last ones alone are of three kinds; this is a restriction [implying] "except for applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra)."

Since applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) have the nature of the associated factor-element (*samprayuktaka-dharmadhātu*), there is the risk of their inclusion here; therefore, they are excluded. For applied thought will be included within the second category, and sustained thought, arising from the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*), is included within the third category.
However, he will explain that anything other than those is not included within any of the three modes.

These elements, beginning with the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and ending with the associated dharma-element (*samprayukta-dharmadhātu*), are accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first dhyāna—including its preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*)—because they are associated with applied and sustained thought.
For this very reason, in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), they are without applied thought, due to the absence of applied thought.

Because they are associated with investigation (*vicāra*) alone, from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), those two are absent; therefore, they are without applied thought (*avitarka*) and without investigation (*avicāra*). Furthermore, the entire unassociated portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is likewise without applied thought and without investigation.

As far as possible, these include the form, mind, and formations dissociated from mind belonging to the three realms, as well as the unconditioned; furthermore, in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is investigation (*vicāra*) but no initial application (*avitarka*) due to the absence of initial application,
and no sustained application (*avicāra*) due to the absence of the second [sustained] application.
Since it is not included within those three types of *vicāra*,
it is "with vitarka and with vicāra" (*savitarkaḥ savicāraḥ*);
for while it can indeed be "with vitarka," it cannot be "with vicāra" because of its non-association (*asamprayoga*) with *vicāra*.
Nor is it included in the second [dhyāna],
because it is "without vitarka and with vicāra only," owing to its association with vitarka.
And because of the absence of the second [factor], investigation (vicāra),
it is not included in the third [dhyāna] either; thus,
it is "without vitarka and without vicāra."

For although that [state] is without investigation (*avicāra*) due to the absence of a second investigation, it is not without applied thought (*avitarka*) because of its association with applied thought;
how, then, should it be described? To this, he says:
It is "without investigation" (*avicāra*) because it lacks the second [mental factor], investigation;
it is "with mere initial inquiry" (*vitarkamātra*) because of its association with initial inquiry (*vitarka*).
"For this very reason" means that on the level of those states accompanied by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), sustained thought alone constitutes the fourth type,
being "without sustained thought and with applied thought only."

"The remaining are devoid of both" means that regarding the ten remaining material elements (*rūpī dhātu*) mentioned, there might be a doubt as to whether they possess vitarka and vicāra, possess only one of them, or are devoid of both; therefore, having determined this, the meaning is that the remaining ones are indeed devoid of both— namely, they are exclusively without vitarka and without vicāra.

How are they said to be "non-conceptual"? Because of the statement that the visual consciousness, in its engagement with an object, cognizes blue but does not think "this is blue," it is said that there are three kinds of conceptualization.
The word "kila" (it is said) is for the purpose of indicating the opinion of another;

his own intention, however, is that *vitarka* is simply a particular kind of volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus there is no other distinct factor (*dharma*) called "conceptualization by nature" (*svabhāvavikalpa*).
For he has stated this in the *Pañcaskandhaka*: [text follows].
What is *vitarka*?
It is a mental discourse that investigates; it is a specific form of volition and wisdom, which is the grossness of the mind.
What is *vicāra*?
The mental discourse that is investigative is likewise the subtlety of the mind;
it is established as volition (*cetanā*) in the state of non-investigation and as wisdom (*prajñā*) in the state of investigation.
Thus, these possess conceptualization by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
The particle *tad* is used here as an introductory marker for the sentence or in the sense of "therefore";

alternatively, discursive thought (*vitarka*) is "conceptualization by way of intrinsic nature" because it has grossness as its characteristic. Thus, it is conceptualization by way of its very nature.
Because this [mental consciousness] is associated with these five groups of consciousness, they are said to be "with conceptualization.

However, they do not possess the other two types of conceptualization—namely, the conceptualization of discernment (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*);
therefore, they are called "without conceptualization."
Just as a horse with one leg is called "legless" when three legs have been cut off— even though one leg remains— so too those who possess a single conceptual construction are called "non-conceptual."

For that is indeed the conceptualization of investigation; it is mental wisdom (*prajñā*) that is not associated [with meditative concentration], consisting of what is derived from hearing, reflection, and innate attainment,
for it exists in the mind and is thus mental.

"Distraught" (*vyagrā*) means having various objects (*vividhāgra*), that is to say, having various focal points (*vividhālambana*); or alternatively, "distraught" means having its excellence departed (*vigatapradhāna*) because it repeatedly relies upon different focal points. Why is it called "discrimination by investigation" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*)?
Because it proceeds in dependence upon names with respect to each respective object—
such as the discernment that "form" or "feeling" is impermanent, suffering, and so forth—
and because meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) occurring in a state of concentration proceeds toward its object without depending on names.
This is not called "conceptualization through investigation" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*);

rather, all memory (*smṛti*) occurs only in the mind. It is said that whether in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or not in a state of concentration (*asamāhita*), it proceeds independently of names, taking as its object merely that which has been previously experienced.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)? It is defined by the characteristic of being an aspiration of the mind.

However, because that which is associated with the five bodies of sensory consciousness does not function as an aspiration for an object already experienced, it is not accepted as the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇavikalpa*).
"Seven have objects" is a double restriction:
only seven have objects, and those that have objects are only these seven;
and "half of the dharmas have objects."
This is stated by way of exclusion from what was previously mentioned;
here too, there is a double restriction:
only half of the factors (dharmas) possess an object.

And because there is the restriction that "only half of the *dharmas* have an object" (*sālambana*)— specifically, the restriction that "only seven [of the eighteen] *dhātus* have an object, and only half of the *dharma-dhātu* has an object"— it is established that the remaining ten material *dhātus* and the portion of the *dharma-dhātu* that is dissociated (*asaṃyukta*) are without an object (*anālambana*). For if this were not restricted, this meaning would not be established.
"Nine are non-appropriated" means that they are exclusively non-appropriated;
"together with half of the eighth" means together with it, so to speak.
"And those eight" means that those seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)— of which half was stated to have an object— are eight;
the mention of "eight" is for the purpose of including the entire dharma-element.
Lest it be understood that half of the *dharmadhātu* is not included, those eight [elements] and sound— these nine— are said to be "unappropriated" (*anupātta*);
the other nine are of two kinds.
The five beginning with the eye and the four beginning with visible form— excluding sound— these nine are of two kinds only;
that is to say, they are both appropriated (*upātta*) and unappropriated (*anupātta*),
and not exclusively appropriated.
And for this purpose,
it is further stated in the sutra that "the other nine are twofold" because they conform to one another through both benefit and injury.

Through the benefit or injury of the eye-element and the other [elements]— characterized by such things as the application of ointment or the striking with the hand— the benefit or injury of the mind and mental factors occurs;
and through the benefit or injury of the mind and mental factors— characterized by such things as joy or dejection—
the benefit or injury of the eye-element and the other [elements] occurs.
Therefore, they are said to be "appropriated" by the mind and mental factors in the sense of being their basis; the meaning is that they are "taken as one's own.
In common worldly usage, this refers to what is "sentient," which means "possessing life.
The statement that "the tangible is of two kinds" is a restriction to these two [categories].

"Tangible objects alone are twofold" and "twofold are tangible objects alone"— this is a double restriction. "The remaining nine material [elements] are derived" and "a portion of the dharma-element is also derived"— here too, there is a double restriction.
And because these two are thus determined,
it is established that the remaining seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), excluding unmanifest form (*avijñapti*), are neither [of the two types],
since the primary elements (*bhūta*) have been determined by their characteristics such as the tetrad of solidity and so forth.

Because of the restriction to four [elements], the earth, water, fire, and wind elements are the four primary elements (*mahābhūta*) within the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), such as smoothness and so forth;
however, the eye and other [senses] therein are not primary elements.
Furthermore, because of the restriction to the characteristics of hardness and so forth, other phenomena such as the eye and others are not included within the earth, water, fire, and wind elements.
How are there four great elements? They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.
What is the earth element? It is solidity, and so forth.
"And because they are tangible" means that those qualities, such as hardness and so forth, are tangible; for they are tangibles,
whereas color and the other [sensory objects] are to be seen, heard, smelled, and tasted.
How is it understood that those [elements] are tangibles?
To this he says:
for hardness and so forth are not perceived by the eye and the other [senses].
If you think that they must therefore be understood as tangibles because they are perceived by the body-faculty alone,
and that consequently color-form and the other [sensory objects] are also tangibles, he says:
Nor are color and so forth grasped by the body-faculty;
rather, the subject under discussion is: "What is grasped [by it]?"
And it is said in the Sūtra, and so forth; it has also been clearly demonstrated in another Sūtra.
How? [This is] explained in detail, up until this was said:

"O Bhikṣu, tangibles are an external sense-field (*bāhyam āyatanam*); they consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*) and that which is derived from the four great elements (*upādāya-rūpam*), being invisible (*anidarśanam*) but offering resistance (*sapratigham*).
This clearly demonstrates that the remaining sense-fields, such as the eye and so forth, are not [composed of] the great elements.
As for what was stated at length in the Sūtra... [the full passage follows].
Regarding that which is "hardness" (*khakkhaṭa*) within the mass of flesh in the eye— the meaning being a type of hardness—

they raise an objection, thinking that the visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) has the nature of hardness; [the response is] that this is a teaching concerning the mass of flesh which exists inseparably from it.

This statement refers to the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that exists inseparably from that visual faculty (*cakṣurindriya*); for even with respect to the physical basis of the eye, there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "eye.
It is for this very reason that it is referred to as a "mass of flesh" (*māṃsapiṇḍa*).

Otherwise, he would have simply said "the two eyes" if it were intended as the sense-faculty itself. Regarding the passage in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* which states in detail, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," and which teaches only the primary elements (*bhūta*) during the stages of the embryo such as the *kalala* and so forth— anticipating the objection that the derived matter (*bhautika*) does not exist, he says:

"For the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substantial entity" means that the four elements, beginning with the earth element, are the fundamental substance precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substantial entity.
Because the five bases of contact beginning with the eye arise from it,
the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is also the fundamental sentient being, since the mind-base of contact (*manaḥ-sparśāyatana*) arises from it;
or else, because they are the supports for the [other] four, these alone are the fundamental sentient being.
How, moreover, is this understood? Because it is stated later in that very same sutra, following the mention of the six bases of contact:
"The six bases of contact" refers to the eye-base of contact up to the mind-base of contact;
from this it is understood that the statement, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," is for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substantiality of a sentient being,
and not because there are merely [the four] great elements.

But is it not the case that, just as the sense-base of mind-contact (*manaḥ-sparśāyatana*) is mentioned again even though it is not distinct from the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*), so too the eye and the other [senses] might be mentioned again even though they are not distinct from the four elements?
Therefore, the existence of derived matter (*bhautika*) distinct from those [elements] is not established by the repeated mention of the six sense-bases of contact. This is not so.
For if the earth element and so forth were themselves the bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), he would have stated that "the primary elements alone are the bases of contact";
but it is not so.
What then?
From the fact that there is the sense-base of eye-contact up to the sense-base of mind-contact,
it is understood that the eye and the other [senses] are distinct from the earth-element and so forth.

As for the consciousness element, it is mentioned again as a "sphere of contact" (sparśāyatana) by way of its connection with the mention of the spheres of contact such as the eye; what is the meaning? The meaning is that it is the basis for contact, which is a mental factor.

And because it would follow that the mind does not exist: if, O monk, this person consisting of the six elements were to be grasped as substances exactly as they are, and not other substances dependent upon them, then this [consequence] follows.

If it is argued that because only the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) is mentioned here, there would be the undesirable consequence of not including the mental factors (caitasika) which depend upon it, and thus this is not a fault since such an exclusion is intended; [we reply:]...
It is not so, because this position is flawed; for this position is indeed flawed,
since it contradicts one's own established tenet that mental factors (*caitasika*) are merely specific states of mind (*citta*).
Therefore, he says:
"And it is not logical to accept that the mental factors (caitta) are nothing other than the mind (citta) itself;
why?"
"Perception and feeling are mental factors; this phenomenon is dependent upon the mind," according to the scriptural statement.
And here the proof is established:
perception and feeling exist as entities distinct from the mind.
Because they are taught separately in the teaching on the aggregates,
just like the aggregate of form;
or else, because perception and feeling are entities distinct from their own basis.
Because it is dependent upon that:
whatever is dependent upon its own substratum is a distinct entity from its own substratum,
just as a painting is a distinct entity from the wall upon which it rests.
And because of the statement regarding minds with passion and so forth:
one understands a mind with passion as "a mind with passion" according to reality;
one understands a mind free from passion as "a mind free from passion" according to reality.
"One understands, as it truly is, a mind with hatred as 'a mind with hatred,'" and so forth;
here, the proof that "the mind is with lust" establishes the mutual distinctness of the mind and lust as separate entities.
Because they are designated in connection with a companion— as in "Caitra is with his son"— just like Caitra when designated in connection with his son,
[the fingers] are said to be "ten" as a collection.
The meaning is that their intrinsic nature consists solely of an accumulation of atoms;
however, since other elements are excluded by this restriction, it is established that they are not accumulated. [Objection:
Of which element is the form "tulyārta" a derivative?
For instance, although the root *tul* in the sense of "weighing" takes the form *tolayati*,
this is not a fault; rather,
this form is accepted as derived from the nominal stem *tulā* in the sense of "one who makes a balance," as in *tulayati*.
And because it is similar in its function, it is "form"; thus,
the four external elements consist of form and the others, excluding sound,
and are designated as "axe," "wood," and so forth.
That which is designated as an axe and so forth cuts that which is designated as wood and so forth;
this is said with reference to their occurrence, for sometimes that which is designated as an axe and so forth is itself cut.
"It also cuts what is designated as wood and so forth, because it produces a connection," and so on;
"producing a connection" (*sambandhotpādin*) means that its nature is to arise through a connection, that is, without separation.
The "stream of aggregation" (*saṃghāta-srotas*) means the continuity of the collection of form and so forth;
the "production of separation" (*vibhakta-utpādana*) or "generation of separation" (*vibhakta-janana*) therein is what constitutes "cutting.
For indeed, even in the absence of axes and the like, cutting occurs for things that are momentary.
However, since the cessation of the continuum occurs by means of an axe and so forth,
it is said that "the axe and so forth cut";
for, by virtue of a specific causal complex, a specific transformation arises.
In that context, it is determined that the four elements either cut or are cut;
and because of this determination, it is established that the other elements are neither.
For this very reason, he says:
"The body-faculty and so forth are not cut," and so on in detail.
In this context, one should have said "the eye-faculty and so forth"; why, then, is the expression "the body-faculty and so forth" used?

It is because the cutting occurs most clearly in the case of the body-faculty, should such a thing as cutting occur; therefore, the faculties are described with the body-faculty as their primary representative.
In the case of the cutting off of all limbs without remainder and the cutting off of all major and minor parts,
because there is no bifurcation of those— the body-faculty and so forth— how, then, is it understood that there is no bifurcation of them?
Therefore, he says again:
"The sense-faculties do not become twofold, because a limb that has been severed and separated from the body is devoid of sense-faculties.
How, then, is this understood?
That limb which has been severed and separated from the body is devoid of sense faculties;

because, depending upon that [severed part] and upon objects such as the tangible, bodily consciousness and the others do not arise. How then, when the severed tip of the nose is joined again, does bodily consciousness arise?
There is no fault, because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) arises again through its connection with the base of the nose.

How is it that here the tails of house-lizards and the like throb even when severed? If the body-faculty does not exist there, one should understand that this is a transformation of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*), and not the activity of the body-faculty.
Nor do they cut, because of their transparency, just as the luster of a gem does not cut due to its transparency;
so it is with the sense faculties.
By the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) in the phrase "it burns and weighs thus," that same external set of four elements is shown to be such [as they appear].
The transformation of wood and other substances caused by fire is "burning," and that does not occur for the sense faculties because of their translucence (*acchatva*), like the luster of a gem.
For those [elements] do not undergo transformation like wood or like leather;
rather,
through connection with them, the continuity of the stream is severed.

Furthermore, it is precisely those four elements that constitute the scales and so forth which perform the weighing, and not the sense faculties, for the same reason [as before], namely their translucence (*acchatva*).
As for the formless elements (*amūrta-dhātu*), because they are indeed formless, cutting and so forth are impossible;
thus, cutting and the like are not considered with respect to them.
Sound is not [an object] to be cut because it is already severed; nor does it cut, nor is it cut, nor does it weigh, because it exists as a continuous stream.
The phrase "the dispute concerns that which is similar to the burner" carries over into what follows as well, [as does] "not sound, because it is not subject to destruction.
Thus, that same set of four elements is both the burner and the similar;
fire, alkali, and so forth are the burners.

The opinion of some is that salt and other such substances are comparable [to the four elements] because they are the cause of transformations such as ash for all four elements here; and even in that case, they are comparable because they are the cause of the bending of a scale when all [four] are present.
Only the fire-element (tejodhātu) is the burner, and only heaviness (gurutva) is what is weighed;
thus, only the fire-element, when its manifest function is present in flames and the like, burns,
because we observe that even though the earth-element and others possess their own manifest functions, they do not burn.
And it is precisely by taking heaviness as the basis that visible form is said to have a manifest function;
for even though the functions of visible form and the other [sensory qualities] are manifest in light substances such as sunlight and the like, they are observed not to be equal.
Thus, it is said: "five are internal."
The mention of "five" is for the purpose of excluding the mind;
the mention of "internal" is for the purpose of excluding form and so forth.
The restriction is that the five internal [bases] are exclusively born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and accumulative (*aupacayika*), and not outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).
Why?
Because there is no outflow (*naiṣyandika*) apart from those;
for although the results of maturation (*vipākaja*) and those derived from accumulation (*aupacayika*) are not outflows, [they are included here].

Since it is said that "an outflow is similar to its cause," those [dharmas] are not considered outflows because they are subsumed solely under the categories of being born of maturation (*vipākaja*) or accumulative (*aupacayika*).
However, those which resemble their own causes, and are neither born of maturation (*vipākaja*) nor accumulative (*aupacayika*),
are intended here as "outflowing" (*naiṣyandika*);
and the eyes and so forth are not of such a nature.

Rather, they are either born of maturation (*vipākaja*) or accumulative (*aupacayika*); therefore, they are described in this way because there is no outflow (*niṣyanda*) distinct from those two. But how is it known that they do not possess an outflowing nature?
Because [the elements] persist after death;
for the eye-element and so forth do not persist in one who is dead,
since they are born from a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The cause of the fruit that is maturation is the "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*).
Those born from the maturation cause are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*),
by the elision of the middle term— the word "cause"— just as in the case of "ox-cart" (*go-ratha*).
Just as a chariot yoked with oxen is called an "ox-chariot," so too [is] karma that has reached the time of its fruition;
the meaning is that it exists in the moment immediately following the arising of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
It is called "maturation" (*vipāka*) because it matures (*vipacyate*);
the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the agent (*karmakartṛ*), or alternatively, the term for the cause is metaphorically applied to the fruit— such is the detailed explanation.
Even though its intrinsic nature is non-maturation, the cause characterized by karma is called "maturation" because it produces that [maturation],
just as the term "cause" is metaphorically applied to the fruit; such is the detailed explanation.
These six spheres of contact, beginning with the eye, are called "ancient karma" (*paurāṇaṃ karma*). Karma that occurred in a previous birth is "ancient," or simply "ancient" itself;
these spheres of contact, although not having ancient karma as their intrinsic nature, are nonetheless called "ancient karma" because they are produced from it.
In this context, the metaphorical application of "perversion" (viparyaya) should be understood as follows:

those [formations] accumulated by means of specific types of nutriment, processing, sleep, and meditative concentration are called "accumulative" (aupacayika); here, the word "specific" (viśeṣa) is to be connected with each [term].
In this context, food and sleep are well-known in the world;
conditioning consists of the nature of anointing, bathing, oil-massage, and so forth;
and meditative concentration is characterized by one-pointedness of mind.
Accumulation (*upacaya*) is that which is heaped together (*caya*).
Those things arising from accumulation are "accumulative" (*aupacayika*), like soldiers;
or alternatively, they are "accumulative" because they are themselves accumulations, like trained horses (*vainayika*).
Some say it is because the secondary suffix is prescribed in its own sense [as "brahmacarya"], and because of the phrase "and by celibacy";
for it is observed that the bodies of those practicing celibacy (*brahmacārin*) whose senses are tranquil undergo growth.
However, by that [practice], there would be merely the absence of injury;
for through unchastity there is a decline of the body,
whereas through chastity there is no decline of the body.
Therefore he said:
by that celibacy there would be merely non-harming, but no accumulation;
accumulation, however, occurs only through food and so forth.
Why, then, does the physical decline of some who have gone forth occur? This [decline] would be due to the exhaustion caused by the fever of sensual desire;
it is like a protective rampart for guarding [the mind].
Protection [of the body] occurs because the continuity of accumulation (*upacaya-santāna*) remains surrounding the continuity of maturation (*vipāka-santāna*);
sound is [produced by] accumulation because no excellence of sound is observed in a body that has not been accumulated;
and because it proceeds according to one's will.
Sound proceeds by virtue of the desire "May sound arise for me," but it does not proceed without such desire; however,
a phenomenon born of maturation (vipākaja) proceeds even for one who has no such desire.
Therefore, sound is not born of maturation;
and here the proof is stated:
"Sound is not born of maturation."
Because it proceeds from desire,
like the mental factor of appropriate attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*);
however, that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is not so.
Its activity does not proceed by its own desire, just as in the case of the visual faculty;
"then what [is it]? and so forth is the detailed explanation.
By this, he points out that the proposition contradicts his own established tenet:
"This third succession is one," and so forth;
for the elements (*bhūta*) of the path of action consisting in abstention from harsh speech arise in the throat with the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

From those [primary elements], sound arises. Even in the second position, from the karma-born primary elements, there arise nourishment-born (aupacayika) primary elements— either through the accumulation of food or through the accumulation of meditative concentration—
and from those, there arise outflow-born (naiṣyandika) primary elements, which are distinct from the previous primary elements and are adventitious (āgantuka).

Is "sound" [the result] derived from them through a traditional succession? However, with reference to the intention of the cessation of human effort, it was stated that the quality of possessing the voice of Brahmā arises from the cessation of vocal activity;
by this, the contradiction of that proposition with one's own established doctrine is avoided.
If there were a contradiction with reasoning—
namely, that sound proceeds from desire— then it would not be said to be born of maturation (*vipākaja*) because of its contradiction with the reasoning regarding maturation;
likewise, if bodily sensation also proceeded from desire, it would not be born of maturation.
But it does not proceed from desire;
rather,
it proceeds even without desire.
The intention is that, like the eye and so forth, it is logical for it to be "born of maturation" (vipākaja); but what, then, is that [maturation]?

That which proceeds even without the application of conditions for pleasure or pain is "outflowing" (*naiṣyandika*), meaning it is produced by similar and omnipresent causes (*sabhāga-sarvatraga-hetu*);
this is a restriction stating that it is produced by similar and omnipresent causes alone, and not by the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
"Born of maturation" (*vipākaja*) means produced by the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*);
that is, they are indeed produced by the cause of maturation, but the restriction "produced by the cause of maturation alone" does not apply,
for things born of maturation are also produced by the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
In that regard, it is determined that the eight non-obstructive [elements] are exclusively outflowing (*naiṣyandika*) and born of maturation (*vipākaja*);
they are not accumulative (*aupacayika*), because there is no accumulation,
meaning that their nature is not one of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
"Of three kinds" means that they are indeed of three kinds; this is what is being determined.
Among them, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are inseparable from the sense faculties (*indriya*).

Because it is stated that "maturation (vipāka) is an indeterminate (avyākṛta) phenomenon pertaining to sentient beings," [the faculties] are not outflowing (naiṣyandika) or accumulative (aupacayika), even though they are distinct from the sense organs.
How, then, is it known that there are also outflowing [phenomena] even when dissociated from the sense faculties? Because their persistence is observed even in one who is dead.
For those not classified as sentient beings are not admitted to be born of maturation;
since there is no second substance,
the restriction is that there is only one possessor of substance.

Because they are essential, they are called "substances"; because they are indestructible, they last for one moment; and because they are non-outflowing, they are produced by a non-homogeneous cause for that single moment.
The intended meaning is that they are "momentary" because there is no preceding moment of uncontaminated [consciousness], and not because they perish at the end of another moment;
otherwise, since the restriction would be that only the final elements are momentary, it would follow that all other elements are non-momentary.

But how can the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) both exist simultaneously within the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti)?
For it is neither accepted nor stated that there is a simultaneous conjunction of two consciousnesses;
rather, what is the case?
The meaning is that here a single consciousness is established as two elements and is spoken of by two names;

therefore, he explains: "the mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering is both the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*)."

"The remaining [factors] are the dharma-element co-arising with it" means that, within that complex of receptivity (*kṣānti-kalāpa*), the factors other than the mind are the "remaining ones," which are co-arising with that receptivity.

That is to say, one acquires possession of the outflow-free restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), which consists of form (*rūpa*), as well as the associated factors such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*sañjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), along with their acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth; this is the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, one attains possession.
The meaning is that he attains a [state] not previously attained;
does he also [attain it] by means of the visual consciousness element?
The phrase "attains possession" (*samanvāgamam pratilabhate*) is the subject under discussion.
By the expression "separate attainment" (*pṛthag lābha*), the first and second alternatives (*koṭi*) are shown;
by the expression "also together" (*sahāpi ca*), the third alternative is shown.

The fourth [type], however, is "excluded from what has been mentioned"; it is not explicitly shown because it is easy to understand, or rather, it is also indicated by the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "not separate and not together."
Regarding "gradually acquiring the eye-faculty in the desire realm":

this refers to a person situated in the desire realm who, through the gradual process of the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, or through the process of death, gradually acquires the eye-faculty; with what is it associated?
Is it associated only with the desire realm?
No, it is said:
when one acquires [the eye-element]— whether associated with the desire realm or the form realm—
during the stages of the embryo (kalala) and so forth, or likewise at the time of gradual death or of death without consciousness, one is not possessed of the eye-element.
In the state of the *kalala* and so forth, or during the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), one now acquires possession (*samanvāgama*) of it; however,

one does not acquire possession of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) while previously being devoid of it, because at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the intermediate existence, that person was already possessed of the past and future [visual consciousness] which is both wholesome and afflicted.
For this refers to the state of being deprived (*viprakṛtāvasthā*), not the state of having already obtained or about to obtain it, as explained in detail.

One who has been reborn in the second dhyāna or higher lacks the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) there; thus, having previously been non-endowed with it, he now, while bringing into manifestation a visual consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna—which is by nature unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—obtains possession (*samanvāgama*) of that visual consciousness element.
But it is not the case that one who was previously unendowed with the eye-element attains its possession;
for he is already endowed with it as if it were attained, since he has fallen away from it and is being reborn in a lower realm.

One who has fallen from the second or higher meditations and is being reborn below— in the first meditation or in the desire realm— attains possession of the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) with which he was previously unendowed;
this occurs through the wholesome or afflicted [consciousness] of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) during the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhāna*), pertaining to the past and future,
but he does not attain possession of the visual faculty element (*cakṣurdhātu*) with which he was previously unendowed.
"Because of being both possessed of and having acquired [them], it would be by both ways," and so forth;
one who has passed away from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) was previously not possessed of both the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) and the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu).

At the very moment of linking with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one acquires possession of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)—whether wholesome or afflicted—which is directed toward arising, even though it is past or future;
for those in the intermediate state possess unimpaired faculties.
However, this does not apply to both [the eye-element and the consciousness-element] simultaneously, setting aside these specific cases.
The meaning is: having abandoned the categories of phenomena mentioned in the three groups [of the three realms].
One who has passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is being reborn in that very same realm is "not possessed of both" [the possession and the non-possession];
there is non-possession there, but no acquisition of possession.
Furthermore, one born in the second dhyāna or above, who does not manifest visual consciousness, does not acquire possession of both [the eye-faculty and visual consciousness] simultaneously;
how so?
Even if he acquires possession of the eye-faculty, he was not previously non-possessed of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
Although one who is not endowed with the visual consciousness element does not acquire such endowment [therein], it is because he does not bring it into manifestation;

however, a sighted person dwelling in the desire realm, through immediate death and at the reconnection of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), is not unendowed with both [the eye faculty and the visual consciousness element] and acquires endowment with them,
because he is already endowed with both.

"One who is endowed with the eye-element is also endowed with the eye-consciousness-element"— by this very sūtra, which states "attainment is both separate and simultaneous," this fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is also formulated;
for "attainment" (lābha) means acquisition (pratilambha).

Even when referring merely to acquisition (*prāpti*), depending on the speaker's intention, it sometimes occurs that "acquisition" (*pratilambha*) is intended in the first fourfold set (*catuḥ-koṭika*), whereas in the second, "merely acquisition" (*prāpti-mātra*) is the first point; such is the detailed explanation.
One born in the second dhyāna or above is necessarily endowed with the visual element (*cakṣurdhātu*) because of the completeness of their faculties; however,
they are not endowed with the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) there,
because it is absent in those realms.
Because eye-consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is not being manifested, one is said to have "not obtained or lost the eye" in the desire realm;
that is, one whose eye is either unobtained or lost is "one who has not obtained or lost the eye."
One who has not yet acquired the eye, being in a state such as that of death or birth,
or one whose eye is lost or destroyed,

is endowed with the element of visual consciousness— whether wholesome or afflicted— which was acquired at the moment of linking to the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is not by means of the eye-element, because that does not exist for him;
"one who has obtained and not lost the eye" means one for whom the eye has been obtained and not lost.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one is endowed with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)— both as previously acquired and now through this neutral (*avyākṛta*) state.
Furthermore, one born in the first dhyāna is endowed with both of these,
because the [eye] belonging to its own level necessarily exists there, and because an eye belonging to another level is possible.
And one who is born in the second or higher dhyānas, while seeing—
that is, bringing into manifestation— the eye-consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; he too is necessarily endowed with both of these.
The fourth [alternative] is "excluding these modes";
one born in the formless realm is to be inferred accordingly as appropriate.
Is one who, not previously possessing the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), acquires its possession, also [one who] possesses the form-element (*rūpadhātu*)?
Or is one who possesses the form-element also [one who] possesses the eye-element?
This would concern the eye-element and the form-element.
There is acquisition both separately and together;
first, there is one who is endowed with the eye-element separately.
There is no such case where one might successively acquire the eye-faculty in the desire realm through the form realm,
[such that] there is the form realm but not the eye-realm; this alternative does not exist.

It may also be that one who was previously unendowed with both [the faculties] acquires their possession when passing away from the formless realm and being reborn in the form realm or the desire realm.
Setting aside these two modes, the "prior-position" (pūrvapādaka) formulation is as follows: "Is one who is endowed with the eye-element also endowed with the form-element?
First, whoever is endowed with the eye-element is also endowed with the form-element.

Could it be that one possesses the form element (*rūpadhātu*) but not the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*)—as in the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, or in the case of one who has not yet acquired the eye or whose eye has been lost—and who, while not possessing the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), acquires its possession? Or could it be that one who acquires the possession of the form element also acquires the possession of the eye-consciousness element? [The answer is: Yes, there could be such a case. One who, in the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, does not possess the eye element but later acquires it, or one whose eye was previously acquired but has since been lost, might acquire the eye-consciousness element while not yet possessing the form element; or conversely, one who acquires the form element might also acquire the eye-consciousness element.
In the same way, for those two, there may be acquisition separately as well as together;
first, [the case] of separate acquisition:
There may be [possession] of the eye-consciousness element but not of the form element,
as in the case of one born in the second or higher dhyānas who brings eye-consciousness into manifestation;
or there may be [possession] of the form element but not of the eye-consciousness element.

One who has passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) and is being reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) may also be simultaneously dispossessed of both [the faculties] and then acquire their possession (*samanvāgama*).
One who has passed away from the formless realm and is being reborn in the desire realm or in the Brahma-world does not possess both [of these characteristics], setting aside these two cases.

Whoever is endowed with the eye-consciousness element is also endowed with the form element; or whoever is endowed with the form element is also endowed with the eye-consciousness element—this is the "prior-position" (pūrvapādaka).
First, one who is endowed with the eye-consciousness element would also be endowed with the form element;
however, there may be one who is endowed with the form element but not with the eye-consciousness element.
One born in the second dhyāna or higher, not manifesting eye-consciousness—

just as this consideration regarding the acquisition and possession of the eye-consciousness and the form-element has been conducted, so too should the consideration regarding the acquisition and possession of the ear-consciousness, the sound-element, and so forth, be carried out.

There may be the separate acquisition of the auditory faculty and the auditory consciousness element, as well as their simultaneous acquisition; thus, beginning with these, there are twelve internal [elements].
Because of this very restriction,
it is established by that same restriction that other things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth are external; thus, [the term] *adhyātma* refers to what is within the self (*ātman*).
"Adhyātmam" means "with reference to the self"; that which pertains to the self is "ādhyātmika," or alternatively,
those things that exist within the self are "ādhyātmika."

Because it is the basis for the conceit of "I," the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self. Proponents of a self (ātmavādins) conceive that the self is the basis for the conceit of "I," and since the mind is the basis for the conceit of "I," it is metaphorically designated as the "self.
To the question "How so? he says:
"For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise man attains heaven"— this is stated in a verse.
But how is it understood that the word "self" (ātman) refers to the mind?
Then he said:
"The Blessed One has spoken of the taming of the mind elsewhere," as it is stated in another verse:
"The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness"—
this is the meaning of that [verse].

Regarding the internal activity of the mind, or with reference to the mind itself as the self, those factors that exist in a state of proximity by way of being its support are "internal" (ādhyātmika);
whereas those that exist by way of being its objects are external.
If they are external,
what then is this state of proximity by which consciousness conforms to their transformation?
For consciousness is observed only in the eyes and other sense organs, not in visible forms and other objects;
thus, the mind is delimited at the location of the body where it is connected to the sense faculties, not at the location of the object.
If this is so, then [the passage] beginning with "the six consciousness-elements" follows in detail.
In this context, first of all, only the five consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu) are taken as present,
because they are simultaneous with their respective sense-faculties and objects;
for the five groups of consciousness have present objects.
The mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is also established here as being only present;
for it is precisely due to the difference in time that the mind element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness element are established separately.
Therefore, they do not qualify as internal.
For when these [past mental factors] have not yet attained the state of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and have not yet attained the state of being past, they do not become the support of the mind;
rather, it is precisely when they have attained those states that they become so. Since they do not deviate from their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), what is established by this statement?
"This has been established by him:

even for these [factors] that are present, there will be the state of being a basis; thus, they possess internality by virtue of having the state of being a future basis," or "of the future and the present," and so forth in detail.

The intended meaning is that whatever is characterized as the mind-element (*manodhātu*) in the past time exists indeed in the future and present times as well; for there is no deviation of a characteristic across the [three] times, nor is there any abandonment of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is the sense.
"Designated as 'dharma,' it is homogeneous (sabhāga)" means that what is designated as dharma is exclusively homogeneous;
this is restricted to that object which is fixed for a particular consciousness.
For example, form is the fixed object of visual consciousness, up to mental phenomena being the fixed object of mental consciousness;
if, in that regard, that visual consciousness has arisen or is subject to arising,
up to if, in that regard, that mental consciousness has arisen or is subject to arising.
That object is called "homogeneous" (sabhāga).

And regarding the phrase "free from its own nature and its co-existent factors" (svabhāva-sahabhū-nirmuktā), this means they are free from both their own nature and their co-existent factors; thus, they are "free from their own nature and their co-existent factors."
All phenomena are the objective support (*ālambana*) of that consciousness,
not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
For indeed, that very fingertip cannot be touched by that same fingertip;
that very edge of a sword cannot be cut by that same edge of a sword; nor can coexistent things [act upon one another].
Whether associated or dissociated [from consciousness],
it is not perceived because of extreme proximity;
for indeed, collyrium applied to the eye is not perceived by that very eye.

Furthermore, since one moment of consciousness does not become the object of another moment of consciousness, those factors that were co-existent with its own nature in the preceding moment—which previously had not been objects—now do become objects;

thus, in two moments, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) become objects. Therefore, the *dharmadhātu* is always "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). For the *dharmadhātu* is restricted exclusively to the mind (*manas*).
"And the remaining [elements] are *sabhāga*.
By the word "and" (*ca*), it is meant that they are *sabhāga*. It is thus determined that only the remaining elements are both *sabhāga* and *tatsabhāga*.

[Objection: But if it is determined that the *dharmadhātu* alone is exclusively *sabhāga*, then it follows by implication that the remaining elements are not *sabhāga*, and thus they will be established as *sabhāga-tatsabhāga*.
They will not succeed even if they are not exactly homogeneous; however,
it is possible that they might be merely "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
To prevent that [misunderstanding], this is undertaken:
"The remaining [elements] are both homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*); they are not exclusively homogeneous, nor are they exclusively partially homogeneous."
That which does not perform its own function is to be connected with the term "tatsabhāga" (homogeneous with that),
because it was mentioned immediately prior in the phrase "and those that are tatsabhāga."
What is meant is this:
that which performs its own function is "homogeneous" (sabhāga).

By implication, the restrictive sense—that only that which does not perform its own function is "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga), or conversely, only that which is non-homogeneous does not perform its own function—establishes that what performs its own function is homogeneous.
Regarding the phrase "he saw forms," one should say "he saw" (adrākṣīt),
for in this way both the recent past and the remote past are included.
Otherwise, the definition would be under-extended;
therefore, this very reading should be regarded as merely an illustration,
and that which has passed since today must also be stated.
In this way, it should be stated for the mind up to its own activity regarding its object; that is, it should be stated by means of its own human-like effort (*puruṣakāra*) toward its object.
How so?
That ear by which one has heard, hears, or will hear sounds is called "functioning" (sabhāga) hearing; this means that all [ears]—
whether associated with consciousness or not— are either connected with consciousness or disconnected from it.

If the eye of one person is "homogeneous" (sabhāga), is it also homogeneous for all others? This question continues to apply; the same is also true for that which is "similarly homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
The meaning is that if the eye of one person is "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga), then it is partially homogeneous for all;
