this is because [the definition] includes the term "attained" (prāpta).
Those odors and so forth which are grasped by Devadatta through their contact with the olfactory and other sense faculties are not grasped by Yajñadatta.
Because they have entered into their own respective [bases] such as the nose and so forth,
and because they are specific to each, it is logical to extend the designation [of "homogeneous"] to these just as in the case of the eye and the other [faculties]:
that which is the odor of one is homogeneous.
It should be stated that for all [the sense objects], it is likewise "partaking of that" (tatsabhāga), but it should not be stated that "as it is with visible form, so it is with odor and the rest."

For this possibility exists: that the very same odors and so forth which might produce olfactory consciousness and the rest for one person would likewise produce them for others, provided they were to reach the olfactory and other sense faculties of Devadatta; in that case, they would produce consciousness in Devadatta.
The meaning is: "Or else, [if] those [objects] reached by the olfactory and other sense-faculties of Yajñadatta were to produce cognition in Yajñadatta;
or else, 'those very same [objects] for others as well'—in that case, they would also produce cognition in those such as the minute insects contained therein."
It is not the case that those odors and so forth belong only to that Devadatta by whom they are reached through the sense-faculties such as the nose;
rather, there is a mutual relationship between the sense-faculties, the objects, and the consciousnesses.
Thus, they proceed by way of being mutually oriented toward one another through the relationship of support (āśraya), object (viṣaya), and supported (āśrayin).
For in this way, the sense-faculty elements (indriya-dhātu) resort to and attend upon the consciousness elements (vijñāna-dhātu) as their basis, according to the case;
and they resort to the object elements (viṣaya-dhātu) as their objects.
Likewise, the object-elements (viṣaya-dhātu) relate to their respective sense-faculty elements (indriya-dhātu) by way of being objects;

however, they relate to the consciousness-elements (vijñāna-dhātu) either by way of being objects or by way of being focal objects (ālambana). Similarly, the consciousness-elements relate to their respective sense-faculty elements by way of being the supported (āśrayin).

And because they partake of the objects and elements (viṣaya-dhātu) by way of being subjects (viṣayin) or by way of being perceivers (ālambaka), there is a "partaking" (bhajana) of one another; this "partaking" (bhāga) is derived from the root *bhaj* with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
Alternatively, "portion" (bhāga) refers to the sharing of activity;
the activity of the eyes and so forth is seeing and so on, while that of the elements of consciousness is the state of being a cognizer.
The state of being an object and a focal point for the elements of the objects is the "partaking of that activity" (kāritrabhajana); the meaning is that they possess this partaking of activity.
This is merely an illustration; the analysis should rather be constructed as follows:
"those which exist together with a portion" are *sabhāga*.

Alternatively, their portion is the same; thus they are "sabhāga" (having a common portion). The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* has been prescribed [in the rule] because of the word *saha* having the same meaning, or because they have the same effect as contact (*sparśa*).
The word "sabhāgāḥ" (homogeneous) is understood here from the context;
the suffix *ghañ* is applied to this verbal root.
It is called a "portion" (*bhāga*) because it is divided;
its analysis (*vigraha*), however, is as before, and the contact is mental (*caitasika*).
The common function of these—the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness—is stated in such passages as:
"Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises;
the conjunction of these three is contact," and so forth.
"Those, however, which are dissimilar," and so forth;

those other eyes and so on which are dissimilar in this manner are "dissimilar" (asabhāga) in relation to those "similar" (sabhāga) ones whose characteristics have been described, being similar to them.
They are "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) because they are similar to them, or because they are similar by means of them; for here the word *sabhāga* is taken in the sense of "equal."
"Abandonable by vision" (*darśanaheya*) means that "vision" (*darśana*) is first the untainted seeing of the truths (*satyadarśana*), comprised of fifteen moments of mind;
"cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is the repeated seeing of that very same [truth].
Or, mundane concentrated knowledge is cultivation; ten and five elements are to be abandoned by cultivation—
namely, the ten and five form-elements and their corresponding consciousness-elements.
How, then, is it understood that these alone are those [elements]?
Because of the statement, "The last three are of three kinds," it is understood that the other fifteen elements, being distinct from the last two, are indeed referred to as "those."
It is determined that these are to be abandoned by cultivation alone;
"of three kinds" means they are [divided into] those to be abandoned by vision, those to be abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned.

These very same [factors] are the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) in three ways: namely, the proclivities such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, distinguished by realm, type, and aspect; their co-arising factors, which are the associated consciousness, feeling, and so forth; the non-associated [characteristics] such as their own characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) along with their attendants.
By that word, "latent dispositions" (anuśaya) and so forth are connected; "their acquisitions" (tat-prāptayaḥ) refers to the acquisitions of those latent dispositions and their co-existent factors,
even though these are indeed co-existent with the latent dispositions.

However, not all acquisitions (prāpti) are co-existent with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and so forth; some are simultaneous with them, while others occur before or after them. Therefore, "acquisition" is mentioned separately.
By the inclusion of the phrase "together with their attendants," their acquisitions (*anuprāpti*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also subsumed.

The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Are these indeed the three final realms? Yes; they are those remaining contaminated factors other than those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*).
These are to be abandoned by cultivation;
which ones, then?
They are the ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya), their co-existent factors, and their acquisitions (prāpti), along with their attendants.
Wholesome contaminated conditioned phenomena, as well as unobscured-neutral conditioned phenomena and contaminated non-informative matter, together with their attendants.
The untainted (anāsrava) are not to be abandoned; thus, they have the nature of the truth of the path and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
But is it not the case that there is more to it?

Ordinary personhood (pṛthagjanatva) is included among those things to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), because its nature consists of unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) conditioned factors (saṃskāra).
Because bodily and vocal karma leading to the miserable realms has the nature of form (*rūpa*), it is said to be abandonable by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
therefore, the Vātsīputrīyas raise this objection:
"Because it is contrary to the Noble Path."

The state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) does not exist when the Noble Path arises; and while there is determinate karma leading to the miserable realms (*apāya*), the Noble Path does not arise;
yet, when the Noble Path arises, karma leading to the miserable realms does not arise.
Therefore, they describe both of these as being abandonable by insight (*darśanaheya*), just like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
in order to refute that [view], although this has already been stated, it is stated again in brief for the sake of easy comprehension.
That which is non-afflicted is not to be abandoned by insight; nor is form, nor that which is not born of the sixth [consciousness].
Insight is vision;
that which is non-afflicted—whether unobscured-neutral or wholesome—is not to be abandoned by insight.
However, even if it is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), form (*rūpa*) is not to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*).
That which is born from the five sense organs—the five consciousnesses—is "not born from the sixth" (*a-ṣaṣṭhaja*); even though that [form] is afflicted, it is not to be abandoned by insight.
Other than that, however, there exists that which is to be abandoned by insight, as has been stated.

And the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), because even those who have severed their roots of virtue (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) and those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) still possess it. Thus, while those who have severed their roots of virtue are held to be non-possessed of virtuous factors (*kuśalair dharmair asamanvāgatāḥ*), they are nevertheless possessed of the state of being a worldling.
Since those [states] are held to be the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), it is therefore not wholesome;
nor is it afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
Because even those who are free from passion (vītarāga) still possess [the seeds of] that [defilement],
the abandonment of a defiled object is held to be the abandonment of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva);
the meaning is that "abandonment" refers to the severance of its acquisition (prāpti).

If the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) were defiled (*kliṣṭa*), then for those who have attained detachment from the world (*laukikavītarāga*), there would be a severance of its acquisition (*prāpti*), and thus they would no longer possess it; yet it is accepted that they do possess it,
for it is held that such worldly detached ones are indeed still ordinary persons.
If there were no distinction between being non-afflicted and being neutral, there would be a fault;
for the abandonment of desire and attachment is held to pertain to what is non-afflicted,
which means the severing of the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that take that [neutral object] as their objective support.
But it is not intended that there is a severance of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that which belongs to its own nature;
for thus it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, whatever desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) there is toward form, abandon it."

"In this way, that form of theirs is abandoned," and so forth; therefore, although the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*)— which is undefiled and neutral— is abandoned for them, it still manifests like the eye and other faculties,
and thus they remain possessed of it.

But what is the reason that the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because it is undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), and bodily and vocal action are likewise [not so abandoned], because they are material (*rūpatva*)? To this he says:

Because there is no misconception regarding the truths and because it is not corrupted by afflictions, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) does not involve misconception regarding the truths such as suffering;
the meaning is that it does not function in a perverted manner.
Furthermore, because bodily and vocal actions lack an object (*anālambaka*), whereas [wrong views] possess an object, they do not function erroneously;
therefore, both of these are not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).

And this reason— "because there is no misconception regarding the truths"— should be applied even to [the state of being] not born from the sixth [consciousness], because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) persisting during the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

This supplementary reason is stated for the purpose of negating that ordinary personhood itself is to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*), since bodily and vocal actions are not directly connected [to it].
During the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the acquisition of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed;
however, it is not yet severed [in its latent state], just like the acquisition of the afflictions to be abandoned by that [path].
Rather, the path, while in the process of ceasing (*nirudhyamāna*), abandons the obscuration to that [state].
Because of this statement,
the acquisition of that [defilement] is severed at the stage of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*);

therefore, due to the continued existence of its acquisition, that person would still be an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*) during the state of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Furthermore, it is not possible to establish that he is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) in that state, because he has realized the Noble Path;
for the definition of being an ordinary person is "the non-attainment of the noble dharmas."
Furthermore, through the acquisition of the noble dharmas, non-acquisition is overturned;
therefore, he is indeed noble.
First of all, this is what you Vaibhāṣikas must be asked.
Is that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) abandoned only through the attainment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
It is said: "No;
moreover, it is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*)."
Therefore, it is abandoned at the stage of abandoning the ninth category of afflictions for each respective bhūmi;
for all non-afflicted [yet] contaminated [states] are abandoned precisely in the ninth path of liberation.
If this were so, then an Ārya in a state where he has not yet abandoned desire would be an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
It is not because the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has been abandoned;
for from the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), that state has indeed already been abandoned.
But it is not abandoned;
what, then, is the distinction between "abandoned" (*vihāna*) and "abandoned by relinquishment" (*prahāṇa*)? Abandonment (*vihāna*) is established as the cutting off of possession (*prāpti*).

However, abandonment is established as occurring upon the attainment of the counteragent; therefore, because of the severance of possession and because of no longer being endowed with that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), one becomes an noble one (*ārya*) in that state and not an ordinary person— thus, there is no fault in this.
Regarding AK(Bh) 1.41: "The eye and a portion of the dharmadhātu are vision (dṛṣṭi).
By this, it is determined that the eye alone, and only that portion of the dharmadhātu, is vision.

"Beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)" refers to the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). "The untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom] of one in training (*śaikṣa*)"—here "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the subject under discussion. "The non-learner's (*aśaikṣa*) wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī*)" means that the untainted wisdom of one beyond training is the "non-learner's [wisdom]. It should be stated that this excludes the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), for it will be said later: "The cognition of destruction and non-arising is not vision (*dṛg*)."

"With clouds" and "without clouds," and so forth in detail, up to: "the vision of phenomena (*dharmadarśana*) by means of views that are afflicted, unafflicted, mundane, of one in training (*śaikṣa*), and of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That which exists in the world is "mundane" (*laukikī*). It is both afflicted and unafflicted; thus, it is "afflicted-unafflicted. And being both afflicted-unafflicted and mundane, it is "afflicted-unafflicted-mundane. Being afflicted-unafflicted-mundane, as well as [the views] of one in training and of one beyond training, constitutes "afflicted-unafflicted-mundane-śaikṣa-aśaikṣa. By means of these, there is the vision of phenomena.

To the question "Of what kind? he says: "Like the perception of forms during the night and day, whether with clouds or without clouds. Just as there is perception of forms at night when there are clouds, so too is there perception of phenomena through afflicted worldly views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the meaning is that it is more indistinct. Just as there is perception of forms at that same night when there are no clouds, so too is there perception of phenomena through unafflicted worldly views; the meaning is that it is indistinct.

Just as the perception of forms on a cloudy day, so is the perception of phenomena through the vision of one in training (*śaikṣa*); it is clear, but not exceedingly so. On the other hand, just as the perception of forms on a cloudless day, so is the perception of phenomena through the vision of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The meaning is that it is exceedingly clear.

"Because of non-investigation" means because of the absence of thorough investigation (*santīraṇa*). Thorough investigation, moreover, is the drawing forth of a certainty preceded by the close observation of an object. For this very reason, it is said: "and other [mental states] as well. The detailed explanation is as follows: for this very reason—because of the absence of thorough investigation—other mental wisdom (*prajñā*), whether afflicted (*kliṣṭā*) and associated with attachment and so forth, or unafflicted (*akliṣṭā*) such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), or the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛtā*), is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Regarding the phrase "in the sense of observing form": the eye is not a view by virtue of being an investigator; rather, it is in the sense of observing form. This demonstrates that wisdom (*prajñā*), however, is a view by virtue of being an investigator.

"One who possesses another consciousness" means a person for whom another consciousness is manifest, that is, one who is occupied with another consciousness. [Such a person] might see with the visual faculty due to the proximity of the object and other conditions. However, for one who holds the position that "visual consciousness sees," there is no fault, because that [other] consciousness is impossible [at that time].
Let it be that the consciousness itself, supported by the eye, sees, since seeing occurs when that [consciousness] exists and does not occur when it is absent.
For it is said that a visible form is not seen when it is obstructed. (1.42cd)
Thus [it is said]. The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another.

"Because it is non-obstructive" means that consciousness (*vijñāna*), being formless, would see even after passing through walls and the like. The proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*) says: "Indeed, visual consciousness does not arise with respect to what is obstructed," the intention being that this is because the object has not entered into the range of appearance (*anābhāsagatatvāt*).

[The opponent asks: "Why indeed would it not arise? The sense is that, because it is non-obstructive, consciousness would arise with respect to an object as if it were not separated by a wall or the like, having penetrated through the wall and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "but for whom": for me, the Vaibhāṣika, whose position is that "the eye sees," because the eye possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), there is an absence of activity when objects are obstructed by walls and the like. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, for the Vaibhāṣika, would consciousness (*vijñāna*) not also [function] even toward what is obstructed?"—that same Vaibhāṣika replies once more: "There is likewise non-arising of consciousness."

Just as it is logical that the eye has no functioning with respect to what is obstructed, so too is the non-arising of consciousness—the absence of the functioning of consciousness—logical, because it operates upon the same object as its basis. For whatever object is obstructed from the eye would be the very same object for consciousness; thus, the non-arising of consciousness is also logical. But for you, the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), since consciousness is non-obstructive, consciousness should arise even with respect to what is obstructed; yet it does not so arise. Therefore, it is the eye that sees.

It is established that [the eye] does not perceive consciousness. Thus, when the proponent of the Vijñānavāda has been refuted, the Master, adopting their position, asks: "Is it then the case that the eye reaches its object? The detailed explanation is as follows: just as the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) reaches its object and does not grasp an object obstructed by a wall or the like—because of the resistance of the wall and because it is unable to proceed beyond it.

Is it the case that the eye, having reached its object, fails to perceive an object obscured by a wall or the like because it is obstructed by such resistance and is unable to go beyond it? This is not tenable. Therefore, one should not say that the eye does not see what is covered because it is non-obstructive (*asapratigha*). [If so,] how is it that an object separated by glass, a film of clouds, crystal, or water is seen?

How is it that a form (rūpa) intercepted or obstructed by glass, a layer of clouds, crystal, or water is seen? For, according to the established tenet (siddhānta), the eye should not see what is obstructed by glass and the like—since they possess resistance (sapratighatva)—just as it does not see what is obstructed by walls and such; yet, in fact, it does see it.

"Where there is no obstruction of light. For when light exists, the object comes into range of appearance, and thus the arising of consciousness is possible. Indeed, the cause of consciousness is taught as follows: "The visual faculty is unimpaired; the object has come into range of appearance; and the attention born thereof is present. Therefore, when a form is obstructed by glass or other such dark substances, visual consciousness does not arise with respect to that which is so obstructed. Why is this? Because [the light is blocked].
"Because it is unarisen, it does not see when it is obscured. As for what you asked regarding the cause of non-arising—namely, "What indeed does not arise?"—we say that this is its cause.

As for what was said in the Sūtra: [the full passage is] "having seen forms with the eye, one does not grasp at their signs (*nimitta*) nor grasp at their secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*)," and so forth. [The opponent argues: Since it is the eye that sees, the intention is that the person (*pudgala*) sees by means of the eye. The Master says: "By means of that basis (*āśraya*)"—this is the underlying intention here; the intention is precisely "relying upon the eye. The meaning is: "having seen by means of the consciousness (*vijñāna*) which has the eye as its basis."

How is this known? He says: "Just as by means of the mind (*manas*) one cognizes phenomena (*dharmas*). This means that one cognizes by means of the mind, which serves as the basis (*āśraya*), namely, by means of consciousness (*vijñāna*). For the mind that has just passed away does not cognize phenomena; rather, it is in its present state that consciousness performs its function (*kāritra*). Alternatively, the action of the dependent is metaphorically attributed to the basis. The action of the dependent consciousness—namely, seeing—is metaphorically attributed to the basis, the eye. When consciousness sees, there is the metaphorical expression: "the eye sees."

Just as in the expression "the beds cry out. Just as when the men situated on the beds cry out, there is the metaphorical designation (upacāra) that "the beds cry out," so too it is as stated in the Sūtra. The full explanation is as follows: this is also the position of the Vaibhāṣikas—that the eye does not cognize, but rather consciousness cognizes. And yet it is said, "forms cognizable by the eye are desirable"; in that case, one must necessarily accept that the action of the supported is metaphorically attributed to the support.

"Only as a door for the seeing of forms. The intended meaning is that "door" is like a gateway; it signifies a cause or a basis (*āśraya*). By means of this scriptural passage, he supports the very point previously stated: "by means of that eye as a door, consciousness sees. Thus, in the context of seeing, the eye is designated as a "door," as in the passage: "The eye, O Brahmin, is a door only for the seeing of forms. For it is not logical to say, "seeing [itself] is for the seeing of forms. The intention here is that because it lacks a distinct function (*avacanatvāt*), this [latter formulation] is not tenable.

If "vision" (*darśana*) is the instrument—meaning "that by which one sees"—or if it is derived from the agentive sense with the suffix *lyuṭ*, meaning "that which sees"—or if it is a derivation denoting the action itself, meaning "for the sake of seeing," i.e., "vision" as "the act of seeing," for that "sake of vision"—how can this be tenable? Because there is no "seeing" apart from the eye. If you say it is "observation" (*ālocana*), no; because it is not distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*). For observation is indeed consciousness itself; we perceive nothing other than this.
However, if the meaning were taken to be that the eye is a door or an aperture for the sake of the consciousness that perceives forms, then it would be tenable.

For example, it is said that a certain kind of wisdom both "sees" and is also said to "perceive. The word *iti* should be supplied here [after *ucyate*]. By this presentation, he demonstrates that seeing (*darśana*) and cognition (*vijñāna*) are not different in meaning. What, then, is this wisdom that is so described? It is that which has been stated to have the nature of seeing, according to the verse: "The noble intellect other than that is of both kinds" (AK 7.1d). This is because it is also stated in the Sūtra: "For one who knows thus, for one who sees thus..."
By the use of the term "something," it is stated that not every consciousness sees; for it is said that visual consciousness sees, but auditory and other types of consciousness do not.

"What other act of seeing could there be?"—the intention is that for that which possesses the quality of perceiving, seeing is appropriate. "This is not a valid objection," and so forth—the detailed argument is as follows: if consciousness (*vijñāna*) cognizes, then one must state what other act of cognition belongs to consciousness acting as the agent; thus, the same objection would apply. And yet, in that case, there is no distinction between the agent and the action. There is no difference or otherness between the agent, which is consciousness, and the action, which is characterized by consciousness.

Furthermore, there occurs the conventional designation of a relationship between agent and action, such as "consciousness cognizes. It might be the same in this case as well; thus, the statement "the eye sees" is not to be questioned. Others hold that visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is what constitutes seeing. Because it is the support (*āśraya*) for that [seeing], it is said that "the eye sees," just as a bell is said to "ring" because it is the support for the sound. "Because it is the support for consciousness" means because it is the support for visual consciousness. That consciousness is conventionally known in the world as "seeing."

"Seeing" (*darśana*) is a conventional term established in the world, but "cognition" (*vijñāna*) is not so established. How is this known? He says: for when that [seeing] has arisen, it is said that "form is seen," not that "it is cognized. It is also stated in the *Vibhāṣā*; the intention is that the very same meaning is being expressed there. "Attained by the eye" means having come into the range of the eye's light.

But consciousness [acts] by its mere presence; thus he shows that it does not do so by way of being a substratum. Just as the sun is called "the maker of the day": just as the sun is said to make the day by its mere presence, so too consciousness is said to "cognize. Why? Because it is established as such in the world.

"Indeed, this is devoid of activity," and so forth. "Devoid of activity" means without exertion (*nirīha*). By this, he negates an action that would be a separate entity from the agent. "A mere phenomenon (*dharmamātra*)" negates an independent agent. And "a mere cause and effect" demonstrates that even in the absence of an agent, there exists the causal relationship between cause and effect.

In this regard, conventional designations (*upacāra*) are made according to common usage (*chandataḥ*). Whatever entity serves as a factor for worldly discourse (*vyavahārāṅga*), for the sake of establishing that discourse and its objects, even though it is non-existent, it is conceptually constructed (*parikalpya*) as having an existent nature; thus, the formal arrangement of agent, action, and so forth is established—such as "the eye sees" or "consciousness cognizes. One should not become attached here to such notions as "an entity depends on an agent," or "one is other [than the action]," and so on. Regarding the phrase "one should not be attached to local etymologies" (*janapadanirukti*): a local etymology is a fixed and settled expression used in a particular region (*janapada*).

One should not adhere to that [notion]. Therefore, this is the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) here. Or rather, one should not imagine an etymological explanation for everything as being meaningful; one should not override the conventional designations (*saṃjñā*) of the world. One should not superimpose upon the world such designations as "self" (*ātman*) or "living being" (*jīva*). The meaning is that one should not go so far as to claim, through the superimposition of what is unreal, that "the self exists as something distinct from the body and so forth. Alternatively, "one should not override the conventional designations of the world" means one should not transgress them; the meaning is that since the referent does not exist, one should not even imagine that the designation exists. "Overriding" (*atisaraṇa*) and "transgressing" (*atikramaṇa*) have the same meaning.

Regarding AK(Bh) 1.43, "by both as well": because of the word "also" (*api*), there is no restriction here that it must be by both; rather, when both eyes are open, the vision is clearer. What is meant is this: "not due to the alteration of one or the other. This refers to the case where one of the two eyes—either the opened or the half-closed—is altered: if one of the two is altered, such that what was opened is made half-closed or entirely closed.

If that which is half-closed were instead made fully closed or fully opened, then the vision of two moons would not occur. Therefore, it is understood that both eyes have a functional role in the arising of this cognition. The statement "because it is not localized in space, unlike visible form" is a counter-example (*viparītadṛṣṭānta*). Just as in the case of visible form, because it is localized in space, its continuity is interrupted by the separation of its physical basis, such is not the case for consciousness.

For consciousness is not established in a location; rather, it is not established in a location because it is formless (*amūrtatva*). And because it is not established in a location, there is no interruption [of its continuity] due to the separation of its substratum. For instance, one sees a form from afar. Where a form is seen, the visual faculty that perceives it does not exist there, because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) there, just like Devadatta who is absent from that place. As it is with the eye, so too should it be stated for the ear.

The other says: "The eye and the ear reach the location of their own objects, because they are sense-faculties, like the olfactory faculty and so forth. By this inference, he demonstrates that the reason—"not being perceived there [in the object]"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). The Teacher says: "And if there were reaching of the object," and so forth. The detailed explanation is: if it were assumed that the eye and the ear reach their objects, then the divine eye and ear would not arise here among humans who practice meditation.

For if the eye and the ear were to perceive form and sound, respectively, even when they are situated at a great distance or obstructed by walls and the like, then their divine nature would be possible; however, that would not be the case if they function by reaching their objects, as is the case with the nose and other [senses]. Just as the divine [senses] of smell, taste, and touch would not arise for meditators because those senses reach their objects, so it would be here.

By this, he demonstrates that the position that [the senses] reach the location of their own objects is flawed by a contradiction regarding the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*). For while the eyes and ears are subjects that may possess divine power (*divyatva*), the state of lacking divine power is a contradiction of their specific nature. That [contradiction] follows, and thus there is a fault. By means of this fault, he establishes that because it is a matter of inference, its non-perception through that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is proven. Therefore, the eye and the ear have objects that are not reached.

p.120 “If the eye does not reach its object,” and so forth—the detailed argument is as follows: since the non-attainment [of the object] is equal whether it is nearby, extremely distant, or obstructed, it would follow that there should be vision in those cases as well.

Is this a proof for the opponent or a refutation? If it is first a proof, namely: “The extremely distant and the obstructed are perceived by the eye and ear because they are not reached, just like a nearby object,” then that is no proof, because the reason (hetu) is either unestablished (*aniścita*) for the proponent himself or contradicts their own prior commitment (*abhyupagama*).

Now, as for the refutation: [the opponent claims that] the consequence follows that the subjects characterized as the eye and the ear would grasp all things without reaching them; however, that is not a valid refutation, because it is sublated by inference. How so? He says: "How is it, first of all, that a magnet does not attract all iron that has not been reached?"

Having introduced the illustration of the magnet by way of a question, he establishes that the eye and the ear do not grasp all things with which they are not in contact: "The eye and the ear do not grasp everything with which they are not in contact, because they lack the power to grasp everything with which they are not in contact, like a magnet. For a magnet grasps—that is, attracts—iron even though it is not in contact; yet it does not grasp everything [even when not in contact]. The eye and the ear are just like that."

This [objection] applies equally even in the case of reaching the object (*prāptaviṣayatva*). An object that is not too distant and not obstructed is perceived by the eye and the ear because it is unfit for perception, like a stick of collyrium that has been brought into contact. Alternatively, the eye and the ear do not perceive everything that is reachable, due to the inherent nature of the sense organs (*indriyasvābhāvya*), just like the olfactory organ and the others. For the objects of the olfactory organ and the rest are indeed reached, yet not all of them; for they do not perceive odors and so forth that coexist with the organ itself.
Indeed, odors, tastes, and tangibles that coexist with the olfactory organ and the others are not perceived by those very organs. Such is the capacity of the sense organs.

"But because the mind is formless. Since the property of "reaching" (prāptatva) can only be established for things that possess form and not for those that are formless, no further investigation is made regarding the mind's non-reaching of its object.

"Three are otherwise. This undertaking is for the purpose of establishing the intended restriction that these three [faculties] have only reached objects. For otherwise, it might be suspected that they have both reached and not reached their objects, since one who is breathless does not perceive odors. When the subtle set of four primary elements has come to the nose along with the breath, its odor is smelled by the nose. Others maintain that another odor has arisen in the air.

They would either merge completely or occupy the same location. Now, regarding "by one part": the question remains, "would they touch? How, then, is the production of sound [accounted for]? The intention is that if they do not touch, then in the absence of impact (*anabhighāta*), the production of sound would not occur. For this very reason, the Kaśmīris [hold that atoms do not touch]: for if they were to touch, a hand struck against a hand would stick to it, just as one piece of lac sticks to another.

How is it that an accumulation, when struck, does not fall apart? How is it that a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*) which do not touch one another does not disintegrate when struck by the hand or other objects? Their very state of being without interval (*nirantaratva*) is such that there is nothing in between; because there is no space or anything else in the middle, their state of being without interval is established. And that alone constitutes their state of contact (*prāptatva*), and not otherwise.

"Moreover" (*api khalu*) means "furthermore" (*api ca*). There is no fault in [the claim] that aggregates (*saṅghāta*) touch because they possess parts. As for the fault that was stated: "If they were to touch with their entire essence (*sarvātmanā*), substances would become intermingled; or if they touched by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*), it would follow that they have parts. [This fault does not apply to us.]

"Regarding the cause": whatever kind of cause something has, that is its cause; whether it be touched or untouched, he says "at times," and so forth—namely, "having a touched cause. That which has another [particle] as its cause through mutual contact is "having a touched cause"; likewise for "having an untouched cause. When it disintegrates, it is, for example, like dry clay being ground into powder.
When it undergoes accumulation, it is, for example, like snow; for that is initially subtle and later becomes large.
"Accumulation belongs to those things that possess accumulation," as for example when two lumps of clay meet.
[One might think] that there would be a state of duration into the subsequent moment because of the contact upon arising;

however, the Venerable [Bhadanta] maintains that the designation "contact" applies only when there is no interval. And it is the opinion of the Venerable that should be accepted. Why, then, should the Vaibhāṣika opinion not be accepted?

But have not the Vaibhāṣikas also said this: "That which consists in there being nothing in between is precisely what constitutes their state of being contiguous"? Indeed, it is so; however, that statement is open to qualification. When the Vaibhāṣikas say "there is nothing in between," they mean that there is no light or the like in the middle; they do not, however, say that there is no room for another atom to enter. For otherwise, if atoms were separated by intervals, what would obstruct the movement of things possessing motion through those empty intervals? The phrase "of things possessing motion" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

And there is this further fault: aggregates are not something other than atoms, as the Vaibhāṣikas imagine. It is those very atoms in aggregate that are touched, just as they are said to be "form-possessing" (*rūpin*). The meaning is that it is the aggregates themselves, not a single [unitary] entity.

"And if [it is argued] regarding the atom," and so forth. Desiring to state that the atom is not ultimately established, the Master investigates: "If a distinction of directional parts—such as east and so on—is imagined for a single atom, whether it is in contact with another or not in contact, there follows the consequence that it must possess parts (*sāvayavatva*). If not—if there is no such distinction of directional parts—then what follows? The phrase 'distinction of directional parts' carries over; [the consequence would be] that even for one in contact, there is no such consequence. Of what? Of having parts."

The proof here is as follows: "An atom is not partless, because it possesses distinctions of spatial divisions (*digbhāgabheda*), like a heap of beans. The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this possession of spatial divisions. For they maintain that spatial division is postulated only for things that have the nature of aggregates (*saṅghātarūpa*). They explain it thus: "This is simply the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that resistant (*sapratigha*) entities occupy distinct locations; lest there be non-distinctness of location due to their existing in immediate proximity (*nairantarya*), even those [atoms] that are separated by intervals are understood to have their movement obstructed by virtue of being resistant. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 1.44)

"And by rapid succession, as in the case of a whirling firebrand and the like. [The author] states the reasoning for such perception, having raised the objection: "If it is maintained that only an object equal in size to the self is perceived, how is it that large objects such as mountains appear to be perceived all at once rather than sequentially?"—[the answer being] "And by rapid succession," and so forth. Just as the perception of a whirling firebrand and the like, though occurring sequentially, appears as if simultaneous, so too does the perception of mountains, rivers, sounds, and so on occur through rapid succession.

"Or rather, [is it] of that which is equal and unequal? The intention is this: in the case of seeing a grape fruit and so forth, it is of the equal; in the case of seeing a mountain and so forth, which are like the tip of a hair, it is of the unequal.

"Merely by opening [the eyes]" means not according to the principle of sequential perception. "In the same way with the ear," and so forth: sometimes they are fewer, when one hears the sound of a mosquito; sometimes they are equal, when one hears the sound of someone whose magnitude is equal to the atoms of the ear; sometimes they are more numerous, when one hears the sound of thunderclouds.
"Situated like the flowers of the *ajājī* (cumin) plant" means situated like the flowers of black cumin (*kālajīraka*), that is to say, situated on a single surface.
"Situated within the *bhūrja*" means: that which has the color and shape of a *bhūrja* leaf within the ear is called "*bhūrja*"; the atoms of the auditory faculty are situated within that.
"Within the *ghāṭā*"—the *ghāṭā* refers to the nostrils. "Situated like a garland" means situated in a circle in a single row.
The word *kila* is used for the purpose of indicating an authoritative tradition (*āgama*), as in the phrase "it is said to be the size of a hair-tip. "Indistinct" means unextended.

Regarding the phrase "by all [atoms] indeed," he indicates his lack of approval with the word *kila*, on the grounds that non-disintegration would occur solely through the efficacy of the action (*karman*).
"Because it has a composite basis and a composite object" means because it has a composite basis (*sañcitāśrayatva*) and because it has a composite object (*sañcitālambanatva*).
"The basis of the last [consciousness] is past" (AK I 44c).

This is a restriction meaning that it is *only* past. For this very reason it is said: since the five groups of consciousness have two types of bases—the bases of the sense organs such as the eye, and the basis of the mind organ (*manas*)—therefore, a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) arises.

The first alternative is "the eye. This is because the eye serves as the support (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness, but not as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). For the eye does not have the nature of mind or mental factors (*cittacaitta*). The definition of an immediately preceding condition is that "mind and mental factors which have arisen and are not the final ones" constitute such a condition; this is the second alternative. Furthermore, the mental factor (*caitasika*) within the *dharmadhātu* that has just passed away constitutes it [visual consciousness] by way of being its immediately preceding condition. Indeed, only six supports for consciousness are accepted—the eye up to the mind—and no others.

The third [category] is the mind that has just passed away, because it possesses both characteristics. The fourth consists of those phenomena excluded from what has been mentioned—namely, those dissociated from mind, such as the non-associated formations, the unconditioned, and so forth, which are free from the three aforementioned limits.

In this way, up to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), its own respective faculty (*indriya*) should be stated. Regarding that which is the basis (*āśraya*) of ear-consciousness, there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) concerning whether it is also the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). The first alternative is the ear. The second is the mental factors (*caitasika*) of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) that have just passed away. The third is the mind (*manas*) that has just passed away. The fourth alternative consists of those phenomena (*dharma*) excluded from what has been mentioned; in this same manner, the others should also be explained.

Regarding the statement "the mental consciousness has a prior basis" (*pūrvapādaka*): that which serves as the basis (*āśraya*) for the mental consciousness also serves as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Thus, it is called "prior-basis. First, that which exists as the basis must necessarily also exist as the immediately preceding condition; therefore, the mind (*manas*) is certainly its immediately preceding condition. However, there may be something that exists as the immediately preceding condition but not as the basis: the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) consisting of mental factors (*caitasika*) that have just passed away. This is because [the mental consciousness] does not have the nature of the six bases such as the eye and so forth. (AKBh 1.45)

"Because they undergo change according to the changes in those [faculties]. This is the detailed explanation: the change of those [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, is "their change" (*tadvikāra*). The change [of consciousness] by means of that change is "change according to their change" (*tadvikāravikāra*). Since these [consciousnesses] possess this [quality], they are "those which undergo change according to the changes in those [faculties]" (*tadvikāravikārīṇi vijñānāni*). The state of being that is "the quality of undergoing change according to the changes in those [faculties]" (*tadvikāravikāritvam*). Therefore, it is determined that the eye and so forth alone are their bases (*āśraya*).

"Because they conform to the sharpness or dullness of benefit and injury. The visual consciousnesses and the others conform to the benefit of the eyes and so forth by means of eye-salve and the like, and to their injury by means of dust and the like, because they arise respectively with pleasure and with pain. They also conform to their sharpness and dullness, because they arise as sharp or dull. Therefore, it is understood that a transformation of consciousness occurs through a transformation of the eye and the other [faculties].

But is it not observed that when a form is sharp, a sharp visual consciousness arises, and when it is dull, a dull one—thus [reflecting] those [factors] such as the eye? Even if the visual consciousness conforms to the sharpness or dullness of the form, in the case of the two discordant states of the eye and the form, the visual consciousness conforms only to the state of the eye, not to the state of the form.

For instance: when the eye is assisted but the object is impaired, the visual consciousness of those who are free from passion for it or who are neutral arises without modification; it does not arise accompanied by suffering. Furthermore, when the object is assisted but the eye is impaired—either by the disease of jaundice, by cataracts, or by other defects—a distorted perception such as seeing yellow or seeing floating hairs and the like occurs. Likewise, when the object is clear but the eye is weakened by old age, a weak visual consciousness arises.

Thus, if the eye is extremely sharp while the form is dull, a sharp visual consciousness arises. For instance, by the very nature of its species, a sharp vulture-eye produces visual consciousness even with respect to a dull corpse-form, even when it is separated by many *yojanas*. The same should be applied to the ear and the other [senses] as well.
Therefore, [the eye is the dominant faculty] because it is uncommon (*asādhāraṇatvāt*). (AK 1.45c)

Therefore, because of its status as a basis (*āśrayabhāva*) and because of its uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*). Since the status as a basis has already been explained, no further attention is paid to it. However, explaining its uniqueness alone, he says: "How is there uniqueness? and so forth. "Also of another's eye-consciousness" means also of the consciousness belonging to another continuum (*santāna*).

It is designated by those very [bases], such as the eye and so forth—from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—and not by [the objects] such as form and so forth—from form-consciousness up to dharma-consciousness—just as one says "sound of a drum" or "barley sprout."

Because they are unique [to that effect], there is a designation based on those two—the drum and the barley—just as in the world one says "the sound of a drum" or "a sprout of barley," but not "the sound of a stick" or "a sprout of a field. For a stick could be the cause of the sound of a *paṭaha* drum and others, and a field could be the cause of the sprouts of rice, wheat, and so forth; because they are common [causes], no designation is made by means of them. However, the designation is made by means of the unique [causes], the drum and the barley; it should be understood in the same way here as well. (AK(Bh) 1.46)

Furthermore, like the eye, consciousness belongs to both [the self and the sentient being], since both are reckoned as sentient beings (*sattvasaṅkhyāta*); whereas form, however, is not reckoned as a sentient being. "Eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*) means consciousness by means of the eye, because the eye serves as its cause. "Eye-consciousness" means consciousness for the sake of the eye, because consciousness associated with the feelings of pleasure and pain functions to benefit or harm the eye. "Eye-consciousness" means consciousness of the eye, because it arises from that [eye] due to its unique (unshared) nature.

Visual consciousness is "eye-consciousness" because the eye alone possesses the status of its owner among those things counted as sentient beings. Alternatively, visual consciousness is "eye-consciousness" because the feeling—whether pleasant or painful—that is associated with it is discerned specifically within the eye itself. This should be applied analogously to the ear and the other [senses]. Thus, it is appropriate to designate consciousness by means of the eye and so forth, but not by means of visible form and so forth.

In the same way, this should be applied to one who sees forms belonging to their own level or to the level of the support with an eye belonging to the stage of the third or fourth dhyāna. This should be applied to that very person born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Likewise, it should be applied to one who sees with an eye of the third dhyāna and so forth; that is, it should be applied to that very person born in the first dhyāna who sees with an eye of the third or fourth dhyāna.
[The Sūtra says: "The eye is not lower than the body" (AK 1.46a).

Thus, "belonging to a lower level" is the meaning. It is permitted that [the visual consciousness] belongs to its own level or to a higher level. For the body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels. "Body" refers to the physical frame. These—body and so forth—belong to five levels: those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those of the first dhyāna level, up to those of the fourth dhyāna level, because they do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Visual consciousness belongs to two levels: that of the desire realm and that of the first dhyāna level.
This is because both possess applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and because visual consciousness necessarily possesses applied and sustained thought.

"Form above is not [the object] of the eye" (AK 1.46b) means that form belonging to a higher level does not become an object of the eye, because form of a higher level is subtle. Form belonging to its own level is permitted, as is consciousness. (AK 1.46c)

What [is meant]? It is the previously mentioned phrase, "not above the eye. For the eye belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), which belongs to a lower level, there is no visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. What is permitted is that it belongs to its own level or to a lower level. For the eye of the desire realm, the visual consciousness is only of its own level, namely, of the desire realm. For the eye belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the visual consciousness is only of the level of the first dhyāna.

For the eye belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, there arises only visual consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; however, visual consciousness belonging to the desire realm does not arise for it.

But was it not said that "the [eye] belonging to a lower stage is permitted"? True, this was said; however, it is intended that when one's own [eye] is absent, that of a lower stage is accepted—not when it is present. For when one's own eye of the second, third, or fourth dhyāna is absent, the visual consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna stage alone serves as the lower [eye], and not that of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), because the latter is far too inferior. It was stated that "the lower-stage [eye] is permitted" only in the sense of what is possible.

"Of this" refers to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) mentioned immediately above (AKBh 1.46cd). For the class of visual consciousness that has arisen, visible form (*rūpa*) is its object in every respect; however, this should be applied according to what is possible. For visual consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), visible form belongs only to its own level. But for visual consciousness belonging to the first dhyāna—which is based on the eye of the first dhyāna—visible form belonging to its own level and to lower levels is its object.

However, for that which has the eye belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna as its support, visible form belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna and all [visible form] belonging to levels below it is the object. Likewise, up to the eye belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, visible form belonging to the level of the second dhyāna and [visible form] belonging to levels below it is the object. Thus, for the class of visual consciousness, visible form becomes an object in the higher, lower, and its own level.

Both form and consciousness exist everywhere in relation to the body. For a body belonging to the desire realm, both form and consciousness may belong to its own level or to higher levels. For a body belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the consciousness belongs only to the level of the first dhyāna; however, the form may belong to its own level, a higher level, or a lower level, just as the eye is the support for its own [consciousness].

The consciousness of a body belonging to the levels of the second dhyāna and above belongs only to a lower level; that is to say, it belongs only to the level of the first dhyāna. However, the form (rūpa) of a body belonging to the levels of the second or third dhyāna belongs to its own level, to a higher level, or to a lower level, according to its respective eye-base (cakṣus). The form of a body belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna belongs only to its own level or to a lower level, because there is no form above that. Ad AK(Bh) 1.47.

"Likewise the ear" (AK 1.47a). Just as the eye has been explained, so too should the ear be analyzed. How so? He says: regarding the body in which one dwells and with which one hears sounds through the ear—do that body, the ear, the sound, and the consciousness all belong to the same level (*bhūmi*), or can they also belong to different levels? He says: there is a distinction among all of them. For one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who hears his own sounds with his own ear, everything belongs to his own level; in this manner, the text should be stated in detail according to this direction. However, this is the fixed rule:
The ear is not lower than the body, nor is sound higher than the ear;
its consciousness [is not higher than the body], but sound and both [the ear and its consciousness] are present everywhere relative to the body.

This should be applied in detail. How so? The ear is not of a lower level than the body. For the body, the ear, and sounds belong to five levels: from those of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) up to those of the fourth dhyāna level. Auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), however, belongs to two levels: that of the desire realm and that of the first dhyāna. In this regard, the ear belongs to the same level as the body or to a higher level, but never to a lower level.
Whatever the level of the ear, its object—sound—belongs to that same level or to a lower level.

Sound is not above [the level of] hearing; for a sound belonging to a higher plane can never be heard by an ear belonging to a lower plane. And consciousness is not above [the level of] the ear, just like the sound. But for this [consciousness], the sound is an object from all sides; and for the body, both sound and consciousness exist from all sides. Regarding "for this": the sound is an object from all sides—above, below, and on its own level—for the ear-consciousness just mentioned. And for the body, both sound and consciousness occur from all sides.

"The mind is undetermined" (AK 1.47d). Just as the eye or the ear are determined—such that the eye or the ear are not of a lower level than the body—the mind is not determined in this way. For this very reason it is said: "Even when the body belongs to five levels, the mind and so forth belong to all levels. Thus, the mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness belong to all levels, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

For example: if one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), immediately after a mind belonging to the desire realm, produces a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that belongs exclusively to the desire realm and has as its object phenomena belonging to the desire realm, then all [the factors] belong to the desire realm. If, at the time of birth or at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), one produces such a consciousness belonging to the desire realm from a level of the first dhyāna up to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—as is possible—then the mind (*manas*) is of that same level, while the remaining [factors] belong to the desire realm.

Then, in that very same place, one produces that consciousness (*vijñāna*). However, the phenomena (*dharma*) are its objects (*ālambana*), ranging from those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). The phenomena are of that same level. The remaining points are as before. In this manner, one who is reborn in the first dhyāna, up to one reborn at the peak of existence, should be described according to the appropriate application. The incidental discussion is concluded. "The eye and a portion of the dharma-element are vision (*dṛṣṭi*)"—this is the governing topic (*adhikāra*).
Now, the discussion beginning with "wherein, situated in the body, one sees forms with the eye" is an incidental digression, as it follows from the connection to the topic of seeing.

Regarding AK(Bh) 1.48, *pañca bāhyā dvivijñeyā* (the five external [elements] are cognizable by two): the mention of "five" is for the purpose of excluding the *dharmadhātu*; the mention of "external" is for the purpose of excluding the eye and so forth. Thus, it is established that there are exactly five external ones. Because of the restriction "cognizable by two," it is proven that the other thirteen elements are cognizable by a single consciousness, since they are not the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

"Permanent phenomena are the unconditioned" (AK 1.48b). This is a restriction meaning that they are exclusively unconditioned. They are permanent because they lack movement through the time periods (*adhvan*). "The elements [are] for the sake of the phenomena, as well as those twelve which are known as internal" (AK 1.48cd). The term "elements" (*dhātu*) is understood from the context.

"Twenty-two faculties have been taught in the Sūtra. Then the brahmin Jātiśroṇa approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa said this to the Blessed One: "Master Gautama, 'faculties, faculties' is what is said. From what, Master Gautama, do the faculties arise?"

To what extent is there a grouping of the faculties (*indriya*)? O Brahmin, these twenty-two are the faculties. Which are the twenty-two? They are: the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the energy faculty, and the mindfulness faculty.

The faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has already known—these, O Brahmin, are the twenty-two faculties. To this extent there is a complete enumeration of the faculties. Then the Brahmin Jātiśroṇa, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, departed from the presence of the Blessed One.

"Half of the dharmas" (dharmārdha) means a portion of the *dharmadhātu*. Some read it as "half-dharma" (*dharmārdham*) using the neuter gender; in their reading, the compound would imply an equal division (*samapravibhāga*), according to the grammatical rule that "a neuter [word] denotes a half" (*ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*), as in the example "half a *pippalī* fruit. However, if the word *ardha*, even when used in the neuter gender, functions in the sense of "a part," then the compound is formed in this way: "it is both a dharma and a half," hence *dharmārdham*; or "a half within the dharma," hence *dharmārdham*.

But the Abhidharmikas, disregarding the established arrangement of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—namely, that the six sense bases consist of the eye base up to the body base and the mind base (*manāyatana*)—recite the mind faculty immediately after the life faculty, because it possesses an object (*sālambanatva*). For they recite the feeling faculties and the others immediately [after the life faculty], as they too possess objects.

The eleven beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are the life-faculty, the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*), and the [five] beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). "And a portion of three" refers to the eight substances—excluding the mind-faculty (*manendriya*)—of the nine-substance faculties beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*); these constitute one part of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). "The five beginning with the eye are mentioned by their own names" means that the five elements beginning with the eye are the five faculties, from the eye-faculty up to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Since the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriye*) are merely portions of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), the five elements beginning with the eye (*cakṣurādidhātu*) constitute seven faculties. The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) constitute the mind faculty (*manaindriya*). Thus, the twelve internal elements (*adhyātmikā dhātavaḥ*) become eight faculties. Because of the restriction that "only the twelve internal elements and half of the dharma-element (*dharmārdha*) are faculties," it is established that the five elements beginning with form (*rūpādayaḥ*) and the portion of the dharma-element other than those are not faculties.
[This concludes] the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by the Master Yaśomitra.
The first chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣyam, titled "Exposition of the Elements" (Dhātunirdeśa).
Chapter 2:
The second chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣyam, titled "Exposition of the Faculties" (Indriyanirdeśa).
Having stated "the faculties have been explained," he says this in order to demonstrate the connection between the first and second chapters of the Abhidharmakośa:
"the faculties have been explained."
The connection is as follows: since it was stated at the conclusion of the first chapter of the *Kośa* that "half of the dharmas are faculties," this [present discussion] follows from that.
Furthermore, as for the meaning of "indriya," since the grammarians have provided a different etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) for the word *indriya*,
he therefore asks:

What, then, is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)? The root *idi* is recited in the sense of "supreme sovereignty"; from that root, the form *indriyāṇi* is to be understood as "those which exercise sovereignty."
How is this so? [The term] *indrāṇi* is derived from the root *ind*, meaning "to rule" (*indanti*), with the suffix *-ra* added according to the *uṇādi* rules;
thus, *indrāṇi* itself becomes *indriyāṇi* by adding the secondary suffix *-gha* in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*).
Alternatively, because they exercise power (*indanti*), it is "the faculty" (*indriya*);
however, due to their plurality, the designation is made in the plural: "those which exercise power are the faculties" (*indriyāṇi*).
Therefore, for this word *indanti*, there is the substitution *indriya*.
How is it that the letter *a* becomes *r*, and the word *ti* undergoes substitution by *iy*,
such that through this etymological derivation it becomes *indriya*?

For example, regarding the word *kuñjara*, grammarians derive it by means of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*), explaining that "it has a *kuñja* (a thicket or temple), therefore it is a *kuñjara*"; however,
etymologists disregard that and establish it through their own method of etymology, stating that "it is a *kuñjara* because it moves within a *kuñja*."
The same should be understood here as well:

for if, according to the system of the Grammarians, *indriya* were derived from *indra* with the sense of "mark" (*liṅga*), the meaning of "sovereignty" (*ādhipatya*) would be lost, whereas it is precisely the meaning of sovereignty that is intended.
Therefore, having observed that the etymology of the word *indriya* must be accepted in this way—
as "because one avoids danger after seeing or hearing"—
one sees a precipice and so forth, and hears the roar of a tiger and so forth.
"Because of the avoidance of dangers such as pits, tigers,
and the like," refers to the two states together with their associated mental factors (*sacaitasika*);
"and of the seeing of forms and hearing of sounds" refers to those very same two.

"The eye sees and the ear hears," and so forth, is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas; therefore, the sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) of the eye and the ear consists in their being the uncommon causes (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*) for seeing and hearing— which are characterized by specific objects— as well as for the beauty of the physical body (*ātmabhāvaśobhā*), as previously stated.
Because beings such as those who feed on odors have unattractive forms— that is, because their physical bodies are unattractive—
it is by means of them that they partake of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Since enjoyment occurs through those [faculties] such as the nose,
how can odor be considered substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)?
It is because the odor is made into mouthfuls by means of the partitioning of the inhalation of odor through the two nostrils.
How is it that the tangible is considered edible food?
Because tangibles such as bathing and anointing the body are taken in mouthfuls by means of being partitioned into morsels through the openings of the pores of the skin.
Regarding the phrase "it is said" (*kila*) in the expression "it is said for two [reasons]," the word *kila* indicates the opinion of another; his own view will be stated later.
The term "of the two" is connected to each [member] respectively; the differentiation of sentient beings is as follows: "woman" and "man"—"woman" constitutes one homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Another [distinction] between those two is "the person" (puruṣa);
"difference in nature" (sattvavikalpa) means a distinction consisting in the alteration of the configuration of the breasts and so forth, as well as the voice and conduct.
Regarding the phrase "of affliction and purification," another [teacher]— namely, a former master (pūrvācārya)—
says that it does not refer to the distinction and conceptualization of sentient beings;
for even without the male faculty, the conceptualization of those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is established.
The intention is that the differentiation of sentient beings is produced by conceptual construction;
"those who are separated and deficient" means those who are both separated and deficient.

Those who are devoid of or deficient in those two—the female and male faculties—are "devoid and deficient in them"; who are they? They are the *ṣaṇḍha*, the *paṇḍaka*, and the hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*).
Those who are devoid of those [faculties] are the *ṣaṇḍha* and *paṇḍaka*; because they lack the female and male faculties,
what further distinction is there between *ṣaṇḍhas* and *paṇḍakas*?
Those who are *ṣaṇḍhas* by nature lack both female and male faculties;
those who are *paṇḍakas* have their faculties impaired by external causes.
However, in the Vinaya, only five types of *paṇḍakas* are enumerated.
The innate impotent,
the envious impotent, and the periodic impotent.
Regarding the "effeminate eunuch" (āsekapaṇḍaka) and the "castrated eunuch" (lūnapaṇḍaka),
it is the "natural eunuch" (prakṛtipaṇḍaka)— the impotent one— who is intended here.
For he who lacks the male organ by nature is a natural paṇḍaka;
the remaining types of paṇḍakas are intended here.
To begin with, it is evident that a *lūnapaṇḍaka* (one whose [sexual organ] has been cut off) is deficient in his faculties because of the severance of those faculties; however,
as for the *pakṣapaṇḍaka* (one who is impotent during certain phases) and others, they are indeed deficient in their faculties due to the inefficiency of those faculties,
and they are established as being deficient even at times when the faculties are efficient.
Because that adaptability of the faculties (*indriyakarmaṇyatva*) does not produce a specific pleasure for a person nor produce offspring,
the term "eunuchs and impotent ones" (*ṣaṇḍhapaṇḍakāḥ*) is recited separately here precisely to exclude the suspicion that the faculties actually exist;
otherwise, just as in the *Vinaya*, they would have been recited here in the *Abhidharma* simply as "impotent ones."

Others explain that those with both sexual organs, as well as those deficient in them, [are not included] because of the deficiency resulting from the loss of their position and the deficiency in being a cause for little pleasure.
Those devoid of that [organ] are eunuchs (ṣaṇḍha);
those deficient in it are impotent (paṇḍaka) due to the impairment resulting from medical intervention.
And those with both sexual organs, as well as those lacking them,
[are excluded] because of the deficiency resulting from the loss of their position and the deficiency resulting from the lack of being a cause for even slight pleasure.
For them, non-restraint and so forth do not exist among humans, excluding those who are eunuchs, impotent, or of dual gender; furthermore,
non-restraint is not admitted for eunuchs and the like, nor for those who have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*).
Because of the lack of shame regarding minor assistance,
a woman cuts [the roots of merit], according to the statement that "a man of [wrong] views does so."
Since those [faculties] belong to women and men,
the female and male faculties have sovereignty over defilement;
and as for restraint, the attainment of fruits, and detachment— restraint is threefold.
Because of the statement: "The Prātimokṣa restraint, the dhyāna restraint, and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint—
none of these constitutes even a single restraint for them,
let alone all the restraints."

For this very reason, it is not possible for them [the non-males] to attain the stages such as stream-entry (*srotāpatti*) or to achieve detachment from the desire realm and so forth; however, since these do occur for women and men,
the female and male faculties exercise sovereignty even with respect to purification (*vyavadāna*).

Regarding "the maintenance of the connection with the homogeneous class" (*nikāyasabhāga*): the predominance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is established in respect to both the arising of the homogeneous class and the maintenance of its connection with that homogeneous class.
And it exercises sovereignty in maintaining the homogeneity of the group (nikāyasabhāga),
because by the power of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) one remains beyond that [death], while by the mind-faculty (manaindriya) there is a connection to renewed existence.
Furthermore, since the defiled [mind] connects one to renewed existence (*punarbhava*), what is its distinction from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
For the life-faculty connects [one] only to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Regarding the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), however, even though it exists at the moment of rebirth, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that effects its connection with the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) simultaneously;
the mental faculty, on the other hand, effects its connection with a future existence even at a different time.
"Conforming to mastery" means that the world or the Dharma conforms to the mastery of the mind, as it has been said in detail:
"By the mind this world is led," and so forth.
It is also said in a verse:
"The world is led by the mind; the world is dragged along by the mind.
All phenomena follow under the sway of this single phenomenon, the mind."
Thus,
because passion and the other [afflictions] adhere to those [states],
they have the habit of adhering to those [feelings] such as pleasure, either by way of their object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*).
These are passion and the other [afflictions] which adhere to that; their state is "adherence to that," and it is because of this.
As it has been said: "Attachment underlies pleasant feeling, aversion underlies painful feeling, and delusion underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
"For by them one is purified" means that by them one becomes cleansed;
thus, it is stated that these [faculties], beginning with faith, exercise sovereignty over the purification from afflictions.
Others say that pleasure and the other [feelings] also have sovereignty over purification; thus,
the sovereignty of pleasure and the others does not belong to them only in regard to defilement,
but rather—
Regarding the phrase "also in purification," the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is as follows:
some Abhidharmikas say that they [the faculties] also possess sovereignty over purification, and they cite this as scriptural authority (*āgama*).
For it is said in the Sūtra that "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated"; thus,
faith has suffering as its proximate cause,
for suffering is its proximate cause.
This faith has suffering as its proximate cause; the meaning is that it has suffering as its cause.
For when suffering exists, faith in the Dharma or in the Three Jewels arises in someone.
Or, if one desires the going forth,
there are six types of mental joy based on renunciation; thus,
there are six joys based on renunciation.
There are six types of mental distress based on renunciation and six types of equanimity based on renunciation;
renunciation is the path, whether with outflows or without outflows.
Others maintain that dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the departure from the realm (*dhātu*) or from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*),

as stated in the Sūtra: "Dependent upon forms cognizable by the eye, there arises mental joy based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*)," which means it has renunciation as its objective support (*ālambana*).
Or, "conducive to renunciation"—in this way, up to: depending on the mind and mental objects, there arises gladness based precisely on renunciation;
and so on, up to the mind.
Likewise, dependent upon forms cognizable by the eye, there arises equanimity based on renunciation; and so on up to the mind.
For some there is gladness, thinking, "I shall attain renunciation," while for others there is dejection, thinking, "I am not making an effort toward renunciation."
For someone, there arises equanimity toward those [objects] such as form through discernment;
however, others say— namely the Sautrāntikas—
that it is "through knowing and avoiding danger."
The intention is that the avoidance of danger is performed by consciousness (*vijñāna*), and not by the eye or the ear;
nor is there any seeing of forms or hearing of sounds other than consciousness.
When examined, no seeing of forms or hearing of sounds is found apart from the nose;
and since the nose is nothing other than consciousness itself,
