that which was stated regarding the sovereignty of the eye and ear consciousnesses, together with their associated mental factors, in their arising [is not contradicted].
The intention is that it becomes that very thing and nothing else; this is its sovereign power, whereas for the mind, however, it is the apprehension of all objects.

Since it is already established by the phrase "due to its sovereignty over the apprehension of all objects," the explicit statement "of the mind (manas) in the apprehension of all objects" is intended to show that the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) does not have the nature of all dharmas;
this has already been explained previously.
Now, one might object: "But do not the objects (arthas) also exercise sovereignty here?"
Because of the statement that "the arising of consciousness is dependent upon a dyad," sovereignty (*prabhutva*) is indeed predominance (*ādhipatya*); thus,
one who is preeminent is the sovereign (*adhipati*), and the state of being such is predominance (*ādhipatya*).
"Because it is the common cause for the perception of all forms" means that the single form of the eye is the cause for the perception of all forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth;
however, a single form [as an object] is not the cause for the perception of all forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
For a blue form does not become the cause for the perception of a yellow form, because perception conforms to the intensity, dullness, and other qualities [of the sense organ];
that is to say, perception conforms to the intensity and dullness of the eye and the other senses.

For example, when the eye is sharp, the perception of it is sharp; when dull, it is dull— and by the word "etcetera," this refers to the conformity with the unwholesome, the wholesome, the pleasant, and the unpleasant.
In an unwholesome mind there is the perception of the unwholesome;
in a wholesome [mind], the wholesome; in that which is with feeling, there is feeling.
In the absence of feeling, there is no perception that conforms to the intensity or dullness of form; therefore, he says: "feeling is not [the perception]."
"By the reversal of that" means that,

therefore, the eyes and so forth possess superior sovereignty, whereas form and so forth do not; likewise, the female and male faculties [possess sovereignty] over the body, but the body does not [possess sovereignty] over them.
In this context, the proof is that the female and male faculties have the nature of the body faculty,
because they generate tactile consciousness.
By way of dissimilarity, like the body-faculty whose nature is neither female nor male faculty,
[it is] like the eye-faculty;
[they] possess the form, voice, gestures, and intentions of a woman.

Since there is thus a reversal between the male intention and the female intention, the predominance of the female and male faculties consists precisely in the conceptualization of a being as female or male;
the predominance of the life faculty consists in the maintenance of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).

But it is not as the Vaibhāṣikas maintain— that feeling has sovereignty over defilement there due to its connection with the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga)— but rather because of the sovereignty of the mind itself.
In this regard, there is agreement with the Vaibhāṣikas;
for it is said, "by them," and so forth.

For by those [faculties] such as faith, when they have entered the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), the afflictions are obstructed, and when they have entered the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so on, the supramundane path is brought forth.

Thus, it has been explained that within the equipment for purification (*vyavadāna-sambhāra*), faith and the other faculties each possess individual predominance (*ādhipatya*). For there is no parinirvāṇa for one whose mind is not liberated; therefore, the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).
And that very [mind] is liberated through liberation from the afflictions and through liberation of the continuum;
for one who has attained it, there occurs *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
Therefore, the sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is established with respect to *nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇa*.
"Regarding the dwelling in happiness in this very life," and so forth; "dṛṣṭadharma" means that which is seen in the present life (dṛṣṭa-dharma).
A pleasant abiding is a "pleasant abiding";
a pleasant abiding in the present life is a "pleasant abiding in the present life. With respect to that, the faculty of one who has already understood (ājñātāvīndriya) exercises sovereignty.
"Because of the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation":
liberation (*vimukti*) is the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
and joy (*prīti*) is mental well-being (*saumanasya*).
The bliss of pliancy is the experience of the bliss of liberation; thus, it is the experience of the bliss of liberation and joy. Therefore...
This is what is meant: the experience of the joy and bliss of liberation itself is the "dwelling in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).
Furthermore, it should be added that speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals are also to be reckoned as faculties (*indriya*).
The Sāṅkhyas postulate vocal organs and others as distinct from the visual organ and the rest; they maintain that the vocal organ is that by which speech is produced,
and the hand-organ is that by which some object is grasped.
The foot-faculty is that by which walking is performed,
meaning strolling; the anus-faculty is that by which the evacuation of excrement is performed.

The faculty of the male organ (*upasthendriya*) is not something distinct from a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*), by means of which a specific pleasure consisting of bliss (*ānanda*) is obtained;
indeed, one should not add ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors to the list as faculties, for it was on that basis that the Blessed One taught there are twenty-two faculties.
Since ignorance and the other [links] are not applicable there, he asks, "What is that object? and replies with the detailed statement: "The basis of the mind is its conceptual differentiation."

The basis of the mind, the conceptualization of that basis, its persistence, its affliction, its purification, the equipment for purification, and purification itself— these constitute the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which are the fundamental substance of a sentient being,
because all other [phenomena] are dependent upon them.
For instance, the basis of the faculties produced through the predominance of the six faculties,
or the six objects, or the groups of consciousness— even this is accepted as a substantial entity of a sentient being, but it is not the fundamental one.
For the six sense bases do not arise solely through the predominance of the physical basis and so forth;
rather, purification occurs through five factors, namely faith and the others,
while purification [itself] occurs through three.

Another interpretation of the process of engagement is that it is the arising of the basis [of consciousness], as detailed in the passage beginning with "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'."
With reference to the side of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and the side of cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is said:
for engagement, which is saṃsāra, there is a basis, an arising, an abiding, and an enjoyment;
and for cessation, which is nirvāṇa, there too is a basis, an arising, an abiding, and an enjoyment.
And since the fulfillment of the human goal is achieved by this much alone,
the postulation of other sense-faculties is useless;
for even in your own system, the fulfillment of the human goal is taught [to be complete] in this way.
Its beginning is the perception of sound and so forth, and its end is the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.

In this regard, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which constitute the fundamental substance of a sentient being, transmigrate; thus, the basis of activity is the process of arising, while the female and male faculties are the point of birth.
It arises from this, thus it is "origination" (utpatti);
why? He says: "because of origination from that."
Of which sixfold sense-base?
Of the mind and the body-faculty, because [the latter] arises directly from those two.
The maintenance of the four [faculties] beginning with the eye occurs through their sequential arising;
their persistence is due to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) because it sustains the six sense bases (ṣadāyatana);
and their enjoyment is by means of the feelings (vedanā), such as pleasure and so forth.
Since faith and the other [faculties] are the basis for cessation,
they constitute the foundation for faith and the rest; therefore,
the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is the source, as it is the first arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
The faculty of "having authority" (*ājñendriya*) is stability because it ensures continuity;
the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is enjoyment,
because through it one experiences the joy and bliss of liberation.
Therefore, the meaning is that there are exactly this many faculties (*indriya*), and thus ignorance (*avidyā*) and the others are not intended to be faculties.
For this very reason, their sequence is as follows—
from the eye-faculty up to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)— because they serve as the basis for engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
Speech, however, does not possess the status of a sense organ,
because its function in speaking depends upon specific training;
for a newborn infant perceives forms with the eye even without such training.
But it does not perform the function of speech; therefore, because it transcends the nature of a sense faculty (*indriya*), speech cannot be considered a sense faculty.
Rather, this action of speech belongs solely to the locus of the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya-adhiṣṭhāna*).

And because the hand and foot are not other than grasping and moving; for it is the very hand that, having arisen in one way and in another place, is called "grasping," and it is the very foot that, having arisen in one way and in another place, is called "moving."
Because of the absence of action and because of the contradiction of an entity acting upon itself,
the hands and feet do not possess the status of sense organs.
Regarding the phrase "of snakes and so forth," this refers to serpents and the like; although they lack hands and feet,
they nevertheless possess the functions of grasping and moving about, yet hands and feet do not constitute sense-faculties (*indriya*) for them.
If it is argued that even for them there exists a subtle [form], we say no, because that remains to be proven.

The anus also does not possess the status of a sense faculty with respect to excretion; for the excretion of an impure substance occurs whenever any heavy object falls into a cavity in space, even elsewhere than at the location of the anus.
Since a heavy object falls by its own weight due to gravity, such falling is not produced by a sense faculty.
And because it is impelled by the wind— meaning that since the impelling of that heavy, impure substance is performed by the wind,
that action would belong to the wind alone, not to the anal faculty.
Because it is not perceived as such, the *upastha* (genital organ) also lacks the status of a sense faculty (*indriya*) with respect to pleasure (*ānanda*);

for the *upastha*— conceived as distinct from both a portion of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)— does not possess the status of a sense faculty in relation to pleasure.
The meaning of the statement is that that afflicted pleasure is produced by the female and male faculties, which constitute a portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*);
the detailed explanation includes [the pleasure of] the throat, teeth, eyelids, and finger joints as well.

If, for the reason already stated, it is not accepted that there are only as many sense-faculties as those mentioned— such as the throat for swallowing and the teeth for chewing— then [the following applies].
It would follow that the eyelid’s opening and closing,

or the joint of a bone in its action of contracting and expanding, would possess the status of a sense faculty— or indeed, everything that serves as a cause [would do so]; such is the detailed argument.

Alternatively, it would follow— given the context— that every cause, such as a seed and so forth, would possess the status of a sense faculty (*indriyatva*) with respect to its own activity, namely the activity of producing its own effect characterized by the sprout and so on,
if it were accepted that whatever possesses human effort (*puruṣakāra*) toward something has the status of a sense faculty with respect to that thing.
And since that previously mentioned cause for restriction is not accepted,
it is therefore illogical for speech and the others to be faculties; therein, [the objection applies] to the eyes and so forth, and so on in detail.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) is used as an introductory phrase; thus,
it is indicated that the eyes and so forth are the translucent forms (*rūpaprasāda*) that serve as the bases for those consciousnesses.
From the body arise the female and male faculties;
consciousness is the distinct cognition [of objects].
Regarding the phrase "of the life-faculty" (*jīvitendriyasya*): life (*jīvita*) is vitality (*āyus*), as stated in the passage, "For that which is the support of heat and consciousness."
Regarding "among the mental factors such as faith" (*śraddhādīnāṃ caitteṣu*), this refers to the section [of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*] beginning with "faith, heedfulness, and pliancy."
But has not feeling (vedanā) already been explained among the mental factors (caitta), and will it not be explained again as "the experience of feeling" in the statement:
"feeling, volition, and perception"?

It has been stated that the general nature of feeling (*vedanā*) is truth (*satya*), and its specific classification will be explained later; however, since the detailed exposition of pleasure (*sukha*) and the other feelings is intended here, it must be set forth.

[An objection is raised: "In that case, the exposition of the faculty of 'I shall come to know' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others need not be done, because the definition of the mind (*manas*) has already been stated."
While [the classification] of faith and the other mental factors will be treated among the mental concomitants (*caitta*),
here [the classification] of pleasure, joy, and equanimity is being made;
for these too must certainly be treated.
Because their nature as consisting of nine substances must be demonstrated;
for in this state these nine substances receive the name of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātām-ājñāsyāmīndriya*),

in this [subsequent] state they receive the name of the faculty of "perfect knowledge" (*ājñendriya*), and in this [final] state they receive the name of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Since this specific state of theirs must be demonstrated, it is well said that [the definition] of pleasure and so forth, as well as of the faculties such as the faculty of knowing (ājñāsyāmīndriya), should be stated.
"Bodily sensation that is unpleasant" (asātā) is used with "unpleasant" (asātā) for the purpose of excluding what is pleasant (sātā).
"Physical" (*kāyikī*) is stated for the purpose of excluding that which is mental (*mānasī*).

In this context, the "body" (*kāya*) refers to the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, because they consist of an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*). That which exists in that body, or that which moves together with the body as its basis (*āśraya*), is "physical."
That painful sensation which is based on the five faculties and is harmful should be understood as the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); pleasure (*sukha*) is that which is agreeable (*sātā*).
In this context, the term "faculty" (indriya) carries over,
and the inclusion of the word "bodily" (kāyikī) and "pleasant" (sātā) is for the purpose of excluding that which is unpleasant (asātā).
This is what is meant:
that faculty of pleasure is the feeling associated with the five sense-faculties which is beneficial.
But in the third dhyāna, that mental [feeling] is the faculty of pleasure;
for in the third dhyāna, even a pleasant mental sensation (*sātā vedanā*) is established as the faculty of pleasure.
Why is it that only mental pleasure is grasped there, and not bodily pleasure?
To this he says: "For there is no bodily feeling there."
Because of the absence of the five groups of sensory consciousness,
why is that [feeling] not the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) in the third dhyāna? To this, he says:
In the third dhyāna, however, because of the absence of passion for joy,
it is exclusively the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and not the faculty of mental happiness (saumanasyendriya).
For it is called happiness because of its continuity,
not joy, because it does not have the aspect of exultation;
thus it is said in the Sūtra:
If it is argued that "he dwells in equanimity through detachment from joy," and so on in detail until "mindful and dwelling in happiness, he attains and dwells in the third dhyāna"—
implying that joy (*prīti*) is something other than mental pleasure (*saumanasya*)— then [the author] says:
For joy is mental ease;
moreover, that which is unpleasant to the mind is mental distress.
Mental feeling that is afflictive is dejection (*daurmanasya*),
whereas equanimity (*upekṣā*) is neutral; thus,
the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is that neutral feeling.
"Neither pleasant nor unpleasant" is the meaning;
"of both kinds" (*ubhayī*) means that it possesses both parts, hence it is "of both kinds."
"Physical and mental" is the meaning;
"due to non-conceptualization" means due to the absence of investigative conceptualization (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).

The inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and born of separation (*viveka*); however, it does not exclude physical [feeling],
for physical pleasure and pain do not arise from conceptualization (*vikalpanā*).
He asks, "For what reason? and replies:
"Because they arise even for Arhats due to the power of objects.
This means that even for Arhats—who have abandoned the conceptual constructions of the pleasant and the unpleasant—physical pleasure and pain arise solely by the power of sensory objects.
Therefore, there is a distinction between those two by way of being faculties;

that is, there is a distinction and separation between those two types of physical and mental pleasure and pain by way of being faculties, such that there is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of mental ease (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), and the faculty of mental unease (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, arises by its own natural flow, without volitional effort and without conceptualization, whether it be physical or mental, and whether born of maturation (*vipākaja*) or outflowing (*naiṣyandika*).

Therefore, they are established as a single faculty; there is no distinction in their status as faculties. It is called the "faculty of equanimity" (*upekṣendriya*) in one sense, and otherwise it is called "bodily" (*kāyika*), and so forth.
By another specific characteristic of its mode of experience, it favors bodily pleasure.
Furthermore, mental [pleasure] is stable, whereas physical [pleasure] is unstable;
indeed, mental [pleasure] is unstable.
Thus, suffering afflicts the physical through one specific mode of experience and the mental through another;
this is with respect to equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the act of being equanimous (*upekṣā-kriyā*).
Because they are non-conceptual and because there is no distinction in their lack of intrinsic nature, there is no difference [between them];
thus it is said: "The path of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning" (AK 2.9ab).
Here, *dṛk* means vision (*darśana*). The path of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning is the path of vision, cultivation, and no-more-learning.

Within those very three paths, the nine substances known as mental pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), faith (*śraddhā*), vigor (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established as follows:

on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) they are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) they are the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) they are the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Depending upon one another, those same nine substances receive their respective names.
The statement "nine" is made with reference to different groups [of mental factors],
for within a single group of consciousness there are not nine substances, because only one of the faculties— pleasure, joy, or equanimity— is present at any given time.

For if that path belongs to the stages of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness,
then there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) therein,
and not the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*) or mental joy (*saumanasya*).
If it belongs to the level of the first or second dhyāna,
there is only the faculty of mental pleasure (saumanasyendriya); if it belongs to the level of the third dhyāna, [there is only the faculty of equanimity].

In that context, it is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) alone and nothing else [that is intended] by the phrase "having set out for what was not yet known" (*anājñātam ājñātum pravṛttaḥ*). Having set out to know—that is, to realize—the Four Truths which were previously unknown, he has begun with the thought, "I shall know them. His faculty is therefore the "faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*). This is a compound formed without the elision of the case-ending (*aluk-samāsa*). Furthermore, this word *ājñāsyāmi* functions as a verbal derivative. On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no new object to be known; rather, one realizes those same Four Truths for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), that is, for the sake of abandoning the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.

For that person who has not yet attained full knowledge (*ājña*), the faculty is either the "faculty of knowing" (*ājñendriya*) or the "faculty of knowing itself" (*ājñam evendriyam*); however, on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), there is the realization "it has been known," which is the "faculty of one who has known" (*ājñātāvī*).
This is merely an explanation of the meaning; however, the grammatical analysis of the word should be performed as follows:
*ājñātam* means "known," and thus *ājñātāvaḥ*.
This form *āva* is derived from the root *avati* with the suffix *ghañ*;
the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) *-in* is added because he possesses this [quality], resulting in *ājñātāvī*.
Alternatively, the suffix *ṇini* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlika*), meaning "one whose nature it is to protect what has been known."
"The faculty of one who has become thus" means the faculty of a person who has become thus,
namely, one who has attained full knowledge (ājñātāvin).

"Pure triad" means that the triad is indeed pure; this is what is being determined. But was this distinction between the untainted (*anāsrava*) and tainted (*sāsrava*) types not already stated in the "Exposition of the Elements" (*dhātunirdeśa*)?
The untainted [dharmas] are the truth of the path;
likewise,
these three [aggregates] are both tainted and untainted, while the remaining ones are tainted.
Because of such statements,
this aforementioned variety of types is indeed spoken of as true;
however, it is spoken of in its general form, not in its specific differentiated form.

Therefore, it should be understood that this distinction of types, beginning with "thus" and so forth, is stated again in the form of individual items for the sake of the student's easy comprehension; thus,

one need not formulate [the rule] as "twofold or ninefold," because "twofold or ninefold" is already established by the very determination of what is exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) and what is contaminated (*sāsrava*).

For if these nine were exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they would be listed among the exclusively uncontaminated faculties such as the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*); likewise, if they were exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), [they would be listed among the contaminated].
They would be taught as exclusively associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) among the material faculties, life-force, suffering, and mental distress;
yet they are not so taught.
Therefore, it is established that nine are of two kinds; this is indeed so.
However, this is stated again— "the nine are twofold"— in order to exclude other opinions;
that is, the nine are as if twofold.
Just as they say that the various [scriptures] are not without outflows (*anāsrava*),
and they cite scripture (*āgama*) for its establishment,
saying, "For whom these [qualities exist]," and so forth in detail.
"In every way, all do not exist" means that in every manner— distinguished as weak, medium, and intense—
all five do not exist.
By the statement, "I say that he stands on the side of ordinary persons," it is implied by the sense of the words that one who possesses these [characteristics] is a noble one (*ārya*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] maintains that this is not an indicator with respect to their being untainted (*anāsrava*),
for he says, "He who has these [faculties]," after having established the classification of noble persons (*āryapudgala*).
How, monks, are these five faculties?
Which are the five?
From the sharpness and perfection of these five faculties—from the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom—one becomes an arhat.
From those that are even more subtle and softer, one becomes a non-returner;
from those that are still more subtle and softer, one becomes a once-returner.

Then, by means of faculties even more subtle and gentler than those, one becomes a stream-enterer; and by means of faculties even more subtle and gentler than those, one becomes a follower of the Dharma.
For thus, monks, depending upon the perfection of the faculties, the perfection of the fruits is made known.
The perfection of the person is known in dependence upon the perfection of the fruit;

him for whom these five faculties do not exist in any way whatsoever, I call an outsider, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Thus, having established the classification of noble persons (*āryapudgala*), the Blessed One said: "him for whom these... and so forth.

Or, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is of two kinds: the internal and the external. One whose roots of merit are not severed is internal, because they are included within the Buddhist fold. However, one whose roots of merit are severed is external, due to the opposite being the case.
For this very reason, the qualification "external" is used;
otherwise, he would have simply said, "I speak of those who stand on the side of the ordinary person."
And it is said in the Sūtra:
"Then, not long after his full enlightenment, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:

'The Dharma realized by me is profound, profound in its appearance, difficult to see, difficult to understand, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, refined, and to be experienced by the wise and the learned.'"
And if I were to explain this to others,
yet they did not understand it,
that would be a source of frustration for me.
There might be fatigue,
and there might be a lack of mental application;
what if I were to dwell alone in the forest, on a slope, devoted to the attainment of dwelling in happiness in this very life?
Then, as Brahmā Sahāpati was dwelling in the Brahma-world, this thought occurred to him:
"Alas, this world is perishing!
Alas, this world is being destroyed!"
It is only at certain times and on rare occasions that Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas appear in the world—
just like the flower of the udumbara tree—
and today the mind of this Blessed One inclines toward dwelling in ease rather than toward teaching the Dharma.
"What if I were to go and entreat him?
Then Brahmā Sahāpati, just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm, [vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One].
In this very way, Brahmā Sahāpati vanished from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One;
then, at that moment, Brahmā spoke this verse:
"Formerly, he appeared among the Magadhans."
For the Dharma is indeed impure and bound by defilements;
open the door to the deathless and speak the Dharma that is stainless and free from passion.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these two verses:
"O Brahmā, I have attained this with great difficulty, having shattered the barren obstructions;
yet this Dharma is not easily awakened to by those overwhelmed by the passion for existence."
"Brahmā said: 'Those who are stained by passion and shrouded by a mass of darkness will not see the path that is like going against the current— profound and exceedingly difficult to perceive.'"

“There are beings in the world who are born in the world and have grown old in the world, who possess sharp faculties, middling faculties, and even dull faculties,” and so on in detail, even before the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion;
by these faculties— faith and the others— they are said to be "capable."
Since it has been stated that there are those with sharp faculties even before the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion, and so forth,
it follows that the [faculties] such as faith and the rest can indeed be contaminated; thus,
the detailed explanation begins with "from the world including the gods," and so on.

"I have not yet, from this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, dwelt extensively with a mind that is liberated, emerged, detached, disengaged, and free from perversion"— such is the detailed statement. Furthermore, this method of examination does not apply to the untainted (*anāsrava*) states,
for it is not appropriate for the untainted to have gratification (*āsvāda*), disadvantage (*ādīnava*), or escape (*niḥsaraṇa*).
One who is an Arhat is not a Non-returner,
because his mental continuum is not liberated from the afflictions.
"One possessed of supernatural power" means one who has attained the higher knowledges; "one who has attained mastery over the mind" means one who is liberated at all times.
"Requisites for life" means that which is a requisite for life because it is conducive to it; "having given and having dedicated that" refers to this.
The meaning is that he "directed his life-force" by forming a resolution in his mind;
as to how, he says:
"whatever karma of mine has its maturation as wealth."
"May that become the maturation of lifespan"—
thus its characteristic will be stated as "the ultimate limit" (prāntakoṭika), meaning it has reached the pinnacle of increase.
"He generates the thought and speaks the words" means that he should employ both mind and speech for its accomplishment, for an effect cannot be achieved by a single cause;
thus, by this, he demonstrates that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is indeed the maturation (*vipāka*).
"May that karma of mine which has the ripening of wealth instead have the ripening of longevity;
for the power of the cultivation of meditative absorption (dhyāna-bhāvanā) is what draws it forth."
"The remainder of the maturation ripens" means that,

due to untimely death, the karma of another birth— which was abandoned before its fruit was fully completed— is drawn forth by the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and experienced; "for them it is of such a kind" refers to those yogins.
"Produced by prior karma and characterized by the momentum of its duration":
"prior karma" (*pūrvakarma*) refers to karma in a previous birth; that which is born from it is "produced by prior karma" (*pūrvakarmaja*).
The duration of the sense faculties and the great elements is their continuity; the time of that duration is "the time of duration" (sthitikāla);
its "projection" (āvedha) is its impelling force.
The "impetus" (*āvedha*) is the capacity for the continuity of moments of saṃsāra for a certain duration; for by means of it,
that period of duration is impelled.

Yogins cause the momentum of the duration produced by prior karma— which pertains to the sense faculties and the great elements— to cease, and they project a new, adventitious momentum born of meditative concentration;
thus, from one question, another question arises.

Now, regarding the question of whose maturation (*vipāka*) the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is when an Arhat monk sustains the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), there arises another question: for what purpose do they sustain the formative forces of life?
[The answer is: for the sake of the welfare of others and for the sake of the endurance of the Teaching.
For the sake of the welfare of others, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
[established] the disciples for the very purpose of maintaining the Teaching, [considering] their own physical existence as being like a disease and so forth.
Being like a disease, a tumor, or a thorn due to its connection with the three types of suffering,
[the question] "where and for whom" is answered by "where": namely, among humans in the three continents.
Regarding the question "Of whom?", the answer is: "Of a woman or a man who is an Arhat liberated at any time (asamayavimukta) and has attained the dhyāna of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika).

For him, indeed—the detailed explanation is that he possesses mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi) because he has attained the dhyāna of the ultimate limit and possesses sharp faculties (tīkṣṇendriya).
And because they have abandoned the afflictions without remainder, their continuums are not supported by the afflictions;
although one who has attained vision possesses mastery over meditative concentration,
his continuum is nevertheless not supported by the afflictions.
Although the mental continuum of one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta) is not supported by the afflictions, he lacks mastery over meditative absorption; however,
for one liberated non-occasionally (asamayavimukta), both qualities are present.
"Plural number" refers to the expression "the life-formations";
that which is such an expression is the plural number.
He asks "Why? and says:
"Of many," and so forth;
because of the relinquishing and the sustaining of many life-formations (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) existing within a continuum.
For there is no purpose in the emission or the sustaining of a single moment, because the accomplishment of another's task occurs through a continuous stream,
and because even a single moment does not cause affliction.

And some say that the plural number is used for the purpose of clarifying that "enduring through another time" means having the nature of persisting through another time— that is, being non-momentary— and that this [entity] is not a substantial entity (*dravya*) such as life-force (*āyus*).
"This [life-force] exists only in many conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra)"— this is the position of the Sautrāntikas;
even in a single moment, there are many such conditioned phenomena upon which the designation "life-force" (āyus) is based.
There is no single substance called "life-force" (*āyus*);
rather, those conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) should be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates or the nature of the four aggregates;
otherwise, the term "conditioned factors" would not have been employed at all.
However, it should have been stated thus:
"The Blessed One, having sustained his vitalities, relinquished his life-span," for the purpose of making known his mastery over death.
Since mastery over death exists,
it lasts for exactly three months and not beyond; thus, the three months taken together constitute "tri-māsam."
The term *traimāsya* means "exactly three months"; here, the accusative case is used according to the rule for expressing the complete connection of time or distance (*kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*).
It does not extend beyond three months, because there is no further task for those to be trained (*vineya*) after that period.
Because the work of a Buddha culminates in Subhadrā, it was for the sake of accomplishing that as well— that is, for the sake of fulfilling his vow;
otherwise, it would have been a mere word.
"Remaining for a *kalpa*,
a full *kalpa*, and a *kalpa* plus more" means a *kalpa* and a fraction;
this refers to the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) and the Māra of death (*maraṇamāra*).
There are four Māras: the Māra of the son of a god, the Māra of afflictions, the Māra of the aggregates, and the Māra of death.
Among these, the Māra of the son of a god was conquered during the first watch;
having surveyed the world with the divine eye during the second watch, the Māra of afflictions was conquered during the third watch.
In Vaiśālī, however, having sustained the formative forces of life for three months, he relinquished the formative forces of longevity;
this was for the sake of conquering the Māra of the aggregates. Once those aggregates were relinquished, he would have had to die.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that [the Buddhas] remain empowered for the sake of conquering Māra at the time of death;
thus concludes the incidental discussion that arose from one question leading to another,
namely, the two ways of the twelve [links of dependent origination].
It is determined that there are exactly twelve [faculties] in two ways,
excluding the final group of eight beginning with faith and ending with the faculty of one who has already understood, as well as the faculty of mental distress.
Excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*), the other twelve faculties are both results of maturation and non-results of maturation.

Among them, the seven beginning with the eye-faculty and ending with the male-faculty are non-results of maturation when they are produced through dreams and the like, as they are not accumulative (*anupacayika*).
[The others include] the mind, suffering, pleasure, and so forth, as detailed below.
Those mental states and so forth that are wholesome or afflicted are without maturation;
and those which, as appropriate, have the nature of postures, crafts, or emanations and are neutral (avyākṛta), are also without maturation.
The phrase "as appropriate" is a qualification.

Since the airyāpathika and other [mental states] are mental in nature, the faculty of suffering is impossible therein; furthermore, since the faculties of pleasure and mental joy are sometimes absent, in that case—within the desire realm—the airyāpathika mental faculty and its associated faculties of mental joy and equanimity are non-resultant (avipāka).
In the form realm, the airyāpathika mental faculty is non-resultant.
The faculty of feeling (vedanendriya) associated with that [mind] is, according to its respective level,
emanation-born (nairmāṇika) and belongs to five levels;
therein, it is exclusively the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya) and is non-resultant (avipāka).

The venerable Anantavarman maintains that those [mental states] pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those pertaining to emanations (*nairmāṇika*) are always associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

As for the others, they are maturation (*vipāka*). Among the mental faculties (*manas-indriya*) and so forth, those other than the ones whose nature consists of the wholesome, the afflicted, the deportmental, the craft-related, and the emanational, are born of maturation; thus, they are maturation.
It is established that the remaining [factors] are not maturation (*avipāka*).

Since it is determined that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the twelve beginning with the eye-faculty are [maturation], it is established by that very determination that the remaining ones are not maturation.
But which are those?
The faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), because it is either wholesome or unwholesome;
for it will be stated later that "only that one [faculty] has maturation."
The group of eight beginning with faith is wholesome, and thus is not a maturation (*avipāka*);
for maturation is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon pertaining to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*),
and these lack the characteristics of maturation.
If [it is argued that] the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*), he shows by this that there is no contradiction with scripture,
[stating] "with reference to being experienced through association" (*samprayoga-vedanīyatām adhikṛtya*); for "to be experienced" (*vedanīya*) means feeling (*vedanā*).

The opponent's intention is this: since "daurmanasya-vedanīya" means "that in which mental distress is to be experienced," and because the terms "saumanasya-vedanīya" and "upekṣā-vedanīya" also refer merely to association (samprayoga), it follows that mental joy and equanimity, like mental distress, would not be [actual] maturation (vipāka).
There is no fault whether it is in association (*samprayoga*) or in ripening (*vipāka*).
Thus, "to be experienced as mental pleasure" (*saumanasya-vedanīya*) refers to karma in this [life] that is to be experienced as mental pleasure;
likewise, for this [karma], mental pleasure is to be experienced as its ripening. Logically, it is determined that mental pleasure is not itself the ripening.
Therefore, it might be explained as follows: "This was stated with reference to the state of being experienced through association (samprayoga-vedanīyatā)";
for this reason, he asks: "What, then, is the reasoning here that mental distress (daurmanasya) is not a maturation (vipāka)?
Or rather, it might be understood thus only out of necessity (agatyā).
If you were to say that in some cases there is experience through association (*samprayoga-vedanīyatā*) and in other cases experience through maturation (*vipāka-vedanīyatā*),
then you must conclude that in all cases it is indeed experience through association.
Therefore, having considered this underlying intention, he said:
"What, then, is the reasoning here that mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*vipāka*"?
For mental distress is produced and pacified by specific conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*), such as thinking about what is undesirable and so forth.
"Joy (*saumanasya*) is also like this," [it is argued];
it is produced and pacified by specific conceptualizations such as thinking of what is desired, and so forth;
[if that were so,] then [joy would also exist] for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*), and so on.
Because mental distress (*daurmanasya*) ceases for those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) and so forth;
for the eye and other [faculties], being of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), do not cease for those free from passion,
yet mental distress does cease.
It is stated in the Sūtra that one who is free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*) is not possessed of mental distress (*daurmanasya*) due to speech;
furthermore, for one who is not free from desire, a twofold arrow of feeling is taught: "He experiences bodily suffering and mental distress."

Because of the statement that for one free from passion (*vītarāga*), there is only a single thorn and they experience only bodily suffering, it follows that they also possess mental joy (*saumanasya*); such is the detailed explanation.
What kind of neutral (*avyākṛta*) mental joy, which is the nature of maturation (*vipāka*), would belong to those free from passion?
It is the mental joy comprised within meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that is possible for them.
And since that [mental pleasure] is wholesome, it is not a maturation;
therefore, it must be explained what kind of mental pleasure constitutes their maturation.
By saying "let it be as it may," he shows that even though it cannot be precisely defined, it certainly exists;
for that [neutral feeling] has the opportunity for maturation (*vipāka*), whereas mental distress (*daurmanasya*) does not.

Since it does not manifest in any way—neither in the state of meditative attainment nor in the state of non-attainment—it is established that the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*). Thus, it belongs to both [realms] and to both [types of action]:
"to both" means to both the happy and miserable destinies; "of both" means of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
"Resultant maturation" (vipāka) is the governing topic.
How is it that this hermaphrodite state, which is considered unwholesome, is the maturation of the wholesome? He says:
"In a happy destiny, one acquires that state [of being a hermaphrodite] through unwholesome karma."
His status has fallen away;
therefore, his acquisition of unwholesome [states] is a dissociated factor (*viprayukta-dharma*).
However, the intention is that both sexual organs (*vyañjana*) are exclusively the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome [karma].
"That one, however, has ripening" means that it alone indeed possesses ripening;
therefore he says:
The word *tu* has the sense of the particle *eva* (only/exclusively) and its position is displaced; thus, the meaning is that it is "situated elsewhere.
For if it were not displaced, the sequence—namely, "that one [is] with maturation (*savipāka*) alone"—would not be broken.
However, this was stated in accordance with the requirements of the verse composition;
for he demonstrates the reasoning for the restriction that "it is indeed accompanied by ripening," showing that it is not otherwise constituted.
For two things are held to be non-resultant:
the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Because it is produced by a specific conceptualization (*vikalpaviśeṣa*), that [indeterminate] is not [truly] indeterminate.

Furthermore, because it is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*), the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); like a rotten seed, it is incapable of yielding a ripened result (*vipāka*). However, the outflow-free is also not capable of yielding a ripened result because it is not moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*); it is like a sound, solid seed that has not been moistened.
By process of elimination, it must be either unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows;
therefore, mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) necessarily has ripening (*savipāka*) and there is no such thing as non-ripening [mental dissatisfaction].
Thus, "the ten are of two kinds."
The restriction "ten indeed" and "twofold, twofold indeed,
ten" means that they are twofold as those with outflowing maturation (*savipāka*) and those without outflowing maturation (*avipāka*),
namely: the mind, the other feelings, and faith and so forth.

"Mind and other sensations, as well as faith and the rest"— here, "other sensations" refers to feelings excluding mental distress (*daurmanasya*), because mental distress has already been mentioned separately.
It is understood that "faith and so forth" refers to faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
and that "the other is without maturation" is established by the restriction [implied] in the previously mentioned [exclusion of] mental distress and the rest.

It is established that life, the [five] forms, the seven faculties beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and the three [faculties] beginning with the faculty of "perfect knowledge" are non-retribution (*avipāka*), because they are respectively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore,
the statement "the eight are wholesome" (*kuśala*) is a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) meaning that these eight are exclusively wholesome.
"Displeasure is of two kinds" means that displeasure is indeed only of two kinds—that is, displeasure alone is twofold—this being a restrictive determination.
"Of two kinds" refers to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; there are other pairs as well.
Since there is both the wholesome and the neutral, as well as the unwholesome and the neutral,
how is it determined that there is both the wholesome and the unwholesome?
The specific distinction is understood through explanation;
or rather, it has been determined that mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is exclusively subject to maturation (*savipāka*).
Therefore, this alone constitutes the twofold division, and nothing else.
And "other sensation" refers to the fourfold sensation excluding mental distress (*daurmanasya*), because that has already been mentioned;
as for "threefold," it means wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

The derivation of the word *edhā* is as follows: from the three types [of suffixes], *tridhā*; and from the two or three [suffixes], *dhamuñ* and *edhāc*, thus *tredhā*. Thus is the etymological formation of the word *edhā*.
Those associated with non-greed and so forth are wholesome; those associated with greed and so forth are unwholesome;
others than these are indeterminate.
"Another is of one kind" means that the eighth [factor], vitality, is determined to be of one kind alone; the meaning is that it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
And for this reason it is stated again;
otherwise, it would be possible for that [state] to be exclusively unwholesome, or exclusively wholesome-neutral, or exclusively unwholesome-neutral.
Therefore, it is stated once more so that the single desired realm may be established.
That for which the state of being a single element (ekadhātutva) occurs— what is it that occurs? It is the state of being indeterminate (avyākṛtatva).
"Excluding the stainless [dharmas] pertaining to the desire realm" means that by excluding only the stainless ones, it pertains to the desire realm,
for those [stainless dharmas] are indeed non-bound (apratisaṃyukta).
The meaning is "exclusively not included within the [three] realms" (*adhātupatita*).
The detailed explanation is that the female and male faculties (*strī-pum-indriya*) belong to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*).
"Female and male" (*strīpumāṃsau*) refers to both the woman and the man.
By the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that "the application of compound suffixes is not mandatory," the compound suffix does not occur;

thus, *indriya* [is used] for those two, namely the female faculty (*strīndriya*) and the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), and for suffering (*duḥkha*). The meaning is that [it refers to] the faculties whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), namely suffering and mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
Having excluded the female and male faculties, the faculties of pain and mental distress, and the untainted faculty when it is present here [in the desire realm],
the remaining faculties belong to the form realm; thus he shows the Sūtra in response to the question, "Where are they said to exist?"
"It is impossible, there is no occasion," and so forth;
the intention here is that in this Sūtra, there exists another state of being a person.
That which occurs among humans in the desire realm— namely, the alteration of the shape of the breasts and so forth, as well as voice and conduct—
is not the faculty of suffering.
Because the basis is translucent, there is no [feeling] born from injury;
and because of the absence of the unwholesome, there is no [feeling] born of maturation;
and because the continuum is supple through calm abiding, the faculty of mental displeasure does not exist.

And because, through the meditative concentration of calm abiding (*śamatha*), there is no harshness in the mental continuum due to the departure of aversion (*pratigha*), therefore the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) does not exist.
"And because of the absence of the objects of malice":
malice (*āghāta*) is anger; its object, or domain, is the "object of malice" (*āghātavastu*).
There are nine bases of malice (*āghātavastu*):
"He has done, is doing, and will do me harm"—this is the first triad of bases of malice;
"He has done, is doing, and will do harm to my friend"—this is another triad of bases of malice.
"He has done, is doing, and will do what is beneficial for my enemy"— this is another triad of objects of malice (*āghātavastu*).
By the absence of these nine objects of malice, he shows that there is no mental distress (*daurmanasya*) caused by external objects, not only that which is caused by internal causes.
For that which is produced by its own continuum and acts as an obstruction is "caused by a cause" (*hetu-kṛta*),
while that which is produced by the nine bases of malice is "caused by conditions" (*pratyaya-kṛta*);
thus, [the verse says] "having excluded [it] from pleasure and from the material."
By the word "and" (ca), the previously mentioned [phrase] is drawn forward;
therefore he says that [the phrase] "excluding the female and male faculties, suffering, and the immaculate" continues [to apply].
Regarding "in pleasure":
this refers to the faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*), which have the nature of pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā-svabhāva*),
as well as the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) such as the eye and so forth.
The three feelings are pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

That faculty of pleasure which belongs to the level of the third dhyāna and is associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*) is itself to be abandoned by insight.

In that same context, other than those, the contaminated [factors] belonging to the five groups of consciousness in the desire realm, and those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna which consist of three groups of consciousness, are to be abandoned by cultivation.
The untainted faculty of pleasure is not to be abandoned; mental joy associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing is abandoned by seeing;
other than that, tainted [mental joy] is abandoned by cultivation.
The untainted faculty of equanimity is not to be abandoned and is all-pervading, which is easy to understand; however,
mental distress is to be abandoned by both [paths].
Due to the association with mental distress (*daurmanasya*), one is "mentally distressed" (*daurmanaska*); the state of being so is "mental distressfulness" (*daurmanasyatā*),
which means mental distress (*daurmanasya*).

For according to the grammatical rule, "the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that quality (*guṇa*) because of whose presence a word is applied to a substance," that which is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) is itself "to be abandoned by seeing" (*darśanaheya*).
Therefore, other [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation;
they are not to be abandoned [by insight] because they are not concentrated.
In the desire realm, two results of maturation are obtained at the beginning.
Because desire is predominant, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is designated as "desire" (*kāma*); this will be explained later.
Among beings born from eggs, from a womb, or from moisture, two faculties that are of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) are first obtained at the very beginning in the realm of desire:
the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Why?
Because at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are necessarily afflicted;
therefore, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is afflicted by all the defilements belonging to its own level.
Because of this statement,
and because the eyes and other sense organs do not exist in that state, the term "by those born spontaneously" (*upapāduka*) serves as an exception (*apavāda*).
Since there is no qualification, it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*) would likewise obtain only those two;
therefore, does this prohibition mean that those two are not obtained at all by those born spontaneously?
However, not only two are obtained;
therefore he says,
"by them six," and so forth.
If they are without sexual organs,
that is, if they lack the male or female faculties, as was the case with those of the first eon.
Based on the statement that "in the past, beings born at the beginning of the eon were possessed of form," which six [qualities] are meant?
"The five beginning with the eye and life as the sixth," as in the case of gods and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), hell-beings and others are also included.
These are first obtained at the stage of the linking of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*); furthermore,
since even those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) may possess both sexual organs,
there is the arising of inferior organs of existence.
The intention of the objection— "How can there be a union of these two, given that the mode of birth (*upapādukā yoni*) is distinguished [from them]"— is as follows:
the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is designated as "forms" (*rūpāṇi*) because form is its primary characteristic.
"Because form is predominant" means that forms are translucent and luminous;
or alternatively, the realm of form (rūpadhātu) does not have the qualities of sensual pleasure as its predominance.
What then? It is characterized primarily by form alone, nor is it characterized primarily by the absence of form, as is the case with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
This is also seen in the Sūtra;
he shows that this is not my own invention alone:
"Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless..."
"They too are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change," and so forth;
[they are] "without gender" means they are born spontaneously (*upapāduka*), such as those of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*);
and "because of being beyond meditative attainment" means because they are superior to it.
Since the attainment of the form realm comes first and the attainment of the formless realm comes later,
the formless realm is superior to the form realm.
And because it is more preeminent in terms of rebirth;
for, in terms of rebirth, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is more preeminent than the form realm (rūpadhātu),
since there its extremely peaceful maturation (vipāka) lasts for many thousands of eons (kalpa).
Therefore, this [attainment] is superior even for that reason, and not merely because of the place of rebirth;
for it is said that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is "without location," and that one brings about cessation while passing away.

One dying in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) ceases these same three faculties; however, this should be understood as having an exception, because of the statement: "In all cases of the wholesome, there are five."
"In the form realm, eight": in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), these same [eight] should be ceased together with the five [faculties], beginning with the eye.
Because death occurs with all faculties complete at once,
for this very reason it is said:
"For all those born by spontaneous generation (upapāduka) are born and die with all their faculties complete."
"In the realm of desire, ten, nine, or eight":
one who possesses both sexual organs ceases ten faculties,
provided they possess all five [sensory] faculties intact.

If one has one sexual organ, there are nine [possibilities]; if one is without sexual organs, there are eight; however, if one has impaired faculties—such as being blind or deaf—[the count is different].
At that time, that faculty must be abandoned;
furthermore, this exception is to be understood as applying only within the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
He states that exception:

Regarding the statement "there are four for gradual death," the intention is that there is no separate cessation for these [faculties], because within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no cessation through mutual separation among them.
"In all cases of the auspicious, there are five" means that for everything previously mentioned regarding the process of death,
as one ceases or comes to rest in the formless realm (*ārūpya*), the life-faculty (*jīvita*) and the mind (*manas*) [cease].
This is an exception to the aforementioned [rule];
for the mind at death can be of three kinds: afflicted, neutral, or wholesome.
In that regard, the procedure for death with a defiled or neutral mind has been explained according to the general rule;
however, in the case of death with a wholesome mind, five additional factors— faith and the rest— must be added,
for these qualities, beginning with faith, necessarily exist in a wholesome state of mind.
Therefore, where three are mentioned, there eight are [meant];
where eight, there thirteen;
and where ten, there fifteen.
"Where there are four, there are nine," and so on in detail; this enumeration shows that there is no gradual death in the realms of form and formlessness,
because in the section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*), all phenomena pertaining to the faculties are being investigated.
Regarding this section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*) being composed here,
some explain that all the properties of the faculties, or specific states of the faculties, or specific modes of activity are being investigated;
others, however, explain as follows:

In the section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*) within the *Indriyaskandhaka*, all phenomena pertaining to the faculties—whether as specific states or as specific activities—are investigated; therefore, they are investigated here as well, because of their close connection to this treatise. This is the intended meaning.
"Attainment by nine" refers to the two final fruits; "attainment by nine" means attainment by means of nine faculties— of what?
Of the two final fruits: "final" means occurring at the end;
the two fruits that are final are the "two final fruits."
Of those two,
which are the last?
The fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of arhatship are the ones that occur at the end.
The fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning occur in the middle;
the attainment of those two final fruits occurs by means of exactly nine faculties.
He asks: which nine? He says:

By nine [faculties]— namely, those beginning with faith (śraddhā) excluding the faculty of one who has already fully known (ājñātāvīndriya), together with the mental faculty (manas) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya)—
the sequence of clear realization (abhisamaya) therein is as follows.
Receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering,
the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering,
and receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering.
Subsequent knowledge regarding suffering,
receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding origination,
and dharma-knowledge regarding origination.
The receptivity to subsequent knowledge regarding origination,
the subsequent knowledge regarding origination,
and the receptivity to dharma-knowledge regarding cessation.
Dharma-knowledge regarding cessation,
subsequent dharma-patience regarding cessation,
and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
Receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path,
the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path,
and receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path.
The sixteenth moment, "subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*), is called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*).

Among these, the fifteen moments— from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*)— constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Because it is stated that "the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments therein for one who has seen what was previously unseen," that is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
The subsequent knowledge regarding the path is the sixteenth; that is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

From that point until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), whatever untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) there may be, all of that is the path of cultivation, and it is called the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñendriya*).
From the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) onwards, the entire untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) is the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
and that is called the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Among these, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is attained during the stage of the receptivity to subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*).

Furthermore, the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) are necessarily present in this state because it is wholesome; moreover, this subsequent cognition of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti), while currently occurring, has the nature of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
The mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is associated with it,
and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is necessarily present as well, because [this state] has the *anāgamya* as its basis,
and the *anāgamya* is associated with the faculty of equanimity.
However, in this state, the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) on the path exists as being oriented toward arising with the nature of the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*);

therefore, that fruit is attained by nine [faculties]: by the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), by the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), by the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*), and by the faculties of mind (*manas*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
For its attainment occurs through both of these.

In that context, attainment occurs through the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) by way of the nature of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), and through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) by way of the nature of the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*); this is because these two serve respectively as the bringer and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*),
since the path of uninterrupted transition brings about that attainment of dissociation.
Because it is the producer of the path of liberation, and because it is its support— that is to say, its basis.
And by means of two [factors], like the expulsion of a thief and the closing of the door:
for just as when two men are present, one expels the thief while the second closes the door for him.

Likewise, by means of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) is summoned; having taken up the acquisition of the afflictions, it is brought to cessation.
Then, by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is maintained, because the acquisition of dissociation arises simultaneously [with it].
Furthermore, the fruit of arhatship is attained in the state of the diamond-like samādhi by means of the faculties beginning with faith— excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know"—
as well as the mind-faculty, all of which function as previously described.
In that state, the vajra-like concentration (vajropamasamādhi) is the uninterrupted path (ānantaryamārga), existing with the nature of the faculty of perfect knowledge (ājñendriya),
and one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity, provided that arhatship is attained by relying upon the third dhyāna.
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is present there;
furthermore, based on the first or second *dhyāna*, the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) is present;

or else, based on any one of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate *dhyāna* (*dhyānāntara*), the fourth *dhyāna*, or the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness (*ākāśavijñānākiñcanyāyatana*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is present there.

However, at this stage, the collection of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)—which is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and has the nature of the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—is oriented toward arising.

Therefore, that fruit is attained by nine [faculties]: by the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), by the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*), by the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), by the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), and by whichever one among the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity is appropriate.
Its attainment occurs through both the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation; the explanation is as before.
The completion of the sentence is: "The attainment of two [fruits] occurs by means of seven, eight, or nine [paths].
The detailed explanation is that this applies to each [fruit] individually;
specifically, the attainment of the fruit of once-returning occurs by means of seven, eight, or nine [paths].
Explaining that [attainment] of the fruit of non-returning in this way, he says:
first, as for the fruit of once-returning, if one who follows the gradual path attains it, and if he does so by means of the mundane path—
The mundane path has the aspects of being peaceful and so forth, or sublime and so forth,
because of the statement that "those having the aspects of being peaceful and so forth, or sublime and so forth, have the higher and lower as their respective objects."
Therefore, in this context, the yogi views the higher stage as peaceful, sublime, and a state of deliverance,
while he views the lower stage as coarse, painful, and like a thick wall;
and this [viewing] is described as being of four kinds.
The path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
Among these, the path of preparation is that from which the path of uninterrupted transition arises;
furthermore, it is that by which one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) also arises immediately after the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*);
it is the basis for the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*). The special path (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is a distinguished path superior to that.
By that path, nine grades of afflictions are to be abandoned:
the intense-intense, the intense-middling, the intense-weak, the middling-intense, the middling-middling, the middling-weak, the weak-intense, the weak-middling, and the weak-weak.

If an ordinary person abandons the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation by mixing them together, they abandon them by dividing them into nine grades according to those distinctions of weak-middling, intense, and so forth.

By means of the weak-weak paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one abandons the strongest-of-the-strong category of afflictions (*kleśa*); in this manner, up to the point where by means of the strongest-of-the-strong paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation, one abandons the weakest-of-the-weak category of afflictions.
The Noble One (*ārya*), however, likewise divides the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) into nine categories and abandons them in that same way.
Since those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing have already been abandoned by the path of seeing,
the supramundane path of cultivation likewise possesses sixteen aspects,
due to the distinction of the aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
And that [path] is likewise fourfold due to the distinctions of the paths of preparation and so forth;

here too, by means of the two weakest-weak uninterrupted and liberation paths, one abandons the strongest-strongest category of afflictions, and so on, until by means of the two strongest-strongest uninterrupted and liberation paths, one abandons the weakest-weak category of afflictions.
This is merely a brief indication of the mundane and supramundane paths.
That fruit of the once-returner may be attained either by one who proceeds through the gradual stages (*ānupūrvika*) or by one who is already largely free from passion (*bhūyovītarāga*).
Among these, the gradualist is one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry, subsequently attains the fruit of once-returning in due order.
And who is this person?

It is one who is bound by all fetters, or one whose [fetters] have been attenuated by one type and so forth, provided that he has not attenuated the sixth type; such a person enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*) at the sixteenth moment of mind and becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
For one who is to abandon [the defilements] through cultivation—up to the sixth category—he, because he practices primarily tranquility (śamatha), generates even the mundane path;
upon the abandonment of that sixth category, he attains the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala).

The attainment of that fruit is by means of seven faculties: the five beginning with faith, the mental faculty, and the seventh, the faculty of equanimity, because it has the threshold concentration (anāgamya) as its support.
Now, by means of the supramundane path, its attainment is through eight faculties:
those same [seven] with the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*) as the eighth;
for those very seven faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), receive the designation of the faculty of "one who has known."
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), [it is called] "one who has further become free from passion" (*bhūyovītarāga*),
referring to one who, while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), had already undergone the removal of six categories [of afflictions] by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
He is called "one who has largely abandoned passion" because he has abandoned passion in a greater measure;
if he attains the fruit of a once-returner, [he is so designated].
How does he attain it?

By means of the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) through the previously mentioned path; he attains it at the stage of the acceptance of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*), just as [one attains] the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) by means of nine [moments].

The explanation is as before: [he is endowed] with faith and the other faculties, excluding the faculty of one who has already fully known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), together with the mental faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
For this person becomes a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*) in the sixteenth moment, even without having previously attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
Regarding the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), if one attains it by way of gradual succession (*ānupūrvaka*):

here, "one who proceeds by gradual succession" refers to either one who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), attains the fruit of non-returning;

or one who, having become largely free from passion (*bhūyovītarāga*), attains the fruit of non-returning without having previously obtained the fruit of stream-entry and having obtained only the fruit of once-returning.
And if he attains it by means of the mundane path, his attainment is by way of seven faculties,
as is intended in the case of the fruit of once-returning for one who follows the gradual sequence.
The meaning is: by means of the five [faculties] beginning with faith, together with the faculties of mind and equanimity.
Now, regarding the supramundane path, "for him [it is] likewise by eight" means that, just as for the fruit of the once-returner, it is by means of eight.
The faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*) becomes the eighth.

Now, regarding the term "one who is free from passion" (*vītarāga*): this refers to one who has become free from passion for the desire realm alone by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) when the ninth category [of defilements] has been abandoned; or alternatively, it refers to one who has become free from passion even up to the first *dhyāna*, or even up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanya*), and who attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
Its attainment is by means of nine [paths], just as the fruit of stream-entry is attained;
for the fruit of stream-entry is indeed attained through the path of seeing.
And since its attainment occurs through the path of seeing alone, it is similar [to the others];
however, this is the distinction: it possesses one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity.
Regarding the phrase "due to a distinction in the basis":
if one enters the path of certainty (niyāma) by relying on the third dhyāna,
the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) exists there.

Now, when this person follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), as the text explains in detail: based upon the first and second dhyānas, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) exists there; whereas based upon any one of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), or the fourth dhyāna, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) exists there.
Even when this practitioner of the gradual path, who has previously attained a fruit and possesses sharp faculties,
enters the fundamental dhyāna by means of a mundane path during the ninth path of liberation, he then attains the fruit of non-returning through eight faculties;
in that case, the path of liberation is comprised within the fundamental dhyāna.

And in that case, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) belongs exclusively to the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) which is comprised within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*); if it does not enter therein, then only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is present, and not otherwise.
Its attainment is by means of eight faculties: the five beginning with faith, as well as the mental faculty, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculty of mental pleasure;
thus its attainment is by both, namely, by the path of immediate succession and the path of liberation.
This has been explained as being "like the expulsion of thieves and the closing of the door.
