Now, regarding the statement "he enters by means of the supramundane [path]," he should be understood as that same gradual practitioner who possesses sharp faculties, because the context continues from what preceded.
Its attainment is by means of nine faculties: by those very faculties just mentioned, and by the ninth, the faculty of one who has known (*ājñendriya*).
For those same faculties, being untainted (*anāsrava*), receive the designation "faculty of one who has known."

This is raised as an objection here: why is it stated thus only regarding one who proceeds through the stages in succession (*ānupūrvika*), and not regarding one who was previously free from passion (*vītarāgapūrvī*)?

For it is not the case that one who was previously free from passion, having generated the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), enters the fundamental first dhyāna at the sixteenth moment of mind.
In that case, because of disregard for what has already been attained,

one who proceeds by way of the successive stages (ānupūrvika) seeks the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), since those have not been previously attained; therefore, it is possible that he enters directly into the fundamental state itself.

However, one who was previously free from passion (vītarāgapūrvī) has already applied himself toward the vision of the Four Truths and not toward meditative absorption (dhyāna); therefore, the intention is that he does not enter into the fundamental absorption (maula-dhyāna) at that sixteenth moment of mind.
This contradicts what was stated [previously] regarding "the non-attainment of the two final fruits," since it is said in the Abhidharma:
In the *Jñānaprasthāna*, it is asked: "By how many faculties does one attain arhatship?
To this, he says:
The intention [of the objection] is: "How is this not contradicted by the statement 'by eleven'?"—
[the response being] "because it is possible for one [to possess them]."

The possibility belongs to only a certain individual, not to everyone; for it was said with reference to one who, having weak faculties, might attain arhatship through various successive states of bliss, mental ease, and equanimity, by means of specific bases after repeatedly falling away.
"By eleven" means that there is no possibility of the simultaneous occurrence (*samavadhāna*) of pleasure (*sukha*), mental ease (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) at one time,
because mental states (*citta-caitta*) arise as individual substances (*ekaika-dravya*).
For whichever person of dull faculties might attain arhatship by relying on the *anāgamya* stage or another basis for the faculty of equanimity,
their attainment of it occurs through that faculty of equanimity; from that state, they may subsequently fall away.
Then, relying upon the third dhyāna, he may again attain arhatship;
his attainment of that state occurs through the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Thus, in each case of attaining a fruit therein, exactly nine faculties necessarily function.
The five faculties beginning with faith, the faculty of one who has known the unknown (*anājñātājñātāvīndriya*), and any one of the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, or equanimity— thus,
because these are acquired again and again, it is said that [the fruit] is attained by eleven.
How is it that this same contingency does not apply even to the non-returner (*anāgāmin*)?
Why is it stated in that treatise that the fruit of arhatship alone is attained by means of eleven [faculties],
and it is not stated that the fruit of non-returning is also [attained] in this way?
For one who has fallen away from it never attains it by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
This non-returner, having fallen away from the attainment of the stages above the third dhyāna,
has indeed fallen away from those higher stages;
however, he is not said to have fallen away from the fruit of non-returning.
In this manner, up to the second dhyāna,
when one has fallen away from the first [dhyāna].
Then he is said to have fallen away from the fruit of the non-returner;
for the fruit of the non-returner is established precisely through the abandonment of the five lower fetters,
and at that time he has fallen away from his detachment from the realm of desire.
In that case, he does not possess the third dhyāna;
how then could he attain the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) by means of the faculty of pleasure? To this, he says:
For it is never the case that one who has fallen away from this [state] attains the faculty of pleasure; so how could such a person attain it by means of the faculty of mental joy?
Since this would result in the negation of the pleasure faculty itself if one were to enter the fundamental dhyāna during the ninth path of liberation,
this is not the case.
For whoever has fallen away is one of dull faculties,
and whoever is of dull faculties [is one who has fallen away].
He is unable to enter the fundamental dhyāna during the ninth path of liberation;
however, one with sharp faculties is able to do so,
because the transformation of the faculties is difficult to accomplish.
This is true; however,

if that person of dull faculties who follows the gradual path, having attained the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) and subsequently fallen away from it, were to undergo a transformation of the faculties (indriyasañcāra),

and having become one of sharp faculties through that transformation of the faculties, were to attain the fruit of a non-returner again by the very same previous sequence and enter the fundamental [dhyāna] during the ninth path of liberation (vimuktimārga).

Then, his attainment of the fruit of non-returning occurs through eight faculties: the five beginning with faith, the faculty of mind, the faculty of equanimity included within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the faculty of mental pleasure included within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of the fundamental dhyāna.
This is so provided that he enters the fundamental dhyāna by means of the supramundane path.
It should be understood that [the fruit] is attained by these eight faculties, with the faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*) as the ninth;
therefore, it is well said that one who has not fallen away from it never attains it through the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
In that case, one who was previously free from passion would attain it by means of eleven [faculties]. How so?
A person of dull faculties who has attained the third dhyāna, relying upon that third dhyāna, enters into the fixed course of rightness (niyāma).
In the sixteenth moment of consciousness, he becomes a non-returner (anāgāmī);

that attainment of the fruit [is characterized] by the faculty of pleasure, the five beginning with faith, and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya).

Having abandoned that fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) and having made himself one of sharp faculties through the refinement of the faculties (*indriyottāpana*), he attains the fruit of non-returning by relying precisely on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*). Upon the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), he would enter the fundamental [dhyāna].

His attainment of that fruit occurs, as before, by means of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*), the five beginning with faith (*śraddhādi*), and the eighth, the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*); and because it is a supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), it also occurs by means of the ninth, the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñendriya*).
Thus, one might think that such a person could attain that fruit of non-returning through eleven faculties at two different times;
therefore, to preclude this, he said:
"And one who was previously free from passion does not fall away."
Because that detachment leads to both paths; furthermore, one who is free from passion for the desire realm and has entered the path of certainty (*niyāma*) by means of some basis does not fall away.
Why?
Because that detachment brings about two paths—
namely, the attainment of both the mundane and supramundane paths— the fruit here is twofold.
Because of the statement: "The conditioned and the unconditioned constitute the fruit of the conditioned and the unconditioned."
In this case, that unconditioned fruit of non-returning, characterized by dissociation,
was previously attained through the mundane path,
and it is attained once again through the supramundane path upon entering the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*).
For its attainment is twofold—
both mundane and supramundane—
and therefore that detachment is stable.
Therefore, one does not fall away from this [state].
Now, is it not the case that there is no falling away from the fruit itself?
There is indeed another reason for this: because those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing lack a real objective basis (*avastuka*).
It must also be explained why this was not stated here;
for indeed, another might argue that there should be no falling away from the detachment attained through the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision.
Why would there not be a falling away from the detachment that abandons only those afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation for one who has fallen away?
For it is through the abandonment of the five lower fetters that the fruit of non-returning is attained,
and among those [five], the view of a self-identity, the misapprehension of precepts and vows, and doubt are to be abandoned by seeing.
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);

and for one who was previously free from passion regarding these two, at the end of the realization (*abhisamaya*), in the sixteenth moment of mind, there occurs the abandonment of those [defilements] by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*). By the power of that [abandonment], there subsequently arises an untainted attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*), because the untainted lineages (*gotra*) have been acquired.

For at that stage, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), which has the nature of the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) abandonment of sensual desire and so forth, are obtained;
therefore, the Noble One stated this very reason: "because that detachment is attained through two paths."
The meaning is that because the abandonment of sensual desire and so forth is brought about by two paths,
one who is endowed with the life-faculty, the mind-faculty, and attention is necessarily possessed of all three.
In relation to [the state] endowed with life or mind, one is necessarily possessed of all three; that is, by those very natures of equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), and mind (*manas*).
For there is no possession of these without their mutual presence; thus, when there is possession of one, there is possession of all.
Therefore, there is also possession (*samanvāgama*) for these two;
thus, the determination of possession is established for them,
but it is not so established for the eye and the other [faculties].
Therefore, he says:
"By the faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that one born in the realm of Ābhāsvara is not possessed of the faculties of eye, ear, nose, and tongue, the faculty of body (*kāyendriya*) is not mentioned therein.

And in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because this sense of "accumulation" (*upacaya*)— referring to those [faculties] which have not been acquired or have been lost— is possible only in the case of the eye and so forth, and not in the case of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*); otherwise, one born in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) would simply be said to be "not endowed" with the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*),
rather than being said to have "not acquired" them during stages such as the embryo (*kalala*).

Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not possessed [of these faculties] because they have lost them through their destruction or because they are in a state such as blindness, or due to gradual death; this qualification is used because a noble one (*ārya*) is necessarily possessed of them.
For there is no abandonment of untainted pleasure through a transition between stages; nor is one who is free from passion for the desire realm [disjoined] from mental distress.
Thus, whether abiding here [in the desire realm] or in another realm, whether an ordinary person or an noble one, one is not disjoined from it.

Those who abide in the fruits of ordinary persons are those abiding in the fruits, such as stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and so forth; because they have already abandoned [that faculty] at the conclusion of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they are not endowed with that faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Those abiding on the path of seeing are not possessed of the faculty of perfect knowledge because they have not yet attained it;
those abiding on the path of no-more-learning are not possessed of it because it has been relinquished upon the attainment of the fruit.
In states other than these two exceptions, possession should be understood to occur as previously described.
The meaning is that in those states which are not prohibited regarding the possession of the sense-faculties such as the eye,
one should be understood to be possessed of whichever specific faculties have been mentioned for those respective states.

For example, excluding the states of not having acquired or having lost them within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one who is endowed with the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the tongue is endowed with the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) when born in the desire or form realms (*rūpadhātu*), and so forth, [along] with four [faculties] including pleasure (*sukha*) and the body faculty.

The word "proper" (yukta) continues [from the previous context], as does the word "necessarily" (avaśyam). However, when there is no intention to specify number or sequence, the mention of pleasure and so forth (*sukhādi*) immediately follows that [word] with the word "by them" (*taiḥ*).
Regarding the statement "endowed with the faculty of pleasure" (*sukhendriya*):
with the exception of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), everyone is endowed with the faculty of pleasure;
however, they are not necessarily endowed with it by way of other [faculties].

There is non-possession (asamanvāgama) of the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the tongue-faculty in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) and in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) during the states of non-acquisition or loss; likewise,
there is non-possession of the body-faculty in the formless realm,
and of the female and male faculties in both the form and formless realms.
In the desire realm, when not yet acquired or having been lost, [the ordinary person] possesses the faculty of suffering; in the form and formless realms,
the ordinary person born in the third dhyāna possesses the faculty of mental pleasure.
With the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), [it is] in the state of being free from passion for the desire realm;

with the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), in the state when the roots of merit have been severed; and with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), in the states of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and one established in the fruits [of the path].

One who is not endowed with the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) on the path of seeing or during the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),

and who is not endowed with the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) during the stages of an ordinary person or one in training (*śaikṣa*), is also endowed with four [faculties]— the same as those associated with the faculty of body (*kāyendriya*).

One born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who is endowed with the body-faculty (kāyendriya) is not necessarily endowed with others, such as the eye-faculty (cakṣus) and so forth; for in the desire realm, there is non-possession (asamanvāgama) during states where these have not yet been acquired or have been lost.
There is non-possession of the female and male faculties in this very state, and also in the realm of form (rūpadhātu);
there is non-possession of suffering in this very state, and of pleasure in the case of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) born in the fourth dhyāna.
An ordinary person born in the third or fourth dhyāna is not possessed of mental joy (*saumanasya*);
likewise, it should be stated that they are not possessed of mental grief (*daurmanasya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and the other [faculties], as previously described;
one who possesses the eye and so forth is possessed of five [faculties].
The meaning is "the eye, ear, nose, and tongue";
and by that [means].
When that eye exists, the body-faculty necessarily exists,
but not the ear-faculty and the others.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because the states of not having obtained or having lost [the faculties] are possible, the same exceptions as previously stated must be mentioned for the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) and so forth;
likewise for the ear, nose, and tongue faculties (*śrotraghrāṇajihvendriya*).

Whoever possesses the ear-faculty necessarily possesses five [faculties]: equanimity, life, mind, body, and that [ear-faculty] itself; thus should all [other cases] be understood, including mental joy (*saumanasya*).
Regarding the question of what one is necessarily endowed with by means of the five [faculties],
why has mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) not been included among the eye and the other [faculties] themselves?

Because it is recited in another location, if it were inserted here by means of the word "etc. (ādi), the arrangement would become confused; for instance, with whom is one born in the second dhyāna but not yet having attained the third endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)?
The faculty of pleasure exists in the desire realm as belonging to the five groups of consciousness,
and in the first dhyāna as belonging to three groups of consciousness; however, in the third dhyāna, it is mental.

Therefore, considering that one born in the second dhyāna is not endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) of a lower level because it has been abandoned through the transition to that higher level,
nor with that belonging to the third dhyāna level because of its non-attainment, he raises an objection.
With what faculty of pleasure is he endowed?
It is said: with the defiled [faculty] belonging to the stage of the third dhyāna.
For it is an established tenet that all beings born in a lower stage are endowed with the defiled [faculties] of the higher stages as long as they have not been abandoned;
the deviation regarding the remaining faculties should be stated as before,
but one who possesses suffering is endowed with seven.
Thus,
since this person is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), they necessarily possess the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and the four feeling-faculties (vedanendriya).
Excluding mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), [these faculties] exist in the state of one who is free from passion; for in that state, mental dissatisfaction is absent,
while the mind-faculty (*mana-indriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are present.
Thus, one is necessarily endowed with seven faculties;
however, the variability regarding the remaining faculties should be stated as before:
one who possesses the female faculty and so forth is endowed with eight or more.
Thus, "possessing the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom" refers to one who possesses the faculties of womanhood or manhood,
as well as the faculties of life, mind, pleasure, pain, mental ease, and equanimity, since these have already been mentioned.
And since the three beginning with the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) will be explained later,
the inclusion here is only of these eight faculties: "he who is endowed with the female faculty."
Is he necessarily one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) because of possessing the female faculty (*strīndriya*)?
Therefore, he is necessarily endowed with eight faculties; as to which ones, he says:
With those seven, together with the female faculty—
namely, the body, life, mind, and the four faculties of sensation— making eight including the female faculty as the eighth;
for the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule.

As it was stated, because of reasons such as the possible deficiency of the eye and other faculties, one who possesses the male faculty should be described in the same way as one who possesses the female faculty; likewise,
one born in the realm of desire who is not free from passion for desire should be described as possessing mental distress (*daurmanasya*) by means of those same seven [faculties] and mental distress.

One who possesses faith is also a sentient being belonging to the three realms; thus, they are endowed with those five beginning with faith—which are inseparable from them—as well as with equanimity, the life-faculty, and the mind-faculty.
As for the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule, as before.
Just as it is with one who possesses faith, so it is up to one who possesses wisdom.
"The faculty of one who has known, the faculty of one who has known"—
the faculty of one who has indeed known is the "faculty of one who has known" (*ājñātendriya*);
the meaning is the faculty of that which has been known without remainder.

For the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*) is indeed the faculty of one who has known (*ājñātendriya*), but not [the faculty] of one who has known without remainder, because that which is to be abandoned still remains;
or else, by taking a part of the word, the person who has realized (*ājñātāvī*) is called "one who has known," and his faculty is the "faculty of having known."
Whoever possesses the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñendriya*) necessarily possesses eleven [faculties].
A learner (*śaikṣa*) established in the fruit who possesses the faculty of "one who has known" exists in all three realms;
yet, how can one born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (*ārūpya*) be endowed with the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*)?
Because a noble one necessarily acquires the faculty of mental pleasure upon detachment from the desire realm,
and the faculty of physical pleasure upon detachment from the second dhyāna, and these two are not abandoned even when shifting between levels.
For it will be stated:

"The wholesome [attainment] acquired through dhyāna is abandoned through changing levels and through loss; likewise that acquired through the formless realms. But the noble [attainment] is abandoned through the acquisition of a fruit, through refinement, and through loss."
Thus, although these two— the path of the candidate and the path of the one with dull faculties— are abandoned even upon the attainment of the fruit and the sharpening of the faculties,
nevertheless, others— consisting in the nature of the path of one abiding in the fruit who possesses sharp faculties— are acquired.

Therefore, because those two—pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*)—are not abandoned even when shifting levels, a noble one (*ārya*) born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms (*ārūpya*) remains endowed with them.
For the remaining [faculties], as before, there is no fixed rule; however, one who possesses the faculty "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is endowed with thirteen.
This is the detailed explanation:

a being belonging to the desire realm who is endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) [is so endowed] because that faculty has arisen within the desire realm itself; for it is stated that due to a lack of spiritual urgency (*asaṃvega*), there is "arrangement here and completion there."

Therefore, he necessarily possesses the body-faculty and the four feelings, excluding mental distress (*daurmanasya*), because those [feelings] are absent in his state of being free from passion (*vītarāga*).
In this context, the word "necessarily" (avaśyam) carries over;
it is determined that one is necessarily endowed with these thirteen faculties,
but not that one is endowed with *only* thirteen.
Regarding the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule,
because the path of seeing can occur even in those who are blind and so forth; however, if there is a deficiency of the female or male faculty, how can the path of seeing arise?
Some indeed say that for those who are deficient and deprived of the female and male faculties, there is no attainment of restraint, the fruits [of the path], or detachment; however,
for those who have already acquired restraint, the attainment of the fruits does occur.
For the abandonment of the Prātimokṣa restraint occurs through the arising of both sexual organs,

not through their deficiency or through gradual death; even when the female or male faculty ceases, the arising of the Path of Seeing occurs for one who has cultivated the levels conducive to penetration.
Others, however, say that here it is the person in general who is under discussion,
and not the necessary possession and variability [of faculties] as restricted to a single case alone.
How is it that one who is endowed with equanimity, life-faculty, and mind-nature is necessarily possessed of all three?
This is the meaning.

Is every person endowed with equanimity (upekṣā)—whether born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) up to being born at the peak of existence (bhavāgra)—necessarily endowed with these three? Regarding the variability of the eye and so forth, while it is possible for some to lack them, it is not the case that everyone lacks them; for indeed, only one who is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is devoid of the material sense-faculties (rūpīndriya).
But it is not the case that whoever is born in the form realm— extensively, up to whoever is someone lacking in faith and so forth, such as one whose roots of merit are severed—
is necessarily the same person who is born in the formless realm.
Likewise here as well, whoever is endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is necessarily possessed of all these thirteen faculties as previously described;
however, deviation is possible for some,
for instance, someone who is blind lacks the eye-faculty (cakṣurindriya).
Someone who is deaf by means of the auditory faculty;
likewise, [those who are so] by the olfactory and other faculties up to someone who is male by means of the female faculty.

It should be understood in this very way: that for some person, [the object] is a woman by means of the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), and for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*), it is by means of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*).
"By the very minimum, one devoid of merit [is endowed] with eight"—
this refers to a single person who is endowed with the fewest of all.
With how few [factors] is he endowed? It is said:
he who is devoid of merit is one whose roots of goodness are severed, and he exists only within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
A woman cuts [the bonds] through the conduct of her gaze, and likewise a man;
thus, detachment from desire is not possible here [in this world].
Therefore, this [being] possesses all five feeling-faculties,
as well as the body-faculty, the life-faculty, and the mind-faculty; these indeed exist everywhere, whereas the eye-faculty and the others do not.

Because they do not exist during the state of gradual death or the state of blindness and so forth, [the term is used] in the sense of "it will be said"; thus, *vid* is derived from the root *vid* with the suffix *kvip* in the active sense (*kartari*),
or it is derived from the root *vid* meaning "cognition" (*vedanam*) as an abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*) with the *uṇādi* suffix *kvip*.
He shows the indicative proof:
just as "attainment" (*sampadana*) is [expressed by] "attainment" (*sampad*),
so too "formlessness" (*ārūpya*)— the mere number— is connected with the word "so" (*tathā*).
Because they are exclusively wholesome (*ekāntakuśala*), faith and the others are included by the mention of "the wholesome" (*śubha*);
thus, they are only wholesome and not unwholesome or neutral. This means that those which are wholesome are intended;
[otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others as well.
Since those [other factors] are also exclusively wholesome, it would follow that they too should be included; therefore, this is not [the case].
Regarding the phrase "from the context of eight," [it refers to] "the unwholesome [mind] with eight";

by this, [the inclusion of] the eight— equanimity, life-faculty, mind-faculty, and the wholesome [faculties]— is established, thereby effecting the exclusion of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others.
Because the limit is established by the word "eight" and because it pertains to the section on children,
the child is the one qualified here.
Because of the statement, "The fool is likewise formless," and because an ordinary person exists in the absence of the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others,
what is this state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
Because of the statement "the non-attainment of the noble dharmas," there is no application [of this definition] to those untainted states; thus,
one who possesses both sexual organs is one whose faculties are complete.
For even one with two sexual organs, provided they possess the complete set of faculties such as the eye and so forth,
is endowed with nineteen [faculties] and not otherwise;
that is, the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya), the two [sexual organs], and either one of the other two.
Because it involves passion (*rāgitva*), the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) must be excluded absolutely;

furthermore, because the noble one (*ārya*) necessarily possesses the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the [faculty of] knowledge (*ājñendriya*) in alternation, that which is the faculty of "I shall come to know" [is also excluded].

That which is the faculty of one who has already known is not the faculty of "I shall come to know"; that which is the faculty of "I shall come to know" is not the faculty of one who has already known.
Having explained in detail the classification of the faculties as they arose in the context of the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*), [the author now asks]:
among the eighteen elements, how many are faculties and how many are not? In this context of the analysis of the elements:
*Half of the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) is a faculty, as are those which are known as the twelve internal [elements].* (AK 1.48cd)
Thus [it is said].
The faculties have arrived;
their classification [is as follows].
It has been explained in detail that "the three are pure" and so forth;
what are these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) which were previously designated as aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
Just as they have distinct characteristics: "it is manifested" (rūpyate) thus it is form (rūpa);
experience is feeling (vedanā).
Is the grasping of signs, such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth,
a grasping of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) because it possesses origination, or rather, do they also necessarily arise simultaneously?
Some exist;
for indeed some things arise together, yet not necessarily together, such as those that arise together with the eye and so forth.
Because those consciousnesses and so forth exist as both "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) with respect to the eyes and other faculties,
he therefore asks:
"All these phenomena are fivefold."
In this way, the inclusion of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) is established by means of the system of the five categories (*pañcavastuka*);
the teaching of the Dharma by way of the group beginning with form (*rūpa*) is for the sake of easy comprehension.
In that regard, since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) never arises,
no rule concerning simultaneous arising is considered with respect to it;
rather, the most subtle aggregate of matter (*rūpasaṅghāta*) is the atom (*paramāṇu*).
The aggregate atom (*saṅghātaparamāṇu*) is not the substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*);
for that substance which is devoid of all form and has no preceding or succeeding part is intended to be the substantial atom.
Therefore, he specifies that in the desire realm, an atom is a composite consisting of eight substances, excluding sound.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when sound does not arise therein,
it necessarily consists of exactly eight substances (*aṣṭadravyaka*) and no more; this is because there is no other sense faculty (*aparendriya*).
"One who possesses another faculty" (*aparendriya*) means one who has the eye-faculty (*cakṣus*) and so forth;
for wherever there is the eye, the ear, or the like, there must also be the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), because the functioning of the eye and the other faculties is dependent upon it.

Furthermore, these atoms accompanied by sound—namely those consisting of eight substances and so forth—are "aggregated atoms" (*saṅghātaparamāṇu*). When they arise with sound, they arise respectively as consisting of nine, ten, or eleven substances;
that which consists of eight substances becomes one consisting of nine substances.
That which consists of nine substances consists of ten substances;
that which consists of ten substances [consists of nine].
It consists of eleven substances;
for there is indeed sound that is inseparable from the sense-faculties—
that which cannot be separated from the sense-faculty.
The meaning is that this sound is inseparable from the sense faculty, existing not apart from the sense faculty;
some read the word as *avinirbhogī*, using the root *bhuji*.
How is it that, although the primary elements are inseparable, a certain aggregate is solid and so forth—
such that the earth element is solid and the water element is fluid?
Heat is the fire element (tejo-dhātu) and motion is the wind element (vāyu-dhātu);
the intention is that because the primary elements are equal in their existence, the composites formed by them must likewise be equal in form.
"Whatever is most intense therein," and so forth:

whatever substance characterized by earth and so on is most intense— that is, most manifest— within a particular aggregate by way of its influence (*prabhāva*) or capacity (*śakti*), but not by way of its substantiality (*dravya*), having arisen or become manifest.
The perception of that [substance] therein means the perception—
that is, the apprehension— of that substance within that aggregate,
like the touch of a bundle of fine needles.
In this context, "needles" (*sūcyaḥ*) are known in the world to be made of iron;
"bristles" (*tūlyaḥ*) are the stalks of the roots and flowers of *vīraṇa* grass and other plants, which are commonly recognized by ordinary people as *siṅkā*.
The cluster of those needles and tufts is "the cluster of needles and tufts";
its touch is "the touch of the cluster of needles and tufts," and the perception thereof is "the perception of that."
By the force of that most intense [feeling], the suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule "as that,
so in this" (*tasyeva tatra*),
signifying that which has arisen from it.
This is what is meant:
just as when there is an equal presence of bundles of needles and cotton, the touch of the needles alone is clearly perceived because of their sharpness,
while that of the cotton is not, due to its lack of sharpness.
Likewise, hardness is perceived only in certain aggregates such as wood, liquidity in water, and heat in fire.
In some cases there is movement in the wind,
yet the four great elements are not absent from each respective aggregate,
just as in the case of the taste of flour, salt, and powder.
Just as there is a perception of the taste of barley-meal powder and salt powder,
it is the taste of the salt powder alone that is clearly perceived, and not the taste of the barley-meal powder.
The same applies here as well; thus,
from "gathering, supporting, ripening,
and expanding," the existence of the water element is understood through its function of gathering in relation to [the earth] and so forth.

Otherwise, it would fall apart like a handful of dust if the water element were not present there; the existence of the earth element within water is inferred by its function of supporting boats and other such objects.
The existence of the fire element is understood through the activity of cooking;
for if it did not exist, wood and other such things would not undergo putrefaction.
The existence of the wind element is understood through the activity of expansion.

For there would be no spreading forth or growth for it if the wind-element were not present therein; the same should be applied elsewhere as well, provided that the necessary conditions are obtained— this is the detailed explanation.
When conditions such as fire and so forth are obtained, there occurs the liquefaction of solid substances and so on; that is, because of the occurrence of states such as fluidity and solidity—
for example, when fire is present, the liquefaction of solid iron.
By that it is known that the iron-element exists;
likewise, when a substance acquires the cognition of coldness and so forth, hardness is thereby known to indicate the existence of the earth-element therein.
Likewise, because heat is perceived through the friction of solid objects,
the existence of the fire element (*tejodhātu*) therein is inferred;
this same principle should be applied accordingly to other cases as well.
"Another [teacher], the Venerable Śrīlāta, says that heat is perceived in water due to an excess of coldness;
for since water is perceived as cold, colder, and coldest,
it is known from this that there is an excess of coldness there due to the production of some other portion of fire."
And by that, it is understood there [in that case] "it exists" when there is no differentiation; such is the detailed explanation. The Master refutes that view.

Just as there is no intermingling or mixing of sound with another substance, yet there is an intensification due to a difference in its own nature— such that a sound is "clear," "clearer," or "clearest"—
so too it would be here;
and just as for sensation there is no intermingling with any other substance, yet there is an intensification by way of degrees due to a difference in its own nature.
So it is here as well;
by this [statement], the existence of fire is not understood,
for those very waters are some cold, some colder, and some coldest.
The Sautrāntikas maintain that "the existence of those [past and future dharmas] in those [present ones] is by way of seed, not by way of intrinsic nature";
"by way of seed" means by way of capacity or potentiality,
and "not by way of intrinsic nature" means not as a substantial entity (*dravya*).
For indeed, there exists a manifold potency by which yogins, through their specific resolve (*adhimokṣa*), produce elements such as gold-element, silver-element, copper-element, and so forth.
Why is this? He says: because of the statement, "In this block of wood there are various elements."

For the potencies of the elements have been described by the Blessed One in that very way; indeed, there is no room therein for many things such as gold and silver in their own essential form. Thus, the Vaibhāṣikas raise this objection: "How can color exist in wind? And they ask: "Given the rule that [matter] in the desire realm consists of eight substances, how is it determined that color exists in wind?"
For no color whatsoever is perceived there;
this matter is to be accepted by faith, not established by inference—such is the view of the Vaibhāṣikas.
The intention is that this matter was spoken by the supreme authorities and must be understood as such; it is not something to be proven through inference.
He shows that there is indeed inference based on either "from association" or "from the perception of odor," stating:
"But odor is perceived due to the contact of the air with a substance possessing odor."
And that fragrance does not deviate from its color;
for wherever there is fragrance, there must also be color.
And here, regarding the statement of the proof—
"Air possesses color because it possesses odor, like a flower of a species"—
it has been stated that odor and taste do not exist in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Because of the statement, "excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness," it follows that the atoms (paramāṇu) present there consist of six, seven, or eight substances (dravyaka).
"Those located there" means atoms located there; "atoms" refers here to aggregate-atoms (*saṃghāta-paramāṇu*),
which are said here to consist of eight substances, being devoid of sense-faculties and lacking sound.
In that case, it consists of six substances;
where there is the body-faculty, it consists of seven substances.
That which consists of ten substances and possesses another sense faculty consists of eight substances;
furthermore, it should be understood that these [atoms], when accompanied by sound, consist of seven, eight, or nine substances.

The meaning is that because they have already been stated in their proper form, they are not stated again; because they are as if already said (*ukta-kalpatvāt*), they are not formulated as sūtras once more.
Furthermore, what is the substance here? Is it indeed substance? This is the detailed explanation.
In its primary sense, when a substance has its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*),
is that substance to be understood as such, or rather is it the sense-field (*āyatana*) that is intended as the substance?
It can also be said that an *āyatana* is a substance (*dravya*), because the characteristics of both the general and the particular exist therein. What follows from this?
What is the fault in this? This is the meaning [of the question], provided that "substance" is understood here as referring strictly to a substantial entity (*dravya*).

If the substance of atoms of earth and so forth is taken as having the characteristic of being limited by form (*rūpa*), then it is said that this [definition] stating "consisting of eight substances" and so on is far too narrow.
Since shape, heaviness, lightness, smoothness, roughness, cold, hunger, and thirst may exist as distinct substances in certain instances,
this being the case, that which consists of eight substances might consist of nine, up to fourteen; thus, the rule of "eight substances" is violated.
In this way, it should be applied to those [atoms] consisting of nine substances and so forth;
likewise, even in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), the distinctions in the fixed number of six, seven, or eight substances must be stated,
for it should be stated that [an atom there] consists of four substances.
Because even the primary elements, such as earth and so forth, are the sense-field of the tangible, according to the statement that "the tangible is twofold."
Therefore, it should be stated that in the desire realm, sound consists of four substances—
namely, visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible—
whereas sound together with itself consists of five substances.
That which serves as the basis refers to the four [elements] beginning with earth;
that which serves as the supported refers to [the derived matter].
Visible form, odor, taste, and a portion of the tangible—
since shape is thus included within visible form,
and weight and so forth are included within the tangible.
This is said to be neither too little nor too much,
because it extracts the tangible bases (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) that serve as the foundation [of the body] and explains them in four ways.
"Even so, they are more numerous," and so forth;

that which is the fourfold primary element (*bhūtacatuṣka*) as the support for one derived form (*upādāyarūpa*), such as blue or yellow, is not the same [fourfold primary element] that serves as the support for another derived form, such as odor or taste.
Rather,
the Vaibhāṣika tenet is that its basis is a distinct set of the four great elements;
furthermore, in that case, it is a substantial entity (dravya) by way of its genus (jāti).
Here, the "arising of the four great elements" is intended;
for whatever is the arising of one set of four great elements,
other sets of four great elements do not transcend that.
Thus, in order to speak by way of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*),
"substance" here is taken in one sense as that which serves as the basis (*āśrayabhūta*),
and in another sense as the substance of the sense-field (*āyatanadravya*) which serves as the supported (*āśrayibhūta*).
And since that which constitutes an influx (āśrava) is grasped by way of its genus,
the application of words occurs according to one's intention.
But the meaning must be examined;
for words proceed according to one's own will or desire, following either a concise or an elaborate formulation,
yet it is their meaning that must be scrutinized.
Do these [elements and derived matter] necessarily arise together in this way, or not?
However, the Yogācāra-Cittamātrins describe a rule regarding the coexistence of the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika) within the state of an aggregate.
How so? It is said:
there is a composite consisting of a single primary element, such as, for example, a dry lump of clay.
There is that very same [lump of clay] which consists of two elements when it is moist;
there is that which consists of three elements when it is hot;
and there is that which consists of all [four] elements when that very same lump of clay is both moist and hot in the state of moving.
Regarding derived matter as well, it should be understood that whatever derived matter is perceived within a particular aggregate exists therein;
there is even an aggregate consisting of a single type of derived matter.
For example, light possesses derived matter consisting of two [elements],
such as wind accompanied by sound and odor.
It consists of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
just as smoke does, because it is manifested by specific qualities of visible form, odor, and tangibility.
Furthermore, the specific quality of the tangible (spraṣṭavyaviśeṣa) here should be understood as lightness,
consisting of the four derived forms of matter (upādāyarūpa),
such as, for example, a ball of molasses.
It consists of the five derived forms;
for example, that very same [base] with sound,
and so forth— this also should be stated.
Regarding the remaining [factors], it must be stated: for mind and mental factors, as well as the dissociated factors, mind and mental factors necessarily arise together;
thus, mind does not arise without mental factors.
Nor is it determined that mental factors do not exist without the mind;
however, it is not the case that every mind necessarily arises simultaneously with all mental factors, nor that all mental factors necessarily arise simultaneously with every mind.
"Everything by means of the characteristics of the conditioned" means that which is endowed with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
All that necessarily arises together with those conditioned characteristics, such as birth and so forth.
What, then, is that? He says:
whatever arises—whether form, mind, mental factors, or factors dissociated from mind.
For since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has already been excluded [from the context] previously, and because of the statement that "the unconditioned does not arise at all" therein,
the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*).
There is a distinction that some [phenomena] arise together with acquisition (*prāpti*)—namely those reckoned as sentient beings—and some do not—namely those not reckoned as sentient beings.

Although acquisition exists for both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), these two do not arise [as acquisitions]; therefore, they are not included [in this category].
For this undertaking is a rule of simultaneous arising;
what is the reason that there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) for that which is reckoned as non-sentient?
Because it is common to all sentient beings.
And it should be understood that one who possesses attainment arises simultaneously with that very attainment, not at a prior or subsequent time;
this is the scope of the [textual] passage.
The meaning is "the domain of arising.
They are called "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmikā*) because their greatness consists in their presence in all states of consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "these, it is said" (*ime kila*),
the word *kila* indicates the opinion of another;
for [according to] his own view, however, the mental factors such as desire (*chanda*) and so forth do not exist in every state of consciousness.
For it has been written by this very same teacher in the *Pañcaskandhaka*:
"What is desire (*chanda*)? It is the longing for an intended object."
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)? It is the determination of a determined object exactly as it is, and so forth;
it is volition (*cetanā*), that is, mental formation (*abhisaṃskāra*).
The "vibration of the mind" (*citta-praspanda*) means a vibration as it were;
"the grasping of the cause that is the object" (*viṣaya-nimitta-grāha*) means the grasping of the specific form of the object.
Contact (*sparśa*) is the "touch" (*spṛṣṭi*) born from the coming together of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness;
it is the touch produced from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness,
which is called "contact" because it is like a touch.
That through the conjunction of which the sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses seem to touch one another is contact (*sparśa*).
It is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); it is called "investigation" (*pravicaya*) because it investigates.
Alternatively, *pravicaya* (discernment) is that by which phenomena (*dharmas*) are discerned;
the meaning is that by means of it, phenomena—which are as if mixed together—are discerned or selected, like flowers, such that one recognizes:
"These are with outflows (*sāsrava*); these are without outflows (*anāsrava*)."
The discernment of phenomena—such as "these are material" and "these are immaterial"—is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

Since it is well-known [in the world], it should be called "wisdom" (*prajñā*); however, for the sake of conforming to the metrical composition of the verse, it is stated in the *kārikā* as "intellect" (*mati*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the object; through its connection with this, the mind does not forget the object and,
as it were, speaks of it.

That mindfulness is attention (*manaskāra*), which is the mental application (*ābhoga*) toward an object; the meaning is the turning of the mind toward an object and its focused determination. "Attention" (*manaskāra*) is the action of the mind (*manasaḥ kāraḥ*). Alternatively, it is called attention because it causes the mind to act, that is, to turn toward [the object].
Resolute confidence (*adhimukti*) is the determination of that object by way of its qualities.
Others say it is "inclination";
the Yogācāras maintain it is "retention according to one's resolve";
and [others] say it is "concentration," which is one-pointedness of mind.
"Supreme object" (agram ālambanam) and "one-pointedness" (ekāgra) have the same meaning;
that by which the mind proceeds continuously toward a single object is *samādhi*.
If concentration exists in every state of mind, for what purpose is effort made toward those in meditative absorption?
It is for the sake of accomplishing a powerful concentration.
How is it understood that ten mental factors (*caitta*) with distinct characteristics exist within a single moment of mind? To this, he says:

"For the distinction between mind and mental factors is subtle," and so forth. This very distinction between mind and mental factors is difficult to discern even in their continuous streams (*prabandha*), let alone in moments (*kṣaṇa*), which are characterized by the limits of time.

Even among material medicinal herbs, such as *harītakī* and others—which possess many flavors and the six tastes (*ṣaḍ-rasa*) and are perceptible by the sense faculties, specifically the faculty of taste—these [flavors] are difficult to ascertain and difficult to distinguish;
how much more so for those phenomena (*dharma*) which are immaterial, graspable only by the intellect (*buddhi*), and graspable only by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
Therefore, the intention is that since they have been taught by a reliable authority (*āpta*), they should be accepted exactly as they are.
Faith is the clarity of the mind;
the mind, which has been turbid due to the afflictions and secondary afflictions, becomes clear through its connection with faith,
just as water becomes clear through its connection with the water-clearing gem.
"Others say that faith is conviction regarding the truths, the jewels, karma, and its results"—this is the definition of faith by way of its characteristic.
It is conviction and firm acceptance that these four truths, three jewels, and the wholesome and unwholesome karmas along with their desirable and undesirable results truly exist. This is faith.
Heedfulness is the cultivation of wholesome dharmas;
thus, "cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to the nature of the acquisition and practice of wholesome states,
which are known as the two types of cultivation of the beautiful conditioned (śubha-saṃskṛta-bhāvanā).
Based on this statement, how can that [non-negligence] be the mental factor called *apramāda* (non-negligence)?
That in whose presence the cultivation of acquisition and practice occurs—
that is non-negligence, characterized by earnest application (*tātparya*).
Therefore he says:
"that attentiveness toward them.
This being so, this is a metaphorical designation of cultivation applied to the cause of cultivation.
"Guarding the mind" refers to that which guards the mind against factors conducive to affliction;
this is heedfulness.
"Mental pliancy" (cittakarmaṇyatā) means that through which the mind becomes pliant; it is mental pliancy, the sense being lightness of mind.

But is it not the case that bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) is also mentioned in the Sūtra? What then is the distinction such that there are two factors of enlightenment called pliancy— namely, bodily pliancy and mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*)?
In that regard, whatever bodily pliancy there is, that too is the factor of enlightenment that is pliancy; it conduces to higher knowledge, to perfect awakening, and to nirvāṇa.
And whatever mental pliancy there is [is likewise].
Since that factor of enlightenment, pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), likewise conduces to higher knowledge (*abhijñā*), awakening (*sambodhi*), and nirvāṇa,
why is it alone described as "the workability of the mind" (*cittakarmaṇyatā*)?

But as for the statement "that is bodily feeling," just as mental feeling is also called "bodily" because it has as its basis the sense-faculties which consist of an accumulation of atoms, so too should this pliancy (praśrabdhi) be understood. [The opponent] asks: how will that be applicable among the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), given that the five groups of consciousness (vijñānakāya) are not concentrated? Thus he asks.
In that case, then, the detailed explanation is as follows:

in that Sūtra, bodily confidence (*kāyavaiśāradya*) is indeed bodily pliancy (*kāyakarmaṇyatā*), characterized by a specific state of being [the body] permeated by joy (*prīti*), because of the statement: "The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes pliant."
The intention is that it is not logical for it to be a limb of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) because it is a separate category and because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
"Joy and the factors conducive to joy are the limb of enlightenment consisting of joy," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
It is said that the non-Buddhist teachers spoke thus to the disciples of the Blessed One:
"Sirs, the ascetic Gautama says this:
'O monks, having abandoned the five hindrances which are defilements of the mind and causes of weakness in wisdom, you should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.'"
We too say this:
"In that regard, what is the distinction between us and the ascetic Gautama concerning the teaching of the Dharma?
To them, the Blessed One taught this.
When there are five, they become ten;
when there are ten, they are established as five.
Resistance and the cause of resistance, along with the nine bases of malice, are called the hindrance of ill-will by the Blessed One.
Because they are conducive to that, there are seven in that way, yet they become fourteen;
and while there are fourteen, they are established as seven.
Because it conforms to that [object] through this distinction— that is, as "joy" and "the cause of joy"—
neither resolve (*saṅkalpa*) nor exertion (*vyāyāma*) have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Since those two have, respectively, the nature of applied thought (*vitarka*) and vigor (*vīrya*),
they do not have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*);

and when the path is established as three aggregates— namely, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi*), and the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā*)— [these two are assigned accordingly].
In that regard, regarding the exposition of the aggregate of wisdom, it was said:
"What is the aggregate of wisdom? It is right view, right resolve, and right effort."

Equanimity is the evenness of mind; that through the application of which the mind proceeds evenly and without effort is called equanimity, specifically the formative force of equanimity (*saṃskāra-upekṣā*).
For equanimity is indeed threefold: equanimity as feeling (*vedanopekṣā*), equanimity as a formative factor (*saṃskāropekṣā*), and equanimity as an immeasurable state (*apramāṇopekṣā*).
But was it not said that the distinction between these is difficult to discern?
For the distinction between mind and mental factors is subtle;
as stated in such passages as "this is difficult to discern even within [mental] continuums," it is known with difficulty and is thus hard to know (*durjñāna*).
For indeed, even that which is difficult to know is known if it is not contradictory with another factor, such as contact (*sparśa*), within a single moment of consciousness;
but this, truly, is extremely difficult to know— that there is no contradiction even where there is contradiction.
The ellipsis of the sentence is that the non-contradiction of effort (*ābhoga*) and effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) within a single moment of consciousness (*cittakṣaṇa*) is established;
for it is not observed that two contradictory states, such as pleasure and pain, exist within a single moment of consciousness.
Therefore, elsewhere there is effort.
There is no contradiction in [the mind] being directed toward one object while not being directed toward another;
other instances of this kind will also arise here,
such as the pair of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), which are of a contradictory nature.
For their defining characteristics are that vitarka is coarseness of mind and vicāra is subtlety of mind; thus, vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety [of mental states]. (AK 2.33ab)
Because of this statement,
the principle regarding the contradiction between those two within a single moment of mind will be explained later.
The intention is that these two function alternately, as expressed by the phrase "so ?asyāpi"; furthermore, shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) will be explained later.
"Shamelessness (ahrī) is a lack of respect for what is blameworthy, and a lack of seeing fear even in that [blameworthy act]";
since this is understood by reversing the [definitions of] the opposites,
it consists of the nature of wisdom (prajñā).
But that non-delusion has wisdom as its intrinsic nature,
and since wisdom is a universal mental factor (mahābhūmika),
it follows from the statement "it is attention, it is mindfulness" [that it is not distinct from them].
This is not called a "great wholesome ground" (kuśalamahābhūmika) alone;
rather,
it is also [a factor] belonging to the grounds of the unwholesome (akuśala) and so forth.
Non-harming (*aviheṭhanā*) is that mental factor which, through its association, another is not harmed; it is non-violence (*avihiṃsā*), the antidote to violence (*vihiṃsā*).
"Exertion of the mind" refers to that exertion of the mind toward wholesome activity; that is vigor (*vīrya*).
However, that mental exertion toward unwholesome actions and the like is not vigor;
it is indeed laziness.
It is recited in the teaching that [it] has the nature of sinking;
for it was thus said by the Blessed One:

Whatever vigor belongs to those outside [this teaching] is actually just indolence; thus, what is called "delusion" is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a distinct factor that is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is what is meant by "ignorance."

Later, it is explained that "the phenomenon which is the opposite of cultivation" is stated so that there might not be an understanding of cultivation as being merely its non-existence. Thus, he says "the opposite of cultivation."
In the same way, this should also be explained regarding laziness and so forth;
"heaviness of body" and "heaviness of mind" refer to the state that is the opposite of pliancy.
Just as bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*)—
wherein feeling is explained as "bodily" because it relies upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*)—
so too is bodily torpor (*kāyikaṃ styānam*).

Lethargy associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness is called "bodily"; excitement is the lack of tranquility of the mind. It is a mental factor whose function is to provide a basis for excitement such as dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as erotic dress and ornaments.

And since *styāna* (sloth) is not recited here [in the list], the "Beloved of the Gods" (*devānāṃ priyaḥ*)—who knows the *Abhidharma*—knows only the formal acquisition (*prāpti*) and not the intended meaning;

thus, by the mere authority of the textual recitation, he concludes that there are ten great ground-elements of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*). In this way, the "Beloved of the Gods" knows only this formal acquisition (*prāpti*), but does not know the intention or desire of the Teachers (*ācāryas*).
Who is this so-called "beloved of the gods"?
Some explain that the "beloved of the gods" is one who is upright by nature;
for indeed, one who is not deceitful becomes beloved of the gods.
Others say that "the fool is the beloved of the gods," meaning that he who is favored by the lords does not learn through being struck,
and thus becomes a fool.

"Just as non-delusion" means that just as non-delusion is established as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*) because it has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its intrinsic nature and is a root of virtue, yet it is not restricted to being only a virtuous universal factor (*kuśalamahābhūmika*); for that reason,
it is not included among the virtuous universal factors.

Likewise, since the five beginning with forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they are not restricted to being exclusively universal afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*);
therefore, these are not recited among the universal afflictions.
To the question "How so?", he says:
For it is precisely afflicted mindfulness that is "loss of mindfulness," and precisely afflicted concentration that is "distraction," and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that afflicted wisdom itself is "lack of clear comprehension."
It shows that attention itself when afflicted is improper attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*), and resolve itself when afflicted is false resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*);
for this very reason it is said, and so forth.
Since mindfulness and so forth, as well as forgetfulness and so forth, are established in this very way and are not distinct from these [factors],
it is therefore said that there are four alternatives (catuṣkoṭika).

He asks rhetorically: "Are those which are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) also those which are universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*)? There would be four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*): those that are universal mental factors but not universal afflictive factors; and those that are universal afflictive factors [but not universal mental factors].
There may be factors that are neither universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) nor universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*);
these are the third category, beginning with mindfulness (*smṛti*),
namely the five [defilements] such as forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*) as previously described.
For these are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), and these are the universal defiled mental factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*).

"Excluding these four modes" refers to those factors mentioned as being excluded, namely the universal wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) and so forth, as well as other [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) and the like.
For them, the fourfold alternative is otherwise; distraction (vikṣepa) should be inserted into the second alternative,
but not into the third.
Therefore, it should be stated as follows:
the first category is as before;
the second consists of lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*).
The third [category] consists of the four beginning with mindfulness—

namely, forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), and wrong resolve (*mithyādhimokṣa*)— which is the meaning; the fourth is as before.
As for what was said— that torpor (*styāna*) is not recited here— he replies to them:
"Torpor, moreover, is accepted," and so forth in detail.
Regarding its non-recitation, whose fault is it? Is it my fault for not reciting this [text], or is it the fault of the Abhidharmika?
The intention is that "this is the fault of the author of the Abhidharma, not mine," because *styāna* (sloth) is considered to be associated with all afflictions;
thus they say.
Regarding that, the Abhidharmikas state the reason for the non-inclusion of *styāna* (sloth) in that treatise:
"It is said to be more quickly [dispelled]. The word "it is said" (*kila*) is used here to express uncertainty (*asambhāvanā*).
For how indeed could an afflicted state be conducive to pure concentration?
Since lethargy and excitement are obstacles to concentration, how can that which is itself an obstacle be conducive to what it opposes?
For these two never abandon their state of coexistence;

that is to say, lethargy and restlessness never relinquish their nature of being concomitant factors. Nevertheless, whichever of the two is predominant in a given case [is designated as the defilement].
Furthermore, if a person has either sloth (*styāna*) or restlessness (*auddhatya*) in excess,
that person should be understood as having that as their temperament— either one of sloth-temperament or restlessness-temperament—
since in some mental complexes (*kalāpa*), a particular factor becomes predominant.
"Not elsewhere" means [they do not exist] among the wholesome factors and so forth; however,
regarding the unwholesome, "lack of shame" (*āhrīkya*) and "lack of dread" (*anapatrāpya*)— the word "but" (*tu*) here functions as either a qualifier or a restriction.
"Only unwholesome" means that the minor defilement-ground factors are "minor," that is,
small.
What is this "mere ignorance"?
It means ignorance alone, nothing else;
therefore, it is said "by that mere ignorance."
It is not by another affliction such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth that is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
nor by one that is to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).
"Only by that which belongs to the mental level (*mano-bhūmika*)," meaning not by that which belongs to the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāyika*),
because these secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger and the like belong exclusively to the mental level.
Therefore, because they are associated with the mind (*manas*), they are called "minor defilement-ground" (*parīttakleśabhūmika*) factors;
for within the complex of passion (*rāga*) and the other [defilements], ignorance (*avidyā*) must necessarily be present, so that passion and the rest are not minor.
Thus, those which are present in every mental state (*caitasika*)...
Those which belong to the great ground are the universal mental factors; those which belong only to the wholesome are the great wholesome ground factors.
Those [factors] which exist in the afflicted, the obscured-unwholesome, and the unwholesome are the great ground factors of affliction (kleśamahābhūmika);
those, however, which exist only in the unwholesome...

Those which are associated with the limited defilements in the mind are the limited defilement-ground factors. Those which are associated with the great unwholesome [factors] in the mind are the great unwholesome ground factors.
However, the detailed explanation of these will be given among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); thus,
in the exposition of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
it is said that there are others as well that are indeterminate (*aniyata*).
Since factors such as *middha* (torpor) occur sometimes in a wholesome mind, sometimes in an unwholesome mind, and sometimes in an indeterminate mind, the word "etc.

(*ādi*) includes secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as discontent (*arati*), yawning (*vijṛmbhikā*), drowsiness (*tandrī*), and irregularity of appetite (*bhakte ’samatā*), as well as the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) such as attachment (*rāga*) and others, which are understood to be distinct from those [three types of minds].
For these factors, such as attachment and the rest, are not restricted to any one of the five categories;
they are not universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) because they are absent from every state of mind,
nor are they universal wholesome factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) because they are incompatible with wholesomeness.
The great ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*) factors do not exist in every afflicted state, because they are absent there;
for instance, attachment does not exist in a mind accompanied by hostility, nor does hostility exist in a mind accompanied by attachment.
The same should be said for the other afflictions as well.
Regarding this, the teacher Vasumitra states a summary verse:
"Doubt, regret, torpor, hostility,
attachment, pride, and doubt— these eight are known as the indeterminate [mental factors]."
Thus,
we do not understand this statement regarding the eight non-fixed [factors];
why are the views also not accepted as non-fixed?

For false view does not arise in a mind that is accompanied by resistance (*sapratigha*) or accompanied by doubt (*savicikitsa*), nor in the unshared (*āveṇika*) unwholesome [mind]. In a mind associated with views, there are twenty [mental factors];
with the four afflictions and the others beginning with anger (*krodha*), there are twenty-one, along with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Because of this statement,
we see that whatever was said here refers to that;
first of all, the realm of desire (kāmāvacara) is fivefold.
The wholesome is one;
the unwholesome is of two kinds:
that which is unique and associated with ignorance alone, and that which is associated with other afflictions such as attachment.
The indeterminate is also of two kinds:
obscured-indeterminate, which is associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes;
and unobscured-indeterminate, such as that born of maturation and so forth.
"Kaukṛtya" means the state of having done what is ill-done; since it is the property (*dharma*) of that which has been ill-done,
and that [ill-done act] is a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is not [directly] connected [to the mind].
Therefore he says:
"But here, moreover, what is the intrinsic nature of the dharma that has remorse as its object? He replies:
Regarding the phrase "remorse of mind":
if the mental factor that has remorse as its object is called "remorse," then other associated mental states and mental factors would also incur the designation of "remorse."
They do not obtain [those states] because of their lack of predominance;
for in the state of remorse (*vipratisāra*), the mental factor characterized by regret (*kaukṛtya*) has its activity manifested in the form of regret.
Other mental states and mental factors conform to its aspect;
for they explain that within a particular collection of mental states, a certain dharma alone holds predominance—
thus, the door of liberation that has emptiness as its object is called "emptiness."

The gate of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), which is a specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*) having as its object the aggregates (*skandhas*) devoid of an internal active person (*puruṣa*), is called "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
Non-attachment (*alobha*) having as its object the impurities such as the livid-blue and the bloated is called "the foul" (*aśubhā*);
the feminine gender is used because it is connected with cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Just as "the cultivation of the foul" is a designation for the mental factor that takes the foul as its object, so too here, "remorse" is a designation for the mental factor that takes remorse as its object;
this is an extension of the name from the locus to the occupant.
When it is said, "the entire village has arrived," the term "village" refers to a collection of houses together with their grounds;
when the inhabitants have arrived, people say, "the entire village has arrived."
In this way, every location has arrived;
and since remorse (*kaukṛtya*) serves as the basis for regret (*vipratisāra*), it is so called because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) for regret.
Therefore, such a designation is logical;
or rather, it is a metaphorical application of the cause to the fruit,
meaning that regret is the cause.
The fruit is remorse;
the cause is metaphorically designated by that fruit.
The meaning is that the fruit is expressed by a word denoting the cause.
Just as these six bases of contact are called "ancient karma," meaning that the six bases of contact, such as the eye and so forth, are the fruits of ancient karma performed in a previous birth,
so too is karma metaphorically attributed to them.
In the same way,
how can that which has an unperformed object be regret?
Thinking that what is unmade is not made, he objects:
"Even in the case of the unmade, there occurs the designation 'made'."
How is it that the word "done" is used even when an action has not been performed? To this he says:
"That which was done by me was not well done; therefore, it is as if it were not done."
"Thinking 'it was done' regarding that which should have been done" means that one feels remorse for not having performed wholesome deeds;
that is, having failed to perform wholesome acts such as giving and so forth, one later becomes tormented by regret.
Having performed that which is wholesome and unwholesome, why does one feel remorse? This is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, that which one regrets after having committed unwholesome acts such as taking life is wholesome;
by contrast, the opposite is unwholesome.
That which consists in regretting after having failed to do what is unwholesome and having done what is wholesome— namely,
that one becomes remorseful after not having committed a sin, thinking, "It was not well done by me that I did not perform it."
That remorse which is unwholesome,
as well as that which is wholesome— namely, when after having performed acts such as giving one later feels regret, thinking, "It was not well done by me that I performed acts such as giving"—
that too is unwholesome.
Thus, both of these have both as their basis;
that is to say, this remorse (kaukṛtya) is both wholesome and unwholesome, and it has both as its basis according to the manner previously described,
being "unshared" (āveṇika).
The meaning is that [it] is distinct from passion and so forth;
and the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "and [in the mind] associated with views" is for the purpose of drawing in the term "unwholesome."
A certain specific type of wisdom among the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) is "view" (dṛṣṭi); that wisdom which is investigative is view.
And since it is the unwholesome [view] that is intended here, he says:
"and false view," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "twenty-one by means of remorse" (*kaukṛtyenaikaviṃśatiḥ*), one should understand that the particle *ca* ("and") has been elided; thus, it should be read as "by means of remorse and [the others].
In expressions such as "by the four afflictions" (*kleśaiś caturbhiḥ*), it should be understood that the syntactical completion applies to each individual term.
For the Abhidharmikas maintain that passion and the other [afflictions] do not associate with one another; thus, there are twenty:

the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the six universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the two universal unwholesome factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
And that affliction— consisting of attachment, aversion, pride, and doubt— is indeed twenty-one; thus,
it should be understood that this is an emphatic restriction (*kriyāvadhāraṇa*) regarding the number being exactly twenty-one,
even when including anger and the others.
When the mind is associated with anger, enmity, deceit, envy, malice, concealment, avarice, guile, intoxication, and harmfulness, there are likewise exactly twenty-one mental factors.
Those [mental factors] are called "unshared" as previously stated;
and that [unshared factor] is an affliction (*upakleśa*), either anger (*krodha*) up to harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
When associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), those aforementioned factors and that remorse itself constitute twenty-one.
For remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is also considered an independent secondary affliction (*upakleśa*); in brief, it is an exclusive [affliction], and so forth.
In an unwholesome mind associated solely with ignorance, or in an unwholesome mind associated with [wrong] views, there are twenty [mental factors];
however, in an unwholesome mind associated with other primary or secondary afflictions, there are twenty-one.
As for the obscured-unspecified [mind], it is as follows.
That which is obscured by afflictions and is indeterminate as being either wholesome or unwholesome is called "obscured-indeterminate" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*);
