that which is not so obscured is "unobscured-indeterminate" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), having as its intrinsic nature [states] born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those pertaining to emanations (*nairmāṇika*).
The outsiders (bahirdeśaka) maintain that remorse (kaukṛtya) can also be indeterminate (avyākṛta);
those who reside outside the region of Kaśmīra are the "outsiders."
Regarding the statement "thirteen": in certain cases, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is added as a thirteenth [mental factor] to the unobscured-neutral category,
because the treatise states that *middha* (torpor) is included when one is in a state of nodding off or dreaming, since it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
"How should sleep be described—is it to be called wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
He replied:
"It may be called wholesome, it may be called unwholesome, and it may be called indeterminate."
Where there are twenty-two,
there are twenty-three, and so forth;
where it was stated that there are twenty-two mental factors.
In that context, "that middha" means the twenty-third, which completes the number twenty-three;
for in some cases, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is added as the twenty-third.
In that regard, that *middha* (drowsiness) is the twenty-fourth [factor];
likewise, up until the other [category], where it is considered that there are twelve indeterminate factors, *middha* should be stated as the thirteenth.
However, according to the opinion of the outsiders (*bahirdeśaka*), when *kautṛtya* (remorse) is added, *middha* becomes the fourteenth; this is how it should be applied.

"Therefore, from what has been stated" means that because of the aforementioned necessity of the simultaneous arising of mental factors (*caitta*), regret (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*middha*) do not exist at all.
Since it is neither wholesome nor indeterminate, how could it possibly be unwholesome?
Thus, in every respect, torpor and remorse do not exist;
likewise, deceit, arrogance, and guile are to be excluded.

Deceit (*śāṭhya*) belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), while lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and pride (*mada*) belong to both the realm of desire and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because they deceive Brahmā;

this is stated [in the *Abhidharmakośa*] as: "Lethargy, restlessness, and pride exist in the three realms. Furthermore, [deceit] exists in the two meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) starting from the realm of desire.
These [three] are excluded because they exist therein;
all else is exactly as before.
Thus, in a wholesome mind, there are twenty-two [mental factors], as previously stated.
In the case of the unique [minds] and those associated with views that are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), there are eighteen [mental factors], as in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In minds associated with attachment, pride, doubt, or other primary afflictions (*kleśa*), and in those associated with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), and arrogance (*mada*), there are nineteen;
that specific affliction or secondary affliction becomes the nineteenth therein.

In the unobscured-neutral [states]— namely, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to magical emanation (*nairmāṇika*)— there are twelve as previously stated;
in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there is also applied thought (*vitarka*).
Regarding the phrase "and [the unwholesome states of] regret and torpor," the question is: why does the word "and" (ca) not imply that [these two] do not exist?

The remainder is exactly as before, but with the exception of applied thought (*vitarka*); that is to say, as has been prohibited, they do not exist— meaning that remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and unwholesome applied thoughts (*akuśala-vitarka*) are absent.

Regarding the phrase "and *vicāra*, and *māyā-śāṭhya*," because of the word "also" (*api*), although one would have had to say merely "and *vicāra*," by the addition of the word "also" in saying "and *vicāra* also," there is an increase in meaning;
thus, another sense is obtained: that even *māyā-śāṭhya* does not exist therein.
But pride (*mada*) is not excluded from the state of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), because of the force of the statement: "Excitement and pride exist in the three realms."
The remainder is exactly the same; thus, in the wholesome [mind], there are twenty factors excluding vitarka and vicāra,
while in the unique [unwholesome mind] associated with views, there are sixteen.

In a state associated with afflictions such as attachment, and in one associated with the secondary affliction of intoxication, there are seventeen [mental factors]: the ten universal factors, the six universal afflictive factors,
that primary affliction itself, and those secondary afflictions.
It should be understood that in the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) state, there are only the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).
For it is said in detail: "from pride up to deceit" (*śāṭhya*);
therein, because it is preceded by deceit, guile (*māyā*) is also included.
Regarding the phrase "not beyond [this life] due to connection with an assembly":
for those who possess an assembly,
deceit and guile arise for the sake of maintaining that assembly.
Eight assemblies are enumerated:

the assembly of kṣatriyas, the assembly of brāhmaṇas, the assembly of householders, the assembly of śramaṇas, the assembly of the four great kings, the assembly of the thirty-three gods, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.
Not even one of these exists beyond this; thus, there is an absence of deceit and guile.
But Brahmā has an assembly;
therefore it is said that he,
while seated in his own assembly, was questioned by the monk Aśvajit who had gone to the Brahma-world.

Not knowing where these four great elements cease without remainder, and failing to understand that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) the four great elements cease without remainder, he initiated this digressive discourse,
saying in detail, "I am Brahmā."
Having said "Brahmā," the statement "Mahābrahmā" is for the purpose of demonstrating his superiority over other Brahmās;

"Īśvara" (the Lord), "Īśāna" (the Ruler), "Kartā" (the Doer), "Nirmātā" (the Fashioner), "Sraṣṭā" (the Creator), and "Sṛja" (the Procreator) are synonyms, or rather, they are connected as successive explanations of one another.
Like a father, for what states of being is he the father?
"This has been stated," and so forth; that is to say,

it has been stated that whatever the level (bhūmi), whatever the mind (citta), and however many mental factors (caitta) there are— that level, that mind, and those many mental factors [are mutually concomitant].
Regarding that, some read "vihitam" as "śāstre vihitam," meaning "prescribed in the treatise";
this is precisely the intended meaning here.
Regarding "qualities and the objects of qualities":
this refers to qualities such as loving-kindness and compassion within one's own and others' continuums,
as well as the persons who are the objects of those qualities— those who are perfected in conduct and sphere of activity.
That through whose connection one does not show respect is "disrespect" (*agauravatā*);
he who has no respect is "disrespectful" (*agauravaḥ*).
Its nature is lack of respect (*agauravatā*), which is a specific mental factor (*caitasika-viśeṣa*). They state the synonyms for what this is:
"Absence of dependence" (apratiśatā) means not being subject to fear;
"dependence" (pratīśa) refers to one who is desired by a disciple, that is, one who stands in the position of a teacher.
"One who has no expectation" is *apratīśaḥ*;
the state of being that is *apratīśatā*.
By the mention of the abstract state (*bhāva*), a mental factor (*caitta*) is understood.
Fear (*bhaya*) is a mental factor (*caitta*) belonging to the mind.
One who has the habit of being under the sway of fear is "one subject to fear" (*bhayavaśavartī*);
one who is not subject to fear is "not subject to fear" (*abhayavaśavartī*), and the state of being so is "the condition of not being subject to fear" (*abhayavaśavartitā*).
That very thing is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*);
one who lacks shame (*hrī*) is "shameless" (*ahrīka*), and the state of being such is "lack of shame."
And that quality is the opposite of reverence (gaurava),
not merely its absence;
for even in this case, fear is seen toward what is blameworthy.
Therefore, he said that what is blameworthy is unspeakable;
for "blameworthy" (avadya) is that which is censured by the virtuous.
In that context, "lack of dread of blame" (*anapatrāpya*) means not seeing the undesirable results in what is blameworthy; here,
the word *bhaya* (fear) is used in the sense of the ablative case (*apādāna*), as in "one is afraid of this."
Therefore, by the word "fear," an undesirable result is expressed; "the vision of fearlessness" means the state of one who sees fearlessness—this is the detailed explanation.
If, for the time being, it were formulated thus: "fear is not fear."
One whose nature is to see fearlessness is "one who sees fearlessness" (*abhayadarśin*); the state of being that is "fearlessness-seeing-ness" (*abhayadarśitā*),
which is understood here to be wisdom (*prajñā*).
For through wisdom one sees fearlessness;
yet, if it is further done in this way— that "one whose nature is to see fear" is a "fear-seer"— then one who is not a fear-seer is a "fearlessness-seer."
The state of that is "seeing fearlessness"; thus,
ignorance (avidyā) will be understood as "seeing fearlessness," for through connection with ignorance, one does not see fear.
For indeed, vision is not the seer, and so forth; it is neither wisdom nor ignorance—
what then?
Of those two, wisdom and ignorance, that which is the cause of the secondary afflictions is the perception of fearlessness, and that is lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*).
*Apattrāpya* is that by which one feels shame;
according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, *na apattrāpyam* is *anapatrāpyam*.

Regarding the two verbal roots *hrī* and *trap*, both meaning "shame" (*lajjā*)—how can these two, which have the same meaning, function as denoters of different meanings? Dissatisfied with this, others say:
"In relation to oneself," and so forth.
Even so, how will two simultaneous relations be established?
Observing that even in this position the simultaneous occurrence of two dependencies is impossible, the objector says,
"Even so" (*evam api*).
By the word "even" (*api*), the intention is that this position, too, is flawed.

Considering how shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) can both exist in a single moment of consciousness, one might object: "How can two points of reference be established simultaneously? To this it is replied:
"It is certainly not said that one refers to oneself and another at the same time," and so forth in detail.
He shows the functioning of these two by way of alternative perspectives:
for some person, even when considering their own faults, shame does not arise; whereas for another, it arises when considering others.
"Shame and dread are the opposite," and so forth.
First, according to the initial interpretation: lack of shame (*ahrī*) is a lack of respect toward what is blameworthy; lack of dread (*atrapā*) is the failure to see fear [in such acts].
By this [phrase],
"with respect for the teacher," and so forth, the detailed exposition of the perception of fear is intended;
the meaning is that *apatrāpya* (moral dread) is the perception of fear as its defining characteristic.

According to the second interpretation, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is the absence of embarrassment regarding one's faults with respect to oneself, while lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is the same with respect to others; by this [second view],
shame (*hrī*) is embarrassment regarding one's faults with respect to oneself, and dread (*apatrāpya*) is the same with respect to others.
In this way, the objection and its refutation regarding the two types of dependence should be stated in detail.
Some consider affection (*prema*) and reverence (*gaurava*) to be one and the same;
therefore, he says [the following] in order to demonstrate the distinction between them.
"Love and faith"— love itself is faith; it is not reverence,
nor is faith merely love.
Therefore, he said:
"For affection (prema) is of two kinds: afflicted and unafflicted," and so forth;
thus there is a fourfold alternative (catuḥ-koṭika) regarding whether faith (śraddhā) might not be affection.
In the case of the truths of suffering and its origin, faith alone takes the form of conviction (*abhisampratyaya*); it is not affection (*prema*), because these two are not objects of longing.
There may be affection that is not faith;
thus, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the form of endearment does not take the form of conviction, and therefore it is not faith.
The meaning is that both— faith and love— constitute the nature of the truths of cessation and the path because they consist of conviction and because they are desirable;
"neither" refers to those [mental states] excluding these aspects.
Other mental factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, as well as those dissociated from mind (*viprayukta*) and so forth—

having thus established a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) for affection and faith that have phenomena (*dharma*) as their object— he now establishes a fourfold alternative for those having persons (*pudgala*) as their object, beginning with "among persons," and so forth in detail.

In this context, "co-residents" (sārdhavihārin) are those disciples who dwell together; "resident pupils" (antevāsin) are those who, having gone forth, live in the presence of their teacher, being connected to him through dependence and study.

Regarding those [objects] such as sons and so forth, affection (*prema*) may be either afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*), whereas respect (*gaurava*) is possible in both ways. Respect is not necessarily affection; for respect is defined as "reverence" (*gurutva*), which will be explained by its characteristics later on, and thus it is not affection. However, there are cases where both affection and respect coexist.
The meaning is that it consists of both;
having set aside these two forms, there is neither affection nor reverence for any other person who is unrelated and devoid of qualities.
And that which is preceded by it is "dearness," namely love (*prema*);
thus, dearness is preceded by the estimation of qualities, and that is love.
Therefore, the Teacher [states] that this very faith (*śraddhā*) is not love.
Gravity is modesty;
as it has been stated, that which is called modesty is a state of reverence, a sense of propriety, and being under the influence of fear [of wrongdoing].

That veneration and that very affection are characterized by faith; however, it has been stated that veneration is characterized by a sense of shame (*hrī*). Thus, the distinction between the two is explained.
In the same way, there is also "having respect"; likewise, there is also "moral shame" (*hrī*) with respect to both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*),
as well as those forms of faith and moral shame that have persons as their object.

"Those two do not exist there"—thus, with respect to the person as an object, faith (*śraddhā*) and moral shame (*hrī*) are the ones under discussion. Those who consider them to be unified [with the self] maintain that they do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), but exist only in the desire and form realms (*kāma-rūpadhātu*).
This was stated in AK(Bh) 2.33.
But how can there be a conjunction (*yoga*) of these two in a single moment of mind?
It is not so; for it is not logical that the very same mind should be both gross and subtle due to that conjunction, because of the contradiction [involved], as it has been stated: "it is ejected."

This form *niṣṭhyūtam* is derived from the verb *ṣṭhīvati* preceded by the prefix *nis*; its meaning is "spat out," that is, "not vomited. It does not become excessively thick or excessively constipated.
The meaning is that it is in a middle state: it is neither too dissolved, nor does it become too fluid, nor does it become too subtle, nor is it too gross.
"In that case, they are the causes (*nimitta*)," and so forth;

just as water and heat are the causes for the solidification and liquefaction of ghee, yet they do not themselves possess the nature of those states— that is, the nature of solidification or liquefaction.

Thus, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the signs (*nimitta*) of the mind’s coarseness and subtlety, but they do not themselves have the nature of coarseness and subtlety. Therefore, it should be stated that applied thought is the cause of the mind’s coarseness.
If you were to say that "sustained mental application" (vicāra) is the cause of the subtlety of the mind, and thus there is no fault because this is an accepted tenet,
he states the following further objection:
And what is relative? It is grossness and subtlety, and so forth;
this is due to the distinction of levels and the distinction of types—that is, from the difference in levels and the difference in types.
First, by way of the distinction of stages: in comparison with the first dhyāna, the desire realm is coarse because it involves greater volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*);
in comparison with the desire realm, the first dhyāna is subtle because it involves less volitional effort, and is thus tranquil.
That same [defilement] is coarse when compared to the second dhyāna,
and so on up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), where it is subtle; furthermore,
by way of its various types, within those very types— ranging from weak, medium, and intense— the most intense defilement among them, from the desire realm up to the peak of existence, is coarse.
"Soft" and "subtle" refer to the qualities by way of the reversal of the afflictions;
thus, depending on the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*), there are coarseness and subtlety, and so coarseness and subtlety would exist up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
And this is undesirable because initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*) belong to the levels of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna respectively;
furthermore, it is not logical that there should be a distinction of type based on coarseness (*audārika*) and subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*).
A difference in genus is maintained between applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), such that applied thought is one thing and sustained thought is another;
yet, it is not logical that the distinction in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) should be based respectively on coarseness and subtlety.
For what reason?
Because feeling and perception, though distinct by nature, possess respectively grossness and subtlety.
Furthermore, the distinction between their intrinsic natures is not merely due to being gross or subtle;
rather,
the distinction between their intrinsic natures consists in the characteristic of experiencing and the characteristic of grasping signs.
Therefore, for these two as well, there is no separate characteristic;
however, others say— namely, the Sautrāntikas—
that they are "vocal formations" (vāk-saṃskāra).
The meaning is that they are the originators of speech;
for one speaks words after having applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*), not without having applied thought and sustained investigation,
thinking, "I shall speak in such and such a manner" by means of those very applications of thought and sustained investigations.
In that regard, those which are gross are *vitarkas*, the formative factors of speech (*vāk-saṃskāras*);
their intrinsic nature is illuminated by their function, for it is not possible to demonstrate their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in any other way.
Thus, those subtle investigations (vicāra),
in this conceptualization, take the form of a composite whole, wherein applied thought (vitarka) and investigation (vicāra) occur as alternating states.
Since the complex of mind and mental factors is that which originates speech, how can it be said that these two are conjoined within a single moment of consciousness?
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣika says:

And if, in a single moment of mind, one factor is gross, and so forth— in a single moment of mind, *vitarka* is a factor whose nature is gross, while *vicāra* is another factor whose nature is subtle;
and because they are respectively the causes of the mind’s grossness and subtlety, they are called the "grossness" and "subtlety" of the mind.

Or rather, [it refers to] the mind: grossness of the mind, the state of being gross in the mind, the quality of being gross in the mind; in the same way, subtlety of the mind should also be explained—what contradiction is there here?

There would be no contradiction if there were a difference in genus between applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
For feeling is gross and perception is subtle;
however, since there is indeed a difference in genus between those two, there is no contradiction even in their coexistence as gross and subtle within a single moment of consciousness.

However, when a single class [of phenomena]—whose characteristics are not fixed—is apprehended as a unity, the states of mildness and intensity, characterized by coarseness and subtlety, cannot exist simultaneously; thus, by implication, it is said that they occur non-simultaneously.
For instance, feeling (*vedanā*) or any other phenomenon undergoes mildness and intensity only successively (*paryāyeṇa*);
it does not become manifest in such a way [that both would occur at once].
What is the distinction between the castes, and from what does it arise?
Because each class [of beings] possesses both weak and intense [faculties],
feeling is indeed either gross or subtle, depending on the distinction of relative comparison.
How so?
Feeling is gross in comparison to perception,
and subtle in comparison to form.
Likewise, perception is gross in relation to mental formations,
while it is subtle in relation to feeling;
or it is like initial and sustained thought.

For even according to your own view, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) belonging to the desire realm are coarse, those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are subtle,
and in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), sustained thought is even more subtle; thus,
each of these classes possesses degrees of mildness and intensity.
"It does not become manifest" means that the distinction between types [of faculties] based on their being weak or superior does not become manifest;
regarding this, Master Saṅghabhadra says:
Furthermore, grossness and subtlety occur within a single moment of mind without contradiction, because their periods of predominance differ;
for when *vitarka* (applied thought) is active within the complex of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittakalāpa*), [subtlety is present].
At that time, when there is investigation (vicāra), the mind becomes gross;
at that time, it is subtle.
Just as there is a designation based on the predominance of either passion or delusion, so too,

even when passion and delusion occur simultaneously, one is designated as "one whose conduct is dominated by passion" or "one whose conduct is dominated by delusion," because of the association with the more manifest activity of one or the other.
"In this case as well, it should be viewed in the same way.
To this we reply:
in a certain collection [of factors], there occurs the state of a particular dharma having its activity manifest.
However, since the definition of these two has not been distinguished,
this is of no consequence; for have not vitarka and vicāra been stated to have the characteristics of grossness and subtlety of the mind?

It has been truly stated that the coarseness and subtlety of each of the classes [of mental factors] ought to constitute the characteristics of coarseness and subtlety, as previously explained; however, this does not satisfy us,
for another teacher— the Master [Vasubandhu]— holds the view that vitarka and vicāra do not occur together in a single moment of mind.
In this view, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not occur;
however, what is the distinction between these two that function as synonyms?
Regarding this, the former teachers say:

What is *vitarka*? It is a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that investigates, based either on volition (*cetanā*) or on wisdom (*prajñā*). It is, respectively, the state of non-investigation and investigation; and it is the grossness of the mind.
What is *vicāra*?

Is it a mental discourse (*manojalpa*) that is either based on volition (*cetanā*) or wisdom (*prajñā*), occurring respectively in the states of non-investigation and investigation? And is that [discourse] the subtlety of the mind?

According to this position, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are held to be of a single nature and to exist as a composite whole; they function as synonyms, yet are distinguished merely by their modes of searching and investigating.
Regarding this, some provide the following illustration:
For example, when many jars are standing there, the deliberation made by striking them with the fist—thinking, "Which one here is solid? Which one is cracked?"—is *vitarka*.
The final apprehension that "this many are cracked or solid" is *vicāra*.
If that [first dhyāna] is [only] investigation (*vicāra*), how then is it said in detail that "the first dhyāna has five factors"?

For in the Sūtra it is stated that it has five factors: "detached from sensual desires, detached from evil and unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion."
How then is it said that those five factors exist according to the stages (*bhūmi*) and not according to the moments (*kṣaṇa*)?
It is because the stage of the first dhyāna is sometimes interspersed with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sometimes with sustained thought (*vicāra*).

Thus, there is no fault in stating that the five factors are taught with reference to the continuum (*saṃtāna*) and not with reference to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Pride (*māna*) is the mental factor consisting of an inflation of the mind based on some imagined excellence attributed to oneself by another—whether real or unreal—such as thinking, "I am brave," "I am wealthy," "I am virtuous," or "I am endowed with intelligence. This pride is the mental state of self-elevation resulting from such an imagined superiority over others.

Regarding the phrase "the exhaustion of the mind," the word "but" (*tu*) should be understood as serving a qualifying purpose and as being displaced in its position; for this very reason, he says in detail: "But intoxication [belongs] to one who is attached precisely to one's own qualities."

"Exhaustion of the mind" refers to that by which the mind, being attached to its own qualities such as physical beauty and valor, is exhausted— that is, it is completely restrained; this is intoxication (*mada*), which is the outflow of passion (*rāga*).

Ācārya Saṅghabhadra maintains that *mada* (intoxication) is the withdrawal from the performance of wholesome dharmas due to the depletion [of merit] of one who is attached solely to their own duties and possesses a haughty mind;
it is a specific kind of intense exhilaration,
intended as afflicted mental joy (*kliṣṭa-saumanasya*).
The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this,
because mental joy (*saumanasya*) exists up to the second dhyāna, and intoxication (*mada*) belongs to all three realms.
Because it is stated that "sloth, restlessness, and pride [occur] in all three realms," it is thus explained how mental factors (caitta) arise together with the mind (citta) in various ways.

Mind (*citta*) has already been explained in various ways, such as "consciousness is the representation of each object" and so forth, through its own characteristics and its divisions into aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), wholesome states, and so on.

Mental factors (*caitta*) likewise [have been explained] by way of their own characteristics and their mutual distinctions, as well as by way of the determination of their number within the mind and the divisions of the levels (*bhūmi*) such as the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
Thus, they are one in meaning.
"That which is mind (citta), that itself is intellect (manas), that itself is consciousness (vijñāna)"— this is its single meaning; thus it is "single-meaning" (ekārtha),
though different etymological explanations are stated.
It is called "citta" because it accumulates (*cinoti*);
the meaning is that it accumulates either the wholesome or the unwholesome.
This is established by means of etymological derivation (*nairukta*).
It is called *manas* because it "thinks" (*manute*); this form *manas* is derived from the root *man*, meaning "to know," with an *auṇādika* suffix.
It is *vijñāna* because it "cognizes" (*vijānāti*) the object; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent.
"Mind by means of pure and impure elements" means that,
according to the Sautrāntika or Yogācāra perspective through the application of cultivation (*bhāvanā*),

the mind (*citta*) consists of the *manas* as the basis (*āśraya-bhūta*) and the *vijñāna* as that which is supported (*āśrita-bhūta*); thus, the *manas* is defined in relation to its state as a basis.
For that consciousness which has just ceased immediately prior to the six [consciousnesses] is the mind (*manas*),
because of the inclusion of this meaning; thus,
consciousness is dependent upon its support.
Because of the statement that "the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality," mind and mental factors possess a basis, an object, and an aspect, and they are associated.
The word "ca" (and) serves to draw in [the preceding term];
for those very same things designated by the expression "mind and mental factors" are also designated by this expression "possessing a basis."
Thus, they possess objects, possess aspects, and are associated;
therein, they possess bases because they depend on the sense faculties (*indriya*),
meaning that they depend on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
They possess an object (*sālambana*) because they grasp an objective field;
for mind and mental factors do not arise without an object,
and they possess an aspect (*sākāra*) because they take on the mode of that very object as their aspect.
Because they possess an object by grasping that very object in its various aspects,
how does consciousness cognize— that is, perceive— an object such as blue or yellow? This is the meaning.
That very same object, as such an objective basis, is experienced by feeling,
delimited by perception,
and conditioned by volition, and so forth.

Alternatively, with respect to that very object, consciousness grasps it in its general form as the nature of being perceived; feeling grasps it in its specific form as the nature of being experienced; perception grasps it in its specific form as the nature of being discerned, and so forth.
They are "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they are applied equally;
they are "equal" (*sama*) and "not dissociated" (*aviprayukta*) from one another,
being associated by way of equality of basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), time (*kāla*), and substance (*dravya*).
By whatever basis the mind arises,
by that very same basis feeling, perception, volition, and so forth arise;
likewise, by whatever object the mind [arises].
Feeling and the other [mental factors] are exactly as the mind is in its particular mode; feeling and the others are precisely in that same mode.
For if the feeling and other factors associated with it arise having precisely the form of blue, and if at the very time when the mind arises, the feeling and other factors do so as well—
just as a single substance of mind arises and not two or three— then [the concomitance is established].
In the same way, only one substance of feeling (*vedanā-dravya*) arises, not two or three;
likewise for the substance of perception (*saṃjñā-dravya*), the substance of volition (*cetanā-dravya*), and so forth.
Therefore, he explains that this very [point] is the final difficulty.
Just as the mind is singular, so too each mental factor (caitta) is singular;

thus, wishing to speak of the dissociated factors (viprayukta), the Teacher provides an introduction. His intention is this: "The mind and mental factors have been explained with their detailed classifications; now, having reached their proper turn, the dissociated factors are being discussed.
This refers to the phrase "with their detailed classifications."
"Extensive and detailed" (*vistaraprabheda*) means both the extensive (*vistara*) and the detailed (*prabheda*);

"together with the extensive and detailed" means accompanied by both the extensive and the detailed. Alternatively, "extensive detail" (*vistaraprabheda*) refers to a detailed [explanation] by way of extensiveness.
Together with their detailed classifications, they are "with detailed classifications.
Among them, the mind (*citta*) has first been explained with its detailed classifications as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), "discernment" (*prativijñapti*), and the "mind-base" (*manāyatana*).

By such means, starting from "the mental factors (caitta) are also the experience of feeling" up to "the mental factors are fivefold," [the text] explains in detail the sets of names (nāmakāya) and so forth.

The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to indicate other such unmanifested dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), such as schism in the Saṅgha (*saṅghabheda*) and so forth; for these are accepted as being dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) in substance. Furthermore, because it is stated in the *Śāstra* that "those which are of this same class" are also dissociated from mind, the inclusion of the term "mind" (*citta*) is for the purpose of indicating those things that belong to the same category as mind.
The meaning is that they are dissociated from the mind as the mind itself is;
furthermore, their commonality with the mind consists in the fact that these [factors] are formless.
Indeed, it is precisely because of its material nature (*rūpitva*) that form (*rūpa*), even though it is dissociated (*viprayukta*), does not receive the designation "dissociated.
As for their status as "name" (*nāman*)—such that these are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)—it is because they share the same genus as the mind;
the mental factors (*caitta*) are likewise of the same genus as the mind.
However, since these [factors] are associated with the mind (citta) regarding a common object, the term "dissociated" (viprayukta) is employed for the purpose of distinguishing them [from the mind].

Furthermore, because unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), which are of the same genus as those [conditioned factors], also lack an object, the term "conditioned" (saṃskāra) is used to exclude them. For this very reason, it is said:
"These conditioned forces (saṃskāras) are not associated with the mind, nor do they have the nature of matter (rūpa); therefore, they are called 'dissociated from mind' (cittaviprayukta)."
In this context, "tatra" (therein) is used for the introduction of a statement or for specification;
the word "tāvat" (first/now) refers to sequence;
"prāpti" (attainment) means acquisition; and "samanvaya" (correlation) means connection.
"Attainment" (*prāpti*) is a general designation,
while "acquisition" (*lābha*) and "possession" (*samanvaya*) are specific designations;
"acquisition" (*lābha*) and "attainment" (*pratilambha*) have the same meaning.

"Possession" (*samanvaya*) and "endowment" (*samanvāgama*) are not different in meaning; however, when "acquisition" (*pratilambha*) is mentioned, "endowment" is not included, and when "endowment" is mentioned, "acquisition" is not included.
"And being endowed with what has been obtained" means:
that which is unobtained and that which has been lost constitute "unobtained-and-lost"; the acquisition of that which was unobtained-and-lost is [what is meant].
Regarding that which has not yet been attained, it is as follows: for instance, the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*.

Regarding that which has been lost, it is as follows: for instance, when one who has abandoned the [attainment] pertaining to the desire realm through detachment from desire regains it by returning to that realm or through falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Furthermore, there is possession (*samanvāgama*) of what has already been attained during the second and subsequent moments.
Because it follows after that [acquisition],

both that which is the obtaining (*pratilambha*) and that which is the possession (*samanvāgama*) constitute the twofold "attainment" (*prāpti*); thus, the term "attainment" (*prāpti*) applies to both obtaining and possession.
When there is no intention to distinguish between them, however, "attainment" (*prāpti*), "acquisition" (*pratilambha*), and "possession" (*samanvāgama*) have one and the same meaning;
for instance, in the first moment, the attainment and acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is accepted,
and that is also called possession.

A noble person (āryapudgala) abiding in the first moment is said to be "endowed with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), because of such statements as: "He is possessed of the faculty of 'I shall come to know' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and endowed with thirteen [faculties]."
How is this a definition of characteristics?
For even when one intends to express a distinction, a definition of characteristics is not appropriate by means of a synonymous term;
what, then, is acquisition (*prāpti*)?
The expressions "acquisition" (*pratilambha*) and "possession" (*samanvāgama*) are synonymous terms,
yet they may sometimes be used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*), just as the words "flame," "born-of-wood," and "fire" are used interchangeably.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: "What is ignorance?
It is non-knowledge regarding the past, non-knowledge regarding the future," and so forth;
thus it is established that non-attainment results precisely from perversion.
The intention is that since non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is established by the very opposite [of attainment], this sūtra need not be composed for that purpose.
Non-attainment, non-acquisition (*apratilambha*), and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*)—these three are understood from their opposites;
likewise, the general designation "non-attainment" applies to both non-acquisition and non-possession.

Therefore, it should be stated in this way: non-possession (aprāpti) is twofold— the non-acquisition (apratilambha) of those things not previously acquired, and the non-endowment (asamanvāgama) of those things already acquired but subsequently lost.

Alternatively, "non-acquisition" (*apratilambha*) refers to the initial non-attainment of that which has not yet been acquired or which has been lost; "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*), on the other hand, refers to the state of one who has neither acquired nor lost [the quality] during the second and subsequent moments.
Thus, acquisition and non-acquisition pertain to those factors belonging to one's own continuum.
Thus,
it is determined that the acquisition and non-acquisition of conditioned phenomena belong only to those [phenomena] included within one's own continuum,
and not to those included within the continua of others.
The meaning is that possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) do not occur for dharmas belonging to the continuum of another being within one's own continuum;
therefore, he says:
For no one is endowed with things belonging to another; thus,
"nor those not included within a continuum" means those not included within the continuum of a sentient being.
Therefore it is said:

"For no one is endowed with those things reckoned as non-sentient," referring to such items as garlands and ornaments, as well as visible forms and so forth residing in wood, walls, and the like, which are reckoned as non-sentient.

The eyes and so forth are reckoned as belonging to sentient beings; likewise, hair and so forth, being connected with the material sense faculties, should be understood as being reckoned as belonging to sentient beings as well, because they conform to the transformation resulting from their benefit or injury.
For it is observed that through the injury to the material sense faculties, transformations such as graying occur in the hair and other parts.

The established doctrine is that through the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and other such means, there is the restoration of conditions such as graying hair; thus, the attainment [of these qualities] occurs for all those classified as sentient beings (*sattva-saṅkhyāta*).

Regarding the two types of cessation (*nirodha*)—namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*)—which are classified as non-sentient (*asattva-saṅkhyāta*), both attainment and non-attainment occur.
All sentient beings are endowed with cessation not through deliberation, according to the deficiency of their respective conditions.
"Excluding those abiding in the initial moment [of the path] regarding all fetters and so forth" means:
first, the "moment" refers to the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti-kṣaṇa*);
those situated therein are "abiding in the initial moment."
Those whose bonds are complete are "those with complete bonds," meaning those who have not abandoned any type of affliction;
and those who are both "with complete bonds" and "abiding in the first moment" are "those with complete bonds abiding in the first moment."
They are to be avoided by these [persons], or they are to be avoided by them; who are all those noble ones (āryas) who avoid those [states] existing at the moment of complete bondage and so forth?
Those noble ones who abide in the first moment [of the path of seeing], while still possessing all fetters, are not yet endowed with analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);
for in that state, the afflictions to be abandoned by receptivity (*kṣānti*) are being severed, but have not yet been severed.

Its cessation is also attained, yet it is not attained while it is in the process of ceasing; rather, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is the Path that abandons its obscuration.

However, those noble ones who have inscribed [the cessation] in a single manner and so forth are endowed with that cessation attained through the mundane path at that stage; from then on, in the second and subsequent moments, they remain indeed endowed with it. Furthermore, some ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are also endowed with the cessation attained through the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*); thus, they are categorized as "those who have inscribed [the cessation] in a single manner" and so forth.
But since no one is possessed of space due to the lack of a connection,
whereas there is a connection with the two cessations,
therefore there is no acquisition of space.
And for that which has no acquisition (*prāpti*), there is also no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Vaibhāṣikas.
From where does this [tenet] come?
Because its own nature and its activity are not perceived, as is the case with form (*rūpa*) and the eye (*cakṣus*) and so forth; thus he asks.
The Vaibhāṣika establishes the very explanation "from the Sūtra" with the detailed passage beginning, "of the ten dharmas of one beyond training."

The ten qualities of one in training (śaikṣadharma) and the eight factors of the noble path (āryamārgāṅga) of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), together with right liberation (samyagvimukti) and right knowledge (samyagjñāna);
through their arising and manifestation.
From the initial acquisition, from the attainment,
and subsequently from the possession after attainment,
one is devoid of the five factors.
The meaning is "one who has abandoned five factors.

As for the five factors— namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*)—
it is not tenable that these are abandoned at the attainment of the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

However, we observe that these five factors being applied are the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*), namely: attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because of his connection with "acquisition" (*prāpti*) which serves as a substitute [for the abandonment of these], even an Arhat who remains in his natural state (*prakṛtistha*) is called a Noble One (*ārya*); and the proof for this is as follows:
The teacher says in response to the argument that "possession exists substantially because it is mentioned in the Sūtra, just like the substances of the sense-bases (*āyatana*)," that "in that case,

possession would also have to exist substantially with respect to things not classified as sentient beings, such as wheels and chariots, and even with respect to other sentient beings, such as the 'jewel-woman' (*strī-ratna*) and so forth."
Because it is stated in the Sūtra,
he shows the Sūtra, beginning with "The king" and continuing at length.
Monks, a wheel-turning monarch is endowed with seven treasures;

these are his seven treasures, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh—thus it is said in detail.
He shows the inconclusiveness [of the opponent's position] by pointing out that the possession of these seven jewels is mentioned in the Sūtra but does not exist substantially;
furthermore, he seizes upon this as a flaw in the proposition because it contradicts inference.
How so? It is said:

"The possession of the ten qualities of one in training (*śaikṣadharma*) is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because its nature is that of a possession, like the possession of the seven treasures of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
By this, he subverts the essential nature of the property in the proposition.
"Mastery is acting according to one's will"— does this mean conformity to desire? In that regard, mastery is defined as such in the *Cakravarti-sūtra*.
Furthermore, as for the statement that it is "something else" (a distinct substance),
what is the inconsistency in this [position] regarding the *Sūtra on the Endowment with the Ten Dharmas of a Learner*?
For in the teaching, two kinds of entities are accepted: substantially existent (*dravyasat*) and nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*). [The Vaibhāṣikas ask: "How is it unreasonable?
The Master says:
"This is illogical," and so forth.
In this context, whatever entity exists as a substantial reality must be either apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or apprehended by inference (*anumāna*).
Among these, that which is apprehended by direct perception includes visible form (*rūpa*), sound (*śabda*), and so forth, because they are apprehended by the five sense faculties;
furthermore, some things apprehended by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are also direct perceptions.
Attachment, aversion, and so forth are self-cognizable;
the eye, ear, and so forth, however, are graspable through inference, because they are inferable from the functions of visual consciousness and the rest,
since those [functions] exist when they exist and do not exist when they do not.

Furthermore, acquisition (*prāpti*) is neither graspable by direct perception nor graspable by inference, because no faultless inference establishing it is observed. Therefore, since it cannot possess the properties of a substance, its non-existence is established. Now, the Master [Vasubandhu], repeatedly raising that position, refutes it.
"The cause of arising," and so forth:
that which has acquisition (*prāpti*) arises because of the existence of its cause;
however, there would be no acquisition of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the unconditioned does not arise.
Those factors such as the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and so forth that have not yet been attained;
and those that have been abandoned through the transition of stages (*bhūmisañcāra*) or through detachment (*vairāgya*),
such as the non-afflicted states of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) abandoned by being reborn in a higher stage, and the afflicted states abandoned through detachment.
How could there be the arising of those [dharmas] through the re-attainment of their elements or through falling away?
For they have no acquisition (*prāpti*),
because they are unarisen and ceased.
If their arising is intended to be caused by the attainment of the co-emergent (sahaja), then what [is the nature] of that arising?
Since the co-emergent acquisition (*sahajā prāpti*) that arises now is what produces them, he asks:
"What does birth (*jāti*) do now, or what does the birth-of-birth (*jātijāti*) do?"
What is the function of birth? Birth produces the characterized phenomenon (dharma),
whereas the "birth of birth" (jātijāti) produces that characteristic itself, namely birth.
Therefore, if the arising of the characterized phenomena (*lakṣya*) were said to be caused by acquisition (*prāpti*), then what would birth (*jāti*) do in that case?
Or, if the arising of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) itself were said to be caused by that [acquisition],
then he says:
Or is it the conceptualization that "what does birth-of-birth do?"?
Or else, if you should imagine that birth produces the phenomenon (dharma).
Furthermore, since acquisition (prāpti) produces birth (jāti), it is asked in that regard: what does "birth-of-birth" (jātijāti) do?
"Indeed, for those with all fetters," and so forth; those for whom not even a single type of affliction has been abandoned are "those with all fetters."
Furthermore, for those who possess all fetters, there would indeed be no distinction in the arising of weak, medium, or intense afflictions;
why?
Because there is no distinction in their possession (*prāpti*).

For those whose fetters are incomplete, a distinction in the arising of weak, medium, or intense afflictions might be postulated due to the deficiency in their acquisitions; however, such a distinction could not exist for those whose fetters are complete,
because their acquisitions are equal,
or else it would have to be that very [deficiency] which constitutes the distinction.
Or for whatever reason— whether from habituation or otherwise—
that distinction is intense for some who possess all fetters, while it is moderate for others.
Let the arising of some [afflictions] that are weak occur from that very cause of differentiation; let there be the arising of those afflictions, such as the weak ones and so forth.
"Therefore, possession (*prāpti*) is not a cause of arising," says the Vaibhāṣika;
"And who says this?"— thus the detailed argument continues.
Acquisition (*prāpti*) is the cause of differentiation;
for if acquisition did not exist, [there would be no distinction] regarding those things belonging to the worldly mind (*laukika-mānasa*).
"Worldly" (*laukika*) means that which exists in the world (*loka*).
The mind itself is the mental;
those noble ones and ordinary persons who possess this mundane mind are called "those with mundane minds."

The inclusion of "worldly mind" (*laukikamanas*) applies to both noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); the qualification "noble" is used because ordinary persons possess a worldly mind at all times,
or else it may serve as a qualification for ordinary persons in the states of the attainment of non-perception (*āsañjñika*) or the attainment of cessation (*asañjñisamāpatti*).

Regarding the phrase "of those noble ones and ordinary persons," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used either for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*) or to indicate a relationship (*sambandha*).
There would be no determination— that is, no delimitation— of those [factors];
that which constitutes such a determination is acquisition (*prāpti*).
"Due to the distinction between having abandoned and not having abandoned the afflictions":
the noble ones (ārya) have abandoned the afflictions, while ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) have not abandoned them.
The specific distinction between those states is that very [distinction] itself;
thus, it is the distinction regarding whether the afflictions have been abandoned or not abandoned.
Therefore,
this must be the established rule;
for is it not the case that even some ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) have abandoned their afflictions?
How is it determined that only the noble ones have abandoned the afflictions?
It is stated thus precisely because of the expression "complete eradication."
And how is this so?
How will this established distinction— that "the afflictions of these have been abandoned" and "the afflictions of those have not been abandoned"— come to be?
But when possession (*prāpti*) exists, this formal distinction is established by means of the possession of afflictions; that is to say,

by the removal or non-removal of that [possession], meaning by the severance or non-severance of the possession of afflictions— [a distinction] which applies to those for whom there is the removal of that possession.
Those who have not abandoned [the defilements] are noble ones; those who have not abandoned them are ordinary persons.

But surely, for some ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) as well, the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) has been repeatedly removed; yet it was not by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*).

How, then, is that distinction produced by the supramundane path discerned—namely, that "this possession of afflictions has been removed by the supramundane [path]," whereas "this [has been removed] by the mundane [path]"?

This is established through the distinction between the attainment of dissociation from the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), and through the excellence of the basis (*āśraya*). Thus, it is established by way of the excellence of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) that for some the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been abandoned, while for others they have not been abandoned.
"Thus transformed" means it has become otherwise; that is,
those [afflictions] which are to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "like rice burnt by fire":
just as rice burnt by fire becomes non-seed,
so too, when the basis (āśraya) has become non-seed for the afflictions (kleśa) through the aforementioned principle, one is said to be "one whose afflictions are abandoned."
Or, "the basis" refers to the state of having its seeds impaired;
by that, it can be said that [the defilement] has been abandoned by the mundane path.
Because there is merely the state of the seed being impaired,
its opposite is "not abandoned," meaning that the seed has not been burnt away in the basis, or that the nature of the seed remains unimpaired.
And as for "that which is not abandoned," and so forth:

one is possessed of that which is not abandoned according to the method just described— whether it be [afflictions] belonging to the desire realm up to the peak of existence that are to be abandoned by seeing, or those belonging to the desire realm up to the peak of existence that are to be abandoned by cultivation.
And that which has been abandoned, up to and including that belonging to the peak of existence—
it is designated as "not being possessed" by that [person].
This shows that this is a conventional designation (*prajñaptidharma*).

"The wholesome are also of two kinds," and so forth; the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is either for the purpose of conjunction— as in how the afflicted are of two kinds— or it means "and the wholesome."
"Because of the non-destruction of their seed-state":
the "seed of those" refers to the seeds of those wholesome states acquired through birth;
that is the "seed," and its state as such is the "seed-state."
The non-affliction of that seed-state within a certain basis is what is meant by "the non-affliction of the seed-state."
Therefore, because the state of their seeds has not been destroyed, one is "endowed" with them.
By what? With the [defilements].
Who is said to be "not possessed" (asamanvāgata) due to the impairment of those wholesome states that arise without effort? To this he says:
Regarding the phrase "of one whose roots of merit are severed," it should be understood that the impairment of the state of those seeds within that basis occurs through wrong view, and not otherwise.
Therefore he says:

"But indeed, there is no absolute eradication of the state of being a seed of wholesome factors within the continuum, as there is an absolute eradication of the afflictions within the continuum by means of the Noble Path"—this is the intended meaning.
As for the passage beginning with "But those who," it is explained in detail.
Those which are preparatory; by their having arisen,
there is the arising of those [subsequent states], which is "their arising" (tadutpatti).
Mastery over its arising is a specific capacity;
because of the non-obstruction of that [capacity], of what [is there obstruction]?
By whom is "possession" (samanvāgama) said to belong to the continuum (saṃtati)?
Since it is thus by those wholesome states arising through effort,

therefore, in this state of possession (*samanvāgama*), the seed itself— that is, the specific capacity— is neither removed by the Noble Path nor destroyed by the mundane path with respect to afflicted phenomena.

And one acquires— that which is referred to as "possession" (samanvāgama)— the seeds of wholesome factors that arise effortlessly and those wholesome factors that arise with effort during a time of mastery, even when these seeds have been nourished by wrong view.
There is no other substance whatsoever that is imagined by the Vaibhāṣikas;
what, then, is this so-called "seed"?
Out of suspicion regarding the substantiality [of the entity], he asks:
that name-and-form which is capable of producing a fruit—
that form consisting of the five aggregates which is capable of producing a fruit— whether directly, immediately, through a succession, or from afar.
"What is this so-called transformation?"—
with this doubt regarding the Sāṅkhya theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*), he asks:
"It is the alteration of the continuum."
Otherwise, what is this "arising" and what is this "continuum"?

Is it like the Sāṅkhyas' view, wherein there is the disappearance of one attribute and the appearance of another attribute within a persisting substance, such that there is a change of state within a persisting continuum?
It is said that they are not; what then?
They are characterized as cause and effect.

Cause and effect constitute "causality"; thus, the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the three time periods, which proceed in uninterrupted succession, are established as a "continuum" (*santati*).
As for where it was stated [in the Sūtra], the full passage is as follows:

But regarding that which is stated in the Sūtra, he asks: "Why? It says: "One who is possessed of greed is incapable and unfit to produce the four foundations of mindfulness, beginning with the foundation of mindfulness of the body."
If "possession" (*prāpti*) were the seed,
then since the seed exists eternally, there would be no arising of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
this would apply equally even to your own theory of possession, for in that case too, their arising would not occur.
Therefore, both [parties] must state that "concordance" (*adhivāsana*) therein means either the non-dispelling of greed or its possession; "concordance" (*adhivāsana*) is consent (*abhyanujñāna*).
Non-dispelling and non-quiescence—in every respect, this is a designated phenomenon (*prajñapti-dharma*) and not a substantial phenomenon (*dravya-dharma*).

Whether it be a cause of arising, a cause of establishment, a specific basis, or even an acceptance or non-dispelling, in every way it is a designated phenomenon; that is, a phenomenon by designation, by convention, and by worldly usage. It is a designated phenomenon and not a substantial phenomenon; the meaning is that it is not a phenomenon as an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in terms of substance.

Alternatively, "substantial phenomenon" (*dravyadharma*) means that which is both a substance and a phenomenon; the meaning is that it is not a phenomenon whose intrinsic characteristic exists [as a real entity] like form (*rūpa*) and so forth. And its negation: the negation of that phenomenon of designation (*prajñaptidharma*) is "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*). Master Saṅghabhadra states that "possession" (*prāpti*) is the mark of the cognition "this belongs to this," and the cause for the non-loss of acquired phenomena.
The claim that "this is the mark of the cognition 'this belongs to this'" is unestablished;

we maintain that such cognition arises through a specific basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*). Furthermore, if "attainment" (*prāpti*) is intended to be the cause for the non-disappearance of acquired factors (*dharma*), [then the following applies].
There would be no abandoning of what has been attained; since there is such abandoning, this [reasoning] is therefore not a valid cause.
And he refutes that very state of being a seed, defined as a specific capacity (śaktiviśeṣa), which was established by the Teacher; [he asks]:
"Is this specific capacity something different from the mind, or not different? And what follows from this?"
If it is a different object,
then [the object] is established and there is no attainment; however, the dispute is merely over the name.
If it is not a different thing, then has it not been admitted that the seed of the unwholesome is wholesome, and the seed of the wholesome is unwholesome?
For who indeed, when heat is not distinct from fire, would determine that heat alone is the burner and not the fire?
For the seed of the wholesome exists in an unwholesome mind or in a neutral one;
likewise, the seed of the unwholesome exists in a wholesome mind or in a neutral one.
In the same way, the seed of the indeterminate also exists in both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
and the contaminated seed [exists] in the uncontaminated, while the uncontaminated seed exists in the contaminated mind. Thus, the fault of confusion (sāṅkarya) would follow.
To this, we reply:
If it were not a distinct entity, there would be the fault of confusion;
therefore, that seed must be said to be neither different from the mind nor non-different from it.
Because it is of the nature of a dependent designation (upādāyaprajñapti),

even if there is no separate entity (anarthāntarabhāva), there is still no fault; for when a wholesome mind has arisen, it would deposit a seed in another mind of its own continuum, whether of the same kind or of a different kind.
Therefore, because of a specific cause there arises a specific effect; thus, that distinguished mind would arise,
and that distinguished mind would arise as capable of performing the function of the seeds of the wholesome.

In this way, even by an unwholesome [mind], a seed would be deposited in a mind of its own continuum— whether of the same class or a different class— and that mind, distinguished by it, would arise as capable of performing the function of the unwholesome seed.
Likewise, even by an indeterminate mind, a seed would be deposited in a mind of its own continuum— whether of the same class or a different class.

And that [mind] would arise as distinguished by that [seed], capable of performing the function of the seed of the indeterminate; thus, even in an outflowing (sāsrava) mind, a seed for the non-outflowing (anāsrava) would be deposited, and in a non-outflowing mind, one for the outflowing— so that mind, arising from another mind, functions as both the mutual depositor of seeds and the mutual producer, through the relationship of the perfumed and the perfumer.
Nor is a specific capacity (śaktiviśeṣa) deposited in an unwholesome mind by a wholesome [mind], such that that unwholesome [mind] would become wholesome,
or that wholesome [mind] would become unwholesome;
for it is merely a specific capacity.
"Power," "seed," and "latent impression" (vāsanā) have this single meaning;

likewise, the latent impressions of the unwholesome and so forth must also be explained, up to the point where a specific power is imparted by the contaminated (sāsrava) into the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Even when a special capacity is imparted to a contaminated [phenomenon] by means of an uncontaminated one,
that contaminated phenomenon does not thereby become uncontaminated, nor does the uncontaminated become contaminated.
This must also be considered by you Vaibhāṣikas:
when an uncontaminated mind arises immediately after a contaminated mind, or a contaminated mind arises immediately after an uncontaminated mind,

is the preceding contaminated complex or the uncontaminated complex capable of producing the subsequent complex by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth, or is it incapable?
And what follows from this?
If it were devoid of capacity, its status as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth would be lost; if, on the other hand, it possesses capacity...
Is that capacity within a contaminated mind itself contaminated or is it uncontaminated?
And would that [capacity] serve as the condition of immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*) and so forth for another contaminated or uncontaminated mind,
or [would it serve] for the uncontaminated [mind] by means of that very [capacity]?

If it were by that very same power, how could there not be a confusion of the effects of the powers? Or, if it were by another power— that one being for the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the other for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)— to produce the state of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth,
how could it be logical for these two powers, which are non-different from that single mind, to possess distinct natures and distinct effects?
If it is argued that even for us, there will be the abiding of various powers non-different from the mind and a differentiation of their effects,

then in the same way, for the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind as well— which occurs by way of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for both tainted and untainted minds— one must likewise state a difference in the nature of the two powers and a differentiation of their effects.
Therefore, what was said—that "would it not follow that the unwholesome is admitted to be the seed of the wholesome," and so forth—is incorrect.
For it is not the case that the unwholesome, being distinguished by a specific capacity deposited by the wholesome, performs the function of a seed of the unwholesome;
rather, what does?
It performs only the function of the wholesome seed,
yet by means of its own specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*), that unwholesome [seed] performs the function of its own seed;
how then can this be said?

If you were to say that the unwholesome is the seed of the wholesome, then how could that wholesome seed, once planted within an unwholesome mind, not become unwholesome? It is clear, therefore, that you do not understand the true nature of a seed.

By means of a wholesome mind that is ceasing, an unwholesome mind is produced with such a specific capacity (*śaktiviśiṣṭa*) that it will become capable of its own arising, either directly or through a succession; thus, it is only this specific capacity that is the seed (*bīja*),
for there is no such thing as a "seed" apart from being a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).
For this very reason, acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) are said to be conventional truths (*prajñaptisatya*);
however, the Vaibhāṣikas describe them as substantial truths (*dravyasatya*),
stating in detail that there is even past acquisition for past phenomena (*dharmas*).
Regarding past phenomena— for example, those that are afflicted— their past acquisition may be one that has arisen and ceased; it may be prior, simultaneous,
or even subsequent.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of those very [dharmas] that have not yet arisen is future; that which has arisen but not yet ceased is present. Furthermore, the acquisition of future [dharmas] is past when it has arisen and ceased as the first-born [preceding moment].
That which is future is unarisen;
that which is present is arisen and has not yet ceased. Likewise, for present [dharmas], there is also past acquisition (*prāpti*) which is arisen and has ceased prior to them.
This was stated by taking into account the commonality of the types [of causes] such as the future, the unarisen, the present, those that are co-arising, and the past.

However, for a single past [dharma], there is not necessarily a threefold acquisition (*prāpti*); for it is impossible for a future or past acquisition to exist for that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because of the statement: "Acquisition is either non-produced (*avākṛta*) or simultaneous (*sahaja*)."

If, however, the determination of possession (*prāpti*) were made with respect to each individual substance, this would be the case regarding possibility: for afflicted states and for wholesome states acquired through birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), past and so forth, there are necessarily past and so forth possessions.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is no past or present possession of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) that has not yet arisen.
And this general rule should be understood as having an exception,
because of the statement that "the acquisition of the indeterminate is simultaneous";
however, for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the acquisition is past, having arisen and ceased.
Those that have not yet arisen are future;
those that have arisen but not yet ceased are present.
Because this is easy to understand, it has not been set forth in a formal sutra.
The acquisitions of those belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms are, respectively, of the desire, form, and formless realms.
Thus, for one born in the desire realm, there is an acquisition of the desire-realm type for dharmas of the desire realm;
for that same person, there is an acquisition of the form-realm type for dharmas of the form realm.
For those very [beings] belonging to the formless realm, it is of the formless realm;
for one born in the realm of form, it is of the desire realm— as, for example, the desire-realm consciousnesses of those who possess emanation-minds (nirmāṇacitta).
For those belonging to the realm of form, the acquisition (prāpti) belongs to the realm of form;
for those belonging to the formless realm, it belongs to the formless realm;
and for one born in the formless realm, the acquisition of factors belonging to that realm is itself of that same realm.
Regarding those not included within the realms (*anāpta*), there are four kinds;
that is, for conditioned and unconditioned phenomena not included within the realms—namely, those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)—there is a fourfold acquisition (*prāpti*:
belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, and the untainted).
"In brief" means having combined all those that are not included;
however, since they are not each of four kinds individually, he says:
Regarding that, the detailed explanation of "non-analytical cessation" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is as follows:

for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of non-analytical cessation of factors belonging to the desire realm and so forth, according to what is possible, and this acquisition belongs to the desire realm;
for one born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is the acquisition of non-analytical cessation of factors belonging to the form realm and so forth, and this acquisition belongs to the form realm.

For one born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the acquisition of the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) of factors belonging to the formless realm and so forth is established as belonging to the formless realm solely by virtue of the continuum of the sentient being;
it is not established by virtue of those factors for which there is non-analytical cessation.
For if this were the case, then the attainment of non-analytical cessation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) of the truth of the path would be untainted (anāsrava),
and the attainment of analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) would belong to the realms of form and formlessness as well as being untainted, but not to the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Because it is not an antidote to the desire realm,

the acquisition of that which is attained by a path belonging to the form realm is itself form-realm-acquisition; likewise, that which is attained by a path belonging to the formless realm is formless-realm-acquisition.

However, for a Noble One, the acquisitions of dissociation (visaṃyogaprāpti) obtained through the untainted path are untainted; those obtained through a path belonging to the form realm are both of the form realm and untainted; those obtained through a path belonging to the formless realm are both of the formless realm and untainted; and in the case of a Noble One’s detachment from passion by means of the mundane path, the acquisitions of dissociation are of two kinds.
By this statement,
[the author] indicates that the truth of the path possesses only the untainted (*anāsrava*) acquisition, thereby precluding its worldly (*laukika*) acquisition.
"This fourfold [classification] is in brief" thus concludes the meaning already stated— that it consists of both that belonging to the three realms and that which is untainted—
with the words "of those in training."
The dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa) are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of one in training;
the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are the untainted dharmas of one beyond training.
These should be understood as being of the very nature of the truth of the path (mārgasatya).
However, those other than the learners (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*),
as well as the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, are held to be neither learners nor non-learners;
their possession (*prāpti*) is of three kinds, according to the distinction of being learner and so forth.
[It is] that of the learner, the non-learner, and that which is neither of the learner nor the non-learner;
"attained by one who is not noble" means attained by an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

"By that very [path] which is of one beyond training" means that the acquisition of that very analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) obtained by a path of one in training (śaikṣa) is "of one in training," while that obtained by a path of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is "of one beyond training."

Because it serves as the basis for the attainment of dissociation (visaṃyoga-prāpti) obtained through the path associated with the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), although that [attainment] is reached by the diamond-like (vajropama) path of a trainee (śaikṣa) since it brings it about, it is not said to be "of the trainee" when describing its attainment; rather, the attainment of one beyond training (aśaikṣī prāptiḥ) is thereby distinguished from the attainment of a trainee. Thus, it is not said to be "of the trainee" by virtue of that trainee's path.
"Of that very [cessation] attained through the noble path, they are untainted" means that for that very analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) attained through the noble path,
as well as for the truth of the path, there is an untainted acquisition (anāsravā prāpti); this is what is being discussed.

Is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*)—which has not been attained by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*)—contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)?
He says: it is both ways.
Why, then, was it not mentioned [in the verse]?
The remaining portion of the commentary will be shown later:
"In the case of worldly noble detachment, the acquisitions of dissociation are twofold."
It should be understood that this is not what is being stated; rather, it is the unmixed attainment (*prāpti*) that is intended here,
because [the former] is difficult to obtain.
The two supernormal knowledges— the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye and the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear— are weak because they lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāravattvāt*).
And one should connect [the sentence] as follows: "Excluding the mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta),
is the acquisition of the indeterminate (avyākṛta) simultaneous?"
"Because they are powerful," and so forth;
for because those [supernormal powers], such as the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the others, are powerful, what [is the consequence]?
Acquisition occurs prior to, after, or simultaneously with [the attainment],
because it is accomplished through a specific application;
thus, accomplishment through a specific application refers to the superknowledges (abhijñā) such as the divine eye and so forth.

The connection of the meaning is as follows: because it is accomplished through a specific application, it possesses strength; and because of that strength, there is an attainment occurring prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously [with the action].
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that even for someone engaged in the arts, such as Viśvakarman,
and for one engaged in postures, such as the Elder Aśvajit,
[the mind arises] when it has been practiced to an extreme degree and thoroughly mastered.
Is attainment (prāpti) prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with [the dharma], and what is the case regarding obscured form (nivṛta-rūpa)?
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction; it conjoins the statement that "attainment is innate.
Furthermore, that afflicted matter should be understood as belonging exclusively to the level of the first dhyāna, and it is informative matter (vijñapti-rūpa).
Therefore, because there is no motivator for it in other stages,
[it is said] "even by a superior [mind]," and so forth;
that is, even by a superior mind, a concealed (*nivṛta*) informative action (*vijñapti*) is motivated.
And that very same intense mind of informative action does not give rise to non-informative action; therefore, its weakness is established.
Because of that establishment of its weakness, its acquisition (*prāpti*) is indeed innate (*sahaja*).
