"Acquisition is differentiated" means that for those [dharmas] born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and so forth, which are non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), acquisition is simultaneous (*sahajā*); however,
for the substances of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth, acquisition is prior, posterior, or simultaneous— this is their differentiation.
Regarding the phrase "prior to speech" (*vāg-agraja*) for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*):

this means that for the wholesome or unwholesome informative and non-informative matter (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) belonging to the desire realm, there is absolutely no prior acquisition (*agraja-prāpti*), whether it be wholesome or unwholesome; the meaning is that it simply does not exist in any way whatsoever.
It is both simultaneous and subsequent; thus, as is possible:

for the first moment of informative and non-informative [action], there is a simultaneous acquisition (*prāpti*) at its beginning, while in the second and subsequent moments, there is a subsequent acquisition of that very same first moment.
In this way, for the other moments beginning with the second, it should be understood that possession (*prāpti*) is both simultaneous and subsequent.

Since possession that arises prior to the form belonging to the desire realm is prohibited, there certainly exists a prior possession of the form of the dhyāna and untainted restraints (*anāsrava-saṃvara*);
thus, non-possession (*aprāpti*) is set aside, and all of it is exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Why is it established?
If non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the afflictions were itself afflicted,
then for one who has abandoned the afflictions, it would not exist, just as the afflictions themselves do not exist.
If it were wholesome, it would not belong to one whose roots of virtue are severed; furthermore, if the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena were itself untainted,
what would be the consequence?
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would never exist, because they would always be endowed with the noble qualities (*āryadharma*);
therefore, by process of elimination, it is established that non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, there is no non-acquisition of a present phenomenon, for that which is present is not [non-]acquired.
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of a present phenomenon exists;
therefore, it has no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), because the coexistence of its acquisition and non-acquisition is impossible in the present.
Regarding the past and future, however, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) pertains to all three time periods.

For those qualities acquired through application (*prāyogika*) that have not yet been attained or have been lost, as well as for the future faculties such as the eye and so forth—indeed, for all those things which lack acquisition—there exists non-acquisition in the past, in the future, and in the present.
This is because their non-acquisition arises and ceases according to the principle of a stream (*sroto-nyāya*), persisting even in the state of the future.

And [the phrase] "of those pertaining to the desire realm and so forth, and of the immaculate" includes the word "threefold" by means of the particle *ca* (and). "Pertaining to the desire realm and so forth" (*kāmādyāpta*) refers to those that are obtained (*āpta*), meaning not dissociated, within the realms such as the desire realm.
The non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of those factors belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as of the untainted (*amala*) factors, is of three kinds;
for it is established by virtue of the place of rebirth (*upapatti*) and the basis (*āśraya*),
since non-acquisition is indeed established in relation to the factors that coexist with it.
It is not established by the power of the dharma in the same manner as possession (*prāpti*);

therefore, for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of dharmas belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, belongs to the desire realm;
for one born in the form realm, it belongs to the form realm.

For one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of those qualities belonging to the formless sphere (*ārūpyāvacara*), such as the acquired qualities of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, for one born in the desire realm, there is the non-acquisition of the qualities obtained through application (*prāyogika*) and those obtained by birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) during the state when wholesome roots are severed; there is the non-acquisition of the unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*) qualities of the form and formless spheres because of the lack of freedom from passion (*avītarāgatva*); and there is the non-acquisition of the untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities because of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). All these are [non-acquisitions] belonging to the desire realm.

Similarly, for one born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) belonging to the realm of form of the qualities pertaining to the desire realm that have been abandoned through changing levels, as well as of the preparatory (*prāyogika*) qualities pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness; and likewise, due to being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), there is non-acquisition of the untainted (*anāsrava*) qualities.

And similarly, for one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is non-acquisition belonging to the formless realm of the qualities pertaining to the desire and form realms that have been abandoned through changing levels, as well as of the preparatory qualities pertaining to the formless realm; and likewise, due to being an ordinary person, there is non-acquisition of the untainted qualities. What, then, is this "being an ordinary person"?
By this scriptural reading, "the non-attainment of the noble dharmas," [the author] shows that non-attainment (*aprāpti*) lacks the quality of being untainted (*anāsrava*).
To the question, "Of which noble dharmas is there non-attainment?

[the answer is: the noble dharmas consist of the entire untainted path, beginning with the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); therefore, he asks thus.
Because it is stated without distinction for all [of them];
why is there the non-attainment of all— the dharmajñānakṣānti and so forth, as well as the jñānas of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa)— with respect to suffering?
Because it is not specified in this way,

if [it were so], then even when the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering has arisen, since there would still be a non-acquisition of the remaining noble dharmas, one would be a non-noble person;
therefore, he said this.
But as for that which is "without gain," that non-gain which exists without gain is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

"Otherwise, indeed," and so forth; for if ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) were held to be the non-possession of other dharmas even when there is the possession of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), then even a Buddha would be a non-noble one (*anārya*), since he does not possess the noble dharmas belonging to the mental continuums of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
However, this undesirable consequence does not follow if "non-possession" alone is what is intended.
In that case, the word *eva* must be read [in the text],
meaning "the non-attainment of the noble dharmas alone," for even single words can function as exclusives (*avadhāraṇa*).
The meaning is that even isolated words [can be used]; for instance,
in the case of "one who subsists on water" or "one who subsists on air," it is not meant that he is *only* one who subsists on water or *only* one who subsists on air.
The meaning of the word *eva* is understood here as well, just as in that [other] case;
or else, he who eats only water is an *abbhakṣa*.
Just as in the expression "one who eats only air is an air-eater" (*vāyu-bhakṣa*),
where the restrictive sense of the particle *eva*— though omitted— is understood, so too here [the meaning is] "only non-attainment."
"Regarding the statement 'of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma concerning suffering and its co-nascent factors,' the full explanation is as follows:

in this position, the non-acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma concerning suffering and of the factors co-nascent with it—such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth—is what constitutes the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*). As for the fault previously stated—that even when the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma concerning suffering has arisen, one would still be a non-noble (*anārya*) because of the non-acquisition of the remaining noble factors (*āryadharma*)—[that fault does not apply here]."
That is not possible;

for when there is the attainment of a fruit, there is the abandonment of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors. To avoid the fault that [the practitioner] would thereby become a non-noble one (*anārya*) upon attaining the fruit, he says:
Nor does the consequence of non-nobility follow from the abandonment of that [attainment], nor from the abandonment of those [factors] co-arising with patience,
because the non-acquisition of that [attainment] has been utterly destroyed.
Since that non-attainment is absolutely abandoned,
how is it utterly destroyed? Because it will not arise again within his mental continuum.
In that case, since there are three lineages— namely, the lineages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas— for whom is there this non-attainment?
"Of all" refers to those belonging to the lineages of the śrāvakas and so forth;
if that is the case, then the same fault remains.

The meaning is that even a Buddha would be a non-noble one (*anārya*) due to not having attained the three lineages (*tri-gotra*); furthermore, that same rebuttal applies, as before, with the elaboration starting from "but he who [is so] without attainment" up to "just as, for example, one who subsists on water or subsists on air."
In that case, the effort [to define *pṛthagjanatva*] would be futile;

for if one were to argue that a person would remain a non-noble (*anārya*) because of the continued existence of the non-acquisition of the noble dharmas remaining after the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), then the effort made to avoid this fault—namely, that "the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the non-acquisition of patience and its co-arising factors"—would be in vain.
This [definition] is adopted precisely as a means to avoid the fault of the prima facie argument.

"The continuum in which noble dharmas have not arisen" means that the continuum in which noble dharmas have not arisen is "the continuum in which noble dharmas have not arisen"; this refers to the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*),
meaning the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantati*) in which the noble path has not arisen.

It is stated that the continuum in which the noble dharmas have arisen by virtue of the [transformation] is "noble-ness" (*āryatva*), because of the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); furthermore,
this "non-attainment" (*aprāpti*) is asserted to be the non-attainment of all dharmas.
"The non-attainment of the qualities of a woman" is an example of how it is, first of all.
"By the acquisition of that, it is abandoned":

by the acquisition of that noble path (*āryamārga*), that state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)—which is characterized by non-possession—is abandoned. To which realm does that state of being an ordinary person belong?

Some say it belongs to the three realms; but surely, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)— which has non-acquisition as its intrinsic nature— is established by virtue of the basis of rebirth?

Therefore, we see that it is illogical to say that this being belonging to the desire realm possesses only the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) pertaining to the desire realm, and not those pertaining to the form or formless realms; for [if that were so], one would be abandoning the state of an ordinary person across all three realms, which is untenable.
Furthermore, if it is considered that one has attained the state of non-arising (anutpattidharmatā), and thus the triple world is abandoned, let this be a conceptual metaphor;
it is not refuted.

However, we understand that there is the acquisition of only one state of being an ordinary person belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), which is abandoned during the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*);
and that [state] is abandoned upon the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in the process of becoming detached from the desire realm.

However, for a noble one (*ārya*) being born in the form or formless realms, as well as for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) residing in each respective level, no acquisition (*prāpti*) arises at all due to the power of having attained the noble path;
rather, it should be understood that their abandonment occurs in the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) on each level,
and also through the transition between levels (*bhūmisañcāra*).
And when, having attained detachment from the desire realm, one enters the first dhyāna,
at that time that state of being an ordinary person belonging to the desire realm is abandoned,
yet one does not become an *ārya*.
Because the state of being an ordinary person belonging to the level of the first dhyāna arises,

in this way, by moving from the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), the state of being an ordinary person belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) is abandoned; and when one moves from a higher level to a lower level, it should be stated that the state of being an ordinary person belonging to the higher level is abandoned.
The same should be applied to others as well;

just as through the attainment of the Noble Path, the non-attainment of the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is abandoned, so too should it be applied that through the attainment of other qualities such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*), their respective non-attainments are abandoned.

How is it that non-possession (*aprāpti*) is abandoned through the acquisition (*prāpti-lābha*) of factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), such as those consisting of hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā-maya*),
and how is the non-possession of wholesome states acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) abandoned by the acquisition of those [wholesome states] for one whose wholesome roots have been severed?
Furthermore, through the transition between stages, when one passes away from the desire realm and transitions by rebirth into the first dhyāna,
then the non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the aggregates belonging to that stage which are included within the [five] destinies is abandoned.

For it will be stated that the destinies (*gati*) are exclusively non-afflicted and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), and it has already been said that "the acquisition of the neutral is innate. In this way, the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the qualities belonging to the level of the first dhyāna that are produced through application (*prāyogika*) is abandoned.

And because of the transition between stages (*bhūmisañcārāt*), one is deprived of the aggregates (*skandha*) belonging to higher stages that are included within the destiny (*gati*) through that transition to another stage; thus,
we perceive this illustration of the explanation of the transition between stages given by some to be indistinct in that regard.
The non-attainment of the aggregates belonging to higher planes that are included within the [five] destinies is lost not only through the transition between planes,
but also through the loss of their attainment.
Let us consider this unambiguous example:

for instance, there exists the non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) of the preparatory states (*prāyogika*) belonging to the levels of the second dhyāna and above by a being of the desire realm who has not yet attained them; if that being, having become free from passion for the desire realm, is reborn in the first dhyāna.
That non-acquisition of theirs is lost through the transition to another stage,
but the non-acquisition belonging to the level of the first dhyāna arises for them;
in this same manner, it should be applied to the others as well.
But in that case, would it not follow that there is an infinite regress of acquisitions, such that for every acquisition there is another acquisition,
and for that one yet another?
If there were yet another [possession] for that one as well, there would be an infinite regress;
rather, it is through mutual association— that is,
by virtue of the connection with the possession of possession— that one is possessed of the primary possession.
The meaning is that one is "endowed" (samanvāgata) through the acquisition of acquisition;
the detailed explanation is "due to the arising of acquisition," meaning that due to the arising of acquisition, one becomes endowed with that dharma or with the mind.
The phrase "is endowed with the acquisition of acquisition" continues [from the previous context];
because the acquisition of acquisition arises, one becomes endowed with the [primary] acquisition itself. Thus, acquisition functions in both cases.
However, since the acquisition of acquisition (*prāptiprāpti*) occurs in only one place, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) for the wholesome and the afflicted;
these two are thus included because they possess acquisitions that arise respectively prior to and posterior to them.

For the possession (*prāpti*) of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma is indeed innate; thus, "in the second moment," and so forth, means that in the second moment there are three possessions: the possession of that dharma, the possession of its possession (*prāptiprāpti*), and [the possession] of that [possession of the possession].
For one becomes possessed of those [dharmas] through the connection with their acquisition (*prāpti*);

and for the sake of being possessed of those three acquisitions, three further "secondary acquisitions" (*anuprāpti*) arise. Thus, there are six acquisitions for the entities produced in the first and second moments.
Together with the dharma itself, there are nine acquisitions (*prāpti*) for the nine substances; together with the secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*), they become eighteen.
Thus, by way of the consequence of ever-increasing growth—this is the detailed explanation—the growth of each subsequent moment occurs through acquisitions.
Or else, there would be the consequence of an increase in acquisitions in each successive moment; that is, the consequence of an ever-increasing growth, by which [it follows].
We shall demonstrate merely the general direction that these acquisitions spread by means of a continuous process of successive increase.
In the fourth moment, there must be the three factors produced in the first moment, together with their acquisitions (*prāpti*) and secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*);

furthermore, there must be the six acquisitions and secondary acquisitions produced in the second moment, which themselves possess further acquisitions and secondary acquisitions. Thus, in the fourth moment, there are twenty-seven acquisitions arising from the first, second, and third moments, along with an equal number of secondary acquisitions, making fifty-four acquisitions in total.

In the fifth moment, however, there arise fifty-four acquisitions (*prāpti*) and secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*) produced in the first, second, and third moments, and fifty-two acquisitions and secondary acquisitions produced in the fourth moment; thus, three sets of fifty-four amount to one hundred and sixty-two acquisitions that come into being. In this manner, the consequence of an ever-increasing proliferation must be explained.
In the phrase "of those past and future," the present is not mentioned because it is not necessary;
and in the phrase "and of those acquired through birth," the acquired-through-exertion (prāyogika) is not mentioned for the very same reason that it is not necessary.

"Of those associated and co-existent" means of those such as feeling (vedanā) and the like, as well as their homogeneous causes (sajāti) and so forth, which are included within the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), encompassed throughout a saṃsāra that has neither beginning nor end.
Infinite and immeasurable acquisitions arise for a single living being moment by moment; how much more so, then, for many?
The meaning is that they consist of infinite substances, that is, they consist of infinite substances of acquisition (*prāpti*);
oh, how great indeed is this festival of acquisitions!
This is merely a statement made in jest;
for since they are formless (*arūpin*), acquisitions (*prāpti*) do not encounter resistance and thus find space [to exist].
Likewise, "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) is the similarity among sentient beings, and so forth.
"Sabhāga" means that their portion (*bhāga*) or sharing (*bhajana*) is common;
the state of being such is "sabhāgatā.
Alternatively, a common portion or sharing is "sabhāga."
Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is precisely that which is homogeneous; it is the substance by connection with which one becomes homogeneous.
The meaning is that "equality" (*sāmya*), "commonality" (*sāmānya*), and "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) refer to sentient beings.
The inclusion of the term "sentient beings" is for the purpose of excluding non-sentient things.
The similarity among sentient beings and those factors reckoned as sentient is "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
Since it is not accepted that there is a *nikāyasabhāga* for things not reckoned as sentient beings, such as rice, barley, and so forth, this term is a designation used in the treatises; thus,
in the *Jñānaprasthāna* and other treatises, this dissociated mental factor (*cittaviprayukta*) is indicated by the name "homogeneity of the group" (*nikāyasabhāga*).
But here, for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse, the intention is that it is by this designation "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*);
furthermore, that [homogeneity] is both undifferentiated and differentiated— that which exists among all sentient beings.
Although it is different with respect to each individual being, it is said to be non-different because of its similarity;
for it is not, as the Vaiśeṣikas maintain, a single eternal entity that exists in some places and does not exist in others.
Then he says,
"Furthermore, they are divided," and so forth;
the three realms are those beginning with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The destinies (*gati*) are the five beginning with the hells;
the modes of birth (*yoni*) are the four beginning with those born from eggs;
and the castes (*jāti*) are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth.
By the word "etcetera," laywomen (*upāsikā*), nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), those who are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), and so forth are included;

thus there is a homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), ranging from the homogeneity of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the homogeneity of the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
"Undifferentiated" means having a universal form,
and it is also a designation.
And the meaning is that there is also the designation (*abhidhāna*).
In this way, the cognitions (*buddhi*) and designations (*prajñapti*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth should also be applied accordingly.

For if the substance (*dravya*) of the homogeneity of the aggregates (*skandhasabhāgatā*) did not remain as a residual entity, then there would be no non-differentiated cognition or designation—such as "aggregate, aggregate"—with respect to the aggregates which are distinct from one another by their specific differences.
Some read that "the same [analysis] should be applied to the conceptual designations of the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth.
To them, this must be said:

if there were no such thing as "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*), then—in detail, up to the point where the elements are distinguished by their mutual differences—there would be neither a non-differentiated cognition nor a designation, such as "this belongs to the desire realm" and "that belongs to the desire realm," among those very elements.
Regarding the fourfold alternative (*catuḥ-koṭika*):
there may be one who would pass away and be reborn, yet neither abandon nor acquire the homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattva-sabhāgatā*).
This refers to the homogeneity of sentient beings.

The "homogeneity of sentient beings" (*sattvasabhāgatā*) is the commonality among sentient beings characterized by being human and so forth. The inclusion of the term "sentient beings" is for the purpose of qualifying the phenomena (*dharma*);
for it is the homogeneity of sentient beings, not the homogeneity of phenomena (*dharmasabhāgatā*), that is intended here in this fourfold proposition (*catuṣkoṭika*).
However, what is intended is not a similarity of aspect consisting in the thought "a sentient being is a sentient being";
for if that were intended,

the third alternative would not be established, because even during the transition between realms of existence (*gati*), that homogeneity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) remains in its original state.
Regarding the phrase "being reborn right there":
for example, one who has passed away from the human realm and is being reborn in the very same human realm;
having died from the human realm, they are reborn in that same state due to the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*).

And he neither abandons nor acquires that human *sabhāgatā*, because that human *sabhāgatā* remains in its original state; secondly, when entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*), he abandons the *sabhāgatā* whose intrinsic nature is the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and acquires another *sabhāgatā* whose intrinsic nature is the state of an noble one (*ārya*).
The third [type of] movement is due to the transition from one state of existence to another;
for example, when one passes away from the human state and is reborn in the divine state,
one dies and is likewise reborn through the linking of the new existence.
One abandons the generic similarity of sentient beings characterized by the generic similarity of humans,
and acquires another, characterized by the generic similarity of gods;
this is the fourth [case], setting aside these aforementioned modes.
The meaning is: "excluding the aforementioned modes of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the categories.

For example, whether one is a living ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or an noble one (ārya), if there were a real entity (dravya) called "ordinary-person-homogeneity" (pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā), then what further need would there be for a postulated "ordinariness" whose intrinsic nature is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas? This is the remainder of the sentence.

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be defined as such solely by way of the homogeneity of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*), just as a human is defined solely by way of the homogeneity of a human (*manuṣya-sabhāgatā*);

for the Vaibhāṣikas do not conceive of "human-ness" as something other than the homogeneity of a human, nor do they consider it to have a separate intrinsic nature (*anyasvabhāva*) like [the state of] non-acquisition (*alābha*). And regarding this, the proof is as follows:
Ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) is nothing other than its own homogeneous character (*svasabhāgatā*), because it is denoted by the condition of that very homogeneous character,
just like humanity (*manuṣyatva*).
Furthermore, the world does not perceive *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity) because it is formless;
thus, the world does not see *sabhāgatā* with the eye because it is formless—meaning it lacks physical form or has the nature of being non-material.
Just as it does not see it, so too it does not hear it, and so on, up to it does not touch it.
By this, he shows that [the object] is not established through direct perception;
and by the statement "nor does one discern it through wisdom," he shows that it is not established even by inference.
And since one perceives the diversity of birth among sentient beings,
how could that [perception] have any function there [regarding the absence of such diversity],
given that there is already a perception of the diversity of birth in the perception of the diversity of birth?

That [notion], however, is not produced by a "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) conceived as a distinct entity, because such an entity is not perceived by any means of valid cognition and therefore lacks causal efficacy; yet you might argue that a cognition of a universal cannot exist without a cause.
Therefore, since there is a basis for that general cognition,
we also maintain that this general cognition is accompanied by a real entity called "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*).
For that cognition is produced by similarity,
and we maintain that this similarity is not a separate substance;
therefore it is said.
Furthermore, why is it not accepted that there is also a "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) among non-sentient things? This is explained at length:

the general cognition "this is a sentient being, this is a sentient being" does not have as its cause a homogeneity that is a separate substantial entity (*dravyāntara*), because it functions through a general mental aspect (*sāmānyākāra*).
Just as there is a common cognition of rice, barley, mung beans,
black gram, and so forth, this common cognition is produced by the similarity within their own respective classes;
and that similarity within their own class does not exist as something distinct from the things themselves.

"And of those homogeneities," and so forth: since it is maintained that homogeneities are mutually distinct— such that the homogeneity of sentient beings is one thing, the homogeneity of realms is another, and the homogeneity of destinies is yet another—
how is it that you apply the designation "homogeneity" to them without distinction, saying, "this is homogeneity" and "that is homogeneity"?

How could conventional usage and cognition arise if, even in this case, another "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) were to be postulated as the basis for the general cognition of homogeneity? This would be a flawed position, because it contradicts the previous position.

The meaning is that the Vaiśeṣikas have likewise been illuminated— that is, set ablaze and refuted— because they too are proponents of the category of "generality" (*sāmānya*). Thus, even they are included.
However, this is the specific distinction of those Vaiśeṣikas:
that even a single [entity] resides in many, like a garland or a thread, or like a quality residing in the neck of a living being.
If they are not illuminated because [the opponent] asserts general categories (*sāmānyapadārtha*),
and if they are not illuminated because [the opponent] asserts specific qualities such as oneness, multiplicity, permanence, impermanence,
and so forth— [for] the existence of the next world and other such matters are certainly not [among those general categories].
Since these are merely imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, they are not established as definitive;
yet, if such a state were to occur,
one would be reborn in the hells through the practice, cultivation, and frequent repetition of the taking of life.
If one returns to this state, one attains the commonality of human beings; through the taking of life, one becomes short-lived—this is the detailed explanation.
"This state" (*itthantva*) means being thus; its condition is "being thusness" (*itthantva*).

The teacher Saṅghabhadra maintains that "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) is the cause of similarity in body, sense-faculties, configuration, activity, food, and so forth, as well as the basis for mutual connection; however,
this has already been refuted by the very same [argument],
for we also accept it in this way.
But that homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is not a separate substance;
for it is those very conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) themselves that assume such a causal state.
Thus, the state of non-conception (*āsañjñika*) among the non-conceptual beings is the cessation of mind and mental factors.
Thus is the detailed explanation:
this is "non-ideation" (āsañjñika) because it belongs to those without ideation, or it is "non-ideation" because it exists among those without ideation.
It is called cessation (*nirodha*) because by means of it the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are ceased, or because it causes the mind and mental factors to cease; by means of it,
the mind and mental factors that exist in the future time are completely restrained for a certain period of time.
The meaning is that they do not obtain birth; that substance called "non-perception" (āsañjñika) is like the obstruction of river water.
The meaning is "like a bridge";
"like the intermediate dhyāna" means,
for example, those gods named Brahmapurohitas, some of whom— namely the Mahābrahmās— reside in a particular region within the intermediate dhyāna.

Likewise, those gods named Bṛhatphala are such that the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva) exist in their region, not in another realm; it should be understood that they possess perception at the time of birth and at the time of death.
Because of the binding of rebirth by the afflicted mind,
and because of the rule that death and birth occur in a state of equanimity,
[death occurs] due to the exhaustion of the formative forces of the previous meditative attainment.
The meaning is: "due to the exhaustion of the ripening cause characterized by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of the previous meditative attainment," because the fruit has been fully realized.
Others explain it as "due to the exhaustion of the projection (*āvedha*) of the formative forces of the previous meditative attainment."
"And because there is no accumulation of the unprecedented"—
the intention is that, due to the absence of consciousness, karma is not accumulated;
they are like arrows shot [into the air] whose momentum has been exhausted as they fall to the earth.
The word *upapadyante* was previously used in its primary sense of "being born";
now, by the force of the context, it has the sense of "going."
They "attain" means they "go";
the completion of the sentence is "they go to the earth," according to others.
The attainment of non-percipient beings, or the attainment that is non-perception, is the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This much is drawn along by the word "thus" (tathā),
because no specific meaning such as "maturation" (vipāka) and so forth is intended;
for the state of non-perception (āsañjñika) is indeed exclusively indeterminate (avyākṛta).
And it will be stated that this attainment is exclusively wholesome;
for it is said that "the five aggregates are maturation" because at the time of death and rebirth, there exists the state of maturation for the mind and mental factors.

Does one obtain that [attainment] from that very [state]? Because, even though one has fallen away, one is reborn among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) after having produced it again, therefore one obtains that [attainment]. One does not enter the fixed course of rightness (*niyāma*);

for it is only an Noble One who has entered the fixed course who attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of rebirth in the miserable destinies, among the non-percipient beings, as a Great Brahmā, or as a Kaurava, as well as of an eighth existence, and so forth.
"They view her as if she were a place of downfall" means they view her as if she were a state of miserable rebirth (apāya);
others say it is like a place of falling, such as a mountain precipice.
The meaning is that ordinary persons enter into that [attainment] perceiving it as an escape, perceiving it as liberation;
however, the noble ones do not attain it with such a perverted perception.
Regarding the phrase "like meditation":

because they have attained the fourth meditation (*dhyāna*), yogins obtain the past and future fourth meditation that was previously obtained during beginningless *saṃsāra*. Therefore, he asks: do they likewise obtain that [past and future] in the same manner?
If even others do not obtain them—
meaning that even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not obtain the past or future [attainments] of which they themselves possess this meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
how much less so the noble ones (*ārya*), for whom these are not their own?

"Even though it is appropriate" means that although it has been obtained previously in beginningless *saṃsāra*, it must be accomplished through great formative effort (*mahābhisaṃskāra*) and produced with great exertion;
furthermore, this is because it is a state of non-mentation (*acittakatva*).
The meaning is that it is acquired as belonging to a single time period (*ekādhvika*) and obtained as belonging to that same time period (*samānādhvika*),
just as in the case of the *prātimokṣa* restraint;
for even though the *prātimokṣa* restraint is of eight kinds, when it is formally undertaken...
Then that [attainment] is acquired,
and its acquisition arises at that very moment;
however, by means of that attained meditative attainment, one becomes possessed of it in the second and subsequent moments, just like the Prātimokṣa restraint.
As long as one does not abandon that meditative attainment,

it is not cultivated in the future; its abandonment occurs either through falling away (*parihāṇi*) or by shifting to another stage (*bhūmi-sañcāra*), and because it is without mental factors (*acaittika*), it is not cultivated in the future.

For a future wholesome mind is cultivated, but this [attainment] is not "without mind"; therefore, that which is called cessation is not cultivated in the same way as the future [wholesome mind]. Thus it is.
The word "attainment" (samāpatti) indeed carries over [from the previous context];
the particle "atha" is used for emphasis,

just as in the explanation of the attainment of non-perception (asañjñi-samāpatti), where by the word "atha" it is extended [to mean] that [this attainment] is the cessation of mind and mental factors (citta-caitta).
In the same way, here too, in the exposition of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), that very same type [of process] is extended by analogy:
"by means of mental attention preceded by the perception of a peaceful dwelling" (*vihāra*); here, *vihāra* refers to a dwelling such as a pleasure-grove (*krīḍāvihāra*).
A specific concentration that is peaceful is a peaceful dwelling;
the perception regarding the peaceful dwelling is the perception of peaceful dwelling.

"Preceded by the perception of peaceful abiding" means that the mental application (manasikāra) is preceded by the perception of peaceful abiding; this is expressed as "that mental application" (*sa manasikāra*) through an *aluk* compound.

For those who possess the perception of peaceful abiding become exhausted by the activity of perception and feeling (*sañjñā-vedita*), and it is by means of such mental application that they enter this attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
But that attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*) is preceded by the perception of deliverance— that is, preceded by the perception of liberation—
and it is "to be experienced in a subsequent existence" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*), where "subsequent existence" (*aparaparyāya*) refers to birth in the third lifetime or thereafter.
In that regard, how is it "to be experienced"?
It is when a noble one, having produced the attainment of cessation in the desire realm, is reborn in the peak of existence.
For him, that [attainment] is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) as it fulfills [the conditions for his birth].

However, for one who falls away from that state, is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and after some time again reaches the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), producing the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or not, and is subsequently reborn at the peak of existence— for him, that [attainment] becomes to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
But for one who would attain parinirvāṇa here,
their [attainment] is indefinite,
because of their fear of annihilation.
Because they fear the annihilation of their entire personal existence,
fools indeed suffer from the prospect of non-rebirth, as if from falling over a precipice;
why, then, does the fear of annihilation not arise regarding the attainment of non-perception?
In that state, because matter exists, they indeed form the notion of a self with respect to matter and enter into it;

however, in the attainment of cessation, since it belongs to the formless realm, matter is also absent. Seeing thus the absence of all personal existence, they do not venture to enter that attainment.

But surely, since dissociated factors such as the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exist in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), why do they not enter those attainments by adhering to the notion of a self (*ātmasañjñā*) therein?
[The answer is: because dissociated factors are invisible.
And because it is produced by the power of the noble path, how is it known that its production is by the power of the noble path? To this he says:
"Because of the conviction in that [nirvāṇa] by one who has attained nirvāṇa in the present life."
Nirvāṇa in the present life is "nirvāṇa in the seen dharma" (dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇa),
because of his resolute conviction in that.
"Tad" means resolve; "tad-adhimukti" means resolve upon that, or resolve by means of that. "Tad-adhimukteḥ" means from that resolve upon that.
The Noble One is convinced that "this is nirvāṇa in the present life";
however, some read it thus:
"because of his conviction in that [nirvāṇa] which has been seen."
And they explain it thus:
"Nirvāṇa has been seen by him," hence he is one who has "seen Nirvāṇa" (dṛṣṭanirvāṇa);
the resolute conviction of that noble one toward that [Nirvāṇa] is "resolute conviction in that" (tadadhimukti).
"Because of his resolve toward that, because of his resolve toward that"—
this is what is meant:
the Noble One who has seen nirvāṇa resolves upon it, and no one else.
But surely even an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) has seen nirvāṇa by means of the mundane path; yet, an ordinary person who has seen nirvāṇa would not be one who has attained nirvāṇa.
For an ordinary person, perceiving the stage immediately above that as peaceful, attains detachment but not Nirvana; thus, this objection is not valid.

This attainment is indeed obtainable through preparatory effort (*prayoga*), and like the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it is to be accomplished by means of great volitional effort (*mahābhisaṃskāra*).
In the same way, how is that which belongs to a single time-period obtained? To this he says: "And that which is past is not obtained."
When one who has fallen away from it produces it again, it is then obtained as something entirely new through formal application,
just like the *prātimokṣa* restraint; this should be explained in detail.
"By the power of the mind, through its cultivation"— this means by the power of the mind, through the cultivation of the future [state];
"attainable as enlightenment by the Sage."
This is an exception to the general rule that "this [knowledge] is obtainable only through preparatory practice" (*prayogalabhya*);
for, considering that this is the method for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, he will state that "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) consists of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Therefore, it is said in detail: "simultaneous with the knowledge of destruction" (*kṣayajñāna*).
And the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, attain these [qualities] together with the knowledge of destruction, which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
There is nothing for the Buddhas that is called "resulting from application" (*prāyogika*),
as it was said by the author of the hymn:
"O you who have reached the end of all that is wholesome, there is no wholesome [deed] of yours that results from application."
Since his power to resolve at will is bound by mere wish,
how then is the Blessed One "liberated in both ways"?
The obscuration of afflictions and the obscuration to meditative attainments constitute the two parts;
one who is liberated from these succeeds, just as if [the attainment] had already been produced.
The Blessed One, who is liberated in both ways, accomplishes it because he has attained mastery over it— as if it were previously manifested—
due to his possession of the capacity to bring it into manifestation.
"How much more so [the case of] her," and so forth.

This is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that a bodhisattva in his final existence, having attained the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and having generated the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) by relying on the fourth dhyāna, emerges from that and enters the peak of existence, and thereafter enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Then, having emerged from that state and again relying upon the fourth dhyāna, he effects the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). From the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) onward, he becomes one who is perfectly and unsurpassedly awakened (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbuddha*); thus, according to the Westerners (*pāścātyāḥ*), those who lived after the region of Kaśmīra, he produces that [knowledge] during the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*). "Netrīpada" is the name of the treatise belonging to the Elder Upagupta, in which this statement occurs: [The text continues with the citation: "Having attained the fruit of Arhatship, he does not produce the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) at that time; rather, he produces it later, when he has arisen from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Why? Because he has not yet abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation. Therefore, while still in the stage of a learner, he produces that [knowledge of non-arising]. This is the position of the Westerners. The term *pāścātyāḥ* refers to those who existed after (*paścād bhavāḥ*) the land of Kaśmīra. *Netrīpada* is the title of the treatise of the Elder Upagupta, in which this very passage is found.
It should be stated that having produced the attainment of cessation, one produces the knowledge of destruction; thus, regarding the Tathāgata,
it is said that [the realization] occurs through sixteen moments during the clear realization of the truths,
starting from the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the subsequent knowledge of the path— this being by means of sixteen mental moments.

And regarding detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are eighteen [moments]; that is, for the abandonment of the nine types of afflictions belonging to the peak of existence which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Thus, by means of these eighteen, these [moments] total thirty-four—namely, sixteen and eighteen.

The afflictions of the lower stages are not to be abandoned again; for since the afflictions belonging to the desire realm and so forth have already been abandoned during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) by means of the mundane path,
if this were the rule, then it would follow that one need not produce an antidote for afflictions already abandoned.

Now, for what purpose does one produce at the time of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*), which is the antidote to those afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm that have already been abandoned?
It is because the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*) is inseparable from it;
for without the arising of the category of dharma-knowledge, the manifestation of the category of subsequent knowledge is not possible.
For this is what constitutes the "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna) of subsequent knowledge—that it occurs after this [dharma-knowledge];
thus say the Westerners (pāścātya).
"What, then, would happen?"—this is the full statement.
"What fault would there be if one were to manifest a dissimilar, outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) in the interval?
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"There would be an intention to emerge [from meditative absorption]," and so forth.
Others say that a bodhisattva should have the intention to emerge [from meditative absorption] and should be skilled in emerging;
for the meaning of the basis (āśraya) is the meaning of the roots of virtue (kuśalamūla).
This is what is meant:

such are the roots of merit belonging to Bodhisattvas that, once they have become manifest, they do not rise from them until they have attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment while still on that very same seat;
so say the outsiders.
The truth is that it is based on non-arising, but not as you describe it;
rather, they have already described it previously according to the position that it occurs simultaneously with the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).
Although there are many kinds of distinctions between these two— such as one being in the final dhyāna and the other arising from the peak of existence (bhavāgra)— nevertheless...
One enters the first [attainment] with the perception of renunciation, while one enters the other out of a desire for abiding; such are the many kinds of distinctions between them.
However, their similarity lies in both having the realm of desire and the realm of form as their basis.
"Could there be a form-existence (*rūpabhava*)? and so forth.
Is every existence that is a form-existence necessarily an existence consisting of five aggregates (*pañcavyavacāra*)? This is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*):
there may be a form-existence that is not an existence consisting of five aggregates.

The existence (*bhava*) that belongs to the gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) who possess perception (*saññin*) while abiding in a dissimilar state of mind (*visabhāga-citta*), or those who have entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaññi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the gods without perception (*asaññin*) when the state of non-perception has been attained—
this is an existence consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-vyavacāra*) which is not an existence of the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*).
Likewise, it refers to the state of beings belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) who abide in a similar state of mind (*sabhāga-citta*).
There may be existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*), and that existence consists of five constituents.

This refers to the existence of gods belonging to the realm of form who possess perception and abide in a homogeneous state of mind, as well as the existence of non-perceiving gods (*asaṃjñisattva*) when the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) has not yet been attained. There may also be an existence that is neither existence in the realm of form nor an existence consisting of five constituents. This refers to the existence of those who have attained the state of non-perception.

The first alternative is illustrated by the existence of beings belonging to the desire realm who abide in a dissimilar state of mind, as well as those who have entered the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation, and by existence in the formless realm.
Form-existence (rūpabhava) is the fivefold aggregate belonging to the form realm;
"fivefold investigation" means the pentad of aggregates.
"Discrimination" (*vyavacāra*), according to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, refers to the specific engagement with the notion of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃjñā*);
"discrimination" means deception through a state of alteration.
The term *vyavacāra* means "that which possesses this [deceit]";
the suffix *a*, as in the rule *arśādibhyo 'c*, has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*),
meaning "deceptive."
Because form is like a mass of foam and feeling is like a bubble, and so forth, [the aggregates] are deceptive; therefore,
if the attainment of non-perception were not admitted in the realm of form, it would not have been stated that [beings] have entered the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation.
Therefore, it is reckoned as the attainment of non-perception belonging to the realm of form;
however, even there, this distinction exists—
meaning that despite the similarity in that regard, a distinction nevertheless occurs.

"Later, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu)" means that those noble ones who, having produced the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and subsequently fallen away from it, obtain meditative absorption (dhyāna) and are reborn in the realm of form—
they, having previously fallen away, would produce the attainment of cessation in the realm of form by virtue of their prior practice.

However, the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*) is produced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) even for the first time within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); this is its distinction.
Furthermore, because there is some possibility of falling away from it, this attainment is similar to *nirvāṇa*.
"How can there be falling away from this?"— thinking it impossible, he asks regarding the Udāyi-sūtra;
this sūtra was spoken by the noble Śāriputra.
However, because Udāyin was an obstacle in that matter, it is called the "Udāyi Sūtra.
How so?
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
Thereupon, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks:
"In this case, venerable ones, a monk is endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom;
he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling."
He understands as it truly is that "this possibility exists";
yet he does not attain final knowledge (ājñā) either in this very life while practicing,
nor at the time of death.

And through the dissolution of the body, having transcended the gods who subsist on physical food, he is reborn in a certain divine, mind-made body. Having been reborn there, he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling,
and he understands, as it truly is, that "this state exists."
Now at that time, the venerable Udāyin was seated and present in that very assembly. Then the venerable Udāyin said this to the venerable Śāriputra:

"It is impossible, venerable Śāriputra, it is out of the question, that a monk who has been reborn in some divine mind-made body should repeatedly enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling, yet know as it really is that such a thing is possible."
A second and even a third time, the Venerable Udāyin said this to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"This is impossible, Venerable Sir," as before.
Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Even though I have spoken to this monk up to three times, he continues to reject and oppose my words; yet not a single fellow-celibate among us approves of what I have said."
"What if I were now to approach the Blessed One?
Then the Venerable Śāriputra approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the monks:
"In this case, venerable ones, a monk is endowed with ethical discipline, as described previously."
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, as before, said this to the Venerable Śāriputra a second and a third time,
just as previously described.
Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Even before my Teacher, this monk has rejected and contradicted what was spoken up to three times,
and not a single fellow-practitioner of the holy life has approved of what I have said."
"What if I were to remain silent?
Then the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Udāyin.
"But which other divine, mind-made body do you perceive, Udāyin? Is it not simply one that is formless and consists of perception?
"It is so, Venerable Sir."

"Since you, being merely a blind man of delusion and lacking eyes, think you should converse on the Abhidharma and the Vinaya with the sighted monk Śāriputra," the Blessed One, having thus rebuked the Venerable Udāyin in his presence, addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda,
do you too overlook this elder monk while he is being harassed?"
"O deluded man, has even compassion not arisen in you toward an elder monk who is being harassed?
Having thus rebuked the Venerable Udāyin and the Venerable Ānanda in their presence, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"In this case, monks, a monk is endowed with virtuous conduct."
"He was perfected in concentration," and so on in detail, up until "he entered into seclusion.
At this point, the Venerable Udāyin, reflecting that "this mind-made body is said to belong to the formless realm," raised an objection;
for in that [formless realm], there is no form.
But the mind alone, together with its associated mental factors, exists; therefore, it is the "mind-made body.
And his intention is that this meditative attainment does not enter into that [body].
For the noble Śāriputra, however, the divine mind-made body belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) is intended, because it manifests without depending upon semen and blood;
for this very reason, the Blessed One asked the venerable Udāyin: "Udāyin, which other divine mind-made body do you perceive?"

Now, [it might be argued: "Since [the body] is formless and consists of perception," the Venerable Udāyin accepted this by saying, "So it is, Bhadanta. Yet the Blessed One, intending only the divine, mind-made body belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), supported the view of the noble Śāriputra and thereby rebuked that venerable Udāyin.

You, being merely a blind man of delusion, yet think that you should converse with the sighted monk Śāriputra regarding the Abhidharma and the Vinaya; and there is indeed this possibility— that you truly understand and practice this matter, namely the attainment and emergence from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)— meaning, as it has been from the very beginning.

The meaning is that one realizes the command, which is to say, one attains ultimate reality (*aty-arthatattva*). And this attainment belongs to the Peak of Existence (*bhāvāgrika*); such is the detailed explanation.
The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) belongs to the Peak of Existence.
And for one who attains that [attainment], rebirth would occur only at the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) and not in the realm of form (rūpadhātu);
and it is said in the Sūtra:
Having been reborn there in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñāveditanirodha);
therefore, it is understood that there is falling away from that state,
and this is indeed logical for the Vaibhāṣikas.
But for the Sautrāntikas, how is this [to be explained]?
For it is the established tenet of the Sautrāntikas that only an Ārya attains the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and there is no falling away from the Ārya-path;
yet, how can it be maintained that such an Ārya falls away from the Ārya-path belonging to a higher stage?
For them as well, this sūtra is not contradicted;
for how could anyone who has attained the peak of existence enter into the path of certainty?
Being a non-returner, he might produce the attainment of cessation; yet he could fall away from the peak of existence and from the attainment of cessation,
but not from the path.
Because the noble path of a higher stage has not necessarily been produced [previously],
one who has fallen away might produce a dhyāna and be reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu);
therefore, while there is falling away from this [attainment], there is no falling away from the noble path itself, and thus there is no contradiction with our own established doctrine.
The nine successive attainments refer to the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the attainment of cessation,
with respect to the first aeon.
The meaning, based on the rule for the attainment [of non-perception] from the beginning,
is that it is "to be experienced in both ways" because the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*) is necessarily to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya*).
The attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is to be experienced in both ways; the meaning is that it is both determinate and indeterminate as to when it will be experienced.
It is determinately experienced by non-returners (anāgāmin), and indeterminately experienced by arhats, because they attain final nirvana (parinirvāṇa) right here.
Regarding "also by way of initial production":
some first produce the attainment of non-perception among human beings, while others do so in the realm of form.
One produces the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) only among humans; however, one who has fallen away from it may produce it in the form realm (rūpadhātu).
Now, for what reason does one produce it only among humans?

An Anāgāmin who has become weary of the mental activity consisting of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and so forth, through the gateway of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*), produces the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with the thought, "May I dwell happily in that state.

However, an Anāgāmin reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) does not produce it for the first time there, because he is not so afflicted by the activity of the mental factors belonging to that realm due to the tranquility of the form realm;
yet, if he has fallen away from it, he produces it again through his previous practice.

Even one born in the formless realm does not produce [the thought of awakening] for this very reason, because of its tranquility; nor does one born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception produce it, lest there be the consequence of entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
For in that state, matter (*rūpa*) is absent, and if the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) were to cease, it would be his final passing away (*parinirvāṇa*).
Because mental factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) lack the capacity to exist in isolation,

and because they persist as obstacles to the completion of the fruit of karma that is necessarily to be experienced (*niyatavedanīya*), the possibility of final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) does not arise [from them]. However,
regarding the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), there arises the notion of liberation (*mokṣasañjñā*) due to the presence of the notion of escape (*niḥsaraṇasañjñā*).

However, one enters the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*) through a mental application preceded by the notion of deliverance, based on the notion that it is liberation; therefore, one enters it for the first time even within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the detailed question "Why, then, these two?"—the intention is that both of these attainments must be described as having the nature of the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittanirodha*).

"Because one practices for those two attainments by way of being adverse to them" means that because one practices for those two attainments by way of being adverse to perception and feeling, there is the practice for the attainment of non-perception by way of being adverse to perception, [as it is said]:
"Perception is a disease, perception is a thorn, perception is an abscess; this is peaceful, this is sublime," and so forth.

The application for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) by way of aversion toward perception and feeling is like the statement regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*);
for just as in the case of the statement regarding the knowledge of others' minds, it is not that minds are never known by means of that knowledge of others' minds.

And yet, because one first applies oneself with the thought, "I shall know the mind of another," it is called "knowledge of another's mind" (*paracittajñāna*) and not "knowledge of another's mental factors" (*paracittacaittajñāna*); likewise, here too, there is such a designation for these two attainments.

Regarding this, there is a difference in established doctrine: the Vaibhāṣikas and others maintain that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) are indeed without mind;
the Sthavira Vasumitra and others hold that they possess mind through a subtle and indistinct mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);
and the Yogācāras maintain that they possess mind through the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Therefore, this is proposed:
"How now [can it arise] from that which has ceased for a long time," and so forth.
The mention of "ceased for a long time" is for the purpose of excluding that which has ceased immediately prior.
The Vaibhāṣikas ask: "If you now accept that what has just ceased exists immediately after it has ceased, why do you not also accept that what has ceased long ago exists? [The opponent replies:

We do not say that there is existence of what has just ceased; rather, the present mind, having established itself as the causal condition for another mind, ceases while another arises, like the simultaneous lowering and raising of the ends of a balance scale.

That [mind] has ceased and another mind has arisen; thus, it is said that "one mind arises from a mind that has just ceased," because of the principle that "what is proximate to the present is treated as if it were present. Others, however—the Sautrāntikas—say:
"How, then, for those born in the formless realm," and so forth—
the word "first" (*tāvat*) signifies sequence;
the meaning is that this very point must first be stated as an illustration.
For the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is not admitted for matter;
how then does it arise? We say that it is born from that very mind, and not from matter.

Regarding the inquiry: "For these two are mutually seed-bearing; thus, the seed of the body together with its sense faculties exists in the mind, and the seed of the mind exists in the body together with its sense faculties."
The treatise named *Paripṛcchā* is the work of the Elder Vasumitra;
in it he states that he also possesses other treatises, such as the *Pañcavastuka*.
Therefore, he specifies that "the fault belongs to him alone";
what, then, is that fault?
Now, what is this that was said regarding "the conjunction of the three"— namely, the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness— arising from a mind that has already ceased for a long time?
The Venerable Vasumitra holds this view: that even though that attainment of cessation possesses mind, there would otherwise be no cessation of perception and feeling therein;
therefore, in that attainment of cessation, there is indeed the cessation of perception and feeling.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka formulates this logical consequence:
"born of contact associated with ignorance" means that contact conjoined with ignorance is "contact associated with ignorance."
Therefore, that which is born from it is born from contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*),
but not [at the moment] of the arising of feeling (*vedanā*); thus,
at the time of the arising of feeling, contact is not specified in such a way as "this kind of contact is the condition for feeling."
The Venerable Ghoṣaka himself summarizes this:
"Therefore, they are without mind.
[An objection is raised: "How can that which is without mind be an attainment (*samāpatti*)?"

It deserves to be called "attainment" (samāpatti) such as the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and so forth, because by means of concentration (samādhi), the mind and mental factors are made even (sama) and focused on a single object; thinking thus, he asks:
"because of the production of the equilibrium of the great elements."
What is "attainment" (*samāpatti*)? It is that by which the great elements (*mahābhūta*) reach a state of equilibrium.
Thus, this state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), as well as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth, possess the nature of an attainment.
But what, in this context, is the equilibrium of the great elements?
They come together with those states that are contrary to the arising of the thought of enlightenment;
thus, they enter into them, they come together with them— therefore it is "attainment" (*samāpatti*), a term derived from the object of the action (*karmasādhana*).
The meditations (*dhyāna*) and so forth also arise for the yogin;
therefore, the meditations and so forth also possess the nature of attainment (*samāpatti*) as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) by way of their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).
Because they obstruct the arising of the thought of enlightenment,
since they prevent the arising of that thought.
"By the very mind of attainment"—
this is not so;
why?
The meaning is that it is by means of the very mind of attainment (*samāpatti-citta*) that there is an obstruction to that [mind],
namely, an obstruction to the arising of the mind; he explains how this is so as follows:
"For it is the very mind of attainment," and so forth;
that very mind of attainment arises, and no other substance, as something opposed to other minds— that is, opposed to future minds.
By means of that mind, there occurs for a period of time a mere non-occurrence that is not absolute;
the word "mere" (mātra) is intended to exclude any other substance,
because it brings about a substratum opposed to that [mind].
Because it brings about a continuum of a basis that is opposed to the mind,
this mere non-occurrence is designated as "meditative attainment" (samāpatti).

The meaning is that this is a phenomenon of designation (*prajñapti-dharma*) and not a substantial phenomenon (*dravya-dharma*). If it is not a substantial phenomenon, how is it designated as "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)? To this he says:
"And that is merely non-occurrence."

"It did not exist previously, nor does it exist for the yogin who has emerged from it"— thus, whether it be the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), this meditative attainment is designated as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) by way of conventional usage, but not as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
"Or rather," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The meaning of "this attainment" is that which is produced by an attainment;
and since that specific state did not exist previously and does not exist afterwards for one who has emerged from it, its conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) is established—this is the meaning.
The same applies to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), and so forth.

The intention is that this yogi designates "mind" itself as being opposed to the activity of mind within those [beings] lacking perception (*asañjñin*), but it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*).
As for the detailed explanation beginning with "of heat," the activity of both heat and consciousness is dependent upon life-force (*jīvita*).

Therefore, vitality is said to be the support of heat and consciousness; it is their cause of persistence. [If it were otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of their never ceasing, and thus a perpetual stream of these would result.

The "projection of the duration of existence for the homogeneous class" (nikāyasabhāga) has been explained; that homogeneous class consists of those very conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) whose intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the aggregates (skandha) such as form (rūpa) and so forth.
Their "duration" is the continuity;
its "time" is as long as they must remain, which consists of exactly that many moments of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Its "propulsion" (āvedha) consists in the establishment of the state of being a cause for the karma of a previous birth at the moment of rebirth-linking;
what, then, is this cause?
It is a specific capacity (sāmarthya-viśeṣa).
For it is the cause of the duration characterized by the continuity of the aggregates through a succession of moments;
for this very reason, it is called the "impulse of the period of duration," because its characteristic is the projection of the stream for that length of time.
It remains for that long;
that homogeneous class [of beings] is like the momentum of grain toward the time of its ripening.

Just as the momentum that impels the ripening time of crops— a specific capacity inherent in the seed— is imparted to the sprout itself, which, through a succession of moments, becomes the cause of the series of the crop until the time of ripening; so too is this [the case with the arrow], like the momentum that impels the duration of flight of a discharged arrow.
Just as the "staying" (*sthiti*) of a discharged arrow is its arising in successive points of space, which is a continuity of a series;
the "time" (*kāla*) is the limit (*maryādā*) beyond which that [staying] does not occur; and the "impelling cause" (*āvedha*) is the establishment of the causal condition for it.
What, then, is this cause? It is a specific capacity produced by the element of wind (vāyu-dhātu), which arises from an excellence of effort;
just as the momentum (āvedha) that sustains the flight-time of a discharged arrow is not a separate substance, so too should this momentum characterized as life-span (āyus) be understood.
But as for the Vaiśeṣika who thinks that "saṃskāra" (impulse) is a specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*),

[he holds that] this Vaiśeṣika quality called *saṃskāra*— which is born of action and is the cause of action, known by the second name "velocity" (*vega*)— is produced in an arrow within the earth and other elements.
Regarding that quality by virtue of which the arrow's motion continues until its fall,
this is not a valid example;
for indeed, there exists a distinct entity called "impulse" (*saṃskāra*).
Thinking that lifespan might also be thus, the Master refutes that view with the words "of that," and so forth.
For that Vaiśeṣika, because of the oneness of that [soul], because of the oneness of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*),
and because of the absence of an obstruction— that is, the absence of an obstruction characterized by the rebounding against wood and so forth—
what [would happen]?
There would be no possibility of differences in the time of arrival— whether it be a swift, swifter, or swiftest arrival— at various other locations;
for by what means could there be such a swift, swifter, or swiftest arrival?
Its time, along with other locations such as points of space and so forth,
constitutes its differentiation.
Its non-occurrence is as follows:

reaching various other locations at speeds that are fast, faster, and fastest is not possible due to these two previously mentioned reasons; furthermore, because the momentum (*saṃskāra*) remains undifferentiated, a falling down is also impossible.
Furthermore, the falling of the arrow is not possible as long as the formative force (*saṃskāra*) exists;
for it is not accepted that an effect does not arise when its cause is present.
If it is argued that there is an obstruction by the wind—that is, the opinion might be that the wind acts as an obstacle here—[the response follows].

Regarding the statement, "Due to specific obstructions, differences in the time of reaching [the goal]—whether faster, slower, or most rapid—as well as falling, are possible," it is here replied: there would be the consequence of falling prematurely; that is, immediately after the separation from the bowstring, or even before [the arrow reaches its destination], it would fall due to contact with the wind. If, on the other hand, it were obstructed by the wind and thus did not fall prematurely, it would either never fall at all, or else it would not fall even later. This is the meaning.
For what reason? Because there is no distinction in wind;
for just as there is wind nearby, so too is there wind at a distance.

The fourth [reason] is "due to the avoidance of irregularity," meaning that when life has been exhausted through the avoidance of irregularities such as overeating, the exhaustion of merit has no efficacy regarding death.
Therefore, the third alternative is not attained;
thus, when there is the destruction of both, death occurs "from the destruction of both," which means "when there is the destruction of both."

This meaning—that death occurs from the exhaustion of both—should be understood as having been stated here; how is it known that death also occurs from the exhaustion of the life-span? It is known through the analogy with crops and the like.

For when the penetration of the seed of crops and the like has perished, even though other conditions such as soil and water are present, the cessation of the continuum is observed; this occurs because the seed has not reached the time of fruition or the time of ripening due to its lack of substantiality,
and even when a substantial seed is projected, the cessation of the continuum is observed due to the absence of conditions for its persistence and growth, such as water and so forth.
It is observed that even in the absence of the conditions for the projection, maintenance, and growth of the substantial seed,
when the projection of the seed has come to an end and there is an absence of water—

even though the projection of the substantial seed and the conditions for its maintenance and growth by means of water and so forth are present— the cessation of the continuum of crops and the like is observed due to the intervention of mobile beings and other factors.
This is the opinion of the Bahirdeśikas: that [vitality] is the basis of which, when impaired, [the body] is impaired, because [the body] is dependent upon its continuity;
thus, that vitality is the obstruction to the continuity of the basis, and is therefore said to be "bound to the continuity."
Even in the view of the Kaśmīras, the meaning is the same;
only the terminology differs, as they speak of it as "with an interval" (sāntarāya) or "without an interval" (nirantarāya).

Alternatively, "bound to a continuity" means bound to one's own continuity; it exists only as part of a continuum and does not remain having arisen all at once. Thus, by this scriptural passage, it is said to be "interrupted. Showing that untimely death is possible, he says in the Sūtra: "There are four ways of obtaining a personal existence," and so forth.
It should be stated that there is volition directed toward oneself, which is killing by oneself; volition directed toward another, which is killing by another; and [the case] of the Buddhas.
