Does one's own volition alone proceed [toward death], since death occurs spontaneously?
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are generally characterized by being beyond harm and have attained mastery over the relinquishing of their lifespan;
the inclusion of the word "generally" is for the purpose of excluding those mentioned in the fourth category, such as hell-beings and intermediate state beings,
while "royal sages" refers to those who previously were universal monarchs and later went forth into homelessness.

A messenger of the Victor (*jinadūta*) is anyone dispatched as a messenger by the Blessed Buddha; for example, a certain parrot sent by the Blessed One to Āmrapālī, who was seen by the Licchavis while they were practicing [archery] and could not be killed even though they covered him with a net of arrows?

For as long as he does not perform his duty as a messenger, neither one’s own intention (*ātmasañcetanā*) nor another’s intention (*parasañcetanā*) can take effect—[the former because] he has been commanded by the Victor that "he must live for this long," and [the latter because] he has not yet been seen by the Blessed One.
Dharmila and others are to be understood as having come from those who know the previous yogas; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), others are also to be understood as having come from that same source.
For them, neither self-intention (*ātmasaṃcetanā*) nor the intention of another (*parasamcetanā*) operates.
And for those in their final existence who attain arhatship in that very same birth— for the mother of a bodhisattva who is pregnant with a bodhisattva,
and for the mother of a wheel-turning monarch who is pregnant with a wheel-turning monarch— there is neither volition by oneself nor volition by another.
If, then, for all those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness there is neither self-intention nor intention by another, why was it said in the Sūtra [as detailed above]?

And because both are absent there—in that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)—the noble path belonging to that level does not exist, since it is stated: "As long as there is the attainment of perception, so long is there the penetration of full knowledge."

Nor is it the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of a higher level, because there is no noble path belonging to a level above that; rather, it belongs to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*),
due to the manifestation of the noble path of nothingness, while at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Because of this statement,
since "paryanta" (limit/end) is included,
the word "tarhi" is a particle used when one intends to express a different meaning [from what has preceded].

Regarding the phrase "the comprehension of that and so forth": the "beginning" (*ādi*) of that culminating sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) consists of the four dhyānas and the remaining three formless attainments (*ārūpya*);
however, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not its beginning, because it is dissimilar due to its lack of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*).

Alternatively, from the perspective of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it refers specifically to the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) because of the statement that "the nine successive attainments have those as their beginning"; thus,
conviction regarding them is "conviction regarding that beginning."
"Is this seen elsewhere as well? He replied, "It exists," beginning with "in some places" and ending with "at the limit," and so forth;
for example, "the gods of the Brahma-body."

The gods of the Brahma-realm (brahmakāyika), and by including those up to that limit, the Brahmapurohitas and Mahābrahmās constitute the first "arising of happiness" (sukhopapatti); for example, as with the Ābhāsvara gods— by including those starting from the Ābhāsvaras, the Parīttābhas and Apramāṇābhas constitute the second "arising of happiness."

For it is said: "There are exactly three rebirths in happiness; there are nine rebirths in happiness consisting of the three levels of the three dhyānas. Thus, only three are accepted as rebirths in happiness.
For this is the nature of an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntadharma*):
it is the practice of an illustration that one points out even a single instance of that type, and not everything, yet there is a comprehension of the remainder;
for example: "Sound is impermanent."
Because of being produced,
just as a jar; by this [statement], cloth and so forth are also included, since the word "tadyathā" (for example/just as) expresses an illustrative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"This is an *anupasaṃhāra*" means that it is without an example;
[the subjects are] "human beings and certain gods."

Thus, some say that there are only the gods of the six desire-realm heavens and the gods born in the first dhyāna—excluding those who have just been reborn—and that these alone are the beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; there are no others besides these. Therefore, this word *tadyathā* (for example) is not used here to express an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); rather, it should be understood as being for the purpose of demonstration (*upadarśana*).
And since it serves the purpose of demonstration, that very point remains established.
Because the mention of the "end" implies the understanding of that which precedes it,
[the term] "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) is used by way of contrast,
since these [characteristics] do not exist therein.
If it is asked, "Is that unconditioned?"— surely stability (*sthiti*) is a characteristic of the unconditioned;
yet there is no stability of the unconditioned that exists as a distinct entity (*dravyāntara*).
Since the conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are intended here as being of the nature of distinct entities (*dravyāntara*), this is not to be questioned.
But how is it that [the text] says, "These three," and so forth? [How can they be three if they are distinct entities?]
In the Sūtra it is said: "O monks, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
What are the three?
O monks, the arising of the conditioned is also discerned."
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that since both decay and the alteration of duration are also discerned, a fourth [characteristic] should also be mentioned here.
Furthermore, what has not been stated here? The opponent asks this, and the Vaibhāṣikas reply: "It is 'stability' (sthiti).
[The opponent objects: "In that case, since this term 'stability' is heard here in the phrase 'change of stability' (sthity-anyathātva), [how can it be said that it was not mentioned]?"
The intention of the objector is this: "How can it be said that 'stability' is not mentioned?
This is a synonym for aging; thus, this aging has been described as 'the alteration of stability' (*sthity-anyathātva*)."
Just as "arising" is a synonym for birth and "passing away" is a synonym for impermanence, so too "alteration of state" is a synonym for aging.
But why, when there are four characteristics, did the Blessed One speak of only three? To this he says:
"For those phenomena... and so forth.
The characteristics of phenomena—birth, aging, and impermanence—have been taught for the purpose of instilling a sense of urgency in those to be trained;
for the teaching in the Sūtras is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), not definitive in its characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*) as it is in the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, aging and impermanence [are defined] as that which passes from the present into the past.
The governing term "transfers" (*sañcārayati*) continues [from the previous context]. Aging and impermanence transfer [the conditioned entity] from the present time-period to the past time-period;
why? Because they weaken it and obstruct it.
Since it is said that "aging weakens" and "impermanence destroys," is it not impermanence itself that causes a phenomenon to transition from the present time-period to the past time-period?
It is not old age that is old age;
for it is merely old age that weakens the Dharma.
Why, then, is it said thus?

Regarding aging and impermanence: since they cause [a dharma] to transition from the present to the past, it is said that even the act of weakening functions solely for the sake of that transition between time-periods (*adhvan*); for there is no transition between time-periods for that which has not been weakened. Thus, aging is also established as being involved in that transition.

Furthermore, because even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) possesses the state of abiding in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇasthitibhāva*), its "abiding" (*sthiti*) was not established as a [separate] characteristic;

for [if it were], it would be identical to the characteristic of abiding that is defined by the non-distinction of being unconditioned. Thus, the intention of the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, was that he did not state a [separate] characteristic for that unconditioned entity, in order to avoid the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it becoming conditioned.
Others, however,
imagine that even in the Sūtra stability (sthiti) is mentioned;
they say that by combining both stability and aging, the Sūtra has stated a single characteristic by combining them as "stability" and "alteration of stability" (*sthity-anyathātva*).
Why not [distinguish them] individually?
Because it would entail a contradiction with the statement: "These three are the characteristics of the conditioned."
To the question, "What is the purpose here?", he says:
"For this is the basis of attachment among these," and so forth.

For this state (*sthiti*) is the locus of attachment, the place of clinging, among these [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and the rest; the intention is that by means of this [state], phenomena (*dharma*) abide. Just as one might show prosperity accompanied by the "ear of death" (*kālakarṇī*), or fortune accompanied by misfortune, the Blessed One showed this state to be accompanied by misfortune, for the sake of non-attachment toward that state.
"One should not form an attachment to this [body], because it is bound by impermanence, like prosperity that is followed by misfortune"—this is one interpretation;
others, however, explain:
"One should not cultivate [attachment] toward this [body], because it is bound by old age, like prosperity that is followed by misfortune."
For, because this [conditioned thing] is unified with aging— which is characterized by change— rather than with impermanence, there are therefore exactly four characteristics of the conditioned;
this is the conclusion for both positions.
Since it must be accompanied by other factors such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth,
by the power of birth, some conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arises; thus,
birth itself is also conditioned.
Therefore, that [birth] must also have another birth, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself,
and because of the established tenet that "everything is characterized by the conditioned characteristics.
The same logic should be applied to aging and the others as well.
"Birth-of-birth and so forth are for them," and "and birth-of-birth and so forth are for them"— here the word "and" (ca) should be understood as having been elided.
Now, as for the passage beginning with "for each one," and so forth...
For each individual characteristic, there would result a "four-characteristic set" (catur-lakṣaṇī)— that is, a collection of four characteristics—

and there would follow the fault of infinite regress (aparyavasāna-doṣa) and the fault of non-termination (aniṣṭhā-doṣa), because those secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) would again entail further [characteristics] such as birth (jāti) and so forth.
Because of the consequence that for every birth there would be a birth of birth, and so on up to impermanence, an impermanence of impermanence, and an impermanence of that impermanence— therefore,
these [characteristics] function upon a single dharma;
the masculine gender used in the word "te" (they) is employed because of its connection with the word "dharmas."
Those phenomena, such as birth and so forth, which have as their intrinsic nature the "birth of birth" and so on, function respectively with respect to eight phenomena and one phenomenon:
the functions of birth and the others pertain to eight phenomena, while the functions of the "birth of birth" and the others pertain to one phenomenon.
For it is said thus with reference to the primary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), taking the self as the ninth;

for it is not the case that, according to possibility, acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth, or the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*), do not arise there in the desire realm. [In that case,] it consists of eight substances (*aṣṭadravyaka*) when sound is absent.
"Everything [is associated] with the characteristics of the conditioned or with acquisition," and so forth; thus,
birth [exists] apart from itself, and so on in detail.
Because there is a contradiction in [a factor] acting upon itself, it therefore produces eight factors excluding itself.
Which eight?

It produces that factor—whether it be matter (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)—as well as its subsistence (*sthiti*), aging (*jarā*), impermanence (*anityatā*), birth-of-birth (*jātijāti*), subsistence-of-subsistence (*sthitisthiti*), aging-of-aging (*jarājarā*), and impermanence-of-impermanence (*anityatānityatā*).
But birth gives rise to that very birth;
in the same way, old age and impermanence are also to be applied accordingly.
Thus, old age, setting itself aside, causes eight factors to decay.
Furthermore, decay-within-decay, having separated itself from that very decay, destroys eight factors; and impermanence, in turn,
destroys that very impermanence.
The intention here is that "this space is being split" means it is being divided;
space is merely the absence of any resistant substance.
Just as there is no such thing called "space" that can be divided, nor is it possible or logical to do so,
even so these non-existent phenomena such as birth and the rest cannot be divided, nor is it possible or logical to do so.
Then he says,
"For these do not exist," and so forth;
for these do not exist as substantial entities with their own specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) in the manner in which they are analyzed.
Birth produces eight factors excluding itself; thus they are analyzed in detail, just as in the case of the factors such as form (*rūpa*).
Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of sound and so forth, feeling and so forth, and the eye and so forth.
In this regard, form, sound, and so forth are first apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is characterized as visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) and the rest;
feeling (*vedanā*) and the other [mental factors] are also apprehended by direct perception itself because they are self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*);
however, the eye and the other [faculties] are inferred by inference (*anumāna*) based on visual consciousness and the rest.
The supports for visual consciousness and the others are the ten material forms, such as the eye and so forth; because when these exist or do not exist, those [consciousnesses] exist or do not exist.
There is also scripture to this effect: "Having seen forms with the eye," and so forth;
likewise, "having heard sounds with the ear," and so forth in detail; and the same should be applied to odors and the rest.
Likewise, whatever form there is—past, future, or present—and so forth; this same principle should be applied to feeling and the other aggregates as well.

However, the existence of non-material phenomena such as feeling belonging to another continuum is inferred from observing a change in one's own body and recognizing its correspondence [to those mental states].
Scripture also states: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; simultaneously born with it are feeling, perception, and volition," and so forth.
However, birth and the other [characteristics] are not perceived directly by the visual faculty and the like, nor is there any inference capable of establishing their existence.
Nor is scripture [the sole authority] for existence as a substantial entity;
for it has been stated in detail in the Sūtra, "That which was said in the Sūtra," and so forth,
and the Blessed One has declared that the meaning (*artha*) is the refuge.
Monks, there are these four reliances.
What are the four?
The Dharma is the reliance, not the person.
The meaning is the reliance, not the letter;
the sūtra of definitive meaning is the reliance, not the one of interpretable meaning; primordial wisdom is the reliance, not consciousness.
In that way, one relies on the meaning and not on the letter;
but what, then, is the meaning of this?
He states the meaning of this cited Sūtra on the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇasūtra*) as follows: "For the foolish are blinded by ignorance," and so forth.

The meaning is that those who are convinced of the continuity of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-prabandha*) as being the self or belonging to the self, having developed a taste for them, become attached to them.
"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) are synonyms; that which is produced by conditions coming together and combining is "conditioned."
"Dependent-origination" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) means that which has arisen in dependence upon this or that condition;
it does not refer to a single moment.
Desiring to show that conditionedness (*saṃskṛtatva*) belongs only to the continuum (*pravāha*), he says this.

But the conditioned nature of a moment [is not established], for the characteristics of a moment—namely the phenomena characterized by arising, cessation, duration, and change—are not perceived; this is because a moment is difficult to discern. If you should say that even though these are not being perceived, they ought to be the characteristics, he says:
And these, not being perceived, cannot constitute a characteristic;
for only that which is perceived constitutes a characteristic, just as, for example, the crane is the characteristic of water.
For this very reason, the word "is known" (*prajñāta*) is included here in this sūtra;
otherwise, he would have simply said: "The conditioned has arising, passing away, and change-while-enduring."

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of the conditioned," the term "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is mentioned again in order to grasp the meaning that these are the characteristics *of* the conditioned. This is an example by way of contrast (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), like a crane and water: just as a crane is a characteristic for the existence of water, but it is not a characteristic for the "waterness" of the water itself.
Let it not be understood thus:
that these characteristics exist at the very beginning of a conditioned entity.
Or, regarding goodness and badness, it is like the characteristics of a maiden;
just as a maiden has auspicious and inauspicious characteristics, so too are there characteristics for goodness and badness.
For if these were accepted as characteristics for the existence, goodness, or badness of a conditioned thing, then one would say, "These three are the characteristics of the conditioned."
If it were not stated that "the conditioned has the characteristics of the conditioned," then by the very fact that they have been so stated,
it would be understood that these are the characteristics of being conditioned.
But how, then, are birth and the other [characteristics], which do not exist [as separate entities], established or discerned within the continuum?
We do not say that birth and the others do not exist; rather, we say that they are not differentiated as having the nature of substantial entities (*dravya*).
We say that they do not exist in such a manner as they appear to you; therefore, let it be explained how they do exist for you.
Therefore he says:
"The beginning of the stream is arising," and so forth;
"the cessation is passing away."
The cessation of the flow is its passing away;
that very flow, as it continues,
is the "continuing" flow due to the persistence of similar moments.
"Stability" is so called;
its "distinction between earlier and later" refers to the distinction of the later moment from the preceding one.

The "distinction between the preceding and succeeding moments" refers to the difference between those two moments; and it was stated with this understanding in mind— that is, by treating arising and so forth as having the nature of a continuous flow— that the discourse concerning the Venerable Sundarananda began by establishing the constant presence of mindfulness regarding impermanence.

For his sensations, occurring as a continuous flow, arise as if already known, persist as if already known, and reach their exhaustion and termination as if already known; they do not occur as discrete moments,
because a moment is difficult to discern and because it is impossible for a known moment to endure.
Summarizing this very point in two verses, he says:
"Birth is the beginning of the stream," and so forth; all has been stated.
But "abiding" (sthiti) is that very [stream]; thus, that same flow is abiding.
"Of that very [stream]" means of that very stream; "its cessation" means its cutting off.
"The cessation of the continuity of a momentary phenomenon," so says the verse.
The meaning is that a phenomenon, being momentary, would perish without [any] duration.
If you think that stability exists,
even that dharma perishes; for despite the presence of stability, it nonetheless vanishes due to its momentariness.
Because there is no cause for destruction,
the conceptualization of that [destruction] is therefore futile;
the meaning is that it is purposeless with respect to the conceptualization of duration.
For the conceptualization of "staying" would not be in vain only if it existed through the persistence of subsequent moments;
therefore, the stream itself is staying,
because for a phenomenon that is momentary, the conceptualization of staying is indeed useless.
And having established it thus, the meaning of "this too" is that stability is merely a continuous flow;
for there is no non-destruction of a moment once it has arisen.
In this regard, someone might have the following thought:
"Because of the existence of duration, there is non-destruction for one moment of a dharma that has arisen;
for if duration did not exist..."
Even that single moment would not exist,
because its existence is preceded by causes and conditions.

If it should be thought that "stability" (sthiti) sustains [a phenomenon] because of the statement, "When this exists, that comes to be," such that stability sustains the phenomenon arising from causes and conditions;
If stability were not to sustain it, what would happen?
The self-existence of the phenomenon would not exist;
thus, stability would result in being merely a producer, not a stabilizer.
If it is argued that [the cause] "establishes the continuum," then the designation "stability" would apply to the causes and conditions,
because the causes and conditions are the cause of the continuum.

The intention is that it is logical for the mind to belong to a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*); thus, even though there are many minds within a single homogeneous class, they are called "one" because they have arisen from the same homogeneous class.
That mind can be said to be "one mind" because otherwise, how could there be birth, death, and alteration within a single moment of consciousness? Furthermore,
its persistence (*sthiti*) is defined as the continuous succession of subsequent moments.
The subsequent moment is a substitute for the preceding moment because of its similarity;
therefore, considering that the preceding moment still persists as it were, the subsequent moment is called "staying" (*sthiti*).
This is so when similar [moments] arise.
When things arise as similar,
there is no dissimilarity;
and this dissimilarity is said to be the alteration of duration (*sthity-anyathātva*).

Therefore, the intention is that if [change] were produced from something similar, there would be no "alteration of duration" (*sthityanyathātva*), and thus the definition would be underinclusive (*avyāpin*).
This is explained in detail by the phrase "of what is thrown, not thrown, strongly thrown, or weakly thrown":
that which is both thrown (*kṣipta*) and not thrown (*akṣipta*) is "thrown-and-not-thrown" (*kṣiptākṣipta*).
That which is thrown by the strong and the weak is "thrown-by-the-strong-and-weak";
that which is both thrown and not thrown is "thrown-and-not-thrown"; and that which is both thrown-and-not-thrown and thrown-by-the-strong-and-weak—what is that?
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "vajra etc.," iron, stone, and so forth are included;
others, however, analyze the compound in this way:
"Thrown" (*kṣipta*) and "not thrown" (*akṣipta*) constitute the pair "thrown and not thrown.
These two are thrown by the strong and the weak, respectively; thus, "thrown by the strong" and "thrown by the weak" are a twofold division of that which is simply "thrown."

In this analysis— *kṣiptākṣipta* (thrown and not thrown), *balidurbalakṣipta* (thrown by the strong and the weak), and *kṣiptākṣiptabalidurbalakṣipta* (thrown and not thrown by the strong and the weak)—
the term "vajra" and so forth is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for that which begins with the vajra. Thus, in this compound, "vajra" and so forth [is the qualifier].
The object to be qualified is that which is thrown by one who is either weak or strong;
for such [an object] as a vajra and so forth, there is a falling—either slow or quick—according to the circumstances.
In the case of what is thrown by a weak person, the fall is slow.
That which is not projected falls after a long time; that which is projected with weakness falls quickly;
that which is projected with strength falls even more quickly.
Its time is the division of time,
due to the distinction between long and short durations of falling away.

It is a specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) such as diamond and so forth that constitute those [substances]; by means of which, for a thrown object, there is a transformation into another state such that its fall is delayed,
and likewise, up to a heavy object, there is a transformation into another state such that its fall is more rapid.
The establishment of that specific transformation;
because of the establishment of that specific transformation, they do not remain without distinction—this is the subject under discussion.
"Then [what of] the last one? and so forth is the detailed explanation.

Regarding sound and the flame of a lamp or similar phenomena, at the final moment— whether at the time of the cessation of the continuum or at the time of nirvana without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa)— there is no duration for that sixfold sense-base (ṣaḍāyatana), because there is no subsequent moment.

Since there is no duration, there is no "alteration of duration"; thus, the definition established as "the state of being dissimilar from that which has duration is the alteration of duration" results in a definition that is not universally applicable.
It is said that change necessarily occurs for that which lacks the alteration of its duration;
for this was stated in the Sūtra with reference to the possibility [of such change], namely: "There are these three characteristics of the conditioned."

Therefore, another teacher says that for the final moment of a sound, a flame, and so forth, only two characteristics— arising and passing away— are intended; however, for others, there is also the characteristic of duration-alteration (*sthityanyathātva*).
Even for those things such as the final sound or the momentary flame, there is duration, which is their own abiding;
and there is their alteration relative to the preceding moment.
Therefore, the three characteristics of the conditioned are established for them as well.
How is it now that the very same dharma is both the characterized object (*lakṣya*) and its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*);
for those who perceive the characterized and the characteristic as distinct from one another— like a crane and the water [upon which it stands]— raise this objection.
Challenging this [position], the Sautrāntikas say: "How then [can it be said that] the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa) [are not distinct from the person]?
Because the marks of a Great Man are comprised within the Great Man himself, they are not other than him."
One might say: "A Great Person is not merely the marks of a Great Person;
rather, it is merely a phenomenon (dharma) that comes into being after not having been, and ceases to be after having been. To this we reply: this is without an illustrative example.
This is exactly the same:

for just as the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa) are called both "Great Man" and "marks of a Great Man," so too a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) is called both "conditioned" and a "characteristic of the conditioned" (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa).
For that phenomenon (dharma) is characterized by a specific state such as arising and so forth; and when a state characterized by a continuum is established,
then the whole (samudāya) is characterized by its constituent parts (samudāyin).
Just as the collection designated as a "great man" is [defined] by the great-man marks which are its constituent parts,
by this the same is explained for the characteristics such as the dewlap and so forth, as well as for those such as hardness and so forth; such is the detailed explanation.
This example is established for both [parties], because it is established by the scriptural tradition;
for the earth-element is said to have the characteristic of hardness,
and there is no hardness other than the earth-element.
In this way, it should be applied everywhere:
for that very earth-element, being perceived as hardness, is called the characteristic of hardness;
and this very same conditioned thing, being perceived as having existed after not having existed and having ceased to exist after having existed, is called the characteristic of the conditioned.
It is called a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) because it is that by which something is characterized; yet it is not distinct from that [which it characterizes],
just as in the detailed explanation beginning with "by upward movement."

For the Vaibhāṣika who maintains the doctrine of momentariness, the upward movement of smoke is nothing other than that very same smoke arising continuously in successive points of space above; it receives the designation "upward movement," and thus that upward movement appears as if distinct from the smoke itself.
And the upward movement of smoke is not held to be something other [than smoke],
nor is that [movement] different from it;
nor is that upward movement other than that smoke.
The same logic applies here:
thus, arising, destruction, and alteration appear as if distinct from it,
yet there is no conditioned phenomenon that exists apart from the conditioned itself.

Furthermore, the conditioned nature of conditioned phenomena such as form and so forth is not perceived even by one who grasps their intrinsic nature, as long as their prior non-existence is not known— that is,
as long as the absence of those forms and so forth prior to their arising is not known.
And since it continues that "the distinction is not known until later," therefore, a thing is not characterized by itself; that is,
being-conditioned (saṃskṛtatva) is not characterized by that very same state of being conditioned.
Rather, that state of being conditioned (*saṃskṛtatva*) is characterized by prior non-existence and so forth;

for if one were to grasp it as "conditioned" while grasping the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and the other aggregates, then—without knowing their prior non-existence, their subsequent non-existence, and the distinction within the continuum—it would be characterized by that [nature] alone. But since one does not know it in this way, it is not characterized by that [nature] alone.
Furthermore, genus (*jāti*) and the other [characteristics] do not exist as substances distinct from the three, such as form (*rūpa*),
because it is stated in detail that "genus is the beginning of the stream."
Because these [factors], such as birth (jāti) and so forth, are co-existent— that is, because they arise at the same time— there is no distinction in their timing of activity.
This is not so;
why? Because of the difference in the time of their activity.
The meaning is that this is due to the difference between human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and time. Demonstrating this, he says:
"For birth (*jāti*) performs its activity (*kāritra*) while still in the future," and so forth.
As for the question of whether the future exists as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) or not—it will first be demonstrated that the future itself does not exist substantially;
the intention [of the author] is: how could a future birth (*jāti*) perform its activity (*kāritra*)?
"But even though that exists" means:
but even though *jāti* exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) in the future state, performing its activity (*kāritra*) in the future condition, how is it established as being "future"?
For the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that what has not yet attained its activity is "future."
That would be contradictory;
therefore, it must be explained how the present [time] is established.
The past is held to be that whose activity has ceased, and the future is likewise [that whose activity has not yet arisen].
For if [activity] were past while it was still in its present state, it would follow that it could not be present; therefore, the definition of the present must be stated.
If it is argued that the present is that whose activity is not yet completed, then even the past would be present;
for the activity of giving its fruit is also admitted in the case of the past.
For when it is thus, as stated in detail, "this is its stability," the functions of stability,
decay, and destruction are mutually contradictory;
indeed, it is not logical to establish that the very same dharma both endures, decays, and perishes.
Its momentariness would otherwise be contradicted; thus,
first stability establishes it,
and then decay causes it to age.
Then impermanence destroys it; because it would persist for three moments,
its momentariness is contradicted.
"For this very moment of ours" means that it is characterized by the completion of the task to be done, not by the characteristic of perishing immediately after arising;
such is the meaning of "even so," and so forth.
It is not logical for things that arise simultaneously to exercise their activity sequentially; why is this so?
First of all, duration causes [the thing] to endure.

But at that time, neither does old age cause it to decay, nor does impermanence destroy it; by what, then, is its weakness [established] later? By what is its weakness established such that impermanence strikes down this "stability" (sthiti) together with the dharma, along with that very dharma to which that stability belongs?
Furthermore, that which has already performed its function (*kṛtakṛtya*) cannot perform it again, just as birth (*jāti*).
For instance, once birth has performed its function, how could it bring about the born entity (*janya*) again? This would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*).
However, it is indeed possible for duration (*sthiti*) to establish what is to be established, by means of establishing it absolutely.
Since destruction is characterized by the obstruction of stability,
those very [factors] are aging and impermanence; thus,
those very [factors] constitute the obstruction of aging and impermanence.
The Master says that because of this, stability cannot establish what is to be established permanently; for old age weakens stability, and impermanence destroys what has been weakened.
If all this were so—
if indeed old age and impermanence were more powerful, they would have already occurred at the very time of the activity of abiding;
for that abiding would not be able to perform its function.
"In the case of [the characteristic] whose activity has ceased," and so forth:
when the characteristic of duration has ceased its activity,
then those two— aging and impermanence— also do not remain.
And that dharma, too,
is established as their "staying" (sthiti) only because of the activity of staying;
therefore, they also do not stay.
How could aging and impermanence, not being themselves established, exert their activity toward a substratum (*dharmin*) that is likewise unestablished? Furthermore, what is there left for those two—
aging and impermanence— to do,
since by virtue of the power of stability (*sthiti*), that phenomenon (*dharma*), as soon as it has arisen, does not perish?
If that entity is being neglected and not established by that state of abiding whose functional activity has ceased, it will certainly not remain;
thus, this very non-abiding is its destruction.
What, then, would be the purpose of aging and impermanence? This is the intended meaning.
And it is not logical for that [entity] to have another mode of being; for if it is that very same thing, it cannot be otherwise,
and if it is otherwise, it is not that very same thing.
For it is observed that whenever there is a difference between two things, there is a difference between them, as in the case of Devadatta and Yajñadatta.
As for the one who says "a member of another school," he refers to the Āryasaṃmatīya.
He considers that the destruction of a jar or similar object is caused by a hammer or other such instruments, for its form persists until another time;
however, the mind and mental factors are momentary,
and therefore it is said:

Furthermore, since it is accepted that mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are momentary, and because their impermanence does not depend on a cause of destruction but rather consists in their inherent perishability, both duration (*sthiti*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) would simultaneously exercise their functions.
Consequently, for a single mind or mental factor, simultaneous existence and destruction—which are mutually contradictory—would result;
thus, this Sūtra is well-expounded.
"Monks, regarding these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned:
because [the effect] exists when there is a collection [of causes],
and does not exist when it is absent."
Since the produced entity exists when there is a completeness of causes and conditions,
and does not exist when it is absent, what [contribution] does the genus (jāti) have?
"We observe its capacity," [one might argue].
But this is not the case, for even when the totality of causes and conditions is present, that which is to be produced sometimes occurs and sometimes does not;
regarding this, the Venerable Ānantavarman says:
Just as the eye does not produce visual consciousness without the eye-base and other factors,
yet it is not the case that it is not a cause for its arising,
so too birth does not produce a phenomenon without causes and conditions.
And it is not the case that, because [the effect] arises from that, there is no cause; to this it is replied:
this is not analogous.

For the visual faculty has its efficacy demonstrated: since, even when light and other conditions are present, one observes the non-arising and arising of visual consciousness in the blind and the non-blind respectively;
but birth is not like this, for the intrinsic natures of phenomena are indeed subtle.
For example, the intrinsic natures or essences (*prakṛti*, *svabhāva*) of mental factors such as contact are subtle because they are difficult to discern;
even so, it is just like this:
although a certain phenomenon (*dharma*) is not perceived, it is determined by its activity (*kāritra*).
But birth is not determined by its activity in this way;
for the activity of contact has been determined by the Blessed One himself:
"Whatever constitutes the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, or the aggregate of mental formations."
"All that [is felt] arises dependent on contact," and so forth;
however, there would not even be the notion "it has arisen" if arising did not exist.
Thus, the cognition of form with respect to form depends upon its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
However, the cognition "born" does not depend on a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because such a cognition occurs even with respect to feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth;
therefore, it is determined that this cognition "born" depends on a substance (*dravya*) consisting of a universal (*jāti*) that is a distinct entity.
Furthermore, there would be no use for the genitive case in the expression "the arising of form" (*rūpasyotpāda*),
just as one does not say "the form of form";
this is an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Just as, because form is not other than form, the use of the genitive case does not occur in the expression "the form of form," so too there would not be [the expression] "the arising of form. Therefore,
it is understood that this use of the genitive case is based on the cause of origination (*jāti*).
In this way, it should be stated up to impermanence (*anityatā*) as appropriate; however,

it would simply not be established that there is "staying" (*sthiti*), and in the absence of staying, the use of the genitive case— as in "the staying of form" (*rūpasya sthitiḥ*)— would be impossible, just as one cannot say "the form of form" (*rūpasya rūpam*).
But "it is worn out" would not exist in the absence of aging; furthermore, there would be no use for the genitive case in the expression "the aging of form," just as there is none in "the form.
Likewise, "it is destroyed" would not exist in the absence of impermanence.
And as for the use of the genitive case, such as "the destruction of form" (*rūpasya vināśaḥ*), just like [one says] "the form of form" (*rūpasya rūpam*);
therefore, in detail,

if birth and so forth are postulated for the sake of establishing cognitions such as "birth" and for the sake of prescribing the genitive case, then "selflessness" (*anātmatva*) must also be accepted.
For a cognition of non-self cannot possibly exist without a cause;
therefore, if non-selfhood is held to be a conceptual construct (*prajñaptisat*), then the cognition of non-self must have that as its cause.
Birth and so forth must also be accepted as being conceptually existent (prajñaptisat),
and the cognition of birth and so forth has those [conceptual entities] as its objective cause; this is the proof in this case.
Birth and so forth exist as designations because they are apprehended in dependence upon substantial entities,
just like selflessness.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "existence and so forth," one grasps substance-ness (*dravyatva*), form-ness (*rūpatva*), pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), and so on;
[the qualities are] one form, two forms, large, small, distinct, conjoined, disjoined, distant, near, and the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*).
Likewise, for the sake of establishing such cognitions as "this substance is form" or "this is a jar," one must also accept number and the other categories imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas;
and for the purpose of providing the sixth case ending, the mention of "conjunction" in the phrase "the conjunction of form" is merely an illustration.
The classification of form (*rūpa*), such as "remoteness" (*paratva*) and "nearness" (*aparatva*), and so forth, should also be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, how is this genitive case to be understood in the expression "the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form"?
For the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept that the intrinsic nature of form is something other than form itself.

The designation "it has arisen" is made for the purpose of making known that what has arisen has indeed arisen and has not perished— that is, to indicate its existence after having been non-existent; thus,
it is a conceptual construction involving many conceptual elaborations.
Since there are many divisions [of conditioned phenomena] due to the distinctions between form, feeling, and so forth,
they employ the genitive case— saying "the arising of form"— in order to specify that it is the arising of form and not the arising of feeling and the rest,
so that it may be understood that the arising designated as "form" is indeed distinct from that designated as "feeling" and so on.

They cite the examples of "the fragrance and so forth of sandalwood" and "the body of a stone statue," wherein the use of the genitive case is employed even though there is no difference in meaning between the terms.
For the Buddhist tenet is that "sandalwood" is merely a collection of odor and other qualities;
however, from the perspective of the Vaiśeṣika tenet, "sandalwood" is not established [as a substance]. Thus, the example "the body of a stone-son" is adduced.
Even in the established doctrine of the Vaiśeṣikas, there is no state of being a different entity between the body and a stone statue, yet the use of the genitive case occurs;
for such a designation is made by way of conceptualizing them as different entities.
In the same way, [the dharmas] such as duration (sthiti) and so forth should also be understood according to their respective applications.
Therefore, this is merely a designation (*prajñapti-mātra*) made for the purpose of making known the state of continuity; it is said that "it remains" (*sthitam*).
Furthermore, that stability (*sthiti*), characterized by the state of continuity, possesses many conceptual variations;
in order to specify it, they employ the genitive case, saying "the stability of form" (*rūpasya sthitiḥ*).
Just as the state designated as "form" (rūpa) is perceived as nothing other than that very state,
so too this is merely a conceptual designation (prajñaptimātra) established for the purpose of making known the distinction between earlier and later states— that it is "aged.
And that aging, characterized by the distinction between earlier and later states, possesses many varieties.

To qualify it, they employ the genitive case in the expression "aging of form" (*rūpasya jarā*), so that aging may be understood as belonging specifically to what is designated as "form," and not something else.
Likewise, this [term] is used merely as a designation to make known the cessation of the continuum, [expressing] that "it has perished."
Furthermore, that destruction characterized by the cessation of the stream has many conceptual variations;
for the purpose of specifying it, they employ the genitive case in the expression "destruction of form" (*rūpasya vināśa*),
so that the destruction designated as "form" alone may be understood, and not some other.
And in every case, two examples should be stated: namely,
"the fragrance and so forth of sandalwood" and "the body of a stone statue," as well as "in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."

The meaning is: *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), *dharmaprakṛtiḥ* (the fundamental nature of phenomena), *dharma-svabhāvaḥ* (the intrinsic nature of phenomena), and *dharma-śailī* (the disposition of phenomena).
Why is it said that "the nature of phenomena is the fundamental nature of phenomena"?
Because the eye, when fully developed, is empty of anything permanent, stable, eternal, unchanging by nature, or belonging to a self or what belongs to a self.
For what reason? Because this is its very nature;
and because, according to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), not everything is held to possess birth, such as space and so forth.
Likewise, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), it must be accepted that not everything arises;
for there is no reason here why only a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*) should arise even in the absence of arising.
It is not the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

For example, among certain [factors] such as form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) which possess a common genus, there are conditions for the arising of form that are distinct from those conditions for the arising of feeling;
those other conditions are incapable of producing anything other than what they are intended for.
Is that other thing, distinct from those [factors] such as feeling and so forth,
form?
Just as those other conditions, such as sensation and so forth, are not capable of producing that [unconditioned thing],
so too all conditions— form, sensation, and the rest— would be incapable of producing unconditioned phenomena such as space.

Previously it was stated by way of the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*), whereas now it is stated by way of the restriction of capacity (*śakti-niyama*); for there are no such critics [as would object]. This is the detailed explanation:
just as barley is not sown because deer exist, [it follows that] they are indeed sown; such is the meaning.
Two negations convey the original meaning;
for example, "Flies do not fly" means that sweets are indeed eaten—
what else?
They are indeed being devoured;
thus, the scriptural tradition (*āgama*) and the Abhidharma treatises are cast aside on the grounds that there are no critics.
Therefore, one must provide a remedy for these faults.
The intention is that when faults have been leveled against [the opponent's position], a rebuttal must be stated,
and one’s own established tenets (*siddhānta*) must be followed rather than abandoned.
The "sets of names" (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are collections of designations, sentences, and phonemes.
Thus,
the collections of designations are the sets of names;
the collections of sentences are the sets of phrases.
The collections of syllables are the body of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*);
"designation" (*sañjñākaraṇa*) is a worldly expression,
and "name" (*nāmadheya*) is its synonym.
For thus people in the world say: "The making of a name for Devadatta" (*devadatta ity asya sañjñā-karaṇam*);
that is, the making (*karaṇa*) of a name (*sañjñā*) is the "making of a name" (*sañjñā-karaṇa*).
That by which the mental factor of perception (*saṃjñā*) is made or produced,
or that which is the instrument of perception itself, is "the instrument of perception" (*saṃjñākaraṇa*);
the inclusion of the term "perception" is for the purpose of excluding other instruments.
The inclusion of the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) is for the purpose of distinguishing [it from] mental factors (*caitasika*);
for if it were merely said to be "perception" (*saṃjñā*) or "name" (*nāman*), it might be suspected of being a mental factor as well.
Furthermore, that which is the instrument of perception—the name—is form, sound, taste, smell, and so forth.
Regarding the statement "a sentence is a word":
a word (*pada*) is so called because it is "traversed" or "understood" (*padyate gamyate*); here, however, by "word" is meant that which ends in a nominal suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*).
Therefore he said:

"As far as the completion of the meaning extends, such as 'Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent,' and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [he includes] "they are subject to arising and passing away; for having arisen, they cease."
"Their subsiding is happiness," and so forth—
thus they explain the meaning of this verse;
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent" is the thesis.
"Characterized by arising and ceasing" is the reason;
because they possess the nature of arising and ceasing, they are determined to be impermanent. "For having arisen, they cease" is the example:
those things which arise and cease are impermanent.
Others, however, explain it thus: "Just as jars and so forth [are impermanent], so too are the formative forces (saṃskāra)."
How is it understood that this is for the purpose of proving an unestablished reason—
that "they possess the nature of arising and ceasing"— because these [things] are seen to arise and then cease?
Others describe it thus:
"Alas, conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are subject to arising and passing away"—this is stated as a pair of synonyms.
He asks "Why? and says:
because they arise and cease—this is the statement of the reason.
Their subsiding is bliss; for those things which are impermanent are suffering, therefore [their cessation is bliss].
He enjoins those to be trained with the thought, "Their pacification is happiness," whereby the specific relations of action, quality, and time are understood.
Those who know the nature of sentences declare that a sentence consists of an indeclinable, a noun (kāraka), and an adjective (viśeṣaṇa);

for example: *pacati* (he cooks), *paṭhati* (he reads), *gacchati* (he goes); *kṛṣṇaḥ* (black), *gauraḥ* (fair), *raktaḥ* (red); *pacati* (he cooks), *pakṣyati* (he will cook), *apākṣīt* (he cooked). In these cases, specific relations among action, quality, and time are understood; such is a word (*pada*).
For they say that if words, which generally abide in universals, come to rest in a particular, that is the sentence-meaning.

Thus, it is stated that a "name" (*nāman*) is that which indicates a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while a "word" (*pada*) is that which indicates the specific relation to action and so forth.
A "phoneme" (*vyañjana*) is a "syllable" (*akṣara*); the meaning is "letter" (*varṇa*).
But it is not only the consonants [that are intended], for the vowels are also accepted as being produced by consonants.
Now, one might object: "Are not the syllables (*akṣara*) also the names of the components of writing?
Thus, the 'writings' (*lipi*) are those which are inscribed by humans and others upon leaves and other materials."
Just as there is a cognition of form upon the grasping of the names of those letters, so too there is a cognition of the script upon the grasping of the phonemes (*vyañjana*);
therefore, since the phoneme also becomes the name for the components of the script, there is a confusion of definitions.
And therefore, that which was intended— that the phoneme (*vyañjana*) or syllable (*akṣara*) is something entirely distinct and separate from the name— is not tenable;
for it is not [the case] regarding the components of writing, and so forth.
He explains that this is the opposite:

as for the claim that there is a cognition of writing upon the apprehension of phonemes, that is because [writing] has been conventionally established through the relationship of signifier and signified.
But liberation does not [result] from the mere existence of that name;
for the word *samukti* is derived from the verbal root *uc* (in the sense of "to come together") with the suffix *ktin*,
and thus the form *samukti* has the same meaning as *samavāya*.
Thus, "object" (artha), "conventional expression" (samukti), and "inherence" (samavāya) are synonyms;
however, the phrase "but those [are... is the statement of the Sautrāntikas.
"These are not of the nature of speech," and so on, is the detailed statement of the Vaibhāṣikas;
nor is the meaning understood by mere sound— that is, by a sound that does not consist of syllables.
Rather,
speech operates upon the name, and by bringing about, as it were, the identity of the name with its own form, it causes the object-nature to appear.
The Sautrāntika says: "Having taken up that speech, it illuminates and causes the understanding of the meaning of the words"— this is the sense.
"Speech is certainly not merely sound," and so forth;
we do not describe speech as being merely sound,
but rather that certain sounds consist of phonemes (varṇa).
That very speech is that which has established limits and fixed boundaries regarding objects;
by this it is shown that a word conveys its meaning in dependence upon convention (*saṅketa*).
He shows that it is not just any word [that conveys meaning],
but rather that a word for which a convention has been established conveys an object;
and this is established by the mere word from which the object is understood.

And it is maintained that this [dharma], which illuminates such meaning and expresses universals (jāti) and so forth, arises as a mental non-associated factor when there is sound devoid of name; therefore, the following is suspected:
if it produces [the name], then even every mere sound, such as the bellowing of a bull and the like, would produce a name, on the grounds that speech has the nature of sound.
You might say that it is specifically the distinguished sound consisting of phonemes, when it has been brought into being, that produces the name;
to this, it is replied:
The intention is that whatever specific sound is intended to be the producer of a name, that very [sound] will be the illuminator of the object;
however, it is not a [separate entity] dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta*).
Now, regarding the passage "it illuminates," and so forth:
if it is maintained that this factor dissociated from mind arises simultaneously with the sound as it is produced, and that it illuminates that sound for the purpose of revealing its meaning;
To this it is replied: "Everything will be revealed as being merely sound," which should be stated as before;
for indeed, there is no such thing as a collection of sounds.
That name which consists of multiple syllables is a conceptual construction of its arising; it depends upon multiple sounds,
and for that reason, it is investigated in this way.
In this world, sounds perish as soon as they are uttered;
therefore, there is no simultaneous existence of them.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity existing as a substantial reality (*dravyasat*) to arise part by part or fragment by fragment, as is imagined in the case of things existing as mere designations (*prajñaptisat*), such as jars or cloths. Thus, how could speech, while being produced, produce a name?
The meaning of the sentence is: when that [speech] produces it, how does it produce it?
For speech, being present, would not produce what is already being produced.
Furthermore, not all phonetic moments of speech occur simultaneously;
for when the sound *ra* in the word "rūpa" is present, then the sounds *ū*, *pa*, and *a* are yet to come.
When the letter *ū* is present,
then the sound *ra* is past and the letters *pa* and *a* are future.
In this way, when the phonemes *pa* and *ka* are present in succession, the others are not present; thus,
that speech called "name" would not produce [the object] at all.

If you were to say that the sound *ra*, while existing, produces the first part of that word "rūpa," and the sound *ū*, while also existing, produces the second part, and so on until the sound *a* produces its fourth part—
that is incorrect.
It has already been stated that it is impossible for a single dharma to arise in parts;
how then can the final moment of informative action (*vijñapti*), depending on those preceding moments, produce non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
In the undertaking of the Prātimokṣa restraint, bodily and vocal informative acts (vijñapti) proceed;
there is no simultaneity among them,

yet the final moment of informative act, depending upon the preceding moments of past bodily and vocal informative acts, produces the non-informative act (avijñapti) comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint.

In this way, the final sound-moment, depending upon the past sound-moments, produces the name. Thus, as for the detailed explanation: since the name is produced by the final sound alone, even one who hears only that single [final] sound—namely, the very last sound—would hear the form "rūpa."
He too would understand the object; he too would grasp the object through its name and form,
because of the arising of that name.
And since one does not practice in this way,
it is therefore illogical;
furthermore, even if it were to be conceived in this manner, [the objection remains], as explained in detail.
Another alternative position is proposed: that speech consisting of phonemes appears momentarily, and the phoneme also appears as such;
[according to this view], speech produces the phoneme, while the phoneme produces the name (*nāman*).
In this case as well, the same undesirable consequence follows: since there is no collection of phonemes,
how indeed could there be a collection of phonemes?
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single dharma to arise in parts; thus, how could a manifesting sound produce a name as it arises?
First of all, how does the final moment of informative intimation (*vijñapti*), depending on those that have passed, produce the non-informative (*avijñapti*)?

If that were so, since the name would be produced only by the final manifesting sound, then even one who hears only that single final sound which produces the manifesting [name] [would produce the name].
Or, if one hears only that single final phoneme, would he not also comprehend the meaning? This same consequence applies to speech in its capacity as the manifestor of the name.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a collection of sounds, nor is it logical for a single dharma to be manifested part by part; so how could that which is called "speech" manifest anything?
First of all, how does the final moment of informative intimation, depending upon the preceding moments, manifest the non-informative [intimation]?
In that case, since the name is manifested only by the final sound, even one who hears that single final sound alone would understand the meaning; yet,
it might be argued as follows:
Speech reveals the phoneme (*vyañjana*),
and the phoneme [reveals] the name (*nāman*); here too, the same objection applies because of the impossibility of the simultaneous assembly of phonemes.

In that case, for one for whom a name consists of mere sound and a name consists of multiple syllables, and wherein there is no simultaneous totality of sounds, how does the name convey its meaning? [The answer is:
because the comprehension of the meaning occurs immediately after the recollection of all the syllables.

For this very reason, by the logic of invariable concomitance (*nāntarīyaka*), at the very moment of hearing the first syllable, someone indeed apprehends the meaning through the power of recollecting the remaining syllables.
Thus, it is not logical that speech (*vāc*) is either the producer or the manifestor even of the phoneme (*vyañjana*).
Therefore, having previously accepted that the phoneme is either something produced by sound or something manifested by sound, the fault was pointed out.
Now, since it is not perceived apart from sound, its status as either produced (*utpādya*) or manifested (*vyaṅgya*) is also non-existent; thus, that very point is uprooted.
One should not, however, state the fault that this is because of the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for sounds, for the apprehension of manifestation does not depend upon multiple sounds.
Furthermore, since speech has the nature of sound, every mere sound will produce or manifest a phoneme;
or rather, whatever specific kind of sound is accepted as the producer or manifester of a phoneme, that alone will effect the meaning of the phoneme.
Furthermore, it is argued at length that the name is considered to be co-nascent with the object, just like the [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth.

Now, thinking that if the name is conceived as co-nascent, there will be no undesirable consequence (such as the name being something produced by speech or something revealed by it), this alternative view is formulated:
just as the characteristics such as birth are held to be co-nascent with the object, they do not exist in the present for an object that is past or future.
If this very [definition] were accepted, there would be no present name for a past or future object;
consequently, it would be impossible to carry out linguistic usage regarding past and future objects.
For a name cannot illuminate an object that is past or future,
just as past or future speech cannot produce or manifest a name;
moreover, if there were a multiplicity of names, the innate name would not be distinguishable.

Since unconditioned phenomena lack the quality of arising, they could not possess an innate name; therefore, this [proposed] position is untenable. The intention is that this position must not be maintained—it is not at all acceptable. Thus, it is said: "Verses are dependent upon names."

A verse (*gāthā*) is a sentence (*vākya*), and that [sentence] is dependent upon names (*nāman*); since it exists when names have arisen, there is room for the statement: "Therefore, names and sentences exist. To this, he says:
Regarding that, "a word that has established a limit with respect to objects is a name," and so forth;
the meaning is that a verse (*gāthā*) is a particular arrangement of names whose intrinsic nature consists of words that have established limits with respect to objects,
which is to say, a particular mode of composition.
"As with a row" means that just as a row is a particular arrangement of ants and so forth, and no separate substance arises from them, so it is here.

Observing that there might be an opportunity for the objection that there is a disparity— since a specific arrangement of birds, ants, and so forth existing at one time is called a "row," whereas there is no such specific arrangement of words existing sequentially— the second example is introduced:
"and like the sequence of thoughts."
Just as there is no sequential order (ānupūrvya) other than the piled-up [bricks] that exist in a specific sequence, so too the postulation of such a thing is purposeless.
The meaning is that it is purposeless to imagine a different referent for names and words;
for not all phenomena are accessible through reasoning—
only some are accessible through reasoning, not all.

The intention is that those who have indeed fallen within the range of the Tathāgata’s wisdom are not accessible to ratiocination; this is introduced with the desire to explain the various classifications of the factors dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta*).
Now, regarding the detailed explanation of "associated with what":
in which realm are they associated? With what are they associated?
Are they designated as sentient beings or not designated as sentient beings? What is meant by this?
"Those pertaining to the desire and form realms, designated as sentient beings, are outflows, indeterminate"—
this is a restrictive definition meaning that they pertain only to the desire and form realms, are only designated as sentient beings, are only outflows, and are only indeterminate.
"But they are inexpressible" means that those sets of names and so forth belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*) cannot be expressed because speech is absent there;
how, then, is it understood that they exist?
When these [factors] are not expressed [as such],
the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that they belong only to the realms of desire and form, and not to the formless realm;
furthermore, they are designated as "sentient beings" because their intrinsic nature consists of color and so forth, which are produced by the effort of sentient beings.
And that being who illuminates is not visible as being endowed with those [qualities];
likewise, it is the illuminator alone who is endowed with them, not the object illuminated.
They are outflowing because they are produced by a homogeneous cause;
they are not born of maturation because they proceed from desire; and they are not accumulative because there is no accumulation for those that are formless.
And why are the non-obscured-neutral states neither wholesome nor unwholesome?
For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even those who have severed their roots of merit and are free from desire for the realm of sensuality would still possess them;
for if that were not the case, then when one whose roots of merit are severed manifests wholesome dharmas,
he would at that time possess those wholesome dharmas.
In the same way, this should also be applied to the manifestation of unwholesome factors (*akuśaladharma*) for one who is already free from passion for sense-pleasures (*kāmavītarāga*);
therefore, they are indeed non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), because there is no contradiction between the non-obscured-unspecified and the wholesome or unwholesome.

The phrase "likewise homogeneous" (tathā sabhāgā) uses the word "likewise" (tathā) to extend the same quality to *sabhāgatā*— namely, that it is called a sentient being (*sattvākhya*), is a result of outflow (*naiḥsyandika*), and is neutral (*avyākṛta*)—
because it will be stated later as an exception that it is obtained in all three realms (*tridhātv-āpta*).
Regarding the phrase "but that," the word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of specification; for homogeneous character (sabhāgatā) is distinguished from the sets of names and so forth.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Even those born of maturation" (*vipākāpi*), which means "even those produced from maturation" (*vipākajāpi*).
This is not only outflowing;
rather,
it is also born of maturation.
But it is not accumulative (*aupacayikī*), precisely because there is no accumulation [of it].

Regarding the statement "possessions (*prāpti*) are of two kinds," the word "two kinds" refers specifically to the distinction between being non-spatial (*naiṣyandika*) and being born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
since other distinctions have already been stated.
The same two divisions must likewise be stated for the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth:
non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) is non-acquisition (*aprāpti*);
it is also unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), but it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
For even the non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) of a ripened result (*vipāka*) cannot itself be a ripened result;
for it is accepted that the ripened result belongs to the unwholesome and to the wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava*),
and the non-attainment (*aprāpti*) of these two cannot be a ripened result.
For whatever phenomenon (*dharma*) is preceded by intelligence (*buddhi*), consists of volition (*cetanā*), or arises in association with or from that [volition],
is a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*); and since non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) is not produced by such intentional action, it is therefore not born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

"The remainder of these has been stated" means that what was to be said regarding their acquisition (*prāpti*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) has been spoken; that which was to be explained has been explained.
What, then, is that "remainder"?

How is it that [the acquisition] is said to belong to the realms, to be designated as pertaining to sentient beings or non-sentient things, and to be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? Furthermore,
regarding acquisition (*prāpti*), its belonging to the realms has already been stated.

Because of the statement, "It belongs to its own realm for those who have attained it," its designation as belonging to sentient beings is stated by means of the mention of possession (*samanvāgama*).

For there are no acquisitions (*samanvāgama*), attainments (*prāpti*), or non-attainments (*aprāpti*) with respect to conditioned phenomena not included among sentient beings, according to the statement: "Attainments belong to those [phenomena] acquired within one's own continuum."
How is it that the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral nature [of phenomena] is stated?
Because of the statement: "The wholesome and so forth [of the objects] are themselves wholesome and so forth."
The characteristics are also said to be associated with the three realms,
because of the statement: "everything [is associated] with the characteristics of the conditioned."
These very same [factors] are said to be designated as "sentient" and "non-sentient" because they coexist with all conditioned phenomena;
for this very reason, they are also said to be wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

The mental factors, the two types of restraint, and their characteristics are followers of the mind (cittānuvartinaḥ), according to the statement: "By way of time, fruit, and so forth, as well as by virtue of being wholesome and so on."
The attainment of non-perception is stated to belong to the form realm because of the statement, "in the final dhyāna."
Because it is stated that "skillfulness is also auspicious."

For this very reason, because it is stated that "it is also designated as belonging to sentient beings and is to be experienced only upon rebirth," it is taught that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is born of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
According to this statement,
skillfulness is also auspicious.
Because of this statement,
it is designated as "sentient" for precisely this reason:
because it is wholesome and conditioned.

The non-possession (asamanvāgama) is said to belong to the three realms because of the statement: "And [it belongs] to those things belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as to the untainted (amala)."
Because it is stated that [non-possession] belongs to sentient beings (*sattvākhyatā*), its neutral nature (*avyākṛtatā*) is also implied;
for non-possession is unafflicted and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*).
Because of this statement,
what [is the nature] of the two remaining [factors], namely the non-percipient state and the life-force?
The phrase "what was to be said has been said" continues [from the previous context].

Regarding the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*), it has been stated that it belongs to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*), is designated as a sentient being (*sattvākhyā*), is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), and is morally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Its maturation occurs among the Bṛhatphala [deities].
From this statement,
it is taught that vitality belongs to the three realms;
vitality is life-force (*āyus*).
From this statement,
because life-force belongs to the three realms, it is also said to be designated as belonging to sentient beings.
According to the Sūtra stating "life is maturation," for maturation belongs only to what is designated as a sentient being.

Because of the statement, "Maturation (vipāka) is an indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharma, designated as a sentient being, and arising from the determinate," for this very reason its state of being non-obscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta) has also been stated.
The view which was to be stated by the Teacher has now been explained;
how is it that acquisition (*prāpti*) and the other [factors] are said to be designated as belonging to sentient beings?
From the statement regarding "possession" (*samanvāgama*) and so forth,
[it follows that] what are these causes (*hetu*) and what are the conditions (*pratyaya*);
what, then, is the specific distinction between causes and conditions?
"No one [is the cause]," he said;
for thus it was stated by the Blessed One:
"There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view."
What are the two?
The voice from another and internal wise attention (*yoniso-manaskāra*).
These are the cause, the condition, the source, the reason, the sign, the mark, and the proximate cause; such are the conditions.
The word *upaniṣad*, however, is sometimes used in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) and sometimes in a prominent manner;
for example, as in "the gods [know] the Sūryopaniṣad," where there is both the usage of *upāṃśu* and the usage of *upaniṣad*.

If there is no distinction, for what purpose are causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*) taught separately? Is there not some other specific meaning by which the teaching on causes is distinct from the teaching on conditions?
For the teaching on causes has been stated to refer to a specific meaning such as non-obstructiveness, coexistence, similarity, and so forth.
For in the explanation of conditions (*pratyaya*), specific meanings such as being non-obstructive, co-arising, and similarity have been stated;

however, in the explanation of causes (*hetu*), another set of specific meanings has been stated by way of being the immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and so forth. Thus, how are six causes explained in this sutra?
"For all Abhidharma is the meaning of the Sūtras, the touchstone of the Sūtras, and the commentary on the Sūtras.
"That Sūtra has disappeared," say the Vaibhāṣikas; for in the Ekottarikāgama, there was an exposition of the Dharma extending up to one hundred [items].
Now, however, they say that [these] are seen up to ten;
nevertheless, there are sūtras that express specific causes, which we shall cite.
"Visual consciousness arises depending upon the eye and visible forms"— this is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*),
for it is established by way of its state as a non-obstructing factor in production.
These three factors of the path revolve around right view.

The feeling, perception, and volition born together with them constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), for this is established on the basis of their mutual accompaniment and single function. This person is endowed with both wholesome and unwholesome factors, as long as there exists even a subtle root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) accompanying him that is not yet severed; from that root of goodness, another root of goodness will arise for him.
Thus, this person will possess the qualities of purification in the future; this is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
For it is established for the sake of producing its own fruit from past and present phenomena.
This is called faith rooted in vision, which is associated with knowledge born of realization (*avetyajñāna*).
"That which one cognizes, one discerns"— this is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*),
for it is established by virtue of its function of having a single object (*ekālambana*).
Whatever bodily action, whatever vocal action, whatever volition, whatever aspiration, and whatever formative factors (saṃskāra) follow from that person of wrong view—
all these phenomena lead to what is undesirable, to what is unlovely, to what is unpleasant, and to what is disagreeable. For what reason?

For his view is evil, namely false view; this is the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*), which is established here in the sense that it generates a continuity of both similar and dissimilar afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*).
Thus, they experience the maturation (*vipāka*) there of wholesome, contaminated karma performed in this life that consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
The ripening of intentional karma that has been performed and accumulated is the "ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*);
for this is established by virtue of its projecting a dissimilar fruit.
Therefore, these six causes are well-known precisely from the Sūtras.
The intention is that the Vaibhāṣikas maintain there are six kinds of causes;
"other than itself" means other than one's own self.
Because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself, its own self is not a cause.
All phenomena—both conditioned and unconditioned—are the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*); thus, the efficient cause is simply the cause that acts as a condition.
That cause which is not designated by a specific name, but is stated by adopting the general state of being a cause,
is the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
