For among the other causes defined by specific designations, it is that which is not specified [by a particular name] and yet is a cause.
That very same qualification applies to it,
as was stated regarding the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*):
"because it exists in a state that does not act as an obstacle to arising."
Because other phenomena exist as non-obstructive states with respect to the arising of those things that possess arising,
they are therefore called the "causal condition" (*kāraṇahetu*). But is it not the case, as stated in detail, that "those which [one] does not know..."?
"If these [defilements] do not arise through knowledge,
then the outflows will arise"— this is the meaning of the conditional mood (*lṛṅ*) in detail;
therefore, he says:

For this person who does not know—this individual for whom the paths of seeing and cultivation have not yet arisen—the outflows such as attachment that would arise and are to be abandoned by the paths of seeing and cultivation do not arise for this person who knows and for whom the paths of seeing and cultivation have already arisen; since they are rendered barren [by those paths], they do not arise.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says:
Knowledge— comprised within the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)— creates an obstacle to their arising;
and just as it is established that the light of the sun creates an obstacle to the arising of the perception of luminous bodies,
if this is so, how can all phenomena, with the exception of themselves, be the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) of conditioned things?
Because knowledge is not the causal condition for the arising of the outflows,
just as sunlight is not the causal condition for the arising of the perception of light;
thus, knowledge is not the causal condition for the arising of the outflows.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of the perception of light, it should be stated that it is indeed the radiance of the sun; likewise, regarding the arising of the outflows (*āsrava*), all phenomena (*dharma*), with the exception of the knowledge of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvajñāna*), are the causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*).
Furthermore, at the time of the arising of the perception of light, all phenomena— excluding their own nature and the radiance of the sun— are the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*),

because they abide in a state of non-obstruction toward that which is arising; thus, when the causes and conditions are complete, a phenomenon that arises immediately thereafter is said to be "arising."
It should be understood that regarding the arising of that [knowledge] which is currently emerging, all phenomena indeed abide as non-obstructive, but this does not apply to everything;
furthermore, when that knowledge exists, those outflows (āsravas) do not arise.
Since the causal complex (*pratyaya-sāmagrī*) is absent due to the non-existence of acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth,
it should be understood that even the vision of light does not arise precisely because of the deficiency of conditions.
Therefore, in this state, all phenomena (*dharma*), with the exception of their own nature (*svabhāva*), serve as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
It is as follows: "a non-oppressor, a provider of sustenance," and so forth; with reference to a village headman who causes no affliction, people would say, "We are happy because of our master."
Why do they speak in this way? Because although he is capable of causing harm, he does not cause it—
just as, for example, with nirvāṇa and those phenomena that are by nature unarisen.
What is the nature of the cause for the arising of all things?
And how is there the nature of a cause for the arising of hell-beings and so forth— those belonging to the realms of hell, animals, and so on— as well as for the arising of the formless aggregates?

The inclusion of "those in hell" and so forth implies that for humans and others, [the attainment of such states] might sometimes occur through instruction and the like; for even though they are non-existent,
these things such as nirvāṇa are nonetheless just so.
Just as those that are existent and present would be incapable of creating an obstacle,
therefore, in their ability to create an obstacle to these [factors] such as nirvāṇa, there is no distinction between the non-existent and the existent;
the meaning is that they are equivalent to the non-existent.
"Even when [he is] incapable," and so forth;
even when the village headman is incapable of causing harm, the villagers speak thus:
"We are made happy by our master."
The very same example that was given previously applies here;

therefore, by this very example, the status of being a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) is established for things such as *nirvāṇa*, because they remain in a state of non-obstruction even though they are incapable of obstructing.
Why, then, is the causality of *nirvāṇa* and so forth—things which are equivalent to non-existence—accepted?
Furthermore, it is not the case that non-existent things such as a hare's horn can serve as examples of the non-existent, for there are no instances of the non-existent;
indeed, villagers do not speak of a non-existent village headman.
The objection is this: "Are we made happy by our master," or "Are we made happy by a hare's horn?"—
this is the challenge.
The explanation is given in general terms;
that is, with reference to both the primary cause-condition (*kāraṇahetu*) and the non-primary one, it is stated:
"Other than itself, all [factors] are the cause-condition."
Thus,
that which is the primary producer is the efficient cause (kāraṇahetu).
It remains far more free from obstacles than other types of nutriment; for it is not only other food that is capable of producing the body, as is established by the statement:
"From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body."
Because of their connection with the transformation of sap and so forth,
seeds and the like [are the causes] of sprouts and the like; thus,
they are capable of producing seeds, sprouts, stalks, nodes, flowers, fruits, and so on.
"But as for those who object in this way," and so forth;
thinking that "when a cause exists, the effect must necessarily arise," one objects:
"Why does the production of everything not occur simultaneously?"
And why is it that not everyone becomes a partaker in killing simply by being like one who commits the act of killing?
It is not by virtue of being an agent.
He shows that this [cause] does not possess causality in a primary sense:
"Therefore, it follows that everything would arise simultaneously, because [if this were the case], nothing would fail to arise due to the absence of a complete collection of conditions."
Furthermore, there is no engagement in taking life because of being a non-agent;
for whoever is the agent is indeed a participant in the taking of life.
Mental consciousness arises as wholesome or unwholesome; thus,
mental consciousness is called "wholesome" because it takes nirvana as its object,
for from that which is wholesome or unwholesome— having nirvana as its object— mental consciousness arises.
Then, through the sequence beginning with visual consciousness, because it also serves as a condition for that very nirvāṇa, where is its efficacy not present?
With "eye-consciousness" being the subject under discussion,
it should be understood in the same way for others as well; thus,
even those such as hell-beings possess the capacity for the arising of the formless aggregates (*ārūpya-skandha*).

"How indeed do these beings, such as hell-beings and hungry ghosts, suffer so intensely?"— from this, a wholesome mental consciousness arises taking hell-beings and others as its object, by virtue of which one who is gradually established in ethical discipline applies himself to cultivation, whereby the formless attainments and rebirth therein come to pass.
"Coexistent are those which are mutual fruits"— here, "cause" is understood [from the previous context].
Co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) are those phenomena (*dharma*) that are mutual effects; the meaning is that they are reciprocal effects.
It is not stated [in the verse] that "co-existent causes are co-existent," because [the definition already implies this].
Why is this?
For there are indeed certain phenomena that are co-existent, yet not a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*);
for example, derivative form such as blue and so forth is co-existent with the primary elements (*bhūta*).
And they are not mutually co-existent causes; therefore, they do not have mutual results.
Such is the comprehension of the meaning;
and since this definition is incomplete,
he will say [the following].
Furthermore, even in the absence of mutual fruitfulness, it should be added that the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas) are co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu) of the dharma,
but that dharma is not [the cause] of them; and the reason for this addition is to demonstrate the status of this as a great treatise.
For great treatises such as grammar are seen to be "as if they had already come into being" (bhūtavat); thus,
the suffix -vat is used in the sense of "like" (tadyathārthe).
And having established this, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are, according to their respective application, co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*);
for since the characteristics of the conditioned are the co-existent cause of the characterized (*lakṣya*), the latter are also [the co-existent cause] of those [characteristics].

Therefore, according to their respective applications and possibilities, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) of [other] conditioned phenomena, because they possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇavat*), and because the characterized (*lakṣya*) and its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) stand in a relationship of mutual co-existent causality;
however, this is not the case for everything in relation to everything else.

Because they are not co-existent causes (*asahabhūhetu*) with other characteristics, they are to be understood according to their respective application. "And those which belong to them"— meaning those [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth belonging to the mind—

and "of those associated with the mind," meaning of volition (*cetanā*) and so forth, as well as the four dharmas such as birth and so forth belonging to the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*), are called the "factors that follow the mind" (*cittānuparivartin*).
"By way of time, fruit, and so forth, as well as by way of wholesomeness and so forth" means:
by way of time, and by way of fruit and so forth, and by way of wholesomeness and so forth.
"By way of time, first, through [factors] such as the ripening at the proper time and their wholesomeness," and so forth;
these arise together with the mind, persist together, and cease together.
The state of being that consists in their having a single arising, abiding, and cessation; thus, "fallen into one time period" means fallen into a single temporal period (*adhvan*).
Their state [of being] by means of that fourth [condition], namely by virtue of falling within the same temporal period (*ekādhvapatitatva*),
the mental factors revolve along with the mind in terms of time.
They follow the mind by way of having a single fruit, a single maturation, and a single outflow;

here, "fruit" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*), since the fruits of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*) have been treated separately.
However, the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) is not counted because it is common to all;

furthermore, this word "one" (*eka*) refers either to enumeration or to being common, as in the case of "having a single fruit," whereas the preceding word "one" has the sense of "together," meaning that they arise, abide, and cease together with the mind.
For in this case, the sense of numerical counting is not possible;
for that which is the arising of the mind is not itself [identical to] those factors that follow along with the mind.
Or rather, that which belongs to them belongs to the mind;
thus, it is by means of these ten reasons.
From the perspective of time, [they are equal] by virtue of arising together, abiding together, ceasing together, and falling within the same temporal period (*adhvan*).
But is it not the case that by the phrase "by virtue of arising, abiding, and ceasing together," the fact of falling within the same temporal period is already stated?
It is true that this alone states it, but it does not state everything.
For when the mind has the nature of non-arising, those mental factors that follow it fall into the same time period;
they do not have a simultaneous arising, abiding, and cessation.
Therefore, falling into the same time period is stated as the fourth reason.

"By way of having a single ripening of fruit and outflow," and "by way of being wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate"— thus, by another three; it is said "by ten" with reference to the occurrence through these ten modes or the [ten] births.
For ten causes do not exist within a single moment of mind;
for in a wholesome mind, the two causes [of the unwholesome and the neutral] do not exist,
nor do they exist in an unwholesome or neutral mind that is subject to non-arising.

In the case of an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) that is subject to non-arising (*anutpatti-dharmin*), [it is similar] by way of four factors: by virtue of belonging to the same time period (*ekādhva-patitatva*), by virtue of being the outflow of the same fruit (*eka-phala-niṣyandatā*), and by virtue of being indeterminate (*avyākṛtatva*).

However, in the case of one subject to arising (*utpatti-dharmin*), it is by way of these same four plus seven—namely, by virtue of having the same arising, abiding, and cessation (*eka-utpāda-sthiti-nirodhatā*)—making eleven.
It is the same for the untainted (*anāsrava*) mind as well.
However, having merely removed its neutral character (*avyākṛtatā*) and added the quality of wholesomeness (*kuśalatā*), [the following applies]:

in the case of an unwholesome state or a wholesome state with outflows (*sāsrava*) that is subject to non-arising (*anutpattikadharmiṇi*), it is characterized by five factors—namely, by its unwholesomeness or wholesomeness according to the actual state of affairs, and by its belonging to the same time period (*ekādhvapatitatva*), and by its having the same fruit, ripening (*vipāka*), and outflow (*niṣyanda*). But in the case of such a state that is subject to arising (*utpattidharmiṇi*), it is characterized by these same five factors plus [the three of] simultaneous arising, abiding, and ceasing (*ekotpādasthitinirodhatā*), making eight factors in total.
"The most minimal mind" means that among all [minds], that mind which has the smallest retinue is called the most minimal.
Furthermore, what is that?
From the second dhyāna upwards, the mind is unobstructed-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); therein, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not exist.

Nor is it the case that only the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) exist as such, for there are also the wholesome universal factors (kuśala-mahābhūmika) and others characterized by those same marks.
It does not [arise] from the characteristics of the ten universal mental factors because they are remote;
however, it does arise from their own secondary characteristics because they are proximate.
Therefore he says:
"and of the eight [mental factors], their own-characteristics and secondary-characteristics," meaning "excluding their own secondary-characteristics."
The secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) function upon the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas),
but they do not function upon the distinguished mind; thus, those [secondary characteristics] are fewer.
For the mind acts as a king over the primary and secondary characteristics;
therefore, the mind is the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) of the secondary characteristics,
but they are not [the cause] of the mind.

However, others hold that because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) do have an operation upon the mind, they constitute the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind; thus there are fourteen [characteristics],
whereas the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*) have no operation upon the primary dharma.
Rather,
because [these] are among the characteristics of a phenomenon (dharma), that phenomenon is not accepted as being their cause.

The intention of others is that the activity of those characteristics (lakṣaṇas) occurs only with respect to the associated [mental states] and not with respect to the mind; therefore, they are not the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu) of the mind.
However, since the mind is like a king to them, it is their co-existent cause. Thus is the view of others.

For otherwise, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise would be contradicted; for if those forty characteristics of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) were not accepted as the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind, since it is stated in the *Prakaraṇas*: [text continues]
Regarding the four noble truths— the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path—

how many have the view of a self-identity as their cause but are not causes for the view of a self-identity; and how many are causes for the view of a self-identity but do not have the view of a self-identity as their cause?

When the question is asked: "How many have the view of a self-identity as their cause and are themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity? And how many neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity? he provides the answer:
"Two neither have the view of a self-identity as their cause nor are they the cause of the view of a self-identity."
The distinction between the two truths of cessation and the path is the detailed analysis of the truths of suffering and its origin.
How so? The truth of suffering would be caused by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) but not itself a cause of the view of a self-identity;
[rather, it would be] both caused by the view of a self-identity and a cause of the view of a self-identity.

There may be that which is neither caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) nor is a cause for the view of a self-identity; this constitutes a threefold alternative (*trikoṭika*), of which there is no second alternative—
that which is caused by the view of a self-identity but is not itself a cause for the view of a self-identity.
Excluding the past and present proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the truth of suffering associated with them;
excluding the past and present universal proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of origin and the truth of suffering associated with them;
and excluding the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Excluding the birth and impermanence of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and those factors associated with it, that which remains is the other afflicted truth of suffering which has the view of a self-identity as its cause and is itself a cause for the view of a self-identity; this is what was excluded. Furthermore, the non-afflicted truth of suffering is neither caused by the view of a self-identity nor is it a cause for the view of a self-identity.
"Just as it is with the truth of suffering, so it is with the truth of origination"—this is the text of the *Prakaraṇa*; we shall now explain its meaning:

those ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and which are past or present.
Those [factors] have been set aside;
the truth of suffering associated with those ten underlying tendencies, such as sensation and so forth, has been set aside— what, then, remains unset aside here?

These very same ten future latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), as well as the associated feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth— excluding the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), for that will be set aside—
[constitute the category], because of the statement: "and having set aside the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity."

Furthermore, the birth (*jāti*) and other characteristics of that [attainment] are not established, with the exception of the birth and so forth of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the factors associated with it;
for it is stated: "Having excluded the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity and the factors associated with it, [the others are established]."

Thus, first of all, that which is future latent disposition (*anuśaya*) and that which is associated with it—excluding what has been set aside—is called "other than that" (*tad-anyat*), namely, the defiled (*kliṣṭa*). It is "caused by the view of a self-identity" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-hetuka*);
that is to say, that for which the view of a self-identity is the cause is "caused by the view of a self-identity."
Because it has as its cause the past and present *satkāyadṛṣṭi* by way of both the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*),
it is not itself the cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*; for a future phenomenon is not established as either a homogeneous cause or a pervasive cause,
nor is it possible for it to be a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) or an associated cause (*samprayuktahetu*) in this case.
For the view of a self-identity does not exist together with, nor is it associated with, another view of a self-identity,
because there is no second view of a self-identity within a single mental complex;
nor does it exist together with, nor is it associated with, the view of grasping at extremes and so forth.
Because they belong to distinct sets,
the acquisitions (*prāpti*) and [the characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) of those past and present factors to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*) are excluded; these,
along with the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) factors other than those that have been set aside, are [what remain].
Those [defilements] as well, by way of being universal causes, have the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause;
however, they are not the cause of the view of a self-identity.
Why is that?
First, acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not established as universal because they exist outside of their own universal [factors], like the bark of a tree;
and because they lack the nature of being universal, they are not the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Although the universal [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth are also accepted as being universal—
on the basis of the established tenet that "those which coexist with these [universal factors], excluding their acquisitions (*prāpti*), are also universal"— [they are not included here].

However, they are not the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) for subsequent minds and mental factors in the same way that minds and mental factors are; for, being secondary due to their primary engagement with their own specific objects, they lack the universal activity (*sarvatrapuruṣakāra*) toward other minds and mental factors. As for the designation of those [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth as "universal," it is because they serve as the universal cause within their own continuum.
Therefore, it is understood from the meaning of the treatise that these are not the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
If so, why is it not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)?
For the establishment of a homogeneous cause depends also upon human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
For when a certain dharma possesses the human effort (puruṣakāra) for the production of another dharma, that [effort] is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of that [dharma];
and this very point is the indicator that the establishment of the homogeneous cause is according to one's preference.
In the *Vibhāṣā* it is also stated thus:
"The eye is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the eye; Devadatta’s eye is a homogeneous cause of Devadatta’s eye;
the right [eye] is [the cause] of the right, and the left of the left, up to the point that a substance of the eye is [the cause] of another substance of the eye."
Even among external things, barley is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of barley and rice of rice;
for if every eye were intended to be the homogeneous cause of every [other] eye—on the grounds that their neutral nature (*avyākṛtatva*) is equal—then such a qualification would not have been stated.
Therefore, it should be understood that those [neutral eyes] are not the homogeneous cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
But others say:
this commentary is incomplete;

therefore, it should be understood that those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) such as those of the same class (*sajāti*), as well as the factors (*dharma*) associated with them, are established [as being included].

For those factors (dharmas) that constitute the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu)— namely, the birth and other characteristics (jāty-ādi) of a factor and its associated [factors]— those factors, when they have arisen previously, become either universal causes (sarvatraga-hetu) or homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu),
with the exception of acquisitions (prāpti). Furthermore, those co-existent factors which are associated with these [universal or homogeneous factors] are also universal [factors].
According to this established tenet,

it is for this very reason that it has been stated: "excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and of the mental factors associated with it."
Therefore, it should be understood that some [factors] such as birth and so forth have been established, while others are not established; the reasoning for this should be examined here.
From this reasoning,

it should be understood that those universal [defilements] which are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin, as well as the truth of suffering associated with them— whether past or present, such as feeling and so forth— are likewise [abandoned].
What else is established therein that is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin? It is that which is not established:
all pervasive [defilements] in their future state, and the truth of suffering associated with them, such as feeling and so forth.
That which has not been established includes those non-universal factors such as attachment and so forth belonging to the three time periods,
as well as the acquisitions (prāpti) of all of them.
Those [factors] such as birth and so forth were not established by you in one position;
however, in another position, some of them were indeed established.
Some [factors] were not established;

all of these that were not established are to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and they have the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) as their pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
because they have the previously arisen view of a self-identity as their cause.
But it is not the cause of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
because the universal [factors] and their co-existent factors, being future, do not function as universal causes;

and because passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions], which are non-universal, along with their co-existent factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, and with birth (*jāti*) and the rest, and with all acquisitions (*prāpti*) in one category, are themselves non-universal.

The defiled latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation— including their associated factors, their co-arisen factors, and their intrinsic nature such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth— are not set aside;
they have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*),
but they are not themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity.

Because it is impossible for it to be a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) and because it is incompatible with other causes, that which has been set aside— namely, those ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) whether past or present, the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) associated with them, and birth and so forth belonging to another category— is caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and is itself a cause of the view of a self-identity.
That [result] has as its cause the previous view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) by way of both the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) and the omnipresent cause (sarvatragahetu);
and those factors such as the birth and so forth of the view of a self-identity, as well as the birth and so forth associated with it,
have that as their cause by way of the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) and the two previously mentioned causes.

Furthermore, those [factors] associated with the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) have that as their cause by way of the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu) and by way of the previously mentioned causes;
and likewise, they are the cause of the view of a self-entity.

Furthermore, those universal [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin that are past or present, as well as their co-existent factors such as feeling and so forth, and their secondary factors such as birth and so forth— according to another school— all these have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their cause solely by way of the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*),
and they are also the cause of the view of a self-identity.
For the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is their cause,

and they [the present ones] are the cause of the previously arisen view of a self-identity; however, the non-afflicted truth of suffering— whether wholesome or unobscured-neutral— is neither caused by the view of a self-identity nor is it a cause for the view of a self-identity.
Because the fivefold causality is impossible here,
it is the generative cause (*janakahetu*) that is intended,
not the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
Because it is common to all [beings],
the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not applicable here; for the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), being obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), does not produce ripening.

In this regard, what has been stated— namely, that "excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the factors associated with it"— would be contradicted if the birth and so forth of the factors associated with the view of a self-identity were not co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu); for they would not have been excluded [from the category of co-existent causes].
For those which have been established are caused by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and are themselves the cause of the view of a self-identity.
Regarding those who do not recite the phrase "of those associated with that," one must supply the words, "How would their *Prakaraṇa* treatise be contradicted?
For they recite as follows: "having set aside birth, aging, duration, and impermanence from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)."

The intention of those who argue thus is that the characteristics (lakṣaṇas) operate only upon those [factors] associated with it, and not upon the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi); therefore, they are not co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu) for that [view].
They too must recite this;
since there is a fault in not reciting it thus, they must further recite this:
"and of those associated with that."

For those [factors] associated with it are conceived as a self by way of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because they share the same object and perform the same function; therefore, just as these characteristics are the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) among those associated factors,
so too are they in the case of the view of a self-identity— this is the intention of the Vaibhāṣikas.
Alternatively, it should be understood in this way by implication (*arthataḥ*):

by the mention of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), those associated with the view of a self-identity are also included; or, because the context continues, it should be understood that by those [afflictions] themselves, as well as those associated with them, [the same applies].
This shows that the Kashmiris do not hold [the view] of those from outside countries;
for they maintain that even that which is co-existent, such as mental factors (caitta) and so forth, is [of the same nature].

For the mental factors (*caitta*) and those characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) of the mind; and those secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are co-existent with the primary characteristic of a phenomenon (*dharma*), such as the "birth of birth" (*jātijāti*) and so forth—this is the detailed explanation. These are co-existent with the phenomenon.
It is not a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) because it is temporally remote;
for their activity operates upon the [four] characteristics such as birth (*jāti*), and not upon the primary dharma itself.
Furthermore, those [primary characteristics] and the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) are mutually co-existent because they operate upon the [four] characteristics such as birth.
A dharma is not a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu); rather, it becomes their co-existent cause due to its predominance.

For just as a king on a journey proceeds with his retinue, drawing along his entire circle of servants, so too do the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) proceed as they follow the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇas), which themselves follow the mind. Thus, the mental factors (caittas)— namely, the dhyāna-restraints and the outflow-free restraints (anāsrava-saṃvara)— which follow the mind, as well as their primary and secondary characteristics, are co-existent with the mind in that very same way.
But it is not by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) that it is a cause;
rather, the word "cause" is for the purpose of indicating the meaning.
And those secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), being co-existent, revolve around one another.
However,

that which is with resistance (*sapratigha*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)— consisting of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible— is co-existent (*sahabhū*) within atoms (*paramāṇu*) composed of eight substances and so forth,
yet it is not a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

The inclusion of the term "with resistance" (sapratigha) is for the purpose of excluding that which is without resistance; for the non-resistant form of restraint— consisting of the seven types of non-informative matter (avijñapti)— is mutually co-existent and is a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu).
And "all by the primary elements" means that derived matter— both resistant and non-resistant— is co-existent with its own respective primary elements,
but it is not a cause [for them] by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

And why are acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are simultaneous with the dharma they acquire not considered co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*), even though they arise together? Because acquisitions produced at earlier or later times are not co-existent; thus, to avoid the undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) of them being co-existent causes, the qualification "simultaneous" (*sahaja*) is added.
He asks "Why? and says:
"Because they have multiple results of maturation (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*).

This is because those [non-acquisitions] do not share a single result—either a result of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) or a result of maturation—with that which possesses the acquisition, since, like the bark of a tree, they flow separately.

Nor is there a single fruition of maturation (vipākaphala) in the two mindless attainments (acittasamāpatti), because of the statement: "The projective [karmas] and acquisitions (prāpti) do not [have such a fruition]."

Nor do they have a single outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*), for the acquisitions (*prāpti*) themselves are the outflow-results [of their respective dharmas] because they belong to a separate continuum;
it is held that only those factors that follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*) have a single result, namely both a ripening-result (*vipāka-phala*) and an outflow-result, but not the acquisitions.
Those [mental factors] are not concomitants— that is, they do not have the nature of accompanying— the mind; for all of this would be the case,
as has been stated in detail, that "whatever is a cause by way of being a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*)."
Regarding the phrase "of seeds, etc.," the word "etc. includes the sprout, stalk, stem, and so forth;
this principle has not been observed [to apply].
The principle characterized by the relationship of cause and effect is not observed between two things that arise simultaneously;
for previously there is the seed and subsequently the sprout, and previously there is the impact and subsequently the sound.
For example, as in the case of a lamp and its light, or a sprout and its shadow—
does there exist a relationship of cause and effect? Thus it continues.
A lamp arises only with its radiance, not without it;
yet when a sprout arises in the sunlight, there is shadow.
Nevertheless, the lamp is the cause of the radiance that arises simultaneously with it, and the sprout is the cause of the shadow.
"In the same way,
it must first be thoroughly examined," and so forth;
this is the opponent's intention, namely that the illustrative example is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Because the very same previously arisen collection of causes, such as the wick and the oil, is the cause for the arising of the lamp together with its light;
that same collection is the cause for both the lamp and its light,
and it is not maintained that the lamp is the cause of the light.

Thus, regarding the production of a sprout accompanied by its shadow, it must necessarily be stated that the previously arisen causal complex— consisting of the seed, soil, and so forth— is the cause;
for when a certain phenomenon exists, another phenomenon necessarily exists, and not by mere chance.
That is the cause;
the other is the possessor of the cause, meaning it is the property of the effect, as is the case with co-existent phenomena.

For example, in the case of the four primary elements (*bhūta*), those that follow the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), and those characterized and their characteristics (*lakṣyalakṣaṇa*), when one exists all exist, and when one is absent all are absent; thus, a causal relationship (*hetuphalabhāva*) would be logical for those that arise simultaneously (*sahotpanna*). This is the detailed explanation: a causal relationship among those that arise simultaneously is accepted.
For example, although the eye arises simultaneously with the visual consciousness, it serves as the cause for its arising; however, how is it not the case that they are mutual causes?
For indeed, the visual consciousness does not serve as the cause for that eye.
He said:

For this very reason, the meaning is that because existence and non-existence possess those [qualities], mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth are also causes of the mind; for when they exist, the mind exists, and when they are absent, the mind is absent.
"If that is so," and so forth;
if, when one exists, all exist, and when all are absent, one is absent, then there would be a mutual relationship of cause and effect among them in the desire realm, consisting of eight substances.

Thus, even though they are invariably concomitant, this undesirable consequence applies to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)— which has the nature of form, taste, odor, and tangibility— namely, that they would be mutual co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*); that is to say,
there is the consequence that derived matter would be a co-existent cause with respect to the primary elements (*bhūta*).
And regarding "of the secondary characteristics of mind, etc.":
by the word "etc.," the secondary characteristics that follow the mind are included;
and [the phrase] "with the mind and so forth" [is used].

Here too, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one must state that there is the consequence of mutual causality with those factors that follow the mind (*cittānuparivartin*); and by that same word "etcetera," it should be stated that this same consequence applies to the possessors of acquisitions (*prāptimat*) together with their acquisitions (*prāpti*)— whether simultaneous or otherwise— just as three staffs stand supported by one another's strength.
Abiding by mutual strength is "abiding by mutual strength";
it is like the abiding by mutual strength of a tripod of three staffs. In this way, the causal relationship of simultaneously arising mental states, mental factors, and so forth, is established.
"This must first be investigated," and so forth;
the intention is that this example has not yet been established and must be examined.

The three staffs arise simultaneously; by what power do they abide? Is it by that power which arises simultaneously with them, or rather is their arising such due to the force of a prior causal complex?
Or rather, he shows that just as their coexistence previously occurred by the power of a causal complex characterized by the assembly of primary elements and derived matter,
so too does their production occur later while mutually dependent; and furthermore,
there is something else involved therein, and not merely mutual strength alone.
If one asks what that is, he says:
it is a cord, or three rods fixed together, or a peg or a wedge; such is the meaning.
Just as the earth is the supporter of these [elements] below,

so too for these co-existent factors, there are other causes— namely, the homogeneous (*sabhāga*), pervasive (*sarvatraga*), and retributive (*vipāka*) causes— which serve as their foundation, like the threads of a cloth; thus, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) is established.

"Defiled [dharmas] are the [homogeneous cause] of defiled [dharmas]" means that defiled dharmas— namely, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)— function as homogeneous causes by virtue of their commonality of being defiled;
thus, unwholesome [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause of unwholesome [dharmas].

It is thus shown that obscured-unspecified [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause of obscured-unspecified [dharmas], and that unwholesome [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause of both obscured-unspecified and unwholesome [dharmas].
"Indeterminate [dharmas] are the [homogeneous cause] of indeterminate [dharmas]" means that non-obscured-indeterminate [dharmas] are the homogeneous cause of non-obscured-indeterminate [dharmas].
Form is indeterminate; the indeterminate aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the homogeneous cause of the five aggregates.
However, the four aggregates beginning with feeling are not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of form, because they are superior;
for it is not accepted that something superior is the homogeneous cause of something inferior,
[but rather] of what is equal or superior.
According to this statement,

because wholesome and unwholesome matter is produced through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*), it is both equal and superior; thus, there are four [types] that serve as its homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
such as the *kalala* being the cause for the *kalala* and so forth.

The five embryonic stages—the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*—and the five postnatal stages—the stages of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age: these ten constitute the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the ten stages;
that is, the *kalala* is the cause for another *kalala* up to old age, and the *arbuda* is the cause for another *arbuda* up to old age.
In this manner, it should be stated for the old, and for the old itself, by decreasing one by one and omitting one by one, until it reaches a single homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*);
and for other homogeneous classes of the same kind, when from a human birth only a human birth arises.
At that time, all ten stages—
even the stage of old age among those ten stages— are [the cause] for the other nine stages;
for that stage of old age is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the stage of old age produced in the subsequent moment.

However, it should be understood that the final [moment] of a birth is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for all ten stages, beginning with the *kalala* of a subsequent life; this applies even to external things, as in the detailed case where barley is the homogeneous cause of barley,
but not of rice.

By the statement, "Rice [is the cause] of rice alone, not of barley," he shows that although they are equal in being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the state of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetutva*) exists only within one's own continuum and not in another's continuum, due to the absence of the power to produce [it]. Thus, it is said:
"Past great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for future great elements."
The meaning is that the acquisitions are the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
Because they do not exist simultaneously, they are not the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*);
for this very reason, and because they are neither mind nor mental factors, they are also not the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).
Because it is not omnipresent, it is not an omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*);
because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*);
by process of elimination, it is understood that it is exclusively a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
If similar things are the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of similar things,
then it would follow that what arises later could be the homogeneous cause of what arose earlier,
and what arises simultaneously could be the homogeneous cause of what arises simultaneously.
Since it is said that "even the unarisen [is the cause] of the unarisen," he says: "Are even those not all [causes]? Rather, what then?"
Those born earlier— whether past or present— are the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*); by implication,
it is stated that those born later [in the future] are not the similar cause.

Thus, regarding past [dharmas] in relation to past and present [dharmas]: those that arose earlier are past, while those explained later are past and present; these are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for future [dharmas].
But it has not been stated that future [dharmas] are [the cause] of future [dharmas]; therefore, it is understood that there is no similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu) in the future,
and thus [it does not exist] at any time.
The phrase "never not a cause" is understood as meaning "it is indeed a cause";
therefore, the intention is that the future homogeneous cause exists.
"Co-existent," and so forth: the intention or underlying purpose refers to the co-existent, associated, and retributive causes; it is by virtue of this that the statement is made.
Therefore, because this statement was made with the intention of referring to the co-existent, associated, and retributive causes, there is no fault in saying that [the mind] is never not a cause;
for this explanation is intended as being based on the majority of cases, having in mind the final state.
The meaning is that [the opponent] intends the "last" [cause] to be in a future state;
his intention is that [a cause] exists as a cause even within all three time periods (*adhvan*). This is not a valid rebuttal to him—such is the detailed explanation.
This is not a valid rebuttal for that proponent;
why?
Because that dharma, having previously been a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) in the state prior to its arising, subsequently comes to exist [as such].
The meaning is that it is not eternally a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
Among the many future states, only one—the final state—is fixed as a homogeneous cause;
the many others besides it remain unfixed in that regard.
And since it was stated there in general that "it is never not a cause," this is not a valid rebuttal;
for even in a single state, one could indeed say that it is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The meaning is that when one phenomenon is the immediate antecedent of another phenomenon, it is called the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*);
this can be understood through such a conceptual construction.

That dharma, in its state of arising, becomes fixed as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); therefore, it is possible to speak with this intention (*abhisaṃdhāya*) regarding that final state, saying that there is never a time when it is not an immediately preceding condition—
why then did he say this?
If that dharma has not arisen— meaning,
if that dharma is future— it does not serve as a *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition); this is the meaning if one speaks of the final state.
"For the purpose of showing two aspects," and so forth;
just as in that case, a phenomenon which is the cause of another phenomenon is not at some time the cause of that same phenomenon.
He said,
"Never";
likewise, it should be done here as well.
He said: "A phenomenon that is the immediate antecedent of another phenomenon may, at some time, not be the immediate antecedent of that phenomenon."
One should never act with the thought,
"As it is here, so it shall be there.
How [could this be]?
If a phenomenon is the immediate antecedent of another phenomenon, could that [first] phenomenon ever not be the immediate antecedent of that [second] phenomenon?
He replied: No.
If that phenomenon has not arisen,
how should one act in that regard?
If a phenomenon that is the cause of another phenomenon is at some time not the cause of that phenomenon, he said: [no].
"If that dharma has not arisen" means that if that dharma is future, it does not constitute a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
regarding this, the Master says:
"If this were so, what benefit [would there be]?"—this is the full statement.
By demonstrating these two perspectives, no benefit whatsoever is obtained;

for in its actual state of arising, that phenomenon (*dharma*) does not function as a cause or as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara*) in a primary sense. Thus, it is considered unskillful on the part of the author of the treatise to have proposed such a thing.
In some cases it is with scope, and in others it is without scope;
first, that which is said to be "with scope" is as follows:
If a phenomenon that is the cause of another phenomenon is at some time not the cause of that phenomenon, he said: [Is this so?]
Regarding the phrase "never," how is it that [the cause] is not never a cause? Having stated this, he further explains that in its final state, it is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If that dharma has not arisen, it is without opportunity and is not the immediate antecedent;
however, once arisen, it is the immediate antecedent—
this is the intended meaning here, for having established a definitive meaning, he then proceeds otherwise.
Therefore, this previous resolution alone is correct;
since the statement was made with the intention of referring to the co-existent, associated, and ripening causes (*sahabhū-samprayuktaka-vipāka-hetu*), there is no fault.
As for that which was said [in the sūtra], "this... and so forth, [the detailed explanation follows].
From where does this come?
It was stated that what is future is certainly not a similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
If that which is future is indeed not a similar-cause, why then was the future view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) set aside [from being a cause]?
For it has been explained that whatever is established [as a cause] is both a cause for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and a cause arising from the view of a self-identity;
in that regard, how can future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* be a cause for *satkāyadṛṣṭi*?
To begin with, it cannot be a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) or an associated cause (samprayuktakahetu), because it does not exist simultaneously [with its effect].
It cannot be a ripening cause (vipākahetu), because it is indeterminate (avyākṛta). Nor can it be an efficient cause (kāraṇahetu), because it is not counted as being common [to all things].
By process of elimination, it would follow that [the future self-view] must be either a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) or a pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*);
and since in this context only the homogeneous cause is [intended as] the pervasive cause,
if the future self-view is not a homogeneous cause of the [present] self-view, why was it established for the sake of the third category?
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"Setting aside the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity"—this is how it should be formulated;
thus, only that which is associated with the view of a self-identity should be set aside.
But the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is not [the cause of that];

for those [factors] such as feeling are caused by the view of a self-identity through either the co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) or the associated cause (samprayuktakahetu), and they are also the cause of the view of a self-identity,
but not through the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).

The reading "for this [person] has destroyed the future view of a self-identity" (vinaṣṭako hy ayam anāgatāṃ satkāyadṛṣṭim) should not be recited together with the word *tat* located in the subsequent clause; rather,
these two words should be recited as a compound for the purpose of qualifying the associated truth of suffering.
"Associated with future *satkāyadṛṣṭi*"—
this should be understood by implication even if such a reading is not explicitly stated;
the intention is that a reading produced merely as a response to an objection in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is not authoritative.
How is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it says, "All phenomena are fixed within the fourfold [classification]"?
It means that regarding a cause, a phenomenon is fixed as the cause of another phenomenon; that phenomenon never fails to be the cause of that [other] phenomenon.
The meaning is that [the cause] exists in all three times.

In this way, one should apply [this principle] to the fruit: whichever phenomenon has which phenomenon as its fruit—such as human effort (puruṣakāra) and so forth—that phenomenon is fixed with respect to the fruit.

Likewise, one should apply it to the basis: whichever phenomenon, such as visual consciousness and so forth, has which phenomenon as its basis—such as the eye and so forth—that phenomenon is fixed with respect to the basis.
"In this way, [the cause] is restricted to its object: for a given phenomenon such as visual consciousness, the phenomenon that serves as its object—such as visible form—is to be applied accordingly.
Since phenomena are thus restricted to their causes, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) exists in all three time periods; such is the intention of the objector.
To show that there is no fault here because it does not intend to apply this to every type of cause, the Vaibhāṣika says:

In this context, the cause is the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the coexistent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), but not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*),
because these are not established in the future state;
nor is it the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because no immovable (*anāniñjya*) karma yields its maturation even in another realm of existence,
its fruit consists of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*),
since these two are the fruits of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).
The Vaibhāṣikas hold this view that the future exists and arises;
therefore, he raises this objection.

But if this were the case, it would follow—that is, it would entail—that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), having not previously existed, becomes a cause in its future state [and remains so] in its present state. This is precisely what is accepted with respect to the state (*avasthā*), but not with respect to the substance (*dravya*).
That is to say, it is indeed accepted that the state of being a homogeneous cause for a homogeneous cause did not exist before, but exists now.
However, it is not the case that the substantial particular (dravyasvalakṣaṇa) did not exist previously and now comes into being;
for the causal totality (sāmagrī) has the state (avasthā) as its fruit, not the substance (dravya) as its fruit.
Thus, through the totality of causes and conditions, the fruit is the present state, not the substance.
Because that dharma exists substantially even when it is future, and not only when it is present, the opponent says:
"What would be the consequence? and so forth—the Vaibhāṣika says:
"There would be its inclusion in the Treatise."
There is no apprehension of that future homogeneous cause,
for it is not so stated in that treatise.
Future roots of goodness are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of future roots of goodness; thus says the opponent, "For that which... and so forth.
The intention of the objector is this:
although a future homogeneous cause exists, it is not capable of the activity of giving or receiving a fruit;
for only that which is capable of the activity of giving a fruit and capable of the activity of projecting a fruit [is a true cause].

Is there no fault because only that homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) which is past or present is included? No, for the future homogeneous cause is not included because it lacks the capacity for the activity of giving and grasping its fruit.
"Therefore, the future homogeneous cause exists,
even though it is not mentioned in the treatise," so says the Vaibhāṣika.
"This is not so," and so forth;
this is not tenable,
for the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) possesses its fruit by means of the outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala).
The outflow of both the homogeneous and the omnipresent [causes] is [their] outflow,
because it is said that "outflow is similar to its cause."
And that is untenable for what is future;
it is untenable as a flow-result (niṣyandaphala).
Why?
Because of the absence of priority and posteriority,
in the future state, it cannot be determined that "this is prior" and "this is posterior," owing to their being dispersed;
and in the absence of priority and posteriority, it is not logical for one similar thing to be the outflow (niṣyanda) of another similar thing.
Now, if it is thought that a past or present [dharma] which has arisen is the outflow (niṣyanda) of a future one,
therefore he says:
Furthermore, it is not logical for what has already arisen to be the outflow of what is yet to come;
just as the past is not the outflow of the present,
so too that which has arisen cannot be the outflow of what is future.
He asks "Why? and says:
"Lest there be the fault that the fruit exists prior to the cause," because it is impossible for the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) to exist either before or simultaneously [with its cause].

Let it not be that the fruit exists prior to the cause; thus, there is no prior connection, nor is there a simultaneous connection. For in the future state, the fruit of a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not perceived as co-arisen, as is the case with a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) in the present state.
Therefore,

regarding the future time, because there is no distinction of priority and posteriority and because the future time is disordered, it is not logical for the cause of maturation to exist first and the fruit of maturation later.
And for that reason, just like the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) would also not be possible in the future;
to this the Vaibhāṣika says:
"This is not so, as it was stated that the ripening cause is likewise [restricted]."
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a state of mutual outflow (*niṣyanda*);
for how could that very same dharma which is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of another similar dharma be considered its outflow at that very same time?
For a son does not become the father of his own father at that very same moment;
why is it not so for the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu)?
The state of being mutual cause and effect does not follow—does not obtain—without a temporal sequence of prior and posterior;
why? Because the cause and the effect have distinct characteristics (*bhinnalakṣaṇatvāt*); that is to say, the characteristic of the cause is its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Its characteristic is either unwholesomeness or being wholesome yet contaminated;
and the characteristic of its fruit is different, namely, being unobscured-indeterminate.
The ripening cause consists of the unwholesome and the wholesome-contaminated dharmas.
Because of the statement that "maturation is an indeterminate phenomenon," therefore [it is so],
and so forth.
The homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) is established precisely by way of its state;
being established within a state,
it is a homogeneous cause when in a past state or a present state, but not when in a future state.
However, the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is established by its characteristic;
being established by its characteristic as having the aforementioned definition throughout all three times, even a future ripening cause is neither excluded nor prohibited.
This is what is investigated here.

Is it because, in the future time, similar phenomena are so dispersed that it is impossible to determine that "this is the cause" and "this is its outflow-result," and for this reason the future is not established as a similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)? Or rather,
[is it because] whichever phenomenon might be the similar-cause of another phenomenon...
That dharma would be its outflow-result (*niṣyandaphala*) by virtue of causes and conditions;
therefore, the future similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) is not established.
This has not been examined by the authors of the commentaries.
But as for me, this former position alone appears plausible;
so what is this restriction? Is it determined that [the object] must belong to its own level alone?
The intention is that it does not exist otherwise;
rather, the path consists of the nine stages mutually.
The word "but" (tu) functions as a qualifier;
by the term "path," the truth of the path is intended,
thereby distinguishing the truth of the path from that which is associated with outflows (sāsrava).

For a contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) only within its own level (*svabhūmika*), not in another level; however, the Path (*mārga*), even when belonging to another level, is a homogeneous cause.
Here, by the mention of "level," both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are included.
But since [the rule] regarding the inclusion of the *dhātus* applies only to that which is *sāsrava*, he says:

"That which is *sāsrava* and the Path—given that their distinction of levels (*bhūmi*) is the same—the Path alone, consisting of nine levels, is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for one another, but not the *sāsrava* [factors]. Why is this so? He says:
For that [path] is adventitious to those stages and does not fall within their realm,
because it is not appropriated by the cravings belonging to those stages;
indeed, the cravings of the desire, form, and formless realms do not appropriate uncontaminated phenomena in the way they appropriate contaminated ones.
When one then desires nirvana or the path, that is wholesome desire for the Dharma (dharmacchanda) and not passion (rāga),
because of the statement: "for that [passion] is to be abandoned."
"Of that which is of the same kind" means of that which is of the same kind as the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If that were so, then everything would follow as being the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of everything;
therefore, he says:
If that is so, then what is the purpose of the mutual inclusion in the phrase "of the equal and the superior"?
Its meaning is that there is mutual [inclusion] between those belonging to higher levels and those belonging to lower levels.

A [dharma] belonging to a higher level is also a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for two [dharmas] belonging to lower levels that are either equal or superior; likewise, one belonging to a lower level is also a homogeneous cause for two belonging to higher levels—
as it is explained in detail.

The receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of that very same receptivity when it is future, and also of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe anvayajñāna*), up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), provided they are superior; however,
it is not the cause of anything inferior.

For the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering is not the homogeneous cause of the future receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering; [this is because] the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning are [the causes] of three, two, and one [categories of dharmas], respectively.
The path of seeing is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for the subsequent path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning; thus it is the cause for three [subsequent paths].

The path of cultivation is the homogeneous cause for the subsequent path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning, but not for the path of seeing; thus it is the cause for two [subsequent paths].

The path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for another path of no-more-learning, but not for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

In that regard as well— meaning within those [paths] such as the path of seeing— the path of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriyamārga*), which has the nature of the path of seeing, is the homogeneous cause only for a path of the same nature that possesses either dull or sharp faculties.
The path of those with sharp faculties is the cause only for the path of those with sharp faculties, not for the path of those with dull faculties, because of its inferiority;
the same should be stated regarding the path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"It is as follows," and so forth;
for even a single person of dull faculties possesses six paths.

For one of naturally sharp faculties, there are three [types of paths]. Among them, the path of faith-follower (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for its own subsequent path of faith-follower; for its own path of dharma-follower (*dharmānusāri-mārga*); and for six other paths of its own that exist in a future state—namely, the paths of the faith-resolved (*śraddhādhimukta*), the view-attained (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the timely-liberated (*samayavimukta*), and the untimely-liberated (*asamayavimukta*)—according to their respective natures as being subject to arising or not subject to arising. Thus, it is the homogeneous cause for these six.

The path of one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for four [paths]: another path of one liberated through faith, and the paths of those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the timely-liberated (*samayavimukta*), and the untimely-liberated (*asamayavimukta*). The path of one timely-liberated is the homogeneous cause for two: another path of one timely-liberated and the path of one untimely-liberated. However, the path of one liberated through faith is not the cause for the paths of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) or the follower by Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) exists at a prior time.
And because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is superior,
the same principle should be applied elsewhere:

the path of the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for three paths— the subsequent path of the follower by dharma, as well as the paths of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) and one who is liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*).

The path of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāptamārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of two [subsequent paths]: another path of one who has attained through vision and the path of one liberated at any time (*asamayavimuktamārga*). The path of one liberated at any time is the homogeneous cause of only one [subsequent path]: another path of one liberated at any time.
However, the path of one who follows through the Dharma (*dharmānusārimārga*) is not the homogeneous cause of the path of one who follows through faith (*śraddhānusārimārga*).
Since the path of the follower by Dharma (dharmānusāri-mārga) is distinguished by its faculties,
nor is the path of one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta-mārga) distinguished by its faculties,

it would follow that the path of one temporarily liberated (samayavimukta-mārga) is the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the path of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta-mārga), which is distinguished by its faculties.
It does not obtain [the status of a fruit],
because it is comprised within the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣamārga);
for a cause that occurs at a later time cannot have a fruit that occurred at an earlier time.

Furthermore, the path of one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta-mārga) is not a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for the path of one liberated by occasion (samaya-vimukta-mārga), because it is inferior in terms of the faculties (indriya). How so? This is the detailed explanation.

Furthermore, how can a path belonging to a lower stage— from the stage of the *anāgamya* up to the stage of the *vijñānānantyāyatana*— be, as the case may be, equal to or superior to a path belonging to a higher stage, from the second *dhyāna* up to the stage of the *ākiñcanyāyatana*, whether it be a path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), a path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), or a path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)?
For it must be understood that [the higher path] is somehow inferior due to its lower stage.

In terms of both the faculties (*indriya*) and the accumulation of causes (*hetūpacaya*), first, regarding the faculties: one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna is equal to that same path of following by faith belonging to a lower level. Or, [one may be] superior.
Because both possess dull faculties,
the follower-of-dharma path belonging to that very same lower stage is superior due to its sharpness of faculty.

Likewise, the path of the follower of dharma (*dharmānusāri-mārga*) belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna is equal to the path of the follower of dharma belonging to the lower stages. In this way, these two—the paths of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*) and the follower of dharma—belonging to the stages of the fourth dhyāna, should each be applied as appropriate to the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*), which are distinguished by their respective stages and faculties, as being either equal or superior. Similarly, on the path of cultivation, the path of one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta-mārga*) belonging to a lower stage is equal to the path of one resolved through faith belonging to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
Because both have dull faculties,
likewise his very path of occasional liberation belonging to a lower stage is equal,
because both have dull faculties.
For that same [person], the path of occasional liberation belonging to a lower stage is superior due to the sharpness of their faculties.

Likewise, regarding the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), it should be applied as appropriate whether the path of no-more-learning belonging to a lower stage is equal to or superior to the path of no-more-learning belonging to the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana).
In this manner, all the stages (bhūmi) are to be applied.
How, by way of the diminution of causes, does a path belonging to a lower stage become equal to or superior to one belonging to a higher stage? To this, the following is said:
In that context, the phrase "of the paths of seeing and so forth" is an elaboration;
by the inclusion of "and so forth," the path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning are subsumed.

Compared to the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering belonging to a higher stage, the dharma-knowledge of suffering belonging to a lower stage is superior by way of the accumulation of causes.

From the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) of an upper stage, the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance (anvaya-jñānakṣānti) of a lower stage— up to the subsequent-knowledge-acceptance of the path (mārga-anvaya-jñānakṣānti) from the dharma-knowledge of the path of an upper stage— is superior by way of the accumulation of causes, because it is accumulated through one additional similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) at each step. Furthermore,
the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) of a lower stage is superior to the path of seeing (darśanamārga) of an upper stage by way of the accumulation of causes.

For the path of seeing is accumulated by causes that are themselves the path of seeing, whereas the path of cultivation is accumulated by causes that are both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Consequently, the path of no-more-learning belonging to a lower stage is superior in terms of the accumulation of causes compared to the paths of seeing and cultivation belonging to higher stages,
because it is accumulated by the causes of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
The path of seeing belonging to a lower stage is equal, in terms of the accumulation of causes, to the path of seeing belonging to a higher stage when considering moments of equal duration;
likewise, the path of cultivation is [equal] to the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning is [equal] to the path of no-more-learning.
Thus, in this way, a certain [path] may be equal in terms of its faculties but superior in terms of the accumulation of causes, even though it belongs to a lower stage.

For example, compared to the path of one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the paths of one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) belonging to a lower level may, from the perspective of the accumulation of causes, be equal, yet be superior in terms of their faculties (*indriya*); for instance,

compared to the path of one who follows by faith and so forth belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, the path of one who follows the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) and so forth belonging to a lower level is [superior] when considering an equivalent moment.

A certain [path] is superior in terms of its faculties and the accumulation of causes; for example, compared to the path of one who follows by faith belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna, the paths of one who has attained through views and one who is liberated at any time belonging to a lower level are superior, because each subsequent stage possesses a greater accumulation of causes, such as the "soft-soft" and other degrees of the faculties.
Excluding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the [nine] grades beginning with "weak-weak" are impossible therein,
from the "weak-weak" grade of that [path], even the "weak-medium" grade of a lower stage [arises] up to the "strong-strong" grade from the "medium-strong" grade of a higher stage.

In relation to moments that are either similar or dissimilar, [the path] becomes equal or superior due to the accumulation of causes, because it is accumulated by causes consisting of one additional type at each stage. As it was stated that "the path of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of six [paths]," how can the path of the follower by faith be the homogeneous cause of the path of the follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusāri-mārga*)?
For there is no simultaneous manifestation of those two within a single continuum;
therefore he said:
"Even though the paths of the follower by faith and the follower by dharma are impossible within a single continuum..."
But that which has arisen is the cause of that which is yet to come;
for here "impossibility" refers to the state of not being present,
not to non-existence.
For those of dull faculties, there exist paths belonging to their own continuum that are of sharp faculties— just like the path of dull faculties—

and even the paths of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or the path of one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), which might become manifest within their continuum if a transformation of the faculties (*indriyasañcāra*) were performed.

Therefore, the path of one who follows by faith (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*), having arisen, is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)—as appropriate—for the future paths of one who follows by dharma (*dharmānusāri-mārga*) that are subject to non-arising, as well as for the paths of those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those liberated at times (*samayavimukta*), and those liberated independent of time (*asamayavimukta*), whether they are destined to arise or not, and whether they are equal or superior.
Thus says the Master Vasumitra.

The arisen path of the faith-follower (*śraddhānusāri-mārga*) is the cause for the unarisen path of the Dharma-follower (*dharmānusāri-mārga*) or the path of one who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta-mārga*). [Objection: When those such as the faith-followers transform their faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*) and bring forth the path of the Dharma-follower and so on, that is incorrect;
for the faculties of a faith-follower do not undergo transformation.
However, those such as the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and others may transition;
they are called "preparatory" (*prāyogika*) because they have arisen through preparatory effort (*prayoga*).
Thus, they are "preparatory" in the sense of being produced by application.
The inclusion of the term "resulting from application" (prāyogika) is for the purpose of excluding those acquired at birth;
"consisting of hearing" (śrutamaya) refers to those belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) which have emerged through hearing the word of the Buddha.
Those consisting of hearing are [the causes] for those consisting of reflection; thus,
