they are the causes for those consisting of reflection alone, not for those consisting of hearing.
Because of the statement "of those two [minds] which are equal or superior," there is an absence of that which consists of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya).

Because the desire realm is not a state of meditative concentration, there are no [insights] consisting of cultivation; and because there is an absence of those consisting of reflection, for when they begin to reflect, [they do so through the power of hearing].
Therefore, for them as well, the cause for the absence of that which consists of reflection is simply that meditative concentration (samādhi) arises;
this refers to those [stages] beginning with that which consists of hearing.

"Those that are weak-weak are the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for all"—that is, they are the cause for other weak-weak factors of the same kind, as well as for the eight superior types beginning with the weak-medium and so forth. Why are the weak-medium factors the cause for only eight, excluding the weak-weak variety? Because the latter is inferior [to them].
This is the principle:

for example, among the seven [levels of] weak-intense [defilements], those that are medium-weak are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of six; continuing in this way down to the intense-intense, they are the cause of one [of their own kind].
Thus, by excluding each preceding category, they serve as the cause for the subsequent ones because of their relative inferiority.
Regarding the phrase "wholesome states acquired at birth" (*upapattipratilambhikāḥ*): acquisition through birth is "acquisition at birth";
those which possess this [acquisition] are "those acquired at birth."
By the rule "ata ini-ṭhanau," the suffix *ṭhan* is applied; thus,
all those nine types [of wholesome roots] are mutually homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*),
from the weak-weak up to the intense-intense.
The extremely superior [state] is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) of those that are weak-weak, up to the extremely superior;
it is not [the cause] of only those that are equal or superior,
because it is unconditioned (anābhisaṃskārika).

For it is not admitted that the fruit of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*) is inferior; this is also the case for those produced without volitional effort (*anābhisaṃskārika*), even if they are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
All nine types are mutually homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) because they are not produced through effort;
all those that have arisen previously are the homogeneous cause for all subsequent ones belonging to the same level (*samāna-bhūmika*),
and in this case, neither equality nor superiority are taken into account.
These are, respectively, the homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) of four, three, two, and one [categories]:
those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are the homogeneous cause of the four, beginning with those born of maturation;
those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) are [the cause] of only the three, beginning with those pertaining to deportment.
Because those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are inferior due to their lack of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskārika*),
the [mind] pertaining to craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) is the cause for two: that pertaining to craftsmanship and that pertaining to emanation (*nairmāṇika*).
The emanated [bodies] belong only to those who are emanated;
they do not belong to the preceding ones,
because the succeeding ones are produced through volitional effort.
The transformation mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire realm is also the fruit of the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

Thus, being the fruit of the four *dhyānas*—namely, the fruit of the first, second, third, and fourth *dhyānas*—the transformation mind of the desire realm is of four types. It follows that these are, respectively, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for four, three, two, and one [higher] states.
The fruit of the first dhyāna is the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) for four fruits: those of the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The fruit of the second dhyāna is [the cause] for three: the fruits of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
The fruit of the third dhyāna is [the cause] for two: the fruits of the third and fourth dhyānas.
The fruit of the fourth dhyāna is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) only for another fruit of the fourth dhyāna;
what is the reasoning here for such a restriction? Desiring to point out that reasoning, he says:
"The fruit of a higher dhyāna is not [the cause] of the fruit of a lower dhyāna," and so forth.

A transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire realm that is the fruit of the fourth dhyāna is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for a transformation-mind of the desire realm that is the fruit of the first dhyāna, nor for those up to the transformation-mind of the desire realm that is the fruit of the third dhyāna. Why? It is said:
for there can be no inferior fruit—produced without great effort—from a homogeneous cause that is produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*) and requires great exertion to accomplish.
For the fourth dhyāna is not accomplished by the same specific kind of effort as that by which the first dhyāna up to the third dhyāna is accomplished;
what then?
Since it is produced by a more excellent specific effort,
it is understood that its fruit is produced by a still more excellent specific effort;
therefore, the fruit of a lower dhyāna is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the fruit of a higher dhyāna.
But the fruit of a higher dhyāna is not [the cause] of the fruit of a lower dhyāna;
and just as the fruit of the fourth dhyāna has been applied [as a cause],
so too should the fruits of the third and second dhyānas be applied.
"Therefore they say" means that because there is no inferior fruit for a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) produced through volitional effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*),
therefore they say so.
"What do they say?
They say: "It would be something that has arisen," and so forth.
The untainted *duḥkhe dharmajñāna* that has arisen is not the cause of those untainted *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntis* which are of the nature of non-arising.

Because the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is distinguished from the receptivities to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) by its being a product of volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*),
it is indeed distinguished in this way: that it arises simultaneously with the attainment of dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyogaprāpti*).
And that which is superior is not the cause of that which is inferior;

for example, the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) that has already arisen is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the subsequently arising paths of once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returners (*anāgāmin*), because it has been abandoned through the state of arhatship.
"It may be determined within a single continuum as previously acquired," and so forth.

The future receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) are acquired in the very first moment; they belong to a single continuum. The knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), which arises in the second moment, [is likewise].
Those [moments] are not its cause, because the fruit does not exist prior to it;
for the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering exists only after the receptivities to the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering.
Because that [dharma] has already arisen while those [future dharmas] have not yet arisen, a future dharma is therefore not a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
The future receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntayaḥ*) have indeed been acquired in immeasurable numbers, yet they have not arisen;
[if one asks] whether they were previously arisen, the detailed explanation is that the question concerns a phenomenon that was merely previously acquired, not one that had arisen.
Since that which is unarisen does not constitute a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*),
one now asks with a specific intent whether even that which has arisen previously might fail to be a similar cause;
[the answer is] "that which is superior [is the cause] of that which is inferior."

The meaning is that a superior [path] belongs to one who has fallen away from a lower fruit; for example, in the case of one who has fallen away from the fruit of Arhatship, the fruit of Non-returner, or the fruit of Once-returner, when a lower fruit becomes manifest— whether it be the manifestation of the fruit of Non-returner or the manifestation of the fruit of Once-returner—
the previously arisen Arhat-path that is of superior degree [is the one that arises].
It is not a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for a subsequently arisen fruit of non-returning or a fruit of once-returning,
because it is inferior;
likewise, for one who has fallen away from the fruit of non-returning, that which is the path to the fruit of non-returning [is not a homogeneous cause].
That which has arisen previously is not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for a once-returner fruit that arises later,
because it is inferior;
and so too is the acquisition of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānaprāpti*), and so forth in detail.

Regarding the acquisition of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna-prāpti*) that has arisen previously: it is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those acquisitions of the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna-kṣānti-prāpti*) that arise simultaneously with subsequent moments—namely, from the moment of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) up until [the moment] simultaneous with the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*). What is the reason?
Because of their inferiority and her superiority,
how then is there the inferiority of those [others] and the superiority of her?

The acquisition of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is superior to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), because it is liberated from the possession of the afflictions to be abandoned by that receptivity and because its causes have been further accumulated.

Therefore, the acquisition of the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering is superior even to the acquisitions of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, despite the latter having more accumulated causes.
And these [subsequent acquisitions] are inferior because they are acquisitions of that [preceding state].

Furthermore, the acquisition of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is superior to the acquisition of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) which arose in the first moment; yet, for those same two reasons, that acquisition of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering is [in turn] inferior [to its own subsequent acquisition].

Therefore, even other [factors] that arise subsequently together with the later moments— such as the attainment of the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)— are indeed inferior, despite their being more highly accumulated as causes; thus, that [attainment] is not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of those [subsequent factors],
whereas the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*), however, consists of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).
The word "iti" here signifies restriction, and its position is displaced; thus, it means that only mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) are the associated cause (samprayuktaka-hetu).
"If this were so," and so forth;

if it were merely stated that "mind and mental factors alone are the associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), it would follow as an over-extension (*samprasajyate*) that even those arising at different times are associated causes with those arising at different times, and even those arising in different continua are associated causes with those arising in different continua.
It is not that they do not become mind and mental factors because they are distinct in terms of time and continuum;
rather, it is because they possess the same aspect and object.

Thus, if mind and mental factors have the same aspect—such as the single aspect of blue—and the same object—the single object of blue—it is in this way that they constitute the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and not otherwise.
The intention is that by this, the states of being born at different times and being born from different continua are excluded;
nevertheless, the same undesirable consequence remains:
namely, the consequence that those born at different times and from different continua would be mutual associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) for one another. This is the meaning.
For it is possible that mental states (citta) and mental factors (caitta) produced in different times and continua could share the same aspect and object;
however, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even those produced in different continua could do so.
Therefore, "being produced at the same time" is specified as a single defining condition.
For when many people see the new moon and so forth, their minds and mental factors proceed with a single mode of apprehension and a common basis; thus,
because their basis (*āśraya*) is equal— that is, undifferentiated— they are called "having a common basis" (*samāśraya*).
For if the word *sama* were used in the sense of "equal," then because of the equality of their genus (*jāti*), that same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow—
namely, [that they would be mutually causes] by virtue of having mutual fruits— as is detailed at length;
just as for travelers in a caravan who proceed on the road through their mutual strength.

In this way, the mind is the fruit of the mental factor, and the mental factor is also the fruit of the mind; thus, they are mutual fruits. For that reason, it is a co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) "with five [factors]," and so forth.
The meaning is that [the associated cause] consists of fivefold equalities— namely, the equalities of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance;
it is called the "associated cause" (samprayuktaka-hetu) in the sense of having an identical application and an identical activity.
Just as those very merchants, traveling along the road by mutual support, have an equal application toward the act of enjoying food, drink, bathing, bedding, and so forth;
in that same way, there is a state of equal application among these [perfections] for one another.
For this very reason, he says:

For indeed, not even one [of them] is associated without all [the others]; thus, they are "previously omnipresent" (*pūrvasarvagāḥ*), meaning that which is both "previous" (*pūrva*) and "omnipresent" (*sarvaga*).
Therefore, they are called "all-previous-omnipresent" (*sarvapūrvagāḥ*).

"Previously arisen and all-pervading" means that the previously arisen universal (*sarvatraga*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), whether past or present, belonging to their own level, are the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) for subsequent defiled states— those whose nature is affliction, as well as those associated with or originated by them— whether they are future, present, or past. We shall explain this further.
"The universal [defilements] are the views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause,
as well as doubt together with those [views], and that ignorance which is associated with them"— this we shall explain in the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
"By way of being the general cause of afflicted phenomena," and so forth;
because this universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) pertains generally only to afflicted phenomena across all five categories,
whereas the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) pertains to both afflicted and non-afflicted phenomena.
Therefore, it is established separately;
explaining how this [ignorance] serves as the general cause for afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*), he says:
"Because it is also the cause for those belonging to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*)."
For it is by the power of these [universal factors] that the afflictions such as attachment and so forth, which belong to a different category and exist within a different category, arise.

Furthermore, which are those factors belonging to other categories that are to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, and which constitute the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) for that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering?

And which are those factors belonging to other categories that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, cessation, and the path, and which constitute the universal cause for that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin?

They are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*) because they go toward and associate with all categories of afflictions (*kleśa-nikāya*) regarding their objects, or because they become the causal state for all categories of afflictions;
therefore it has been said:
All afflictions have the view of a self-identity as their root, originate from the view of a self-identity, and arise from the view of a self-identity;
since passion, pride, aversion, and so forth manifest by way of grasping at a self,
[one might ask] does this apply even to a noble person?
Thinking that for an noble person (āryapudgala), all universal [defilements] have been entirely abandoned because they are to be abandoned by insight (darśanaprahātavya),
whereas for those in training (śaikṣa), lust and the other [defilements] still manifest— and that these lusts and so forth do not have universal [defilements] as their cause— one asks thus.

Since "defiled phenomena" (*kliṣṭā dharmāḥ*) are mentioned without qualification, it is understood that they arise within the continuums of both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*);
this also includes whatever is the maturation (*vipāka*) of those phenomena to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
This was stated for the purpose of completing the argument;
it is not an example [intended] to show that conditioned phenomena are indeterminate.
Both the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are included.

The obscured-unspecified refers to the factors associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extreme attachment (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as well as those originating from them, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it also includes all afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) factors belonging to the form and formless realms.
The inclusion of the term "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) is for the purpose of excluding space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*).
Regarding the phrase "in the supreme, neutral, and constant," because those two are neutral (*avyākṛta*),

the afflicted factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) have as their neutral causes precisely those [afflictions] such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) which function as their homogeneous, pervasive, co-arising, and associated causes, as appropriate; they do not have other [neutral causes] such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth.

But as for those belonging to the higher stages, it is easy to understand that they are also [produced] by other causes; the non-obscured-unspecified [dharmas] have non-obscured-unspecified [dharmas] as their homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu),
while the unwholesome [dharmas], such as attachment and so forth belonging to the desire realm, have unwholesome [dharmas] as their cause.
And those [defilements] have the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth as their pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu);
this is the illustration here.
Furthermore, because it is not specified that they are unwholesome, both those to be abandoned by seeing (darśanaprahātavya) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāprahātavya) are included.
This is the second indicator here:
that "the other afflicted truth of suffering" is the third indicator;

for by that [third indicator], the other afflicted truth of suffering—both that which is to be abandoned by vision and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation—is included, since no distinction has been made.

For it has been explained that, by way of the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*), even for the noble ones—as well as for ordinary persons—the [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation are caused by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), yet they are not themselves causes of the view of a self-identity.
If this is so, then how is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it says:

"If unwholesome [states] also have neutral (*avyākṛta*) causes, and not only unwholesome causes"? [This refers to the following: "The unwholesome roots are causes of the unwholesome, and the unwholesome roots are causes of the neutral. How is this statement in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be understood?
It may be that an noble person (*āryapudgala*), while falling away from detachment from the desire realm (*kāmavairāgya*), first brings forth a defiled volition (*kliṣṭā cetanā*).

For at the time of falling away from detachment from the desire realm, that volition of the noble person has only unwholesome roots (*akuśalahetu*) by way of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).

He raises this objection with the following intention: "The meaning of the *Prajñapti-bhāṣya* appears to be that [the afflictions] do not have neutral states as their cause, because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) have already been abandoned."
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"This was stated with reference to a cause that has not been abandoned.

That is to say, this passage from the *Prajñapti-bhāṣya* was spoken with the intention and reference to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), both of which have not yet been abandoned.
For the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*), are the cause of that volition;
because they have been abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are not mentioned in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya*.
As for the statement "unwholesome and wholesome-with-outflows" (*akuśala* and *kuśalasāsrava*), since unwholesome states are necessarily with-outflows (*sāsrava*), they are not specified separately.
Wholesome states, however, are of two kinds— contaminated and uncontaminated— and thus they are further distinguished;
those wholesome states that are contaminated [are now being discussed].
They are the cause of maturation (vipāka-hetu) and not untainted (anāsrava),
because they possess the nature of maturation; that is to say, because their intrinsic nature is to ripen.

"Because of their weakness, like rotten seeds," and so forth. Just as rotten seeds, even when moistened, do not become the cause for the production of a sprout due to their weakness, so too neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, even when moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), do not become the cause for the production of maturation (*vipāka*) because of their weakness.
Even though they are powerful, the untainted [dharmas] do not produce a maturation because they are not moistened by craving;
just as dry seeds, even if potent and substantial, do not produce a sprout because they are not moistened by water, so it is in this case.
The deficiency of the former’s own power and the deficiency of the latter’s auxiliary causes— what are they associated with?
To what are they associated?

Regarding what is associated with which realm: can those who are dissociated from the realms of desire and so forth—being dissociated and untainted (*anāsrava*)—bring about a maturation (*vipāka*) that is dissociated?
It must be a maturation associated with a specific realm, not one that is dissociated.
"Because they have the nature of phenomena associated with the desire realm and so forth, but the remaining ones... and so on;

the meaning is that the remaining [factors]—both the unwholesome and the wholesome-with-outflows—are of both kinds, because they possess both modes, that is, because they possess the mode of being strongly moistened.
They bring about maturation just as seeds, when moistened by moisture, produce a sprout; such is the detailed explanation of the cause of maturation.
If "vipāka" is a noun derived from the root with the suffix -ghañ in the sense of the action itself— meaning "vipakti" (the process of ripening)—
then it is a genitive compound meaning "the cause of ripening."

Now, [in the phrase] "it ripens by itself" (*vipacyate svayam*), the suffix *ghañ* has the sense of an object (*karmasādhana*). In that case, since it is an object-based derivation, "ripening" (*vipāka*) itself is the cause; thus, [the term] is "the cause of ripening" (*vipākahetu*).
What follows from this? What fault arises from this?
If "cause of maturation" is understood as a noun-based derivation (*bhāvasādhana*),
then the expression "the eye born of maturation" would not be tenable,
for the eye is not produced from maturation itself.
What, then, is meant? It means "of karma that has reached maturation," for [the mind] is not the cause of maturation itself.

Now, if the cause is indeed the fruition itself, then the interpretation [of the compound] as an action-noun (*karmasādhana*) is established; for that eye is "born of fruition" because the fruition is precisely the karma,
since it is the karma that ripens.
However, [the expression] "the ripening of action" (karmaṇo vipākaḥ) is not tenable.

For ripening (vipāka) is said to be action itself, not the process of ripening; and here, in the phrase "the ripening of action," the sense intended is one that establishes the state (*bhāvasādhana*), not one that establishes the action (*karmasādhana*). Therefore, the expression "the ripening of action" is not tenable.

It was stated previously that "in both ways there is yoga," and it was said here [in this verse] that "the five internal [elements] are born of maturation and accumulation"; those born from the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
Because of the elision of the middle term, as in the case of "ox-cart" (*goratha*), the term is understood as a derivation based on the state (*bhāva-sādhana*);
or else, karma that has reached the time of its fruition is called "ripening" (*vipāka*),
because it is said to "ripen" (*vipacyate*).
Therefore, "born from that" means "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*); this is the adoption of the instrumental derivation (*karmasādhana*).
Alternatively, since maturation itself is the fruit, when there is a desire to express the fruit, it is adopted as a nominal derivation (*bhāvasādhana*)—this is the meaning.

Therefore, the expression "the eye born of maturation" (*vipākajaṃ cakṣuḥ*) is established either by the elision of the middle term or by adopting it as an instrumental derivation (meaning "that by which maturation is produced"),
and it is also established as a nominal derivation (meaning "maturation itself") in the sense that maturation is the result of karma.
Since the comprehension of words is preceded by the intention to speak,
"vipāka" (ripening) means a dissimilar result from a dissimilar cause.
For the cause is indeed determinate,
whereas the fruit is indeed indeterminate;
however, since the maturation of simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) and the others is strictly similar [to their own nature], the qualification [“determinate”] is applied.
In the Abhidharma treatise, it is explained in this way; therefore, this is prescribed:
"A ripening cause consisting of a single aggregate has a single fruit," and so forth.
Here, the acquisitions (*prāpti*) exist separately from the mind and other factors, like the bark of a tree.
According to the principle of fulfilling those [causes], the individual fruit is described:
"having one aggregate" (*ekaskandhaka*) refers to a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) in which the acquisitions (*prāpti*) reside within a single aggregate.
And since its birth and other [characteristics] belong to that very same [dharma], it consists of a single aggregate (*ekaskandhaka*);
and since the fruit of acquisitions (*prāpti*) is the very same as the fruit of their birth and other characteristics,
they possess a common fruit and are thus "single-fruited" (*ekaphala*).
The "two-aggregate" [cause] has a single fruit:
the ripening cause consists of bodily and vocal karma, as well as their birth-characteristics (*jāti*) and so forth.

It is called "two-aggregate" because bodily and vocal karma are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), while their birth-characteristics and so forth are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
And they have a single fruit because their fruits are not distinct; thus,
the four aggregates consisting of wholesome and unwholesome mind and mental factors have a single fruit.
"Along with birth and so forth" means that those minds and mental factors are, as appropriate, comprised within the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness;
and since birth and so forth are comprised within the aggregate of formations, the retributive cause consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit because it possesses a common fruit.

For there is no fruit of the mind that is distinct from that of the mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth; because they are not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*), there is no ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) consisting of the five aggregates in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
This is because, in this realm, bodily and vocal action—which are subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—do not share a single fruit with the mind and its mental factors.

However, because they constitute separate groups (*kalāpa*), the "three-aggregate" (*tri-skandhaka*) does not exist in any of the three realms, since mind and mental factors necessarily have a single fruit and possess,
as the case may be, the nature of four aggregates.
"In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is [an action] consisting of a single aggregate," and so forth.
Since acquisition (*prāpti*) together with its [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) is comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), it consists of a single aggregate;
likewise, because it has a common fruit, it has a single fruit.

The attainment of non-perception (asañjñisamāpatti) should also be described in the same way, together with birth and the other [characteristics], because informative action (vijñapti) is included within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
and because birth and the others have the nature of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).

A two-aggregate [action] has one fruit, as before, in the case of a wholesome mind that is not in meditative absorption (*asamāhita*); because there is no concomitant matter (*anuparivarti-rūpa*), it consists of four aggregates, being comprised of the aggregates of feeling and so forth, excluding the aggregate of matter. In the case of a mind in meditative absorption (*samāhita*), it consists of five aggregates.
Because the concomitant form (anuparivarti-rūpa) functions simultaneously with the mind and other factors,
[the text says] "in the formless realm" and so forth;
therein, since all form is absent, the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu) consists of either one aggregate or four aggregates.
Regarding "acquisition" (*prāpti*):
there, together with its own birth-characteristic (*jāti*) and so forth, it consists of a single aggregate (*skandha*), as previously described.

Cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is also, together with its own birth-characteristic and so forth, a single aggregate; thus, it is easy to understand that it is a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) with a single fruit.

"There is karma," and so forth; for that karma whose maturation (*vipāka*) is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), that life-faculty and its concomitants, such as birth (*jāti*) and so on, must necessarily be the maturation associated with that [karma].
And all of this is comprised within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); thus, one sphere ripens as maturation (*vipāka*).
For that [person] for whom there is the sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*), there are two: the sphere of the mind and the sphere of mental objects.

For within that aggregate of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), there are necessarily co-arising factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, as well as [factors] such as birth (*jāti*) which are of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).

Since these factors—feeling and so forth, as well as birth and so forth—are subsumed under the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), those two—the mind-base and the dharma-base—are indeed what ripen as maturation.
The same applies to that for which the tangible-base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) is [the cause].

Since that tangible object necessarily possesses [the factors] such as birth and so forth, the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) also ripens for it, not merely the sphere of tangibles; thus, two spheres ripen for it.
For one who possesses the sphere of the body (kāyāyatana), three [spheres] ripen:
that very sphere of the body, the sphere of tangibles, and the four primary elements (bhūtacatuṣka) which serve as its basis.
Since that very [result] must necessarily be based on the four primary elements (bhūtacatuṣka),
and since those [elements] must possess birth and so forth, the dharma-āyatana also ripens there as the third; such is the detailed explanation.
Thus, for one whose maturation (*vipāka*) consists of any one of the bases of form, odor, or taste, three bases constitute that maturation:

that very base which is any one of form and so forth, the base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) which has as its nature the primary elements (*bhūta*) that serve as its support, and the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) which has as its nature the birth-moment (*jāti*) and other such factors associated with it.
For one who possesses the sense-base of the eye, there are four [sense-bases]:
that very eye and the body-base, because their functioning is necessarily dependent upon both the eye and the body.
And regarding the sense bases of the tangible and mental phenomena, it is just as before;
thus, "for whomsoever," and so forth,
means for whomsoever one of the [faculties] such as the ear is the maturation.
For that [mind] as well, four bases (*āyatana*) are the maturation (*vipāka*):
namely, any one of those bases beginning with the ear, as well as the body-base, the tangible-object-base, and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*), as previously described;
"there exists such karma," and so forth in detail.
From five up to eleven bases (*āyatana*) are [results of] maturation (*vipāka*) according to possibility, but not all twelve bases,
because the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*) is by nature not a result of maturation.
Regarding this, Ācārya Vasumitra explains:
there is karma for which only a single sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) ripens as its maturation (*vipāka*); why is this not possible? What is the reason?
Since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the fruit of projecting karma (*ākṣepakakarma*), if life is ripening as a maturation (*vipāka*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
then in that case the body-faculty and the life-faculty necessarily exist during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, even before the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen.
Once the six sense bases have arisen, there must be seven bases:
the six beginning with the eye, and the mind base (*manāyatana*).

Thus, there must necessarily be seven in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there must be at least two: the mind base and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).
Since the life-faculty has as its fruit the projection of an entire birth, we ask: which realm (dhātu) is intended here? We reply: the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
But surely, since the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the fruit of projecting karma (*ākṣepakakarma*), there must necessarily also be the mind-base (*manāyatana*);
yet it is not the case that the life-faculty alone ripens as maturation (*vipāka*).
It is not the case that the life-faculty alone ripens as maturation.
Since maturation (vipāka) has sensation as its manifestation, it follows that sensation must also be present there;
to this it is replied: this was said with reference to the arising of a single moment.

At the moment when the resultant mind (*vipākaja-citta*) of one born in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) does not manifest, at that moment only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) ripens as a result; because only the resultant life-faculty arises and the mind-base (*manāyatana*) does not manifest, for what reason does another mind-base not exist when it should manifest? [The answer is: "For him, there are two bases: the mind-base and the dharma-base."
This is now investigated:
if it is thus the case that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the maturation (*vipāka*) of the projecting karma,
then when the life-faculty is maturing, the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and so forth must also mature.
It is not the maturation in another sense-field that is being denied here; rather, it is the cause of maturation (vipākahetu) that is being considered,
for such karma exists.

It is held that for one whose single sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) alone ripens and no other sphere does, this much is what has ripened; that is, it is the thought that the mental spheres (*manāyatana*) and so forth existing therein are the maturation of precisely that same karma which projected the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and not of any other karma.
What is the basis for this restriction?
For it is indeed possible that the maturation of one karma is the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*), while that of another is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
And you might say that the mind-base and so forth belong to something else; just as when it is said that for one whose eye-base exists,
there are the eye, body, tangible, and mental-object bases, [it follows] that for whom the eye-base is a maturation.
Because its body-base (*kāyāyatana*) is necessarily [the result of that],
and likewise its mind-base (*manāyatana*) and so forth are also the maturation (*vipāka*) of that very same karma— this is not so.

Because the functioning [of one] is dependent upon another in certain cases—for indeed, there is no manifestation of the eye-faculty without the body-faculty—whereas even when there is no maturation (vipāka), there is the manifestation of the life-faculty in the mind; therefore, this is not equal. However, the Master Saṅghabhadra says:
There is karma whose maturation ripens as the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) alone; there is that whose maturation ripens as the life-faculty (jīvitendriya);
and there is that whose maturation ripens as the eye-sphere (cakṣurāyatana).
For that [person], there are five sense bases— namely, the eye, body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects— and so on up to the tongue base.
For one who possesses the sense-base of the body, there are four:
the sense-bases of the body, visible forms, tangibles, and mental objects.

Because it is inseparable from form (*rūpa*), some other school maintains that the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is also the maturation (*vipāka*) of that very same karma which produces the eye; however,

the Master [Vasubandhu], holding the view that the sense-sphere of form is not necessarily the maturation of that specific karma, adopts another position regarding that for which there is the sense-sphere of the body (*kāyāyatana*).
Of those three,
for one whose sense-base is the eye, there are four.

The intention is that factors such as the life-faculty (*jīvita*) and the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), which are mutually inseparable, are not necessarily the maturation (*vipāka*) of one and the same karma.
These two positions were recorded by the authors of the *Vibhāṣā*; whichever of them is pleasing to someone, let him accept it.
It is encompassed by that;
enough of this digression.
Now, how is it that the maturation of a certain karma ripens as a single sense-base (*āyatana*)?
Regarding the statement "for some [it is] up to eleven," he says:
"Because karma has variegated and non-variegated fruits, like external seeds," and so forth.
The seeds of lotuses, pomegranates, nyagrodha trees, and others have variegated fruits.

Indeed, silver is seen as the root, sprout, stalk, leaf, filament, and pericarp of lotus seeds and the like; furthermore, trees such as the *nyagrodha*, which possess an abundance of many trunks, branches, boughs, shoots, sprouts, flowers, and fruits, appear like clouds.
Some have undiversified fruits,
such as the seeds of barley, wheat, and so forth, because their fruits are of a single form.
This is the nature of seeds:
the maturation of a single-temporal action— whether past— ripens as a maturation spanning the three times (past,
present, and future), but not as a maturation of a dual-temporal action (both past and present) ripening in a single time (the future).
"But not from the reverse" means that a single-moment result should not arise from multi-moment karma,
lest the fruit be excessively inferior to its cause.
Furthermore, maturation does not ripen simultaneously with the action, because the simultaneous (sahabhū) and associated (samprayuktaka) causes operate upon what has arisen together [with them],
whereas the cause of maturation depends upon a dissimilar ripening.
Nor does the maturation ripen immediately thereafter;
for what reason? Because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the power of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and not by the power of the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*), even though that immediately preceding condition may itself be a ripening cause; for this very reason, the immediately succeeding moment— arising from the immediately preceding condition which is a ripening cause— is sometimes wholesome, sometimes unwholesome, and sometimes indeterminate.

Otherwise, it would indeed be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Alternatively, the intention is that because the immediately succeeding moment—which is by nature not a maturation—is drawn forth by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*) depends upon a continuous stream; for when there is a stream of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), the cause of maturation bestows its maturation once that stream has passed away.
The intended meaning is that this is simply the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
It was stated [above] that "there is a restriction regarding their sequence in terms of meaning";
the meaning is that it was stated in terms of meaning, not in terms of the literal words.
For speech is of two kinds: that expressed by its own words and that implied by the meaning.
How is it a "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāgahetu*)? [It is so] because those born earlier are similar to those belonging to their own category and level.
Likewise,
that which is called "pervasive" (sarvatraga) is the cause of defiled states within its own level, according to the statement: "The previous pervasive [factors] are [the causes] of the defiled."

The similar (sabhāga) and pervasive (sarvatraga) causes exist only in the past and present, not in the future; this is because they are mentioned without qualification. By implication, it is stated that the co-existent (sahabhū), associated (samprayuktaka), and retributive (vipāka) causes belong to all three time periods;
for it is only the similar and pervasive causes that must have arisen previously.
Furthermore, because of the restriction that "these two have arisen previously," because of the statement that they are mutual fruits,
and because of their intrinsic nature as unwholesome states such as reflection (*cintā*) and so forth, they do not belong to the [three] time periods (*adhvan*).
How is it stated that "it is formulated as a sutra"?
For a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) is indeed fruitful by means of its outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala).

And that [arising] of a future [dharma] is illogical because of the absence of priority and posteriority; this and other such reasons that have been stated for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) should be understood as applying to the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) as well, in the same manner.
For the pervasive cause is indeed like the homogeneous cause;
for while the homogeneous cause is defiled for defiled [dharmas],
the pervasive cause is also defiled for defiled [dharmas] alone.

However, it has been stated that this [cause] is established separately as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) because it is a general cause for afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*). Furthermore, just like a homogeneous cause, this one does not exist in the future, and it possesses a fruit, namely the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*).
In the same way, its news is that there are three belonging to the three time periods.

Because of the restriction that "only those belonging to the three time periods are the three," and "only the three are those belonging to the three time periods," the cause as a reason (kāraṇahetu) becomes otherwise;
and how is it otherwise?

"Belonging to all time periods and yet free from time periods"—is this [the case] by its own nature? For all other phenomena, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*);
therefore, it is exactly thus and not otherwise.
Since these two—cause and fruit—are mutually dependent, he asks:
"What, then, is that fruit of which these are the causes?
The fruit consists of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and dissociation (*visamyoga*).
Thus,
it is stated that all phenomena, with the exception of space and analytical cessation, are results;
"if this is so," and so forth.
Since the unconditioned is a fruit, and considering that the fruit is unconditioned, it must have a cause— either itself or something other than itself—
of which that unconditioned fruit is the effect;
and because the unconditioned is a cause, it must also have a fruit— either itself or something other than itself.
That unconditioned [phenomenon] which is the cause of a certain fruit—
those two, cause and fruit, do not belong to the unconditioned;
for the unconditioned, characterized by analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), does not have the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
And it has no cause because it is unproduced;
yet it is considered a cause because it exists as a state that does not obstruct the arising of conditioned phenomena,
and yet no fruit is established for it.
Furthermore, because it is incapable of receiving a fruit or giving one,

and for that very reason because the six kinds of causes are impossible— this is the detailed explanation— it cannot be its co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) or its associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).
Because the unconditioned is incomparable and because it is impossible for it to belong to the same level,
for this very reason it does not have a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
And because this is non-defiled,
it does not have a ripening cause,
since the unconditioned has the nature of being without ripening.
For maturation (*vipāka*) is a phenomenon (*dharma*) comprised within the category of sentient beings and included within the [real] elements (*dhātu*);
and because it is unproduced (*anutpādyatva*), these [other] causes do not exist for it,
and precisely because it is unproduced, it does not have a causal cause (*kāraṇahetu*).
Therefore it is asked: why is the path not accepted as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of dissociation?
Because it is established as such by virtue of its being a non-obstruction to arising.
Furthermore, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) does not possess origination;
and because it does not fall within the temporal paths (adhvan), it has no causes,
for a cause is established only for a phenomenon that falls within the temporal paths.
Thus, because the six kinds of causes are impossible for it, the unconditioned has no cause;
and because the five kinds of fruits are impossible for it, the unconditioned has no fruit.
Why?
Generally speaking, that which is dissociated from the time periods is incapable of receiving or giving a fruit;
for it has been said:
"The five present [factors] receive a fruit, and two give [a fruit]."
Regarding such passages as these,
furthermore, that [result] cannot be a dominant result (*adhipatiphala*),
for a dominant result is held to be either co-arisen (*sahotpanna*) or subsequently arisen (*paścādutpanna*).
Since that which is unconditioned is not itself conditioned, it cannot be the dominant fruit of a conditioned [cause];
furthermore,
because it is non-arising, it possesses neither a simultaneous nor a subsequently arisen fruit.
Precisely because it is characterized by non-arising,
there is no outflow fruit;
for an outflow fruit is a similar phenomenon that arises from that which has arisen.
For this very reason, there is no fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because of the absence of human effort in the unconditioned;
for that by whose power something arises or is attained is the fruit of human effort for that [power].
And for this very reason, dissociation is not the fruit of the path;
for dissociation is attained solely through the power of the path,
and the path is not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Nor is it the fruit of maturation,
because it differs in nature from the cause of maturation;
for the cause of maturation is indeed with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the unconditioned is not associated with outflows;
alternatively, because of the dissimilarity to the five kinds of causes, the five kinds of fruits are impossible, and thus no fruit of the unconditioned is possible.
If the Path is not accepted as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), then whose fruit would it be?
For there must be a fruit possessed of a cause; or rather, in what manner or by what means is that fruit?

As for what was said regarding "in what manner is that fruit," the meaning is that the fruit arises through its power—that is, through the power of the path—by way of attainment. Alternatively, the connection between the words is as follows: "Of what is that the fruit?"
How is that the fruit of the path, or in what sense is it its fruit?
Because it is attained through the power of that [path].
In that case, it follows that attainment alone is the fruit of the path,
because the efficacy of that path resides in that very attainment; why then is dissociation not [the fruit]?
The phrase "the fruit of the path" is the subject under discussion;
therein, "due to incapacity" means that the path lacks the capacity with respect to that dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
Therefore, the path is not in any way its cause; indeed, none of the six types of causes constitutes a cause for it,
and its fruit is dissociation (visaṃyoga).
The intended meaning is that the fruit to be attained is not something produced;
for some maintain that there are five kinds of causes:
the producer (*kāraka*), the informer (*jñāpaka*), the manifester (*vyañjaka*), the destroyer (*dhvaṃsaka*), and the attainer (*prāpaka*).
The cause that produces is like a seed to a sprout;
the cause that makes known is like smoke to fire;
the cause that manifests is like a lamp to a jar.
Just as a hammer is the destroyer of a jar,
and a chariot is the bringer of that which is to be reached in another place,
so too is the path the bringer of this [nirvāṇa].
It is thus shown that the cause is not a producer and that the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala) is not something produced;
this is the detailed explanation beginning with "if there were no sovereign fruit" (adhipatiphala).
If the unconditioned were to have a fruit, it would be a dominant fruit, because it is established as being a causal condition; however,
those [fruits] do not belong to the unconditioned.
Because of this statement, that [result] is also excluded for him; thus, when [the matter] has been determined, the interlocutor asks:
"If there is no sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala), how can the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) be a causal condition (kāraṇahetu)?
It is a causal condition by virtue of being a non-obstruction to arising."

By the statement that it is "the state of being an unobstructed cause for arising," it is shown that this *kāraṇahetu* (efficient cause) is established only with respect to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
and not with respect to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why is its fruit not established because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)? To this he says:
"And it has no fruit, because that which is devoid of the time-periods (*adhvan*) is incapable of receiving or giving a fruit."
For only a dharma that is comprised within the time-periods possesses the capacity to receive and give a fruit, and not any other;
as it will be stated:
"The five [causes] grasp the fruit when present; two give it."
The meaning is that although it was stated by way of a synonym— that it is a "cause"— it was not stated by its own specific term.
"Those too are impermanent" means "those too are indeed impermanent"; by this restriction, it is implied that the cause is not permanent,
and the same applies to the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as well.

Just as causes (*hetu*) here have been stated to be impermanent, so too conditions (*pratyaya*) have been stated to be impermanent, because of the statement: "whatever are causes, whatever are conditions.
Therefore, it follows that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be an objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Because of the restriction "for the sake of arising," those causes and those conditions for the arising of form are also impermanent.
But as for those [factors] for the sake of non-arising,
conditions are indeed twofold:
productive and non-productive.
Furthermore, objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*) are not productive [of the dharma], because they are merely objects;
for an objective condition exerts its activity (*kāritra*) upon a dharma that is currently being produced,
since it is grasped by present minds and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).
Is it not the case that [the causes] also [act], because of the statement: "When [a dharma] is ceasing, two causes exercise their activity"? This is the full extent of the argument.
A cause is both productive and non-productive;
therefore, because the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) exists merely as a state of non-obstruction, its status as a causal condition (kāraṇahetu) is not denied, even though it is non-productive.
Thus, the objective condition (ālambanapratyaya) has been explained according to the Sūtra.
Regarding the statement "there are four conditions" in this sutra, [the Buddha] did not prohibit [it];
the intention is that there is no fault because it does not contradict the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, many sūtras have disappeared due to the loss of the original communal recitations; therefore,
the Master does not insist on this point.
There is no contradiction with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
rather, it is precisely the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that is being investigated— whether it exists or not—
and thus everything is indeed unconditioned.
Not only is analytical cessation [unconditioned],
like form, sensation, and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), perception and the others are included.
Just as feeling is a distinct entity from form, and perception from feeling, up to consciousness being a distinct entity from the formations,
so too there is no unconditioned thing that exists as a distinct entity from the five [aggregates] beginning with form;
therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that the unconditioned is not a substantial reality (*dravya*).
"Merely the absence of the tangible" means merely the absence of a resistant substance;
"not finding" means not obtaining.

Regarding the cessation of arisen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and birth: when there is the cessation of arisen latent dispositions and of birth through the power of discernment—that is, the power of wisdom—the non-arising of other latent dispositions and of further birth is "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). Thus, it is stated that the cessation of latent dispositions is the cessation of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), and the cessation of birth is the cessation of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Furthermore, the mention of both types of cessation is for the purpose of establishing the distinction between nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).
According to the Sautrāntika system, what are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*),

how is there the cessation of birth through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyābala*), and what is the latent tendency of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā-anuśaya*) among the ninety-eight latent dispositions?

Whichever path is the antidote to a particular latent tendency (*anuśaya*), through that analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) and simultaneously with it, that latent tendency arises in the first moment;
by its power, its cessation occurs in the second and subsequent moments.

And by the power of that very [knowledge], there is the cessation of rebirth without further connection, just as in the case of the remainder of the *nikāyasabhāga*; this is the full explanation. The *nikāyasabhāga* is characterized by such states as humanity and so forth.
Or, the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) characterized by the five aggregates—
when that which remains of it, being of that very same nature, arises [in the next life],

there is a non-arising due to the deficiency of conditions during an intermediate death (*antarāmaraṇa*), even before the lifespan of that remaining group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) has been fully exhausted.
What, then, is cessation through non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*)?

It is the deficiency of conditions; specifically, it is the incapacity of the final aggregates—known as the state of death—to connect with a new homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), due to the incompleteness of auxiliary conditions such as the necessary equipment. Therefore, this is called cessation through non-analytical discernment.
The element of nirvana with remainder is the non-arising of suffering;
the one without remainder is also the non-arising of suffering.
That which is called "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is not established without deliberation (pratisaṅkhyā),
because the deficiency of the latent tendencies (anuśaya)— which are the cause of arising— is not produced by deliberation.
Therefore, this is precisely cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), because it is a cessation by its own nature;
that is to say, it is a cessation by its own essence, not through the power of wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Because it does not exist when that has not perished" means that as long as that latent disposition (*anuśaya*) has not perished, there is an absence of that analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*),
because the obstruction to its arising has not been established.

The phrase "akṛte utpattau pratibandha eṣām" means that there is an obstruction to their arising when [the cause] has not been performed; thus, they are "those for whom there is an obstruction to arising when it has not been performed," and the state of being such an obstruction to their arising is what is meant by "akṛtotpattipratibandhabhāvaḥ."
This is the efficacy of analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyā*) in this context:
if it is indeed non-arising (*anutpāda*), then— according to the detailed explanation— the intended abandonment is *nirvāṇa*.

If it is said that nirvāṇa is the non-arising of only that which is yet to come, then since the past and the present have already arisen, they cannot be said to have non-arising; how then is this statement in the Sūtra to be interpreted: "They lead to the abandonment of suffering that is past, future, and present"? How is that scriptural passage to be understood?

Furthermore, for one who holds that *nirvāṇa* is a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*), it would follow that *nirvāṇa* is attained even through past and present [moments] by means of cultivating that [substance] and so forth; thus, this Sūtra would become poorly interpreted.
Therefore, [the Sūtra says] "by the abandonment of the afflictions having that as their object" (*tad-ālambana-kleśa-prahāṇāt*).
The meaning is: because of the abandonment of afflictions that take as their object past and present suffering.
As for "desire and lust for form" (*rūpe chandarāga*), desire (*chanda*) is the longing for a future object.
Attachment (*rāga*), however, is the determination regarding an object already attained;
in detail, it extends up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It is the desire-attachment toward feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*sañjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Abandon that;
when desire and passion are abandoned, thus will that consciousness of yours be abandoned,
and likewise the suffering of the three times.
The abandonment of desire and attachment is itself the abandonment of the suffering of form and so forth,
and through that, there occurs the non-arising of future desire and attachment;
thus, he demonstrates that the abandonment of suffering belonging even to the three time periods is logically established.
"This very same principle applies" means that even if the reading is "of the abandonment of past, future, and present afflictions," this very same principle applies there as well.
"One should abandon whatever desire or attachment there is toward afflictions, whether passion or hatred," and so forth;
thus, through the abandonment of the afflictions that take those [afflictions] as their object, there is also the abandonment of the affliction itself.
The meaning is that the abandonment of even the afflictions belonging to the three time periods is logical because they do not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Alternatively, the detailed explanation begins with "in a previous birth": existence in a previous birth is "pertaining to a previous birth" (*pūrvajanmika*).
That which occurs in this life is "belonging to this life" (*aihajanmika*);
thus, the affliction (*kleśa*) is excluded as being momentary.
How is this to be understood?

All afflictions belonging to previous births are connected [to this life], as are those belonging to the present birth, but not those belonging to a single moment; therefore, he says: "Just as craving [is explained] in the *Vicarita*," and so forth.

Since it is seen elsewhere as well, it should be understood in this way: how are the eighteen investigations of craving applied to a single moment in the past time? Therefore, with reference to a past birth, it is said that there are eighteen investigations of craving.
"Monks, when one thinks 'I am,' there arises the thought 'I am thus,' 'I am in this way,' 'I am otherwise,' 'I am existent,' or 'I am non-existent';
and the thought 'I shall be' occurs to him."
"I shall not be," "I shall be thus," "I shall be in this way," "I shall be otherwise"—such thoughts occur to him;
"May I be," such a thought occurs to him; "May I be thus," "May I be even so," "May I be otherwise"—such thoughts occur to him.
The thought "May I be" arises for him;
the thoughts "May I be thus," "May I be in this way," and "May I be otherwise" arise for him,
and so on up to the present.

Likewise here too, the entire stream of afflictions from previous lives and those of this life are connected; it is not momentary. Thus, he speaks with the intention of establishing that very point, saying "by those two types of afflictions," and so forth.

By these two types of afflictions—those belonging to previous births and those belonging to this birth—a capacity characterized by the nature of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is deposited as the state of a seed within the present continuum for the sake of the arising of future [afflictions]. Through the abandonment of this state of the seed, those two types of afflictions also become abandoned;
just as it is metaphorically said that "karma is exhausted" through the exhaustion of its maturation (*vipāka*) by means of experiencing that maturation, so it is here.
How, then, is the abandonment of the future established?
For [it might be argued that] no seed-state has been deposited in the continuum by that [past factor], such that its abandonment would constitute an abandonment. To this he says:
"Furthermore, the abandonment of future suffering or affliction is their absolute non-arising due to the absence of a seed."
And because of the absence of seeds, [cessation] occurs through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*);
for when cessation has already passed, or when it is present and facing cessation, effort in producing the antidote is neither meaningful nor purposeful—this is the sense.
Among these, dispassion (*virāga*) is supreme.
The meaning is that the destruction of passion (*rāgakṣaya*) is dispassion (*virāga*), which is analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
How can that which is non-existent be the foremost among non-existent things?
That is to say, how can the non-existent unconditioned dispassion be the foremost among the non-existent unconditioned things such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth?
He states the reply to this:
"Even non-existence is something," and so forth;
and [the reply] to the second [objection] is...

Immediately after the second truth, the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), what would be the third of the three ancient [truths]—seen by oneself through wisdom and taught to others through instruction?
What would be the fault? This is the meaning.
"Furthermore, what would there be?
means "What quality would there be? He asks this as an inquiry regarding a further quality.
As for what was said—that the Vaibhāṣika position would be upheld—what would that entail? What would be the fault? To this it is replied:
[the object] would then be an unreal mental construction (*parikalpita*).
The meaning is that there would be a fault,
as in the case of form, sensation, and so forth; this is established through direct perception.
"Like the eye and so forth" means by way of action, that is, by inference;
this has been explained more than once.
"Of a thing" means of a thing such as passion and so forth;
[it is said] because of the impossibility of its existing in the nature of cause and effect and so on.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the relationships of owner and owned, part and whole, and so forth are included;
for when a thing ceases, there is no cause-effect relationship, nor the relation of part and whole, and so on—
this is the detailed explanation of how its attainment is now restricted.
Regarding this restriction of the attainment of that cessation—
namely, that the attainment belongs to this very cessation and not to another— what is the cause for that restriction of attainment?
For there is no connection whatsoever between cessation and its attainment, because it is impossible for them to stand in the relation of cause and effect or any such relation.
"One who has attained nirvana in this very life" means one who abides in nirvana with a remainder of substrate;
if [nirvana] were non-existence, how could there be its attainment?
"By way of attainment," and so forth:
by the attainment of the noble path, because one has acquired a basis that is absolutely opposed to the arising of both afflictions and renewed existence, it is said that "nirvāṇa is attained";
[yet] its nature is merely non-existence.
The word *mātra* is for the purpose of excluding [the existence of] another substance.
The detailed explanation beginning with "that which indeed belongs to this" and ending with "non-appearance" consists of these synonymous terms, from "abandonment" up to "non-appearance."

The example "it is clear" (*sphuṭam*) is stated [in the commentary] as "non-appearance" (*aprādurbhāva*); because there is no appearance in this [state], they show that *aprādurbhāva* is an instrumental noun derived from the locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*), and not that *aprādurbhāva* is a verbal noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*) meaning "the state of not appearing. This is the meaning.

Since that attainment is postulated from whichever path abandonment is attained, then when that path exists or when that attainment has been reached, let the non-appearance of suffering be accepted; what is the use of postulating another nirvana?
"His mind is liberated" refers to the time of the Blessed One’s nirvana without remainder,
in accordance with the actual state of things and in accordance with the object of focus.
The object of conjunction is that wherein one is conjoined with affliction; these are called "dharmas with a basis" (vastukā dharma) because they possess a cause.
It is called "appropriation" (parigraha) because the object of appropriation is grasped.
That very same thing is the "object of appropriation" (*parigrahavastu*),
because it is mentioned at the end; thus,
the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) is recited at the end of the verse.
Its ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*) is precisely the aforementioned efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), because it was mentioned at the beginning of the verse;
its dominant fruit (*adhipaja-phala*) is [the same].
*Adhipati* means the sovereign; that which is born from that is *adhipaja*, meaning the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Some read *pūrvasyādhipatam* instead.
The result of the dominant [condition] is "dominant" (*ādhipata*);

however, the form *ādhipatya* is obtained by the exception (*apavāda*) [of Pāṇini 4.1.85], which prescribes the suffix *ṇya* after words ending in *aditi*, *aditya*, *āditya*, or those having such as their final member.
Now, if it were the case that even in the domain of an exception (apavāda) there is the inclusion of a general rule (utsarga),
then this very [exception] would constitute that form of sovereignty (adhipatya).
The meaning is that when there is the state of mere non-obstruction, there is also the state of being a factor (*aṅgībhāva*),
which implies both the state of being primary (*pradhānabhāva*) and the state of being a producer (*janakabhāva*).

Thus, by this it is shown that for both kinds of efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*)—whether it be an active agent or a passive observer—there exists a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), with the exception of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For he will say:
"A conditioned [phenomenon] is the dominant fruit of a conditioned [phenomenon], but only one that is unprecedented."
Thus,
regarding the ten bases (āyatana),
from the eye and form bases up to the body and tangible object bases.

Because of the statement, "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises; ... up to ... dependent upon the body and tangibles, body-consciousness arises," this is indeed a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*);
for it is not possible for the sense bases such as the eye to be any of the five causes—such as the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*)—of visual consciousness and the others.

However, since the mind-base (*manāyatana*) can function as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and so forth for mental consciousness, and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) can also function as a concomitant cause (*sahabhūhetu*), an associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*), and so forth, it is not restricted to being only a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*). Therefore, it was stated that [the causal condition] pertains to ten bases, and not to twelve.
And regarding the receptacle world, is there a state of being a constituent part of karmas through the cause that is the efficient cause? This is what is under discussion.
For the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), although produced by wholesome and unwholesome karma, is not accepted as a fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*),
because of the defining characteristic that "maturation is what is designated as a sentient being" (*sattvākhya*).
Therefore, this [receptacle world] is the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of that causal factor (*kāraṇahetu*).
Is it not the case that the ear and the other [faculties], not only the eye,
also possess a dominant influence, albeit indirectly, in the arising of visual consciousness?
It is not directly [perceived], as is the case with the eye;
how is this known? He says:
because the desire to see arises after having heard.

The intention is that visual consciousness arises when there is a desire to see; in this manner, [the formula] should be applied, such as "because the desire to smell arises after having smelled," and so forth. This is how it should be applied.
The phrase "the outflow fruit belongs to the similar and universal [causes]" continues; thus,
it is determined that the outflow fruit belongs exclusively to the similar cause and the universal cause.

For the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) also arises immediately after those two; thus, the restriction "the fruit of human effort belongs to the two" means that it belongs specifically to the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*).
The fruit of human effort is "pauruṣa," meaning the fruit of human effort;
because it is not distinct from the state of being a person (*puruṣabhāva*), human effort is not separate from the state of being a person.
For human effort (*puruṣakāra*) is indeed just human action (*puruṣakarma*); it is not something other than the person.
For Buddhists do not maintain that action is distinct from those who possess action.
Therefore, whatever is the fruit of human effort—
That which belongs to the person alone is called "the person";
that which is the activity of a given dharma is its function, its action, or its operation.
That is his "human effort" (puruṣakāra); this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: since there is no internal active person (puruṣa) and only a mere phenomenon (dharma) constitutes the "person," it would follow that it is a "phenomenon-effort" (dharmakāra) rather than a "human effort. To this, he says:

For "human effort" (puruṣakāra) is like [the effort of] a person; just as in the world there is the human effort of a person who is conceptually constructed, so too is there the human effort of a dharma— thus it is called "human effort."
He tells an illustration:
"The *kākajaṅghā* herb," and so forth; the herb that has the shape of a crow's leg is called *kākajaṅghā*.
Is that man who was seen as a hero like a rutting elephant truly a rutting elephant,
or is he so only to others?

Since other causes also exist— namely, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)— it is said that [the result] exists for these as well.
Why is this stated except for the ripening cause? He says:
because the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) arises either simultaneously with or immediately after [the cause].
For it has been stated that the fruit arising simultaneously belongs to both the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*),
and that [fruit] is exclusively the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
indeed, there is no other fruit that arises simultaneously.
The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) arises immediately after [the cause] only for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*);
however, for the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), it occurs in both ways.
But is the fruit of human effort distinct from the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) or the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*)?
No, it is said;
for that very same fruit receives various names according to its function.
Thus, because it arises similar to its cause, it is called the "outflow fruit" (niṣyandaphala).
Because it arises through the power of that [cause], it is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
and because it arises by remaining in a state of non-obstruction, it is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
however, it is not a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*).
Is it that which arises simultaneously or that which arises immediately subsequent? This refers to the statement, "maturation is an indeterminate dharma," and so forth.
The restriction is that it is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), exclusively designated as a sentient being (*sattvākhya*), and exclusively arising from the determinate; thus,
by "indeterminate," the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is intended,
and by "sentient being," that which has a designation (*ākhyā*) is meant.
It is called "sentient" (sattvākhya),
meaning it arises from the continuum of a sentient being;
it is "born of the determinate" (vyākṛtodbhava) because it originates from that which is determinate.
But those that are non-accumulative and outflowing do not arise from the determinate;
yet is it not the case that for one who has attained a specific meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there is an accumulation of the sense-faculties and the great elements,
and this too arises from the determinate?
That [resultant mind] becomes a maturation,
and the emanation-mind is likewise so, because it is produced from a mind in meditative concentration.
This is not a fault;
in the expression "arising from the determined" (*vyākṛtodbhava*), the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) signifies a later time.
It refers to that which arises at a later time from a determined [state], whether wholesome or unwholesome, and not simultaneously or immediately [thereafter].
That is maturation;
however, that which arises from concentration is accumulation,
and it occurs both simultaneously with the concentration and immediately after it.

The mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), however, arises immediately [after the transformative mind], and it is intended that the maturation (*vipāka*) belongs to the same level; yet since both of these can also belong to different levels, there is no undesirable consequence regarding maturation.
Outflow (*niṣyanda*) is similar to its cause.
Thus,
with reference to the similarity between the wholesome, the afflicted, and the unobscured-neutral,
if this were so, then an uncontaminated outflowing fruit would result from a contaminated wholesome cause, due to their similarity as wholesome.
It is not so, because of the absence of similarity of category;
for it is held that a homogeneous cause belongs to the same category.
Not all [factors] are similar to this universal cause by way of their level and their defiled nature; thus,
the similarity of this universal cause consists in its level and its defiled nature.
