With what [is it associated],
with its own fruit,
and how?
In terms of the levels (*bhūmi*), the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*) ranges from the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgrika*);
its fruit likewise ranges from the desire realm up to the peak of existence.
Furthermore, by virtue of being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), the universal cause is itself afflicted.
That fruit is also afflicted (*kliṣṭa*),
yet its similarity is not by way of its specific mode (*prakāra*), as is the case with the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*);
whereas for that [other cause], there is similarity even by way of its specific mode.
That universal cause (sarvatragahetu) which possesses similarity even in terms of its mode with its own fruit is indeed accepted as being a homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu);
for it becomes a universal cause precisely because of the similarity in terms of its level (bhūmi) and its afflicted nature (kliṣṭatva).
And it is also a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) by way of similarity in its mode;
for this very reason, a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established because of the possibility of a third category due to its possessing the nature of both.
The first alternative is that which is a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) but not a pervasive cause (*asarvatraga*); this refers to the homogeneous cause consisting of attachment and so forth,
for it is indeed a homogeneous cause of the afflictions belonging to its own category.
However, the universal cause (sarvatragahetu) is not [the same] because it does not have a non-universal nature; rather,
the universal cause belonging to a second category is the universal [defilement] such as the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth.

For that [universal defilement] is indeed a universal cause because its nature is universal and because it is the cause of defiled states belonging to other categories; however, it is not a homogeneous cause.
In the case of a defiled dharma belonging to a different category (*anyanaikāyika*), because it lacks the nature of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*),
the third [type of cause] applies: the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) is that which belongs to the same category, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

For it is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of a defilement belonging to the same category, by virtue of being a defiled cause within that same category and by virtue of being a universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*); and the fourth [alternative] is established by excluding these aforementioned modes.

The meaning is: "having excluded those types of phenomena that are stated in the three categories. For example, afflicted phenomena are not the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of wholesome phenomena because they are dissimilar;
nor are they the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
For this very reason, because wholesome states are undefiled, the same applies to wholesome states being [the cause] of defiled ones; likewise,
defiled states are also not a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for defiled states.

Nor do they constitute universal causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*), such as lust and so forth, [which are] not universal causes for the defiled states belonging to other categories, because they belong to different categories; nor are lust and so forth universal causes, because they themselves are not universal.

Even universal factors (*sarvatragā dharmāḥ*) are neither similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) nor universal-cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) for those defiled factors belonging to the same category, provided that they are future; this should be applied accordingly.
Disjunction (*visaṃyoga*) is the destruction [of defilements] by means of wisdom (*dhiyā*).
The meaning is that cessation, which is attained through wisdom, is the fruit of dissociation;
"by that" means for that reason.
Since "destruction" (kṣaya) means cessation (nirodha) and "intellect" (dhi) means wisdom (prajñā),
for that reason it is stated that analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyoga-phala); thus he explains [the verse] with the words,
"by whose power it arises," and so forth.
The compound *yadbalaṃ yasya* is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

That conditioned phenomenon which arises from whose power is the "fruit" (*phala*) belonging to that [power]. It is "born of human effort" (*puruṣakāraja*), meaning born from human effort (*puruṣakārāt jātam*); thus, it is the "fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāraphala*).
He provides an illustration:

for example, when a preparatory mind belonging to a lower level—either the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) or the first dhyāna level—attains a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a higher level, whether belonging to the first or second dhyāna level, that absorption is the fruit born of human effort (*puruṣakāraja*); this is what is intended here.
The outflow-free emanation-mind of the mind in meditative absorption belonging to the essential dharma becomes that very fruit;
by the word "etcetera," other [results] are also included.

For example, from a death-consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), the first moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises; such instances of heterogeneous examples are given for the purpose of distinguishing the outflow-result (*niṣyandaphala*).

For the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of a higher level is not the outflow-result of a preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) of a lower level, because that which belongs to a different level is not similar to its cause.
Nor should it be said that the uncontaminated arises from the contaminated;

however, not everything is a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), for that which arises through the power of something else— being similar to it, belonging to the same level, and occurring immediately after— is a result of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
That constitutes for him both the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*);
and in this regard, there is a fourfold alternative (*catuḥ-koṭika*):
there is that which is solely the fruit of human effort and not the flow-on fruit.
As has been stated, there is only the outflow fruit (niṣyandaphala) and not the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala),
because the fruit of the similar cause (sabhāgahetu) and the pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu) is separated [from its cause].
There is a case where both [causes] have arisen immediately prior as the fruit of two similar causes (sabhāga-hetu); there is also a case where neither has so arisen.

For example, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is accepted as resulting from the cause of maturation (*vipākahetu*), and analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) is also accepted as the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*);
yet this [cessation] does not arise through the power of a cause because it is eternal. Therefore, that which was not mentioned in the verse is here added as a supplement.
However, it must be stated that analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) is attained by means of a certain power;
for analytical cessation is attained through the power of analysis (pratisaṅkhyā).
Therefore, it is the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) resulting from analysis.
"Unprecedented," and so forth;
"unprecedented" means other than what has previously arisen—
what, then, is this?
Neither that which arises simultaneously nor that which arises later can be the cause after the fruit has already arisen;
for only a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomenon, and not an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) one, is a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
It belongs only to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the latter lacks the capacity to receive or bestow a fruit;
"of all" refers to both that which produces [the fruit] and that which exists in a state of non-obstruction.
"The fruit of human effort belongs to the agent," because of the statement: "That which arises by the power of something, that fruit is born of human effort."
Even for one who is not the agent, there is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*);
for it is stated that the sovereign fruit of a conditioned phenomenon is exclusively a conditioned phenomenon that is not its predecessor (*apūrva*).
And for others, it is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*);

that is, for those who are not artisans but remain in a state of non-obstruction regarding that craft, that craft is exclusively the sovereign fruit and not the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Thus, there are four logical alternatives (*catuḥ-koṭika*).
There is that which is only the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and not the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala),
namely the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala);
there is also that which is only the sovereign fruit and not the fruit of human effort.
For a neutral cause, the fruit is both separated and simultaneous;
for an agentive cause, it is both co-arisen and immediately arisen.
Neither [is it] both,
as in the case of space and cessation not through deliberation; thus, the present [factors] are five fruits.
The restriction that "only those that are present take up the fruit" means that they accept [the fruit] and persist by way of being its cause.
The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is also like this:
it receives its fruit only when present, neither when past nor when future;
however, because it does not necessarily possess a fruit, it is not mentioned [in that context].
For thus, the unconditioned is accepted as a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*),
yet it has no fruit;
and the future is also a causal condition.
And it is not the case that a dharma previously arisen gives its two fruits; rather,
the two present ones are intended here.
It is logical that the co-existent and associated causes yield their fruit only when they are present; however,
it is stated that these two are "possessed of fruit" by means of the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) even when they are past.
Since it is stated that "the outflow [result] belongs to the similar and the universal [causes]," how then do these two,
being present, bestow an outflow result?
For their outflow is not observed while they are in the present state; thus he says,
with reference to what fruit they bestow, [the answer is] "because they produce immediately after."
And since those two have also passed away, O Bharata,
because cause and effect do not coexist,
it is not the case that "that very same thing" is given again.
The meaning is that they do not, however, bestow that same fruit again;
for the verbal form *datta* (given), being in the dual number,
refers only to the state of having been given in the present.
For that which has been brought to the state of the present cannot be brought again;
and when those two past [karmas] bestow their fruit,
they bestow their own respective fruits at that very moment.
For the fruit is actually accomplished at the very moment of its arising, and not otherwise;
however, it should be understood that this fruit is merely obstructed.
This is because one who is severing the roots of wholesome merit relinquishes those acquisitions (*prāpti*) last of all.
In this case, the roots of merit are severed gradually;
how then is wrong view of nine types?
From the weakest-of-the-weak up to the strongest-of-the-strong,

the roots of wholesome merit (*kuśalamūla*) are likewise of nine grades; conversely, by the weakest-of-the-weak wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the strongest-of-the-strong roots of wholesome merit are severed, and so on, until by the strongest-of-the-strong wrong view, the weakest-of-the-weak roots of wholesome merit are completely severed,
just like the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
In that final state, the very weak wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) do not manifest,
yet their very weak acquisitions (*prāpti*) do manifest;
he then abandons those acquisitions at the very last moment.

The meaning is that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those acquisitions brings about their cessation; those acquisitions in their final state are the wholesome similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) which "receives" the fruit— that is,
it performs the grasping of the fruit.
The second alternative is that it does not give its own outflow fruit, because there is no other moment of wholesome [dharma] to be produced.
Regarding the statement "he gives but does not receive":
it refers to those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one first obtains when reconnecting the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*),
and which one obtains prior to all others.
The skilled one [understands] that the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) gives its fruit; thus,
it produces its own outflow (svaniṣyanda), namely acquisition (prāpti),
but it does not "take" [it], because it has already been taken previously.

However, this second point of explanation is faulty; for at the time of reconnecting the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*), the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all nine types of roots of goodness—past, future, and present—are obtained simultaneously. Among those, as for the past acquisitions...
It is logical that this wholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) gives forth its fruit but does not receive it, because it has already been received; however,
how is it determined that this wholesome homogeneous cause consists of those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which are present and have been obtained in that very same way?
"It gives fruit but does not receive"—
for it both receives and gives;
since it is not specified in this way, this second alternative is faulty.
Therefore, the Teacher said:
"But it should be stated thus:
'for one who reconnects those very [skandhas]'."

Those very acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are wholesome are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*); they only give their fruit because they give their outflow-fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), but they do not receive it because it has already been received previously. This is the third alternative.
One both receives and gives the fruit in the remaining states for one whose roots of merit are not severed,
excluding two states.
In whichever state one severs the roots of wholesome merit (*kuśalamūla*), those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one abandons last of all;
and in whichever state one reconnects the roots of wholesome merit, those which one acquires first of all—
just as the wholesome acquisitions of people like us receive and give forth their fruit.

It should not be stated that [the homogeneous cause] must be uninterrupted by another moment of a different class; for even when there is an intervention by another moment of a different class, it is possible for the homogeneous cause— characterized as "possession" (*prāpti*)— to receive and give forth its fruit.
The fourth [case] is setting aside these aspects;

for example, when one has fallen away from a higher level, those acquisitions (prāpti) of the wholesome factors belonging to that higher level do not take up a fruit as a wholesome similar cause (sabhāga-hetu).
Because it was previously acquired, one does not give it;
for one who has fallen away from that stage, there is an absence of possession (*prāpti*) of the wholesome roots and dharmas belonging to that stage.
The same should be stated regarding the state of having completely severed the roots of virtue (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*).
On this point, the Master Saṅghabhadra says:
"What was stated is not tenable."
But it should rather be stated thus:
"of one who is reconnecting those very [skandhas]";
why?

For it is not the case that the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) belongs only to those [roots] which were abandoned last of all, such that one who reconnects [the roots] obtains them as the very first thing.
For even though the continuum of its acquisition has already ceased previously, that [result] is its outflow (*niṣyanda*);
therefore, how could the entire *sabhāga-hetu* be grasped merely by the taking of its fruit? It is for this very purpose that it is stated;
thus, it is better to leave it exactly as it was originally formulated.
Since both readings have been cited as faulty, which reading is superior?
Here we see that the Abhidharma reading alone is superior.
But was it not already stated?

Since there is no distinction [between the states], the acquisitions (*prāpti*) obtained at the time of reconnecting the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*) are present and thus both give and receive their fruit; however, it is not the case that they only give and do not receive. There is indeed the fault [of over-extension] if one were to say so. When it is said, "reconnecting the roots of merit," this refers to the state in which the acquisition of the roots of merit is currently arising (*utpadyamānāvasthā*), and not to the state of being already present (*vartamānāvasthā*).
And in that case, since no acquisitions of wholesome roots (kuśalamūla-prāpti) exist in the present, it cannot be said how they could receive or give forth a fruit; however,
all past acquisitions of wholesome roots within one's own continuum, being homogeneous causes (sabhāga-hetu), do indeed give forth their outflowing fruit (niṣyanda-phala) at that time.
They do not receive [them] according to the principle of immediate production,
because they have already been received previously.
Thus, by this reasoning, we support the very reading of the Abhidharma.

But surely, if the reading were not thus specified, there would be the undesirable consequence that the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of future roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) would also fall under the second category;
for they too, at that time, are acquired just like past acquisitions.
This is not a fault,

because future [phenomena] lack the status of being homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*), and because the homogeneous cause is specifically intended here; even so, it should not be said that only acquisitions (*prāpti*) are [the factors].
"Those which one first acquires" means those wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*);
for even the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) are acquired at the very beginning during the reconnection of the wholesome (*kuśalapratisaṃdhāna*).
It is not only that those [attainments] exist for the sake of attaining that;
rather, this statement is made precisely because attainments (*prāpti*) themselves are indispensable for the reconnection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of wholesome states.
For the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of wholesome states necessarily arise when there is a reconnection with the wholesome, whether by means of right view or even by doubt;

however, they explain that while the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not yet arise when there is a reconnection with the wholesome through doubt, it is only the acquisitions themselves that arise— this applies to the unwholesome as well, and so forth.
The non-virtuous homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is also fourfold.
There is a non-virtuous homogeneous cause that receives its fruit but does not give it; this is the first alternative, explained in detail.
When one attains detachment from the desire realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) that is abandoned last of all—
the unwholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*)— receives its fruit but does not give it; how is this so?
In this context, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are of nine types,
and the path (*mārga*) is also of nine types; therein,
the most intense type of affliction is abandoned by the weakest-weak path.
Up to the point where the weakest-weak [defilement] is abandoned by the strongest-strong [counteractive],
its acquisitions are likewise abandoned;
when one attains detachment from the desire realm, the acquisition of the weakest-weak unwholesome states is the very last to be relinquished.
Those unwholesome [dharmas] are a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) that receives a fruit but does not give one,
because there is no intervening moment of the acquisition of the unwholesome; this is the second [case].

When one falls away from detachment from the realm of desire (*kāmavairāgya*), those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of unwholesome states that one first obtains constitute an unwholesome similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*); it gives forth its fruit but does not receive it. This should be explained as before.
Regarding this, the Master says:
However, it should be stated thus:
"those very [attainments] of one who is falling away," meaning that those very attainments which one had acquired upon reaching detachment from the desire realm, one abandons last of all.
For, because they have already been accepted, they do not accept them; rather, they simply yield their fruit.
In the first reading, the second alternative (koṭi) is not possible, as was stated previously.
On this point, the master Saṃghabhadra likewise refutes it,
stating that "this is not tenable," as is the same as what was said previously.
Everything is to be elaborated [in this way]:
the third [category] pertains to one who is not yet free from passion for the desire realm, while the remaining states pertain to others.
Excluding these two states already mentioned— the first and second states— in the remaining states, it is just as it is for us.
Those acquisitions (prāpti) which are unwholesome (akuśala) constitute the fourth [category]: the unwholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) both receives and gives its fruit.
Setting aside these aforementioned modes,
for example, the acquisitions of unwholesome states belonging to one who is free from passion for the desire realm and is of a nature not subject to falling away—
this unwholesome homogeneous cause does not take up a fruit.
Because it was previously accepted, one does not give it back, as there is no longer any possession of it.
The same applies to the obscured-unspecified [state], as the detailed explanation continues:
in this way, the formulation of the four alternatives for the obscured-unspecified should also be applied accordingly, based on the attainment of arhatship and the falling away from arhatship.
There is a case of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) which receives its fruit but does not give it; this is the first alternative (*koṭi*).
It refers to the acquisitions (*prāpti*) that one who is attaining Arhatship abandons last of all.
That obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) receives its fruit but does not give it,
because there is no other afflicted moment [to receive it]; this is the second [case].
Regarding one falling away from arhatship, it should rather be stated that those [roots] which are acquired for the very first time are the same as those of one who is falling away.
For in this way, the granting of the fruit alone is established;
the justification for the previous reading must also be stated by that same sequence, [and thus] the third [point].
For one who is free from passion regarding the peak of existence, in the remaining states, there is the fourth [type of knowledge], excluding these aforementioned aspects.

For example, for one who has attained arhatship, those acquisitions (*prāpti*) of the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states belonging to the three realms— which, as the case may be, constitute that obscured-unspecified similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*)— do not "take up" a fruit,
because it has already been taken up.
It does not give [the result],
because it has been abandoned; thus,
for the unobscured-unspecified [state], there is no subsequent member.
Since the definition of the "consequent member" (paścātpāda) has already been explained, it is not stated again.
As for that which is unconditioned and indeterminate (*anirvṛtāvyākṛta*) homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), does it receive its fruit and also give it?
He says: [it does].
First, one who both gives and receives [the gift] possesses it as an unobstructed-neutral state, because it remains present until final nirvana.
It may be that one receives but does not give;
this refers to the final aggregates of an Arhat, because, due to the relinquishment of all substrates, there is an absence of unobstructed-unspecified outflows.
However, according to the rule regarding objects of perception, this occurs moment by moment.

Previously, a rule was stated regarding the possibility of [dharmas] being without an object; however, by means of the rule concerning those with an object, it is said that only mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) possess the nature of a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu). This refers to moment by moment in relation to subsequent moments, and not in terms of total exhaustion or final cessation—this is the meaning of the detailed passage beginning with "immediately after wholesome minds."
When one brings forth a defiled or neutral mind immediately after wholesome minds,

at that time that wholesome mind "takes up" its fruit; for from it will arise a future wholesome fruit— either subject to arising or of a nature not to arise— that falls within its own continuum, even though it is separated [from the cause].
Because there is no wholesome state whatsoever immediately following it,
the similar cause (sabhāga-hetu) is held to be fruitful only through a result that is of a similar kind.
The second [case] is by way of the reverse:
when one brings a wholesome mind into manifestation immediately after a defiled or unobstructed-neutral mind.
Then, that wholesome mind by which that wholesome mind had previously been accepted as its fruit gives it; it does not accept it,
because it has already been accepted.
The third [case] refers to making manifest that which is wholesome immediately after a wholesome mind; this is the subject under discussion.
That preceding wholesome mind receives and gives the second mind as its fruit,
because it arises immediately thereafter.
The fourth [alternative] is "setting aside these modes," which refers to when one brings forth either a defiled or an indeterminate mind immediately after a defiled or indeterminate mind.
At that time, this wholesome homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), being accompanied by an object (sālambana), neither receives a fruit because it has already been received,
nor does it give one.

Since this applies to the manifestation of afflicted and neutral minds, the same should be applied to unwholesome [minds] and so forth. Thus, there is an unwholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) with an object that receives its fruit but does not give it; this constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuḥ-koṭika*).
The first alternative is when one brings forth a wholesome or unobstructed-neutral mind immediately after an unwholesome mind;
the second [alternative]...
By way of reversal,
the third [case] is:
immediately after an unwholesome [state], there is only an unwholesome [state].

The fourth [category] is established by setting aside these aforementioned modes; by the word "etcetera," the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) are to be applied.
First, regarding the obscured [unspecified], there is the first alternative (*prathamā-koṭi*).
Immediately after a defiled-neutral mind, one brings forth either a wholesome mind or an undefiled-neutral mind;
the second case is the reverse.
The third [alternative] is that immediately after a defiled-neutral mind, there arises only a defiled-neutral mind;
this is the fourth [case].
Excluding these unwholesome states, the first alternative is that immediately after an unobscured-neutral state, one brings forth either a wholesome or an afflicted mind.
The third [is established] by the reversal of the second.
Immediately after the unobscured-neutral, there arises only the unobscured-neutral;
this is the fourth [case], setting aside these aforementioned modes.

"Because it attains the state of being its seed" means because it attains the state of being the cause of that fruit; this is a metaphorical expression according to the system of the Sautrāntikas. In some manuscripts, this reading does not exist at all.
"Just as the water-circle," and so forth;
"just as" indicates an illustration:
the water-circle is the fruit that is the support for the wind-circle.
By the word "up to" (yāvat), the topic extends from the golden earth of the water-circle,
and from that golden earth, the fruits of establishment such as crops, medicinal herbs, and so forth; and [furthermore],
starting from the applications of mindfulness regarding the foul (aśubha-smṛty-upasthāna) up to the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
In the same way, the result of other applications such as mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) should also be applied;
the result of a totality of conditions is called the "result of the totality" (sāmagrīphala).
Regarding the phrase "of the eye and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes the eye, visible form, light, and attention;
thus, the compound "the fruit of cultivation" (bhāvanā-phalam) means the fruit that is the result of cultivation.
"But all this," and so forth,
means that these four kinds of fruits are included within the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*),
[namely] the fruit of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā-phala*).

Included within the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala) are the afflicted [dharmas] belonging to the fruit of application (prayogaphala) and so forth, as well as the fruits of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the dominant fruit; such is the detailed explanation.
Defiled [dharmas] are those associated with or originated from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Those born of the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) are "born of maturation" (*vipākaja*).
The first untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] are the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors.

And from those three— namely, the afflicted and so forth— the remaining [states] are the neutral ones, excluding the maturation [result], which are the states of deportment, the states of craftsmanship, and the states of emanation, as well as the wholesome states, excluding the first moment of the untainted.
By the inclusion of the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*), both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are included.

It should be understood that therein, all wholesome factors—namely, the entire complex of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna-kalāpa*) and so forth, as well as all paths of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the worldly wholesome factors—are [the first category]. The remaining factors here constitute the third heap;
therefore, he says:
These four types of dharmas— the afflicted, those born of maturation, the remaining [non-defiled non-maturation], and the first noble ones—
arise respectively from all causes except for maturation, the pervasive, and those two [pervasive and maturation] together with the homogeneous.

Thus, regarding "maturation" (*vipāka*): defiled phenomena arise from the remaining five causes— the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)— excluding the maturation cause (*vipāka-hetu*), according to their respective possibilities.
From the cause as efficient condition (*kāraṇahetu*), which consists of the characteristics of all phenomena excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
from the cause as co-existent condition (*sahabhūhetu*), which consists of the characteristics of one's own collection [of factors], mind, and so forth;
and from the cause as homogeneous condition (*sabhāgahetu*), which consists of the defiled characteristics of one's own continuum that have arisen previously.
Because they arise from the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) characterized by their own group of mental factors (*svakalāpa-citta*),
and because they are produced from the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) characterized by previously arisen views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*),
and not from the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
For the retributive cause is fruitful by means of its retribution fruit;
however, since afflicted phenomena do not have retribution as their intrinsic nature, they are not born from that [cause].
Excluding the omnipresent cause, they are born only from the remaining five causes.
However, it is not [the result] of the universal cause (*sarvatragahetu*),
because those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are non-defiled;
for the characteristic of the universal cause is that it is the cause of defiled phenomena.
Although [dharmas] born of maturation arise from universal [defilements] such as wrong view and so forth,
they do not arise from them by virtue of being the universal cause; rather, how then do they arise?
"Of the ripening cause,
the rest," and so forth;
because the remaining [factors] do not have the nature of maturation, there is no ripening cause for them.
And because their intrinsic nature is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*), they do not have a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Therefore, excluding those two—the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) and the pervasive cause—[the afflicted dharmas] arise from the remaining four causes;
the explanation is as before.

The first pure (anāsrava) dharmas arise, as appropriate, from the remaining causes—namely, the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*)—excluding the two previously mentioned, the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*), and also excluding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), which is implied by the word "and" (*ca*).
This is because pure dharmas do not have the nature of ripening; therefore, there is no ripening cause for them.
Because it is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*), it is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);
because the Path has not previously arisen, there is no homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Indeed, it is not logical for the contaminated supreme mundane dharmas (*anāsrava-agradharma*) to be the homogeneous cause of a group of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors.
Therefore, since mental states and mental factors do not arise from those [material phenomena],
the mention of "mental states and mental factors" is for the purpose of establishing the existence of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).

The factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*), such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and birth (*jāti*), as well as the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which has a material nature (*rūpisvabhāva*), are to be understood as being among the untainted (*anāsrava*). These dissociated factors and those with material nature are distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); they include the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth, those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), and all others comprised within the first moment of the untainted. They arise in the same manner as mind and mental factors.
However, they are excluded from arising solely by way of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), because their intrinsic nature is dissociated;
thus, they do not arise from the associated cause.
How so?

In the case of defiled [dharmas], excluding the dissociated and material causes, as well as the ripening and associated causes, they arise from the remaining four causes. Even those born of ripening, excluding the associated and omnipresent causes, arise from exactly the same remaining four causes.
As for the remaining [dharmas], excluding the ripening, omnipresent, and associated causes, they arise from the remaining three causes.

The first pure [dharmas] arise from the remaining two causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*). There is no such thing as arising from a single cause, because the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) are necessarily inseparable. (AK(Bh) 2.61c)

It has been stated [in verse 2.46cd]: "The birth of a person is not [possible] for a person without causes and conditions" (AK 2.46cd). Therefore, immediately after the detailed explanation of the causes, he asks: "What are the conditions?
The term *pratyayajāti* means the category of conditions (*pratyayatā*), that is, the various types of conditions; it is like the word *gotā* (the state of being a cow).

Regarding the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*), the full statement is: "mind and mental factors," and so forth. The restriction is that only mind and mental factors are the immediately preceding [condition]. The inclusion of the term "not final" (*acarama*) is because those that have a superior [subsequent state] possess the quality of being immediately preceding. The inclusion of the term "arisen" (*utpanna*) is for the purpose of excluding future [phenomena]. It is called the "immediately preceding condition" because it is both equal (*sama*) and immediate (*anantara*). The prefix *sam-* has the sense of "equal. Regarding the phrase "of form belonging to the desire realm":

Regarding non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*), sometimes both desire-realm (*kāmāvacara*) non-informative matter and form-realm (*rūpāvacara*) non-informative matter arise for one who has undertaken the vows when a contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna becomes manifest; sometimes both desire-realm and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [non-informative matter] arise when an uncontaminated dhyāna becomes manifest. However, it is not the case that immediately after a desire-realm mind, a desire-realm and form-realm mind, or a desire-realm and uncontaminated mind, ever arise simultaneously; thus, the manifestation of matter is not disordered.

"Because of the arising of a second [moment]" means because of the arising of a second moment of the accumulative (*aupacayika*). For when one sleeps after eating, or enters into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), then that which is born of food is accumulative, and that which is born of sleep or born of meditative concentration is also accumulative; thus, a second [moment] arises. "Because of the arising of less or more"—what is this? It refers to the context that matter (*rūpa*) is not an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The Venerable Elder is a Sautrāntika.
[This applies] to minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.

In a wholesome mind of the desire realm accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, there are twenty-two mental factors; occasionally, remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is added. However, in an unwholesome mind that is independent (*āveṇika*) or associated with [wrong] views, there are twenty.
With the four afflictions (*kleśa*), such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, and with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), there are twenty-one.
In the obscured (*nivṛta*) [neutral mind], eighteen; elsewhere, in the non-defined (*avyākṛta*), twelve are held.
By this sequence, sometimes from many mental factors (*caitta*), twenty-three, twenty-one, eighteen, or twelve arise as few mental factors; sometimes from few, many arise by way of the reverse.

And regarding the three types of meditative concentration—those with applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savīcāra*), and so forth—there is a concentration with both applied and sustained thought; there is one without applied thought but with sustained thought alone; and there is one without either applied or sustained thought. In these three concentrations, mental factors (*caitta*) arise in varying degrees of frequency. Consequently, even the mind and its mental factors would not function as immediate antecedent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

There is production with respect to another genus (*jātyantara*), but not with respect to its own genus (*svajāti*). There is production of fewer or more [factors] with respect to another genus, but not with respect to its own genus. For in certain minds, there occurs the activity or non-activity of vitarka, vicāra, and so forth, which exist as belonging to different genera.

Never, however, is there a greater number of feelings (*vedanā*); for never does one feeling occur in one mind, while two or three occur in another. But in the case of matter (*rūpa*), there is production of fewer or more [units] with respect to its own genus.

Furthermore, why [is it said] "only from its own kind"? Does feeling (*vedanā*) serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) only for feeling? Because [feeling alone] lacks the capacity for the arising of multiple feelings. The same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others. It is not from another kind; feeling is not [the condition] for perception and so forth, because otherwise the arising of mental factors (*caitta*) in greater or lesser numbers would not be accounted for. "But those belonging to the same continuum" and so forth: the mind (*citta*) is the immediately preceding condition for another mental factor, but not for feeling; feeling is [the condition] for another feeling, but not for the mind. Thus, "belonging to the same continuum" means that they are similar causes (*sabhāgahetu*).

Those who play with or engage in discourse according to the commonality of the continuum (*santānasabhāga*) are the *santānasabhāgikas*, certain Abhidharmikas. If the continuum is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for another continuum, then when a defiled state arises immediately after an undefiled one, how is the status of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) established therein? To this he says: "But when [it arises] immediately after an undefiled [state]," and so forth.

They establish that for a subsequent defilement, the previously ceased defilement—though separated by another moment—is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), because it is not interrupted by another mind of a different kind. However, an interruption by a non-defiled mind does not constitute an interruption at all, because it is of a dissimilar kind.

This is just as the mind of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is established as the immediately preceding condition for the mind of emergence, because it is not interrupted by another [defiled] mind, even though it is separated by the substance of the meditative attainment; it is exactly like that.

"Because those [factors] not bound to the three realms manifest simultaneously. For a noble one (*ārya*) who is not yet free from passion for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), immediately after the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a state belonging to the desire realm, acquisitions of factors not bound to the three realms arise, because he is still possessed of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. In this way, their birth (*jāti*) and other characteristics also arise; thus, because of this confused simultaneous manifestation, even the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—namely, acquisition, birth, and so forth—are not the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Why [is it said that] "the future [is not]"? [The full passage begins: "Those that have arisen are the equal-and-immediate [condition]. (AK 2.62b)

Thus, it was previously stated that only the past and present [dharmas] constitute the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); for this very reason, he asks as follows. "Because of disorder" means that the future is not accepted as the immediately preceding condition due to its disorder. Furthermore, the disorder of the future time-period (*adhvan*) arises because there is no prior or subsequent [order], that is, because it lacks the state of being prior and subsequent. For it can be said that the present is prior to the future and the past is prior to the present, owing to their connection with prior and subsequent times; however, the future has no such priority or posteriority.

For this very reason, a present [moment] is not accepted as the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for another present [moment], because there is no priority or posteriority between them due to their being simultaneous; rather, it is through inference from the past and the present. He says, "one infers by means of the past," providing the detailed explanation: "one indeed sees the past path. He says, "one infers by means of the present," providing the detailed explanation: "and this [present moment] is also of such a nature right now.
The intention is that if one did not know the future limit (*aparānta*), one's status as omniscient would be lost.

"Being the sign of the fruit" means being the mark of the fruit. It is not a direct realizer, nor is it one who directly perceives. When it was stated that a future [dharma] is not accepted as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) because of its disorderliness and the absence of priority and posteriority, someone asked: "Why [is it not so] immediately after the *anāgāmidharma*? and so forth. To this, the Vaibhāṣika provides the rebuttal: "Because the arising of whatever [dharma] is dependent upon whatever [other dharma]," and so forth.

When the arising of a particular dharma—such as the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering—is dependent upon another dharma—such as the supreme mundane dharma—that [latter] arises immediately after it. This is just as sprouts and so forth arise from seeds and so forth; for the arising of a sprout is dependent upon the seed, and therefore it arises immediately after it. Thus it is with stalks and so forth in relation to sprouts and so forth, even in the absence of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), that is, even when the immediately preceding condition does not exist.

The intention [of using] the word "api" (also/even) is that when the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) exists, [the effect] arises all the more readily. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence is that there is no fixed state of sequential order, yet there is likewise a fixed rule for immediate succession.

"Why are [the moments] of an Arhat called 'final'? This question arises because of the statement that they are "not non-final. "Because of the lack of connection with another mind" means that immediately after them, no other mind is connected. "The mind is characterized by its state as a basis" means that just as the eye, once arisen, exists in the state of being the basis for visual consciousness—if, due to the deficiency of other causes, visual consciousness does not arise, the eye is not at fault in that regard.

In this way, even for an Arhat, the final [moment of consciousness] remains as a basis (*āśraya*). However, because of the deficiency of other causes, another consciousness does not arise; thus, that [final moment] is not at fault. For its meaning is this: it is not characterized by causal efficiency (*kāritra*), nor is it characterized by the human effort of production (*janana-puruṣakāra*). If it were characterized by production, then that mind would exist only when the effect is actually arising. But this is not the case. Therefore, even when there is no further thing to be produced, that mind certainly exists.

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), however, is defined by its functional activity (*kāritra*). It becomes an immediately preceding condition only when there is something to be produced, and not when there is nothing.

Therefore, regarding that dharma which has been grasped as a fruit by that immediately preceding condition—[the condition] thinking, "Let this dharma arise"—it cannot be obstructed by any dharmas, even by all insentient things or by all sentient beings acting with deliberate intent, such that it would fail to arise or would not be produced.

"Those dharmas which have the mind as their immediate antecedent," and so forth. "Mind-immediate" (*cittasamanantara*) means produced by a mind that serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). They are called "mind-immediate" because they are both equal (*samā*) to the mind and immediate (*anantara*) to it. Alternatively, they are called "mind-immediate" because the mind is their immediate antecedent, serving as their immediately preceding condition. Furthermore, they are "uninterrupted by the mind" (*cittanirantara*) because they are not separated from the mind by another moment.

Furthermore, those [factors] that have mind as their immediate antecedent are mind and mental factors, as well as the two attainments—the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation. The state of non-perception (*āsañjñika*) is not taught in the treatise as having mind as its immediate antecedent, because it arises through the power of karma.

"The first alternative," and so forth in detail. The mind of emergence from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is produced by the mind that enters the attainment; therefore, it is "immediately following the mind" (*cittasamanantara*) but not "without an interval from the mind" (*cittanirantara*), because it is separated by the moments of the attainment itself. As for the second and subsequent moments of the attainment—meaning those excluding the first moment—they are "immediately following the mind" because they are produced by that [preceding] condition, but they are not "without an interval from the mind" because they are separated, as the case may be, by the first and other preceding moments.

The second [alternative]: the birth (*jāti*) and other [characteristics] of the first moment of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are "immediately following thought" (*cittānantara*) because they are not separated by another moment; however, they are not "immediately preceded by thought" (*cittasamanantara*), because their nature is that of being immediately preceded by non-thought (*acitta*). For it is only mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), together with the two types of meditative attainments, that are intended as "immediately preceded by thought. Furthermore, the birth and other characteristics exist during states possessed of mind (*sacittika-avasthā*). Since these are not specified, the birth and other characteristics belong to all of them—mind, mental factors, and so forth.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) are included, with the exception of the two attainments (*samāpatti*). These, in the same manner, are immediately following thought (*citta-nirantara*), but not having thought as their immediate antecedent (*citta-samanantara*). The explanation is as before.

Regarding the "state with thought" (*sacittikāvasthā*): when one thought arises from another thought, then the subsequent thoughts and mental factors (*caitta*) are both immediately following thought (*citta-samanantara*) and immediately succeeding thought (*citta-nirantara*) by virtue of the preceding thought.

The fourth [category] consists of the birth and other characteristics (*jāti-ādi*) of the second and subsequent moments of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and of the mind of emergence (*vyutthāna-citta*); these are not "immediately preceded by mind" (*citta-samanantara*), because their nature is that of being immediately preceded by non-mind; nor are they "uninterrupted by mind" (*citta-nirantara*), because they are separated by the first moment of attainment and so forth.

Those which are the third and fourth [moments] are the first and second [categories], and so on in detail. The first limit (*koṭi*) is the first moment of attainment and the state possessed of mind (*sacittikā avasthā*).
For these [moments] are immediately preceded by mind because they are produced by an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
they are not immediately preceded by the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
because the first moment of the attainment lacks any prior moment of attainment, and thus there is no immediate succession with respect to that.
And because there is no meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) during the state of having a mind (*sacittikāvasthā*),
the second [characteristic] refers to the birth and other [phases] of the second and subsequent moments of attainment, as well as those of the mind of emergence (*vyutthānacitta*).
These factors have meditative attainment as their immediate antecedent, but not mind as their immediate antecedent; namely,
the emerging mind from the third mindless attainment and the second and subsequent moments of that attainment.

These are immediately preceded by mind and are also immediately followed by meditative attainments; they include the birth-moment and so forth of the first moment of an attainment, as well as those occurring during a state possessed of mind.
These phenomena are neither immediately preceded by mind nor immediately followed by meditative attainment,
because they have the nature of being non-mental as their immediate antecedent and because there is an absence of the preceding moment of meditative attainment.
Because that which is accompanied by its associates— that is, together with mental factors— is characterized in such a way;
that is to say, because it has the characteristic of being an object of cognition.
"By way of the restriction of the bases, substances, and moments" means:
the bases (*āyatana*), the substances (*dravya*), and the moments (*kṣaṇa*); by that very restriction of them.
Those mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are restricted to their own respective objects (*ālambana*);
for instance, visual consciousness together with its associated factors is restricted to the object-base (*āyatana*) of visible form, and not to the object-base of sound and so forth—
thus they are restricted by way of the sense-bases.

In that sense-field as well, by way of the restriction of substance, visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors is restricted to apprehending only blue form when [the object] is blue form,
and not to anything else such as yellow and so forth;
thus it is by way of the restriction of substance.
In that case as well, regarding the blue form as the object, whichever moment of blue form is the object of a [cognition],
it belongs to that [cognition] alone and not to any other.
Thus, by way of this restriction of moments,
the auditory consciousness and so forth, together with their associated mental factors, should likewise be applied to the sense-base of sound and the others;
should this also be understood as a restriction of the basis?
Are these minds and mental factors restricted by the restriction of their bases, such as the eye and so forth?
He says "Yes," which means "It is so."

The objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) consists of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) with respect to mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). It is called the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) because it is a superior (*adhika*) condition.
Regarding the causes and conditions such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*):
for the causal condition consists of five types of causes, whereas the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not possible for co-existent factors; thus, it is not an addition.
Alternatively, it is a compound meaning "the condition for that which is superior"; previously, the superior [condition] was called the *adhipati*, and thus it is a compound meaning "that condition."

Now, as for the term *adhipatipratyaya*, how is this compound formed? He explains: [it is] "the lord (*pati*) of that which is additional (*adhika*) and more extensive (*bhūyas*); that is the condition (*pratyaya*)," thus [it is] "the dominant condition" (*adhipatipratyaya*).
"Everything," and so forth:

everything, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for everything else—excluding its own self-nature—whether that [thing] has an object (*sālambana*) or lacks an object (*anālambana*). However, the objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) belongs only to that which has an object, not to that which lacks an object.
In the first analysis, the excessiveness of the suffix is shown; in the second, it is shown that the activity belongs to that which possesses the suffix while it is being ceased.

The restriction "only while ceasing" is applied because the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and associated (*samprayuktaka*) causes are respectively mutual fruits and have a common basis; thus, there are three [conditions] for that which is being born.
The restriction "only while being born" implies that the other two conditions are the reverse of that.
The previously mentioned immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) relies on the subsequently mentioned restriction regarding the time of its activity,
meaning that it performs its activity while [the effect] is arising;
the subsequently mentioned object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) relies on the previously mentioned restriction regarding the time of its activity.
The meaning is that they perform their activity while in the process of ceasing;
thus, by way of reversal, those two perform their activity.
Therefore, he says:
The immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) performs its activity at the moment [the dharma] is arising, by providing space;
the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) performs its activity at the moment [the dharma] is ceasing, because present minds and mental factors grasp the present.
For the objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is established in the sense of being grasped;
yet future mental states and mental factors do not grasp the object to be grasped,
and this alone constitutes its functional activity (kāritra).

The intention is that because it is easy to understand, the restriction of the time of the activity of this sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)— namely, that its activity consists precisely in its persistence in every state by way of being non-obstructive— is not explicitly indicated; thus,
"the cause is of two kinds."
Because associated, omnipresent, and ripening causes are impossible [in this case],
wholesome factors belonging to the same level— namely,
the wholesome factors of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)— are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*) for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The immediate antecedent condition for the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*)— which belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna and by whose power those attainments occur— is the mind of attainment together with its associated mental factors (*sasamprayoga*).
Because all moments of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and all moments of the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*) are not separated by any other state of mind,
[the definition] is as before:
all phenomena (*dharmas*), with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Because it is born from the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*)" means because it is born from the mental application (*cittābhoga*);
it is not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) because it constitutes an obstacle to the arising of the mind.
Because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the cause for the arising of consciousness,
the phrase "but the others from two" uses the word *tu* (but) for emphasis and has a distinct function.

Other phenomena—excluding the mind, mental factors, and the two meditative attainments—are produced by only two conditions: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the list] includes God (*īśvara*), the Primordial Spirit (*puruṣa*), the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), time (*kāla*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that "for this very reason," then in the case where God alone is the cause, or the Puruṣa is the cause, what is the reason? If a reason is sought by taking a cause other than God as the basis for establishing that [Puruṣa], then it becomes admitted [that there is another cause].

And by accepting that [position], the refutation—that is, the abandonment—of the doctrine that "the Lord (Īśvara) or the Primordial Person (Puruṣa) alone is the cause of the entire world" follows; this is the general meaning of the sentence.
[The phrase] "not from the Lord and so forth, because of the sequence and so on" means that entities do not arise from the Lord and so forth.
Why [is it said] "by sequence and so forth"?
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of place, time, and the rest.
Alternatively, the inclusion of [theories such as] the denial of other persons, time, and so forth is due to the consequence of an infinite regress resulting from having multiple causes;
for if there were only one cause—this being the detailed explanation—the meaning is: if God alone, or Mahādeva, or Vāsudeva, or some other [principle] such as the *puruṣa*, were the sole cause.
The entire world would have to come into existence simultaneously because of the presence of its cause;
for it is not accepted that an effect does not arise when its cause exists.
Furthermore, the sequential arising of entities such as the embryo (*kalala*) and so forth, as well as sprouts and so forth, is observed;
therefore, it is understood that these are produced by a succession of their own causes and do not have God or any other [single] cause.

For one who asserts that the world has God or another single cause as its cause is characterized by a defect in his thesis, as indicated by the specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) consisting in being produced through a sequence of its own causes.
If that is so, then [one might ask]: "Does that variation in sequence arise from the power of [the Lord's] will? He says how this would be so: "From the power of the will of the Lord."
"Now let this entity arise," "let it arise until this [other] arises later"—
such is the intention of those who hold that God is the cause, namely that the successive arising of entities is caused by God; this is the detailed explanation of the difference in their assertions.

Furthermore, due to the diversity of the Lord’s will and because of the acceptance of a single cause, a contradiction with the previous position arises; thus, a reversal of the nature of dharma occurs for that position as well—
this is the detailed explanation— and moreover,
that diversity of will would have to exist simultaneously.
The meaning is that because the Lord—the cause of that [creation], who is the cause of the diversity of desires—is undivided, that is, one;
and consequently, that aforementioned fault would occur simultaneously.
Now, if you think:
If it is argued that God depends upon some other distinct cause for the production of that [effect], this is stated:
"And if there is dependence on a distinction among other causes," and so forth;
for if one accepts that God alone is not the cause, that same fault remains.
"And as for those [others] also," and so forth.

If the sequential arising of even those other causes is desired, then because those various distinct causes would themselves require further distinct causes, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
There would be the consequence of no finality, such that those [causes] which depend on further distinct causes would themselves require yet further distinct causes.
"The reasoning of the Śākyaputrīyas alone" means that even if [the two were] simultaneous,
one would not have transgressed the reasoning of the Śākyaputrīyas, namely that "saṃsāra is beginningless"; such is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, it might be argued: even if the wills of the Lord were simultaneous, why would there not be simultaneity in the world?
Because it arises according to one's wish— namely,
the wish that "may this [desire] arise right now"— it arises at this very moment from that very desire.
For that which is to arise later, its arising is subsequent to that [preceding moment];
and because this is indeed subsequent in such a manner, its arising is likewise subsequent to that.
And that [desire] does not belong to them later, because there is no distinction;
for there is no distinction whatsoever among those desires later on.
Just as they did not begin previously, so too they would not begin afterwards;
or else, just as they do begin afterwards.
Likewise, it was so previously;
or rather, since there is only one creator and no other, there is no distinction among them.
Therefore, the simultaneity of entities follows as a matter of course, just like the simultaneous desires of Īśvara.

Alternatively, if the specific volitions depend upon other causes, the same fault as before would apply; thus, God would not be the cause of that pleasure, because without a means, He lacks the power to produce its cause.
This is the lordship of the Lord:
that he might act in one way depending on other causes,
and likewise in another way.
Just as he is not the master over pleasure, so too he is inferred by the three worlds to be not the master over anything else; "and if he were the master," and so forth, is the detailed argument.

Having created beings in the hells and other realms, and having created those beings afflicted by many spirits (*cetis*)— meaning afflicted by many various kinds of calamities such as diseases— if he were to take pleasure [in this], then "homage be to him" is a statement of derision.
"And well-sung," and so forth;
this verse in the *Śatarudrīya* was composed by Vyāsa concerning that Lord, beginning with him, which [states]:
"That which burns..."
Because it burns [all things], as stated in such passages, it is therefore called Rudra; this applies everywhere to others as well.
The manifest human effort exerted by seeds and so forth toward sprouts and so forth would be negated,
because no activity of anything other than the causes is observed;

for when visual consciousness and so forth arise from the eye, visible form, light, attention, and so on, and when sprouts and so forth arise from seeds, soil, water, and so on, no activity of anything else is perceived.

For just as the activity of the eyes and so forth is observed in the production of visual consciousness and the like, and that of seeds and so forth in the production of sprouts and the like— since these occur when those [causes] are present and do not occur when they are absent—
it is not the case that the absence of visual consciousness, sprouts, and so forth is observed upon the absence of God, even when the eyes, seeds, and so forth are present.
Furthermore, since its existence occurs when that [other cause] exists, it is understood that this [other cause] also has an operation (*vyāpāra*) in its production;
therefore, for those who postulate God as the cause along with other causes because they do not perceive His operation, it would be a mere expression of devotion (*bhaktivāda*).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And as for the auxiliary causes," [the question is]:
as for those other auxiliary causes of that Lord (īśvara), would the Lord not be the Lord with respect to them?

For those [causes] operate by their own capacity toward the production of the effect; however, regarding other auxiliary factors, God would be the cause— this inclusion of the word "others" implies that the initial creation is caused by God.

For in this way, there would be no denial of the visible human effort [as a cause]; moreover, there is no fault in the fact that no operation other than [human] causes is observed; and as for the claim that God is the cause of the world, that too is untenable because He, like everything else, would not depend on any other cause.

Since that initial creation also does not depend on any other cause, God alone is the sole cause and nothing else; thus, there follows the undesirable consequence that [the world] is beginningless, just like God.
And this is undesirable; therefore, God is not the cause.
This should be applied accordingly to the *pradhāna* as well;
thus, the *pradhāna* is insentient.
Therefore, having set aside the conceptualization of desire in that regard, the rule of negation for the remainder should be applied:
if the primary cause were indeed such [as you claim], then the entire world would have to come into existence simultaneously.
Furthermore, the sequential arising of entities is observed;
if this depends on a difference in other causes, then *pradhāna* alone could not be the cause.
For if those [other causes] also arise sequentially by depending on a difference in yet other causes, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*); such is the detailed argument.
Furthermore, by thus grasping at a single cause for the world, one would be denying the perceptible human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of other factors; moreover,
for those who postulate *pradhāna* as the primary cause even alongside other causes, it would be a mere expression of devotion,
since no activity distinct from the [other] causes is observed.
Furthermore, among other auxiliary causes, that [Pradhāna] would be either primary or non-primary. If the initial creation were caused by Pradhāna, then because that initial creation—
which has the nature of producing Mahat and the rest— is itself characterized as an "initial" [event], it follows that, like Pradhāna, it must also be beginningless.
For the Pradhāna is eternal, and since the Pradhāna is the cause of the Mahat, it is established that the Pradhāna exists first and the Mahat afterwards;
moreover, the Pradhāna is by nature productive, and therefore it must proceed eternally because it is independent of any other cause—
for illumination, once it has illuminated an object, does not fail to illuminate it again.
For intrinsic nature does not overlook the state of having accomplished its purpose;
"those of unrefined intellect" means those whose intellects have not been cultivated by the treatises on ultimate reality.
The elements are twofold, and that is their cause.

Thus, the primary elements (*bhūta*) that have arisen previously are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)— the latter by virtue of being inseparable— for those [elements] arising later within their own continuum,
because they conform to the primary elements.
The derivative material follows the primary elements because it undergoes modification when they do;
this is like depending on a teacher and so forth.
Just as a monk relies upon a teacher (*ācārya*) and, by the word "and so forth," relies upon a preceptor (*upādhyāya*),
so it is in that same way.

The primary elements (bhūta) depend upon the derivative matter (bhautika); such is the detailed explanation of how this is so. It has been declared that these primary elements are the cause of birth for derivative matter, because the latter arises from them.
It is the cause of transformation because it conforms to that [transformation];
it is the cause of support because it serves as a substratum;
it is the cause of stability because it is the cause of non-interruption.
The state of being a cause of increase is due to its being a cause of nourishment;
"because it operates without distinction" means that by remaining in a state of non-obstruction, it serves as a cause for others as well;
thus, bodily and vocal actions follow the mind reciprocally.

Bodily action that follows the mind, comprised within the dhyāna and untainted (anāsrava) restraints, is threefold, distinguished by the abstinence from taking life, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. Verbal action that also follows the mind, likewise comprised within the dhyāna and untainted restraints, is fourfold, distinguished by the abstinence from false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter.
Thus, these sevenfold bodily and vocal actions are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

The abstention from taking life is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and is the co-existent cause of the other six; those six are likewise the co-existent cause of that [abstention]. This should be applied to all cases accordingly.

The phrase "not other" means that all derived matter (upādāyarūpa), such as the eye and so forth— even including that which is comprised within the Prātimokṣa restraint and the like— is not a co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) for one another, because they belong to distinct aggregates (pṛthag-kalāpa).
This applies even to those of the same class (sabhāga).
The wholesome [action] is the cause of the wholesome within one's own continuum, and the afflicted [action] is the cause of the afflicted, and so forth;
this applies as appropriate to whichever bodily or vocal karma— whether of the nature of informative or non-informative [action], and whether concentrated or unconcentrated.
The restriction "that [result] is indeed of one kind" means that the ripening cause alone is singular;
this is because the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is likewise not counted [as a single result].

Because they belong to separate sets (*pṛthak-kalāpa*), and because [the factors] such as the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) are incompatible, there is no unwholesome state in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

This is because of the scriptural statement: "Detached from sensual desires, detached from evil and unwholesome states, he, possessing applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of detachment and characterized by joy and bliss."
In that realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is no unwholesome state; for that which is born from seclusion from the unwholesome— namely, the wholesome—
is called "seclusion."
And since the fruit is just as the cause is,
it is understood that even in that rebirth there is nothing unwholesome.

In the realms of form and formlessness, all afflictions and secondary afflictions are exclusively obscured (*nivṛta*) because they are not results of maturation (*avipāka*), and are not unwholesome (*akuśala*). This will be explained later in the verse; therefore, it should be connected here.

"At the time of attainment, it is wholesome" means that immediately following a wholesome mind of the desire realm belonging to the stage of preparatory effort (*prayoga*), there arises a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna— either of the threshold (*sāmantaka*) or the fundamental (*maula*) stage.
"At the time of rebirth-linking, it is obscured" means...

Immediately after the death-consciousness acquired at birth in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), a defiled-neutral mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*);
for it is stated that "the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is afflicted by all the afflictions belonging to its own level."
In this context, "arising" (upapatti) is intended to mean arising from the intermediate state;
likewise, the linking of rebirth (pratisandhi) in the intermediate state should be understood as afflicted.
It is said to be "distant" by way of the four kinds of distance.

In this regard, "remoteness of basis" (āśrayadūratā) means that no dharma whatsoever belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) is brought into manifestation by a basis belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara),
just as a mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta) belonging to the desire realm is brought into manifestation by a basis belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara).
By this remoteness of basis, the formless realms are remote from the desire realm;
as for remoteness of aspect,
it is that the desire realm is not taken as an object by a mind belonging to the formless realm.
Just as there is remoteness of the object by means of a form-sphere mind through aspects such as "grossness," so too there is no apprehension of the desire realm by a formless-sphere mind.
Just as the form realm is not apprehended by a mind belonging to the formless realm,
so too the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have the lower tainted realms as their object.

Since this is stated [in the scriptures], how can it be said that "the formless realms are distant from the desire realm" alone? It is true that the form realm is not taken as an object by a mind belonging to the fundamental (maula) formless levels;
rather, the fourth dhyāna is taken as an object by the preparatory (sāmantaka) mind of the sphere of infinite space through aspects such as coarseness (audārika).

Therefore, unlike the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are not established as being distant from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in terms of distance as an antidote (*pratipakṣadūratā*),
since the formless realms are not the antidote to the desire realm.

Just as the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is distant from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so too are the formless realms distant from the desire realm by way of basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), support (*pratītya*), and difficulty (*dūratā*); therefore,
a wholesome state belonging to the formless realm does not arise immediately after a wholesome state belonging to the desire realm.
Regarding "the learner's and the non-learner's":
immediately after a wholesome preparatory mind of the desire realm, at the time of meditative attainment, the previously acquired learner's [mind] arises,
and likewise the non-learner's [mind].
"Of one oppressed by an afflicted attainment" means:
for a yogin oppressed by an afflicted attainment, there arises a wholesome mind even from the obscured-unspecified [state] by resorting to a lower wholesome stage;
for a lower wholesome stage is better than a higher afflicted one.
"From all [four] wholesome and neutral minds of the form and formless realms" means that since death can occur from a wholesome or neutral mind, there are four [minds] arising from it.

Therefore, from that unwholesome state, there arise only four states belonging to its own level; for it is impossible for an unwholesome state to serve as the preparation for a wholesome state of a higher level, and because it has not been abandoned, a mind of rebirth in a higher level does not arise.
A wholesome state arises immediately after the mind of transformation.
At the time of emergence from the transformation [body], immediately following that, there are eleven; thus,
at the times of rebirth-linking, meditative attainment, emergence from that, and entry into the transformation [body], the arising of eleven moments of mind is possible.
How are the three [minds] belonging to one's own level and those belonging to the desire realm wholesome at the time of emergence?
At the time of rebirth-linking, there are two defiled [minds], the unobscured-unspecified [mind], the mind of transformation,
and the obscured-unspecified [mind] belonging to the formless realm at the time of rebirth-linking.
And it is wholesome at the time of attainment, as well as that of the learner (śaikṣa) and the non-learner (aśaikṣa);
however, it is not the unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara).
Because it is necessarily non-afflicted and because it lacks connection with meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and so forth,
