it is not obtained through preparatory application (*prayoga*), unlike the transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
Excluding the two defiled [minds] of the desire realm and the non-obscured-unspecified [mind] of the formless realm,
a wholesome mind of the form realm does not arise from the two defiled minds of the desire realm,
because those two defiled minds are incapable of serving as its preparation (*prayoga*).

For this very reason, that [mind] does not arise from an unobscured-unspecified mind belonging to the formless realm; nor does it arise from the two types of afflicted minds of the desire realm, because there is no linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-bandha*) with a wholesome mind; and this is stated excluding the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
From the two types of afflicted [minds] belonging to the desire realm, the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) mind of the form realm does not arise;
because as long as those [afflicted minds] have not been abandoned, there is no possibility of an obscured-unspecified mind due to the absence of rebirth-linking in the form realm.
Nor does it arise from the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Because it is impossible to emerge from that defiled state,
the phrase "and those belonging to the desire realm" refers to three [types of minds].
At the time of rebirth-linking, there are two defiled [minds]; and for one oppressed by defiled meditative absorption, there is the wholesome [mind],
as well as the defiled [minds] of the desire realm and the formless realm— at the time of rebirth-linking.
At the time of rebirth-linking, the defiled states belonging to the lower realms,
or those from the formless realm up to the wholesome states, do not arise; rather, only the three [types of mind] belonging to one's own level arise.
Wholesome [mind] of the form realm [arises] at the time of entering and emerging from that attainment, and during retrogressive attainment;
defiled [minds] of lower stages [arise] at the time of rebirth-linking; and the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) [also arise].
Excluding the wholesome [states] of the desire realm and the unobstructed-neutral states of the desire and form realms,
it is not possible to emerge from that attainment by means of a wholesome state of the desire realm because of its extreme remoteness;
for this very reason, it is also not possible by means of the unobstructed-neutral state because of its lack of clarity.

For this very reason, there is no emergence from [the meditative attainment] by means of an unobstructed-indeterminate state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), nor is there a connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) through these; thus, these do not arise from that. The phrase "immediately after the six" continues to apply here.
"From the wholesome [mind] of the form realm" refers to the time of entering meditative attainment;
"and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training" refers to the time of emerging from it.
"Defiled of the form realm" refers to that which is obscured (*nivṛta*) for one oppressed by defiled concentration (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*), and so forth.
At the time of rebirth-linking,

one excludes the defiled states belonging to the desire and form realms, as well as the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is because for one who has not yet abandoned passion for the lower planes, there is no rebirth-linking by means of those [higher] states.
Furthermore, because it is impossible to emerge from [the meditative attainments] by means of either the *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa* states, that [attainment] does not arise from them;
rather, at the time of emergence, there are three wholesome states belonging to the three realms— namely, those four [wholesome states of the form realm] and the *aśaikṣa* state.

The learner's [cognition] occurs in the stream immediately after the diamond-like concentration, namely the cognition of destruction; and the non-learner's [cognition] follows from that very same fivefold set mentioned immediately above. Thus, there are five.

From the wholesome states of the three realms, there are four [results]: at the time of entering meditative attainment, upon the immediate arising of the diamond-like concentration, and during the continuous flow; therefore, there are four from that.
Excluding the state of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
for the state of one in training does not arise from the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) at the time of falling away; how is it that it does not arise?
Because it is separated by the arising of afflictions, and because there is falling away only for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption],
it is both acquired through application and acquired at birth.
The *prāyogika* (attained through application) is that which is obtained through practice (*prayoga*),
consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as applicable in the three realms;
the *upapatti-lābhika* (attained at birth) is that whose acquisition first arises at the moment of linking to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the desire and form realms.

And in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), regarding the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), there arises for someone the acquisition (*prāpti*) of [minds] born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*);
this distinction [of types of minds] exists due to the difference between causes and karma.
That which is born from a ripening cause is "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*);
that which exists in the modes of conduct—lying down, sitting, standing, and walking—is "pertaining to deportment" (*airyāpathika*);
that which exists in the fields of arts and crafts is "pertaining to arts and crafts" (*śailpasthānika*).
The mind that creates emanations is "emanation-mind" (*nirmāṇacitta*);
or, that which exists within an emanation (*nirmite*) or emanations (*nirmāṇe*) is called "pertaining to emanation" (*nairmita*) or "emanational" (*nairmāṇika*). Thus it is expressed.
How is it that they become twenty again? He says:
by dividing the wholesome into six types and the unobscured-neutral into seven types.

Having divided the wholesome [states] in the three realms into six types by way of the distinction between those acquired through application and those acquired at birth, and having divided the non-obscured neutral states in the desire and form realms into seven types by way of the distinctions between the resultant, the postures, the arts and crafts, and the emanated [states] in the desire realm;
And in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is a distinction between those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), and those that are emanated (*nairmāṇika*);

thus, these thirteen remain, while the other seven are indeed undifferentiated, namely: the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

There are twenty types of consciousness: the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) of the form realm (rūpāvacara), the obscured-unspecified and the unobscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) of the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), as well as the consciousness of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
this is because [in the formless realm] there is an absence of bodily postures and the like.
Due to the absence of deportment, the bases of the arts, and emanation,
these three do not exist in the formless realm because of the absence of form that could serve as an object of perception.
Visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are the objects (*ālambana*) of these [mental states].
Among them, the visible forms and so forth of bedding and seating, as well as the visible forms and so forth of the parts of one's own body, are the objects of the *airyāpathika* (postural) state;

the visible forms and so forth of the craftsman’s workshop are the objects of the *śailpasthānika* (artisanal) state; and the visible forms and so forth of emanations are the objects of the *nairmāṇika* (emanative) state.
But for that which pertains to the stage of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), there is also sound;

the word "but" (*tu*) serves as a qualification, and by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, as well as sound, are its objects of perception (*ālambana*).
By taking the word "instruction in the arts" as an object, one learns the art through mental consciousness;
since there is no mention of [consciousness] born of maturation, it should be understood that all [objects], such as visible forms and so forth, are the objects of mental consciousnesses alone.
The three types beginning with the deportment-mind (*airyāpathika*), which have the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
are so because they function in the formation of conceptualization;
since the result-of-ripening (*vipākaja*) is not mentioned [as a separate category], it is thereby indicated that [the mind] has the nature of the six consciousnesses.
Those five bodies of consciousness are "preparatory" (*prāyogika*) in relation to the [minds] of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the [minds] of crafts (*śailpasthānika*),
because they exist during the stage of preparation for those;
for they arise after having seen, and so on, up to having touched.
There is no preliminary application for the ripening [result],
because it flows spontaneously through the efficacy of karma; it is "produced by the postural" (airyāpathika), and so forth.

Others maintain that the mental consciousness projected and produced by the consciousness of postures (*airyāpathika*) is a mental consciousness that has the twelve sense-bases as its object— ranging from the eye-base as its object up to the dharma-base as its object— and which is of an unobscured-neutral nature;
they demonstrate it in this way.
There is also another unobscured-neutral [state] that is not included among those such as the functional (airyāpathika) and so forth;
this must be understood in exactly this way,
for otherwise, that which he will say later—

The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action (vijñapti), belonging to the second dhyāna and above, are obtained in their first [level]; they are undefiled-neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta).
Emanation occurs by means of [the mind] of its own level, but speech by means of [the mind] of a lower level.
Thus, with these and other such [statements], by which of these four are those consciousnesses subsumed?
They are not, first of all, born of maturation (*vipākaja*).
Because for those who have arisen in a higher realm, there is no possibility of maturation belonging to a lower level;
nor do [the minds] such as the *airyāpathika* exist, because of the absence of postures (*īryāpatha*) and so forth.

And where should the mind, which consists of the latencies of ignorance and so forth, be made to enter? Even the Venerable Anantavarman stated in his *Vibhāṣā-vyākhyāna* that there exist indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) consciousnesses distinct from these four; therefore, it should be understood that this scriptural explanation is incomplete.
"Except for the fruit of supernormal knowledge" means that a mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm arises immediately after a preparatory mind of the form realm,
but not immediately after a preparatory mind of the desire realm.
The form-sphere [mind]— namely, the preparatory, the learner's, and the non-learner's— at the time of attainment,
arises from its own wholesome and afflicted [minds].

Because at the time of preparatory application, there are both wholesome and afflicted states, and because for one who is weary of the afflictions, the preparatory state arises from the absence of [active] afflictions.
It does not arise from the non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) states because they are weak and lack volitional effort (anabhisaṃskārita);
nor from the two states belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), namely the preparatory (prāyogika) and the afflicted (kliṣṭa),
[meaning] from the preparatory and from the afflicted.
And at the time of emergence from both the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* [attainments],
for one oppressed by afflicted concentration,
there is the arising of the afflicted [mind] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
For at the time of rebirth-linking, death occurs for the mind acquired at birth,
as previously described.
The meaning is "except for the fruit of the supernormal powers" (*abhijñā-phala*);

for that [fruit] arises immediately after the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), as it was stated previously in detail: "and from the two [minds] of the form realm," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "immediately after the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified":
it should be analyzed as "immediately after the unwholesome" and "immediately after the obscured-unspecified," for since they are equal [in this respect], they are mentioned together.
From the four [minds] of the form realm— excluding the preparatory mind and the fruit of supernormal knowledge— at the time of rebirth-linking.
For one established in the preparatory stage (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*), there is no death;
therefore, those two do not give rise to the two types of afflicted [minds].
However, for one established in the remaining [stages], there is death.

Therefore, those two defiled [minds] arise from them at the time of rebirth-linking; in the same way, it should be explained that this also occurs elsewhere, except in the case of the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*).
Six [minds] arise from others, excluding the preparatory mind and the fruit of superknowledge;
because these two are weak and lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāraka*), the preparatory mind does not arise immediately after them.

Furthermore, because they arise immediately after the preparatory stage (*prāyogika*) of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and their fruits do not arise from those two; nor do they arise from the defiled states (*kliṣṭa*) of the form and formless realms. Thus, at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), six [minds] arise immediately after the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Because death is impossible for one situated therein, just as with the *airyāpathika* and *vipākaja* [minds], here— during the period of the flow— the defiled minds belonging to the realms of form and formlessness are impossible, as is its own fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*).
And the preparatory [attainment] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara-prāyogika*); for upon emerging from that,
there is no emergence from the fruit of the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*) without having entered meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
That too [arises] from this very pair; that is, the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñā-phala*) arises both during its flow and at the time of entering into it,
within the wholesome states of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-kuśala*).
For at the time of emergence,
there is indeed the possibility of emerging from meditative attainment even by means of that [wholesome state] acquired at birth, because of its clarity;
therefore, both types of wholesome states are included.

And the fruit of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*): this refers to the mind of transformation belonging to the desire realm, the preparatory mind belonging to the formless realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) at the time of meditative attainment.
"Except for those born of deportment and those born of maturation," because those two are weak and unconditioned;
"by means of those that are preparatory and afflicted," [is the meaning].
At times when one is oppressed by emergence from meditative absorption or by afflicted attainment,
[the mind] is afflicted belonging to the desire realm; that is, at the time of rebirth-linking,
except for the result of superknowledge.
Because the transformation mind arises immediately after a preparatory mind,
it is a defiled state belonging to the formless realm at the time of rebirth-linking.
"Wholesome and afflicted" (*kuśalakliṣṭāni*) is a compound meaning "in the wholesome and in the afflicted";
it is "wholesome" because of relying on a basis belonging to a wholesome lower stage.
But at the time of rebirth-linking, when [the mind] is afflicted,
it is from those belonging to the desire realm; such is the detailed explanation regarding the time of rebirth-linking.

Since there is no death in the states of the preparatory, the artisanal, or the fruits of supernormal knowledge, there is no [arising] from them into the afflicted states of the desire realm at the time of rebirth-linking.

Even the afflicted [mind] belonging to the formless realm does not arise from this very same [state], because its own preparatory [mind] belongs to that [realm]; likewise, the mind born of maturation does not arise, because the mind pertaining to postures is weak and, being unconditioned, is unfit for preparatory effort.
Just as it was stated regarding the [minds] belonging to deportment (*airyāpathika*),

so too here, following those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), seven [minds] arise, with the exception of the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*); thus, the meaning of the text is the same.
Immediately after the fruit of the higher knowledges (*abhijñā*), there are two [minds] belonging to one's own level;
that is, during emergence from meditative absorption and during the flow [of the subsequent state], those too arise from these very two.
At the time of entry and during the flow, it is the preparatory [attainment] of the form realm; this refers to the time of emergence from meditative absorption.

In this way, the wholesome consists of the [minds] of those in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and its own four [types]; it is clearly afflicted at the time of relishing (āsvādana).
But the obscured-unspecified [mind] arises at the time of emergence from the preparatory [meditation] belonging to the form realm,
and at the time of meditative attainment.
The reason for the phrase "except for that which is born of maturation" will be stated as being because it is weak and proceeds without volitional effort;
and [the reason] for the phrase "and by those who are in training and those beyond training" [will also be stated].
At the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*),
there are [formative forces] belonging to the lower realms and those that are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*);
at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), there are those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) and the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Regarding "the preparatory and the afflicted":
the preparatory is [so called] because it is produced by the pressure of the afflicted concentration; the afflicted occurs at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*).

Regarding the defiled [minds] of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), it is precisely at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) that they arise from those of the desire and form realms; this is the detailed explanation,
because death is possible while that mind is present.
"Except for the preparatory [mind]" means that because a preparatory mind does not arise immediately after a mind born of maturation,
the three lower defiled minds [do not follow it].
At the time of rebirth-linking, those belonging to two realms— the desire realm being acquired through birth—
are sharp; therefore, this mind of emergence from training can arise [from them].

He will state the reason as "because of its sharpness" (*paṭutvāt*); however, since the [wisdoms] acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) belonging to the form and formless realms are not sharp, they do not occur [as such], nor does the wisdom of one in training (*śaikṣa*) occur in the stream, nor does the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) occur immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama*).
"Excluding one of the *śaikṣa*" means that a *śaikṣa* state does not arise from an *aśaikṣa* state;
therefore, five [minds] follow immediately after an *aśaikṣa*.
But it is not six, as in the case of the *śaikṣa*; and those five should be explained like the *śaikṣa*.

Here are summary verses in the form of aphorisms for the twenty states of mind that serve as the immediately preceding conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*), which were not explicitly formulated [in the root text].

From the wholesome [state] acquired through application in the desire realm, ten [minds] arise; from others than that, nine [arise] from the wholesome, and eleven from that [wholesome]; from the afflicted, seven arise separately;
and from those fourteen, eight arise—namely, the functional and the resultant.

From those seven, six arise from the sphere of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*); from that [six], two arise from the emanated (*nairmita*). From these two, this [arises] from the wholesome (*śubha*) acquired through application (*prāyogika*) in the form realm;
from these twelve, eight arise from the wholesome not produced through effort (*ayatnajāta*).
From those five, nine arise from the defiled; from that [defiled], eleven arise again. From the resultant and the postural, seven arise; from those seven, two arise.
From the mind that is the fruit of supernormal knowledge, two arise; likewise, from those two, it arises in the same way.

In the formless realm, from the effortful wholesome mind, seven [minds] arise; from that same effortless wholesome mind, six arise. From the defiled mind, eight arise; from those eight, ten minds arise; and from those ten, six minds arise, including the resultant-of-maturation.

That [unwholesome mind] arises immediately from four [minds], while those of one in training (śaikṣa) arise from six; furthermore, that [mind of one beyond training] arises from four, and that [mind of one beyond training] likewise arises from five,
because it proceeds from the performance of deportment and artistic crafts.
It is under discussion that preparatory [thought] (*prāyogika*) does not arise from these;
therefore, because of this impossibility, preparatory thought does not arise immediately after the thought of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or the thought of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*),
for the intention is that those two are engaged in the performance of other formative activities (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*).
Because the *airyāpathika* [consciousness] is engaged in the performance of postures, having the form of walking and so forth,
and the *śailpasthānika* [consciousness] is engaged in the performance of crafts.

Because it proceeds with such modes as "I am doing this" or "I am doing that," and because it flows without weak volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the *prāyogika* (preparatory) mind does not arise immediately after a *vipākaja* (resultant-of-maturation) mind;
for that resultant-of-maturation mind is weak due to its being morally neutral (*avyākṛta*).
Is it "proceeding without volitional effort" because it proceeds effortlessly due to the projection of prior karma?
Or rather, because it proceeds through the volitional effort of postures and crafts?

Immediately after the states of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and the arts (*śailpasthānika*), the preparatory state (*prāyogika*) does not arise, because they proceed with weakness and lack volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Furthermore, immediately after the states of deportment, the arts, and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the preparatory state does not arise,
because all of these are weak due to being neutral (*avyākṛta*).

And because it proceeds without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), it belongs only to that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*); or alternatively, even for those belonging to deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), since there is an absence of preparatory volitional effort (*prāyogikābhisaṃskāra*), their engagement in volitional formation (*abhisaṃskaraṇapravṛttatva*) is said to consist merely in being intent upon other activities.
Or rather, this is the intended connection of this very statement.

Because they are engaged in the performance of postures (*īryāpatha*), crafts (*śilpa*), and formative activities (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*), and because they proceed with weak formative effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), these— namely those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*)— are not preparatory (*prāyogika*). Therefore, it should be connected [to the previous statement] that a preparatory state does not arise immediately after them.
The mind of departure (*niṣkramaṇacitta*), however, flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*); it is that mind which is other than the stream of preparatory minds (*prāyogikacittapravāha*).
This is the mind of departure.

For indeed, because that yogi has descended from that stream, it is logical that his mind of emergence flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and flows without exertion (*anābhoga*). Thus, it is fitting that this mind of emergence—which possesses one of the natures such as being born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—arises immediately after a mind of application (*prāyogika-citta*).
"In that case," [it is said].
If [it is argued that] the preparatory mind does not arise immediately after the result-of-maturation and so forth because they are not conducive to the preparatory, then in that case,
the preparatory mind would also not arise after defiled minds, because of their incompatibility.
For the meaning is that a defiled dharma is incompatible with the wholesome, as it is contrary to it.
"Nevertheless," and so forth:

even though that [state] is deficient in qualities, nevertheless, for the yogin who is weary of the active manifestation of the afflictions (*kleśasamudācāra*), the manifestation of the preparatory mind (*prāyogika*) is appropriate because of the thorough knowledge of that—that is, the thorough knowledge of the active manifestation of the afflictions;
for the thorough knowledge of that itself is the preparatory mind.
"Because of its sharpness":
the innate [mind] belonging to the desire realm is sharp; it can arise as the mind of emergence from the states of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth.
For this very reason, one who is oppressed by afflicted concentration takes recourse in that [innate mind].
However, because it flows without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), the states of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth do not arise from it.
On the other hand, the state acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) is not as sharp as that of the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*);
therefore, for one who is oppressed by afflicted concentration (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*), there is no recourse to it.
Only that which is produced through application (*prāyogika*) is relied upon;
for minds arise immediately one after another, and they arise by the power of mental attention (*manaskāra*). Therefore, mental attention is introduced.
"Three [types of knowledge arise] from mental attention," and so forth.
Mental attention to a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-manaskāra*) is the mental attention directed toward a specific characteristic;
for example, "the characteristic of visible forms is form," and so on.
By the word "etcetera," [it is meant] that feeling is characterized by experience, and so forth; thus,
the mental attention directed toward impermanence and other such qualities is the mental attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-manaskāra*), which is associated with sixteen aspects,
from "impermanence" up to "leading to liberation."
Mental attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*) is the mental attention that does not engage with the object as it truly is;
this includes [mental attention] toward the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) up to the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the resolute conviction in lightness and so forth during the accomplishment of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and other qualities is included.

For example, one who possesses great supernatural power and great majesty can, if he so desires, resolve upon a limited perception of earth or even an immeasurable perception, and thereby cause the earth to shake; such is the detailed account.
"Accompanied by the foul" means connected with the foul; this is what is meant:
immediately after the mental attention directed toward the foul, one cultivates, generates, and produces the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness.
Since the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is indeed the noble path,
he says this to show that there is the arising of the noble path immediately following the mental attention of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manaskāra*).

If one brings the Noble Path into manifestation immediately after a mental application of general characteristics (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) and not after a mental application of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimanaskāra*), how is this [scriptural statement] to be understood:
"He cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness accompanied by the meditation on the foul"?
Therefore, this is said:
"Having tamed the mind by means of the foul," and so forth.

Having tamed the mind by means of the foul during the stage of preparation (*prāyogāvasthā*), up until the end, immediately after the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*), one brings the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra; thus,
[the phrase] "even immediately after the noble path" is explained in detail,
meaning that one brings the noble path into manifestation not only immediately after ordinary mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*).
Others maintain that even immediately after the noble path, one brings forth only the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*);
this is the detailed explanation beginning with "it might be so" and continuing with "the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and so forth."

By the word "etcetera," it is meant that when one enters the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) by relying on the three stages—the *anāgamya*, the first dhyāna, and the intermediate dhyāna—one would, immediately after that [supramundane] path, manifest a general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) belonging to the desire realm, whether consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya*) or reflection (*cintāmaya*), because it is proximate.

Now, if one enters the path of certainty by relying on the second dhyāna and so forth—specifically by relying on the second, third, or fourth dhyānas—how does one manifest the general mental attention immediately after the noble path? How does one bring it into presence?
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "for it is not possible to bring [the desire-realm state] into manifestation.
Why?
Because it is too remote, being separated by the first dhyāna.
If you should say that one brings into manifestation only that which belongs to the levels of the second dhyāna and above, he says in response:
"And it is not obtained as belonging to those levels, except for the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya)."

The untainted path belonging to the stages of the second dhyāna and so forth, or the stage of the *anāgamya* and so forth—excluding the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)—had not previously been attained;
however, the mundane path that had fallen into [specific] mental aspects (*ākāra*) had been attained.
Therefore, it is pleasing to the Noble One for the purpose of emerging from meditative absorption.
"In that case, he will bring face-to-face the general mental attention that is conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
To this he says:
"And the noble one does not [bring] the stage conducive to penetration," and so forth.
If it is asked, "For what purpose? he says:
"For it is not logical that one who has already attained the fruit should bring its preparatory application (prayoga) into manifestation."
Because the preparatory application has already fulfilled its purpose and because it is inferior, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are the preparation for the Noble Path;
thus, another [type of attention] of the same kind as these exists, namely,
that which is a general mental engagement (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) of the same nature as the aids to penetration, since it takes the [Four] Truths as its object and undergoes cultivation.
The meaning is that it is attained at the time of the arising of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
How is it that "nirvāṇa is peaceful"? It is because the mental application of generality (*sāmānyamanaskāra*) has all of nirvāṇa as its object.

They do not describe this [view] as: "He will bring that face-to-face," meaning that immediately after the path of cultivation, he will bring face-to-face either that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," or "all phenomena are non-self," or "nirvana is peace."

Why is this? Because these mental orientations of that same class, which are conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), are bound to cultivation; it is said that they are not bound to the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*).
Thus, the detailed explanation is: "relying on the *anāgamya*," and so forth.
"Belonging to that level" means belonging to the level of the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
or belonging to that level, or belonging to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
The mind of emergence belongs either to the level of the sphere of nothingness or to the peak of existence if one is reborn at the peak of existence;
in other levels, the mind of emergence belongs exclusively to its own level and not to another level.
Because that which belongs to another stage must be accomplished through preparatory effort (*prayoga*),
whereas that which belongs to one's own stage occurs without volitional exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra*); thus,
it is because [the former] is dependent upon preparatory effort.
Of which noble path does the state of manifestation of the innate [wholesome mind] belonging to the desire realm occur immediately after? This is the subject under discussion.
Regarding the acquisition of the defiled [dharmas] of the three realms, the teaching is given according to their respective order: "of six, of six, and of two."
In the case of a defiled mind of the desire realm, there is the acquisition— that is, the attainment— of six minds;
in the case of the form realm, [there is the acquisition] of six.
"In the formless realm, [it arises] from two" means that he said,
"For in the desire realm, it is defiled," and so forth.
"Of one who is not possessed of those"—
how is it for a person who is not possessed of those six types of mind?
In this case, for those who reconnect with wholesome states— whether by means of right view or by doubt—
if they reconnect through doubt,
then when a defiled mind associated with doubt has become manifest, they return from the form realm or the formless realm to the desire realm.

Then, when his mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi-citta*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is necessarily defiled, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of that wholesome [state] by one who was previously not endowed with it;
this refers to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), as detailed in the full passage.

Both the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), because of the context and because the obscured [state] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) is mentioned separately.
Regarding those two— the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified— it is the subject under discussion as to what is acquired of the afflicted [mind] belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).
How is there attainment? It is said:
"Through returning to a realm and through falling away.
This refers to when one returns from the form realm or the formless realm to the desire realm.

Then, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), which is necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), when either the unwholesome (*akuśala*) or the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of those two— the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified— because they were previously lost. Furthermore, for one who was not previously endowed with them,

there is the acquisition of the afflicted [states] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), because of the return to the realm [of desire], when one returns from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Then, in his intermediate state (*antarābhava*) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), which is necessarily defiled, there is the acquisition of a previously abandoned defiled [state] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), because he was not previously endowed with it and has fallen away from it when he falls away from detachment from the form realm by means of a mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

Then there is the acquisition of that afflicted [state] belonging to the realm of form which has been abandoned through detachment; and by means of that, there is the acquisition of the afflicted [state] belonging to the formless realm with which one was previously endowed,
due to falling away from detachment from the formless realm when one falls away from it by means of a mind belonging to the realm of desire.
At that time, there is the acquisition of that afflicted [state] belonging to the formless realm for one who was previously not endowed with it;
and this applies to the case of a learner (śaikṣa) who falls away from arhatship due to a mind belonging to the desire realm.
Then there is the acquisition of that mind of one in training (*śaikṣacitta*) by one who was previously not endowed with it.

Thus, first, when a defiled mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) has become manifest, the acquisition of six minds by one who was not previously endowed with them has been explained; likewise, when a defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition of six minds by one who was not previously endowed with them.

"Of those belonging to the realm of form," and so forth: when one returns from the formless realm to the realm of form, at that time, in his mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the realm of form—which is necessarily defiled—there are necessarily three [types of] mental states belonging to the realm of form: the wholesome acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), the defiled, and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Because of the existence of the attainment of the first [moment] of the transformation-mind (nirmāṇacitta),

there is the acquisition of the desire-realm (kāmāvacara) non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) transformation-mind itself, as well as the formless-realm (ārūpyāvacara) afflicted mind, and the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
Regarding falling away from arhatship by means of a mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), for one who falls away and is not yet possessed of that [arhatship],
the acquisition of six [defilements] is likewise stated for the defiled [minds] of the form realm.
However, regarding the defiled [mind] of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), there is the acquisition of two, for one who was previously not possessed of them.

Regarding falling away: for one falling away from arhatship by means of a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), it is a portion of the afflicted [mind] that has become manifest; and for a trainee (*śaikṣa*), it is likewise.
Thus, in the wholesome [mind] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), there are three [types].
"Wholesome" (*kuśala*) is a designation for a genus;
how is it possible that there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of three [wholesome factors] in some wholesome state belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)?

First, when a wholesome mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition (*lābha*) of that very same wholesome mind of the form realm for one who was previously not endowed with it. Furthermore, when a wholesome mind comprised within the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition of the two types of unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to the desire and form realms for one who was previously not endowed with them.
Thus, it is said that when a wholesome mind of the form realm becomes manifest, there is the acquisition of three [types of minds].
But it is not a simultaneous acquisition; thus,

regarding "four in the state of training" (*śaikṣa*), when a mind of training is manifest— specifically, a mind of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)— there is the acquisition of that very same [receptivity] which has the nature of the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering, for one who was previously not endowed with it.
Regarding the non-obscured-unspecified [states] of the desire and form realms and the wholesome [state] of the formless realm—in which group [of factors] do they occur? It is said:
at the point of detachment from the desire and form realms by means of the noble path.
How so? When one attains detachment from the desire realm by means of the noble path belonging to the stage of *anāgamya*, then,

when the learner’s mind (*śaikṣacitta*) comprised within the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) has become manifest, there is the acquisition of the two unobstructed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) pertaining to the desire and form realms, for one who was previously not endowed with them.

But when one effects detachment from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) by means of any one of the noble paths (*āryamārga*) belonging to the six stages, then— at the moment the first type of mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) becomes manifest— one acquires the wholesome [state] pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), according to the principle of the acquisition of past and future [states]. The mention of "the noble" (*ārya*) is for the purpose of excluding the tainted mind (*sāsravacitta*).
When a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) has arisen, this acquisition (*lābha*) is described.
Here, the master Guṇamati explains:

[there is the acquisition] of four [minds] when that very mind of one in training arises, as well as of the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds belonging to the desire and form realms, and of the wholesome (*kuśala*) mind belonging to the formless realm.
To the question "How so?", he says:

regarding detachment from the realms of desire and form by means of the noble path, when one effects detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by means of the noble path belonging to the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*),
that which is the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
In that [moment], one acquires a previously unobtained *śaikṣa* state belonging to the level of the fundamental dhyānas; thus, it is called "the acquisition of the *śaikṣa*" for the learner.
Furthermore, in that [moment], there is the acquisition of the two types of unobstructed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) pertaining to the desire and form realms.
However, by means of the noble path (*āryamārga*) belonging to the six levels, during the detachment from the desire and form realms, there is the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
In that [context], he acquires wholesome [states] belonging to the formless realm;
thus, even his disciple, the Master Vasumitra, writes down that very same meaning with those same words and syllables.
This explanation is incorrect.
For in this way, the explained meaning does not fit within a single sentence;
rather, it fits through a division of sentences.
"The attainment of that very same trainee"—this is one sentence.
And there is another statement: "up to the point of detachment from the desire and form realms for those belonging to the desire and form realms.

This is not a qualification of that same aforementioned "learner" (śaikṣa) by means of the distinction "detachment from the desire and form realms through the noble path," because it is a separate sentence.
For this acquisition of mind is described as belonging to one who does not yet possess [that detachment].
For how can it be so, given the statement: "The attainment of mind belongs to one who does not possess it"?

In the ninth path of liberation, the acquisition of a learner’s mind (*śaikṣacitta*) is established for a person who possesses that learner’s mind; however, it was not stated that a previously unobtained learner’s mind belonging to the level of the fundamental dhyānas is acquired, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
It would follow that even a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), belonging to the level of the fundamental dhyānas, would be considered "attained" when it is acquired for the first time;
regarding this, Master Vasumitra says:

for one who abides in a mind of training (*śaikṣacitta*) and is becoming detached from the desire realm, the wholesome [mind] of the form realm is not counted as attained because it was already acquired at the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) during the entry into the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*).
That is incorrect, because even the *śaikṣa* [path] would then result in not being counted;
for since the *śaikṣa* path is also obtained during the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it follows that you should not establish it in such a manner.
Therefore, it is certain that this is a misinterpretation, because the Master himself wrote in his commentary on the *Miśraka-śloka*:
"Of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), [there is the attainment] of the entry into the fixed course and of arhatship."
To show that "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) and "that which has been made a remainder" (*kṛtaśeṣita*) are forms derived from nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and verbal roots (*dhātu*):
In which mind the acquisition is not explained,
how is it that there is the acquisition of that very [mind]? How is this so?

First, regarding the wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), it has not been explained as the acquisition of so many minds; for in that case, there is the acquisition of that very [wholesome mind] itself and not of others.

This is as follows: when a wholesome mind of the desire realm becomes manifest through the reconnection of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*) by means of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is the acquisition of that very wholesome mind for one who was previously not endowed with it.
It is not [the acquisition] of other afflicted states of the three realms either, because they have already been previously obtained;
nor is it that of the unobscured-unspecified state belonging to the desire realm.
Because those born of maturation and so forth possess simultaneous acquisition (*sahajā-prāpti*),
whereas the mind of emanation lacks acquisition,
and because there is no acquisition for the wholesome states and so forth belonging to the form and formless realms, nor for those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
The acquisition of the unobscured-unspecified mind belonging to the desire realm has also not been explained; for in that case,
there is the acquisition of that very [mind] by one who was previously not endowed with it,
which is an innate attainment of the unspecified.
Thinking thus, [it is] not so for others, such as the wholesome factors and so forth, because they have been previously acquired,
and likewise because some lack their acquisition altogether.

However, when a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) has become manifest, it should not be said that there is no acquisition (*lābha*) for anyone; for that [state] in which there is no acquisition for anyone— whether in a defiled state or otherwise— is not what is being discussed here.

For indeed, in the three realms, there is the acquisition of all six [types of minds] only when they are defiled; however, this restriction—that it is not necessarily so—applies to the non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind of the form realm as well. When that very [non-obscured-unspecified mind] becomes manifest, there is the acquisition of that alone, and not of the others; this should be explained as previously stated.

Likewise, when a wholesome mind belonging to the formless realm— specifically that included in the first category of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*)— is manifested, there is the acquisition of that very mind for one who was previously unendowed with it; however, there is no acquisition of any others,
because some were already previously acquired and others lack the conditions for their attainment.
Thus [it is said] regarding the unobscured-unspecified and the learner;
others, however, say this without making such distinctions— whom are they?
The author of the *Miśraka* says "without distinction" because the defiled states and so forth belonging to the three realms are not separated;
however, in the case of the six [mental factors] in a wholesome mind—
Thus,
what was stated is an incomplete definition.
For the wholesome [mind] of the three realms is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava);
in that context, it should be said that there are seven [mental factors] in a wholesome mind, not six. Demonstrating this, he says: "of the desire-realm [wholesome mind]," and so forth.
This has been explained as "due to the reconnection of the roots of merit.

Regarding the phrase "through detachment from the non-obscured-neutral [states]," it means that through either the mundane or supramundane path, upon attaining detachment from the desire realm in the ninth path of liberation, there is the acquisition of the two types of emanation-minds belonging to the desire and form realms for one who was previously not endowed with them.
Regarding the wholesome states of the form and formless realms, it is "by way of attaining the concentration pertaining to them":
when one first attains the *anāgamya* stage of the form realm,
at that time there is the attainment of the wholesome state of the form realm.

When one first attains the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of the sphere of infinite space, there is the acquisition of wholesome states belonging to the formless realm, as well as the acquisition of those of a learner (śaikṣa) and a non-learner (aśaikṣa), occurring respectively at the entry into the fixed course [toward liberation] and at the attainment of arhatship.
When one enters the fixed course of determination,
there is the acquisition of the complex of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering for the trainee; this occurs when one attains arhatship.
At that time, there is the acquisition of the complex of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Thus, in these states, by means of these seven aforementioned minds, one who was previously unendowed [with them] attains their possession;
the remainder should be understood from this very explanation.
Therefore, the remainder should be understood from my own commentary:
for when the mind is afflicted, there is the acquisition of nine [roots], of which one is [the root of] equanimity.
"Indeed, [the question] regarding that very same [matter] is indeterminate"— this is the second [point],
and this is the remainder.
How is there the acquisition of nine [types of minds] in a defiled mind of the three realms?

There is the acquisition, as appropriate, of nine— namely, four of the desire realm, three of the form realm, one of the formless realm which is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*), and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*)— for one who was previously not endowed with them.
What is the meaning of "according to application" (*yathāyogārtha*)?

It is the acquisition of wholesome states belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) through either the reconnection of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*) or the return to that realm (*dhātu-pratyāgamana*); and the acquisition of the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) states through either the return to that realm or through falling away (*parihāṇi*).

Only when a defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises is there the acquisition of a wholesome mind of the form realm and of the two non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms—namely, the transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*)—due to returning to that realm.

When a defiled mind of the desire or form realm arises, there is the acquisition of a defiled mind of the form realm due to returning to that realm or due to falling away (*parihāṇi*). When a defiled mind of the desire, form, or formless realm arises, there is the acquisition of a defiled mind of the formless realm and of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) due to falling away.
Thus is the meaning according to the application;
indeed, "in that very [case]" refers to the indeterminate.
Whatever remains is similar, as before;
for when any one of the indeterminate [dharmas] belonging to the three realms becomes manifest, there is the acquisition of that very same indeterminate [dharma].

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), for one who has not yet acquired [a state] by means of this or that [path], the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is innate (*sahaja*);
this is the summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
Thus,
all this is established through reasoning.
Because of the statement "due to returning to the realm," and because of such statements as "of that very same wholesome state" regarding the meditative attainment.

Because of the statement "from the attainment of that concentration," and because of the statement "in regard to detachment" meaning "in regard to detachment from the desire realm and the form realm."
Because of the statement "in falling away, [it is] by way of falling away," and also because of the reconnection of wholesome [roots].
Because of the statement, "By means of doubt and right view, there is the reconnection of the roots of merit," there is the attainment of the mind,
which is the acquisition of the mind.
"Because of the statement: 'of a person who does not possess them, and who is not endowed with them,'" [as stated] in the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
The second chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the Faculties," is completed.
Chapter 3:
The third chapter of the Treasury, titled "Exposition of the World."
This must now be explained;
thus, in order to demonstrate the connection between the second and third chapters (*kośasthāna*), it is said:
"The exposition of mind and the other [factors] has been made according to the fixed determination (*naiyamya*) of the desire, form, and formless realms."
*Naiyamya* is the state of being restricted (*niyama*) or restriction itself;
by means of that, the description of the mind and so forth as wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, or unobscured within the realm of desire is established.
Because of the statement, "In the realms of form and formlessness, [there are] other than the unwholesome," the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes mental factors (caitta) and so forth.

Because it is accompanied by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), remorse, torpor, and other unwholesome states do not exist in the first *dhyāna* when the wholesome mind of the desire realm is present; therefore,
applied thought and sustained thought also cease from the intermediate *dhyāna* onwards.
According to this statement, the faculties (indriya) are designated according to their restriction by desire and so forth:
those pertaining to the realm of desire (kāmāpta), excluding the stainless (amala) ones; and those pertaining to the realm of form (rūpāpta), excluding the female and male faculties.

Because of the statement, "Having abandoned [the factors] belonging to the formless realm in suffering itself, and having excluded those in pleasure and in the form realm," the characteristics of the desire, form, and formless realms have not been stated; therefore, he asks.
In that regard, what are those realms of desire, form, and formlessness? To this it is said:
hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Thus it is said in detail:
"The four destinies" refers to the four destinies of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and humans; these four are entirely included within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
But the divine realm is not exhaustive;
rather, he shows that it consists of six classes of gods.
In this context, "nīryantaḥ" [is derived as follows]: from the root *nṛ* in the sense of "guiding" (*naye*); from *rañjeḥ* [it means] "they do not delight" (*na rañjayanti*);
and "narer" is a form of the root *ṛ* in the sense of "going" (*gati*) and "seeking" (*eṣaṇā*), preceded by the negative particle *na*.
They are called "hells" (*naraka*) because beings are led out (*nīryante*) from them due to demerit;
others say they are called "hells" because one does not find pleasure (*na rañjayanti*) there; yet others say this is a form derived from the root *nṛ*, meaning "to reach" or "to encounter."
"They do not delight in them, they do not long for them as a refuge, [thinking] 'these are hells'— thus says the Master Saṅghabhadra.
Because they have gone far from here and do not return, they are called *preta*s."
Others say they are called *tiryag-yoni* because they move horizontally; they are called *manuṣyas* because the mind has arisen [in them].
"Offspring of Manu," so say the worldly people;
"those whose abode is heaven" are the *divaukasas*;
and he will explain that the realm governed by desire is the *kāmadhātu*.

The four great kings, the world-protectors—Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vaiśravaṇa—their inhabitants are the Cāturmahārājikas; the meaning is that they are situated among them. Just as "reborn among the gods" means one is born in the midst of the gods.

Others say that the Cāturmahārājikas are those who exist in the place of the Four Great Kings, [the term being formed] by eliding the middle word, as in the case of "ox-cart" (*goratha*). The Trayastriṃśas are so called because they are reborn here through shared meritorious deeds;
the meaning is that they possess equal merit.

Others maintain that because there are eight Vasus, two Aśvins, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas, they are called "the thirty-three" (trayastriṃśāḥ) due to their preeminence; and accordingly, this same designation is used in the sacred teachings (pravacana). Furthermore, they are called Yāmas because they have gone (yātāḥ) from suffering by means of merit.
They are called *yāmas* because they restrain (*yāmayanti*) sufferings;
they are called *tuṣitas* because they have gone (*itāḥ*) by means of contentment (*tuṣṭyā*), or because "contentment" (*tuṣa*) exists within them.

Because their delight lies in emanations created by themselves, they are called "Those Who Delight in Emanations" (Nirmāṇarati). Because it is their habit to exercise mastery over enjoyments created by others, they are called "Those Who Exercise Mastery over Creations by Others" (Paranirmitavaśavartin).
The words "abodes" (sthānāni) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Those twenty places constitute the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
however, if one were to apply the elision of the final member of the compound, it would be expressed as "twenty" (*viṃśati*), meaning "that which consists of twenty places."

For example, it is called *Pītatoya* because its waters are drunk by horses; it is called *Pīta* because [the horses] have drunk [them]; and *Sañjīva* is so named because there the winds revive sentient beings who are dying;
and *Kālasūtra* is so named because there sentient beings are cut after lines of black cord have been laid down.
*Saṅghāta* is where mountains and other objects in the shape of rams descend from both sides and crush sentient beings;
*Raurava* is where sentient beings, being driven about, cry out in extreme distress; and where they do so especially intensely, that is *Mahāraurava*.
*Tapana* is where beings are tormented by fire and other means; *Pratāpana*, however, is that specific hell where they are especially tormented.
*Avīci* is where there is no interval (*vīci*) of happiness for beings embraced by the excessively intense flames of fire.
Jambūdvīpa is the continent marked by the Jambu tree;
Pūrvavideha is to the east of Sumeru;
and Avaragodānīya is to the west.
To the north is Uttarakuru;
these are the continents well-known in the world, as well as the six classes of gods mentioned immediately above.
Thus, these are the twenty locations:

the eight hells, the four continents, and the six realms previously mentioned beginning with the Cāturmahārājikas; since the hungry ghosts and animals are not subdivided, the desire realm consists of twenty locations, extending down to the circle of wind.
Below, where the water-element sphere (ap-maṇḍala) abides, is the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The realm characterized by form consists of distinct meditative absorptions (dhyāna) comprising three stages each; therein, however, the fourth [dhyāna] comprises eight stages.

Thus, in that realm of the form-dhātu (rūpadhātu), even among sentient beings, each of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) is divided into three levels according to the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense:
the first is the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
The Limited Light, the Immeasurable Light, and the Radiant Light constitute the second [station];
the Limited Purity, the Immeasurable Purity, and the All-Pervading Purity constitute the third;
the Cloudless, the Merit-Born, and the Vast Fruit constitute the fourth.

However, through the intermingling of that very same superior [level] of untainted meditative absorption—which is further divided into the distinctions of weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest—there are five other locations:
the Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha.
For this reason, the fourth dhyāna is said to consist of eight stages.
In that regard, because he has emerged from vast roots of merit, he is Brahmā;
and who is he? He who is called Mahābrahmā.

Because they have attained the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because they attain death and rebirth both later and earlier [than others], and because of distinctions such as their physical dimensions, they possess a great body as their dwelling; thus they are the *Brahmakāyikas*.
Because Brahmā is placed at their head (*purodhīyate*), they are the *Brahmapurohitas*.

They are called Mahābrahmās because Great Brahmā possesses excellence in terms of lifespan, complexion, and other qualities in relation to them. They are called Parīttābhās (Limited Radiance) because their radiance is limited when compared to the level of Ābhāsvara. They are called Apramāṇābhās (Immeasurable Radiance) because the measure of their radiance cannot be determined.
They are called Ābhāsvara because they illuminate all other abodes.
The bliss belonging to the mental level is called "pure" (śubha);
since that bliss is limited (parītta) when compared to other levels, they are the Parīttaśubhas.
Their purity is immeasurable, thus they are the "Immeasurable-Purity" (Apramāṇaśubha) gods; their purity is all-pervading, thus they are the "All-Pervading-Purity" (Śubhakṛtsna) gods—
the intention being that there is no happiness superior to theirs elsewhere.
They are called Anabhrakas because they have no connection with the earth, like clouds;
for according to the statement, "Together with the sentient beings, their celestial palaces arise and perish," there is no other level of earth above them, thus they are Anabhrakas.
Others say they are Anabhrakas because, like a cloud, there is no connection with the earth above them.

Because they arise from immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*), their production is from merits; thus they are the "Merit-Born" (*puṇyaprasava*). Because a vast fruit, which is the most excellent among those belonging to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and connected to a specific station, arises for them, they are the "Vast-Fruit" (*bṛhatphala*). Because their dwelling is pure due to being unmixed with ordinary persons, they are the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*).

They are called the Abṛhas because they are not surpassed by other Śuddhāvāsa realms and thus are not "increased" (abṛṃhita); or alternatively, they are called Abṛhas because they do not abandon their own station for a short time.
They are called the Atapas because, due to the attainment of distinguished meditative concentration, the afflictions do not torment them there.
Because their intentions are virtuous, they do not cause others to suffer; thus they are the "Heatless" (Atapa).
Because their vision is completely pure, they see clearly; thus they are the "Beautiful-to-see" (Sudṛśa).
Because their vision is excellent, they are the "Good-to-beheld" (Sudarśana).

Because there is no other realm superior to them, they are not "inferior" (*kan-iṣṭha*), and thus they are called *Akaniṣṭha*. Since these inhabitants are designated as the most eminent (*jyeṣṭha*), how can it be said that "these are seventeen realms"? [The answer follows:]...
Since the location is indicated by the word "sthānin" (the occupant), there is no fault;
thus, according to the system of the outsiders, there are seventeen locations, whereas the Kashmiris maintain that the realm of form consists of sixteen.
The Kashmiris maintain that the realm of form (rūpadhātu) consists of sixteen locations, like a terrace or like a stepped embankment.
Others say it is a forest fort, but not a frontier territory— that is,
not one connected with a foreign realm.

For it is said that past, future, non-informative (avijñapti), and formless (arūpin) dharmas do not abide in a location; therefore, even past and future form-possessing (rūpin) dharmas do not abide in a location,
and non-informative matter, though present, does not abide in a location.
Likewise, formless phenomena such as feeling, even when present, do not occupy a location;
how much more so those that are past or future?
Thus, by way of their arising, they are of four kinds.
Thus, rebirth (*upapatti*) is the emergence of the aggregates (*skandha*) in another life, brought about by karma;
by that [rebirth], the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is fourfold, consisting of four types.
That is to say, "the sphere of infinite space," and so forth.

Because at the time of the preparatory practice for meditative attainment one takes as the mental aspect that "space is infinite," it is called the "sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantya-āyatana*); and because that very [space] is its objective basis (*āyatana*), it is so designated.

Likewise, because one takes as the mental aspect that "consciousness is infinite" or "there is nothing whatsoever," it is called the "sphere of infinite consciousness" (*vijñānānantya-āyatana*) and the "sphere of nothingness" (*ākiñcanya-āyatana*).

"Perception is a boil; perception is a thorn; the state of non-perception is delusion"—because of the arising of such dullness of perception, it is called the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," but there is no spatial hierarchy among these [realms] because they do not occupy a location, unlike those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpin*), and so forth.

What is the basis for this doubt? Since there is no self (nairātmya), one might suppose that the activity of the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) in the desire and form realms depends upon matter;
however, in the formless realms, matter does not exist.
In this regard, in order to dispel the doubt that there should be no occurrence of mind and mental factors, it is said:
"The continuum of mind here is dependent upon the group-homogeneity and the life-faculty."
By the word "and" (ca), the non-possession (*asamanvāgama*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) are included,
because they are weak in the continuum of a certain [person].

The mental continuum of material beings is weak because the perception of form has not yet been transcended; therefore, it does not function without form, but functions by depending upon form. How, then, could there be strength in that [continuum]?
For what reason does that [concentration] belonging to the formless realm possess strength? To this he says:
"Because it is born from a distinguished meditative attainment," and so forth.
"Having transcended the perception of form" means being free from the perception of form;
therefore, the mental continuum of the formless realm (*ārūpya*) arising therefrom also proceeds independently of form.
The intention is that, precisely because it is powerful and produced by a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), it will proceed without depending on anything else,
just as in the case of those possessing form (*rūpin*), and so forth.

Just as for material phenomena, the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) depend upon material form, so too for non-material phenomena, upon what do they depend? This is the meaning of the sentence; thus, these two are mutually dependent.
The homogeneous group (nikāyasabhāga) proceeds depending upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), and the life-faculty [proceeds] depending upon the homogeneous group;
for what reason, then, are these two not mutually [dependent]?

The intention is: "What is the basis for form? In that context, "now" refers to the formless realm; by what means do those two—the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)—possess strength there?
Since this is the same in the continuum of consciousness,
that continuum of consciousness also arises from a specific meditative attainment; thus, it will not proceed by depending on both,
but will proceed without any support at all.
Or rather, it is the same regarding the mind and mental factors; this is what is under discussion.
But what is the same? It is their mutual dependence, just as the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) proceeds depending upon the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Likewise, mental factors arise depending on the mind, and the mind arises depending on mental factors; therefore,
the postulation of a basis other than these two is purposeless.
"Of whichever mental continuum," and so forth.
The "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*) is the cause that projects the mental continuum; it is characterized by karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).
One from whom craving has departed is "one free from craving" (*vītatṛṣṇa*).
Is he not free from craving? He is not free from craving for form.
The meaning is that the activity [of the mind] proceeds by depending on form which arises together with that mental continuum;
this is because the projecting cause is turned away from form (*tadvimukhatvāt*).
That is to say, it is because the projecting cause is turned away from form.
"Like a *vajravālaka*" means a *vālaka*— whether a ring (*aṅgulīyaka*) or a bracelet (*kaṭaka*)— joined with a diamond (*vajra*),
as well as a drink of black pepper (*marica*).
Just as a drink mixed with black pepper is called "black-pepper drink" (*maricapānaka*) through the elision of the middle term, so it is in this case.
The realm associated with desire is the "desire realm" (*kāmadhātu*), and so forth; or,
it is that which is "subject to transformation," meaning that which is subject to affliction.
And because it is associated with form, it can be obstructed;
its state is "formless" (ārūpya) when this is a compound with "realm" (dhātu) as the final member.

Then it is appropriate to call it the "formless realm" (ārūpyadhātu); however, when the term "formless" (ārūpya) is used in its supreme sense— as in the expression "having transcended forms, they are formless"— then [it refers to that].
In that case, one should understand "formless" (*ārūpya*) as "those which are formless" (*ārūpyāḥ*), taking the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in its own sense;
or alternatively, one may view it as "those suitable for the formless" (*ārūpye sādhavaḥ*).
Or else, one establishes it through a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) as "the realm of desires" (*kāmānāṃ dhātuḥ*), even without the elision of the word *pratisaṃyukta*.
And what is this realm of desires?
He says: "That which holds desires.
In this way, the realms of form and formlessness are to be understood.
The realm of forms is the "form-realm" (*rūpadhātu*),
meaning that which holds forms;
the realm of the formless is the "formless-realm" (*ārūpyadhātu*), meaning that which holds the formless.
"Attachment associated with edible food and sexual intercourse": that which is made into mouthfuls is "edible" (*kavaḍīkāra*);
that itself is the food.
Edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*);
sexual existence (*maithuna*) is the state of copulation,
such as embracing in pairs and so forth.

Or, it is called "sensual desire" (*kāma*) because it is a passion associated with physical food and sexual intercourse, produced through a connection associated with physical food and sexual intercourse;
for it is by means of this that one desires (*kāmyate*). Thus, it is "sensual desire."
"How is this understood?"— this meaning is shown by the verse spoken by the Elder Śāriputra,
beginning with "Those which are not desires are yours," and so forth;
[this was] the verse stated by the Ājīvaka in another passage.
The Elder accepted that for a monk who entertains thoughts of sensual desire, there is the state of being a consumer of sensual pleasures.
For the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is threefold—
by way of body, speech, and mind—
and even if one who has not abandoned passion enjoys sensual pleasures through the mind, he does not cease to be a monk.
However, his conduct alone remains impure;
for he who, having transgressed the boundary of the training rules of the Tathāgata through body or speech, indulges in sensual desires, becomes a consumer of desires and is no longer a monk.
Therefore, he states another fault:
"If those desires," and so forth.
If, for you,
the objects such as form and so forth are manifold;
The position that "desires exist" implies that you have accepted that the Teacher is not free from passion.
Even your teacher will become one who indulges in sensual pleasures.
Even while seeing delightful forms and experiencing those sense objects with the body as well, one would be [perpetually] attached;
yet this is not accepted.
Therefore,
it is established that desire for a person is passion born of conceptualization.
"Kecanā" means "some";
he says "no."
For it prohibits [the occurrence] because the phenomena (dharmas) belonging to one realm manifest in another realm, and those not included within any realm [also manifest];
for in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the phenomena belonging to all three realms as well as the untainted (anāsrava) phenomena manifest.

In this way, in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), a mind of emanation belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) operates there; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), minds belonging to the formless realm and the untainted (*anāsrava*) operate; therefore, it does not obstruct them.
What then?
Those [factors] in which the attachments of the desire, form, and formless realms lie latent—
those in which attachment to the desire realm lies latent, whether by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*), as the case may be.
Those which are associated with the desire realm are those in which the latent tendencies of attachment to form and the formless are present;
these are, respectively, associated with the form and formless realms.
"This is now that which belongs to the horse-tetherer"—
the horse and the horse-tetherer together constitute "horse-tetherer";
like a horse-tetherer is "horse-tetherer-ish" (*aśvabandhīya*).
Alternatively, regarding this term *aśvabandhīya*, meaning "belonging to the horse-tetherer," if someone asks, "To whom does this horse-tetherer belong? another person replies to him:
He to whom this horse belongs asks again, "To whom does this horse belong?"
The other, however, says,
"He to whom this horse-tether belongs," yet neither of these two things is known.
Just as in the case of "horse-tether" and "horse," where these two are not defined by one another because both are unestablished,
so too here the elements are not established by the passions.
And as for the claim that "passions [arise] from the realms," neither of these two points is established;
for the locations within the desire realm have already been specified as being the hells,
hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and the six classes of celestial beings.

The desire realm consists of twenty locations, distinguished by the various hells and continents; as has been explained regarding the desire realm, it is the attachment of one who is not free from passion toward those locations.
For those states have already been defined as "passion for sensual desire," and likewise as "passion for form" and "passion for the formless."
Above the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are seventeen realms, which constitute the form realm (rūpadhātu).
The attachment of one who is not free from passion toward those [realms] is "attachment to form" (rūparāga);
the same explanation applies to the arising [of beings] in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is without location; it is fourfold by way of rebirth.
It is the attachment of one who is not free from passion toward those [realms].
"That is attachment to the formless" means "according to the case," which refers to the specification of the respective locations.
"Attachment to the meditations and the formless realms" refers to attachment toward the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the rebirths (*upapatti*) of the form realm;
likewise for attachment to the formless realm.
Regarding the question of how there can be desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) in a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*):

how could there be desire for sense-pleasures in a mind of emanation belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), which is the fruit of meditative absorption (*dhyānaphala*), for those who are already free from desire for sense-pleasures (*vītarāga*), given that its nature is to belong to the realm of desire? For it is only when one is not yet free from desire that such a mind arises.
At that time, the mind of emanation does not manifest;
when the mind of emanation manifests,
then no passion arises in him.
The meaning is: how is its status as belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) established in the absence of sensual passion (*kāmarāga*)?
