Having heard [of it] and having abandoned it, because of relishing that [attainment], passion for it arises in him from another [being] when it is a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Or, having abandoned one's own emanation-mind,

because of the non-perception of that [object], passion arises with that as its object when one who meditates in this way hears that "one creates a desire-sphere emanation by means of a desire-sphere emanation-mind."
And by recollecting one's own [past], passion arises there through the power of emanation;

thus, having seen a captivating emanation, passion arises either toward the mind that emanates it or toward the mind of the emanator, thinking, "Such is the emanating mind of this person whose emanation is like this."
Or, as for the phrase "due to the manifestation of odors and tastes," that mind which belongs to the desire realm and produces the manifestations of the desire realm is [the one in question].
Because it is the cause of dharmas belonging to the desire realm,
like the mind that is the cause of a jar;
however, that which does not belong to the desire realm [is different].
That is not the cause of dharmas belonging to the desire realm;
for example, a mind belonging to the form realm.
For this very reason, he said:
Because those two are not emanated by a mind belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
Why, then, are those two—odor and taste—not emanated by a mind belonging to the realm of form?
Because those two, odor and taste, have the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
And because one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) is free from passion (vītarāga),
it is called "the support for the plow-pole" (īśādhāra), meaning the support for rain of the measure of a plow-pole (īṣā).
By stating "there is no interval or gap," he demonstrates continuity,
but it was not specified whether this refers to above or below.
Thus, it is shown that the world-systems are situated only horizontally;
and by the phrase "a portion of the fifth," the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm within the divine destiny are indicated.
The remaining [beings] belong to the realms of form and formlessness;
for otherwise, there would be a confusion of destinies, which constitutes a mixing of destinies.
If wholesome and afflicted states were also [to constitute] destinies, there would be a confusion of destinies;
for instance, a human being might perform karma leading to rebirth in hell up to karma leading to rebirth as a god. Consequently, the human destiny would also be the hell destiny.
Even their destiny as gods is included within those [same] karmas because it is comprised within that destiny;

furthermore, one born in the desire realm is possessed of the afflictions belonging to the higher stages and is also possessed of the defiled states pertaining to all destinies belonging to the desire realm.

That very same human being becomes a hell-being, and so forth; thus, they are designated as "sentient beings" because, according to their karma, they go to those states by way of their personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Therefore it has been said:
"They will go according to their karma, reaping the fruits of merit and demerit."

In order to demonstrate that [the intermediate state] is neither of the nature of a vessel nor of the nature of an intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), they cite the evidence stated in the *Prajñapti* treatises, and so forth.
"Having causes and having a going":
the cause is *karmabhava* (existence as karma),
and the "going" is *antarābhava* (intermediate existence).

It is called "going" (*gati*) because one goes by means of it; however, since that which is gone to is itself "going," the existence as karma (*karmabhava*), being the cause of that, is excluded from those [five destinies].
Because they exclude from those destinies the existence resulting from wholesome and unwholesome karma,
those who dwell in Kaśmīra— the Kāśmīrakas— recite the Sūtra.
The intention is that only they, and no others, recite that *muktaka* sūtra;
"of the hell-beings" (*nārakāṇām*) is the full expression, meaning those who are suited to the hells are "hell-beings."

"Of these," and so forth, refers to the crookednesses of body, speech, and mind— actions arising from deceit (*śāṭhya*)— and the defects and impurities (*doṣakaṣāya*) arising from hatred (*dveṣa*) and attachment (*rāga*);
for this reason as well, the destinies (*gati*) are indeed only unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Since it has been stated that "when the maturation has ceased, one comes to be reckoned as a hell-being," the treatise passages stating that "all latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere within the realms of existence" must be addressed;
the meaning is that a refutation must be stated.
Because it would lead to a contradiction;
for if the five types of dharmas were of the nature of a destiny (*gati*), then all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) would become latent.
If, however, the destinies were exclusively non-obscured-indeterminate (anivṛtāvyākṛta),
then it should have been stated that they are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya) and are universal (sarvatraga).

For conditioned phenomena that are unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) are exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); and within them, all latent tendencies of attachment (*sarva-rāga-anuśaya*) and other latent tendencies adhere, either by way of being the object (*ālambana*) or by way of application (*prayoga*),
but not others.
By this it is known that the destinies (*gati*) are not exclusively non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*);
for the linking-minds (*saṃdhicitta*) of the destinies are of five types, and these linking-minds constitute the entry into the destinies.
Since these [defilements] are of five types—
ranging from those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering to those to be abandoned by cultivation—
it is logical that all latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere therein.
"Like the inclusion of the vicinity of a village" means like the inclusion of the surroundings of a village;
[this refers to] "in the five turbidities."
There are five degenerations: the degeneration of lifespan, the degeneration of afflictions, the degeneration of views, the degeneration of the eon, and the degeneration of sentient beings;
among these—

The defilement of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*) and the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*) are mentioned separately; the meaning is that the defilement of views is stated apart from the defilement of afflictions.
These two are spoken of separately because they pertain respectively to the categories of householders and renunciants.
The phrase "for the purpose of making known the cause of the destinies" means that since karma is the cause of the destinies,
this same [causal] consequence would apply even to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
In this way, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would also be a destiny (*gati*), and there would be a separate mention of it for the purpose of making known the going to that destiny; thus,
they go.
The inclusion [of the intermediate state] as a means of accomplishing karma is not appropriate in this way; therefore, it is not a destination,
nor are the formless realms, according to the detailed explanation.
The formless realms (ārūpya) cannot be considered "destinies" (gati), because birth occurs precisely at the place of death;
for those going to the formless realms die wherever they may be— in a monastery, at the foot of a tree, or even up to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
If they arise in that very place,
then, like the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there would be no [distinct] realm of rebirth (*gati*); "if that were so," [it is said].

The Vaibhāṣikas say that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not itself a destiny (*gati*), because they abandon the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and adopt another view, establishing the name "intermediate existence" based on its literal meaning: it exists in the interval, in between two destinies. Thus, the intermediate state is not a destiny.
Regarding the passage beginning with "What then," and so forth:
the intention behind the statement that "when the ripening has occurred" is that because of the use of the term "ripening" (*vipāka*), the destiny (*gati*) has the nature of ripening;
thus the other [opponent] says.
When the maturation has ceased, one is established as a hell-being; however, it was not said that the maturation itself [is the hell-being],
nor was it said that the destiny is of the very nature of maturation.

What then? The nature of the realms of existence (gati) consists of both that which is fruition (vipāka) and that which is not fruition; therefore, the intention is that the realms of existence can also be wholesome or afflicted.
The Vaibhāṣika, however,
says: "As for what was stated there," and so forth,
[it means] "other than those dharmas."
The intended meaning is "from those born of maturation" (*vipākaja*);
however, this does not imply a negation of other aggregates (*skandha*). This is the subject under discussion, as expressed in the detailed passage beginning with "And those... (*tāś ca*).
Even in the case of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), there is a twofold nature;
by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that they possess both the nature of accumulation (*aupacayika*) and the nature of maturation (*vipāka*).
As it has been said:
"Vipāka is life; it is twofold, and twelve [types] exist."

However, Master Saṃghabhadra maintains that the outflowing [phenomena] are not included because they possess the nature of maturation alone; he thus prefers the former position regarding the six [mental factors] belonging to the desire realm and those of the first dhyāna.

According to the system of the outsiders (Bahirdeśakas), which are they? They are the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, and the Mahābrahmans, excluding those who were first produced [at the beginning of the aeon].
According to the system of the Kaśmīris, however, they are the Brahmakāyikas and the Brahmapurohitas, excluding those who were first produced.

For, according to their system, the Mahābrahmās are included within the Brahmapurohitas themselves and do not constitute a separate station, because they possess various colors, marks, and shapes; here,
"color" refers to blueness and so forth.
The *liṅga* consists of clothing, ornaments, and so forth;
its configuration (*saṃsthāna*) refers to length and the like; and its height (*āroha*) refers to its elevation.
Circumference is the horizontal measurement;
"form-body" (ākṛtivigraha) means a body characterized by form.
When specified in this way, the "body" of feeling and the other [aggregates] is excluded.
The analysis of the compound is "it is not characterized by form"; furthermore, it refers to the body,
speech, or the utterance of speech.
"How now? and so forth:
by returning to the first dhyāna, they have abandoned that [state] belonging to the second [dhyāna], namely, that which belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.
How did they recollect their former abodes?

It was not by means of a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, because that is not its object; nor by means of a mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, because that has not yet been attained.
If it is argued that [it] is obtained again, he says in response:
"And when it has been obtained," and so forth.
If it is argued that the view of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*), which has Mahābrahmā as its object, is logically restricted to the level of the first dhyāna,
and that because it is abandoned through the attainment of the second dhyāna, it does not manifest when belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
Not [from a lower realm], because it is impossible for it to have a lower object;
for no affliction whatsoever is admitted to have a lower level as its object.
"Being in the intermediate state, they saw" means that while in the intermediate state, upon seeing that Mahābrahmā, they said:
"We have seen this being."
This position also does not hold;

for even in that intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is impossible to remain for a long duration because there is no obstacle to rebirth and because they do not depend upon semen and blood. How, then, could they have this thought: "We have seen this being who is long-lived and remains for a long duration"?
The meaning is that the realization of his remaining for a long duration would not occur;
therefore, the detailed explanation is that they [saw him] while remaining right there—
namely, while staying on the level of the first dhyāna— they saw that Mahābrahmā, who had arisen previously, remaining for a long time.
And having seen [them], subsequently at a later time, the thought "we have seen them" arose for them— this is the completion of the sentence.
But this being the case, the following objection remains unrefuted:
And as this being had thus made a mental vow,
"May we also be reborn [there]," they, by means of a mind acquired at birth belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, recollected that very mental vow of Mahābrahmā.
Because they belong to the same level,
this is not a fault;
or rather, [it is so] because of hearing [the teaching] from him.
But would this same consequence not also apply to the Śubhakṛtsna deities?
How could they be "unified in body but diverse in perception"?
As it has been said:

"For they, being weary of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) on the fundamental stage (*maulyāṃ bhūmau*), bring forth the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*)," and so on, should be explained in detail; furthermore, that "they possess a single body and a single perception" will be stated later.
"By that pleasure" means by that which belongs to the level of the third dhyāna, because it causes the mind to leap up with joy.
Because it produces exhilaration,
because it is characterized by the perception of arrival and departure,
and because for those recently reborn, it is characterized by the perception of arrival.
Because those who have been reborn for a long time have the perception of departure,
or because those who have recently been reborn have the perception of arrival, or because those who have been reborn for a long time have the perception of both arrival and departure,
or because they have the perception of being afraid or not afraid.
Respectively, because they have been reborn for a short or long time, they possess diverse perceptions (*nānātvasaṃjñin*),

and not because they possess perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain, as stated by the Vaibhāṣikas regarding the first dhyāna— that is, by means of afflicted perception (*kliṣṭasaṃjñā*).
Because one is attached to what is not a cause as being a cause due to the [view] associated with the adherence to rules and rituals,
it is "with wholesome perception" in the second [dhyāna],
because it is comprised of both the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stage (*maula*).
"In the third [dhyāna], by means of the perception born of maturation" means that because it is associated with pleasure born of maturation,
the three formless attainments are as stated in the Sūtra.
There are formless beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, thinking "space is infinite," dwell having attained the sphere of infinite space;

just as the gods of the sphere of infinite space. Having transcended the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," they dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This is the sixth station of consciousness:

there are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," attain and dwell in the sphere of nothingness; namely, the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness.
"This is the seventh station of consciousness" refers to the five aggregates and four aggregates as appropriate;
that is, the four aggregates associated with the three [formless attainments] beginning with the sphere of infinite space.
The five aggregates associated with other [realms] are the remainder, because they are its disintegration;
for "disintegration" (*paribheda*) means that by which something is broken apart.
The destruction of that consciousness is "its destruction" (*tat-paribheda*);
because that [destruction] exists in this [state], it is "possessing its destruction" (*tat-paribhedavat*).
The remainder refers to the miserable destinies (*durgati*) and so forth.
And since both [qualities] are absent in the states of woe, those staying here have no desire to go there,
nor do those staying there have any desire to depart.
Because its activity is not sharp— meaning that because the activity of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) here is sluggish—
it is logical to say that consciousness (*vijñāna*), being weak, does not persist.
It is stated in the Sūtra that there are nine abodes of beings, including those at the peak of existence and the non-percipient beings; thus,
there are nine abodes of beings.
Which nine are the beings possessing form who have diversity of body and diversity of perception? Namely, human beings and certain gods.
This is the first abode of beings;
the second, third, and fourth should also be described in the same manner as the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
But this is the distinction:
there are material beings who are without perception and without discernment,
namely, the non-percipient gods (asaṃjñisattva-devāḥ).
This is the fifth abode of beings.
Regarding the abodes of formless beings, three should be described in the same manner as the stations of consciousness;

however, the fourth formless [abode] is: there are formless beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

For example, it is said that "the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception constitute the ninth abode of beings. Are those other than the non-percipient beings who have reached the fourth dhyāna also abodes of beings, or not?
"No," they say; "why was it said thus by the Teacher? Who, then, are these others?"

"Unfortunate states" (apāya) is merely a partial designation; it should also be stated that they include those belonging to the fourth dhyāna who are not comprised among the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva).
In this case as well, the same reason must be stated that was explained regarding the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*):
for those dwelling here there is no longing to go to the states of woe (*apāya*),
and for those dwelling there there is no desire for material things (*vastu*).

The miserable realms (apāya) are not abodes of sentient beings; nor are the Great Fruit (bṛhatphala) heavens, which do not include the non-percipient beings (asaṃjñisattva). Although those dwelling here may have a desire to go there, ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) dwelling there seek to enter the state of non-perception (āsañjnika).

But for the noble ones, even among the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, and the Śuddhāvāsas, there is a desire to enter the formless realms and a wish for final nirvana; this is also true for those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens themselves.
Thus, they have no intention of remaining there.
Therefore, those [places] are not abodes of sentient beings; thus says the Master Saṃghabhadra.
Others, however, explain:
"Who, then, are these others?"
By the specific mention of "the states of woe" (apāya), it is understood that the Master [Vasubandhu] accepts the Anabhraka and other such abodes of beings as being among them; therefore,
the logical justification for this must be sought by comparing them to places of imprisonment.
Just as places of confinement are not abodes of sentient beings because one dwells there against one's will, so it is with the states of woe; thus,
the station of consciousness for those who have reached the realm of form is explained.
"Consciousness abides in this" means it is a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*);
"it approaches" (*upagā*) means it moves in the vicinity of consciousness— this is the meaning.
"That which is form and that which approaches it is 'approaching form' (rūpopagā)";
and so on, up to "those which are formations and that which approaches them is 'approaching formations' (saṃskāropagā)," thus explains Bhagavadviśeṣa.
In that context, the station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) is the non-interruption of the continuity of existence;
"matter" (*rūpa*) is the approach (*upaga*) of this station of consciousness, and thus it is called "approaching matter" (*rūpopagā*).

"Approaching" (*upaga*) means that it is approached as being "one's own"; thus, up to the point where the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are the approach of this station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), it is therefore called "approached by formative forces" (*saṃskāropagā*).
Alternatively, craving is the "abiding" because by means of it consciousness abides through the non-interruption of the continuity of renewed existence.
Thus, having established this, the stationing of consciousness is the "station of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*).
That [consciousness] approaches form (*rūpa*) because it flows toward it; thus it is "approaching form.
This continues in the same way up to "approaching formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, [the author] refutes [this view], stating that according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, the sense of "agent" (kāraka) cannot be applied;
here we say:
in both of these explanations, a station of consciousness (vijñānasthiti) distinct from form and so forth is stated.
For they are indeed the four contaminated aggregates.
The inclusion [of all things] within the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) is thus entirely refuted; therefore, this is another fault,
and for that reason, the previous explanation alone is correct.

We describe this as the Vaibhāṣika explanation; however, they did not explain it in this way—that "consciousness abiding" (vijñānasthiti) is so called because consciousness approaches form (rūpa), and so forth.
Others, moreover, explain it differently.
"The station of consciousness that approaches form" means having form as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
as it is stated elsewhere.

The phrase "that which has reached the state of hardness" (khakkhaṭakharagata) refers to the meaning of intrinsic nature (svabhāva); the intention is that the root *gam* here signifies "to go," in the sense of excluding that which remains stationary.
The meaning is that the one who stands in the world— such as Devadatta and others— is distinct from the standing itself— the location, such as a house and so forth; or rather,
it means that consciousness causes [the body] to move and proceed.
According to the analogy of the boatman and the boat,
just as a boatman steers a boat, so it is in this case.
The meaning is not that consciousness, having mounted upon consciousness itself, causes it to proceed;
for within a single continuum, two consciousnesses do not coexist simultaneously, even though the consciousness of another continuum may occur at the same time.
But since it does not exist in proximity to anything other than that, it does not constitute its station; [likewise] delight (*nandī*) and mental well-being (*saumanasya*),
as well as the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), which have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature— how is that so?

Since it is accepted that the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature, how is it that consciousness itself is not accepted as a station of consciousness?
To this, [the author] says: "In that case," and so forth;

that is, when the aggregates such as form and the rest—comprised within the bases of rebirth (*upapattyāyatana*) and comprised within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of humans and so on—are considered without distinction, as a single unified mass.
When consciousness proceeds accompanied by delight and attachment, that consciousness is intended as a "station of consciousness" in the teaching on the seven stations of consciousness;
however, individually, each [station] corresponds to a single aggregate (*skandha*), just as form and the other aggregates serve to defile consciousness.
Because it has approached [the state of being] by way of being the basis, the associated factor, and the co-existent factor,
how could consciousness alone be separate in this way?
What is it?
It is understood that this leads to affliction;
why?
Because it is impossible for [the two] to function as a basis simultaneously.
Therefore, in the teaching on the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), consciousness alone is not declared to be a station;
for, depending on the disciples to be trained (*vineyajana*), the station of consciousness is described in one way in one sutra and in another way in another.
Therefore he says:
"Moreover, by way of being a field," and so forth.

By way of being the field for consciousness, the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)—which have the nature of form, feeling, perception, and mental formations (*saṃskāra*)—have been taught.

Consciousness, together with its appropriation, accompanied by craving through the thirst belonging to its own level, is taught as being entirely present within the continuum in the form of a seed— that is, in the form of something to be sown; thus,
the Blessed One did not establish a seed as the field for another seed.
For in the world, a seed is not established as being the nature of a field;
and as for those factors, and so forth—
those factors such as form and the rest which coexist with consciousness.
These very [mental factors] become more effective as the field-nature,
for in the world a field is seen to coexist with the seed;
however, consciousness does not coexist with consciousness, because they do not exist simultaneously.
In that case, do past and future forms and so forth not become stations of consciousness?
Even those [past and future factors], according to their respective natures, serve as stations for past and future consciousnesses.
Therefore, it should be understood that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) forms and so forth within their own level constitute stations of consciousness.
"The first alternative," and so forth;
"that which is consciousness among the seven" refers to the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) because they have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature.
In that case, consciousness is not included, because consciousness is not apprehended therein among the four [elements].
Regarding the statement "the aggregates excluding consciousness," even in the miserable destinies (*apāya*) and so forth, consciousness is not included among the four [aggregates],
nor among the seven; this is because consciousness is not apprehended as a distinct category within the miserable destinies and so forth.
Regarding the statement "in seven there are four aggregates":
those four aggregates mentioned in the context of the seven stations of consciousness, excluding consciousness itself,
are included within all four stations of consciousness as well.
The third alternative is that which is included in both;
the fourth is "setting aside these modes," namely,
the consciousness in the states of woe, in the fourth dhyāna, and at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), as well as the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
And as for this [existence] which is divided by the distinctions of the realms of rebirth (*gati*) and so forth—

the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the receptacle world (*bhājana*), the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the stages of existence (*bhūmi*), and so on— there is the *jarāyu*, that by which the embryo remains enveloped within the mother's womb.
Therefore, those born from a womb are called *jarāyu-ja*.

As for those born from the moisture of the elements (*bhūta-saṃsveda-ja*), they are so called because they are born from the moisture of the elements— earth and so forth— which is characterized by fluidity.
They are "unimpaired" because their visual faculty and other senses are not deficient;

they are "possessed of unimpaired faculties" because of the absence of being one-eyed, cross-eyed, or otherwise defective; and they are "endowed with all limbs" because they possess hands, feet, and so forth.
And they are born all at once, endowed with all their minor limbs such as the fingers and so forth,
not through a sequence beginning with the *kalala* and so on, unlike those born from eggs and the like.

They are called "spontaneously born" (*upapāduka*) because they are produced all at once without depending on semen, blood, or other such materials, owing to their excellence in action regarding rebirth and the process of arising.
"Born from Krauñcī," and so forth;
it is said that two merchants whose ship was wrecked reached the Krauñcī mountain on the seashore,
and from her were born the two elders Śaila and Upaśaila.
Regarding the king of Pañcāla,
five hundred eggs were born to his chief queen;
the king placed them in a chest and cast them into the Ganges.
While the Licchavi king, together with his harem, was bathing, he saw that chest being carried along; it was opened,
and within it five hundred boys were seen and taken up— such as Māndhātṛ and others, who are moisture-born (saṃsvedaja).
It is said that a tumor grew on the head of King Upoṣadha;
as it increased, matured, and burst open, a boy was born.
Thus, this Māndhātṛ is born from moisture;
indeed, two swellings arose above the knees of King Māndhātṛ, and as they grew, as previously described, two boys were born,
these two being Cāru and Upacāru.
It is said that a boil arose on the chest of King Brahmadatta;
as it grew, as previously described, until finally a girl was born—
she is this very one.
It is heard that Āmrapālī, known as Kapotamālinī, was also born from the trunk of a plantain tree,
as was the case with those of the first eon.
From the statement that "in former times beings were like those with form," *suparṇī* refers to *garuḍa*.
The detailed passage beginning with "O Long-lived One" is stated for the purpose of establishing that pretas are born from a womb;
how is it understood that this is for the purpose of establishing their status as womb-born?
From the statement, "having undergone death at night," it is understood that this is indeed for the purpose of establishing the fact of being spontaneously born (*upapāduka*).
"Five at night and five likewise by day— nevertheless, there is no satisfaction for me," so he said.
For satisfaction would come from begging for those born from a womb;
it is for the sake of accomplishing what is born from a womb,
not for the sake of accomplishing what is spontaneously born.
It is not contradictory for five [beings] to be born at once during the night and another five during the day;
for that duration of time, their individual existences (*ātmabhāva*) are fully developed.
Furthermore, it is not contradictory for five to be born during the night and another five during the day, even if occurring sequentially.
"That species of being is such, and the ripening of karmas is inconceivable"; yet,

because of the fault of having an excessively increased desire to kill, there is no satisfaction even for one who has attained mastery over rebirth— by this [statement], he demonstrates the impossibility of the force of karma acting upon birth from a womb (*jarāyu-ja*).
"Just as other heterodox teachers slander" means that other heterodox teachers, such as Maskari and others—
as stated in the *Nirgrantha-śāstra*— "Venerable sir, who displays supernatural power?"
Regarding the statement "Gautama is a magician," it is said elsewhere with reference to the Blessed One himself:
"At the end of a hundred eons, such a magician appears in the world, and as a magician he devours the world."
The meaning is "it subsists";
"because of the absence of external seeds" means because of the absence of external [factors] such as the mire of semen and blood.
"Based on resolve" (ādhiṣṭhānikī) means that which one resolves upon, thinking "let this be thus," is the resolve (adhiṣṭhāna);
the supernormal power (ṛddhi) that has that as its purpose, or that which exists therein, is the power based on resolve.
For those Buddhists who accept that [position], this refutation which was stated is not tenable; which one is it?
From the question, "For the purpose of establishing the bodily relics," another question arises; thus, the question "Why is it that the Bodhisattva in his final existence... is stated in detail.
And it was stated therein,
"for the purpose of establishing the bodily elements," and so forth;
from that question, this other question arises.
Regarding the passage beginning "If [it refers] to those born by transformation," and so forth: the "destruction of the body" (kāyanidhana) means the dissolution of the body.
Why are there two qualifiers—namely, "the transformation-born garuḍa" (upapādukaḥ suparṇī) and "the transformation-born nāga" (upapādukaṃ nāgam)?
Are there also non-embryonically born (*anupāduka*) *suparṇins* and *nāgas*?
They say that there are;
for *garuḍas* and *nāgas* are of four kinds, according to the divisions of being born from eggs and so forth.
Among them, those of miraculous birth are the highest;
those born from moisture are next highest;
those born from a womb are middling; and those born from eggs are the lowest.
Therein, the spontaneously born *suparṇī* seizes all beings beginning with the spontaneously born for the purpose of eating;
the moisture-born seizes three types beginning with the moisture-born;
and the womb-born seizes two types, namely the womb-born and the egg-born.
They describe the egg-born as being indeed egg-born,
as long as it is not dead; when it dies...
This demonstrates that at that time the flesh and so forth do not disappear;
however, it does not mean that one is satiated by this dead person,
nor that one is satiated by means of this dead person— this is the meaning.
Regarding the rule "tṛpipūrau vibhāṣā," a genitive in the sense of optionality (*vibhāṣā-ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended;
thus, it should be understood that one does not become satiated by eating the flesh of a deceased being, because it vanishes like the flesh of a lump of meat eaten within space.
For that [realm] consists of two destinies: the hellish destiny and the celestial destiny.
And "a portion of the three" refers to the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, and humans,
because they constitute the intermediate states between [the higher] destinies.

Is it not the case that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is intended to be exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), because it exists between two destinies (*gati*), whereas the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is invariably afflicted (*kliṣṭa*)?
The state of death (*maraṇabhava*) may sometimes be wholesome or afflicted, but it is not a "destination" (*gati*).
How then can the term "destination" be metaphorically applied to those two? It is said [to be so] because they exist in the interval between destinations.
This is not a fault,

because at that time there exist the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) factors— such as the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth—
which constitute the nature of the destinies (*gati*) within both the desire and form realms, and because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also necessarily present.
Furthermore, unlike the state of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*), the state of death (*maraṇa-bhava*) is neither necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) nor necessarily wholesome (*kuśala*).
Therefore, applying the term "destiny" (*gati*) to those [two states], it was stated that they are "intermediate between destinies" (*gaty-antarālatvāt*),
because the word *gati* has the sense of "going."
The root *pad* is recited in the sense of "going";
by this, he shows that the word *upapanna* has the meaning of "having gone," and thus the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not [yet] arrived.
Rather,
"being born" (upapadyamāna) refers to manifestation and completion.
The manifestation of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) occurs through projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), while its completion occurs through fulfilling karma (*paripūraka*);
because both types of karma function throughout the entire birth,
one [karma] projects a single birth, while many [karmas] fulfill it.
According to this statement,
or alternatively, it is the place where there occurs the manifestation— that is, the appearance— of the ripening of name-and-form projected by karma,
as well as its completion through the fulfillment of the six sense bases.
That location is to be understood as being analogous to the continuum of rice-grains;
such is the detailed explanation.

*Saṃbandhana* means continuity (*tāna*); *saṃtāna* is a series, such as a series of rice (*vrīhisantāna*). Because of this similarity, there is no arising of an existence that is disconnected—that which has departed [from its cause].

And that in which it arises is preceded by the continuum existing in the intermediate state; it has the nature of the form of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*), because its intrinsic nature consists of the continuum of the form of its own appropriated [aggregates].
For it is observed that phenomena existing within a continuum manifest in different locations through uninterrupted arising in those locations, like the successive forms in a stream of rice;
just as, for example, occurs in the case of a stream of rice.
For the form that follows in the continuum of rice, since it departs from one location and arises in another location,
it arises preceded by the forms existing in the intervening continuum.

For this is our established doctrine, we who maintain the theory of momentariness: when rice is carried from one village to another, that rice does not cease in the former village and then arise in the other village—separated by many *yojanas*—without arising in the intervening space. Rather, it arises in the other village.
Rather,
it arises in another village through a sequence of production and cessation in contiguous points of space,
and its intrinsic nature consists of the continuum of the form of its own material cause.

Likewise, regarding the statement that "the form of existence at birth (upapattibhava-rūpa) also arises," here the teacher Guṇamati, together with his disciple the teacher Vasumitra— whose minds were conditioned by attachment to their own school— set aside the task of exposition and remained intent only on opposition;
we, however, take care to provide an explanation of the meaning of this treatise.
That refutation will not arise,
because it is devoid of substance and for fear of having too much to say;
"bhaviṣṇu" means having the nature of coming into being.
"Even though it is separated," and so forth;
by stating that "from the original object (*bimba*) [arises] a reflection (*pratibimba*) in mirrors and the like"—

meaning that in mirrors, water, and so on, a reflection in the form of a shadow of the face is seen arising as something distinct from the original face— he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) [of the opponent's argument].
Or he performs a counter-argument,
[showing] from where it departs and where it arises.
The form of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava-rūpa*) is not preceded by the form existing in the continuum of the intermediate state (*antarāla-santāna*),
because it has as its intrinsic nature the form of the continuum of its own appropriated form (*svopādāna-rūpa-santāna-rūpa-svabhāvatva*),
like the form of a reflection.
The claim that "a reflection arises as something else, a distinct entity" is unestablished;
rather, the Master’s intention is that through the power of the original object (*bimba*) alone, a deluded cognition in the form of a reflection arises there in the mirror and so forth.
By stating "there is no such thing as a reflection there," he demonstrates the fault in the example known as the non-establishment of the substratum (*dharmyasiddhi*).
Therefore, there is no inconclusiveness,
nor is this counter-argument valid,
even though [the probandum] has been established.
"Because it is not identical, it is non-demonstrable":

even though the reflection is established as a substantial entity (*dravyasattva*), because it is not identical to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the reflection is "non-demonstrable," meaning it is not a valid example.
Regarding the phrase "how, first of all, is it unestablished," the word "first of all" (*tāvat*) indicates that he is demonstrating the reasoning for its lack of establishment in due order.
"Because of the absence of both identity and duality," and so forth;
for in that very location of the mirror, the form of the mirror itself is seen by one standing at the side, but not the reflection.
And yet, the reflection is seen in that very same place by one standing in front; it is not the form of the mirror itself, nor is there a coexistence of two forms in a single location.
What is the reason?
Because their foundational elements are distinct;
for the foundational elements of those two are indeed different.
Thus, there is no room for the foundational elements of the reflected image's form in that location occupied by the foundational elements of the mirror's form.
Therefore, there is no possibility of two derived forms [existing together];
thus, because two consciousnesses do not exist simultaneously,
and because two derived forms cannot coexist in a single location.
He shows that there is nothing at all [there],
for in whichever place the form of the mirror is seen, the reflected image is seen in that very same place.
But what is the fault in [the case] otherwise? He says:
"And there is no coexistence of two forms in one [place]."
Or it should be stated as before; or rather,
because two [entities] cannot exist together in one place.
The meaning of this sūtra is as follows:
since two persons cannot simultaneously perceive a single form, the reflection of simultaneous perception is unestablished; thus, he states the completion of the sentence by asking "How so? (katham).
By persons situated in different directions— some established in the northern direction and others established in the southern direction—
at a single location in the water of a pond or a single location in the water of a lake,

the forms situated in the region facing themselves [are perceived]; specifically, those forms situated on the upper part of the southern bank are positioned facing the person established in the northern direction.
Is a reflection of both of these perceived by one another?
Those situated in the northern direction perceive a reflection beneath the southern bank,
and those situated in the southern direction likewise perceive a reflection beneath the northern bank;
thus they perceive one another.
The meaning of the sentence is that both [the riverbank and the reflection] are not perceived simultaneously;
for the reflection at the bottom of the bank is not perceived by those standing on one bank, nor even by those looking at the water from all sides.
If it is asked, "What follows from this?", he says:
However, when two persons look at a single form—whether a jar or a cloth—it is not the case that simultaneous perception does not occur; rather, the meaning is that it certainly does occur.
But here [in the case of the visual organ], simultaneous perception does not occur; therefore, it is not logical that another form is produced therein.
Alternatively, this is its meaning:
the coexistence of both shadow and sunlight in a single place is not observed in the world, whether in a pavilion or elsewhere, wherever shadow exists.
Where there is no heat, there is no sun; where there is an open space, there is no shade.
Since the reflection of the sun is perceived in a mirror situated in the shade,
how then could a reflection of the sun arise in a pond?
And when a mirror is placed in a shady pavilion situated on the bank of that pond,
another reflection of the reflection of the sun residing in the pond arises within that mirror;
and as for the reflection of the sun in the pond—
Therefore, that which arises from the sun must necessarily be admitted to have the nature of heat;
and as for the other reflection in the mirror—
Therefore, that which arises as a reflection having the nature of sunlight must necessarily be admitted to have the nature of sunlight;
this being so, there would be a coexistence of shadow and sunlight, yet in the world, no such coexistence of shadow and sunlight is observed elsewhere.
The appearance of this reflection there is illogical,
like water in a well; for example,
just as water is seen deep within a well from a distance.

Likewise, the reflection of the moon is also seen as being contained right here within it, yet the mirror does not possess a physical object corresponding to that result; and while that reflection arises there—
And that reflected image, arising only in the mirror, would not be perceived elsewhere, such as below it;
yet it is indeed perceived there.
Therefore, that [reflection] does not exist at all;
rather, it is the power of the causal complex— characterized by the mirror, the object, and so forth— by which such a perception occurs.
For the differentiation of the powers of phenomena is indeed inconceivable,
as is seen from the fact that iron approaches a magnet while wood and other substances do not.
One must state such things as: "The appearance of the production and flow of water from the moonstone upon the rising of the moon does not occur from charcoal and the like."
Because it is connected to the continuum of the mirror, the reflection is not part of the continuum of the object,
since it is connected to the mirror.
And because it exists simultaneously, like the form of a mirror,
it is like another form that is co-temporal with the reflected image.
Thus, just as the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is a continuum of the state of death (*maraṇabhava*), the reflection is not so of the original object; therefore,
the example of the reflection is devoid of the probans (*sādhanānanvita*).
However, the example of the subsequent form in the continuum of rice is itself part of the continuum of its own preceding forms;
therefore, there is no similarity between the example and the reflection, because the latter arises from two [causes].
Thus is the detailed explanation:
"arising from a pair" means arising from both the object (*bimba*) and the mirror; this is the meaning.
That which is the primary cause, such as a mirror and so forth, depending upon that the reflection arises;
for the mirror and so forth are indeed the primary cause of the reflection, because the reflection conforms to them.
For example, if a sword is placed horizontally, the reflection is also seen as horizontal and elongated;
if it is placed vertically,
the reflection is likewise seen in that same way.

And it is not the case that the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) likewise arises from two causes— namely, from the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) and from another primary cause standing in the place of a mirror, such as the external semen and blood which are the primary causes— if this is argued, we say no, because [semen and blood] are insentient (*acetana*),
and because they are absent in the case of those born by spontaneous generation (*upapāduka*).
Therefore, this example is also dissimilar;
what is shown by this is that when the qualifying attribute has been removed from the reason (*hetu*), this example becomes unequal.
How so?
Because it departs from one place and arises in another.
The form of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava-rūpa*), which exists within the continuum between those two, is preceded by the form [of the previous life];

this is because its nature consists of a continuum of its own appropriated forms that arise without [pre-existing] substantial entities (*adravyotpanna*), just like the subsequent form in a continuum of rice.
This being the case, it has been stated that it is impossible to point out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of this proof, nor can a counter-proof (*pratisādhana*) be formulated; thus,
establishing the existence of an intermediate state (*antarabhāva*) by means of scripture (*āgama*), he says:
The meaning is that [the existence of the self] is established because of its being explicitly stated by its own word;
for this sūtra is not recited by them.
Why is it not recited by those belonging to other schools? Because it is absent from their own scriptures.
Why then is that which is well-known in the scriptures of another school not accepted as authoritative?
Because of the fear that sūtras might have been interpolated due to the loss of the original recitation (mūlasaṅgīti),
[the phrase] "of the three points" refers to the three causes.
The mother is healthy, free from disease, in her fertile season, and possessing a digestive fire for flavors;
this is the first condition.
"Passionate and come together," meaning they engage in the act of sexual intercourse;
this is the second ground.
"The Gandharva has appeared" refers to the third [condition];
"the disintegration of the aggregates has appeared" refers to the state of death (*maraṇabhava*).

These, along with the five non-returners (*pañcānāgāmin*) and the seven destinations of noble persons (*saptasatpuruṣagati*), will be explained in the section of the *Abhidharmakośa* that provides the exposition of individuals (*pudgalanirdeśa*).
If [the term] "upapadya" and so forth were [to be taken as the first member of the compound],
then it would follow that those gods named Upapadyas and so on would be included among the seven destinies of the noble persons (satpuruṣagati).
These same five, when divided threefold according to the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, become seven;

therefore it is said: "Three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are taught, distinguished by differences in time, place, and intensity," namely, by the distinction of the intensity of time and the distinction of the intensity of place, as appropriate.
And the Sūtra is recited here: the setting was at Śrāvastī;
there the Blessed One addressed the monks.

"Monks, I shall teach you the seven destinations of superior persons and the final nirvana without clinging; listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly, and I will speak. What are the seven destinations of superior persons?"
In this case, a monk has practiced in such a way that he thinks:

"May I not be, may it not be mine; may I not come to be, may it not be mine; whatever exists, whatever has come to be—that I shall abandon. Thus he attains equanimity and is not stained by passion for this existence.
He is not attached to this existence,
and through wisdom he penetrates the higher state of peace;
furthermore, that state is realized by him directly with his own body.
If there were those who asked: "What will be the destination of a monk who has practiced in this way? What will be his rebirth? What will be his future state?"
It is just as if, monks, a small spark from a chip of wood were to go out even while it is still turning;

even so, as long as a residue of conceit remains for him— unabandoned and not fully understood— due to that non-abandonment and non-understanding of the residue of conceit, yet through the abandonment of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who attains final Nirvana in the intermediate state.
This is declared to be the first destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk practices in this way:
"May it not be so," as before, up until: "there may be those who ask."
Just as when iron balls or iron spikes, heated by a blazing fire, are struck with an iron hammer and the iron sparks fly up and are extinguished even as they rise—
just so, as before, through the abandoning of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), one becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
this is the second destination of a true person (satpuruṣagati).
Furthermore, a monk practices in such a way—
as previously described— up until: just as a spark of iron, having flown up, would be extinguished without even falling to the ground,
even so, as previously described, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
This is the third destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk practices in this way— as described previously— until, like a spark of iron that flies up and is extinguished as soon as it falls upon the earth,

even so, through the aforementioned process, by the abandoning of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*).
This is the fourth destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).
Furthermore, a monk who has practiced in this way—as described previously—would be like a spark of iron that, having flown up, falls upon a small amount of grass and wood;
it would produce smoke there.

Just as that [fire] might produce a flame, and having produced smoke, it might again produce a flame; and having burned up and exhausted that same small amount of grass and wood, it would go out for lack of fuel— even so, through the aforementioned process up to the abandoning of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), one becomes one who attains final nirvana without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
This is the fifth destination of a superior person.

Furthermore, when a monk has practiced in this way—as described previously—until [the simile]: just as an iron spark, having flown up, might fall upon a great and vast heap of grass and wood, and there it would produce smoke;...

It might produce a flame, and having produced smoke there, it might also produce a flame; then, having burned that very same great and vast heap of grass and wood and exhausted it, it would go out for lack of fuel.
In the same way, as before, through the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*).
This is the sixth destination of a true person (*satpuruṣagati*).

Furthermore, a monk who has practiced in this way—as described previously—until: just as a spark of iron, having flown up, might fall upon a great and vast heap of grass and wood, and there produce smoke and even generate a flame; so too [is it with the monk].

Having produced smoke there and generated a flame, and having burned that very same great and vast heap of grass and wood, it might burn a village, or a part of a village, a city, or a part of a city, a district, or a part of a district, a thicket, a forest, an island, or a grove.

Having burned the village, and so on, up to having burned the grove, and having reached the edge of a road, or the edge of water, or a patch of ground with little greenery, it would be extinguished, exhausted and without fuel.
In the same way, as previously described up to the point of the abandonment of the five lower fetters (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana), one becomes an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvaṃsrotas);
this is declared to be the seventh destination of a true person (satpuruṣagati).
What, then, is parinirvāṇa without clinging (anupādāya parinirvāṇa)?
"In this case, a monk has practiced in such a way," as previously described up to "there would be a spreading out.

For that monk who has practiced in this manner, I do not say there is a destination in the eastern direction, nor in the southern, nor in the western, nor in the northern, nor above, nor below, nor in the intermediate directions;
rather, in this very visible world, he has become shadowless, completely extinguished, cooled, and become Brahman.
"What is this that is called 'parinirvāṇa without clinging'?
O monks, when I said, 'I shall teach you the seven destinations of superior persons and parinirvāṇa without clinging,' this is what was intended by that."
Others, however, say— and so on in detail—
that "the measure of life" is its interval; the meaning is that while that interval of the measure of life has not yet been completed, one dies.
Or, in the interval while going toward the presence of the gods— that is, into the vicinity of the gods, near the gods— one who abandons the afflictions.

As for the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, he further attains parinirvāṇa having entered the realm [of rebirth], being one who has attained it as soon as he has arisen while still in the state of the seeds of the afflictions.
The meaning is that his afflictions do not manifest.
One who attains parinirvāṇa while in the state of the manifestation of the perception of objects— having reached the stage of perception—
attains parinirvāṇa much more slowly than one who has reached the [pure] element.
Or, one who has entered into applied thought (*vitarka*) and attains parinirvāṇa during the state of the active manifestation of applied thought—
this person also attains parinirvāṇa after a longer time than one who has entered into perception (*saṃjñā*).
Thus, by means of the three aforementioned similes, there are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyin*).

The first [type] refers to one who, having taken up the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), has just been born; this is the meaning with reference to which the simile of the "small spark of fire" is given. The second [type] is one who, having experienced the prosperity of the gods, attains final nirvana (*parinirvāti*).
Regarding that for which this simile of the iron spark is given:
having entered the third assembly of the Dharma and having entered into a discussion of the Dharma, he attains parinirvāṇa.
With reference to this, there is the following simile:
just as an iron spark, having flown up, might be extinguished without even falling to the ground,
so too, even without an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyī*).
And just as its threefold distinction has been established by those belonging to other schools (nikāyāntarīya) through three examples,
once that has been established, this objection might be raised: "If one who enters the communal recitation of the Dharma (dharmasaṅgīti) attains final nirvāṇa..."

If one asks, "What kind of person is the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī), given that the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyī) has already been described? he says in response:
"The one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, moreover, enters into a communal recitation (saṅgīti) endowed with excellence and then attains parinirvāṇa.
The intention is that because of this connection with excellence, the term implies the sense of being born [into a superior realm].
Considering that there is no room for the statement "this distinction is not tenable" because of the commonality of entering the communal recitation (*saṅgīti*), he speaks again:
"or, having mostly struck [the wind]," which means that having exhausted most of his lifespan, he attains final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāti*).
"Regarding the phrase 'these [three],' and so forth:
why are all these three— the states of the elements (*dhātu-gata*) and the rest— not connected with the examples of the *śakālika* and others?"
Because there is no distinction in their movement through space— that is,
because there is no specific quality to their spatial movement— indeed, no distinction in their movement through space exists for them.
Because final nirvāṇa occurs in that very same place,
there is no distinction of ten destinies among the three examples mentioned in the Sūtra;
therefore, these [examples] are not connected with those [destinies].
"And even in the formless realms," and so forth.
If those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth were thus established as being those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state,
they would likewise be listed in that same manner within the formless realms.
Because one attains parinirvāṇa within the interval of that lifespan,
and not otherwise,
the meaning of the sūtra is not as [you] have stated.
Regarding the phrase "or at another time during the lifespan" and so forth,
how is it understood that one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is not mentioned among those in the formless realms? To this, he says:
"By means of the meditations, there are four sets of ten," and so forth;
that is, by means of the four meditations, there are four sets of ten meanings of the Sūtras.
Having established the elevenfold sets for the first dhyāna up to the single set for the fourth, one then forms three sevenfold sets with the formless attainments.
Thus,
there are three sets of seven [stages] consisting of the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness;
of these, there are three.
Because of the absence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the absence of the three places of rebirth, there is a non-existence of both;
having established that, the group of six does not exist by means of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Since there is no upward-streamer (*ūrdhva-srotas*) among those same three [types of non-returners], and having excluded that [category], the group becomes complete; the meaning is that it is "bound" (*baddha*).
How so?

In this case, a monk— by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs— having attained and dwelling in the first dhyāna, which is secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and which is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), born of seclusion, and characterized by joy and bliss— he does not indeed attend to those aspects, those marks, or those signs; rather,
he attends to whatever there is therein that pertains to form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
He attends to those phenomena as passion;
he attends to them as a boil, as a thorn, as a calamity, as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.
Having attended to those phenomena as a disease, up to having attended to them as non-self, he causes the mind to become weary of, terrified of, and turns away from those phenomena.
Having caused the mind to become weary of, terrified of, and turned away from those phenomena, he directs it toward the deathless element,
[thinking]: "This is peaceful, this is sublime— namely, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, which is Nirvana."
Having spoken this very same sutra, there is this distinction:

for one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), the mind is liberated from the influx of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).

For one who is liberated, the knowledge and vision arises: "I am liberated. "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further state of existence beyond this."
Having spoken this very sutra, he is not yet liberated; rather,

by that same desire for the Dharma, that same affection for the Dharma, that same love for the Dharma, and that same delight in the Dharma, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state,
or indeed he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Rather, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; indeed, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
but rather he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
He is certainly not one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion;
rather, he is one who goes upstream (ūrdhvaṃsrotas); yet he is certainly not one who goes upstream.
Moreover, by that very same desire for the Dharma, as before, up to: by that very same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Mahābrahmā devas;

indeed, he is not reborn in the company of the Mahābrahmā devas, but rather, by that very same desire for the Dharma, as before, up to: by that very same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Brahmapurohita devas.
He is certainly not reborn in the company of the Brahmapurohita gods;
rather, by that very same desire for the Dharma, as previously described, and by that very delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Brahmakāyika gods.

Here, a monk, through certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and the unification of the mind, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is without applied or sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by rapture and happiness.
He does not indeed direct his mind toward those forms, those marks, or those signs;
rather, he perceives therein—as in the preceding text—up to: the cessation of discursive thought, which is Nirvana.

Having spoken this very sutra, for one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), from the influx of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and from the influx of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*), as previously described, up to: "What was to be done has been done; I know there is no further state of existence beyond this. Having spoken this very sutra, yet [in another case] it is not liberated.
Rather, by that very same desire for the Dharma as before, up to that very same delight in the Dharma, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
indeed, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Furthermore, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; indeed, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
but rather one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
For he is not one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion,
but rather he is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion;
yet he is not even one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
Furthermore, he may become one who flows upwards; indeed, he does not necessarily become one who flows upwards,
but rather, through that same desire for the Dharma as before, and so on, up to that same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Ābhāsvara gods.
Indeed, he is not reborn in the company of the Ābhāsvara gods;
rather, by that very desire for the Dharma and by that same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Apramāṇābha gods, and indeed,
he is not reborn in the company of the Ābhāsvara gods.
Rather, by that very desire for the Dharma— as previously described— up to that very delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the company of the Parīttābha devas.
In this regard, monks, by whatever modes, whatever characteristics, and whatever signs, through the fading away of joy, one dwells in equanimity,
mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body.

When the Noble Ones describe it as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and abiding in happiness, having attained the third dhyāna," he does not indeed attend to those aspects, those marks, or those signs, as previously stated in all the sūtras;
the only difference lies in the homogeneity of the class.
Indeed, he does not become one who flows upwards;
rather, by that very same desire for the Dharma, as before, he is reborn among the company of the Śubhakṛtsna gods,
yet he does not indeed become one who is reborn among the company of the Śubhakṛtsna gods.
Furthermore, by that same [cause], as before, he is reborn in the company of the Apramāṇaśubha gods; indeed, he is not reborn in the company of the Apramāṇaśubha gods,
but rather, as before, he is reborn in the company of the Parīttāśubha gods.

In this case, a monk— by means of those aspects, those marks, and those signs— through the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and through the prior disappearance of mental joy and dejection, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness; he does not indeed [need to] describe those aspects and those marks in detail— all the sūtras should be recited here as before.
However, the rebirths among the classes of gods are distinguished:
by that very delight in the Dharma, one is reborn in the fellowship of the Bṛhatphala gods,
and not, as before, in the fellowship of the Puṇyaprasava gods.

In this case, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, thinking, "Space is infinite.

He does not indeed [retain] those aspects as before; however, instead of reading "pertaining to form" (*rūpagata*), one should simply read "pertaining to form" (*rūpagatam*) [in the context of the previous description].
In that regard, because of the absence of form,
up to "cessation is nirvāṇa"— having stated this very sutra, this is the distinction.

For him who knows thus— as previously described— up to the point where he understands, "There is no further existence beyond this," even after saying this much, he is not yet liberated; rather, by that very desire for the Dharma, up to that very delight in the Dharma, he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī).
He certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
rather, by that very [path], he becomes one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
He certainly does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion; having stated everything up to that point, he does not become one who flows upwards.
Moreover, by that very same process as before,
up until through that very same delight in the Dharma, he is reborn in the fellowship of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite space.

Here, a monk, by means of certain aspects, certain marks, and certain signs, completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
He does not indeed perceive those modes [of perception]— the seven sūtras should be stated here just as in the case of the sphere of infinite space—
but the distinction is that he is reborn in the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

Furthermore, in this case, a monk, by means of certain modes, certain marks, and certain signs, completely transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and, thinking "there is nothing at all," attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
He does not indeed perceive those aspects, as before; thus there are seven sūtras.

Furthermore, "In this case, a monk, by means of which... and so on, up to: having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, he dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
All [the descriptions] should be stated as before, with the exception of only one: the "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

Thus, by means of the four *dhyānas*, there are four sets of ten topics of the Sūtra which have as their intrinsic nature: the application of the mind to the realm of the deathless (*amṛtadhātu*), liberation of the mind, intermediate parinirvāṇa, birth-parinirvāṇa, non-exertion parinirvāṇa, exertion parinirvāṇa, upward movement, and birth in the three higher realms of rebirth.

However, by means of the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), there are three sets of seven topics of the Sūtra which have as their intrinsic nature: the application of the mind to the realm of the deathless, liberation of the mind, birth-parinirvāṇa, non-exertion parinirvāṇa, exertion parinirvāṇa, upward movement, and birth in the higher realms of rebirth.
Having excluded upward movement by means of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a group of six is also stated;
therefore, it is not tenable to say that one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is not one who attains parinirvāṇa within the duration of his lifespan.
For even in the formless realms, the possibility of intermediate death exists,
because it is stated that "intermediate death occurs everywhere except among the Kurus."
Therefore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established not only by reasoning but also by scripture; this is the meaning of the word "also" (*api*).
Regarding the phrase "Dūṣī Māra":

at that time, a disciple of the Tathāgata Krakucchanda named Vidura had a Māra named Dūṣī, who struck him on the head with his fist; by this act, [the existence of the intermediate state] was admitted.
At that very moment, he fell into the great Avīci hell with his very own body;
by the statement "with his very own body," the intention is that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
for he was [consumed] by the flames of the hell-beings while still alive.

While still alive, this Māra fell with his own body because he was embraced by flames of fire rising from hell, resulting in the arising of suffering within the state of his own physical form; however, he did not fall without having completed his lifespan, nor did he remain in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

The intention is that he has not entered the state of existence as rebirth in hell; "extremely intense and complete" means they are extremely intense due to their connection with the excellence of the field and the intention.

The intention is that because they are fully developed, one is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter; thus, based on the statement "immediately thereafter," there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
The intention is that this statement— "without going to another destination"— is primarily intended to exclude other [future] rebirths, not to exclude the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

If it is interpreted according to the literal expression "only five," it would follow that one goes to hell only after having committed all five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), and not by committing just one or two.
From the statement "five," it would follow that immediately after the action and immediately after the subsequent action, one is reborn in the hells;
yet from the statement "having performed and accumulated [them], one is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter," there is no interval of time during which one lives.
Furthermore, who does not accept that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is in the process of being reborn?

The state of being "about to be reborn" (upapadyamāna) is mentioned because of the word [in the sūtra]; for the intention is that one who is facing rebirth is "being reborn," but we do not say that he has already been reborn.
But we do not say that this word "upapadyate" has the meaning of "having been reborn";
therefore, this objection regarding the age [of the person] is not a fault.
Thus is the detailed explanation:
he whose age has reached the vicinity of death is one whose life has been brought to its end.
"O twice-born one"—this was the address;
a certain aged Brahmin was thus addressed: "Indeed, you have not even a garment between [your body and the cold]."
Thus,
the intention here is that this [scriptural passage] serves as the indicator for the non-existence of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
The meaning is that you have no provisions for the journey, no food fit for the road, and no accumulation of merit for the world beyond;
furthermore, there is no intermediate dwelling among humans,
meaning that as you are on the verge of death, there is no place for you to rest among men.
The intended meaning is that for someone here who is coming to a standstill;
"due to the cessation of going" means due to the stopping of motion.
The intention here is this: that which you describe as "there is an intermediate state" (antarābhava) is not the same intention as that which I describe.
That there is no intermediate state—
how is this so? From what cause does this arise?
This inquiry is equal for you as well; this question is the same for you as well— this is the meaning— because there is no contradiction with the sūtra as it has been stated.
Because it does not contradict the *Dūṣīmāra-sūtra* and others,
this sūtra is not a proof for the non-existence of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); for indeed, a "proof" is merely a resort when no other way is possible.
That state of existence for which there is no other state of existence is the "state of non-going";
this is what is meant.
If a sūtra or a verse that serves as an indicator is spoken for the purpose of illuminating a certain meaning, [then that meaning is established].
If it illuminates only that very object and no other distinct object, then that indicator, being contrary to it and having no other possible referent, [is established].
"Having the form of the future prior existence" means that which is yet to come (*aiṣyat*).
Why is it called "having the form of the future pre-death existence" (*aiṣyat-pūrvakāla-bhava-ākṛti*)? Because its form is like that of the future pre-death existence (*pūrvakālabhava*).
Because of a single projection (*ekākṣepāt*):
since both the future rebirth (*aiṣyantī gati*) and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that leads to its attainment are projected by that very same single karma,
as is the case for dogs and other such beings.
"Among dogs, pigs, and so forth" means "going to the five destinies," that is, one who goes to the five destinies.
If one were to die even while remaining in the womb, his hellish intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would consume the womb;
for the hell-being is ablaze, and the intermediate state is of that same nature.
"Even in the prior existence," and so forth;
even those hell-beings residing in the prior existence of hell are not constantly burning while wandering through the secondary hells such as the Pit of Hot Ashes (kukūla),
let alone those belonging to the intermediate state.
Or let it be that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a hell-being is "blazing," yet there is no contact [with the womb] because of its location within the belly.
Because the bodies of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are transparent, they do not obstruct one another;
and because of the obstruction of karma—that is, due to the obstruction of that specific karma—there is no burning. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the womb of a dog or similar animal does not burn, and hundreds of millions of four-continent world-systems are illuminated;

because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a Bodhisattva is like that of a full-grown youth, endowed with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), he— desiring to enter his mother’s womb while remaining in the intermediate state— illuminated the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system, regarding it as his own field.
