If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) had the form of the previous existence that was to follow, why did the mother of the Bodhisattva see a white elephant calf of such a form?
That is merely a sign for that Bodhisattva, because he has long since turned away from rebirth as an animal;
from the time he begins to perform the deeds that ripen into the [thirty-two] marks, when a hundred eons remain, from that point on all his miserable destinies have been averted.
For example, King Kṛkī saw ten dreams as mere omens of future events;
these ten dreams are recited in the Vinaya.
It is said that King Kṛkin saw ten dreams:
an elephant emerged from a window and clung to its tail;
a well pursued a thirsty man from behind.
A prastha of pearls is obtained for a prastha of barley meal; sandalwood is sold at the price of common wood;
and groves abounding in flowers and fruits have all their blossoms and fruit carried off by those who take what is not given.
Young elephants are terrified by scent-elephants;
a monkey smeared with filth defiles others;
the consecration of monkeys takes place.
"A cloth is being pulled by eighteen men;
a great multitude of people have fallen into mutual destruction through quarreling, brawling, strife, and dispute.
And they reported this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
And the Blessed One has prophesied:

"In a future time, there will be a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni. His disciples, having renounced their extensive circles of kinsmen and relatives and gone forth into homelessness, will give rise to the notion of 'home' within monasteries and form attachments, like elephants whose tails become snagged as they exit through a window.
By means of the dream of a well, those very disciples will approach brahmins and householders and teach them the Dharma."
This shows that their desire to hear [the Dharma] will not be established;

by the dream of the measure of flour and pearls, it shows that those very disciples will proclaim the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and so forth, even for the sake of a begging bowl of flour;

and by the dream of the churning-stick, it shows that those very disciples, having failed to cultivate body, morality, and wisdom, will adopt the doctrines of the non-Buddhist heretics and equate them with the words of the Buddha.

By the dream of the garden, it is shown that those very disciples, making their dwellings their refuge, will repeatedly sell whatever flowers, fruits, or surplus goods belong to the Saṅgha to make a living, and with that they will provide hospitality to householders;
by the dream of the young elephant, it is shown that those very disciples will become immoral and of evil character.

This is shown by the dream of the monkey smeared with impurity: those monks who are elders, possessed of virtue, and of noble character will be expelled from their dwellings; for it is precisely those disciples of his who, being of immoral conduct and evil nature, [will act against] those monks who are virtuous.
This shows that they will revile them with false faults;
by the dream of the monkey-consecration, it shows that those very disciples will perform the consecration of neighboring kings in the monasteries,
and also that eunuchs will exercise sovereign rule in the world.
By the dream of the cloth, he shows that his teaching itself will undergo division into eighteen schools, yet the cloth of liberation will not be torn;
by the dream of the quarrel, he shows that his disciples themselves, through their adherence to specific sects, will fall into mutual dispute.
The summary verse: An elephant, a well, groats, sandalwood, a young elephant, a garden, likewise the consecration of a monkey,
an impure monkey, a cloth, and a quarrel— these are the ten dreams seen by King Kṛkin.
Because of the predominance of moral dread (*apatrāpya*)— that is, because of the intensity of moral dread—

the moment of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) occurs at the very instant of reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*); any existence subsequent to that moment of reconnection is "existence during the prior period" (*pūrvakālabhava*).

If it is said that "beings are reborn among those with form," this specific qualification— "by those of the same class"— is stated because there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
A hell-being intermediate state is seen only by hell-being intermediate states; likewise, up to a divine intermediate state being seen only by divine intermediate states—
thus it is "perfectly pure."
The divine eye is free from eleven defects;

those defects are: doubt, lack of attention, physical rigidity, sloth and torpor, restlessness, over-exertion of energy, elation, timidity, perception of diversity, excessive talkativeness, and preoccupation with objects of knowledge as described in the Sūtras.
It consists of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
The meaning is that it consists of cultivation having the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) as its intrinsic nature;
furthermore, although the divine [perception] of gods and others is admitted to be obtained by birth (*upapattipratilambhika*),
it is not considered to be perfectly pure.
"Regarding the intermediate state of the gods," and so forth;
others say that the intermediate state is not perceived by those of the same class alone.
Rather, one belonging to the intermediate state of the gods sees all those belonging to the intermediate states of the gods and so forth,
excluding each preceding category— namely, those belonging to the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings.

How is it that one in the intermediate state of a human, setting aside those in the intermediate state of a deity, sees those in the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings; and how is it that one in the intermediate state of a hungry ghost, setting aside the previous two— those in the intermediate states of deities and humans— sees those in the intermediate states of hungry ghosts, animals, and hell-beings?

In this way, even up to a being in the intermediate state of hell, having set aside those in the intermediate states of the gods and so forth who precede them, sees only those in the intermediate state of hell,
because the destinies become progressively more degraded;
for this very reason, it is called a *gandharva*.
Because he has gone to the fragrance, he is a *gandharva*; the meaning is that he "seeks" (*arvati*) or "consumes" (*bhakṣyai*) the fragrance,
since verbal roots have multiple meanings.
This root *arv* does not function solely in the sense of motion; rather, it also functions in the sense of eating. Thus, there is no fault even if the sense of motion is accepted.

It is called *gandharva* because it goes (*arvati*) toward fragrance (*gandha*) in order to consume it; the shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule for *śakandhu* and *karkandhu*, as it ends in a primary suffix (*kṛt*).
Just as the formation of the single substitute *pararūpa* is established in the cases of *śakandhu* and *karkandhu* due to the substitution of the subsequent form,
so too is it established here in the case of *gandharva*.
"Alpeśākhya" means one who is not noble, that is, of low birth;
"īśa" means one who rules (*īṣṭe*), and "alpeśa" means one who has little power to rule (*alpa īśaḥ*).
One who has the designation "of little power" is called *alpeśākhya*; one who possesses the opposite is called *maheśākhya*,
because they belong to the same homogeneous class (*ekanikāyasabhāgatva*).

The existence of the prior period (*pūrvakālabhava*) and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) that leads to it share one and the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*). Therefore, because they belong to the same homogeneous class,
by the very same life-projecting karma (*āyuṣya-karma*) that projects the lifespan of the prior period-existence, [the lifespan of the intermediate existence is also projected].
By that very [karma], the intermediate state [is projected];
for otherwise,
if there were a separate projection for the lifespan of that intermediate state, [it would follow that there is a second death].
Furthermore, at what point in that intermediate state life would death-existence (maraṇabhava) occur, as it does in the case of prior-time existence?
Therefore, there is no fixed rule; thus says the Venerable One.
Having smelled that odor, their craving for odors and tastes increases—this is the full explanation.

When those small creatures smell that odor and recollect the taste experienced as accompanying it, they become greedy for the odor and taste; at the time of death, awakening the karma that leads to rebirth in the class of worms, and turning toward its maturation through that craving for odor and taste, they are born among the worms by means of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Thus, the time is indeed abundant with those conditions.
In a time abundant with conditions for worms, those karmas conducive to that [birth]—karmas conducive to being born as a worm—obtain their operation in the production of maturation;
the meaning is that they become oriented toward the giving of maturation.
Indeed, having reached the collection of conditions and the [proper] time, the fruits of embodied beings surely ripen.
According to this statement,
[this applies] not elsewhere, nor at a time when that [state] is not predominant.
"Not in another" means that the appearance of a Wheel-turning Monarch does not occur among those of short lifespan, nor below the height of eight thousand [yojanas].
Because of this statement,
for this very reason—

that is, because even those karmas conducive to becoming a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), though they exist, only occasionally obtain their operation at the time of the actualization of their maturation (*vipāka*).
Because they depend on many conditions,
because they seek existence, and because they desire rebirth,
it is karma alone that brings about the assembly of conditions.
Due to the predominance of karma, sexual intercourse occurs even at another time, having transgressed the established time [of conception],
because it is projected by a single karma; that is,
by the very same karma by which the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) of cattle and so forth is projected.
Since that very karma projects that intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
this must be explained regarding what was said: "by which [karma] one is to be reborn among cattle at another time."
It is reborn among the gavayas; thus, in detail,
its status as a single-projecting [karman] is not lost despite the difference in the class [of beings],
because that karman is of a single type.

Master Saṅghabhadra maintains that this fault does not apply, because even for those karmas fixed to a particular destiny, a variety of rebirths is observed without abandoning the specific form and configuration of that destiny, as in the case of Kalmāṣapāda and others.
Regarding the phrase "one whose mind is perverted," he says the following to demonstrate how one becomes perverted in mind through a thought accompanied by either attachment or aversion.

Regarding the passage beginning "there, for his parents," and so forth: when the intermediate state being is male, a male passion arises toward his mother— that is, toward the sexual union of his parents characterized by the conjunction of the two organs— just as one might feel toward a wife.
In a woman, this feminine passion arises toward her father; conversely, in a man, aversion arises toward him as if toward a brother.
A male hostility, arising from envy, occurs toward the father as if he were a rival man,
while a female hostility arises toward the mother as if she were a rival woman.

Distorted by those two perverted states of mind, through the desire for pleasure and the desire for the act of sexual intercourse, he embraces that place— the location of the two organs— and, having entered that state, he falsely imagines that state to be himself.

Thinking, "I am performing this action," it enters and takes its stand— that is, it settles— within that impure semen and blood when they have reached the site of the womb, specifically in the space between the stomach and the large intestine;
the meaning is that it faces the back and remains in a squatting position.
Being nourished and increasing through the union with the activity of self-conceit consisting of sexual intercourse, [it thinks],
"these very [are my possessions]."
The great elements of semen and blood are indeed other elements,
being distinct from semen and blood.

According to the principle of the cessation of the seed and the arising of the sprout, the seed ceases and the sprout arises in one and the same moment; because destruction and arising are simultaneous, like the lowering and raising of the ends of a balance scale,
that which is designated as the *kalala* [occurs at that time].
Because of the scriptural statement beginning with, "The *kalala* comes first;
from the *kalala*, the *arbuda* is born," and so forth.
And having established it thus, the scriptural passage says:

"O Bhikṣu, 'anthill' is a designation for this body—material, gross, composed of the four great elements, nourished by boiled rice and gruel, produced from the impure *kalala* of mother and father," and so forth;
[the *kalala*] arises indeed from the impurity of the mother and father.
The meaning is "of that which has arisen from that";
*kaṭasi* refers to a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
"The drop of blood fell"—
this is the example [given] because of its having attained the state of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
There are indeed other primary elements distinct from the semen and blood,
just as in the case of the leaf-worm; for instance,
just as in the case of the leaf-worm, other primary elements arise through karma by depending upon the primary elements of the leaf.
Those which become of the nature of sense-faculties are not the great elements of the leaves,
because of the multiplicity of those worms.
And since the leaf [of the scripture] is not seen in its entirety, how then is the scriptural passage—"born from the impure *kalala* of mother and father"—to be interpreted? To this he says:
"However, because the statement regarding the *kalala* was made with the intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) of referring to its arising based upon the impure, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra."
The arising of other primary elements (bhūta) based upon the impure;
therein lies the intention (abhisaṃdhi), the underlying purpose (abhiprāya), by which the statement regarding the *kalala* was made.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with this Sūtra passage stating that [the embryo] is produced from the impure *kalala* of the mother and father;
what is meant is that, based upon the semen and blood, other primary elements (*bhūta*) called *kalala*, which possess sense-faculties, arise simultaneously with the semen and blood.

"Just as, by depending on a leaf, worm-like great elements (*mahābhūta*) together with sense-faculties arise at the same time as the leaf—though they are said to be 'other' [than the leaf]—so too should it be stated according to the circumstances.
Thus say the Abhidharma masters: "In other cases, namely for the two modes of birth—the womb-born and the spontaneously born—it should be explained according to the circumstances."
And regarding this, the Teacher says that "this application would be seen" and "coldness in the hells," at the time of rebirth in the cold hells.
"In what state" means in the state of a butcher of sheep and so forth;

having seen such beings—as that karma which was previously performed to be experienced by him truly is—in a manner like a dream, he runs toward hell. This is the view of the former masters, the Yogācāras, beginning with the noble Āsaṅga.
"Rising as it were from his seat" means that because he goes to a higher place of rebirth, he is like a human being or others who rise from a seat.
Just as a human, an animal, and a hungry ghost pass away,
so it is with those who speak in opposition to the sages.
"Abusers" means revilers;
because of the inclusion of the word "always" in the phrase "always egg-born," there is no such restriction regarding the term "all" in the phrase "all are deluded."
However, it is taught in reverse order even for one who possesses full awareness;
for in the Sūtra, it says that one who performs all [the stages] without full awareness [is described first].
This first descent into the womb has been explained;
however, as for those who will be born according to the sequence already specified, there are three [other types].
"He too is egg-born" means that he will be born from an egg; this is the intended meaning,
for a future state is necessarily expressed as if it were already accomplished.
For example, someone might say to another: "The present tense may be used for what is proximate to the present, or the past tense may be used for an expression of hope."
"Know me as one who has already come even while coming"—
therefore, this is not a fault;
one born from an egg, one yet to be born, and one currently being born is called "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*).
Because of the rule stating "it is also seen after other [roots]," Master Saṅghabhadra says that this is therefore not faulty;
or else, it is because a designation may be applied even to what is yet to come.
An indication is also made by means of a designation that is yet to come;
for example, one says "he conditions the conditioned," even though it becomes conditioned only at the state of having been produced.
It is not in the state of being produced, for the further conditioning of that which is already conditioned is not logical; rather,
it is designated as such by means of a future name.

In this way, [the phrase] "he cooks rice," and so forth, should be applied. Furthermore, as for the detailed explanation of how one enters the mother's womb without clear comprehension (*asamprajānan*): it means that with a perverted mind, one goes to the place of rebirth in its proximate state.
The remote state is resolution (*adhimokṣa*), which is conviction (*adhimukti*): "I stand thus, I go forth thus.
How is it that even while standing thus, one thinks, "I am standing in these"?
Others, however, say that even when departing from these [realms], thinking "I am going forth"— this is the distinction between these two types of misconception.
It is not only through passion and hatred that one with a perverted mind goes to the place of birth;
rather,
it is also otherwise.
"How so? [He asks:
"The wind blows, the god rains," and so forth;
likewise, "I enter the grove and the garden," and so forth.
But one who is fully conscious correctly understands [the process],
such as "they enter the mother's womb," and so forth.
If he understands it correctly in this way, how can the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) be established by means of an afflicted mind alone?
The mind becomes afflicted due to the presence of maternal affection and so forth;
another says that for one entering the mother's womb, there are such perverted perceptions and convictions (*saṃjñā-adhimokṣa*).
Immediately upon being reborn, this occurs: "The wind blows," and so on, up to "I shall go to the foot of a tree and the base of a wall";
and even while standing, [the thought] "I am standing" arises.
"Even as he was departing from these [palaces], thinking 'I am going forth,' and so on—
therein, 'the first' refers to the Cakravartin; this is the detailed explanation."
That one who enters [the womb] with full awareness is the first; the second is that of a Pratyekabuddha.
This third [state] of the Buddha is that which remains even as another [being] departs;
this is that which remains even as another departs.

In this case as well, the phrase "those who will exist" refers to those who are not cakravartins and so forth at that time; rather, it is said that "these very ones" are the cakravartins and so forth— this is merely a difference in expression.
The intended meaning is that the object remains the same;
the conventions are the established relations between cause and effect,
which are conditioned by afflictions and karma.
The meaning is that it is "perfumed by afflictions and karma";
"like a lamp" refers to the five aggregates (skandhas) which proceed by way of a continuous stream.
He shows that it is like a lamp because of its momentariness,
according to the projection [of its cause].
"Projection" (*ākṣepa*) refers to a continuity for that duration;

and this qualification is stated because of the distinction between the karma that constitutes life-force (*āyuṣya*) and the karma conducive to life-force (*āyuḥ-saṃvartanīya*), [as well as] because the primary characteristics (*vyañjana*) appear in succession.
The "limbs" (vyañjanāni) are the bases of the eye and so forth; for by means of them, the eye and other faculties are supported, as if in a cesspool.
"Mahākāya-nāḍī-vraṇa" is a term of reproach;
it means "nāḍī-vraṇas," so called because they are like a sinus ulcer (nāḍī-vraṇa).
It is fierce and foul-smelling, being the most foul-smelling of all; it is darkness because it is devoid of light;
and it is a pool because it is like a pool for those who are equal [in their suffering].
In that [body], which requires constant remediation and whose purification must be performed perpetually,
there is semen belonging to the male and blood belonging to the female.
Completely soaked, meaning thoroughly saturated on all sides by lymph— which is characterized as a specific liquid— and by impurities;
and excessively decomposed, meaning particularly putrefied.

When that [excrement] has become boiled, putrid, and slimy, they thrust their hands into it and, having torn limb from limb— cutting off the hands, feet, and other parts— they pull them out and drag them away,
like a fresh wound that is painful.

Behaving as if he were a fresh wound, thus acting like a fresh wound; [the term] *taruṇavraṇāyamānātmānaṃ* means "one whose self (*ātman*) acts like a fresh wound"; [the compound] *śastrakṣāraṃ* refers to both the weapon and the caustic alkali. The child and the weapon-and-alkali.

Thinking, "I shall treat myself as if it were that [medicine]," and perceiving the touch of these two hands to be like a surgical instrument or caustic alkali (*śastra-kṣāra*), they take hold of him with those hands— which feel like a surgical instrument or caustic alkali— and bathe him.
Because of the following— that is, the continuous occurrence— of its increase, it is causeless; that is,
the beginning is causeless.
And if this [arising] were causeless, then everything would manifest as being causeless just like that;
yet, the efficacy of seeds and so forth with respect to sprouts and the like is observed.
Why is there the capacity within the sprout, stalk, stem, leaf, and so forth, to produce the seed, sprout, stalk, stem, and so forth?
It is because of the specific determination of place and time.
However, because place and time are restricted,
there is a restriction of place in that [production] because production occurs only in a place connected with the seed and so forth;
and there is a restriction of time because production occurs immediately after the seed.

The causal capacity of fire and so forth— such as fire, cold, heat, impact, the eye, and so on— with respect to products of maturation and so forth— such as the sensations of pleasure and pain produced by maturation, sound, visual consciousness, and so on— is observed to be restricted by place and time. For if manifestation were causeless,

seeds and the like would not possess the capacity for production in sprouts and the like, nor would fire and the like possess the capacity for production in products of maturation and the like, according to the restriction of place and time.
Everything would arise everywhere and at all times,
yet this is not observed; therefore, there is no causeless manifestation,
and the doctrine asserting the existence of a permanent cause has already been refuted.
Because of the statement "not from a creator god (īśvara) and so forth, due to [the occurrence of] succession and so on," the remaining eight [links] are understood to be in the middle:

namely, the factors of consciousness (vijñāna), name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), sensation (vedanā), craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming (bhava).
Nor does it belong to the realms of form or formlessness;
for in the realm of form, since the members of name-and-form and the six sense-bases exist precisely at the time of the member of consciousness, there are not eight intermediate members.
Furthermore, because the factors of name-and-form and the six sense bases do not exist for those belonging to the formless realm, it is stated in the *Mahānidānaparyāya-sūtra*:
"Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would that name-and-form coagulate into the state of the embryo (kalala)?"
"No, Venerable Sir," and so forth— that sūtra is recited because the descent into the mother's womb occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
due to the inclusion of both the prior and subsequent limits together with their respective causes and fruits.
This is in sequence because it includes the past limit together with its fruit and the future limit together with its cause;
therein, ignorance and formative forces constitute the cause in the past limit.
Its fruit consists of five members:
from consciousness up to feeling, and in the future limit, birth and old age and death; this is the fruit.
Its three members—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*)—are the causes.
Thus, it is explained that there are seven members in total: five belonging to the prior limit (*paurvāntika*) and two belonging to the posterior limit (*aparāntika*).
Now, what are these [members] beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*)?
In response to the doubt— whether it is ignorance alone, or all the afflictions, or rather the state of the afflictions— he asks,
"Because of their association," since the afflictions accompany ignorance.
And because those [defilements] manifest under its influence,
and because those defilements manifest through the power of ignorance,
that [ignorance] is their subsequent occurrence.
For the manifestation of afflictions belongs to one who is deluded, not to one who is undeluded, as in the detailed explanation regarding the statement "the king is coming";
just as when it is said, "The king is coming."
Because they follow him, the arrival of the servants is established; due to their association with him, their conduct is determined by his influence,
and this case is just like that.
Thus, by the power of ignorance, the state of affliction is a limb of ignorance;
therefore it is said that the prior state of affliction is ignorance.
Thus,
it was not stated that the prior stage of ignorance is "ignorance" [itself], nor that it is the "state of meritorious and other karmas."
The meaning is that the state of karma consists of merit and demerit;
it should be stated that this occurs prior to the arising of the four sense-bases (*āyatana*),
because the sense-bases of mind (*manas*) and body (*kāya*) arise only at the moment of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
"At that time, because of their establishment" means that at the time of the arising of the sense-bases (āyatana) such as the eye, the body-base and the mind-base are established;
this occurs prior to the conjunction of the triad.

Thus, that member of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) [is defined] prior to the conjunction of the triad; the meaning is: prior to the coming together of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness.
"Contact occurs prior [to sensation]" means that contact is established in the stage of birth as the conjunction of the six sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness,
due to the existence of this conjunction when the six sense bases are complete.
From what point prior [to this] does he become a fool?

It is from the time when, regarding the causes of pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations, he possesses the capacity for knowledge, yet is not yet able to discern: "This is the cause of pleasant sensation; this is the cause of painful sensation; and this is the cause of neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation."
That state is called contact (*sparśa*);

for instance, an infant might even touch fire without discerning that it is a cause of suffering. When there is the capacity for such discernment, the experience [of that object] is feeling (*vedanā*); this is the meaning.
From what point is it "eastward"?
From the time before sexual intercourse,
as long as sexual desire has not yet arisen.
That state is called "feeling" (vedanā),
for that state is characterized by feeling because it feels the cause of feeling.
"Those who thirst and are lustful for enjoyments and sexual union" refers to enjoyments characterized by the qualities of desire, such as visible forms and so forth.
And regarding sexual intercourse as it is commonly understood in the world, that state in which passion arises in a passionate person is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*),
because he has entered into a state of seeking.

The form *upādāna* is derived from the verbal root *upādā*, meaning "to take up" (*upādīyate*). Since the self-nature of objects is taken up by this, the fourfold affliction (*kleśa*) in its various states is called *upādāna*.
"That which will be the fruit of future existence" is the designation for that which runs about.
"Future existence is its fruit"— thus, "karma that has future existence as its fruit" means karma that leads to renewed existence (*paunarbhavika*); that is "existence" (*bhava*).
"Becoming" (*bhava*) is so called because one comes to be by means of it; it is a synonym for karma.
"Up to old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇam āvidaḥ*) means up to the member of sensation (*vedanā-aṅga*).
Old age and death have the four members beginning with name-and-form as their intrinsic nature;
however, for the purpose of causing revulsion in those to be trained, the Blessed One spoke of these four members by the term "old age and death," [saying]:
"O monks, that which is the arising of form..."
That which is the arising of old age and death,
and so on down to consciousness,
is momentary; it exists for a single moment.
Alternatively, "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) means that which possesses a moment (*kṣaṇa*); "prolonged" (*prākarṣika*) means that which plays or acts with intensity,
in the sense of being connected with a continuous stream (*prabandha*).
Thus, "relating to connection" (sāmbandhika) means being endowed with the connection between cause and fruit;
likewise, "relating to states" (āvasthika) means the twelve states consisting of the five aggregates.
"Co-existent with consciousness," and so forth:
here, "form" refers to the co-existent manifest and unmanifest [karma] and so on, while the "name" refers to the three aggregates beginning with perception.
The sense faculties are established within name-and-form because their functioning is dependent upon it; alternatively, they are established within "name" by virtue of being its support.
Contact is the convergence of the six sense bases;
"convergence" refers to the engagement of the eye and the other faculties with their respective objects,
which occurs as far as possible.
That which at that time occurs as an impact should be understood as its contact;
the outbursts associated with it are grasping.

The outbursts (paryavasthāna) such as lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya), which are associated with that craving, are "clinging" (upādāna) because they are originated by it; thus,
they are originated by craving.
Others say that "arising from volition" refers to emergence, which is birth; and "ripening" refers to aging,
which is the impairment of the capacity to project a fruit.
Alternatively, death is the cessation in relation to the preceding moment;
it is the destruction of that very moment.
Others say that "destruction" (bhaṅga) refers to the state of being oriented toward destruction;
[this is] both momentary and relational, as in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
How so?
In the *Prakaraṇapāda*, it is asked: "What is dependent origination?
It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
In that context, because conditioned phenomena are associated with destruction at every moment, dependent origination is momentary (*kṣaṇika*).

The "relational" (*sāmbandhika*) dependent origination arises from the connection between two moments that function as cause and fruit; the "situational" (*āvasthika*) dependent origination refers to the twelve states consisting of the five aggregates, which are connected across three uninterrupted births— that is, connected across past, future, and present lives.
The inclusion of the term "uninterrupted" (nirantara) is for the purpose of establishing the three sections;
that very [type] is the "prolonged" (prākarṣika), and that same [type] is the "situational" (āvasthika); it is called "prolonged" because of its connection with prolongation.
It is "intentional" (ābhiprāyika) because it pertains to multiple moments or multiple births;
that which exists in the intention is "intentional."
The meaning is that it was taught in such a way by virtue of the intention of those to be trained (*vineya*).
Is it not the case that the *Abhidharma* is "definitional" (*lākṣaṇika*) because it prioritizes definitions?
Indeed, in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, dependent origination is described as pertaining to both sentient and non-sentient beings, since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are included therein.
Because it serves as the cause for all conditioned phenomena,
the twelvefold dependent origination— pertaining specifically to what is designated as "sentient beings"— was taught as the cause for the removal of the delusion of those to be trained;
therefore, he says:
"Because it is for the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the prior, the posterior, and the middle limits,
it is therefore called 'three-sectioned' (trikāṇḍa)."
"Section" means a part;
what indeed was I before?
"Was I a god or a human? means "In what manner, by what means, or by what application did I come to be so?"
"What indeed shall I become in the future time? and so forth;
"What indeed shall I become in the future time, or rather, shall I not become?"
"What indeed shall I become?
How indeed shall I become?"—the meaning is: "In what manner? By what method?"
"What indeed is this?"— thus he investigates the substance of the personal existence;
"How indeed is this?"— thus [he investigates].
In what manner and by what reasoning does one fail to ascertain that very substance of the personal existence,
[thinking] "who am I?"?
"One does not determine in this way according to the sequence in the Sūtra: 'Who are we now that exist, and who shall we become?'"
Ignorance and the formative forces are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the past;
birth and old age and death are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the future; and consciousness up to existence are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the middle.
"For it has been stated thus in the Sūtra," and so forth;
by saying "it is shown in this very way even in the Sūtra," he supports his own explanation with the authority of the Sūtra.
He does not pursue the past, thinking, "Did I indeed exist in past time? and so forth; he does not run back toward the prior limit.

The meaning is that by means of the vision of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as it truly is, one is not deluded regarding the past, thinking, "Did I indeed exist in the past? By the word "in detail," it is meant that he does not pursue the future limit (aparānta).
"What indeed shall I become in future time?"— this is the detailed [passage].
Likewise, he does not resort to the middle limit [thinking],
"What indeed is this?"— this is the detailed [passage].
"Craving, grasping, and becoming as well"—

all these [factors of] craving, grasping, and becoming are for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the future limit (aparānta), not for the purpose of dispelling delusion regarding the middle [limit].
As previously taught, [the links] begin with consciousness and end with existence;
what, then, is the reasoning here? He says:
"For these are the causes of that very [consciousness]."
Because these causes are like those of the future limit (*aparānta*),

meaning that the seven members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are the bases (*vastu*) or substrata (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for afflictions and karma, since they serve as the support for afflictions and karma.

"Likewise, the fruit" refers to the seven members themselves: the members of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the fruits of ignorance and volitional formations;
while birth and old age and death are the fruits of craving, grasping, and becoming.
The five that function as causes are ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and existence,
because they have the nature of karma and afflictions.
Ignorance, craving, and grasping have the nature of afflictions (*kleśa*),
while formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*) have the nature of karma;
this is because the entity is divided into five categories.
Consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling;
and of the afflictions, there are two: namely, craving and grasping.
In the future time, the fruit is summarized by way of a twofold division as "birth" and "aging-and-death";
in the past time, the cause is summarized by teaching it through a single aspect, namely, the afflictions.
The meaning is that this is because the afflictions beginning with ignorance are taught [as future];
however, the fruit in the future time is not expanded in this fivefold way,
nor is the cause in the past time expanded in this twofold way.
Because the Blessed One has demonstrated here [the sequence] beginning with "from affliction,
affliction," and so forth.
This is the method regarding the factors of existence;
therefore, it is a real entity.
From that, action;
from that, again, the object;
from that object, the object.
And the afflictions arise; the word "from the entity" (*vastunaḥ*) is understood [as the source], and the particle *iti* is to be supplied after the word "arise" (*jāyante*).
It has been made known that [affliction arises] either from an object or from another affliction;
for it is observed that affliction arising from an object occurs, as in "from feeling,
craving [arises]," and likewise it is observed that affliction [arises] from another affliction, as in "from craving, grasping [arises]."
And since ignorance is declared to have the nature of all afflictions of the past limit,
it is understood that if grasping arises from craving, it arises from that [ignorance];
or else, it is understood that craving arises from that very object.
Therefore, it is made known that ignorance, being of the nature of an affliction (*kleśa*), arises either from a thing (*vastu*) or from an affliction;

and it has been explained that old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are a thing consisting of four factors. Furthermore, in this context, an affliction arising from a thing is observed, as in the statement: "craving (*tṛṣṇā*) has feeling (*vedanā*) as its condition."
Therefore, it is made known that from that [cause] affliction will come to be;
nothing further needs to be added here because it has been made known in this way.
To the question, "How, then, is it understood that this method has been shown? he says:
Because of the statement, "In this way there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering," for otherwise, what would be its efficacy if this aforementioned method did not exist?
From affliction arise both further affliction and action; from that, the objective basis; and from that, once again, the objective basis and afflictions are born—one should state only this much.
One should not say, "With ignorance as condition, the formative forces arise, up to: with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair come into being;
thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering," because "origination" (samudaya) and "arising" (utpāda) are not different in meaning.
Therefore, it is understood that its capacity is to illuminate the manner described above; thus,
in the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna-sūtra*, ignorance is stated to have improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) as its cause.
How, monks,
is ignorance accompanied by cause, accompanied by condition, and accompanied by source? And what, monks, is the cause of ignorance, what is its condition, what is its source?
"Monks, improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance, improper mental attention is the condition, and improper mental attention is the source"— because of this statement in the Sūtra,
and because it is stated in another Sūtra that "improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause," this is the point under discussion.

Because it is stated in the Sūtra that "dependent upon the eye and visible forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion," for what reason is this not mentioned here? And why does it not become another limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*)? To this, he says:
And since that [defiled attention] is also included within the category of clinging (*upādāna*), it is mentioned here as well;
"that" refers to defiled attention,
and "here" refers to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
How was it stated?
Because it is included within the *upādānas* (appropriations);
for *upādāna* is the state in which the afflictions (*kleśa*) are active for the sake of obtaining enjoyments (*bhoga*).
And in that regard, improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*)— which is the application of a distorted mind— is said to be included [within ignorance];
therefore, ignorance is not without a cause,
nor is there any need to add another member beyond the twelve beginning with ignorance.
"And there is no consequence of infinite regress because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) has ignorance as its cause"—
thus said the Elder Vasubandhu, the teacher and preceptor of Ācārya Manoratha.
The Teacher asks: "How so? This is the detailed inquiry:
how is it that improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manaskāra) is included within grasping (upādāna)?
For improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) does not have the nature of grasping (*upādāna*).

If you maintain that it is included within grasping because improper mental attention is associated with grasping by way of association (*samprayoga*), then [it follows that] you accept its inclusion within grasping for that reason.
It would follow that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is also included within those two members of dependent origination, namely craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*),
for it is associated with both craving and ignorance;
and therefore, it should have been stated in that way.
And since that [ignorance] is also included within ignorance, craving, and grasping here, it is thereby stated;
however, one should not say that "it is also stated here because it is included within grasping."
The intention is that one should not maintain such a restriction regarding inclusion within the *upādānas*;
furthermore, even if there were inclusion— as we say even while conceding an inclusion that is impossible— this remains the case.

How is it that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*)? This is understood through scriptural authority (*vijñapti*), for there is no such statement in the Sūtra; for [it would have been stated] "by way of inclusion," and so forth.
If, because improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is included within clinging (*upādāna*),
it is thereby made known that improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*),
then it need not be stated as a separate member [of the dependent origination formula].
Since that [craving] is established by the very mention of "clinging" (*upādāna*),
do craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) also then fall within clinging?
Therefore, because those two are also included therein, it would be possible not to treat them as separate members [of dependent origination].
Since that [ignorance] is established by the very mention of "clinging" (upādāna), and since craving (tṛṣṇā) and ignorance (avidyā) have already been stated as separate factors (aṅga),
this is not a valid rebuttal.
But another says: the Venerable Śrīlāta maintains that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is stated in another sutra to be the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*),
namely in the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna-sūtra*.
"Monks, ignorance also has a cause, has a condition, and has a source," and so on in detail;
"and that too... and so on in detail;
and that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) was taught at the time of contact (*sparśakāla*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Dependent upon the eye and visible forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion"—
this refers to the time of contact, which is the very time of the arising of visual consciousness.
Turbid attention is so called because it proceeds from an improper basis or because it is born of delusion;
"born of delusion" means that which arises from delusion,
as in the phrase "feeling born of contact with ignorance."
Feeling born from contact associated with ignorance is "feeling born of ignorance-contact";
wherever there is feeling born of ignorance-contact,
ignorance is necessarily associated therein.
For feeling that is not associated with ignorance does not become a cause for craving;

thus, it is made known that improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manaskāra), occurring at the time of contact, is established as the condition for the ignorance that co-exists with feeling— this being what is meant by "ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause."
Therefore, ignorance is not without a cause,
because it has improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) as its cause;
nor is any other member [of dependent origination] to be added beyond the twelve.
Because the improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) existing at the time of contact is established as the condition for the ignorance (*avidyā*) that co-exists with feeling (*vedanā*),
there is no consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*),
since that improper mental attention is also said to be born from delusion (*moha*).
"Defiled attention is born of delusion"—
thus this is described as a cycle:
from improper attention comes ignorance, and from ignorance comes improper attention.
Seeing that this rebuttal, moreover, is faulty, the Master begins a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) in order to manifest that fault,
saying "In that case, then," and so forth— that is,
as it was stated in detail according to the Sūtra or by reasoning: "Improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance," and so on.
In that case, when there is the intention to express a different meaning, "now" (tarhi) means "at this time"; this is a specific point of the Blessed One’s teaching.
This was stated elsewhere in a sutra, but it must now be explained here in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
When asked, "By what reasoning does the Venerable Śīlāṭa say that it should not be stated?
the Venerable Śrīlāṭa replied:
"For it is not so," and so forth;
for Arhats possess sensation, yet that sensation does not become a condition for craving.
It is understood that ignorance itself is the condition for feeling and craving;
and since contact is not non-perverted [with respect] to afflicted feeling,
it is understood that contact, too, is indeed accompanied by ignorance.
Since that which was stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* as the condition for feeling is understood to be ignorance, which is the cause of this contact,
it follows by this reasoning that in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, feeling has contact accompanied by ignorance as its condition.
And it is understood that craving has ignorance-conditioned feeling as its condition;

therefore, by the reasoning already stated, and since that [ignorance] was also specified at the time of contact, dependent origination is established here in detail: that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) is the cause of ignorance.

Here it is objected: if, by such statements as "feeling devoid of ignorance does not become a condition for craving," it is understood through internal reasoning alone that improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance and ignorance is the cause of improper mental attention,
then what is the purpose of relying on another sutra to demonstrate the mutual causality between ignorance and improper mental attention?
To this it is replied: This is true;
however, this is merely a logical argument within the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
Since this reasoning is not explicitly stated [here], it must be understood that the purpose of citing another sūtra is to establish this reasoning through explicit statement in that other sūtra;
otherwise, the author of the treatise observes that an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would result.
How is this an over-extension? He says:

it is taught in another sutra that "craving arises dependent on feeling born from contact associated with ignorance," yet for an Arhat who is free from ignorance, feeling does not become a condition for craving.

Furthermore, there is no non-perverted contact for an afflicted feeling, nor is there a perverted contact for an Arhat who is free from ignorance. By this reasoning, even though these two members called contact and feeling are not explicitly mentioned here in this *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, they are understood because they have been taught elsewhere; thus, it follows that these two members need not be stated here, as they have already been taught in another sutra.
If he performs meritorious volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), his consciousness (*vijñāna*) becomes one that leads to merit;
likewise, it becomes one that leads to demerit or one that leads to imperturbability (*āniñjya*).
However, for an Arhat who is free from ignorance regarding volitional formations, there is no consciousness leading to merit, nor any up to consciousness leading to imperturbability.
It follows that this member, *saṃskāra*, is established by reasoning and need not be stated here; likewise,
it is understood through reasoning that aging and death do not occur in the absence of birth.

Otherwise, an undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) would follow, such as that the factor of birth (jāty-aṅga) need not be mentioned; however, this is not at all a valid objection, as has been explained in detail.
The Teacher states his own view:
"How [does one go] from the world beyond to this world? and so forth;
therein, this world is connected with ignorance and formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
In this world, the factors of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are connected to the next world by way of craving, grasping, and becoming;
and that next world consists of birth, as well as aging and death.
Because this much meaning was intended for those to be trained here in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
and because this meaning has already been explained previously.

Because it has been stated, "In order to turn back delusion regarding the prior, the posterior, and the middle," this [objection] is indeed not to be raised; the connection [of the argument] extends in detail up to the point that "the exposition is not incomplete."

For both [categories] consist of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṭadharma*); thus, all conditioned phenomena belonging to the three time periods are dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and for that very reason they are "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). There is no distinction whatsoever between them.
How, then, can they be called "unproduced"?
The intention is that just as future conditioned phenomena are referred to by a prospective designation as "conditioned," so too are they called "dependently originated."
"By means of volition that is formative" (ābhisaṃskārikayā cetanāya):
by saying "formative," he illuminates the specific characteristic of all volitions,
for that [volition] is [the thought], "I shall come to be," "I shall become a human being," and so forth.
Because they are conceived by that [volition] and because they are intended—
such as "I shall become a god" or "I shall become a human"—
therefore future conditioned phenomena are so called.
But this does not contradict the intention that [the designation] is by way of a future name;
for how could those [factors] that are with-outflows (sāsrava) be appropriately intended as such when they are yet to come? Only those that are with-outflows [in the present] can be so intended.
"But as for those [factors] that are untainted and future,
how is it appropriate for them to be intended?
The challenger asks:
If those [factors] were also willed by a wholesome volition with the thought,
"May the untainted factors be attained," then it would follow that even Nirvana could be attained.
If it is argued that even *nirvāṇa* would entail being conditioned (*saṃskṛtatva*) because it is intended as something to be attained— such that one would attain *nirvāṇa*— then,
for this reason, a further argument is presented to show the fault in establishing the conditioned nature of things that have not yet come into existence.
"Because they belong to that same class," and so forth.

Just as there is an extension [of the definition] stating that what is future is not yet "formed" (*rūpyate*) because it belongs to the same class as that which is being formed, so too there is this extension for these future factors:

that because they belong to the same class as phenomena arisen through conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna*), even future factors are "arisen through conditions. Thus, this extension applies to those future ones.
"Because of the state of being cause and fruit" means that since a very same member [of dependent origination] is both the cause and the fruit,
there is no lack of systematic order when this is the case.
Like the near shore and the far shore,
or like cause and effect,
dependent origination is not non-established; nor is that which is dependently originated [non-established], because it depends upon distinct factors.
The cause and effect therein are like that of a mango fruit or like that of a father and son; it is,
for example, like a seed and its sprout.
Just as that in relation to which a cause is established is not the same in relation to which an effect is established,
so too that in relation to which an effect is established [is not the same in relation to which a cause is established].
It is not in relation to that [result] that something is established as a cause;
rather,
it is in relation to the result that a cause is established.
And just as the effect depends upon the cause,
so too, that which one depends upon to be a father is not what one depends upon to be a son.
That in relation to whom one is a son,
in relation to him one is not a father;
what then?
He is called "father" in relation to his son,
and "son" in relation to his father;
yet that [relationship] is not fixed.
In the same way, "this indeed is so" refers to the first alternative regarding impossibility: the future phenomena.
Because they are the cause of other phenomena, they are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) on the grounds that [phenomena] arise from them; however,
they are not themselves "dependently originated" (*pratītyasamutpanna*), because they have not [yet] arisen,
just like the final [moments] of a second Arhat.
Because it has already arisen and because no further fruit arises from it,
the third [alternative] is "other than that."
For an Arhat, the past and present dharmas other than the final [moments] are the fourth [category], namely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
because they lack that fruit and because they are non-arising.
Why indeed are these called "wishes" (*iṣṭayaḥ*)?

[They refer to] dependent origination according to states (*āvasthika-pratītyasamutpāda*), such as: "There is dependent origination, but not dependently originated [phenomena]," and so forth, regarding ignorance concerning the past (*pūrvānta*).
Since it is stated that ignorance alone [is the limb] and not the other aggregates, he shows that this is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), namely, that ignorance alone is the limb.
"Of definitive meaning" means that its meaning has been analyzed;
the Sūtra on the Simile of the Elephant's Footprint exists,
and therein there are also other [elements] such as form and so forth.
Just as among those [parts] such as hair and body hair it is not merely the earth-element,
so too here the designation should be according to what is predominant.
Likewise, here too in the Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra, among the twelve states consisting of the five aggregates, there would be a designation of whichever [factor] is predominant in whichever [state].
In the state where ignorance is predominant, there would be the designation "ignorance";
in those states where formations and so forth are predominant, there would be the designation of "formations" and so forth;
yet, even there, other factors such as form, feeling, and the rest do exist.
"For it is not there," and so forth;
for in that sūtra, hair and the rest are not indicated by means of the earth-element, as in the question:
"What are hair and the rest? They are the earth-element."
Since this would be an incomplete description of these [parts] such as hair and so forth—
because there are indeed other things there such as visible form (*rūpa*)—
hair and the rest must have the nature of visible form and so on, and not merely the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*). Which [is it]?
Regarding "hair and body hair," the internal earth element does not exist apart from or beyond hair and so forth; thus,
this is the complete definition of the earth element.

In the same way here as well, in this sutra, the exposition of ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth, is indeed complete and not incomplete; tears, snot,
and the like are not recited therein in that sutra.
Therefore, he shows that the earth element contained therein has not been mentioned and is thus incomplete,
by saying "or let it be exactly so," and so forth;
for just as there is a remainder of the earth element in tears, snot, and so on, because they were not mentioned.
In the same way, let ignorance remain as the remainder, since one employs the word "if" thinking that it might be possible to demonstrate [the remainder] but it cannot be demonstrated;

for all such bases of ignorance have already been stated, namely: ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, ignorance regarding the intermediate period, ignorance regarding cause, ignorance regarding the Dharma, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha, and so forth.

But as for the inclusion of other categories such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth within ignorance (*avidyā*), what is its basis? [The position is that] "ignorance is the state of the five aggregates," for it is not logical that feeling and the others should themselves be ignorance;
thus, there is a fixed rule regarding existence and non-existence.
That for which the existence and non-existence are respectively determined by the existence and non-existence of another is indeed the [causal] member.
Since the existence of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) occurs when ignorance (*avidyā*) exists, and their non-existence occurs when it does not, ignorance alone is the member,
and not feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
For it is not the case that, when feeling and the other [factors] exist, there are in Arhats those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) which produce the member of consciousness; this is the meaning.
Therefore, he says:
And even though the five aggregates exist, conditioned phenomena do not arise; this is the detailed explanation.
Even though the five aggregates exist, in the state of arhatship, consciousness that leads to merit, up to consciousness that leads to the imperturbable, does not arise.
The meaning is that there is no rebirth-linking consciousness;
it goes to this or that birth, thus it is "approaching," as in "merit-approaching consciousness" (*puṇyopaga-vijñāna*). It approaches merit.
In this way, up to the attainment of the imperturbable (*āniñjyopaga*), even though the five aggregates exist, craving, grasping, and so forth do not occur during the state free from ignorance; thus,
the meaning of the Sūtra is exactly as it has been explained.
The meaning is that only those factors beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) as they have been enumerated are to be understood;
therefore, even though the aggregates (*skandhas*) exist, they are not conditions for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, and thus they are not a "limb" [of dependent origination].
If, however, they were future, they would not be dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
As for what was said— that the first alternative, "future phenomena," contradicts the Sūtra—
it would follow that birth, old age, and death would not be dependently originated.
And it has been said: "Ignorance [extends] up to birth, aging, and death. Alternatively, as for the detailed explanation:
if even the members of birth, aging, and death are accepted as being dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), [then what need is there to mention the others?]
If one were to maintain that there is no establishment of those two in the future time,
then the arrangement of the three sections would be disrupted—
namely, two each for the prior and posterior limits, and eight in the middle.
Thus say the followers of other schools, namely the noble Mahīśāsakas,
because arising is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
This arising which is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is conceived as permanent by those belonging to other schools; however,
it has been stated that there are these three conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) of the conditioned.
The intention is that because origination, cessation, and the alteration of duration are also perceived in the conditioned,
it is impermanent due to possessing the characteristics of the conditioned; yet you might say that even these characteristics are permanent.
Therefore, he says:
"And it is not logical for an eternal distinct entity to be the characteristic of the impermanent;
for neither nirvāṇa nor space is the characteristic of anything impermanent."
For prior to the arising of the characterized object, to what would that characteristic belong as its characteristic?
And once the characterized object has perished, to what would it belong? Thus, [the notion] that there is "arising" is not tenable; such is the detailed argument.

Furthermore, according to the Sautrāntika system, origination (*utpāda*) is characterized by the coming into being of what was previously non-existent; since the arising of a phenomenon occurs only at that very moment,
how could this unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) origination, according to your own view, have any connection with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors?

Just as there is a relationship between rice and cooking characterized by agent and action, such that one says "the cooking of rice" and not "the cooking of space," in the same way, what is this relationship of [suffering] with ignorance and the rest?

Since the dependent origination of those factors, such as ignorance and the rest, is thus described, and since the meaning of the term [pratītyasamutpāda] would otherwise be incoherent, it is "arising having reached conditions" (pratyayaṃ prāpya samudbhavaḥ).
Regarding the meaning of the term *pratītyasamutpāda*:
how can it be both "eternal" (*nitya*) and yet "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?
[For] the prefix *prati* has the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*).
The meaning is that it indicates attainment;
the root *iti* has the sense of "going," according to the meaning of the verbal root.
Regarding the phrase "because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*):
verbal roots indeed have multiple meanings, and the prefix *prati* indicates attainment; thus, this root *iti*, having abandoned its sense of motion, comes to mean attainment.
The root *pad* means "existence" (*sattā*), as in the statement "the root *pad* is used in the sense of existence";
by that [root], for that reason.
Because the rule for the suffix *ktvā* applies when there is a prior action,
according to the statement "for two actions having the same agent, the one occurring at the earlier time [takes *ktvā*]," and because,
according to the Sautrāntika school, no such thing exists prior to its arising.
Furthermore, since there is no action without an agent,
and because the establishment of action depends upon the existence of an agent,
he says here: "And regarding this..."
The Teacher sets forth this objection of the grammarian in a verse: "If [the effect] exists prior to its arising, it would have already attained [its existence]."
Because it does not exist, [an agent] is not tenable;
for one who is non-existent is never observed performing actions such as bathing.
If you think that [the agent] performs the action of dependence and the action of origination simultaneously—thus:
Having performed [the action], why is the suffix *ktvā* not established here?
Because of the rule regarding priority in time—

that is, because of the statement that the suffix *ktvā* occurs when there are two actions with the same agent and the one [expressed by it] is prior in time— the suffix *ktvā* would not be established.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of further arising": if one imagines that what has already arisen arises yet again, there follows the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),
because it would arise repeatedly in the second, third, and subsequent moments, leading to the consequence of non-termination (*aniṣṭhā*).

Now, regarding the detailed explanation "the future": if the future has not yet acquired its own nature (*alabdhātmaka*), how can agency (*kartṛtva*) be established for that which is non-existent and has not acquired its own being? Or, how can an action (*kriyā*) be established if it is without an agent?
Since this is so, therefore, in whatever state a thing arises for a grammarian who knows words,
in that very same state he perceives it;
what then are these states?
"What is its state? "In what state is it?
"It is facing production; it is the future.
Not every future thing, however, is produced.
What then?
It is that which is facing toward arising;
it is directed toward arising.
The meaning is "desirous of arising"; it is said that while in that very state— specifically, the state of being oriented toward arising— it is perceived.
"This is not established," and so forth;
why is this grammatical system of the grammarians— the formal arrangement of the agent and the action— [not established]?

Since no difference is observed between the "becoming" (bhūti) conceived as an action and the "worthy one" (arhat) conceived as the agent of becoming, there is therefore no fallacy in such expressions as "it becomes," "it arises," or "it comes into being";
and regarding this, he says: "And here [the Sūtra] states..."
He demonstrates the process according to that established tenet with the detailed passage beginning: "Just as that which is non-existent arises."
The meaning is that just as a non-existent thing, one whose self-nature has not been acquired, arises,
so too does it "approach" (pratyeti) while being non-existent.
If it is conceived that what already exists, or what has already attained its own nature, arises,
then one would have to say that what has already arisen arises; this leads to an infinite regress.
If that which has already arisen arises again, there would be an infinite regress; because of this, another undesirable consequence follows.
For, according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine, only what exists arises, not what does not exist. With reference to this, he says: "Or [if it were] existent even previously."
The word "vā" (or) signifies an alternative view:
if your position is that "the existent arises," then for us as well, the existent arises.
Since, according to the Vaibhāṣika system, future phenomena exist,
and according to the Sautrāntika system, the seeds of the producing dharmas are present, why is this [objection] stated?
And there is nothing whatsoever that exists prior to its arising which, having depended [on conditions], arises at a later time;
or else, if it is the case that only what already exists arises.
It follows that the jar must exist as established by itself even prior [to its production], without depending on the lump of clay and so forth;
others, however, explain:
"Or it exists even before, though not yet having reached completion."
Thus,
lest there be the undesirable consequence [of non-arising],
one maintains that "the non-existent arises."
Furthermore, that very same point is restated: "Just as that which is non-existent arises, so too does it pass away"; thus our position is established, as should be stated as before.

Regarding what was also stated— that the rule for the suffix *ktvā* applies when there are two actions by a single agent, specifically to the action occurring at the earlier time— he says, in order to demonstrate that this is not invariably so: "The suffix *ktvā* occurs even in cases of simultaneity," and so forth.
The rule for the suffix *ktvā* is observed even when the actions are simultaneous;
for example:
"Having reached the lamp, the darkness departed."
Thus,
in this context, the meaning is not that darkness first reaches the lamp and afterwards departs and perishes;
what then?
At that very moment, darkness perishes upon reaching the lamp;
if it is thought that this occurs immediately after and not simultaneously, that is not so.
Therefore, this is further stated:
"Or he sleeps with his mouth wide open."
For he does not first open his mouth— that is, gape— and afterwards lie down;
rather,
it is one who lies down while opening his mouth.
It is said, "He sleeps having opened his mouth";
now, if it is thought that he first opens his mouth and afterwards sleeps, therefore [the author] says:
If [the action] occurs later, why would one not say that someone who opens his mouth and then lies down after closing it again "lies down with his mouth open"?
And it is not said by him that one who sleeps with his mouth open is known [to be so].
"He lies with his mouth open"— so it is said;
however, others,
such as the Venerable Śrīlāta, maintain that the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*).
The desire to pervade all various readings and legal cases by means of both action and quality is *vīpsā*; the prefix *prati* expresses this.
Those who are effective (*sādhu*) in going (*iti*) or moving are called *ityāḥ*.
In this context, the suffix *yat* is used in the sense of "suitable for" (*sādhur*); thus, "perishing in going" (*itau vinaṣṭau*) means they are non-abiding (*anavasthāyinaḥ*).
The prefix *sam-* indicates the sense of conjunction (*samavāya*), while the root *pad-* preceded by the prefix *ut-* signifies manifestation (*prādurbhāva*),
due to a modification of the root's original meaning.
The repetition [of the word] *prati* in the phrase "toward each respective collection" (*tāṃ tāṃ sāmagrīṃ prati*) indicates its distributive sense;
thus, there is the arising of these perishable things through their aggregation.
No single phenomenon arises by itself, because form and the other [aggregates] are necessarily co-arising.
In the desire realm, an atom that is without sound consists of eight substances;
likewise, mind and mental factors necessarily arise together.
By this rule,
"this is the conceptualization," and so forth— the detailed exposition beginning with "the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*)"— is found right here in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.
In this case, how will [the expression] "visual consciousness arises depending upon the eye and visible forms" be possible?
For a compound such as *pratītyacakṣūṃṣi*—meaning "the eyes that are depended upon"—is not possible because the meaning is untenable;
rather, the meaning understood is that visual consciousness arises having depended upon, that is, having reached, the eye and visible forms.
Therefore, that objection remains exactly as it was; the statement made at length— that "this meaning of the word is not logical,
for how can the rule for the suffix *ktvā* apply to the earlier of two actions performed by a single agent"— is not tenable.
One does not eat after having bathed;
likewise, visual consciousness does not exist prior to its arising,
such that it could arise at a later time depending upon the eye and visible forms as its preceding conditions.
Nor is it the case that an action is without an agent;
therefore, he states two synonymous expressions for the sake of emphasis:
"when this exists," were only this much to be said...
It is understood that formations do not arise only when ignorance exists,
but also when something else exists,
just as visual consciousness arises when the eye exists.
It is not restricted to the meaning "only when the eye exists," for by that [first formulation] it is understood that [the visual consciousness arises] also when the visible form exists;
however, by the second formulation, "from the arising of this, that arises," one restricts the meaning precisely to the previous formulation.
Or it is to demonstrate the succession of the members [of dependent origination], showing that "from the arising of this very thing, this arises, and not from anything else."

When this member exists— that is, when the member of ignorance exists— this member of volitional formations comes to be; furthermore, from the arising of this member of volitional formations, this member of consciousness arises.
In this way, the succession of the other factors should also be stated,
or rather, the succession of births.
What [is the point]?
It continues: "He spoke two formulations in order to demonstrate.

The full explanation is as follows: he spoke two formulations in order to demonstrate the status of ignorance and the other factors as conditions, both directly and through a succession in the continuum.
The phrase "this being, that comes to be" (*asmin satīdaṃ bhavati*) demonstrates the state of being a direct condition,
while "from the arising of this, that arises" (*asyotpādād idam utpadyate*) demonstrates it through a succession. In that context,
when immediately after ignorance (*avidyā*) afflicted formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise, that is the direct [condition].
But when wholesome states arise through a succession [of causes],
because of the absence of ignorance during that wholesome state,
what [more] is there?
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the direct condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and [it is] for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the subsequent members through a mediated succession.
This is what is meant:

when the member of ignorance exists, the member of the formative forces comes to be; from the arising of this member of the formative forces, this member of consciousness arises—[arising] directly conditioned by ignorance in the case of the first, and mediately in the case of the others.
The elder Vasuvarman states that all of this is intended as a refutation of the teacher's [Vasubandhu's] view; specifically,
the first formulation is for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), which holds that an entity comes into being even in the absence of a cause.

In order to refute the doctrine of an eternal cause, the Teacher stated with the second [verse], "And nothing arises from that which is eternal and unproduced, such as *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and so forth," and he elaborated on this with the words,
"But in this conceptualization... and so on.
The inclusion of the first formulation is redundant;

for by this very formulation—"it arises in this"—the existence of the cause and the causality of that which possesses arising are established through the refutation of both positions characterized by "no-cause" and "eternal-cause. Consequently, the first formulation becomes purposeless.
"There are some, then," and so forth;

there are certain proponents who, when the self exists—that is, when it exists as a basis, serving as the basis for ignorance—imagine the existence, that is, the arising, of the formative forces and so on: namely, the formative forces, consciousness, name-and-form, and the rest.
And because they postulate the arising of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth from the arising of ignorance and the rest— namely, ignorance, formative forces, and so on—
it follows from this reason that [the Blessed One] established and reiterated this in order to set aside and refute the conceptual construction of those proponents.
What did he say?
"From the arising of which, up to the origination of the aggregates"—
that is to say, from the arising of which something arises,
when that very thing exists, this comes to be.
It is not in another self;
that is to say, conditioned formations have ignorance as their condition,
for it is only when ignorance exists that conditioned formations come to be.
Not from anything else; thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering:
how is it that, conditioned by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair come to be?
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering;
for it is only when there is birth that aging, death, and the rest come to be, and not in the presence of any other self.
For otherwise, if it were stated merely that "when this exists, that comes to be," speakers might say:
"When the self exists as a support, and when ignorance and the other factors exist, the formative forces and so forth come to be.
On the other hand, if one were to state only the second formulation—"from the arising of this, that arises"—[the same misunderstanding would follow].
Even so, they might still imagine that it is true that formations and the rest arise from the arising of ignorance and the other [links],
while the self exists as their substratum.
Therefore, he determines it by means of two formulations:
that from whose arising something arises,
and when that very thing exists, this comes to be.
The former masters (pūrvācāryāḥ) maintain that it does not exist as a support while another self exists;
they say this for the purpose of making known that [the self] has not been abandoned and for the purpose of making known its arising.
He shows by means of the second [member] that when ignorance exists and has not been abandoned, the formative forces (saṃskāra) come to be and are not abandoned;
and so on, up until: when birth exists and has not been abandoned, old age, death, and so forth come to be.
"They are not abandoned;
rather, they arise precisely because of its arising"— this is for the purpose of demonstrating duration and arising, according to another, namely, the Venerable Śrīlāta.
To that end, he states two formulations:
first, "As long as there is a stream of causes, so long is there a stream of effects";
and second, "Because of the very arising of the cause, the effect arises."
