But since the subject under discussion is "arising"—
in the context of the statement, "O monks, I shall teach you dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)—
what occasion or what relevance is there for a statement concerning "stability"?

By the statement "when this exists, that comes to be," it is described that as long as the stream of causes persists, so long does the stream of effects persist; thus the meaning of its "abiding" is explained.
Furthermore, for what purpose would the Blessed One state this in a reversed order, since arising necessarily occurs first?
Since stability is dependent upon arising— considering that stability is [only] subsequent to arising—
one would have to state first: "from the arising of this, that arises."
Subsequently, [one understands]: "When this exists, that comes to be;
however, it is not thus, therefore this meaning is not so."
"He says again" refers to that same venerable teacher, Bhadanta Śrīlāta, who replies.
The phrase "If this...
and so forth shows that it would have been more appropriate to state simply, "When this exists, this does not exist," rather than employing a negative formulation to indicate non-existence.
And previously, he would have stated that "the effect arises" as "from the arising of this,
that arises," because destruction is preceded by arising.

It is stated in the Sūtra: "Conditioned by birth, aging, death, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and despair arise. It should be understood that these are indeed subsumed within aging and death, and thus do not constitute a separate limb.
Among them, these occur due to the transformation of objects—whether categorized as sentient or non-sentient—and due to the transformation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
Discursive thought associated with mental distress is sorrow;
lamentation is the outburst of speech arising from sorrow.
Suffering and mental distress have already been explained.
Distress (*upāyāsa*) is dejection (*daurmanasya*) whose momentum has been interrupted, preceded by sorrow and lamentation; others say that distress is exhaustion (*śrama*).
"For the fool," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
The fool, an ordinary person, not understanding that there is "merely formations"— the inclusion of the word "merely" being for the purpose of negating a self—
thereby demonstrates unshared ignorance (*āveṇiky-avidyā*).

Adhering to and established in the view of self and the conceit "I am," one undertakes through the body and so forth— namely, by means of body, speech, and mind— the threefold karma characterized as meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
Regarding the term *āniñjya*, it is a different verbal root, *ig*, of which this is the form.
This form of *ejati* is either *āneñjya* (the immovable) or read as *puṇyaṃ āyatisukhārtham* (merit for the sake of future happiness),
meaning for the sake of happiness in a future birth.
Is wholesome karma belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) for the sake of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure called "immovable" (*āniñjya*)?
Wholesome karma pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness is for the sake of pleasure up to the third dhyāna;
above that, it is for the sake of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
"Non-meritorious [action] for the sake of happiness in this life" means that it is performed out of regard for the happiness of this world, and not out of regard for future happiness;
"by the force of the projection of karma" means by the force of the momentum imparted by the aforementioned karma.
It goes to each respective destination, such as the hells and so forth, by way of the movement of a flame;
just as it is said that a flame attached to long grass moves along.

Likewise, because the series of consciousnesses is connected with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it goes to this or that destination (*gati*)—even one in an extremely remote location—by means of that connection with the intermediate state.

And having established it thus: if, starting from the mind of rebirth-linking in the intermediate state which has the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition, up until the moment of birth, this entire series of consciousness consisting of the six groups of consciousness is intended as the "consciousness conditioned by the formative forces," then [the scriptural statement] becomes logically consistent.
In the explanation of the limb of consciousness— that is, the explanation of the third limb—
what is consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness.
Otherwise, if the continuity of the six groups of consciousness were not intended,
then "consciousness conditioned by formative forces" would have been intended as referring only to the mind at rebirth;
in that case, it would not have been stated that there are "six groups of consciousness."
However, it should be stated thus: "What is consciousness?
It is mental consciousness."
For at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*), the occurrence of the five groups of sensory consciousness is not possible,
because the connection of rebirth is established by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone;
[the same applies to] the severance and reconnection [of roots of merit], detachment, falling away, death, and rebirth.
Because it is stated that "it is intended as mental consciousness alone," and because it is explained in this way in the *Vibhaṅga*.
Because in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, the division of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is explained as follows:
"What is name?
It consists of the four formless aggregates (*skandha*)."
What is form? Whatever is form— in detail, as far as this which is both form and name.
Both of these together are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa);
"craving for sensual pleasures" (kāmatṛṣṇā) refers to craving belonging to the realm of sensual desire (kāmāvacarī tṛṣṇā).
Craving for form refers to that which exists in the three dhyānas of pleasure and in the fourth [dhyāna] of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Craving for the state that is neither painful nor pleasant is craving for the formless realm;
this constitutes the grasping of desire and the other [clingings] pertaining to the formless realm.
The meaning is that "clinging" (upādāna) refers to sensual desire, views, rules and observances, and the doctrine of self.
Regarding the "five strands of sensual pleasure" (pañca kāmaguṇāḥ): they are called "sensual pleasures" (kāmāḥ) because they are desired.
They are called "guṇas" because they are multiplied; thus, the desires themselves are the guṇas, and these are the "qualities of desire.
But what, then, are they?
Regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles,
as for the sixty-two views, they are to be understood through the Brahmajāla Sūtra, according to the Brahmajāla.
Regarding "the dog-vow, the cow-vow, and so forth," by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the deer-vow and others are included;
these belong to the Nirgranthas and other such [ascetics].

By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of Pāṇḍarabhikṣu and others; the detailed explanation beginning with "brāhmaṇa" refers to the staff and deerskin of the Brāhmaṇas, and the matted hair and ashes of the Pāśupatas.

The triple staff and tonsure of the wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and by the two initial words [of the compound], the carrying of skulls and so forth by the *kāpālika*s and others are included; the undertaking of these is the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*).
The "doctrine of self" (ātmavāda) is so called because there is a discourse regarding a self within this [context],
as it has been said:
"Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive a self..."
"All of them perceive these very five aggregates of clinging," and so forth.
Others say that the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) constitute the "doctrine of self" (*ātmavāda*).
By stating that there is an "appropriation of the doctrine of self" because of the non-existence of a self, he demonstrates the purpose for introducing the word "doctrine" (*vāda*).
The "fool" refers to the unlearned ordinary person;
he is a fool who lacks the wisdom acquired at birth, which arises from the latencies of previous practice.
He who lacks that which is born of scripture is unlearned;
he who lacks that which is born of realization— that is, born of the clear comprehension of the truths— is likewise [unlearned].
That ordinary person has fallen into conventional designation; thus according to perception and according to worldly usage.
The meaning is "followed in that manner";
"of them" refers to desire and so forth;
"desire-attachment" (chanda-rāga) [is the specific state].
Chanda is the longing for objects not yet attained;
rāga is passion for those [objects] already attained; that which is chanda-rāga toward those [objects] such as sensual pleasures (kāma) and so forth—[that is what is meant here].
That is the grasping;
however, it is not simply ignorance as previously described, because of the distinction between the two types of views.
The intention is that "appropriations" means that which pertains to renewed existence, i.e., that which has rebirth as its fruit.
"This here is of existence" means that this is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of existence;
[it is said] by way of the descent of consciousness (*vijñānāvakrānti*).

By way of the progression of a flame and through connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), future birth is "birth" (*jāti*), which consists of the five aggregates because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As for "aging-and-death" (*jarāmaraṇa*), it is as explained in the Sūtra;
therein, what is aging?
That which is baldness, graying of hair, and so forth;
what is death?
It is the passing away, the falling away of those various sentient beings from their respective states, and so forth.
He shows the meaning of "of the solitary," which is "devoid of a self," by [the phrase] "of the great" (mahataḥ),
meaning "of the mass of suffering" (duḥkhaskandhasya), that is, of the aggregate of suffering, which is without beginning or end.

But that very Vaibhāṣika principle which was stated previously— that the twelve states consisting of five aggregates are the twelve links— is what applies here, such that "ignorance" (avidyā) is not [the mere absence of knowledge].
There would also be the undesirable consequence [of applying this definition] to the eye and so forth;
for the eye, ear, and other [senses] would then follow as being ignorance,
on the grounds that they too are not knowledge (*vidyā*).
If ignorance (*avidyā*) were the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*), meaning that it would be a non-entity (*adravya*),
this would not be tenable.
By teaching [the term] in the sense of being a condition (*pratyaya*),
he shows that the negative particle *naÑ* expresses opposition, as in the case of "the opposite of that" (*tadvipakṣa*).
He shows that it is not merely an exclusion (paryudāsa) in the sense that "anyone other than a friend" is meant,
nor is it a simple negation (abhāva) of the measure.
He shows that it does not mean "non-existence" by stating:
"and non-dharma, non-benefit, non-action, etc."; by the word "etc.," illogicality, non-conventionality, non-humanity, and so forth are included.
"Being the opposites of dharma and so forth" means being the opposites of dharma, artha, kārya, yukti, vyavahāra, manuṣya, and so on;
it does not mean any other things such as the eyes and so forth that are distinct from dharma and the rest.
Nor is there an absence of phenomena and so forth; likewise for ignorance—this is the detailed explanation.
From where is this [known]?
Because they are taught as being conditions— namely, "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces"—
it is not logical that ignorance should be taught as a condition for other things such as the eye and so forth.
Because conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impossible for Arhats,
and because non-existents such as a rabbit's horn lack the status of being conditions (pratyaya).
Since it is stated in the sūtras that "from the fetter (saṃyojana) up to the bond (yoga), ignorance (avidyā) is spoken of"— that is, from the fetter of ignorance up to the bond of ignorance—
it cannot be the case that [ignorance] is merely a non-existence.
The meaning is that [the eye and so forth] cannot be the fetters and so on;
nor can the eye and so forth be of such a nature, as is the subject under discussion;
and since that [view] has the nature of a view, it is not logical for it to be ignorance.
Since view (*dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are listed separately as fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth,
that which is not a view is the afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) associated with attachment (*rāga*) and the other [defilements].
"Because of its association with that view" means because of its association with ignorance (*avidyā*).

And how is it that view is associated with ignorance? Because delusion, which has the characteristic of ignorance, is recited among the universal defilements (kleśamahābhūmi), and all those belonging to the universal defilement stage are associated with the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).
It is understood that ignorance is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other views, which have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature;
therefore, ignorance is not wisdom,
because two distinct substances of wisdom cannot be associated.
"Wisdom defiled by ignorance does not become pure"—
this is the illustration by which it is shown that ignorance is a distinct entity from wisdom.

Furthermore, it is not logical that wisdom itself should be a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) of that very same wisdom; for in the teaching on the secondary afflictions of wisdom, ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a distinct entity from wisdom, is specified as the secondary affliction.
Therefore, it says "just as [the mind] is other than passion," and so forth.

"Being intermingled, it is not purified" means that wholesome wisdom (*kuśalā prajñā*) arising in a subsequent moment is not purified when it is being intermingled by afflicted wisdom (*kliṣṭā prajñā*) arising in the intervening moments.
Why is that necessarily "enveloped by passion" (*rāgaparyavasthita*)?
The meaning is that it is associated with passion; however,
it is "afflicted" by passion in such a way that the passion is not actively manifesting.

By the implantation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), that [mind] becomes impaired; when one exerts effort to turn away those predispositions—that is, that functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*)—that mind is liberated.
Thus, afflicted wisdom (*prajñā*) impaired by ignorance does not become pure.
Therefore, he shows that there is no fault in either wisdom or ignorance,
for who can prevent one from conceptualizing?
He states that this is merely a conceptual construction, independent of any scriptural authority.
As for the Venerable Śrīlāta, who maintains that all afflictions are ignorance—
it is he who thinks thus.
"Ignorance" (avidyā) is a general designation for all afflictions;
there is no such thing as "ignorance" existing apart from the afflictions such as attachment and the rest. Why, then, should it be considered in this way?
"From the Buddha’s sūtra:
'O Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, because one does not understand and does not understand, it is therefore called ignorance (avidyā).
Thus, even afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have the nature of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*), for they are misapprehensions."
"For that [opponent] also, for this very reason," and so forth;
for that venerable teacher (*bhadanta*), by this very statement of negation, there is a refutation— that is, a denial— of his own position, as the words "of his view" must be supplied.
To the question "How so?", he says:
For if it were of the nature of all afflictions (*kleśa*), it would not be mentioned separately among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth;
that is, it would not be mentioned separately as the "fetter of ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) among the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) and the others.
Because they are not distinct from the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*),
after stating "attachment is a bond" and "aversion is a bond," [it says] "delusion is a bond";
and after stating "the latent tendency of sensual desire" (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) and so forth, [it says] "the latent tendency of ignorance" (*avidyānuśaya*).
Why is it that among the floods (*ogha*) "the flood of ignorance" is not mentioned separately, as it is among the yokes (*yoga*) where "the yoke of ignorance" is mentioned?
Because they do not associate with one another;
for vision does not associate with vision, nor does passion associate with passion.

Furthermore, ignorance associated with views and so forth has been described as belonging to the great ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*); because of the rule regarding association with the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the mind would also have to be described as being defiled by ignorance alone.

It would not have been said that "the mind defiled by passion is not liberated," because the fact that it is defiled by passion and so forth is already established by the very statement that it is defiled by ignorance.
If it is thought that it was stated in that way for the sake of specification, [we reply:]...
If it were said that "the mind defiled by ignorance characterized by attachment is not liberated," then one would have to provide a qualification for wisdom as well—
specifying whether it is by attachment, aversion, or pride— lest there be the undesirable consequence of [wisdom] being understood as including all afflictions.
If it is argued that [the qualification] is intended [only for the mind],
then the qualification should not be applied to the mind either;
one would simply have to say, "The mind defiled by ignorance is not liberated."
"Clear manifestation," "wisdom," and "knowledge" have one and the same meaning;
likewise, the fault is the same as in the case of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, what is the meaning of "non-manifestation"?
If it is non-manifestation,
then there is the undesirable consequence that it would apply to the eyes and so forth as well;
if, on the other hand, it is the absence of manifestation, then [the same fault follows].
This being so, if nothing [were the case],
it would not be logical; therefore,
it must be another distinct entity that is the opposite of clear manifestation (*samprakhyāna*).
Thus, this very thing is not known in the same way that it is not known what ignorance (avidyā) is.
"Of such a kind" means, in detail,
that it is manifested by the power of karma;
therefore, the intrinsic nature of ignorance is to be understood through its functional activity.
There exists a certain dharma which is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*); thus, its function is to be the opposite of knowledge.
For example: "What is the eye?
It is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that is the basis of visual consciousness."
But is it not the case that its definition as "translucent matter" (*rūpaprasāda*) is established by its intrinsic nature?
No, because it is not perceptible.
And because it is always inferable from visual consciousness,
the notion "I am" is the state of being a sentient being; this is for the purpose of making it known.
The meaning intended by that Elder was not grasped;
furthermore, the Sautrāntikas describe ignorance— or pride— as being distinguished by its various modes.

"That which is stated in the Sūtra," and so forth; the intention of Bhadanta Dharmatrāta is that the term "of the *mayatās*" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) in its various divisions, because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and the others are taught separately.
The Teacher said:
"This state of 'mayatā' exists;
the state of 'mayatā' is mentioned in the Sūtra."
In that context, since it is indicated by a genus-term, it is expressed in the singular;
but for what reason is it determined that "it" refers to ignorance?
"It is ignorance," says the Venerable Dharmatrāta, clarifying his own intention because it cannot be said to be any other affliction.
Why is it not possible?
Because craving, views, and the conceit "I am" are mentioned separately; thus the Teacher says:

The intention is that it would indeed be another form of pride; distinct from the pride of "I am" (asmimāna), it would be one of the other six types of pride, and thus it is *mayatā*, not ignorance (*avidyā*).
But here, when further investigated, much that must be said arises;
for when this branch of "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is further investigated, this extensive treatise arises,
as has been stated.
Therefore, let this matter rest; let it be just this much.
Or rather, it would simply be another form of valid cognition (māna), and not ignorance (avidyā).
If one were to further investigate by asking, "From where does this [follow]? and so forth, much would have to be said by way of successive replies;
therefore, let this rest—meaning, enough with further investigation.
Now, regarding "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*):
immediately after the designation of the member of ignorance (*avidyā*), the member of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) should be designated,
and following that, the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Why has this been introduced by bypassing that [previous point]? Regarding this matter, the Teacher will say here:
"That which was said, and that which is yet to be said, is other."
Thus form has been explained in detail:
"Form consists of the five sense-faculties, the five objects, and non-informative matter alone."
Regarding this, the detailed explanation is "by way of name, faculty, and object":
by way of name, by way of faculty, and by way of object, it bends toward objects such as form and so forth; thus it is called "name" (*nāma*).
To the question, "By the power of which name? he asks because of the two-fold nature of names; he explains it as being by the power of the conventional name (*ācara*).
"That which is known in the world," and so forth; [this refers to] that which causes the cognition of a collection, such as "cow" or "horse."
"Form," "taste"— these,
which cause the cognition of a single object, namely this tetrad of aggregates beginning with feeling, are expressed by the word "name."

Because, by virtue of that name and by virtue of the formation of a conceptual designation (*saṃjñākaraṇa*), one inclines toward or proceeds toward objects even when they are not directly perceived, thinking, "This is the meaning of this name"; whereas, by virtue of the sense-faculties and their objects, one inclines toward or arises [with cognition] toward visible forms and so forth when they are directly perceived— this is the meaning.
And with respect to the name as well, it inclines by virtue of its object, thinking, "This is the name of this object";
but for what reason does it possess the status of being a name?

For what reason does this name, characterized by the act of producing a designation, possess the quality of being a "name" (*nāmatva*) with respect to those various objects? It is because that name— which consists of the four aggregates— bends toward (*namayati*), that is, directs itself toward, those objects.
Therefore, its status as a "name" (nāman) is established by the fact that it causes [the mind] to bend; having thus considered it a name, it is placed here— this is the detailed explanation.
At the time of death, when the body has been cast aside, the formless aggregates—feeling and the rest—are called "name" (nāman) because they bend toward and go toward another birth.
As it has been said:

"Indeed, when one has died and passed away, his kinsmen either burn this putrid body with fire, or cast it into water, or bury it in the earth; or it undergoes drying up, destruction, and total exhaustion by wind and sun."

Furthermore, that which is called "mind," or "intellect," or "consciousness"— when it is cultivated by faith and cultivated by ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom— that becomes upward-tending, tending toward distinction, and leading to rebirth in heaven in the future.

The six sense bases have been explained: the eye and so forth are the translucent forms that serve as the supports for their respective consciousnesses; consciousness is the individual representation [of objects], and it is also the mind base (*manāyatana*).
In this regard,

how can there be a conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) of the mental faculty (*manas*), which has already ceased, with a future phenomenon such as form (*rūpa*) that is yet to arise, and with the present mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
This [conjunction] is the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
The effect is mental consciousness;
the causes are the mind-faculty and the phenomena, such as form and so forth.
Or, "having a single purpose" (*ekakāryārtha*) means that the purpose itself is a single purpose; the meaning is "the state of having a single purpose."
How is it that they have a single purpose? It is said: all three of them—the mind-faculty and the others—become conducive and favorable toward the arising of contact;
thus, this is the "six-by-six" exposition of the Dharma.
"Six sextads are in this" means it is a "six-sextad" because of the occurrence of the sixfold sets of internal and external [bases], consciousness, contact, feeling, and craving;
this serves as the indicator for the "six groups of contact."

For if there were non-difference [between them], then when the sense-faculties, objects, and consciousnesses have already been mentioned, the mention of the group of contacts and speech would be redundant;
consequently, the "sixfold-six" nature [of the bases] would be lost, lest feeling and craving become separate from the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
If separate existence were to result from separate designation,
then since feeling and craving are also designated separately from the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*),
those two— feeling and craving— would also have to exist separately from the sphere of mental objects.
And their separate existence is not admitted because they are included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*); thus there is no fault— this is the detailed explanation.

"This is not a fault," as has been stated; for even apart from sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), there exists—that is, is present—the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) which has the nature of perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth.
"And it is not thus," and so on in detail:

for you who assert that "contact (*sparśa*) is the coming together of these three," there cannot exist another triad of organ, object, and consciousness that is not contact, distinct from the triad of organ, object, and consciousness that constitutes contact itself.
If there were to be an inclusion here in this sūtra of that which remains—

namely, "the six groups of contact"— then, even though feeling and craving are not separate from those three elements that constitute contact due to their functional necessity, it is nevertheless appropriate to designate them separately for the sake of the needs of those to be trained.

However, for you who maintain that contact is merely the conjunction [of the three], it is not logical to designate the "six groups of contact" as a separate category for any purpose; because by the expression "six groups of contact," the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness is already stated, it follows that those [three] would not be mentioned separately. Therefore, the "Dharma-discourse of the six hexads" would not be established for you, whereas for me, it is established.

Even though there is mention of a hexad consisting of contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), since there exists a hexad of sense-faculties, consciousnesses, and objects— such as the sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and so forth— which are distinct from those [three], it is established that because of the separate designation "six groups of contact" (*ṣaṭ sparśakāyāḥ*), there is a distinct factor (*dharmāntara*) associated with the mind called "contact. Now, he might say this:
In this sutra, the sense-faculties and their objects are taught as being devoid of consciousness,
because of the statement that there are six internal and six external [bases].
Therefore, the inclusion [of the elements] here must be for the purpose of making known the remainder— that the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness constitutes contact (*sparśa*).
Regarding the phrase "the six groups of contact," this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of refuting that meditative absorption,
even though the sense-faculties and their objects might exist without consciousness.
The meaning is that they are "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga),
but consciousness is not, however, devoid of sense-faculties and objects;
for consciousness necessarily possesses both sense-faculties and objects.
And that consciousness has already been indicated here by the phrase "the six groups of consciousness";
therefore, when the faculty, the object, and the consciousness have been specified, the further mention of "contact" by way of the expression "the six groups of contact" would result in redundancy.
Therefore, it is established that contact is something other than the coming together [of the three].
Regarding this, the Venerable Śrīlāta says:
"Certainly not," and so forth.
The eye and visible form that have arisen previously are the cause, but not those that arise simultaneously with consciousness,
nor is it every instance of visual consciousness.
That which arises later does not [arise] simultaneously with the preceding eye and form; therefore, there exists between them the relationship of cause and effect.
Otherwise, this would not have been made known;
nor indeed do they recite it thus—
the word "vai" being a particle.
The meaning is that they do not recite it in this way;
how, then, do they recite it?
"That which has arisen from the conjunction, the meeting, and the assembly of these phenomena."
They recite "that contact" (*sa sparśa*); or rather, this is a metaphorical designation of the effect for the cause—
meaning that "contact" is used as a metaphor for the cause, namely the conjunction (*saṅgati*), the coming together (*saṃnipāta*), or the coalescence (*samavāya*).
Just as the arising of the Buddhas is blissful.
Because its moral discipline (*śīla*) extends through a manner of exceedingly great detail, it is called "extending through a manner of exceedingly great detail" (*atibahuvistaraprakāravisāriṇī*).
It is termed a "designation" (*adhivacana*);
it is called a designation because one speaks by means of it (*adhyucyate ’nena*).
Speech operates upon the name and illuminates the object through the name; thus, "designation" (*adhivacana*) is the name.
It is said that this name is the predominant and most frequent objective support (*ālambana*) for this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with which it is associated.
Therefore, "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) and "contact" (*saṃsparśa*) have the same meaning; for example,
one cognizes blue by means of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The meaning is that one cognizes the denotable object;
and when one cognizes "it is blue," one cognizes that "this is the name for this object."

"One is characterized by its basis" means that the first is characterized by its basis; it is contact having resistance as its basis, or contact that is the resistance itself, which is "resistance-contact.
It is "characterized by its object."
Contact with designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) means contact with an object (*ālambana-saṃsparśa*), or contact within designation;
it refers to the engagement of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) with objects such as form and so forth, having taken speech as its basis and having determined the meaning of that speech.
It is not the case that the five [consciousnesses], such as visual consciousness and the rest, engage with objects by taking speech as their basis.

Therefore, is that very designation (*adhivacana*) the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) operating upon the designation? Because it is associated with that [designation], or because it belongs to that contact, it is "contact of designation" (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*).
And for this reason, this second type of contact is said to be "distinguished by association" (*samprayogaprabhāvita*).
"Contact with knowledge, ignorance, and that which is other than both"—
thus, "knowledge, ignorance, and that which is other than both" refers to knowledge, ignorance, and the other.
Those very same contacts are "contacts of knowledge,
ignorance, and the other": that is to say, those called knowledge, those called ignorance, and those other than these two.
"Knowledge" (vidyā) is untainted wisdom (anāsravā prajñā);
"ignorance" (avidyā) is afflicted non-knowledge (kliṣṭam ajñānam);
that which is neither knowledge nor ignorance is wholesome tainted wisdom and that which is unobscured-neutral wisdom.
These contacts associated with that [ignorance] should be understood respectively as follows:

furthermore, regarding the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), there is a portion that is frequently active and constantly active, being associated with all the afflictions (*sarvakleśa*). This is the detailed explanation.
Regarding the contact of ignorance, which is associated with all the afflictions, there is a portion that manifests repeatedly and manifests constantly.
From the inclusion of that [unwholesome mind], two types of contact arise—
namely, the contact of ill-will and the contact of attachment— and the three [types] beginning with that which is to be experienced as pleasure.
The experience of pleasure is *sukhaveda*;
that which is appropriate for the experience of pleasure is *sukhavedya*. Alternatively, it is *sukhavedya* because pleasure (*sukha*) is what is to be experienced (*vedya*) therein.
He is the first among these, thus [they are called] "to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukhavedya*) and so forth;
because they are conducive to pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*) and the like,
that which is conducive to pleasant feeling is "to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukhavedanīya*).
The suffix *cha* is prescribed after a word ending in *prāk-kṛta*;
by stating "it is to be known" (*vedyate*) or "it is possible to make it known" (*vedayituṃ śakyam*),
he demonstrates that the gerundive (*kṛtya*) is used here in the sense of the mere object (*karmamātre*).
By the rule "kṛtya-ctṛcaś ca," he shows that the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of "capable of being felt";
thus, these sixteen—
namely, from eye-contact up to mind-contact— constitute six.

Furthermore, sixteen types of contact (*sparśa*) have been taught: contact of resistance (*pratigha-sparśa*), contact of designation (*adhivacana-sparśa*), contact of knowledge (*vidyā-sparśa*), contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*), contact of malice (*vyāpāda-sparśa*), contact of attachment (*anunaya-sparśa*), and contact to be experienced as pleasure, contact to be experienced as pain, and contact to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Since it was stated that "contact is to be explained as feeling (*vedanā*)," has feeling not already been explained?
"Feeling is experience"— this is stated even though it has already been said.
In that case, one should not say: "I will not speak that which has been said and that which is yet to be said."
And because of the statement, "that which has been said and that which will be said," there is no fault, as it is a specification of the various types.
The characteristic was stated previously; now, the mode [is discussed], as in the detailed explanation beginning with "for when [the effect] has arisen.
For when the dharma to be produced has already arisen, the producing dharma possesses no efficacy, because they have arisen simultaneously.
"Non-distinct from the thesis" (*pratijñāviśiṣṭa*) means that this proof is not distinct from the thesis;
[this is said] if a proof non-distinct from the thesis is not accepted.
If there is the consequence that they would be mutual producers,
then how is it established— in this context— that there is a relationship of producer and produced between two things that have arisen simultaneously?
By this, the fault of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) is raised:
"The proposition that there exists a relationship of producer and produced between two things that have arisen simultaneously contradicts what was previously accepted. [To this, it is replied:
"This is not a fault, because it is [already] intended [by us]."
He shows the prior admission:
"This is accepted [by us], but it is not accepted in the Sūtra."
This is accepted in the Abhidharma:
"Co-existent [factors] are those which are mutual fruits."
Demonstrating that this is undesirable according to the Sūtra, he says:
"Dependent upon eye-contact, there arises feeling born of eye-contact."

Having refuted the state of being mutual fruits by means of the authority of the Sūtra, and fearing the destruction of the relationship between simultaneously arisen cause and effect, he says: "And it is incorrect because it transgresses the nature of a producer. For this is the well-established nature of a producer: that it must exist at a different time [from its effect].
Just as, for example, first there is the seed and afterwards the sprout, and so forth;
likewise, in that case as well, first there are the sense faculty and the object, and afterwards the consciousness.
Thus, the sense faculty and the object arise in the first moment, while the consciousness arises in the second moment.
In that case, as with the shadow and the sprout,
is there a relationship of producer and produced between two things that have arisen simultaneously?
For indeed, a sprout produces its shadow as soon as it has arisen;
it is not the case that in the first moment the sprout is without a shadow and only in the second moment it comes to have a shadow.
The same applies to contact and sensation as well.
It can also be said that for these two—the shadow and the sprout—the preceding causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause;
however, since this point has already been stated in the explanation of the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), it is not repeated here.
As for the statement, "feeling occurs at a time subsequent to contact," this is the view of the Venerable Śrīlāta.
Thus, that conjunction of the three is contact (*sparśa*),
which is the relationship between producer and produced;
sensation (*vedanā*) occurs in the third moment.

The first moment is that of the sense faculty and its object; the second moment is the arising of consciousness; and the third moment is the arising of feeling. Thus, it follows that feeling does not occur in every instance of consciousness, because feeling is absent in the second moment of consciousness.
Nor is every consciousness contact;
in the third moment, which is the moment of feeling, consciousness is not contact,
whereas in the preceding two moments, it is established as being precisely contact.
For feeling in a subsequent contact is caused by a preceding contact;

that is to say, in this second moment which has just been described as being of the nature of contact, a feeling arises caused by the preceding contact— that is, caused by the consciousness of the first moment.
Even when preceded by that contact, sensation occurs in another [moment]; thus, in every case of consciousness, sensation would follow,
and since all consciousness is contact,
those contacts would be accompanied by sensation— this is the detailed argument regarding two [moments] having different objects.
The objective support (*ālambana*) of these two is distinct; thus, they have distinct objective supports:

for the former, visible form (*rūpa*) is the objective support, and for the latter, sound (*śabda*). Of those two with distinct objective supports, that feeling (*vedanā*) which arises in the subsequent contact (*sparśa*) having sound as its objective support is caused by the preceding contact—that is, it is caused by the contact having visible form as its objective support.

"How is this incorrect?"— with these words he reveals the fault: "Feeling, which arises from contact having an object of a different kind— that is, from contact having as its object a specific type of form— would then have a different object."
It will have sound as its object because of the discordance of the cause;
for when a sensation arises from contact having form as its object, that sensation will indeed have form as its object, and thus there is no possibility of [a sensation] having sound as its object.
In that case, it would be logical that feeling arises from contact in a subsequent moment caused by a preceding contact;
however, when feeling arises from a contact having form as its object, yet has sound as its object,
how will this be consistent?
For in the world, an effect is seen to correspond to its cause;

now, if it is thought that a feeling produced from a contact having visible form as its object remains one having visible form as its object even when associated with a contact having sound as its object,
therefore he says this:
Or, they have an object different from that mind with which they are associated; thus,
"different from that" means they have an object different from the mind whose object is sound.
The meaning is that because it has arisen with form as its object, it therefore has that same object;
and how is it said to be associated with that?
For those that are associated are indeed associated;
if [it is argued] that they are distinct because of having different bases, how could that which has arisen with the ear as its basis have visible form as its object? And how could it not be so?

Because the mind and mental factors function with a single object by virtue of having a common basis, the fault regarding sensation— even though its objective support is distinct [from that of the mind]— is now demonstrated.
If, first of all, a feeling produced from a contact having visible form as its object were to take another object such as sound and so forth,
then it would not be possible to designate that contact having visible form as its object as "to be experienced as pleasure" up to "to be experienced as neither-pain-nor-pleasure";
however, such a designation is logical only when the feeling has a single object.
"Let it be so," and so forth;
if there is such a fault, then let it be at that time.
At what time? At the time when sound is the object, consciousness, which has become contact, is without feeling.
And therefore, that consciousness accompanied by feeling which precedes the cognition having sound as its object is not contact;
for in this way it remains faultless.
Otherwise, if the previously arisen consciousness accompanied by feeling were contact, [it would lead to a logical inconsistency].
In that case, the aforementioned fault would apply— namely, that "feeling has contact as its condition"—
and furthermore,
there would be some consciousness that is without feeling.
And yet, there is no contact due to the deficiency of conditions;
for the conditions remain obstructed by impediments.

For not every immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya) is capable of producing a consciousness that has become contact (sparśabhūta) with feeling as its condition; thus, that consciousness which has a different object is necessarily devoid of feeling,
and that which produces it is not of the nature of contact.

If, however, immediately after a visual consciousness having form as its object, there arises either another visual consciousness or a mental consciousness having form as its object, and that [subsequent one] is accompanied by feeling, then the previously arisen [visual consciousness] is called "contact."
If this were so,
the rule regarding the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) would be violated,
because there is a fixed rule that contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) occur in alternation.
The three stages are as follows:
the realm of desire and the first dhyāna possess both vitarka and vicāra;
the intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka and possesses only vicāra.
The stage that is without applied thought and without sustained thought, from the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra),
consists of wholesome levels and wholesome dharmas; likewise, there are unwholesome and neutral [levels and dharmas].
The stage of the learner consists of the untainted dharmas of one in training;
the stage of the non-learner consists of the untainted dharmas of one beyond training;
and the stage of neither-learner-nor-non-learner consists of tainted dharmas.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) states are not mentioned here because of their connection with mental factors (caitta); thus,
"that which is in this [consciousness]" and so forth is the detailed explanation.
The word "that" (tad) is used to introduce the statement;
"which" (ya) refers to those mental factors (caitasika) that exist in this entire stage (bhūmi).
From the stage characterized by applied and sustained thought up to the stage of neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
those factors such as feeling, volition, and so forth, as previously described, are the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).
Those which exist only on wholesome levels are the great wholesome ground factors, such as faith and so forth; those which exist only on afflicted levels [are the great afflictive ground factors].

Those [factors] such as ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, which have been described, are indeed the great ground of afflictions (kleśamahābhūmika); furthermore, they occur according to their possibility— this is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, those [factors] such as the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) which are possible in a particular [mental state] occur in that state successively.
But others say that they do not all occur simultaneously;
for example, although feeling exists in all stages, it does not occur simultaneously with perception, volition, contact, attention, and so forth.
Likewise, contact [is associated] with feeling and so forth;
likewise, in wholesome [states], there are applied thought and so forth—
others, moreover, explain it in this way.
This should be understood exactly as it is written in the *Pañcaskandhaka*:
for example, what is desire (*chanda*)?
The intention is that desire exists for an intended object, but there is no *chanda* for what is not intended;
what then is initial liberation?
What is mindfulness? It is the ascertainment of a determined object as being exactly so;
it is the non-forgetting of a familiar object.
What is concentration that expresses itself through the mind? It is the one-pointedness of the mind upon an object to be examined.
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)?

It is discernment (*pravicaya*) regarding that very [object], whether it is applied correctly or incorrectly, or otherwise—and so forth; the *Pañcaskandhaka* treatise should be consulted for this, for therein it is stated that there are five universal [mental factors].
Feeling, perception, contact, attention, and volition— these five have specific objects;
as do desire, resolve, concentration, wisdom, and so forth.
The unwholesome universal mental factors (akuśalamahābhūmika), however, are not included here because they are mentioned in connection with the context of their recitation;
for they are recited in the Sūtras and other texts simply as "wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate," thus being linked only within that specific context of recitation.
The meaning is that they were added later;

previously, they were not recited, for in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, only four types were recited: the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikā*), the wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmikā*), the afflictive universal factors (*kleśamahābhūmikā*), and the minor afflictive universal factors (*parīttakleśamahābhūmikā*).
They are said to be "co-arisen," but not "co-arisen with contact";
because they are not so specified, these [factors] beginning with feeling are co-arisen with one another.
The meaning is that the Sūtra must be explained by adopting the sense that "it is not [perceived] by touch.

Regarding the phrase "accompanied by loving-kindness" (*maitrī-sahagata*), this word *saha* is not necessarily seen only in the sense of simultaneous occurrence; it is also observed in the sense of immediate succession (*samanantara*).
For there is no coexistence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*),
because loving-kindness is exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*),
whereas the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness is exclusively without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Therefore, this [statement] that they are "conjoined" does not prove [the point], for the intended meaning is that they are "co-arisen."
For in that very Sūtra it is stated in detail:
"Whatever is feeling, whatever is volition, and whatever is perception... and so forth.
In that regard, the meaning of "sūtra" is not understood, as the full passage states: "Is this, first of all,
a restriction of these [factors] such as feeling (vedanā) regarding their objects— that is, a restriction with respect to the object?"
Does one will that very same object which one feels, up to the point where consciousness cognizes it;
or rather, is there a restriction of moments, such that in the very same moment one feels, [one wills]?
We say that this very [cognition] lasts as long as it discerns; this is the restriction regarding the object.
Therefore, the intention is that there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
The Teacher says:
"In that very Sūtra, because of the statement regarding the 'conjoined' nature of vitality and heat in their coexistence, the restriction to a single moment is established."
By stating that "vitality and heat are conjoined;
these two factors are not disjoined," it is expressed that vitality and heat arise simultaneously.
Since those two lack an objective support (*anālambana*),
it is thus established that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) necessarily arise simultaneously.
In that sutra, because it is stated using the expression "intermingled," [it is said] "like life-force and heat";
how is that so? This is the detailed explanation.
How then can consciousness exist without the conjunction of the three— sense faculty, object, and consciousness?
Therefore, if consciousness exists, the conjunction must necessarily be admitted.
And since for you "contact" is the coming together [of the three],
this contradicts your position that not every consciousness is contact.
Alternatively, one should see that "or [the conjunction] is not contact" (*saṃnipāto vā na sparśaḥ*) is intended here as a further connection; thus,
because the elision of the *s* is not established by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, the *guṇa* substitution does not apply.
But the resolution is this: this negative particle (*nañ*) should be understood in the sense of "slight" (*īṣad-artha*).
Thus, because it is "not unestablished"—meaning it is slightly established—the elision of the *s* occurs due to its being established.
"This very one is Rāma, the son of Daśaratha," just as in the detailed explanation of the six mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*):
having seen forms with the eye, one applies oneself to those forms which are a basis for joy.
Having heard sounds with the ear, one dwells upon those sounds that are conducive to mental pleasure;
and so on, up to having cognized mental objects with the mind, one dwells upon those mental objects that are conducive to mental pleasure.
In the same way, having seen forms with the eye, one [dwells upon] those that are conducive to mental displeasure and those that are conducive to equanimity; this should be applied in detail.
"There will be three" because of the threefold nature consisting of joy (*saumanasya*), dejection (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*);
"one" [is said] because of its unity.
They are six because they are associated exclusively with mental consciousness,
due to the distinction between the six objects, such as form and so forth.
Regarding the statement "by all three there is establishment":

that single substance of feeling which is associated solely with the mental consciousness is divided into three types according to the distinction of its three intrinsic natures, such as joy (*saumanasya*) and the rest.
Furthermore, since each of those is divided sixfold according to the distinction of the six objects,
there are eighteen;
for if their establishment by way of intrinsic nature were not [stated], there would be no such thing as the mental applications of joy, grief, and equanimity.
If there were no establishment by way of association, they would not be called "mental applications" (manopavicāra),
and they would also be distinct from the eighteen [dhātus], because they would be established by taking the six objects such as form as their objective support.
If they did not exist individually, there would not be eighteen mental explorations (manopavicāra) through the sixfold division of joy and so forth;
therefore, it is established that they are determined by all three [feelings] and have unmixed objects (asambhinnālambana).
The three mental applications to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) have unmixed objects; they are of both kinds—
namely, those that have as their object phenomena distinct from the fivefold objects such as visible form and so forth.
Those mental applications regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) that have unmixed objects are those which take two,
three, up to all six objects— form and so forth— as their objective support; these are the ones with mixed objects (*sambhinnālambana*).
Regarding the phrase "the mind, indeed" (*manaḥ kila*), the word *kila* indicates the opinion of another (*paramata*).
The meaning is that the mind, having depended upon— that is, relying on— the objects, ranges over them and takes them as its objective support (*ālambate*).
"They investigate" means they set [the mind] in motion.
How so? He says:
"Because of the repeated investigation of objects by the mind under the influence of feeling. The meaning of the prefix *upa-* is "repeatedly."
"Nor is it investigative" means it is non-examining;
"incompatibility" means impossibility.
If feeling based on the mind alone is a mental application (manopavicāra), then the pleasure in the third dhyāna must also be based on the mind alone.
Since it does not depend on the visual faculty and so forth,
why is it not included among the mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) from the beginning? This is the detailed explanation.
"In the beginning," that is, from the very start, according to the opinion of others,
there is no pleasure belonging to the mental level within the realm of desire.
Therefore, that is not a mental application (*manopavicāra*).
Consequently, even though the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in the third dhyāna is dependent on the mind, it is not included among the mental applications,
just as the mental application of displeasure (*daurmanasyopavicāra*) is excluded as the counterpart to the mental application of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*).
In this way, there is no mental application of suffering as the direct opposite of the mental application of pleasure,
because suffering is based upon the mental consciousness.
Therefore, that pleasure is not a mental application (manopavicāra) in all cases; rather,
"conducive to joy" means those things which produce joy.
"Five," and so forth;

this means they are produced—that is, generated—by the five groups of consciousness. However, these belong to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), just as, for example, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*).
It is not derived from visual consciousness because it arises prior to the perception of the livid corpse and so forth,
and it belongs to the mental level because it is in a state of meditative concentration; however,
this is not the case.
This is not to be questioned on the grounds of the statement: "Having seen forms with the eye... up to: having touched tangibles with the body.

For it would only be subject to such objection if it had been said that "one mentally explores (*upavicarati*) forms that are bases for joy with the eye," and so on, up to "touching tangibles with the body."
One might raise the objection that this has not been stated in such a way, but this is not at all an objection,
as shown by the detailed explanation beginning with "even one who, having not seen... and so forth.
Even those who, having heard from another, mentally attend to and take as an object [those sounds], these too are his mental explorations (*manopavicāra*);
otherwise, [it would not be so], and so forth in detail.
The mental explorations (*upavicāra*) of visible forms and so forth would not have the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) as their object,
because for one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the visible forms and other objects belonging to the realm of form are not directly perceived.
Furthermore, the mental explorations of odors, tastes, and tangibles would not have the desire realm as their object for one born in the realm of form.
Because odors and the like are not its objects,
it has been explained in the manner that is most clearly evident.
Because the mental applications (*manopavicāra*) that have as their objects forms and so forth directly perceived by the senses are more manifest,
even one who, having seen forms, applies himself to the desires associated with them— this too is a mental application of his.
It has been stated in such a way that it is not confused; and as to how it is not confused, he says:

"By way of the differentiation of sense faculties and objects" means that it is stated through the differentiation of the sense faculties, such as the eye, and the differentiation of the objects, such as visible form.
Otherwise, there would be confusion;
for [the Sūtra] says, "Having seen forms with the eye, one investigates the desires that are a basis for mental pleasure," and so forth.
Thus, it is by way of delimiting the continuum that [these distinctions] exist.
Having observed the mental continuum of a certain being, whatever therein is a basis for joy,
up to and including a basis for equanimity.
But what object is being restricted?
For what reason?
Because that very same object of perception may be a basis for mental pleasure for one person, yet not for another.
In this way, up to those associated with the formless realm:
how many are associated with the form realm,
and of those, how many have what as their object?
How many are associated with the formless realm?
And among those, how many have what as their object? [The answer is:
All those that have the desire realm as their own object.
Thus,
regarding the sense-desires, all eighteen mental explorations of those belonging to the desire realm exist;
and that very same desire realm is the object of support for all of them.
The analysis of the words of the verse is as follows: "those whose objective support (*ālambana*) is their own realm (*sva-dhātu*)" are called *svālambana*.
[And] "the twelve have the material (*rūpin*) as their sphere (*gocara*)."

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the objective range (*gocara*) for twelve mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the six explorations of odor and taste; that is to say,

excluding the two explorations of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*) that have odor and taste as their objects, excluding the two explorations of grief (*daurmanasyopavicāra*) that have odor and taste as their objects, and excluding the two explorations of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) that likewise have those same [odor and taste] as their objects.
Why?
Because in that realm of form (rūpadhātu), those two—odor and taste—are absent; [and thus they do not exist] without the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.
Because of this statement,
it is the answer to the three.

The higher realm, the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), is the object of the three mental applications (upavicāra) of joy, grief, and equanimity pertaining to the desire realm (kāmāvacara); because of the absence of visible forms and so forth there,
[these three] exist in the two [upper] dhyānas as twelve.
Thus,
because of the absence of the six mental applications of dejection,
its own [sphere] is the object.
Thus,
there are eight objects of focus; it is called "the eightfold object" because it excludes the four mental applications (*upavicāra*) directed toward odors and tastes.
The meaning is that, excluding the two mental applications (*manopavicāra*) having odor as their object and the two having taste as their object—
because those two do not exist there—
the formless realms (*ārūpya*) possess two.
Thus,

for the mental applications (*upavicāra*) of joy (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is their object (*ālambana*), because of the absence of visible forms and so forth therein.
There are only six applications of equanimity and no others; that is to say,
there are only applications of equanimity having visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena as their objects,
because there are no applications of mental joy in the third or the fourth dhyāna.
However, it should be understood that the two [consciousnesses] having odor and taste as their objects there have as their objects odors and tastes belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*);

and that "four" are mentioned there because the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space has the fourth dhyāna as its object.
And because form, sound, tangible objects, and mental phenomena exist there,

for those teachers according to whose opinion that neighboring stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*) has a "delimited object" (*vyavacchinnālambana*), the meaning is that it has separate objects such as form and so forth, rather than a collective object.
According to the opinion of some masters, that [preparatory stage] takes the fourth dhyāna as its object through aspects such as "grossness" (*audārika*). However,

according to the opinion of those masters for whom that preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*) has only a collective object— that is, it takes as its object the five aggregates belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna— [the situation is as follows].
In that regard, there is only one mental application on phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) with a mixed object; thus,
there is only one that moves upward.
On whose side are those for whom there are four formless neighboring [deities]?
Such is the position:

"For the fundamental [formless attainments]," and so forth; that is to say, for the fundamental formless states, a lower realm is not an object of perception; the meaning is that a thing belonging to a lower level is not an object.
Thinking, "I shall explain this later," [the author notes that] the fundamental wholesome [mental factors] do not have the lower realms or the contaminated as their objects.
"Of the first," and so forth;
he is endowed with eight belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas,
and with four belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas.
To the question "Which ones?", he says: excluding those that have odors and tastes as their objects, because they are afflicted.
In that regard, since odors and tastes are absent there, how can it be said that the first and second dhyānas possess twelve applications of attention?
Because the mental applications (*upavicāra*) of joy and equanimity are established as having the six objects as their cognitive domains,
among them, there are four afflicted mental applications of joy that have their own level as their domain and have visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and phenomena as their objects.
And as for those four afflicted applications of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*), one born in the desire realm who has not yet attained the wholesome states of the form realm is endowed with them;
for one born in a lower stage is indeed endowed with the afflicted states belonging to the higher stages.

But it is not by means of the four distinguished [minds] having odor and taste as their objects, because those are undefiled and because there is no acquisition of undefiled factors belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), as one has not yet acquired the wholesome [factors] of that realm.
One is not endowed with those [defiled states];
furthermore, it is taught that even for those belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas, there are only six applications of equanimity,
among which those that have their own level as an object are defiled.
One endowed with those [faculties] is likewise;
however, those two which have odor and taste as their objects are not afflicted.
Therefore, by the very same reasoning stated previously, one is not possessed of those two [roots] through the afflicted alone;
nor is one possessed of them through the non-afflicted, because of the absence of the wholesome [root].
"One who has attained [a mind] of the form realm," and so forth:

one born in the desire realm who has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm comprised within the *anāgamya* stage, yet is not free from passion for the desire realm, is endowed with all eighteen [mental factors] of the desire realm,
as well as with ten belonging to the level of the first dhyāna.
To the question "How [is it] by ten?", he says:

"By excluding those with afflicted mental applications (*saumanasyopavicāra*) that have odors and tastes as their objects. Thus, afflicted mental applications do not exist in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
Because the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya),
one is therefore endowed with only the four afflicted mental explorations (saumanasyopavicāra) that are included within the fundamental [dhyānas] and have their own level as their object.
However, it is not [attained] through the objects of smell and taste,
because there is no acquisition of the undefiled by means of the acquisition of the fundamental wholesome [states];
for there is no defiled dhyāna that has a lower realm as its object.

Regarding the statement "by means of the six equanimity-meditations belonging to the stage of the *anāgamya*," since no distinction is specified here, one is endowed with even the four afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) equanimity-meditations included within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*),
as well as with the six wholesome (*kuśala*) equanimity-meditations that have the desire realm as their object and those that have their own stage as their object.
"By those born in the second, third, fourth dhyānas and the formless realms, as before"—

how is it that one born in the desire realm who has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm, yet is not free from passion, [is endowed] with eight [minds] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna?
By those very [mental applications] which,

having excluded the objects of smell and taste, are associated with the four afflicted [mental applications] belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas, one who has not yet attained [the higher stages] [is bound].
Having excluded those [cognitions] that have odor and taste as their objects,
one should follow the remainder by this same method and path, using only a single defiled [cognition] belonging to the formless realm.

How is it that one born in the first dhyāna, who has not yet attained a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, is nevertheless endowed with all [factors] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna,
as well as with the eight afflicted factors belonging to the level of the second dhyāna?
By means of [the minds] born of the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless attainments, as before;

one who has acquired a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the second dhyāna but is not yet free from passion for that level possesses all [the minds] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna and eight belonging to the level of the second dhyāna.

Excluding those having odor and taste as their objects, [they are associated] with four afflicted mental applications of joy and with four mental applications of equanimity included within the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna.
By means of the four defiled [mental states] belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, having excluded those that take odor and taste as their objects;
likewise by means of those belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna.

One born in the second dhyāna who possesses only one defiled mind belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), and who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the level of the third dhyāna, is endowed with all [the factors] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna,
as well as with four defiled [factors] belonging to the level of the third dhyāna.

Regarding those born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realms (*ārūpya*), as before: one who has attained a wholesome mind belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, yet is not free from passion for that level, possesses all the four afflicted mental applications (*upekṣopavicāra*) belonging to the level of the second dhyāna and the level of the third dhyāna, excluding those having odor and taste as their objects.
And with the twenty-four mental applications of equanimity included in the preparatory stage of the third dhyāna,
as well as those born of the fourth dhyāna and the formless attainments— as before— this is the general principle.

Following this same method, for one born in the third and subsequent dhyānas, one should apply the possession of afflicted and wholesome mental applications of equanimity belonging to their own level and to higher levels as appropriate;

this is because the transformation-mind (nirmāṇacitta) of the desire realm is associated with equanimity, specifically through the mental application of equanimity toward phenomena (upekṣā-dharmopavicāra).
Another says:
"This very author of the treatise [says] 'for that which [arises] from that which... and so forth.
Whatever person is free from passion for a certain form or other object, he does not mentally engage with that form or object as an objective support; how then could he mentally engage with it?
In that regard, one either leads [the mind] away, or obstructs it,
or neglects it through a lack of discernment; thus it is said.
When one remains indifferent without discernment and does not apply oneself,
it is then unwholesome;
therefore, the qualification "without discernment" (*apratisaṅkhyā*) is used.
Therefore, not all things that are with-outflows (sāsrava) are [defiled];
rather,
it is those that are defiling (sāṅkleśika).

Those which exist in the defiled state are "defiled" (sāṅkleśika), meaning they are conducive to defilement; by means of these, such as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth, the mind ranges over its objects.

Those which, as their antidote, are the six constant abidings (*sātatyavihāra*); that is, those which exist constantly by way of being the counter-array against those [states] associated with defilement (*sāṅkleśika*).
The meditative abidings (vihāra) are specific types of yoga; as for how there are six of them, he says:
Having seen forms with the eye, one is neither pleased nor led away; one is neither displeased nor repelled.
He becomes equanimous and does not partake;
how does he not partake?
Does he do so without discernment or rather with discernment?
To specify this, he says:
"mindful and clearly comprehending," which means examining with wisdom associated with mindfulness.
In this way, up to "having cognized mental objects with the mind," there are six *sātalās* due to the distinction of the sixfold objects;
for it is not so for an Arhat, and so forth.

An Arhat possesses mundane wholesome mental joy (*saumanasya*) that has as its object the *dharma* with outflows (*sāsrava*), namely the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) or the dharma of realization (*adhigama-dharma*).
For when he brings before him the qualities belonging to the continuum of a Buddha, wholesome mental joy arises;
therefore, it is not logical to exclude this [type of joy] from him.
Then to whom does this prohibition apply? It is observed that it applies to that which is defiling and constitutes a mental application (*manopavicāra*).
Therefore, not all mental factors such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, even if they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), are "mental applications" (*upavicāra*).
Regarding this, the Venerable Ānantavarman says:
"This is incorrect."
Why?
Because of a different explanation in the Sūtra;
for in the Sūtra, the Blessed One did not state that the mental explorations (*upavicāra*) are exclusively defiled (*sāṅkleśika*).
For thus it is said: "In this regard, monks, those six applications of mental joy— relying upon them and established upon them."
Monks, having abandoned these six applications of mental joy,
there are these six applications of equanimity.
Having relied upon them and having established himself in them,
he abandons these six applications of equanimity.
Monks, there are two kinds of equanimity:
that which is based on diversity and that which is based on unity.
Of these, monks, that which is based on unity is as follows:
"Relying upon that, abiding in that,
abandon this equanimity which is based on diversity."
It is known from this sūtra that the mental applications (*upavicāra*) such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth are exclusively defiled (*saṅkleśika*). However,
this is not a definitive proof, because even when the word "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) is used, their status as being defiled is not thereby excluded.
For even if it is stated that one is abandoned by means of the other as its support, the defiled nature of these mental explorations does not cease,
because they cannot possibly exist otherwise;
thus he said.
"Conceit must be abandoned by relying on conceit itself;
however, conceit can never, in any case, be a factor of purification.
Therefore, because afflictions function in mutual opposition and because [conceit] possesses a quality relative to another mode of functioning,"
There is no fault because the statement in the Sūtra was made with a view toward relative gravity and lightness;
Nanda and others are the illustrations here,
and for this reason, it is thus.
Since the Blessed One taught that the mental applications of equanimity serve as the very basis for abandoning the mental applications of equanimity—
based on such statements as, "O monks, there are two kinds of equanimity"— is it not established,

according to the Vaibhāṣika school, that these [mental applications] are both defiled and purified, given the statement that there are thirty-six categories of the Teacher's words distinguished by those based on attachment and those based on renunciation?
There is no fault;

for even in the case of the teacher (ācārya), there exist there mental factors such as satisfaction (saumanasya) and so forth that are distinct from the mental explorations (manopavicāra), and these are indeed the same [as those previously mentioned], and so on in detail.
These same eighteen mental applications (upavicāra) are, some, based on worldly existence (bhava) and based on attachment (abhiṣvaṅga), while others are based on renunciation (naiṣkramya);
renunciation is the state of departing from affliction (saṃkleśa) or from the suffering of saṃsāra.

Through the distinction between those based on attachment (*gardha*) and those based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*), there are two sets of eighteen, making thirty-six "Teacher's words" (*śāstṛ-pada*);
for the Teacher, the Buddha, has brought forth and taught this twofold division of those mental applications (*manopavicāra*) according to the Sūtra.
"It is designated as 'afflictions, karma, and bases' because of the statement:
'The afflictions are three, karma is two, and the bases are seven.'"
Thus, regarding the arising of maturation (*vipāka*), karma is the proximate cause; this is the subject under discussion. For affliction (*kleśa*) is also a cause of maturation.
But that [existence] is remote,
and those two have already been explained; thus, that which exists here between the existence of death and the existence of rebirth is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, because it is stated that "it occurs before death and after the moment of rebirth," it is explained that [the afflictions] do not exist as independent outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
Their independence [is established] because they are not associated with other afflictions that are liberated from ignorance, such as envy, avarice, anger, and hypocrisy.
Since ignorance is indeed present everywhere, there is no lack of independence due to association with it; however,
the connection to rebirth is not prevented by shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and other such factors when they are associated with other afflictions.
"Even though that state is dull," and so forth;
even though that state of death is [associated] with equanimity because of the lack of clarity in the activity of the mind and mental factors at the time of passing away and rebirth.
Thus, due to the dullness of sensation,
whichever affliction a person has habitually and constantly practiced and engaged in, at that time— when death is near—
that very same affliction, even if it be wrong view or the like, manifests and arises for that person at the moment of death.
The meaning is: due to a prior impulse, a prior projection, or a prior habituation;
or else, it refers to that affliction which arises at that time.
Because it was previously grasped and projected as a result-state, it manifests at that time;
this is because the desire and form realms have not been excluded [from the context].
All four states of existence indeed exist;
however, there are only three in the formless realms,
and those three exist only within the formless realms.
Because of this restriction,
it is understood that for these two other realms, there is no set of four types of existence (*bhava*), due to the absence of outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The meaning is "due to the absence of urine and feces";
and as for the phrase "subtle among the subtle," that is the subtle food of the subtle beings.
"Infants" refers to those just born, such as sweat-born insects and the like; "lice and so forth" includes, by the word "and so forth," those residing in the womb.
Regarding the statement "sensual pleasures are edible food," why is there this restriction that edible food exists only in the desire realm? To this he says:
For those who are free from passion—specifically those free from passion for solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)—there is rebirth in those two realms, the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).
Because of eating by taking [food] in mouthfuls—that is, because of swallowing after having made it into a lump—it is called "solid" (*kavaḍīkāra*).
