Furthermore, eating by taking [food] in mouthfuls occurs through the partitioning of morsels by means of the mouth and nose. Thus, when it is said that the sense-bases of odor, taste, and the tangible are themselves the "solid," he asks: how can those odors and so forth constitute food in the case of shadows, sunlight, flames, and light?
Since there is no consumption of the odors and so forth found there by means of making them into morsels, it is said that this description refers primarily [to those realms]; thus,
one understands that the odors and so forth found there do not constitute the nature of "morsel food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
However, this designation is based on the majority of cases:
"In the desire realm, it consists of three bases."
The word "kila" indicates that this is the opinion of another, whereas his own intention is expressed by the phrase "but those which... and so forth;
for even those things which are not consumed, such as shadows and the like, provide stability and provide sustenance.
These too are subtle food,
like bathing and anointing;
for just as bathing and anointing are not consumed by being made into mouthfuls, so it is with them.
And food is likewise [a cause of bondage],
because there is no restraint over those who have not liberated their own senses.
Thus,
because of his failure to favor his own sense organ— that is, his own faculty— and because of [the absence of such favor] in the case of those who are liberated.
Because it does not provide sustenance for those in the desire realm who have attained the stage of non-returner or arhatship,
the sphere of visible form is not nutriment;
furthermore, the sphere of visible form is the time of ingestion.
At the time when food that has entered the mouth is being consumed, having passed beyond the range of the eye,
at that time one's own faculty— the eye-faculty— and those great elements which are the basis of that faculty [are to be understood].
Since it does not benefit that form-sphere (*rūpāyatana*),
how much less will it benefit other faculties such as the ear and so forth, because they are not its objects?
For the visible sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not within the range of the ear and other [senses].
[Objection: "In that case, will it not provide benefit at the time of eating? To this he says: "And even when it is being seen," and so forth.

Now, how is it understood that at that time also, it is the contact (sparśa) associated with pleasant feeling (sukhavedanīya) which has that as its object (ālambana) that is the nutriment, and not matter (rūpa)? To this he says:
"Of those who are liberated," and so forth:
if that which is being seen were to perform the function of nutriment,
it would provide benefit even to those liberated ones— non-returners and arhats— who are free from desire for edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra) when they behold even most agreeable food.
Just as the bases of odor, taste, and tangibles provide nourishment for the sense faculties and the primary elements at the time of ingestion,

it is therefore established that contact— which is to be experienced as pleasant and has those [objects] as its objective support— is nutriment; thus, contact, volition, and consciousness [are established as nutriments].
Thus,
"vijñā" ending in -ā means "prajñā," in the sense that it is like consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It is established that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is *sāsrava* (with-outflows) because it consists of three bases (*āyatana*). However,
since the other three— contact (*sparśa*) and so forth— can be either *sāsrava* or *anāsrava* (without-outflows), they alone are specified [in the verse].
They are "with outflows," and likewise, the dharmas are "without outflows."

And it is not the case that these [desires] lead to the stability and maintenance of beings, nor to the favoring of those seeking rebirth; for they are born from the mind, and thus result in cessation (nirvṛtti), rather than in arising (upapatti).
The word "mind" (*mana*) is used for the sake of emphasis;
for this very reason, he says that it exists even without depending on any external material cause such as semen, blood, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), mud, flowers, and so forth are included.
Because it is oriented toward rebirth (*upapatti*), it is called "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*);
thus, arising is that which has birth as its manifestation, being oriented toward rebirth.
"With affliction" means with suffering; "having brought about that which is with affliction"—
this is the indicator here.
"Manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*) is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)," and "thus there exists a person (*pudgala*)," and so forth;
from this sūtra consisting of four alternatives, it follows that manifestation is the intermediate state.
There is a person for whom the fetter of manifestation has been abandoned, but not the fetter of rebirth;
there is one for whom the fetter of rebirth has been abandoned, but not the fetter of manifestation;
and there is one for whom both the fetter of manifestation and the fetter of rebirth have been abandoned.
There is one for whom neither the fetter of actualization nor the fetter of rebirth has been abandoned, namely, one who is free from passion for both realms—
that is, one who is free from passion for the desire realm and the form realm.
The qualification "non-returner" is used because ordinary persons have not completely abandoned the fetters of the intermediate state;
for it is said: "O monks, that which is abandoned by noble wisdom is truly abandoned."
Furthermore, because that [result] is subject to further cultivation,
the first alternative refers to a non-returner who is detached from the two realms,
while the second refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
The third [type] belongs to the Arhat;
the fourth belongs to others, such as ourselves, who are ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).

The previous synonym "beings who are worthy" has already been explained; [the term] "beings" refers to those who have arisen, namely, those seeking rebirth who exist in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Now, here is another formulation:
"beings" refers to Arhats because they are free from passion for the three realms;
"those seeking rebirth" refers to those possessed of craving.
Because they seek birth within the three realms,
[the perfections] are called "stabilities" for the purpose of establishing [themselves therein].
"For the sake of favor" means for the sake of renewed existence and for the sake of arising;
all [these] are in both ways.
All four nutriments serve for the maintenance and the welfare of beings who have come into existence, as well as for those seeking rebirth.
It is reasonable that mental volition (*manaḥ-saṃcetanā*) has the nature of karma; and consciousness (*vijñāna*), being manifested by it, is the seed;
furthermore, contact (*sparśa*), being associated with it, also serves as a support.
But how does edible food (kavaḍīkāra) provide benefit to those seeking rebirth?
To this it is said:
"For even edible food," and so forth.
The phrase "for those who possess passion for that" is introduced in this sūtra passage in order to make known that [craving] leads to renewed existence for those who possess passion for edible food.
For it was said by the Blessed One, and so forth;
therein, the five aggregates of clinging were described as being like a disease,
and the four nutriments are the root of that disease.
By the statement "the root is the cause," it is established that even edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*) leads to renewed existence for those who are attached to it;
others, however, cite this very same example as a condition for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*),
with the intention that aging and death are established as occurring beyond this present birth.
It is logical that even edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) serves for the maintenance of beings existing here, because this is directly perceived;
likewise, it has been stated that contact conducive to pleasure and consciousness are also supportive.
Now, how is it that mental volition (*manaḥ-saṃcetanā*) is so?
Therefore, this is said:
"And mental volition as well," and so forth;
for this very reason, by the mention of mental volition (*manaḥ-sañcetanā*), both contact (*sparśa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also included.
Because they are associated with that, they are called "rushed forth" (*pradruta*); thus, in the Abhidharma treatise, they are referred to by the synonym *prasṛta*, meaning "extended."
For their nourishment, there is contact (*sparśa*), because it provides benefit through that which is to be experienced as pleasant;
whatever constitutes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Because of the statement, "All that [suffering] arises dependent upon contact," mental volition (manaḥ-sañcetanā) projects rebirth,
since it has the nature of karma.

And how, moreover, is rebirth projected by that [volition]? It is through the production [of the new existence] from the seed of consciousness permeated by karma, due to the state of mutual conformity among the conditions for its arising.
The meaning is that the arising of renewed existence is like that of a sprout from a seed. To the question, "Is whatever is edible food necessarily nutriment? he replies:
"There may be something that is edible food but not nutriment."
There is a fourfold alternative: there may be nutriment that is not physical food (kavaḍīkāra), there may be both, and there may be neither.
The second category consists of the three nutriments— namely, mental volition, contact, and consciousness;
the fourth is that which excludes these aforementioned modes.
Sound, all mental states and mental factors associated with painful feeling, and likewise contact and so forth— fourfold alternatives (catuṣkoṭika) should be formulated accordingly for each; thus,
whatever contact there may be...
"All that is nutriment is contact, but not all contact is nutriment"— this constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).
The same applies to whatever mental volition (*manaḥ-saṃcetanā*) there may be.
"All that is nutriment is mental volition, but not all mental volition is nutriment"— this is a fourfold alternative;
likewise for whatever consciousness there may be.
Regarding the statement that "all of that would be nutriment, but consciousness is not nutriment," there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika);
first, concerning contact (sparśa), the first alternative is as follows:
That contact, dependent upon which there is the decline of the sense faculties and the disintegration of the great elements—
this is the second of the three nutriments.
The third is that contact depending upon which there is the nourishment of the sense faculties and the growth of the great elements;
the fourth is excluding these modes.
In this way, up to consciousness, there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika).

The first alternative is that consciousness which, depending on the sense-faculties, results in the diminution of the great elements and their disintegration. The second alternative consists of the three nutriments, excluding consciousness.
The third is that consciousness depending upon which there is the accumulation of the sense faculties and the growth of the great elements;
the fourth is setting aside these modes.
"Could it be that [feeling arises] depending on contact and so forth?"—this is another question stated in detail.
"Contact and so forth" should be understood as referring to the factors of contact, volition, and consciousness;
and the text should be composed accordingly.
It may be that, depending on contact and so forth, there is an accumulation of the sense faculties and an increase of the great elements,
yet these are not [considered] nutriments.
The use of the second case [in the compound] is due to the connection with the phrase "depending on those belonging to another stage and those that are untainted (anāsrava)."
Regarding the passage beginning with "even that which has been consumed," and so forth:
by what connection was this stated?

When it is said that [certain things] are not food when they depend on [factors] belonging to other stages or those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), it follows by implication that this is what is being stated.
It is called "nutriment" because it depends upon the contaminated factors of its own level; and as for that which is consumed here,
the edible food (kavaḍīkāra) brings about affliction for the eater.
What is its nutriment? That nutriment also provides benefit at the time of eating, at the initial moment.
"In all [realms], for everyone, in this way, in all wombs" means that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the existence of the five destinies (*gati*) and the four modes of birth (*yoni*).
The fourfold alternative (catuḥkoṭika) and the treatise (*prakaraṇagrantha*) are contradicted; thus,
regarding this third alternative in the first set of four alternatives:

Since it contradicts the statement that "depending upon which edible food there is the nourishment of the sense faculties and the growth of the great elements," this [definition] is refuted; thus, the fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is also refuted,
for it is not merely that which produces nourishment.
What then?
Does this contradict the *Prakaraṇa* treatise which states that even food that causes diminution is "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)?
To demonstrate what kind of treatise (*prakaraṇagrantha*) this is, he says:

"What is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)? It is that which, depending upon being made into morsels, results in the nourishment of the sense faculties (*indriya*), and so on in detail up to consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

There is no contradiction because the statement was made with the intention of referring to nutriment as accumulation; therefore, both the fourfold classification and the statement in the *Prakaraṇapāda* were spoken with reference to nutriment as accumulation.
There is no contradiction between these two;
for that which leads to accumulation is the primary [meaning].
"Because they have attained the characteristic of being sustenance" means because they have attained the characteristic of being edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); as to how this is so, he says:
For that [food] also is capable of warding off hunger and thirst; thus, it should be understood that food in the form of glowing iron balls is capable of warding off hunger,
while food in the form of molten copper is capable of warding off thirst.
In connection with the topic of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), this is stated:
"The Blessed One said, 'And as for those of the outsiders... and so forth;
[this refers to] Jambudvīpa, the grove of *jambu* trees.
For thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Whatever rivers flow from the Jambu Grove, all of them slope toward the ocean, incline toward the ocean, and tend toward the ocean."
The intention is that those dwelling there, situated in the Jambu grove, are sentient beings endowed with the capacity for digestion and are not in embryonic stages such as the *kalala* and so forth;
however, this is incorrect.

Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of 'one'": if those dwelling in Jambudvīpa who possess bellies were intended [by that term], then one would have to say, "and the ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have gone to the Jambu-grove."
And it has been said: "He who [sees] even one [person] in the Jambu-grove," therefore this meaning does not hold;
what then is the distinction here?
What is the wonder here that feeding many would produce much merit, whereas feeding even a smaller number— meaning no more than a hundred— of those free from passion [would not]?
For the Bodhisattva is proximate [to Buddhahood].
The intention is that a bodhisattva who is close to perfect enlightenment is so from the point at which he performs the actions that produce the marks.
However, this designation is not "anvarthā" (meaning-conforming);
that is to say, it does not follow the meaning, nor is it a word expressive of its own meaning.

Nor was he rebuked; rather, disregarding the literal meaning [of his name], they said, "This Bodhisattva, having gone to the Jambu Grove, has indeed departed to visit the farming village. Thus, the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddha, seated at the foot of a Jambu tree, attained the first dhyāna.
Therefore he says:
"For that ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is connected with detachment from the desire realm";
and indeed, that bodhisattva is also an ordinary person who is free from passion for the desire realm.
And likewise, ordinary worldlings who are free from passion for sense-desires—
by this connection, he is said to be distinguished by a much greater fruit of giving than those outsiders; thus,
he is distinguished from those infinite outsiders.
Because of the statement that "the gift (dakṣiṇā) even to non-noble ones for a bodhisattva is immeasurable," the mention of "a hundred" is, however, due to the previous context.
In that very sutra, the section on the hundred is introduced: "If someone were to give a gift to a hundred beings born in the animal realm,
and another were to give a gift to a single human being who is of immoral conduct..."
Therefore, a hundredfold maturation is to be expected,
up to that which belongs to the outsiders; such is the detailed explanation,
and thus this is indeed so.
And this is so because it is only logical that this very Bodhisattva was seated in the Jambu-grove;
for, setting aside this Bodhisattva,
he [the Buddha] distinguished the one entering the fruit of stream-entry from among those outside [the Buddhist fold].
A gift given to those outside [the Buddhist fold] who are free from passion is more immeasurable than one given to a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry;
it is even more immeasurable than one given to a stream-enterer; and so on, in detail, until a gift to a candidate for the fruit of once-returning is more immeasurable than that.
If he had been one who had reached the stage conducive to penetration while staying in the Jambu Grove,
he would have distinguished himself even from those staying in the Jambu Grove; how [could this otherwise be]?

And if someone were to feed a hundred people belonging to the Jambu-grove, and another were to feed a single person who has entered the path toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, this latter gift bears much greater fruit than that former one.
But it is not so;

because he is far more distinguished than those such as the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphalapratipannaka), it is therefore appropriate that this very Bodhisattva, having entered the Jambu-grove,
[experiences] the exhaustion of his lifespan and so forth.
There is death from the exhaustion of the life-span but not from the exhaustion of merit;
there is [death] from the exhaustion of merit but not from the exhaustion of the life-span, and so forth—
this is the detachment regarding cutting and rejoining.
Thus is the detailed account:
the severance of the roots of merit occurs through wrong view,
and that [wrong view] is exclusively mental.
Because it is investigative in nature, the reconnection of the roots of merit occurs either through right view or through doubt;
and these two belong to the mental faculty.
Detachment from elements or stages— whether detachment from an element or from a stage— is obtained only in the mental consciousness and only in a concentrated mind; therefore,
falling away [from such detachment] is brought about by improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).

Furthermore, since improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), death occurs when there is a consciousness conducive to the interruption of the stream for one whose activity of the five sense-faculties has been withdrawn;
likewise, rebirth also occurs for one of perverted intellect. Therefore, it is logical that these pertain to the mental consciousness alone.

The intention is that the linking of rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is also of the nature already described; thus, although it is not explicitly mentioned because it shares the general characteristics of "linking" (*pratisaṃdhi*), it is considered as if it were already described.
"Death" (*cyuta*) is simply "passing away" (*cyuti*).
It shows that they have the same meaning because the suffix *kta* is produced in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*);
for "pleasure" and "pain" are indeed two distinct types of cognition (*vedanā*).
"Because it belongs to a different level":
since a concentrated mind belongs to the level of concentration, it is of a different nature from the desire realm;
therefore, neither a death-consciousness nor a rebirth-consciousness [arising from that state] is tenable.
If it is argued that when one dies or is reborn in the form realm itself,
the mind at that time will belong to a state of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmika), [the author] says:
"Because it is produced through volitional effort (ābhisaṃskārikatvāt)."
*Abhisaṃskāra* is effort;
that which is produced by *abhisaṃskāra* is *ābhisaṃskārika*; its state is *ābhisaṃskārikatva*.
Therefore,
it is not logical that either the mind at death or the mind at rebirth should be produced by volitional effort,
because of the lack of clarity in the state of dying.
And because it is supportive;
for a concentrated mind is supportive and not conducive to interruption.
Therefore, for one whose mind is concentrated there is no death, nor for one who is without mind; such is the detailed explanation,
including that it is not for one who is without mind.
Is it death or birth? This is the subject under discussion.
One who is without mind— whether having entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), having entered the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti),
or abiding in the ripening (vipāka) thereof—
cannot be harmed or killed by weapons and the like.

Therefore, there is no death for one who is without mind, nor does it occur when his physical basis (āśraya) begins to undergo transformation. According to the treatise, this is because for one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or the attainment of non-perception (asañjñisamāpatti), or for one abiding in the maturation (vipāka) of the attainment of non-perception, the mind— bound to the physical basis— necessarily exists within that basis in the form of a seed (bījabhāva) until the projection of that maturation is fully exhausted, due to the onset of fire or other such causes.
Having manifested that [state], one would subsequently fall away;
what kind of person (pudgala) would fall away?
If the person (pudgala) were the subject under discussion, then because there would be a single agent [for both actions], the rule for the suffix -ktvā would not apply;
therefore, the mind would then pass away.
Or rather, the connection is as follows:

And when the basis begins to undergo transformation—that is, to reach a state of alteration—then for this person, the mind which exists in the form of a seed bound to that basis must necessarily manifest; [this is expressed by] the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇi*), as in the sense of "it will manifest," as in the examples: "there is a wind that causes leaves to grow" (*parṇaruha*) or "there is a wind that causes leaves to wither" (*parṇaśuṣa*).
Thus,
why is it that being without mind is also illogical at the time of rebirth?
Because there is no cause for the severance of the mind,

the mind of rebirth must necessarily be afflicted; otherwise, since it is impossible for the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and so forth to occur, and because [rebirth] cannot arise without affliction (kleśa).
For the connection of rebirth occurs through all the afflictions belonging to that particular stage,
and afflictions never exist without a mind;
therefore, for one who is without mind, there is no rebirth.
It has been stated that the state of death (maraṇabhava) is of three kinds; thus,
the state of rebirth (upapattibhava) is afflicted by all the defilements belonging to its own level.

Because of the restriction that "only the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is afflicted," it is stated that the states of death, the prior limit, the intermediate period, and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;
or alternatively:
As he passes away in the formless realm, he ceases life, mind,
and equanimity;
thus it is explained in detail, up until...
It has been stated that "in all [other] defiled [existences], there are five";
therefore, the general rule is that the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) is of three types.
But an Arhat attains parinirvāṇa in two neutral states;
such is the exception.
If there is equanimity as a maturation in the desire realm,
then according to the opinion of some, there is also a middling [feeling] below that.
"If it does not exist"— thereafter, "the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant" is stated according to another opinion.
"Only pertaining to postures" means that it is of the nature of postural activity; wherein does it cease?
It ceases in the resultant, the postural, the artistic, and the emanated.
It has been explained that the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in the desire realm is not intended to be only fourfold.
For that [state] is conducive to the cutting off of the mind; that is,
it is conducive to the cutting off of the mind without reconnection because of its weakness.
The meaning is "due to extreme dullness.
In the case of the cutting off of the mind accompanied by rebirth-linking (*sapratisaṃdhika*), both wholesome and unwholesome minds are possible for them,
respectively.
The consciousness of those going to the states of woe ceases at the feet;
that of those going to the human realm, at the navel; and that of those going to the divine realms, at the heart.
Since consciousness is formless, it does not abide in a location; how then is it ceased within them?
To this he says: "Because the body-faculty is ceased within them."
Since consciousness in the desire realm and the form realm functions in dependence upon the body-faculty located in those [parts] such as the feet,
the consciousness of those [beings] also ceases in the heart.
This meaning is obtained precisely from the indication according to numerical order (*yathāsaṅkhya*):
"the heart and the heart [are] in the hearts."
The foot, the navel, and the heart— these are the "foot-navel-heart" (pādanābhihṛdayāṇi);
thus there are four items.
"Downward movement," "human," "divine," and "serpent"— these four meanings are established by that [term] according to their respective order;
the inclusion of the word "mostly" (prāyeṇa) is because gods and others generally experience a happy death.
But they are not cut like pieces of wood;
rather,
they are indeed cut by means of intense pains.
Or, they are called "severed" because they do not move again, as if severed;
like limbs that have been cut off, they do not move again, and thus they are said to be "severed. This is the conceptual function of severance.
Since it has been stated that [death occurs] by means of any one of water, fire, or wind through the splitting of the vital points (*marman*), he asks:
"Why not by means of the earth element?"
"Those in which the elements of water, fire, or wind predominate, as appropriate," means according to possibility: phlegm (śleṣman) predominates the water element,
and bile (pitta) predominates the fire element.
Others say that when the wind element is predominant and only wind remains, it is due to the similarity with the destruction of the receptacle world;
thus there are three destructions of the receptacle world: destruction by fire, destruction by water, and destruction by wind.
There are three destructions of the receptacle world: destruction by fire, destruction by water, and destruction by wind.
Since it has been explained in detail that these occur through whichever one of the elements—water, fire, or wind—is similar to them, how is it that [the world] has gone far away?
Because they have attained the acquisition of ultimate dissociation,
whereas ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) possess the acquisition of dissociation but not its ultimate form, they have indeed gone far away.

The meaning is that they would indeed be fixed even in falsehood (*mithyātva*) if they were to commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*); and "but they do not," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, those who have attained the factors conducive to liberation are not restricted by a fixed temporal limit,
as is the case for those such as the "seven-times-at-most" (saptakṛtvaḥparama) and others.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those such as the *kulaṅkula* and *ekavīcika* are included;
the restriction of time for these will be explained in the exposition of the persons (*pudgala*).
Other than these two fixed [types], there are those who are not fixed.
"For they depend on conditions," and so forth;
if they obtain the conditions while combined,
they are fixed in their state of correctness.
Now, those fixed in falsehood,
being fixed in falsehood,
do not find conviction in either.
Even though it does not pertain to either [of the two],
the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka) has been described by means of the sequential instruction beginning with ignorance;
"uśanti" means "they desire."
The wind-circle is sixteen hundred thousand [yojanas] in depth and incalculable;
by way of its depth it is sixteen hundred thousand,
and by way of its circumference it is incalculable.
The meaning is that it is incalculable in its total circumference;
by the sovereign power of karma— that is, by the efficacy of karma— therein is the illustration.
Just as food and drink that have been eaten and drunk do not fall into the receptacle for digested matter while still undigested,
but only when digested do they go to the place of digestion— this is the meaning according to the principle of the "skilled man" (kuśala-nyāya) and the principle of the "stomach" (koṣṭha-nyāya).
The meaning is that it stands all around like a wall;
by way of the curdling of boiled milk, according to the principle of the curdling of boiled milk,
just as there is a solidification (*śarī*) of boiled milk.
The indication of the feminine gender means "an arrow" (śara);
or else, the state of being an arrow (*śarabhāva*) refers to the feminine application, just as this arrow comes into being through the process of solidification (*ghanībhāva*).
Thus, above the water, there is a ground made of gold;

as for the remainder, it is three hundred and twenty thousand [yojanas], which results from subtracting eight [hundred thousand] from eleven hundred and twenty thousand. This is the remainder that remains.
"Three thousand [yojanas] across," and so forth;
this is stated as the measurement of the four-continent world system.
For these two are not equal to the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.
The circle of water and gold, however, is threefold in circumference on all sides.
This [measurement] tripled by way of total circumference applies to both;
this is the rule for every circle:
that the measurement of its total circumference is exactly three times its horizontal measurement.
By that [ocean], the four-continent world-system was encircled; thus it was made a circle (*cakra*), i.e., encircled (*cakrīkṛta*), brought to the state of having the form of a wheel.
For this very reason, it is called Cakravāḍa; it is made of iron (śastraka) and consists of metal,
[forming] four sides respectively.
The side facing Uttarakuru is made of gold, the side facing Pūrvavideha is made of silver,
the side facing Jambūdvīpa is made of lapis lazuli,
and the side facing Avaragodānī is made of crystal.

"Containing various kinds of seeds" means being endowed with various types of capacities; "by winds distinguished by manifold powers" means by winds distinguished by many kinds of capacities for producing those [seeds]. This is the meaning.
"By non-conjunction" means by way of not existing simultaneously;
for it is not the case that when the effect [exists], [the cause exists].
At that time, the cause does not persist,
for there is no persistence of a substance consisting of form, taste, and so forth.
"In the cessation of one property" means that upon the cessation of the milk,
there is the manifestation of another property.
Is that very same substratum (dharmin) which has yogurt as its origin,
or is it not?
A phenomenon distinct from the substrata such as milk— which consist of form and other qualities— is transformation; it is unarisen and undestroyed even while those [substrata] arise and perish,
just as the state of curd exists upon the cessation of milk.
If it were the case that "this is that very thing," then curd would be identical to milk;
however, this is not so.
And this curd is not that very same milk, as was stated regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*).
If it is argued that this is not so,
because of the statement that "transformation is merely the becoming otherwise of that very substance," then this formulation of speech is unprecedented.
The intention is that it is contradicted by one's own words;
for a difference between the preceding and succeeding moments is asserted, and it is observed that whatever undergoes change is distinct [from itself].
Just as in the case of Devadatta and Yajñadatta, therefore, gold and other such things must exist as distinct from their causes and effects.
Gold, silver, jewels, earth, and so forth have a height of six million yojanas;
this means that their height is one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.
"Endowed with eight qualities":
that water which is cool, clear, light, sweet, soft, and free from foul odor;
when drunk, it does not distress the stomach nor does it irritate the throat. That is [the ideal] water.
Thus says the verse from the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha*:
"But it becomes threefold by the side, when measured along the shore of Yugandhara.
This refers to the fact that this inner ocean, when its length is calculated along the side of Yugandhara, is threefold.

The length on the side of Yugandhara is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas; on both sides, because of the width of the boundary rivers in the directions of the two Cetas mountains, there are two further eighty [thousand], making three eighty-thousands,
which together with the original amount becomes two hundred and forty thousand.
Three hundred thousand, twenty-two thousand—
that is the measurement of the outer ocean in one direction between Nimindhara and Cakravāḍa.
In this case, it should be stated that there are one thousand, two hundred, and eighty-four [others],
because of the deficiency;
the same should be stated for the other direction.
Thus, when two thousand five hundred and seventy-five *yojanas* are added, that aforementioned Ādāra ocean becomes full—
[the one] which was stated to be three thousand four hundred and fifty *yojanas* across.
And "the twelve hundred thousand [yojanas] of the water and golden mandalas" is because, according to this enumeration of the four continents, it exceeds [the measurement] as they are arranged.
This is answered as follows:
this is not a fault,
because the water and the golden disk outside the Cakravāḍa mountains are exceeded by this much.

In that case, it should be understood that the four-continent world is not encircled by that Cakravāḍa mountain range; rather, it is the upper landmass that is encircled by it, not the circle of water.
Another says:
mountains such as Sumeru and others do not possess cliffs that are absolutely severed from their height and density;
rather, what then?

Having stated that, according to the analogy of a mountain, they are of uniform height and mass because their lower portions slightly protrude and their specific distinctions are difficult to perceive;

Therefore, since those various lower parts slightly exceed [the rest], that which is to be supported—Mount Sumeru and so forth—pervades its support, consisting of the water and golden mandalas; thus, there is no contradiction in this, as explained at length by others.

Furthermore, there is no support other than the basis of the Bodhisattva, nor is there any location other than the site of the Vajrāsana capable of sustaining that diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
And that a continent has whatever shape it does is a matter of direct perception; the diversity of sentient beings arises from the power of the earth.
Among the Kirātas and Śabaras dwelling in the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, fair and dark complexions are seen;
[there are] the Videhas and the Kurus.
Because there are many inhabitants, the location is also indicated in the plural;
and "one [is surrounded] by Rākṣasas" refers to either Amarāvatī or Cāmara.
"From the nine Kīṭa mountains" means from the nine mountains shaped like insects;
it is on account of them that this is called Jambūdvīpa.
Jambudvīpa is so called either because it is marked by the Jambu tree according to the section on the Jambu tree, or because of its fruit according to the section on the fruit.
Or, by the rule "the suffix *lup* may optionally be applied after *jambū*," the fruit is also called *jambū*; thus, the meaning is that Jambudvīpa is so named because it is marked by those fruits.
"Catuskandhāḥ" means "of four kinds";
others say it means "having a fourfold configuration."
"Encircled by iron walls" means surrounded by iron walls.
"Covered with iron" means they are shielded from above by iron.
Others say that "the doors are closed with iron" means they are "burst open," which is to say they are pervaded,
as described previously.
The meaning is that when the foot is lifted, skin, flesh, and blood are produced once again; thus,
there are three [types of paths], beginning with the razor-path.
The razor-path, the forest of sword-leaves, and the forest of *śālmalī* trees— these three, along with the dark-spotted dogs that devour [the sinners],
are included within the forest of sword-leaves.
And "iron-beaked crows" refers to spears,
javelins, and the like contained within the Śālmali forest.

They are called *utsada* because they are places of excessive torment; the prefix *ut-* has the sense of "excessive," and they are called *utsada* because beings are tormented excessively (*sīdyante*) there.
But how is there an excess of torment? To this he says: "In the hells," and so forth;
"another" refers to [the following].
The Elder Manoratha says that the prefix *ud-* has the sense of "above";

thus he says that because they are released from the confinement of the hells— from the confinement of the Avīci hell and so forth— they sink down into these [other hells] such as Kukūla and the rest, which are above [them].
Therefore, following the question "Why are they called 'abounding in those'?", another question is posed;
having stated this, [the Buddha] says: "Which are the sixteen abodes of abundance?"

The fourth protrusion is the Vaitaraṇī river, in which those beings are prevented from reaching either bank by men with swords, spears, and javelins in their hands; even as they go upward, they are steamed and cooked.
From this, the following further question arises.
"What are these hell-wardens? and so forth;
"like the winds of world-evolution" means just as the winds during the evolution of the world exert themselves for the purpose of bringing about the formation of the receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*).
In the same way, those who consist merely of the primary elements and their derivatives— namely, the hell-wardens, the Yama-rākṣasas,
and beings of evil karma— are born as hell-wardens; this is the meaning.

Those inhabitants of the realm of King Yama who, by means of the instruction spoken in the *Devadūtīya-sūtra*— "those who [are instructed] by Yama"— have been so instructed, cast those beings into the places of hell.
These are called the Yama-rākṣasas,
but they are not those who, with swords, spears, and darts in hand, inflict the tortures; where, then, is the ripening of that karma?
Where is the ripening of the karma created by the hell-guardians?
It is in those very [hells], and so on in detail;
for it is in those [hells] that there is room for the ripening of the karma of those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*).
What obstacle is there for those hell-guardians in those hells?
This is what is meant:
even for those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), there is room within the hells for the exceedingly great ripening of their immense immediate karma.
How much more so, then, regarding the hell-wardens (*naraka-pāla*)— considering that they perform their actions as the cause for [others] to undergo them—
and because they have set limits, having established a boundary such that these [beings] must not be burned by the hell-wardens.
Or rather, due to the production of a specific kind of primary element (*bhūta-viśeṣa*),
those specific elements are produced by their respective karmas such that they are not burned by that fire.

"Corresponding to the transformations of body and sound" means they correspond to the transformations of the body; the names *arbuda*, *nirbuda*, *utpala*, *padma*, and *mahāpadma* are given because the bodies of the sentient beings dwelling there take on the forms of an *arbuda* and so forth.
The names *aṭhaṭhaḥ*, *hahavaḥ*, and *huhuvaḥ* correspond to the modifications of sound;
they are so called precisely because of their downward expansion, like a heap of grain.
"Externally" means not internal;
it consists of the fiery [element] in the form of sun-crystals and the watery [element] in the form of moon-crystals,
as the case may be.

Both of those mandalas exist for the purpose of benefiting or harming the visual faculty and the others, in accordance with differences of place, time, and state; this same principle should be applied to other cases as well—
how so?
When it is night in Pūrvavideha,
then it is sunset in Jambūdvīpa, midday in Avaragodānīya, and sunrise in Uttarakuru; this same principle should be applied elsewhere as well,
[specifically] on the ninth day of the latter half of the second month of the rainy season.
Thus,
the four months of the rainy season begin with Mārgaśīrṣa and end with Phālguna;
therein, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, [the moon] wanes by one *nilavaṃlavaṃla*.
When there is continuous connection with time or distance, the second case ending is used; thus,
as the shadow of a lamp falling upon a pillar reveals a partial circle, so too does the shadow falling on the opposite side reveal a distorted orb.
Just as the pillar comes closer,
so too is the pillar covered by its own shadow;
for when the lamp is situated at a distance, the pillar is seen in its entirety.
When it is somewhat near, it diminishes somewhat; as long as it is near, the pillar remains in a state where its form has vanished—
such is that practice of yoga.
Furthermore, according to the Yogācāras, through the process of horizontal tilting and rising, the lower portion of the moon’s orb wanes while the upper portion waxes;
these are the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, so called because they constitute the host (kāya) of the four Great Kings.
Therein, the beings belonging to the Four Great Kings' realm [reside] on the terraces of Mount Sumeru and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the Yugandhara mountains and others are included.
"Intervals of ten thousand" means that the intervals have a measurement of ten thousand *yojanas*; thus,
"half is projected."
The half-verse "sadāmadā" is [an instance of] *avaṣṭabdha*;

although it should have been stated as "sadāmattāḥ," it was expressed as "sadāmadāḥ" for the sake of conforming to the requirements of the verse composition (*ślokabandha*), since the meaning remains the same.
The four Great Kings themselves dwell in the four [palaces]; namely,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the eastern quarter and Virūḍhaka in the south.
Virūpākṣa is in the west and Vaiśravaṇa is in the north; this sequence is to be understood as that which was stated regarding the gods of the Four Great Kings (cāturmahārājika).
Because the four Great Kings themselves reside on the fourth terrace,
it is thus said that they are the "Mahārājika gods," meaning they exist among the Great Kings; [the term] *mahiṣṭha* means the greatest or most extensive.
If it is thus that the directions are twenty thousand [yojanas], how was it stated that they are equal in height and thickness?
Their intention is that this was stated thus with reference specifically to the middle portion,
namely "one and a half."
That which has an additional half is "adhyardha";
that which has one and a half yojanas is "adhyardhayojana."
The word "in height" (samucchrāyeṇa) is to be supplied;
[it refers to] a hundred elements, a hundred colors,
and the perfection of the arrangement of various jewel-locations.
By means of its perfection in the arrangement of various jewels and its perfection in the arrangement of various locations,
it causes the splendors— the majesties and greatnesses— of all other dwellings to feel ashamed; that is to say, it produces shame in them.
In length it is two hundred and fifty yojanas;
each side is of this measure, and even the fourth side is of this same measure.
"Subhūminī" means those whose grounds (*bhūmi*) are beautiful; thus,
"subhūminī" refers to pleasure-grounds in the four directions.
"Of this [place] there are four directions" means "in the four directions";
according to the opinion of Bhāguri, the word *dik* ends in the vowel *ā*.
Thus, it means that after traversing twenty *yojanas*, there are pleasure grounds.
It is said that they are separated by twenty yojanas;
"of the Trayastriṃśas" means those who dwell among them are the Trayastriṃśas.

It was said with reference to the fact that those trees do not exceed [the height of] them, that they are the abode of the excellence of sensual delight and the place for the specific enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
That fragrance persists without exceeding that *kovidāra* tree;

its branches, leaves, and foliage extend for fifty *yojanas*. Thus, with reference to the fact that it does not exceed the tree, it was said that "the fragrance wafts fifty *yojanas* against the wind.
To this, they offer the following reply:
For indeed, there is no such thing as a wind blowing against the wind; it perishes at the very place where it arises.
It does not extend the continuum to another location,
for it has been stated that [the scent reaches] fifty yojanas even against the wind; therefore, this is not a valid solution.
Therefore, he states this other point regarding meditative concentration:
"But of that very [fragrance]," and so forth.
What, then, is the reason that here the fragrance blows for a hundred *yojanas* with the wind, but for fifty *yojanas* against the wind?
"Not beyond that" is why he says,
"because they begin in a progressively weaker, weaker, and weakest manner," and so forth;
because they are obstructed by a gentle breeze, their onset is progressively weaker, weaker, and weakest.
Consequently, that very continuum of fragrance is cut off;
for this reason, it does not spread to such a distant distance as a measure of a hundred *yojanas*.
Or rather, is it that the wind arises already perfumed?
Just as from the scent of flowers in sesame seeds another scent arises that is distinct [from the original], such that it is not the floral scent itself— so he said:
"If the fragrance wafts against the wind for fifty yojanas,
then what of that which was spoken by the Blessed One?"
"The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind," and so forth;
this refers to the fundamental fragrance.
The phrase "mustādiḥ kṛtyākṛtyaṃ samarthayantaḥ" means that they deliberate upon what ought and ought not to be done; that is to say, they reflect upon what is to be performed and what is not.
In brief, it is said that "for whom the vessel is known," meaning the vessel is the location;
in detail, there are also other gods such as the Krīḍāpramoṣakas, the Prahāsakas, and so forth.
Therefore, it has been stated in brief by means of a dvandva compound that their sexual union extends up to looking; thus, they are [the five types of union]:
embracing, joining hands, laughing, and looking.
"For all through sexual union" means that for all six classes of desire-realm beings, the cessation of burning passion occurs through sexual union;
however, the specific duration of time is stated in the *Prajñapti*.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that during the same amount of time it takes for [beings] to engage in coupling, embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing, there occurs, respectively, the sexual union of those inhabitants of the earth-related realms—the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin gods.
This is the detailed explanation of the phrase "as much as... as much as."

The intention is that to the extent that the objects of the senses become increasingly intense for those higher and higher [realms], passion also becomes more intense; to that same extent, there is sexual intercourse. Furthermore, these are the four classes of gods.
From the gods of the Four Great Kings up to the Tuṣita gods,
they possess enjoyment according to how they have arisen; thus they are "those who enjoy according to their arising," and that is their state.
Therefore,
he enjoys that which has been fashioned by himself according to his own desire.
As before,
it is because of the enjoyment of what is created by oneself and by others according to one's wish; that is,
[enjoyment] of what is fashioned by oneself and by another.

Some read: "The enjoyment of those two [deities] in what is created by themselves and others according to their wish is as before, because they enjoy what is created by others according to their wish."
In that reading, the analysis of the compound is as follows:
"that which is created by others according to one's desire" is *paranirmita*; the enjoyment of that is [the meaning].
As before,
it does not succeed for the Nirmāṇarati gods to enjoy the pleasures created by others;
thus, the distinction of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods from the Nirmāṇaratis is demonstrated.

And here, the manifestation of external objects such as forms and so forth should be understood as arising from the first dhyāna stage, which is born of seclusion because it is secluded from unwholesome states.
And by means of the joy and bliss belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration, because of the departure of applied and sustained thought.
By means of the happiness characterized by joy and the happiness free from joy,
there is the disappearance of mental gladness.
"Inhabiting happiness" means that "happily" is an adverbial modifier;
it should be understood as the state of the arising of happiness.
If it is argued that because there is an absence of pleasure (*sukha*), one cannot say that the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is a rebirth in pleasure—
since it cannot be established as a "rebirth in pleasure" on the grounds that it merely resembles pleasure due to being a wholesome maturation (*kuśalavipāka*)—
then it would follow that even in the fourth dhyāna there would be a rebirth in pleasure.
The meaning is that this must be investigated and thoroughly deliberated upon, because there is no absence of happiness on that level.
In the same way, the remaining [beings] would go to Tuṣita by means of their supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), or they would go there if they were led by one possessing supernatural power.
But those belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings who share the same level as the deity residing there go to the Heaven of the Thirty-three;
having arrived there, one might see a being born in a higher realm.
"Belonging to the same level, not to a higher level" means that one born in the first dhyāna does not [perceive] one born in the second dhyāna, and so forth,
according to their wish.
"By the desire for rebirth in the higher realms, as if [it were] here"— thus,
"of this world" (*ihatyam*) means belonging to this existence (*ihabhava*).
The meaning is "belonging to a lower level. According to other schools, one should see [it] as if it were present here;
the phrase "as if to the touch" is merely an illustration.

Just as in the case of the word "sound," it should also be understood that for the four [heavens] of the desire realm, such as the Yāma and others, [the height] increases twofold at each successive stage.
The Tuṣita realm is twice the size of the Yāma realm, and so forth;
however, the fourth [realm] is immeasurable.
The intention is that its immeasurability is possible because its celestial palaces (vimānas) are connected to the *atala* subterranean vaults, like stars.
"A thousand Brahma-worlds" means [a thousand worlds] of the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmapurohitas, and the Mahābrahmans.
Because it is so recognized in the world, it is called "cūlika"; and because it serves as the crest (cūḍā) of the great world-system, it is called "cūlika."
For *sambhava* is indeed *vivarta*;
*vivarta* is a manifold turning (*vividhavartana*),
or it is called *vivarta* because various things turn within it (*vividhā vā vartante 'smin*).
*Saṃvarta* means dissolution (*saṃvartana*).

It is called *saṃvarta* because beings dissolve (*saṃvartante*) or gather together (*saṅgacchanti*) within it; for at that time, sentient beings dissolve—that is, they come together—in a single meditative absorption, either the third or the fourth.
And regarding the dissolution, it remains dissolved and dissolves simultaneously;
we shall explain this further below.
As for the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa, their measurement is four and three-and-a-half cubits.
Thus,
some have bodies measuring three and a half cubits, while others have bodies measuring four cubits.
"Pūrvagodottarāhvayāḥ" means that their names are Pūrva, Goda, and Uttara.
Those known as Pūrva, Godā, and Uttara have,
respectively, a height of eight cubits for the inhabitants of Pūrvavideha, sixteen cubits for those of Aparagodānīya, and thirty-two cubits for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
"By increasing by a quarter," and so forth;
since it will be stated later that "up to one and a half *krośas*," it is understood that "quarter" refers to a quarter of a *krośa*.
The body of the gods of the Four Great Kings is the measure of one-fourth of a *krośa*;
that of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is two *pādas*; and so on, up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, whose bodies are one and a half *krośas*.
Each subsequent realm is double the size of the preceding one, less three *yojanas*.
Having doubled [the previous measure], three *yojanas* are to be subtracted; thus,
the body-measure of the Anabhrakas is one hundred and twenty-five *yojanas*,
and that of the Puṇyaprasavas is the same.
The body size of the Puṇyaprasava deities is two hundred and fifty yojanas,
and that of the Bṛhatphala deities is five hundred yojanas; this should be calculated as being like the white and red lotuses.
Just as here the night-lotuses close during the day and bloom at night, while the day-lotuses do the reverse,
so too there the distinction between day and night is established by the closing of certain flowers and their blooming during the day.
From the singing or not singing of birds: silence indicates night, and singing indicates dawn;
or it may be the reverse, according to the specific species of bird.
And from the departure of and arrival at sleep,
night is known through the arrival of sleep;
from the departure of sleep, it is known as dawn.
"More and more" means twenty is added.
The meaning is that it becomes greater;
therefore he says:
"Thus, their lifespan is respectively forty thousand, sixty thousand, and eighty thousand kalpas."
In the sphere of infinite consciousness there are forty;
in the sphere of nothingness, sixty; and at the peak of existence, eighty.
Therefore, "half of a great kalpa below that," and so forth: eighty intermediate kalpas constitute a great kalpa;
half of that is forty intermediate kalpas.
Of that half of a great eon (mahākalpa) which is constituted as an eon, the half consisting of twenty intermediate eons (antarakalpa) is the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika gods;
that same half-eon, when calculated as an eon, consists of forty intermediate eons.
That is the lifespan of the Brahmapurohitas; half of that is the lifespan of Mahābrahmā,
which is indeed called one and a half kalpas, numbering sixty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpas).
Regarding the phrase "of Mahābrahmā and the others," by the word "others" (ādi), there is an inclusion— moving in reverse order— of the Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmakāyikas;
half [of that] is below it.
Thus, because it refers to the description "from the divine host of Parīttābha," the measure of their lifespan has been stated;
[this applies] to those Mahābrahmās, Brahmapurohitas, and Brahmakāyikas.
"Equal to the lifespan of the Kāmadevas," and so forth;
this refers to the measure of the lifespan that has been stated for the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm.
In Sañjīva, that [lifespan] constitutes a single day and night;
thus, up to the lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods as it has been described,
that becomes a single day and night in Tapana.
"Like Kāmadeva" means "like the Kāmadevas"; [the suffix] *vat* is used here in the sense of "as for that, it is like that."

"By that [measure] up to twelve months" means: by that day-and-night of theirs, with thirty such nights making a month, and twelve such months making a year, their lifespan is five hundred divine years of that place;
and so on—this should be applied accordingly to the others as well—namely, the measure of the lifespan of the Yāma gods.
In that Saṅghāta great hell, one night and day is equivalent to that measure;
by such nights and days, the lifespan there is two thousand years.
In this same manner, it should be applied accordingly to the other hells as well.

"Monks, these eight," [the Buddha said], "are these eight monks who are *nāgas*, great *nāgas*, who endure for an eon (*kalpastha*), who support the earth (*dharaṇīdhara*), and who cannot be driven away even by Suparṇin, the king of birds; they even experience and even counteract the battle between the gods and the asuras. Who, then, are they?"

They are as follows: Nanda the Naga king, Upananda the Naga king, Aśvatarī the Naga king, Mucilinda the Naga king, Manasvin the Naga king, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Naga king, Mahākāla the Naga king, and Elāpattra the Naga king— those who are bound by a crest,
bound by a topknot, and bound by a single birth.
"One whose Buddhahood is bound to a single birth" refers to one in their final existence (*caramabhavika*), that is, one in their last birth,
by whom Arhatship must be realized in that very same life.
For him, there is no death in the interval until he attains arhatship;

for the followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the followers by dharma (dharmānusārin), there is no death in the interval until they become those resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta); this applies to those who are in the womb as well.
For a Bodhisattva and a Cakravartin, there is no death in the interval between their parents until those two have been born;
such is the case for these and others.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that for those who have entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), as well as for those who have entered the meditative absorptions of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, there is no death in the interim as long as they do not emerge from that concentration;
this refers to the human hand at the time when the Abhidharma statement, "twenty-four finger-breadths make a cubit," is being uttered.
It should be understood by that [calculation] through which the determination of the measure of the four-continent world system and so forth during the winter months is established.
Just as the plural form "varṣāḥ" (rains) is well-established even for a single meaning, so too should "hemantāḥ" (winters) and "grīṣmāḥ" (summers) be understood;
in the sacred teaching (pravacana), there are only three seasons, not six as in common worldly usage.
For the cool season (śiśira) is called winter (hemanta) due to the commonality of cold; spring (vasanta) is also called summer (grīṣma) due to the commonality of heat;
and autumn (śarad) is also called the rainy season (varṣā) due to the commonality of rain.
Regarding the seasons of winter, summer, and the rainy season,
for all Buddhists, winter is the first season.
Summer is the second [season],
the rainy season is the third;
since it has one additional half [month] therein, it is called "one and a half" (adhyardha) months.
When one and a half months of Mārgaśīrṣa had passed and half of Pauṣa had elapsed.
In the remaining half-month of Pauṣa, when half [of that month] still remains, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
there is an intercalary day (ūnarātra).
It is caused to fall by learned Buddhists.
The meaning is that it is discarded.
Here, the monks perform the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day.
Thus, when half of Phālguna has passed in the month of Māgha, and the remaining half-month of Phālguna remains, another intercalary night (*ūnarātra*) is again subtracted.
Likewise, during the summer months, two further omitted nights (*ūnarātra*) are subtracted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha and on the fourteenth day of Āṣāḍha;
and during the rainy season as well, two further omitted nights are subtracted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada and on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika—
this is the "dissolution of the world" (*gatisaṃvartanī*).
The five destinies, beginning with the hells, dissolve— that is, they become unified— within a single portion of the destinies, namely the destiny of the gods;
this refers to both the dissolution of the realms (*dhātu-saṃvartanī*) and so forth.

The destruction of the desire realm within the form realm is called the "destruction of sentient beings" (sattvasaṃvartanī) when sentient beings themselves undergo destruction and become unified in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna).
But it does not mean that the receptacle worlds have already dissolved;
rather, the meaning is that they are in the process of perishing— this is what is meant by "the dissolution of the receptacle world."
When only the receptacle worlds dissolve, but not the sentient beings—
because not even a single sentient being remains there— the phrase "this world," and so forth, is used in detail.

The meaning is that when this world has remained evolved for twenty intermediate aeons (*antarakalpa*), from the time it first arose until the emergence of beings in the hells, it is said to have reached its completion.
"It should be stated that this has been entered upon" means it should be stated that the process of dissolution (saṃvartana) has begun;
in the same way, the dissolution of animals and the dissolution of hungry ghosts (pretas) should also be stated.

When not even a single being remains among the animals, to this extent this world has become dissolved through the dissolution of the animal realm; at that time, however, any karma necessarily to be experienced as an animal that still persists [remains].

He is cast among the animals in other world-systems; in the same way, the destruction of the hungry ghosts (preta-saṃvartanī) should be applied when [it occurs] among the hungry ghosts, and so on in detail,
up to those who dwell together with humans.
Cattle, buffalo, and other such animals that have the habit of associating with humans possess [this state] through the attainment of the nature of things (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*).
"Dharmatā" refers to a specific transformation of wholesome factors at that time;
"attained through dharmatā" means that one possesses [the quality] by means of that [transformation],
as it occurs among human beings.
The intention is "among the humans of Jambūdvīpa";
in this same way, the destructions of Pūrvavideha and Godānīya are to be applied,
but the destruction of Uttarakuru must be stated as follows:
That is the time when humans in Uttarakuru pass away but are no longer reborn;
when not even a single sentient being remains there,
to this extent this world has become dissolved.
Why should it be stated as "the destruction of Uttarakuru" and not, as in the case of "the destruction of Jambudvīpa" and so forth? To this he says:
Because there is an absence of detachment there— namely,
because there is an absence of detachment in Uttarakuru—
it is from this very preliminary stage (sāmantaka).

The meaning is "from the vicinity of the four continents. "When the karma that projects that [world] is exhausted" means that when the karma that projects the receptacle world— that is, the karma that produces the receptacle world— is exhausted.
The meaning is that the flame, burning the Brahma-palace, "goes forth," that is, departs; and that flame belongs to that very level, namely,
it belongs to the level of the first dhyāna.
He asks, "Why? and says:
for heterogeneous and dissimilar calamities (*apakṣāla*), such as fire and the like, do not advance—that is, they do not burn—[in that manner].
He says:
If this is so, why is it said, "and from that very [source]," and so forth? To this it is replied: "because it arises in connection with that," and so forth.
Because the flame belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara) has become connected with— that is, produced by— that flame of the lower realm of desire (kāmāvara),
its state [is so called]; it is because of that.

"Thus in another" means that just as it was explained regarding the destruction by fire (*tejaḥ-saṃvartanī*), so too in the case of the other [destructions], namely the destruction by water (*ap-saṃvartanī*) and the destruction by wind (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*), it should be understood according to what is applicable.
How so?

Having described the dissolution beginning with the hells as previously stated, up until this point the world has become dissolved through the dissolution of sentient beings; thereafter, in the empty receptacle-world, the innate water-element arises, which dissolves that receptacle-world like salt.
That water-element belonging to the desire realm connects with the water-element belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
that, in turn, connects with the water-element belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
and even though that water-element belongs to three levels, it disappears together with its respective receptacle world.
In the same way, regarding the destruction by wind, it should be stated that the innate wind arises;
having explained how this occurs as previously described, up until the point where the innate wind-element arises.

Desiring to explain the eon of evolution (*vivartakalpa*) in detail, he says: "He who gradually scatters and destroys that receptacle-world (*bhājanaloka*), from the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) up to the level of the third dhyāna, like a heap of dust, until it disappears along with him."
"For thus the world has come to be," and so forth;
"thus" means as it has been described;
"then," and so forth.
From the time when gentle breezes begin to stir in the sky,
it should be said that this world has emerged from its state of dissolution and reached the completion of those twenty intermediate kalpas during which it remained dissolved.
The meaning is that "it should be spoken when it has arrived" means "it should be spoken when it has been commenced," according to the prescribed sequence as stated.
Everything arises according to the sequence and the procedure as described;
the sequence as described is: the wind-mandala, the water-mandala, then the golden earth, and then Sumeru and the rest.
As for the procedure as described, it refers to whatever procedure was stated for each thing, characterized by its length, depth, circumference, and shape.
All that is born in that manner first as the Brahma-world, and so forth,
before it subsequently undergoes dissolution.
The established position is that it evolves first;
therefore, he says:
"But first, the Brahmā celestial palace arises."

Then, by the word "up to" in the phrase "up to the realm of the Yāmas," it is meant that immediately after the celestial palaces of Brahmā, the celestial palaces of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods arise; immediately after those, the celestial palaces of the Nirmāṇarati gods; and immediately after those, up to the celestial palaces of the Yāmas.
Then, immediately after the arising of the celestial palaces of the Yāmas, the wind-circle and the other [elements] arise.
That is to say, he shows that it is the evolution of the receptacle world (*bhājanavivartanī*), not the evolution of sentient beings (*sattvavivartanī*), when he says:
"He is born in an empty Brahma-palace," [referring] to Mahābrahmā and other sentient beings who are his retinue.
Having passed away from there, [one is reborn] among the Brahmapurohitas;
thus it emerges from the Ābhāsvaras.
The meaning is that the evolution of the world has reached its completion;
"it has arrived" means that the state of having evolved has been initiated.

"Nineteen intermediate kalpas for those of immeasurable lifespan" means that one intermediate kalpa has already passed with the completion of the formation of the receptacle world, such as the celestial palaces of the Brahma-world; thus, nineteen remaining intermediate kalpas pass for humans of immeasurable lifespan until the appearance of beings in the hells,
and this should be understood as the period of the world's evolution (vivartamānāvasthā) having been completed.

When a being has appeared in hell, the state of evolution (vivṛttāvasthā) has begun; this is called the intermediate aeon of evolution (vivṛttāntarakalpa), during which the lifespan decreases from being immeasurable down to ten years. This constitutes one intermediate aeon of evolution.
Therefore he said:
"Of those that have evolved and are remaining, the first is an intermediate kalpa," and after that,
eighteen.
There are increases and decreases;
thus, with one period of increase,
the state of evolution (vivṛttāvasthā) is to be understood as having a duration of twenty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa).
A conceptual construction (kalpa) has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature;
these very [aggregates] are the time-periods (adhvan) and the basis of discourse (kathāvastu).
"Detached" (muktaka) means that it is not included within the four Āgamas;
[it is said] "the *Aṣṭaka* was forgotten from among them."
Since eight places have been lost somewhere and were not recited by him,
there are fifty-two places here;
yet, there ought to be sixty numerical places.
One should oneself create some names for those eight [places] and recite them,
so that the sixty numerical positions may be completed;
thus they are called "the incalculable" (asaṅkhyā).
Incalculable means that which is incalculable by calculation; thus,
they are called "incalculables" (asaṃkhyā).
Because of the use of the plural number, even those [elements] not explicitly mentioned are included;
if that is so,
then it arises from the three times (asaṅkhyatraya).

If this is so, how was it said that "there is no number beyond these"? There is no fault here; it means that the eons (kalpas) are incalculable, yet they are accompanied by that which is to be calculated.
"Immeasurable" (asaṅkhya) means those that are immeasurable, and "three immeasurables" (asaṅkhyatraya) refers to the arising of three such immeasurable eons (kalpa).
"Buddhahood arises from three incalculable eons"— this is how it should be explained,
because that is his intended meaning.
Because that benefit for others is desired; for whatever is desired is seen to be one's own interest.
"Because of that" means because of self-attachment;
"self-attachment toward them," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Having turned away from self-attachment toward those conditioned phenomena belonging to one's own continuum, and having increased the regard characterized by compassion, one should understand that it is possible for them to bear sufferings for that cause— that is, for the sake of that regard— whereas the person of middling capacity seeks only the cessation of suffering.
The Pratyekabuddha and the Śrāvaka seek only the cessation of suffering, that is, liberation itself, and not the worldly happiness of saṃsāra.
Why?
Because that worldly pleasure is a locus of suffering; that is to say, it becomes a station of pain.
The excellent bodhisattva [exchanges] the sufferings occurring within his own continuum for the worldly happiness of others.
And he seeks for others the very cessation of suffering, which is the nature of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa),
and indeed the very cessation of suffering.
Why does he pray for his own Buddha-characteristics, which serve as the means for accomplishing the welfare of others? He says:
because he is one who suffers from their suffering.
Thus,
because that bodhisattva becomes sorrowful through the sufferings of others, for that very reason he seeks happiness in its two forms.
"Below the period of decline," and so forth;
the meaning is that below the hundred-year mark, the five corruptions (*kaṣāya*) become manifest, that is, they become excessive.
Even after a hundred years, they are merely *utsada* (increased) and not *abhyutsada* (greatly increased), as in the case below; thus,
the *āyus-kaṣāya* (corruption of lifespan) is a dross-like, inferior corruption.
The corruption of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) is simply the corruption that is lifespan; likewise for the corruptions of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) and so forth, in their respective order.

Failure of life occurs through the corruption of lifespan; failure of requisites occurs through the corruption of the eon, for those requisites— such as grain, flowers, fruits, and medicinal herbs— become deficient in taste, potency, ripening, and efficacy.
Or rather, they do not exist at all;
for the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities occurs through two [impurities]: the impurity of afflictions and the impurity of views.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of the context of devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure and self-mortification.
Here, "sensual pleasure" (*kāmasukhallikā*) is simply sensual pleasure itself (*kāmasukha*).
"Adherence to sensual pleasure" means either sensual craving or the pursuit of sensual pleasure, by which one becomes attached to sensual pleasure;
"self-mortification" means self-affliction or self-torment.
The "devotion to" or "cultivation of" both the pursuit of sensual pleasure and self-mortification [is what is meant].
Therefore, his qualification [for that] has been stated.
With reference to devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasures or devotion to self-mortification, the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities occurs through the two stains of afflictions and views;
thus, first of all, it is stated without distinction regarding both the factions of householders and those who have gone forth.
The failure of the side of householders due to the defilement of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*), and the failure of the side of renunciants due to the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*),
correspond respectively to the fact that householders are primarily characterized by sensual desire (*kāma*) and renunciants are primarily characterized by views (*dṛṣṭi*).
"By one" refers to the defilement of sentient beings;
for there are two kinds of *pratyekabuddhas*,
since even those who move in groups (*vargacārin*) were formerly disciples (*śrāvaka*).
It is not only those who are like the rhinoceros horn [who are solitary];

therefore, their arising even during a period of excellence is not contradictory, for there are those who, having already produced the fruit of stream-entry and the fruit of once-returning, personally realize arhatship when the Buddha's teaching has disappeared.
They were practitioners who moved in groups,
and because they had already experienced spiritual urgency (*samvega*) at the time of the previous Buddha's appearance, they did not need to be stirred to urgency again;
this was due to the demonstration of his [the Buddha's] deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Because Pratyekabuddhas manifest the deportment [of a recluse] and manifest the form of meditative absorption in the cross-legged posture, one might think that being noble ones they would not undergo arduous austerities; however,
this is not so, because at the very time of seeing the Truths, their view of attachment to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*) has already been abandoned.
And because their practice of arduous asceticism is preceded by the view of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*),
they are like the rhinoceros horn; that is,
just as the horns of a rhinoceros are solitary.
Thus, because they dwell unmixed with householders, renunciants, and other pratyekabuddhas,
they are called "those who are like the rhinoceros horn" and "those whose lineage extends for a hundred eons."
The meaning is that he has established the cause for awakening over a hundred eons;
for this very reason, [the author] explains:
"He has practiced and applied himself to the provisions for awakening—characterized by ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom—for a hundred great eons."
"And it is possible for them," and so forth;
even if they were not yet possessed of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*),
nevertheless, by means of their knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), they would be able to teach the Dharma by recollecting the previous Buddhas.
"Because of the manifestation of supernatural power" means because of the display of powers such as traveling through space for the sake of benefiting sentient beings;
nor is it because of the incapacity of sentient beings.
The ellipsis of the sentence is "they do not teach the Dharma.
To the question "Why?", he says:
"For thus," and so forth in detail.
The intention is that since worldly persons free from passion exist at that time, those who are supramundane and free from passion must also be possible;
provided, of course, that these [other factors] are not the causes for the non-performance of the teaching of the Dharma.
What, then, is the cause? He says:
"What then? and so forth in detail;
it is because of the power of previous habituation—that is, the power of habituation to non-association—and because of being resolved upon having little eagerness.
The meaning is: because they have taken pleasure in that [worldly life];
and furthermore, for the sake of avoiding the consequence of attracting a retinue, they do not venture to exert themselves in causing others to grasp the profound Dharma.
If there were such an operation, the group would have to be drawn out;
why, then, do they avoid the consequence of drawing out the group?
Because of their fear of distraction and social contact.
Due to fear of distraction and social contact,
"distraction" (*vyākṣepa*) refers to non-engagement in the intended activity such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
while "social contact" (*saṃsarga*) refers to association with others.
Furthermore, the fear of distraction and social contact arises from the force of previous habituation;
this is a conventional designation (*prajñaptika*), according to the instruction of the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
