that there are four types of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).

In the Sūtra, however, only the Golden Wheel-turning King is mentioned because of his preeminence; "impossible" (*asthāna*) refers to the present time, while "no occasion" (*anavakāśa*) refers to the future.
Because they can occur simultaneously even in the future time,
they are "without priority or posteriority";
thus, one is not prior and the other is not subsequent.
What then?
The meaning is "together with";
"equal and equal" is an intensive repetition (vīpsā).
Alternatively, he is "equal to the equals" (samasama) because he is equal to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are equal toward all sentient beings;
and he is so called because he perceives that many world-systems without effort (anābhoga), that is, without deliberate exertion (anabhisaṃskāra).
"Those of other schools" refers to the Mahāsāṃghikas and so forth;
"not in one place" means not within a single world-system during the human lifespan.
"Puruṣāyuṣam" means the lifespan of a person; "bearing that" is what is understood here. "This faculty" refers to faith and the others.
Regarding the phrase "of this factor," that is, "of this condition": what is the meaning of "with reference to one world-system"?
The intention is to ask whether this was said with reference to a single *cāturdvīpaka* (four-continent) world-system or a *trisāhasramahāsāhasra* (trichiliocosm) world-system.
And [the passage] beginning with "and even for a wheel-turning monarch" is the detailed explanation.

"It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, neither before nor after the other, should arise in the world"— by this, there is no prohibition against their arising in other world-systems,
because such a statement regarding Tathāgatas is made in the same way as it is regarding universal monarchs (cakravartins).
For even universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) are spoken of in that way;
ordinary people think it is impossible and there is no occasion for two universal monarchs, neither before nor after the other, to arise in the world simultaneously.
But wise men wield weapons and raise them;
the householder-treasure belongs to the class of treasury officials.
The counselor-jewel is of the nature of a commander-in-chief;
being "of a kind related to that," he is connected with that universal monarch.

That which leads to the dissolution of what is connected to that [wheel-turning king], or which is conducive to or favorable toward it by virtue of that connection, is called "leading to the dissolution of what is connected to that";
this refers to the karma accumulated by a sentient being when that wheel-turning king has arisen.
One's own very own mental states and actions produce him;
however, the sentient being does not become the causal condition for the arising of the wholesome maturation of a universal monarch,
and it should be understood that this wholesome maturation belongs to the universal monarch alone.
"More firmly established" means that their positions are unshakable,
more intense, more radiant, more complete, and of unimpaired form.

In connection with the topic of the universal monarch (*cakravartirāja*), this is investigated: "Indeed, up to 'together with his retinue of kings,' were they like those belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*)? To demonstrate this point, he cites the Sūtra.
It is stated in the Sūtra, and so forth:
because they have a visible form, they are "material" (rūpin); because they are born spontaneously, they are "mind-made" (manomaya).
Because they possess hands, feet, and their respective fingers and so forth, they are "endowed with all major and minor limbs"; because they possess all sense faculties, they are "unimpaired";
and because they lack conditions such as being one-eyed or having wandering vision, they have "unimpaired faculties."
They are beautiful because of their pleasing form; they are abiding in color because of their lovely hue;
and they are self-luminous because they do not depend on the light of the sun or other sources.
Because they travel through space by means of the miraculous power of karma, they are called "those who move through the air" (*vihāyaṃgamāḥ*);
because they do not depend on solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), "feeding on joy" (*prītibhakṣāḥ*) and "having joy as their nutriment" (*prītyāhārāḥ*) are synonyms.
Likewise, "those of long life remain for a long duration" means that its taste is as sweet as honey;
that is, its taste is like the sweet flavor of honey.

For sentient beings who have fallen into the prey of improper mental attention— which has become a seizing grasper— sensual desire itself is the grasper; its onset is the commencement [of that grasping],
as in the expression "for the sake of the evening meal."
For the sake of eating in the afternoon,
for the sake of eating in the morning— that is, for the sake of the morning meal.
The accumulation of stores and the gathering [of wealth]—

by dividing the fields and providing a livelihood through rice that is sown without plowing, the designations of "Kṣatriya" and so forth are established according to the method of etymological derivation (*nairukta*).
"Niryaṇa" means completion;
"those stained by passion for what is not the Dharma" refers to those who are intent upon the passion of sexual misconduct.

"Overcome by the affliction of improper greed," "enveloped by false teachings," "proclaimers of perverted teachings," "those who do not recognize their mothers, those who do not recognize their fathers," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the "time of the eon's conclusion," it is said here that there are three conclusions of an eon:
weapons, disease, and famine.
Do the three exits occur sequentially for a single ten-year lifespan kalpa, or does each exit occur sequentially for each [individual] lifespan? Regarding this,
some first say:
Others, however, say that each one [of the three] occurs sequentially for a single person.
"First famine, immediately after that disease, and immediately after that the sword"—
we see that this former position is accepted [by others],
[but we hold it to be] "by those very same faults," namely by unrighteousness (*adharma*) and so forth, as well as by passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
Non-human beings, such as piśācas and others, release calamities such as diseases and the like, or they steal vitality,
or by their power they corrupt the great elements of flowers, fruits, medicinal herbs, and so forth.
From which incurable diseases arise for them, and from which they die— such is the detailed account.
When there is killing by weapons here in Jambūdvīpa,
then malice reaches its peak in the two continents of Pūrvavideha and Avaragodānīya; and when there is disease here, [the same occurs there].
At that time, their weakness is as follows: famine here is their hunger and thirst.
The Tīrthakāras, such as Kaṇabhuj and others,
have stated that "the wind is the seed," because of the statement that [the world] is churned by winds distinguished by various powers.

"Of that, it is the cause" means that the wind of the form realm, which has not yet perished, is the cause of the wind produced in the first moment at the time of the evolution of the desire realm; thus, seeds are brought forth.
There are five kinds of seeds, beginning with root-seeds:
root-seed, joint-seed, seed-seed, tip-seed, and trunk-seed; it is thus.

Even though seeds are brought forth, they do not assert that the production of gross entities—such as sprouts and so forth—from seeds and the like, or of stalks and so forth from sprouts and the like, occurs [in such a manner].
For they hold that seeds and the like are the efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) of those things, not the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*); and yet, there must be inherent causes.
Therefore he says:
"What then? [It arises] from its own parts alone," and so forth.

For example, a composite whole such as a sprout arises from its own parts; those parts of the sprout likewise arise from their own respective parts, and those too from their own, continuing in this manner down to the atoms.
The intention is that, apart from the approaching of atoms,
seeds and the like possess no capacity whatsoever for production; rather,
their capacity is asserted only through the approaching of the atoms of the sprout and so forth.
"For there would be no restriction" means that [otherwise] mats and the like might arise even from threads and so forth;
[this is avoided] because of the restriction of causal capacity (*śakti*).
Just as, due to the restriction of the capacities of seeds and so forth, [an effect] will not arise indeterminately—
just as sound arises from heterogeneous causes such as impact— so too [is the case here].
And yet, they do not arise from just any heterogeneous cause such as odor or taste,
because only heterogeneous causes such as impact possess the capacity to produce them;
likewise, color and other qualities born of maturation (pākaja) arise from heterogeneous causes such as fire.
And yet, they do not arise from just anything heterogeneous, such as the eye and so forth,
because only fire and the like possess the capacity to produce them; thus says the Vaiśeṣika.
The quality of color (citra) indeed arises from both homogeneous and heterogeneous causes;
first, with respect to homogeneous causes, color, taste, smell, touch, and so forth, being preceded by their own causes, arise only from color, taste, smell, touch, and so forth.
Even from heterogeneous causes—such as conjunction, disjunction, and those produced by heat—from actions and so forth [qualities arise];
thus, the property of a quality is not an illustration for the property of a substance, for it is precisely those [substances] that exist in such a manner; this is the detailed explanation.
For it is the *vīraṇa* grass and so forth themselves that, being arranged and situated in such a manner—
that is, in the form of a mat and so on— receive the designation "mat," just like a row of ants.
Just as ants,
being arranged in a certain way, receive the designation "row," yet there is no substance "row" other than them, so it is in your own established doctrine as well.

How is it understood that those vīraṇa-grasses and so forth, when arranged in such a manner, receive the designation "mat" and the like, and yet are not separate substances from them? To this, he says:

Because a cloth is not perceived when there is a connection with only a single thread— since, according to your view, when a single thread that has begun its effect is conjoined with both the eye and touch, the cloth would also be in close proximity to those two, and thus it too should be perceived in that same way—
if one were to say this:
If it is argued that its non-perception is due to an obstruction,
he says in response:
"For what could there be as an obstruction to the perception of that cloth when it exists and is present?"
The intention is that there is no connection;
therefore, the view might be that there is no distinct substance called "cloth."
In each individual thread, the cloth exists only by way of a portion and not by its entire self;
therefore it is said,
"existing non-wholly," and so forth.
If it is assumed that the cloth exists only partially, then only a portion of the cloth would exist in each individual thread, and not the cloth itself; if one asks what follows from this,
he says:

It follows that the mere collection [of parts] would not be the cloth; for if one part exists in one thread and another part in another, then it results that the cloth is merely the aggregate of the many parts residing in the threads,
which is not accepted.

And those who follow the Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika) must be asked: "What part of the cloth is other than the threads? by which part this [cloth] would exist in a thread that is in contact with the sense organ;
therefore, even having constructed this conceptualization, no cloth other than these [threads] is established.
This might be thought:
The cloth exists even in each individual thread; however, the perception of the cloth is caused by the contact between the cloth and the sense organ,
which depends upon the conjunction of the cloth with multiple substrates.
Therefore, if one assumes that perception depends on a conjunction with multiple substrates, then when a mere collection of parts is grasped, the cloth should be perceived;
yet it is not so perceived, because the middle part of the cloth and other such portions are not seen.
Now, if it is thought that even at that time the middle and other parts are not in contact with the sense organ,
and therefore the perception of the cloth does not occur when there is a mere collection of threads;
To this, it is replied:
"Or rather, never," and so forth;
that is to say, there would never be the perception of a cloth.
Because the middle and rear parts [of an object] are not in contact with the sense organ,
it is simply impossible for all those middle and rear parts that constitute it to be in contact with the sense organ;
and if that were the case, this same consequence would apply even to threads and the like, such that no effect whatsoever could be perceived.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning "And in the case of successive contact," it means that when the eye or the tactile organ perceives a cloth in succession,
there would be no perception of the cloth as a whole.
Because there is no simultaneous conjunction with multiple substrates, there would likewise be no perception of other parts by the sense organs of sight and touch; such is the detailed argument.

Since the cognition of a cloth or the cognition of a mat occurs only successively, therefore that cognition— the cognition of a cloth or the cognition of a mat— arises with respect to the parts themselves, namely the parts of the cloth or the parts of the mat, by the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
like the circle of a whirling firebrand.
Just as a firebrand, due to its rapid movement, gives rise to the cognition of a circle of fire as it appears in various places,
so too is the proof in this case.
The cloth does not exist as a substantial entity,
because its apprehension is dependent upon the apprehension of its parts,
like a fire-brand wheel.
"In those of different form, genus, and action," and so forth;
that is, in threads of different forms due to distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so on,
and in [threads] of different genera due to distinctions such as *dukūla* silk and cotton.
Regarding the different actions: due to the distinction between upward and downward movement,
and because color and other qualities cannot exist in a cloth [when it is moving],
what kind of "form" (rūpa) could there be in that case— is it a genus (jāti) or an action (kriyā)?
It might be thought: "Its color and other qualities are variegated.
But if its color and other qualities are thus conceived as being variegated, there would also be the production of heterogeneous effects;
even from threads and vīraṇa grass, a mat could be produced.
If that were the case, it would follow that there is a reversal of the specific properties of things;
the meaning is that substances would come to possess the capacity to originate something of an entirely different genus.
Furthermore, on the other side which is not variegated, the cloth—which is variegated on one side—would not be perceived.
Because that [color] is considered to have a variegated form,
the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that upon the perception of color, there is the apprehension of the substance which is its substratum;
for they hold that perception occurs when there is magnitude, possession of multiple substances, and color.
Because it is stated that air is not perceived due to the absence of the formation of color-form (*rūpa-saṃskāra*),
the perception of variegated color-form would have to occur on a side that is not variegated if the cloth were visible;
for its color-form is held to be variegated.
If action is also manifold,
then it is not the case that "this single substance possesses manifold actions" is without fault;
for when there is diversity of action, a difference among the substances intended to possess those actions is necessarily admitted.
"And in the case of the difference between heat and light," and so forth.

In the case of a whole characterized by fire and its radiance, when there is a difference in heat and light among the constituent parts at the beginning, middle, and end, a difference in touch is observed;
and that difference therein is, respectively, intense, moderate, and dull.
Those two—color and touch—are not possible for that composite substance consisting of light;
for it is not logical that a single composite should possess multiple colors or touches.
Therefore, there is no composite substance distinct from its parts.
Now, it might be thought: if the composite whole, such as a cloth, does not exist as something distinct from its parts, such as the threads,
because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses;
And since the sensory object is not composed of those parts,
the entire world would be imperceptible;
yet cows and other such things are seen to be perceptible.
Therefore, it is established that another distinct object, which is perceptible by the senses, is commenced by the atoms which are themselves imperceptible; to this it is replied:
"Even though the atoms are beyond the senses," and so forth.
Just as for you Vaiśeṣikas, although they are beyond the senses, the atoms in their aggregate state possess the capacity to originate an effect, but not when they are separate.
In this way, for us as well, perceptibility belongs only to atoms when they are combined, not when they are separate, even though there is no "whole" (*avayavin*) existing as a distinct entity.

Just as the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention—when combined—are the causes for the arising of visual consciousness, but not individually; so too, although atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), they possess perceptibility when combined, but not each one individually.
And for people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), a mass of scattered and unconnected hairs is perceived even when no composite whole (*avayavin*) has been produced;
yet for those afflicted with ophthalmia, each individual hair is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), just like an atom (*paramāṇu*).
Therefore, there is no other substance for you;
thus, having refuted the whole (avayavin), he who wishes to refute that the possessor of qualities (guṇin) is a distinct entity from the qualities such as form (rūpa) and so forth, says:
"And precisely in form and so forth," and so on in detail.
The Vaiśeṣikas say that the designation "atom" (paramāṇu) is applied only to form and the other [sensory objects];
therefore, when those [objects] perish— that is, when form and the others perish— the destruction of the atom is established.
For substance (*dravya*) is indeed the atom (*paramāṇu*), and substance is distinct from [qualities] such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth,
according to established doctrinal statements such as "earth possesses form, odor, taste, and tangibility."

Its distinctness is not established because these—earth, water, and fire—and these qualities of theirs, such as color and so forth (namely, color, taste, smell, and touch), cannot be discerned by anyone as being "these are the earth and the others" or "these are their qualities.
Since they are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), they cannot be determined; therefore, he says:
And since those [elements] such as earth and so forth are asserted to be perceivable by sight and touch,
the phrase "and when they are burned," and so forth,
refers to the Pailikas, who maintain that composite substances such as wool and the like are not burned.
What is meant is this:
when the previous qualities cease and qualities produced by baking arise, the substances that serve as their substrates remain in that very same state;
thus, the cognition of wool and so forth would occur in exactly that manner.
And it does not exist;
therefore, because there is no cognition of that substance,
the cognition of it occurs only with respect to form and so forth, and not with respect to a substance that is a separate entity.

For if a substance such as wool were other than its color and other qualities, it would remain in its own state; thus, when the color and other qualities are consumed by heat through contact with fire, there would still be a cognition of "wool" and so forth. But this is not the case;
therefore, the cognition of wool and the like occurs only with respect to the color and other qualities themselves.
The Vaiśeṣikas say:
"If a jar were merely its form and other qualities, then when different forms and so forth produced by baking arise through contact with fire, one would not recognize that 'this is that same jar.

But for one who holds that through baking only the forms and so forth arise and cease while the jar itself remains in that very state, the recognition of it as such is logical; therefore, this is said:"
Regarding the recognition of a jar upon the arising of that produced by baking (*pākaja*),
it is due to the similarity of its configuration;
this means it is due to the similarity of the form and so forth of its shape.
Just as in the case of a row, for you there exists no substance called a "row" distinct from the ants;
nevertheless, because of the similarity of the configuration of the preceding row, there occurs the cognition of it in another [row].
"This is that very same line of ants"—
how is this understood?

Regarding the claim that "recognition occurs due to the similarity of configuration, but not due to the persistence of the same state," it is replied here: [this is so] because there is no recognition for one who does not perceive the characteristic mark (*cihna*).
Since the cognition of that [earth] does not occur for one who does not perceive marks such as brokenness, depressions, or elevations,
it is established that [the cognition arises] from the generality of shape (*saṃsthānasāmānya*);
and "that" [is the earth], and so forth in detail.
And that joy, through its association with pliancy (*prasrabdhi*)—
since pliancy of the mind arises from joy— is like water because it makes the basis (the body) supple through that association with pliancy;
and for this very reason, [the verse says] "and thus," and so forth.
Because the basis is made supple,
in that second meditative attainment, due to the departure of all bodily rigidity, the cessation of the faculty of suffering is stated.

And because of the statement: "With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of mental joy and mental grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness."
"Because it is free from internal defects" refers to those eight internal defects, namely: applied thought (*vitarka*),
sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the four beginning with breath— namely, inhalation, exhalation, pleasure, and so forth.
The meaning is "because it is devoid of that";
"unshakable" (*ānejya*) is a form derived from the verbal root *ejṛ*, which means "to shake. Thus, it is called "unshakable" (*ānejya*).
But when the reading is *āniñjyam*, then this form should be understood as belonging to a different verbal root, *iṅg*,
for it is not possible for those belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host to enter the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
Because they are characterized by insight (vipaśyanā),
those whose conduct is tranquility (śamatha) do not go to the formless realms (ārūpya), nor do they go elsewhere to a superior stage.
Because it proceeds toward a higher distinction by this sequence— that is,
by the manner already described— immediately after the seven destructions by fire, there occurs one destruction by water.
Furthermore, immediately after seven destructions by fire, there occurs a second destruction by water;
and in this manner, up to a seventh destruction by water, when seven such cycles by water have thus passed, again—
After that, there is a sequence of seven [destructions] by fire, followed by one destruction by wind.
What is the reason? Because, as it has been described, a destruction occurs even after a vast duration of time.
Because the wind-destruction (*vāyu-saṃvartanī*) lasts for a much longer period than even that, it is said:
"For just as, among them," and so forth;

that is, just as there is a specific distinction in the duration of the personal existences belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, due to the excellence of the attainment of the second dhyāna over the first dhyāna.
The lifespan of those born in the first dhyāna is half of a great aeon (ardha-mahākalpa), while that of those born in the second dhyāna is two aeons;
the same applies to their receptacle worlds as well.
What is this "distinction in stability"?
In this way, the distinction of the third dhyāna must also be stated relative to the second.
And having established it thus—

since there are eight cycles of destruction by fire (tejaḥ-saṃvartanī), which constitute fifty-six destructions by fire, seven destructions by water (ap-saṃvartanī), and one destruction by wind (vāyu-saṃvartanī), making sixty-four destructions in total— it follows that what was stated in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* is correct: "The measure of the lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna deities is sixty-four eons (kalpa)."
That is well said:
just as the physical basis [of the body] is superior to the Parīttābha deities.
Regarding the statement "doubling, doubling," it has been stated there that the body size of the Śubhakṛtsna gods is sixty-four yojanas,
and their lifespan is stated to be equal to that body size.

But as for the lifespan, it is measured in kalpas according to the statement "its own basis [is measured] by kalpas," on the grounds that each individual period of destruction (saṃvartanī) constitutes a great kalpa (mahā-kalpa).
For it is at the end of this much time that their lifespan reaches its completion;
thus ends the third treasury-location in the *Sphuṭārthā* commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* composed by the master Yaśomitra.
CHAPTER 4: Exposition of Karma (Karmanirdeśa)

Having had doubts aroused by the misconceptions of the *tīrthakaras*, he asks: "Now, as for this... and so forth. In that regard, the diversity of sentient beings is due to distinctions such as realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and modes of birth (*yoni*); the diversity of the receptacle world is due to distinctions such as Mount Meru and the continents; and [the diversity] of those who perform mixed actions is likewise.

Now, why is it that for those who perform wholesome and unwholesome deeds, their physical bases (āśraya) are not delightful, while their enjoyments (bhoga) are delightful? For if this were the case, the enjoyment of sense objects would be possible; for if the physical base itself were delightful, what remedy would there be for the enjoyment of sense objects? As for those who perform mixed deeds—namely, the gods of the form realm (rūpāvacara)—the gods of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are also like those who perform unmixed deeds, in that their physical bases and sense objects are delightful. This is because they have performed two kinds of karma that cause such delight: first, through volition (*cetayitvā*), thinking "I shall do this," and second, through the actual performance of the deed.

If [action] were defined by its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then since verbal action would be one [type], speech itself would be the action; however, the other two would not possess the status of action, for there is no action of the body by means of the body, nor is there bodily action, and likewise no mental action. Thus, action is not established by its intrinsic nature alone. Rather, the three [types of action]—body, speech, and mind—are established by way of three causes: by way of basis (*āśraya*), by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and by way of origination (*samutthāna*).

Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind: in terms of their basis (*āśraya*), bodily action is "action based on the body" (*kāyāśrayaṃ karma*); in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), vocal action is "speech itself as action" (*vāg eva karma*); and in terms of its origination (*samutthāna*), mental action is "that which is originated by the mind" (*manaḥ-samutthitam*). Others, such as the Vātsīputrīyas, maintain that "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to a "coming-into-being" (*ātmalābha*) that perishes immediately thereafter. According to the etymological method (*nairukta*), that which has a coming-into-being that perishes immediately is designated by the word "moment. Alternatively, a "moment" is the limit of time (*kālaparyanta*); that which possesses this duration of its own abiding is "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).

Therefore, by the rule *ata ini-ṭhanau*, the suffix *ṭhan* is applied; since that which has been produced must necessarily perish, destruction occurs immediately after arising—just like the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*). For the destruction of entities is indeed spontaneous (*akasmika*).

"Accidental" (*ākasmika*) means occurring without cause; the proof for this is: "Destruction is causeless because it is a non-entity (*abhāva*), like absolute non-existence. The detailed explanation continues: "The destruction of wood and so forth is indeed observed [to be caused]. By the word "and so forth," visible form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are included. [The opponent claims: "Destruction is observed to result from contact with fire. This points out the flaw in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*), namely that it contradicts the actual nature of things as established through perception. For this very reason, he says: "There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more weighty than what is observed. The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition more authoritative than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The Teacher, demonstrating the opponents' misconception regarding perception, says:

How, then, do you think? For the destruction of wood and such things is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the same way that color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities are. Those who maintain the non-momentary theory (*akṣaṇikavādin*) say: "Because they are no longer seen. This means: because those [things] such as wood are no longer seen. Thus, he demonstrates its establishment through inference (*anumāna*): "The destruction of wood and such things has conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) as its cause. When [fire] occurs, [destruction] exists; whatever exists when something occurs has that thing as its cause. For example, a sprout is produced when a seed occurs. However, this must first be carefully considered.

He demonstrates the lack of invariable concomitance: for it is not the case that whatever destruction occurs upon the arrival of something X is caused by that X. Indeed, when there is contact with wind, the lamp is destroyed; yet that destruction is not produced by the contact with wind. This is because, since the momentariness of the lamp is admitted, its destruction is held to be spontaneous. For the lamp, being destroyed as soon as it has arisen, perishes of its own accord. It is simply not seen because another [moment] does not arise due to the obstruction by the wind; it is not "destroyed" by that [wind]. Likewise, the sound of a bell is admitted to be momentary.

When there is a falling together of hands, the sound of the bell perishes; yet that [perishing] is not caused by that [impact]. For the sound of the bell perishes of its own accord due to its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Because it obstructs another [sound], the latter is not perceived; it is not, however, because of that [impact] that the [first] sound perishes. Therefore, this point is to be established through inference (*anumāna*), and it is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); such is the intention. Consequently, the following is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): "Whatever destruction occurs upon the falling of this [hand] is caused by that. What, then, is the inference here?

Regarding the point that destruction is causeless, what is the inference? It has already been stated: "Because non-existence is not an effect, destruction is causeless. It is causeless because it is not an effect, like space; and it is not an effect because its nature is non-existence, like absolute non-existence.

"Of nothing whatsoever without a cause" means "of nothing whatsoever by chance. The phrase "like arising" (*utpādavat*) is a comparison by way of contrast; for just as arising, which is characterized by the acquisition of self-nature, is necessarily with a cause and not without a cause, so too would its destruction be [with a cause]. But this is not the case. How so? He says: "And the destruction of momentary things—such as cognitions, sounds, and flames—is seen to be accidental (*ākasmika*). Thus, [the opponent's position] falls into the reach of inference (*anumāna*).

The Vaiśeṣikas hold that the destruction of wood and other things is spontaneous, being a reversal of their essential nature (*dharmasvarūpaviparyaya*), because they possess the inherent property of perishability, just like the destruction of cognitions (*buddhi*) and so forth. They maintain that a preceding cognition is destroyed by a subsequent cognition that has arisen, while another [subsequent] cognition is destroyed by the preceding one; the same should be said for sound. [The author] says: This is not tenable. Why? Because of the non-coexistence (*asamavadhāna*) of two cognitions; the meaning is that they do not exist simultaneously. For a cause does not destroy that which is to be destroyed if it is no longer present. How, then, is it known that there is no coexistence of two cognitions?

Therefore, he says: "For the coexistence of doubtful and certain cognitions is not logical," and so forth. This is to be personally experienced (*svasaṃvedya*): when there is a doubtful cognition, there is no certain cognition; when there is a certain cognition, there is no doubtful cognition. In this same way, the non-coexistence of pleasure and pain, as well as of attachment and aversion, is to be applied. And just as there is no coexistence of contradictory [states], so too there is no coexistence of even non-contradictory cognitions.

"And when... and so forth in detail. Even if there were a conjunction [of conditions], nevertheless, the dull intellect and sound would not harm the sharp ones, because they belong to the same class as that which is weak; for it is never observed that one belonging to the same class as a weak thing harms what is strong. However, one that is of a different class might harm even if it is weak, such as water [harming] fire. As for the claim that "it is also because of the absence of a cause for the persistence of flames,"...

The Elder Vasubandhu and others have stated that the destruction of entities occurs because there is no cause for their continued existence; however, that reason is incorrect, for non-existence cannot function as a cause. Furthermore, regarding the Vaiśeṣika claim that it occurs "by the power of merit and demerit," [the author] replies: "Nor [is it due to] the causes of arising and destruction. This means that for the causes of arising and destruction—namely, demerit—the state is moment by moment (*kṣaṇe kṣaṇa eva*). The meaning is: at every single moment.

The acquisition of activity and the obstruction of activity—the acquisition of activity and the obstruction of activity—cannot occur moment by moment. Why so? Because when a flame arises, it would have to be assisted by someone such as Caitra or Maitra, whose nature has attained activity, and thus [the flame] produces that [flame]; in this way, there would be a cause for its production. Furthermore, regarding the cause of destruction: if its destruction were to receive assistance from that [agent], [then the same logic would apply].

In the state of darkness, even so, when there is non-dharma (*adharma*)—and for one who experiences harm upon the arising of a flame, that non-dharma has acquired its activity and produces it—even if it is the cause of its destruction, if that destruction also brings about a benefit for it during the state of darkness, then because both have acquired their activity, the arising of the flames occurs; and since their activity is not obstructed by those two, their destruction does not take place at that very same moment by those two alone.

In every moment, the occurrence of both the acquisition and the obstruction of activity is not tenable for these two; furthermore, this conceptualization of a cause is impossible, as is explained at length. The conceptualization of a cause—that there is a destruction of merit and demerit—can be applied everywhere to all conditioned things, such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and the like, to impermanent phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), and to action (*karman*); therefore, this [conceptualization] should not be asserted.

From such [reasoning] as "the destruction of wood and so forth results from conjunction with fire," the momentariness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is established; for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) do not depend on any other cause for their destruction. Enough of this dispute! [If you argue: "In that very case, or by some similar means—if it is conceived that the conjunction with fire, having removed the blackness of the jar, produces redness, and that same [conjunction], having removed the redness, produces a deeper redness—then the cause itself would be the destroyer."

Now, if it is imagined that because flames are momentary, one [flame] is the producer of their conjunction and another is the destroyer, then the destroyer would be indistinguishable from the cause; and this is not logical. Thus, regarding all other flames, even though there is a difference in their causes, the Vaiśeṣikas might still imagine such a conceptualization—that because flames are momentary, one is the producer and another is the destroyer.

But when a specific transformation produced by heating arises due to the pressure of an alkaline substance and so forth, what kind of conceptual construction could they possibly imagine? For for them, the alkaline substances and such are not momentary; thus, the cause itself would have to be the destroyer. As for the detailed explanation beginning with "If [it is argued] that water," the intention is: if water is not destroyed even when in contact with fire, how then is it that water diminishes when being boiled? [The answer is: It is the element of fire (*tejodhātu*). This refers to its growth in inseparable association [with the water]; by its power, the mass of water becomes increasingly diminished. Thus, from a specific cause, a specific effect arises.

It becomes increasingly emaciated until it reaches a state of extreme emaciation; at the end, it does not continue its series (*santāna*) nor perform its function, but rather the meaning is that it does not produce non-existence. "Because of its fragile nature" is the elaboration:

because it has the character of breaking, perishing by itself, and having no destruction produced by another, these [entities], being existent, perish as soon as they have arisen, having obtained their self-nature for a single moment, like a grass-flame.
Just as, although a grass-flame is momentary, there is the misconception of motion when it arises uninterruptedly in different locations, such that one says "it burns the grass."

Just as flames move, so too the means of accomplishment—the entities such as form and so forth that arise continuously in another location without having a [physical] motion—are momentary; therefore, the Vaibhāṣika statement that "bodily intimation is shape, like a flame of grass" [is accepted].

"Facing one direction" (*ekadiṅmukha*) means that which has one direction as its face; in that which is "more," that is, more extensive—thus "all"—when there is more toward the upper direction facing one way, it is designated as "elevated" (*unnata*); when there is more below, it is [designated] as "depressed" (*avanata*). This direction is not substantially existent (*dravyasat*), because its configuration is like a whirling firebrand (*alāta*); for it is grasped through the grasping of color (*varṇa*), and because it is grasped by way of a mental construct (*pakṣa*), it is like a circle of fire (*tālātacakra*).

Alternatively, [it might be argued that] shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not a substantial entity (*dravya*), because it is perceived through a different form and because it is grasped by two [senses], like a heap of grain; thus, it would follow that its perception occurs via two [senses]. To this, the Vaibhāṣika might say: "Length and so forth are not perceived by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). Rather, when the parts of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) are arranged in such a way, the perception of length and so forth occurs. Therefore, it does not follow that its perception occurs via two [senses]. To this, the following is said: "Or, just as the tangible," and so forth. What [is meant]?

The meaning is as follows: just as there is the perception of length, shortness, and so forth regarding the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), yet shape (*saṃsthāna*) is not included within the sense-sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), so too should one consider that the perception of length and so forth regarding color (*varṇa*) might likewise exist, even though shape would not be a separate entity included within the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*). Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣika says: "In that case, it is mere memory," and so forth. This means that in that regard, concerning shape, it is merely memory because of its association with touch—that is, because of its state of co-occurrence with tangibles such as smoothness and the like.

But there is no direct perception of shape, such as length and so forth, as is the case when, having seen the color of fire, a recollection of that fire’s heat arises due to their constant association; this is what is meant by “it is appropriate here,” and so forth. It is appropriate here because heat is never found apart from fire, and thus there is a recollection of one thing through another—namely, of heat through the color of fire, or of its color through the fragrance of a flower. But it is not the case that any [tangible quality] such as smoothness and so forth exists anywhere in a shape such as length and so forth; this is the full meaning. However, no tangible quality such as smoothness and so forth exists anywhere within a shape such as length and so forth.

Since, in this case, when one has touched a tangible object, the recollection of its shape necessarily occurs—just as where there is the form of fire, it must be accompanied by heat, and where there is the fragrance of a *campaka* flower, it must be accompanied by that color—it does not follow that wherever there is smoothness or roughness, there must be length or shortness. Therefore, while a necessary connection is appropriate between that [tangible] and its heat or color, a necessary recollection of the shape does not obtain, even though such a thing may exist.

If there were a rule of concomitance (*sāhacarya-niyama*) between the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) and the shape (*saṃsthāna*), then the recollection of the shape would necessarily occur upon touching the tangible; [and by parity of reasoning] the recollection of the color (*varṇa*) would also necessarily occur. Thus, the meaning is that one would necessarily remember the color after having touched the tangible. Alternatively, if the recollection of the color occurs without necessity, then the recollection of the shape would likewise occur without necessity—just as with the color—such that one might think "short" when there is "long," or "long" when there is "short."

What is the reason? For regarding color (*varṇa*), recollection occurs without restriction; from a tangible object, one might sometimes recollect "yellow" when it was red, or "red" when it was yellow. But this does not happen [regarding shape]. Why does it not happen in this way? [Because] just as recollection regarding color does not occur with restriction, so too would it be unrestricted regarding shape (*saṃsthāna*). What then? It is incorrect to say that while recollection regarding color is not restricted, recollection regarding shape is restricted.

How, then, does the recollection of this shape arise from the tangible? It has been stated: when a greater number of colors or tangibles are perceived in a particular direction, there arises a conceptual cognition of "long," whereas when they are fewer, there arises a conceptual cognition of "short. This and other such cases are to be understood through the example of a variegated painting (*citram*), and so forth. Or, by means of a variegated painting—where many types of multiple colors and shapes are seen—there is a perception of multiple shapes.

Is it seen as long and so forth? Because multiple shapes are perceived, [the atom] would have to occupy the same location as many shapes; for one perceives length in this very place and shortness and so forth in that very place, and that is illogical. Furthermore, just as color does not occupy a single location because it possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), so too shape [would not]. This being the case, the position that "shape exists substantially" becomes flawed, because it contradicts the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*). And that [shape] does not exist in an atom, just as blue and other colors do not.
In an atom consisting of eight substances and so forth, [color and shape] do not exist; likewise, in an atom, shapes such as long and so forth do not exist.

How, then, is it understood that shape does not exist in the atom? Because when a long shape is diminished, the cognition of "long" ceases to exist. For if one perceives a long staff, the cognition of "long" would not cease even as that very staff is being diminished; for when a substance such as blue is perceived, the cognition of "yellow" does not arise as that substance is diminished. However, when a long substance is diminished, the cognition of "short" arises, not the cognition of "long. And it is not tenable to say that the shape itself remains.

"Because it produces the cognition of long and so forth, as well as short and so forth, therefore [the term] 'only in many' applies; thus, the full argument is as follows. The intention is this: it is precisely the atoms of shape (*saṃsthāna-paramāṇu*) that, when arranged in such a manner—following a sequence toward a single direction and so on—become designated as "long" and so forth. For things that do not have that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are not capable of being perceived with that designation when arranged in that way. Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of the parts of shape is not established in the same way as that of color (*varṇa*) and so forth, because there are no parts of color.

The [atoms] of color and so forth have well-established intrinsic natures because they are perceived in each individual part as being blue and so on; however, atoms of shape are not perceived in each individual part as being long and so on. Therefore, they do not have well-established intrinsic natures.

But if those atoms of color and so forth do not possess the nature of length and so on, yet become the causes for the cognition of length and so on due to a particular arrangement (*saṃniveśa-viśeṣa*), then why is it not accepted that the atoms of color themselves, through a particular arrangement, become the causes for the cognition of length and so on? As for the point that "it is non-different from the state of being color" (*varṇatva-abhinna*): if shape (*saṃsthāna*) were merely the arrangement of color, then there would be no difference in shape when there is no difference in color, because clay vessels such as jars and the like are not distinct entities [from the clay]. Now, as for what was said in detail: "Just as... [the following applies].

When a color is situated facing a single direction, the designation "long" and so forth is applied; and regarding the phrase "and a color," the full explanation is as follows: just as in the case of ants and so forth, where ants and the like are of a uniform form, yet their "line" appears different in one place and different again in another—just as there is such a distinction among wheels and the like—and likewise, even though there is no difference in the color, there may be a difference in shape. As for the passage beginning with "then, in the dark": when, in the dark, they do not see the color...

The ellipsis of the sentence is: "How is it that they perceive the length, shortness, circularity, and so forth of posts, persons, elephants, and the like? If, then, shape were not a distinct category from color, then just as they do not perceive color as "blue" or "yellow," they likewise would not perceive shape as "long" or "short. Yet they do perceive it at times; therefore, shape is a distinct category. This is like the conceptualization of a row or an army: for example, when one sees birds or ants indistinctly in the dark, one perceives them as "a long row."

Or just as, having seen elephants and so forth indistinctly in the very midst of darkness, people imagine, "This army is stationed in a circular formation," so too is this understood to be the case: as has just been stated, even though there is no distinct shape (*saṃsthāna*) other than the color itself, they nevertheless perceive that indistinct color and form mental constructions such as "long" and so on—this is what is meant by the phrase "when [the object] is not being determined with its boundaries. This is the detailed explanation. "With its delimitation not being determined" means...

Just as one does not postulate any other substance, so too shape (*saṃsthāna*) should not be postulated as something distinct from color (*varṇa*). [This refers to] a mere collection whose configuration is not being determined, which is unmanifest and whose blueness and so forth are not being perceived; and just as it is held that there exists a sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) distinct from both color and configuration, because of the statement "it is seen by the eye," yet no other substance is postulated—so too shape should not be postulated as distinct from color. In this context, "those venerable ones" means "those venerable ones. [The opponent asks: "How do they designate bodily action (*kāyakarman*), given that [shape] is seen by others? Thinking that bodily action is untenable because it exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), he asks: "Is it the basis of the body (*kāyādhiṣṭhāna*)?"

The meaning is that it has the body as its objective support (*ālambana*). For that action whose body is to be set in motion has the body as its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*); thus he says: "What is the volition (*cetanā*) that leads the body here and there? This is to be understood according to the circumstances. Likewise, action having speech as its basis is vocal action; mental action, however, is the action of the mind, or action associated with the mind—this is called "mental action" according to the circumstances. The detailed explanation is that "because of the absence of informative intimation (*vijñapti*). If informative intimation did not exist, then even non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm would not exist.

For non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) would indeed be dependent upon informative matter (*vijñapti*), and not following the mind (*cittānuparivartin*). And if that were so, great faults would follow: the fault of the non-existence of restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); the fault of the non-existence of the increase of merit through the seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), and so forth. These are the consequential faults (*anuṣaṅga*). Furthermore, there are counter-consequents (*pratyanuṣaṅga*) to these faults; the meaning is that these will serve as their refutations. [The phrase] "from what is designated as bodily action" (*kāyakarma-saṃśabdita*)...

The meaning is "due to the basis of the body. [The Sautrāntikas say: "Like non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*). Just as non-informative matter in a state of concentration follows the mind, so too would non-informative matter characterized by the Prātimokṣa vows and so forth follow the mind. The Sautrāntikas reply: "It will not be so; it will not follow the mind. Because of the specific nature of volition (*cetanā*) that is not in a state of concentration, there is a specific projection of it; the meaning is that there is a projection of non-informative matter that is not in a state of concentration. Furthermore, even that informative matter (*vijñapti*) of yours, being existent and present, [is the cause] of the non-informative matter..."

In this context, one observes—that is, depends upon—the strength and efficacy of the volition that initiates [the action]. Why? Because of its insentience and lack of clarity; without the power of that volition, one is unable to produce that non-informative action (*avijñapti*). For an informative action (*vijñapti*) that arises by chance does not produce a non-informative action when the volition of formal undertaking (*samādāna-cetanā*) is absent.

However, the word "but" (*tu*) serves as a qualification: unlike bodily informative action, which consists of shape (*saṃsthāna*), vocal informative action is not like that. What then? It means that vocal informative action is sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*), having the nature of speech.
As for the non-informative action, it has already been explained previously.

Those two have been described as informative and non-informative; therein, the informative has been explained, and the non-informative is now to be discussed, though it has already been mentioned previously.

Because of the statement, "even for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind," that [non-informative action] also does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). That informative action (*vijñapti*) also does not exist as a substantial entity; the word "also" (*api*) implies that it is not only the informative action [that lacks substance]. Because it is merely the undertaking of non-doing—namely, having undertaken, "From this day forward, I shall abstain from taking life and so forth"—the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is merely the non-doing of those [unwholesome acts] thereafter. Thus, the Sautrāntikas maintain that it does not exist as a substantial entity. Furthermore, regarding those past great elements (*mahābhūta*), there is no such thing as a present intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in what is past; this will be demonstrated in the fifth chapter of the *Kośa*.

How can that which does not exist be its basis? Therefore, it does not exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*). Because it lacks the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), it is called "form" (*rūpyate*) [only figuratively]; and since that characteristic of form does not exist for it due to its non-obstructive nature (*apratighatva*), it does not exist substantially. Thus, it is said to be "threefold," and so forth. It is threefold and stainless (*amala*); this is the expression of the threefold stainless form. "The path of one who does not act" (*akurvat-patha*) means an action performed by another on behalf of one who is not acting themselves. These—namely, the expression of the threefold stainless form, increase (*vṛddhi*), and the path of one who does not act—are the first among these.

The mention of the three kinds [of form], pure form, and the increase [of form], as well as the path of the non-doer, and so forth—by the word "and so forth," the statement "O Bhikṣu, this is the Dharma" is also included, as is the mention of the Noble Eightfold Path and the mention of the Prātimokṣa restraint as a dam. Regarding the inclusion of form within form: the inclusion of form occurs by means of form alone, and not by other [aggregates] such as feeling and so on. There is form that is visible and resistant, namely the eye and the other [sense organs]; there is form cognizable by consciousness; there is form that is invisible and resistant, namely the eye and the other [sense objects]. Furthermore, that...

There are nine bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) that are invisible and non-obstructive, which are cognizable by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), namely, non-informative form (*avijñaptirūpa*) included within the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). This is the detailed explanation: apart from non-informative form, there is no form that is invisible and non-obstructive, as stated in the *Rūpasaṅgraha-sūtra*. Nor is there any untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*) apart from non-informative form; for it would not be logical for one who has attained the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) to possess the form of bodily or vocal informative action (*vijñaptirūpa*).

"By seven material [gains]"—*upadhi* refers to parks, monasteries, and so forth; that which arises therein is "material. Because of the absence of such *upadhi*, it is "non-material. Constantly, repeatedly, continuously, and uninterruptedly. Herein is the Sūtra: The Blessed One was dwelling at Kauśāmbī in the Ghosira Park. Then the Venerable Mahācunda approached the Blessed One; having approached and bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Mahācunda [addressed] the Blessed One...

He said this: "Venerable Sir, is it possible to designate a basis for meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*) that is of great fruit, great benefit, great splendor, and great expansion? "Cunda, it is possible," the Blessed One said to him. "Cunda, there are these seven bases for meritorious action consisting of material things that are of great fruit, up to being of great expansion, with which a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family—whether walking, standing, sleeping, or waking—is endowed."

Merit increases constantly and continuously; merit is indeed produced. Cunda, there are seven bases of meritorious action here for a faithful son or daughter of good family who dedicates a monastery to the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions. Cunda, this is the first basis of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), which is of great fruit, and so on, up to being very extensive. For a son of good family endowed with this, [the merit]—to be described in detail—is such that merit is indeed produced. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful...

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family establishes a monastery in that very same grove, this is the second basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, which has great fruit and results in the continuous arising of merit. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or a daughter of good family provides bedding and seating in that very same monastery.

That is to say, he gives a couch, a stool, a mattress, a woolen rug, a pillow, or a square bolster; Cunda, this is the third basis for meritorious action consisting of material things, as described before. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son or daughter of good family establishes a permanent alms-provision in that very monastery as a suitable offering; Cunda, this is the fourth basis for meritorious action consisting of material things, which is of great fruit, as described before. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son or daughter of good family...

Or if a daughter of good family gives a gift to a newcomer or to one about to depart—this, Cunda, is the fifth basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, as before. Furthermore, Cunda, if a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family gives a gift to one who is ill or to an attendant of the sick—this, Cunda, is the sixth basis of meritorious action consisting of material things, as before. Furthermore, Cunda, if a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family [gives] during those times that are cold or stormy...

Or refreshments, or drinks of gruel—having prepared these for the Saṅgha, he presents them, saying: "May the Noble Ones, who do not neglect their duties toward us and whose robes have not been rained upon, enjoy these and dwell in comfort. And this, Cunda, is the seventh basis of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), which is of great fruit; indeed, merit continues to arise for a faithful son or daughter of good family who is endowed with these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things.

It is not possible to grasp the measure of this merit—whether it be the merit itself, the fruit of the merit, or the maturation of the merit—but because of the vastness of the merit, it is called a "great mass of merit."

"It is reckoned," and so on; for a second time, the Venerable Mahācunda said this to the Blessed One: "Is it possible, venerable sir, to designate a basis for meritorious action that is free from substrate (*niraupadhika*) as having great fruit, up to being of great extent? "It is possible, Cunda," the Blessed One said to him. "Cunda, there are these seven bases for meritorious action free from substrate, endowed with which a faithful son or daughter of good family—whether walking or standing—[attains] [great fruit], and so on in detail."

To whatever extent merit indeed arises, Cunda, when a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears that "the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is dwelling in dependence upon such-and-such a village or field," and having heard it, experiences a sublime, wholesome, and noble joy associated with renunciation—this, Cunda, is the first basis of meritorious action not involving material substratum (*niraupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), as previously described; to whatever extent merit indeed arises. Furthermore:

Cunda, when a faithful son or daughter of good family hears that the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is preparing to arrive, and having heard it, they go out to meet them—as previously described—this, Cunda, is the second basis of meritorious action not involving material substrates. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son or daughter of good family hears that the very same Tathāgata or disciple of the Tathāgata has set out on a journey and has arrived at that very village or field.

And having heard it, he further attains it—as before—this, Cunda, is the third basis of meritorious action free from substrate, wherein merit continues to arise. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears that a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata has arrived in that very village or field; and having heard it, he further attains it—as before—this, Cunda, is the fourth basis of meritorious action free from substrate, as before, up to where merit continues to arise.

Furthermore, merit indeed arises: when a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family approaches that very Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata for the purpose of seeing him, and having seen him, attains [realization] as previously described—Cunda, this is the fifth basis of meritorious action consisting of the non-material (*niraupadhika*). Furthermore, Cunda, when a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family [hears] the Dharma from that very Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata...

"He hears it, and having heard it, he further masters it," as before. Cunda, this is the sixth basis of meritorious action that is free from worldly attachment. Furthermore, Cunda, a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family hears the Dharma from that very Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata; having heard it, he goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma, goes for refuge to the Saṅgha, and undertakes the precepts. Cunda, this is the seventh [basis of meritorious action].

"The basis of meritorious action that is without substrate (*niraupadhika*) has great fruit," as before; [the full text] is not written here for fear of excessive bulk. For the informative act of commanding (*ājñāpanavijñapti*) does not constitute the path of action (*karmapatha*), because that action—such as killing and so forth—has not yet been performed. It might be thought: "Once that action has been performed, will that informative act of commanding then become the path of action? To this, it is said: "Even when that [action] has been performed, there is no difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Even when that action has been performed by another, there is no change in the nature of that [informative act].

In the informative act of commanding (*ājñāpanavijñapti*), there is no specific difference in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by which a sequential path of action (*kramapatha*) could exist at that time. Therefore, just as previously, because there is no difference in its intrinsic nature, the path of action is not established as it was before; likewise, it is not established afterwards either. Consequently, one must admit that there exists something which arises at that time and is comprised within the path of action, [which] is not comprised within the eleven bases (*āyatana*).

The meaning is that [the unmanifest] is impossible because, excluding the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), speech, action, and livelihood—which are of the nature of consciousness (*vijñapti*)—cannot exist. As for the detailed passage beginning with "But as for what was said," what is its connection? Or rather, if it is thought: "If the unmanifest did not exist, this Eightfold Path would not exist, because manifest action (*vijñapti*) is impossible therein; therefore, the unmanifest exists"—then why is it stated in detail, from "But as for what was said" up to "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*)? It was already stated previously.

"And of this" means prior to the time of attainment (*samāpatti*) for the entire path; the intention is that those [factors] have been described as having the nature of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*). The Vaibhāṣikas offer a rebuttal: "Detachment through the mundane path," and so forth.

This was said with reference to this informative matter (vijñapti-rūpa) which has speech and so forth as its intrinsic nature during the state of detachment through the mundane path; however, it is not the case that at the time of the [supramundane] path, the non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) comprised within it does not exist. It is called "matter consisting of the object of concentration" (samādhi-viṣaya-rūpa), meaning it is the objective support (ālambana) of concentration. It is "non-obstructive" (apratigha) because it does not obstruct places such as saṅkala and the like. That matter which obstructs a place is "obstructive" (pratigha); by contrast, the opposite is established as "non-obstructive. Now, how is that "matter"? If it cannot be manifested (rūpayituṃ) [as a physical form],...

The intended meaning is that "it is possible. This is the same regarding non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); for it is likewise the case that non-informative matter does not obstruct space. In the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), when a practitioner of yoga (*yogācāra*) brings the untainted path into manifestation, he acquires a corresponding intention (*āśaya*) and basis (*āśraya*), by virtue of which he abides in the state of natural morality (*prakṛti-śīlatā*). Alternatively, even in the untainted concentration, those masters maintain that such a kind of form exists—namely, the form of an Arhat and external form, as others hold.

Other teachers explain: "The form of an Arhat, as well as external forms such as wood and walls, are untainted (*anāsrava*) form. Why? Because they are not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*). For neither the form belonging to the continuum of an Arhat nor external form is a basis for the outflows, which are the afflictions (*kleśa*). If this is so, then how is it that the Sūtra states without distinction: "Which are the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*)? They are: the eye, up to and including visible forms," and so forth?

Furthermore, that [form] is said to be "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) because it is not an antidote to the outflows (*āsrava*). For it is stated by way of a synonym that "the specific states of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-viśeṣa*) are the antidotes to the outflows. In this regard, the detailed explanation is as follows: that very same form of an Arhat, as well as external form, is "with-outflows" because it is not an antidote to the outflows; yet it is "without-outflows" (*anāsrava*) because it is not a basis for the outflows—meaning those forms which are sense-bases (*āyatana*). This continues in detail up until the statement: "Those phenomena (*dharma*) which are with-outflows and subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*) are the objects of mental stubbornness and hypocrisy"; therefore, there exist [forms] that are without-outflows.

Furthermore, which are those bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*sopādāna*)? They are the forms of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), because they are the support for the outflows and are not the antidote to them. Which are those that are without-outflows (*anāsrava*)? They are the forms of an Arhat and external forms, because they are not the support for the outflows. For this is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is the beginningless capacity of dharmas. "Due to a specific excellence of qualities" means due to the specific excellence of qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and due to a specific excellence of assistance.

"Because of the specific qualities of the body, such as its color and strength, it has that as its object," and so forth. This [volition] has an object accompanied by a recipient; thus, "it has that as its object. By means of the volitions of giving, which have been cultivated, the mental continuities attain a subtle, specific transformation that serves as the cause for the arising of the fruit. How will this come to be?

The intention is: "How will there be the production of even greater fruit? For in this case, the gifts of the donors are not being consumed; rather, through the specific qualities and specific benefits [derived] from that consumption by the recipients—even when the donors have other thoughts—their [mental] continuums undergo a subtle, specific transformation through the repeated practice of volition directed toward those [recipients], and so forth, until they become capable [of producing fruit], or as long as merit continues to arise. This is due to the repeated practice of volition directed toward the Tathāgatas and their disciples.

By means of these, they become capable of producing even greater results in the future, whether walking, standing, waking, or properly engaged; but how is this so when one is sleeping? To this he says: "Even in dreams, those volitions continue as accompanying tendencies."

But for the Vaibhāṣika who maintains the doctrine of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), how could there be non-informative action in the case of a basis of meritorious activity that is "without material substratum" (*niraupadhika*)—wherein no informative action exists and one merely attains vast, wholesome joy and gladness upon hearing of it—since for that listener, both informative action and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are impossible? For non-informative action would arise either from informative action or from meditative concentration; this applies even in the case of bases with material substratum (*aupadhika*), such as the gift of a grove and so forth, because of the repeated cultivation of volition (*cetanā*) directed toward that object. In this case, the recipient is the object of this volition, as explained previously.

He said: "If this is so even regarding material things (*aupadhika*)—that through the repeated practice of volition (*cetanā*) directed toward that object, there is [great fruit]—then as for the Sūtra," and so forth. It shows that for a donor whose volition has that [immeasurable state] as its object, there is an immeasurable outflow of merit (*puṇyābhiṣyanda*), specifically the particular volition associated with the immeasurable concentrations of the mind (*cetahsamādhi*), such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Regarding the phrase "upon the completion of the action and its fruit": the preliminary application (*prayoga*) of the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) is the "action"; the fundamental path of action is the "fruit. Upon the completion of that, this same principle applies.

Thus, through one's own application, because of the specific injury inflicted upon others, a subtle, specific transformation of the continuum (*santatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*) arises in the agent. Since all effects are metaphorically designated by the name of their cause, this specific transformation of the continuum constitutes the "path of action" (*karmapatha*). The effect—the specific transformation of the continuum—is the path of action, while the cause is that very application of body and speech. For that [application] is the path for the action characterized by volition (*cetanā*). Thus, with respect to that effect, the term "path of action" is used metaphorically for the cause.

However, that [action] is designated as "bodily" or "verbal" because that particular transformation of the continuum is the fruit of those actions; the meaning is that it is the fruit of body and speech. This is just as for the Vaibhāṣikas, who maintain the doctrine of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), non-informative action is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*) by metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the effect.

However, its status as bodily or vocal is due to it being the fruit of those actions; thus, demonstrating by another method that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is not a substantial entity, the Venerable One said: "In the appropriated aggregates," and so forth. This means that a killer is touched by the fault of taking life through a volition belonging to the three times, directed toward the present aggregates included within the category of sentient beings.

How [is it] "in the three times"? He says: when there arises in him [the thought], "I shall kill," "I am killing," and "it has been killed"—thus, in this case, it is volition (*cetanā*) alone that is said to be action (*karman*). The Master (*ācārya*), showing that the Venerable One’s (*bhadanta*) position is intended in one respect and not intended in another respect, says: "But not by this much alone," and so forth. If someone were to instigate [another] in this way, "Kill my mother," and once the killer has set out, the thought should arise in that instigator, "That is my mother," regarding that person who possesses the conceit of having killed.

There would be no immediate karma (*ānantarya-karma*) [in that case]; therefore, the Venerable One must specify [the agent] by saying "killing himself. For this very reason, he says: "But for one who kills himself," and so forth. "This extent of the manifestation of volition (*cetanā-samudācāra*)"—namely, "I shall kill," "I am killing," and "it has been killed"—is "proper" (*yuktarūpa*). The suffix *-rūpa* is used here in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), as in the expression "properly so. Some explain that *nāmadheya* is simply another name for *nāman* (name), just as "name" is synonymous with "designation. Alternatively, *yuktarūpa* means "of excellent form" (*praśastarūpa*), or "whose nature (*svabhāva*) is proper."

It is appropriate that it is likewise unperceived; just as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is difficult to comprehend, so too is this specific transformation of the continuum (*santatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*). "By means of bodily application following the mind" means by means of a bodily application preceded by the mind. "Distinct from those two" means distinct from both mind and body. "Arising from an application performed by someone" means that which is performed by someone (*yat-kṛta*); the completion of the action (*kriyā-parisamāpti*), that is, the completion of the path of action (*karmapatha*), arises from such an application performed by that person. It belongs to that very [person].
There occurs a transformation of the continuum, caused by that [action] and having as its cause the application of the mind and mental factors which are the agents.

The ellipsis of the sentence is: "Is there satisfaction for us? [The answer is] no. And because the fruit arises in the future from the continuum of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-santāna*), there is no such thing as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). The phrase "is there satisfaction" continues to apply here. Because of the absence of informative matter (*vijñapti*) and so forth, the meaning is that due to the absence of the originating factor (*samutthāpaka-dharma*), there is an absence of the originated factor (*samutthāpya-dharma*). This has been established: that non-informative matter does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravya*). By the word "and so forth," [it is meant that it is] merely the non-performance [of an action] after having made a commitment; and because it is designated based upon past great elements (*mahābhūta*), those [elements]...

Because it does not exist [as a substantial entity], let it be included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). That which has been described as the form that arises for meditators as the object of their concentration through the power of concentration—that, indeed, is invisible and non-obstructive; at least, let this much be said.

Regarding the phrase "non-opposition of the limbs" (*aṅgāprātilomya*), some say: "Come now, let him explain! means "Come now, let him speak! From this [it follows] "on account of the cause," and so forth. Since this is so, therefore, with respect to the informative act (*vijñapti*) which is the cause, there is a metaphorical designation of the effect; that is to say, there is a metaphorical designation of "right speech" and so on. Thus, even though it is non-informative (*avijñapti*), it is at that time designated as "right speech, action, and livelihood"—the meaning is that these names are applied to it. [The text mentions] "both the intention (*āśaya*) and the basis (*āśraya*)."

*Āśaya* (intention) refers to the intention not to commit killing and so forth, or the intention of faith and so forth. *Āśraya* (basis) refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). Therefore, by applying the designation of the effect to the cause—namely, to the intention and the basis—one applies the designations of "right speech" and so forth, and thus the eight path-factors are established. If [the opponent asks]: "Is that merely non-action? [The answer is: "It is merely the non-action of wrong speech and so forth.
