To the question, "What is that?", he says: "That which is this... and so forth. If a factor is merely non-action, how can it be untainted (*anāsrava*)? To this he says: "That... and so forth.

If it is argued that [the path] is "untainted" (*anāsrava*) because it is obtained by relying on the untainted path, then if the "limb" (*aṅga*) were merely the non-performance [of unwholesome acts], it would not exist as a substantial entity (*adravyasat*); how then could there be eight limbs? To this he replies: "For it is not in all cases," and so forth. "Preceded by a formal rule" (*vidhipūrvam*) means preceded by the formal act of undertaking the precepts (*śīla*). [He adds: "Otherwise, one would not be restrained when possessed of another thought. This volition (*cetanā*) is the restraint (*saṃvara*). Therefore, when one possesses a thought other than that volitional mind, one would not be restrained; for the volition which restrains body and speech does not exist at that time.

"By the cultivation of that," and so forth: it is not as you say. By the cultivation of that—that is, by the cultivation of the mental continuum—at the time of action, when a thought of killing or the like has arisen, one remembers, "I am abstaining from killing and so forth. For one whose mindfulness is thus present, through the manifestation of that volition (*cetanā*) by which one restrains body and speech, there is the actualization of that [restraint]; this is precisely the meaning of its formal undertaking (*samādāna*).

"How might this person, having recollected his vow of non-action, not commit misconduct?"—thinking thus, so that no one with impaired mindfulness might break the training, there exists at that time that *avijñapti* which, acting as a dam, obstructs misconduct. For it is not the case that the very same collection [of elements] is both; the detailed explanation is as follows: it is not the same collection of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as the earth element and so forth, which serve as the basis for informative action (*vijñapti*), that has a subtle fruit, because its fruit is the invisible and non-obstructive *avijñapti*, while [the collection of the great elements] also has a gross fruit.

Because it has as its fruit a non-manifest [form] that is visible and resistant, it is logical that a non-manifest [form] arises based on entirely different great elements than those of the manifest [form] at that time; this is the detailed explanation. "The manifest [form] at that time" means the manifest [form] which exists at that time. Likewise, "the great elements at that time" refers to the great elements produced at the same time as the manifest [form]. Does the non-manifest [form] arise based on only those great elements produced at the same time as the manifest [form]? [The answer is: everything. All form—whether manifest or non-manifest—is based on everything.

The [derived matter] comprised within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as the eye, ear, visible forms, sounds, and so forth, generally exist by depending upon primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that are simultaneous with them. The inclusion of the word "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is for the purpose of excluding certain types of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). For this very reason, he says: "Some [derived matter] exists by depending upon past primary elements. To demonstrate what kind of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is such, he says: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.10ab: "Derived matter consists of the five sense organs, their five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*). (AKB 2.10ab) [Commentary: Among these, the five sense organs—eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—are the supports for the five consciousnesses, respectively. Their respective objects are visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. Unmanifest form is that which has previously been explained. All of these are called "derived matter" because they are derived from the four great elements. Furthermore, the five sense organs are derived matter because they are derived from the four great elements as their material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Visible form and the others are also derived matter because they are derived from the four great elements as their generative cause (*janaka-kāraṇa*). Unmanifest form is derived matter because it is derived from the four great elements as its support (*āśraya*). Regarding the phrase "derived matter": it is called "derived" (*upādāya*) because it arises depending on the great elements; it is called "matter" (*rūpa*) because it possesses the characteristic of transformation (*rūpaṇa*). It is called "derived matter" (*upādāyarūpa*) because it is both derived and matter. Alternatively, it is called "derived matter" because it is matter that is derived from the great elements. Among these, the five sense organs are exclusively derived matter. Visible form and the other objects are both primary and derived matter. Unmanifest form is exclusively derived matter. Therefore, it is said that derived matter is of three kinds: that which is exclusively derived, that which is both primary and derived, and that which is exclusively derived. Furthermore, regarding the statement "derived matter consists of the five sense organs," one might ask: why are the sense organs alone specified? It is because the sense organs are the most prominent among derived matters. Moreover, since the sense organs are the basis for the five consciousnesses, they are the most significant. Also, because they are the supports for the mental consciousness, they are the most important. Furthermore, because they are the bases for the acquisition of the fruits of the path, they are the most essential. Thus, the sense organs are mentioned first. Regarding the statement "their five objects": the objects of the five consciousnesses are, respectively, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. Among these, visible form is that which is perceived by the eye. Sound is that which is perceived by the ear. Odor is that which is perceived by the nose. Taste is that which is perceived by the tongue. Tangible objects are those perceived by the body. These are the objects of the five consciousnesses. Regarding "unmanifest form": it is that which was previously explained as being included within the category of discipline (*saṃvara*). It is called "unmanifest" because it does not manifest itself to others as it does when one performs an action. It is called "form" because it is derived from the great elements. It is called "unmanifest form" because it is both unmanifest and form. Thus, derived matter is established as consisting of these three categories. This concludes the explanation of derived matter. Now, to show how many types of derived matter there are, he says: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.10cd: "There are twenty-one kinds of derived matter. (AKB 2.10cd) [Commentary: Derived matter is of twenty-one kinds. What are they? They are the five sense organs, the five objects, and the twelve types of unmanifest form. Among these, the five sense organs are as previously described. The five objects are also as previously described. Regarding the twelve types of unmanifest form: they are the eight types of restraint (*saṃvara*) and the four types of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). The eight types of restraint are: the restraint of the Prātimokṣa, the restraint of meditation (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), the restraint of fasting (*upavāsa-saṃvara*), the restraint of the intermediate state (*antarāla-saṃvara*), the restraint of the vow (*praṇidhāna-saṃvara*), the restraint of the observance (*anuśamsā-saṃvara*), and the restraint of the specific undertaking (*pratiniyama-saṃvara*). The four types of non-restraint are: the non-restraint of killing, the non-restraint of stealing, the non-restraint of sexual misconduct, and the non-restraint of false speech. These constitute the twenty-one kinds of derived matter. Now, to explain the characteristics of these derived matters, he says: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.11: "The eye is that which is clear (*prasāda*) derived from the four great elements, and it is the basis for the visual consciousness. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body. (AKB 2.11) [Commentary: The eye is a subtle, translucent matter derived from the four great elements. It is the support for the visual consciousness. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body. That is to say, the ear is the support for the auditory consciousness, the nose for the olfactory consciousness, the tongue for the gustatory consciousness, and the body for the tactile consciousness. All of these are derived from the four great elements and are translucent matter. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.12: "Visible form is that which is derived from the four great elements and serves as the object of the visual consciousness. The same applies to sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. (AKB 2.12) [Commentary: Visible form is derived from the four great elements and is the object of the visual consciousness. The same applies to sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects. That is to say, sound is derived from the four great elements and is the object of the auditory consciousness; odor is derived from the four great elements and is the object of the olfactory consciousness; taste is derived from the four great elements and is the object of the gustatory consciousness; and tangible objects are derived from the four great elements and are the objects of the tactile consciousness. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.13: "Unmanifest form is that which is derived from the four great elements and is included within the aggregate of form, yet it does not manifest itself externally. (AKB 2.13) [Commentary: Unmanifest form is derived from the four great elements. Although it is included within the aggregate of form, it does not manifest itself externally like the other forms. It is called "unmanifest" because it is not perceived by others as a physical manifestation of action. It is called "form" because it is derived from the great elements. It is called "unmanifest form" because it is both unmanifest and form. This concludes the explanation of the twenty-one kinds of derived matter. Now, to clarify the relationship between derived matter and the great elements, he says: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.14: "Derived matter exists simultaneously with the great elements upon which it depends, except for certain cases in the desire realm. (AKB 2.14) [Commentary: Generally, derived matter exists at the same time as the great elements that serve as its material cause. However, there are exceptions. Specifically, certain non-informative matters in the desire realm may exist by depending upon past great elements. What, then, is this derived matter that exists in such a manner? To show this, he says: *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 2.15: "Derived matter consists of the five sense organs, their five objects, and unmanifest form. Among these, the five sense organs are derived matter that exists simultaneously with the great elements. The five objects are also derived matter that exists simultaneously with the great elements. Unmanifest form, however, may exist by depending upon past great elements. (AKB 2.15) [Commentary: The five sense organs are derived matter that exists simultaneously with the great elements. The five objects—visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects—are also derived matter that exists simultaneously with the great elements

After the first moment, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm arises based on past primary elements. At the time of undertaking the restraint of the desire realm and so forth, the non-informative arises having produced co-nascent primary elements; likewise, other non-informative matter also arises based on those very same [past] ones. This is because they exist for it in the sense of being its basis (*āśraya*). Just as present primary elements are the basis for other derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*), so too the past primary elements are the basis for this [non-informative], because they are respectively the causes of its initial activity and its subsequent persistence.

The past great elements (*mahābhūta*) function as the basis in the sense of being the cause of origination (*pravṛtti-kāraṇa*) and the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-kāraṇa*); the present great elements of the body function as the basis in the sense of being the cause of persistence (*anuvṛtti-kāraṇa*) and the cause of support (*adhiṣṭhāna-kāraṇa*), just like a wheel. This is the detailed explanation. Just as the hand’s impulse is the cause of the wheel’s origination, so too is [the past] the cause of this [present body’s] origination; just as the ground is [the cause], so too is [the past] the cause of its persistence. Having explained the determination of time, he asks about the determination of the level (*bhūmi*): "Now, from which [level] do they arise? and so on, up to "belonging to the level of the fourth dhyāna."

Because in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) there is an absence of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derivative matter (*bhautika*), and because [untainted phenomena] do not fall within the realms (*adhātu-patita*); the intention is that since untainted bodily and vocal action (*kāya-vāk-karman*) is not connected to any realm, it does not exist as a rule [in the formless realms]. [Objection: "In that case, why does it not arise by depending on untainted great elements (*mahābhūta*)? To this he says: "And because there is an absence of untainted great elements."

Furthermore, what function do the great elements (mahābhūta) have for this [unmanifest action]? To this he says: "And because it arises by their power. This means it arises by the power of the great elements. Now, why does its arising not occur through the power of the mind alone? Because it would follow that it is not derived matter (anupādāyarūpa). [For] unmanifest action is non-appropriated (anaupāttika); because it is formless (amūrta), it is incapable of serving as a basis for the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta). And it is "outflowing" (naiṣyandikī) because it is wholesome or unwholesome; it is not born of maturation (vipākaja).

Because of the statement that there is no neutral (*avyākṛta*) non-informative (*avijñapti*), and because that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is neutral—given the statement that "maturation is a neutral dharma"—it is not born of accumulation (*aupacayikī*), since there is an absence of accumulation. By process of elimination, it is born of outflow (*naiṣyandikī*). It is designated as belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhyā*) because it falls within the continuum of sentient beings. It is born from great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are outflow-born and appropriated (*upātta*), because it depends upon the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*), and because it is produced by informative action (*vijñapti*) and so forth that arise from a non-concentrated (*asamāhita*) mind. Therefore, it is not born from great elements that are accumulated through dreams, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth; for this very reason, it is also not born from great elements that are born of maturation.

"Born of meditative concentration" (*samādhija*) is the full expression. Because they are born from both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) restraint born of dhyāna and the outflows is called "born of concentration. Furthermore, it is said to be "derived from the great elements that are not appropriated" (*anupātta*). This is because, by the power of the concentrated mind, [the restraint] follows the mind in that body; for the great elements that are not appropriated continue to exist even in states such as the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), even in the absence of the mind. The phrase "up to the point of confused conduct" (*yāvat sambhinnapralāpāt*)—by the word "up to" (*yāvat*)—is meant to include stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, slander, and harsh speech.

Regarding "from [the great elements] of confused speech" (*sambhinnapralāpa*), just as the mind is undifferentiated, so too are the great elements that produce it undifferentiated; for just as the mind that produces it is not distinct, so the great elements that produce it are likewise not distinct. Furthermore, the great elements are not the support (*āśraya*) of the non-informative (*avijñapti*) in the sense of being its substratum; rather, they are its support in the sense of being the cause of its occurrence. Therefore, the statement that it arises from undifferentiated great elements is not contradictory. However, in the case of the Prātimokṣa vows, the great elements are distinct for each instance.

Since it does not follow the mind (*acittānuparivartanīyatva*), is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) indeed outflowing (*naiṣyandika*)? Because it continues by the force of a projection (*ākṣepa*). But is it appropriated (*upātta*) as bodily? It is not vocal; this is the meaning. For it is bodily because it exists inseparably from the great elements of the body, and thus its foundational elements are appropriated; but it is not vocal because it exists separately from them. Regarding this, they raise an objection: "This contradicts the treatise (*śāstra*), for it says: 'Of these five training rules (*śikṣāpada*) of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), how many are appropriated and how many are unappropriated? He replied: 'All.'"

There is no fault [in the statement] that they are "unappropriated" (*anupātta*), because this description is either intended to refer to the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) characterized as non-informative (*avijñapti*), or because such a designation is the general rule. Furthermore, the claim that this is not Vaibhāṣika because of its continuous succession is incorrect; for when one shape arises, the other shapes do not cease. How, then, in detail, can two shapes be established? [This continues] up until the point where it is explained.

Because they provide mutual space for one another and because they are pervaded by those great elements (*mahābhūta*), how could informative action (*vijñapti*) be made manifest by the great elements of informative action through the entire limb? For it cannot be said that it is not manifested by a single part of the body, nor that it is not manifested by the whole body; this is because the great elements that serve as the basis for informative action do not remain without pervading that limb, since there is space for them within the body due to its porous nature.

Even in the case of pervading [the body], it should not be larger than the limb [it occupies], because it enters the body through its porosity; nor, therefore, should that limb become swollen or heavy, because of its subtlety. If it is argued that [action] is said to be twofold, threefold, and fivefold:
it is twofold because of the statement, "It is volition and what is produced by it";
it is threefold because of the statement, "Volition is mental action (manas-karman), and those born from it are vocal and bodily action (vāk-kāya-karman)."

However, because there is a distinction between the informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) aspects of bodily and vocal action, and because action consisting of volition (*cetanā*) itself constitutes five types, it is said that [action] is fivefold.

It is implied that non-informative action does not exist as neutral (*avyākṛta*); rather, the meaning is that non-informative action is exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*). Thus, it is stated that powerful action—characterized by non-informative form—exists even in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

By the word "api" (also), which has the sense of "iti ca" (and thus), the term "kāma" (desire) is drawn in; that is, just as in the case of untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter (*avijñapti*): although there are no untainted great elements (*mahābhūta*) for untainted non-informative matter, nevertheless, when one produces it in a particular stage (*bhūmi*), it arises depending upon the great elements belonging to that stage; likewise, although there would be no formless (*ārūpya*) great elements, nevertheless, when one born in a particular stage produces the formless [non-informative matter], it arises depending upon the great elements belonging to that stage.

It might be argued that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) will exist [therein]; however, this is not so because it does not fall within the realms (*adhātu-patita*). Since it is not included here among the realms, how can untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter belong to the desire, form, or formless realms? Because it is not appropriated by the cravings (*tṛṣṇā*) of those realms, its great elements (*mahābhūta*) are neither similar nor dissimilar to them in terms of realm or level (*bhūmi*). Therefore, it arises depending upon those great elements born where it itself is born. However, non-informative matter belonging to the formless realm cannot depend upon great elements belonging to the desire or form realms.

The intention is that [the formless attainments] cannot arise based on dissimilar primary elements (*mahābhūta*), because they fall within the realm of their own nature (*dhātupatita*). Furthermore, because of its turning away from all form, the formless attainment is not capable of producing form. Is it not the case that the untainted (*anāsrava*) attainment belonging to the formless level is capable of producing form? The meaning is: it is capable of producing informative action (*vijñapti*). Why? The intention is: "Because of its turning away from all form. And how is there a turning away from all form for the formless attainment? To this he says: "Because the perception of form has been transcended" (*vibhūtarūpasañjñatvāt*).

The meaning is: "because of being free from the perception of form" (*vigatarūpasañjñatvāt*). Regarding the statement "morality (*śīla*) is the antidote to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*)," and so forth: since immorality belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) because it originates from unwholesome states, it is logical that morality belonging to the level of the form realm (*rūpabhūmika*), characterized as non-informative (*avijñapti-lakṣaṇa*), serves as its antidote. If it is argued that the same would apply to [immorality] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), he says: "And the formless [realms] are [far] from the desire realm," and so forth. Because the formless realms are far from the desire realm by way of four types of distance, morality comprised within the formless realms is [not the antidote].

It is not possible [for this] in the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, since the four types of distance (*dūratā*) have already been explained previously, they are not explained again here. In this context, the example for "distance as an antidote" (*pratipakṣadūratā*) is informative action (*vijñapti*) in the two levels with discursive thought (*savicāra*). The undertaking of the restriction "only in the two levels with discursive thought" is for the purpose of defining the scope. Because bodily and vocal actions are preceded by initial thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), [informative action] does not exist even in the desire realm; thus, he shows that it is not only absent in the levels without discursive thought (*avicārāsu bhūmiṣu*). By saying "it exists only in the Brahma-world," it is implied that it does not exist above that.

The statement that "above the Brahma-world, the sphere of sound (śabdāyatana) of wind and so forth is caused by external primary elements" is intended primarily to exclude *vijñapti*-sound; it does not mean that [sound] is caused exclusively by external primary elements. For even the sound of limbs such as hands occurs in the second and higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Treatise (*śāstra*). Thus, the Treatise asks: "Who is endowed with the sound-element? It replies: "One belonging to the Desire or Form Realms. It asks again: "Who is endowed with it? It replies: "One belonging to the Formless Realm. Indeed, it is not logical for one to be endowed with something external that is reckoned as non-sentient.

Because of the statement that "acquisition and non-acquisition pertain to those [dharmas] included within one's own continuum," and for the sake of avoiding that very fault, others say: "There is also informative action (*vijñapti*) in the second and subsequent meditations. To what level does this belong? It belongs to the level of the first meditation; this is precisely the Vaibhāṣika position, and not another position, regarding the body, eye, and ear consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action.

In that case, [the non-informative action] in the second dhyāna and above is pervaded by [the absence of thought], and it is established as being undefiled-neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*). If this is so, then regarding the question of whether that which belongs to the level of the second dhyāna and above is "determined" (*vyākṛtā*) or "undetermined" (*avyākṛtā*), he says: it is "unobstructed-undetermined" (*anivṛtāvyākṛtā*), but neither wholesome (*kuśalā*) nor afflicted (*kliṣṭā*). For those who are engaged in mutual conversation and the like, there arises for them an undetermined informative action (*vijñapti*). What is the reason it is neither wholesome nor afflicted? Because they have not attained [wholesome or afflicted states], and so forth; for [such states] do not exist in the second dhyāna and above.

One born in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) brings forth a mind of a similar nature—belonging to a lower stage and characterized as either wholesome or afflicted—by means of which mind one might produce a wholesome or afflicted informative act (vijñapti). Why? It is said: because of its inferiority and because of its lack of proficiency.

Because wholesome states belonging to a lower level are inferior and have already been abandoned, one does not bring them into manifestation; by implication, this means that one brings into manifestation a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind belonging to a lower level, and by means of that, one originates that [informative action]. This is what is meant by saying that informative action belonging to a higher level is originated by a mind belonging to a lower level. The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this, for they maintain that such informative action belongs exclusively to the first dhyāna.

Because it is originated by a mind belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, he therefore says: "But they explain it as being only prior. And that [mind] exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, that obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind which is to be abandoned by cultivation does not exist in the desire realm; for in the desire realm, the obscured-unspecified mind is held to be associated only with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). And by that [mind], informative action (*vijñapti*) is not originated, because it functions inwardly by its very nature—that is, because it is supremely secure within itself.

Because there is an absence of even a trace of insecurity due to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*samprayoga*), and origination (*samutthāna*), that which is wholesome is said to be the ultimate security; for those things that are not associated [with such factors] lack wholesomeness.

Because mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth that are not associated with the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) lack the quality of being virtuous, the virtue of their association with those [roots] is established. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "associated with those very roots of virtue and so forth," shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are included. It is like milk produced from a cow that has drunk medicinal water; that is, the milk of a cow that has drunk medicinal water is "produced from medicinal water. As for the detailed explanation regarding "those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which are virtuous," it refers to the acquisitions of virtues that have been originated by a dissimilar mind (*visabhāgacitta*). A dissimilar mind is...

Regarding the acquisition (*prāpti*) of wholesome states that occurs when reconnecting the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*) through doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding what is other than the wholesome: their wholesomeness does not first arise from being ultimate security (*paramārtha-kṣema*), as is the case with *parinirvāṇa*; nor do they possess wholesomeness by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as is the case with non-greed (*alobha*) and so forth, because they do not have that as their intrinsic nature; nor do they possess it by way of association (*samprayoga*), as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, because they are dissociated (*viprayukta*); nor do they possess it by way of origination (*samutthāna*), because the mind that originates them is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). Likewise, this applies to the acquisitions of innate wholesome states (*upapatti-pratilambhika-kuśala*) during the reconnection of rebirth (*punarbhava-pratisaṃdhi*).

It must be explained how these [factors] possess wholesomeness (*kuśalatva*); this is what must be addressed here, and effort should be exerted on this point—this is the intended meaning. Here they provide the following rebuttal: because they are to be originated by wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*), they become wholesome precisely while in the future state. It is not the case that their wholesomeness is compromised simply because an obstacle to their acquisition (*prāpti*) is removed by a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*). [The phrase] "because its nature consists in the proceeding of all suffering" means that the proceeding of all suffering is its essence (*ātman*), that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Samsara consists of the attainment of body, speech, karma, birth, and so forth; it is essentially the occurrence of all suffering, and thus, in the ultimate sense, it is insecurity.

Bodily and vocal actions, which consist of the nature of informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*), are comprised within the categories of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint, and restraint (*saṃvara*). The [characteristics] such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth have the nature of the characteristics of birth, aging, duration, and impermanence, as well as the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). The acquisitions (*prāpti*) of unwholesome states are comparable to diseases, unwholesome food, and [inaffective] medicine; thus, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is comparable to disease. Because they depend on other associated factors for their origination, those [factors] associated with them—bodily and vocal actions, birth, and the acquisitions—are comparable to water mixed with unwholesome medicine.

They are comparable to milk produced from drinking wholesome medicine and water. "In that case," and so forth in detail: if, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*), then nothing contaminated (*sāsrava*) would be neutral (*avyākṛta*) or wholesome (*kuśala*), because the contaminated is included within cyclic existence; this was stated in the ultimate sense. This is accepted: "All that is comprised within cyclic existence is unwholesome. However, "with respect to maturation (*vipāka*)," and so forth in detail: that which is not defined with respect to maturation as "this has maturation" is [what is meant by] "that."

It is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). What is meant by this is as follows: that which is with-outflows (*sāsrava*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*) because it is ultimately insecure; however, in the sense of not being defined in terms of its maturation (*vipāka*), it is "indeterminate. Wholesomeness (*kuśala*) should likewise be understood in the same way [as indeterminate], yet it is wholesome because its maturation is desirable. "If by virtue of the motivating cause (*samutthāna*)" and so forth: with the intention that only volition (*cetanā*) itself possesses wholesomeness or unwholesomeness, he examines whether the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of bodily and vocal action [is derived from the motivating cause] or not, asking: "Why not [of] the great elements (*mahābhūta*)?"

The state of being wholesome or unwholesome [belongs to the great elements] because bodily and vocal action is originated by a wholesome or unwholesome mind; thus the Vaibhāṣika says: "For the agent's intention is directed toward the action, not toward the great elements. One does not think, 'I shall produce these great elements,' but rather, 'I shall perform this action. Therefore, the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of the great elements is not like that of the action."

The Teacher says: For one who is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), there is no intention (*abhiprāya*) such as "I shall produce an unmanifest action" (*avijñapti*) with respect to that unmanifest action; nor does a non-concentrated mind exist that could give rise to it and thereby form such an intention, because of its dissimilarity (*visabhāgatva*) and its lack of correspondence (*visadṛśatva*) to the state of concentration due to the difference in level (*bhūmi*). How then can that concentrated unmanifest action be wholesome? The implication is that because it consists of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it could not possess wholesomeness. Alternatively, it would follow that even the divine eye and ear would be wholesome.
If, even in the absence of that intention, the non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) is considered wholesome, then this is its connection:

if its wholesomeness were due to the power of a mind of a different class (*visabhāga-citta*)—that is, a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*)—then it would follow that the divine eye and ear are also wholesome, because at the time of their preliminary application (*prayoga*), that intention is possible; yet they are not wholesome.

Because of the statement that "the supernormal powers of the ear and eye are indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*), those who assert that "the mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) does not originate informative action (*vijñapti*)," on the grounds that it "functions inwardly," contradict what was said by the Blessed One. This is the meaning of the explanation: "What was said by the Blessed One? It is stated: "From that false view," and so forth. How is it that from false view—which is to be abandoned by seeing—there arises false speech whose nature is informative action, and false conduct which has that very same nature? Thus it is explained.

The term *hetu-tat-kṣaṇotthāna-sañjñita* means that which is designated as "the arising from causes and the arising at that very moment. It is "designated" (*sañjñita*) because it is produced by a designation (*sañjñā-kṛtam*). Alternatively, it refers to that for which "the arising from causes and the arising at that very moment" is the designation; thus, it is "made into the designation 'arising from causes and arising at that very moment'" (*hetu-tat-kṣaṇotthāna-sañjñī-kṛtam*).

What is meant by "origination by cause" (*hetu-samutthāna*)? It is designated as such because it arises from that [cause]. It is called "origination" (*samutthāna*) because one originates by means of it; it is both the cause (*hetu*) and the origination (*samutthāna*), hence "origination by cause. What is "origination at that very moment" (*tat-kṣaṇa-samutthāna*)? That "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) refers to the moment of action (*kriyā-kṣaṇa*). "Origination at that very moment" means origination occurring at that same moment. The meaning is that because origination exists at that very moment—the moment of action—there is the presence of origination-at-that-moment precisely at that moment of action. Why is this so? Because of its "projecting nature" (*ākṣepakatva*), which means its quality of producing [the effect]. What [is produced]?

"‘Now’ [is] the detailed explanation: the capacity of that momentary origination (*tat-kṣaṇasamutthāna*) for that act of communication (*vijñāpanakriyā*), by which it is said to be its ‘concomitant’ (*anuvartaka*) at that time. ‘For by that,’ [is] the detailed explanation: for indeed, without that momentary origination, this informative intimation (*vijñapti*) would not exist—just as in the case of one who is dead—even though it has been projected and produced by causal origination (*hetusamutthāna*). It is like someone who, having projected the action with the thought ‘I shall go to a village,’ might die in the interval; because of the absence of a concomitant mind, there is no going."

"Then how can it be for one whose mind is absent? This is the full statement. If, due to the absence of that momentary origination (*tat-kṣaṇasamutthāna*), this [informative action] were not to exist—as in the case of one who is dead—then how could there be bodily informative action (*kāyavijñapti*) belonging to the restraint (*saṃvara*) included within that restraint, at the time of the conclusion of the ritual proclamation (*karmavācanā*) during the production of the restraint for someone who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and is undergoing ordination, since he is without mind because the attainment of cessation is present at that time? How does it come to be, and how is it produced?

The meaning is that [the manifestation] occurs without the momentary arising (*tat-kṣaṇa-samutthāna*). When [this] is thus contradicted, another concentration (*samādhi*) is resorted to. [The opponent says: "In that case, it is even more manifest. [The author replies: By means of the momentary arising, the informative action (*vijñapti*) of one who possesses mind (*sacittaka*) becomes more distinct; this is its efficacy (*sāmarthya*).

"Initiating [action] is to be abandoned by insight"—this restricts that only the initiating [action] is to be abandoned by insight. How, then, is it initiating? He says: because it serves as the primary cause (*nidāna*), that is, the causal condition (*hetu*), for the *vijñapti* (informative action) which gives rise to *vitarka* and *vicāra*; thus it is initiating, but not conforming. This is the detailed explanation. "Because of its absence" means because of the absence of that initiating [action] which is to be abandoned by insight. Therefore, it is not conforming. And in this way, another...

"The fault [is that] the form produced by that [mind] would also [be so]," and so forth. If that [form] were to follow the nature of the mind, then the bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti-rūpa) produced by a mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) would itself be abandoned by seeing—just as bodily and vocal action produced by a mind to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) is abandoned by cultivation. What would be the consequence? The opponent asks. The Vaibhāṣika replies: "The Abhidharma would be contradicted."

Because of the statement that "what is non-afflicted is not to be abandoned by vision, nor is form," what then is ignorance (*avidyā*)? It means that because there is no contradiction with knowledge—that is, with the path of vision—there is no abandonment of that form, unlike the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth. Furthermore, even for those who have seen the truths, they remain possessed of that [form]; therefore, there is no form to be abandoned by vision. And because there is no contradiction with ignorance, form is also not contradicted by ignorance; for indeed, [ignorance] does not contradict it while afflicted or non-afflicted form is active, nor while its acquisition (*prāpti*) is in a continuous flow.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is opposed [to knowledge] because it does not arise during the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), or because it is abandoned when it does arise during the state of an Arya. Thus, although it is like the untainted (*anāsrava*) in that it is not something to be abandoned, it is nevertheless not the case that it is not to be abandoned. If it is not not to be abandoned, and it is also not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), then by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established that it is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Another says: "This position—that form (*rūpa*) is not opposed to knowledge—is yet to be proven. For how can one who maintains that form is to be abandoned by insight [accept] that it is opposed to knowledge?

The Vaibhāṣika will maintain that there is no contradiction regarding matter (*rūpa*). He says: "The primary elements (*bhūta*) as well," and so forth. If that matter were to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) because it was originated by a mind to be abandoned by seeing, then its supporting primary elements would also have to be abandoned by seeing. Why? Because they are originated by the same mind; for that very mind which originates the matter also originates its supporting primary elements. And yet, those [elements] cannot be such [abandoned by seeing].

Because they are undefiled and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), they are not susceptible to being abandoned by insight (*darśanaprahātavya*); and because those things to be abandoned by insight are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it will not be the case that [these] would be abandonable by insight.

How so? He says: just as [the elements] do not become wholesome or unwholesome—just as by whichever wholesome or unwholesome mind a wholesome or unwholesome form is produced, by that very same [mind] its constituent elements (*bhūta*) are also produced—and yet that form, which consists of bodily and vocal action, is wholesome or unwholesome, whereas its constituent elements are not; in the same way, he again turns back and says: "Or rather, let them be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*. The Vaibhāṣika replies: "It cannot be so."

The ellipsis of the sentence is "to be abandoned by vision. Why? Because there is no contradiction with ignorance (*avidyā*) for an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) dharma. For a non-afflicted dharma—namely, the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*)—is not contradicted by knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, by the outflow-free path (*anāsrava-mārga*), in the same way that afflicted dharmas are contradicted through the severance of their acquisition (*prāpti*). However, contradiction is not denied in the case of [the non-afflicted] being contradicted by the afflictions that take it as an object (*ālambana*), due to the severance of the acquisition of those afflictions. Nor is it contradicted by ignorance; [this refers to] the affliction that takes it as an object through the severance of its acquisition.

Regarding that which was stated—"or rather, let them be [unreal and] non-afflicted"—that is incorrect. Thus, the proof is established here: the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for afflicted form (*rūpa*) are not themselves afflicted, because they are non-afflicted, just like afflicted minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*). Thus says the Vaibhāṣika.

Having established—with both objection and resolution—that consciousness which is to be abandoned by insight (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) is the initiator (*pravartaka*), he concludes: "Therefore, [consciousness] is the origination from causes," and so forth. Thus, there is no contradiction with that Sūtra which states: "From wrong view comes wrong intention, up to wrong action. This is because [consciousness] is both the initiator and the follower (*anuvartaka*), due to its functioning directed both inwardly and outwardly.

The restriction that "the five [faculties] are only conformers" is because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). It is not the case that both [the initiator and the conformer] are untainted (*anāsrava*); thus, [the untainted mind] is neither an initiator nor a conformer, because it functions inwardly while in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). Regarding the term *mlāyamāna*, it means "not declining" (*ahīyamāna*), as this word ends in the suffix *-anaṭ*. "Wholesome one-pointedness" (*kuśalaikatānā*) means a wholesome continuity (*kuśalaikaprabandha*). In the Sūtra, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is called a "Nāga. Having spoken at length, saying, "O Udāyin, how is the Tathāgata in the world with its gods and its Māras... he says: "He commits no offense (*āgas*) by body, speech, or mind; therefore, he is called a Nāga."

"He does not commit a transgression" means he does not commit an offense. "Because of his lack of desire" means that because the mind of this Buddha does not wander—due to its non-dispersal toward sense objects—it is said, in detail, that "while walking, he is concentrated like an elephant. Because he possesses established mindfulness while thinking "I am walking" during the four modes of conduct, up to "I am sitting," he is called "ever-concentrated"; this is because [his concentration] proceeds without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*).

For the absence of formative activity (*saṃskāra*), that is, of effort (*prayatna*), carries [the mind] without formative activity; thus, its state is "carrying without formative activity. Therefore, it is not the case that everything to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*) is an instigator. This would be so if all that is to be abandoned by seeing were accepted as an instigator; however, not everything is so. What then? Only false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the like are instigators of representation (*vijñapti*), and not the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the like. For this reason, the qualification "not all" is stated.

It must be stated whether such [an action] is instigating (*pravartaka*) or not; that is, for one whose mind is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*). When someone is being ordained (*upasampādyamāna*), by some means, the informative act (*vijñapti*) of the Prātimokṣa restraint—such as the joining of palms and so forth—which belongs to an unwholesome or neutral mind, would not be wholesome. This is because the following mind (*anuvartaka-citta*) is unwholesome or neutral. Thus, it is said "according to the instigator" (*yathā pravartakaṃ*); the full explanation is that just as the instigating mind is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), so too is the informative act established, and not according to [the nature of the following mind].

Why is that which is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) established as the initiator (*pravartaka*)? Because it is separated from [the action] by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). How so? Having first determined, "I must make others understand that 'the self exists'," one then utters speech with a mind that has turned outward, which is to be abandoned by cultivation, and which is accompanied by vitarka and vicāra; thus, the initiator to be abandoned by seeing is separated [from the result] by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

"He says 'the self exists' and so forth; therefore, [it is] according to what initiates [the action]," and so on in detail. Thus, immediately after an initiator that is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), there must necessarily arise an initiator that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), whether it be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. And by virtue of that, the informative action (*vijñapti*) possesses the quality of being wholesome and so forth. However, it should be stated as follows in detail: "It should be stated as follows: this was said with reference to a causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*) separated by another—that is, separated by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation. The meaning is: "with reference to an indirect causal origination (*paramparā-hetu-samutthāna*)."

"Non-informative [matter] is of three kinds," and so forth. Having indicated that it is "threefold," he explains it as "restraint, non-restraint, and that which is other than these. The compound is analyzed as follows: it is both restraint and non-restraint (*saṃvaraś ca saḥ asaṃvaraś ca saḥ*), and it is both restraint and non-restraint (*saṃvarāsaṃvaraḥ*), and it is that which is other than restraint and non-restraint (*saṃvarāsaṃvaretarā*). This is because its characteristics are specifically determined.

The definition of the monk's restraint (*bhikṣu-saṃvara*) is distinct [from the others], and likewise the definition of the fast-day restraint (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) is distinct; for it will be stated that [the latter] arises from undertaking the abstention from five, eight, ten, or all things to be avoided.

If there were eight types—lay follower (*upāsaka*), one observing the fast (*upavāsastha*), novice monk (*śramaṇoddeśa*), and monk (*bhikṣu*)—then confusion would arise; for that which is the *bhikṣu* restraint (*saṃvara*) would be the very same as the *bhikṣuṇī* restraint, and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the *śikṣamāṇā*: when a *śrāmaṇerī* changes gender, she becomes a *śrāmaṇera*; and when a *śikṣamāṇā* changes gender, she likewise becomes a *śrāmaṇera*. Why is this not accepted? [The opponent asks: Does a monk who changes gender abandon the *bhikṣu* restraint and [take] the *bhikṣuṇī* restraint?

And because one does not acquire [it again], he says: "Nor upon the transformation of the sexual organs," and so forth. When the sexual organs of a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*) appear, there is no cause for the abandonment of the previous restraint (*saṃvara*). [The causes for the abandonment of the Prātimokṣa discipline are: "Through the renunciation of the training, through death, through the appearance of both sexual organs, through the cutting of the roots [of merit], and through the passing of the night. This is what was stated as the cause here. It continues: "Nor is there a cause for the acquisition of a restraint not previously possessed. This refers to what was stated regarding that which is called the *Prātimokṣa*.

Because of [the rules] such as making others understand, it is known that the *bhikṣuṇī*-saṃvara is not different from the *bhikṣu*-saṃvara. The same should be stated for the *śrāmaṇera* and so forth. Therefore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four—namely, the *bhikṣuṇī*, *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇerī*, and *upāsikā*—saṃvaras is not distinct from the three—namely, the *bhikṣu*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *upāsaka*—saṃvaras. What are these saṃvaras? This is the detailed explanation. Just as when five other items are added to the number five, it becomes ten through the addition of those five.

When fifteen in number, by adding another five, they become twenty. Just as a *dīnāra* together with a *satera* becomes [twenty], so too in the world, regarding a second *dīnāra* or the value of a *dīnāra* as an addition to the value of the first *dīnāra*, a speaker might say, "I have obtained a *dīnāra-satera*," which means "I have obtained two *dīnāras*. Is this so?

The vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) are designated as distinct from one another because of the addition of further abstentions, while the abstentions from killing and so forth remain exactly as they were. Specifically, the vow of a novice monk is distinct from that of a lay follower, and the vow of a fully ordained monk is distinct from that of a novice monk, due to the addition of new abstentions such as those from dancing, singing, and so on. The meaning is that their respective definitions are established through the application of these eleven specific distinctions. Alternatively, do these arise as entirely separate and distinct entities? No, they do not.

The abstinences from killing living beings and so forth for a lay follower (*upāsaka*) are distinct; those for a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) are distinct from them; and those for a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) are distinct from those. Thus, within the single continuum of a monk, there are three [sets of] abstinences from killing living beings and so forth, as well as abstinences from taking what is not given, and so on. The same applies to the remaining [precepts], such as the abstinence from dancing, singing, and so forth. "From intoxication and negligence" means from high beds and the like, from drinking liquor and the like—from many more causes of killing living beings and so forth than those for a lay follower. A novice monk [abstains] from many more [such causes] than a lay follower.

One should desist from the causes of taking life and so forth; for example, if eating at improper times were a cause for taking life, from that a *śrāmaṇera* would desist, but not a lay follower (*upāsaka*)—this is how it should be applied. And this being so, the meaning is "if it were not thus. One who renounces or abandons the *bhikṣu* restraint would also abandon all three, beginning with the *upāsaka* restraint, because the two—the *upāsaka* and *śrāmaṇera* restraints—are included within that *bhikṣu* restraint due to the undertaking of abstinence.

"Thus, it will be stated that 'abstention' (virati) consists of informative action (*vijñapti*) and non-informative action (*avijñapti*). This means "because of its accomplishment" (*samāpādanāt*), which has the sense of "because of its establishment" (*pratisaṃsthāpanāt*). For evil karma proceeds in a harmful manner toward sentient beings; yet, that [abstention] is also performed by means of both informative action and the mind. That which is comprised within the *prātimokṣa* restraint is performed by informative action, while the non-informative action comprised within the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints is performed by the mind. The meaning is that it is performed by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, because it is performed in this way, it is called "action" (*kriyā*); this is a derivation based on the object (*karman-sādhana*). It is so called because it is the cause of performing [the abstention].

Because it is the cause of action, one who abides in restraint initiates an action characterized by informative intimation (*vijñapti*) for the sake of protecting that restraint; and because it is the fruit of action—meaning, because it is the fruit of an action characterized by informative intimation. How can that which is produced from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) be an action? Because it is the fruit of volition (*cetanā*) born of concentration, that too is an action. Or, in the context of the Prātimokṣa restraint, it is not merely the mind [that is the action]. Thus, in this way, the Prātimokṣa restraint is designated without distinction.

The first moment, as well as the second and subsequent moments, are called *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* (the restraint of individual liberation); however, the nature of *prātimokṣa* itself belongs only to the first moment. To this effect, he says again: "In the first [moment], both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) are called *prātimokṣa*, because by means of it there is liberation (*pratimokṣaṇa*) from evil. The meaning is that by the very first moment, evil is liberated—that is, it is relinquished and abandoned. Although the form *pratimokṣa* would be expected, the word *prātimokṣa* is used with the prefix *pra-* added for the sake of the rule regarding vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in its own sense.

The meaning is: because an augment (*vṛddhi*) is applied by means of a suffix (*pratyaya*). Just as *vaikṛta* is that which is transformed (*vikṛta*), and *vaiśasa* is that which is killing (*viśasa*), so too is *prātimokṣa*. It is also called *prātimokṣasaṃvara*; the meaning is that it is both *prātimokṣa* and *saṃvara*, in the sense of restraining body and speech. It is also called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*), meaning it is the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*). In the second and subsequent moments, there is only *prātimokṣasaṃvara*, which belongs to the same category as *prātimokṣa* and arises from *prātimokṣa*.

Or, the restraint that has arisen is the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*, not simply *prātimokṣa*. Why? Because by means of it, one is liberated from evil (*pāpa*); for it effects liberation at the very first moment. Regarding the restriction "only eight classes," he asks: "What about those outside [the Buddhist fold]? and so forth. The qualification "morality of undertaking" (*samādāna-śīla*) is used because there are two kinds of morality. For morality is twofold: morality of undertaking and morality acquired through the nature of things (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*). Among these, morality of undertaking is that which is formally received, specifying "this and this, and not that."

The meditative restraint acquired through the natural law (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) are based on existence; thus, even for those seeking liberation, because they are afflicted by wrong views and the like, for some among them, "liberation" is merely a particular state of existence.

Their morality is based solely on existence; therefore, they possess the morality of undertaking [vows], but not the Prātimokṣa restraint. Here, even the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of dhyāna is included under the term "dhyāna. This is because both the dhyāna restraint and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraint are accepted as existing even in the preparatory stage; thus, it is accepted that even the preparatory stage of dhyāna is expressed here by the word "dhyāna. By the use of the word "also" (*api*), the fundamental (*maula*) stage is certainly included as well when the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is being discussed. Regarding the statement, "the mental factors (*caitta*) and the two restraints among them," there are three [categories] here.

Thus, because the Prātimokṣa restraint, the dhyāna restraint, and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint continue even for one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind; because of the statement "even for one whose mind is distracted or without mind"; because of the inclusion of "not having attained" [the first dhyāna], since [this restraint] is the antidote specifically to the immorality belonging to the desire realm; because of the phrase "in the paths of immediate succession" (ānantarya-mārga), since those paths are paths of abandonment; because of the phrase "of those that originate it," meaning those that originate immorality; and for this very reason—namely, because its establishment occurs precisely in the paths of immediate succession of the Not-Yet-Arrived (anāgāmin)—therefore...

A fourfold alternative (catuḥ-koṭika) is established: The first alternative is the meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara), excluding the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) of the threshold stage (anāgamya). This refers to the meditative restraint existing in the paths of liberation, preparation, and excellence belonging to the threshold stage, or in the fundamental first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, within their respective paths of immediate succession, liberation, preparation, and excellence. This is meditative restraint but not the restraint of abandonment (prahāṇa-saṃvara), because by it there is no abandonment of immorality (dauḥśīlya) nor of the afflictions (kleśa) that give rise to it. The second [alternative] concerns the paths of immediate succession of the threshold stage...

The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is this restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*), because by it there is the abandonment of immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) and so forth; it is not the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) because it is untainted. In the third [category], within the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), there is the tainted restraint (*sāsrava-saṃvara*) and this restraint of abandonment, because by it there is the abandonment of immorality and so forth; and it is also the meditative restraint because it is born from tainted concentration (*samādhi*). In the fourth [category], excluding the paths of immediate succession of the threshold stage (*anāgamya*), there is the untainted restraint; this is neither the meditative restraint because it is untainted, nor the restraint of abandonment because by it—

Because of the abandonment of immorality and so forth, that same untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which exists within the paths of liberation, preparation, and excellence belonging to the stage of the *anāgamya*—is described in detail by way of its restriction as "restraint. Otherwise, other factors would also have to be mentioned; for instance, there might be the case where there is untainted restraint but not the restraint of abandonment. Thus, there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*): the first alternative is the untainted restraint excluding the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the *anāgamya*, as well as the restraint of mind (*manaḥ-saṃvara*), which has the nature of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛti-samprajñāna*).

Since the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*) also has mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajñāna*) as its intrinsic nature, the word "two" is used twice in order to indicate that it possesses these two natures; for indeed, duality is established by the very mention of the dual number. How, then, is it understood that these two have such an intrinsic nature? It is from scripture (*āgama*). It is said that a certain deity spoke to a monk who was letting his senses wander among sense objects: "O monk, O monk, do not create a wound!"

The monk said: "I shall cover it, O deity. "The deity replied: 'O monk, having made a wound as large as a jar, with what will you cover it? The monk said: "I shall cover it, O deity, with mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*samprajanya*)," [this applies] as long as one does not abandon that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). [This concerns] the abandonment of the training (*śikṣā-nikṣepa*), and so forth. After the preceding moment, having passed beyond, it is stated that in the first moment one is possessed of [the non-informative matter] only as it exists in the present. "One who possesses the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) always [possesses it] through the past and the unborn"—one who possesses the restraint of meditative absorption, what [does he possess]?

Whether an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or an noble one (*ārya*), because [the text] does not specify otherwise, it is said that both are endowed with past and future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). Regarding its characteristic: since the context concerns the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*), it is understood that it has the characteristic of the restraint of meditative absorption. The phrase "abandoned in another birth" is intended merely as an illustration; for even that which is abandoned in this very life is included. However, the noble one, in the first [moment], is not endowed with the past [non-informative matter]. A noble one is always endowed with past and unborn non-informative matter. Regarding its characteristic: it is the untainted (*anāsrava*) [non-informative matter], because the context concerns the noble ones. For this very reason, it is said: "The noble person (*āryapudgala*) likewise possesses the untainted [non-informative matter]."

But this is the distinction; he shows the meaning of the word "tu" (but) as follows: "And that [non-informative action] is displaced in its sequence. The meaning is that in the first moment—the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering—one is not possessed of past non-informative action. Why? Because in beginningless *saṃsāra*, the Path has not previously been produced. [Objection: But surely, at the time of attaining a fruit or at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), when the previous path is abandoned, one is not held to be possessed of past non-informative action? [Response: If that is so, then that [non-informative action] belongs to the path of the fruit as well.

The first moment occurs there; it should be explained that one is not possessed of past non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) because the path of the fruit has not previously arisen. However, Master Vasumitra states the resolution to this objection: "The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is the subject under discussion here, and it is acquired precisely at the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). Therefore, in the first moment, one is not possessed of it as past; in the second moment and thereafter, one is possessed of it as both past and future. But as for what follows...

Regarding the attainment of another path: since there is a similarity to the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) therein, it is not mentioned [in that context]. We do not understand what kind of similarity exists here such that it would be [implied] as existing. Is the intention that the tainted [restraint] (*sāsrava*) exists? Even at the time of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), that [tainted restraint] exists; thus, the prohibition stating "one is not endowed with the past" would be untenable. Alternatively, if the intention is that the past untainted restraint exists at the time of attaining the fruit, how can it be said that it exists when it has already been discarded? This must be considered.

His intention is as follows: "Abiding in the concentrated noble path" means abiding in both the worldly concentrated path and the noble path; that is to say, one who abides in the concentrated noble path is endowed with both the meditative (*dhyāna*) restraint and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraint. Here, "abiding in the noble path" should be understood as being mounted upon the noble path, according to the analogy of standing on a boat: just as one who has boarded a boat is said to be "standing on the boat," so too one who has mounted and entered the noble path is said to be "abiding in the noble path. Otherwise, [the definition would not hold].

[Objection: Even one who is endowed with the noble path (āryamārga) is considered "abiding in the noble path"; thus, it follows that even a noble one (*ārya*) who is not yet abiding [in the meditative state] (*aprakṛtistha*) is possessed of the present non-outflowing non-informative matter (*anāsravā avijñapti*). [Response: Another, avoiding this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), explains as follows: "In this case, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is employed: both 'one who is concentrated' (*samāhita*) and 'one who abides in the concentrated noble path' (*samāhitāryamārgastha*) constitute the two paths; those two are 'the concentrated noble paths. Abiding in those two, they are respectively possessed of the present non-informative matter of the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara-avijñapti*) and the non-outflowing restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*)."

And one is endowed with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), yet not when emerged [from meditative absorption], nor when emerged from that path; for one is endowed with it while it is present, because it follows the mind. This is how it is explained. As for what was raised by the Master Saṅghabhadra: "How is the present state of non-informative matter understood? Simply from the statement 'one who abides in the Noble Path'? If you say, "This refers only to one who has entered that [path], and there is no consequence of stating that one is endowed with it [at other times]," [the answer is: because of the context of dhyāna, and because non-informative matter does not exist therein. Whoever...

One who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint is called "neutral" (*madhyastha*); such a person is neither a monk (*bhikṣu*) and so forth, nor a fisherman and so forth. [The term] "comprised of good conduct, the limbs of morality, and so forth" refers to bad conduct (*dauḥśīlya*), such as killing and so forth; the "limbs of morality" refer to abstaining from killing and so forth. By the word "and so forth," it is understood that non-information (*avijñapti*) regarding actions such as bowing to a stupa or striking with a whip or a hand is not comprised within either restraint or non-restraint. Thus, the two types of persons—those established in non-restraint and those established in restraint—are established in unwholesome and wholesome dharmas respectively. Regarding these two:

Not conceiving of the opposite possibility, he asks: "What about one who abides in non-restraint? and so forth. "As long as those [impulses] continue": this refers to the force of faith or the force of affliction. "In others, even by means of the past" means that in the second moment and subsequent moments, from the moment after the first until its abandonment, one is endowed with that past informative action (*vijñapti*). How is there an abandonment of informative action characterized as restraint? It occurs through such acts as the renunciation of the training (*śikṣānikṣepa*). Until that abandonment, one remains endowed with that past informative action.

One who is endowed [with non-restraint] abandons it through the undertaking of restraint and so forth; therefore, one is endowed with this until that abandonment. One who is endowed with that which is characterized as neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint abandons it through the cutting off of the force of faith, afflictions, and so forth; therefore, one is endowed with this until that abandonment. For whoever is endowed with the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of restraint and so forth, they are necessarily endowed from the moment after [the first] with the past unmanifest whose nature is the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*); however, no one is endowed with a future manifest (*vijñapti*).

“Endowed with” means that because [the acquisition] does not follow after the mind, there would otherwise be no acquisition even for the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind; the meaning is that it should not be a continuous follower. Why? He says: “For informative action (*vijñapti*) is insentient (*jaḍa*) because it lacks an object (*anālambana*), and it is dependent because it is dependent upon the mind. But the mind is not like this”; the meaning is that it is neither insentient nor dependent. Why? Because it is the opposite of that: it is even weaker than the weak obscured-unspecified mind by which it was produced.

If it is argued that this is because [the action] is included within the primary [volition], we say no, because that [volition] has that [action] as its object. One who is neutral (madhyastha) is endowed with the informative act (*vijñapti*) alone when performing [an action] with weak volition (*mṛdu-cetanā*). The mention of "neutral" is for the purpose of excluding those established in restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), for those established in restraint or non-restraint are necessarily endowed with both informative and non-informative acts. The mention of "weak volition" is for the purpose of excluding intense volition (*tīvra-cetanā*); for one performing an informative act with intense volition would give rise to a non-informative act, let alone an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) one. Thus, [it is by means of] the weak [volition].

When one performs an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) action by means of volition (*cetanā*), specifically in cases other than when one—abiding in neither restraint nor non-restraint—performs a wholesome or unwholesome action with weak volition and is endowed only with informative action (*vijñapti*) and not with non-informative action (*avijñapti*), because there is no possibility for the arising of non-informative action; this is the detailed explanation. "Other than" refers to the seven material bases of meritorious activity (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*) and the paths of action (*karmapatha*) beginning with taking life. For in those cases, even while performing an indeterminate action, one is endowed with non-informative action.

Because of the statement in the Sūtra: "Whether walking or standing, [the noble person] is constantly and continuously possessed of merit," and because even when performing the paths of action such as taking life with a weak volition, the noble person (*āryapudgala*) remains endowed with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and so forth in detail; furthermore, for a noble person who has changed births—such as during the embryonic stages of the *kalala* and so on, or upon rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—or when non-informative matter has been lost, [informative matter] does not yet exist.

Furthermore, for one who is devoid of the informative action (*vijñapti*) originated by an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛtacitta*), there is no continuous acquisition (*prāpti*) of that [action]; this applies even to one who has built a stupa or the like, because upon the destruction of that object, he abandons even the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) at that time, let alone the informative action.

In these states, upon the transition to another birth, the noble person (*āryapudgala*) is endowed with non-outflowing non-informative action (*anāsravā-avijñapti*) acquired in that other birth, but not with informative action (*vijñapti*). Now, this rule is also possible for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), yet it is not mentioned because it is not necessary; for only one who has attained meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), has undergone the transition to another birth, and either has not performed an informative action or is devoid of having performed one in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), can be so [endowed], and no other.

Or, because the statement refers specifically to beings of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), or because the noble person (*āryapudgala*) was mentioned as an illustration, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) should also be understood in the same way. For this very reason, it was stated: "One who is neutral and possesses weak volition is endowed with [the action] through informative intimation (*vijñapti*) alone. Since this statement excludes the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*) and the paths of action (*karmapatha*), it is made with reservations. Thus, the first and second alternatives are explicitly formulated in the sutra, while the third and fourth should be applied accordingly. This is the third [alternative].

Those abiding in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state, while performing wholesome or unwholesome actions with intense volition, constitute the fourth [category]. It is that by which, upon the transition to another birth, even an ordinary person has not yet manifested, or having manifested it, has not lost it; because it is co-existent, since the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) exists together with the meditative mind. "Another informs" means one causes another to understand; "other than the person" refers to the restraints of the novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), the novice nun (*śrāmaṇerī*), the layman (*upāsaka*), the laywoman (*upāsikā*), and the fast-day restraint (*upavāsa-saṃvara*). [The restraint of the noble ones] arises through entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*).

By means of introducing [them] to the Noble Path, [the Buddha ordained] the group of five, Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others, with the "Come, monk" formula—namely, by the Blessed One’s words, "Come, monk; lead the holy life. When the Protector Sugata said "Come," he became shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes. This refers to the acceptance of Mahākāśyapa by the Teacher. It is said that whenever Mahākāśyapa would bow to a certain image of a deity, the image would fall into ruin. Knowing this intention, the Blessed One urged him, saying, "Bow down, Kāśyapa! (to the image).

Having thus paid homage to the Blessed One by saying "Tathāgata," he saw that the Blessed One’s physical form was unaltered; thinking, "This is my Teacher," he accepted the Blessed One. His full ordination (*upasampad*) was through the satisfaction of the question, as in the case of Sodāyin; for the Blessed One was satisfied by Sodāyin’s answering of the questions, and through that satisfaction his full ordination was granted. It was also [granted] by the acceptance of the qualities of a teacher (*gurudharma*).

The eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*): 1. Full ordination (*upasampadā*) for *bhikṣuṇīs* must be received from a *bhikṣu*; this is the status of a *bhikṣuṇī*. 2. Every half-month, instruction (*avavāda*) must be received from a *bhikṣu*. 3. One must not enter the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) in a residence where there are no *bhikṣus*. 4. At the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*), both Saṅghas must perform the invitation with respect to three matters. 5. A *bhikṣu* who has committed an offense must not be accused [by a *bhikṣuṇī*], nor should he be reviled. 6. Upon committing an offense against a weighty rule, a *mānāpya* penance of half a month must be performed even by a *bhikṣuṇī* who has been ordained for a hundred years.

A monk ordained at that very moment is to be saluted; furthermore, a nun must never, under any circumstances, reprove a monk. Full ordination (*upasampad*) for her is attained through the acceptance of these [rules], as was the case with Dharmadinnā by means of a messenger. It is said that while she was still within the inner apartments, she sent a messenger to the Buddha for the sake of going forth (*pravrajyā*). "With a fifth person who is a holder of the Vinaya" means that the Saṅgha consists of four monks, and there, ordination is conferred by the fifth person acting as the proclaimer of the motion (*jñaptivācaka*). This applies in the border regions (*pratyantika-janapada*); however, in the central countries (*madhyama*), [the requirements are different].

In the countryside, ordination is conferred by a tenth person acting as the proclaimer of the formal motion (*jñaptivācaka*). Regarding those ordained by the group of sixty "Noble Ones" (*bhadravarga*): the term *bhadravargāṇām* means "those for whom the group is noble. These were sixty sons of good family who were ordained by that group—that is, by the assembly—as a collective. Their ordination was performed through the threefold formula of going for refuge, by saying "We go for refuge to the Buddha" three times. For them, [the ordination] was not necessarily dependent upon a formal motion (*vijñapti*). This is the opinion of those masters of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*): that the Prātimokṣa restraint is not necessarily dependent upon a formal motion.

Because [the discipline] of the Buddhas and others does not depend on informative action (*vijñapti*), or because for those who have no informative action during the rite of full ordination (*upasampad*), there exists a portion of restraint (*saṃvara*) that is a permanent entity; anticipating this doubt, he asks: "What is this phenomenon called 'time'?"
