The meaning of the question "What is the referent of this designation 'time'? is as follows: this is a term that illuminates the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). It is a name that indicates the past, future, and present formative forces; for example, by [the expressions] "past time" up to "present [time]," only the formative forces belonging to the three time periods are understood. Furthermore, because there is no application [of the vow] therein by means of that [past basis], and because there is no recollection by means of that basis, the undertaking of that [vow] does not occur through that dissimilar basis.

The Vaibhāṣika master Smṛti says: "Because there is no contradiction with reason even in the arising of restraint (*saṃvara*) after [the initial period]," thus reason is not contradicted here. Just as there is a contradiction with reason regarding the arising of restraint after one's life has ended—even though there may be a formal undertaking—because the basis (*āśraya*) is of a different nature, and so forth; likewise, non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). Like non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), non-restraint also does not exist substantially, just as it was established that non-informative matter does not exist substantially. This applies to that which is ruined at another time, such as for a day and night, or for as long as the intention to act persists. Thus, non-restraint also lacks substantial existence.

The intended meaning is that [it] exists substantially as something distinct from volition (*cetanā*). "Intent toward a sinful action" means an intention for a sinful action. "With its continuity" means together with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*). The meaning is that non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is a specific kind of volition accompanied by latent tendencies. Because of that continuity, one who possesses it is said to be "possessing non-restraint," which is to say, one is a person of non-restraint (*asaṃvarika*). "Because of its not being discarded" means because that intention, along with its continuity, has not been discarded; the meaning is that it has not been impaired by a volition contrary to it. That...

One may take up the vow even after having eaten; the restraint (*saṃvara*) arises precisely at sunrise because it is that which arouses the mind of commitment and restriction. However, the mention of "having eaten" is for the sake of clarification, as it is a mere token (*kapataka*).

By placing the four fingers, excluding the thumb, into the space between the thumb and forefinger of the other hand, one forms the *kapataka* (the "clapping" or "seal") gesture. *Śīla* is the absence of *pārājika* offenses and the absence of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and so forth; *vrata* refers to a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Because of the absence of that [rule], both [virtue and restraint] would not exist due to eating at improper times—this is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) regarding the lack of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). However, the Master [Vasubandhu], in detail, refutes the Vaibhāṣika position through reasoning, but he does not refute those very factors such as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the rest.

The meaning is that only when there is the factor of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and the awakening-factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), along with concentration (*samādhi*), do right view and the others become fit or appropriate to be "factors" (*aṅga*). Why? Because it would contradict the scriptural statement if it were established that the preceding [moments of] right view and so forth are factors for the subsequent [moments of] right view and so forth. If this were the case, the Noble Path arising in the first moment would not be eightfold; for in that instance, there is no previously arisen right view to serve as a factor, and thus it would be sevenfold.

It might be argued that even among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the final moment would not be a factor of enlightenment; for there is no other awakening (*bodhi*) subsequent to it of which that [moment] could be a factor. Thus, it is held that it is a factor of that future awakening.

Future enlightenment would not exist; thus, this meditative absorption (samādhi) should be applied. Except for ignorance—meaning due to the forgetfulness or lack of understanding of either the giver or the receiver, or for one who is doubtful, whose intention has failed, or who takes refuge without respect—the restraint (saṃvara) does not arise. "Householder" is the term of general indication (uddeśapada); "one wearing white garments" is the term of specific explanation (nirdeśapada). "Man" is the term of general indication; "endowed with the male faculty" is its term of specific explanation. If one becomes a lay follower (upāsaka) even without the restraint, then what [of the following]?

It is stated in the Sūtra: "By this much one becomes an upāsaka. The completion of the sentence is: "How so? [The author] replies: "There is no contradiction with the Sūtra here. As for the statement in the *Mahānāma-sūtra* that "[the upāsaka's undertaking] is like that of a bhikṣu," this refers to the statement regarding the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) of an upāsaka. Just as a bhikṣu, even though he has already obtained the vows (*saṃvara*), is made to grasp and be informed of the training precepts in their gross form through the formal ritual (*jñapticaturtha-karman*)—[being told], "Your restraint is from this and from that, such as the *pārājika* offenses and others"—so too for the other [precepts].

Thinking, "My fellow religious practitioners will speak [of me]," the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is made to take up the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). Even though he has already obtained the vows (*saṃvara*), it is at the very moment he previously undertakes: "I, named so-and-so, follow in the renunciation of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha Śākyamuni, the Sovereign King of the Śākyas who has gone forth; I abandon the marks of a householder and assume the marks of one who has gone forth; maintain me as a novice (*śramaṇoddeśa*). In this way, up to three times, he likewise becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

Even one who has obtained the vows by saying, "I go for refuge to the Buddha... up to... I go for refuge to the Saṅgha," a second and a third time, nevertheless receives the training precepts (*śikṣāpada*) again, [reciting]: "Having abandoned the taking of life, I abstain from taking life," and so forth in detail. One who practices a single portion observes one precept; one who practices a limited portion observes two; one who practices the majority observes three or four; and one who practices in full observes all five. Such a person is said to be "one who acts accordingly" (*tatkārī*).

The meaning is: "one who practices one part" up to "one who practices in full. For the reading of the *Mahānāma-sūtra* is not like this; for the reading of the *Mahānāma-sūtra* does not state, "for as long as life lasts, [he is] free from taking life," but rather: "And because, Mahānāman, a householder... [up to] 'may you hold me as a lay follower'—to this extent one becomes a lay follower. However, where there is this reading—in another sutra where the reading is: "For as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge with faith, being free from taking life"—therein are those persons who have seen the truths.

He demonstrates that, as a consequence of and caused by verified faith (*avetyaprasāda*), one approaches the True Dharma even at the cost of life and even for the sake of living; [he does so] to show that such persons are incapable of abandoning this Dharma. However, this is not an instruction on the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of the restraint (*saṃvara*); the meaning is that the definition is not being set forth by this Sūtra. Furthermore, the phrase "devoid of life" (*prāṇāpeta*) is not recited anywhere—not in the *Mahānāma-sūtra*, nor in the *Dṛṣṭasatya-sūtra*. Who indeed would recite something of such unclear meaning?

Because of this ambiguity arising from the optional elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*), it is not known whether *prāṇāpeta* means "deprived of life-breaths," or "departed from life-breaths," or rather "devoid of the taking of life" and so forth; thus, the very question is not tenable. As for this question—"To what extent, Venerable Sir, is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) a partial practitioner, and to what extent is he a complete practitioner?"—this question is not tenable. Why? Because the answer [is already established]: here, Mahānāman, a lay follower, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from the taking of life.

"Mahānāman, by this much a lay follower becomes one who practices a single portion of the training; by abstaining from two training rules in detail, he becomes one who practices a partial portion; by abstaining from three or four, he becomes one who practices the majority; and by abstaining from five, he becomes one who practices the complete portion. This explanation is not entirely appropriate; rather, this question would be appropriate regarding the capacity for only that much of the training—namely, for one training rule, two, or more than that.

Or, even without the formal restraint (*saṃvara*), one is designated an Upāsaka by another through the mere expression "I am patient," as stated in the *Mahānāma-sūtra*: "Indeed, Mahānāma, a householder clad in white garments... and so forth. Even for an Arhat, the Prātimokṣa restraint may be weak if his motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) is weak; conversely, it may be intense (*adhimātra*) for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) if his mind is intense. Except in cases of ignorance, there can be no Upāsaka without taking refuge, nor without the donor and recipient being free from disrespect.
[This applies to] those who perform the acts that constitute a Buddha.

Precisely because they are the causes for the designation "Buddha," it is said that that very personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is called "the Buddha. For other qualities also reside therein, though not as primary ones; or rather, it is by the acquisition of these—such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth—that he is so designated.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*) are included. By including them along with their retinues, the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are understood. This is because there is no difference in the physical body (*rūpakāya*) before and after [attainment].

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Why does one not go for refuge to the form-body (*rūpakāya*)? The intention is that because the form-body is of the same nature as it was during the stage of a Bodhisattva, it remains so afterwards; thus, one goes for refuge to all Buddhas by way of their *characteristics* (*lakṣaṇa*), and not merely by way of explicit verbal statement. This is because the path is non-distinct: since the mundane path, characterized by the equipment of merit and knowledge, and the supramundane path, characterized by the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, are non-distinct—that is, equal—therefore all [Buddhas] have equal characteristics, such as lifespan, birth, and the rest.

They are called "Buddhas" because they become a *saṅgha* due to being indivisible; that is, because they are indivisible with respect to the Path even by the world including the gods, they become a *saṅgha*, meaning they exist in a state of complete harmony. This should be explained according to the characteristics as previously [stated]. Regarding the passage beginning "He who will be," and so forth: there, the Blessed One addressed the two merchants Trapusa and Bhallika: "Go for refuge to this Buddha and to the Dharma; and also to that which will be known as the *Saṅgha* in the future time."

When it was said, "Go for refuge," at a time when the Saṅgha did not yet exist, this was spoken with reference to the future Saṅgha. How, then, is this not contradicted by the statement that he goes for refuge to the entire Saṅgha? It is because [the Saṅgha] will become manifest; the meaning is that the Jewel of the Saṅgha, which will become manifest to those two, the Bhallikas, immediately after the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, will be the very one intended [by the command], for the purpose of highlighting and proclaiming it through its qualities. This is because [the Saṅgha] has the single characteristic of peace (*śānti*).

Thus, the "characteristic of peace" (*śānty-ekalakṣaṇa*) refers to that which has the characteristic of the pacification of the afflictions and suffering belonging to one’s own and others’ continuums; *nirvāṇa* is that very state. Therefore, he goes to all *nirvāṇa* through the "destruction of the basis" (*āśrayavipādana*). The "basis" of those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); by its destruction—that is, its disruption—the qualities that constitute a Buddha (*buddhakārakā dharmāḥ*), which depend upon that basis, are also destroyed. However, the treatise does not say this, and so forth; the Abhidharma treatise does not speak in such a way, nor does it show it in such a way, [but rather] that the qualities beyond training themselves are the Buddha.

What then? "Those which produce a Buddha"—what are those that produce a Buddha? They are the mundane and supramundane dharmas that are the causes of Buddhahood and the designation of a Buddha; these are called "Buddhas."

Therefore, since the basis—characterized by the five mundane aggregates—is not excluded from being the Buddha, this objection is indeed invalid: namely, "If only the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the Buddha, how can there be an immediate offense (*ānantarya*) for shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind? Otherwise, as the detailed explanation goes: if only the dharmas of one beyond training were the Buddha, and only the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training were the Saṅgha, then one abiding in a mundane state of mind would be neither the Buddha nor the Saṅgha. Why? Because a mundane mind is not [the Buddha].

Could it be that the *aśaikṣa* dharmas are the cause, while the basis (*āśraya*) is not? It is precisely the morality known as the *bhikṣu-saṃvara* that makes one a monk; the basis itself would not be the monk. [Objection: If the basis also possesses Buddhahood, why did the Teacher say, "One goes for refuge to the Buddha"? [Response: He said this so that one might go for refuge to the *aśaikṣa* dharmas that constitute a Buddha; thus, he restricts the reference to the *aśaikṣa* dharmas alone. When the Vaibhāṣika has spoken thus, the Master (Vasubandhu) provides a resolution by means of an analogy: "Just as when one honors a monk..."

The detailed explanation is as follows: Just as one who honors a monk honors the monk-making virtue (*śīla*) by way of that virtue, yet the virtue itself is not the monk; likewise, one who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to the *aśaikṣa* (beyond-training) factors that constitute a Buddha by way of those *aśaikṣa* factors, but the *aśaikṣa* factors existing within one's own continuum are not themselves the Buddha. Therefore, there is no fault in this: when one goes for refuge to the Buddha, one goes for refuge to the *aśaikṣa* factors that constitute a Buddha.

"Going" refers to the eighteen unique [qualities] (*āveṇika*); the intention is that they are so called because they are not shared [with others]. "Having the nature of vocal intimation" (*vāg-vijñapti-svabhāva*) is said with reference to the time of grasping [the vow]. "And the *caitya*-trees" (*caityavṛkṣān*): trees that are designated as *caityas* are *caitya*-trees; [the phrase] "those" refers to them.

For this very reason—namely, because by resorting to this refuge one is liberated from all suffering—it follows that [the others] serve as gateways for the undertaking of all vows, meaning for the undertaking of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth. Furthermore, because sexual misconduct leads exclusively to the miserable states (*apāya*), being conducive to rebirth in those states, whereas celibacy does not; for the restraint of non-action consists in the rule of non-performance.

The restriction (*niyama*) regarding non-action—that is, non-performance—is the "restriction of non-action" (*akriyā-niyama*). This is the restraint (*saṃvara*) characterized by non-performance; it does not mean a restraint consisting of formal undertaking (*samādānika-saṃvara*). According to the Sautrāntika system, this is merely a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*); however, according to the Vaibhāṣika system, it is the unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) that constitutes a limb of morality (*śīla-aṅga*). Thus, the detailed explanation begins: "those who, being lay followers (*upāsaka*),..."—meaning those who, having already taken the five precepts (*pañca-śikṣā-pada*), subsequently take wives and marry them. Do these lay followers possess restraint even with respect to those women?

"Obtained" means previously obtained; however, the context here is "if not obtained. The Vaibhāṣika says: "It is obtained," lest it be considered partial. This is because one vows, "I abstain from all unapproachable [sexual] acts" (*agamyā*), meaning "I abstain from sexual misconduct" (*kāmamithyācāra*). The intention is not "I abstain from unapproachable acts toward this particular person," but rather "I abstain from unapproachable acts within this [specific] continuum (*santāna*). For this very reason, he says: "But not with respect to this continuum."

The detailed explanation: "That which is blameworthy by way of rejection" means that for one who performs an action prohibited by the Blessed One—which is blameworthy by way of prohibition—sin arises due to disregard for the Blessed One's teaching. When an Abhidharmika says, "It is not afflicted [karma] when one drinks knowing it to be merely non-intoxicating," the Vinaya-holders establish that it is "blameworthy by nature" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Upāli, setting aside what is blameworthy by nature, [one is] not to be treated with medicine by means of an action that is blameworthy by nature, but rather by means of what is blameworthy by designation (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).

The intention is that [alcohol] is to be treated medically. Since drinking intoxicants was not permitted even among the Śākyas who were ill, it is understood that this is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*). For if it were a conventional transgression (*prajñaptisāvadya*), it would have been permitted for the sake of attending to sick Śākyas; yet it was not so permitted. Therefore, it is a natural transgression. Furthermore, this has been stated by those who hold me as their teacher and designate Śākyamuni as our teacher: "Alcohol must not be drunk even with the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass. Thus, it is a natural transgression.

The Blessed One prohibited that [intoxicant], but he did not prohibit intoxication itself; for even a blade of *kuśa* grass [when consumed] is not intoxicating. Furthermore, [it is prohibited] by the Noble Ones (*ārya*), and so forth. The proof is that alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), because it is never practiced even by Noble Ones who have passed into other births, just like the killing of living beings and so on. Another proof is that it is called a bodily misconduct (*kāya-duścarita*). Alcohol is a natural transgression because it is designated as a bodily misconduct, just like the killing of living beings and so on. For in the *Nandika-sūtra* and other texts, bodily misconduct is said to be fourfold.

It has been stated: "Killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and the occasion of negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants. This refers to that which is generally prescribed (*utsarga-vihita*). [The opponent asks: "How so? and so forth, in detail. By this, they resolve the contradiction between the earlier and later statements of the Blessed One: the general statement regarding the drinking of intoxicants is the *utsarga* (general rule), while the statement "among the Śākyas, when ill, the drinking of intoxicants is not permitted" is the *apavāda* (exception). It is understood that even in a state of illness, the drinking of intoxicants is not permitted; thus, it is an exception.

Furthermore, in order to avoid the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that drinking liquor even once might lead to addiction, the Blessed One said: "For one who indulges in these three things, there is no satisfaction, nor an end, nor a limit: namely, liquor, unchastity, and sloth-torpor. Why does he say this to avoid such a consequence? Because there is no fixed rule for the amount that causes intoxication; for that very same amount may be intoxicating or non-intoxicating depending on the substance, the time, the constitution, and the state of the body. And for this very reason...

The prohibition against drinking from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass is an exaggerated statement; it was spoken by the Blessed One as something to be avoided not because it is inherently faulty (*prakṛtisāvadya*), but rather with the intention that "it is so," and thus [otherwise] it would be a fault of over-extension (*prasaṅgadoṣa*). It is shown that the Noble Ones do not practice such things out of a sense of shame (*hrīmattva*). In the Sūtra, five powers of the trainee (*śaikṣa*) are recited. Which five? They are: the power of faith (*śraddhābala*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), the power of shame (*hrībalam*), the power of dread of blame (*apatrāpyabalam*), and the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*). Therefore, they do not drink out of a sense of shame, but not because it is inherently faulty.

If it is argued that because intoxicants are inherently blameworthy (*prakṛtisāvadya*) and one possesses a sense of shame (*hrīmattva*), one does not consume them—yet why do they not drink [water and so forth] when those are unknown [to be blameworthy]? To this he says: "And because of the loss of mindfulness (*smṛtināśāt*). For in one who drinks intoxicants, the mindfulness of what ought and ought not to be done (*kāryākāryasmṛti*) is destroyed. If this is so, then let them drink a small amount, in such a measure that mindfulness is not lost; to this he says: "Because there is no restriction on drinking even a small amount, like poison. Just as poison sometimes kills due to the combination of time, constitution, and potency, so too is intoxication.

The statement that intoxicants "cause intoxication" refers to misconduct because they are a basis for negligence (*pramādasthāna*). Here, the designation "basis for negligence" is applied because one fails to avoid unwholesome states and fails to perform wholesome ones due to intoxication; this designation does not apply to other [bases of negligence].

In this very training rule (*śikṣāpada*), there is the inclusion of the term "basis of negligence" (*pramādasthāna*), because of the statement: "Having abandoned the basis of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, I abstain from the basis of negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants. However, in other training rules such as the abstinence from taking life (*prāṇātipāta-virati*) and so forth, there is no inclusion of the term "basis of negligence," nor is the phrase "basis of negligence" recited [there]. Rather, it is said: "Having abandoned taking life, [I abstain] from taking life."

"I shall abstain"—in this way, [the formula] for taking what is not given and so forth should be applied accordingly. Why? He says: "Because they are inherently reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). This means that because those training rules (*śikṣā-pada*), such as the abstinence from taking life and so forth, are inherently reprehensible, it is said: "This is a basis for negligence (*pramāda-sthāna*)," and thus one must abstain from drinking intoxicants; however, it is not because this [drinking] is inherently reprehensible.

"By excessive indulgence," and so forth; for it is stated in the *Nandika-sūtra*: "By indulging in, cultivating, and frequently practicing surā, maireya, and intoxicating liquors—the basis of negligence—one is reborn in the hells after the dissolution of the body. Thus, the statement that one goes to an evil destiny through the excessive drinking of intoxicants refers to the continuous engagement in a stream of unwholesome states (*akuśala-santati*) due to addiction to drinking—meaning, by constant and uninterrupted involvement with intoxicants. This leads to the arising of unprecedented states pertaining to the miserable destinies (*apāyika*), which have the miserable realms as their purpose.

Regarding "due to the projection (*ākṣepa*) of karma" and "due to the attainment of activity (*vṛtti-lābha*)," this should be connected as follows: because of the projection, or because of the attainment of activity for the sake of yielding fruit, there is the mention of going to an evil rebirth (*durgati*) when previously accumulated karma attains its activity at the stage of death. As for "fermented liquors" (*āsava*): those made from rice are *taṇḍulakṛta-āsava*; those made from sugarcane juice and so forth are *dravāsava*. The phrase "or those" refers to the detailed explanation. *Surā* and *maireya* are sometimes in a state where the nature of intoxicant has not yet been reached, which is when they are fresh; and sometimes they have lost the nature of intoxicant, which is when they are stale.

Regarding the phrase "atipurāṇe bhavataḥ" (they become very old), the inclusion of the term *madya* (intoxicant) implies that if it is intoxicating, then there is a fault; this applies even to substances such as the juice of betel nuts (*pūgaphala*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), *niṣpāva* and other such grains are included. Regarding the drinking of intoxicants (*madyapāna*), there is no fault even when one is not currently intoxicated; the meaning is that there is a fault in drinking *surā* and *maireya*, which are intoxicants by their very nature. It is called a "basis for negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) because it is the locus, the foundation, and the support for all forms of negligence—that is, for all instances of the loss of mindfulness that serve as causes for unwholesome acts such as taking life. "Because [the full offense] is obtained from one" means that it is obtained from the fundamental [act] (*maula*) and so forth.

The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained from things designated as sentient and non-sentient; the remaining two—the meditative (dhyāna) and the outflow-free (anāsrava) restraints—are obtained from the fundamental, the preliminary, and the subsequent [stages]. From unwholesome actions consisting of the fundamental, preliminary, and subsequent stages, there are obtained, respectively, the informative and non-informative [acts] known as the Prātimokṣa restraint, which serve as their antidotes and consist of the nature of the fundamental, preliminary, and subsequent stages, and which arise from bases designated as sentient and non-sentient.

Regarding actions characterized by having living beings, plants, and so forth as their basis, and those characterized by being naturally reprehensible (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) such as killing living beings or destroying plants; both of these possess two types of bases: they are both naturally reprehensible and based on sentient beings, as well as based on non-sentient things. Furthermore, proscribed offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) are also based on sentient beings and based on non-sentient things. However, it should not be understood that naturally reprehensible actions are exclusively based on sentient beings.

Regarding the fault of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), it is based on non-sentient things (*asattvādhiṣṭhāna*). In that regard, first, natural faults (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are based on sentient beings; likewise, even designated faults (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) such as killing living beings are based on sentient beings. However, for a monk, grasping the hand of a woman and so forth, or sleeping in the same house [with a woman], are natural faults based on non-sentient things. Cutting leaves from trees and so forth, as well as the instructions regarding food and so forth mentioned in the Vinaya for a monk, proceed by being based on sentient beings—that is, they proceed by being based on the designation (*prajñapti*) of sentient beings.

This is the intended meaning: only present phenomena (*dharma*) serve as the basis for the designation of a sentient being (*sattva-prajñapti*), not those that are past or future, because the latter are equivalent to non-entities (*nirupākhya*). For this very reason, [the Prātimokṣa restraint] is not derived from past or future [phenomena], since they are reckoned as non-existent (*asattva-saṅkhyāta*). [Objection: But does not the Prātimokṣa restraint also proceed with respect to the basis for the designation of a non-sentient being? For it is stated that "it is obtained from those designated as sentient and non-sentient," and that [restraint] is likewise not prohibited [in such cases]. Indeed, just as [restraint] is [obtained] from those designated as sentient who are present...

It is said that [it] is obtained; likewise, it is said that it is obtained from those very present things designated as non-sentient. Likewise, it should be stated that it is also obtained from those present things designated as non-sentient. For by this statement, it is precisely the basis in the present that is extended [by analogy]. It is not from those following upon formal application (*prayoga*), because in the state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*) there is exclusively the fundamental [path]; and because in the state of absorption there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), how much less could there be [restraint] from those [factors] consisting of mere designation (*prajñapti*)?
And [it is obtained] from all times, because there is no [doctrinal] admission [to the contrary].

Because one also obtains the past and future restraints (*saṃvara*) precisely through the mind and its mental concomitants that coexist with them—since these restraints are obtained in the manner described in detail—a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established. In detail: there are those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) from which the meditative (*dhyāna*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) restraints are obtained, but not the *prātimokṣa* restraint; there are those from which the *prātimokṣa* restraint is obtained, but not the meditative and uncontaminated restraints; there are those from which both are obtained; and there are those [from which neither is obtained].

The detailed meaning is that from those [factors] neither [type of restraint] is obtained; this is the first alternative (*koṭi*). The restraint that arises from present preparatory (*prayoga*) and consecutive (*pṛṣṭha*) actions such as taking life, and from prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) such as cutting down trees, is the *prātimokṣa* restraint. Because of the statement "from all [objects] and both [types of action]," the meditative (*dhyāna*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) restraints do not arise from the preparatory and consecutive stages. The second [alternative] consists of the bodily and vocal fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*), such as killing and so forth, belonging to the past and future.

The two restraints—the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) restraints—are [restrained] from the seven [bases]. Because of the statement "from the fundamental [actions] at all times," the Prātimokṣa restraint is not [restrained] from the past or future; rather, it is from the third [category], namely the present, because it consists of present paths of action (*karmapatha*). Furthermore, because they consist of the fundamental paths of action, the meditative and outflow-free restraints are [restrained] from the fourth [category]: the past and future, as well as the preliminary (*sāmantaka*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages.

Because they are past or future, there is no Prātimokṣa restraint; because they lack the preliminary and subsequent stages, there is no dhyāna or untainted (anāsrava) restraint. Seeing that it is not logical for restraint to exist toward courses of action (*karmapatha*) currently present within one's own continuum, the Teacher instructs: "However, at the time of acquiring restraint, present courses of action do not exist; therefore, it should be said that [restraint is] from those courses of action as they were when they served as the basis for the present. This is because one abstains from that very object.

Because the present state is impossible for those [actions] that are past and present, restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*) of these is not logical, since they have already arisen; for it is not possible to effect the non-arising of what has already arisen. However, it is possible for future [actions]; therefore, the intention of the Teacher is that restraint is logical only for those [future actions]. As for the Vaibhāṣikas, their intention in speaking thus appears to be as follows: the preliminary (*prayoga*), main (*maula*), and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages of the Prātimokṣa restraint proceed respectively for the sake of restraining the preliminary, main, and subsequent stages of killing and so forth, with the thought: "May these [unwholesome actions] not arise."

These [factors] arise as antidotes to the Arhat himself, as if obstructing them; the preliminary application (*prayoga*) speaks as it were to the preliminary application: "I am obstructing you; do you rise! In this way, up to the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*), it speaks to the subsequent action: "Do you act thus! Likewise, when one obstructs the present natures of the preliminary application, the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent action of the paths of karma (*karmapatha*) regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), the Prātimokṣa restraint is said to be obtained from those present factors. Therefore, it should not be stated in that manner.

"Someone [receives it] from all," and so forth. The *bhikṣu-saṃvara* (monastic restraint) is obtained from all paths of action; the meaning is that all paths of action are to be avoided. "Someone [receives it] from four": other than that, i.e., other than the *bhikṣu-saṃvara*, the *saṃvara* of a *śrāmaṇera* and so forth is obtained from only four factors—namely, the three bodily [factors] such as taking life and the verbal [factor] of false speech. Since non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are the causes, the causes of *saṃvara* are twofold.

Are non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, or weak, medium, and intense states of mind, intended as the causes? If the former alternative is accepted—that restraint is acquired through all the causes whose nature consists of non-greed and so forth—then restraint is obtained when the wholesome motivating mind possesses them simultaneously, because they exist together. If, however, weak and other such states of mind are intended as the causes, then it is obtained through a single cause, because they do not exist simultaneously. Thus, according to the latter alternative—the position that the causes are weak and so forth—one who abides in restraint exists [only] through one of these.

The vow is extensive because it is restricted to all sentient beings; for when a virtuous intention (*kalyāṇāśaya*) directed toward all sentient beings exists, the vow arises. It is not [complete] in terms of all factors (*sarvāṅga*), because the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and so forth do not involve abstention from all factors. Nor is it [complete] in terms of all causes (*sarvakāraṇa*), because weak and other [levels of] mental states cannot exist simultaneously as causes. However, the monastic vow (*bhikṣusaṃvara*) is indeed complete in all factors, because it involves abstention from all factors. Regarding the statement that one undertakes the three vows with a threefold mind: for example, one undertakes the lay follower’s vow with a weak mind.

One undertakes the *śrāmaṇera* vow with a medium degree of resolve and the *bhikṣu* vow with a superior degree; this is so in terms of all the causes (*kāraṇa*), but not in terms of all the limbs (*aṅga*). This is because each of the vows, such as that of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), has one of the degrees—weak and so forth—as its respective cause for one who takes them in that way. Regarding the act of undertaking [the vow] through the fivefold restriction, how is there the acquisition of the vow from those "unavoidable" beings? By "unavoidable" is meant those beings whom it is simply impossible to kill; how, then, is there the attainment of the vow from such unavoidable sentient beings? Here, the Master provides the resolution.

"Because of the undertaking [of the vow] with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of not harming the life of any sentient being. Because the restraint (*saṃvara*) is undertaken with the resolute intention of not harming the life of all sentient beings, the Vaibhāṣikas also state another answer to this very question: "If, however, it were only toward those who are capable," and so forth. It would be subject to increase and decrease: when these sentient beings become capable [of being harmed], the restraint would decrease; when they become incapable, it would increase—referring to those who are capable or incapable, such as humans and gods, respectively.

Seeing that this Vaibhāṣika rebuttal—that gods and others migrate into the state of humans and so forth, while humans and others migrate into the state of gods and so forth through mutual transmigration—is subject to qualification, the Master says: "It will not be thus," and so on at length. And in this way, the restraint (*saṃvara*) will not be characterized by increase or decrease. How so? For just as when previously non-existent grass and such arise, or when grass and such wither—even though restraint is obtained from those very grasses and so forth—nevertheless there is no increase or decrease of the restraint; so it is here.

The meaning is that even when there is a transition between what is possible and what is impossible, there would be no increase or decrease—that is, no accumulation or diminution. Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas say that restraint (saṃvara) is obtained from the very elements (dhātus), and thus this fault would not arise. "Not from sentient beings," and so forth; it is not so. For as it was stated at length: "just as in the case of the arising of previously non-existent grass and so on. What is the reason? Because sentient beings existed both before and after their migration, whereas grass, firebrands, and the like did not exist before or after. Therefore, it is not [the case that restraint arises from sentient beings].

By the example of grass and so forth, the fault of increase and decrease is indeed averted. Thus, it has been stated that there is merely a difference in nature (*vaidharmya*), and not a proof for the thesis (*sādhya*) by means of the reason (*sādhana*). However, the Teacher further says: "When they have entered final nirvāṇa, they simply do not exist," and so forth. Therefore, the previous reason alone is correct, because [the vow] is undertaken with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) of not harming the life of any living being.

Therefore, it is established that restraint is obtained from those who are capable and those who are incapable. If this is so, and if the *prātimokṣa* restraint is obtained from all sentient beings, then there would be a deficiency in one's morality because of the non-obtainment [of restraint] from the Buddhas who have previously entered parinirvāṇa, since those sentient beings are fewer than those [previously existing]. The Master says: "Because it is obtained from all sentient beings without distinction, whether the Buddhas arose previously or later. For if they too had not entered parinirvāṇa, one would obtain [restraint] from them even now. [This applies] to all paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Regarding bodily and vocal [actions], there is no such thing as being endowed with a deficient non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). For instance, one is not endowed with non-restraint through killing alone while lacking taking what is not given, and so forth; rather, one is endowed with even a mild non-restraint because it was previously acquired. But as for what one is endowed with by means of an intense (*adhimātra*) informative act (*vijñapti*) of killing—this refers to the specific distinction of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). This should be applied similarly to the medium and intense degrees. Thus, he who acquires non-restraint with a medium mind may also deprive a living being of life with an intense mind.

When depriving [a being] of life through a medium [level of] non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), one is endowed with that [non-restraint]; however, by means of an intense informative act (*vijñapti*) of taking life, one is likewise endowed with an intense non-restraint, up to the point where one is endowed with an intense non-restraint and an intense informative act of taking life. This same principle should also be applied as follows: he who acquires non-restraint with an intense mind, even when depriving a living being of life with a weak mind, is endowed with an intense non-restraint and a weak [informative act].

However, by means of the informative act (*vijñapti*) of taking life and so forth—such as elephant-trainers, elephant-keepers, or those called *vāgurika* (trappers)—who kill a species of living beings called *pampā* [or *pampaka*] using what is known as a snare (*vāgurā*), they are *vāgurika*s; in actual meaning, they are those characterized by non-restraint (*asaṃvarika*). Kings and judicial officials, although not explicitly mentioned here, should also be understood as being characterized by non-restraint because they exercise the administration of punishment. Other cases should be applied in the same manner.

Having explained at length in detail [the categories] such as "those who kill chickens are *kaurkuṭikas*," and so forth, up until the question is asked: "How is it that non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is applicable toward all sentient beings?"—the Vaibhāṣika offers the following response: "For even one's mother and so forth... and so on. The Master (Vasubandhu) says: "It is not the case that they are those very same persons. This means that people would not kill their mothers and others if they recognized them as such; therefore, how can non-restraint be applicable toward those who are not to be killed? Furthermore, for those who have become noble ones (*ārya*), there is no possibility of becoming animals again.

There is no possibility [of non-restraint] toward them, because it is impossible for them to be reborn as sheep and so forth; how, then, could there be non-restraint toward them? Or, if one were to say that non-restraint exists toward present parents and others on the basis of future existences—thinking that they will become sheep and so forth—then those butchers would never, under any circumstances, kill their own sons who have become sheep in a future birth. Thus, there would be no non-restraint toward those sheep. The Vaibhāṣika asks: "How indeed could it be that those who intend to kill... and so forth. The Master (Ācārya) says: "This... [and continues].

"Equal with respect to [the killing of] one's mother and so forth," and so on in detail. For how indeed could there be non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward those mothers and others for butchers and the like, who do not intend to kill those who have become their own children and so forth? It would be incomplete as a constituent of the path of action (*karmapatha*). It would also be partial, because of the non-cessation of even a single constituent through the application of restrictions regarding sentient beings, place, time, and occasion; and since there is partial abstinence, the restraint (*saṃvara*) would likewise be incomplete and partial. Why is this so? Because it is excluded from the previously mentioned eightfold Prātimokṣa restraint. Why? Because it merely counteracts immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) in relation to that specific [limited] morality.
Non-restraint obstructs that very [virtuous] conduct, and restraint obstructs misconduct; therefore, it is said, "by those of that family."

[Non-virtue arises] from those belonging to the families of the undisciplined (*āsaṃvarika*). "From the field, the undertaking, and the earnest application" (*kṣetrādānādarehanāt*)—the compound is analyzed as: the field (*kṣetra*), the undertaking (*ādāna*), and the earnest application (*ādarehana*); from these, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises. This is the detailed explanation. "The meal for a guest" (*tithibhakta*) means a meal [offered] up to half a month; such is the understanding of the meaning. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the making of mandalas and so forth are included. Or, "with earnestness" (*ādareṇa*) means by way of that specific form; the meaning is: by means of intense affliction (*kleśa*) and intense clarity (*prasāda*). This is because of the arising of an informative action (*vijñapti*) that is contrary to the formal undertaking (*samādāna*).

The abandonment of the *prātimokṣa* restraint occurs through the first cause, which is the arising of a contrary manifestation (*vijñapti*) due to the undertaking [of a vow] such as, "I shall abstain from taking life and so forth for as long as life lasts. It occurs through the second cause, which is the abandonment of the basis (*āśraya*), meaning that the restraint is abandoned upon death because the very basis by which the restraint was undertaken has been relinquished. It occurs through the third cause, which is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayavikopana*), meaning that the restraint no longer exists because the basis by which it was acquired has undergone a change.

Its abandonment is through the cutting off of the cause (*nidāna*); that is, through the cutting off of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*), which is the fourth reason for its abandonment. Furthermore, because of the projection (*ākṣepa*) for only that long—namely, the projection of the fast-restraint (*upavāsasaṃvara*) for a day and night—this is the fifth reason for the abandonment of that fast-restraint. It is also through the four previously mentioned reasons, and by means of a "cause of falling" (*patanīya*). By these aforementioned five reasons and by the cause of falling—that is, that by which one falls—is what constitutes a "cause of falling."

The fourfold unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*) consists of [sexual intercourse] according to the stated measure, taking what is not given (*adattādāna*), killing a human being, and false speech regarding superhuman qualities (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*). However, the Kashmiris maintain that one who has committed [an offense] is like a debtor; this is accepted based on scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Regarding this, the following is the scripture: it is stated in the *Vinaya* that "if a monk who is immoral (*duḥśīla*) instructs other monks, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."

For a monk who has committed a *pārājika* offense is intended here as one who is "of bad character" (*duḥśīla*), not one who has not committed a *pārājika* and remains in his natural state as a virtuous person; this is understood from the contrary statement [in the text]. Therefore, it is understood that even for one who is of bad character, the status of being a monk (*bhikṣubhāva*) still exists, because it is stated that "he falls into a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This reasoning is also correct, because it is not logical to abandon the entire vow (*saṃvara*) due to the disturbance of a single part. "Even for one who has fallen into a fundamental offense" means even for one who has fallen into a downfall involving expulsion (*patanīya*); it is certainly not [the case that the vows are lost].

"And another offense" refers to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or similar offense. Regarding the phrase "when it has been disclosed," meaning when it has been confessed, the text continues with the detailed passage beginning, "What then was said by the Blessed One," up to "he is defeated. How is this to be understood? The sentence must be supplied as follows: "This was said with reference to ultimate (*paramārtha*) monkhood. This is because one who has committed such an offense is incapable of seeing the Truth (*satyadarśana*), and thus cannot attain ultimate monkhood. Having understood that even through a fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*) the status of a monk is not destroyed for those with many afflictions (*kleśa*), such as Nanda and others, they might otherwise commit such an offense. [Therefore, the rule was established.]
The meaning of the sentence is as follows: "A monk by designation" refers to one who, though not fully ordained, has the name and claim of being a monk;

"a monk by bad conduct" refers to one who engages in unchaste behavior and the like; "a monk by begging" refers to a mendicant; and "a monk because of having shattered the afflictions" refers to one who has destroyed the defilements (*kleśa*).

Regarding what the Blessed One said concerning the Arhat—"he becomes no longer a monk, no longer a śramaṇa," and so forth—in this sense as explained, this fifth type of monk, who is fully ordained by means of the *jñapticaturtha* [formal act], is indeed distinct from those four previously mentioned monks. Furthermore, as for the statement that this was said with reference to the state of being a monk in the ultimate sense (*paramārthabhikṣutva*), he refutes that by saying: "He was not previously a monk in the ultimate sense; therefore, he does not subsequently become 'no longer a monk' or 'no longer a śramaṇa'."

By making the comparison "like [the palm fruit] from its stalk," he who makes the comparison to the palmyra fruit with its head cut off has already provided the answer in the scripture itself; thus, the question is resolved—this is the meaning. The connection is that there is the consumption of food in a single mouthful, and the movement about in a space occupied by a single foot. Furthermore, he has been excluded from all communal enjoyment with the monks by the Teacher; that is, he has been excluded by the Buddha from all shared activities with the monks, such as eating in the same row. [The phrase] "do not destroy the *kāraṇḍava* duck" [is used].

Just as the *kāraṇḍavaka* is a particular kind of grass that has the appearance of barley and is called "barley-ruiner" (*yavadūṣī*), so too is this one a non-monk who merely has the appearance of a monk.

"Kaśambaka" refers to rotten wood; likewise, this monk has become rotten. "Expel him from the community of those endowed with virtue"—thus the Blessed One commanded the monks. Furthermore, "drive out the *utplāvī*"; the *utplāvī* is a grain that, though appearing among rice, lacks the inner kernel. Likewise, this monk is devoid of the essence of virtue, being a mere semblance of a monk. "Drive him out" means to expel him. [The Buddha is] the Victor on the path, the one in training (*śaikṣa*), and the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The Buddha is the teacher of the path; he who lives by the path is the virtuous one.

A monk who pursues the signs of the path, who lives for the sake of his own livelihood, and who corrupts the path—being of immoral conduct—is the example here. The detailed explanation is: "like burnt wood. Just as that which is burnt is no longer wood, yet it is still called "burnt wood" because of its similarity to the mere remaining shape of the former wood; and just as a lake, even when dried up, is still called a "lake"; and just as a "parrot-beak" (śukanāsā) fashioned by a sculptor on houses and such things is called a "parrot-beak" because it has the form of a parrot-beak; so too, this person is called a "śramaṇa" because of the mere remaining similarity to the outward appearance of a monk.

It has been said: just as a rotten seed, because it does not produce a sprout, is called "not a seed" even though it is [formally] a seed—since only its shape remains—and just as a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) is called a "wheel" because it has the form of a wheel; likewise, a deceased being is called a "being" (*sattva*) even though he is no longer a being, because only the mere appearance of a being remains. In the same way, this case is to be understood: a monk named Śikṣādattaka, having committed unchaste conduct with a woman due to excessive passion, immediately thereafter felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "Alas, a grievous thing has been done by me," and even in that single instance...

If, without having produced a mind of concealment, one approaches the community of monks and confesses, "This evil was committed by me," and then, following the instruction of the noble community, performs the disciplinary penance (*daṇḍakarma*) such as being placed at the end of the entire assembly of monks, he is called a *śikṣādattaka*. If he were indeed no longer a monk due to his immorality (*dauḥśīlya*), he would not be so; for he is not ordained (*upasampadā*) again. Yet he is established as a monk. Therefore, we do not say that one ceases to be a monk through immorality.

The detailed explanation: We do not say that one becomes a *pārājika* immediately upon committing unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*) together with the transgression; rather, [it is so] by means of the intention to conceal it. Why is he not ordained again? One must supply the words "one who has not relinquished the training. Because his mental continuum (*santati*) has been ruined by intense lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*), and because his continuum has been thus ruined, there is an incapacity for the restraint (*saṃvara*). Therefore, the point is that he is not ordained again; however, it is certainly not [the case that he cannot be ordained at all].

It is not, however, because of his status as a monk that he is not ordained; rather, it is because his status as a monk no longer exists. For even one who has committed a defeat (*pārājika*) or has renounced the training (*nikṣipta-śikṣa*) is not ordained, because his mental continuum (*santati*) has been corrupted by intense lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*). The term "attained through meditation" (*dhyānāpta*) is intended to refer to both that which has a material nature (*rūpa-svabhāva*) and that which has an immaterial nature (*arūpa-svabhāva*). For this very reason, he explains [the text] with the words "all indeed. Regarding the phrase "by means of two," it means either by way of rebirth (*upapatti*) or by way of falling away (*parihāṇi*). Thus he says, "by way of rebirth," and so forth. Above...

When being reborn, one abandons what is below; and when being reborn in a lower realm, one abandons what belongs to the higher stages. Thus, through falling away from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), the wholesome state comprised by that attainment is abandoned. Furthermore, through the abandonment of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), certain factors are abandoned—namely, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) which were produced during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) up until the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Even in the absence of a change of plane, these are abandoned through the abandonment of the homogeneous class when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in that very same realm, as will be explained.

Indeed, the Noble One abandons those [attainments] by abandoning the stage (*bhūmi*); however, the Non-Noble One abandons them through death. The "path of the candidate" (*pratipannaka-mārga*)—which consists of the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*)—is the path under discussion here as being either the fruit or a path superior to the fruit. For example, if a Non-Returner (*anāgāmī*) falls away from the fruit of Non-Returner, he abandons that fruit, which is the superior path. But if a Non-Returner attains the second *dhyāna* and then falls away from it, he [abandons] that path superior to the fruit.

The meaning is that [the restraint] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna is abandoned by the power of causes and conditions—that is, by the power of homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and by the power of another's voice—and one either obtains the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) [again] or [loses it].

It is not said that one obtains the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), because by the prior arising of the dhyāna-restraint itself, there is the intention to abandon that [unwholesome action]. Even with the intention, "I shall not perform this action," if one abandons the entire web of the treatises (*śāstra-jāla*) without taking up the restraint, there is no cutting off of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Just as, even if one avoids the cause of a disease, there is no cessation of that advanced malady without medicine, so it is in this case. Thus it is said: when there is the desire to abandon non-restraint, restraint must be taken up, and not otherwise; such is the acquisition of it.

Regarding the acquisition of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), one should state that it consists of both non-informative (*avijñapti*) and informative (*vijñapti*) action; for even in the case of informative action produced by oneself, its possession (*prāpti*) is severed at that very moment [of death]. However, it should be recited: "The intermediate [state] is [lost] through momentum, undertaking, action, purpose, life, or the cutting off of the roots. This means it is neither restraint nor non-restraint. Furthermore, if only the non-informative is mentioned, the reason for not mentioning the informative must be stated; thus it is said: because the informative is not necessary, for instance—

He will say: "The six unwholesome [paths] are non-informative (*avijñapti*); one is of two kinds. And since the mention of informative action (*vijñapti*) is established by the mention of non-informative action, that [informative action] is not mentioned. Others, however, say: "There is no acquisition (*prāpti*) that follows an informative action which has ceased and is comprised within neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint; therefore, this cause for abandonment is stated only with respect to non-informative action."

"Like the motion of a potter's wheel"—this means that just as the motion of a potter's wheel and the motion of an arrow are projected by a specific formative force (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), they are cut off when that [force] is severed; so too is that [unmanifest action]. Regarding "by the undertaking": this refers to the statement of a vow, such as "I shall not eat without having first paid homage to the Buddha or without having made a mandala. For one who eats without having done so, that intermediate unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) is severed. "By a mechanical trap and so forth" refers to [the cessation of the unmanifest action through such means].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [things such as] the poison of the treatises are included. By saying "he begins to cut off the roots of merit," it is shown that [the roots] are severed precisely at the stage of beginning the cutting off of the roots of merit, and not at the stage when they have already been completely severed. Regarding the phrase "unmanifest wholesome" (*kuśalārūpa*), the inclusion of the term "unmanifest" (*arūpa*) is because the cutting off of manifest form (*rūpa*) has already been stated. In this context—[referring to the verse] "by the cutting of the roots, by birth in a higher realm"—it should be stated that "and by detachment from passion (*vairāgyataḥ*), some [are abandoned]. This is just as [it was said regarding] the wholesome faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*); and [it applies to] "all" [of them].

The path of abandonment pertaining to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—whether it be the path of seeing or the path of cultivation, and whether mundane or supramundane according to the case—is this [path] together with its retinue.

This type of secondary affliction (*upakleśa*), together with its co-arising [factors], its acquisition (*prāpti*), and its attendants—this inclusion of "the type of secondary affliction" is for the purpose of encompassing all [afflictions] by treating even the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) as secondary afflictions; for it is stated in the treatise: "Whatever are primary afflictions, those are also secondary afflictions; however, there are secondary afflictions that are not primary afflictions. "Based on both" is the detailed explanation: because the primary affliction based on both women and men is excessive, and because of the incapacity for discernment (*apratisaṅkhyāna*) characterized by the cultivation of its antidote, and because of its intensity.

Because they lack a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*), they do not possess restraint (*saṃvara*). This is because non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exists as the opposite (*pratidvaṃdva*) of restraint; therefore, wherever there is restraint, there alone can there be non-restraint. For those such as the *ṣaṇḍha* (eunuchs) and others, the second reason for the absence of non-restraint is the absence of both formal undertaking (*samādāna*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Due to the absence of formal undertaking, the Prātimokṣa restraint does not exist; and due to the absence of meditative concentration, the restraints of dhyāna and the untainted (*anāsrava*) do not exist. Their absence, moreover, is due to a deficiency in wholesome states.

Because of a lack of discernment and because of the absence of evil actions, there is no non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Regarding the phrase "through association with which and through the destruction of which": by association with which sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*), and by the destruction of which sense of shame and dread of blame, restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint would respectively come to be—that intense sense of shame and dread of blame does not exist among those in the miserable states (*āpāyika*). Thus, if restraint and non-restraint do not exist for those in the miserable states, then as for what was stated at length in the Sūtra, how is that? [The answer is: The Prātimokṣa restraint belongs only to humans.

However, because the gods lack a sense of spiritual urgency (*asaṃvega*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*)—due to their causes, karma, dharmas, and cultivation—are [respectively] both temporary and ultimate. That which has a desirable maturation is "secure" (*kṣema*) because it provides protection from suffering for that duration; that which leads to the attainment of *nirvāṇa* is "secure" because it provides ultimate protection from suffering. For one who has attained final *parinirvāṇa*, there is no suffering at all times. But have the Blessed One not stated that the first three meditative absorptions are "shaken" (*señjita*)? When it is said, "Whatever is here thought out (*vitarkita*) or deliberated upon (*vicārita*)" and so forth, the Noble Ones call this "shaking" (*iñjita*) in this context.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), that which was stated regarding the second [dhyāna] is indicated: "Whatever joy (*prīti*) has not yet vanished here—this, the Noble Ones (*ārya*) call 'movement' (*iñjita*)"; and regarding the third [dhyāna]: "Whatever 'pleasure, pleasure' (*sukhaṃ sukham*) is here as a mental engagement (*cetasa abhoga*)—this, the Noble Ones call 'movement'.

Now, why is all wholesome (*kuśala*) karma belonging to the realms of form (*rūpa*) and formlessness (*arūpya*) called "unshakable" (*āniñjya*)? He says: "Because it leads to unshakable conditions" (*āniñjyapratyayagāminam*).

The meaning is: "with reference to the path that partakes of the immovable (*āniñjya*) and partakes of the unshakable (*akampya*). But what is the reason that elsewhere [the same] is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*) even though it is actually "shaken" (*señjita*) due to having the defects of meditative concentration? He says: because in those stages, karma does not move with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*), such as the production of enjoyments and so forth.

"Enjoyment" is understood by the term "abundance of wealth" and so forth, as well as "beauty, melodious voice," and so on—this is the detailed explanation. That which would ripen among the gods is precisely that which has been extensively cultivated; such is the case for that which consists of morality (*śīlamaya*) and that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). And it occurs to him: "O, may I be reborn in the company of those who are fortunate among the gods or those who are fortunate among humans. Eventually, he is reborn there. Thus, [the realms] are the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the three dhyānas.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna, bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental joy (*caitasika-saumanasya*) constitute pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*). In the second dhyāna, mental joy constitutes pleasant feeling. In the third dhyāna, there is mental pleasure. The word "that" (*tat*) is used here to refer back to suffering (*duḥkha*), for the purpose of making known its absence [in those states]. The inclusion of the word "here" (*iha*) is for the purpose of making known that this [bodily] suffering exists only in the desire realm. Regarding the phrase "with its equipment" (*sasambhāraiḥ*): it is so called because by means of these [factors], [the result] is gathered together (*sambhriyate*) or produced.

The "provision" (*sambhāra*) is characterized by the sense faculties, their objects, and their bases; thus, feeling together with its provision is the fruit. Regarding the phrase "due to the maturation (*vipāka*) of the intermediate dhyāna": since there must be a felt maturation when the intermediate dhyāna arises from the karma of the intermediate dhyāna, and since neither pleasant nor painful feeling exists there, it follows that its maturation is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. [Objection: Is there not also karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant below the fourth dhyāna? [Response: Or else, there would be no feeling that is the maturation of some other karma in the intermediate dhyāna. No.

For it is not tenable to say that the maturation of karma belonging to the level of the fundamental first dhyāna—which is to be experienced as pleasure—occurs in the *dhyānāntara* (intermediate dhyāna), because the fundamental [dhyānas] are inferior to the *dhyānāntara* due to the presence of applied thought (*savitarka*). Nor does it belong to karma of the desire realm to be experienced as suffering, precisely because of the difference in level, and for the same reason, nor to karma belonging to the levels of the fourth dhyāna and so forth, because of being free from passion (*vītarāga*) with respect to those levels. Wishing to avoid these faults, it is held that the faculty of pleasure is the maturation of the karma of the *dhyānāntara* within the dhyāna itself.

Some say that the maturation (*vipāka*) of that karma of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is not feeling (*vedanā*); rather, others say it is form (*rūpa*) and so forth. [The opponent asks: Is there no feeling at all for those born in the intermediate dhyāna? [The reply is: There is, but it does not have the nature of maturation; rather, it is outflowing (*naiṣyandika*). Regarding this, the Master says: Both of these statements—that the maturation of the karma of the intermediate dhyāna is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) within the dhyāna itself, and that its maturation is not feeling at all—are contrary to the treatise (*ucchāstra*).

Explaining this, he says: "For it is recited in the Śāstra," and so forth. "By means of action without vitarka" means by means of the action of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). Therefore, because of the restriction that "only mental feeling matures as the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome action without vitarka," it is understood that for that action, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not the maturation within the [first] dhyāna itself, nor is it anything other than feeling. For action without vitarka begins from the intermediate dhyāna upward.

"Neither prior nor posterior" means not before, not after, but simultaneous. "The form of that which is to be experienced as pleasure" refers to the eye and so forth. "Those [factors] associated with the mind and mental states of that which is to be experienced as suffering" refers to those belonging to the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), because mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation (*avipāka*). "Those dissociated from the mind of that which is to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth. "Not elsewhere than in the desire realm" is said because karma to be experienced as suffering does not exist elsewhere; what, then, is that?

"If that is so, [then] there is karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant even below the fourth dhyāna," and so forth. If there exists wholesome karma to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant even below the fourth dhyāna, this contradicts the statement: "Wholesome [karma] to be experienced as pleasure [extends] up to the third dhyāna. For it is not only wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasure that extends up to the third dhyāna; rather, there is also [wholesome karma] to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. This also contradicts the statement: "Wholesome [karma] has desirable maturation," for it is not only wholesome karma that has desirable maturation.
The statement that "there is also wholesome [karma] whose ripening is contrary to the desirable and undesirable" means that this is a teaching based on the majority;

the sense is that it is taught in this way because it is the most frequent case. Wholesome [karma] up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasure, and it is wholesome because its ripening is desirable.

But how can that which has the nature of non-feeling (*avedanā-svabhāva*) be experienced as pleasure? It is asked thus, having considered whether it is not karma. "To be experienced as pleasant" (*sukhavedanīya*) means that which is conducive to the arising of a pleasant feeling; it is like a bathing powder (*snānīyakaṣāya*). Just as that by which one bathes is called a "bathing powder," so too that karma by which one experiences a pleasant ripening (*vipāka*) is "to be experienced as pleasant. Because the suffix *vedanīya* is prescribed even in the sense of the agent (the instrument), it is thus.

"To be experienced as suffering" (*duḥkhavedanīya*) means that which is conducive to the sensation of suffering; "to be experienced as suffering" should be applied in detail as before. Likewise, "to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure" (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya*) refers to the state of being experienced by way of its own nature (*svabhāvavedanīyatā*), meaning its nature is to be experienced through the characteristic of experiencing the sensation of its own nature. This should be applied in the same way up to "to be experienced through manifestation" (*saṃmukhībhāvena vedanīyatā*). "Contact to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukhavedanīyaḥ sparśaḥ*) means that contact in which pleasure—conducive to the sensation of pleasure—is to be experienced; this is "to be experienced as pleasure. [The term] "to be experienced as an object" (*ālambanavedanīyatā*)...

"Objects to be felt" (*itivedanīyā viṣayāḥ*) means "objects to be taken as focal points" (*ālambanīyā*). "Experiencing form, but not experiencing passion for form" (*rūpapratisaṃvedī no tu rūparāgapratisaṃvedī*) means "experiencing form directly, but not experiencing passion for form. Alternatively, it means "he does not experience or take form as a focal point through passion. "To be felt in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) means that its characteristic is maturation (*vipāka*) to be experienced in the present birth; thus it is "karma to be felt in the present life," and so forth. "In which time," and so forth, refers to in which [time].
At that time, one experiences and feels a pleasant feeling; at that time, his two other feelings—the painful and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant—have ceased.

"By virtue of the commencement" means that because the maturation (vipāka) commences in this very life; "the establishment of its name" means the establishment of the name "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*). The phrase "for there exists... and so forth provides the examples: for karma with a proximate fruit, the *suvarcalā* plant serves as the illustration; for karma with a remote fruit, barley, wheat, and so on serve as the illustrations. These are the Sautrāntikas. For those who describe the first and second alternatives (*koṭi*) in this manner, karma is eightfold, including that which is to be experienced in the present life.

With respect to ripening (*vipāka*), there is both determinate (*niyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*) [karma]. Thus, up to "indeterminate-to-be-experienced" (*aniyataveditavya*): [namely] karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) is both determinate and indeterminate with respect to ripening; karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) is also both determinate and indeterminate; and karma to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*)—which is that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and so forth—is also both determinate and indeterminate. Thus, one would project eight kinds of karma, which are fourfold. The meaning is that one would project four kinds of karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth. How so?

It might be said that when one has incited another to commit three [acts]—killing, stealing, and false speech—and has personally engaged in sexual misconduct oneself, and these actions are completed simultaneously, one would be karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), another to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), another to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and yet another of indeterminate timing (*aniyatavedanīya*).

Regarding "of the wholesome and the unwholesome according to possibility": this means that where there is the possibility of the unwholesome, it occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not elsewhere. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule (*utsarga*) that [karma exists] "in all destinies" (*sarvāsu gatiṣu*). Regarding the statement "the wholesome is threefold in hell": the restriction "only threefold" (*tridhaiva*) means that in the hells, only the three types of wholesome karma are projected, and not the fourfold type; this is because, setting aside that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), there is no desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*) in the hells. This is why the term "wholesome" (*śubha*) is employed here.

For the purpose of excluding the unwholesome (*aśubha*), it is because the projection (*ākṣepa*) of all four types of unwholesome [karma] into the hells is possible. The compound "one who is detached from that which he is firm in as a fool" (*yadviraktaḥ sthiro bālaḥ*) means "one who is detached from that from which he is detached. The inclusion of the term "firm" (*sthira*) is for the purpose of excluding one whose nature is subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*); for such a person, karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in that stage is possible. The inclusion of the term "fool" (*bāla*) is for the purpose of excluding the Noble One (*ārya*); for a Noble One, neither karma to be experienced upon rebirth nor karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) exists there.

Because he is destined not to return [to the lower realms], the Noble One does not perform [karma] to be experienced in another birth, nor does he perform [karma] to be experienced upon rebirth; this is the meaning. Demonstrating the reasoning for this, he says: "For he is not capable of returning again to a lower level. For that Noble One who possesses the quality of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*) is one from whom passion has departed; therefore, he is not capable of returning to a lower level—that is, to a level below his current state. However, one who possesses the quality of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is capable [of such a return]. For example, a Noble One who has attained the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

One of a nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is one who, having fallen away, would be reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); for such a person, both karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) are possible, as stated in the Udāyi-sūtra:

"one may perform indeterminate [karma]. Furthermore, a noble one (*ārya*) of a nature not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*) may also perform karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) in the very place where he has been reborn—provided he is free from passion (*vītarāga*) with respect to either the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

"One who is free from passion for the desire realm" refers to the non-returner (*anāgāmī*); "one who is free from passion for the peak of existence" refers to the arhat. We shall explain these two later regarding the desire realm and the peak of existence. [The statement] "one who has fallen from the fruit does not die" and so forth concerns the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Regarding what is to be experienced there, is it determinate (*niyata*) or indeterminate (*aniyata*)? That which is determinate has been stated to be of eleven kinds; as for that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), it is as follows.

Karma to be experienced in the *kalala* stage, up to karma to be experienced in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is fixed—these, along with the ten stages that follow them, constitute four types of karma: karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*). This was not mentioned here because the intermediate state is projected by the very same [karma] that projects rebirth. Since it has been stated that karma is both fixed and indeterminate, he asks: "What kind of karma, then, is fixed?"

The detailed explanation: "One who has attained the excellence of the fruit and the meditative attainments" refers to one who has attained the fruit of the path of seeing and one who has attained the fruit of arhatship; these are considered to have attained the excellence of the fruit.
