The inclusion of the term "excellence" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of including those fruits obtained through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). "One who has attained the excellence of the meditative attainments" refers to one who has acquired the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the attainment of non-contention (*araṇā*), and the attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*); here too, the inclusion of the term "excellence" is for the purpose of distinguishing these from other mundane (*laukika*) attainments. "In whatever way"—whether by a mind of merit or by hatred and so forth—even a Persian (*pārasika*)...

If one kills a mother or a father with the mere thought that it is meritorious, that unwholesome action becomes a fixed *ānantarya* (immediate) karma; nothing else does. This is because [the opposite case]—such as an act performed with weak afflictions or faith, or the utterance of a false accusation against the Saṅgha—is excluded by the phrase "and so forth."

It is said that a certain monk, having been defeated in a legal dispute, addressed the Saṅgha, saying, "You are women! In that very life, his male characteristics vanished and female characteristics appeared. This occurs due to the excellence of the field (*kṣetra-viśeṣāt*); it becomes experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*) because of the excellence of the intention (*āśaya-viśeṣāt*). For example, when Śānta saw cattle about to be castrated, he thought, "Such suffering as this [castration] is for me," and with such an intense intention, he brought about the castration of those cattle.

In the very same lifetime as one who has been restrained by the Prātimokṣa, the male organ manifests; because of this particularity of intention, this becomes karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*). Furthermore, due to the absolute detachment from that level, even that karma which was to be experienced in a future life becomes karma to be experienced in the present life—just as in the case of Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arhats, [karma] performed in a state not yet free from passion [becomes so]. This is because they do not return to a lower level and because they attain final Nirvana without further grasping; however, it does not occur in every state.

Thus, that which is "undetermined" (*aniyata*)—meaning not determined by states such as the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and so forth—is nevertheless determined by its maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, that very [karma] becomes "to-be-experienced-in-the-present-life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). For this reason, he says: "But what if it is determined in another state, such as the present life? The meaning is that for one who possesses [such karma], there is no possibility of attaining ultimate detachment (*atyantavairāgya*) from that level, because the maturation of that karma—being determined for another state—must occur in that very other state. Since it was stated, "due to the excellence of the field" (*kṣetraviśeṣāt*), he asks: "What kind of field, then, is it?"

"Of one who has emerged from *araṇā*," and so forth. Regarding the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), there is a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) and a purpose (*abhiprāya*) that benefits sentient beings through *araṇā*. One's mental continuum (*santati*) proceeds as accompanied by—that is, permeated by—that exceedingly exalted, sharp, and immeasurable merit; and it is also accompanied by *araṇā*, which will be explained later. In the context of "the knowledge of the vow (*praṇidhijñāna*) [of one who has emerged] from *maitrī*," and so forth: the resolute intention is the thought, "May happiness arise for immeasurable sentient beings. One's mental continuum proceeds as accompanied by—that is, permeated by—that exceedingly exalted [merit]; all [is thus explained].

"As before, [the continuum] is stainless due to the transformation of the fresh basis. "Fresh" means new, because it has recently emerged from meditative equipoise; thus, through the transformation of the "fresh basis," which is the body, the continuum becomes stainless. This shows that for these individuals, the fruit of benefits or harms—of assistance or injury—performed toward them, whether wholesome or unwholesome, is obtained in this very life, in this very existence; hence, it is called "immediate" (*sadyas*) because it is as if it were immediate. As for the passage beginning "But of the remainder," the detailed explanation is as follows: the "remainder" refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

The state of having an incomplete nature or an incomplete fruit—that which brings about the fruits of once-returning and non-returning—is "incomplete-nature-and-fruit. What, then, is its completeness of nature and completeness of fruit? Completeness of nature is the state of being beyond training (*aśaikṣatva*); for that path has the nature of one beyond training by which arhatship is attained. Completeness of fruit is the attainment of arhatship; for that is the path of fruition, possessing fruit through the three fruits.

Alternatively, the path comprised within the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) possesses a perfected nature and fruit; for the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) has a perfected nature because its fruit is complete, being a fruit without remainder. For those who have emerged from that [path], this refers to those who have emerged from the remaining path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Those who have emerged from that are not such a field of merit as those who have emerged from arhatship, let alone those who have emerged from the mundane path (*laukikamārga*). Indeed, this distinction arises from the abandonment—either with remainder or without remainder—of the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by cultivation.

It should be understood that this has been stated because it necessarily possesses both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). For it is a fixed rule that the five sensory consciousness-elements possess vitarka and vicāra; and since vitarka and vicāra have the intermediate dhyāna and so forth as their nature, it is not possible for a maturation of an action without vitarka to be a maturation characterized by vitarka and vicāra belonging to a lower stage. For, in detail, painful feeling is the maturation of that [action]; specifically, painful feeling is held to be the maturation of that unwholesome [action], because its fruit is undesirable, and [because] the mental painful feeling...

It has been explained in the *Indriyanirdeśa* that feeling (*vedanā*) is of two kinds, and that there is no other [feeling] besides mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), and furthermore, that mental dissatisfaction is not a maturation (*vipāka*). "Life is maturation; twelve are of two kinds, excluding the last eight. Not accepting the statement that "mental dissatisfaction is not maturation," he says: "If, then... and so forth. If mental dissatisfaction is not maturation, then when there is a derangement of the mind (*cittakṣepa*) among sentient beings, in which state of mind does it occur, and by what cause? This is his [response].

The intention is as follows: mental derangement (*cittakṣepa*) does not occur within the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*), because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). Furthermore, since that [derangement] has unwholesome roots as its cause and is undesirable, it must therefore arise as the result of maturation (*vipāka*) in the form of mental distress (*daurmanasya*).

Regarding the phrase "because they are non-conceptual": this is because the five groups of sensory consciousness lack both the conceptualization of discernment (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) and the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). Moreover, since mental derangement is characterized by false conceptualization, [it cannot occur in the sensory consciousnesses]. As for the expression "they release fire into the forest fires," *deva* refers to a specific region consisting of thickets of grass and the like; or it may refer to someone else entirely.
"Through the experience of undesirable sensations and so forth, [there was suffering] for Vasiṣṭhī and others.

Thus the Blessed One was dwelling at Mithilā, in the Mithilā Mango Grove. Now at that time, six sons of a brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan had died. Because of their death, she became naked, insane, and deranged in mind; wandering here and there, she approached the Mithilā Mango Grove. At that very time, the Blessed One was seated before an assembly of many hundreds of monks, teaching the Dharma. The brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan saw him.

Having seen the Blessed One from afar, the Brahmin woman, feeling ashamed, rose up from her crouching position and regained her mindfulness. The Blessed One saw the Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan from afar, and having seen her, he addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, give the upper robe to the Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan; I shall teach her the Dharma. The venerable Ānanda gave the upper robe to the Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan.

Then a Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan, having put on her upper robe, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As she was sitting to one side, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the Brahmin woman of the Vasiṣṭha clan with a discourse on the Dharma. For fear of excessive length, the entire sutra has not been written here; this is the meaning therein: the Blessed One [spoke] to her.

Having delivered a discourse on generosity and so forth, he taught the Four Noble Truths until she attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). Once she had attained it and departed from the presence of the Blessed One, at another time her seventh son died. She did not grieve over his passing. Seeing her not grieving, her husband said to her: "Previously you were consumed with grief at the death of a son; now you are not consumed with grief. Surely your sons have been eaten by you, since you do not grieve. She [replied] to him:

He replied: "O Brahmin, on this long journey, thousands of sons and grandsons and hundreds of groups of kinsmen have been devoured by me, and likewise by you, in various successive births. Knowing the escape from existence and knowing birth and death, who would grieve, suffer, or lament? I do not grieve, nor do I suffer, because the teaching of the Buddha has been accomplished. [If this were the case], how could it be that mental feeling does not become the maturation (*vipāka*) of that unwholesome karma?

"Of karma" is the completion of the sentence. "The disturbance of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is the ripening (*vipāka*). Ripening means the process of ripening; therefore, that which is born from that is "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*). For this very reason, it is said that "it is born of the ripening of karma," but it is not said that "it is born of karma. "If this is so," and so forth in detail: because a mind ranging up to one whose mindfulness has been lost proceeds by means of what is born of karma, therefore this fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is appropriate. "Both [are] the defiled mind of one with a deranged mind"—this alone is the example there, for... [the rest of the sentence is not provided in the source].

A defiled mind is consistent with being a *vipāka* (maturation), because of the statement that "maturation is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharma. Those who are driven out or oppressed, as well as those who lament and wail, should be cited here as examples of hell-beings whose minds are deranged. It is said that hell-beings have deranged minds, except for the Buddha; because he possesses a great accumulation of merit, the Buddha’s mind is not deranged even by an imbalance of the elements. Is the mind of the Noble Ones (*āryas*) ever deranged? Only by an imbalance of the elements, and for no other reason. Why is this? He says: because of what is fixed (*niyata*).

Because of the non-ripening of that karma which was previously undetermined during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and because of its ripening [only] during the stage of an *ārya*, it is for this very reason called "undetermined. Regarding the phrase "due to the complete transcendence of the five fears," the five fears are: fear for one's livelihood, fear of ill repute, fear of timidity before an assembly, fear of death, and fear of an evil rebirth. Among these, "fear of ill repute" is the fear of infamy; "fear of timidity before an assembly" is shrinking back in a gathering, as is the case for one who lacks inspiring qualities.

Because of his direct realization of the nature of phenomena—that all that is with outflows is suffering, all conditioned things are impermanent, and all phenomena are without self—and because of his realization of the underlying continuity of crookedness, [he knows] the nature of karma that does not lead to clarity.

Because crookedness is the probandum due to its having crooked causes, and because it follows from coloring—just as dye is the cause of coloring—it is said "likewise" (*tathāpi*) on account of that similarity. By the term "belonging to the desire realm" (*kāmāpta*), the wholesome (*śubha*) is qualified; the unwholesome (*aśubha*) is not, because it necessarily belongs to the desire realm. Why is that which belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*) not mentioned? For even that is not intermingled with, nor mixed with, the unwholesome; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "where, indeed," etc., the word "indeed" (*kila*) refers to the opinion of others (*paramate*); "where, indeed, [the being] belonging to the intermediate state... [and so forth].

In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), existence is indeed a maturation (*vipāka*). Is it the same for the existence at rebirth (*aupapattibhavika*)? Furthermore, there is the maturation of the threefold action of body, speech, and mind; and because bodily and vocal actions included within the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) exist even in the second and higher meditations, it is stated in that very [text] that "white action has a white maturation. That too, however, is stated in another Sūtra: "There is also action pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*) that is white with a white maturation, such as in the first meditation, and so on up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)."

By this, he reveals his own intention, for which reason he employed the word "kila" (it is said): "This is established by way of the continuum (*santāna*"; that is to say, because within a single continuum both the wholesome and the unwholesome operate, the wholesome is intermingled with the unwholesome due to their mutual contradiction).

The two-fold nature—that the wholesome is overcome by the unwholesome and the unwholesome by the wholesome—is not tenable; for it is not necessarily the case that the unwholesome is intermingled with the wholesome, and so forth. It is not necessarily intermingled because, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the unwholesome is powerful due to the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as its antidote, and for that very reason, the wholesome is weak. Thus, in the realm of desire, the roots of the wholesome are severed by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), but not by right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

The eradication of wrong view occurs; for this term "non-white" (*aśukla*) is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), meaning that because of the absence of white ripening (*vipāka*), it is "non-white," but not that it is "not white at all. Furthermore, it is "non-white" in the sense that what was called "white" does not exist [in that state]. This is stated in the *Mahāśūnyatārthasūtra*: "Unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*); and since ripening falls within the realms, therefore untainted (*anāsrava*) karma is without ripening. Why is this so? He says: "Because it is opposed to the process of cyclic existence (*pravṛtti*)."

For untainted (*anāsrava*) karma obstructs the activity of those phenomena that fall within the realms (*dhātu*), but it does not produce them; thus, it is "karma for the destruction of karma. The repetition of the word "karma" is for the purpose of illuminating this fourth type of karma—that which was designated as "that karma exists"—meaning that such karma, being real, existing, and possessing an unaltered intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), leads to the destruction of karma. Alternatively, this is an instance of distributive repetition (*avīpsā*); the meaning is that it leads to the destruction of each and every karma. Among the four [types of karma]...

Thus is the detailed explanation. The mention of "receptivity to the Dharma" (*dharma-kṣānti*) and the mention of the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) regarding detachment from the desire realm (*kāma-vairāgya*) are because these constitute the path for abandoning black karma belonging to the desire realm; furthermore, since it is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) that is under discussion here, the worldly uninterrupted paths—which, though they effect its abandonment—are not included. Regarding the phrase "of the white [karma] during detachment from the dhyānas," it is restricted to the wholesome alone, because there is no black [karma] therein. The abandonment of afflicted formations (*kliṣṭa-saṃskāra*) occurs through eight [moments]; however, by the ninth, even the wholesome is abandoned, for it is not [abandoned] by that [ninth moment].

"Abandonment by way of intrinsic nature" refers to abandonment through the severance of acquisition (*prāpti*). Even though a wholesome state has been abandoned, because it can still manifest, [the term] "abandonment by way of its object" means that through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) which have that [wholesome state] as their object, there occurs the abandonment of that wholesome state. And this abandonment of the afflictions having that as their object occurs when the ninth category of afflictions having that as their object is abandoned; thus, it is precisely the volition of the ninth path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) that leads to the destruction of black-and-white karma. For at that time, of the ninth...

When the possession (*prāpti*) of a type of affliction is severed, the possession of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises; and for that black-and-white karma, as well as for other non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, the possession of dissociation arises—so they explain. This should also be stated regarding the detachment from the four dhyānas. Therefore, it is "to be experienced by that" (*tad-vedanīya*); by that cause which determines the hell-realm, it is "to be experienced in hell," meaning it is to be experienced in the hells. "Elsewhere than that," and so forth, means elsewhere than from that hell-realm.

Except in the human and other destinies within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the ripening (*vipāka*) of both unwholesome and wholesome karma. Because of that specific restriction regarding destiny (*gatinaiyamyakāraṇa*), these two—both of which are to be experienced in other parts of the desire realm—are described as "black-and-white" (*kṛṣṇaśukla*) by mixing them together without distinction. However, this should not be understood to mean that the wholesome is black-and-white, nor that the unwholesome is likewise so; for the wholesome is unmixed with the unwholesome. Indeed, there is no wholesome [karma] that is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*), because of the rule: "That which is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*) is not to be abandoned by seeing. In that regard:

It is specified that "belonging to the desire realm" (*kāmāvacara*) must be stated [in the verse] as a qualification for "black" (*kṛṣṇa*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of stating that even that which is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) belonging to the form and formless realms has black ripening (*kṛṣṇa-vipāka*). It should not be said [that this is implied]. "But the other is black-and-white, born of desire" (*kṛṣṇa-śuklaṃ tu kāma-jam*). Because the term "born of desire" (*kāma-ja*) qualifies both [black and white], it means: "That which is born of desire and to be abandoned by seeing is black; the other, born of desire, is black-and-white. For that, in detail, is the wholesome and unwholesome [action] belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Having combined both possibilities, it is stated that [the third] is both black and white; however, it is not the case that there are three *mauneyas* (states of sagehood) individually. *Mauneya* refers either to the state of being a sage (*munitā*) or to the action of a sage (*munikarma*), just like the term *kāpeya*. Regarding the "threefold silence" (*maunatraya*): this silence belongs to a sage (*muneḥ idam maunam*). It is the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth. The non-informative (*avijñapti*) bodily action of one beyond training, which has the nature of non-informative matter, is precisely "bodily silence. Likewise for vocal silence. Now, why is only the non-informative (*avijñapti*) taken here, and not the informative (*vijñapti*) as well? Because it is impossible for an informative action to be both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and belong to one beyond training (*aśaikṣatva*).

Thus, "mental silence" (*mano-mauna*) is formed by applying the suffix *vṛddhi* in its own sense; for the mind is indeed the ultimate sage (*paramārtha-muni*) because it has ceased all conceptual proliferation of the afflictions (*kleśa*). He will state the reason for this: it is inferred to be "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) by means of the two types of action—bodily and vocal—which belong to one beyond training.

"How is the Tathāgata to be inferred? By his peaceful bodily action and his peaceful vocal action"—because of this statement in the Sūtra, the Master [Vasubandhu], having indicated the Vaibhāṣika position with the word "kila" (it is said), states his own view in detail with the words "api khalu" (but indeed). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of mental non-informative action" (*cittāvijñaptyabhāvāt*): since there is no non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of the mind, [mental action] does not have the nature of abstention (*virati*). Furthermore, regarding the term "silence" (*mauna*) in the sense of "restraint" (*virama*): the intention is that "silence" (*mauna*) means restraint in the sense of abstaining from all unwholesome things; therefore, [the silence of the mind is... the mind...

Thus, one who has desisted from all unwholesome states is called "one who has desisted. Because of the cessation of the conceptual proliferation (*jalpa*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and because afflictions are called "proliferations" due to their conceptualizing of false objects, an Arhat is one for whom these have ceased; thus, an Arhat is a sage in the ultimate sense (*paramārthamuni*). Regarding "purifications" (*śauceyāni*): the state of being pure is "purity" (*śauceya*), which means "purity" (*śauca*). The inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of encompassing both wholesome conduct with outflows (*sāsrava*) and wholesome conduct without outflows (*anāsrava*). The phrase "for a limited time and absolutely" refers to that which removes the stains of misconduct for a limited time by means of [conduct] with outflows.

"By means of the three types of good conduct, and ultimately by the untainted [path], O monks, that which is abandoned through noble wisdom"—this statement in the Sūtra is for the purpose of distinguishing those who are devoted to false silence and false purity. Those who see purification through mere silence are devoted to false silence; those who see purification through the mere removal of bodily impurities are devoted to false purity. The "distinguishing" of these is the causing of them to fall away from that view. This is because it is stated in the *Saṃcetanīya-sūtra*: "For this purpose, these [actions] were performed intentionally. Thus, it is "intentional" (*saṃcetanīya*).

"Having performed and accumulated karma, one is reborn in the hells. And how, monks, is intentional karma performed and accumulated? Here, monks, a certain person intentionally performs and accumulates threefold karma by way of the body, fourfold by way of speech, and threefold by way of the mind. Having spoken thus in detail, he said: "And how, monks, is threefold intentional karma performed and accumulated by way of the mind? It is when, for example, a certain person here is malicious and possesses a mind of ill-will."

“Monks, as for wrong view, there is indeed one person here who possesses perverted vision,” and so forth in detail. Since no mental action other than covetousness and the rest is mentioned therein, the Dārṣṭāntikas—meaning a specific group of Sautrāntikas—hold that covetousness and the others are themselves mental actions. However, if this were the case, there would be an identity between karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Covetousness (*abhidhyā*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are afflictions (*kleśa*); if these alone were actions (*karman*), there would be an identity between them. This is not so, for there is no affliction whatsoever that could be an action. [This is because] it is stated in the Sūtra: "Action is volition (*cetanā*) and what is willed after having willed. However, in the Sūtra, those things to be willed are indicated by means of covetousness and so forth, because [volition] proceeds through their medium; thus, by means of covetousness and the rest, it demonstrates that volition: "O monks, one indeed becomes covetous," and so on in detail. Otherwise, O monks, I declare that action is volition and what is willed after having willed.

This is refuted [by the argument]: "If karma and afflictions were identical, there would be a contradiction with the Abhidharma, because there would be an absence of the intention to benefit or harm others," and so forth. If there is an absence of the intention to benefit or harm others, how can right view and wrong view be wholesome and unwholesome respectively?

Therefore, he says: "Because they are rooted in that. This means that right view and wrong view are the roots—that is, the causes—of the intention to benefit others and the intention to harm others, respectively. Consequently, their status as wholesome or unwholesome is according to what is appropriate; that is, as the case may be. To explain how this is so, he says: "The wholesome [arise] from good conduct, and the unwholesome from bad conduct."

And other afflicted [actions] as well—because [actions such as] beating and binding are not extremely coarse; that is to say, because other afflicted actions that constitute the preliminary or subsequent stages are also not extremely coarse, and because mental misconduct is not included within volition (cetanā). Regarding "abstention from alcohol and so forth, giving, sacrifice, and so on": by the first word "and so forth" (*ādi*), abstention from beating, binding, and the like is included; by the second [word "and so forth"], bathing, anointing, providing uneven assistance, and so on are included; and by the word "and so forth" [in "pleasant speech and so on"], [pleasant speech and the like are included].

The teaching of the Dharma, the exposition of the path, and so forth, are included; however, the volition (*cetanā*) of mental good conduct is not included—this is the sense. "Six are non-informative" (*avijñapti*): this means that six are necessarily non-informative, but it is not a restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) that only the six are non-informative. This is because there is no primary informative action (*maula-vijñapti*). For the Vaibhāṣika tenet is that while there is no informative action included within the primary paths of action (*karmapatha*), there is indeed an informative action of commanding (*ājñāpana-vijñapti*) which is included within the preliminary application (*prayoga*). "One is of two kinds": the meaning of the restriction is that one [the mind] is exclusively of two kinds.

The undertaking [of the precepts] occurs at the time of death with consciousness (*vijñapti*); however, in the case of death at a later time, there is only non-informative action (*avijñapti*). The seven wholesome [paths of action] are of two kinds; this restriction—that they are indeed of two kinds—is because the morality of formal undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) is dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*). For morality is twofold: the morality of formal undertaking, which is the Prātimokṣa restraint, and the morality of natural law (*dharmatā-śīla*), which consists of the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints. The morality of formal undertaking is dependent on informative action, for it is received from another; however, the morality of natural law is not.

Because it is dependent on mental representation (*vijñapti*), being dependent solely upon the mind, he says for that very reason: "Non-representation (*avijñapti*) arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*)," whereas the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) of the paths of action belonging to the desire realm are necessarily *vijñapti*, but not necessarily *avijñapti*; therefore he says: "It may or may not be non-representation, depending on the presence of an outburst (*paryavasthāna*)."

"By means of the thick essence of shamelessness and so forth"—that is, by means of a thick force. "One should act in accordance with its *anudharma*"—that is, an action similar to that path of action (*karmapatha*). For example, even after the living being has died, [acts such as] dealing further blows, cutting open [the body], or tearing out the flesh; such things are meant. The word *kṣīṇa* (exhausted) signifies the removal of the subsequent [factor]; the meaning of the preceding [term] should be understood as having a different sense. And "when the fruit is fully completed"—this refers to the fact that for one who does not produce the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) following the preliminary application (*prayoga*), [the fruit is not yet complete].

There is the fruit of the preliminary application (*prayoga*), but not yet the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala-paripūri*). It is the same with other [actions] as well. For example, suppose someone here, desiring to steal another's property, rises from his bed, takes up a weapon, goes to another's house, listens to see whether [the owner] is asleep or awake, and touches the other's property—up until the point where he does not yet displace it from its place, that is the preliminary application (*prayoga*). But at the moment when he displaces it from its place, or [at the moment of] the informative act (*vijñapti*) therein, and the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) belonging to that moment—this is the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) consisting of two [factors].

For two reasons, one is touched by the fault of taking what is not given: through the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and through the completion of the result (*phala-paripūri*). Beyond that, the moments of non-informative action (*avijñapti-kṣaṇa*) constitute the "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*). Furthermore, as long as one divides, sells, hides, or boasts about that property belonging to another, even the moments of informative action (*vijñapti-kṣaṇa*) for that person constitute the "consequent. This should be applied accordingly to the other five [courses of action] as well, up to the point of being situated in the state of death (*maraṇabhava*).

"This is not the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). [The opponent objects: "Since the fundamental [path of action] does not exist for one who has already died, because another basis [the new body] has arisen, this should not be stated. [The author replies: It is not improper to say "he deprives [it of life]" (*vyaparopayati*) in the state of being currently undergoing the act; rather, it should be stated thus: "The informative intimation (*vijñapti*) that occurs when a living being is dead, and the non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*) of that same moment—this is the fundamental path of action. And as for the passage beginning with "And also this," the Vaibhāṣikas have explained the meaning of this scriptural statement in the treatise as follows: [in this treatise...]

By the word "preparatory act" (*prayoga*), the "aftermath" (*pṛṣṭha*) is meant; thus, "like a preparatory act" means a "preparatory act," i.e., an action similar to a preparatory act. Why is this interpretation contradictory? Because, at that time, the fundamental path of action is established only for one whose self has not yet been obstructed while the living being still exists. This is the intended meaning here. The Vaibhāṣika says: "Let it be so, in such a way that there is no fault. And how is there no fault? The Master [Vasubandhu] asks this, and the Vaibhāṣika replies again: "In this case, it is the fundamental act itself that is expressed by the word 'preparatory act' (*prayoga*)."

Where would this question arise: "The living being has been killed, yet the taking of life has not ceased"? In this case, the "subsequent" (pṛṣṭha) is expressed by the term "preparatory effort" (prayoga). Is this position entirely abandoned? No, it is not entirely abandoned; for both possibilities exist. If the living being exists in the moment immediately following the state of death (maraṇabhava), then it is accepted that what is expressed here by the term "preparatory effort" is the fundamental act (maula); however, beyond that, it is the "subsequent."

The Teacher asks: "In that case, how does the informative act (*vijñapti*) at that time become a fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), since once the living being is dead, the informative act is ineffective? For one cannot kill again a being who has already been killed by that striking of the informative act. Thinking thus, he asks this question. Why does he not ask about the non-informative act (*avijñapti*)? Because, the Vaibhāṣika replies, "Since it is invisible (*anidarśana*) and non-obstructive (*apratigha*), it is not designated as a 'striking' (*prahāra*). When the Vaibhāṣika has stated this, his own underlying intention is not seen.

Thus the Vaibhāṣika says: "How can non-informative action (*avijñapti*) now be a fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*) if it lacks causal efficacy? Because non-informative action becomes a fundamental path of action even when lacking efficacy, therefore—at the time of the completion of the fruit of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*), that is, at the time of the full accomplishment of the fundamental path of action, during the state when the living being has died—that both [actions] called informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) would be the path of action; this is the meaning of how it would be logical. In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to other cases as well. Just as...

Desiring to steal another's property for the sake of accomplishing his purpose, he should take what belongs to another and perform a sacrificial offering with that animal; he should also commit adultery with his wife. For the sake of seizing that property, he should create a rift between him and his friends by means of falsehood, slander, harshness, flattery, and sowing dissension. He should also harbor covetousness toward those who might be capable of protecting him, and malice toward the owner of that property. He should cultivate wrong views. In this same manner, [the other unwholesome actions] such as sexual misconduct should be applied as appropriate. This is the general direction; it is not detailed here.

The completion (*niṣṭhā*) of all paths of action (*karmapatha*) occurs through greed (*lobha*) and the other [roots]. However, not all [paths] are completed by greed; rather, only some, such as sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), are so completed. Nor are all [paths] completed by malice (*vyāpāda*); rather, only some, such as killing (*prāṇātipāta*), are so completed. Likewise, not all are completed by delusion (*moha*); rather, only some, such as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), are so completed. [Regarding the phrase] "the Triambukas, Varatas," etc.: the word "etc. includes tigers and other [beasts]. Furthermore, that which is instigated by wrong view—meaning one kills without regard [for consequences], thinking "there is no other world"—this too is born of delusion. [Also, that which is done] for the sake of other gain, honor, or fame [is likewise born of delusion].

One who steals the property of another for the sake of some other gain—such as a horse-thief—or for the sake of performing a ritual or for the sake of fame, this too is taking what is not given born of greed. And that which is prompted by wrong view is also taking what is not given born of delusion, because delusion predominates therein. "He approaches his mother for the sake of unchastity"—the phrase "he approaches his sister" follows [from the context]; "sister" means a female sibling. "He approaches one of the same lineage"—this means one of the same *gotra*. "The sacrificer and those who say... [and so forth].

The detailed explanation is as follows: "Women are like mortars and other such objects. Just as mortars and the like are common property to be used by all, so too is the female sex; therefore, there is no fault for those who approach them. False speech and the others [the ten non-virtues] arise from greed and hatred, as previously described. False speech, slander, and frivolous chatter arise from greed when intended for the sake of another's gain, honor, or fame, or for the sake of protecting oneself or one's friends; they arise from hatred for the sake of retaliating against an enemy. [False speech] is not [permitted] when joined with jesting.

That which is joined with derision and incited by false views—namely, the unbridled false speech [claiming] "there is no other world"—is born of delusion (*moha*). Furthermore, slander and so forth, as well as malicious speech, backbiting, and idle chatter (*abaddha-pralāpa*), are born of delusion just like false speech; and as for the detailed explanation: that which is the improper prattle of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and others, that too is idle chatter born of delusion. And of that... [the rest follows].

To enter the various dwellings of one with a virtuous mind means to enter the maṇḍala; for indeed, various dwellings exist within that great boundary-maṇḍala. Regarding the third formal act (*karmavācana*): by the formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is ordained. Therein, by the motion (*jñapti*), it is said: "The Saṅgha shall ordain this person named so-and-so"—this expresses the sense of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). By the formal act (*karmavācana*), the sense of the indicative suffix (*laṭ*) is expressed: "The Saṅgha ordains this person. In that regard, the formal act is recited three times; [the third time is] for the third [proclamation].

The preliminary stage (*prayoga*) of the path of action (*karmapatha*) is to be understood as lasting until the formal proclamation (*karmavācanā*) is completed. However, at its conclusion, the informative act (*vijñapti*) or the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) of that very moment constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*). Thereafter, as long as the four requisites (*niśraya*) are announced—namely, robes, alms-food, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick according to the prescribed rule—for that person who has been ordained, one performs the informative act based on those [requisites] and the informative act based on the requisites themselves.

The meaning is that one performs an informative act (*vijñapti*). And as for non-informative action (*avijñapti*), it persists as long as the restraint is not abandoned; this is the meaning. This is the "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*). "By hatred alone" means by hatred itself; this is a restrictive determination. "Because of the manifestation of a mind of abandonment and harshness" means: the completion of killing is through hatred because of the manifestation of a mind of abandonment; however, the completion of malice and harsh speech is through the manifestation of a harsh mind. They are said to be [completed] by four stages; that is, by four.

How are they explained by way of their parts? The first section states: "The completion of killing, malicious intent, and harsh speech is through hatred. The second section states: "The completion of sexual misconduct with another's wife, covetousness, and taking what is not given is through greed. The third section states: "But the completion of wrong view is through delusion. The fourth section states: "For the remaining [paths of action], it is held that [completion occurs] through all three. Regarding the phrase "having enjoyment as their basis": this means having objects as their basis. Regarding the phrase "having name-and-form as their basis": this means having the five aggregates as their basis. For "name" refers to the aggregates such as feeling and so forth, while "form" is...

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and the object (*viṣaya*) are not different in meaning. Since false speech and the like have the collection of names (*nāmakāya*) as their basis, and because it is established that speech operates upon names, it is understood from the prohibition [of such acts] being "principal" (*maula*) that they are also not "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*). This is because a consequence presupposes a principal act; furthermore, one is not touched by the fault of taking life through such [speech], which is the intended meaning of the phrase "not by the principal. Regarding the phrase "because of the arising from another basis," the meaning is "because of the arising from a dissimilar basis. For those [Arhats] are mutual instigators; thus, they do not [act] by means of speech.

[Question: Are they mutual agents? [Answer: No; rather, because of the undertaking to commit the taking of life against an Arhat, they are so called due to their having a single objective (*ekakāryatva*), meaning they have distinguished [the victim] by name. "Not having mistaken another" means that one does not kill another through delusion. Regarding "in the momentary aggregates (*skandha*)," the intention is: since the aggregates perish by their own inherent nature (*svarasa*), how can their cessation be brought about by another? "Life-force (*prāṇa*)" refers to the vital wind (*vāyu*) which functions in dependence upon the body and the mind.

How does the wind proceed supported by the mind? Because its activity is bound to the mind; for it does not proceed in one who has entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), nor in one who is dead. It is also stated in the *Śāstra*: "Regarding these inhalations and exhalations, should it be said that they proceed supported by the body? It should be said that they proceed supported by the mind. Should it be said that they do not proceed supported by either body or mind? It should be said that they proceed supported by both body and mind."

It should be stated that they "proceed depending upon body and mind," and so forth. "He causes that [life] to fall" means he destroys that vital breath (*prāṇa*). Because it obstructs the arising of what has not yet come into existence by means of the natural cessation of what has already arisen, it is said that he "extinguishes" it—just as one extinguishes a lamp or the sound of a bell. Even though [the sound] is momentary, how does he extinguish it? By obstructing the arising of what is yet to come. Or, [he extinguishes] the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which is the vital breath.

Thus, he demonstrates that this [life-force] has a nature dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta-svabhāva*): "To whom does that life belong, by whose absence one is dead? That living being who becomes dead through the absence of life-force does not exist for the Buddhists, because they are proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*). Therefore, he asks: "To whom? This is the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Regarding the refutation of the person (*pudgala*) in the section on the doctrine of the person: "In the absence of a self, to whom does this memory belong? What is the purpose of this genitive? I shall consider this point later; let this general discussion stand for now.

The intention is this: by stating that "the body with sense-faculties lives," it demonstrates that life belongs only to the body possessing sense-faculties and not to a self; and that very same [body], when devoid of sense-faculties, is dead.

"Even from that which is not preceded by conscious intent," and so forth. Even from the taking of life performed unintentionally, demerit accrues to the agent, just as burning occurs from contact with fire even when it is not preceded by conscious intent and is performed unintentionally. This refers to the Nirgranthas, the naked ascetics (*nagnāṭakas*). For those Nirgranthas who hold such a doctrine, there would be this same consequence—even though not preceded by conscious intent—regarding the seeing or touching of another's wife; the meaning is that there would be the consequence of sin. Furthermore, based on the example of fire, there would also be [the consequence of sin] regarding the plucking of hair from a Nirgrantha’s head, that is, the tearing out of the hair on a Nirgrantha’s head.

Even in the absence of the intention to produce suffering, there would follow the consequence of demerit (*adharma*). For example, just as in the case of setting fire [to a house], there would be the consequence of demerit for the teacher of the *Nirgranthas* when he prescribes painful asceticism, because—regardless of his intention—causing suffering to another results in demerit. Furthermore, in the case of death from cholera, there would be the consequence of demerit for the giver of food if a *Nirgrantha* dies of cholera due to indigestion, because the act of giving food is the cause of death; for even killing a living being, though not preceded by the conscious intent [to kill], is a cause [of demerit].

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of demerit (*adharma*) for unrighteousness itself, as well as for the mother and the one staying in the womb, because they are the mutual causes of suffering for one another; and for that very reason, by the analogy of fire, there would also be the consequence of demerit for the killer due to his connection with that action—namely, the action of taking life—for when a victim exists, the action of taking life belongs to the slayer. Just as fire burns its own support, fire indeed does not burn only other people, but rather it also burns its own support, the fuel; likewise, [the killer is affected]. For it is not the case that...

A distinction in intention (*cetanā*) must be taken into account for those who cause another to perform acts such as killing; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*) of demerit (*adharma*) falling upon the one who causes the act. For instance, when one causes another to touch fire, the one who touches it does not incur the fault of the fire's nature because he has accepted the properties of fire. Furthermore, there would be the consequence of sin for wood, clods of earth, bamboo, and other insentient things if they were to kill living beings situated inside a house during its collapse. This is because no specific mental state (*buddhiviśeṣa*) is being made the criterion, nor can this point be established by mere analogy without a valid reason. This is stated elsewhere.

If it is argued that [theft] occurs due to a confusion of perception—such as when one intends to take the property of Devadatta but instead takes the property of Yajñadatta—that is not considered theft. Regarding the statement "taken at the time of final nirvāṇa": this is for the sake of favoring the merit of the donor; for if there were no recipient, a gift to a stūpa would be fruitless due to the absence of one who accepts it. "Transfer" refers to the robes and other belongings of a deceased monk after the formal ritual (*jñaptikarman*) has been performed. "In the case of approaching a pregnant woman" means causing obstruction to the fetus. "She who is nursing" [refers to a woman giving suck].

Regarding the state of consuming breast milk: if a woman who is like a foster-mother (*putrikā*) engages in unchaste conduct, her breast milk is depleted; or, for the sake of the child's nourishment, that milk does not become [suitable] breast milk. This is like the case of taking life (*prāṇātipāta*). Just as when one intends to kill Devadatta but kills Yajñadatta instead, no taking of life occurs, so too here: if the application (*prayoga*) was intended toward one object, but another object is consumed, others say there would be no sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*). Finally, "if [the act is committed] against the king... means if...
There is no other protector whatsoever, even ultimately from the king himself; therefore, that sexual misconduct must certainly not be tolerated by him.

Or rather, is it that he is capable of cognizing? For even one who is capable of cognizing an object can be said to be "one who has cognized the object," because the intention is directed toward the state of having already cognized the object, or because the meaning of the sentence is the object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Thus, when it is said, "Devadatta is here" or "is not here," the word is first cognized by the auditory consciousness; immediately thereafter, however, Devadatta—the referent of the sentence—is [cognized] by the mental consciousness through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is a collection of the visual and other sensory faculties.

Because of this [non-perception], non-informative action (*avijñapti*) alone would be the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), since vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*) is held to cease simultaneously with auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*). Furthermore, it is maintained that the fundamental path of action has the nature of both informative and non-informative action; therefore, these [objects] are called "dead" (*mata*). Relying on the etymological method (*nairukta-vidhi*), the Vaibhāṣikas explain: "They are 'dead' (*mata*) because they have been reached by their respective sense-faculties. Master Saṅghabhadra says: "[This applies] in detail up to mental objects (*dharma*) being reached by the mind. But as for those odors which were not smelled by you...

"Odors have been smelled by the nose, tastes have not been tasted by the tongue, tangibles have not been touched by the body," and so on, up to "those phenomena (*dharma*) which have not been cognized by you with the mind. Since the terms "seen," "heard," and "cognized" are applied respectively to the three objects—form, sound, and phenomena—the designation "known" (*mata*) is understood to apply, in due order, to odors, tastes, and tangibles; they are expressed by the word *mata*. If this were not accepted—that is, if the designation "known" were not accepted for odors and the rest—then because odors and the rest would fall outside the states of being "seen" and so forth, they would lack the characteristic of form (*arūpalakṣaṇatvena*).

Because they are external to the state of being seen, and because they lack the characteristics of the sphere of sound (*śabdadharmāyatana*) and thus are external to the states of being heard or cognized, there would be no conventional usage regarding odors and so forth such as "seen" or even "cognized. This is the logical argument [for why] the name "known" (*mata*) applies to them. The Master says: "First, the Sūtra... and so on. "Because it has another meaning" means that the meaning of the Sūtra is indeed different. He explains the meaning of the Sūtra here: "And in this regard, for you, in the sixfold object—form and so forth—in four [of them]..."

In the conventional usages of "seen," "heard," "thought," and "cognized"—that is, in the usages regarding what is seen, heard, thought, and cognized—there will be merely the usage of "seen" and so forth. Thus, regarding form, there will be the usage "it is seen," and so on up to "it is cognized. Likewise, O Mālakīmātṛ, regarding the six objects, when they are seen there will be merely the state of being "seen"; when the six objects are heard, merely the state of being "heard"; when they are thought, merely the state of being "thought"; and when the six objects are cognized, merely the state of being "cognized. This is the intended meaning as that phrase of the Sūtra is explained; for indeed...

"The meaning of the Sūtra is that there will be for you the superimposition of the signs of the pleasant and the unpleasant. Now, it may be objected: "But those forms which were not seen by you with the eye were stated as such, but they were not stated as 'not heard' up to 'not cognized'; likewise, sounds were stated as 'not heard,' but they were not stated as 'not seen' up to 'not cognized'; and so on, up to mental phenomena (*dharmas*), which were stated as 'not cognized,' but they were not stated as 'not seen' up to 'not touched. This is not a fault, for this was stated merely by way of illustration."

Just as it was stated by the Blessed One that "forms have not been seen," so too should it be said that they have "not been heard," and so on, up to "not been cognized. The same should be stated regarding sounds and the other [objects]. By this very [principle], the definition is expressed: "that which [is perceived] by the five sense-faculties," and so forth. That form and so on which is directly perceived by the five sense-faculties is "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). That group of six objects which has been received from another is "heard" (*śruta*). That which is approved and intended through logical inference (*yukty-anumāna*) is "thought" (*mata*). "Logical inference" (*yukty-anumāna*) means...

Infallible inference has six objects as its domain; the sixth object is "that which is seen elsewhere," namely *dharma*. Excluding the conventional usage of "seen," it is designated by the three conventional usages beginning with "heard. Therefore, there is no consequence of the absence of conventional usage regarding odors and so forth. Consequently, this reasoning put forward by the Vaibhāṣikas—beginning with "if it were not accepted in this way"—is not logical, because conventional usage regarding odors and so forth occurs even otherwise.

"Perceived with the eye" does not mean by all five sense-faculties. That which is "heard with the ear" and that which is "received from another" (scriptural authority)—both of these are intended. That which is "individually experienced" refers to pleasure and so forth perceived by a mind not in meditative equipoise; however, that which is "attained" by a mind in equipoise is mundane (*laukika*) and not supramundane (*lokottara*). It is mundane because it pertains to worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). Thus, even according to the system of the Yogācāras, each of these six objects is "seen" as appropriate to its possibility.

They are conventionally designated as "heard," "thought," or "known" precisely because of this; therefore, there is no consequence of the non-existence of the established categories regarding odors and so forth. As for the phrase "one who acts otherwise by means of the body," it refers to one who conveys a meaning through the perception of the body; for such a person, false speech would also apply. "One who acts by means of speech" means that one would kill another by means of speech. However, since the taking of life here is bodily in nature, only the bodily *avijñapti* (non-informative action) is included within the fundamental [course of action], not the vocal. Nor, in this case, could there be a bodily *vijñapti* (informative action), as in the expression "one who acts by means of the body."

In this context, since false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) is vocal in nature, it should be understood that only the vocal non-informative action (*vācikī avijñapti*) is included within the fundamental [course of action]. Alternatively, it may be said to be "by both types of fault," meaning by the faults of body and speech. For the sages, through mental malice, there is a connection with the fault of the body; and here the illustration of the *poṣadha* shows a connection with the fault of speech. For during the *bhikṣu-poṣadha*, when the keeper of the discipline (*vinayadhara*) proclaims, "Are you all pure?", if any monk does not disclose an existing offense but should consent by remaining silent, he would be a speaker of falsehood.
How is the path of action established for those two?
How is it that, even though the sage and the monk do not exert themselves through body or speech, the taking of life and the speaking of falsehood are respectively established as paths of action?

"Effort must be made here" means that the Vaibhāṣikas must apply themselves with concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding this, the Master Saṅghabhadra states the following concentration: "The sages (*ṛṣi*) are, in effect, commanders. For when non-human beings perceive that those [sages] have developed a sinful intention (*pāpāśaya*) directed toward abandoning sentient beings, they exert themselves physically out of devotion to them, whereby a course of action (*karmapatha*) arises for those sages. How? It is 'by means of another's informative intimation' (*paravijñapti*). There necessarily occur such transformations of body and speech; moreover, they utter curses."

Furthermore, in that case, there must necessarily be some movement of body or speech. However, others say: "In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not every non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is necessarily dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*). This is because the arising of the *prātimokṣa* restraint for those who have already attained the five [precepts] and so forth occurs simultaneously with the very attainment of the fruit. Thus, some unwholesome [non-informative action] of this kind might exist even without an informative action, as they had previously informed [others]. Therefore, it will certainly exist in other cases as well. As for the sages (*ṛṣi*), it has been stated regarding the *poṣadha* [vow], even in the case of a lie..."

When one who is impure enters into the midst of the Saṅgha, sits down, assumes his proper deportment, or says anything connected therewith, that constitutes his "prior intimation" (*pūrvavijñapti*). All such afflicted speech is frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*). This includes not only the other three [vices] beginning with lying (*mṛṣāvāda*), but even when they are not present, that very state is frivolous chatter. For according to the rule: "The suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to express that quality by virtue of whose presence a word is applied to a substance," this suffix is employed here.

Idle chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*) is said to have the characteristic of defiled speech. For through its connection—that is, through the connection with idle chatter—that person becomes one who engages in idle chatter. Having stated that idle chatter is any other defiled speech apart from the three types of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), he says [the following] to show an illustration: "Like flattery, song, and dance, and like bad treatises"—this means that one performs such "flattery" by uttering words that manifest servility for the sake of gain, fame, and ritual action (*karma*). "Lamentation, socializing, and so forth" refers to [other forms of idle chatter].

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that discourse other than lamentation and socializing—namely, any conversation of those with afflicted minds—is included, because of the existence of talk concerning weddings, marriages, and so forth.

*Āvāha* is the coming of the girl to the boy’s house; *vivāha* is the coming of the boy to the girl’s house. Others say that *āvāha* is the entry (*praveśanaka*) and *vivāha* is the marriage ceremony (*pariṇayana*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the conversation of those with lustful minds. "In an improper and unjust manner" (*viṣameṇānyāyena*)—these are two synonyms in the form of a brief statement and its detailed explanation. "For instance" (*tathā hi*) is the elaboration: because, in the context of the five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*), referring specifically to sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), which has the nature of craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*), it was said: "Having abandoned covetousness (*abhidhyā*) in the world, with a mind free from covetousness..."

Having abandoned ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt regarding the world, he dwells externally; he has crossed over uncertainty, crossed over doubt, and is free from hesitation regarding wholesome states. Because it says "having abandoned these five hindrances" and so forth, it is known that all craving belonging to the desire realm is ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because they include only the gross forms of misconduct, among the ten unwholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*), only that which is gross misconduct is included therein, not everything; the same applies to the wholesome paths. Therefore, not all covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is a path of action. Rather, according to the opinion of others, only that improper longing for the property of others is a path of action. This is so that the covetousness of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru does not become a path of action; for while desire-realm craving (*tṛṣṇā*) exists there, the unwholesome paths of action do not.

This [view] is accepted as a denial of action, its fruit, the noble ones, and the transcendent state in its entirety; for it is recited thus: "There is no gift, there is no sacrifice, there is no oblation, there is no good conduct, there is no evil conduct, there is no ripening of the fruit of actions consisting of good and evil conduct, there is no this world, there is no other world, there is no mother, there is no father, there are no spontaneously born beings, and there are no Arhats in the world. In that context, from "there is no gift" up to "there is no evil conduct," it is a denial of action (*karmāpavādikā*); likewise, "there is no... [is a denial of fruit].

"There is no mother, there is no father"—this is a denial of action (*karmāpavādika*). "There is no ripening of the fruit of well-performed or ill-performed actions; there is no this world, there is no other world; likewise, there are no spontaneously born beings"—these are denials of the fruit (*phalāpavādikā*). "There are no Arhats in the world"—this is a denial of the noble ones (*āryāpavādikā*). However, only the beginning has been shown in the verse. Regarding the view that "there is no [result of] the auspicious or inauspicious," this is merely an illustration; for the "paths of action" refers to the paths of the action known as volition (*cetanā*). How so? [As follows:]...

For volition associated with those [three]—namely, that associated with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and so forth—flows along by means of the flow, that is, the movement, of those very factors such as covetousness; the meaning is that it proceeds by their power. Because one performs formative acts (*abhisaṃskaroti*) in that manner under their influence, volition forms—that is, intends—in accordance with them. This is because they are, respectively, the causes for attachment, aversion, and the false leading astray, and so on. Therefore, it flows along by means of their flow, since its nature consists of bodily and vocal action, and because action is designated as volition.

"Paths" refers to the paths of action (*karmapatha*). [This is said] because the volition that originates them—the volition that originates the actions of body and speech—proceeds by taking those [actions], such as killing and so forth, as its basis. Furthermore, although they are not identical in form, the grammatical rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) is established here; for it is accepted that single remainder applies to words that are identical either in their phonetic form or in their meaning, as in "tree and tree" becoming "two trees" (*vṛkṣau*), or "crooked and curved" becoming "two crooked things" (*vakrau*). However, in this case, since we have "action" (*karman*) and "paths of action" (*karmapathāḥ*), the rule of single remainder does not apply to the word "action" and the word "path of action."

There is no formal identity (*sārūpya*) either in terms of sound or in terms of meaning, because the object of the action (*karma-artha*) and the object of the path of action (*karmapatha-artha*) are distinct; therefore, the rule of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) does not apply. The meaning is that the single remainder is established and intended for those that are dissimilar in their entirety but similar in one part. For example, regarding the rule *guṇo yaṇ-ṅ-lukoḥ*: one cannot say *yaṇ* and *yaṇ-luk* are *yaṇ-lukau*, nor can one say *yaṇ* and *luk* are *yaṇ-lukau*, because this *luk* is an elision (*niṣṭhā*). However, due to partial similarity (*ekadeśa-sārūpya*), [the form] *yaṇ* [is understood].

Because of the similarity between the term *yaṅ* and the elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ*, the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) of both *yaṅ* and its elision is established by the rule "of those that are similar. Subsequently, there is again a single-remainder formation of similar forms: "the paths of action" (*karmapathāḥ*) refers to both covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and the [other] paths of action such as killing (*prāṇātipāta*). Alternatively, the construction is as follows: "paths of action" (*karmapathāḥ*) means the paths (*pathāḥ*) of action (*karman*); "actions and paths of action" (*karmakarmapathāḥ*) means those which are both actions and paths of action; thus, covetousness and the others are the paths of action, while killing and the others are both actions and paths of action—hence they are called "paths of action" (*karmapathāḥ*). It is in this way.

"Non-covetousness and so forth," and so on in detail; the wholesome paths of action (*karmapatha*) are to be applied in exactly the same way. For non-covetousness and the others are indeed paths of action, as are the abstentions from taking life and so forth. And because they are both actions and paths of action—this is the meaning of "for that purpose," and so on in detail—since the preliminary applications (*prayoga*) proceed for the sake of the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*), and since the subsequent stages (*pṛṣṭha*) proceed for the sake of the fundamental paths of action, therefore they are not themselves paths of action, even though [they may be wholesome].

It has been stated that even one course of action (*karmapatha*) can be the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for another course of action; however, that [specific instance] is called a "course of action" because of its grossness (*audārikatva*), and not because it constitutes the preliminary or the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*). This is as was previously stated: "Because of the inclusion of the gross. According to the statement, "The ten courses of action are taught because of the inclusion of the gross," those which are preliminary applications or subsequent stages are not included. And as for those... [the full passage continues]: through the increase or decrease of those fundamental (*maula*) [actions], there occurs in the world the increase or decrease of internal and external entities; but it is not [the case that]...

Therefore, only those [three] are the paths of action (*karmapatha*) for the preliminary (*prayoga*) and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages. He will explain that the increase or decrease of those [paths of action] results in the increase or decrease of them [the preliminary and subsequent stages]. Are all [stages] givers of dominant (*adhipati*), outflow (*niṣyanda*), and ripening (*vipāka*) fruits? In this regard, the preliminary and subsequent stages are not themselves paths of action. How then are they called "paths of action"? For there is no mental action (*manas-karma*) other than covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and so forth; since covetousness and the rest are the paths of that volition (*cetanā*) which is the action, they would be "paths of action. They alone [the three roots] should be questioned; by means of those very [roots], [they are so designated].

A rebuttal must be stated: "But it is possible," and so forth; by this, he supports that position according to his own view. Or, as for the phrase "because they mutually induce one another"—what is the context?
It is the statement that "covetousness and the others are paths of action" (*karmapatha*). Covetousness induces ill-will and wrong view, and those two [in turn] induce it [covetousness].

Because they are both actions (*karman*) and paths (*patha*) for either of those actions, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). Desiring to state the meaning that "the roots of the wholesome are severed by wrong view," he speaks this introductory summary: "All these... and so forth, [ending with] "...of the wholesome. [The phrase] "by the supreme and complete [wrong view]" refers to the highest degree of fulfillment.

The meaning is "by the strongest of the strong. What, then, is stated in the treatise? If the severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) is by means of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and not by the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), then as for that which is stated in the treatise—"those unwholesome roots by which one severs the roots of merit," and so forth—the meaning is that these [unwholesome roots] have greed (*lobha*) and so on as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and do not have wrong view as their intrinsic nature. The detailed explanation is: "because they are brought about by the unwholesome roots," etc.; that is, wrong view is [brought about] by the strongest unwholesome roots, such as greed and so on.

Because that wrong view has drawn in and removed those roots of merit, the teaching on that karma is given specifically with respect to them—that is, the teaching on that karma which cuts off the roots of merit within those very unwholesome roots. How, then, is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it explains: "If the roots of merit belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are cut off, [it is because] they are not possessed by those belonging to the form and formless realms"? This refers to the distancing of their acquisition (*prāpti*), meaning the distancing of the acquisition of those [roots of merit] belonging to the form and formless realms.

This was said with reference to the distancing of that person's [acquisition of] wholesome roots of the three realms, which have been severed. Furthermore, how is there a distancing of their acquisition? It is by bringing about the fact that the continuum is no longer a fit vessel for them; because this continuum was previously a fit vessel for those acquisitions, but now, due to the severance of the wholesome roots, it has been rendered an unfit vessel for those acquisitions. Thus, their acquisition is distanced, since one has already fallen away from the acquired states resulting from application (*prāyogika*).

The meaning is that even before [the attainment of] those preparatory states (*prāyogika*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he has already fallen away from them in their weakest-weak stage; at that very moment, there is a severance of their acquisition. In this context, the view that denies the cause stands in the place of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the view that denies the fruit stands in the place of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). What is being said is this: both of these—denying the cause and denying the fruit—are operative in the total eradication of wrong views and unwholesome states, and not just one of them alone. Thus says another [teacher].

The position is that [the cutting off of the roots of unwholesomeness] occurs only through [a path] having a contaminated object—that is, having suffering and origin as its object—not through one having an uncontaminated object, nor through one having cessation or the path as its object; and it occurs only by having the same realm as its object—that is, only by having the desire realm as its object—not by having a different realm as its object, nor by having the form or formless realms as its object. This refers to the fact that the roots of unwholesomeness are cut off. Why is this so? He says: because they are weak, since [the defilements] persist merely as associated [with the mind].

That wrong view which has the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object and that which has a dissimilar realm (*visabhāga-dhātu*) as its object, dwells within the associated factors merely by way of association (*samprayoga*), not by way of the object (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is weak; consequently, the roots of merit are not severed by it. Thus the Vaibhāṣikas explain: "In every respect"—that is, by whichever [wrong view] denies the cause, whichever denies the fruit, whichever takes a similar realm as its object, whichever takes a dissimilar realm as its object, whichever takes the tainted (*sāsrava*) as its object, and whichever takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object—it is by all such [wrong views] that [the roots of merit are severed].

"They are severed like those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision" means that just as the nine types of afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the other truths are all abandoned simultaneously upon the vision of the truths such as suffering, so too the nine types of roots of goodness are all severed at once; according to some, this is like the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Just as the nine types of afflictions are abandoned by the ninefold path—whereby the most intense type of affliction is abandoned by the weakest-weak path, and so on—[so too are the roots of goodness severed].

By the strongest-of-the-strong [grade of wrong view], the weakest-of-the-weak [grade of wholesome root] is severed; thus, by all nine grades of wrong view, the nine grades of wholesome roots are completely cut off. By the weakest-of-the-weak wrong view, the strongest-of-the-strong grade of wholesome root is severed, continuing down to the point where by the strongest-of-the-strong wrong view, the weakest-of-the-weak grade of wholesome root is severed. In this way, this textual passage is preserved if they are severed as described—like the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation—even when they are associated with subtle [tendencies].

The statement that one "severs the very soft and very subtle roots of wholesome merit" refers to the severance of the roots of wholesome merit by means of the most intense (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) unwholesome roots; the intention is that this does not occur through the very soft (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and other [lesser grades] of unwholesome roots. If they are severed gradually, then how is it that the phrase "of this person" (*asya tarhi*) and so forth is spoken? This was said with reference to the completion [of the process].

This was stated in detail with reference to the completion of the severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda-samāpti*), saying that [the actions] are "excessive" (*adhimātra*). Although the severance of the "weak-weak" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) and other grades has not been explicitly mentioned, it should nevertheless be understood. Therefore, this was said specifically with reference to the completion [of the process]. Because of them, there is a severance without remainder; for by those nine types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), there occurs a severance of the roots of merit without remainder. For even if a single type among them were not severed—the ninth type, which is "weak-weak"—it would serve as the cause for the re-arising of all nine types.

Therefore, with reference to its completion, it is said: "by both," meaning by both emergence and non-emergence. "From the abandonment of that, there is the abandonment of it" means that when there is the abandonment—that is, the total severance—of that very weak mind with which the restraint was undertaken, namely the very weak mind associated with very weak roots of merit, there occurs the abandonment of that restraint. This applies likewise up to the case where the restraint was undertaken with a very intense mind; from the abandonment of that [mind], there is the abandonment of it.
This is because the fruit of karma is directly perceived.

For a son of the gods who has recently been reborn, three thoughts arise: "From where have I passed away? Where have I been reborn? By what karma? Because he thus perceives the results of karma directly, the roots of wholesome merit (*kuśalamūla*) are not severed among the gods. [The reason they are severed] specifically in Jambūdvīpa is because of their inclination toward speculative reasoning (*tārkikatva*); this is the intended meaning. He is endowed with at least eight faculties: the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), as well as the faculties of body, life, and mind; this applies specifically to one whose roots of wholesome merit have been severed.

For indeed, faith and the other [faculties] are completely severed; and because of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the faculties of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and so forth do not exist; nor do the eye and the other [senses] exist, either due to their deficiency or in the state of gradual death—just as it is for one from Pūrvavideha or Godānīya.

By means of this extension (*atideśa*), he shows that for these two [the female and male] as well, there is the severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*). Regarding the statement "a woman or a man severs," the word "and" (*ca*) is indicated as being elided; thus, one who is endowed with the female faculty (*strīndriya*) is necessarily endowed with eight faculties: the four feeling faculties (*vedanendriya*), the three faculties of body, life, and mind (*kāya-jīvita-manas*), and the female faculty as the eighth. The faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are excluded in the state where the roots of virtue have been severed.

This very point is contradicted here: the eyes and so forth are also subject to deviation, as previously stated for them as well. Among those aforementioned destroyers, one whose conduct is driven by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*) does not completely cut them off, because his underlying intention (*āśaya*) is firm, hidden, and evil. The compound is analyzed as: "one whose intention—meaning purpose—is firm, hidden, and evil. "Firm" means stable; "hidden" means concealed; "evil" means unwholesome.
