This is because he belongs to the class of those whose conduct is driven by craving; that is to say, because he is of the same nature as one whose conduct is driven by craving. Just as one whose conduct is driven by craving has a wavering intention, so too do those such as the eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others.

Just as those bound for the miserable realms (*āpāyika*) do not sever the roots of goodness because their wisdom—whether afflicted or non-afflicted—is not firm, so too [the case of] eunuchs and others is the same. Regarding the term *pratisaṃdhitāni*, some read it as *pratisaṃhitāni* (meaning "rejoined" or "connected"), while others read it as *pratisaṃdhikṛtāni* (meaning "made by way of reconnection"). It is like the recovery of health and the acquisition of strength: just as health comes first and the acquisition of strength follows in sequence, so it is here. "Not one who commits an immediate transgression" means that only those who commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) are excluded from this [attainment].

"Rebirth occurs"—this means that for one who has committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), rebirth occurs here [in this very life]. "While abiding in the intermediate state" means while abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for the sake of going to hell. "Facing death from hell" means facing death from hell. "By the power of the cause" means by the power of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), because for those individuals false view is pleasing to them of its own accord. "By the power of conditions" means by the power of the voice of another, because for those individuals false view is pleasing to them through external influence. This refers to the power of the cause.

Because of its essential nature, one who [falls] by the power of his own [reasoning]—that is, by the power of his own logic—is one who falls away; one who [falls] by the power of another—that is, by the power of what has been heard from others—is one who is reborn. One who is "ruined in intention" (*āśaya-vipanna*) is ruined and destroyed through the manifestation of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); he takes rebirth in this very life, in the present existence. One who is "ruined in both intention and application" (*āśaya-prayoga-vipanna*)—that is, one who is ruined through the manifestation of wrong view and through the commission of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-kriyā*)—takes rebirth after the breaking up of the body. And herein, one who [falls] by his own power...

"By the power of another" (*parabala*) is a synonym for what was previously stated; likewise, "one who has fallen away from view" (*dṛṣṭivipanna*) and "one who has fallen away from both view and conduct" (*dṛṣṭi-śīlavipanna*) should be understood as synonyms for what was stated immediately prior. [The reference to] "Pūraṇa and others" refers to those very individuals.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), six teachers are included, namely: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambala, Kakuda Kātyāyana, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. These have their roots of merit completely severed because of their nihilism; yet they are not fixed in falsehood (*mithyātvaniyata*) because they have not committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*), for those who commit an immediate transgression are indeed fixed in falsehood. Ajātaśatru is fixed in falsehood because he has committed an immediate transgression, as is Devadatta, who has also had his roots of merit completely severed.

And one fixed in falsehood [is so] because of causing a schism in the Saṅgha and because of shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind. "Excluding these four modes" refers to ourselves and others. "Without another" means that when covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and the others manifest in the absence of another path of action (*karmapatha*), such as killing (*prāṇātipāta*) and so forth—that volition (*cetanā*) coexists with one path of action: either with covetousness, or with malice (*vyāpāda*), or with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), or with an unafflicted mind.

When that practitioner, possessing a wholesome or neutral mind, brings to completion any one of the material [unwholesome actions] such as killing and so forth—excluding sexual misconduct—by means of his preparatory effort, volition (cetanā) operates together with that single [action]. Or it should be stated: when he possesses a defiled mind other than covetousness and the like, for in his case too this same rule applies; for instance, "the killing of a living being by one whose mind is malicious," and so forth. [In such a case, volition] operates together with two: through malice (vyāpāda) and through killing. [It also operates] with two in the cases of sexual misconduct and frivolous speech (sambhinnapralāpa).

Or, when it occurs together with two [factors]: with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), or with frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*) and any one of covetousness and the others—it is precisely regarding these two that this objection is raised: "Is the killing of a living being by one whose mind is corrupted [the result of] covetousness? And is the taking of what is not given [the result] of one who is possessed by covetousness?"

What is this that is said regarding one who acts by oneself, or rather, regarding one who causes another to act? If it refers to one who acts by oneself, then the qualification "of one with a malevolent mind" (*vyāpannacitta*) and "possessed by covetousness" (*abhidhyāviṣṭa*) would be inappropriate; for in the case of killing a living being, malevolence is necessarily present, and in the case of taking what is not given, covetousness is necessarily present. Indeed, a qualification is desired only when there is a possibility of deviation. Alternatively, if it refers to one who causes another to act, then [the offense occurs] when one possesses a mind characterized by any one of covetousness, malevolence, or wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), while another commits killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, or frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).

It is said that [the agent] must be stated as "one who acts himself. Now, was it not argued that the qualification is not appropriate? This is not a fault. For this is not a qualification; rather, it is a description of the essential nature [of the act]. What is being stated here is the existence of the two factors—malice (*vyāpāda*) and covetousness (*abhidhyā*)—which constitute the second part [of the path of action]. Even so, for one whose mind is established in covetousness and the like, when causing those [acts] such as taking life to be committed, it would follow that the volition (*cetanā*) occurs together with two [factors]; therefore, that too must be stated, and it must be stated truly.

This has been stated merely as an illustration; thus there is no fault. Regarding the simultaneous occurrence of the killing and the taking away of a living being by one with a malicious mind (*vyāpannacitta*): where the taking away is accomplished by the very act of killing, the paths of action (*karmapatha*) of malice, killing, and taking what is not given (*adattādāna*) occur simultaneously. "Then that is not so," and so forth: if malice (*vyāpāda*) arises at the time of taking another's property, then the completion (*niṣṭhā*) of the taking of what is not given is not established through greed (*lobha*) alone; [therefore, both] greed and hatred [are required].

"Because they do not exist simultaneously for one whose mind is not otherwise [directed]"—this is the full statement. That rule should be understood to apply specifically to one who possesses the intent to steal; that is, when the completion of the act of taking what is not given is achieved through that very intent. [The completion of] sexual misconduct with another's wife and covetousness occurs through greed (*lobha*). However, for one whose mind is otherwise directed—such as one possessing the intent to kill—this rule does not apply. Likewise, "false speech [is completed] by the intention to cause a schism."

Because it is intended for the purpose of causing division, that very [speech] becomes malicious speech (*paiśunya*) and that same [speech] becomes frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*). According to the established tenet that "all that is afflicted is frivolous chatter," because it is intended for the purpose of causing division, that very harsh speech (*paruṣavacana*) is both malicious speech and frivolous chatter; thus, it occurs together with four [unwholesome paths of action]. How so? He says: for in that case, there is one mental [path of action] and three vocal ones.

In the case of false speech (*anṛtavacana*), there may be covetousness (*abhidhyā*) or ill-will (*vyāpāda*); thus there are three verbal [actions]: lying, slander, and frivolous chatter (*sambhinnapralāpa*). In the case of harsh speech (*paruṣavacana*) as well, there is one mental [action], namely ill-will; there are three verbal [actions]: harsh speech, slander, and frivolous chatter. Thus, by name alone there are three, but not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For that very same false speech is called "slander" and "frivolous chatter," yet it does not possess three distinct intrinsic natures. In the same way, harsh speech also possesses three names.

Others, however, explain that there is also a distinction in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); for the non-informative acts (*avijñapti*) of false speech, slander, and frivolous chatter are distinct, and likewise, the non-informative acts of harsh speech, slander, and frivolous chatter are distinct.

"Of one who has entered into covetousness and so forth," and so on in detail. For one who has entered into covetousness and so forth, [an unwholesome action] may coexist with four [paths of action]. In that case, there is one mental [path], namely any one of covetousness and the rest; and by means of its application—that is, through the application of covetousness and so forth—when another three paths of action such as killing living beings reach their completion at the time of their final consummation, it should be applied in this way with five, six, or seven [paths]. How can volition coexist with five? First, it coexists with five when one who has entered into covetousness and so forth, through the application of that [covetousness], reaches the other four [paths of action]. It is thus.

When one who has fallen into covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and so forth brings another five or six courses of action to completion, it coexists with six or seven [courses of action]. It coexists with eight when, having initiated the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for the six [actions] such as killing and so forth, one who has fallen into covetousness personally commits sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*), and they reach completion simultaneously. However, this is not the case; for there is no simultaneous occurrence of the mental courses of action. It does not coexist with one, eight, or five. That is to say, it does not coexist with only one mental [course of action] when the mind is virtuous (*kuśala*).

Because non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*) and non-malice (*avyāpāda*) necessarily exist [in every wholesome state], volition (*cetanā*) does not operate together with even a single material path of action (*karmapatha*) included within the restraint (*saṃvara*). This is because, even in states of mind that are afflicted or neutral, these four—killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech—are necessarily present in the lay follower’s restraint (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) and others. Furthermore, when the mind is wholesome, these two—non-covetousness and non-malice—necessarily coexist; and among those paths of action included in the restraint, such as killing and the rest, these four [non-covetousness, non-malice, non-killing, and non-stealing] necessarily coexist.

Because they necessarily coexist, [the restraint] is said to occur together with two or more [factors]. Since those factors comprised within the *bhikṣu-saṃvara* that are bodily and vocal can only exist as seven in a defiled or neutral state—due to the impossibility of non-covetousness and non-malice in such states—and can exist as nine or ten in a wholesome mental state, it follows by elimination that they occur together with two or more. In this regard, "together with two" is explained in detail: therein, in the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), there are non-covetousness and non-malice, but not [non-wrong view].

Right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)—according to the established tenet that "the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not [right] view because it does not judge"—therefore, in this case, it functions together with only two [mental factors], namely non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*) and non-malice (*avyāpāda*); and likewise in the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), it co-exists with the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

And in the case of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) as comprised within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they coexist with these same two [mental paths of action]. Because the knowledge of destruction and non-arising is not "vision" (*dṛg*), right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) is absent therein; therefore, the mention of "formless attainments" is for the purpose of excluding the sevenfold bodily and vocal untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) which constitutes the nature of the paths of action when comprised within the dhyāna attainments. The mention of "knowledge of destruction and non-arising" is for the purpose of excluding right view from those two knowledges.

Because it has the nature of wrong view (*asamyagdṛṣṭi*), it operates together with three [mental factors]; the elliptical completion of the sentence is that there is an absence of the material paths of action (*rūpi-karmapatha*) when the mental consciousness is associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). For in that case, only the three [mental] paths of action—non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*), non-malice (*avyāpāda*), and right view—exist. "With four," and so forth; by the qualification "of one whose mind is unwholesome or neutral" (*akuśala-vyākṛta-citta*), it is shown that there are no [material paths of action] for the mind. This applies to the undertaking of the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) and a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).

The upavāsa restraint (upavāsa-saṃvara) should be understood as having the form already described, consisting of exactly four courses of action (karmapatha) characterized by abstention from killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech. This is because abstentions such as from drinking intoxicants are not included within the ten courses of action, and because abstentions such as from slander are not comprised within the vows of a lay follower (upāsaka) or a novice monk (śrāmaṇera). Furthermore, since there is a mention of undertaking the śrāmaṇera vows, the undertaking of the upavāsa vows must be understood in the manner stated. However, in the undertaking of the śrāmaṇera vows, abstention from unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*) constitutes the third course of action; and in that regard—

Sexual misconduct is indeed included within the six [wholesome courses of action]. In the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), it is included by means of those four as previously stated, along with non-covetousness and non-malice—thus by six. This is because right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is absent in the five sensory consciousnesses. In the wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is included by seven: by those same aforementioned ones, plus right view as the seventh, specifically when undertaking the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*).

For when this path of action exists within a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is present. However, when one undertakes the monastic vows (*bhikṣusaṃvara*) with an unwholesome or neutral mind, [the restraint] consists of only the seven material factors and not the mental ones, because the mind is unwholesome or neutral. When undertaking the monastic vows during the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*), it consists of nine factors; yet, even there, right view is absent because right view does not exist within those five consciousnesses. Furthermore, when the mental consciousness is associated with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*), it likewise operates with those same nine factors, for right view is also absent therein. And in that very case...

Only when associated with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, and by means of the mental consciousness included within the dhyānas, is there possession of ten factors: the seven material factors included within the dhyāna-restraint, as well as non-covetousness and non-malice; but in cases other than that, it is otherwise.

In a wholesome mental consciousness that is devoid of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), specifically at the moment of undertaking the *bhikṣu* vow, "all" [karma-paths] exist—this is the full statement. All volition (*cetanā*) that co-exists with the meditative (*dhyāna*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) states, provided it is not associated with the knowledge of destruction or non-arising, co-exists with ten [paths]: namely, the seven bodily and vocal paths included within the meditative and untainted vows, and the three mental ones. Thus, it is shown that volition operates only together with the paths of action included within the vows; however, [it operates] with those excluded from the vows...

But how could there be [co-existence] even with a single [path of action] for one who is free from the eightfold restraint? To this he says: "of another mind" (*anyacittasya*). This means: of a mind other than that which originates the wholesome courses of action free from those restraints; that is, of a defiled or neutral mind. When undertaking the abstention from a single limb—whether it be the abstention from taking life or the abstention from taking what is not given—it co-exists with that single course of action. It also co-exists with five or eight [courses of action].

In the case of a person with a wholesome mental consciousness (*kuśalamanovijñāna*) who undertakes two members simultaneously—namely, the three mental ones and the two material ones—it is by way of five; and in the case of undertaking five members simultaneously—namely, those same five material ones and the three mental ones—it is by way of eight. This has been stated as an illustrative example; for otherwise, it can also be said that for one with a defiled or neutral mind (*kliṣṭāvyākṛtacitta*), when undertaking five members not included within the vows (*saṃvara*), it coexists with five, because of the absence of any object to be attached to (*rañjanīyavastu*).

In the [Northern] Continent (Kuru), because there is an absence of objects that cause passion (*rañjanīya-vastu*), covetousness (*abhidhyā*) does not manifest; and because the fruits of karma are directly perceived, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) does not exist. For these very reasons, because there is no purpose for it, malicious speech (*paiśunya*) does not exist; and because they are eternally separated from one another due to the absence of mutual affection and so forth, and because there is no sense of "mine" or possession, covetousness as a path of action does not manifest in Kuru. Furthermore, because their mental continuum is gentle and because there is an absence of objects that provoke malice, ill will (*vyāpāda*) does not exist; and because they lack an evil disposition, wrong view does not exist. These three...

Furthermore, these [actions] such as covetousness and so forth do not exist. Regarding the explanation that "even by oneself" means "through their manifestation," because his underlying intention is free from evil, none of the six [unwholesome paths of action], beginning with taking life, manifest. Because his lifespan is fixed, there is no taking of life. Because he lacks the possession of material goods and women, respectively, there is neither taking what is not given nor sexual misconduct. And because he lacks a motive, there is no false speech, slander, or harsh speech. If there is no possession, how can there be unchaste conduct for them?

"He asks: 'Released from restraint' means not comprised within either restraint or non-restraint. But he kills one situated in another realm" means that even gods die from the cutting off of the head or the torso; for although it is said that "a god does not kill a god," the intention is that gods are not subject to being killed [in the sense of total destruction], since the limbs and members of gods, though cut off again and again, grow back. Even if this is so, nevertheless..."

The intention is that there is no death for the gods because of the severing of the head, the severing of the body, or the severing of the middle; [there is no reconnection after such cuts]. Regarding the phrase "that which has the earth as its basis," the detailed explanation is as follows: there are five levels, from the level of the desire realm up to the level of the fourth dhyāna. That which has the earth as its basis means that which has a particular level as its support. Untainted (*anāsrava*) morality produced by a noble one (*ārya*)—having been produced and then ceased, having been produced and sent to the present time, or having been ceased and sent to the past time—has a single level as its basis, and so on.

One is endowed with [the restraint] based on the four levels through the past wind [attainment] in the formless realms; however, one is endowed with that based on the five levels through the future [wind attainment]. This is based on the support of the desire realm up to the support of the fourth dhyāna—whether one is born there or not born there—with the exception of the hells and Uttarakuru, because of the absence of undertaken morality (*samādāna-śīla*) there. In other cases, it is both ways.

Elsewhere—in the desire realm among the gods, and among humans with the exception of those in Uttarakuru—there are those who are free from both types of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). There, the threefold restraint (*saṃvara*) comprised of vows should be understood as occurring according to possibility: the Prātimokṣa restraint, the Dhyāna restraint, and the Anāsrava restraint. Regarding the phrase "by practicing, cultivating, and frequently performing [these]," this refers to the states of preparation (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*). If one asks, "How is it that by such [actions] one becomes short-lived? it is shown that because of the meagerness of the life-span, it is a result of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*). External entities—such as medicinal herbs, the earth, and so forth—possess little vitality (*ojas*) and little potency (*vīrya*), and are abundant in lightning and dust.

"Thunderbolt" refers to a rain of stones; "dust" refers to a shower of dust or a rain of alkaline matter; "destruction of crops and so forth by wind" refers to the scattering of dust. "Covered with dust" means that dust has arisen. "High and low" means uneven, consisting of saline soil (*ūṣara*) and wasteland (*jaṅgala*). These refer to external things; these lands are intended here. "Repulsive" means censured. "Irregular seasonal transformations" means those for whom the seasonal transformations are irregular—namely, the crops and medicinal herbs—in which season it ought to rain, in that [season they do not].

When it ought to rain, it does not rain; where cold ought to be, there is no cold; and where heat ought to be, that does not occur—this is to be understood as the *vipākaphala* (fruition of maturation). That which occurs within the continuum of a sentient being is the *niṣyandaphala* (fruition of outflow), whereas that which is an external object is not the *vipākaphala*, because it arises from the application [of the action] (*prayoga*). This is the detailed explanation. Through the application of taking life in hell, one experiences intense suffering; for through the application of taking life, the living being who is killed experiences extremely intense suffering.

In this case, one becomes short-lived through the fundamental [path of action] (*maula*), just as the life of that living being is impaired by the act of killing. Since the fundamental path of action is momentary, and there is no painful sensation therein, it is logical to say here "through the fundamental. If it is asked: "If it is by the fundamental in this case, why was it stated [in the Sūtra] 'by the taking of life' (*prāṇātipātena maulena*)?"—one who perceives the meaning of the Sūtra asks this because of the inclusion of the "retinue" (*saparivāra*). Thus, the taking of life is the fundamental itself; its preliminary application (*prayoga*) is [the preparatory stage].

Regarding the retinue: in that application, having performed the preparatory act (*upacāra*) of taking life, it is stated "by taking life," and so forth. This does not transcend the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Considering that the fruit of maturation occurs within one's own continuum while the sovereign fruit occurs elsewhere, it is nevertheless stated thus because of a specific similarity. That is, due to a specific similarity characterized by the cutting off of desired life, the ruin of wealth, and so on, it is stated thus: "If he comes to such a state, [he attains] the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of human beings."

"By taking life one becomes short-lived; by taking what is not given one becomes deprived of wealth," and so on in detail. For in this case, there is a similarity between the cause and the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). The same should be stated regarding wholesome [actions]. The outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) does not transcend these two types of fruits; however, it is described in that way because of a specific kind of similarity. "If he comes to such a state, entering into the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of human beings, through abstaining from taking life he becomes long-lived," and so on in detail. Vitality (*ojas*) is destroyed; vitality resides in the region of the heart. The same should be applied to the others as well.

Indeed, by one who commits taking what is not given (*adattādāna*), suffering is produced for the owner of the property, the loss of enjoyment is caused, and vitality (*ojas*) is destroyed. Therefore, because of causing suffering, depriving [the owner] of enjoyment, and destroying vitality, there is a threefold result. How is vitality destroyed? By the destruction of its cause and by the impairment of that [vitality] through the loss of enjoyment. For this very reason it was said: "Through taking what is not given, there is an abundance of thunderbolts and dust. Thus, by that, his vitality becomes impaired. Likewise, by one who approaches another's wife, suffering is produced for the other.

By [this] one, having made his wife subject to rivals, his vitality (*ojas*) was destroyed; because of that vitality, he is called "radiant" (*tejasvin*) in the world. For this very reason it is said: "By sexual misconduct, they are scattered with passion (*rajas*). In this same way, it should be applied to the others as well. This is the general direction: everything should be applied by means of the reversal of what is wholesome (*kuśala*).

How is it that by practicing, cultivating, and frequently developing the abstention from taking what is not given, one is reborn among the gods? And if one returns to this state and enters into the common lot of human beings, one does not become destitute of wealth. Having spoken thus in detail regarding the abstention from sexual misconduct—practiced, cultivated, and so forth—up until: "if one enters into the common lot of human beings, one does not become subject to much calumny. Following this direction, all [the other precepts] should be applied accordingly. By one who abstains from taking life, suffering has not been produced for another, nor...

"Killed" means vitality has been destroyed; thus, there is this threefold result. Likewise, for one who abstains from taking what is not given, no suffering is produced for the owner of the wealth, no loss of enjoyment is caused, and no vitality is destroyed; therefore, for him there is this threefold result. For one who abstains from sexual misconduct, no suffering is produced for another, that person is not made to have a rival wife, and no vitality is destroyed; therefore, for him there is this threefold result. In the same way, it should be applied to other cases as well.
"By one whose conduct depends on others" refers to one who looks to various [external] views, such as omens, auspicious signs, lunar days, moments, and constellations.

The causes for the maintenance of the body—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and so forth—are dependent upon others for a monk, because of the statement, "relying on alms-food. For that monk whose livelihood is thus dependent on others, there may arise wrong modes of livelihood (*mithyājīva*), such as hypocrisy (*kuhana*), hinting (*lapanā*), seeking signs (*naimittikatā*), and pressuring (*naiṣpeṣikatā*)—the desire to obtain gain by means of gain. These applications of livelihood are difficult to purify. This is stated in the *Śīlaskandhikā*, a section of the *Vinaya* known as the *Śīlaskandhikā-nipāta*. Therein it is said: "O Tridaṇḍin, just as some ascetics and brahmins..."
Having consumed what was given in faith, they dwell devoted to the pursuit of various philosophical systems, as follows:

In elephant-fighting, horse-fighting, chariot-fighting, infantry-fighting, staff-fighting, fist-fighting, fighting with the *sārasa* bird, bull-fighting, buffalo-fighting, goat-fighting, ram-fighting, cock-fighting, quail-fighting, and duck-fighting; in women’s combat, men’s combat, boys’ combat, and girls’ combat; in the sport of *iṭgālava*, in the tossing of the ball, at the tip of a banner, at the head of an army, in military arrays, in the clash of troops, or in great assemblies—some experience such things as these, yet the ascetic [remains detached].

He abstains from the practice of engaging in various spectacles for sight. For instance, Tridaṇḍin, there are certain ascetics and brahmins who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, dwell devoted to the practice of engaging in listening to various sounds, such as: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of infantry, the sound of conchs, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of ḍambara drums, the sound of dancing, the sound of singing, the sound of snapping fingers, the sound of hand-clapping, and the sound of musical instruments like the kumbha and tūṇīra.

Some desire to hear stories connected with the Lokāyata, consisting of variegated syllables, variegated phrases, and variegated expressions; thus, a śramaṇa abstains from such undertakings involving the hearing of various sounds. Because of the enjoyment of false objects—that is, the enjoyment of improper objects—the five fruits previously mentioned [arise]: the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala), the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala), the concordant fruit (niṣyandaphala), the ripening fruit (vipākaphala), and the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala). This is the path for the sake of abandonment.

The path is a "means of abandonment" (*bhāvasādhana*), as in the analysis: "the path of abandonment" (*prahāṇamārga*) means that by which [defilements] are abandoned; this is an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*). Furthermore, the analysis is: "the path that is abandonment. The inclusion of the term "born of concentration" (*samādhija*) is for the purpose of excluding those not born of concentration. The inclusion of the term "similar" (*sadṛśa*) is for the purpose of excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*). The term "co-existent" (*sahabhū*) refers to both the associated factors (*samprayukta*), such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, and the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*), such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth. As for the phrase "that which is cultivated in the future," it refers to the future states that are produced.

Because a future dharma is attained by its power, that [attainment] is its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); for this very reason, that abandonment is established as a fruit of human effort and not merely as a fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*). Regarding the phrase "excluding those previously arisen," this is because a previously arisen result is not tenable; for it has been said: "Only a conditioned [dharma] is established as the fruit of a conditioned [cause], provided it is not prior. This excludes the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Because that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) has no ripening (*avipāka*), its outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) consists of similar subsequent states born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); its fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*) is disjunction itself, which is that abandonment (*prahāṇa*); its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) consists of those states drawn forth by it, such as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), its co-existent factors, and that future state which is cultivated; and its sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) other than its own nature, excluding those previously arisen. As for "whatever is wholesome or unwholesome," this refers to any tainted (*sāsrava*) karma other than the path of abandonment.

Whether it be concentrated (*samāhita*) or unconcentrated (*asamāhita*), that too possesses fruit through four fruits—excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*) because this is not a path of abandonment (*aprahāṇa-mārga*). For it has no fruit of dissociation; its fruit of ripening (*vipāka-phala*) is the desirable or undesirable ripening within its own level; its fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) consists of subsequent similar factors; its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) consists of those factors drawn forth by it, whether co-existent or immediately subsequent; and its dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is as previously described. Furthermore, regarding "the rest is untainted" (*anāsrava*): the inclusion of the word "rest" (*śeṣa*) [is for the purpose of excluding the aforementioned categories].

In order to exclude the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), how then is the remainder [to be understood]? Because it is not a path of abandonment, there is no fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) in the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣa*); and because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). The remainder is as previously explained: that which is neutral (*avyākṛta*), whether obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), is also endowed with three fruits. Because it is not a path of abandonment, it has no fruit of dissociation; and because it is neutral, it has no fruit of maturation. The remainder exists exactly as before. [The verse says: "Four, two, and likewise... (IV.87ab)

Regarding the three wholesome [dharmas], they are as follows in sequence: for a wholesome [dharma], there are four fruits of wholesome dharmas; for that same [wholesome dharma] when it is unwholesome, there are two fruits; for that same [wholesome dharma] when it is neutral (avyākṛta), there are three fruits—excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala), because maturation is neutral. For an unwholesome [dharma], there are two [fruits]: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala); there is no fruit of outflow (niṣyandaphala), because wholesome dharmas are not similar causes (sabhāgahetu) for unwholesome ones; there is no fruit of maturation, because maturation is neutral. And for an unwholesome [dharma], [there is no fruit of maturation] with respect to maturation...

They are not explained [as having] the fruit of dissociation because they are unwholesome; by process of elimination, they are only the fruits of human effort and dominance, and these are to be explained as before. Furthermore, the indeterminate [dharmas] have four [fruits].

How can neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena be the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of the unwholesome (*akuśala*), and why should they not be so? Because they are dissimilar; for unwholesome and neutral phenomena are indeed dissimilar, being respectively with and without maturation (*savipāka* and *avipāka*). This is not a fault. For there is a similarity between unwholesome and obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena by virtue of their commonality as afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). Therefore, it is logical that obscured-neutral phenomena are the outflow fruit of unwholesome ones, and unwholesome phenomena are the outflow fruit of obscured-neutral ones. Thus he says, "In the case of the neutral," and so forth, referring to the universal (*sarvatraga*) unwholesome [defilements].

The outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of passion and the other afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin of suffering consists of the views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); it is the outflow fruit of both the similar-type (*sabhāga*) and the universal (*sarvatraga*) [causes].

"Unwholesome," and so forth in detail: unwholesome [dharmas] are those belonging to the five categories that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the other [truths]. Among the neutral [dharmas], the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) belongs to the two views—the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). These same three fruits [are obtained] excluding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the disconnection fruit (*visaṃyogaphala*). For past karma, the dharmas belonging to the three time periods—past, future, and present—are each four fruits, excluding the disconnection fruit because it does not fall within the time periods (*adhvan*). How so? For past karma, its ripening occurs later as something past.

The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) consists of those [dharmas] drawn forth by it, whether they are co-arisen and past, or immediately subsequent and past; excluding its own nature, these are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*). Those that arise together with it and those that arise subsequently and are past are the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Similar dharmas that arise subsequently and are past are the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Regarding the past, the future is its fruit of maturation; that future dharma which is obtained through its power is the fruit of human effort and the dominant fruit. That which is similar to it is the outflowing fruit.

In this same way, for that past [action], four fruits of the present [dharmas] are to be applied. For the middle [present action] as well, future dharmas are its four fruits; the meaning is that these are exactly the same, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*). Those [fruits] are also to be applied in this very same manner. Present dharmas are two fruits of a present [action]: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). For that which arises simultaneously with it is born by its power; thus it is the fruit of human effort, and it is also the dominant fruit.

It is indeed not a fruit of disjunction, because its nature is non-disjunction; it is not a fruit of disjunction because of the absence of preceding and succeeding [moments]; it is not a fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*) because maturation (*vipāka*) depends upon a continuous stream; and there is no present [fruit] of a present [cause], excluding the fruits of outflow and disjunction.

Regarding the future [dharma]: it is not the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of the future, because the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) do not exist in the future; for since those [causes] are scattered, it is impossible to determine that "this is its fruit" on the basis of similarity. It is not the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyogaphala*), because disconnection does not exist in the future. However, it may be the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) of the future, for the ripening fruit of a future unwholesome or wholesome-with-outflows dharma is that which will arise later in the future. It is also the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), namely that which arises simultaneously.

It is easy to understand that the future [result] and that which arises immediately [after] are the dominant result (*adhipatiphala*); thus, they are not stated again. Dharmas belonging to one's own level (*svabhūmika*) are not the result of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*), because dissociation does not have the nature of a level. If they are untainted (*anāsrava*), there are three results, because the third result—the outflowing result (*niṣyandaphala*)—is possible. For the established tenet is that "the Path of the nine levels is mutual [cause and effect]. Regarding the action of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the dharmas of one in training are three results; for the result of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is not of one in training, nor is dissociation.

Regarding the *śaikṣa* [path], it is neither *aśaikṣa* nor *naivāśaikṣanāśaikṣa*. It possesses three fruits: it has no fruition fruit (*vipākaphala*) because the *śaikṣa* state is not a fruition; it has no outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) because the *naivāśaikṣanāśaikṣa* is dissimilar to the *śaikṣa*; however, it does have a disjunction fruit (*visaṃyogaphala*), because disjunction has the nature of being neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*, and it also has a human-effort fruit (*puruṣakāraphala*), because it is possible for the *naivāśaikṣanāśaikṣa* to be drawn forth by the *śaikṣa*. Furthermore, there is certainly a sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*); thus, three fruits are possible. As for the *aśaikṣa*... [text ends].

In detail: for one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the factors of one in training (*śaikṣa*) constitute a single dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*); they are not a flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) because [the latter] would be inferior. This is because of the statement that [a cause produces a result] that is equal or superior. They are not a fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) because there is no simultaneous or immediate arising; for a factor of one in training does not arise immediately after a factor beyond training, even at the time of falling away (*parihāṇi*), because it is interrupted by the manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, they are neither a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) nor a fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*), as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is neither that of one in training nor beyond training. Moreover, since there is no ripening for one beyond training, [these factors of one in training] do not constitute those fruits.

The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) consists of the three [fruits] belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). These are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), and the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). They do not include the fruit of maturation or the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyogaphala*), because these two do not have the nature of being neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*); furthermore, that which has the nature of being beyond training is what is under consideration here. The two fruits of human effort and the dominant fruit belong to those who are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training. Regarding the fruit of human effort: for example, the dharmas that arise immediately following and are drawn forth by that [action]. As for the dominant fruit, it is as previously stated; because of the reasons already explained, there are not three fruits [in this case]. Those beyond training are also like this; thus, there are two.

The meaning is "as the fruit of human effort and sovereign power. "Those and so forth" refers to those [factors] to be abandoned by seeing and so on. "Those" refers to those to be abandoned by seeing and so on. "Two are to be abandoned by cultivation."

Regarding the statement that at the emergence from the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), the wholesome factors to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*), and so forth—the phrase "as in the beginning and the end" (*ādyantavat*) is used to indicate that it is as it is in the middle, just as it is in the beginning and the end. Why was the word *anukrama* (sequence) employed in the beginning? Because of the statement: "Of the unwholesome, there are two, three, and four [results] respectively, starting with the wholesome. It was also employed there; likewise, for the [factors] not to be abandoned, it is said: "Those [results] are one, two, and four respectively. Thus it is.

The meaning for the beginning and the end has been stated according to their respective order; likewise, it should be understood for the middle as well, for this is the rule of abbreviation (*peyāla-dharma*). This is the method of summary (*abhisaṅkṣepa-nyāya*); otherwise, in cases such as "for the indeterminate there are two, three, and three [results] respectively" and so forth, one would have to state "according to their respective order" in every instance, because they arise from improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*).

That mental attention which proceeds by way of non-origination, by way of injustice, and through the conjunction with the afflictions; that which has arisen therein, its state, and from that—by means of which, and in whatever manner one should go, and by whichever person, and in whatever manner one should go—if one does not go in that manner, this is "action performed through improper application" (*ayogavihitam karma*). It is also "that which deviates from the rule" (*vidhibhraṣṭam*).

By the word "also" (*api*), "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*) is also included; thus, that which is other than both is "neither. It is neither prescribed by rule (*yogavihita*) nor not prescribed by rule. Furthermore, what is that other? It is neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma—neutral being that which is other than both [the prescribed and the non-prescribed]. "Birth" (*janman*) is a designation for the homogeneous group (*nikāyasabhāga*); the intention is that this refers to a formation dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and not to the [specific] birth-moment itself. As for the phrase "if, then": if one single karma projects only one single birth, then as for what was stated by the Elder Aniruddha...

The meaning of the sentence "How is this not contradicted by the detailed account that 'I was he'? is as follows: In another life, alms-food (*piṇḍapāta*) was given to the Pratyekabuddha Tagaraśikhi; by him [the Buddha] it was said, "I was he," and so forth. Having brought that to completion means having established it. Even though human birth is equal, one person has all their faculties (*sakalendriya*) while another has deficient faculties (*vikalendriya*); because of the difference in the completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*), that [objection] is untenable, since it is the fruit of the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*).

For the six sense bases, beginning with the eye, are projected [by the projecting karma]; however, it is logical to say that visible form and so forth are the fruit of the completing karma. Even though humanity is equal, why is it that one possesses beauty while another does not? There is no contradiction, because this occurs through the power of the completing karma once the conditions obstructing its arising have been avoided. Otherwise, if there were projection of birth, no one would ever be deficient in their faculties.

Furthermore, other [factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth possess maturation (*savipāka*). This is because those two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) do not coexist with the action known as volition (*cetanā*); nor are they projected by bodily or vocal actions, since [the states of attainment] are devoid of mind (*acittika*); nor are they projected by acquisitions (*prāpti*), even though these are themselves subject to maturation, because [acquisitions] have multiple fruits and thus do not share a single fruit with the projecting action. For acquisitions exist externally, like the bark of a tree; therefore, they constitute an "obstruction of action" (*karmāvaraṇa*).

Karma itself is an obscuration, afflictions themselves are an obscuration, and maturation itself is an obscuration—[these] refer to the roots of virtue belonging to those practicing the preparatory stages for the Noble Path, such as the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth. By the word "etcetera," one should understand that this includes karma fixed for the miserable realms—that is, karma fixed for rebirth as hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—as well as karma fixed for the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the Great Brahmā realm. Furthermore, one must mention karma fixed for [rebirth as] eunuchs, impotent men, or those with both sexual organs; likewise, one must mention karma fixed for birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and birth as a woman. For Noble Ones are not reborn in the hells and other such states, nor in the egg-born or moisture-born modes of birth.

They do not undergo womanhood, nor will they undergo an eighth existence, because they have at most seven more births (*saptakṛtvobhavaparamatvāt*). They are "easily seen" (*sudarśakāni*); that is, they are easily seen by others, hence *sudarsāni*; *sudarsāni* itself is *sudarśakāni*. Likewise, they are easily made known to themselves, hence *suprajñeyāni*; *suprajñeyāni* itself is *suprajñapakāni*, with the suffix *ka* used in the sense of the base meaning. These two terms—*sudarśakāni* and *suprajñapakāni*—are synonyms. [This is] from the perspective of their basis (*adhiṣṭhānataḥ*).

Regarding the paths of action (*karmapatha*): among the three bases of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), killing (*prāṇātipāta*) is the path of action and the basis for one; false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) is the path of action and the basis for the second; and the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) for killing is the path of action and the basis for the fifth. Thus, they are easy to see and easy to understand by way of their bases. They are easy to understand by way of their fruit, because all of them have undesirable fruits; by way of their destiny, because they lead to rebirth in the hell realm; by way of their mode of birth, because they are to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*); and by way of the individual, because they arise from the most grievous afflictions (*kleśa*). They are well-known [for these reasons].
"This person is one who has committed patricide, up to and including one who has shed the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind."

Others, however, explain [the distinction] as follows: by way of basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as before; by way of fruit (*phala*), because its fruit is hell; by way of destiny (*gati*), because it causes one to enter the human destiny; by way of rebirth (*upapatti*), because it is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) in that very same way—as stated in the passage "immediate [karma] exists in the three continents"; and by way of person (*pudgala*), because it is performed by a male or a female, and not by a *ṣaṇḍha* or a *paṇḍaka*. Thus, these [actions] are easy to see and easy to explain by means of these five reasons; however, those actions fixed for the miserable destinies (*apāya*) are not easy to see by means of these five reasons.

These have been described as being well-defined because they are brought forth in successive order; for the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) brings about the obscuration of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and the obscuration of karma brings about an undesirable maturation (*vipāka*) in the miserable states of existence (*apāya*). Among these, the obscuration of afflictions is the most grave, followed by the obscuration of karma, and then the obscuration of maturation. This is because the operation of the obscuration of maturation occurs only in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), not in a second [future] life. Regarding the naming of that factor—such as patricide and so forth—by whose connection one becomes "immediate" (*ānantarya*), in its designation:

The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) [in *śrāmaṇya*] signifies "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*). Just as in the case of *śrāmaṇyavat*, when one becomes a recluse (*śramaṇa*) through union with a particular untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), the abstract suffix is used to denote that [path]. "Śrāmaṇya is the stainless path"—thus it is said. Furthermore, [it does not exist] in Uttarakuru because of the fixed lifespan, natural morality, and the absence of the Teaching there. And whatever is the reason for the absence of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) there—namely, the instability of intention regarding evil—it is for this very reason that restraint (*saṃvara*) exists there; for even non-restraint exists there by virtue of its existence as an opposite.

Non-restraint does not exist for eunuchs and others. Regarding the statement "because of the destruction [of shame]," it means that because of the destruction—that is, the corruption—of that sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-vyapatrāpya*) by which [normally] eunuchs and others would be touched by immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), such shame and dread do not become intense toward their own mother and father; therefore, immediate retribution is not admitted for them. This is because, since they are the cause of a defective physical existence, they provide little benefit.

Therefore, the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) is not admitted for them; even for women or men who are blind from birth and so forth, there would be no immediate retribution for killing their mother or others, because what is intended here is a deficiency of the physical basis (*ātmabhāva-vai-kalya*) that is incompatible with the attainment of the Dharma. That deficiency which is opposed to the attainment of the Dharma is what is under discussion; and by that alone is the lack of affection toward one's mother [defined], not by a deficiency such as being blind from birth. For this very reason, it is also not admitted for animals or hungry ghosts (*preta*). It is said: "Precisely because of little benefit and a lack of shame, it would apply to those of sharp intelligence, like a well-bred horse."

The immediate [karma] (*ānantarya*) applies even to animals and hungry ghosts (*preta*); this is the subject under discussion. It is heard that it is like the case of a noble horse (*ājāneya*): for instance, a certain distinguished noble horse, thinking "I must not mate with my mother," had his face covered with a cloth and was led to his mother; having later realized this, he tore out his own genitals. Such a noble horse possesses a sharp intelligence; the intention is that such a being would incur the immediate karma. Furthermore, for a human who kills non-human parents, there would certainly be no immediate karma.

The meaning is: "How could there be an immediate [retribution] (ānantarya)? Because one is not ashamed of a minor benefit; for a non-human is not capable of performing a benefit corresponding to that of a human. Furthermore, intense moral shame (hrī) and dread of blame (vyapatrāpya) do not abide toward the mother and father who are non-humans, because affection is slight due to the difference in their respective realms of existence (gati). Regarding the four actions of body: these are the killing of the mother and so forth. One action of speech: this is the schism of the Saṅgha (saṅghabheda). Three are the taking of life: these are the killing of the mother and so forth. One [action of mind].

False speech, schism in the Saṅgha, one instance of the preparatory effort for taking life, and causing blood to flow from the body of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind—why are these not considered the actual taking of life? It is said that this is because Tathāgatas are of a nature that cannot be harmed; the meaning is that they are of a nature such that death cannot be brought about by the assault of another. This is because the term for the fruit is applied metaphorically to the cause. False speech is the cause of the schism in the Saṅgha, which is characterized as a factor dissociated from thought (*cittaviprayukta-dharma*); thus, the term for the fruit is applied metaphorically to that cause. The factor dissociated from thought is metaphorically designated as "schism in the Saṅgha" (*saṅghabheda*), either because it is the schism itself or because it is that by which the Saṅgha is split.

Alternatively, by adopting the analysis of the means (*karaṇasādhana*), false speech is called "schism in the Saṅgha" (*saṅghabheda*); for it is by false speech that the Saṅgha is split, but [the term] "schism in the Saṅgha" does not adopt the analysis of the state (*bhāvasādhana*). However, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, schism in the Saṅgha is primarily the lack of concord (*asāmagrī*); thus, it has substantial existence (*dravyasattā*). Therefore he says: "Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is a dissociated factor (*viprayuktaka*)," meaning it is a dharma that is non-defiled and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*). [The question is: "Will this then be an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)? The meaning is that it does not become an immediate transgression characterized in such a way; nor indeed is it [an immediate transgression] by means of that.

The intention is that the schismatic is not possessed of that [act] by means of a dissociated dharma; therefore, this is not an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). Furthermore, that false speech is born simultaneously with the schism in the Saṃgha, or born simultaneously with the dissociated dharma; its nature consists of vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) and non-intimation (*avijñapti*). This is the meaning. "A monk causes the schism."

Because the Buddha is a monk and because the schismatic acts in rivalry with him, he is a monk; laypeople, nuns, and others are not [the ones who can cause a schism], because they lack a foundation worthy of acceptance. Furthermore, he is one whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), because his basis is firm and hidden. He is "one whose conduct is dominated by views" because he has practiced and is engaged in the five [wrong] views, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, he is "one whose conduct is dominated by views" because views are his conduct. For, by virtue of his capacity for reasoning and refutation, he is able to lead others to accept another teacher and another path; he is not one whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*).

Because their resolve regarding the sides of affliction and purification is unstable; because they are difficult to endure; because they are difficult to overcome; and because they have directly realized the Dharma.

The meaning is: because of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāritva*) of the two dharmas—the dharma of scripture (*āgama*) and the dharma of realization (*adhigama*). "Not one who has attained receptivity" (*kṣānti-lābhin*) means not one who has attained the receptivity that is a part of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kṣānti*), because such a person is equivalent to one who has seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*). "He does not dwell" (*na vivasati*) means he does not spend that night there. Regarding the statement "it becomes split" (*bhinnaṃ bhavati*), if one asks how it is split, [the answer is]: "Because it obstructs the proceeding of the Path" (*mārgapravṛttiviṣṭhāpanāt*), which means because it hinders the proceeding of the Path. For as long as the Saṅgha is not reunited, the proceeding of the Path [is obstructed].

The meaning is that the Path does not become manifest in the mental continuum of anyone [remaining in the original group]. Because it is the cause for the schism of the wheel (*cakrabheda*), the schism of the Saṅgha is called the "schism of the wheel. For the Saṅgha must necessarily be divided into two factions.

The meaning is that one must stand on the side of the Buddha and on the side of the schismatic. For the *saṃgha* consists of four monks; and since there must be two *saṃghas*, there must be eight monks to be split, plus the ninth who is the schismatic. As for "another kind of *saṃghabheda*," this refers to a schism other than a schism of the wheel (*cakrabheda*); the intention is that in this case there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), because that [other kind] arises from a schism of ritual action (*karmabheda*). "Dissension" means having diverse opinions; "rites" refers to the communal rites of the *saṃgha*, such as the *poṣadha* and so forth. [This occurs] with eight or more [monks].
In this case as well, there must be two groups of sixteen; the schismatic, imagining himself a Teacher, must consist of exactly eight monks and not nine or more; thus he becomes of one accord.

The meaning is that one becomes undistracted and of a single-minded intent. In the former state, joy and gladness arise; in the latter state, there arises an intense agitation and a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) in the mind. Regarding the phrase "prior to the *arbuda*": the fault is the *arbuda*. Is it a *dṛṣṭyarbuda* (a tumor of views) or a *śīlārbuda* (a tumor of morality)? Here, it is a *dṛṣṭyarbuda*, as it has been stated. As it was said: "As I understand the meaning of what was spoken by the Blessed One, those things described by the Blessed One as obstructive factors (*antarāyika-dharma*) are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction when they are indulged in"—such is that very mind.

It "wanders" and "transmigrates," and so forth; it is called an *arbuda* because of its nature of being connected with immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) up to that point, and because it is capable of being linked again by that pair of disciples. The meaning is that it is to be linked again by that pair of disciples. Furthermore, all Buddhas necessarily have a pair of disciples: one is the foremost among those possessed of wisdom, and the second is the foremost among those possessed of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). In this case, for Śākyamuni, the noble Śāradvatīputra is the foremost among those possessed of wisdom, and the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost among those possessed of supernatural power. This is because there is no rival [to them] after [the Buddha] has entered *parinirvāṇa*.

In the Blessed One, there exists no adversary for that schismatic when the boundary is unbonded—that is, within the boundary of the maṇḍala; for it is by performing separate ritual acts within a single boundary that a schism in the Saṅgha occurs. Now, while it is true that natural boundaries such as villages and cities exist, it is only when the *jñapti*-boundary exists that the natural boundary is established; thus, it should be understood that its bonding is indeed established, because it is dependent upon the ritual act (*karman*). By means of this [schism], one brings about the division of the community of disciples.

The karma that has been performed results in a schism for that very person alone, and not for another. It is said that while the Śākyamuni was still in the state of a Bodhisattva, he caused a schism in the assembly of a rishi who possessed the five superknowledges; it is because of this that it is said "the Saṅgha was split by Devadatta," and not because of other [offenses] such as the killing of an ordinary woman. [This occurs] "due to the rejection and destruction of the field of benefactors and the field of qualities. Because of the rejection—that is, the abandonment—of the field of benefactors or the field of qualities, as in the case of the killing of mother or father, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) from its destruction.

The immediate [karmic offense] resulting from the destruction of a Tathāgata’s body, as well as the immediate offense resulting from maliciously drawing blood from him, and likewise that which consists in the schism of the Saṅgha—this too is an immediate offense. This is stated because they are fields of benefit and fields of virtue; since their rejection and destruction are equivalent to the killing of one's mother and so forth, it is an immediate offense in these cases alone and not otherwise. Furthermore, if the mother’s sexual characteristics were to change, or the father’s—if, through the transformation of sexual characteristics, that state of being a mother or that state of being a father is lost—then [the act would no longer be an immediate offense] regarding the mother...

He asks out of the apprehension that there might be no *ānantarya* [immediate retribution] due to the absence of killing the father, or due to the absence of killing the mother—[asking], "From whose blood is he born? (*yac-choṇitodbhava*). The meaning of "he who is born from her blood" (*yac-choṇitodbhava*) is that she is to be regarded as such in all maternal duties; the intention is that she is to be looked upon as a mother in all matters appropriate for a mother. Because she is like a mother, she is the nourisher, the one who carries the womb, the fosterer, and the wet-nurse—this is the sense. The "fosterer" (*poṣikā*) is the one who brings about growth through the habituation of coarse food.

Regarding the avoidance of bathing and anointing: for example, a son, thinking "a man is sleeping here" because he had spread a coverlet over a bed where his mother was actually hidden beneath the bed-mat, struck her with a weapon; by that stroke of the weapon, the mother hidden beneath the bed-mat was killed—this is to be cited as an instance [of killing]. Furthermore, a washerman’s son, intending "I shall kill a mosquito," kills his father through the application of a mosquito-spray; these are two cases of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

The non-informative [action] of the immediate [offense], as well as the non-informative [action] of mere killing—however, the non-informative [action] is indeed the immediate [offense] itself; the meaning is that it is subsumed within that alone and not by anything else. Of that too, there is only one.

"Go and tell Śikhaṇḍin: 'Arhat-vadha! Thus, in the city of Rauruka, a king named Udrāyaṇa, having consecrated his son named Śikhaṇḍin as king, went forth into homelessness. Having attained the state of an Arhat through that renunciation, he arrived in the vicinity of Rauruka and desired the kingdom once more. At the instigation of his ministers, King Śikhaṇḍin killed his own father. While he was being killed, he said to the man who was killing him, "Go and tell Śikhaṇḍin," and so on, with these two [verses].

It should be stated that [this is] "by two causes. Thus one should go and say to Śikhaṇḍin: "You have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) by means of two immediate causes. He should reply: "Or rather, I was reviled from two mouths. The intention is that because there are two mouths, there is a metaphorical designation of two immediate transgressions; for that immediate transgression is more grave due to the duality of its causes, since the basis (*āśraya*) is absolutely opposed to them. This is because the basis of one in whom the Noble Path has arisen is utterly incompatible with those courses of action (*karmapatha*).

Because of its contradictory nature, the story of Cheka serves as an illustration here. It is said that a certain clever Śākya man, out of fear of Virūḍhaka, took refuge in a rugged forest region and adopted the livelihood of a hunter. While the Blessed One was spending the three-month rains retreat among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, he descended from there and taught the Dharma to Cheka and his family. Through that teaching, Cheka attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). His sons, who had already attained the fruits [of the path], had previously set out snares, nets, and other traps for deer; and by means of those very devices...

Even when deer are being slaughtered, because they obtain the fruit [of their actions], they are not touched again by unwholesome paths of action. Thus, the fifth, the third, and the first are the most serious. This is the sequence of the teaching on the immediate (ānantarya) karmas: matricide, patricide, schism in the Saṅgha, and causing the blood of a Tathāgata to flow with a malicious mind. Among these, the fifth—causing the blood of a Tathāgata to flow with a malicious mind—is more serious than the remaining four, excluding schism in the Saṅgha. The third—patricide—is more serious than those [remaining].

Between the two—killing one's mother and killing one's father—killing one's mother is more serious than killing one's father; therefore, he says that killing one's father is the lightest of all. This refers to the restriction [of the gravity of offenses]. Having ascertained this very point, the meaning is as follows: with respect to the full extent of the ripening [of karma], causing a schism in the Saṅgha is said to be the most blameworthy, because it yields a ripening lasting for an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*). With respect to the slaughter of a great multitude of people, the mental rod (*manodaṇḍa*) is [the most serious], because it causes the desertion of places such as the Daṇḍaka forest. For by no other bodily or vocal action could so many people be [destroyed].

Malice arises with respect to the cutting off of the roots of virtue; false view is the most blameworthy because no other unwholesome root cuts off the roots of virtue, since [other unwholesome roots] are only opposed to their manifestation and not to their very existence. However, it is not immediately [after death] that one is born in hell; rather, they are called "similar" (*sabhāga*) to those [immediate transgressions] because of their similarity to them, and not because of immediate rebirth there. For otherwise, they would simply be "immediate" (*ānantarya*) transgressions themselves—this is the opinion of others. Even though they are produced immediately [after the act], they are not [immediate transgressions].

These [actions] are indeed *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses because their maturation occurs at a time that is not equal [to other karmic results]; this is the rebuttal of those who hold the first position. The refutation [of the second position] is as follows: killing one's mother who is an Arhat is similar to the *ānantarya* of matricide; killing a Bodhisattva who has entered the state of certainty is similar to the *ānantarya* of patricide; killing a Śaikṣa is similar to the *ānantarya* of killing an Arhat; stealing the means of subsistence from the Saṅgha is similar to the *ānantarya* of causing a schism in the Saṅgha; and destroying a stūpa is [similar to the *ānantarya* of destroying a Buddha-body].

Master Vasumitra says that stealing from the Sangha’s gateway for requisites is equivalent to the immediate offense of shedding the Tathāgata’s blood with a malicious mind; furthermore, he explains that it is the theft of the Sangha’s inexhaustible endowment (*akṣayanīvī*). However, others explain it as "stealing from the gateway for requisites for comfort," meaning the theft of those things used for comfort by which the Sangha maintains its livelihood. This is because of the transgression of the ground of its maturation (*vipākabhūmi*); just as one who has attained *kṣānti* does not go to the miserable realms (*apāya*) because they have transcended the ground of the miserable realms, so too [this act] is defined by the transgression of the ground of its maturation. It is like a man who abandons his country.

The meaning is that as he acts, the creditors likewise rise up. "Born into a great *śāla* family" means born into a family with great ramparts. From "born into a great *kṣatriya śāla* family" up to "born into a great householder (*gṛhapati*) *śāla* family," the meaning is born into a great householder family. "Harassment" refers to the infliction of suffering and mental distress upon another through the activity of body and speech preceded by great contempt; with respect to that [suffering], the restraint [of such activity] is called "constraint. [This was said] ninety-one eons ago.

"Taking as a starting point" (*upādāya*) refers to the completion of the ninety-first *kalpa*. Taking that [period] as the starting point, the Blessed One was addressed by the village headman Aśibaddhaka, a disciple of the Nirgranthas: "For what purpose, O Gautama, have you set out for the ruin of these families, that in such a famine you wander for alms with such a large community of monks, destroying them like a thunderbolt? The Blessed One replied: "From this time forward, O village headman, for ninety-one *kalpas*... and so on in detail. [He spoke thus] regarding these four faults.

It turns away the faults of rebirth in miserable states, the fault of low birth, the fault of impaired faculties, and the fault of being female; and one acquires two qualities: the quality of recollecting past lives and the quality of non-retrogression—provided one excludes those Bodhisattvas who are already near [to enlightenment]. Regarding the statement that "the three-thousandfold world system is produced by the karma that ripens into the marks," and that its magnitude corresponds to the sovereign power (*adhipatya*) of the karma of all sentient beings, such that the great trichiliocosm appears through that power—it is this [magnitude] that was described as the measure of merit.

The measure of these [meritorious acts] is such that one hundred of them, thus measured, produce a single mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*). This continues in this manner up to the thirty-second mark. Some explain it as follows: through the manifestation of mental attention directed toward the Buddha as its object, there arise fifty volitions (*cetanā*); then another fifty [arise] with the thought, "May I too become like this. In this way, there is a hundredfold merit. Others describe it thus: the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) has twenty places, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) has sixteen, and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has four; and [these constitute] eight.

There are forty-eight varieties of the cold hells; thus, the triple world consists of forty-eight [divisions]. Taking that as its object, this bodhisattva’s mind of compassion arises. Consequently, there are forty-eight volitions associated with that [compassion]. Immediately thereafter, a volition having the Buddha as its object arises, [thinking]: "In this way, sentient beings have been liberated by him from this triple world"—this is one volition. Immediately thereafter, a second volition arises: "May I also liberate them in this same way."

There are fifty volitions (*cetanā*) that have the self as their object (*ātmālambana*). Because these manifest twice, they are endowed with five causes. The five causes are: purity of the fundamental path of action (*maulakarmapatha*), purity of the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*), non-affliction by discursive thought (*vitarka*), being sustained by mindfulness (*smṛti*), and being dedicated toward *nirvāṇa*. Thus, there are also five volitions that have those [five causes] as their objects. In this way, there are ten sets of five volitions having the ten paths of action as their objects, making fifty volitions in total. Of these...

Because [the Buddha] appeared twice, there arose a hundredfold volition; this constitutes a "hundredfold merit. Thinking, "Just as this Blessed One is born from the uncommon ten wholesome actions, may I also become so," and because this is the case, it is established that each [mark] is born from a hundredfold merit. Regarding the form *paryupāsayāmāsa*, this is the form of the root *ās* with the suffix *āṃ* (perfect tense) following *pari-upa-ā*; its meaning is "he attended upon" (*paryupāsitavān*). As for the passage beginning "wherein by the Blessed One... and so forth, it refers to the one named Prabhāsa.

When he was a potter’s apprentice, having served [the Buddha] with pleasant water and massages, he made his first vow. At that time, the perfection of patience and the perfection of ethical discipline were fulfilled: the fulfillment of the perfection of patience occurred through a mind free from anger; the fulfillment of the perfection of ethical discipline occurred by not committing misdeeds through body or speech. "Neither in heaven nor on earth"—this is stated according to the method of a summary heading. "Neither in this world, nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, nor in the celestial palace of the gods."

These phrases of specification are intended to clarify those divine abodes: "in this world" refers to the human world; "the abode of Vaiśravaṇa" refers to the station of the Cāturmahārājika gods; "the realm of the Maruts" means the abode of the Maruts, that is, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. He speaks thus in order to make known the absence of anything like them even in other world-systems, such as the divine abodes of Yāma and so forth. "If one does not believe this, let some man traverse this entire, flourishing earth in every direction and intermediate direction."

The intention is that he himself surveyed [the world] together with its mountains and forests, inhabited by many beings. Furthermore, nine eons were turned back; because the perfection of vigor was fulfilled through ninety-one eons by means of that exertion of vigor, for this very reason it is said that [the merit] was projected during ninety-one eons, immediately prior to enlightenment.

What is the immediate preceding cause for awakening, which is characterized by the knowledge of destruction and non-arising? It is because one attains awakening through the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*), and not through their non-fulfillment; thus, it is "according to what is appropriate."

Some are merit, action, and object; some are merit and action; some are only merit and action; some are merit and object; and some are only the object. How so? He says: "For example," and so forth. The seven courses of action (*karmapatha*), such as killing and the rest, are both actions and paths because they have the nature of action and because they are the paths for volition (*cetanā*). However, the three beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) are only paths, since they are the paths along which that which is called volition proceeds. [Thus,] bodily and vocal action are [both action and path].

It is of three kinds. First, regarding merit (*puṇya*): because it has a desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*), it is an action (*kriyā*); because its intrinsic nature is karma (*karmasvabhāva*), it is a thing (*vastu*).
