This is because the volition (*cetanā*) that originates it proceeds by taking that [action] as its basis; and the volition that originates it is the originator of bodily and vocal actions. Because it has a desirable maturation, it is merit; because it is mental action (*manaskarma*), it is not a thing, nor is it an action, because it lacks the characteristic of being a basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Furthermore, the co-arising factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth are merit alone because they have a desirable maturation, but they are neither action nor a basis, due to the absence of those characteristics. Regarding "consisting of ethical discipline" (*śīlamaya*), it is as explained previously.

The threefold application [of merit] should be joined as before: "merit" refers to the basis of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*) associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and the volition (*cetanā*) associated with loving-kindness. Because of the formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) and the intentional impulse (*abhisañcetana*) by way of loving-kindness and through the power of loving-kindness, the volition co-arising with it and the morality (*śīla*) comprised within the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) constitute both merit and action, as previously explained. For volition does not proceed by taking a formal resolve such as, "I shall initiate the meditative restraint. Therefore, it is not so.

What is the basis of action (*kriyādhiṣṭhāna*)? Others [hold it to be] the feelings (*vedanā*) and so forth that coexist with it; this is merit alone, as before. Thus, in the case of that which consists in giving (*dānamaya*), there is merit, action, and the basis of action; merit and action, and the basis of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*). In the case of that which consists in ethical discipline (*śīlamaya*), there is merit and action, and the basis of action; merit and action, and the basis of meritorious action. In the case of that which consists in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), there is the basis of meritorious action, merit, and action—merit and action. Even for those [words] whose individual components are similar in form, a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is accepted, as in the rule "the quality [is retained] when the *yaṅ* affix is elided," and likewise in other cases.

That by which something is given is "giving" (*dāna*); thus, taking the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), it refers to the object to be given. However, in this context, "giving" is intended to mean that which is wholesome (*kuśala*). For the objects to be given, such as clothing and so forth, are neutral (*avyākṛta*), since they can be given even out of passion (*rāga*) and the like; by the word "and the like," anger, envy, and so on are included. "With the desire for worship and assistance": worship is directed toward shrines (*caitya*) and those who have attained final nirvāṇa; assistance is the desire to benefit the sense faculties and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). "By that collection" refers to the collection of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittakalāpa*). "Wholesome aggregates" refers to the five [aggregates].

The aggregates (*skandha*)—namely, bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) as well as non-intimation (*avijñapti*)—are to be understood as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). The suffix *-maya* here denotes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), not a transformation (*vikāra*) or the like. For example, in the expression "a house made of grass" (*tṛṇamayaṃ gṛham*), it does not mean that the house is a transformation of the grass; rather, since the house is constructed from those very grasses which remain untransformed, it is understood that "made of grass" (*tṛṇamaya*) means having the nature of grass (*tṛṇasvabhāva*). Even though this [nature] exists as its own essence, the intention is that the suffix *-maya* is applied by conceptually imagining a state of transformation despite that essential nature. Alternatively, this is according to the rule: "the suffix *-maya* is used to express the material cause (*prakṛti*)."

By way of definition, a *maya*-suffix is prescribed; thus, this too must be stated: "a vessel made of leaves" (*parṇamayaṃ bhājanam*). Having set aside [the case of] that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), it is set aside for the sake of both [types of karma], because it has completely transcended the level of maturation (*vipākabhūmi*)—that is to say, because it has completely transcended the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). For the realm of desire is indeed the level of maturation for giving, and [the realm of form] is endowed with qualities such as hearing and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is meant that one endowed with qualities such as renunciation, wisdom, and fewness of desires gives with respect and so forth. Thus, "respectful giving" (*satkṛtya*) and so on are qualifiers of the action for whom this applies; these are the four distinctions in their respective order. One who gives respectfully becomes a recipient of honor. One who gives with one's own hand acquires a taste for sublime enjoyments. One who gives at the proper time obtains enjoyments at the proper time, and because they do not give after the time has passed, they are not even unable to enjoy them. One who gives without having seized from others obtains enjoyments that cannot be confiscated.
Her limbs obtain a touch pleasant to the season—warm when it is cold, temperate when it is moderate, and cool during the *śītalikā* and other such [cold] periods.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand that as stated in the Sūtras regarding the *vardalikā* (rainy-season) and *varṣalikā* (annual) [observances], and as in the case of mother and father—the meaning is that because of their particular quality of being benefactors, benefit and harm toward them result in great fruit. This "maturation" (*vipāka*) is understood from examples such as the *Ṛkṣa-jātaka* and *Mṛga-jātaka*: by doing harm to those who were benefactors—such as by entering the cave of a bear or a deer and providing the heat of one's body or by helping them cross a river being carried away—one's limbs fall off immediately. By the word "etcetera," examples such as the *Kapi-jātaka* should be cited; for instance, "having given to one possessed of virtue, the maturation is a hundred-thousandfold," and so forth.

By the word "etcetera," it is meant that having given [a gift] to one who has entered the path toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala-pratipannaka*), the maturation (*vipāka*) is immeasurable; it is even more immeasurable for one who is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), and so forth—this being set aside.

The aforementioned generosity of the bodhisattva is for the sake of perfect enlightenment and for the benefit of all sentient beings; because it is easy to understand, it has not been analyzed in detail. Regarding this, [the first type of giving] is "this gift was given to me"; [the second] is "he gave to me in the past"; [the third] is "he will give me a gift"; [the fourth] is "it was given to me by my fathers and grandfathers in the past"; [the fifth] is "giving for the sake of heaven"; and [the sixth] is "giving for the sake of fame."

Giving for the sake of the seventh ornament of the mind, up to the attainment of the supreme goal—this is the eighth ornament of the mind. For the sake of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), for the sake of the equipment of the mind, there are eight equipment-factors of the mind. For the sake of the limbs of the path, for the sake of the equipment for yoga, and for the sake of the foundation of yoga—the attainment of the supreme goal is the attainment of Arhatship or Nirvana; therefore, giving for the sake of that attainment, though fourfold, constitutes a single eighth [category]. Considering that this indeed leads to the attainment of Nirvana, it is easy to understand.

The Master has stated that there are four types of distinguished fields: the field of destiny (*gati*), the field of suffering (*duḥkha*), the field of benefactors (*upakārin*), and the field of virtues (*guṇa*). To which of these categories does [the field of the Arhat] belong? Since for him neither the state of being a field of destiny nor a field of virtue is possible, he asks: "having revealed the even and the uneven. This means because of the fixed establishment of the maturation (*vipāka*) of dharma and adharma; that is to say, because of the fixed establishment of the yielding of maturation. "For some, solely by the power of the field" refers, for example, to the killing of a father compared to the killing of an ordinary person;
and furthermore, within that very same field, by the power of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

To explain how [the gravity of an action] depends on the path of action (*karmapatha*), I say: "By killing one's mother or father, the karma is grave; however, it is not so by taking what is not given (*adattādāna*) and so forth. For the act of seizing the property of one's mother or father does not become as grave as the act of killing them, because that killing possesses the nature of an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), lying, slander, and the rest are included. In this way, other cases should also be applied accordingly:

for some, an action becomes grave due to a particularity of its preliminary application (*prayoga*); for some, due to a particularity of the volition (*cetanā*) through the fixed state of its maturation (*vipāka-naiyamyāvasthāna*); and for some, due to a particularity of intention (*āśaya*). It is not the case that an action performed unintentionally or impulsively is grave.

Alternatively, that which is done unintentionally—that is, performed without having reflected, "I shall do this"—is not accumulated (*upacita*), for such action is neutral (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, even if an act is done intentionally, if it is not done impulsively—such as when one practices lying and so forth due to the force of habituation—that is unwholesome (*akuśala*) but not accumulated, up to the point of [the mention of] the three [factors].

"By means of misconduct of body, speech, and mind, and being without an antidote"—this refers to the absence of antidotes such as confession (*pratideśanā*) and so forth; "unwholesome and accompanied by unwholesome associates"—this refers to one who, having committed [an act], also rejoices in it; "certain in yielding its maturation"—this refers to the production of the characteristics of fully developed unwholesomeness. The same should be applied to the wholesome as well.

How is it that an action is performed intentionally and with deliberation, rather than being done without prior reflection? For example, if one were to give a lump of gold while intending to give a stone with an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) mind, that would be "done" but not "accumulated. Indeed, such an action is indeterminate because it was not performed impulsively. Likewise, if someone utters the truth as a result of being prompted by speech, that is wholesome (*kuśala*), yet it is not accumulated. Furthermore, some go to a good rebirth through a single good deed, some through as many as three, and some through just one.

Regarding the path of action (*karmapatha*), it ranges from one up to ten; in this regard, as long as one proceeds [toward its completion], the karma performed is not yet accumulated (*upacita*); once completed, it is indeed accumulated. Thus, it should be applied according to possibility, up to the point where it is fixed in the yielding of its maturation (*vipāka*). As for the detailed explanation "of one who possesses passion (*sarāga*) toward a shrine (*caitya*)," and so forth: regarding the statement "for the sake of oneself, others, or both," he says that even in this case, merit (*puṇya*) follows from relinquishment (*tyāgānvaya*) alone, because there is no benefit to anyone else. For if there were a recipient, it would be logical that merit following from relinquishment exists therein.

It is argued that one who accepts [a gift] is joined with merit through the favor of affection (*prīty-anugraha*). [The opponent replies: "Like loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, merit arises even for one who does not accept. Just as in the case of loving-kindness and the like, merit occurs even when there is no recipient who accepts; likewise, even in the absence of favoring another, merit arises from the empowerment of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) and other factors. For instance, even toward a Tathāgata or another virtuous person who has passed away, an offering made to a shrine (*caitya*) out of devotion constitutes merit. [The opponent objects: "In that case, the act of giving and honoring would become useless, if merit were to arise from one's own mind alone, since giving and honoring would be accomplished by the mind itself."

Furthermore, merit is obtained precisely from that [performance of the action], because devotion (*bhakti*) which motivates that action is more excellent. Why is this so? Because the devotion of one who performs acts of giving and honor is more excellent than the devotion of one who merely contemplates giving and honor with the mind alone; for it sets both bodily and vocal actions into motion. Indeed, devotion contemplated by the mind alone does not set bodily and vocal actions into motion. As it is said in detail: "Just as, for example, 'I shall kill the enemy'..."

When someone who has formed an intention performs bodily or vocal action arising from that [intention]—arising from the thought "this person is an enemy" and with the perception "this enemy has not yet died"—then even if that person is already dead, a much greater demerit arises due to the continuity of the volition (*cetanā*), and not merely by the intention alone when it is devoid of action. For instance, even though the Blessed One has passed away and entered final nirvāṇa, the subsequent performance of acts of giving and honoring, which arise from devotion to him—that is, from devotion to the Teacher—is likewise [meritorious].

For one who acts in this way, a much greater merit arises than from mere devotion devoid of action; otherwise, in a "bad field" (*ku-kṣetra*), there would be an undesirable result. Thus, the Nirgranthas [hold] that giving to thieves and the like results in an undesirable fruit. They maintain that in a "good field" (*su-kṣetra*) there is a desirable fruit, whereas in a bad field the opposite occurs; therefore, he says: "In a bad field as well, there is a desirable fruit, because of the non-reversal of the seed and its fruit. We do not say that the desirable fruit comes from the excellence of the field; rather, it is distinguished by something else. For indeed, in a good field... [the text continues].

It is accepted that from the seed of killing and so forth, a desirable fruit arises even in a bad field; for even in the case of a fruit, such as the grape-fruit, no reversal is observed from its seed—that is to say, the grape-fruit is seen to be sweet, and not the nimba-fruit. Likewise, from a nimba-seed, only a nimba-fruit arises, which is bitter. Thus, the grape-seed is an illustration of the wholesome (*kuśala*), while the nimba-seed is an illustration of the unwholesome (*akuśala*). Immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) is unwholesome form (*rūpa*); it is characterized by killing and so forth, and is a transgression by nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

"Immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) is form (*rūpa*). Because it is a transgression by designation (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) prohibited by the Buddha, immorality arises for one who has undertaken the training through the transgression of that [training], due to disregard for the words of the Blessed One by one who has accepted the abstention from it; the meaning is stated [implicitly] that for one who has not undertaken the training, there is no immorality. "But it is pure and possesses four qualities": that which has these four qualities is "four-qualified. By means of the aforementioned immorality—that is, immorality is unwholesome form.

"By means of non-greed and so forth" means that it is not impaired by those causes of misconduct (*dauḥśīlya*) when they are active; the meaning is that it relies upon the opposites of misconduct. "Pure through the fundamental paths of action" means it is unbroken by the fundamental [acts] such as taking life. "Pure through the preliminary stages" means it is untainted by the preliminary applications (*prayoga*) of taking life and so forth. "By discursive thoughts" refers to discursive thoughts of sensual desire and so forth. "Sustained by mindfulness" means it is strengthened by the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) regarding the body and so forth, or it is sustained by the mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla*). This is the "ethical discipline of aspiration."

"Hope" (āśā) means expectation; "desire" (astiḥ) means prayer. That which is produced by craving for existence, enjoyments, and honor—meaning that which has been undertaken through craving for existence, enjoyments, and honor—is [the action] of those possessing right view.

For those of other sects who have entered the Buddha’s teaching, [their practice] is not conducive to the accumulation of awakening because of their adherence to false views. The term "concentrated" (*samāhita*) is used for the sake of excluding what is unconcentrated; the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is used for the sake of excluding defiled meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) associated with the relishing (*āsvādana*) of concentration. That which arises similar to that wholesome concentrated state—meaning that which has concentration as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and co-exists with it—is "concentrated. This is the meaning: it is that which possesses the nature of concentration and exists together with it. Indeed, that is concentrated.

Thus is the detailed explanation. That wholesome state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) thoroughly perfumes (*saṃvāsayati*) and cultivates (*bhāvayati*) the mind; even when not in a state of concentration (*asamāhita*), it perfumes it, though not to such an extreme degree. To show this, he asks: "How so? and replies: "Because the mental continuum (*santati*) is made to consist of those qualities. Since the continuum of the mind is made to consist of the qualities of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he provides an illustration: "Like the perfuming of sesame seeds with flowers. Just as sesame seeds are cultivated by flowers through being made to consist of the fragrance of the flowers, so too is this explained:
cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is perfuming (*vāsanā*); merit consisting of that [perfuming] is called "consisting of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Now, he asks for the sake of completing the sentence: "To what do ethical discipline (*śīla*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) lead? [The answer is: "Ethical discipline leads primarily to heaven. This means that ethical discipline is, by its preeminence, conducive to heaven; however, other things are not conducive to heaven by way of their preeminence. What else? Generosity (*dāna*). For generosity also leads to heaven, and ethical discipline also leads to dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), because ethical discipline is the foundation for calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); whereas cultivation is [conducive to heaven] by its preeminence.

Because it does not directly bring about dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), or because it is comprised within the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), this is introduced in connection with the topic of non-meritorious actions (*apuṇyakriyāvastu*). It is stated in the Sūtra: "There are four types of persons who generate Brahma-merit (*brāhmaṃ puṇyaṃ*): one who establishes a stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Tathāgata on a spot of ground that is not already occupied; this is the first person who generates Brahma-merit. One who dedicates a grove (*ārāma*) to the Saṅgha of monks from the four quarters, and in that very grove, a monastery (*vihāra*)."

He establishes [the Sangha]; this is the second person who generates Brahma-merit. He reunites a divided Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples; this is the third person who generates Brahma-merit. With a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—free from enmity, free from rivalry, free from ill-will, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having resolved upon and suffused one direction, and likewise the second, the third, and the fourth.

"Pervading and suffusing this entire world—above, below, across, and everywhere—he dwells; this is the fourth person who generates Brahma-merit. This refers to what was stated in order to indicate the measure of the karma that results in the maturation of the marks [of a Great Being]. Furthermore, as for what was said—that "excluding a proximate Bodhisattva, [the merit] is equal to the fruit of enjoyment of all sentient beings," and so forth—this is what constitutes Brahma-merit.

This is the merit of the Brahmās (*brāhma-puṇya*). Here, the term "Brahmā" refers to the Brahma-purohitas; why? Because the lifespan of the Brahma-purohitas is one *kalpa*. For it is said that the lifespan of the Brahma-purohitas is a *kalpa*, and by this karma, one rejoices in the heavens for a *kalpa*. According to the reading in another school (*nikāyāntara*), it says: "One generates the merit of the Brahmās and rejoices in the heavens for a *kalpa*. Due to its similarity to that [lifespan], this is called the "merit of the Brahmās. [Objection: But surely, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karma lasting for a *kalpa*.

Thus, it is true that for a single [person], there are many volitions based on non-belief (*nāstikya*), through which a heavenly fruit equal in measure to an eon (*kalpa*) is successively produced. Furthermore, because one who has passed away reconnects with birth in that very same place, others say it is "great merit" (*bṛhatpuṇya*) pertaining to the Brahma realm. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "of the Sūtras, etc.," there is the inclusion of the twelve limbs (*aṅga*). These twelve limbs are: Sūtra, Geya, Vyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Nidāna, Avadāna, Itivṛttaka, Jātaka, Vaipulya, Adbhutadharma, and Upadeśa. This is the teaching that is undefiled (*akliṣṭadeśanā*).

The meaning is "arisen from an unafflicted mind. Regarding the term *puṇyabhāgīya*: "part of merit" (*puṇyabhāga*) means the attainment of merit; that is, the attainment of a desirable fruit. That which is beneficial for this is *puṇyabhāgīya*. For this very reason it is said that it has a desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*); that is, it is conducive to the attainment of that [desirable fruit].

Alternatively, there are three portions (*bhāga*): the meritorious portion (*puṇya-bhāga*), the non-meritorious portion (*apuṇya-bhāga*), and the imperturbable portion (*aniñjya-bhāga*). That which is beneficial for that [meritorious portion] is "conducive to merit" (*puṇyabhāgīya*). Alternatively, one who possesses merit is "merit-possessing" (*puṇyabhāk*); that which belongs to a merit-possessor is *puṇyabhāgīya*, with the suffix *-ka* used in the sense of the base itself. Likewise for "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*). Alternatively, there are two portions: the portion of saṃsāra and the portion of liberation. In that context, that which is beneficial for the portion of liberation is "conducive to liberation. Or, the attainment of liberation is the "portion of liberation"; that which is beneficial for it—that is, favorable to its attainment—is [conducive to liberation].

The characteristic of that which is conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) will be explained later; in the same way, that which is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) should also be applied, as we shall explain subsequently. Therefore, regarding the statement "the arising of the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*) occurs," here, within the context of action (*karman*), the characteristic of these things whose nature is action is stated: "That which is in the world," and so forth. "Together with its origination" (*sasamutthāna*) means together with the aggregate of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-kalāpa*); by means of which that bodily action is originated—that bodily action, together with its origination, is set in motion by application (*yoga*). Writing and seals are mentioned because the effect is metaphorically designated by the cause. For by means of which... [text fragment ends].

By means of bodily action (*kāyakarman*), writing (*lipi*) is inscribed or a seal (*mudrā*) is carved. Regarding that writing and seal, according to what is intended in the treatise: in the world, a sign consisting of syllables (*akṣara*) on books and so forth is accepted as "writing" (*lipi*); a sign consisting of non-syllables (*anakṣara*) is "seal" (*mudrā*). Calculation (*gaṇanā*) and poetry (*kāvyam*) are [forms of] vocal action (*vāk-karman*) set in motion through application; the phrase "together with their origination" (*sasamutthānam*) continues [to apply here]. Thus, having the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their intrinsic nature: for writing and seals, bodily action is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); for calculation and poetry, vocal action is the aggregate of form; [the remaining factors] such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth [are the other aggregates].

In both cases, these have the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhasvabhāva*), because they consist of the four aggregates that serve as the originating basis (*samutthāna*). Regarding the mental synthesis of phenomena (*dharmāṇām*) such as "one, two, three," and so forth—that is *saṃkhyā* (calculation). However, the Abhidharmikas maintain that when this is done by speech rather than by mind, it is *gaṇanā* (counting). Furthermore, because this calculation includes the associated factors (*saparivāra-grahaṇāt*), it has the nature of the four aggregates; and by way of the incidental explanation of the characteristics of writing and so forth, it also includes phenomena such as those that are faulty (*sāvadya*) and so on.

The presentation of the definition of characteristics: these synonyms are taught in the *Dharmaskandhakavibhāṣā*. Another [teacher] states the connection as follows: "These synonyms are presented because this [treatise] is closely related to that. They are "with fault" (*sāvadya*) because they exist together with the characteristic of affliction (*kleśa*). They are "obscured" (*nivṛta*) because even the afflictions themselves are obscured by other associated afflictions. They are "inferior" (*hīna*) because they have been extracted [from the path] or because they have been abandoned by the Noble Ones (*ārya*). However, the "afflicted" (*kliṣṭa*) should be understood as being due to their association with afflictions; whereas the "pure" (*śubha*) are "stainless" (*amala*).

Those that are wholesome and untainted (*kuśalānāsrava*) are "excellent" (*praṇīta*), because they have reached the pinnacle of purity. It is established that those other than the excellent are "intermediate" (*madhya*).

Since it is determined that only the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) are "inferior" (*hīna*) and only the wholesome and untainted are "excellent," it follows that those other than these are neither inferior nor excellent; thus, they are established as intermediate. Conditioned wholesome states (*saṃskṛta-śubha*) are to be cultivated (*sevya*). Without distinction, whether tainted or untainted, they are to be cultivated and attended to by way of their being superimposed upon one's own continuum. The remainder are not to be cultivated.

What are the remaining unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena? They are those which are neither wholesome (*kuśala*) nor afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), meaning they are obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). [They are called "unconditioned"] because they are not to be cultivated (*anabhyasanīyatva*), meaning they cannot be produced repeatedly; so say others, because they are not to be produced (*anutpādyatva*). And because they are without fruit (*aphalatva*): for the conditioned has cause and fruit, whereas the unconditioned does not. They are "with superior" (*sottara*), meaning they possess something higher. Unwholesome states are "with superior" compared to the obscured-unspecified, because the obscured-unspecified lack undesirable maturation (*aniṣṭavipāka*). The obscured-unspecified are "with superior" compared to the unobscured-unspecified conditioned states.

They are "surpassable" (*sottara*) because they are undefiled; yet even those [undefiled] are surpassable by wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*), because the latter have desirable fruits. Those [wholesome-with-outflows] are also surpassable by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), because the latter are free from afflictions. Even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) outflow-free states are surpassable by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the unconditioned are eternal. Furthermore, among the unconditioned, space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) are surpassable by cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), because cessation through deliberation is both wholesome and eternal. But liberation (*mokṣa*) is unsurpassable (*anuttara*); for there is nothing more excellent than *nirvāṇa*.

It exists; for it has been said: "O monks, whatever dharmas there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, among them this is declared to be the foremost"—namely, analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). For because it is eternal, it is superior to all conditioned things; and because it is wholesome, it is even more excellent than the other two unconditioned things, space and non-analytical cessation. Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
Chapter 5.
The fifth chapter, titled "Exposition of the Latent Dispositions" (Anuśayanirdeśa),
begins: It was stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter that "the variety of the world is born of karma."
Therefore, he demonstrates the connection by showing that the presentation of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) follows this sequence:

those actions, which possess the aforementioned characteristics and divisions, undergo accumulation through the power of the latent dispositions and arise here with a fixed certainty of maturation (*vipāka*).

The meaning is that they become fixed for the giving of their maturation (*vipāka*). Furthermore, without the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), or in the absence of underlying tendencies, wholesome or unwholesome karmas are not capable of bringing about—that is, producing—existence, which is birth.
For, in reality, there are no karmas leading to rebirth that are not fixed.
However, due to the absence of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are no longer capable of producing renewed existence;
for this very reason, their indeterminacy is established.
Furthermore, the particle *ca* here should be read in the sense of "but" (*he*).

Since they are not capable of producing existence (*bhava*) without the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the intended meaning is that they undergo accumulation by the power of the underlying tendencies.
Others, however, explain these two sentences as follows:
And those actions accumulate by the power of the latent dispositions (anuśaya);
the meaning is that those actions which have not yet been performed accumulate for the production of renewed existence through the power of the latent dispositions.

For the actions of Arhats do not accumulate toward the production of renewed existence; and apart from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those actions which have been performed are not capable of producing renewed existence.
Even those [karmas] are not capable of producing existence in the absence of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
for it is not the case that the wholesome and unwholesome, rebirth-inducing, and indeterminate karmas performed by an Arhat during his stage as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) do not exist.
However, due to the deficiency of latent dispositions, they are not capable of producing existence.
Thus, because the meanings are stated separately,
this conjunction (*ca*) is used in a cumulative sense;
such is the root of existence, namely the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

The intention is that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of renewed existence (*punar-bhava*) or of existence as karma (*karmabhava*), because they are the causes for its accumulation and origination.
"He makes the root firm" means that acquisition (*prāpti*) is indeed the root;
the sense is that he makes it firm by way of its non-interruption.
"It establishes a continuity" means that it establishes a succession of afflictions through a continuous series;
"it brings about a field" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that it makes the basis conformable to its own production;
"it brings about an outflow" means it generates a secondary affliction as its own outflow.
For example, attachment gives rise to shamelessness, restlessness, and stinginess;
hatred gives rise to anger and envy; and so forth—it brings about the existence of karma.
Karma itself is existence; "karmabhava" means that it produces [existence] for the sake of the manifestation of renewed existence (punarbhava);
this is its meaning.
"The underlying tendencies are the root of existence"— this is the demonstration of the meaning; thus, one grasps one's own equipment.
One's own equipment is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) regarding the afflictions; it "grasps" that [affliction],
meaning it remains as the causal state for its future occurrence.
It causes delusion regarding the object of focus; that is,
it causes delusion because of either a failure to grasp things as they truly are or an impairment of the intellect.
"It bends the stream of consciousness" means that it bends the continuum of consciousness either toward an object or toward rebirth, if [it so directs].
"Because it is the root of existence"— this refers to the grasping for renewed existence; this is an illustration of how it causes one to deviate from the side of the wholesome.
It causes one to fall away from the side of wholesome qualities and pervades for the sake of bondage;
the meaning is that it extends over and encompasses the function of bondage.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"By way of not transcending the realm," which means by the manner of not transcending the realm;
this is what is being stated.
Another [teacher] says that there are sixteen [afflictions], adding six to these, on the grounds that whichever affliction belongs to a particular realm does not transcend that realm.
It produces corruption of the basis by bringing about unworkability;
it hates virtuous qualities because they are its opposites;
and it provides a foothold for slanders by instigating bodily actions that are censured by the wise.
Service to a perverted teacher turns one away from the true path by causing one to face [it];
it plants the seed of manifold misfortunes, because all the calamities of saṃsāra originate from that;
and through its sovereign fruit, it brings about what is undesirable for the world, as it leads to the transformation of external states by its force.
"By the power of attachment, [the others] also [arise] in others" means that wherever there is attachment toward an object, other [defilements] such as aversion also lie latent therein.
From attachment, hatred arises, as do pride and the other [afflictions]; this is the Sūtra.
For this very reason, because there is no latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of passion (*rāga*), the afflictions do not lie latent in the untainted (*anāsrava*) or in a dissimilar realm (*visabhāgadhātu*);
and we shall explain this further below.
For when an object has been appropriated by the view of self and craving,
other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also able to adhere to it,
just as dust settles upon a moist cloth; this we shall demonstrate.
Or rather, is it that desire for sensual pleasure itself is the latent tendency?
According to the Vaibhāṣika system, the outburst itself is the latent tendency;
according to the Vātsīputrīya system, possession is the latent tendency.
According to the Sautrāntika system, "seed" means the subsequent emergence, that is, the later emergence.
"By means of strength" means well-completely driven out; "by means of power" means thoroughly and correctly driven out;
thus, it is abandoned along with its latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*).
This is the illustration here: this is what is contradicted here,
namely that distinctness is observed in a compound expressing association (sahayoga-samāsa),
as for example, "Devadatta with his son" (saputra).
And this being so, there would be contradiction with the Sūtra and contradiction with the Abhidharma; thus,
the latent tendency of sensual desire is associated with three faculties.
"With which three?
With the faculties of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity.
For it is not possible for that which is dissociated—characterized by acquisition—to be associated with these faculties; thus, [to claim otherwise] would contradict the Teacher’s teaching.
"With latent tendency" (*sānuśaya*) means "with a continuous connection" (*sānubandha*). Thus, by the word "latent tendency," the connection of sensual desire is expressed;
furthermore, this "connection" is the state of remaining in a manner conducive to the arising of other afflictions (*kleśa*).
Alternatively, the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is non-occurrence; that which possesses the latent tendency is abandoned,
meaning that the affliction (*saṃkleśa*) does not recur.
Or is the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) used metaphorically? That which exists by way of metaphor is "metaphorical.
Where is it metaphorical? He says: it is metaphorical with respect to possession (*prāpti*).
The term *anuśaya* (latent tendency) applies primarily to the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
but it is used figuratively for their acquisition (*prāpti*) because that acquisition serves as the cause for the latent tendency.
Just as fire is called "suffering" because it is the cause of the sensation of suffering,
so too,
in the Abhidharma, the term *anuśaya* is used in its technical sense.
That which exists in a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), or that which shines by means of a characteristic,
is "characteristic-based" (*lākṣaṇika*); thus he says that it is indeed the affliction (*kleśa*).
They are called "proclivities" (anuśaya) because they adhere [to the mind] both by way of their object and by way of association;
therefore, only those that are associated are proclivities.
Regarding this point, they cite a verse:

Because they cause affliction of the mind, because they are obstructions, because they are opposed to wholesome states, and because the wholesome is observed [only when they are absent], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) here are not dissociated from consciousness.
The explanation of the phrase "because it causes affliction of the mind" is that the mind becomes afflicted by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The explanation of this phrase is: "The mind does not become afflicted by the dissociated [factors] because they are obstructions."
"New wholesome [states] do not arise" means that in a mind accompanied by latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*), new wholesome states do not arise because they are opposed to the unwholesome.
The explanation of this term is that one falls away from what has arisen; thus,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are opposed to wholesome states.
Since one falls away from the affliction that has arisen,
the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are therefore opposed to the wholesome; thus, they are not dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Because the aforementioned defiled states and so forth cannot occur through those [factors] existing in the mind when they are dissociated,
whereas all of this is logical when they are associated;
therefore, it might be thought that the same would apply even to those that are dissociated.
By means of the dissociated [factors], the mind becomes afflicted;
previously non-existent wholesome states do not arise,
and one falls away from those already arisen.
If that were so, the wholesome would never be perceived at all,
because those dissociated factors are always present;
for since those dissociated factors exist in a defiled state, a wholesome state, or any other state, the wholesome would nevertheless be perceived.
Therefore,
because wholesome states are also perceived, it is established that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) here are dissociated [from the mind].
The Master said: "This which has been stated by the Vaibhāṣikas is merely an authoritative injunction."
"Because it causes affliction of the mind," and so forth;
for the Vātsīputrīya, who maintains that there is a dissociated latent disposition (*anuśaya*),
holds all of this [to be true].
The phrase "desires only that which is produced by affliction, such as the defilement of the mind" means that it is produced solely by the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) of the afflictions.
Furthermore, since the active outburst (*paryavasthāna*) is not constantly present, the attainment of wholesome states is established;

thus, in accepting the position that the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire exists, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra regarding the statement that "that which is accompanied by a latent tendency is abandoned. However, it follows that the latent tendency must be dissociated (*viprayukta*).
Therefore he says:
"And the latent disposition (anuśaya) is neither associated nor dissociated.
To the question "How so? he says:
Because it is not a separate substance;
that is, because the seed in the form of a potentiality is not a different entity from passion and so forth,
[it is] the basis of the personal existence.
Born of afflictions (*kleśaja*) means produced by previously arisen afflictions;
it is the capacity for the arising of afflictions,
just as the capacity for the arising of memory born from the knowledge of experience is not a separate substantial entity.

Having raised the objection that, in the same way, there must be some distinct entity among the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) that serves as the cause for the arising of memory, he presents another analogy,
stating: "And just as in the case of sprouts and so forth," and so on in detail.

And just as the power of sprouts and the like to produce another grain of rice— which arises from a previously produced grain of rice— is not a separate substance, so it is with that which is referred to by "yas tu" (but that which...).
The Vātsīputrīya: If it is held that the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is the affliction (*kleśa*),
then how is it that in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra* the affliction itself is stated to be the latent disposition?
It is said that for this person, there is a latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) toward pleasant feeling; however,
it is not stated that attachment itself is the latent tendency, because attachment only manifests (*samudācarati*) during the state of pleasant feeling.
The intention [of the author] is not that this is its seed;
for since it is stated that "it does not become a latent tendency (anuśaya) at that very moment," it is said that this is precisely the latent tendency of attachment.
Because of the statement that "passion does not exist," it follows that in that state, there is a latent tendency (anuśaya) for the passion that is arising.
The intention is that what is being described here is the state of the seed's own nature (prakṛti), wherein the seed arises but has not yet arisen.
When, then, does it exist?
The meaning is: when does the latent disposition (anuśaya) exist?
It is when it is dormant.
The meaning is "when it has ceased";
or, since the term is used metaphorically for its cause,
the metaphorical designation of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is applied here to the cause that precedes it.
For passion is the cause of the latent tendency of passion; for it has been said that the capacity to produce passion born of passion is called the "latent tendency of passion" (rāgānuśaya).
This is what is meant by that statement.
In some places the term *anuśaya* refers to the seed, while in others it refers to the active outburst (*paryavasthāna*),
for among them, attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti-rāga*) is generally predominant.
In the dhyāna associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*), there is generally attachment (*rāga*) to those [objects];
since there is also attachment to celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and so forth, the term "generally" (*prāyeṇa*) is employed.
Furthermore, that [attachment] functions inwardly because it has a concentrated nature.

And this being so, the notion of liberation arises; in order to dispel that [notion], the Blessed One taught such things as "sensual lust" and "lust for existence," [showing] that this is indeed lust for existence.
"This desire for the Dharma is not skillful regarding liberation;
rather, it is the very personal existence itself that constitutes existence"— this is the opinion of the Master.
Regarding the phrase "the attainment together with its basis":
those who relish the attainment together with its personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) are, in fact, relishing the personal existence itself.
Because he is free from passion for the qualities of sensual desire, he does not [cling] to them;
thus, it is shown that his passion is called "passion for existence" (*bhavarāga*) and not "passion for sensual desire" (*kāmarāga*).
The intention is that "Abhidharma" does not mean "Sūtra"; thus,
[the view] "there are seven [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of the collection" [is stated].

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) takes as its object the five aggregates of clinging which have become the fruit; therefore, it is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*).

Likewise, the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering, because it grasps those very same aggregates as being either eternal or subject to annihilation.

Furthermore, the misapprehension of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) also takes those very same aggregates as its object in terms of purity, liberation, and deliverance; thus, it is not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaheya*).
In the same way, those [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are also to be applied;
as for those to be abandoned by the vision of the path,
one adds to them the additional [affliction of] adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Because one is mistaken in thinking that purity is attained by abandoning the path and instead relying on another form of moral discipline and austerity (*śīlavrata*),
it is to be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*).

For whatever affliction has arisen for the purpose of denying a particular truth, that affliction is abandoned upon the direct perception of that truth, just as the delusion of a snake is abandoned upon seeing the rope.
The intention is that [defilements] are abandoned by the mere vision of the truths, not by repeated practice;
for they are abandoned through the practice of the path subsequent to having seen the truths.
The governing topic is whether these [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Thus, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) means repeated practice, that is, repeated production;
and the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is of one type.

Because it is a misconception regarding suffering by way of the aspects of "self" and "mine," the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is to be abandoned precisely through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*). Likewise,

since this [view] also superimposes the extremes of eternalism and nihilism upon the entity conceived as a self, it is a misconception regarding suffering itself and is therefore to be abandoned precisely through the vision of suffering.
False view (mithyādṛṣṭi) is of four kinds;
because it functions by way of denying the characteristics of the truths such as suffering, it is in error regarding all four truths and is therefore to be abandoned by the vision of the four truths.
In the same way, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is also of four kinds;
for it is the viewing of what is inferior as supreme.
Among those [four], that which has as its object the truths of origin, cessation, and the path is to be abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path.
The remainder is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering alone.
Likewise, doubt (*vicikitsā*)—being of the nature of uncertainty everywhere—is to be abandoned by the vision of all four truths because it is mistaken regarding everything.
Adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two types.
The grasping at causes in regard to non-causes such as Īśvara and so forth proceeds from the perversions of permanence and self; thus, it is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
The view of a path where there is no path is to be abandoned by the vision of the path. As for what these [perversions] are like:

The four afflictions beginning with attachment— namely, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance— are indeed being examined; these are the ones just mentioned, and they are to be abandoned by insight.
"These [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation" is difficult to distinguish; however, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth are not being considered here,
for those are misapprehensions regarding the truth of suffering.

Those [afflictions] which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, and so on up to those which are mistaken regarding the truth of the path—those are to be abandoned by the vision of the path; this is well-determined.
In that context, "those" refers to attachment and the other [afflictions].
The vision of that truth, which is the vision itself,
and those things to be abandoned by that vision— these are their objective supports.
Those [defilements] such as attachment and so forth, which have as their objective support that which is to be abandoned by seeing,
are themselves to be abandoned by seeing.
The vision of that truth is "tad-darśana";
those things to be abandoned by that vision are "tad-darśana-heyāḥ. This is what is meant.

Those afflictions such as attachment and so forth that take as their object an affliction to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to one to be abandoned by the vision of the path are "to be abandoned by the vision of those [truths]";
thus it should be stated: "whatever they take as an object, and whatever is the object to be abandoned by the vision of which."
It should not be said that the latent tendency of ignorance has the four noble truths as its object,
because this is established by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of two identical terms).
That which is truth and those afflictions to be abandoned by seeing [that truth] are their objects; thus,
these are "those whose objects are to be abandoned by seeing," and they are therefore "to be abandoned by seeing that."

But is it not the case that the universal latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), which is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin [of suffering], also has as its objects those things to be abandoned by the vision of the truths such as the cessation of suffering, because it takes all five categories as its object? Consequently, would it not follow that this [ignorance] must also be abandoned by the vision of the truths such as the cessation of suffering?
There is no fault;

for although that [cognition] has the five aggregates as its object, it apprehends those aggregates by way of the aspect of their form as "origination" (*samudaya*); therefore, because it takes them as such an object, it is indeed to be abandoned by the vision of origination.
In this way, even that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) should be included.

And this being so, those who explain that "whatever has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of [a particular truth], all of that is subject to abandonment by vision" are referring to all [factors] to be abandoned by vision, not merely to attachment (*rāga*) and the rest.
In explaining those [points] as well, these very same objections and responses must be stated:
because of the absence of suffering in the form and formless realms, there is an absence of resistance (*pratigha*);
for resistance underlies painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
And because that [pleasure] does not exist above,
there is also harsh aversion, like the disease of wind (vāta).
These two [passion and aversion] are present.
Sentient beings whose mental continuums are moistened by tranquility [do not experience this],
because there is no karmic maturation; for its maturation is indeed undesirable.
In those two realms, the ripening of undesirable results has ceased, and because there is an absence of any basis for malice,
neither external things such as weeds, alkaline soil, or thorns exist there, nor internal afflictions such as fever or epilepsy.
Because they are produced from roots of virtue such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and because they lack [the sense of] appropriation,
[they are distinguished] by way of their aspects (*ākāra*), types (*prakāra*), and realms (*dhātu*).
Thus, there is a distinction of aspect among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The categories of views such as the view of self and what belongs to self, the views of permanence and annihilation, and the views of non-existence, inferiority, and superiority— such varieties of distinctions constitute the group [of afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.
The division of the elements consists of those belonging to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
In that regard, the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) is of fifteen kinds through the distinctions of its modes and realms;
yet there is no mutual difference in its aspect (*ākāra*),
for all attachment has the aspect of clinging.
Therefore, the latent tendency of repulsion (*pratighānuśaya*) is not established by way of a difference in aspect (*ākāra*); although it is fivefold due to a difference in type (*prakāra*),
there is no mutual difference in aspect among them.
Because everything has the aspect of resistance (*pratigha*), there is no distinction between the realms (*dhātu*),
since that [resistance] is absent in both the form and formless realms.
The latent tendency of pride is of fifteen types based on the distinctions of its modes and elements;
there is no distinction of aspect,
because all of them have the aspect of loftiness.
Likewise, ignorance is of fifteen kinds;
there is no difference in their aspects from those [two] alone.
Because all [of these] have the aspect of non-apprehension,
doubt is twelvefold by means of those very same [factors].
There is no difference in aspect for all [latent dispositions], because they all have the aspect of doubt; however,
the latent disposition of views is of thirty-six kinds through the distinctions of aspect, type, and realm.

"Those born at the peak of existence are to be abandoned by patience"— the inclusion of the phrase "to be abandoned by patience" is for the purpose of excluding those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The mention of "the highest stage" (bhavāgra) is for the purpose of distinguishing it from other stages;
for there is no mundane path of cultivation that serves as an antidote to the highest stage,
[and thus the restriction applies] to the remaining stages.

"From the desire realm up to the stage of the sphere of nothingness, as appropriate" means that in the desire realm, [the afflictions] are to be abandoned by the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Thereafter, in the remaining stages, those [defilements] to be abandoned by the subsequent cognition-receptivities (anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti) are abandoned through vision for the noble ones (āryas), while those same [defilements] are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) for ordinary persons (pṛthagjanas);
for the path of cultivation is indeed twofold.
It is both mundane and supramundane;
for it is stated in the treatise that "a disciple of the Blessed One abandons [defilements] through vision."
An ordinary person abandons [defilements] through cultivation; thus,
those not to be slain by patience are abandoned by cultivation alone.
The mention of "those to be destroyed by non-forbearance" (akṣāntivadhyāḥ) is for the purpose of including those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya),
across all stages from the desire realm (kāmadhātu) up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).

Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) of attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance which, as the case may be, are not to be destroyed by patience (akṣānti-vadhya) but are to be destroyed by knowledge (jñāna-vadhya),

are always to be abandoned only through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), whether by the mundane or the supramundane path of cultivation, for both noble ones (ārya) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
At the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), however, [defilements] are abandoned only by the supramundane path, because there is no mundane path belonging to a higher level;
for indeed, among outsiders (*bāhyaka*), those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing are never abandoned.
Only those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation are suppressed for them,
whereas those to be abandoned by insight are to be destroyed by the supramundane path in all stages;
for it is said thus in the Mahākarmavibhāga-sūtra:
It has been stated that even for those free from passion, views having the desire realm as their object can still manifest:
"In this case, Ānanda, a certain person abstains from taking life, up to and including abstaining from wrong view."

In this world, one who abstains from right conduct is reborn after the dissolution of the body, after death, in a state of deprivation, an evil destination, ruin, and the hells; yet a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, or an external heretic who possesses supernatural power, divine vision, and knowledge of others' minds, perceives him in this way.
It occurs to him:
"There is no good conduct of body, there is no ripening of the result of bodily conduct; there is no good conduct of speech or mind."
"There is no ripening of good conduct of speech and mind," and so forth;
this is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which has the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object,
because that karma belongs to the desire realm.

And because hell arises in that very place, it is stated in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* that for those who speculate about the past and hold eternalist views, there is the active manifestation of views that take the desire realm as their object, even though they are free from passion.

Based on their lack of penetration regarding the vision of past lives, those who have thus developed such views are the many proponents of eternalism among those who speculate about the past, as described therein.
We shall show one example of these:
here, a certain ascetic or brahmin, having gone to the forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, through the sequence of non-heating and the sequence of abandonment...
Through the sequence of cultivation, through the sequence of frequent practice, and through the sequence of correct mental attention,
he touches that kind of peaceful meditative concentration such that,
with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects twenty eons of world-dissolution and evolution.
It occurs to him:
"This self and this world are eternal.
Thus, all these proponents of the past limit are eternalists.
By means of this eternalist view, those who take the self and the world as their object also take the desire realm as their object;
thus, the manifestation of views having the desire realm as their object has been explained.

Likewise, in that very *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the manifestation of views having the desire realm as their object is explained for certain eternalists who speculate about the past and are free from passion [for the higher realms].
Monks, what is that occasion when this world undergoes dissolution?
When the world is dissolving, for the most part, sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods.

There they become beings with form, mind-made, complete, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all limbs and minor members, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the air, feeding on joy, nourished by joy, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration. Monks, this is the time when this world is evolving; as the world evolves, an empty Brahmā-palace appears in space.

Then, another being, through the exhaustion of his lifespan, the exhaustion of his merit, and the exhaustion of his karma, passed away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods and was reborn in an empty Brahmā-palace. There he remained alone, without a second, without attendants, long-lived, for a long duration of time. Then, after the passing of that long period, craving arose in that being and dissatisfaction was born within him.
"O, would that other beings also might be reborn here in my very same state!
Thus was the mental aspiration of that being;

and other beings, through the exhaustion of their lifespan, the exhaustion of their merit, and the exhaustion of their karma, having passed away from the Ābhāsvara host of gods, were reborn in the state of that being.
Then this thought occurred to that being:
"I am alone, without a second, without an attendant, yet long-lived; would that other beings also might be reborn here in my very same state of existence"—such was his mental aspiration.
And these beings born here in my own likeness— these beings have been created by me;
I am the lord of these beings, the maker, the fashioner, the creator, the progenitor, and the father of all things."
Those beings also thought thus: "We have seen this being alone, without a companion, without an attendant, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration of time;
after the passing of that long period, thirst arose in this being and dissatisfaction was born."
"O, would that other beings also might be reborn here in my very same state of existence!
And thus was the mental aspiration of that being:
"May we also be reborn here in this being's very same state of existence."
"We have been created by this being;
this being is our lord, even as a father to all things.
Then, another being, due to the exhaustion of his lifespan and the exhaustion of his merit, [passed away].
Due to the exhaustion of their karma, having passed away from that state, they come to such a condition as this: into the common lot of human beings.

Following his growth and through the maturation of his faculties, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on saffron-colored robes, and with genuine faith goes forth from the home to the homeless life. Having gone to the forest or to the root of a tree—and so on in detail—until he touches such a peaceful concentration of mind.
When his mind is thus concentrated, he recollects his former existence and thinks to himself:
"That Brahmā by whom we were created— "
"He is eternal, stable, everlasting, and of an unchanging nature; but we, who have been created by that Brahmā,
are impermanent, unstable, non-eternal, and of a changing nature."

Thus, in this way, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also taken as an object by that view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); therefore, the active manifestation of views having the desire realm as their object has been explained.
Likewise, in that very *Brahmajālasūtra*, it is stated regarding those who speculate about the past concerning the causeless arising [of phenomena].
It has been stated that there is the active manifestation of views among those free from passion that take the desire realm as their object;
how then can there be gods in the form realm known as the "unconscious beings"?
Due to the arising of perception, those beings undergo death from that place;
then, one or another being, having passed away from that place, comes into this state among the human community,
as previously described, up until he recollects his former existence.
It occurs to him:
"The self and the world have arisen without a cause";
thus it occurs to him in this very way.

Taking the self and the world to be "arisen without cause" (*ahetusamutpanna*), they take even the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object through that false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Thus, the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of these views which have the desire realm as their object has been explained. Furthermore, how does the false view arise in this way: "The self and the world are arisen without cause"?

Thinking that there might be an opening for the statement, "For those who are free from passion for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), those views would belong to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)," because they thus deny that previously performed wholesome or unwholesome actions are the cause of oneself or the world,
he says: "And the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm do not have the desire realm as their object (*ālambana*), because [those beings] are free from passion."
Some offer this defense: "These views belonging to the desire realm are not false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*)," but that is incorrect for them.
The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that they have fallen away because they possess that same view, just like Devadatta;
for instance, Devadatta fell away from his supernormal powers due to the arising of an evil desire to lead the community of monks away from the Blessed One’s state of dwelling with few concerns.
Because it is stated in the Sūtra;
for thus it is recited in the Sūtra:
"Then, Devadatta, overcome by gain and honor, this kind of evil desire arose in him: 'O, that the Blessed One would relinquish the community of monks to me!'"

"May the Blessed One dwell with little concern, while I lead the community of monks," and as soon as that thought arose, Devadatta fell away from that supernatural power— this is the detailed account.
In this way, they too fell away at the very moment the [wrong] view arose.
For their grasping at a self with respect to those [aggregates] is preceded by this; thus, it is entirely preceded by the notion of a permanent, unitary whole.
The fivefold [view] is also called "satkāya" (the existing body) with respect to the five aggregates of clinging.

For indeed, every view that functions with a nature of inverted perception is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) because it is a false contemplation, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; yet others are superimposing views (*samāropikā*).
How, then, is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) a superimposing view?
The noble one is designated as "one who possesses abundance" because of having abandoned [the defilements],
that is, because of having relinquished them.

Because the verbal root *ohāk*, meaning "to abandon," is employed here, the initial syllable has been elided; thus, "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to the view that regards the aggregates of appropriation— such as vision and the rest— as supreme or preeminent.
Master Saṅghabhadra maintains that by the use of the word "para" (other), this sense of "excessive" is obtained;
thus, the view of a cause where there is no cause is said to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*).
And "the view of a path where there is no path" is to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
[as is] "mere morality and vows."

Even the moral conduct and observances (*śīlavratam*) of Buddhists lead to the attainment of liberation, yet they do not consist of that alone; therefore, the view of others holds that the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) applies here as well.
What is the reason that the adherence to rules and observances and so forth is called "adherence to rules and observances"?

Since moral conduct and ascetic observances (*śīlavrata*) are comprised within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including the other aggregates;
why, then, is this [view] not to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*)?
The intention is that because there is a misconception regarding the cause,
the attachment to a cause produced by that [misconception] also exists;
the meaning is that it is also produced by the grasping at a permanent, unitary self as the agent.
"It is abandoned by that very [vision]" means it is abandoned by the vision of suffering alone;
what then of one who perceives the attainment of heaven through such acts as entering water or fire?
How is this adherence to causes— the notion that purity is achieved through moral discipline or ascetic observances—
abandoned by means of the vision of suffering?
"Therefore, this [view] must be abandoned precisely by the vision of the origin"—this is the intention [of the opponent].
The Vaibhāṣika says:
"That too is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering," and so forth; the Vaibhāṣikas [state this] because it is a misconception regarding suffering.
Furthermore, how is it that one is mistaken regarding suffering?
Because of that [mistaken view], there would be an over-extension [of the definition of a view of self] due to seeing purification in going to heaven; thus the Teacher explains in detail.

For all [afflictions] that have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and whose nature is not that of a view (*adṛṣṭisvabhāva*), yet are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and so forth, there would follow the consequence that they must be abandoned by the vision of suffering alone, because they are all mistaken regarding suffering— since every contaminated thing is suffering. And if that were the case, nothing at all would be to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya*) and the other truths.
Furthermore, this other point must be stated:

what kind of other adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned by the vision of the path? For one must also explain that [adherence] which views purification as occurring through the "cow-vow" (*go-śīla*) and so forth, up to the attainment of the transcendence of pleasure and pain.

The Vaibhāṣika says: "This [view] would also have to be recited as 'the adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering,' because it perceives that which is not a cause as being a cause;
rather, it is that which has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of the path."

The teacher [Vasubandhu] maintains that the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which takes as its object the eight [afflictions] beginning with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)— which are to be abandoned by the vision of the path— is itself to be abandoned by the vision of the path; for even that, he says, is a misconception regarding suffering.

For the eight underlying tendencies beginning with wrong view, which are to be abandoned by the vision of the path, are the objective support for the adherence to rules and rituals; and since they are associated with outflows, they are subsumed under the truth of suffering,
and it is in regard to these that [the adherent] is mistaken.
The intention is that [such a view] would be abandonable solely by the vision of suffering; and as for the phrase "of whom," the detailed explanation is:
of whichever person there is no [correct] path—that is, who possesses a false view or doubt directed toward the path as its object.
That person, either seeing that there is no path to liberation or being doubtful, wonders:
"Does the path exist?"
Doubting that [anything] exists,
how could he accept or practice purification through that wrong view, thinking, "By this wrong view" or "by this doubt"?
For precisely because of his association with wrong view and doubt, there is no attainment of purification for him.
"Now, another," and so forth:
having scrutinized and grasped another path to liberation imagined by the Sāṅkhyas and others,
he says, "This Buddhist path to liberation does not exist."
He too,
that non-Buddhist, believes in purification through that very other [means] imagined by the Sāṃkhyas and others.

It is not because it is a wrong view that this adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of his is established as having for its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
what then?
Furthermore, there is this other fault: that it would have as its object only a path imagined through numbers and so forth;
this is what is meant by the detailed passage beginning with "and also... (yaś cāpi).
Furthermore, why is it that one who possesses wrong view and believes in purification through a wrong view to be abandoned by the vision of origin and cessation—
that adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)— is not itself to be abandoned by the vision of those [truths]? This is the meaning.
Therefore, this matter must be examined,

because this adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) cannot be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), nor can it be abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).

Because of faults such as over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), this matter— the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)— must be examined as to whether it is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) or by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*); thus,
the Master has raised this point of doubt.
This is not his own view; others say it was formulated out of regard for the Yogācāra perspective,
for the Yogācāras describe one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*).

For just as these ten underlying tendencies (anuśaya)— namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)— are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśana), so too [are the others].
False view,
adherence to views, and adherence to rules and observances.
Doubt, attachment, and aversion.
Pride and ignorance— these ten are likewise to be abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].
In the same way, there are ten to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and ten to be abandoned by the vision of the path; thus,
there are forty [afflictions] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by vision.
However, those to be abandoned by cultivation are the six:
the false view of a self-entity and the view of nihilism.
Innate attachment, aversion, and pride.
Including ignorance, there are forty-six latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm;
however, there are forty-one belonging to the form realm, which are these same [forty-six] excluding hostility (pratigha).
Just as it is with those belonging to the form realm, so it is with those belonging to the formless realm; regarding this, someone has stated a meditative concentration.

Regarding what was said— that there would be an over-extension [of the definition] because all those whose objects are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are mistaken with respect to suffering— we reply: there is no over-extension, because the misconception occurs specifically by way of [the aspects of] suffering and so forth.
Although those with outflows have objects of perception that are mistaken regarding the truth of suffering,
nevertheless, some are mistaken by way of the aspect of suffering, while others are mistaken by way of the aspect of its origin.
Some are those who are mistaken regarding cessation, while others are those who are mistaken regarding the path;
therein, those who are mistaken regarding suffering by way of the aspect of suffering [are as follows].
Those [afflictions] are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering,
as is the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); because one misapprehends suffering through the gateway of suffering by grasping at it as permanent and as a self,
it is therefore to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

But as for those who have gone astray regarding the path— such as the Sāṅkhyas, Nirgranthas, and others— who, having adopted a path of their own fabrication, give rise to the false view that "there is no path to liberation for the Buddhists," and regard that false view as being foremost [in its excellence], this is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of theirs is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*),
because it is a perversion due to being mistaken regarding the path;
however, there is no such adherence to rules and observances that would constitute a perversion by way of the origin [of suffering].
Nor could one who is mistaken regarding [the truths] by way of cessation be considered mistaken;
therefore, the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) must be abandoned precisely through the vision of suffering and the path.
But how is it that one does not become mistaken by way of the origin and cessation?
Regarding this, the Master Saṅghabhadra says:

"The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned through the vision of the origin and the cessation [of suffering], because its essential nature cannot be established;
for it is an attachment to what is not a cause as being a cause."
Furthermore, the adherence to what is not the path as being the path constitutes the body of the "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);

and within the false view that negates origination (*samudayāpavādikā mithyādṛṣṭi*), there is the adherence to [such practices] as purification. Would it not then follow for him that the perception of birth occurs without cause?
In some cases, because there is no cognition of a cause,
and since suffering and its origin are not distinct in substance, even the aggregates such as the Lord (Īśvara) and so forth would be excluded by that [definition].

However, regarding the false view that denies cessation (*nirodhāpavādikā mithyādṛṣṭi*), since one has returned to [the notion of] purification, the very conception of a means for cessation is impossible;
how could there be no cessation? For, following upon such a view, the conception of a means for it would be futile.
And thus, the body of the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is untenable;
for even the adherence to rules and rituals that is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*) is not possible in this way,
because it is impossible to falsely imagine a path following the vision [of the truth] with the thought, "The path does not exist."

For one who possesses wrong view or doubt regarding the path as its object— either seeing that "there is no path to liberation" or being uncertain— how could such a person expect purification through it? Thus, it is entirely logical that there is an adherence to purification within this wrong view that denies the Noble Path.
