For by grasping that [view] through reasoning, another path to liberation is indeed established in his heart; for this reason,
a notion of "reasoning" arises in him toward false view, which denies the truly existent path.
This is the logical principle: that there is no other path to liberation,

and that one who doubts whether another path to liberation exists or not is acting according to logic, for it is only through such logic that the adoption of the means to purification becomes possible.

Furthermore, that other path to liberation which has been established in his heart is not at all the object of that adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path,
because it takes as its objective support only that which belongs to its own category.
Now, it might be thought that even that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is practiced due to the power of conceptualizing it;
for another place of liberation has been established within his heart by him.
Since he has, by way of logic, grasped this false view which denies the existence of true liberation,
therefore [the opponent's claim] that "this is the same" is incorrect.
Because it is impossible for there to be an adherence to purity when that [purity] is negated by the universal apprehension of eternal peace;
for indeed, when there is a distinction in the realization of substance and non-substance, someone seeks the means to liberation, and the certainty arises: "Liberation certainly exists for him."
And for one who possesses a firm certainty regarding liberation, there is necessarily a constant grasping for that [state],
because otherwise a longing for it would be impossible.

In this regard, just as there is a distinction among those who follow unrighteous paths regarding whether *nirvāṇa* is a substantial entity or a non-entity— due to the commonality of grasping it as eternally peaceful— and yet a fault is seen in their denial of it; likewise,

even for one who has placed some state of liberation within his heart, because of the commonality of grasping it as eternally peaceful, the adoption of the correct principle (*nyāya*) is appropriate when that [erroneous] view of liberation is refuted.
For ethical discipline, ascetic observances, and so forth, are indeed distinct from the noble path both by way of their intrinsic nature and their aspects; however,
since there is no distinction in the apprehension of eternal tranquility,
there is no commonality of conceptual construction.

Therefore, it is possible that the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned only by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*), and not by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*); thus,
in this context, the Abhidharmikas maintain that the adherence to rites and rituals is of two types.
In this regard, what kind of adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is established as being abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*),
and what kind is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*)?
For even one who believes that purity is attained through the "cow-vow" (*go-śīla*) and so forth [is included].

Likewise, that adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) which perceives a path where there is no path— having as its object such things as [the mistaken belief that] morality and observances are the cause of suffering—
is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*).
That which has the wrong practice regarding the path as its object is to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
that which has [wrong] conduct and vows, etc., as its object is [to be abandoned by the vision of suffering].
It does not obstruct as much as that which has the misconception regarding the path as its object.
Because the object consisting of moral precepts, vows, and so forth is coarse,
not far-reaching, not firm in its underlying intention, and easily destroyed with little effort;
whereas its opposite is the object of the deviation from the path.
"From the three views, there are the four perversions" indicates that the perversions have the three views as their intrinsic nature.

The intention is that because of the view of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryadṛṣṭi*), there is the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the inversion regarding the self (*ātmaviparyāsa*), but not the view of "mine" (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*);
this is the opinion of another [teacher].
The meaning is that the entire view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—namely, the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*)—is a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
The Vaibhāṣika asks: "How is the view of what belongs to a self a perversion?"
"For it is not called the 'perverse view of what belongs to self' (ātmīya-viparyāsa);
and why should it not exist?"— thus the Vaibhāṣika replies, citing the *Viparyāsa-sūtra*.

Because of the scriptural statement that "the notion of a self in what is not-self is a perversion," there is indeed such a scriptural teaching [regarding the self], but not regarding "what belongs to a self."
Furthermore, how is it that this [view of self] is not something distinct from the view of a self?
For by seeing the self itself as the ruler within those very five aggregates of clinging, one sees what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).

The meaning is that it does not only perceive the self, but also perceives what belongs to the self; thus, this very "view of self" is two-faced. That is to say, it is a single [view] that exists as a substantial entity, possessing two faces: the face of "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*) and the face of "mine-making" (*mamakāra*).
Now, from this [view] first mentioned as "I," there would be another view mentioned with the genitive case as "mine";
likewise, "by me" and "for me" would also be another view— this is the context.
Because of the mention of the instrumental case in "mayā" and the mention of the dative case in "mahyam," this [interpretation] is undesirable;
therefore, it is established that [the word] is "sakala."

Why are the other afflictions not considered inversions? [They are not] because, apart from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the others— namely, the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment (*rāga*), and so forth— are [not inversions] for three reasons.
The establishment of the perversions occurs through the superimpositions of inverted investigation,
wherein all these causes are present.
Those [factors] are established as inversions;
however, where they are not all present,
it is said that they are not inversions.
"Because of taking as an object the purity of that alone" means that one takes as an object and determines that purity comes through mere morality and observances (*śīlavratamātra*).
Therefore, the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively perverted;
for it is not that the rule and observance itself is not a cause of purification, but rather that it alone is not [sufficient].
How is this [ignorance] a superimposition?
Because it superimposes the state of being a cause of purification upon that which is merely [the object].
If non-investigation were not a perversion, then what about that which was stated in the Sūtra?
How then is it that neither perception nor mind are the twelve perversions?
Regarding the four inversions, how is it said that each consists of the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*)?
It is explained as follows: "the permanent in the impermanent," and so forth, up to "the self in the non-self."
There are three perversions of perception, view, and mind regarding suffering as being pleasure;
these same three regarding the impure as being pure, and likewise these same three regarding what is not-self as being self. Thus, there are exactly three for each.
In that regard, eight are to be abandoned by vision:
the perversion of perception, mind, and view consisting in [taking] the impermanent to be permanent;
and the perversion of view consisting in [taking] the impure to be pure.
Which four are to be abandoned by cultivation? It is said:
the perversions of perception and thought regarding suffering, and likewise regarding the impure.
The two inversions of perception and mind regarding suffering as pleasure,
and the other two inversions of perception and mind regarding the impure as pure— these four belong to a noble one who is not yet free from passion.
For the stream-enterer and the once-returner as well, there are those two opposites,
because of the manifestation of the perception of a sentient being and the manifestation of the mind of a sentient being.
The intention is: why are their opposites not also accepted?
Why are the misconceptions regarding perception and mind that take sentient beings as their object not also accepted?
And why are the misconceptions regarding a self not also accepted?
They ask: "For what reason? [The answer is:
"Because sensual desire is not possible toward a woman or toward oneself without the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*).

Therefore, it follows that these two—the misconception of self in what is not-self (*anātman*) and the corresponding perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*)—are also to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Because of the word "in detail" (*vistara*), it should be understood as follows: the perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), the perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*)—namely, [perceiving] pleasure in suffering, purity in the impure, and so on up to a self in the non-self—are abandoned.
Therefore, these perversions of perception and mind occur only when they arise from views and are associated with views, not otherwise.
The meaning is "not associated with wrong view";
what is being said is that there exists this confusion of perception and mind.
But it is not a perversion,
because that [view] does not arise from a [fundamental] view;
if one asks why, he says:
The phrase "because it is merely an error at that time" means that at the time of seeing the woman, it is merely an error;
for it is precisely at that very moment— the moment of seeing— that the noble ones (āryas) experience an error.
Likewise, false cognition occurs like the delusion of a whirling firebrand or a painted yakṣa;
just as when a firebrand is whirled rapidly, a delusion arises that it is a wheel for the mere duration of that time.
It is just as when one sees a yakṣa painted on a wall later on, and at that very moment, the delusion arises that it is a yakṣa.
Because the Noble One contemplates this [state], there arises for a brief moment the delusion of pleasure or purity, or the delusion of a sentient being;
however, this is not a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, lapses of mindfulness do indeed arise in the learned noble disciple, but they are slow."
And yet, they quickly go to their setting, exhaustion, and total disappearance.

If that is merely a delusion of perception and mind and not a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*), then what about the passage beginning with "the Elder Ānanda"? This was said by the noble Vāgīśa to the Elder Ānanda.
"Because I am overcome by sensual desire, my mind is burning;
O Gautama, please tell me how to attain peace out of compassion."
The noble Ānanda replied to him:
"Your mind is being consumed by perceptions that are perverted;
therefore, abandon the sign associated with passion for what is beautiful."
Thus, he is indeed a stream-enterer; and by this verse, the existence of the perversions is elucidated.
Therefore, [the passage] beginning with "therefore" is explained in detail.
Since the doctrine of other schools is contradicted by the Vaibhāṣikas through scripture, and the Vaibhāṣika doctrine is likewise contradicted by those of other schools,
others maintain that all eight distortions of perception and mind remain uneliminated in one who is still in training (śaikṣa).
Some who belong to the third position also avoid the contradiction with the Sūtra, asking:
"Of which Sūtra?"

As for this sūtra cited by the Vaibhāṣikas, beginning with "the learned noble disciple" and continuing in detail up to "is abandoned," as well as that which begins with "of the noble truths" and so forth— [these are the proofs].
Furthermore, those eight distortions of perception and mind are abandoned through the knowledge of the noble truths, such as suffering and so forth, exactly as they are;
they are not abandoned without that knowledge of reality as it is.

Thus, because of the explanation of the means and the application of those means, there is no contradiction in that Sūtra which states: "This is the noble truth of suffering; this is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
This was not stated with reference to the path of seeing alone.
What then?
It is also the path of cultivation;
for the path of cultivation is likewise untainted and has precisely the four noble truths as its object.
"Due to the difference in activity" means "due to the difference in aspect";
[this refers to] "the attainment of a distinction that was not previously attained."

The "attainment of distinction" (*viśeṣādhigama*) refers to the realization and direct manifestation of those distinguished phenomena— both contaminated and uncontaminated— which are based upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
this occurs when such attainment has not yet been reached or brought face-to-face.
The conceit "I have attained this special realization" is pride;
the conceit "I am virtuous" in one who lacks virtue,
or "I am possessed of virtues" in one who is not endowed with virtues, is pride with a perverted object, which is false pride (*mithyāmāna*).

What is the specific distinction between false pride (*mithyāmāna*) and overweening pride (*abhimāna*)? Overweening pride is the intention regarding a quality that merely resembles the attainment of a superior distinction one has actually acquired; it is "with a basis" (*savastuka*). False pride, however, is the thought "I possess qualities" when one is actually devoid of qualities; it is "without a basis" (*nirvastuka*).
"Types of pride" (mānavidhā) means varieties of pride. One should say:

"the type of pride thinking 'I am equal,' the type of pride thinking 'I am inferior,' and the type of pride thinking 'I am superior. (Note: *sadṛśo* and *hīno* appear to be scribal errors for *sadṛśo* and *viśiṣṭo* respectively). Thus, the types of pride are to be stated as: "I am equal," "I am inferior," and "I am superior."
"The three based on views" refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*); they are said to be "based on views" because the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) first arises as "I."
Immediately thereafter, these types of pride—excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride (*māna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*)—arise in their respective order.
How so? "I am superior" is a form of pride based upon a [wrong] view; this is excessive pride (*atimāna*).
The conceit based on views consisting in the thought "I am equal" is conceit (*māna*). The conceit based on views consisting in the thought "I am inferior" is the conceit of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).

This second triad is to be understood in reverse order, respectively, as being based on views: "There is one superior to me," "There is one equal to me," and "There is one inferior to me"—these being the conceit of inferiority, conceit (*māna*), and excessive conceit (*atimāna*).

The third [type of pride] consists of the views based on [the notions]: "There is none superior to me," "There is no one equal to me," and "There is no one inferior to me"—these being, respectively, pride (māna), overweening pride (atimāna), and pride of inferiority (ūnamāna).
However, this is according to the explanation found in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
What is this "explanation of the presentation of the chapters" that was mentioned previously?
The instruction that "I am superior to the inferior" or "equal to the equal," and so forth,

may also constitute the pride of thinking "I am better," because the definition of pride includes such thoughts as "I am superior to the inferior" or "equal to the equal" in relation to those who are inferior.
This might also be overweening pride (*atimāna*), because the definition of overweening pride is "I am superior to one who is equal";
it might also be pride-beyond-pride (*mānātimāna*), because [it occurs] in relation to one who is superior.

Because of the definition of the characteristics of pride (*māna*) and excessive pride (*atimāna*) as "I am superior to one who is superior," the inclusion of the term "all" implies that the pride of self-existence (*asmimāna*) is also to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
not merely the remaining types.
The phrase "not necessarily" is used to demonstrate that the other [defilements] are also to be abandoned by vision, not merely the conceit "I am."
The rule is that what has been abandoned does not manifest;
for instance, faith and so forth, as well as the faculty of sleep, the faculty of suffering, and the eye-faculty and others, continue to manifest even though they have been abandoned,
because those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing are inward-looking.
Since informative action (*vijñapti*) is instigated by attachment, aversion, and delusion which have as their objective support only that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),
the obsession with killing and so forth is itself to be abandoned only by cultivation.
Thus, it is called "the obsession with killing and so forth" which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech;
these are to be abandoned by cultivation because they have as their object those phenomena that are to be abandoned by cultivation.

Since the factors such as killing and so forth, which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), are its object (*ālambana*), one might ask why the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and others are not also considered to be abandoned by cultivation. Although these too take factors abandoned by cultivation as their objects, they do not consist *exclusively* of factors abandoned by cultivation; therefore, they themselves are not abandoned by cultivation, and thus there is no aspiration for them therein.
In that regard, concerning the impermanence of the three realms, if one asks whether there is also a longing for that [impermanence],
he says: "There is."

As it is said in the Sūtra: "As long as this self lives, remains, subsists, and maintains itself, so long is it accompanied by disease, accompanied by abscesses, accompanied by arrows, accompanied by fever, and accompanied by burning sensations."
And because one grasps at this self as being annihilated, perishing, and no longer existing,
thinking "to this extent this self is completely and utterly annihilated," a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) is thereby apprehended.
The craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*)—such as "O, would that I were Airāvaṇa, the king of elephants"—does not manifest.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [desires] such as "May I be Kuvera" or "May I be a woman" are included;
by mentioning these specific instances, it is shown that [cravings] such as "May I be Indra" do indeed manifest.
It has been stated that even those [defilements] belonging to the realm of desire are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*),
because of the statement: "They are destroyed by vision and cultivation" (*dṛgbhāvanā-kṣaya*).
Furthermore, since the modes [of affliction] such as *vidhā* and so forth do not occur for a noble one (*ārya*),
it was previously stated that the term "to be abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) includes [only those afflictions] that are not *asmitā*.
The abandonments through vision and cultivation, the outbursts such as killing, and likewise the desire for non-existence are to be abandoned through cultivation.
By this passage,
the noble conduct (*āryasamudācāra*) of those [persons] such as the *vidha* is now being described; however, the *vidha* and so forth do not actually exist for a noble one (*ārya*).
By the inclusion of the phrase "not 'I'" and so forth, there is the inclusion of everything up to the craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*);
the meaning is that this includes the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing, the craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*), a portion [of the latter], and the craving for existence itself.
They do not arise and do not manifest because they are nourished by [wrong] views.
Because it is preceded by that [wrong view] and reinforced by it,

the outburst of killing and so forth is nourished by wrong view; the meaning is that through the habitual practice of that [view], one denies the results of karma, and thus, due to the absence of anything to sustain it, its back is broken.
Regret is universal because it has as its object those factors that are to be abandoned by cultivation, and it is itself to be abandoned by cultivation.
They are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) because they go everywhere;
the meaning is that they take all five categories as their object.
Others maintain that they exist as the causal condition for all five categories.
For he will say: "By the power of these, even afflictions belonging to other categories arise," and so on in detail regarding the eleven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
There are seven views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*), namely the five beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
There are two views to be abandoned by the vision of the origin: false view and the view of holding [wrong] views as supreme;
seven [factors], namely two doubts to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin, and two ignorances to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin.

They exist partially and not in their entirety; for those two types of ignorance— namely, that which is associated with the universal [defilements] and that which is independent— are present only in part.
These two alone are universal, not those associated with attachment and so forth;
thus, eleven latent dispositions (anuśaya) are universal,
while nine latent dispositions are universal in their entirety.
Since two are [identical] in part,
why is it that, by way of the distinction of elements (*dhātu*), there are thirty-three [qualities] called "unshared" (*āveṇikī*)? What is the meaning?
Thus they say:
"Contact is called *veṇi*;
that which is not *veṇi* is *aveṇi*."
The meaning is "separateness. For it has been said: "The Blessed One is distinct, the community of monks is distinct";
the intention is that the Blessed One is separate and the community of monks is separate.
It functions as a unique [mental factor],
meaning it does not coexist with other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*);
this is because its object of cognition (*ālambana*) is the entirety of its own realm.
Because these [defilements] take their entire own realm as their object, they are called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*).
As for the phrase "by what is it 'entire'?", the detailed explanation follows.

Who would believe that purification comes from the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), or who would regard the entire realm of desire—which is not a cause—as a cause? This is the point under discussion; therefore, the intention is that the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
It is not said that they apprehend their own realm in its entirety, without remainder, and in its many diverse divisions simultaneously;
rather, they apprehend all five types simultaneously,
from those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to those to be abandoned by cultivation.

"This word 'all' (sarva) should be understood as referring to all modes" is the Vaibhāṣika resolution [to the objection] that "the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) consists in [clinging to] the five aggregates of grasping (pañca-upādānaskandha)."

In that regard, their craving for a self arises because [the aggregates] are the basis for the adherence to a self; and regarding that object characterized by the five aggregates of clinging, where there is the view of excellence and the view of purification, there is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The view of purification is the adherence to rules and observances;
therein, the longing is characterized by craving.
Regarding this, some read the text as "the longing for that."
In that regard, "desire for that object" means the desire of that person for that [object];
and "pride by means of that" means pride by means of that object.
The meaning is that there is elevation by way of that;
"this being so" means this being the case when craving and pride are universal.

Because they have as their objects those things to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation—just like the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and so forth—these two, characterized by the fire of craving, must be abandoned: what is to be abandoned, and by what means?
Is it to be abandoned by seeing, or rather by cultivation?
[This applies to] those which have as their objects that which is to be abandoned by seeing.
Having in mind the rule that "those [defilements] are to be abandoned by seeing that," he asks;
for otherwise, just like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, both of these would necessarily be abandonable only by seeing—so what would there be to ask?
For it is not the case that the view of a self-identity and the others do not have objects that are abandonable by both seeing and cultivation.
And it is not the case that these are not to be abandoned by seeing;
regarding this, the Master states the resolution:
"Because that which is to be abandoned by cultivation has a mixed object."
If craving and pride were to have only those things abandoned by seeing as their objects, they would themselves be abandoned by seeing;
however, this is not the case.
Therefore, because their objects are mixed, they are to be abandoned by cultivation.
"Or rather, because of the restriction of the definition that the remaining [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya)."
That same teacher, turning back, speaks again: "Let it be [furthermore] that which is to be abandoned by vision;
what [is the point]?"
The phrase "both of these" carries over from the previous context; therefore, he says:
"because they proceed by the power of being sustained by vision."
The strengthening of view is its capacity;

that which has the habit of operating by means of the strengthening of view is "operating through the strengthening of view" (*dṛṣṭibalādhānavarti*); both of those [terms] constitute that state (*tadbhāva*).
Therefore,
let both of those be abandoned by vision;
thus the Vaibhāṣika now establishes his own position.
These two are afflictions with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*); they do not become universal afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*).
Therefore, they are not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*), wherever the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) occurs.
In that regard, craving and pride do not arise simultaneously in all [objects],
because they are afflictions with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*).
For those two have a limited scope as their object;
therefore, they are not universal,
and if they are not universal, [they do not constitute universal outflows].

Therefore, it is established that those two which have as their objects what is to be abandoned by seeing are themselves to be abandoned by seeing, while the remaining ones are to be abandoned by cultivation.
It has not been stated that it sometimes takes one dissimilar realm as its object, sometimes two, or sometimes three realms.
However, those residing in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) sometimes take as their object a dissimilar single realm, either the form realm (rūpadhātu) or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
and sometimes both the form and formless realms;
this is because they do not grasp them as "self" or "belonging to self."
Because one does not grasp that Brahmā as "self" or "belonging to self," there is no view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) regarding Brahmā;
and because the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises from the view of a real body.
Therefore, even the view of eternity regarding that Brahman is not a view that grasps at extremes;
what then is this view?
It is the view of existence regarding Brahman.
And this is not the view of eternalism; rather, because its object is inverted, this is a false cognition. Thus, it is a false cognition.
For not every wisdom that has a perverted object is considered a "view" (dṛṣṭi).
Wisdom that is perverted in the sense of [perceiving] a self in what is non-self is considered the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi),
as well as the view of permanence (nityadṛṣṭi) and the view of grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) which are produced by that [self-view].
For there is no other;
indeed, that which serves as the basis for ego-conceit is itself the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Furthermore, the view of a sentient being in the Great Brahmā realm does not serve as a basis for the conceit "I am";
therefore it was said [in the sūtra], "because of not grasping [him] as self or belonging to self.
Thus, those factors that arise simultaneously [with the afflictions] are excluded from [the category of] acquisition (*prāpti*).
Thus,
while sensation and the other [factors] are as described, acquisitions (prāpti) are not so, because they have multiple fruits.
For it has been stated that acquisitions (*prāpti*) possess multiple fruits— namely, fruition (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*);
therefore, the acquisitions of universal factors (*sarvatragadharma*) are not established as being universal themselves,
and for this very reason [it is said].
Since even co-existent [factors] are established as universal,
a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is formulated:
the first alternative consists of the future universal proclivities (anuśaya).
Because these possess the nature of being universal,

they are not a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) in their future state, since a universal cause is not established while in the future; the second category consists of those co-arising factors in the past and present.

The universal [factors] and those that arise simultaneously are universal causes because they are past or present; however, the universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) themselves are not [the cause], because their intrinsic nature is not that of a proclivity. The third and fourth [categories] should be applied accordingly.
The third [category] consists of the omnipresent latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the past and the present;
the fourth consists of those same aspects excluding them, namely, the future ones and their co-existent factors such as acquisitions (prāpti) and so forth.
"Six have the uncontaminated as their object" is a restriction meaning that there are exactly six.

Therefore, it is not logical for passion and the other afflictions to have the untainted as their object; for passion is not such an object because it is to be abandoned, and because of such statements as "not due to non-harmfulness," and so forth.
And ignorance [associated] with those two refers to that ignorance which is associated with wrong view and doubt,
as well as the independent ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

That single latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) consists of three [types] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), which have only the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;
likewise, those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) are also these same three. Thus, there are six [latent tendencies] for each stage (*bhūmi*).
They are the objects of those whose range is that; thus, since cessation and the path are their range, they are called "those whose range is that."
For those three, respectively,
there is cessation within their own level.
The cessation of its own level is the range and the object of focus.

But how is it that the Path— consisting of the six stages belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge and the nine stages belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge— is the objective support for the other three latent tendencies that have the Path as their domain? How so?
These three latent dispositions (anuśaya) have cessation as their object; they belong to nine stages, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
Among them, for those belonging to the desire realm, only the cessation of phenomena belonging to the desire realm is their object.

For those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the object of focus is precisely the cessation of phenomena belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; likewise, for those up to the level of the peak of existence (bhavāgra), the object of focus is precisely the cessation of phenomena belonging to the level of the peak of existence.
However, the path belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) pertains to six levels.
That which belongs to the stages of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), as well as that belonging to the four dhyāna stages—
all of these are the objective support (*ālambana*) for these three proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm;
furthermore, that which pertains to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) belongs to nine stages.

That which belongs to the stages of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness—
each and every one of these is exclusively the object (*ālambana*) of these three underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna,
and so on up to those belonging to the stage of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

Why, then, is only the cessation of its own level the object-sphere (*gocara*) and focal point (*ālambana*) for those [afflictions], whereas the Path (*mārga*), even when belonging to six levels or nine levels, is also their object? To this he shows:
"For the Path is mutually causal."
How is it that the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge, which pertains to the six stages, is mutually causal? It serves as the cause for both the lower and the higher paths;
likewise, that [path] belonging to the category of anvaya-knowledge, which pertains to the nine stages, should be applied accordingly. This has been explained in detail.

Regarding the statement, "The path of each other's nine stages is [the object] for the equal and the superior," this means that for those [paths] belonging to the desire realm which have the path as their object, the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna-pakṣya) belonging to the stage of the threshold concentration (anāgamya-bhūmika) up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna serves as the object.

The path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), whether it belongs to the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) up to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), is indeed the object of those [afflictions] belonging to the first dhyāna stage that take the path as their object; and so on, up to those belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

This is the case if the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) that take the path as their object—such as false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and others—also take as their object the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) known as cessation and the path, which is the antidote to the form and formless realms.

Since the entire category of the side of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣya*) is mutually causal, why do those very [afflictions] such as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth not also take as their object the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣya*), given that dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge are mutually causal? To this he says:
"Even though dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge... and so on.
Since subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is not an antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
those [beings] do not take it as their object; however,
since dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) is an antidote to the desire realm, it also takes the antidotes to the form and formless realms as its object.
"In that case, [it is] dharma-knowledge," and so forth;
that dharma-knowledge which pertains to cessation or the path on the path of cultivation is the antidote to the three realms.

According to this established tenet (*siddhānta*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the realms of form and formlessness; because of its existence, it will serve as the object (*ālambana*) for those factors belonging to those levels—namely, the realms of form and formlessness—such as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, but not in their entirety. To elaborate:
that knowledge of phenomena is not the antidote to the realms of form and formlessness in their totality.
What then? What is the reason?

It is because the knowledge of the dharma regarding the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudayadharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*), when included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), do not serve as antidotes to these [two realms];
that is to say, they are not antidotes to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).

Therefore, the knowledge of those phenomena (dharmajñāna) is not the object of false views and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, nor is it [the object] of both realms in their entirety; this is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, that knowledge of phenomena is not the antidote for the entirety of the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the reason?
Because it is not an antidote to those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing;
thus, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding cessation or the path belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because of this statement, there is no conclusion here that "it is not an object-support" (*ālambana*) due to the absence of the first [two];

for, among the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, the two former— the dharma-knowledge of suffering and the dharma-knowledge of origin— lack the nature of being antidotes to the form and formless realms as previously described.

Because that *dharmajñāna* lacks the nature of being an antidote (*pratipakṣatva*) toward the defilements of the form and formless realms— whether they are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) or by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)— among those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing in the first [moment],
it does not serve as an object for the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth belonging to those levels which take the Path as their object.

Thus, it is established that, excluding those eighteen untainted (*anāsrava*) objects belonging to the three realms, the remaining eighty latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have tainted (*sāsrava*) objects.
"It should not be abandoned" means that it should not be relinquished by the severance of its acquisition (*prāpti*),
just as the wholesome desire for the Dharma, which consists of aspiration, is not to be relinquished by the severance of its acquisition because it is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
In the same way, this [hatred] would not have uncontaminated phenomena as its object, because there is no harm [to be done].
Nor is it hatred, because there is no injury.
Thus,
because cessation and the path are free from the characteristics of the nine bases of malice, there is no hatred toward them,
as they are pure in their true nature.
Purity in the sense of ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) is cessation (*nirodha*),
because it is the abandonment of the stains of the afflictions (*kleśamala*);
the path (*mārga*) is also purity in the ultimate sense (*paramārthaśuddhi*), because one becomes pure through it by way of the ultimate.
It is not tenable to establish that the grasping at those two as purity is "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*),
because they are supreme; and they are supreme because cessation and the path are supreme in terms of their being the reality of purity.

Furthermore, if the two types of misapprehension (*parāmarśa*) were to have uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects, they would partake of the characteristics of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), because uncontaminated phenomena are pure and supreme.

Consequently, they would not be abandonable by seeing (*darśana-heya*). For it is logical that the "misapprehension of views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists in grasping at what is inferior as being supreme.
And since cessation and the path are not thus [perceived], the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)— which consists in grasping them as supreme— does not occur with respect to them;
how many [defilements] adhere by way of their object?
He does not ask with the restriction "how many only through association" or "how many only through the object," because those which increase by way of the object [also increase] through association.
Those which necessarily adhere through association—
namely, those that adhere solely by way of association—
do not adhere by way of object; these are the latent dispositions (anuśaya) whose objects are the untainted (anāsrava) or those belonging to a different level (visabhāga-bhūmi).
In this context, the meaning of "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is the sense of "conformity.
It is not the case that the conditions belonging to that [particular] level exist in conformity for the sake of its arising,
nor is it that they are favorable to it.
Furthermore, cessation and the other [truths] are not conducive to those [defilements] such as false view,
just as dry food is not conducive to one suffering from wind-disorder;
for when it is said that "dry food does not agree with one suffering from wind-disorder," it is understood that it does not function in accordance with the body's needs.
In the former position, however, it is for the sake of attaining a foundation, because of the statement that "one does not find a foundation in them";
[the phrase] "by which dharma" refers to feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
And that [cause] does not exist for those two;
thus, that suffering does not exist for those two, the realms of form and formlessness.
Why?
Because of the absence of a cause for harming others; "harming others" refers to malice and so forth, and because of the non-existence of that.
"This is the foremost of the views" means that this is distinguished from other types of views because it is not excessively blameworthy.
Liberation is the secret doctrine of the path, whereas annihilation is intended to be without cause; thus, due to delusion, there is necessarily a view of annihilation—this is the distinction.
Regarding "because of being deluded about one's own substance":

because of grasping the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) that constitute one's own continuum as "self" and "belonging to self," the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is deluded regarding its own substance.
For them, the view of grasping at the extremes of eternalism and nihilism is likewise; and just as that view is,
so too is the ignorance associated with it.
And because they proceed without afflicting others,
why are the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) considered indeterminate? This is the subject under discussion.
For those two indeed do not cause any harm to others;

yet this same [charge of being neutral] would apply to craving for rebirth in heaven and to pride as well, because they are not in contradiction with giving and so forth, and because—due to being deluded regarding one's own property and due to not engaging in harming others—they are neutral. With this intention, he presents the opinion of the former masters (pūrvācārya).
"Innate view of a self-existent body" and so forth;
however, that which is "conceptualized" as unwholesome is that which has been conceptualized by those who propound a self, such as Kapila, Ulūka, and others.
Is that indeterminate? Rather, it is unwholesome.
The view of grasping at extremes, which is also conceptualized by them,
is likewise unwholesome.
Because it is preceded by that [previous statement], it is understood even if not explicitly stated that "the remaining ones here are impure," as they belong to the same category.
The word "here" (*iha*) is used for the purpose of including the remainder of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*); thus,
it is determined that in the desire realm, the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*), such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).

How many of these sixty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), and how many are not? This distinction is made as follows: among those [sixty-eight], in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the unwholesome roots are attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), and delusion (*mūḍhi*).
Thus,
in the desire realm, those [afflictions] which are attachment, aversion, and delusion—
all of them without exception— are the five types of unwholesome roots.
Because it is established as the adversary to the roots of virtue,
it is not [simply] other latent dispositions;
"delusion" (mūḍhi) is a synonym for ignorance (moha).

Since all delusion is included here [within the category of ignorance] by virtue of being associated with the delusion connected to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), why is it not stated in the Sūtra that "the foul" (*aśubhā*) is obtained here?
Thus, because of the governing context and because of the indication of a single part,
it is for this very reason said:
"If that which is unwholesome is intended to be the root of the unwholesome itself."

Because of the restrictive determination "only these [are unwholesome roots]," it is established that the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), such as false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth, are not unwholesome roots;
thus, among these ninety-eight latent dispositions, three are neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*).
Regarding the statement "there are three neutral roots," the inclusion of the number "three" is for the purpose of distinguishing this from the opinion of the outsiders (Bahirdeśakas).
It is thus shown that there are exactly three and not four; as to which three they are, he says:
craving, ignorance, and that [which is] understanding.
By saying "that" (*sā*), he shows its indeterminate nature;
by the phrase "indeterminate roots" (*avyākṛtamūlāni*),
he shows that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) are qualified by this term "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) alone.
And here, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that even a state of mind whose intrinsic nature is free from affliction is considered a root of the indeterminate—
namely, whatever indeterminate craving arises in the case of the dhyānas and formless attainments associated with relish, or at the time of rebirth within celestial palaces and the like.

Whatever ignorance there may be in the form and formless realms, as well as in the desire realm, that is associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
likewise, whatever wisdom there may be that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
even including that born of maturation (*vipākaja*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mind of maturation (*vipākaja*), the deportment (*airyāpathika*), the occupational (*śailpasthānika*), and the transformative (*nirmāṇa*), as well as that associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), wisdom associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*) and associated with [minds] such as those born of maturation, is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) according to its occurrence, because it functions in two ways.
Dvaidha is the state of being twofold; it is the function [of the mind] within that state of duality.
Doubt cannot be the root [of unwholesome states] because it wavers due to its dualistic mode of operation, characterized by fluctuation.
The characteristic of rising is that by means of it,
there is upward movement.
Therefore, the mind cannot be the root,
because roots are firm and grow downwards; thus, due to this dissimilarity with a root, doubt is not the root because it lacks stability.
"It should be said by you that pride is not [included] because it does not function downwards;
thus, craving is indeterminate (avyākṛta), and [the other factors] are indeterminate."
In the realms of form and formlessness,
there is also [only] view; and in those two realms as well as in the realm of desire, all [eighteen elements] exist.
Regarding those who practice meditation dominated by craving, views, and pride:
one who practices meditation associated with relishing is one who practices meditation dominated by craving.
One who, relying on meditative absorption, gives rise to views such as eternalism and so forth,
is one who practices meditation dominated by views and one who practices meditation dominated by pride.

He who, because of that [attainment], thinks, "I am a master of this dhyāna, and others are not so," is one who practices dhyāna with pride as the preeminent factor; therein, craving is the preeminent factor, and craving is what stands above it.
One whose nature is to meditate thus is a "meditator dominated by craving," and likewise a "meditator dominated by views" and a "meditator dominated by pride."
And they come to be through the power of ignorance;
thus those three meditators, by virtue of ignorance—that is, through association with ignorance—come to be in such a way.
Therefore, ignorance also is an indeterminate root.

And he inquires by way of connection with the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), [asking] how these states of the manifestation of afflictions for those who have entered meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) constitute the root cause of indeterminate phenomena—
namely, the fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) mentioned in detail in the Sūtra.
"The world is eternal," "the world is non-eternal," and so forth.
Why is it that because they are indeterminate (avyākṛta),
those things are neither wholesome nor unwholesome? Is it because they are indeterminate that they are not designated as indeterminate entities?
A question to be set aside is explained as follows: that which is not explained— that is, not stated—
by way of being set aside is an unexplained question.
Its basis is the entity;
thus, in connection with that, this is introduced:
"For there are four kinds of questions," and so forth.
"Like death, birth, distinction, self, otherness,
and so forth" means like death, like birth, like distinction, and like self, otherness, and so forth.
The examples for the categorical (ekāṃśa) and other types of responses are given in their respective order: "They will die" is the example for a categorical response;
"Those with afflictions will be born, not those free from afflictions" is the example for birth in the case of a response that requires analysis (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa).

"Regarding whom do you ask? is an example of answering by asking for clarification (*paripṛcchāvyākaraṇa*). "Is the sentient being other than the aggregates? is an example of answering by setting aside (*sthāpanīyavyākaraṇa*), [as it refers to a non-existent self]. "Will all sentient beings die? is to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśena vyākartavya*) [in the affirmative].
As it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, short is the life of humans; the world beyond must be traversed; one must practice what is wholesome."
Since there is no immortality for one who is born, is the sentient being other than the aggregates or not other? This is to be set aside,
as stated by the Blessed One.
"But, O Gautama, does he who acts experience [the result]?
This is undeclared, Brahmin;
or does one act and another experience [the result]?"

When asked, "O Brahmin, is it undeclared that he who acts is the same one who experiences [the result]? you say, "This is undeclared. When asked, "Is it undeclared that one acts and another experiences [the result]? you say, "This is undeclared."
In this regard, what indeed is the meaning of this statement of yours, venerable Gautama: "He who acts is he who experiences"? To say this, O Brahmin, leads to eternalism;
to say "one acts and another experiences" leads to annihilationism.
"Having followed these two extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma by means of the middle way," so said the Venerable Rāma;
this too must be answered categorically.
"Not all will be born"—
this is not to be answered categorically; rather, "all sentient beings will die," as the Teacher has explained in detail.
But if someone were to ask in this manner, "Will those who are going to die be born again?",
for him there would be an analytical explanation.
Not all will be born;
rather,
those possessed of afflictions will be born.
It is not the case that they are free from afflictions;
therefore, what was said— that this must be answered categorically by saying "not all will be born"— is untenable.
The intention is that, for this reason, the example cited by the Vaibhāṣikas is indeed appropriate; thus, the same Venerable Rāma said:
"And among humans, both [conditions] exist."

Inferiority and superiority—both of these are relative; therefore, both must be explained categorically. For example, when asked whether consciousness is an effect or a cause, it is explained categorically as being both cause and effect, depending on the relationship between cause and fruit.
In that regard, as for what was said— that one must answer by asking back, "Is the human inferior or superior? after first asking, "With respect to whom do you ask this?"—
that is incorrect.
Because this question is to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśena*),
the Master supports the Vaibhāṣika position by stating that [the Buddha] asks with absolute certainty:
"Is a human being exclusively inferior or exclusively superior?"
Because it is not a categorical answer, it is appropriate to analyze whether [the person] is inferior or superior; thus, one asks, "With reference to whom do you ask?
In that regard, it was stated in detail that both [inferiority and superiority] exist only among humans.
That is incorrect;
for he himself has stated that the sentient being is other than the aggregates. All of this [is thus untenable].
As for that which is to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*), the Master has stated this according to the Vaibhāṣika system; "the Abhidharmikas say" refers to these fourfold examples.
For one who has merely studied the six-footed Abhidharma,
there is the designation of suffering up to the designation of the path; that is,
the designation of the four noble truths according to the sūtra.
"Because it is connected with the goal" means "because it is associated with the goal";
this very [phrase] refers to the deceitful person.

Venerable Rāma said that this very statement regarding a question to be answered by analysis should be understood as an answer-by-questioning for an insincere questioner who intends to cause vexation.
"When those two," and so forth in detail:
when those two, the deceitful and the non-deceitful, do not ask anything at all, but merely request, "Speak the Dharma."
And regarding those two, the deceitful and the non-deceitful, nothing is explained as to whether these phenomena—form and so forth—are with their full details and distinctions;
they are merely asked, "Which ones shall I speak of?
How, then, can this be considered a question from these two, the deceitful and the non-deceitful?
And how is the explanation of the Abhidharmika?
For the Master [Vasubandhu] has explained this in detail, beginning with "For he who says,
'Tell me the path,'" to which one ignorant of that [matter] replies.
The intention is this: by the very act of requesting, has he not already asked about the path?
For when one says, "Tell me the way," it is effectively as good as saying, "Which is the way?"
When one says, "Speak thus of the dharmas," it is implied by the question, "Which dharmas?

that there is an answer; and because the answer to that question—or the explanation of those dharmas—is given only after asking, "There are many dharmas; which ones shall I speak of?", the multiplicity of dharmas is considered to be undeclared (*avyākṛta*).
How is it that "not answering by way of questioning" means "answering after having questioned"?
In this regard, it has been stated that of those two [questions], something is explained only after they have been questioned; as for how the explanation is given: [it is as follows].
That is incorrect;
the Teacher said,
"Precisely from the Sūtra," and so forth.
However, it is explained in this way in the Sūtra: having established [the matter] in the refined language (saṃskṛta), it is recited:
"Having performed an intentional action (sañcetanīya-karma), what does one experience?"
When asked, "Is it pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure?", this is a question to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*).
This is because volitional action (*saṃcetanīyakarma*) is divided into categories such as wholesome and so forth;
having performed a wholesome, yet tainted (*sāsrava*), volitional action, one experiences either pleasure or neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

If one were to say, "Having performed an unwholesome intentional action, one experiences suffering," [then] if it is said that this is "gross," there would be no detailed analysis of material form (*rūpi*) and so forth, up to the point of [the view] that the soul (*jīva*) is something other [than the body].
By the word "up to" (yāvat), it is not necessary to state everything;
for example: "The Tathāgata exists after death, and the Tathāgata does not exist after death."
The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; "the soul is that same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another."
The meaning is that because he is conjoined with that [defilement] therein, it is indeed known that the person is bound by that latent tendency (*anuśaya*);
and [this applies to] those afflictions which have their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to an object such as that which is to be experienced as pleasant; since attachment arises there by taking only an object to be experienced as pleasant as its objective support (*ālambana*), it is called an affliction of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*).

Because arrogance arises when that object conducive to pleasant feeling is taken as an objective support, pride (*māna*) is also called a specific affliction (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*). Likewise, because hostility (*pratigha*) arises by taking an object conducive to painful feeling as an objective support, hostility is also called a specific affliction,
as well as a general affliction (*sāmānyakleśa*).
Views, doubt, and so forth are called "universal afflictions" (sāmānyakleśa) because they are afflictions in a general sense;
for these arise without distinction toward objects such as those to be experienced as pleasant.
Therefore, those that have arisen by taking such [objects] as their focal point are called universal afflictions.
"By those past and present" means by those belonging to the past and the present.

"Regarding the detailed explanation, 'in whatever object attachment, aversion, and pride have arisen,' these [afflictions] such as attachment and so forth, although belonging to the six groups of consciousness, because they are considered without distinction, arise— according to their respective application— in whatever object belonging to the three time periods, from that which is to be abandoned by seeing suffering up to that which is to be abandoned by cultivation,
and they have not yet been abandoned."
In that object, one is bound by those afflictions such as attachment,
like an ox tied to a stake by a rope;
for since these are afflictions with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*), they do not necessarily arise in every person, nor in every situation.
The meaning is that they arise in someone with respect to something;
therefore,
those [defilements] which have arisen and have not been abandoned in a particular case...
Thus, that qualification "not abandoned" is a qualification because [the person] was previously bound to a certain object by means of those [defilements], such as attachment and so forth.
If those [defilements] were abandoned, one would not be bound by them in all respects, because they would have been abandoned and their objects would no longer possess latent tendencies; thus,
one would not be bound by these future mental [defilements] in all respects.
Thus, the inclusion of the mental [consciousness] is for the sake of those belonging to its own sphere; for the five groups of sensory consciousnesses are established differently by others.
This is a qualification of attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*);
since pride (*māna*) is necessarily [associated with] the mind,
one is bound by these future [defilements] everywhere— across all three time periods and even within the five classes [of dharmas]— each according to its own nature.
For that entity is not substantial which, even by a defilement as subtle as its own characteristic, is not possessed of passion through attachment, nor possessed of hatred through aversion.
Furthermore, it is not the same as pride (*māna*),
for future instances of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, which have all contaminated things (*sāsrava-vastu*) as their objects, arise in their respective ways in unlimited numbers; thus,
by means of other future instances of passion or aversion (*pratigha*), one is bound to a future object itself.
Since all minds and mental factors are restricted to their respective objects, they are bound to future entities alone by virtue of having the nature of arising;
this is because the five groups of consciousness have the present as their domain.
The mention of "attachment and aversion" [in this context] implies the inclusion of pride, because pride belongs to the mental faculty (*mānasa*),
as stated in the passage: "Those [defilements] to be abandoned by insight (*dṛg-gheya*) are equal to torpor (*middha*) and belong to the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmikā*)."
The word "also" (*api*) indicates that [the latent dispositions] are associated not only with mental [consciousnesses] but also with those belonging to the five groups of sensory consciousness;
they are bound to all objects throughout the three times. For these [dispositions] characterized by non-arising exist only in the future time-period.

Furthermore, their objects shift along with the afflictions (kleśa) and their associated mental factors; for those [afflictions] characterized by non-arising remain directed toward their objects like the *suvarcalā* plant. Thus, those characterized by non-arising do not arise by taking an object as their support.
Therefore, for some, the object of focus is past;
for some, it is present; and for some, it is future.
For their non-arising does not occur solely because of the non-arising of the object;
rather,
it occurs due to the deficiency of conditions.
For the established doctrine is that the totality [of causes] is the fruit of the state, not the fruit of a substance;
however, by all the remaining [factors], it is conjoined with everything everywhere.

The meaning of "bound" (*saṃyukta*) is that one is bound even by views and so forth belonging to the three time periods, even those belonging to various realms, and even with respect to an object of five kinds belonging to the three time periods.
He asks: what is the reason?
And he says: because they are universal afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*).
For these [defilements] arise in everyone with respect to everything,
because they have the five aggregates of clinging as their object; how then can one be bound to that [object] by means of that [defilement]?
How can one be bound to, or liberated from, a past or future object by means of that past or future latent disposition (*anuśaya*)?
Or how are they established in the states of being un-abandoned and abandoned through their connection with the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*)?
Because the characteristics of the conditioned, such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth, function for the sake of the movement of the objects of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, their impermanence is asserted; this is the initial reading of the sutra beginning with "O monks, if form... [which states]:
"Form, whether past or future, is impermanent."
What need is there to mention the present?
Thus seeing, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form and does not delight in future form.
One practices for the sake of revulsion toward, dispassion toward, and cessation of present form.
Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be indifferent toward past form;
however, since past form does exist, [he is indifferent].
Therefore, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form;
and if future form were not to exist, the learned noble disciple would not delight in future form.
But since future form does indeed exist, [he is indifferent toward it].
Therefore, the learned noble disciple does not delight in future form;
and if, monks, past form had not existed— this is the full passage—
it would follow that the learned noble disciple would not have been indifferent toward past form.
The meaning is that because [the object] is free from poison at the time of dispassion, the noble disciple’s mind would not be without expectation regarding past objects;
for when a past form is expected, there is attachment to it.
"Would he have rejoiced? means "would he have desired.

Monks, if present form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not have practiced for the sake of revulsion toward, detachment from, and the cessation of present form; therefore, this was not said, because [the existence of both] is established by both parties. From these two [reasons].
Thus it was previously shown that [this] was stated explicitly;
now, however, the distinction is that it is [stated] by implication and not explicitly:
"mental consciousness would not arise in dependence upon a duality."
If it were specified that [consciousness] has the past and future as its object,
then consciousness itself would not exist due to the absence of an object;
for it is on the basis of there being something to be known (*vijñeya*) that there is consciousness.
And the proof here is that mental consciousness has only an existent object, because its nature is that of apprehension.
"Like visual consciousness" means "from the result."
Past karma, whether wholesome or unwholesome, possesses its own existing characteristic because it produces a fruit at the time of ripening, just like a present dharma.
"The alteration of the state" (bhāvanyathātva) means that there is an alteration of the state of a phenomenon (bhāva) belonging to the past, future, or present;
it does not mean an alteration of the substance (dravya).

The meaning is that there is no alteration in the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth; for when the future [dharma] enters the present time-period, it abandons its future state and acquires its present state.
Even while existing in the present,

gold and milk serve as two examples, respectively, for the purpose of making known the transformation of form and the transformation of quality; for one who maintains that there is a change in characteristics (*lakṣaṇānyathika*), conventional usage depends upon the acquisition of the operation of a characteristic.
Therefore he says: "Dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods, when past is endowed with the characteristic of the past,
yet is not separated from the characteristics of the future and the present," and so forth.
If the future were separated from the past and the present,
then it would follow that the future itself has already arisen or is past; likewise,
if the past were separated from the future and the present, [the same consequence would follow].
The future would become the present, and the present would become the past; the present would be devoid of both the past and the future;

and the future itself would be the present, while the present itself would be the past. For it is by being endowed with a characteristic that has attained its functional activity that something is established [as being in a particular temporal state].
The meaning is that he is not separated from anything other than that;
for this very reason, he provides an illustration:
"For example."
A man is attached to one woman but not detached from the rest; thus,
while his firm resolve of passion (*rāgādhyavasāna*) operates toward that one woman, there is merely the presence of passion (*rāgaprāpti*) toward the other women.

"Not in active operation" refers to the conventional designation made in relation to a particular state by one who maintains that there is a change of state; it means that in whichever state that dharma does not perform its activity (*kāritra*).
In that [time], it is called the future;
in that [time] in which one acts, one is present.
Having entered into that state in which it was obstructed, it is designated as "past"; thus, having reached various states, it is designated differently:
having reached the future state it is "future," and so on, until having reached the past state it is "past."

The meaning is that [the dharma] is designated by terms such as "future" and so forth solely because it has reached states such as the future, being characterized by non-difference rather than being a different substance;
for this very reason, he provides an illustration.
"Just as a single counting-stick," and so forth;
just as a single small ball placed in the unit-place, established in the position of ones, is called "one," so too [it is called] "one hundred" when placed in the hundred-place.
It is said that there are a thousand in a thousand-fold array;
this is with respect to its state,
but not because of any alteration in its intrinsic nature.
Rather,
it is because of the distinction of different positions that another name arises which indicates a difference in number; thus,
with respect to what precedes and follows, they are said to be mutually distinct.
The past and future are designated in dependence upon what precedes and what follows;
that is, the present is designated in dependence upon either what precedes it, namely the past, or what follows it, namely the future;
and the past is designated in dependence upon what follows it, namely the present, or the future.
The conventional usage of the "proponent of change" (anyathānyathika) depends upon the prior and the posterior;
for this very reason, he provides the example:
"Just as one and the same woman is called both mother and daughter."

Just as a single woman is called a "mother" in relation to her daughter and a "daughter" in relation to her mother, so these designations arise through dependence on what precedes and follows, and not because she is a different substance.
That which is the refutation of the Sāṃkhya position is itself the refutation of that position; it should be categorized as belonging to the Sāṃkhya side.
The intention is that the Sāṅkhya position has already been refuted;

furthermore, for the second [position]— that of the Venerable Ghoṣaka as well— a confusion of the time-periods (adhvasaṅkara) would result, such that what is intended as the past time-period [would become indistinct].
How does that which is present also obtain the status of being future? By way of this:
while it is endowed with the characteristics of the past, it is not devoid of the characteristics of the future and the present.

The meaning is that it is indeed endowed [with all characteristics]: even the future is endowed with the characteristic of the future, yet not separated from the characteristics of the past and the present; likewise, the present is endowed with the characteristic of the present, yet not separated from the characteristics of the past and the future—this being the case.
Since each [dharma] possesses the three characteristics, it would follow that it is past, future, and present simultaneously;
thus, the same logic should be applied to the future and the present as well.
What, then, is the similarity here?
Is there a person who possesses only one [of these],
or does a single characteristic of a phenomenon exist,
or rather do no characteristics exist at all?
Since it is stated thus, there is no parity [with our position];
for even according to the Venerable Buddhadeva, who holds that the three time-periods exist within a single time-period, it would follow that the three time-periods occur in one and the same period.
Thus, within a single past period, there exists the distinction between prior and subsequent moments.
In that regard, the preceding and succeeding moments are the past and the future;
the preceding moment is the past, the succeeding moment is the future,
and the middle one is the present.
Thus, in the past time, three times would be obtained;
therefore, for all of these,
the third is the best.
"How is the Vaibhāṣika position thus established as correct? he asks; [the author] replies:
"Because for him..."
The time periods are established by way of their activity (*kāritra*);
furthermore, the activity of the eye and so forth consists of seeing and so on, while for visible forms and so forth, being the objective domain of the sense faculties is their activity.
"If it is so," and so forth:
if they are established by way of their activity (*kāritra*),
then what is the activity of an eye that is "similar to its own kind" (*tatsabhāga*)?
For that which does not perform its own function according to its characteristic of activity (*kāritra-lakṣaṇa*) is "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*);
and since such [an eye] lacks the activity characterized by seeing, the intention [of the objection] is: "How can that be present?"
Regarding "the giving and receiving of the fruit":
that eye receives its own outflowing fruit (*svaniṣyandaphala*) and projects it,
yet it does not perform the activity of seeing the fruit.
But since it produces another fruit,
and because of the existence of its grasping and giving of that fruit, it is established as being present;
for this would also apply to past causes such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and others.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the ripening cause (vipāka-hetu) and others are included;
because they bestow their fruit,
two— namely the present and the past— and one— the past— bestow it.
From this statement, it follows that there is activity,
because activity exists.

Furthermore, it would follow that these [causes], such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and others, when past, would possess the status of being present, because their activity (*kāritra*) exists just as it does in the present; thus, there would be a confusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṅkara*). You might argue: "This applies only to those [causes] for which both the grasping of a fruit (*phalaparigraha*) and the giving of a fruit (*phaladāna*) exist."
Those who are currently existing,
for whom neither [of these two] is the case, are not those who are currently existing.
Therefore, this is stated:
"Or [the consequence] of half-performed activity," which is governed by the context of the *prasaṅga*.
Or else, it follows that they would have only half their activity,
or that they would be half-present; for those [dharmas] are established as past because they possess the characteristic of the past, since their activity of grasping the fruit has ceased.
And because they possess the activity of yielding present results, they are endowed with the characteristic of the present; thus,
there is that very same fault of the confusion of characteristics,
for this is held to be the definition of the past and other time-periods.
The past has its activity ceased; the future has not yet attained its activity; and the present has its activity attained and not yet ceased. What is the obstacle? This word-form is neuter.
"What is the obstruction? is the meaning; "what is the hindrance for this [action]? Others say, "What is the obstructive activity?
If it is argued that it is the incompleteness of the conditions (*pratyaya-asāmagrya*), [we reply: no.

In this regard, it might be argued that because the conditions— such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and so forth— are not present as a complete totality, they do not exercise their activity at all times.
Since it is not admitted that [the self] exists eternally,
it is not logical to postulate the primacy of the conditions.
Because here you constantly admit the existence of conditions, since existing things are not destroyed,
and that activity is "past," and so forth.

Regarding that activity which is called past, future, or present— since the established doctrine states that "the past is that whose activity has ceased," and so forth— is there yet another activity belonging to this activity, by virtue of which its being past and so on is described?

If [you argue that] there is the consequence of an infinite regress, and if it is not so, then is the future-ness and so forth of activity merely in relation to the existence of its own nature? In that case, the future-ness and so forth of entities will also exist in the same way; what is the use of postulating a separate "activity"?
"How is that past? and so forth;

"Now, if it is not at all past," and so on in detail—that which is neither past, nor future, nor present is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because it is unconditioned, it follows that it exists eternally.
The topic under discussion is "activity" (*kāritra*);
therefore, he asks "What follows from that? and replies:
"Consequently, it need not be stated."
When a dharma does not perform its activity (*kāritra*), it is then called "future";
however, since this would entail that the activity is impossible to perform, this fault would arise— such is the detailed argument.

This fault might arise— namely, the over-extension that activity would require another activity, or the consequence of [activity] being unconditioned— if activity were distinct from the dharma; however, since activity is indeed not distinct [from the dharma],
this fault does not apply.
"By that very self" means by that which is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the present.
