If one asks, "What did this not have previously?"— meaning that in its future state,
because the activity is non-different [from the entity], it would be said that the entity itself did not exist;
and furthermore, "What does it not have later?"— meaning in its past state.
If it were said that the activity (kāritra) does not exist at all as a phenomenon (dharma),
because there is no difference between the phenomenon and its activity,
then if it is not accepted that [the activity] comes into being after having not existed, the present would not be established.
Furthermore, if it is not accepted that "having come into being, one ceases to be," then the past time is not established; however,
it follows by implication that the future is that which has not yet come into being after having been non-existent.
The meaning of the statement is that the three times are established in this way, and not otherwise;
for existence at all times renders the occurrence of arising and destruction impossible. Thus, because it exists at all times, there is no possibility of arising or destruction.

Therefore, this is a mere verbal assertion; the claim that "there is no consequence of eternalism because of the connection with the characteristics of the conditioned" is an unprecedented mode of expression—
meaning it is a mode of expression that contradicts its own preceding and succeeding statements.
And because it exists at all times while being subject to arising and destruction,
its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists at all times.
If it is maintained that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form and so forth exists at all times,
then, since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth would exist eternally, it follows that the entity of form and so forth must be permanent.
Therefore he says:
"An entity is not admitted to be eternal;
this being so, an entity must surely be other than that intrinsic nature."
Therefore he says:
"And an entity is not other than its intrinsic nature."
This, therefore, is clearly the act of the Lord, arising from mere will;
there is no logical reasoning here.

But by saying "the past is that which has previously existed," he shows that it does not exist by way of its own characteristic; and by saying "the future is that which will exist when the cause is present," [he shows the same].

He shows that even though something is non-existent, it is established by virtue of the existence of its cause; for it is said that "it exists" by way of considering what was previously existent or what will exist in the future.
However, it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) in this way;

rather, it was stated that "the past exists" for the purpose of refuting the view that denies cause (*hetv-apavāda-dṛṣṭi*). This is for the purpose of refuting the view that denies cause and effect (*hetu-phalāpavāda-dṛṣṭi*).

In order to refute the view that denies the fruit (*phalāpavādadṛṣṭi*), it is said, "the future exists. While one might say "the past was" and "the future will be," the use of the word "exists" (*asti*) is intended; for since the word *asti* is an indeclinable particle (*nipāta*), and an indeclinable particle can refer to all three times.
It occurs with respect to the past and also with respect to the future;
as in the detailed explanation,
"the lamp exists," just as speakers say, "there was the prior non-existence of the lamp" and "there will be its subsequent non-existence."
And it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) in the way that it exists;
for people say, "That lamp has ceased, but it was not extinguished by me."
And it is not the case that this [attainment] exists even when it has ceased through application;
for does the Vaibhāṣika not hold that this exists even when it has ceased?
True, it exists.
But it is not the case that it exists while merely maintaining the nature of a lamp;
thus it is said that the past and future exist, even though they lack substantial existence (*dravyasattva*),
for otherwise the very categories of the past and future could not be established.
The meaning is that if [the past and future] were to exist by that very same characteristic, then the past and future themselves would not be established.
As for the passage beginning "If the past is what has previously occurred," and so forth: the *laguḍaśikhīyaka* wanderers [asked about] women as the causal basis (*nidāna*).
In Nālandā, those who were learned stated that the Buddha had spoken a sūtra in the *Saṃyuktāgama* concerning the killing of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Because it is recited in the Sūtra itself regarding the statement "he has not killed us" as follows:
"The wandering mendicants of Laguḍaśikhīya, who have committed an act of immediate retribution, hold the view that 'whatever karma has passed away does not exist'"; and so forth.
Do those wandering mendicants of Laguḍaśikhīya not accept that this action was previously committed?
By this it is meant that they did indeed accept that this action had been previously committed.
However, they are in disagreement regarding that action— specifically concerning its nature as a substance—
because they maintain that no such past action exists, whereas the Blessed One [affirms it] in its intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
"That past karma exists," and so on in detail;
therefore, "the past exists by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*)," and so on in detail.
Furthermore, regarding that which was formerly karma in that very sutra:
It was not with the intention that "that very [action] which has passed away exists" that it was said "that action exists";
rather, what exists is that which was deposited— that is, brought about— by that previously performed action.
"How is it understood that this was said with the intention of referring to the capacity for yielding fruit within that continuum? To this he says:
"For otherwise, a past [dharma] existing in its own nature would not be established."

The intention is that if an action existing by way of its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) were to exist as something past by way of a present characteristic, then the past would not be established; rather, only the present would be established.
However, when it is stated in detail that "it was deposited by that [action]," it is thereby established that the past action exists.
And this is so because, as has been explained in detail, the future does not exist substantially, nor does the past,
within the present time-period.
The meaning is that [a dharma] comes into being after not having been, by way of its present state;
it is not [the case that this occurs] because of a change in the time-period (*adhvan*), since the time-period is not a different entity from the state of being (*bhāva*).
It is not the case that this very thing [is the present time], because the existence of the present path is not distinct from the entity designated as "eye";
the meaning is that it is not a separate substance.
That which is the present time is itself the entity;
how then could that very same [entity], being present, come into existence within its own time after having not existed?
For it has been said:
"Those very [factors] are the time-periods (adhvan) and the bases of discourse (kathāvastu)."
Now, since the eye does not exist as the eye within its own self, it is established that the future eye does not exist;
[the phrase] "merely an object" uses the word "mere" (*mātra*) for the purpose of excluding its status as a producer.
The intended meaning is that phenomena (dharmas) are the objective support (ālambana) because they arise in the form of those [phenomena];
as for the statement "the future by the thousands," it is not logical that even a proximate future [object] can be a producer.
How much less so after a very long time,
since it is not logical for a cause existing at a later time to produce a result that existed at an earlier time; thus,
[the attainment of] nirvāṇa [would be impossible].
The intention is that consciousness in nirvāṇa would not produce [anything], because the progression of saṃsāra has been ceased; thus,
it "has been" and "will be."

How is it known that the meaning is "that form which existed in the present state and will exist [in the future] is the object," and that it is apprehended in this way rather than as something currently existing? To this, he says:
For no one, when recollecting past form or feeling, perceives it as "it exists";
rather, they recollect that form as "it was," and feeling exactly as it was seen and experienced through the power of the experience of visual consciousness.
Regarding this, the Master himself has stated the reason for his argument in detail, beginning with the words, "Just as indeed... and so forth.
The intention is that the past and the future are apprehended as if they were present in form;
and if they exist in exactly that way, then it follows that the past and the future would become present.
Now, if that [object] does not exist, then it is established that even a non-existent thing becomes an object of cognition, because its form is absent— just like that of a present object—
and yet it is being remembered.
"That very thing is scattered" means that which is present is itself what is scattered as past and future.
"This is not tenable because that which is scattered cannot be apprehended."
Because that which was previously not scattered is not grasped as "this form was not scattered before, but is scattered now," and because it is not grasped in this way;
and furthermore, [the argument] "if that were indeed that very same thing," and so forth.
And if form, which exists as a solid mass in its present state,
is divided into atoms in its past and future states, then those very same things that exist in the past are not identical to those in the present;
and this being so, it follows that there is merely the aggregation and disintegration of atoms.
However, if one were to maintain that there is neither any arising nor any cessation, the doctrine of the Ājīvikas or other heretics would be accepted;
and if that were desired, the Sūtra would be discarded, for it says:
"Monks, when the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere."
"Monks, when it ceases, the eye does not go to any accumulation; for the eye, having not been, comes to be, and having been, it passes away.
How, then, is this sutra cast aside or contradicted?

Because the eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere by way of its own nature— this statement is contradicted— and when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation— this statement is also contradicted,
since it is accepted that those atoms are dispersed in past time.
Regarding the phrase "of those not accumulated from atoms":
how could there be a state of being scattered for things such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, which do not consist of atoms?
For accumulation or scattering can belong only to material things (*mūrta*), not to immaterial ones.
And since those [past objects] too are remembered as they were experienced when they arose,
they are remembered as having precisely the form of the present, provided that they exist in that very same way.
If present things were eternal,
or if they did not exist in that form, then it would be established that even a non-existent object is an objective support;
thus, even a thirteenth sense-field (*āyatana*) could become an objective support.
The completion of the thirteen bases would require a thirteenth base,
which would then be the object of that consciousness; or, if a non-existent object were admitted, then that consciousness would have a non-existent object.
When the Vaibhāṣika had spoken thus, the Master said:
"Now, as for the thirteenth," and so forth;
"This very name [is what is meant]," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
If this thirteenth base called "name" were merely an object of cognition, then it would follow that name itself does not exist.

Nor is the denotable object characterized by the non-existence of the thirteen sense-bases; furthermore, what is the objective support for that which takes the prior non-existence of sound as its support?
The phrase "it exists" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Thus, regarding the subject at hand, the Vaibhāṣika says that sound alone is the object of cognition; this is the subject under discussion.
"In that case," the Master explains at length,
"the very sound which one takes as the object of its prior non-existence becomes the very thing apprehended by that [non-existence]."
Prior non-existence does not become attained for one who seeks the absence of sound.
If it should be thought that for one who possesses this prior non-existence, only the sound itself ought to be produced, [then it would follow] that it is not in its original state.
Since it is in a future state that it is apprehended by that [cognition],
therefore, for one who seeks the absence of sound, it would not be the case that the sound itself must be produced.
To this it is said:
"How can there be the cognition 'it does not exist' when [the object] exists?
That is to say, while that sound is present, how can there be for someone the cognition "it does not exist" which takes its prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*) as its objective support?

If it is argued that "the present does not exist," then this would be the case: because of the identity [of the object], the cognition of non-existence arises from that very object, thinking "the present does not exist."
That which is future becomes that very same thing when present;
it is not something other than that.
How can the cognition "it does not exist" arise with respect to that very same thing while it is present?
Or what is its distinction [from the past],
or what is the subsequent distinction of that future thing when it reaches the state of being present?
In that case, when [the object] exists in its particular state, the cognition "it does not exist" arises;
this establishes its existence after having previously been non-existent—
that is, the existence of that particular state after it was previously absent.
The sense of its "accomplishment" (siddhi) is that it is both existence and non-existence;
it is existence in its present state and non-existence in its past and future states.
"Thus, both [existence and non-existence] become the object of consciousness;
if non-existence is the object of consciousness..."— this is the full passage spoken thus by the Bodhisattva in his final existence.

By stating, "There is no possibility that I shall know what does not exist in the world," it is shown that [this knowledge] does not have non-existence as its object; thus the Master, demonstrating that this Sūtra has another underlying intention, says:
"Others are conceited," and so forth. Regarding impure meditative concentration (*apariśuddha-samādhi*), others become conceited;
even though the radiance—the radiance of the divine eye—is non-existent during the stage of preparatory application, they perceive it as if it were actually present.

"But as for me, I see that there truly exists a manifestation which is the precursor to the divine eye"—this is the intended meaning in that Sūtra. How could there be any such inquiry [as you suggest]?
For when it is established that all cognitions have real objects as their domain, how could there be any investigation, deliberation, or doubt regarding this?
That is to say, regarding the detailed statement that "it does not exist in the world," this investigation concerning whether cognitions have existent or non-existent objects is possible,
and not otherwise.
Or what is the distinction?
What indeed is the distinction of the bodhisattva from others,
if they too perceive only an existing appearance and not a non-existing one?
For if cognitions have both existent and non-existent things as their objects, this distinction arises:
such being the case, one might think, "This cognition has a non-existent object," [but] it will know the existent as existent and the non-existent as non-existent; this is the illustration here.
Since one will seek and know a real entity as being existent, and an unreal entity as being non-existent— thus it is established that cognitions have non-existent objects—
it follows that this [argument] stated by the Bodhisattva is also not a valid reason.
"From that which is preceded by it" means from a specific mental continuum preceded by karma; thus, there is the refutation of the doctrine of a self.
At the conclusion of the treatise, in the refutation of the Vātsīputrīya doctrine,
it is established that arising occurs as "having not been, it comes to be"; thus, arising previously did not exist and now exists, which constitutes prior manifestation.
Because origination shares the same status as that which originates,
if everything exists,
then origination also exists— not only the cause, but also the future effect; such is the intended meaning.
Now, whose capacity is it, and where?
For what cause is there capacity for what fruit?
And the cause has been explained as arising; thus, the fruit exists in the future.
The Vaibhāṣika maintains that it is made present because it exists;
for this very reason, he asks as follows.
If you think that the drawing [of the effect] to another location by means of a cause is the bringing of the effect into the present state,
we say this in response:
The ellipsis of the sentence is "the fruit is eternally attached";
it is merely a drawing from one place to another,
and nothing new whatsoever is produced.
Since [the self] is eternal, pervasive, and formless, how could there be the drawing of feelings and so forth to another location?
The intention is that because it is formless and does not abide in a location, that [action] is not tenable;

and as for that drawing toward [an object] which is designated as "action," since it comes into being after having not existed, the proof of its existence through prior non-existence (*abhūtvābhāva*) is established— this is the intended meaning.

If you think that it is a qualification of the intrinsic nature— that is, if you believe that the intrinsic nature of this fruit is qualified by the cause, and therefore it becomes a qualification of the fruit— then [the following applies].
To this we reply: it is established that "coming into being after not having been" means the coming into being—
that is, the manifestation— of a qualification after it has not previously existed.
Or rather, regarding the question of whether all three time periods exist,
it has been explained here how they do indeed exist.
That which has previously occurred is the past;
that which will occur when the cause exists is the future.
That which, having come into being, has not perished is "present";
in this way, the Sarvāstivāda doctrine becomes sound within the Teaching.
How is one bound by that, or how is one bound to that? How is one bound by that past or future affliction, or to that past or future object?
It is because of the state of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) born from that [affliction] and having that as their cause. Thus, one is bound by the affliction.
Therefore, that which is born from the past is "born from that" (*tajja*);
it is the cause of that future [moment], thus it is "the cause of that" (*taddhetu*);
being both "born from that" and "the cause of that," it is "born-from-that-and-cause-of-that" (*tajjataddhetu*).
The latent disposition (*anuśaya*) which has that as its source and that as its cause is the "latent disposition having that as its source and that as its cause"; because of its existence,
one is bound by past and future afflictions respectively.

That past or future thing is the object (*ālambana*) of this [affliction]; thus, it is "having that as its object. The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) belongs to that affliction; because of the existence of that [tendency], one is "bound" (*saṃyukta*) to the past and future thing respectively—this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*).

Since the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmas*) exists within the established framework of the temporal periods such as the past and so forth, [the author] says "there is a way of expression" (*asti paryāya*) and so on, for the purpose of explaining their conventional usage.
There is a sequence of statements:
having stated that "whatever arises, that ceases," [he then says...]
He states an illustration:
"Form arises; form ceases. Since it is not other than the substance, is it that one thing arises and another ceases?
Does the future arise? It is different [from the present] because it is oriented toward arising. Does the present cease? It is different [from the past] because it is oriented toward cessation.

Furthermore, the time period (*adhvan*) also arises; the meaning is that for a dharma that is in the process of arising, it is subsumed within a time period because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the time periods.
Because they are defined as "the path" (*adhvan*) and "the basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*), a phenomenon (*dharma*) also arises from the path, which is of the nature of appropriation (*upādāna*).
He asks "Why? and replies:
"Because the future time consists of multiple moments," meaning that from among the many future moments existing as a collection, only a certain moment arises.
Therefore, it is said that [the mind] arises even from the path;
this has been discussed as an incidental point.
However, by means of all the remaining [factors], [it arises] everywhere.
The investigation into the past and future, which arose as a consequence [of the discussion],
beginning with the statement "that which has been abandoned," refers here to abandonment (*prahāṇa*) by virtue of the disappearance of its acquisition (*prāpti*).
Disjunction [is attained] through the abandonment of the afflictions that take those [objects] as their focal point;
this refers to the paths of seeing and cultivation regarding that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering when it has been abandoned.
"Thus, etc. refers to what was previously stated; "in the case of what has been abandoned, etc.
refers to the rest by all [the remaining paths].
Thus,
by means of the remaining universal afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the origin, along with their objects, [the defilements are abandoned].

This means: by those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) whose objects have been abandoned according to their respective types. For example, when the highest-of-the-high type has been abandoned, one is still bound by the remaining un-abandoned latent dispositions, such as the high-middling and so forth.
For indeed, although he is dissociated from that category of affliction which has been abandoned at the highest-of-the-high degree, he remains as if bound by the remaining ones;
this is what they mean when they provide a "comprehensive analysis" (*piṇḍavibhāṣa*), that is, when they provide a concise explanation.
And who are the sixteen Vaibhāṣikas?
There are five types of [defilements] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*):
four to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, and the fifth to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In this way, up to those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are five types each; thus, there are fifteen.
And the sixteen [moments] are untainted; thus, these sixteen dharmas— and those dharmas which are to be abandoned by vision—
have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature.
Those [factors] which are to be abandoned by cultivation have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature; how so?
Those feelings which are associated with the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) to be abandoned by vision constitute the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), as do those perceptions (saṃjñā).

That aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) consists of those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those mental factors such as volition (*cetanā*) associated with them, and the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of all these mental factors beginning with feeling (*vedanā*), as well as the dissociated factors (*viprayukta*)— namely, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—
that constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
And the mental consciousness associated with these is the aggregate of consciousness;
thus, those [factors] which have the nature of the four aggregates are to be abandoned by vision.
Furthermore, what are the other contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation?
All contaminated form, whether external or internal, is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Furthermore, the aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of the untainted—are to be understood as having the nature of the five aggregates and as being abandonable through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). These sixteen moments of mind are also precisely these:

namely, the five minds belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), ranging from that to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) up to that which is abandonable through cultivation.
In this way, there are sixteen states of consciousness— five belonging to the form realm, five belonging to the formless realm, and the untainted (anāsrava) consciousness—
and these are described as having those sixteen categories of phenomena as their objects, such that "in this [consciousness], there are this many underlying tendencies (anuśaya)."
Regarding this dharma, one should consider how many latent tendencies (anuśaya) are associated with that mind— whether by way of being an object (ālambana) or by way of association (samprayoga)—
and that these are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its cause (duḥkha-hetu-dṛg-abhāsa-praheya), arising from the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The meaning is that those [factors] belonging to the desire realm which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, and by cultivation—
this is the type of analysis;
and there are the three [categories] of one's own [realm], those obtained in the single form [realm], and the untainted (*anāsrava*).

The consciousnesses belonging to their own realm, the three realms, the formless realm, and the immaculate [uncontaminated] are the consciousnesses belonging to their own realm, the three realms, the formless realm, and the immaculate; of these...
"First, the objects belonging to the realm of desire," and so forth;

that is to say, the ten and seven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) belonging to the realm of desire, which are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin, respectively.

The four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), together with their co-existent factors and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) along with their attendants; and all contaminated form (*rūpa*) together with its co-existent factors and its acquisitions along with their attendants.
And other non-afflicted dharmas— of which of the five types of consciousness are these dharmas the object? To this he says:
Regarding those three belonging to one's own realm— namely,
those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and by cultivation— how is this so?

First, those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are the objects of: that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and is associated with both universal and non-universal [defilements],
that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin and is associated with universal [defilements],
and that which is wholesome and to be abandoned by cultivation.
Of one [defilement] of the form realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation alone:

for one born in the desire realm, during the state of taking dharmas of the desire realm as an object; and for one born in the form realm, during the state of seeing the desire realm, [it is abandoned] by means of the mundane path.
And they also become the objects of five minds— namely, the uncontaminated [minds] belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge—

but they do not become the objects of the two minds belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, because those two have only the contaminated as their object, and [these five] have only the [truths of] cessation and the path as their objects.
Because defiled states belonging to higher levels do not have lower levels as their objects,
there is no wholesome state belonging to the formless realm [that takes them as objects].
Because they are distant by way of the four types of distance,

those [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of origin are likewise [distant] from two kinds: that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin and that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, both of which are associated with the universal [defilements].
Of one wholesome state belonging to the form realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation, and of the untainted [state] which is likewise to be abandoned by cultivation alone.
They become the objects of precisely five [consciousnesses],
and their explanation should be made exactly as before;
those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) also become the objects of precisely five [consciousnesses].

[The objects] of the two minds to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin— which are associated with universal [defilements], as well as the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral mind to be abandoned by cultivation; and, as applicable, the single mind of the form realm to be abandoned by cultivation alone, and the untainted (anāsrava) mind.
As before, it should be stated:
"of one's own [level], the three below, and the one above, which are stainless."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one's own and those of the lower [realms]" refers to the three [categories] of one's own and the three of the lower; "one of the higher" and "the untainted" (*amala*) are added.

These same three types of factors belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) are intended here, because they are subject to abandonment through the vision of suffering and its origin, and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

These eight [types of] minds are the objects of three [minds] belonging to their own realm— namely, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and by cultivation— as was explained previously;
and they are also the objects of three [minds] belonging to the lower realm— namely, those same ones.

Among those, [the objects] are: the two minds associated with universal [defilements] belonging to a different realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin; the mind to be abandoned by cultivation which is either consisting of hearing or reflection; the mind belonging to a higher realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation alone and is comprised within the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space;
and the side of subsequent knowledge that is untainted (*anāsrava*).

"Having as their objects those belonging to the three realms, the three [types] belonging to the three realms, and the untainted" means that they have as their objects the three types belonging to the three realms and the untainted.
"Those very same" means those very same [defilements] to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, and through cultivation, which were under discussion;
"of those very same" refers to those of the three types.

Of which [factors] among those belonging to the desire and form realms— namely, the four associated with the universal [defilements] of a different realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, the two to be abandoned by cultivation,
and the three belonging to their own realm?

The objects of the ten minds— namely, those associated with both universal and non-universal [defilements], as appropriate for the two [categories of] those to be abandoned by cultivation, and the untainted—
are the spheres of all their own respective superior levels, excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.
Thus,
this universal censure is for the purpose of including the three realms,
as it pertains to one's own superior sphere of activity.

From this statement, it follows by implication that they are the objects (*gocara*) of those previously mentioned; or alternatively, "svādhikagocara" means the objects of those that have their own as an addition (*svādhika*).
"By that which is superior" means by that which is associated with attachment and so forth,
not by that which is associated with wrong view and so forth.
Because it always has cessation and the path as its object,
[it takes] those previously mentioned five— namely, three of the desire realm.

Of those [factors] belonging to the two groups, the universal, the associated, and those to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as that which belongs to the form realm and is to be abandoned by cultivation alone, and the untainted (anāsrava).
Since those [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of the path are also like this,
how then is it that these six minds have such objects?
They become the objects of nine and eleven minds respectively;
that is to say, those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path become the objects of nine minds,
while those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) become the objects of eleven.

How are the factors of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) related to the three types of factors of the desire realm— those to be abandoned by the universal [afflictions] of a different realm (*visabhāga-dhātu-sarvatraga*), those associated with them, and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)— and to the three types of factors belonging to its own realm (*svadhātuka*), which are to be abandoned by the two classes of universal [afflictions], those associated with them, and those to be abandoned by cultivation?
[It is the object] of a mind belonging to the formless realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation, comprised within the sphere of infinite space,
as well as the untainted [mind] on the side of subsequent knowledge;
and furthermore, of that very same [mind] which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation or to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

Thus, the factors belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) are each the object of nine [minds]. Furthermore, the factors belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) are each the object of eleven minds:

namely, the six [minds] belonging to the desire and form realms that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), together with the universal (*sarvatraga*) and associated (*samprayukta*) [minds] of a different realm.

And of the three belonging to one's own realm— namely, those to be abandoned by seeing the two [truths of suffering and origin], the universal [afflictions], and those associated with cultivation— and of each of the additional ones to be abandoned by seeing cessation and the path, as well as the untainted side of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).
Thus, these eleven are the objects of the untainted [dharmas]; the untainted [dharmas] are the domain of the last three [categories] of each of the three realms and of the untainted [dharmas].
The untainted [factors], such as cessation and so forth,
which are the last three among those to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and cultivation within the three realms,
are, as appropriate, the objects of the untainted [cognition].
How so?

First, it should be understood that analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and noble cessation (*ārya-nirodha*)—the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) being included therein—are respectively the objects of those [defilements] associated with false view, doubt, and ignorance which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as the object of the untainted category of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (*anāsrava-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna-pakṣa*), according to their respective applications.

However, space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) are to be understood as the objects only of the non-afflicted mind (*akliṣṭa-citta*) that is to be abandoned by cultivation.
However, Ācārya Guṇamati and Vasumitra explain that space and non-analytical cessation are the objects of the defiled and undefiled [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation;
that is incorrect,
because wrong view and doubt are associated with those two, as is ignorance both when associated and when solitary.
Because of the rule that the six [objects] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have the uncontaminated as their domain,
it is established as the tenet that the defiled mind does not have cultivation as its object.

Those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*)— namely, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, and those to be abandoned by cultivation— are the objects of five, eight, ten, and ten consciousnesses respectively. These are the objects of the five [consciousnesses].
Those belonging to the form realm are conditions for eight;
those belonging to the formless realm are conditions for ten;
and the pure [dharmas] are also conditions for ten.
These sixteen layers should be applied according to the previous explanation; they become thirty-six,

consisting of [the factors] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin in the desire realm, including those associated with non-universal [defilements], those associated with both homogeneous and heterogeneous universal [defilements], and those associated with universal [defilements].

Thus, in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), that which is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) is of three types each; in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is likewise, except for those associated with the universal [defilements] of a different realm and level (*visabhāga-dhātu-bhūmi-sarvatraga-samprayukta*).

In all three realms, that which is to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-heya*) is of two types each: both the side of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) and the side of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*), even though they are contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The faculty of pleasure belonging to the realm of desire that is to be abandoned by cultivation consists of five types;
that belonging to the realm of form is of five kinds.
Comprising that which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna consisting of the three groups of consciousness,

and that which belongs to the level of the third dhyāna consisting of the mental consciousness— summarizing these as appropriate— there are five types [of sensation]: those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering up to those to be abandoned by cultivation, as well as the untainted [sensation], all of which belong specifically to the level of the third dhyāna.
Regarding the four types of [defilements] belonging to the desire realm—
that is, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, by the path, and by cultivation—
the faculty of pleasure becomes the object for those two which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin.

Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), whether belonging to its own level or a higher level, which is comprised within the truths of suffering and origination, serves as the object (*ālambana*) for [afflictions] such as the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*);
and because the faculty of pleasure comprised within the truth of the path, associated with false view and so forth, serves as the object for [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing the path;

and because that faculty of pleasure belonging to the fivefold body of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāyika*) serves as the object for the mind associated with attachment and so forth, which are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
Thus, that is the object of these four types [of afflictions],
but not of the mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*),
because false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the others therein have cessation as their object.
And because adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the other [afflictions] have their own category as their object,
and because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) does not exist therein,
it is therefore stated: "except for those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*)."
Regarding the fivefold [defilement] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*):
because there exists a fivefold faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) comprised within the third dhyāna,
which is to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of the path (*mārgadarśanabhāvanā-heya*).

The faculty of pleasure included within the Path is the object of a mind belonging to the formless realm that is to be abandoned by the vision of the Path and is associated with false view and so forth;
it is also the object of a wholesome mind of the same realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation, and it becomes the object of all untainted minds as well.
In that context, "according to possibility" means that because latent dispositions do not adhere within the untainted state,
and because only certain dispositions adhere in certain cases.
Therefore, it is said "according to possibility.
In that consciousness, there are four categories belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).

For example, when the faculty of pleasure is the object associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) lie latent (*anuśerate*) either by way of the object or by way of association, according to possibility.

In this way, those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin and those to be abandoned by the vision of the path also underlie the consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure as its object.
For in a consciousness associated with false view and so forth that takes the faculty of pleasure belonging to the path as its object, false views and the rest underlie it through association.
The adherence to views and the other [proclivities] also persist by way of their object;
therefore, that category [of proclivities] also persists there,
and even the category to be abandoned by cultivation persists here.
In that regard, because passion (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions] are associated with the objects of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the objects of consciousness,
the category of those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaprahātavya*) does not adhere there,
due to the absence of a consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object.
Since those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) have conditioned phenomena as their object,
there exists a fivefold form-realm object for the faculty of pleasure;
it is easy to understand that the four categories of defilements adhere (*anuśerate*) therein.

But how do those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, which have conditioned phenomena as their object— such as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth— become latent (*anuśerate*) in the third dhyāna when they are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*),
and how can they take one another as objects?

In this regard, the two categories belonging to the formless realm— namely, those to be abandoned by the vision of the path and those to be abandoned by cultivation— adhere to the consciousness that takes the faculty of pleasure as its object, either through association or through its objective support.
When the faculty of pleasure on the path is associated with wrong view and so forth, wrong view and the like adhere [to it] through association (*samprayoga*);

however, adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the rest adhere there through the object (*ālambana*). Furthermore, the category [of defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) also adheres.
For a wholesome mind that is to be abandoned by cultivation takes the Path as its object;

it should be understood that in that case, the group [of defilements] beginning with attachment (*rāga*) lies latent there, as do the omnipresent (*sarvatraga*) latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), or they lie latent in that very consciousness, or in a consciousness associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth that has the Path as its object.
Of those very twelve types— namely,
the fourfold type belonging to the desire realm (excluding that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation),

the fivefold type belonging to the form realm, the twofold type belonging to the formless realm (both to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation), and the untainted type— it is through the connection of being mutual objects that consciousness having the faculty of pleasure as its object becomes an object for that [untainted consciousness].
Furthermore, that consciousness which has the faculty of pleasure as its object becomes the object of two further types of [consciousness] belonging to the formless realm; of which ones? He says:
"of those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin."

For the consciousness associated with the universal [defilements] of the formless realm— which is of two types due to the distinction between those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin— has as its object the consciousness associated with false view and so forth belonging to the path of the formless realm that is to be abandoned by vision, as well as the wholesome [consciousness] of the formless realm that is to be abandoned by cultivation;
thus, this fourteen-fold consciousness has the faculty of pleasure as its object, wherein the two [types] of the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin are added.

Previously, it was stated that only the universal [defilements] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) adhere to a consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object;

however, when there is a consciousness that has as its object the object of the faculty of pleasure, both categories of defilements belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) adhere to it.

Therefore, in a mind associated with the universal [defilements], the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin adhere [to it] either through association (*samprayoga*) or through the object (*ālambana*), as the case may be.
The remaining cases should be applied as before; by this method, other instances should also be understood,
and by this path, other matters should likewise be comprehended.
When the question arises as to how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) adhere to the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya) as their object, one must investigate this:

the faculty of suffering is of a single type, belonging to the realm of desire (kāmāvacara), and is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), because it consists of the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañcavijñānakāyika).
In brief, that serves as the object for five kinds of consciousness:

for the three types of consciousness belonging to the desire realm— namely, those associated with universal [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.

And this fivefold consciousness that has the faculty of suffering as its object belongs to the realm of form (rūpāvacara), is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), and is also untainted (anāsrava).

In that regard, as far as possible, the three categories belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)— those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, and those to be abandoned by cultivation— are [present] there. For in that state, within a mind associated with universal [defilements] and within a mind to be abandoned by cultivation, the two categories to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin adhere [to it] through association (*samprayoga*) or through being the object (*ālambana*), as the case may be.
And when it is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), a category [of defilement] to be abandoned by cultivation underlies it; specifically,
one category belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) which is to be abandoned by cultivation underlies that mind to be abandoned by cultivation.
It should be understood that the universal [defilements] belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) reside in that very same [consciousness].
Regarding the consciousness that has as its object the consciousness which itself has the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) as its object, how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere?
Furthermore, of which consciousness is that consciousness—which has the faculty of suffering as its object—the object?
By way of mutual objectification, that very [object] becomes the object of those five types [of afflictions],

as well as of the further [afflictions] of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of the path which have the untainted as their object, and of the universal [afflictions] associated with the form realm.

Therefore, the wholesome [consciousness] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) which has the faculty of suffering as its object and is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) takes as its object [the consciousness of the formless realm];

furthermore, that which belongs to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) takes as its object the faculty of suffering characterized by aspects such as "coarseness" (*audārika*).
This is the eightfold consciousness that has the faculty of suffering as its object-of-object (*ālambanālambana*).
In that regard, there are four classes belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)— those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and the path, and those to be abandoned by cultivation—
and three classes belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

It should be understood that among those belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara), one category of defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya) and the universal underlying tendencies (sarvatraga-anuśaya) persist as latent proclivities.

Consciousness having the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object is of eleven kinds: five each belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the fivefold untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousness;
thus, in brief, this becomes the object of thirteen kinds of consciousness.
Of the five types belonging to the desire realm that have conditioned objects as their focus, [it is the antidote] because those objects are themselves conditioned;
likewise for those belonging to the form realm,
and for the two types belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path and by cultivation.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this thirteenfold consciousness which has the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) as its object— being untainted (*anāsrava*)— is the locus where, according to possibility, the five classes belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) adhere (*anuśerate*).
In the consciousness that takes as its object the object of the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*), how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere?

Furthermore, that [consciousness] which takes the faculty of mental pleasure as its object consists of thirteen types of consciousness; of which consciousness is it the object? It is the object of those very same thirteen kinds.
Furthermore, for the two types of consciousness belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin—
making fifteen kinds in total— this consciousness has the faculty of mental pleasure as its object;
in this context, the two types from the formless realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin are added.
It should be understood that the latent dispositions (anuśaya) belonging to the desire realm and the form realm which have conditioned phenomena as their object,
as well as the four categories belonging to the formless realm— excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation—
persist as latent tendencies.
In this manner, other cases should also be understood;
thus, afflicted [states] are of two kinds, being accompanied by latent tendencies (*sānuśaya*).
The meaning is that a defiled mind is "with latent dispositions" (*sānuśaya*) by virtue of both those latent dispositions that are currently active and those that are not;
because it is accompanied by them and they are constantly present.
A non-defiled mind is "with latent dispositions" only by virtue of those [dispositions] that are currently active, since [the dispositions] can be dissociated from it.
For it will be stated thus:
"The affliction to be abandoned consists in the nature of the object."
Because it is possible for anything to arise immediately after anything else, there is no universal rule regarding the sequence of their arising.
The phrase "having set aside the aggregates as suffering" refers to the misconception of a self, thinking "this is not suffering."
For one who holds the view that "form is the self," the view of grasping at feeling and so forth as the self remains uneliminated and unknown;
thus it is "uneliminated" because its acquisition has not been severed.
Because they are not fully understood and because their antidote does not arise,

they are "conducive to the obsession of sensual desire"; they are called *paryavasthānīya* (conducive to obsession) because one becomes obsessed by means of them, just like [substances] used for bathing (*snānīya*).
"Conducive to the outburst of sensual desire" means they are favorable to it;
or, the outburst itself is sensual desire, and thus "the outburst of sensual desire" refers to that, while "conducive to the outburst of sensual desire" means beneficial for it.
Furthermore, those objects such as form and so forth "come into appearance" means that they come to assume the nature of objects;
and in that regard, there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*).
In that context, the meaning is that when objects have appeared, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is perverted.
Regarding the powers of cause, object, and application:
the power of the cause (*hetubala*) refers to the latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) being neither abandoned nor fully understood for the arising of sensual desire.
The power of the object conducive to the outburst of sensual desire,
as well as improper mental attention therein, constitute the power of application;
in this same way, other afflictions also arise.
The latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*) is neither abandoned nor fully understood;
objects conducive to the outburst of aversion (*pratighaparyavasthānīya-dharma*) come into range,
and there occurs improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*)— this is the principle.
These very same are the four yokes: the yoke of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*), the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*), the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*), and the yoke of ignorance (*avidyāyoga*),
excluding delusion (*moha*).
Thus,
because ignorance (avidyā) is mentioned separately as an outflow (āsrava),
there are forty-one entities when it is taken together with the secondary afflictions (paryavasthāna) such as lack of shame (āhrīkya) and the others that will be described hereafter.
Regarding the thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are twelve views (*dṛṣṭi*);
five are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*).
There are two [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of the origin,
two to be abandoned by the vision of cessation,
and three to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
There are four types of doubt,
five types of attachment, and likewise [five] types of aversion and pride.
The ten outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); thus, there are exactly forty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding the *paryavasthānas*; thus, there are twenty-six *anuśayas*:
namely, twelve views (*dṛṣṭi*), four doubts (*vicikitsā*), five attachments (*rāga*), and five prides (*māna*).

But is it not the case that even there, in those two realms, there are two types of outbursts (*paryavasthāna*)? [The answer is: In those two, namely the form and formless realms, there are torpor, restlessness, and pride; [these three] belong to all three realms.
Given this statement,
why is that pair of *paryavasthānas* not included here?
Regarding the phrase "due to lack of independence":
how is there a lack of independence?
Because it is associated with passion and so forth, like envy and the rest, and because it is not associated with mere ignorance.
For these two are associated with passion and the other [afflictions],
whereas envy, avarice, regret, anger, and hypocrisy are independent.
"Because of association with mere ignorance"—
the meaning is that both of them, even those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*), [are included].
"Operating toward the internal face" means that they do not have sensory objects as their primary focus;
and for the very same reason, attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*) was mentioned.
Because it is inward-looking, this [term] was employed to turn back the notion that it is liberation;
and by this, it is called the "outflow of existence" (*bhavāsrava*).
"It is established that ignorance is an outflow" means that ignorance is excluded from the two previously mentioned outflows;
therefore, it is established that even though ignorance belongs to the three realms, it is nonetheless called the "outflow of ignorance."
"There are fifteen substances" means that since ignorance is of five types in each of the three realms, this applies to all of them.
For it has been stated that ignorance is the cause of the outflows of desire and so forth, as well as of cyclic existence; indeed,
whatever miserable destinies there may be in this world or the next, they all arise from it.
All [defilements] have ignorance as their root; they arise from desire and greed,
and likewise from the floods and yokes.
Thus,
the outflows themselves are the floods and the yokes;
they are simply that.
It is explained how the views are established separately:
the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) itself is the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāmayoga*).

In this way, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) itself is the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*); however, the flood and yoke of ignorance (*avidyā*) are to be understood exactly as before.
Here, the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*) is stated as the fourth.
Therefore he says, "except for views," and as for the phrase "it is said that those [views]," the word *kila* indicates the opinion of another.
However, the intention that the "yoke of views" (dṛṣṭiyoga) is mentioned separately is appropriate because of the needs of those to be trained (vineyajana).
To the question of why views (dṛṣṭi) were not established separately among the outflows (āsrava), he says:
[they were not] among the outflows because they are not independent.
The meaning of this and so forth is that for views that are without support, there is no conformity to sitting— that is, no conformity to remaining— due to their mobility and acuteness;
nor is there conformity to reclining.
When the form *āsa* is reached, by the rule of Āpiśali, the form *āsyā* arises;
this means that these views, when without companions, are not conducive to sitting (*āsana*), but when accompanied by companions, they become conducive to sitting.
Therefore, these [defilements] are said to be "with companions" (sasahāya) among the outflows;
the meaning is that they are stated by being combined.
He asks: for what purpose? And he says:

The etymological definition of *āsravas* (outflows) is that they "cause one to settle" (*āsayanti*); this will be explained later. Therefore, the intention is that they must exist in the sense of "settling" within the *āsravas*.
Thus, the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) consists of twenty-nine entities;
because the twelve views have been removed, it does not consist of forty-one entities as the *āsravas* do.
What then? There are twenty-nine substances.
How so? He says:
"Lust, hostility, and pride," and so on for all of them.
The flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) consists of twenty-eight substances;
thus, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) is said to consist of fifty-two substances.
From these, having removed the twenty-four views (*dṛṣṭi*), there remain twenty-eight substances.
Regarding "twenty [types] of attachment and pride": there are ten attachments belonging to the two realms, and pride is likewise ten; thus, there are twenty.
As for the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*), it consists of thirty-six entities.
In the three realms, there are twelve views in three groups; thus,
the flood of ignorance consists of fifteen entities,
as previously described.
The yokes (yoga) are like the floods (ogha);
the yoke of sensual desire consists of twenty-nine entities:
fifteen instances of attachment, aversion, and pride; four instances of doubt; and ten instances of the secondary afflictions (paryavasthāna).
The yoke of existence consists of twenty-eight substances:
attachment and pride are twenty; doubt is eight; the yoke of views consists of thirty-six substances;
and the yoke of ignorance consists of fifteen substances.
"Those very [factors] as previously described constitute ignorance," and so forth;
which ones are those previously described?

The term "yogas" is the subject under discussion; therefore, it is explained that the yoga of desire (*kāmayoga*) itself, together with ignorance (*avidyā*), constitutes the appropriation of desire (*kāmopādāna*).
Thus, ignorance is included within its respective categories of the appropriation of desire and the appropriation of the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda*).
Because views are divided into two, there are four types of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to the doctrine of self.
Having extracted the attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) from the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*),

there are thirty substances for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*): having extracted the six attachments to rules and observances from the attachment to views— which consists of thirty-six substances— according to the distinction of the realms (*dhātu*).
The clinging to rules and observances consists of six entities in the desire realm, and likewise two each in the form realm and the formless realm,
because it is the adversary of the Path.
Because liberation is seen to be attained through means such as Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and knowledge, the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) stands in opposition to the path;
and because it deceives both sides— this being the detailed explanation— meaning that it deceives both the side of householders and the side of those who have gone forth.
By the phrase "by fasting and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes [practices such as] throwing oneself into water or fire, silence, the vow of the hero, and so on;
fasting and the others are comprised within [the category of] moral precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata*), as is the avoidance of desired objects.

By means of "avoiding desired objects," one returns to purity through practices such as renouncing flavors, sleeping on the ground, wearing dirty mud, naked wandering, and plucking out the hair; however,
because ignorance is not a grasper [of objects], it is mixed [with the other afflictions].
Thus, [the author] asks: why is it that ignorance alone does not take up existence? He says:
The intention is that because it is dull due to having non-apprehension as its characteristic, it does not grasp [its object] independently;
rather, it grasps by virtue of contact with other afflictions (*kleśa*).
Therefore, it is said "indeed" (*kila*).
The word *kila* indicates the opinion of another; by means of it, one's own position is stated,
[as opposed to] what was spoken by the Blessed One in the Sūtra, as explained in detail.
Thus, up to "the yoke of views" (dṛṣṭiyoga): what is the yoke of views, and which one is it?
In detail, up to: whatever attachment to views, desire for views, and affection for views he has— just as before—
and since desire and attachment are stated in other sūtras to be grasping (*upādāna*), how [is this so]?
What is grasping?
It is that which is here desire and lust;
this is the opinion of the Teacher.
This is what is meant:
here, "yoga" refers either to acquisition (āga) or to appropriation (upādāna).
It is said that there are no other afflictions [besides these], because among desire and the rest, that which is "will and lust" (chanda-rāga) is subtle (aṇu).
Thus, in detail,
they are called *anuśayas* because "they lie down subtly" (*aṇavaḥ śerate*); their establishment is according to this etymological method.
"Because its activity is subtle" means because its functioning is subtle;
but how, then, is the activity subtle?

Because they are formless and difficult to discern, [the afflictions] are like an enemy seeking a vulnerability from the perspective of their objective support (*ālambana*); and like the poison of a gaze or like the poison of touch,
they are [harmful] from the perspective of their association (*samprayoga*), like the heat of molasses-water.
Just as two nurses lie down beside a young child,
so too these [dharmas], increasing their own continuum through their objects or through associated factors, augment it by means of acquisitions (*prāpti*) and bind it.

Others say that they are called *anuśayas* because, like quartan fever or the poison of a rat, they recur again and again due to their manifestation before the person— even if that person has warded them off through deliberate application or has prohibited them through lack of effort— and thus they persist as a continuous bond.
The etymological rule is that they are called *āsravas* because they cause one to dwell (*āsayanti*) in *saṃsāra*, or else because their meaning is "dwelling" (*āsana*).
They flow from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell;
that is, through the six sense-bases— the eye and so forth— which act as wounds, they flow and leak,
going from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell.

Since even one who is free from passion for the peak of existence (bhavāgra) may still experience the manifestation of the afflictions of the Avīci hell, or since it is possible for such a person to be reborn there once those afflictions have arisen,
which underlying tendencies (anuśaya) flow [into that state]?
They are called *āsravas* because they flow; the suffix *-a* is applied here. They are called *oghās* because they carry away; they are called *yogās* because they bind.
"They seize," thus is the meaning of "appropriations" (*upādāna*);
this was stated by the Vaibhāṣikas:
"This form is like a flood (*ogha*)."
They are called floods (*oghāḥ*) because they carry away and transport [the mind] to another state of existence or another object.
They are called yokes (*yogāḥ*) because they join and bind [it] to another state of existence or another object.
They are called clingings (*upādānāni*) because they take up and grasp the continuum of consciousness toward rebirth or toward sensual pleasures and so forth.
"But this would be more correct," "but this would be better"— thus [thinking], the Teacher asks,
"How so? and says:
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because by means of them the continuum—the continuum of consciousness—flows or goes toward sense objects;
this is an instrumental derivation (*karaṇasādhana*).
Through great effort, the mental continuum is led against the current by wholesome factors and is turned away from sense objects.
"By the subsiding of those very formations" means by the cessation of those very efforts;
they are called "floods" because of their excessive velocity.
It shows the similarity to a flood (*ogha*),
considering that they are "floods" (*oghāḥ*) because they conform to it.
Because they conform to passion and so forth, the yokes (yoga) do not manifest excessively; thus he shows the various causes for the floods (ogha) and the yokes.
For those [defilements] which do not manifest intensely are merely "yokes," whereas those which manifest intensely indeed [constitute "floods" and so forth].
Regarding the statement "these are the floods," as for how they are the "yokes," he says:
because of the joining with manifold sufferings; that is to say, because of the joining with various sufferings such as birth and so forth.
Alternatively, they are called "yogas" because of their constant attachment, or because they are constantly joined within the continuum.

"Because of the grasping for sense-pleasures and so forth" means that those things by which sense-pleasures and the rest are grasped are the graspings for sense-pleasures and so forth, consisting of desire and attachment.
Those same underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), having been further described as fivefold by way of the division into outbursts (*paryavasthāna*),
are those very same underlying tendencies that have been described fourfold by way of the division into outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth;

they are again described as fivefold by way of the division into fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) in the Sūtra and the Abhidharma.

But surely, since the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth are taught as being distinct from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how can it be said that the underlying tendencies themselves are the outbursts?
It is true that they exist as distinct from it,
yet they are also accepted as non-distinct; for so he will say:
For even an affliction (*kleśa*) is a state of obsession, as it is stated in the Sūtra: "One experiences suffering conditioned by the obsession of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*).
In this manner, other [statements] should also be applied accordingly, as the case may be.
The fetters of repulsion, envy, and avarice belong to the desire realm;
the fetters of pride, ignorance, views, adherence to views, and doubt belong to the three realms;
and the fetter of views consists of the three [wrong] views.
The view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and false views constitute the fetter of adherence; these are two types of views:
the adherence to views and the adherence to rules and observances.
Therefore it is said:
because three views constitute the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), while two views constitute the secondary fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*), for that very reason it is stated.
The question is stated in detail as "it may be in those associated with views" (*syād dṛṣṭisamprayukteṣu*);

that is, in the case of feeling and so forth associated with views— specifically those associated with the view of grasping— one is bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunayasaṃyojana*), which is [the fetter of] passion (*rāga*).
It is not by means of the fetter of views characterized by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; nor is it that the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of views does not persist there,
nor is it that the latent tendency of views does not persist among those factors associated with views.
What then?
It would persist; for a double negation returns one to the original state.

He said, "It may be," and so forth; this detailed response to the question includes the qualification "when the knowledge of origination has arisen" in order to demonstrate the abandonment of the universal fetter of views,
and [the qualification] "not yet arisen" in regard to the knowledge of cessation.
In order to demonstrate the existence of their association through the non-abandonment of the two views of misapprehension (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*),
[the text says] "in the dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path," namely,
in feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.

For among those, one who is bound by the fetter of attachment— which is to be abandoned either by the vision of cessation or by the vision of the path— by what kind of object is that [attachment] bound?

Because this attachment arises by taking as its object those factors such as feeling— which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing cessation and are associated with the adherence to views and the adherence to rules and observances— one is bound to it by way of the object (*ālambana*),
yet not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
He asks "Why? and replies:
because that which is universal—having the nature of being abandoned through the vision of suffering and the origin—is already abandoned upon the arising of the knowledge of origin;
and because there is no non-universal fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that has that [knowledge] as its object or is associated with it.

For although there exists a fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) that is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*), has the nature of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path,
it does not have as its object the factors such as feeling associated with the view of grasping (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*),
because it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
Therefore, it is not bound by the fetter of views through its object,
nor is it associated with those [factors] such as feeling,
because it constitutes a distinct aggregate.
Therefore, even by way of association, one is not bound by that; and as for the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), how does it persist? To this he says:
Those very two, the views of esteeming [inferior practices] (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*), are [the underlying tendencies] by way of association (*samprayoga*);

that is, the view of esteeming views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) or the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) underlie those factors such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth by way of association,
because they arise from within their own group (*svakalāpa*).
Furthermore, the fetter of views does not underlie those two;
because he stated "the fetter of views regarding those two," when referring to the underlying tendency of views, there is no inclusion of all five views,
whereas when referring to the fetter of views, there is indeed the inclusion of the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and false view alone.
It should be understood that the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is distinct from the two [types of] grasping (*parāmarśa*).
The two views of misapprehension (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*) consist of eighteen substances; the ellipsis to the sentence is "there are three views," meaning they comprise eighteen numerable substances.
The meaning of the sentence "the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and false views" is that there are exactly eighteen substances; this is the subject under discussion,
and two of these are views of misapprehension (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*).
How is it that in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) the two views— personality-belief (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and extreme-view (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)—
are both held to be abandoned only by the vision of suffering (duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya)?
False view is of four types:
that to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to that to be abandoned by the vision of the path;
thus, there are six in the desire realm.
Just as there are six in the desire realm, so too in the form realm and the formless realm; thus, there are eighteen.
How are the two views of grasping (parāmarśadṛṣṭi) exactly eighteen?

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is of four types, from that to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) up to that to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*); likewise,
the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two types, being both to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and to be abandoned by the vision of the path.
Thus, there are six in the desire realm;
as they are in the desire realm, so too in the form realm and the formless realm—
thus, there are exactly eighteen substances.
The views that "there is nothing remaining" are not [included here],
because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) consists of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) due to the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhaka*).
The fetter of adherence is the grasper;
"from which" means from whatever cause.
It is said that among these [factors], [only these two] are mentioned because they are characterized by being exclusively unwholesome and by independence.
Among these envelopments, such as lack of shame and so forth, both envy and avarice have been specifically singled out and mentioned.
For no other type of *paryavasthāna* (envelopment) is of such a nature; thus, lack of shame (*anāhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are exclusively unwholesome,
yet they are not independent, because they are associated with afflictions such as attachment (*rāga*).
Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is also independent because it is associated with ignorance alone;
however, it is not exclusively unwholesome,
for it can also be wholesome.
Stiffness (styāna), restlessness (auddhatya), and torpor (middha) are also not independent, because they are associated with passion and other [afflictions];
however, they are not exclusively unwholesome,
for they can also be wholesome or neutral.
The connection is as follows: "wherein both these [exist]" means that where there is both absolute unwholesomeness and independence, there is no other *paryavasthāna* (outburst) of such a kind.
Furthermore,
for that Vaibhāṣika for whom there are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), both anger (*krodha*) and hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*) are of both types: they are exclusively unwholesome and independent.
Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal;
what then is the rebuttal for that?
To this, the Master Saṅghabhadra says:
Because envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are frequently practiced, they are classified as separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).

For this very reason, even though there are thirty-six fetters in total, it is said: "O Kauśika, among those born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), gods and humans are characterized by the fetters of envy and avarice.
This is because these two afflictions constitute a primary bond within that particular realm of existence.
Alternatively,
