because they are the causes of having little renown and little enjoyment, because they indicate everything [about the roots of unwholesomeness],
and because they constitute defilement for both sides, stinginess and envy are treated separately.
The reason why he, even though born in a happy state, undergoes such intense humiliation is envy and avarice;
for it is thus:
One who is called "of little power" and has "little enjoyment" is considered to be bound by both [types of bonds]; furthermore,
the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are of two kinds, including those accompanied by torment (*santāpa*).
And all those accompanied by delight are indicated by these two;
moreover, the side of householders is exceedingly afflicted by these two bases of enjoyment.
Even the faction of those who have gone forth [into homelessness], due to their support of the Dharma,
suffers excessively for the sake of causing a rift between the factions of gods and asuras;
for this very reason, it was said by the Blessed One:
"Kauśika, gods and humans are fettered by envy and avarice.
Therefore, among those ten fetters, these two alone are the fetters,
for the lower portion is the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).

In comparison with the totality of the three realms, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is inferior and base because it is exclusively non-concentrated, because it contains unwholesome states, rebirth in the miserable destinies, suffering, and mental distress,
and because its afflictions are dense.
"By means of two [factors], there is no transcending of the desire realm," because as long as those [two] are not abandoned, one does not transcend the desire realm.

"Because of their similarity to gatekeepers and attendants" means that sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) are similar to gatekeepers; for they do not permit exit from the prison-house of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the other [afflictions] share the same nature as a gatekeeper;
for just as a man, though having escaped from prison due to the negligence of a gatekeeper, is turned back by the gatekeeper's attendants.
Likewise here also, by means of these three,
[one attains] the inferiority of sentient beings.

By means of the fetters of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*), one does not transcend the inferiority of sentient beings characterized by the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*);

and by means of the two [fetters] of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one does not transcend the inferiority of the realm, which has the nature of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
For ordinary persons are inferior to the noble ones,
and among the realms, the realm of desire is the lowest.
Therefore, other practitioners of yoga (yogācāras) explain that those [fetters] are called "belonging to the lower realm" because they are exhausted by the abandonment of the three fetters;
that is to say, by the abandonment without remainder of the fetters of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the adherence to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā).
"Six afflictions have been abandoned" refers to the five views and doubt,
but not to attachment and the others, because they remain to be abandoned.
"Having abandoned three views" refers specifically to the triad of the view of extremes, false view, and the esteeming of views.
The Blessed One spoke only of this triad: the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the clinging to rules and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), and doubt (vicikitsā). Who said otherwise?
For it is recited in the Sūtra:
"To what extent, Venerable One, is one a stream-enterer? And from what point, Mahānāman, does a noble disciple understand, as it truly is, 'This is the noble truth of suffering'?"
He understands, as it truly is: "This is the origin of suffering, this is the cessation of suffering, and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
Furthermore, his three fetters have been abandoned and fully understood, namely:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Through the abandonment of these three fetters, he becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, destined for full enlightenment, with seven births at most; having transmigrated and wandered among gods and humans seven times at most, he will make an end of suffering.
All this would have to be stated;
the meaning is "it would exist.
There are three types of views regarding the self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the grasping at extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), because they are to be abandoned by the mere vision of suffering alone.
The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of two kinds;
doubt (*vicikitsā*), wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) are of four kinds;
therein, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the gateway for those of one kind.
Therefore, by the inclusion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is also included;
doubt (*vicikitsā*) is the gateway to the four types [of views],
and thus by its inclusion, there is the inclusion of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the esteeming of inferior views (*parāmarśa*).
The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), however, is grasped directly;
as for those [afflictions] such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth that are to be abandoned by insight (*darśanaheya*),
it can be said that they too are indeed grasped because they have that [adherence] as their object.
The view of extremes is set in motion by the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); because it clings to the self as being either eternal or subject to annihilation,
it is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
"Set in motion by the adherence to rules and observances" means that one grasps as supreme that by which one believes purity is attained.
False view is said to be "proceeded from doubt" because,
for one who is doubting, false hearing and reflection give rise to a false certainty;

thus, by the mention of the root [doubt], the inclusion of that which arises from the root is established, and it should be understood that the views of grasping at extremes and so forth are also of the nature already described.
Others, however, say: "In this very way, the Teacher [explains] how there is a deviation from the path;
he says 'by resorting to another path'."
By the mention of the "fetters pertaining to the lower portion" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), it is implied by the sense that there are also those "pertaining to the other portion";
therefore, this is stated:
the fetters pertaining to the higher portion (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) are likewise fivefold.
Thus ends the discussion on the fetters;
furthermore, they are taught as fivefold through the classification of fetters and so forth.

By this connection, following the exposition of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the occasion for the exposition of the bonds (*bandhana*) arises; as for the synonym "all," passion (*rāga*) is a bond in its entirety— both in terms of its modes and in terms of the realms (*dhātu*).
Is all hatred [abandoned] in every way? Is all delusion [abandoned] in every way and according to its elements (dhātu)?
"By way of both the object and association":
attachment underlies pleasant feeling—whether belonging to one's own continuum or that of another—as appropriate;
hatred underlies painful feeling by way of both the object and association alone.
Regarding the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, there is delusion (*moha*).

But surely, since passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) also adhere to that same neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling according to their respective conditions, why is it said that only delusion adheres? To this he says:
Attachment and aversion do not persist in that way;
although attachment and aversion also underlie as latent tendencies, they do not do so in the same manner as delusion does.
For delusion (*moha*), due to its lack of clarity, adheres even more strongly to a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant because it is compatible with it; thus,
the restriction [of its predominance] is either by way of having its own continuum as its object,
or the restriction is such by virtue of the capacity for the experience of pleasure and so forth within one's own continuum.

"For when there is pleasant feeling within one's own continuum, attachment arises; when it is painful, aversion; and when it is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, delusion—this is due to association," so say others, but they explain that it is not thus with attachment and aversion.

Just as attachment underlies pleasure, hatred does not; how much less, then, could hatred underlie pleasure itself? Yet hatred does underlie it by way of its object, as in the case of an enemy's happiness.
And just as hatred underlies suffering, passion does not;
however, does passion also underlie even suffering?
It underlies it by way of its object (*ālambana*), as in the case of the suffering of an enemy.
Alternatively, the restriction is based on having one's own continuum as the object;
or else, attachment underlies [the mind] by way of its object or its association with pleasure belonging to one's own continuum.

Hatred does not underlie [the mind] with respect to the happiness of an enemy belonging to another continuum, nor does it underlie [the mind] with respect to the suffering of one's own continuum; however, it does underlie [the mind] with respect to the suffering of an enemy belonging to another continuum, whether by way of the object (*ālambana*) or by way of association (*samprayoga*).
Thus, by way of having as its object that which belongs to one's own continuum, there is this restriction: attachment underlies pleasant feeling,
while aversion underlies painful feeling by way of both the object and association.
"Because they afflict the mind" means because they cause the mind to be defiled; this refers to those other mental factors as well.
Thus,
the meaning is that they are distinct from the afflictions (*kleśa*);
they are indeed secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they have the form of being near to the afflictions, or because the afflictions are present nearby for them;
this is due to their following after the activity of the afflictions and because they do not possess the full characteristics of the primary afflictions.

The secondary afflictions (upakleśa) are indeed mental factors (caitasika); they are not dissociated from the mind (cittaviprayukta), as they are recited in the section on minor matters (kṣudravastuka) within the portion of the teaching.
Thus, they are those which are recited in the Kṣudravastuka division of the scripture.
The intention is that it is not only volition (*cetanā*) and so forth [that constitute the hindrances].

For example: discontent, yawning, physical rigidity (*kāyadauṣṭhulya*), irritability (*śṛṅgī*), stubbornness (*bhittirīkā*), lack of rectitude, lack of gentleness, lack of conformity to one's own nature, discursive thought regarding sensual desire, discursive thought regarding ill-will, discursive thought regarding harmfulness, discursive thought regarding relatives, discursive thought regarding one’s native land, discursive thought regarding immortality, discursive thought associated with contempt, discursive thought associated with the prosperity of one’s family, sorrow, suffering, mental distress, and despair. Among these, shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) have already been explained.
Lack of shame (ahrī) is a lack of respect for what is blameworthy; likewise, here too, it is the failure to see fear [in wrongdoing].
This refers to the detailed explanation of "Dharma and material goods" (dharmāmiṣa), and so forth.

Mātsarya is the mental state characterized by the thought, "May stinginess not depart from me," which is an attachment of the mind that acts as an obstacle to the giving of the Dharma, material goods, and skillful means; mātsarya is simply the state of being stingy (matsara).
The state of one who is stingy is stinginess;
and since remorse and lethargy have already been explained,
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is the state of having done what is bad (*ku-kṛta*).
In this context, however, when it is stated that "the factors having that as their object are remorse, physical and mental unwieldiness, and lethargy;
and sleep is the contraction of the mind," there would be the unwanted consequence [of these terms] also applying to meditative attainments (*samāpatti*); therefore, they are further specified.
"Unable to sustain the body"—
this refers only to that which is an afflicted (kliṣṭa) entanglement (paryavasthāna); that which is wholesome (kuśala) or neutral (avyākṛta) is not an entanglement.
For sleep is held to be of three kinds,
as is afflicted remorse.
That obsession is not wholesome;
for it is held to be both wholesome and unwholesome.

Malice (*vyāpāda*) is a specific form of resentment toward sentient beings, distinct from malice toward non-sentient things; it is anger (*krodha*) that excludes ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).
Malice proceeds with the mental aspect: "May these beings be killed, or destroyed, or meet with calamity through injustice."
Violence (*vihiṃsā*) consists of engaging in activities such as attracting, terrifying, or threatening sentient beings;
anger (*krodha*) is malice toward sentient or non-sentient objects other than those two,
such as the mental agitation of a monk who desires to train [his mind].
And regarding the provocation by thorns and so forth,
it should be understood in due order as being toward those who are known and unknown;
among those persons known by kings and others, "concealment" (mrakṣa) is the outflow of craving.

Some say that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the outflow of both [ignorance and craving]: the outflow of ignorance is the thought, "May I not lack gain and honor," while lacking faith in the fact that one's own actions are one's own property (*karmasvakatā*), one conceals that fault and does not confess it before another for the sake of purification. Thus, concealment is the outflow of both.
How is lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*) the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of ignorance?
Because,
even in this case, there is a failure to see danger in what is blameworthy.
Thus,
remorse is born of doubt.
That which is afflicted is precisely what constitutes the stains of the afflictions, by virtue of their being categorized as active outbursts (paryavasthāna).
Thus,
just as impurities arise from the body, so too do these [impurities] such as *māyā* arise from the afflictions (*kleśa*); it casts forth and impels them.
Intoxication (mada) is as previously described; intoxication is the total absorption of the mind of one who is attached to his own duty.
And as for the phrase "that which is associated with what is to be abandoned by the vision of that":
the vision of a particular truth is "the vision of that" (*yad-darśanam*);
that which is to be abandoned by means of that vision is "what is to be abandoned by the vision of that" (*yad-darśana-heya*).
That which is associated with it— namely, that which is associated with what is to be abandoned by seeing— is itself to be abandoned by seeing;
it is to be abandoned by the vision of that [specific] truth.
What are shamelessness and so forth?
Those other than these are abandoned only by cultivation.
"Other than those" means that envy and the other [afflictions] distinct from shamelessness and so forth are to be abandoned only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The meaning is that these are not to be abandoned by vision, nor are they independent; rather, they are dependent upon passion and the other [afflictions].

Regarding [the statement] that "stinginess, restlessness, and torpor are unwholesome or neutral," because this occurs in the context of the *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), it is not stated that torpor is also wholesome; rather,
they are [specified as] neutral by others [only] from that point onward.
"Thus,
according to what is possible" means as many [factors] as are possible beyond the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, those qualities such as deceit and guile consist in the manifestation of a false self; thus,
through the manifestation of a false self, Mahābrahmā set out to deceive the Venerable Aśvajit.
When asked, "O Brahmin, where do these great elements cease without remainder?", he, not knowing, made an evasive remark:
"I am Brahmā, Mahābrahmā, the Lord, the Maker, the Fashioner, the Creator, the Originator, the Father of all beings. Thus he began to deceive him through his power of illusion.
Then that Mahābrahmā took Aśvajit by the hand and led him aside; standing in private, he spoke this.
"Thinking that one should question me while the Tathāgata is still present—this is seen as his deceit;
for, out of shame before his own assembly, he acted in such a way while concealing his own ignorance. Thus, even what was said is considered deceitful; for it is as follows:
Because remorse, torpor, and unwholesome states do not exist in the first dhyāna,
it has been stated here [in this context] as a secondary point that they are absent from it.
"Others are indeterminate from that [point] onwards" refers to the consequence;
"having removed five" refers to *māyā*, *śāṭhya*, *styāna*, *auddhatya*, and *mada*.
By these [factors], all those belonging to the mental level— namely, pride and torpor— are secondary afflictions, as are the independent ones.
Thus, envy, avarice, and so forth— those which are mentioned among the universal defilements (*kleśamahābhūmika*)— are indeed lack of faith, laziness, and heedlessness,
and not others, because lethargy and restlessness have already been included here previously.
Because delusion (*moha*) is included by the mention of "afflictions" (*kleśa*),
the phrase "by the two pleasant [faculties]" means by the two faculties whose intrinsic nature is pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).
"Because they function with the aspects of joy and dejection" means that attachment functions with the aspect of joy and aversion functions with the aspect of dejection, respectively;
and "because they belong to the level of the six consciousnesses."
Because they belong to the level of the five sensory consciousnesses, attachment is associated with the faculty of pleasure,
and aversion is associated with the faculty of mental distress,
respectively for those of meritorious karma and those of sinful karma.
For those of meritorious deeds, wrong view is associated with mental distress because they perceive the futility of meritorious actions and the fruitlessness of evil; thus,
there are four views.
Because of its intense attachment to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*),
equanimity (*upekṣā*) remains established; this is because [those views] are weak during the state of destruction.
In whichever stage there are as many faculties—namely, mental joy, pleasure, and equanimity; or equanimity and mental joy;
or pleasure and equanimity; or simply equanimity—these are known to exist in the rebirths of the dhyānas.
Thus it should be understood;
there too, in the higher stages,
those belonging to the four groups of consciousness exist only in the first dhyāna.

In the first dhyāna, there exists the faculty of pleasure belonging to the three groups of consciousness— eye, ear, and body— and the faculty of mental joy belonging to the group of mental consciousness. These belong to the levels of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.
The faculty of equanimity belonging to the four groups of consciousness exists [there], while above that it belongs solely to the mental level;
in the second dhyāna, there are the faculties of mental pleasure and equanimity.
In the third [dhyāna], there is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*);
in the fourth dhyāna and in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there is only the faculty of equanimity.
In all those cases, all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are associated with the respective faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*) according to their nature.
In that state, because the mental continuum is moistened by calm abiding (*śamatha*), there is no distinction between the modes of elation and dejection;
since these factors such as remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and so forth function with a mode of dejection, they are not associated with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*),
and because they belong to the level of the mind (*mano-bhūmika*), they are not associated with the faculty of physical pain (*duḥkhendriya*).
"By way of being a consequence of greed" means by way of having greed as its cause,
that is, arising from greed.
"Intoxication [arises] from the two kinds of pleasure" means from physical pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*).
In the third dhyāna, [the term] "by means of pleasure" is used because of the pride arising from the state of being a mental entity,
just as in the case of ignorance.
Just as there is no prohibition of association with ignorance (*avidyā*) with respect to any affliction (*kleśa*) or secondary affliction (*upakleśa*),
so it is also for equanimity (*upekṣā*);
this is because shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) belong to the great ground of unwholesome states (*akuśalamahābhūmika*).
However, in the unwholesome [mental states], there are lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*);
and because of their status as universal mental factors (*vedanā*) and as universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), there are lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Since the six groups of consciousness arise as unwholesome and afflicted, they can also be associated with all five sense-faculties; therefore, what is the point of asking about those belonging to the three realms? Restlessness and doubt are mentioned [here] because they are taken as representative, since these two belong to all three realms; thus, they alone are singled out and questioned.
"This is exclusively [unwholesome]," and so forth; "O monks, one who speaks correctly would say that this is a mass of unwholesomeness, namely the five hindrances.
For what reason?
Because it is stated in detail that "O monks, this is an entirely complete mass of unwholesomeness, namely the five hindrances," due to their being exclusively unwholesome.
The syntactical unity of the words in the commentary and the sūtra— namely, "the hindrances exist in the realm of desire and nowhere else"—
means that "hindrances" (nīvaraṇa) are the obstructions to the meditative attainments (dhyāna-samāpatti) and so forth.
"By way of having a single function of nourishing the discordant factor" means "because of having the single function of nourishing the discordant factor."
For even without the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), there can be an expression emphasizing the state (*bhāvapradhāna*);
or else, "one" refers to the single function of taking up the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*), and thus [it is called] "from that."

Regarding the phrase "the adverse side" (*vipakṣa*) and "the remedial side" (*pratipakṣa*), for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse, "remedial side" is intended here as the "adverse side"; that is,
it is considered the "adverse side" because it is the side opposed to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the Abhidharma, however, "black" refers to the adverse side (*vipakṣa*), which is the side opposed to the white; it is well known that the white side is the counter-side (*pratipakṣa*),
and that inequality exists within attachment.
The obstruction of the body caused by eating too much food is countered by abstaining from food;
the obstruction of the aggregate of wisdom by sloth and torpor is countered by [the cultivation of] wisdom.
"What is the harm? refers to the subject at hand;
"in this conceptualization," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

The aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhiskandha*), and the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*)— in the very same sequence in which these aggregates are established, in that same sequence their respective opposites, the hindrances (*nivaraṇa*), should be recited.
Since sensual desire, ill will, restlessness-and-remorse, sloth-and-torpor, and doubt [are listed],
it would follow that restlessness-and-remorse should be mentioned before the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor,
because the aggregate of concentration was taught prior to the aggregate of wisdom.
And since this is not the case, the intention is that this [reason] is not the cause.
If one asks, "What then is the cause here?", he says:
"Therefore, respectively, by these two hindrances—namely, torpor-and-drowsiness and restlessness-and-regret—there is an impairment of the aggregates of concentration and wisdom."
How is this so? It is said:
for one engaged in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is fear of sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*) because they are of a nature that obstructs it;
likewise, for one engaged in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), there is fear of restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*).
But others describe it differently, saying that according to the former masters,
"of one who has gone on his rounds" means of one who is wandering for the sake of alms-food,
due to the grasping of signs.
Whether by perceiving it as "the form of a woman" or as the "word 'woman'," for one who has gone to a pleasure grove, or who is staying, sitting, or walking about in seclusion,
there arise [afflictions] preceded by that, preceded by the grasping of signs regarding pleasant and unpleasant objects, or preceded by pleasant and unpleasant objects themselves.
They act as obstacles to calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) respectively;
lethargy and torpor (*styānamiddha*) act as an obstacle to calm abiding because they arise through their close proximity.
Excitement and remorse, along with doubt, create obstacles for insight (*vipaśyanā*).

"Excitement-and-remorse-and-doubt" is a compound formed by first creating a *dvandva* (copulative) compound of excitement and remorse—which undergoes singularization—and then forming another *dvandva* with that result and doubt;
thus: excitement and remorse, and doubt, [making] "excitement, remorse, and doubt."
Furthermore, doubt creates an obstacle even for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption] at the time of reflecting upon the Dharma;
others, however, read the text as follows: "sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt."
And they explain it thus:
lethargy and drowsiness create an obstacle to calm abiding (*śamatha*), while restlessness and remorse create an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
And doubt creates an obstacle for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption] at the time of reflecting on the Dharma;
this refers to the universal [afflictions] belonging to a different realm (*visabhāgadhātu-sarvatraga*), as explained in detail.
These universal afflictions of a different realm are of two types, insofar as they are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*).

When the objects of wrong view and the other [defilements] are fully understood by means of the category of subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin, they are not abandoned at that time while they have the form and formless realms as their objects.

Because they have already been abandoned previously by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudayadharmajñāna*) as appropriate—

since they are to be destroyed by the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñānavadhyā*) due to their belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*)— the objects of the views of misapprehension (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth, which are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodhamārgadarśanaprahātavya*) and which have the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object, namely the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and so forth that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path and whose intrinsic nature consists of the truths of suffering and origination, are fully understood according to their respective realms (*yathādhātu*) by means of the category of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānapakṣa*) or the category of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering and origination.
They are not abandoned at that time because they are to be abandoned by the vision of the path of cessation;
nor is their object perceived in that way, since it has already been known previously.

The intention [of the objection] is: "How is their abandonment [achieved]? It is not logical that their abandonment results from the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the object (*ālambana*). In this regard, through the full comprehension of the object, those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that take their own realm as an object, as well as those belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*), are abandoned.

Among these, for one who perceives the abandonment of those [defilements] taking a dissimilar realm as an object through the full comprehension of the object—namely, at the moments of the receptivities to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudayānvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*)—there is abandonment because both [types of defilements] simultaneously take two realms as their objects.
The qualification "having their own level as their object" is for the purpose of excluding those universal [defilements] belonging to other realms,
because [the latter] are abandoned through the destruction of their objects.

Those universal [defilements] belonging to the homogeneous realm have the universal defilements of other realms—such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth—as their objects; thus they are "those having those as their objects" (the universal defilements of the homogeneous realm). Through the destruction, that is, the abandonment, of these [universal defilements of other realms].
Those universal [defilements] pertaining to dissimilar realms are abandoned through the abandonment of their objects;
that is, by the abandonment of wrong view and the others which have the adherence to views and so forth as their objects, and which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.
Those [defilements] such as the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and so forth, which have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*), are also abandoned;
their destruction occurs through the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

He shows that the destruction of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation occurs only through the arising of their antidote, and not from the thorough knowledge of the object and so forth, stating: "we shall explain this later.
For there are nine types of faults on each level, and likewise [nine] qualities.
Regarding this, he will state that the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) is the "counteractive" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*);
a counteractive is a category (*pakṣa*) that stands in opposition to the discordant factors (*vipakṣa*).
The counteragent for the sake of abandonment is the "counteragent of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*).
For even the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is a counteragent, but it is not [a counteragent] for the sake of abandonment; therefore, this qualification is applied.
Alternatively, it is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) because by means of it, [the defilements] are abandoned.
It is both an abandonment and an antidote;
thus, it is the "antidote of abandonment," such as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*).
It is the "antidote of support" because it follows after that.
Therefore, the path that follows after that path of uninterrupted transition is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
for it is the support (*ādhāra*) of abandonment, because it maintains the possession of that [abandonment].
That by which something is supported is a support (*ādhāra*); that very thing is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), hence "support-antidote" (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*).

For example, following the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) comes the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*); therefore, it is so called.
"By which that was attained," and so forth:

by whichever path that [abandonment] was attained—that is, the abandonment attained by the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga)—it is maintained; because its possession (prāpti) is not severed, it is called the "maintaining counteragent" (ādhāra-pratipakṣa).
"The antidote of distancing," and so forth:
that by which the acquisition of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) is distanced is "distancing"; that very thing is the antidote, hence it is the "antidote of distancing."
Alternatively, *dūrībhāva* means becoming distant; the antidote to that is the *dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*,
which is the path subsequent to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

He shows that the path which follows after that very path of liberation— the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñāna)— namely the path consisting of the subsequent-knowledge-receptivity toward suffering (duḥkhe anvayajñānakṣānti) and so forth, is the counteragent of distancing (dūrībhāvapratipakṣa).
"Another [teacher] says that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is also [the antidote of distancing]"—
and this first path of liberation is called the "antidote of distancing" (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*),
for it also distances that possession of the afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*).
This being the case, it is stated that the path of liberation receives two names: "the counteragent as support" (*ādhārapratipakṣa*) and "the counteragent through distancing" (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*).
The meaning is that one "disgusts" that realm by seeing its defects; that is to say, one causes that realm to be loathed by means of aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
This being the case, it is shown that even that which has suffering and its origin as its object— such as the counteragent of abandonment and so forth— is also a counteragent of revulsion;
however, the Master [Vasubandhu] suggests that this sequence would be more appropriate.
He demonstrates that this sequence is correct because it follows the logic of a staircase and avoids confusion regarding the definitions:
"The path of preparation has suffering and its origin as its objects" means that the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth are included within the path of preparation itself.

It is not [limited to] the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantaryamārga) and so forth, because it is established as such by virtue of being the antidote for abandonment and so on; thus, it is "the entire path of uninterrupted transition."
Furthermore, any other path of liberation belonging to later times is also governed by the term "all," whereas the special path (*viśeṣamārga*) is that which is distinct from these three.
It is grasped here because a defilement cannot be separated from its association; that is,
because it is impossible to separate it from its own constituent group.
First, future [dharmas] can be separated from their objects;
once separated, that object no longer serves as a basis for their arising. For this reason, how is it with the past—that which has already arisen having taken an object as its basis?
For it is not possible to make an object that has been grasped into something that grasps;
this [position] also is not absolute.
Thus, the destruction of the afflictions is held to occur in four ways.
Through the thorough knowledge of the object, through the destruction of that which has it as its object,
through the abandonment of the object, and through the arising of the antidote, there is cessation.
Therefore, because of the thorough knowledge of the object (*ālambana-parijñāna*), this is not an absolute rule;
thus, the meaning is that "this must be stated" or "this must be refuted.
Here, the Master Saṃghabhadra offers a rebuttal.
Defilements are to be abandoned by means of their objects;
for defilements are abandoned through the power of thorough knowledge of the object.
Furthermore, the object of the underlying tendencies is twofold.
There are two types of entities: those associated with conjunction (*saṃyoga-vastu*) and those not associated with conjunction (*asaṃyoga-vastu*).

Among these, regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have as their object entities associated with conjunction, as well as those [dispositions] produced by the power of those [primary] latent dispositions even when they do not have such objects, their acquisition (*prāpti*) proceeds without interruption within the continuum of a person—even in one whose mind is unafflicted—and exists as the cause and fruit of future and past afflictions.

In this way, the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions that have as their object things not associated [with outflows], as well as those that do not have such things as their object but nevertheless arise following upon afflictions directed toward them, should be understood.
For it serves as the cause for the arising of future [afflictions] by providing the necessary conditions,
and it serves as the fruit of past [afflictions] by being their outflow (*niṣyanda*).
And that [attainment] is opposed to the presence of the acquisition of the outflow of the antidote for its abandonment,
because the afflictions are supported by it; thus,

when the acquisition of those [afflictions] ceases upon the arising of the outflow of the antidote for their abandonment— which has them as its object— those afflictions, even though they still have that as their object, are deprived of their cause and fruit.

They are said to be "abandoned" because, as long as some object of affliction is not fully understood, even those afflictions that do not have that specific object will continue to arise within the continuum— functioning as causes and effects for past and future afflictions— by the power of the afflictions directed toward that object, according to the nature of the thing itself; therefore, it is intended that afflictions must be abandoned by means of that objective support (*ālambana*).
But surely it is intended that afflictions are also abandoned through the abandonment of their objects and so forth;
why then was it said that "afflictions are abandoned by the power of thorough knowledge of the object"?
For those [other modes] are also abandoned precisely by the power of thoroughly knowing the Truth of Suffering and the others.
Because their presence or absence is contingent upon the presence or absence of that [defilement],
even those which are said to be abandoned through the arising of an antidote are also to be abandoned by cultivation.

It should be understood that afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned solely through the power of thoroughly knowing the objects of observation, such as the truth of suffering; however, that which was stated— that afflictions are also abandoned by means of abandoning their objects and so forth— is merely a formal classification, and its underlying intention appears to be that [the abandonment of the object facilitates the abandonment of the affliction].
"One's own [afflictions] belonging to one's own continuum are abandoned through the cutting off of their acquisition," and so forth;
that is, an affliction of one's own continuum is to be described as abandoned due to the departure of its acquisition,
whereas an affliction of another's continuum is not abandoned through the cutting off of acquisition.
Because that attainment does not exist within one's own continuum,

what then? It means that [the abandonment occurs] through the abandonment of the afflictions within one's own continuum that take those [afflictions] as their object, by cutting off the afflictions within one's own continuum that take the afflictions in another's continuum as their object.
All form— whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—

as well as non-afflicted dharmas, and likewise wholesome contaminated [dharmas] and the unobscured-neutral, should be said to be abandoned through the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to one's own continuum that take them as their objects.
The word "as if" (*iva*) serves as an illustration here for the types of distance, such as those between [different] elements, moral precepts, locations, and the two time periods.
How so? It should be seen in its actual meaning:
because of their distinctness, there is a distance from defining characteristics, as is the case with the primary elements (*bhūta*).
For the water element has a characteristic distinct from that of the earth element; therefore, the water element is distant from the earth element because it is its opposite,
which is what is meant by "distance due to being an opposite," just as immorality is the opposite of ethical discipline.
Spatial remoteness arises from the separation of locations,
such as that of the western ocean from the eastern ocean;
temporal remoteness arises from time.
For example, regarding the two time periods characterized as past and future—
that which is past and future is said to be "distant"; where is this stated?
In the Abhidharma it is said thus:
"Which are the distant phenomena?"
Past and future phenomena are distant phenomena; which are the present phenomena?
And that which is unconditioned is "distant";
this refers to the past and the future.
"And as it is arising" means that which is future and facing toward origination;
it does not mean by way of being long-past or long-future.
The meaning is that the past is not distant by virtue of having occurred long ago, nor is the future distant by virtue of being yet to occur;
[if that were so], even the present would likewise result in being distant.
Thus, because of the plurality of time-periods (*adhvan*), even the present, as a presently arisen time-period, results in being distant.
Just as the past and the future are called "distant" because the future has not yet attained its activity, so too,
how can the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) be considered "near"?

Because of the scriptural reading in the treatise, "Due to the absence of activity in that [unconditioned state], dharmas and the unconditioned are [not subject to acquisition]," it follows that there is acquisition of that [non-acquisition] everywhere.

Since there is the acquisition (*prāpti*) and arising of that unconditioned state—namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*)—in all locations, even in the past and future, there would be attachment; thus, since the acquisition of the past and future states of the wholesome and so forth is possible in all locations, it follows that even the past and future would possess spatial extension.
And how could space [be explained in this way]?
And how could space be near?
For there is no reaching it;
likewise, the past and the future are [not near] to one another.
The meaning is that the future is distant from the past, and the past is distant from the future;
and the unconditioned is [distant] because it is not intervened by anything,
as it is not separated by anything whatsoever.
Just as the past and future are [known] by means of the present,
so too is its proximity;
it is thus as well.
Even according to this conceptualization,
that which immediately precedes or follows the past and future would, due to its proximity to the present, result in both being [present].
Regarding "distant" and "near":
since that [past] is separated from the present, it follows that it is distant from the future,
and because it is not separated from the present, it follows that it is near.
Thus, this should also be understood to apply to the future;
however, the following would be more appropriate— this is the Master’s own view.
Why is the future distant from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena?
Because it has not yet been attained.
Because its own characteristic has not been attained by that which is future;
or alternatively, because that own-characteristic has not been attained and is not present,
as is the case with the past.
Is it distant from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena because it has fallen away from it?
For that is the specific characteristic of phenomena.
Therefore, that which has fallen away from the past is indeed past, because it has fallen away from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon; thus,
through the arising of the antidote, there is destruction (*kṣaya*).
Since this has been said, he asks:
"Is it because of the grasping of a specific path? and so forth.
"Distinction of abandonment" means that abandonment is distinguished;
the intended meaning here is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), which serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Because the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises simultaneously with it, there is no attainment of dissociation in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
since that path is oriented toward the act of arising; for it can also be established that the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is likewise an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Because it shares a single function with the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), which is the primary antidote;

for it has been said: "The attainment of that [result] occurs by means of both, because [the path of liberation] is the bringer and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*). Thus, there are four fruits.
The mention of "four" is for the purpose of excluding the recognition of eighty-nine fruits,
or alternatively, for the purpose of excluding the recognition of five fruits such as human effort;
furthermore, the attainment of the fruit is understood specifically as occurring in the state of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

Regarding the statement that "the transformation of the faculties (*indriyavivṛddhi*) is the transition of the faculties (*indriyasañcāra*) due to the possession of the existence of the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyogalābha*)," Master Saṅghabhadra maintains that this demonstration of the meaning is intended to refute the notion of an increase in the number of faculties; for the transformation of the faculties is already established by the very mention of the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*).
To this we reply:
it is true that the attainment of the fruit itself is the increase of the faculties;
however, a specific distinction in the attainment of the fruit must be demonstrated, wherein there is the further acquisition of the fruit of dissociation.
Otherwise, even the statement regarding the attainment of the fruit would not need to be made,
since that is already established by the very statement of the arising of the counteragent; so, enough of this excessive wrangling.
For some, up to two—
meaning for certain afflictions, there is the attainment of dissociation at six times;
by the word "up to," for some [it is] at five.
For some it is in four, for some in three, and for some in two.
It was not stated that for some it occurs at one and the same time, because what is under discussion here is the re-attainment of dissociation;
for it is indeed possible for one of sharp faculties to obtain dissociation from the ninth category of the Peak of Existence at precisely the same moment.
However, that is not called "attainment" (*lābha*) again;
for in that regard, one of dull faculties attains dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) at six times:
at the time of the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) for those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

The acquisition of dissociation occurs at six times: at the time of the fruit of stream-entry, the time of the fruit of once-returning, the time of the fruit of non-returning, the time of the fruit of arhatship, and at the time of the transformation of the faculties;
this is stated with reference to what is possible, for one of dull faculties does not necessarily transform the faculties.

For that same person of dull faculties, at the time of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)—which is either the time of the arising of the antidote or the time of attaining the fruit—there is first the acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-lābha*) from those [defilements] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

Furthermore, there is the acquisition of dissociation from the five types of defilements belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—ranging from the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) up to the middle-of-the-middle (*madhya-madhya*)—at five points in time: from the time of attaining the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) up to the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*).
In those same five occasions— excluding the time of the fruit of stream-entry— there is the attainment of dissociation;
however, for the sixth category, which is middling-weak, there is attainment in four occasions,
because the occasion of the arising of the counteragent and the occasion of the attainment of the fruit are one and the same.
At that time, during one of those two occasions— the time of the fruit of non-returning or the time of attaining the fruit of arhatship—
And at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasañcārakāla*):

that is, at the time of the arising of the antidote for that very same [defilement] which is weak-intense (*mṛdv-adhimātra*) and weak-medium (*mṛdu-madhya*), during the seventh and eighth categories; or at the time of the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), up until the time of the transformation of the faculties—thus, the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyogalābha*) occurs in these four times alone;
or else, at the time of the arising of the antidote for that very last category, which is weak-weak (*mṛdu-mṛdu*), or at the time of the attainment of the fruit, whichever it may be.
The acquisition of dissociation occurs at three times: at the time of the fruit of arhatship, at the time of the transformation of the faculties,

and at the time of one who is attaining that very fruit of arhatship, when those nine types of afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness— which are to be abandoned by cultivation— have been abandoned, ranging from the highest-of-the-high to the lowest-of-the-low.

Excluding the final, weakest-of-the-weak category belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), for all other [categories], there is the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-lābha*) at three times:
at the time of the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), at the time of the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattva-phala*), and at the time of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
However, regarding that very same weakest-of-the-weak final category of afflictions belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*):
Because the arising of the counteragent and the attainment of the fruit of arhatship occur at one and the same time, the acquisition of dissociation occurs at either of two times:
namely, at the time of the arising of the counteragent, or at the time of the fruit of arhatship; that is, at the time of the transformation of the faculties (indriya-sañcāra).
Thus, there is the acquisition of dissociation at these two times.

Thus far, what has been said regarding those of dull faculties must now be stated for those of sharp faculties: that for some afflictions [the abandonment occurs] at five times, and for others even down to two.
Excluding one occasion for the transition of the faculties,
for him there is no transition of the faculties at all times; rather, it is at that one specific time that he attains dissociation from the afflictions.
We consider that it should not be said that there is no further acquisition of the softest-of-the-soft category of what is to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the peak of existence; for,
as in the case of metaphorically applying the name of the cause to the fruit, abandonment is the fruit and thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)— which has the nature of cognition— is the cause.
In that abandonment,
which is the fruit, there is a metaphorical designation of the cause as "abandonment" and "thorough knowledge."
For example, these six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), which were previously conditioned and volitionally formed, are to be understood as past karma.
Furthermore, who is it that designates "abandonment" by the word "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) in the Sūtra? For it is recited thus:
And, monks, I shall teach you the phenomena that are to be fully understood,
as well as full understanding itself and the person who possesses full understanding.
What are the phenomena that are to be fully understood?
What is the full understanding of the five aggregates of clinging? It is the abandonment of desire and lust for them.
The transcendence of desire and lust—
this is called "thorough knowledge," and so forth;
it is the destruction of the first two types [of craving], beginning with that for sense-pleasures.
Thus,

thorough knowledge [is attained] through the acquisition of the disjunction from the outflows, the mutilation of the peak of existence, the eradication of the two causes, and the transcendence of the realms.
Regarding this, the reason for establishing "thorough knowledge" will be stated as "the abandonment of the lower fetters," which means the abandonment of the outflows (*āsrava*) of the desire realm.
And this very designation for it is "the abandonment of the outflow of form" (rūpāsrava-prahāṇa),
which means the abandonment of the outflow pertaining to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Regarding the name "thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form" (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*):

although this thorough knowledge is established as the abandonment of other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as pride (*māna*) and so forth belonging to the realm of form,

it is nevertheless called the "thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form" because attachment is predominant therein, specifically referring to the abandonment of the fetter (*saṃyojana*) that binds one to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
The exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādāna*). [The portion from *l* to *l* is missing;
Wogihara supplies it from the Tibetan translation of the Peking edition (a–b).]
The intermediate dhyāna belongs to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space; thus,
even for that mundane state, the fruit of full comprehension (*parijñā*) is established.
Because the attainment of untainted dissociation is possible only for the Noble One, and because of the three fundamental formless attainments,
[this applies] to the untainted.
"There are two [types] of the mundane path" refers to the noble one's detachment from the desire realm and the form realm by means of the mundane path.
For subsequent knowledge as well, there are two [aspects],
namely that which is subsumed within the path of cultivation.
In the west, there are three [aspects] of dharma-knowledge: the thorough knowledge of the exhaustion of passion for form and the thorough knowledge of the total destruction of all fetters.

The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) included within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), whether regarding cessation or the path, which serves as the antidote to the three realms on the path of cultivation, is that [knowledge].
Thus,

why are its last three fruits— the full comprehension consisting in the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), the destruction of passion for the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana*)? He says:
Because they are the antidotes to what is to be abandoned through cultivation in the three realms,
there are six [paths] as their antidotes, or five.
Of those two— dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge—

their respective sides consist of six and five [moments] as appropriate; by the mention of "side," there is the inclusion of both the receptivities and the knowledges, just as in the case of the dharma-knowledge-receptivities and dharma-knowledges.

The compound *dharmajñānakṣāntīnāṃ dharmajñānānāṃ ca* means "of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena and of the knowledges of phenomena. Among these, the three complete knowledges (*parijñā*) as previously described—which have the nature of abandoning what is to be abandoned through seeing in the desire realm—are the fruit of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena; whereas [the remaining ones] are the fruit of the knowledges of phenomena on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

For those [knowledges] comprised within the knowledge of suffering and its origin, there is one thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).

However, for those comprised within cessation and the path, there are all three thorough knowledges: the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters, the thorough knowledge of the destruction of passion for the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya*), and the thorough knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*).
These are precisely the same as those of the subsequent patiences and knowledges (*anvaya-kṣānti-jñāna*).
Why are the receptivities to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*)—

which have as their nature the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through seeing in the form and formless realms— not each considered a single abandonment, given that they consist of the three aforementioned thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) plus the two final ones?

The abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by the vision of origin, and so on in detail up to the abandonment of the weakest-of-the-weak category belonging to the peak of existence— wherein is this not included?
It is included within the attainment of the untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-viyogāpti*).
The meaning is: "due to the attainment of untainted dissociation" and "due to the impairment of the peak of existence."
The meaning is: "by abandoning a portion of the peak of existence," that is,
"by uprooting two causes."
The meaning is: "due to the abandonment of the two types of universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the origin.
The intention is that, because its abandonment occurs through these causes, that abandonment is preeminent; thus, it is established here as "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

Regarding "in other dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges," this refers to the knowledges beginning from the dharma-knowledge of origin up to the knowledge of exhaustion; in these dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges,
the fruit of knowledge is abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
For on the path of cultivation, that [knowledge] is not the fruit of patience,
because it transcends the realm.
And the word "ca" (and) is indicated as elided,
because of the transgression of the verbal root.
For this very reason, it is explained that "and from the fourth," meaning when one transcends a realm—
whether one transcends the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Then it receives the name "thorough knowledge" (parijñā); this is the completion of the sentence.
Why?
Because of detachment from the entire realm (kṛtsnadhātuvairāgyāt).

The intention is that [the abandonment] is thorough because of detachment from the entire realm, and not merely because of partial disintegration; for at that time, there is a complete relinquishment.
"Both conjunction and disjunction" means that conjunction characterized by the afflictions of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is "both conjunctions."
Therefore, the Abhidharmikas say that the fifth cause is the disjunction from both [the object and the fetter], which is the disjunction from their conjunction;
and by this cause, abandonment is called thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

Regarding the category that has been abandoned— whether it be that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, up to that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path, or that which is to be abandoned by cultivation—
if one becomes dissociated from that abandoned category by means of another affliction (kleśa) to be abandoned by vision or cultivation that takes it as its object,
others say that this too is the fifth cause for the establishment of abandonment as thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
"But it is not other," and so forth.

However, that [cessation] is not other [than the cessation of suffering] because of the destruction of both conjunctions and the destruction of both causes; that is, because of the destruction of the universal cause (sarvatragahetu) which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and by the vision of origin, and because of the transcendence of the realm (dhātu). For even when those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering have been abandoned, there is as yet no destruction of the two causes as long as the universal cause to be abandoned by the vision of origin—which has that [same object] as its focal point—remains unabandoned.

Furthermore, even when those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation have been abandoned up to eight types, there is as yet no transcendence of the realm (*dhātu*) until the ninth type is also abandoned; therefore, we say again: "not of one," and so forth. To begin with, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is not at all possessed [of such abandonment].
Because of the absence of the acquisition of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*),
even a noble one (*ārya*) abiding on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)— up to and including the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origin (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*)—

is not at all possessed [of such dissociation]. By the word "up to" (*yāvat*), it is meant that [he is not possessed of it] during the receptivity and knowledge of the subsequent knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmānvayajñānakṣāntijñāneṣu*), as well as during the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origin (*samudaya-dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Because the two causes have not been abandoned, it should be understood that one is endowed with only one [parijñā] during the knowledge of the dharma of origination (*samudayadharmajñāna*), and likewise with only one during the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudayānvayajñānakṣānti*).

However, in the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudayānvayajñāna*), one is endowed with two: the aforementioned single parijñā consisting in the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination in the desire realm, and the parijñā consisting in the abandonment through the vision of suffering and origination in the form and formless realms.
In the case of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñānakṣānti*), it is likewise by means of two [indriyas];
in the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*), it is by means of three.

This should be understood up to five, for one established in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is endowed with five, but not six, because the sixteenth moment is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the statement "by six [knowledges] in the subsequent knowledge of the path," this refers to the previously mentioned [knowledges] together with the thorough knowledge of abandoning through the vision of the paths belonging to the form and formless realms;
for will he not indeed state this later?
The establishment of the four fruits occurs due to the presence of five causes:

the abandonment of the former [path], the attainment of another path, the summation of cessations, the acquisition of the eight knowledges within the fruit, and the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Thus,
there is an accumulation of abandonments but not an accumulation of full understandings; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "until one has attained detachment from the desire realm," the word "until" (yāvat) implies that even when one has abandoned the first category of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation up to the abandonment of the eighth category, one remains endowed with exactly six [faculties], and even when one has fallen away from that state, it remains the same.
For by means of the abandonment through detachment from sensual desire, one is freed from that synthesis; thus,
having attained detachment from sensual desire, it occurs either before or after the path of seeing (abhisamaya),
or before or after [the fruit].

How is it that one who has become free from passion for the desire realm by means of the mundane path, having entered the fixed course (niyāma) upon the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), is endowed with a single thorough knowledge of abandonment pertaining to the lower portion (avarabhāgīya-prahāṇaparijñā)? Because this noble one, having reached the sixteenth moment, becomes an non-returner (anāgāmin).

It is not stated that one is a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), nor that one is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) due to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya*);

therefore, because of the combination of the abandonments of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) and the abandonment of the five lower fetters, one is endowed with only a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*), namely, the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters.

Or, after the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), one who follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*) has attained freedom from passion for the desire realm and is endowed with only a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*)—that of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*);
likewise, one who has attained arhatship is endowed with only a single [thorough knowledge].
This is because, at that time, the thorough knowledges are consolidated.

"Even one who has fallen away [from the fruit] by means of the form realm"— this qualification is for the purpose of excluding the possession of the six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) that occurs when falling away from the desire realm; thus,
"one who has attained detachment from the form realm" means a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is free from passion for the form realm.
Why does the consolidation [of thorough knowledge] not occur through detachment from a realm alone?
Because there is no attainment of the fruit;
it is held that the consolidation of thorough knowledge results from both causes together: detachment from a realm and the attainment of the fruit.
Is it not abandoned by the mere [attainment]?

Even though it is abandoned by that which belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), because one who has attained Arhatship might fall away from Arhatship due to a defilement belonging to the formless realm— thereby regaining the two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) consisting of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the destruction of passion for the form realm (*rūparāgakṣaya*) which were included in the attainment of Arhatship—
one would, upon falling away through a defilement belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), be endowed with only one [thorough knowledge].

And since one would be endowed with six [defilements] by means of a defilement belonging to the desire realm, the mention of "envelopment belonging to the formless realm" refers to the non-returner and the arhat; thus,
the non-returner who is detached from the desire realm is intended here.
Because it is stated that non-returners who are free from passion for the realm of form possess two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*),
they are not "more," meaning they are not more numerous.
The intention is that [the practitioner] is like one who has entered the stream in successive order;
as for the phrase "by their own two causes," it has been explained as a summary— what is the meaning of this?
The meaning of "establishment as a unity" refers to these two states—
the state of one who is free from passion for the desire realm and the state of an arhat; both of these [are established] therein.
"Detachment from the realms and the attainment of the fruit" are said to constitute a single thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).

Thus, for a non-returner who is not yet free from passion for the form realm, there is the single thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters; and for an arhat as well, there is the single thorough knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters.
"One, two," and so forth in detail; someone abandons one.
Thus, the meaning is "he abandons":
some abandon two, some five, and some six;
or [alternatively], he attains them.
It is not the case that one person attains one, another two, another six, and another five;
therefore, he says:
Regarding "five not," no one at all attains even five not.
Such is the method of the meaning of the Sūtra; as for the commentary, it is explained as follows:

one who falls away from Arhatship relinquishes, by means of any [defiled] state of mind whatsoever, that single thorough knowledge which consists in the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-paryādāna-parijñā*).
In the calculation, because each of those exists in the state of Arhatship,

thus one who has fallen away from detachment from the desire realm but is detached from the form realm— an Anāgāmin— abandons two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) while [retaining] only one thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).
Regarding the full comprehension of the abandonment of the lower fetters and the full comprehension of the destruction of desire for the realm of form, he asks:
"What is this? and says:
An Anāgāmin who has become detached from the realm of form, when falling away from detachment from the desire realm,

abandons five [knowledges] at the sixteenth moment of mind during the clear realization (abhisamaya), namely, the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) for one who was previously detached.
For upon the attainment of the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*),

he who has reached the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) abandons the five previous full comprehensions acquired during the fifteen moments by means of his acquisition of the untainted disjunction (*anāsravavisaṃyoga*);

however, he does not abandon the sixth full comprehension, which is the abandonment of what is to be abandoned through the vision of the path regarding the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara-mārga-darśana-heya*).

However, because it is already included within the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) resulting from detachment from the realms and the attainment of the fruit, it is not mentioned here as if it were lost; for one who follows the gradual path and has not previously been detached from passion abandons six [thorough knowledges] due to the cause of detachment from desire—
namely, those thorough knowledges of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) belonging to the three realms.
Thinking that "acquisition is also like this," someone— setting aside the case of acquiring five— acquires one.
As for the statement that "whosoever obtains six," this refers to one who obtains what was not previously obtained;

it concerns either one situated on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or one on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) who, for the first time, obtains a *parijñā* (thorough knowledge) among the nine that had not been obtained before.

He obtains that single [complete] knowledge on the path of cultivation as well; for one who was previously free from passion obtains the single complete knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters at the end of the path of seeing,
and one who follows the gradual sequence also obtains that very same one on the ninth path of liberation during the detachment from the desire realm.
Even an Arhat may obtain another [state],
which shows that he falls away solely from detachment regarding the formless realm (*ārūpya*) and not from detachment regarding other realms.

For he attains both the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters and the thorough knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form; such is the case for one who, being a gradualist *anāgāmin*, falls away from the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
For there is no falling away for one who was previously free from passion, because such a person has attained both paths;
and for this very reason, no one indeed acquires five.
For if there were falling away for one who was previously free from passion, he alone would obtain five knowledges simultaneously;
thus it is stated in the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
The fifth treasury-location, titled "Exposition of the Latent Tendencies," is completed.
Chapter 6:
The sixth treasury-location, titled "Exposition of the Person and the Path."
Demonstrating the connection between the fifth and sixth treasury-locations (kośasthāna), he introduces this [topic] with the words:
"It has been stated how abandonment occurs," and so forth;
that is, how one attains thorough knowledge (parijñā) according to the manner of abandonment.
Because of the statement, "The cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the fruit," that [state] is also declared to be the abandonment of the afflictions.
To explain how this was stated, he says: "Because of the vision and cultivation of the truths."
Thus,
this is a designation of a dvandva compound in the singular;
it is [so called] because of the seeing and cultivation of the truths, or else because of cultivation.

It has been explained in detail that the afflictions (kleśas) are to be abandoned through seeing (darśana-heya) and through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) by reason of the vision of the truths and their subsequent cultivation:
"These ten, seven, seven, and eight— excluding three and two views respectively—
are abandoned in the desire realm through the visions of suffering and the other [truths] in due order."

Since the four [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and so forth, the vision of the truths is accomplished by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) and the cultivation of the truths is accomplished by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); therefore, this is said:

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: "Are these two—the path of seeing and the path of cultivation—now untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*)," which introduces the exposition of the paths;
[the reason for this inquiry is given by the phrase] "because they are the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the three realms," referring to the path of seeing.
Furthermore, if it were worldly, it would not be an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
moreover, because the nine types of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) are abandoned all at once,
it is not like the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The mundane [path] does not possess this power to abandon the three realms or to abandon the various categories [of defilements]; if it were so,
then the supramundane [path] would have the power to abandon the nine categories all at once.
There would also be the undesirable consequence that those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) would be abandoned all at once by the supramundane [path].

However, what is determined is that abandonment by the supramundane [path] occurs all at once, but not that abandonment all at once occurs only by the supramundane [path]; therefore, that consequence does not follow.
For the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are firm because they possess a real objective basis;
therefore, even by means of supramundane [wisdom], there is no simultaneous abandonment of them.
Otherwise, indeed...
If the exposition were not intended to follow the order of realization (*abhisamaya*), then the exposition of the cause would have come first— the exposition of the truth of origin—
because in the world, causes are perceived first.
Just as in the case of the applications of mindfulness, the meditative absorptions, and so forth; that is to say,
the teaching of the applications of mindfulness and so forth is arranged in accordance with their actual arising,
for the application of mindfulness to the body arises first.

Whether by way of the coarseness or subtlety of the object, or by way of the coarse or subtle activity [of the mind], or by way of the state of cause and effect between what precedes and what follows—
therefore, the application of mindfulness to feelings is taught first,
followed by the application of mindfulness to the mind; such is the teaching in accordance with their logical sequence, as it is for the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

By the word "etcetera," it is meant that for some [teachings], such as the liberations (vimokṣa), the bases of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the totalities (kṛtsnāyatana), there is a teaching conducive to rebirth, a teaching conducive to detailed exposition, a teaching conducive to demonstration, and a teaching conducive to comprehension.

Just as it is with the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), so it is with the destruction of the black and white [factors] respectively, due to the distinction between those already arisen and those not yet arisen;
for that which has arisen is easy to understand, whereas that which has not yet arisen is not.
Alternatively, the dark side is easily understood by those to be trained:
how one generates desire, exerts effort, arouses energy, upholds the mind, and applies it for the sake of abandoning evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
"He generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen [states]," as before;
"he generates desire for the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas," as before;
"he generates desire for the stability and non-confusion of arisen [wholesome states]," as before.
For there is no fixed rule that one first generates the desire for the abandoning of those [defilements] already arisen, and only afterwards [the desire] for the non-arising of those not yet arisen;
