what then?
First, one generates the desire for the non-arising of those [unwholesome states] not yet arisen,
and subsequently, for the abandoning of those already arisen; this is the illustration,
and the same should be applied to the white side as well.

However, because [the order of the truths] conforms to their realization (*abhisamaya*), there would be the consequence of explaining the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) first and the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) later, since the cause precedes the fruit; thus he shows this by saying "wherein one is attached," referring to the truth of suffering.
That by which one is afflicted is precisely that [from which] one seeks liberation; thus,
it is from that very Truth of Suffering.
Why is that very [state] first [attained] during the stage of application? He says:
"during the stage of investigation," meaning during the stage of examination, that is to say, during the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
"Having seen illness" means that illness is a metaphor for the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya),
and its cause is a metaphor for the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
The destruction of that [suffering] is the Truth of Cessation;
its remedy is the Truth of the Path.
This is also the illustration of the Truths found in the Sūtra.

In the *Vyādhyādi-sūtra*, how is it that a physician who removes arrows, being endowed with four factors, becomes worthy of a king, fit for a king, and is reckoned as one of the king’s essential attendants?
By which four?
He is skilled regarding the affliction and skilled regarding the origination of the affliction.
Skilled in the abandonment of afflictions and skilled in the non-arising of those abandoned afflictions—
just so, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with these four factors, is called the unsurpassed physician who extracts the arrow.
And by which four?
Here, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, understands as it truly is: "This is the noble truth of suffering," and "This is the origin of suffering."
"One understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering,' and 'This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering'—
this is due to the force of previous momentum."
"Because of the projection of what precedes,
like the unimpeded galloping of a horse on ground already seen. This means that when the ground has been previously perceived, the horse's galloping proceeds without obstruction.
In the same way,
as in the case of "running a horse," every verb meaning "to go" also carries the sense of "to cause to understand."
By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "also substantially" (*dravyato 'pi*), it is shown that [it exists] "also nominally" (*nāmataḥ api*);
"because it is non-perverted" (*aviparītatvāt*) means that it is non-perverted for both the Noble Ones (*ārya*) and others.
It is indeed suffering and nothing else;
however, it is by the Noble Ones that these truths have been seen as they truly are.
The truth of suffering was seen as suffering, impermanent, empty, and non-self; and likewise, up to the path, it was seen as the path, the right method, the practice, and the deliverance—
thus seen by others who were not noble ones.
Therefore, these are called the truths of the noble ones (āryas), but they are not called truths for the non-noble ones;
why is that?
Because of their perverted vision,
they indeed perceive the truth of suffering through such modes as "suffering is not suffering," and they perceive the truth of origination through such modes as "origination is not origination."
By means of such expressions as "cessation is non-cessation" and so forth,
and by means of such expressions as "the path is not the path" and so forth, they understand that [reality] as suffering.
Thus,
just as fools tremble at the truth of cessation as if from a precipice of renewed existence,
the noble ones, however, know it as suffering.
Thus is the pentad of the aggregates of clinging; these two are the noble truths,
namely the truths of suffering and its origin, because they are seen without error.
The two noble truths are noble by virtue of being wholesome and untainted,
and they are the truths of the noble ones.
Because it is seen without error,
and because of this indication by retaining only one term (*ekaśeṣa*), it follows that "among the noble truths" refers to when a portion of feeling has suffering as its intrinsic nature.
A portion of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), consisting of suffering and mental distress as appropriate, is [suffering] without exception.
Even pleasant things are suffering due to the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned formations;
unpleasant things are suffering due to the suffering of suffering and the suffering of conditioned formations;
and other things are suffering solely due to the suffering of conditioned formations—this is the meaning according to their respective applications.
They are called *manāpāḥ* because they are pleasing to the mind;

furthermore, it has been explained that there is a sandhi-conjunction here [as *manāpa-a-manāpebhyaḥ*], meaning "other than those [objects] which are both pleasing and unpleasing. Thus, it means "other than those things that are pleasing and unpleasing."

The three feelings are, in their respective order: pleasant feeling is agreeable; painful feeling is disagreeable; and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is neither agreeable nor disagreeable—this is the meaning.
"By virtue of that" means by virtue of those [feelings].
By the power of feeling (*vedanā*),

even forms, sounds, and so forth— which are not themselves of the nature of feeling— receive the designations "pleasant" and so on because they are conducive to it; thus, through transformation, they constitute the state of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
The meaning is "by way of transformation through impermanence," as it has been said:
"Alas, Caitraratha! Alas, the Mandākinī! Alas, my beloved!"—thus lamenting in distress, even the gods fall to the earth.
"Thus,
by the very nature of suffering" means "by the nature of affliction."
If it is said that "painful feeling is suffering in its arising and suffering in its duration," does this not imply by logical necessity that it is pleasant in its transformation?
And if that were so, there would be a confusion of characteristics.
This is not its defining characteristic;
rather, this instruction is for the purpose of refutation.
Or alternatively, let it indeed exist here.
That very form by which one is repelled is precisely what one depends upon; thus, it becomes nothing but suffering.

Just as pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*), although it is pleasant because its arising and duration are pleasant, is nonetheless reviled as suffering due to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*)— since it is intended to be reviled— so too, "suffering by way of conditioned forces" (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) means precisely by way of conditioning, that is, by way of being produced.
That which is impermanent is suffering; that which does not remain fixed is suffering.
The meaning is that whatever suffering arises and whatever [suffering] perishes, that is suffering.
He said,
"Because it is conditioned by conditions," since it is conditioned by conditions.
Therefore, just as that [feeling] is suffering, so too should the formations (saṃskāra) that are to be felt as such be understood; thus,
the state of suffering of formations to be felt as pleasant consists in their transformation.

Formations to be experienced as pleasant are pleasant at their arising, pleasant in their duration, and painful in their transformation; thus, for formations to be experienced as painful, their state of suffering is due solely to their nature of being experienced as painful;
[likewise], formations to be experienced as painful are painful at their arising and painful in their duration.
The suffering inherent in formations that are to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant is precisely their nature as formations,
because they are conditioned by causes and are impermanent.
That which is "suffering" is suffering itself as the nature of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

by the use of the word "up to," it should be stated that transformation itself is the nature of suffering (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and conditioned formations themselves are the nature of suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This formulation is distinguished by its grammatical analysis alone, not by its meaning;
for it is that very meaning which must be understood here, because of its uniqueness— such is the detailed explanation.
Agreeable conditioned phenomena are not common to the suffering of suffering;
therefore, because they are uncommon, the suffering of change is predicated of them.
Furthermore, disagreeable phenomena are not common to the suffering of change.
Therefore, because they are not common [to all], they are said to be the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);
however, all things, beginning with the pleasant, are suffering by way of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) because that [suffering] is pervasive.
If all things are thus suffering, why do they not all perceive it? To this he says:

It is stated here that "only the Noble Ones (āryas) perceive that [suffering], and no others," and "if all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras) are suffering due to the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), then it would follow that even the Path (mārga) is suffering. Thus, the entire argument is presented as follows. If all conditioned phenomena are indeed suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena, then it would entail the undesirable consequence that the Path is also suffering.
Because it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) means that it is produced by causes and conditions;
since suffering (*duḥkha*) has the defining characteristic of being "contrary" (*pratikūla*), why is it now stated otherwise that the Path (*mārga*) is not suffering?
It was stated previously that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent because they are produced by conditions,
and that whatever is impermanent is suffering.
Furthermore, because the path is conditioned by causes, it would follow that it is impermanent, and therefore suffering—
provided, of course, that "being disagreeable" alone were accepted as the definition of suffering.
That previously mentioned absence of characteristics would itself be characterized by suffering; thus,
this [absence] would not be without characteristics.
This is not a fault;
for how could that which is impermanent be disagreeable to the Noble Ones?
Is this the intended meaning here: that which is suffering?
Furthermore, is this the intended meaning here: that which is impermanent and disagreeable to the Noble Ones is suffering?
Furthermore, what is impermanent is disagreeable to the Noble Ones because it is a contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing.
Why, then, is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) path likewise impermanent yet not disagreeable to the Noble Ones? To this he says:
"For its arising is not disagreeable to the Noble Ones, because it brings about the destruction of all suffering."
For even when a term is used without specifying a particular distinction, a specific understanding is observed in common usage;
for example, "a cow" [is so called] because of its walking, yet a buffalo does not become a cow simply because it walks.
Thus, since the meaning is restricted in this way, why would [the term] "cow" apply [to anything else]?
Just as it is said "it goes," so too here, whatever thing is with-outflows (sāsrava) is disagreeable to the Noble Ones.
Why? Because it is impermanent; for that very reason, it is viewed as suffering.
It should be understood that they perceive the contaminated entity and its very cessation as peace, but not so the path.
"Just as there is the designation 'a heap of beans' even when mung beans and so forth are present"—

just as in common worldly usage, even when mung beans, lentils, peas, and the like exist within a heap of beans, it is designated as "a heap of beans" because the mung beans and others are few in number, so it is here.

"By way of being conducive to the slight pleasure of sprinkling" means: that which is both pleasure and slight is "slight pleasure" (*sukhāṇuka*); [the pleasure] through sprinkling is "slight pleasure of sprinkling" (*pariṣekasukhāṇuka*).
Therefore, the Venerable Kumāralāta indeed said: "Because it is a continuity of suffering and because it is the cause of suffering."
Thus,
pleasure is the cause of suffering because it is associated with karma to be experienced as suffering,
and because it is compounded with no small amount of suffering.
Because an abundance of suffering arises from performing services for others and the like,
and because when such suffering exists, there is a desire for its cessation; and because when suffering caused by hunger, thirst, and so forth exists...
The pleasure produced by food, drink, and so forth is desirable,
and not otherwise;
therefore, for these reasons:
"They determine suffering to be happiness" means "together with happiness."
The word "tu" (but) serves to set aside the prima facie view;

"because it has the single flavor of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations" means because it consists of the single modality of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
How is it now that they view feeling— which is of the nature of pleasure, and thus not of the nature of suffering— as suffering?
It is because [pleasure] is impermanent and therefore contrary [to one's desires].

The meaning is that because they are impermanent, they are disagreeable, and because they are disagreeable, one views them as suffering; this applies just as it does to the perception of form and so forth—
that is, just as one views even the perceptions of form, volitional formations, and consciousness as suffering.
And those [objects] are not suffering in the same way as the feeling of suffering, because the latter has the nature of being injurious.
Or, because they possess that characteristic;
however, as for the Venerable Kumāralāta who thinks [thus], for that Venerable one, this would be the aspect of origination (*samudaya-ākāra*) and not the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*).
Furthermore, because they have seen [the aggregates] as the cause of suffering,
how could the perception of suffering arise for noble non-returners when they are reborn in the form and formless realms?
The meaning is that it does not arise at all.
For those non-returners, the cause of painful feeling— the cause of a painful sensation—
is indeed the aggregates belonging to the realms of form and formlessness.
Why is it not a cause?
Because suffering does not recur;
and for what purpose would the "suffering inherent in conditioned formations" (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā) have been taught in the Sūtra?
If they perceive even pleasure as suffering because it is a cause of suffering—
referring to that which is called the "suffering of conditioned formations" (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā), namely, "that which is impermanent is suffering"— then [this is so].
What is its purpose? Since its purpose is established simply by being a cause of suffering, the proponent of [its] being a cause of suffering says:
"If, then..."

If they see that which is impermanent as suffering because it is impermanent, and not because it is a cause of suffering, then what is the distinction between the aspect of impermanence and the aspect of suffering?
Regarding this, the Master says:
"Because it has the nature of arising and passing away," and so forth.
Explaining how it is suffering because of its disagreeable nature, he says:
"Since that which is seen as impermanent becomes disagreeable, the aspect of impermanence draws forth the aspect of suffering."
This is what is meant:
that which has been stated— namely, "whatever is impermanent is suffering."
It was not stated thus merely because of the identity of their aspect;
rather, for those who see that pleasure as impermanent, it becomes disagreeable,
and because it is disagreeable, they see it as suffering.
"According to some," namely the Venerable Śrīlāta and others,
"this is the characteristic of suffering here" means that this is the defining mark of suffering in this context.
" Pleasant feeling is to be viewed as suffering"—
this is another scriptural passage concerning cold, heat, and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), sour, sweet, and other [tastes] are included; as well as those consumed in excess, those over-indulged in, and those consumed at improper times.
For example: cold in winter, warm in summer,
or temperate— that is, by means of a cause of pleasure.
The same should be stated regarding the distinction of postures (*īryāpatha*):
for those very things such as lying down that are desired as causes of pleasure are exactly those [that become suffering], and so it must be stated for everything up until they reach manifestation.
And since the notion of pleasure arises only in the counteracting of suffering,
how could there not be a pleasant sensation? This is the point at issue regarding the analysis of suffering.
To demonstrate that there is no such thing as a pleasant sensation for one who perceives it as pleasure, but rather that it is merely the counteracting of suffering, he says:
To demonstrate that it is not indeed pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, he says, "and regarding the conceptualization of suffering,
the foolish," and so forth.
When porters shift a burden from one shoulder to the other, they produce the notion that "there is happiness" even while remaining in a state of suffering, thinking that the burden has been relieved;
and this is precisely the logic [the opponent uses]. However, the Teacher [holds] that such sensual pleasure is not intended by the Noble Ones.

Because it would otherwise not be intended [as such], he says the following, demonstrating that meaning through another aspect, namely, the state of being a ground for negligence (pramādapada) and so forth:
"For whatever feeling," and so forth;
"a basis for negligence" means a cause for falling away from the wholesome.
The meaning is that it is accomplished through great effort, subject to transformation, productive of suffering immediately thereafter, and not productive of either suffering or pleasure;
or rather, that it has attained a diminished state.
The meaning is that it is impermanent and subject to destruction,

but certainly not in the form of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). For even for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), there is no contradiction regarding pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) when considered in the form of its beneficial specific characteristic.

And if there were attachment toward that pleasant feeling for anyone, just as there is toward a painful feeling— this is the intended meaning— then [the teaching] would be for the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*).
For this reason, they might perceive her as possessing faults even through another aspect for the sake of dispassion;
otherwise, since the absence of passion would be established without effort, this sūtra passage would have been stated solely for the sake of dispassion,
and he [the Buddha] would have asked in this manner.

Seeing that the statement "whatever is felt, all that is here suffering" was an improper expression, the Elder Ānanda questioned him about that very point; for he considered that "whatever is felt, all that is here suffering" was indeed contradictory.
Had he, however, seen that the [doctrine of] three feelings was improper, [he would have questioned him about that].
He would have asked this very thing: "With what intention did the Blessed One say that there are three feelings? This is indeed contradictory.
And the Blessed One, having been so questioned, would have replied: "It was with this intention that I said there are three feelings," but he did not reply in such a manner.
"Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena and their subject to transformation that I said: 'Whatever is felt, that herein is suffering.'"
But he did not say that;

rather, because of his statement regarding the three feelings, there must indeed be three feelings by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). However, the Blessed One shows that this statement—"Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering"—is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), having spoken it with this underlying intention.
Whatever is felt here is suffering— this is said with the intention of referring to the transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāmatā*),
because they have the nature of transformation and impermanence, that is,
because they possess the quality of transformation and the quality of impermanence.
Furthermore, transformation is alteration;
"objects of desire" is a designation for desirable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
If it is argued that "upapatti" is a designation for a highly desired birth,

and that there is a misconception (*viparyāsa*) on the part of one who views such a birth as having little happiness and much suffering, or as consisting of absolute happiness, because of a failure to turn away from the world;

Now, if it is thought that the statement "there are three feelings" was made merely in conformity with the world's determination regarding feeling—and not because it was spoken with the intention that all that is felt is suffering—this is not so; for the Blessed One has said:
"Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*) and the transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāmatā*) that I spoke."
"Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering"— therefore, this statement of three [truths] is not made in conformity with worldly convention;
rather,
the intention is to determine them according to their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).
And because he speaks according to reality, one might ask: "How is it that he says there are three feelings merely by conforming to worldly convention? To this, he says:
Having stated in detail: "That which is the faculty of pleasure and that which is the faculty of mental joy— this is to be seen as pleasant feeling," and so forth.
That which is the faculty of suffering and that which is the faculty of mental distress— this is the feeling of suffering; that which is the faculty of equanimity— this is the feeling of equanimity.
Having explained in detail, "This is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling," and so forth, [the text says], "By whom these five faculties have been thus seen as they really are through right wisdom.
This is the indicator here for the actual existence of the three types of feeling,
because of the absence of superimposition and denial in the phrase "as they really are" (*yathābhūtam*).

Furthermore, how could the world determine that feeling is threefold—pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant—if, by virtue of its inherent nature as suffering (*duḥkhasvābhāvya*), it were necessarily determined to be suffering alone? This applies to the weak, intense, and moderate [feelings], as explained at length.
Now, if it is thought that there is the notion of pleasure in weak suffering, the notion of pain in intense suffering, and the notion of neither-pain-nor-pleasure in moderate suffering...
To this we reply:
"Because pleasure is also threefold," and so forth;
that is, by way of the distinction between weak, medium, and intense, [pleasure exists] in relation to weak, medium, and intense sufferings.
The meaning is that there would be a perception of intense pleasure, and so forth; that is, there would be a perception of intense, moderate, or mild pleasure.
How could there be a perception of intense pleasure toward a mild suffering, or a perception of moderate pleasure toward a moderate suffering?
If there is a perception of mild pleasure in what is intense,
it is not logical to have a perception of mild pleasure when there is intense suffering;
for what reason?
That suffering would not be intense at all if there were a perception of mild pleasure therein;
and if there were a perception of intense pleasure toward what is actually mild suffering, how could that suffering be considered mild?
For it is not logical that such a clearly manifest experience should be mild.
Observing that the experience of pleasure follows immediately after the neutral state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, he says: "When [pleasure] arises from a specific odor, taste, or tangible object.
For you, the neutral state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is indeed the middle [feeling], which is suffering.
Therefore, it must be explained that there is no mild degree [of suffering]; for what kind of suffering could be so mild that one would have the perception of pleasure toward it?
For that pleasure arises solely through the power of the object,
whether by the power of the immediately preceding condition of mild suffering or by the power of the immediately preceding condition of intense suffering; furthermore,
if you maintain that there is a perception of pleasure in mild suffering, [then consider this].
Regarding the statement "when that slight suffering has not arisen or has perished":
when that slight suffering has not arisen or has perished,
there would be an even greater perception of pleasure, because of the complete disappearance of suffering.

The intention is this: since you desire the notion of happiness even when suffering has been removed only partially, why then would you not do so when suffering has been removed without remainder? For indeed, all suffering has been eliminated.
The same should be said regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure;
just as the pleasure born from specific odors, tastes, and tangibles was described,
so too should it be described regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure.
How can there be a perception of sensual pleasure when the suffering of passion is mild?
Furthermore, that sensual pleasure would be even greater when that suffering of passion has not yet arisen or has already perished.
"And this has not been seen," thus [the question] "how indeed" and so forth;
how indeed can this be tenable?
That which is felt mildly— that is, that which is mild suffering— is what should be stated as being grasped as intense experience;
[yet] it is grasped as pleasure.
Furthermore, "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) in the middle refers to the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*) within middling suffering; this is the meaning.
The intention is that, in the case of mild suffering, it must be unmanifest by virtue of that [feeling].
"And in the three," and so forth;
because of the mention of "pleasure" in the three dhyānas— the first, second, and third—
there is pleasant feeling there, according to the statement in the Sūtra.
There would be mild suffering;
for what reason?
Because of your intention that there is a perception of pleasure within mild suffering.
Since the Sūtra speaks of neither-pain-nor-pleasure in the fourth dhyāna and in the formless realms (ārūpya), would there not be "intermediate suffering" [in the lower stages]? Why?
Because of that specific intention, it is said that "in the middle [level] of suffering there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling]";
therefore, it is not logical to establish the classification of pleasant and other feelings within mild and other degrees of suffering.
For how indeed could there be mild suffering in the lower dhyānas?
"Furthermore, it is said: 'Above, and again in the middle, there is form,' O Mahānāman.

If form, O Mahānāman, were exclusively suffering—neither pleasant, nor accompanied by pleasure, nor joy, nor accompanied by joy, nor experienced as pleasure—then no cause for passion toward form would be discerned."

"Since, therefore, there is form that is pleasant, accompanied by pleasure, and so forth as before, a cause for form is discerned, namely, for the sake of passion"— regarding this [argument] that "pleasure does not exist because its cause is not established," we say:
if, for you, pleasure does not exist because its cause is not established, [then...]
Even suffering would be non-existent because the cause of suffering is not established; furthermore, since the cause of happiness is indeed established, he asks: "How so? and replies:
"For it depends on a specific basis," and so forth.
For if the object alone were the cause, the cause would indeed be indeterminate;
however, the object alone is not the cause.
Since a specific state of the substratum (*āśrayaviśeṣa*) is also a cause,
that very same thing is called "fire";
for example, that very same fire becomes the cause of sweet cooking when the collection of rice grains is in a slightly cooked state due to a specific transformation of the substances to be cooked.
The meaning is that because fire is the cause for cooking the desired rice,
it is itself the cause for cooking it deliciously,
since it is the cause for its burning.

The meaning is this: it is not the case that having reached a certain state of the substance to be cooked—which was previously the cause for its being cooked sweetly—it would later, upon reaching that same state again, no longer be the cause of such sweet cooking;
this is the illustration for the aforementioned subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*).
And how is it that the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are not established as a cause of happiness?
For indeed, those very meditative absorptions—from the first up to the third—even when entered for a long duration, do not become a cause of suffering;
thus, what could there be to counteract the bliss born of meditation?
Indeed, because there is no suffering in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*),
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) it should also be stated that if there were a perception of pleasure (*sukha-buddhi*) only in the remedies for suffering, [it would not be true pleasure].
Mahānāman, if form were exclusively suffering— neither pleasure nor accompanied by pleasure— and so forth, this would not have been said; therefore,
since it is said that "pleasure arises," that feeling which arises is indeed pleasure.
That painful feeling is not imagined as pleasure; rather,
it is that particular state of the body which is conducive to the arising of pleasure.
For otherwise, if pleasure arising from a different state did not arise until such a bodily state had ceased,
then there would subsequently be an even greater perception of pleasure;
[the question remains] "from where [does it come] at the end?"— this is the detailed argument.
Now, if it is thought: "How could there be a perception of suffering at the end of drinking, eating, and so forth, if their beginning and initial commencement did not exist?
To this we reply: it is due to a specific transformation of the body (*kāyapariṇāmaviśeṣāt*).

What is this? He says: through the practice of drinking and so forth, a specific transformation of the body arises later, such that suffering does not arise during the state when pleasure is produced, but it does arise at the end.
Because intoxicants and the like possess sweetness and pleasure at their end—

just as in the case of wine, milk, and so forth— a specific subsequent transformation occurs such that acidity (sourness), which was non-existent during the prior state of sweetness, arises at the end.
Alternatively, just as sweetness arises from a specific transformation of wine and other substances,
and subsequently acidity arises from that very same specific transformation—
here, sweetness is the illustration of pleasure.
That which is the sourness of suffering is precisely what is called the truth of origination.

Because of the statement that those which have become causes constitute the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), or because it was stated in the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* that the world is the origination of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*).
Because of this statement,
since it is craving alone that is mentioned in the Sūtra,
what is the truth of origination?
"That which is craving, accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there"—
the Vaibhāṣika says this is because of its predominance.
Because of the mention of other factors as well—
since in another sutra there is mention of other things such as karma and ignorance— the others too are the origin in the future life.
"In the future" means in the next world;
furthermore, it is said elsewhere in a sutra:
"For when, monks, there are five kinds of seeds that are unbroken, undamaged, not rotten, not destroyed by wind or heat, fresh, substantial, and well-planted."
"There is the earth element and the water element;
in this way, those seeds attain growth, sprouting, and abundance.
For indeed, monks, this simile has been made only for the sake of understanding this matter. Having introduced this illustration, this was said.

"O monks, 'the five kinds of seeds' is a designation for this consciousness accompanied by grasping; 'the earth element' is a designation for the four stations of consciousness. Furthermore, the seed is the cause, and that which is the cause [is the condition]."
That origination is also the foundational cause for the stations of consciousness;
therefore [it is so called].
Since karma and the other [factors] are also stated to be causes, their status as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is established;

therefore, the teaching in the Sūtra concerning craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is "intentional" (*ābhiprāyika*). It is intentional because it exists in the intention, or because it operates by means of the intention. The underlying intention is that this was formulated with reference to a person (*pudgala*) who is dominated by craving.

In the Abhidharma, however, that which pertains to the definition is "definitional" (*lākṣaṇika*). Thus, the definitional exposition in the Abhidharma states: "Every contaminated (*sāsrava*) thing is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*)," because the five contaminated aggregates possess the characteristic of being the truth of origination.
That same Vaibhāṣika, wishing to express that the status of being the truth of origination for craving and so forth is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), says:

However, by speaking at length on the cause of actualization with the words "but rather," the Sūtra— while explaining the cause of birth and actualization along with its conditions— has stated that craving alone is the truth of origination; yet it has also stated that karma, craving, and ignorance [are the causes].

Karma is the cause of rebirth (*upapatti-hetu*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause of actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*) within the realms of existence; furthermore, regarding these two, it is stated in that verse: "Karma is the cause of rebirth, and craving is the cause of actualization."
"Karma is the cause for rebirth; craving is the cause for manifestation"— this is because of such statements in one sutra and another,
as in the detailed explanation beginning with "with cause and with condition."
In this sutra, this explanation is given either in sequential order or in the order of a causal succession within the verse.
Karma, craving, and ignorance are the cause for the formations— the eye and so forth— in the future life;
thus, what is being said is that karma is the cause of rebirth.
Therefore, from this sutra, or rather from the *Sahetu-sapratyaya-krama-sutra*, such is the meaning of this verse.
How, monks, does the eye have a cause, a condition, and a source?
And what, monks, is the cause of the eye, what is its condition?
"Monks, karma also has a cause, it has a condition, and it has a source.
And what, monks, is the cause of craving? Craving is the condition."
Craving is the cause;
monks, craving has a cause, it has conditions, and it has a source.
And what, monks, is the cause of craving?
"What is the condition,
what is the cause of craving, monks? Ignorance is the cause."
Ignorance is the condition,
ignorance is the cause;
monks, ignorance also has a cause, has a condition, and has a source.
And what, monks, is the cause of ignorance, what is its condition,
what is its source?
"Monks, improper mental attention is the cause of ignorance, improper mental attention is the condition,
and improper mental attention is the source."
By explaining the nature of the seed and the field, consciousness and the others have also been mentioned; consciousness is the seed,
and its field consists of the aggregates such as sensation and so forth— these too have been explained as the truth of origination.
It has been established that the teaching in the Sūtra— that it is not only craving and so forth— is intentional (ābhiprāyika);
furthermore, that the nature of origination (samudaya) for all suffering is defined by its characteristics (lākṣaṇika) according to the various types of birth and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the various distinctions of birth, female, male, and so forth are understood;
by "without distinction" (*abhedenā*), the elements, destinies, wombs, and so forth are intended.
Regarding those two in their respective order:
action is the cause of arising (*upapatti*), and craving is the cause of manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*); this is explained in detail by the analogy of the seed and so forth.
A rice seed is the cause for the production of a rice sprout, a barley seed is the cause for the production of a barley sprout, and so forth;
water, however, without distinction,
is the cause for the growth of a rice sprout as well.
In the same way, this applies to the sprout of barley and so forth;
therefore, those [conditions] are the cause for the mere growth of all sprouts,
because without craving there is no birth.
In this context, the proof is the reason [that] craving is the cause of birth,
because [birth] occurs or does not occur depending on its presence or absence.
To explain the meaning of the statement, "Just as a seed [is the cause] of a sprout through the continuity of the series," he says:
"And where there is craving," and so forth.
In whatever object, such as form and so forth, there is a mental continuum accompanied by craving.
In that regard, we observe the mental continuum frequently inclining [toward rebirth]; therefore, it is the same even in a future existence— that is, even in a future existence,
the mental continuum is accompanied by craving.
Therefore, we conclude that it bends toward that [object], and wherever it bends, there it proceeds.
And the proof for this is that the mental continuum proceeds toward rebirth because it inclines due to craving.
Because it has form and other objects as its domain,
it is like the application of a bath-powder of dry lentils (*masūra*); thus,
"lentil" (*masūra*) refers to the bath-powder (*upasnāna*).
Its coating is dry;
"having a dry lentil-bath-paste coating" refers to a limb that is like that—
just as a limb is not grasped by a dry lentil-bath-paste coating.
Thus it is shown that by craving there is the personal existence;
this is the reasoning, namely,
that craving is the cause of production.
In this regard, it is said "like a jar and water" as an incidental discussion on truth, because both are truths in this sense.
The presentation of two examples is for the purpose of demonstrating the two types of division:
those that divide by way of physical form, such as jars and the like,
and those that divide by way of cognition, such as water and the like.
Because it is impossible to extract taste and other qualities from water and such substances by means of physical manipulation;
or rather, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is of two kinds: that which relies on another convention and that which does not rely on another substance.
In that regard, for that [exclusion] which relies upon another conventional designation, both differentiation and the exclusion of others are possible; however,
for that which relies upon a distinct substance...
In that [atom], only the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is possible, not its division;
for it is impossible to effect the disjunction of parts in an atom composed of eight substances.
Thus, it is conventionally real (saṃvṛtisat).
The meaning of "existent" is [existent] by way of conventional usage;
in the same way, feeling and so forth should also be regarded [in this light].
Thus, feeling, volition, perception, and the rest should also be regarded as substantially existent.
How is it that, when one excludes phenomena such as sensation through the intellect, the intellect still arises with respect to the intrinsic nature of sensation? Thus,
sensation is substantially existent.
In this way, perception, volition, and so forth are also to be applied accordingly;
for those who say "the jar exists" and "the water exists," they speak the truth and not a falsehood.
He shows the purpose for speaking of conventional truth,
and it has been said:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths."
There is the conventional truth of the world and the truth in the ultimate sense; thus,
it is called "ultimate truth."
The object of supreme knowledge is the ultimate (paramārtha);
that which is both ultimate and true is ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). Just as it is apprehended by another, namely worldly knowledge, so it is conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).

That which is apprehended through convention (*saṃvṛti*), through worldly discourse (*saṃvyavahāra*), or through cognition—whether afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*)—is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). For according to the Yogācāras, existence (*sat*) is threefold:
ultimate existence (*paramārthasat*), conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*), and substantial existence (*dravyasat*).
"Substantially existent" means existent by way of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
"substantially existent" [is explained] by the passage beginning with "one who abides in conduct," where "conduct" (*vṛtta*) refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*).

That which has been heard as pertaining to the realization of truth— which is the cause of non-attachment, the cause of non-distraction, and the cause of right conduct— is conducive to the vision of truth.
One grasps that which is heard, recites it, or hears its meaning; one understands that meaning through the gateway of the ear. How so?
Showing that the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) has both as its object, he says:
"Sometimes one draws out the meaning by means of the phrasing;
one draws out the meaning by means of the name produced from the phrasing, thinking, 'This is the meaning of this name.'"
Sometimes the phrasing (*vyañjana*) is drawn out by means of the meaning;
the sense is that "this is the phrasing for this particular meaning to be expressed. For this word *vyañjana* is employed here in the sense of "name" (*nāman*).
It is also stated in the Sūtra that [the teaching] is "well-meaning and well-phrased";
however, regarding this conceptualization, the Master has explained it at length.
Since wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) is not established [as distinct],
it is said that the characteristic [of wisdom] is one that is conflated with the characteristics of what consists of hearing (*śrutamayi*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*),
and because it is not unmixed, it is not established.
"Born from the contemplation of reasoning" means that *nidhyāna* is thorough investigation (*nitīraṇa*) by means of reasoning; [the knowledge] is born from that.
"Because the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of 'cause'":
this is the authoritative statement heard; here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed for the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) in the sense that it has hearing as its cause.
Wisdom caused by hearing is "that which consists of hearing" (*śrutamayī*);
likewise, reflection consisting of reasoning is "thought" (*cintā*), and this is the cause of that which consists of thought (*cintāmayī*).
Here, the suffix *-maya-* is prescribed [to denote the cause].
According to the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of its material cause" (*tatprakṛtivacane mayaṭ*), or according to the rule "it denotes a modification" (*tasya vikāraḥ*),
it is a figurative modification.

Furthermore, another definition must be added: "consisting of hearing" (*śrutamayī*) is like a "modification of hearing" (*śrutavikāra*), because we observe such usage in the world as "breaths consisting of food" (*annamayaḥ prāṇāḥ*) and "cows consisting of grass" (*tṛṇamayyo gāvaḥ*);
[this is so] because it causes the removal of contact with unwholesome discursive thoughts (*akuśalavitarka*).
Physical seclusion consists in dwelling alone for the sake of distancing oneself from social contact;
mental seclusion consists in avoiding afflicted thoughts for the sake of distancing oneself from unwholesome thoughts.

Therefore, one is mentally withdrawn [from the world] because of distress regarding what has been obtained— whether it be unexcellent or insufficient; this "distress" (*paritāsa*) is mental anguish (*daurmanasya*).
Therefore, "he is distressed" means that he is exhausted,
either because [the food] is not excellent or because it is insufficient.

According to the opinion of the Master (Ācārya), dissatisfaction (*asantuṣṭi*) is the distress felt regarding what has been obtained; whereas great desire (*mahecchatā*) is the longing or craving for what has not yet been obtained, whether that be excellent or abundant—
these two belong exclusively to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
Because its intrinsic nature consists in the skillfulness regarding gain,
the delight in abandonment and cultivation, and the delight in cessation and the path,
it does not have contentment as its intrinsic nature.

And how is this fourth noble lineage (āryavaṃśa) of the nature of its own essence? To this he says: "Because of turning away from craving for existence (bhavarāga)," that is, because of turning away from craving for becoming.
And because it is an aversion to sensual desire, and this aversion is non-greed; thus,
[it refers to those] who have abandoned their own livelihoods and occupations.
To those who have abandoned their own livelihoods and abandoned their own occupations; therein, "livelihood" (*vṛtti*) refers to that by which one lives through food, drink, and so forth,
while "occupation" (*karmānta*) refers to agriculture, crafts, and the like.
"In this way, for the sake of existence and non-existence"—here, the word "iti" indicates the various modes of existence and non-existence.
Among those, craving regarding the mode of existence is as follows: "O, may I become Indra! May I become a universal monarch (cakravartin)! and so forth.

Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is also craving for annihilation; it is precisely the mindfulness [expressed by] thoughts such as, "O, may I be cut off! May I not exist after death! and so forth, that is what is meant by "remembered" (*smṛtam*).

He shows that the suffix *kta* is prescribed in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*), as in the term *avatāra*, meaning a "ford" (*tīrtha*) by which one descends; thus, it refers to the "proximate ford" for those whose conduct is dominated by passion (*rāgacarita*).

One for whom passion arises quickly with even a slight [stimulus] is one whose temperament is inclined toward passion (*rāgacarita*) in its proximate form; whereas one for whom passion is excessive [only when the stimulus is great] is one whose temperament is inclined toward passion in its predominant form.
Thus, he is excessively prone to passion because of the lack of variety in the object of focus;
for in the case of wind, no variety of color or shape is perceived.
Because it is not directed outward but is directed inward,
it conduces to the cutting off of discursive thought; this is the subject at hand,
because of its close contemplation of that object.
The meaning is "due to the discernment of the objects of the eye.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" in the phrase "having as its object the forms of the livid corpse and so forth," there is the inclusion of the forms of the festering corpse and so on;
"vipatūmakam" refers to that which has generated worms.
The fourfold object of passion does not exist, because it consists of color, shape, touch, and social convention,
and [the mind] is characterized by resolute conviction and partial mental attention.
The meaning is that it is because of its nature as attention consisting of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manasikāra*) and because of its nature as partial attention (*prādeśika-manasikāra*);
this attention has resolute belief as its primary element.
And this [meditation] is partial (*prādeśika*), meaning it is not all-pervasive;
for the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) does not have the five aggregates as its object, nor does it have the entirety of the stages (*bhūmi*) as its object.
What then?
It has as its object a portion of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha),
because that [aggregate] exists.
The meaning is that through the unwholesome there is no abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*), but only their suppression;

for it is said that "one fixes the mind on the parts of one's own limbs," and thus, at the very time of the preliminary practice (*prayoga*), one does not yet fix it on the parts of a woman's body because of the avoidance of the cause of passion. This is shown by the phrase "while purifying the bones."
Removing the flesh from the bones, he beholds the entire skeleton,
just as has been described for a novice monk who is still in training and whose mind has not yet attained stability.
If he wishes to destroy passion, he should go along the path of Śiva; then he should look at the livid corpse, then he should look at the putrefying corpse,
then he should look at the bloated corpse, and even at the skeleton.
Thus, in this regard, briefly stated, there are three types of practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) engaged in the meditation on the foul:

the beginner practitioner of yoga fixes the mind upon a single big toe and perceives that big toe as becoming moist; he then resolves upon [the perception] that "this is flesh," and so on, until he resolves upon the entire body as a skeleton.
But for one who has achieved mastery, it is the same as before up until the mental attention that transcends the half-skull; likewise, he holds the mind between the eyebrows.
However, the "one with expanded mind" expands the bones as far as the ocean, while the "beginner" contracts them; thus, there are three types starting from this point.
And having established this, there arises a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) question regarding those with conquered and unconquered mental attention (*manaskāra*), as explained in detail:

the first alternative is the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) of one who has conquered mental attention, which has one's own body as its object; it is "limited" (*parītta*) by way of the limitation of its object, because the body is small.
The meaning is that because one has mastered mental attention (*jitamanaskāra*) and transcended mental attention (*atikrāntamanasikāra*), there is no limitation of mastery (*vaśitā-parīttatā*).

The second alternative refers to the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) which, for one who has not mastered mental attention, has the ocean as its limit as its object; it is limited because mastery is limited due to the lack of mastery over mental attention.

The third category consists of the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) that has one's own body as its object for one whose mental attention is not yet mastered; it is "limited" both by way of the limitedness of its object,
because the body is small, and because its object is limited, since it does not have the ocean as its limit.

The fourth alternative is for one whose mental application is conquered, because it does not have a limited mastery nor does it have a limited mental application, since its object of focus extends to the limit of the non-sealed (amudra).

"In the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and the intermediate dhyāna" means in the preparatory stages, in the intermediate dhyāna, in the four dhyānas, and in the desire realm; thus they belong to ten levels,
because there are four preparatory stages for the dhyānas.

Therefore, the intention is that they have objects as their objective support (*arthālambana*) because they take color and shape as their objective support; they do not have names as their objective support.
The intention is that since it is established by its very name as having an "unpleasant aspect" (*aśubhākāra*), it need not be formulated [again] for the sake of specifying its aspect.

As for the statement "that which belongs to a particular time has an object belonging to that same time," this is like visual consciousness: for past [non-conceptual wisdom], the object is exclusively past, and so on, up to present [wisdom] having a present object.
Because it is restricted to its own object and because it consists of mental attention through resolute conviction, it is not set forth as a sutra,
due to being [only] partially suitable or unsuitable.
In the beginningless great cycle of existence, because it is habitual, it is "attained through detachment" (*vairāgyalābhikī*);
because it is not habitual, it is "attained through application" (*prāyogikī*).
The applications of mindfulness of the body and so forth have wisdom as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Because they function through the application of the power of that mindfulness— since their activity consists in the application of the power of that mindfulness— the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), such as the foundation of mindfulness of the body, which consist of the substance of wisdom regarding the body and so forth, are called "foundations of mindfulness. Similarly, because the wisdom regarding inhalation and exhalation functions through the application of the power of mindfulness, it is called "mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation" (ānāpānasmṛti).
"In five stages" means in the three preparatory stages (sāmantaka), excluding the fourth preparatory stage, and in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
And why is it said to exist in the five stages including the desire realm?
Because it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Because in the first dhyāna, there is the feeling of equanimity in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and so forth; however, although there is equanimity in the preparatory stage of the fourth dhyāna,
that is not the ground for inhalation and exhalation.
Now, for what reason is this equanimity determined to be associated only with [the third dhyāna]?
To this he says: "Because it is conducive to discursive thought (*vitarka*).

This means that mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which is the antidote to those [discursive thoughts]—that is, the antidote to discursive thought—is not associated with those two, pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, because pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*) are obstacles to focused attention (*avadhāna*) and are contrary to the application of effort (*ābhoga*), and because this mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*) must be accomplished through focused attention, it does not associate with those two.
The word "kila" (it is said) indicates the opinion of another, [the view] that it is because [the mind] is conducive to applied thought (*vitarka*).
Therefore, this alternative position is presented: "But those who [are] in the fundamental [dhyānas]," and so forth;
"by another" means starting from the fourth dhyāna.
It has the desire realm as its basis because,
therein, discursive thought (*vitarka*) is predominant due to the lack of prior cultivation of the preparatory effort.
"Obtained through detachment" means that because they are habituated to these teachings;
"these teachings" refers to the Buddhist teachings, and those who possess them are "those of these teachings."

The meaning is "of those very Buddhists"; for while there is instruction on breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) among outsiders, there is no instruction on mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
And because of the lack of self-awakening to subtle dharmas;
for, without instruction, outsiders do not possess self-awakening to subtle dharmas.
Furthermore, its subtlety is due to its being endowed with six causes.
"Having disregarded the body or the mind" means without attachment;
"the distance of a span or a fathom" is due to the application [of this measure] to beings who are strong or weak.
To follow [the mind] downward as far as the circle of wind,
and upward as far as the Vairambha winds,
is not logical because of the nature of mental attention directed toward reality (*tattva-manasikāra*).
As far as the wind-circle and the Vairambha winds, this conceptualization belongs to the mental application of resolute belief (*adhimukti-manaskāra*); one might ask:
"Are these [winds] beneficial, and so on, up to being warm?"
This should be understood as a mere designation,
because one designates specific qualities such as being "beneficial" with respect to a particular part of the body itself,
[thinking] that the mind and mental factors are dependent upon it.
The meaning is that their activity is bound to those [preceding stages];
"in each subsequent root of merit" refers to the applications of mindfulness, the stages of heat, and so forth.
By the word "etc. in the phrase "in the path of seeing, etc.," the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is included;

by the word "etc. in the phrase "the purification consisting of the knowledge of destruction, etc.," the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) and the right view of one in training (śaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi) are included.

Regarding the phrase "inhalation and exhalation are like the body," this indicates that inhalation and exhalation belong to all stages (sarvabhūmika) by virtue of their connection with mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti).
For whichever level the body belongs to—
ranging from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the third dhyāna— the two [mental applications] belong to that same level and not to any other level.
Regarding the phrase "dependent on specific states of body and mind," he asks:
why are inhalation and exhalation dependent on specific states of body and dependent on specific states of mind? He says:
Because they do not exist for those who have entered the formless realm or the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*,
[these] do not occur for those in the formless realm due to the absence of a body, nor for those in the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*.
Furthermore, they do not exist for those in the stages of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, and so forth, because there is no differentiation of the body and no hollow body; this is the meaning.
Nor do they exist for those who are without consciousness.
Due to the absence of mind,
inhalations and exhalations do not occur even for those who have attained the fourth dhyāna, because of the absence of that specific state of mind which constitutes their basis.
For this very reason, he says:
"If the body is porous," and so forth;
[the reason being] because it is devoid of sense faculties (*indriya*).
The meaning is that they function separately like the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Are they not "nutritive" (*aupacayika*) because they decrease as the body increases?
They are not "resultant of maturation" (*vipākaja*) because inhaled and exhaled breaths, once severed, are reconnected again.

For this [reconnection] does not occur for matter that is a result of maturation (*vipāka-rūpa*), nor for matter whose nature is maturation, such as the eye and so forth; however, the reconnection of non-material phenomena— namely, mind and mental factors— is not prevented by the Nidhāna [sūtra], because it refers to those [phenomena] consisting of postures (*airyāpathika*) or emanations (*nairmāṇika*).

The mind pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*) and the mind pertaining to supernormal transformations (*nairmāṇika*) belonging to a lower stage manifest even for one born in the fourth dhyāna; anticipating this objection, it is said that there is no observation by means of those two minds of a lower stage,
because [the observation] is for the purpose of accomplishing insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The meaning is "for the sake of accomplishing wisdom";

for even for one who has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) are not abandoned without wisdom, according to the statement: "The afflictions are to be slain by knowledge."
But from what [source] is it known that insight is accomplished through the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness?
From the sūtra: "O monks, this is the one-way path, namely, the applications of mindfulness."
From the statement, "This alone is the heap of the wholesome, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness," it follows that "kāyavid" refers to feeling (vedanā).
Their own-nature (*svabhāva*) is their specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
what is the own-nature of the body? It is its being composed of the primary elements and their derivatives.
Feeling has the nature of experiencing,
mind has the nature of apprehension,
and for the others besides these three, there is their respective intrinsic nature.
"The state of suffering of the essential [elements]" refers to what has been explained as suffering characterized by being contrary to the noble ones;
this statement that "phenomena are distinct from the three" is spoken with reference to an unmixed formal arrangement.
But in the case of the mixed arrangement, even the body and so forth are included;
furthermore, all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are to be viewed as the foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature, which is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because this wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth arises in dependence upon association and its object, it is therefore called a "foundation of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
This qualification is used because the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and are not obtained by birth;
for what reason, then, are they said to have the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*)?
Is it said that there is also another kind of application of mindfulness? Yes; others [arise] from association and from objects.
Thus, others— the co-arising factors such as feeling and so forth—
are the application of mindfulness by association; this is the application of mindfulness through association (*saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because it is associated with the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature and because it has that as its object— meaning,
because it has the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature and through association as its object— it is the application of mindfulness as an object.
Which are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena that have those as their objects?
This being so, that foundation of mindfulness as its object (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna) has the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (sarvadharma-svabhāva).
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"O monks, 'all phenomena' is a designation for the four foundations of mindfulness."
For by that thorough knowledge, one who possesses it— the wise one— is made an "anupaśya"; thus, he is called an *anupaśya* because he observes (*anupaśyati*).
The suffix *śa* is applied according to the rule *pā-ghrā-dhmā-dheṭ-dṛśaḥ śa*;

thus, "one who perceives a person" (*anupaśyan pudgalam*) is called an *anupaśyaka*. However, if it refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) [of wisdom], the analysis of the compound is as follows.
The instrument for one who observes is "observing" (*anupaśyanā*);
for by means of that wisdom, the possessor of it— the wise one— is made an observer (*anupaśya*),
just as a person is called "wise" (*prājña*) due to their connection with wisdom.
Since one is called "one who contemplates" (*anupaśyin*) due to the practice of such contemplation (*anupaśyanā*), it is established that contemplation is wisdom (*prajñā*);
for this reason, it was said by the Blessed One:
"He dwells contemplating the body in the body internally and personally."
How is it established that "insight is contemplation" by that [statement]? It is established thus:
"What is its object of contemplation? It is vision."
For "observation" (anupaśya) has the characteristic of seeing;
therefore, the person who observes is like a staff,
and thus it is a locative tatpuruṣa compound.

Regarding "one who contemplates the body" (*kāyānupaśyī*): if the suffix *ṇini* were also prescribed in the sense that "one whose habit is to contemplate the body" is "one who contemplates the body," we observe that this form is established nonetheless because of the predominance of mindfulness (*smṛty-udrekatvāt*).
The meaning is "because of the predominance of mindfulness";
"functioning through the application of the power of mindfulness" refers to the application (*ādhāna*) of that power.

The strengthening of mindfulness is "strengthening of mindfulness" (*smṛtibala-ādhāna*); wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which functions by means of this strengthening of mindfulness, and its state is "the state of strengthening of mindfulness."
Therefore,
just as a split in wood is held together by a sharp wedge driven into the crack,
so too does this wisdom function toward its object through the support of the power of mindfulness.
For if mindfulness holds the object, then wisdom understands it;
thus, because [wisdom] "establishes itself by means of mindfulness," it is called a "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This is the meaning according to the Vaibhāṣikas:
since the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* allows for the suffix *-lyuṭ* (the abstract noun suffix) even in the sense of the agent, [wisdom is the foundation].
"But this is logical," says the Teacher;
for this [term] "smṛti" is an instrument (karaṇa-sādhana), meaning that memory is established by means of this [mind].
This is merely an indication of the meaning; however, the analysis (vigraha) should be made thus:
"That by which one stands near is 'upasthāna'."
Regarding the term *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness),
as to how mindfulness is established by means of this [foundation], he says:
"because of the clear observation (*abhilakṣaṇa*) of that which has been seen."
Because the object, exactly as it has been perceived by wisdom, is expressed and grasped by mindfulness; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, where does it abide?
It abides in the body, and so on, up to the phenomena;
this is the application of mindfulness to the body, the *kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*.
In this way, up to the application of mindfulness regarding phenomena, which is the "application of mindfulness to phenomena" (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*);
and just as it is for the application of mindfulness by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), so it is also for the application of mindfulness by way of association (*saṃsarga*).
For just as mindfulness is established upon the body and so forth by means of wisdom, so too is it by means of those [mental factors] associated with it; thus,

seeing that the definition of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) mentioned in the Sūtra as being formed by the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*) is untenable, he speaks now, wishing to express the meaning through another grammatical factor (*kāraka*).
But as for where it was said,
"and so forth," just as the arising and passing away of the body were explained, so too should those of feeling and the other aggregates be explained.
How is it that from the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling,
and from the cessation of contact there is the disappearance of feeling?
From the arising of name-and-form, there is the arising of the mind;
from the cessation of name-and-form, there is the disappearance of the mind.
From the arising of mental attention, there is the arising of phenomena.

Regarding the statement in this sutra, "Through the cessation of mental attention, there is the disappearance of phenomena," it is precisely the objects of focus— namely the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena— that constitute the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
for mindfulness is established here upon the body and so forth.
Thus, the locative derivation (*adhikaraṇasādhana*) is demonstrated:
"that in which mindfulness stands" is *upasthāna*;
the standing of mindfulness is *smṛtyupasthāna*.
In this way, up to the point where "the foundations of mindfulness are themselves the phenomena" constitutes the analysis of the term *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*.
Furthermore, if the object (*ālambana*) were not intended here in the Sūtra as the foundation of mindfulness,
the Blessed One would not have spoken in this manner.
And how, monks, is there the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness?
Through the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body;
through the cessation of nutriment, there is the passing away of the body—this is the detailed explanation.
For such a statement is appropriate only when the body and so forth constitute the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);
therefore, it is established that the body and so forth are the "foundations of mindfulness" by way of their objects (*ālambana*),
and that their names correspond to those objects.

Among these applications of mindfulness beginning with the body, the designations from "application of mindfulness to the body" up to "application of mindfulness to phenomena" are established in dependence upon their objects, because they take as their objects one's own continuum, another's continuum, both, or neither.
Furthermore, because they take both continuums as their object of focus, each one of these— beginning with the application of mindfulness to the body— is threefold,
according to what is stated in the Sūtra. How so?

He dwells contemplating the body in the internal body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world; he dwells contemplating the body in the external body, ardent... as before.
"He dwells contemplating the body in the internal and external body," as before;
thus, first, there are three modes for the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

In the same way, for the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanāsmṛtyupasthāna*) and the others as well, the three modes should be applied in detail: "He dwells contemplating feeling in internal feeling," and so forth.
"Because the gross is perceived first":
the body is grosser than the other three because it is cognizable by the six consciousnesses.

Of these, perception of the [aggregate of] sensation occurs first because it is coarse in its mode of activity; immediately after that, perception of the [aggregate of] mental factors occurs because they are subtle in their movement and thus difficult to discern. Since mental factors are subtle, perception of the mind occurs prior to them.
"Regarding 'at the forefront of phenomena'":
that is sensual desire;
that is of the mind; that is the longing for feeling.
Because those afflictions have not been abandoned, their lack of self-control occurs respectively in that manner.
The application of mindfulness to the body is the antidote to the perversion of purity;
the application of mindfulness to feelings is the antidote to the perversion of pleasure,
[based on the realization] that whatever is felt, all of it is here suffering.
The application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*) is the antidote to the perversion of permanence,
because the mind changes rapidly;
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is the antidote to the perversion of self.

From the division of the aggregates (*piṇḍa-vibhāga*), because phenomena lack the activity of a self, they are merely phenomena devoid of a self; this is the etymological definition (*nirvacana*) of "phenomena" (*dharma*).
These phenomena exist individually and separately, and there is no independent self whatsoever.
Or, by virtue of that observation,
the fourth foundation of mindfulness— the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena— becomes one whose object is undifferentiated, having an unmixed object, in both ways.
Because it is possible for it to have as its object dharmas distinct from body, sensation, and mind,
it also has a mixed object (*sambhinnālambana*),
as one perceives two, three, or all four of the body and so forth collectively.

If one observes the body and sensation up to the mental objects, that application of mindfulness of phenomena has a mixed object; if one observes the body up to the mental objects, it likewise has a mixed object.
That too is likewise;
furthermore, when one observes the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena all together,
that too is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena with a mixed object.
"Abiding in the universal object" means having synthesized the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena.
"Heat-attained" refers to a type of wholesome root characterized by heat,
so called because it is the prior form— that is, the first sign— of [the path].
Or, because of its prior intrinsic nature,
or because of its excellence—
meaning, because of its continuity.
We shall explain the distinction between these later;
thus, in the seventh chapter of the Kośa,
they are sixteen aspects in terms of substantial entity.
If they too are such as this,
then for what purpose are they taught? To this he says:
But because they are more excellent, they have a different name;
thus, he asks, "Why then are they called 'summits' (mūrdhānaḥ)?
and replies, "Because they are the summits of the fluctuating roots of merit."
This word *mūrdhan* denotes the ultimate limit of excellence; for thus do people say in the world: "His glory has indeed reached its summit (*mūrdhagata*)."

For two roots of goodness— characterized by *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*— are unstable because falling away is possible; the other two— characterized by *kṣānti* and *laukikāgradharma*— are stable because the opposite is the case.
In that regard, whichever of those two is weak is the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata), and whichever is superior is [the stage of "Summits"].
That which is even gentler than the immovable summits is patience.
Those which are the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) of yours are so called because from them there is either a falling back or a transcending.
From the summits (mūrdhan), there is either a fall, a regression, a transcendence, or the manifestation of receptivity (kṣānti),
because the summits are unstable.
For in the world, from the tops of trees and so forth, there may be a falling, an over-falling,
or an upward-reaching; thus, the similarity to a "top" (mūrdhan) consists in the initial onset of the aspects such as impermanence and so on upon those [truths].
The meaning is that they cause those things which have that as their object to proceed;
"by others" as well.
The meaning is that [this occurs] by means of others besides the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*);
"increasing" (*vardhana*) refers to making it more intense through repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), as expressed in the full passage beginning with "he increases."
For a yogin who is increasing [the roots of goodness], through that increase there is the manifestation of distinguished roots of goodness previously acquired,
while there is no manifestation of those that are undistinguished.
Why? Because of a lack of respect;
that is to say, because of a lack of respect due to [perceiving the object] as inferior.
"Because of the superior endurance of the truths" means that from the mild superior endurance of the truths during the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata), patience (kṣānti) arises;
as to how this occurs, he says:
Regarding "due to non-retrogression":
because receptivity (*kṣānti*) does not undergo retrogression,
whereas there is the possibility of retrogression from the summits (*mūrdhan*).
"In the same way, that is twofold" means that the mild and medium levels of receptivity (kṣānti) are likewise.
Just as the summits (*mūrdhan*) were described,

so too [are the patience stages] because of "making" (*akaraṇa*); that is to say, by making the aspects (*ākāra*) within the truths through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The statement "of all" refers to all forms of patience (*kṣānti*)— distinguished by the divisions of weak, medium, and intense—
which are expressed solely through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Not by another [application of mindfulness], such as the application of mindfulness to the body and so forth;
why?
Because it is contiguous with the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).

For the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), because they are contiguous with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), consist solely of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); thus, it is said "because of their contiguity with the supreme mundane dharmas."

Because the receptivity (*kṣānti*) arises immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), which have the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm as their object, it has the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm as its object; for its similarity [to the supreme mundane dharmas] is due to its proximity to them,
since there is no restrictive rule stating otherwise.
Just as with supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), since no specific restriction is stated regarding the objects of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stages and so forth,

how is it that the status of these heat stages and others as having the suffering and other truths of the three realms as their objects is established solely by the determination [of the object] for supreme patience?
Since its object is suffering belonging only to the desire realm,
this is "supreme patience" (adhimātrā kṣānti) whose object is suffering belonging to the desire realm;

because of the restriction "of patience alone," it is established that the others— the levels of heat (uṣmagata) and so forth— have as their objects the suffering and other [truths] of the three realms.
"When, it is said," and so forth; "when, it is said," refers to the antidotes to the form and formless realms, etc.—
by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of the cessation, origin, and suffering of the form and formless realms, as well as the antidotes to the desire realm, and so on.

By the gradual reduction of the aspects and objects of each truth— specifically, by the reduction of each aspect of a truth and each object of a truth, until one attends to only the suffering belonging to the desire realm through two moments—
this entire process, starting from the reduction of the aspects of the antidotes for the form and formless realms, constitutes intermediate patience (*madhyā kṣānti*). How so?
First, one contemplates the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge through these four aspects: as the path, as the correct method, as practice, and as leading to liberation;
then through three aspects, omitting one; and then through two aspects, omitting two.
Then,
having set aside the truth of the path from that [truth of cessation],
he contemplates the cessation of the form and formless realms by means of his own four aspects.
