Then, having practiced the truth of cessation through three, two, and one aspect respectively, and having set aside the truth of origin, he practices it through his own four aspects,
and then through three, two, and one.
In the same way,
having set aside that truth of suffering with its own characteristics, one sets aside that truth as well by means of a single characteristic.
He contemplates the counteragent to the desire realm through its own four aspects, then three, then two, and finally one;
having set that aside,
he likewise contemplates the truths of cessation and origin belonging to the desire realm by means of the process of diminishing their own aspects, and having set those aside as well—
One contemplates the truth of suffering belonging to the desire realm through four aspects,
then through three, and then through two;
thus, from the commencement of this reduction onwards, all these moments are said to be "intermediate patience" (madhyā kṣāntiḥ).
In the third moment, there is the highest degree of receptivity (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) having that same object;

in the fourth, there are the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharmāḥ*) having that same object. However, the weak degree of receptivity (*mṛdvī kṣāntiḥ*) is that which follows immediately after the highest degrees of the summits (*mūrdhānaḥ*), [taking as its objects] the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path within the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
It should be understood that some explain it thus: while one attends to the [objects] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness through all their respective aspects without reduction,
there is first a reduction of the aspects, followed by a reduction of the object.
Others, however,

explain [the process] as "by the reduction of the aspects and objects of each individual truth," but it should not be understood in this way— that is, as a reduction of the aspects of each individual truth and a reduction of the objects one by one.
Rather,
it should be explained as follows: by means of the reduction of the objects of those aspects (ākāra) which belong to each of the truths, such as the antidotes to the realms of form and formlessness.
They describe the intermediate stage of receptivity (*madhyā kṣānti*) as consisting of one hundred and nineteen moments;
for if the object of focus (*ālambana*) were to be reduced prior to the reduction of the mental aspects (*ākāra*), too many moments of consciousness would pass away,
and this is not logical.
For as long as the truths remain present, the abandonment of their aspects is not logical;
however, when the truths have been abandoned,
then the abandonment of their aspects is appropriate.
This being the case, one first reduces the objects (*ālambana*) of the truths and subsequently reduces the aspects (*ākāra*);
for the eight paths of those [truths] are not established unless their fundamental objects have been removed.
Now, another principle is taught regarding the fact that there are thirty-two aspects of these [paths].
How so? When one attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects,
and likewise attends to the antidotes for the [suffering] of the form and formless realms through four aspects, this is "mild patience" (mṛdvī kṣāntiḥ).
Furthermore, when one attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects, and so on, up until one attends to the antidote to the formations of the desire realm through four aspects;
from the point of abandoning the antidote to the formations of the form and formless realms, the medium level of patience (madhyā kṣānti) has begun.
And in that abandonment of the antidote to the formations of the form and formless realms, there are twenty-eight moments of mind.
In the abandonment of the counteractive factors for the formations of the desire realm, there are twenty-four;
in the abandonment of the cessation of the formations of the form and formless realms, there are twenty;
and in the abandonment of the origin of the formations of the desire realm, there are eight.
Upon abandoning the suffering of the form and formless realms, one attends to the suffering of the desire realm through four aspects; thus,
there are four aspects for that [suffering].
And that practitioner of yoga is of two types: one whose temperament is dominated by views and one whose temperament is dominated by craving.
One whose conduct is dominated by views is also of two kinds:
one whose conduct is dominated by the view of self,
and one whose conduct is dominated by the view of what belongs to self.
For one who has practiced the view of a self enters into the determination by way of the aspect of non-self,
whereas one who has practiced the view of "mine" [enters by way of the aspect of emptiness].
Even one whose conduct is dominated by craving, when characterized by the aspect of emptiness, is of two kinds:
that which is afflicted by the conceit "I am."
Furthermore, one who is characterized by excessive laziness and is afflicted by the conceit of "I am" enters into the determination of correctness by means of the aspect of impermanence.

He who is prone to laziness contemplates that [suffering] by way of its aspect of suffering; furthermore, the practitioner of yoga whose conduct is dominated by the view of self contemplates that suffering belonging to the desire realm again through three aspects.
Having set aside one aspect,
he then brings two aspects— those of selflessness and emptiness— into manifestation; thereafter, he brings the single aspect of selflessness into manifestation twice.

Because it is similar to the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*), this is called "intermediate receptivity. In this way, there are one hundred and nineteen moments of mind.

Thus, for one who is resolved upon [the self] as belonging to oneself, when they cultivate [it] through the aspects of emptiness and non-self, they bring the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyākāra*) into manifestation twice.
This is his middle stage of patience (*madhyā-kṣānti*). Thus, there are one hundred and nineteen moments.
In this way, the one whose temperament is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*) is of two types:
that which is afflicted by the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
And it should be stated that one who is excessive in indolence [is also included]; thus, the highest degree of patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) lasts for only a single moment,
and according to the conduct of the individual, its diminution occurs through the aspect of impermanence, the aspect of suffering, or by taking emptiness as its object.

For previously, while reviling the three realms, he took up the entire counteragent; subsequently, because the desire realm must first be abandoned and fully understood, he abides in the suffering belonging specifically to the desire realm,
since the path is drawn forth by the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) directed toward that.
Because, in the absence of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), there would be no prior untainted state;
for it is by the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) that the Truth of the Path is drawn forth.
The supremacy of all worldly things is understood to belong to the supreme dharmas (*agradharma*).
However, because they include their retinues (*saparivāra*), all five aggregates (*skandha*) are included.

Since the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth belong to the level of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), there exists for them the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) characterized by non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). Thus, the stages of heat and so forth consist of the five aggregates; when "including their retinues" is mentioned, they are taken together with their attendants.
"Lest there be [the manifestation] for the Noble One" means:

lest there be the manifestation for a noble person (*āryapudgala*) of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and other stages—which constitute the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for attaining the fruit—due to the manifestation of their acquisition (*prāpti*). Therefore, acquisitions are not included among the heat and so forth;
for it is not logical that a noble one who has already attained the fruit of the application should again bring that application into manifestation.
Regarding the "production of the heat-stage having the three truths as its object":
when producing the heat-stage having suffering, origin, and the path as its objects,
the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
Because the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) alone is capable of taking everything as its object when one fails to perform the task that arises from effort,
whereas the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) and the others are incapable due to having specific objects, all four future applications of mindfulness are cultivated.
Because, by means of the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the body, feelings, and so forth— which are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering and the others— are also grasped,

and because the applications of mindfulness such as the mindfulness of the body have already been previously acquired, therefore all four are cultivated through the arising of their attainment (*prāpti*). Thus, when the Truth of Cessation is the object, that same [application of mindfulness] occurs in both ways.
When one produces the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata) with the truth of cessation as its object,
the present application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is cultivated, and that very same [application] is cultivated for the future.
The applications of mindfulness, such as that of the body, do not exist within the truth of cessation because of the absence of the body and so forth; therefore,
the aspects are similar in all cases.
When the "heat" stage (*ūṣmagata*) has the three truths as its object or the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as its object, similar aspects (*ākāra*) are cultivated; specifically,

when it has the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as its object, only the four aspects of the truth of suffering are cultivated, not the aspects of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) and so forth.
Regarding the object of the aspects of the truth of origination and so forth, only the four aspects of the truth of origination are cultivated and no others;
this is what is meant by "contempt" (vigardhana).
When the three truths are the object, any one of the applications of mindfulness beginning with that of the body may be present;
when the truth of cessation is the object, the last one is present.
In both cases, are all four aspects cultivated, even all sixteen? What is the reason?

"Because of the acquisition of the lineages" means that because one has acquired the types [of practices] such as the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that take the four truths as their objects while abiding in the state of "arising. Regarding the phrase "in the making of the summits" (*mūrdhākaraṇe*),
the detailed explanation is that in every case during the making of the summits, only the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
Because of the capacity of the applications of mindfulness of the body and so forth to act as a source,
even when increasing the cultivation of the cessation as an object, the final application of mindfulness— of phenomena— is present,
since the others are not applicable.
But in the increase of the cultivation having the three truths as its object, one of the four [foundations of mindfulness] is present,
while all four are future; and in all cases, all aspects are cultivated.
It should be understood that this is because the lineages have been acquired;
in all cases, the final [application] pertains to the patiences (*kṣānti*).
Thus, in both the initial production and the increase [of the applications], the final application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present.
For it has been said:
"The increase of all patience is by means of the Dharma," and [this] is the last among the supreme dharmas (agradharma).

When the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) are being manifested, the final application of mindfulness (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is present; four future applications of mindfulness are acquired, which are strictly of the nature of non-arising (*anutpattidharman*); and the aspects (*ākāra*) are likewise only four.
The aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self [are established] because of the absence of others;
that is to say, since the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) do not possess other aspects such as origination and so forth, because they have suffering alone as their object.

If, then, even when the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) whose intrinsic nature is the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma) are not present, future applications of mindfulness and so forth are cultivated during the state of the active engagement (samudācāra) of the supreme mundane dharmas, why is it not accepted that future aspects such as the arising and so forth, whose intrinsic nature is the supreme mundane dharmas, are likewise cultivated? To this, he says again:
"And because of its similarity to the path of seeing (darśanamārga)."
Why are only the four aspects of suffering cultivated?
Because of their similarity to the path of seeing.
For on the path of seeing, only those aspects (ākāra) of whichever truth is being seen are cultivated,
because the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharma) resemble the path of seeing.
What, then, is their similarity to the path of seeing? It is by way of connection:
first of all, they have the suffering of the desire realm as their object in that very same way, or they share the same level;
for it will be said with reference to the path of seeing:

Thus, they belong to the same stage as the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*); or rather, the supreme mundane dharmas serve as the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) for the destruction of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*).

Thus, their similarity to the path of seeing is established by the fact that the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) correspond to the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); such is the detailed classification.
This is the form derived from that verbal root with the suffix *yañ*: "ascertained" (*niścita*) because of the abandonment of doubt,
and "discerning" (*vibhajana*) because of the differentiation of the truths.
"This is suffering" up to "this is the path"— this penetration is the noble path;
its "portion" is a single part of the path of vision.
Because it is beneficial by way of bringing about [the path] and attracting it, the suffix *cha* is applied in the sense of "beneficial for that";
thus, it becomes *nirvedhabhāgīya*,
which belongs to the stages of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, and the [four] dhyānas.
Thus,
because it has as its stages (bhūmi) the threshold (anāgamya), the intermediate (antara), and the dhyānas,
it is called "having the stages of the threshold, the intermediate, and the dhyānas" (anāgamyāntaradhyānabhūmika).
"Higher up" means that the aids to penetration do not exist in the formless realms,
because they are attendants of the path of seeing.
The meaning is: because it is the preparation for the path of seeing;
its absence [in that regard] is due to its having the desire realm as its object.
The absence of that path of seeing is its non-existence;
"where" refers to "above."
The meaning is "in the formless realms";
why?
Because they do not have the desire realm as their object.
Since the formless realms do not take the desire realm as their object,
he asks: "What is the purpose of a path of seeing that has the desire realm as its object?"
Therefore it is said:
"Because that must first be fully known and abandoned," meaning because that suffering-natured realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) must first be fully known.
And since that which has the nature of origination is to be abandoned,
the reason here is that because that yogi is afflicted by suffering belonging to the desire realm, he first seeks liberation from it.
For them, the maturation in the realm of form consists of the five aggregates;
because those aids to penetration belong to the realm of form, if that yogi were to be reborn in the realm of form,
then the maturation consisting of the five aggregates would be produced for him there.
And these [karmas] are only fulfillers (*paripūrikāṇi*), because they produce experience that is desirable;
they are not projectors (*akṣepakāṇi*) of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), because they belong to the realm of existence (*bhava*).
Because they hate existence through aspects such as impermanence,
the first two [levels]— having the nature of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*— are based in the desire realm.
Thus,
because the realization of the truths occurs only here [in the desire realm] and not in another realm,
nor above it, for there is no sense of spiritual urgency (*asaṃvega*) in the path of seeing (*dṛk-patha*).
Regarding the statement "here [there is] the practice and the culmination," based on scripture,
it is explained that this refers to the three continents— excluding Uttarakuru—
and also to the inhabitants of Uttarakuru among the gods.

And these three aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exist only in those [realms] and nowhere else; except for the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), both types— those based on the female and male faculties— are obtained by women and men in this very life upon the transformation of their female or male faculties.
For women, having produced these [roots of goodness], bring to manifestation those based on a female basis when the female state appears in another birth;
however, when the male state appears in another birth, they bring to manifestation those based on a male basis.
This is because it is not impossible for women who have acquired them to possess the female state in another birth.

Men likewise, when there is birth in another life in a female state, bring forth those [factors] based on a female basis; and when there is birth in a male state, they bring forth those based on a male basis.
With reference to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), he says:
"A woman attains the supreme dharmas based on two supports" means that only a female attains the supreme dharmas based on both [supports].
It is not the case that the man [possesses them],
for when a woman has acquired those [faculties], she is endowed with them based on her female basis at that time;
and upon the transformation of another birth, when a male basis appears in the desire realm, that man is endowed with them based on his male basis.
But why does a male obtain only those [faculties] that have the male as their basis? He says:
because he has attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of femininity.

In that birth, womanhood does not exist again even in another birth; thus, there is the attainment of its non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). For it is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that whoever produces the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) will necessarily produce the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) immediately thereafter, and for one who has seen the truths, the reappearance of womanhood does not occur.
"By the abandonment of the stage," and so forth:

this refers to those aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belonging to a particular stage, from those belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna up to those belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna, which have been acquired.

When abandoning that stage—abandoning from the first dhyāna up to the fourth—the noble one abandons those [attainments] belonging respectively to the levels of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna;
not otherwise, nor through death or retrogression, as is the case with an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). This is the meaning.

Furthermore, the abandonment of a stage occurs through the transition to another stage, not through detachment; this is shown by the detailed explanation beginning with "But the ordinary person... and so forth.

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), however, abandons the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) solely by abandoning the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāgatā*), whether or not there is a transition between stages (*bhūmisañcāra*). For instance, when an ordinary person who has attained the aids to penetration belonging to a certain stage is reborn in a higher stage, they abandon those [aids] through death alone, even though there has been a transition of stages.
However, one who is not free from passion abandons [the roots] through death when there is no movement to another stage,
and is reborn only in the desire realm;
but a noble person (āryapudgala) does not do so, because the continuity of their roots of merit has been strengthened by the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
How is it understood that it is only an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who thus abandons [the roots of goodness]?
Because of the statement in the *Śāstra*: "An ordinary person in the stage of the embryo, such as the *aṇḍaka* or *kalala*, is endowed with the body, but not with bodily action."
But Master Vasumitra explains:
"An ordinary person, however, abandons [the roots of goodness] solely by relinquishing the homogeneous class of beings (nikāyasabhāga),
whether or not there is a transition to another stage (bhūmi)."
All meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is included here by the mention of the "stages" (*bhūmi*).

In that regard, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having passed away from among the Brahma-body gods (*brāhmakāyika*), is reborn among the Ministers of Brahmā (*brahmapurohita*), he abandons [the absorption] by abandoning his homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

But when one passes away from the first dhyāna and is reborn in the second, [the claim] that it occurs "by means of both the abandonment of the level and the abandonment of the homogeneous class" is incorrect.
Because those reborn in the Brahma-world lack the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),
for it is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that the aids to penetration arise;
and it is precisely through falling away from the desire realm that they abandon those aids to penetration.
This has also been demonstrated by the Master Saṅghabhadra:

"Is it not the case that even an ordinary person who has attained the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belonging to a particular stage would abandon those aids to penetration when being reborn in a higher [stage]?"
This is not so; they are abandoned simply through the relinquishing of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Therefore, for one being reborn hereafter, that [homogeneous class] no longer exists such that he would have to abandon it.
It is said, "by death alone," as in the case of the *prātimokṣa* restraint;
just as when the *prātimokṣa* restraint is relinquished and then taken up again, it is obtained as something entirely new.
Why?
Because it is to be accomplished through unfamiliar effort,
because it is unfamiliar, and because it is to be accomplished through effort.
Because, in the beginningless cycle of existence, they have not been cultivated— since they are attendants of the Noble Path— they are therefore not obtainable through mere detachment.
Since they must be accomplished through effort, those previously abandoned are not regained; thus,
there is the rule regarding the observation of the boundary.
"Sīmā" means a boundary; its "indicator" (daiśika) is one who teaches it, namely, one who has attained the knowledge resulting from resolution (praṇidhijñāna).
When such a person exists, [the practitioner] produces [the attainment] beyond what was previously acquired and then lost.
The meaning is that it produces what has not yet been produced;
this means that in the absence of a teacher who defines the limits, one begins from the very root, starting from the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata).
Furthermore, regarding these two— loss (*vihāni*) and falling away (*parihāṇi*):
"loss" has been explained by such statements as, "the noble one abandons [it] through the abandonment of the stage."
Because of the statement, "The first two are also subject to falling away (*parihāṇi*)," he indicates that these [two] are so designated.
The term *hāni* includes both "abandonment" (*vihāni*) and "falling away" (*parihāṇi*), as it encompasses their common form; however,
falling away is caused by defects.
The meaning is "produced by afflictions";
it is not necessarily a loss, for that [increase] can also be produced by qualities, not only by defects.
That [loss] is produced by qualities (*guṇa*), such as the abandonment of the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) upon the arising of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);

whereas it is produced by defects (*doṣa*), such as the abandonment of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) through wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), or the abandonment of certain factors (*dharma*) by the mind at rebirth (*pratisandhicitta*).
Thus, that which is falling away is also loss; however, that which is loss [is not necessarily falling away].
This is not necessarily a falling away;
for falling away occurs only from specific qualities,
and thus one attains the state of non-arising.
The meaning is that one attains the cessation through non-analytical discernment (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) of those [factors] such as the destinies;
"but according to the case" refers to that state of non-arising (*anutpatti-dharmatā*).
It continues: "One attains [this] in both the weak and the intense stages of receptivity (kṣānti) as they occur.
How so? By means of the weak receptivity, one attains the state of non-arising (anutpatti-dharmatā) regarding rebirth in the miserable destinies (apāya-gati).
In the highest degree, there is [the obstruction] of the egg-born and moisture-born modes of birth;
in the mild degree, of rebirth among the non-percipient beings and in Uttarakuru or as a Great Brahmā;
and in the highest degree, of having a physical basis that is a eunuch, a paṇḍaka, or one possessing both sexual organs.

In the highest degree [of patience], there is the very state of non-arising (anutpattidharmatā) regarding the eighth and subsequent existences, the eighth, ninth, and subsequent births, and the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.

"But of that very lineage" refers to the Śrāvaka lineage cultivated by means of *kṣānti*; this is the opinion of the Master (Ācārya), the intention being that because it has been cultivated by *kṣānti*, it is irreversible.
"Even the other three" refers to the Pratyekabuddha, who might even turn back from the stage of *kṣānti* belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvaka.
The intention is that they do not plunge into the miserable states for the sake of others;
[it is said] "because of the immovable and powerful concentration" because concentration is called "immovable" due to being free from the eight defects.
For this very reason, or because their faculties are sharp and refined,
for those Abhidharmikas according to whose opinion there is a pratyekabuddha other than the rhinoceros-like (khaḍga), there exists one other than the rhinoceros-like as well.
The intended meaning is that even one who has merely produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is a group-dwelling *pratyekabuddha*.

There is no prohibition against those of that lineage turning away from the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summits" (*mūrdhan*), because the restriction applies only to those who are like the rhinoceros horn (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).
Furthermore, liberation is attained quickly, within three existences.
He who attains liberation quickly would produce the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in one lifetime and the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in the second.
Regarding the third [case], "on the noble path":

it should be understood that one who has accumulated the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in a previous birth may produce both the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and the noble path within a single lifetime.
"Sowing the seed," and so forth: "sowing the seed" is the production of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*);
"the increase of truth" is the arising of the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);
and "the production of the fruit" is the noble path (*āryamārga*).
"In this dharmatā" means that within the dharmatā of the teaching,
there occur entry, maturation, and liberation.
Entry is by means of the factors conducive to liberation;
maturation is by means of the factors conducive to penetration;
and liberation is by means of the noble path.
"Because of being embraced by that vow" means because of being embraced by a mental vow;
furthermore, a vow is a specific kind of volition (*cetanā*).
"Having given even a single alms-meal" refers to bodily action; "and having undertaken even a single training rule" refers to vocal action,
which is in turn originated by mental action.
Even this small amount, having the nature of the three types of action,
projects what is conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) by virtue of providing the strength for the desire for liberation;
"liberation-part" (*mokṣabhāga*) means the portion or attainment of liberation.

That which is beneficial for that [attainment] is "conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*); it does not exist elsewhere because of the absence of wisdom (*prajñā*) and world-weariness (*nirveda*), as the case may be;
thus, for instance, both are absent among the Kurus.
In the miserable realms there is disenchantment but no wisdom;
among the gods there is wisdom but no disenchantment.
Therefore, [the path] is projected only among humans in the three continents.
Nowhere else,
however, has the sequence of realization begun to be explained;
thus, one who is established in conduct and possesses [the wisdoms of] hearing and reflection applies himself to cultivation.

Beginning with this, the sequence of the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) is established; in connection with that, the aids to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya) are introduced. Thus, the receptivity to the dharma (dharmakṣānti) is untainted (anāsrava).
Thus,
even by means of the factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), there is the endurance of the Dharma;
therefore, it is distinguished by its outflow (niṣyanda).

That whose outflow is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti); it is called receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena because it is the receptivity for the sake of the knowledge of phenomena.

Like a tree with flowers and fruit: just as a tree for the sake of flowers is a "flower-tree" and a tree for the sake of fruit is a "fruit-tree," so too in the verse the mention of "receptivity to the Dharma" (*dharmakṣānti*) is by way of taking a single part, just as one says "Datta" for "Devadatta."
It has been said that "rightness is nirvāṇa";
what, then, is rightness? It is that which, having brought [the defilements] to exhaustion, is the abandonment of passion, and so forth.
In that context, *niyama* means *niyāma*.

Regarding that state of correctness (*samyaktva*), *niyama* refers to the state of being fixed (*ekāntībhāva*), and it is called *niyāma*; while its form with the suffix *ghañ* would be *niyāma*, it is instead *niyama* because the suffix *ap* [which yields *niyama*] is optionally prescribed after the root *yama-* when preceded by the prefixes *sam*, *upa*, *ni*, and *vi*.
Its "approach" and "entry" refer to the approach—
that is, the attainment— of that state of exclusivity; because it is the departure from error, it is called "entry into the determination of correctness" (*niyāmāvakrānti*).
And in that [moment], namely in this receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*),
"like the arising of a lamp" means like the arising of a lamp and like the arising of a birth.

Just as a lamp that has not yet arisen possesses the capacity to destroy darkness, and just as a birth that has not yet arisen possesses the capacity to produce what is to be born, so too is it accepted that the future receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) possesses the capacity to eliminate the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).
"Nothing else" refers to the activity of abandoning the afflictions by means of the supreme mundane dharmas; thus says another.
The phrase "the state of being an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva) is averted" is the subject under discussion;
[it is not the case that it is not averted] because that [state] is its intrinsic nature (dharmatā).
It is not logical that there should be a turning back from those [noble states] by means of the worldly supreme dharmas;
why?
Because they too are dharmas of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
How can the dharmas of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) turn back the dharmas of an ordinary person? There is no fault here because they are contradictory;
since the supreme mundane dharmas (agradharmas) are incompatible with the state of being an ordinary person, there is no such fault.
To the question "In what way? he says:
"Like killing an enemy while mounted upon his shoulders."

Just as someone mounted on the shoulders of an enemy might slay that very enemy, so too it is said that the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), mounted upon the shoulders of the enemy that is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), would slay that very state of being an ordinary person; thus,
[the path of seeing arises] by means of both.
How is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) overturned by the mundane supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) and by patience (*kṣānti*)? He says:
"Because they share the same nature as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)."

The similarity of *kṣānti* to the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) is with the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), and its similarity to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is as follows: for just as afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned by the path of immediate succession, so too [is the object abandoned] by *kṣānti*.

It is abandoned by the path of liberation; thus, by means of the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is relinquished. Since it is said to be relinquished by "patience" (*kṣānti*), the context of the untainted (*anāsrava*) applies in all cases.
Therefore, it is understood that right here [in this stage] there is untainted knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); thus,
the treatise shows that the conventional usage of the name "knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) is employed for that very reason.
It has all things as its object because it takes as its objects the suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness;
"because of the initial knowledge of the reality of phenomena" means because of the initial knowledge of the reality of phenomena such as suffering and so forth.
"Because of its concomitance with that" means "because it has that as its cause," since it follows in exactly that manner.

Just as the truth of suffering and so forth, which has been fully understood through the modes of suffering and so on, is followed by the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), in the same way, because it follows upon the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, this is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*); such is the detailed explanation.

In this manner, according to the sequence of immediate succession, one should apply the analysis in detail: "subsequent receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding the remaining origin [of suffering] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness," and so forth.
The masters of other schools, such as the noble Dharmaguptas and others,
maintain that because realization is attained without distinction,
this realization of the truths consists of sixteen moments of mind.

The realization through seeing (*darśanābhisamaya*), the realization through the object (*ālambanābhisamaya*), and the realization through the task (*kāryābhisamaya*)— thus, there is no distinction in the "sixteen-moment mind" [realization].
Regarding "realization through seeing," seeing itself is the realization.
Thus, the realization of the object and the realization of the task constitute the realization through vision; for that,
O monks, is what is "seen" by means of untainted wisdom.
Because of the statement, "that which is seen by untainted wisdom (anāsrava-prajñā)," it is established that wisdom itself is vision; however,
the grasping of the object also occurs through its associated factors, such as feeling (vedanā) and so forth.
From the word "also" (api), it follows that by means of wisdom as well,
the truths are apprehended by the mind and mental factors;
for whatever truth has a particular function to be performed, that function is carried out.
Namely: the full comprehension of suffering, the abandonment of its origin, and the realization of its cessation.
The cultivation of the path occurs through factors dissociated from it, such as morality (*śīla*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth;
by the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that it also occurs through wisdom (*prajñā*) and its associated factors.
For that fourfold function is performed by those [factors] associated with and dissociated from wisdom, such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), other characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and acquisitions (*prāpti*) are included.
This is the detailed explanation beginning with "for in suffering... (*duḥkhe hi*...).
For when suffering is being seen through wisdom,
how is it that there is a threefold realization for the one who realizes that suffering, as previously described? To this he says:

The clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the origin, cessation, and path—whose objects are the origin—is, respectively, abandonment, realization, and cultivation: abandonment of the origin occurs through the severance of the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions; realization of cessation occurs through the arising of its possession;
and cultivation of the path occurs through its manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*).
"Because of the difference in their aspects" means that because each of these— suffering and the others— has a distinct aspect,
it is not logical to perceive origination and the other truths through the aspect of suffering.

If one were to say that there is a vision of all truths through their distinct aspects— that is, even by way of the aspect of selflessness— a proponent of another school might argue this on the grounds that emptiness and selflessness are the common characteristic of all truths.
In that case, there would be no vision of the truths as suffering and so forth—
namely, as suffering, origin, cessation, and path—
and if that were so, one who asserts that all [truths] are seen through the aspect of selflessness (*anātmākāra*) would contradict the Sūtra.
Since it is stated thus in the Sūtra, "of the noble disciple," and so forth;

and if you think there is no contradiction with the Sūtra because [the statement] refers to the stage of preparation prior to the stage of clear realization— namely, that the noble disciple, while attending to suffering as suffering, and so on— therefore, since all [truths] are seen through the aspect of selflessness, there is indeed a single clear realization (*ekābhisamaya*).

And that is incorrect, because of the statement: "The discernment of phenomena is associated with untainted mental attention (*anāsrava-manasikāra*). For untainted mental attention is not possible during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
If it is argued that the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is thus, [the answer is] no; for when a noble disciple attends to suffering as suffering, and so forth in detail,
cultivation is not like seeing (*darśana*).
This is not so;
for just as there was previously the vision of the truths, in that very same way there is subsequently their cultivation.
The meaning is that it becomes the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga);

"because of the attainment of mastery over the remaining [truths]" means that the attainment of mastery is the acquisition of the capacity to manifest the vision of the origin and so forth without further preparatory effort (prayoga). Therefore [it is the path of cultivation].

The intention is that one might wonder whether or not there is emergence from meditative absorption in the intervals [between attainments]; however, because mastery has been attained over the remaining [attainments], one would logically conclude that emergence occurs during those intervals.
Yet, when examined in either way, there is a contradiction with many sūtras.
And how their contradiction is to be understood from the scriptures should be heard [therein],
because it is stated that upon the vision of one, there is the realization of the task for the rest.
Because there is this statement: "When suffering is being seen, its realization is threefold;
for origination and the others, it is the realization of what is to be done."
Because [the path] consists of abandonment, realization, and cultivation, there is no fault, since we also accept this very point.
He says:
"Even if one accepts it, [this constitutes] clear realization (*abhisamaya*)."
The sequential realization of the truths in the Sūtra would thus be contradicted; therefore, it is said in detail: "But with respect to the realization through vision," and so forth.
How is it that three sūtras with their respective similes are recited in the *Saṃyuktāgama*?
Anāthapiṇḍada said:
"Venerable sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths, or rather, a simultaneous realization?"
"Householder, there is a gradual realization of the four noble truths, but not a simultaneous realization.

Householder, if someone were to say: 'Without having realized the noble truth of suffering, I shall realize the noble truth of its origin,' and so on in detail up to, 'I shall realize the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,' he should be told: 'Do not speak thus.'"
For what reason? It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one who has not fully realized the Noble Truth of Suffering will fully realize the Noble Truth of the Origin; as before, up to:
this situation does not exist.
"This is possible," as before;

for example, householder, suppose someone were to say: "Without having established the foundation pillar of a peaked house or a hall with a peaked roof, I shall establish the wall; without having established the wall, I shall establish the floor."
One should say to him: "Do not speak thus, thinking, 'Without establishing a base, I shall establish sandalwood.
For what reason?"
It is impossible, it is out of the question, that [the gable-roofed house]— as before, up to—
"having established the foundation-pile, I shall establish the wall"— as before.
"As long as this is so, householder, it is impossible that one who has not seen the truth of suffering will see the truth of its origin," and so on in detail;
then another monk said:
"Venerable sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths, or rather a simultaneous realization?
The Blessed One replied:
"Of the four truths, O monk," as before, up to: "Just as if, O monk, someone were to say: 'Without having ascended the first step of a four-stepped staircase, I shall ascend the second;
without having ascended the second, I shall ascend the third.'"
"One should say to him: 'Do not speak thus, thinking, "Without ascending the third, I shall sprinkle the fourth.
Why is that?'"
It is impossible, it is out of the question, that one should ascend to the second step of a four-stepped staircase without having first ascended the first step;
likewise, without having ascended the third, one should ascend the fourth—
it is not possible here either.
Regarding the statement that one might see the truth of origination without having seen the truth of suffering, and so forth,
the Venerable Ānanda likewise asked:
"Venerable Sir, is there a gradual realization of the four noble truths?"
Or rather, is it a single realization? This is because of the preceding sūtra, up to...

It is just as if, Ānanda, someone were to say, "I shall ascend to the upper story of a palace without having first climbed the first step of a four-stepped ladder"—one should tell him, "Do not speak thus.

In detail, up to: even so, Ānanda, if someone were to say, "I shall realize the noble truth of the origin of suffering without having realized the noble truth of suffering"—in detail, up to: such a thing is impossible.
Regarding these three sūtras,
beginning with "He who [is without doubt] regarding suffering," and so forth:

if it should be thought that there is a single simultaneous realization (ekābhisamaya) because of the sūtra stating, "He who is without longing and without doubt regarding suffering is likewise [without longing and without doubt] regarding the Buddha."
For how so?
The dharmas of one beyond training are indeed the Buddha;
those very same dharmas of one beyond training are the Path.

Therefore, through the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of suffering, the path is also clearly realized by him; for, as with [the realization of] suffering, he is free from longing and free from doubt regarding the Buddha.
Here, "longing" (*kāṅkṣā*) and "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) are not different in meaning.
Alternatively, "longing" is the desire for certainty, while "doubt" is indecision, characterized as previously described.

It is not so, because the statement regarding "non-manifestation" and "necessary abandonment" is made with a specific intention; for it is said with a specific intention that there is a single realization according to the Sūtra,
as well as [the statements] regarding non-manifestation and necessary abandonment.
When suffering has been fully understood, there is the non-arising and the necessary abandonment of doubt regarding the domain of the Buddha;
therefore, the underlying intention [of the teaching] is that he who is free from uncertainty and free from doubt regarding suffering is likewise so regarding the Buddha.
Furthermore, it was stated previously that these belong to six stages,
because of the statement: "belonging to the stages of the threshold, the intermediate, and the dhyānas."

Regarding the phrase "because it is impossible to obstruct" (*an-antaryaśakyatvāt*): the suffix *kṛtya* is used in the sense of possibility according to the rule *kṛtyāś ca śakī liṅ ca*. Thus, *antarayituṃ śakyāḥ* means "capable of being obstructed," i.e., *antaryāḥ*; those that are not so are *anantaryāḥ*.

They sever the possession of the afflictions; that state of being rendered obstructed by them is intended as the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantaryamārga*). The lengthening of the vowel [in *ānantarya*] is applied according to the rule for the suffix *vṛddhi* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), where the suffix itself carries its own meaning.
The state of being immediate, or the immediate path, is "ānantarya";
the paths toward that are the "ānantarya-mārgas," and there is also the "vimukti-mārga" (path of liberation).
The paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are the paths in the state of liberation from the afflictions;
this is because, by means of two [factors], there is the expulsion of the thief and the closing of the door.
Just as by two people— a thief is expelled by one,
while by the second the door is closed so that he cannot re-enter—
so too, by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), the thief of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is expelled.

By means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the door to the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) is closed through the severance of the acquisition of that [defilement] by way of bringing it into the present.
"If, however," and so forth:

if, moreover, the acquisition of dissociation were to arise together with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe anvayajñānakṣānti*) by means of that very second path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*),
then the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) would not arise at all.

The intention is that whatever ought to be accomplished by this [knowledge] would instead be accomplished by the very receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe anvayajñānakṣānti*).

Consequently, there would be no knowledge arisen with respect to that same object—the suffering belonging to the desire realm—in which doubt has been abandoned; that is, knowledge in which doubt has been eliminated would not have arisen.

For in that case, the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) occurs precisely while accompanied by doubt, because doubt has not yet been abandoned;
nor can it be established that the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) is one in which doubt has been abandoned,
since its object is not that [same] doubt.
"By means of the patiences," and so forth;
this scriptural reading [refers to] the nine groups of fetters, because of the abandonment of the afflictions by means of the patiences.

It is also stated in the Sūtra: "There are groups of fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering, those to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination, those to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of cessation, those to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of the path, those to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering, and the group of fetters to be abandoned by cultivation."
Thus, monks, the afflictions are to be slain by knowledge; since the mind is like lightning, there is a contradiction between them.
For it is not said there that the category of fetters to be abandoned by patience [is abandoned] by the patiences themselves; such is the detailed explanation.
This is not so;
why?
Because the patiences (kṣānti) have knowledge (jñāna) as their retinue.
Since the patiences (*kṣānti*) are the retinue of knowledge (*jñāna*), the category of fetters (*saṃyojana-nikāya*) that is to be abandoned by patience is said to be abandoned by knowledge;
this is like the designation "done by the king" for something done by the king's retinue,
just as some matter accomplished by the king's retinue receives the designation "done by the king."
In the same way, the category of fetters (saṃyojana) that is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya) is indeed to be abandoned by knowledge (jñāna-prahātavya);
for in that case, even the path of immediate succession (ānantarya-mārga) has the nature of knowledge,
and it is specifically the path of immediate succession that is authorized for the abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa).
Regarding the phrase "because of the seeing of the unseen truths": how does the seeing of the unseen truths occur through knowledge?
It occurs because, while one truth remains unseen, another truth is seen; thus, the knowledge existing in the intervals between the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is itself the path of seeing.
This is with reference to the continuous succession [of moments], for by means of that [succession], one sees as if seeing what was previously unseen.

Alternatively, because it is the seeing of what was not previously seen, fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing; for as long as this person’s vision of the unseen continues to operate, those moments of his constitute the path of seeing.

Even though suffering has been seen by him, the vision of what was previously unseen still proceeds with respect to its origin (*samudaya*); thus he says, "the sixteenth moment is indeed the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*), supplying the necessary words to the sentence.
Now, one might ask: "Does he not see with that [sixteenth moment] what was previously unseen? What is that which was unseen? To this he replies:

Regarding "the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path" (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*): the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path, excluding itself, takes as its object the remaining path belonging to the side of subsequent knowledge,
because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself.
Therefore,
it is said that "one sees the previously unseen receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path," which refers to the detailed investigation of the truth.
The reflection concerns truth— whether it has been seen or not seen—
but not regarding the moment, as in whether a particular moment has been seen or not;
why is this?
Since the very same truth characterized by the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that was seen in the fifteenth moment is also seen in the sixteenth,
there is no seeing of a previously unseen truth.
The path of seeing is not established as consisting of sixteen moments;

for it is not the case that by a single moment characterized by the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*) which has not been seen, that truth—the truth of the path—remains unseen.
[To illustrate this,] he provides a worldly example:
Just as a field is not considered unharvested when a single stalk of grain has not been cut— that is, when it has not been severed by a sickle—
the meaning is that it is indeed already harvested.
For instance, some people, out of negligence, say "we have harvested the field" even when a single stalk remains uncut;
this is because it has borne fruit, and so forth.
By such reasons as "because it has borne fruit," [the author] establishes that the sixteenth moment is indeed the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is the sixteenth moment, because it is a conditioned fruit of asceticism (saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala),
like the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) up to the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).

Likewise, because it possesses the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects, because it is free from the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*), and because it is continuous, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)— just like the other fruits— is present in the sixteenth moment;
for in that sixteenth moment, the eight knowledges are cultivated.
From the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*), up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*),

the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*)— beginning with impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth— are cultivated; however, in that very same way, there is no cultivation of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
For in that case, it is precisely the cultivation of the aspects of similar knowledge that are cultivated as they arise, because of the statement: "The patiences and knowledges are seen."

Furthermore, at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), there is the abandonment of the previous path— that is, the path of application (*pratipannakamārga*)— whereas in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) there is no abandonment of the previous path;
thus, this subsequent knowledge of the path is continuous.

Furthermore, because there is no patience (*kṣānti*) or knowledge (*jñāna*) whatsoever that is continuous on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), for this reason as well, the other [opponent] objects: "The subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
the path of seeing consists of sixteen moments."

Or, it refutes the prima facie argument that [the state of being a stream-enterer] is subject to falling away because it is necessarily [liable to decline], just like the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and so forth.

"This thesis is flawed because it contradicts the essential nature of the property (dharma) as established by inference. Even when [the state of] being on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is being proven, the fact that there is no falling away from that [state] follows from this very inference.
Having taken this internal implication into account, he speaks again:

"But there is no falling away," and so forth; because the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing is maintained by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) as its sustaining counteragent (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*),
and if there were falling away from that sixteenth moment— the path of the fruit— there would be falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
And since there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry, one does not fall away from it;
therefore, the other says: "For this very reason."
Is this stated solely as a reason for non-retrogression?
We also maintain this very point.
If it is argued that this is the answer being taken up— that "this is the attainment of realization"—
the Master says:
"Precisely for that reason, it is the path of seeing."

If you think that it is precisely because the maintenance of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing occurs through the knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna) that this [knowledge] is therefore the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
that is not so.
Because it would lead to an over-extension:

if the maintenance of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing were to occur through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), then it would consequently become a path of seeing;
such being the case, there would be an over-extension.

Therefore, if the maintenance of the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing were achieved by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) subsequent to that knowledge of the subsequent dharma of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), then the entire [path] would be the path of seeing;
and this is undesirable,
for you maintain that only sixteen moments constitute the path of seeing.

A moment such as the seventeenth or eighteenth does not arise according to the principle of a continuous flow on the second or third day; that which arises [then] is of a different kind, being comprised within the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*).
That [prior continuity] does not exist.
For even from that [state], there is no falling away; thus, it is shown that the reason stated— namely, "the state of being necessarily without falling away"—
is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because that [reason] is inconclusive, it is not a proof;
nor is it a refutation of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa).

Thus, there are seven knowledges—from the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering up to the dharma-knowledge regarding the path. Why is the eighth, the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) regarding the path, not included in the path of seeing (darśanamārga)? This is the intended meaning.
"Because vision is not yet complete" means that vision is completed at the stage of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*),
since all the truths have been seen.
The vision of the Dharma regarding suffering is completed because all the truths have been seen at that time;
for even though the suffering belonging to the desire realm has been seen when the knowledge of the Dharma regarding suffering arises.

However, the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness have not yet been seen; likewise, as long as the dharma-knowledge of the path has not arisen, the antidote to the realms of form and formlessness has not yet been seen.
"Seeing is not yet complete because it has a remainder" means that it occurs within the interval,
namely, within the interval of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The intention is that because they lie between those two patiences (*kṣānti*), those seven knowledges (*jñāna*) also constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for that yogin, since he still has a desire to see what remains to be seen.
The meaning is that previously, by following the meaning through reliance on others and what was taught by others, one realizes the truths such as suffering;
by the qualification "previously," it is stated that at the time of cultivation, one follows the meaning independently of the instruction of others—
thus [one is called] a "follower of the Dharma."
"Following by means of the dharmas" is *dharmānusāra*;
one who possesses that is a *dharmānusārī*,
or one whose nature it is to follow by means of the dharmas.
Previously, by following the meaning through the twelve branches of the teaching— such as the sūtras and other dharmas— on one's own,
the explanation proceeds as before until the five types [of hindrances] are abandoned.
By the word "up to" (yāvat), if one, two, three, four, or five categories [of defilements] have been abandoned,

they are likewise called candidates for the first fruit (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*), just as those bound by all fetters [are called candidates] up until the destruction of nine [categories] in the second [fruit].
"Thus,
in the second [case]" means "for the sake of the second cause," just as in the expression "one kills a leopard for its skin."
"Down to the destruction of the ninth" means down to the abandonment of the nine types [of defilements]; by excluding the abandonment of the nine types, it is effectively stated that if,
for those two persons, beyond that abandonment of five types, six, seven, or eight types have previously been abandoned by the worldly path.
Those two are "candidates for the second fruit" because of the expression "the second," and they are "beyond" [the first] because they are free from passion for the first dhyāna.
Up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), one may be free from passion,
yet it is impossible to attain arhatship from the very beginning; thus,
without having first attained the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), it is impossible to attain arhatship from the outset.
He asks "Why? and says:
because of the non-abandonment of those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation;
for there is no abandonment of the defilements belonging to the peak of existence that are to be abandoned by cultivation through the path of seeing.

Just as one abiding in the fifteen moments whose nature is the path of seeing would, from the beginning, be a candidate for the third fruit [of non-returning] and a candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship; however, when the sixteenth moment of consciousness has arisen, one would be a non-returner from the beginning and an arhat,
because arhatship is established through the abandonment of the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
He said:

"If there is no abandonment of the defilements belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), then it would be impossible to attain arhatship; therefore, one must have already become a candidate for that fruit (*tat-phala-pratipannaka*) by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) while still in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), through detachment from the peak of existence."
Abiding in those [moments], one will be a candidate for the realization of the fruit of arhatship; however, at the sixteenth moment of mind from the beginning, one becomes an arhat.
Therefore, it is said:
And because detachment from the peak of existence (bhavāgra) is impossible beforehand;
for previously, while in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), detachment from the peak of existence through the mundane path (laukika-mārga) is not possible,
due to the absence of any higher realm.
Therefore, from the very beginning, one who has entered the path would not be an Arhat;

rather, because they are characterized by resolution (*adhimokṣa*) through the predominance of faith (*śraddhā*), and because they are characterized by vision (*dṛṣṭi*) through the predominance of wisdom (*prajñā*),
one who is characterized by resolution through the predominance of faith is called a "one liberated by faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*).
One who is liberated through the predominance of faith is called "liberated by faith-resolve" (śraddhādhimukta) because faith is predominant;
it is not that he lacks wisdom,
but rather that he is not characterized by it [as his primary faculty].
However, it does not receive that name because it is dominated by wisdom (*prajñā*) due to being characterized by views; thus, one is "attained through views" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Yet, as stated previously, it should be said that this does not mean he lacks faith (*śraddhā*).
Others, however, relying on the method of etymological interpretation, explain it thus:
one who is liberated from the [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing through the predominance of faith is "one liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
By virtue of the predominance of view, one who has attained the fruit is called "attained through view" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*); this refers,
in short, to those who have destroyed five categories [of afflictions], as it has been stated.
Therefore, he asks, "What then is the reason? and so forth.
"A path superior to the fruit is not obtained" means that a path superior to the fruit—such as the one for those practicing for the fruit of a once-returner and so on—is not attained.
The meaning is that the path which serves as the antidote to what is to be abandoned through the first and subsequent modes of cultivation is not cultivated; that is to say,

"as long as he does not apply himself toward distinction" means as long as he does not undertake the preparatory application for the sake of attaining another fruit in order to abandon the defilements that have not yet been abandoned.

One is not called a "practitioner" (pratipannaka) as long as one is merely engaged [in practice]; rather, it is implied that one is a practitioner only when one is actually applying oneself [to the path].

For it is the established tenet that at that time, an untainted acquisition (*anāsravā prāpti*) arises for the antidote to previously abandoned afflictions and for that abandonment which was not previously attained;
this should be understood to apply to other fruits as well,
because of the statement that "one is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) at the sixteenth moment of mind."

Since it was stated that one is called a *srotāpanna* [upon the abandonment of the first eight categories of afflictions], it should be understood that this applies elsewhere as well— namely, regarding the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
Even when the eight categories [of afflictions] have been abandoned by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one is still designated merely as a "once-returner" at the sixteenth moment of mind.
One who is practicing for the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmiphala-pratipannaka) is not,

at the sixteenth moment of mind— whether having already become free from passion for the desire realm or being so above it— called one practicing for the fruit of Arhatship (arhattvaphala-pratipannaka), because in a given fruit there is no attainment of a path superior to that fruit.

Because, as stated previously regarding "the fruit of one distinguished by the fruit," there is the possibility that one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna— this being the full elaboration— enters into the determination of correctness (*niyāma*) by relying on a lower stage, namely by relying on the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, or the first or second dhyāna. This is the possibility that exists.
He necessarily brings face-to-face a path distinguished by its fruit, either one comprised within the third dhyāna;
for it is from this that the untainted faculty of pleasure (anāsrava-sukhendriya) comprised within the third dhyāna is obtained,
since there is indeed the possibility that he might bring face-to-face a path distinguished by its fruit.
Since his defilements belonging to the level of the third dhyāna have been abandoned,
it is established that he necessarily brings forth the path distinguished by its fruit;
for otherwise, the meaning would be that he does not bring it forth.
Having been reborn above that,
that noble one would be disjoined from the faculty of pleasure in the fourth dhyāna or in the formless realms, which are above that third dhyāna.
For that faculty of pleasure which is with-outflows (sāsrava) is abandoned through the transition between stages,
as is that which is without-outflows (anāsrava).

If even that were not present, one would be devoid of both [faculties]; however, it is stated that for Noble Ones born in the higher realms, there is necessarily possession of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Furthermore, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (*ārūpya*) does not possess the faculty of pleasure.

Furthermore, because of the statement that "the noble one (ārya) is endowed [with them]," and because of such statements as, "Whoever is endowed with the faculty of mental pleasure (saumanasyendriya) is necessarily endowed with five: the faculties of equanimity (upekṣā), life (jīvita), mind (manas), pleasure (sukha), and mental pleasure," and so forth.
To this we reply:
although this is a position recorded in the Vibhāṣā,
it does not appear to be the established position.
Because of the statement "others say," whoever who has attained the fourth dhyāna and enters into the path of certainty (niyāma) by relying on any one of the six stages becomes endowed,
at the sixteenth moment of mind, with the fruit of a non-returner belonging to those six stages— from that of the stage of the non-returner up to that of the fourth dhyāna.
Likewise, because he is free from passion,
one who has attained the third dhyāna possesses [the faculty] belonging to five stages.
Excluding that which belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna,
in this way, one who has attained the second dhyāna possesses [the faculties] belonging to four levels.
Excluding those belonging to the third and fourth stages,
however, one who is free from passion and has attained the first dhyāna but not the second,
if they attain the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala), [is included].
He is endowed with the fruit of non-returning belonging to three stages—
that of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, and the first dhyāna.
For they explain that even the very lowest non-returner is necessarily endowed with the fruit of non-returning pertaining to these three stages.
Therefore, it would be logical that the Master spoke thus with reference specifically to the latter category;
in this way, the phrase "of those who have largely abandoned desire for the sense realm" refers to those who have largely abandoned desire.

And among those who are free from passion for the realm of desire, one is "largely free from passion" (bhūyovītarāga) whose seven or eight categories [of afflictions] have previously been abandoned by the worldly path; another is one whose nine categories have been abandoned.

He is one who has become free from passion for the realm of desire; among those persons who have further become free from passion, he is established as the second type of Arhat, due to the destruction of the nine [categories of] afflictions.
According to this statement,
for those who are free from passion for the realm of desire,
there is detachment from desires both above and below.
From this statement,
it follows that as long as these [defilements] exist in the desire realm—
up to the point where one has destroyed five types [of defilements] in the second [dhyāna], but before the destruction of the nine [types] below— that is the case.
From the statement "detached from desire," it is taught that there are nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm.
"From cloth" (*cetād*) means from a garment;
"this is the application of an example" (*dṛṣṭāntayoga*)— others say that the application of an example, the connection with an example, is a type of example (*dṛṣṭāntaprakāra*).
Thus, by this reasoning or in this manner, he indicates that another example should also be stated;
otherwise, he would have simply said, "this example [is like] beginningless saṃsāra."

The intention is that in beginningless saṃsāra, these [afflictions] have been burned and increased through a succession of their own causes; therefore, they possess an excessive magnitude. [This refers to] the uprooting of those afflictions by means of cutting off their acquisition (*prāpti*).

For acquisitions (*prāpti*) are of the same nature as the root [defilements] because they constitute a continuity (*prabandha*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*), just like the extraction of *tṛvṛt* by means of a purgative;

that is, just as the extraction of the humors (*doṣa*), such as wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*), which have been accumulated over a very long time, is accomplished by the administration of a *tṛvṛt* purgative.
Thus, even by means of a noble path that is momentary and subtle, there is the destruction of the afflictions;
just as a great darkness is dispelled by a small, momentary lamp, so too are the afflictions destroyed.
"Seven times at most shall I slay him" means that there is a limit of seven births for him,
and not more than that.
The meaning is that one goes to nirvāṇa by means of that path;
for in the world, one travels by means of a stream,
and because of the attainment of the initial path.

The first untainted path is the path of seeing; if, through its attainment, one were a stream-enterer, then even the eighth person would be a stream-enterer, as well as one practicing for the fruit of stream-entry— this is the meaning.

For instance, if one proceeds in reverse order starting from the Arhat among the eight types of persons (*puruṣapudgala*), such as those practicing for the fruit of Arhatship and so forth, then the one practicing for the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala-pratipanna*)— the eighth [type] who is either a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārī*) or a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārī*)— would also be a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) because he has attained the initial path;
and if it is argued that he is a Stream-enterer because he has attained a fruit not previously attained, [then the same would apply].
Furthermore, even one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*)—
that is, a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*) who has abandoned six categories of afflictions at the sixteenth moment— would also be a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Because there is likewise a distinction in its unprecedented fruit, even one who is free from passion for the desire realm would be [considered such];
for him too, that is the first fruit.
Now the rebuttal is stated:
"With reference to one who attains all the fruits, because of the acquisition of the first fruit," thus [it is said] "all the fruits."
One who has the nature of attaining the four fruits, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry, is called "one who has attained all fruits" (*sarvaphalaprāpī*);
or, one who possesses the attainment of all fruits is called "one who has attained all fruits."
Referring to him, with reference to him, because of the attainment of the first fruit and the attainment of a fruit not previously attained, he is called a *srotāpanna*,
and not an *aṣṭamaka*; for he too has entered the stream of the path to liberation.
"Because of the attainment of the path of the candidate and the fruit," and so forth;
for by him (the one on the path of seeing) the sixteenth moment, which is the universal [path], is attained,
whereas by the eighth [moment] only the path of the candidate is attained.
Furthermore, because of the attainment of both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation,
he has acquired that very path of seeing and that very path of cultivation;
however, the eighth person has acquired only the path of seeing.
And because of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the entire stream (*srotas*), at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);

since he has clearly realized the entire stream by seeing even the moment of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*), whereas the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*) has not, for these reasons, only one who has attained all the fruits is called a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*), and not the eighth person.
For such a statement is made on account of preeminence;
just as in the world, he who produces light preeminently is called "Bhāskara" (the Sun).
It is not like a firefly;
therefore, it is other than those.
Therefore, [the Blessed One spoke of] "others" than this present existence as being like the "skill in seven points" and the "seven-leafed tree";
just as, due to the commonality of the number seven, a monk skilled in the seven points is mentioned in the Sūtra.
Having explained it in detail, he said:
"And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the seven points?"
One understands form as it really is;
one understands the arising of form, the cessation of form, the path leading to the cessation of form, the gratification of form, the danger of form, and the escape from form as they really are.
In the same way, one understands feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they really are.
"One understands, as they truly are, the arising of consciousness in detail, up to its escape"— according to this principle, there are five sets of seven, which makes thirty-five; thus,
one becomes proficient in thirty-five [factors].

And just as in the case of the *saptaparṇa* tree, although that tree has many hundreds of leaves, it is called "seven-leaved" (*saptaparṇa*) because each individual leaf resembles a seven-leafed cluster; so it is here.
The first example is established in the teaching (pravacana),

while the second is from the world; the purpose of presenting these two examples is that if [the term] "at most seven times" (saptakṛtvaḥ parama) is explained based on the commonality of the number seven.
If that is so, does this not contradict what was stated in the Sūtra? The intention is that this is a misinterpretation;
there is no contradiction because one does not bring about an eighth existence within a single realm of rebirth (*gati*).
Or, if it were interpreted according to the literal expression—

that "having transmigrated and wandered seven times among gods and humans, one makes an end of suffering"— then because of the mention only of gods and humans, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist; yet, the production of seven existences within the destinies of gods and humans is indeed accepted.
If intermediate states were not counted—
