such that, had the seven existences been counted together with the intermediate states, he would have had only four births— then by this statement of an undesired consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*), he [the author] supports his own interpretation that [the seven existences] pertain to a single realm of rebirth (*gati*).
The other says: "Even so, [the phrase] 'one who flows upwards' and so forth—
if you explain it as meaning that one does not bring about an eighth existence within a single realm of rebirth."

How then is it that for one who has "upward-streaming" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and for whom the summit of existence (*bhavāgra*) is the limit, the production of an eighth existence occurs within a single realm of rebirth (*gati*)? For what purpose is this qualification made,
since the production of an eighth existence is also possible for one who has Akaniṣṭha as the limit?
He is also to be described as a leaper (*pluta*), a half-leaper (*ardhapluta*), one who dies from every state (*sarvaścyuta*), and another who goes to the peak of existence (*bhavāgraga*),
according to the scriptural statement.

We perceive the intention behind the mention of "the summit of existence as the limit" to be that it is intended to express the excellence of existence; for this is stated with reference to the desire realm, and within the desire realm, there is only one destiny: the human destiny.
Or rather, it is in that [desire realm] state of existence as a god that one does not bring about an eighth birth,
but not so in the realms of form or formlessness.
What is the scriptural authority or the reasoning here that this was stated with reference to the desire realm?
"Sūtra" means scripture;
"yukti" here means inference (*anumāna*), by which the challenger has thus questioned: "What is the scriptural authority or the reasoning (*yukti*) for this?"
He said again:
"And here, what is the proof that [the limit is] seven times each among gods and humans? This is the full statement;
it means transmigrating seven times each among gods and humans.
It is not, however, that one is limited to seven times among both gods and humans; rather,
what is meant is that this applies to one who has seen the truth among humans.
Having transmigrated three times among the gods and exactly three times among humans, he then returns to the gods and attains parinirvāṇa;
or alternatively, one who has seen the truth among the gods does so in that very same way.
Having transmigrated three times among humans and exactly three times among gods, he returns from there to the human realm and attains parinirvāṇa;
for it is recited thus: "seven times among gods and humans," which is indeed stated in a general form.
The meaning is that it is not recited as being specified "individually.
Thus, when the Vaibhāṣika position has been placed in a state of doubt, the Master, providing a justification, says:
"But the Kāśyapīyas [hold] even individually," and so forth.
The Kāśyapīyas, belonging to another school, recite thus:
"seven times among the gods, seven times among humans."
In this way, the meaning is obtained for each [term] individually;
thus, both points that were raised—namely, "What is the scriptural authority or the reasoning here? and "Was this said with reference to the desire realm?"—are refuted by this.

And as for what was said: "What is the proof here that it is seven times each among gods and humans?"— for by the very acceptance of the meaning of "each," the intention regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also indicated.
For it is not logical that those born in the realms of form and formlessness should transmigrate seven times among gods and humans,
since non-returners (anāgāmins) born there do not return to the human realm; the underlying reasoning is understood from this very point.
It is precisely on that level where one is described as having "seven births at most" that the prohibition of an eighth birth is appropriate, and not elsewhere; therefore,
one should not be dogmatic about this.
And what here is the proof that it is "of that same kind"?
It is "of that same type."
In that much time, because the continuum necessarily reaches maturity, one does not bring about an eighth existence;
just as one bitten by a seven-step venomous snake dies after having gone seven steps.
That kind of poison does not manifest later nor earlier,
just like a quartan fever.
Just as a quartan fever occurs only on the fourth day, neither later nor earlier,
such is the nature of that class of disease.
In the same way,
the two lower fetters refer to sensual desire and ill will.

Because they have not yet abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), these two— namely, the two types of attachment arising from the form and formless realms— as well as restlessness, pride, and delusion, constitute the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*pañcordhvabhāgīya*).
Thus,
because he does not attain nirvana before that point, nor does he bring about an eighth existence.
"This is not a valid reason because seven fetters remain," says the Master Saṅghabhadra;
for the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*) are not capable of producing birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), since they belong to the higher stages.
To this, those who maintain the [original] reason reply:
Although those [karmas] belong to the higher stages,
nevertheless, by virtue of the capacity for their acquisition (*prāpti*), there occurs the production of that many existences;
for they are not established as causes of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) even in the higher realms.
"Because it is indeterminate" means "without [an intervening cause]," that is, "in the interval" or "prior to";
"attained through the very nature of phenomena" (dharmatā-pratilambhika).
The meaning is that it is obtained through the power of the path of one beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*);
for its very nature is that which joins one with the marks of a monk (*bhikṣuliṅga*), and thus one is "of a nature not subject to falling away" (*avinipātadharmā*).
It is recited in the Sūtra:

"One who has entered the stream (srotāpanna) is of a nature not subject to falling into lower realms, destined for full awakening, and having at most seven more births, after wandering and transmigrating seven times among gods and humans, makes an end of suffering.
To the question, "Why is it so?", he says:
"Because of the non-accumulation of karma leading to that" means:
"falling into misfortune" refers to the states of woe, such as the hells and so forth; "leading to that" means going to those [states].
What is that action which leads to that [state] by going toward it?

Because that [karma] which has not yet arisen does not accumulate, and because the continuum of the noble one lacks the capacity to yield the ripening of what was accumulated during the stage of an ordinary person,
there is a lack of capacity for the continuum to yield the ripening of that karma leading to those states which was accumulated during the stage of an ordinary person and was of indeterminate timing.

It is said that "he becomes one whose nature is not subject to falling into the lower realms" because his continuum of aggregates has been transformed in such a way that it remains incapable of yielding the ripening of any accumulated karma leading to those states.

Why, then, does that continuum of the aggregates remain in such a state due to the deficiency in the capacity of the maturation of the accumulated karma leading to that [state]? To this it is replied: "Because of the perfuming by powerful roots of virtue."
Because this continuum of aggregates has been infused and cultivated by powerful roots of virtue;
and how, moreover, is it infused by powerful roots of virtue?
By means of the purity of application and intention.
It is [distinguished] by purity of application and purity of intention;
therein, purity of application refers to the precepts beloved by the noble ones, and purity of intention refers to verified clarity of faith toward the Buddhas and so forth.
"One should not even give rise to patience" means that one should not give rise to the mind of forbearance,
nor should one give rise to the thought [of it].
The intended meaning is "all the more so regarding the preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
Alternatively,
when one's karma is fixed toward a downfall, that person does not even produce the stage of receptivity (*kṣānti*) characterized as a factor conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How much more so the untainted path?
To demonstrate how one who is permeated by powerful roots of virtue becomes incapable of yielding the ripening of accumulated unwholesome karma, he shows it through this verse:
Having committed even a small [evil], the wise man [is purified];
thus,
the fool [is not purified] even by a small evil.
Having done so, one goes downward to a state of ruin.
The Buddha,
moreover,
is great even though he is small.
Having committed evil,
one brings about misfortune and a state of ruin for living beings.
He establishes those two points in their respective order by means of two examples:
even a small amount of iron, when compacted...
Remaining in the form of a solid mass,
it sinks in water because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
That very same iron, moreover, when fashioned into a vessel, [is no longer called iron].
The great one has been born in the waters.
It floats or crosses over by virtue of the quality of its formative activity (saṃskāra).
Thus, because he has been rendered unworthy by his virtues, the non-enlightened one sinks; however, the enlightened one does not sink because he has been rendered worthy by his virtues,
since for him there is no further suffering.
Because there is no suffering beyond that suffering which is comprised within the various states of existence,
that is the "end of suffering," meaning the final cessation of suffering;
for otherwise, the end of suffering would occur at the time of death.
But that suffering is accompanied by rebirth;
therefore,
he says that the meaning is "he brings about suffering that is without rebirth."
The intention is that it is not logical for nirvāṇa to "act" because it is eternal; rather,
[it is said to act] by way of removing the obstacles to its attainment.
Because it removes the obstacles to the attainment of nirvāṇa,
it brings about nirvāṇa by removing those obstacles— namely, the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) or the substrate (*upadhi*).
This is just as space is not perceived when a pavilion stands [in its midst].
When there is an obstruction to it, by removing that [obstruction], one says that one "makes space," even though space is eternal;
therefore he said:
"Just as there are those who say, 'Make the pavilion like space' or 'Bring it down,' so too there is another, namely the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) whose mental continuum is matured,
but who is not yet fixed [in the path]."
Because he might attain parinirvāṇa right here, or in the intermediate states, it is not said that he has "two or three births";
for "one who has two or three births" (dvitrijanmā) means one who has two or three births.
Some read it thus:
"dvitrajanmā," meaning two or three, [which are] "dvitrāṇi."
Regarding the compound: by the rule *saṅkhyayāvyayāsannādūrādhikasankhyāḥ saṅkhyeye*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
by the rule *bahuvrīhau saṅkhyeye ḍaj*, the suffix *ḍac* is added at the end of the compound.
Thus, "one whose other births are two or three" is *dvitrajanmā*.
But why does he say that in the verse there is a mention of both— the abandonment of afflictions and birth? He says:
For a stream-enterer who proceeds gradually, once the defilements to be abandoned by vision have been abandoned,
when one up to four categories of the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation are subsequently abandoned,

there is the acquisition of the untainted faculty that serves as the antidote to those— one, two, three, or more categories of defilements. Because this is established even without being explicitly stated, it is not mentioned in the verse.
For there is no abandonment of the types of afflictions without an antidote; indeed,
when that noble one abandons the types of afflictions even by means of a mundane path, there is the acquisition of an untainted faculty as its antidote,
though his birth may sometimes be somewhat lessened.
If he were to attain parinirvāṇa right here, or after being reborn in the intermediate state, what would be the reason?
It is because he is destined for a higher [attainment].
Because it is possible [to attain] from the fruit of stream-entry onwards up to once-returning and even arhatship, this birth is specified;
one who has two or three births is a "family-to-family" (kulaṅkula).
Thus,
for the sake of establishing a restrictive rule, this is investigated here:
what is the one who is liberated from one or two types [of fetters]?
Some say that he becomes a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner who is liberated after three or four [births].
The mention [of two types] is for the sake of illustration or for the sake of defining the limit as "not beyond this"; thus,
it has been stated that there are one or two types, while others say there are five or six births.
Since the qualification "one who is freed from three or four [categories of defilements]" is employed,
this has not been examined by the commentators; therefore, it should be investigated why this is not [the case] due to the abandonment of five types [of defilements].
The heading is "What is a *kulaṅkula*? and the detailed explanation begins with "the abandonment of that," and so forth.
Since the sixth type must necessarily be abandoned when the five types are abandoned, he asks "Why? and replies:
"For that single sixth type is not capable of obstructing the fruit, namely the fruit of the once-returner."
The phrase "like that of the ekavīcika" is a counter-example; for instance,
just as for the ekavīcika, a single type— the ninth [defilement]— is capable of obstructing the fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala).
It is not the case that this sixth category of the stream-enterer is capable of obstructing the fruit of the once-returner;
why is this? He says:
"Because there is no transcending of the realm."
For the one who has only one interval remaining (ekavīcika) transcends the desire realm;
therefore, even a single type—the ninth—is capable of obstructing his fruit, because transcending a realm is difficult to accomplish.
However, the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmī) does not transcend a realm.
Not even a single sixth category of affliction is capable of obstructing his fruit; thus,
whether in that [realm] or in another divine assembly—
such as among the Trāyastriṃśas— he sees the truths and, after wandering through two or three families, [attains parinirvāṇa].
There, he attains parinirvāṇa among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, or elsewhere among the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods or the Yāma gods.
In this same way, it should be applied elsewhere as well; for how is it stated in the Sūtra that [the stage] is called "thin" because of the attenuation of passion, hatred, and delusion?
By the abandonment of the three fetters and by the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one becomes a once-returner; this is because only the weak grades remain—
namely, the weak-intense, the weak-medium, and the weak-weak— and because these alone are what remain.

"In one whose seven or eight portions of the defilements have been exhausted": here, "portion of the defilements" (doṣāṃśa) refers to a constituent part of the defilements characterized by seven or eight types.
Furthermore, the third cause here, "by way of the faculties" (*indriyata*), was not set forth in the sūtra; it should be explained in the same manner.
As for the detailed explanation of how this is so:
how is it that for this "one-interval" (*ekavīcika*) practitioner, the ninth category of defilement is capable of acting as an obstacle?
It is said that this is because of the transcendence of the realm (*dhātu*);
for when this ninth category has been abandoned, one has transcended the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, he is not reborn there;

and since that ninth category of karma is to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) together with [the other] karma, he is thus able to obstruct the fruit by transcending the stage of its ripening (*vipāka*) and outflow (*niṣyanda*) fruits.
For it was stated previously that karmas present themselves as obstacles during three stages.
Regarding the statement that "karma creates an extreme obstacle to the attainment of patience, the state of a non-returner, and arhatship," this should here be applied to the afflictions (*kleśas*).
For this very reason, he says:
"Just as with karma, so too with the afflictions," and so forth.
"Because it is separated by only one birth" means that for that once-returner who has destroyed seven or eight categories [of defilements],
nirvana is separated by only one birth.

Or, because his fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is separated by only one type of affliction (kleśaprakāra), he is a "one-intervaller" (ekavīcika); yet, as long as he has not [attained that fruit], he is neither a "family-to-family" (kulaṅkula) nor a "one-intervaller.
Thus, even if one was previously liberated from three or four types [of afflictions] by means of the mundane path (laukikamārga), one is still not a family-to-family practitioner for that long.
Even one who has eliminated seven or eight categories [of afflictions] is not yet a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner,
because they have not yet attained the untainted faculties that serve as the antidote to those [remaining afflictions];
for this very reason, he said:
As long as the path distinguished by the fruit has not been brought face-to-face, [the state of being a *kulaṅkula* or *ekavīcika* does not occur];

however, when that which is distinguished by the fruit— namely, its antidote (*pratipakṣa*) or the antidote to the higher categories— is brought face-to-face, then, due to the acquisition of the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*),
it is implicitly stated that one becomes a *kulaṅkula* or an *ekavīcika*.
"Of the five," and so forth;
because of the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), one is called a "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*) in the Sūtra,
due to the grouping together of those abandonments.
Because the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others is established as a single [event], there are either two or three prior abandonments.

If, first of all, one who is already free from passion for the desire realm enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*), then two [categories of defilements] have been previously abandoned by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*).
Because sensual desire and ill will have been abandoned without exhausting the underlying tendencies such as the view of a self-identity and so forth,
one who follows the gradual path has previously abandoned three [fetters].
By which path of seeing are the view of a self-identity, the misapprehension of precepts and observances, and doubt abandoned?
Therefore, because of the complete abandonment of the five [lower fetters], he is called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon being reborn, with effort, or without effort;
he is a non-returner (anāgāmin).

Because he attains parinirvāṇa through application (*samskāra*) or without application (*asamskāra*) after having arisen in the intermediate state, he is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state through application or without application.
As for what was said regarding "one who has thus arisen," we do not understand that.
How can there be a *bahuvrīhi* compound for "one who has attained parinirvāṇa while already born" (*utpannasyānāgāminaḥ parinirvṛtiḥ*),
since a *bahuvrīhi* is said to function in the sense of another word (*anyapadārtha*) and not in the sense of its own constituent members (*svapadārtha*)?
Therefore, we see the reading here as *evam utpanne 'syeti*; it is likely that the vowel *e* was deleted by a scribe,
for with such a reading, this meaning becomes possible.
"One who attains parinirvāṇa upon being born" (*utpanna-parinirvṛti*) means that parinirvāṇa occurs for him once birth has arisen;
or rather, if the reading were exactly thus,
it would be explained in this way.
The genitive case is used here in the sense of disregard;
thus, the compound is formed in this way:

"one for whom there is the parinirvāṇa of a birth already arisen," namely, an anāgāmin who has attained parinirvāṇa after having been born—thus he is called an "anāgāmin who has attained parinirvāṇa upon being born" (*utpanna-parinirvṛti*).
Alternatively, "of that which has arisen" (*utpannasya*) refers to the genus (*jāti*) of what has arisen;
the meaning of "of those that have arisen" (*utpannānām*) is the same as the meaning of "of that which has arisen" (*utpannasya*).
Therefore, because he possesses the parinirvāṇa of those [defilements] that have arisen, he is one who has attained parinirvāṇa upon arising;
this is distinct from the mere sense of "parinirvāṇa" itself, which refers to the state of a non-returner (anāgāmin).

Even though the referent of the first member of the compound is not distinct [from the referent of the second], they might intend that the word *utpanna*—which is in grammatical apposition with *anāgāmin*—forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the word *parinirvṛti*.
If this were accepted, it would be well-stated:
"That very non-returner (anāgāmin) further becomes fivefold."

He concludes that there are five types— those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyī*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyī*), those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*), those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*)—
because their paths are characterized by being "diligent and swift" (*abhiyukta-vāhi*); "diligent" (*abhiyukta*) means energetic, having initiated vigor (*ārabdhavīrya*).
The path of this [person] is "carrying" (vāhī), thus it is the "carrying path" (vāhi-mārga).
How is the path carrying?
Because it manifests without deliberate effort (abhisaṃskāra).
It is "abhiyuktavāhimārga" because it is both applied (*abhiyukta*) and swift on the path (*vāhimārga*); [the word] refers to that state,
and therefore [it is so called].
Having arisen, he soon attains final nirvana through nirvana with a remainder of substrate; thus,
because there are two kinds of nirvana, he specifies that he attains final nirvana by means of nirvana with a remainder of substrate.
The meaning is that he brings about the destruction of all outflows (*sarvāsravakṣaya*);
this occurs through *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

It is not only the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyī*) who attains parinirvāṇa through *nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa* after reaching the state of an Arhat without having completed his lifespan.
Others say that even one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin) is similar to him,
because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his lifespan.
This is not so; for he too [attains] parinirvāṇa without remainder of substrate.
Why?
Because of his lack of mastery over the relinquishing of life; that is, because he lacks mastery in the relinquishing of his lifespan.
Why, then, does he lack mastery in this regard?
For while one who has attained the fourth meditative absorption of the ultimate limit (prāntakoṭika-caturtha-dhyāna) possesses mastery over the relinquishing of life-span,
that ultimate meditative absorption is produced only among humans in the three continents.

And since he has been reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), does one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) possess mastery over the relinquishing of life-force (āyur-utsarga-vaśitva),
by virtue of which he thus passes into parinirvāṇa without remainder of substrate (nirupadhiśeṣa-parinirvāṇa)?
He also lacks mastery;
for there is no such karma for remaining in the intermediate state as there is for one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
Therefore, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarā-parinirvāyī) attains parinirvāṇa quickly,

whereas the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī) attains parinirvāṇa after remaining for the duration of his lifespan; thus, it is said that only the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth attains parinirvāṇa through nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa),
while the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī) is so called [only] according to tradition.
The word *kila* indicates the Vaibhāṣika position;
for his own view will be stated later in accordance with the Sūtras as "uninterrupted application."
The meaning is that the application is not abandoned due to the momentum of prior application;
it is "with effort" and "with exertion" because it is a path that carries one forward through diligent practice.
Because that yogin is diligent and because it is the path of swift progress, for this very reason he is established as one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī),
rather than without exertion (anabhisaṃskāreṇa).
Because, as the opposite of the former case, the application has been relaxed, there is an absence of a path that carries forth diligent effort.
The meaning is that this is due to the absence of application (*abhiyoga*) and vigor (*vīrya*), as well as the absence of the path of swift progress (*vāhi-mārga*).
Thus, by means of the various distinctions such as application and so forth, the specific differences in parinirvāṇa have been explained.
For one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth possesses both:
application and a swift path;
whereas for one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, there is application [but not a swift path].
But for one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, neither of these two exists:
there is neither application nor a swift path.
"Because of the parinirvāṇa through a path that has conditioned and unconditioned objects":
"conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) and "conditioning" (*saṃskāra*) have the same meaning;
likewise, "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) and "non-conditioning" (*asaṃskāra*) [have the same meaning].
He who abandons the afflictions by means of a path that takes conditioned phenomena as its object— that is, a path taking suffering, origin, or the path as its objects—

is one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion; he who [does so] by means of a path taking the unconditioned as its object— that is, taking cessation as its object— [is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion].
Thus, he is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
however, that is not because of an over-extension [of the term].
That is not so;
why?
Because it would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Furthermore, since both the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth attain parinirvāṇa through paths that have either conditioned or unconditioned phenomena as their object, it would follow that each of them could be classified as both "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion" and "one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
Consequently, there would be only two types of persons residing in those states, rather than five.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*) was previously recited as "one who attains parinirvāṇa through effort" (*panabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*);
thus it is appropriate [to understand] it in that very way, and so forth.

Regarding the two types of persons—those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*)—who correspond respectively to those on the swift and the slow paths:
since the parinirvāṇa of the former is accomplished without exertion and that of the latter is accomplished with exertion, [the author] asks how the latter is accomplished in such a manner. He says:
It is because their parinirvāṇa occurs respectively through attainment with effort and without effort; or rather, the term "of the paths" refers specifically to the two paths: the slow and the swift.
There is no connection between two individuals,
because a flowing path is not to be accomplished through volitional effort, whereas a non-flowing path is to be accomplished through volitional effort,
due to their respective attainment with or without exertion.
Because the former path manifests without effort while the other is attained through effort,
it is therefore logical that the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyī) comes first.
He asked:
"If the path of one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion is 'swift' because it is accomplished without exertion, then the path of one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth is also a 'swift' path;
what, then, is the distinction between the two?"
Therefore it is said:

for one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), the path is more powerful and more mastered than that of one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*); thus, it is superior and accumulated through causes.
Furthermore, because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted by means of the superior path, they are exceedingly subtle; thus,
one is called "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*),
meaning that his course of flow (*srotas*) is directed upwards.
Where it is recited as "ūrdhvam," it means "above both self-restraint and the body."

It should be understood that in the case of *ūrdhvandāmika* and *ūrdhvandaihika*, the word *ūrdhva* is also prescribed with the suffix *-mat* (*mānta*) by virtue of its association with those specific suffixes; others maintain that there exists a conventional form *ūrdhvam* just as there is *cirantana* from the word *cira*.
Even though there exists a word *ūrdhva* ending in the vowel *a*, it is not excluded;
for "because of being mixed or unmixed dhyānas" means because of being combined or uncombined dhyānas.
Because the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dhyāna is mixed with the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), one here becomes detached from the three dhyānas after having mixed the dhyānas; thus,
"mixed dhyāna" is preceded by the mixing of the fourth dhyāna.
Because of the statement "the fourth is mixed first," it is indeed the fourth dhyāna alone that is capable of being mixed at the outset.
Since there is no rebirth in the first and subsequent dhyānas for one who has not fallen away from the fourth dhyāna, it is therefore said that "he has fallen away from the three dhyānas."
And how has he fallen away? It is said: "having relished the first dhyāna," because of not sinking into the middle—that is, not sinking into the intermediate state.

"Named 'Half-Leaper' (ardhapluta)," and so forth; the syntactical connection is as follows: "one who, having bypassed even a single intermediate station, is reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa [deities] and enters the Akaniṣṭha [heaven]," because it is a locus of views (dṛṣṭisthāna).
And for the Great Brahmas and those first reborn among the Great Brahmas, [it is so] because of the conceit of being creators within the Great Brahma realm and because there is only a single creator.
Why is this?
A noble one (*ārya*) is not reborn among the Mahābrahmās;
for if a powerful noble one were to arise there, there would be a duality of leaders,
whereas sovereignty over that realm belongs to one who acts without a rival.
Therefore, it is not accompanied by a rival; thus,

having passed away from the Brahmakāyika realm, one traverses all the other stations— the fourteen intermediate stations beginning with the Brahmapurohita and ending with the Sudarśana— and enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
"Because, having been reborn there, one does not return from that place at all"—
that is, having been reborn in such a place as the first dhyāna.
Because of not returning at all to the desire realm;
likewise, because of not returning at all to where one has been reborn;
and because of not returning at all to that first dhyāna.
Furthermore, his state of non-returning is complete because he will not undergo a second birth there;
for he is one whose practice is characterized by tranquility (śamatha).
He who has reached the peak of existence is one who delights in meditative concentration;
and in the formless realms, meditative concentration is exceedingly tranquil.
Therefore, this person enters the formless realms,
whereas the former one, who was described as having insight (vipaśyanā) as his primary practice, has Akaniṣṭha as his ultimate limit.
"He, being fond of full comprehension, enters the Pure Abodes [and attains] intermediate parinirvāṇa," and so forth;
this has not been definitively established by the authors of the treatises.

And since it has not been prohibited, we see that—due to this lack of prohibition—it is logical for those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and for those whose limit is the *Akaniṣṭha* heaven to enter either the *Akaniṣṭha* or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in the interval and attain final nirvāṇa;
the meaning is that we see the possibility of such an occurrence.
But was it not stated that there are those for whom the *Akaniṣṭha* is the limit and those for whom the Peak of Existence is the limit? To this he says:

However, "having the Akaniṣṭha heaven and the Peak of Existence as the limit" means that there is no further destination beyond them, because there is no going upward from the Akaniṣṭhas or from the Peak of Existence.
This is just as, for a stream-enterer, "seven times at most" does not mean that it is impossible for him to attain parinirvāṇa after having produced two or three more existences.
Beyond that, however, one does not bring about an eighth existence;
thus, it is said that "at most seven times" [is the limit].
Furthermore, that [stream-enterer] is of four kinds, and because there is no such thing as one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyin*), it is not of five kinds.

These are the six non-returners: the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, the one who flows upwards, and the sixth, the one who goes to the formless realm— this being stated without counting the fourfold division of the last.

"One who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyī*) means "one who attains parinirvāṇa in this very birth" (*dṛṣṭajanmaparinirvāyī*). How is it that there are these three? [This is] the detailed explanation.
Not understanding why the three non-returners (*anāgāmin*) were not mentioned after [the discussion on] revulsion (*nirvidya*), the other asks.

The Master, seeing that they have been stated by implication (*arthāpatti*), explains: "The meaning is [the division into] those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*);
and the third is the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*)."

Regarding "due to quick, not-quick, and long-term parinirvāṇa by means of three similes": one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly, one who attains parinirvāṇa not quickly, and one who attains parinirvāṇa after a long time are to be applied to the three similes as follows:
just as a small spark of fire might go out even while it is still being produced; [and likewise for the other two].

Thus is the first, one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly; just as when iron balls or iron ploughshares, heated by a blazing fire, are struck with an iron hammer, an iron spark flies up and is extinguished even as it rises—
such is the second, one who attains parinirvāṇa not quickly.

It is as follows: "Just as with iron balls," and so on as before, up to: "just as an iron spark, having flown up, might be extinguished even before falling to the ground—such is the third type, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*).
And since this sutra has already been written in detail previously, it is not written again here.

The connection is as follows: because of attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*), and without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), there are nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) due to these threefold distinctions.
One who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*) is one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately after being reborn.
However, he does not attain parinirvāṇa through volitional effort or the absence of volitional effort;
rather, one who attains parinirvāṇa with effort (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) does not attain parinirvāṇa immediately upon rebirth,
but instead attains parinirvāṇa through the power of previous volitional effort that has not yet been relaxed.

For although he possesses a swift path, he attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (*adhiyoga*), whereas the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*) does not do so through exertion; this is the distinction.

Furthermore, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*) is one whose previous exertion has subsided and who attains parinirvāṇa without further exertion. This alone is to be understood as the distinction between them.
Showing how even those who attain parinirvāṇa with effort and without effort receive the designation "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth," he says:
"For all these are 'those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth' because they attain parinirvāṇa after being reborn."
"By way of the divisions of *pluta* and so forth" means by way of the divisions of *pluta*, *ardhapluta*, and *sarvacyuta*;
or, [it refers to] all three [of these].

There is a threefold division among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*), based on whether their parinirvāṇa occurs quickly, not quickly, or after a long time. Specifically,
some who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state do so quickly, while others do so not quickly, or after a long time.
In this way, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyī) and the one who flows upwards (ūrdhvasrotas)—
due to these threefold divisions, there are nine non-returners (anāgāmin); this same connection should be stated.
"Furthermore, their distinction," and so forth:

furthermore, regarding those three— the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, and the one who flows upwards— and these nine [others] as well, there is a distinction from what has been described due to each being divided threefold.
Due to the distinction of karma, afflictions, and faculties— that is,
due to the distinction of karma, afflictions, and faculties— it comes to be;
as to how this is so, he says:
"Of the three," and so forth:
"arising" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
because of having accumulated karma to be experienced upon arising, one is an "attainer of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."

Because they have accumulated karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadya-vedanīya-karman*), they are called "those who flow upwards" (*ūrdhva-srotas*). Thus, first, there is a distinction among these three based on the distinction of their karma; second, there is a distinction among these very same ones based on the distinction of their afflictions (*kleśa*), due to the manifestation of weak, medium, and intense afflictions respectively;
and third, there is a distinction among these very same ones based on the distinction of their faculties (*indriya*), due to having superior, medium, and inferior faculties respectively.
For each of those as well, there is a distinction according to the circumstances for that very reason;
this means that for each of those nine distinct [categories], there is a distinction.
For that very reason, due to the distinctions of karma and so forth, they are presented according to their respective applications, not according to a fixed sequential order.
A distinction must be understood;
as to how, he says:
"Of the first two triads," and so forth.

And because of the distinction in afflictions and faculties between those two triads— the triad of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state and the triad of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth.
The distinction [between them] is, respectively, due to the manifestation of weak, medium, and intense afflictions,
and due to having superior, medium, and weak faculties.
But it is not due to a difference in karma,

because for the first triad, the karma to be experienced upon arising (*abhinirvṛtti-vedanīya*) is the same, and for the second triad, the karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*) is the same.
Furthermore, there is a distinction [between these] and the last triad due to the specific nature of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya-karma*);
for the karma to be experienced in subsequent lives of those who leap (*pluta*) and so forth is distinct.
Thus, it is because of this specific nature of karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.

And because of the distinction between afflictions and faculties— due to the inclusion of the word "and" (ca)— there is a distinction based on the manifestation of weak, medium, and intense afflictions,
and due to being of intense, medium, and weak faculties respectively.
The meaning is "in due order.
These [nine types] are so called because of their ninefold afflictions and faculties;
that is, these non-returners (anāgāmin) are distinguished by their ninefold afflictions.
And because there are nine types of faculties, there are nine non-returners;
the mention of "karma" is not intended to be all-inclusive, as it would otherwise be over-extensive.
For there is no distinction between the first two triads due to a difference in their objects;
how then do these afflictions become ninefold?
Here, the affliction is of three types: weak, medium, and intense.

The [faculties] of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are weak; those of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth are middling; and those of those who are "stream-winners heading upward" (ūrdhvasrotas) are superior.

Among them, the first is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, possessing the weakest of weak afflictions; the first of those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth possesses middling-weak afflictions;
and the second, the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, possesses middling-middling afflictions.
The third is one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), possessing medium-strong afflictions (*madhyādhimātra-kleśa*).

Among those who "flow upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), the "leaper" (*pluta*) has strong-weak afflictions (*adhimātra-mṛdu-kleśa*); the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*) has strong-medium afflictions (*adhimātra-madhya-kleśa*);
and the "one who dies in every place" (*sarvasthānacyuta*) has strong-strong afflictions (*adhimātrādhimātra-kleśa*).
How do the faculties become of nine types?
In that same way, the faculty is also of three types—superior and inferior;
the superior belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
The medium [degree] belongs to those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; the weak [degree] belongs to those who go upstream.
Among these, the first is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, possessing the sharpest of sharp faculties.
The second has superior-middle faculties;
the third has superior-weak faculties.
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, the first—those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth—has middle-superior faculties.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion has medium-medium faculties;
the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion has medium-weak faculties;
and among those who "stream upward," the leaper has weak-strong faculties.
If the "half-leaper" has dull faculties on earth,
and the one who dies from all places has very dull faculties,
how then are the destinies of the noble persons (satpuruṣagati) taught in the Sūtra?
"O monks, I shall teach you the seven destinations of the true persons and parinirvāṇa without clinging"—
this entire sutra is written in this section as "according to the sutra" (*sūtrato*), and thus it is not written out again.

And in this sutra, seven destinations of the true persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are taught: three who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), and three who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*); thus, there are six destinations.
"And the seventh is the state of one whose stream flows upwards" (ūrdhvaṃsrotas);
this word form is a derivative ending in a *kṛt* suffix, meaning "one whose nature is to flow upwards."
He shows that this verbal form is for the purpose of specification by stating "and 'ūrdhvam' is an adverbial modifier (kriyāviśeṣaṇa)," because of its indication as non-distinct from that [action].
The meaning is that because the distinctions such as the "leaper" (*pluta*) and so forth have not been specified for one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
For the exposition in the Sūtra is dependent upon the dispositions of those to be trained; there are no other destinies for those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
The meaning is that they do not have the destinies of stream-enterers or once-returners;
for "destiny," "birth," and "future state" are stated in the Sūtra as synonyms,
and [the phrase] "of them" refers to those non-returners.

Furthermore, there is engagement when there is action, because of the non-commission of killing and so forth; and there is non-engagement when there is no action, because of the non-commission of unchastity and so forth,
for it is by means of an unwholesome mind that one commits acts such as unchastity.

However, for those who are free from passion, their activity occurs only when karma exists and not when it is absent, because they have abandoned unwholesome states; thus, there is no returning again to those realms of existence (gatis) in which they were born.

The meaning is that there is an absolute non-returning for them to each respective place; however, this— namely, functioning only when [the cause] exists, not functioning when it does not exist, and the absence of returning again— is not found elsewhere as it has been described here.
This [fault] does not exist in the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*);
the phrase "and for others as well" means that it applies to stream-enterers and once-returners as well.
"Pāryāyika" means that which exists in a particular mode (paryāya); the sense is that it exists in some specific way.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of the attainment of the restraint of absolute non-performance of the fivefold evil.

This means that restraint (*saṃvara*) is the act of restraining (*saṃvaraṇa*) by way of non-performance—that is, by not committing—the fivefold evil characterized by killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the drinking of intoxicants.
Because of its attainment,
the noble ones do not commit these five kinds of evil even in another birth;
this is what is meant by the expression "the restraint of non-doing."
Because the restraint of formal undertaking is not necessary,
[it is said] "for the most part," due to the absolute abandonment of all unwholesome states that are to be abandoned through insight.
And of some [defilements] belonging to the realm of desire that are to be abandoned by cultivation, as far as is possible— of which [it is said], "of those," and so forth;

but for those [defilements] for which there is no other way, nor by any other means, [to attain] the state of a true person (satpuruṣatva), as in the case of the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) or the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
Rather,
it is because of the attainment of the restraint of never again committing any evil whatsoever,
and because of the abandonment of all unwholesome afflictions that are to be abandoned by insight.
And because of the abandonment of all nine grades of those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by cultivation,

these noble persons (satpuruṣa), the non-returners (anāgāmin), are the subject of this sūtra under the heading "the destinies of noble persons" (satpuruṣagati); therefore, the figurative status of being a noble person for others is not excluded.

Furthermore, does this distinction— such as being one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) and so forth— exist even for a non-returner (anāgāmin) who has changed births?

One who is a non-returner having changed births is someone who, having attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) or the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) in the first birth, becomes a non-returner in the second birth.
The qualification "desire" (kāma) is used because one whose birth has occurred in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) sometimes enters the formless realms (ārūpya),
and thus attains final nirvana (parinirvāṇa) in that very birth.
Because of the abundance of suffering in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he possesses intense spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);
thus, the detailed passage beginning with "In that case...
was spoken by Śakra: "Having passed away from here, if I am reborn among humans and do not attain *arhatship* and enter final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*... [he would remain subject to rebirth]).

Thinking, "Those gods who are renowned as the Akaniṣṭhas—when I am finally passing away, my rebirth shall be there," he would indeed be one whose birth is completed after returning from among the gods;

for it is said that one who has attained the stream (*srotāpanna*) among the gods will come to the human realm and attain final nirvana (*parinirvāsyati*). Thus, he would be one who has undergone a single further birth (*parivṛttajanman*).

Since there is a statement of aspiration— namely, "At the end of my current nikāyasabhāga, while I am declining from arhatship through the loss of non-attainment, may my rebirth occur there in the Akaniṣṭha heaven"— it is understood that this demonstrates the existence of going to another realm. How then can it be said that a noble one (ārya) who has undergone a change of birth within the desire realm does not go to another realm?
If you say that the meaning of the Sūtra is evident [therein],
we would reply: it was stated thus by the author because he was unacquainted with the characteristics of the Dharma.
"Therefore, there is no fault.
To this, [the opponent asks]: "If the Blessed One was listening at that very time, why did he not prevent him, saying, 'Do not speak thus'?
To this, it is replied: "The Blessed One's failure to prevent him..."
"Because it is to be gladdened" means that it is to be gladdened by the desire to abandon the suffering of sensual desires;
Master Saṅghabhadra says it is because it is to be gladdened for one who is distressed by the suffering of death and rebirth.
"Because the faculties are more fully matured" means because there is a specific nourishment of the outflow-result (*niṣyandaphala*) of the faculties such as wisdom,
and because of the attainment of a specific basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*).
Furthermore, because one obtains a specific basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*) that is unimpaired and favorable for the manifestation of the Path—

since it is observed that even those with sharp faculties may fall away from their qualities due to a defect in the basis— there is no transformation of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*) because the faculties have become more fully matured through dwelling in another birth,
and there is no falling away because of the attainment of this specific basis; and by this very dwelling in another birth, there is no transition to another realm (*dhātu-antara-gamana*).
"Because the path has not been mastered and has not been brought into manifestation": since the path has not been mastered and thus does not manifest,

for that reason a learner (*śaikṣa*) who is not yet free from passion— namely, a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmī*)— does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
And because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not extremely weak;
since his latent dispositions are not extremely weak, he does not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*). This is the teacher’s resolution.
"What is the Vaibhāṣikas' rebuttal? he asks;
[the author] says: "Because the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is difficult to transcend," according to the Vaibhāṣikas.
How so? It is explained as follows:
For much remains to be done by him:

the abandonment of unwholesome and neutral afflictions must be accomplished by him; and for one who is already free from passion, it is the abandonment of only the neutral afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that remains to be accomplished by the trainee.
"Attainment of two or three fruits of asceticism" means that two or three fruits of asceticism are to be attained;
by a once-returner, two fruits of asceticism are to be attained.
For one who is already free from passion, the fruit of non-returning and the fruit of arhatship must both be attained as a single fruit of arhatship; thus,
the transcendence of the three realms must be accomplished by one who is not yet free from passion.

But for one who is free from passion [for the desire realm] yet not yet free from passion for the form realm, and who is to attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state— being one who must effect the transcendence of two realms—
it is "intermingled," it is "mixed," it is "blended."
The meaning is that the fourth dhyāna with outflows (*sāsrava*) is mixed with the two [dhyānas] without outflows (*anāsava*);
this is because it is the foremost among the easy paths (*sukhapratipad*),
for the four fundamental dhyānas are the easy paths.
Because it is stated that "the path within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) is the easy practice," the fourth absorption is the foremost among them, as it is free from the eight defects.
Regarding the phrase "it is said" (*yadā kila*), the word *kila* indicates the opinion of the Vaibhāṣikas;
his own position, however, he will demonstrate later.
However, the intermingling of moments is impossible; for, in detail, two moments are similar to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*),
namely the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the tainted (*sāsrava*),
while the third is similar to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and is thus untainted.
Those of dull faculties practice the intermingling [of dhyānas] out of fear of the afflictions;
by the word "and," it is implied that they also practice the intermingling for the sake of rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
Those of sharp faculties, however, practice the intermingling solely for the sake of rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.
It is not out of fear of the afflictions (*kleśa*), because for them there is no possibility of falling away;
yet, how is it that they practice the intermingling [of dhyānas] for the sake of not falling away due to fear of the afflictions? To this he says:
"By means of distancing the concentration associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta-samādhi*), it is for the sake of non-retrogression;
[the thought] 'May I not fall away from the fruit'—
thus it is of five kinds," and so forth in detail.
"Mild, medium, intense, more intense, and most intense"—
thus there are three levels of mind in the first [stage]; the capacity of that person is to such an extent, and so it should be stated for the subsequent stages as well.
Regarding the second [set], there are six:
namely, the untainted (*anāsrava*), the tainted (*sāsrava*), and the untainted; then again, the untainted, the tainted, and the untainted—thus there are another three, making six in total.

In the same way, one should apply the sequence as follows: nine in the third, twelve in the fourth, and fifteen in the fifth. Thus, the fruits of those mixed cultivations (vyavakīrṇabhāvanā) are, respectively, the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).
The Avṛha heaven is the fruit of weak cultivation, and likewise up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven being the fruit of the most intense cultivation;
this is because of the predominance of the faculties such as faith. This is the opinion of the Venerable Śrīlāta:
that for cultivation in which faith is predominant, the Avṛha heaven is the fruit.
In this way, up to the cultivation of superior wisdom, Akaniṣṭha is the fruit.
For whoever is a non-returner—
whether one liberated through faith or one who has attained through vision— [attains that fruit].
"Realization by means of the body" means that because of the absence of mind, one realizes by means of the body alone;
as to how it is by means of the body alone, he says:
Because it arises based on the body,
it must be so; this is the Master's own view,
[stated] by means of the attainment and the direct realization of knowledge.

For "direct realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) means making manifest through perception (*pratyakṣīkāra*), because at the time of meditative absorption one directly realizes the attainment of a basis conducive to that [state],
and at the time of emergence one directly realizes the knowledge that experiences it.
The intention is that direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) is appropriate in the state of attaining the tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness;

or rather, through the attainment of the tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness, its acquisition is understood to occur in the state of the tranquility of the body devoid of consciousness—
this is what is meant in the Sūtra regarding "the eighteen learners" (*aṣṭādaśa śaikṣāḥ*).
The householder Anāthapiṇḍada asked the Blessed One,
"Venerable Sir, how many are worthy of offerings?
The Blessed One replied:
"Householder, there are eighteen who are worthy of offerings: the nine trainees and the nine non-trainees.

Which are the eighteen trainees? They are: one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; [and so on through the remaining fruits and stages up to] one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
The stream-enterer,
the one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning, and the once-returner.
One who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of non-returning;
a non-returner;
one who has entered the path for the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
The follower by faith,
the follower by dharma,
and the one resolved through faith.
One who has attained vision, one who goes from family to family, and one who has only one interval remaining.
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth,
and one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion and the one who goes upstream—
these, householder, are the eighteen learners (śaikṣas).
Who are the nine types of non-learners? They are: those subject to falling away, those subject to volition, and so forth.
One whose nature is to guard,
one who is immovable in stability,
and one capable of penetration.
One of unshakable nature, liberated in mind and liberated by wisdom.
"O Householder, these are the nine types of non-learners (aśaikṣa), including the one liberated in both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
There are three trainings and their fruit."
The three trainings— higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom— are characterized by the noble path;
their fruit is dissociation (visaṃyoga),
for it is by way of that distinction that the stages of those in training (śaikṣas) are established.
The meaning is: "by way of the distinction in training and by way of the distinction in its fruit.
But how is that distinction [established]? Because the eighteen types of trainees (*śaikṣa*) are of various kinds, as is their fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Furthermore, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is not a state of training (*śaikṣa*) because its intrinsic nature is not the path of abandonment;
nor is it the fruit of training because its intrinsic nature is not the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*).
Therefore, one is not designated as a "distinguished trainee" (*śaikṣaviśeṣa*) on account of being endowed with that, namely, on account of being endowed with the attainment of cessation.
Just as these eighteen are trainees (śaikṣa),
so too is this person not non-trainee;
in that regard, it is said:

Regarding the statement "there are eighteen learners" (*śaikṣa*) in this Sūtra, for what reason is the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) not mentioned as a learner? It is because [the classification] is stated according to coarse distinctions; thus, there are five who have reached the realm of form (*rūpopaga*).
The one going to the formless realm is of four types; the other attains nirvana here,
and so forth.
"But when [the category] is divided subtly," and so forth;

here the Master, for the purpose of demonstrating the methods of calculation, first explains the distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) according to their faculties (*indriya*), stages (*bhūmi*), lineages (*gotra*), and so on.
What is the reason?

For when their distinctions are calculated, just as there is a distinction among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) due to differences in faculties and so forth, so it is up to those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*); thus, I shall easily apply this analogy,
and therefore there are four distinctions of levels.

These very stages are those of the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, because it is the non-returners who go to the realm of form who are intended here, and their stages are the four dhyānas.
In that regard, from the first *dhyāna* up to the fourth, there are four types of those who attain *parinirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyin*).
There are six [types] due to the distinction of lineages (*gotra*), such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth; these are:

the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the one whose nature is volition (*cetanādharman*), the one whose nature is guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one who is stable and unshakable (*sthitākampya*), the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*), and the one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*).
There are sixteen [heavens] due to the distinction of different locations;
according to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas, these range from the Brahmakāyika heavens up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, as they constitute distinct locations for Mahābrahmā.
Even according to the system of the outsiders (*bahirdeśaka*), since he is not born there even though it is another location, he is not counted [among the inhabitants].
Thus, due to the distinction of different locations, there are sixteen types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*);
and due to the distinction of the stages (*bhūmi*) and degrees of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are thirty-six.

He explains how there are thirty-six types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) due to the distinctions among the stages (*bhūmi*) and the distinctions in their detachment from them (*vairāgyabheda*), starting with the detailed explanation:
"In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one who is bound by all fetters... and so forth.

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), in the first dhyāna, there are nine [types of individuals]: those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), those who have abandoned one type of passion up to those who have abandoned eight types; likewise in the second [dhyāna] there are nine, from those bound by all fetters up to those who have abandoned eight types;
and similarly in the third [dhyāna] there are nine.
Likewise, in the fourth [dhyāna], there are nine; thus four sets of nine make thirty-six,
up to one who is free from passion regarding the eight categories of the fourth dhyāna.
By the word "up to" (yāvat), this detailed meaning is obtained:
one who is free from passion regarding the ninth category of the fourth dhyāna is not mentioned,
because such a person remains fully bound by fetters in the formless realm (ārūpya).
And one who goes to the formless realm is not under consideration here,
because those who go to the realm of form are intended here due to their connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
And this being so, as it is stated in detail: "due to the distinctions of place, lineage, detachment,

and faculty," there are two hundred and ninety-two— that is, two hundred and ninety-two more— of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), owing to the distinctions among places, lineages, degrees of detachment, and faculties.
To explain how they become such, he says:
in one place,
namely among the Brahmapurohitas, there are six lineages (gotra) due to the distinction between those subject to falling away (parihāṇadharma) and so forth.
The phrase "gotra-gotra" is a distributive repetition; it refers to the nine types of persons,
from one bound by all fetters up to one who is free from eight categories of passion, each according to their own station,
such as that of the Brahmapurohita.
There are six groups of nine, because of the inclusion of the ninefold set of persons within the six lineages; there are fifty-four,
because of the inclusion of sixteen sets of fifty-four across sixteen different positions.
Sixty-four and so forth means eight hundred plus sixty-four;
however, due to the distinctions among the faculties, they are tripled by way of the distinctions of weak, medium, and intense.

Having established this, why do [the categories] become two hundred and ninety-two, by which logic nine types of persons (pudgala) are established, ranging from one bound by all fetters up to one who is free from passion regarding eight categories?
Demonstrating that principle, he says: "For one who is free from passion regarding nine categories in a lower dhyāna," and so forth.
For one who is free from passion regarding nine categories in a lower dhyāna—from the first up to the third—is said to be "fully bound" in a higher dhyāna—from the second up to the fourth.
He asks "Why? and says: "For the sake of equal enumeration," meaning so that there may be nine [factors] in each of the four dhyānas.
Otherwise, the calculation would be inconsistent: in the first dhyāna there would be ten [categories], from those bound by all fetters up to those free from passion in nine ways;
in the second [dhyāna] there would be nine, from those free from passion in one way up to those free from passion in nine ways.

Thus, in the third [dhyāna] there are nine; in the fourth, however, there would be eight—from one who is free from passion regarding one type up to one who is free from passion regarding eight types—because one who is free from passion regarding nine types is bound by all the fetters of the formless realm (*ārūpya*). It has been stated thus, up to the case of those who "stream upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

In this way, for those who attain birth [in the form realm] with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra*), without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra*), and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*), there are likewise twenty-five hundred and ninety-two varieties each, based on the distinctions of station (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and faculties (*indriya*). When these are totaled, there are thirteen thousand minus forty varieties of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

However, when combined with those who go to the formless realms (*ārūpyaga*)—which are further divided into the four types beginning with "attaining birth" (*upapadya*)—the number becomes exceedingly vast.
Since it is understood that one proceeds by this very path, it is not written out here.

Regarding the term *ābhavāgrāṣṭabhāgakṣit*: it means "one who destroys eight parts up to the peak of existence" (*ābhavāgra*); that is, one who destroys eight types [of afflictions] up to the peak of existence, meaning one who effects the destruction of the eight categories [of afflictions] at the peak of existence.
This non-returner (anāgāmī), starting from the detachment from one category of the first dhyāna—
because it is from the detachment from the desire realm that one is established as a non-returner—
therefore becomes one who has entered the path toward the fruit of arhatship beyond that point.
Just as a diamond breaks everything, so too this concentration breaks every latent tendency (*anuśaya*); thus, by virtue of its capacity, it is "diamond-like" (*vajropama*).
However, because it has already broken [them], it does not break everything.

If one does not break all eight types—those belonging to the three realms, whether to be abandoned by seeing or by cultivation, ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the peak of existence—why is it said that [the path] "breaks all latent dispositions" (*sarvānuśayabhedin*)? To this he replies:
"But it is capable of breaking them all."
The intention is that this was stated with reference to the possibility (*sambhava*).
The detailed explanation—that they are "comprised within the *anāgamya*"—is as follows:

the attainment of arhatship occurs by relying upon nine stages—the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the thirty formless attainments (*ārūpya*) excluding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). It is for this reason that it is explained in such detail.
There are eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding the origin of suffering;
that is, four associated with the four aspects of the subsequent knowledge having the suffering of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object, and another four.
In the same way, it should be stated that there are eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding cessation and the path.

According to the established tenet that dharma-knowledge regarding cessation or the path on the path of cultivation is the antidote to the three realms, only those two are presented here; there is no inclusion of the dharma-knowledges regarding suffering and its origin.
In this way, up to the word "as far as" (*yāvat*):
by the word "as far as," just as there are four [applications of mindfulness] associated with the aspects having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object,

so too should it be stated that there are four each for those having the cessation of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the peak of existence as their objects.

Regarding the statement that there are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), why is it not said that there are four for each level associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge that takes the path of that specific level as its object? To this he says:
"Because [the subsequent knowledge] takes the entire category of subsequent knowledge as its object."

For the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is undifferentiated, and since the path is mutually the cause for one another by way of being an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it is taken as a whole and not like cessation (*nirodha*); therefore, there are exactly four aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
These [aspects] are distinguished by the differences in their cognitive aspects (*jñānākāra*), objects (*ālambana*), and types.
They are distinguished by the difference in the aspects of cognition and the difference in their objects;
or rather, they are distinguished by the threefold difference of cognitions, aspects, and objects.
First, they are distinguished by the difference in the aspects of cognition.

Because of such statements as "by means of the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and its origin," and because of such statements as "even though distinguished by differences in their objects, [they are distinguished] by having the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence as their objects."
"Forty-two" means that,
starting from "two eights," there are sixteen;
four have the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object, and likewise four are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path— thus, nine sets of four make thirty-six.
Sixteen, thirty-six, and fifty-two [moments] arise,
as is detailed in the case of those comprised within the *anāgamya*. It is called *anāgamya* because the fundamental dhyāna arises without having entered the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage].

In the same manner as the fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) included in the *anāgamya* were described immediately above, there are likewise fifty-two included in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*). How so?
There are eight [moments] included in the intermediate dhyāna, associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the Peak of Existence;
eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path;
and four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object.
In this way, up to the four [moments] having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object,
there are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path,
because they take the entire category of subsequent knowledge as their object.
Thus, these become fifty-two, distinguished by the differences in their aspects, cognitions, and objects;
just as there are fifty-two included within the intermediate dhyāna, so too there are fifty-two included within the first dhyāna, up to fifty-two included within the fourth dhyāna.
"Respectively," and so forth;
twenty-eight are comprised within the sphere of infinite space,
and twenty-four are comprised within the sphere of infinite consciousness.
There are twenty [factors] included within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*); however,
because the noble path (*āryamārga*) does not exist in the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), those [twenty] are not considered to be included therein,
as there is an absence of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) among them.
Because there is an absence of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) in those [realms] such as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*),
and because dharma-knowledge belongs to the six levels, the eight [mental applications] associated with the aspects of the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path do not exist therein.
Furthermore, because there is no subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) that takes the cessation of a lower stage as its object,

those [mental states] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) which take the cessation of the four dhyānas as their object do not occur sixteen times; thus, they become twenty-eight,
since eight and sixteen have been subtracted from fifty-two.

How is it that those [minds] included within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*)— eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin (*duḥkha-samudayānvaya-jñāna*) pertaining to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),

and sixteen associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvaya-jñāna*) having as their objects the cessations of the sphere of infinite space and so forth— are [so described]?
There are four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*);
thus, these become twenty-eight, distinguished by differences in knowledge, aspect, and object.
In the same way, having removed the four [moments] that have the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness as their object, twenty-four are to be applied.

Having further removed those [objects] included in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) that have the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) as their object, there remain twenty.

What, then, is the reason that the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) take only the cessation belonging to their own level or a higher level as their object, and not that of a lower level, unlike the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?
For it is not possible to take the cessation of a lower level as an object without first taking its suffering (*duḥkha*) as an object.
And all suffering is indeed with-outflows (sāsrava);
this is a fixed rule:
the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have lower realms with-outflows as their object.
This is the reason why there is no prohibition against the meditative absorptions (dhyānas), because they involve comprehensive observation;
for he will say:
Since meditation has a wholesome object that exists,
why then do they take cessation alone as their focal point, and not suffering or its origin?
Because he is free from passion for the lower realms down to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
only the ninth category belonging to the peak of existence remains to be destroyed by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama*); thus,
it is the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that is under discussion, as it takes as its object the antidote to the lower realms.
And that [path] should be understood as being associated with the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi),
because that antidote has mutual causality;
for the path of the nine stages is mutually related to those that are equal and superior.
Because of this statement,

all subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has as its object the category of subsequent knowledge belonging to the nine stages; thus [begins] the detailed explanation of the view of those who hold that.

For those Abhidharmikas who maintain that the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), not merely the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), has each individual level as its object of opposition, they add twenty-eight more; thus, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropamasamādhi*) comprised within the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*). How is this so?

The four [mental applications] previously mentioned, which have the entire category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*),
are now established— according to the opinion of some teachers— as having each individual level as their counteractive object (*pratipakṣālambana*).
