These are those included in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), which have the counteractive aspect of the first dhyāna as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path.

In this way, up to the four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) which have as their object the antidote to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), there are twenty-eight additional ones.
Thus, by adding these twenty-eight additional ones, there are fifty-two plus eighty-two [making one hundred and thirty-four].

But what is the reason that the four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path which have as their object the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) are not counted?
He said:

"Is it not the case that there exists an untainted path included within the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) which serves as the antidote to the peak of existence? Indeed, such a path belonging to the level of the first dhyāna does exist."
Up to the level of the sphere of nothingness (*akiñcanyāyatana-bhūmika*),
therefore, they are said to have as their objects only the counteragents (*pratipakṣa*) of those respective levels, and not the counteragent of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Others, however, explain that for those who maintain that even the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has as its object the antidote to each individual stage—
just as the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) is held to do— this is the intended meaning.
Of these, there are eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path;
and four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, having the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object.
Thus, up to those having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object, there are four; making thirty-two in total.
Likewise, those associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) are also thirty-two in the same manner.
Having thus calculated thirty-two for each of the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path, [the total is one hundred and twenty-eight].
By adding twenty-eight more, there are eighty diamond-like (*vajropama*) concentrations included within the "unshakeable" category.

For among those [concentrations], the four which have the entire category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as their object and are associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path do not exist;
however, in their place, there are those that have the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object. Therefore, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations.
In this way, up to those comprised within the fourth dhyāna,
how is it that by adding twenty-eight more, the diamond-like concentrations (vajropama-samādhi) comprised within the intermediate dhyāna become eighty?

Just as those included within the intermediate dhyāna, so too, for each of the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations; this is likewise the case in the sphere of infinite space and the others.
In the three formless realms, excluding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there are respectively forty, thirty-two, and twenty-four [moments]. How so?

First, in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), to the twenty-eight diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama*), one adds four associated with the aspects of subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) having as their object the antidote to the sphere of infinite space, up to four having as their object the antidote to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*). Thus [there are forty].
By adding twelve, they become forty.

Likewise, by adding four that have the counteragent of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) as their object to the twenty-four, and then adding four that have the counteragent of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) as their object, they become thirty-two.
Likewise, by adding four that have the counteragent of the sphere of nothingness as their object to the twenty, they become twenty-four.
He said:
"But has it not been stated that its object is the counteragent of the lower stage,
because they are mutual causes?"

Now, why are those comprised within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth said to have as their objects only the counteractives (*pratipakṣa*) of their own level and higher levels, and not the counteractives of lower levels? To this it is replied:
It has been stated that, without distinction, the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) across the nine stages takes as its object the antidote to the lower stages;
however, it was not stated that [the path] comprised within the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth takes as its object the antidote to the lower stages.
What then?

In that context, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) has as its object only the counteragent belonging to its own level or a higher level; it takes the lower level as its object only in an undifferentiated form,
not in its specific nature.
However, since [subsequent knowledge] can also have its own level and the higher levels as objects in a specific manner,
this former position of the Vaibhāṣikas—
that subsequent knowledge takes the entire category of subsequent knowledge as its object only in a general manner— is the established view.
For thus it was said by the Master Saṅghabhadra:
"Indeed, all subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has as its object the category of subsequent knowledge pertaining to the nine stages";
however, others explain it in this way.

There are sixteen [moments]: eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin pertaining to the peak of existence (*bhāvāgrika*); four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation and having the cessation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) as their object; and likewise, up to four having the cessation of the peak of existence as their object.

There are likewise four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) that have as their object the antidote to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*);

continuing in this manner up to four that have as their object the antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). These sixteen, together with the previously mentioned eight, constitute the thirty-four.
There are forty diamond-like concentrations comprised within the sphere of infinite space;
there are thirty-two comprised within the sphere of infinite consciousness,
formed by removing the eight that have as their object the antidote for the cessation of the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, twenty-four [moments] included within the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) remain,
after excluding another eight that have the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) as their counteractive object;
for they also describe the path of counteraction belonging to a lower level as being [the antidote] to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, since they become more numerous due to the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*),
how is it that those eight who were mentioned first of all [are so designated]?
That which has the suffering of the peak of existence as its object and is associated with the aspect of impermanence— the diamond-like [samādhi]—
is divided into six types due to the distinction of the six lineages (*gotra*).
Likewise, each of the three [diamond-like samādhis] associated with the aspects of suffering and so forth is likewise divided into six types.
Each of these is further divided according to the distinction of weak, medium, and superior faculties;
and just as there are distinctions for each of these based on lineage (gotra) and faculties,
so too for the four [types of knowledge] that take the origin belonging to the Peak of Existence as their object, there is a sixfold division for each based on the distinction of the six lineages.
Furthermore, there is a threefold division due to the difference in faculties (*indriya*).

In this same manner, for all [meditative attainments] included within the stage of Non-returning (*anāgāmin*)— which are distinguished by differences in knowledge, aspect, and object— up to those included within the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), their distinctions should be applied according to this method, based on the differences in spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and faculties.
Or rather, it should be applied in this way:

in the first case, there are fifty-two included in the stage of non-returning (*anāgāmya*), up to twenty included in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*); thus, in total, there are three hundred and eighty-four diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama*).
Multiplying those by six and then by three, they become six thousand nine hundred and twelve;
this is according to the second position, wherein there are eighty at the beginning [of the stages] up to twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
From the single aggregate, there are five hundred and seventy-six [types] due to the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*); when multiplied by six and then by three,
there are ten thousand three hundred and sixty-eight types of diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
For this very reason, why is it called "the knowledge of destruction"? He says:
because it arises for the first time simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows (āsrava).

Because that first knowledge arises simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "knowledge of destruction" (*kṣayajñāna*) through the elision of the middle term.
Alternatively, according to the rules of etymology,
the inclusion of the word "all" is for the purpose of qualifying the knowledge of those such as the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*),
while the inclusion of the word "first" is for the purpose of qualifying the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and so forth.
For the application of the word "hi" (for/indeed) depends upon convention;
for this very reason, [the particle] "sa" (he/that) is used because its own meaning is fully established.
He is an Arhat because he is worthy of performing the welfare of others; the meaning is that he is capable of performing the welfare of others,
and also because he is worthy of worship by all those who possess passion.
Ordinary worldlings and those in training (śaikṣa) possess attachment; because he is worthy of the veneration of all of them, he is established as an Arhat.
Thus, the three who abide in the fruits and the four who are entering toward them have been explained.
Because of the restriction that "only this one is an *aśaikṣa*," it is established that other noble ones (*āryas*) are *śaikṣas*.
To the question, "By what [reason] are they *śaikṣas*?"—
that is, for what reason are those seven persons called *śaikṣas*?— he says:

Because they have the habit of constantly training for the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), their morality is "training" (*śikṣā*); thus, they are called "trainers" (*śaikṣa*). This is their morality.
According to the rule that [the suffix] "na" is not applied after words such as *chattra*,
where is there one whose nature is to train in the three trainings?
What are the three trainings—
the training in higher ethics, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom—
and what is their intrinsic nature? To this he says:
Furthermore, these have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thus, training in ethical discipline is "higher ethical discipline" (*adhiśīla*); likewise, up to training in wisdom is "higher wisdom" (*adhiprajña*).
Since the analysis follows this sequence, it is a *avyayībhāva* compound.

However, because the acts of training are not distinct [from them], he explains that the trainings have morality and so forth as their intrinsic nature; thus, even an ordinary person would become a "learner" (śaikṣa),
since even an ordinary person trains in the trainings taught in the Vinaya.
Because of not knowing the truths as they truly are,
it is not thus.
Why?
Because of the non-cognition and non-comprehension of the truths, such as suffering and so forth, as they truly are;
for it is said: "O monks, that which is seen by noble wisdom is indeed [the truth]."
For thus, after explaining in detail the training in higher ethics or the training in higher mind in the Sūtra, it says:
"What is the training in higher wisdom?
It is to understand, as it truly is, that 'this is the noble truth of suffering.'"
"This is the origin of suffering,
this is the cessation of suffering,
and this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
Because of the wisdom that realizes the truths as they truly are,
and because of training further in those areas where one has already been trained, such as ethical discipline and so forth.

Due to the abandonment of the *prātimokṣa* vows and due to falling away from the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, even though a noble one (*ārya*) may again abandon something, he does not abandon everything;
for at no time is the threefold training ever absent in a noble one.

"A noble one abiding in the natural state" refers to a noble one who, while in the non-concentrated state— which is the natural condition of sentient beings— is engaged in activities such as wandering for alms.
The intention is that one would not be a *śaikṣa* (learner) if they were not habituated to training;
"by intention" means by desire.
Like a traveler who has stopped:
one who travels the road is called a "traveler," and even when standing still, he is still called a "traveler."
Because the desire for going has not been abandoned,
and because of the consequent attachment to attaining that [state].
Furthermore, the attainments of morality, concentration, and wisdom are also associated with one who abides in the natural state;
therefore, even one who abides in the natural state is not necessarily "one whose nature is not to train.
This is stated as a digression following the explanation of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Now, what are the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa)? They are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of one in training that have a conditioned (saṃskṛta) nature.
Likewise, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are those of one beyond training.
The intention [of the question] is: why is *nirvāṇa* not "belonging to those in training" (*śaikṣa*), even though it is attained by one who is in training?
[The answer is: because it is also possessed by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Even an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is joined with the nirvāṇa attained through the mundane path; thus,
one who stands on the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is the first "enterer" (pratipannaka).
"Of the remaining," and so forth:

this refers to the remaining candidates (*pratipannaka*)—namely, those candidates for the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship—because they are not distinct from those established in the three fruits;
that is, they are not distinct from those established in the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning.
The meaning is that those who have entered the path to the fruit of once-returner and so forth are not other than those who have entered the stream and so forth;
this is stated with respect to the gradual attainment [of the fruits], that is,
it is stated with respect to the sequential attainment of the four fruits.

In substance, there are five; furthermore, there may be those who have mostly abandoned passion for the desire realm, and those who have mostly abandoned passion and have eliminated six categories [of defilements].
One who is free from passion for the realm of desire and has exhausted nine categories [of afflictions] would,
respectively, be a candidate for the fruit of once-returner and non-returner during the stage of the path of seeing; however, they would not be a stream-enterer or a once-returner [at that time].
What then? They are distinct from that; and such being the case, there are seven [elements] substantially.

It should be understood that the three who have entered the paths toward the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning, along with the four established in those fruits, constitute only one person entering the fruit of arhatship; this is because the one established in the fruit of non-returning is not distinct from [the one entering the fruit of arhatship]. For it has been stated that the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is twofold, and thus the path of cultivation is twofold, while that which is called the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because of this statement, "due to being underlain by afflictions" (*kleśānuśayitatva*),
it means that the affliction belonging to that level underlies [the path] by way of its object (*ālambana*) within that mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
"For whichever affliction," and so forth, he demonstrates the examples of similarity and dissimilarity:
whichever path belongs to a particular level is not the antidote to the afflictions belonging to that same level.
Because it is not characterized by those afflictions and because it is a different dharma belonging to that stage which is not in a state of meditative equipoise,
it is— by way of contrast— like the preparatory path (*sāmantaka-mārga*) of a higher stage, or like the untainted (*anāsrava*), or like the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).
"By means of the mundane as well as detachment" refers to the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the higher levels;
"by means of the supramundane as well" refers to the transcendent path.
By means of its antidote— the untainted (*anāsrava*) path belonging to its own or a lower stage, as well as the mundane (*laukika*) path— there is the noble detachment (*āryavairāgya*).

For example, when a stream-enterer who practices tranquility (śamatha) proceeds toward detachment by means of the mundane path, for each stage [of detachment], both contaminated and uncontaminated acquisitions of dissociation arise,
based upon meditative absorption (dhyāna).
And because one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) transforms their faculties by relying on six stages,
but not the formless [stages],
whereas one beyond training relies on nine stages, but one in training (śaikṣa) relies on six.

According to this statement, he says that one who, relying on dhyāna, transforms the faculties (indriya-sañcāra) abandons the entire previous path; that is, because of abandoning the previously acquired paths of the formless realm (ārūpya-mārga) which are comprised of dull faculties (mṛdv-indriya).
And because of the attainment of the path to the fruit of isolation— that is, the attainment of the isolated fruit of a non-returner (anāgāmiphala) characterized by sharp faculties—
he attains the fruit after having abandoned the distinguished [lower] fruit, according to the statement: "He attains the fruit while increasing it."

Furthermore, there would be this other fault: by means of the dissociation from the afflictions of the higher stages—that is, the dissociation from the afflictions belonging to the formless realm—one would become non-endowed [with that dissociation];
and once that dissociation from the afflictions of the higher stages has been relinquished, one would again become endowed with those very afflictions of the higher stages.
Just as one who has attained the half-liberation from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and one born above it lack [the possession of] that [defilement],
so too is one "half-liberated" (*ardhavimukta*).
One who is half-liberated from the peak of existence is "one half-liberated from the peak of existence" (*bhavāgrārdhavimukta*).

"Born above" (*ūrdhvajāta*) means born in a higher realm; "one liberated from half of the peak of existence and born above" (*bhavāgrārdhavimuktordhvajāta*) refers to those two [types of individuals], and [the phrase] means "like those two."

The ellipsis of the sentence is: "for one who is half-liberated from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) and for one born above, there is possession (*samanvaya*) of those [attainments]. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of excluding the previously mentioned fault.
Explaining that point, he says:
"In the absence of... and so forth;
for such a person lacks the worldly acquisition (*prāpti*) of dissociation from half of the categories [of afflictions] at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because there is no mundane path that serves as its antidote,

you maintain that the supramundane attainment of dissociation from those [defilements] would be abandoned through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*) based upon meditative absorption (*dhyāna*);
yet, it is accepted by you that one does not again become possessed of those categories of defilements belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
In the same way, this would occur for one born above the level of the first dhyāna— such as one reborn in the second dhyāna or higher—
due to the relinquishing of the possession of dissociation from the afflictions belonging to the desire realm.

Wholesome [dharmas] attained through dhyāna are abandoned by means of changing levels or falling away from the attainment of dissociation belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; likewise for those attained through the formless [attainments].
Because of this rule, there is an abandonment [of those defilements];
therefore, it is accepted that one no longer possesses those afflictions belonging to the desire realm.
In the same way, this would also apply to this person.

The mention of "the ordinary person" (pṛthagjana) is because for a noble one (ārya) who attains detachment from the desire realm or from the realms above it by means of a mundane path, there occurs both a mundane and a supramundane acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions;
therein, the mundane [acquisition] is the acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions belonging to the desire realm.

For one born above that level of the first dhyāna, there is abandonment through the transition to another level, but not so for the supramundane; however, for the noble one, there is abandonment through the attainment of a fruit, the intensification of faculties, or retrogression—
such is the rule regarding abandonment.
And when that supramundane [path] exists, even for a noble one (ārya) born above the first dhyāna, it is impossible for them to be endowed with those [defilements] again;
however, this is not the case for an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). Therefore, the mention of the "ordinary person" is not a proof for that [conclusion].
Regarding what was stated— that when [the path] is abandoned, there is no longer possession of the afflictions—
it occurs "from all," meaning from all levels: one's own, the higher, and the lower.
Because it is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava),
and because of the commonality of the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya),
the faculty of equanimity is equal in both the fourth dhyāna and so forth, as well as in their respective preparatory stages (sāmantaka).
Someone is unable [to do so] because they have dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*),
since the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is difficult; that is,
because it is difficult for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) or the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) to arise immediately after the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Since the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is common to both the fundamental (*maula*) and the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) stages, for what reason does one manifest the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) only from the fundamental stage and not from the preparatory stage?
[It is] because of the high esteem for the level of freedom from passion (*vītarāga-bhūmi*).
"Not for one below, because of being free from passion"—
this is because detachment from the lower realms has already been achieved by means of its preparatory stage (sāmantaka); thus,
it proceeds by way of the aspects of the [noble] truths.
Some say that those [paths] proceeding with the aspects of impermanence and so forth are possible because they view the lower stage as coarse and the higher stage as peaceful by way of its opposite.
Others explain that one sometimes characterizes [the object] by even a single aspect among those such as "peaceful," and not necessarily by all of them together.
"Coarseness" means that which is coarse; "by way of coarseness" means by way of its being not peaceful.
How is it that the lower stage is "unpeaceful"?
Because it involves greater effort;
this "great effort" means that the lower state, along with its path, must be accomplished through exertion.
This higher station, along with its path, also involves great effort;
because it surpasses these two [lower stations], it is characterized by even greater effort—
that is its nature.
Therefore,
because it is a barrenness that is difficult to break through,
a despicable barrenness, it is called "barrenness" (duḥkhila) by virtue of its being a state of barrenness.
How is it that a lower stage is "inferior"? He says:
"Because of its state of being adverse due to having a greater degree of *dauṣṭhulya*.
*Dauṣṭhulya* means the unserviceability (*akarmaṇyatā*) of body and mind, which is to say, a state conducive to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This has much corruption; thus,
this too is a lower state accompanied by much corruption along with its path.
This higher station, along with its path, also possesses much *dauṣṭhulya*;
because it exceeds those two [lower stations] in this regard, it is "possessing even more *dauṣṭhulya*" (*bahu-dauṣṭhulyatara*),
by virtue of that state.
"Having thick walls" means that because of the state of having thick walls,
one cannot escape from that very ground by means of that [same wall].
Because there is no escape from that very same ground for one who remains on that very ground—
just as there is no escape from a wall by means of that very same wall.
Because they are the opposite of those [lower stages] in terms of the space occupied by them—

due to having little effort (*alpābhisaṃskāra*) and being less coarse (*alpadauṣṭhulyatara*), and thus not being disagreeable— and because one emerges from that stage by means of that stage, there are, respectively, the aspects of "peaceful" (*śānta*), "excellent" (*praṇīta*), and "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*).
This incidental discussion is concluded;
now that which arises immediately after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) must be explained.
As a secondary point, however, there is the explanation of the characteristics of the mundane paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation; thus,
if one is immovable, the cognition of non-arising follows from the cognition of destruction.
At that time, the knowledge that there is nothing further to be done arises for him,
because the possibility of falling away still exists.
Because there is still the possibility for the arising of afflictions, the knowledge of non-arising does not arise in him;
what is the reason?
Because falling away is possible.
Because falling away is possible for him,
whereas for one who possesses the knowledge of non-arising, there is no falling away.
Therefore, one becomes a śramaṇa;
one becomes a śramaṇa through connection with the state of a śramaṇa (śrāmaṇya), just as a cloth is called "white" through connection with whiteness (śauklya).
One is a *śramaṇa* because one pacifies the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because they are the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of that state of being a *śramaṇa*— which is characterized by the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*)— the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) are [designated as such] according to their respective roles as outflow fruits and fruits of human effort.
The paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and its fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*);
the unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta*) are only the fruit of human effort,
because that fruit arises through the power of those [paths].
And that which is obtained by the power of something is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); having established this, [the text says] "in that case," and so forth,
just as an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is made to the teaching of Pāṇini for ordinary people.
The meaning of the sentence is that an enumeration must likewise be made for the omniscient Buddha;
"the prior abandonment of the path" is the detailed explanation, wherein "the prior abandonment of the path" refers to the abandonment of the path of the candidate (*pratipannaka-mārga*).
And there is the attainment of the unprecedented path because of the acquisition of the path of fruition;
that is to say, because of the acquisition of a single attainment for everything.

At the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), a single attainment comprised within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is acquired for the abandonment of all [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).

Likewise, at the time of attaining the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*), a single attainment comprised within the fruit of once-returning is obtained for all [the abandonments], namely, the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) and the abandonment of all that is to be abandoned by the sixfold path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The same should be applied to the fruits of non-returning (*anāgāmin*) and arhatship; this applies to the four types of dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*).
Due to the distinction of the truths, there is the simultaneous acquisition of eight knowledges— namely, four types of dharma-knowledge and likewise four types of subsequent knowledge—
and these constitute the two fruits obtained via the mundane path.
The fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning can indeed be attained even by means of a mundane path;
how then is it that the state of a recluse (śrāmaṇya) can be attained by both the untainted path and the mundane path?
How, then, is it logical for the fruit of the ascetic life— which is characterized by the untainted path—

to be abandonment? By the word "also" (*api*), it is understood that the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is abandonment, and the fruit of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is also abandonment.
For both these two types of abandonment, a single attainment (*prāpti*)— whether comprised within the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*)—

is obtained. Therefore, due to its connection with the abandonment that is the fruit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state consisting of the abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) becomes the fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), namely, either the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of non-returning.
The abandonment of the three fetters occurs through the path of seeing;

furthermore, the partial abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—occurs by means of the path of seeing alone.
As for that abandonment, it constitutes the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of the once-returner itself, and the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
By what was this interpolation made?
By that it is known.
It was said by the Blessed One thus because of the mixing with abandonment;
for through its power, there is falling away [from detachment]. Thus, in the case of worldly noble detachment, the acquisitions of dissociation are of two kinds.

Thus, in that case, by means of the untainted attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*), that abandonment which was attained through the mundane path is maintained; the meaning is that it necessarily remains present through the connection of attainment. One does not die having fallen from the fruit.
For in its absence, there would be death for one who has fallen away, just as for a worldly person;

"by its power" means by the power of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga*). And that very acquisition of the untainted state produced by the present worldly path, as well as the future eightfold noble path being attained through the power of the worldly [path], are designated as the conditioned fruit of asceticism (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Because of its preeminence,
even the term *saṃskṛta* (refined) should be understood here;
thus, "brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇya*) arises from the removal of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Because he has driven away various kinds of evil and unwholesome states, he is a *brāhmaṇa*;
the state of being such is *brāhmaṇya*, which is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
How is this the Wheel of Brahmā (*brahmacakra*)? He says: [it is so called because...]
But it is called the Brahma-wheel because it is turned by Brahmā;
since it was set in motion by Brahmā, it is therefore the Brahma-wheel.
"Because of his union with unsurpassed brahminhood" means because of his union with the unsurpassed untainted path (*anāsravamārga*);
for this example— "this Blessed One is indeed a Brahmin"— was spoken by Jīvaka.
"By means of swift movement and so forth,
and by means of spokes and so forth" means by means of swift movement and the like, and by means of spokes and the like.
"Because of its swift movement," and so forth;
this expresses the similarity of the path to the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*),
just as the wheel-treasure moves swiftly.
Thus, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called "swift-moving" because it realizes the truths through fifteen moments of mind, proceeding by way of successive abandonment.
Just as one leaves one place and moves to another place,
so too does this [practitioner] leave the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and move to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
either by way of its manifestation or by way of leaving one truth and moving to another.
Because of the conquest of the unconquered and the dwelling in what has been conquered—
just as one conquers unconquered villages, market towns, and so forth,
and dwells in those already conquered.

In this way, by means of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), one conquers the afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) that have not yet been conquered, through the severance of their acquisition;
and one dwells upon those already conquered by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
through the simultaneous arising of the acquisition of dissociation from the afflictions.
And because of its arising and falling away—
just as it arises in one place and falls away in another—
so too [is there a distinction] due to the repeated manifestation of the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Alternatively, it arises according to the appropriate application from having the objects of the truths such as suffering and the realms such as desire;
it arises from having the form and formless realms as its object, and it falls back from having the desire realm as its object.
"Right view as the hub," and so forth:

here, having established oneself in ethical discipline (*śīla*), one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); from the attainment of concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) speaks of things as they truly are. Therefore, right speech, right action, and right livelihood occupy the position of the hub, because right view and the other factors function in dependence upon them. This is on the grounds that ethical discipline serves as the foundation.
Concentration is like the hub because it holds the others together;
right view and the rest are like the spokes,
as they proceed from this side and that side [of the path].
Whence is this?
Is this the Vaibhāṣikas' own opinion— that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*)— or is it based on scripture (*āgama*),
[namely] that [the wheel] was set in motion upon its arising?

Since it is stated in the Sūtra that "the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion upon the arising of the Path of Seeing," how is it that the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana?
There, the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
"This is the noble truth of suffering," O monks; as I applied my mind thoroughly to these things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, and insight.
"This is the origin of suffering."
"This is the cessation of suffering;

this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering"— as he applied his mind thoroughly to these teachings unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose.

"Indeed, that noble truth of suffering must be fully understood by me through direct knowledge"—as he applied wise attention to these previously unheard-of teachings, the eye arose, as before. "Indeed, that noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned by me through direct knowledge"—as he applied wise attention to these previously unheard-of teachings, it was as before. "Indeed, that noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized by me through direct knowledge"—as he applied wise attention to these previously unheard-of teachings, it was as before.
"Indeed, that noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering is to be cultivated by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described;
"indeed, that noble truth of suffering has been fully understood by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described;
"indeed, that noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned by me through direct knowledge"—regarding these dharmas unheard of before, as previously described.
"Indeed, that noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized by me through direct knowledge," regarding these dharmas unheard of before—just as before;
and furthermore, "that noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated by me through direct knowledge," regarding these dharmas unheard of before—just as before.
Monks, as long as this threefold revolution and twelvefold aspect regarding these four noble truths had not yet arisen as vision for me...

Neither knowledge nor vision nor wisdom had arisen in me so long as I had not dwelt extensively with a mind free from perversion— liberated, emerged, detached, and disjoined— from this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and from this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras;
and it was not until then that I claimed to have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And because, monks, regarding these four noble truths, the eye arose in me in this way—three turnings and twelve aspects—and likewise wisdom arose, from that time forth I dwelt much in seclusion with a mind free from perversion, having departed from the world including its gods; then I knew: "I have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Now, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dharma regarding all phenomena arose in the Venerable Kauṇḍinya and in eighty thousand deities.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Kauṇḍinya:
"Kauṇḍinya, have you understood the Dharma?"
"I have understood it, Blessed One; I have understood the Dharma, Kauṇḍinya;
I have understood it, Sugata."
"Friends, the Dharma has been understood by the Venerable Kauṇḍinya! Thus did the terrestrial yakṣas raise their voices and proclaim this sound:

"O worthy ones, the Blessed One has set in motion at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, the Wheel of Dharma—threefold in its revolution and twelvefold in its aspects—which has never before been set in motion by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā."
Furthermore, it is said in detail that "by some means in accordance with the Dharma for the benefit of many people," and so forth;

thus, when the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) arose in the noble Kauṇḍinya, the deities declared, "The Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion by the Blessed One," according to the statement in the Sūtra.
It is understood that the path of seeing is the wheel of Dharma;
how is it "threefold-turning," and so forth?
"This is the noble truth of suffering" is the first turning.
"Indeed, that must be fully understood"—this is the second;
"Indeed, that has been fully understood"—this is the third.
These are the three turnings.
In each individual turn, regarding the thought "this is suffering," there arose vision, knowledge, science, and awakening; these are the four aspects.
Together with the [four] aspects of "it must be fully understood," these constitute the twelve aspects.
Among them, the untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*) is "vision" because its object is directly perceived.
It is knowledge because it is free from doubt; it is wisdom because its object is reality;
it is intelligence because of its purity.
According to the etymology, "pure" (*viśuddhā*) means wisdom (*dhī*).

Furthermore, the vision of outsiders regarding the [Four] Truths is not an antidote to wrong views, doubt, and ignorance, and it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); therefore, the term "eye" (*cakṣus*) and so forth is employed for the sake of distinction. Moreover, among the three turnings, the first vision is the "eye," and the subsequent investigation of what has been seen is "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
Insofar as it pertains to the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), it is knowledge (*vidyā*) because it grasps things as they actually exist;
insofar as it pertains to the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), it is wisdom (*buddhi*).
Furthermore, because of the realization of the meaning as it truly is,
he says "eye" in order to exclude inferential knowledge regarding phenomena not previously heard,
and he says "knowledge" in order to exclude knowledge based on resolute conviction.
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) is for the purpose of negating conceited knowledge (*ābhimānika-jñāna*),
and "wisdom" (*buddhi*) is for the purpose of negating that which is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*);
thus they exist as such in accordance with reality.
"This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering; that indeed must be abandoned;
that has indeed been abandoned"—these are the three turnings.
In each single turn, "the eye arose, knowledge [arose], wisdom [arose], and awakening [arose]"—these are the twelve aspects.
This should likewise be applied to the truths of cessation and the path; so he said.
If this is truly the case,
then there would be three revolutions and twelve aspects, or twelve revolutions and forty-eight aspects;
why, then, is it said to have "three revolutions and twelve aspects"?
Therefore it is said:
"But because of the similarity between the three and the twelve, it is described as having three turnings and twelve aspects," just like the teaching on the two kinds of skill in the seven bases.

Just as in the teaching on the dyad and as in the teaching on skill in the seven points—having spoken at length accordingly—it was said: "In that case, monk, I shall teach you the dyad; listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak."
What is the dyad?
It is the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental objects; just as here, because of their similarity to a dyad, they are called "the dyad."
Thus, due to the commonality of the three sets of twelve, it is said to have three turnings and twelve aspects;
and just as a monk skilled in the seven points understands form as it really is, as well as the origin of form...
The cessation of form,
the path leading to the cessation of form,
and the gratification and danger of form.
Because he understands, as it truly is, the escape [from suffering],
the monk who is skilled in the seven points and examines the meaning in three ways will quickly understand the end of suffering in this Dharma and Vinaya;
this is because each of the aggregates possesses a commonality with skill in the seven points.
Similarly here too, because of the commonality of three sets of twelve, it is said to have "three turnings and twelve aspects";
and by these [turnings], as detailed in the full passage, it is demonstrated.
Starting from "This is the noble truth of suffering" up until "This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering," the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) has been shown.

Then, starting from "That noble truth of suffering must be fully known through direct knowledge (*abhijñā*)" up until "That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering must be cultivated through direct knowledge," the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) has been shown.

Starting from "That noble truth of suffering has been fully understood through direct knowledge" up until "That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated through direct knowledge," the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) is thus shown;
regarding this, the Master says:
"If that is so," and so forth.
If, by these turnings, the paths of seeing and so forth are shown respectively,
then it is not the path of seeing alone that has three turnings and twelve aspects; what then?
Regarding the statement that "a single revolution has four aspects," how can this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) be established as the wheel of dharma (*dharmacakra*)?
The intention is that in the absence of three revolutions, there is a lack of similarity to a wheel (*cakrasādharmya*), and thus it would not be appropriate to call it a wheel.
Therefore, that very discourse on the Dharma is the Wheel of Dharma;
that very Sūtra is the Wheel of Dharma,
because it reveals the Wheel of Dharma.
It is appropriate that it has three turnings and twelve aspects because it reveals that meaning through three revolutions.
From "suffering" up to "the path" is the first turning, which is to be fully known;
from "fully known" up to "to be cultivated" is the second;
and from "fully known" up to "cultivated" is the third.
"Because of the threefold application to the four truths":

regarding the nature of the truths as suffering, origin, cessation, and path, there is the first mode of application consisting of four aspects, namely: "it is to be fully known," "it is to be abandoned," "it is to be realized," and "it is to be cultivated. Regarding the activity of full knowledge in its functional form, there is the second mode of application consisting of four aspects.
"Fully known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated"— with respect to these perfected activities of full knowledge and so forth, there is a third mode of performance; thus, with four modes,
it becomes twelvefold for that [knowledge], as it were.
The setting forth of this Dharma discourse is its movement into the mental continuums of others; it is its impelling into the mental continuums of those to be trained.
How does it move?

Alternatively, it is because it makes the meaning known; or rather, the entire Noble Path— the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning— is the Wheel of Dharma, because it proceeds through the mental continua of those to be trained.
If the entire Noble Path is considered the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra) because it "turns" (kramaṇāt),
then how is it said that it was "turned" when only the Path of Seeing arose for Ājñātakauṇḍinya?

Therefore it is said: that [wheel], however, because it was begun to be turned by generating the path of seeing in the mental continuum of another— namely, in the continuum of the noble Kauṇḍinya— and was first turned, is called "set in motion" (*pravartita*).
The prefix *pra-* occurs in the sense of an initial action,
as in "the rice has begun to be eaten" (*prabhukta odana*); but why does it not apply to the third [case]?

The intention behind the question— "If one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) were to enter the fixed course of certainty (niyama), why would the attainment of the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) not occur at the sixteenth moment of mind?"— is answered as follows:
For there is no scriptural statement that "the path of vision is indeed upward."
In the formless realms, there can be only the awakening of a śrāvaka, because the awakening of a self-enlightened one (svayambhū) is impossible there;
furthermore, the clear realization of a śrāvaka does not occur without the voice of another.
Furthermore, because they do not take the lower realms as their object,
the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have the contaminated lower realms as their sphere of activity.
Since the path of seeing must have the three realms as its object,
that [object] does not exist therein;
thus, "vidhāna" means a method (*vidhi*) or a means (*upāya*).
One whose nature is subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is one whose very essence is such; likewise,
there is the one whose nature is volition (*cetanādharman*), the one whose nature is self-destruction (*ātma-māraṇadharman*),
and the one whose nature is guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), who is able to guard that liberation.
One who is stable and unshakable (*sthitākampya*) is one who, being established in a particular liberation,
is unshakable therein and is capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*).

One who is capable of transforming the faculties (*indriyasañcārabhavya*) is one whose nature is unshakable; because his nature is unshakable and cannot be diverted, he is "one of unshakable nature" (*akopyadharmā*), and he is of two kinds.
Those who are sharp by nature,
those who become sharp through the transformation of their faculties, and those born from the five types of liberation through faith— these are the five.
The emphatic particle *eva* signifies that they have become those resolved through faith; the meaning is that they have arisen as such,
which amounts to saying that they were previously resolved through faith.
However, it has been explained that the sixth [type of restraint] can also exist otherwise;
it is called "occasional" (*sāmayikī*) because it arises in relation to specific conditions (*samaya*), characterized by particular requisites, health, location, and so forth.
And as for "lovely" (kāntā): why is the liberation of the mind called "lovely"?
For it is observed in the world that what is beloved must be constantly protected because it is to be perpetually guarded;
this is also stated in the Sūtra.

It is just as if the kinsmen of a one-eyed man were to think that his single eye must be protected well and thoroughly, [thinking]: "Let no cold, no heat, and no dust or grit fall into his eye; lest even this one eye that remains unimpaired should also perish. In the very same way, for an Arhat liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), this Dharma is to be protected, cherished, and sustained.
Therefore, an Arhat who is liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), having reflected well and thoroughly upon how he might guard himself,
thinks, "May I not fall away from these qualities," and thus he does not fall away from them.
"Like a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭavat*):
just as a jar full of ghee is called "a jar of ghee" due to the elision of the intermediate word "full" (*pūrṇa*).

Just as one says "a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*), so too here, by the elision of the intermediate word *apekṣā* (dependence), they are called "those liberated through dependence on circumstances" (*samayavimukta*). Furthermore,
it has been stated that "circumstance" (*samaya*) refers to requisites and so forth.
He says "because it is impossible to provoke [them]" by means of the phrase "due to non-retrogression" or "due to liberation at another time or ultimate liberation."
The meaning is that "temporary liberation" (*samayavimukti*) refers to liberation after a period of time,
whereas "non-temporary liberation" (*asamayavimukti*) refers to ultimate liberation.
To the question "How is this so?", he says:
Based on whether or not falling away is possible:
because falling away is possible, one is called "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) due to liberation after a period of time;
because falling away is impossible, one is called "unconditionally liberated" (*atyantavimukta*) and "not liberated by occasion" (*asamayavimukta*).
And he is one who follows from having attained vision,
when, having been a learner (śaikṣa), he transforms his faculties.
He attains the state of one who has attained through vision;
moreover, if he is by nature of sharp faculties, he is already one who has attained through vision at the sixteenth moment of mind.
Therefore, such a person of immovable nature is said to be "one who was previously one who has attained through vision."

However, it should be understood that one who transforms their faculties while in the state of arhatship is not of the immovable nature (akopyadharman) and has not previously been one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta); rather,
such a person was originally of the lineage of those whose nature is volition (cetanādharman).
Thus,
one who has undergone refinement is not called "subject to falling away," because such a person does not exist [among those who have undergone refinement].

Regarding the statement that "some belong to that lineage from the very beginning," what is this so-called *parihāṇadharman* lineage up to the *akopyadharman* lineage? They have not specified the lineages of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharma*) and so forth;
in that regard, some describe them as follows: "The roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are the lineage."
For such wholesome roots belong only to someone who is of the nature to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*) up to one of the unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*).
Others, however, say that the lineage (*gotra*) is the differentiation of the faculties (*indriyabheda*) starting from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

The Sautrāntikas, however, explain that the lineage (*gotra*) is the capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the mind; thus, when the seed of the nature of falling away exists as the cause during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), one is called "of the lineage of the nature of falling away.
Likewise, in the stage of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), because of the acquisition of the functioning of that seed, one is called "of the nature of falling away."
Thus it continues up to "one of immovable nature.
In that context, the detailed explanation begins with "one of the nature of falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*);
"one of the nature of falling away" refers to one who is liable to fall away.
If he were to say only this much—

that it does not possess the quality of being conscious, and so forth— but were not to say that all four of these qualities, beginning with being conscious, are capable of being abandoned, then one of these very qualities would be the "one subject to falling away" (parihāṇadharman).

Since there is no fifth [category] other than those, one who wishes to distinguish this fifth as being indeed distinct from them states that it is "not a dharma such as volition. Furthermore, since the four [types of Arhats], beginning with the one liable to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*), possess the quality of falling away, it follows that this must be stated again, precisely because the specific characteristics of each one have been pointed out.

"One of the nature of volition" (cetanā-dharman) is one capable of intending [to fall away], but not one of the nature of guarding (anurakṣaṇā-dharman), up to one incapable of penetration (prativedhanā-bhavya).
Likewise, "one of the nature of guarding" [does not fall away] except in the presence of a powerful condition for falling away;
the intention is that if there were a powerful condition for falling away, he would indeed fall away.

By this expression "powerful conditions" (balavat-pratyaya), he distinguishes [this type] from the previously mentioned one who is subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman); for one subject to falling away falls away even by a weak condition for falling away. Furthermore, the conditions for falling away are as stated in the Sūtra.
There are five causes and five conditions that lead to the falling away of an Arhat who is liberated by occasion.
What are these five?
He becomes one who is intent upon worldly occupations.
He becomes intent on verbal exposition,
intent on formal debate,
and devoted to the practice of wandering on long journeys.
"And he becomes afflicted by a long-lasting variety of diseases"—
by this phrase, he distinguishes [this person] from one whose nature is to guard [the faculties],
for the latter would not fall away even while guarding them.
"But this one, even without guarding"—
that is, even without guarding that fruit— he is capable of remaining in that fruit and not falling away from that fruit.
Nor can it be increased without application and without vigor, through the attainment of the capacity for penetration;
by this, it is implied that [without these, there is no increase].

If one were to apply effort, it would be possible [for him to penetrate]; thus, because of the possibility of penetration through effort, he is described in this way. For he is capable of penetrating even without effort;
this is the detailed explanation of "the first two."

One of a nature prone to regression (*parihāṇadharman*) is deficient in both constant and respectful application; one of a nature prone to volition (*cetanādharman*) is also deficient in constant application,
but is specifically deficient in respectful application— this is the distinction between these two.
The phrase "one of dull faculties," however, distinguishes [the former] from the sixth [type],
for the sixth possesses sharp faculties;
indeed, the distinction between these two is based on their faculties and not on their application.
"And having done so," and so forth;
because this is not necessarily the case, the intention is that there are six types of arhats in the realms of form and formlessness as well, not only in the realm of desire.
In the realms of form and formlessness, there are two types: the one who is stable and unshakable, and the second, the one of immovable nature.
Regarding the first, the one who is stable and unshakable, he may possess a fixed inclination [toward the realm], yet he lacks the capacity for penetration and is not diligent in practice.
One who is unshakable while abiding in the desire realm does not undergo the state of being capable of penetration; furthermore,
because there is no powerful condition for falling away in the form and formless realms,
such a person does not fall away.
And since the faculties do not shift, he remains one whose lineage is stable and unshakable; furthermore, because of his connection with immovable liberation, he is also one of immovable nature—
thus, there are only these two.
There are no others than these three in the form and formless realms; for, due to the absence of falling away, the volition [to fall], and the transformation of the faculties,
the one of a nature to fall away (*parihāṇadharman*) does not exist there at all.
Because there is no falling away,
even the quality of one who must guard [the attainment] does not exist, since there is no possibility of guarding it when there is no falling away.
For this very reason, due to the absence of the shifting of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*), one is not even "capable of penetration" (*prativedhanābhavya*);
and thus it has been said:
"He, as well as one born in a higher realm, does not possess the shifting of the faculties or falling away."
Thus,
because there is neither self-intention nor intention by another in that state, one does not possess the nature of volition;
this refers to the four [categories] beginning with the nature of volition.
Regarding those of the nature of guarding volition (*cetanā-anurakṣaṇā-dharma*), those established in the nature (*sthitākampya*), and those capable of penetration (*prativedhanā-bhavya*):
one of the nature subject to falling away (*parihāṇa-dharma*) does not fall away from his own lineage (*gotra*),
because that lineage is not artificial.
Regarding the five types beginning with those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*):
because even for one subject to falling away, a fall from the fruit is possible,
since the fruit is adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Not from the previous lineage nor from the fruit.
He does not fall away from that; why is he an Arhat? It is said:
because he has been made firm by both the path of training and the path beyond training.
That lineage which exists in the state of a learner (śaikṣa) has been cultivated by the path of a learner and is further cultivated in the state of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa).
Because it has been made firm by those two, the Arhat does not fall away from that state;
but as for how it is for the Śaikṣa, he says:
"The Śaikṣa, however, because it has been made firm by both the mundane and the supramundane, does not fall away from the first lineage."
That which is one's own original lineage was previously cultivated by the mundane path and subsequently cultivated again by the path of training; therefore,
one does not fall away from it.
Regarding this, someone says: "As for that which is said, 'whatever is one's first lineage'..."
He does not fall away from that [attainment] because it has been made firm by both the paths of the learner and the non-learner; however,
this is not a valid reason,
because even one of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma*) who has reached refinement falls away from that lineage (*gotra*).
Since that lineage has been made firm by both the path of training and the path beyond training, falling away is not possible;
therefore, that lineage itself is of such a nature that one does not fall away from it initially.

As for the statement that one may fall away from what has been reached through refinement (*uttāpanā*), and the further claim that a learner (*śaikṣa*) does not fall away because they have been made firm by both mundane and supramundane [attainments]— this too is not a valid reason, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of falling away even for a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
For the fruit of stream-entry is not made firm by a mundane path;
therefore, one must apply effort here.
In this regard, we shall demonstrate the intention of the Master (Ācārya), by which he spoke thus.
How so?
As for what was previously stated— that one of the nature of volition (cetanā-dharman), having reached refinement (uttāpanā-gata), falls away from that lineage (gotra)— that is incorrect.

For that lineage of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma-gotra*) which was cultivated during the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*) and further cultivated— and thus strengthened— during the stage of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*),
does not fall away even when falling from arhatship,
because it has become primary during the stage of a learner.

And it was said by Ācārya Saṅghabhadra: "Even one who, having attained another lineage (gotra) during the stage of training (śaikṣa), subsequently attains arhatship, abandons that [new] path; yet he does not remain in the lineage reached through refinement (uttāpanā)."

However, as for the lineage of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma-gotra*) which has been attained only now in the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and was not attained in the state of one in training (*śaikṣa*),
one who falls away from it does so because that lineage has not been stabilized across those two states.
Thus, this is not a valid reason;
furthermore, as for what was said— that a trainee (*śaikṣa*) would not fall away because he has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane paths— that too is no reason,
because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) could fall away.
For it is not the case that the fruit of stream-entry has been made firm by both the mundane and the supramundane; thus,
having failed to understand even that, it is stated as the cause for that lineage.
For no other cause will be stated there with respect to the fruit by which one would not fall away from the first fruit.
For there is no fruit whatsoever that is simultaneously strengthened by both paths—

namely, by the present-life "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, or by the path of abandonment belonging to a future life, or by another mundane path, or by the supramundane [path]— because it has already been cultivated during the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
That which is acquired later, however, is [the result of] refinement (*uttāpanā*).
Since the adventitious lineage is attained only later and not in both states, one falls away from it;
having thus indicated the lineage, the fruit is then indicated, as in the detailed explanation: "and for whomsoever there is a certain first fruit," and so forth.
For this very reason, there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).
This is because if the fruit of stream-entry is attained, it necessarily occurs first;

however, the fruits of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and non-returner (*anāgāmin*) may or may not occur first, depending on whether one is already largely free from passion (*bhūyovītarāga*) or entirely free from passion for the realm of desire (*kāmavītarāga*).
Sometimes, if for one who follows the gradual path,
whatever fruit occurs first therein— whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning—
one does not fall away from that.
But as for the fact that one subsequently falls away from the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship—
it is because it has been made [into a conditioned state] in this way.
And since one does not fall away from that which is one's first lineage (*gotra*) or fruit,
there are respectively five, six, and seven types.
For one whose nature is to guard [the attainment], there are five possibilities:

attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that state, the transformation of the faculties, falling away from the state of a learner (śaikṣatva), returning to the lineage of the nature of volition (cetanādharmagotra), and returning to the lineage of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharmagotra).
For one who is stable and unshakable (sthitākampya), there are six possibilities.
These same five, along with the sixth, which is the return to the lineage of those whose nature is to guard [the fruit],
and for one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*), there are seven types;
these same six, plus the seventh, which is the return to the lineage of those established in the state of immovability (*sthitākampya*).
And for whomsoever there was a certain lineage (*gotra*) previously during the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*),
that person, having become a trainee again— this is the ellipsis to be supplied in the sentence.
It remains in that very state and not in another;
for otherwise, by obtaining a specific lineage (*gotra*), that lineage would become superior to the lineage of the stage of training (*śaikṣāvasthā*).
Therefore, due to the acquisition of a superior lineage, there would be only progress for this person (*pudgala*).
How is it that there is no falling away?

For instance, one of the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman) who, while in the state of arhatship, has attained the incapacity for penetration (*prativedhābhavyatā*) through the sharpening of the faculties (*indriyottāpanā*).
Thus, one who falls away from arhatship becomes a learner (śaikṣa); even when falling away from that lineage, he does not remain in the lineage of one who remains steadfast,
nor, in reverse order, would he remain in the lineage of one whose nature is volition (cetanā-dharman).
"Because of the acquisition of a specific lineage" means because of the acquisition of a lineage superior to the lineage of one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
Therefore, when one falls away from arhatship, one necessarily falls away from that lineage even through the sharpening of the faculties (*indriyottāpana*);
what, then, is the reason why there is no falling away from the first fruit?
Whichever is one's first fruit— whether the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*)—
it is so because those things to be abandoned by seeing lack any objective reality (*avastuka*) and lack any basis (*anadhiṣṭhāna*);
the meaning is that these [defilements] proceed with the self as their basis, and so forth.
Why are these [defilements] to be abandoned by insight said to proceed with the self as their basis? He says: because they have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their root.
Because the manifestation of those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing occurs through the power of the view of a self,

and it has been said: "Furthermore, whatever views exist separately in the world, they are rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), originate from the view of a self-identity, belong to the class of the view of a self-identity, and arise from the view of a self-identity."
And since that self does not exist, there is no falling away because there is no objective basis;
this is because it has the truths as its object,
insofar as the truths are grasped as permanent and so forth.

And which affliction is not such that, although it is to be abandoned by cultivation, its object is unreal— such as attachment and so forth— because it takes the truths and other realities as its objects through the aspects of purity, pleasure, and permanence?
They superimpose a selfhood that is unreal,
as it has been said:
"O monks, whoever perceives 'self' or 'belonging to a self,' they perceive [only] these."
"Perceiving these very five aggregates of clinging as self and as belonging to self," and since views such as the grasping at extremes proceed based upon that,
they are said to "proceed based upon the self."
Is the self eternal or subject to annihilation? Or does the self not exist at all?
"This alone is the foremost;

this alone is purity"—those [views] that proceed in such forms as "does he exist or does he not exist? and so forth, which are to be abandoned by insight and are devoid of a real basis, are called "unfounded" (*avastuka*).
The meaning is that they are said to be "without a basis" (niradhiṣṭhāna);

however, by the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), there is not even a trace of a self (ātman) and so forth, nor is there the inclusion of "belonging to a self" (ātmīya), or the inclusion of a Lord (īśvara) and so forth.
It has specific characteristics of being agreeable or disagreeable;

thus, for attachment (*rāga*), which is to be abandoned through cultivation, the object is agreeable, characterized by the beauty of hair, teeth, and so forth; for aversion (*pratigha*), it is disagreeable, characterized by their impurity and so forth.

Even for pride, it is something slightly agreeable; and for ignorance as well, it is that same twofold thing which causes delusion—namely, something indeterminate—but there is no specific, fixed entity characterized as a self (*ātman*) or belonging to a self (*ātmīya*) among those [afflictions] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).
Indeed, there is no such determinate object characterized as "self" or "mine" for those to be abandoned by seeing.
"Except for those [afflictions] such as attachment that have them as their objects;
therefore, they are said to be without a real basis (avastuka)," so says the Master in detail.

In the case of a noble one who is still in training, when not reflecting or investigating, an affliction such as passion arises due to the loss of mindfulness and the association with defiled mindfulness,
but not for one who is reflecting.
Just as the notion of a snake arises for someone who does not closely examine a rope due to a lapse of memory,
but not for one who does closely examine it,
so it is in this case.
Regarding the phrase "of the view of self, etc.," this includes the view of extremes and so forth;
what, then, is the reason for this?
Furthermore, it is not logical for views such as the view of a self to arise in one who is not reflecting, because they are investigative in nature; of what [views] is this true?

Because the afflictions such as the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) do not arise from improper reflection (*anupanidhyāna*), it is not logical for an noble one (*ārya*) to experience the arising of the view of self and so forth; thus,
since there is no cause for falling away, there is no falling away from the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).

"There is no [falling away] even from arhatship" means that there is not only no falling away from the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing, but there is also no falling away from arhatship; this is indicated by the word "even" (api). However, falling away is possible from the two fruits other than the first—that is, from the fruits of once-returner and non-returner.
The intention is that its attainment is possible by means of the mundane path;
and the Master supports this very principle, saying:
"For that, O monks, has been abandoned."
The intention is that what has been abandoned arises again; thus,
the second phrase of the sutra, "and the heedfulness of one in training," and so forth, serves as the proof that there is no falling away from arhatship.
And this is its meaning: "I declare heedfulness as the task for a trainee, for the sake of the sign of heedfulness, so that heedfulness must be practiced by the trainee.
Now, since abandonment also occurs for a trainee through noble wisdom, how can it be taught that there is something for him to do regarding heedfulness?

Since there remains for him another fruit yet to be attained and a worldly path-based abandonment yet to be realized, a Vaibhāṣika might argue that even an Arhat can fall away, because of the scriptural statement: "Ānanda, I declare that gain and honor are obstacles even for an Arhat. To this, the following is said:

Since even for an Arhat, as explained in detail up to this point in the sutra, it is stated that there is falling away from nothing more than the dwelling in happiness in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), how is it that the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda [in a manner suggesting otherwise]?
"Ānanda, I say that even for an Arhat, gain and honor are obstacles.
The Venerable Ānanda said: "For what reason, Blessed One, did you say this?"
"Ānanda, I say that gain and honor are an obstacle even for an Arhat," said the Blessed One; "it is not so, Ānanda, regarding the attainment of what has not yet been attained."

Not for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, nor for the sake of realizing what has not been realized; rather, it is because he has attained these four higher mental states that constitute dwellings in happiness in the present life.
Therefore, I declare that there may be a falling away from one or another of these for one who dwells in company; however,
that unshakable liberation of mind which has been realized by him through his own body— having dwelt alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute— is not subject to falling away.
Therefore, Ānanda, I do not say that there is any way in which such a person can fall away.
For this reason, Ānanda, you should train yourself thus: "I shall overcome gain and honor, and my mind shall not remain overwhelmed by excessive gain and honor."

If a Vaibhāṣika were to say, "Ānanda, you should train yourself thus," on the grounds that the qualification "unshakable" implies there is falling away from the occasional [attainment], [then one should respond as follows:]
Then he says:
"If you say it exists by way of convention,
we too say the same."
He asks: regarding "occasional" (sāmāyikī), does occasional liberation refer to arhatship,
or rather do only the mundane meditative absorptions (dhyāna) constitute occasional liberation?
To the question "Why is this apprehension raised?", he says:
"For the fundamental meditative concentration" (*maulo hi dhyānasamādhiḥ*); that is, the meditation itself is the concentration, hence "meditative concentration" (*dhyānasamādhi*).
The mention of "fundamental dhyānas" is because they are the foremost among the easy paths of practice,
because they manifest at the proper time,
and because they manifest at certain times such as when it is silent and so forth.
Because it exists at a specific time, it is called "temporary liberation" (*sāmayikī vimukti*);
because it must be sought again and again, it is called "delightful" (*kāntā*), meaning that upon each occasion of falling away, it remains desirable and worthy of being prayed for.

"Because it is to be savored," says another—namely, the Venerable Rāma; the intention is that because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is "delightful" (*kānta*) due to its connection with dhyāna not associated with savoring (*āsvādana*).
"But the liberation of Arhatship," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

Arhatship itself is liberation; thus, "liberation consisting of arhatship" is not appropriately described as "occasional" (*sāmayikī*) because it is eternally present through its attainment. By this [statement], he demonstrates that the liberation of arhatship is the opposite of occasional liberation.

By the phrase "it is not lovely because it is not to be longed for again," is there a reversal of "lovely"? The meaning is that the liberation of an Arhat is not "lovely" because it exists as something eternally attained and thus is not to be longed for;
[this applies] specifically to those [liberations] consisting of higher mental states (*adhicaitasika*).
The "higher mental states" (adhicaitasika) are the pleasant dwellings in this very life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra);
for what purpose would he have spoken of falling away from those very states?

Because of the statement, "I declare that there may be falling away from any one of those mental states of abiding in happiness in the present life which have been attained," if there were the possibility of falling away from Arhatship characterized by occasional liberation, [then this statement would not be made].
The meaning is: why would he have spoken of falling away from those very [attainments]?
