He would not have spoken of falling away from those very ones; this is because of the loss of mastery (*vaśitva-vibhraṃśāt*).
The meaning is: "due to the loss of mastery over the manifestation of meditative concentration.

He is called one of "the nature of non-falling away" (*aparihāṇadharman*); that is, one whose nature is not subject to falling away, distinct from one whose nature is immovable (*akopyadharman*), as recited in the Sūtra.
Having explained the eighteen types of those in training in detail, he says:
"Which are the nine types of those in training? Those of a nature to fall away."
One of a nature not to fall away, one of a nature to intend [for higher states], and one of a nature to guard [the attainment].
The one who is stable and unshakable,
the one capable of penetration, and the one of immovable nature.
The one liberated by wisdom and the one liberated in both ways—
these are called the nine types of those beyond training.

He who falls away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life is one of a nature subject to falling away; he who does not fall away from those same states is [one of a nature not subject to falling away].
Thus, one who is of the nature of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*) is established; in the same way, those of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) and the others should also be applied.
How?
One who, out of fear of falling away from meditative concentration, maintains awareness of oneself is "of the nature of volition" (cetana-dharman);
one who somehow protects a particular excellence of qualities is "of the nature of guarding" (anurakṣaṇā-dharman).
Thus, one whose nature is to guard is not shaken even when not guarding, remaining steadfast in whichever quality he is established.
He is "unshakable while established" (*sthitākampya*),
meaning that he penetrates further and produces a specific excellence of qualities.
He who does not become angry and does not fall away from what has arisen is one capable of penetration;
he is of an unshakable nature.
"What is the distinction?"—

asking this because he does not perceive any distinction among the three types, beginning with those of non-falling-away nature (*aparihāṇadharman*), due to their connection with non-falling-away; thus he asks,
"one who has not reached refinement" (*anuttāpanāgata*).
The meaning is that one who is by nature of sharp faculties has not attained the refinement of the faculties;
therefore, he does not waver.
"Therefore, the meaning is 'due to a specific quality';
this specific distinction is observed"— in these words, the Teacher presents his own view.

Now, if a Vaibhāṣika were to say, "Is not the Venerable Gautika one who has fallen away from arhatship?"— it is with reference to this that the following refutation begins, starting with the words "the Venerable Gautika," and so forth;
for while he was still a learner (*śaikṣa*), he was not yet an arhat.
"Maintaining the weapon" means that,
while wielding the weapon,
because he was indifferent toward both body and life for that reason, he attained arhatship at the very moment of death.
The meaning is "at a time subsequent to the support of the weapon";
and he has attained final nirvāṇa by that very blow of the weapon,
and [after] ten more [eons].
He asks what is said in the *Daśottara-nāma-sūtra*, and says:
"One single dharma is to be produced."
To the question "Which one?", he says:
"The temporary, lovely liberation of mind"; the intended meaning is the "pleasant dwelling in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra).
"One dharma is to be realized directly;
which one? he says: "The unshakable liberation of mind."

The intention is that "arhatship" is meant [by the term *cetovimukti*], because it is mentioned separately; for since the nature of arhatship is characterized by unshakable liberation (*akopyavimukti*), it was stated that the liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) does not have arhatship as its intrinsic nature.
Seeing an opening for the Vaibhāṣika position—that the separate mention is due to the two-fold nature of arhatship—he speaks again:
And if it were the case that "arhatship" [is the occasional, pleasant liberation of mind], as the detailed explanation goes—
if arhatship itself were the occasional, pleasant liberation of mind,
for what purpose would there have been a double mention of arhatship in that very same *Daśottara-sūtra*, rather than in another sūtra?
The meaning is that he would not have failed to directly realize this one dharma: the unshakable liberation of the mind.
For if he had intended it thus, he would have said: "One single dharma is to be realized, namely, liberation of mind";
but you say that arhatship is of two kinds.
Therefore, it is stated according to the distinction of the words that "one is to be produced" and "the second is to be realized";
to this we reply:
Nor has it been stated anywhere that arhatship is to be produced;
rather,
it is said that it is to be realized.
Even granting that, we say that it must be produced as included within the category of those with dull faculties in each respective sutra.
What is indicated or stated by this indication?

If it is first [the case that] "it is possible to produce," then this is what is indicated, because of the rule regarding the kṛtya suffixes: *śaki liṅ ca* ("the optative suffix is used after a verb meaning 'to be able'").
Furthermore, it is possible that there is another form of arhatship included among those with sharp faculties;
and if that were the case, the Sūtra would have to state:
"One dharma is to be produced."
By the term "liberation of mind" (*cetovimukti*),
it is indicated that it is worthy of being produced;
this is because of the application of the grammatical rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaś ca* (Pāṇini 3.3.169), which prescribes the use of the suffixes *kṛtya* and *tṛc* in the sense of being worthy (*arha*).
The other [type of] arhatship is even more worthy, because that arhatship comprised by those of sharp faculties is indeed more easily produced due to its immovability; this is the intended meaning.
"How then? and so forth is the detailed explanation.

The intention is that if occasional liberation constitutes arhatship, then it is appropriate to call an arhat "one liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta) because of being endowed with that [liberation];
for the manifestation of meditative concentration depends upon the right occasion.
Because his concentration—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—depends upon conditions characterized by time, place, specific circumstances, and so forth;
and as it is stated in detail in the *Abhidharma*: "The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) remains unabandoned"—this is the illustrative example.
And if it is argued that this example also shows that there is a complete arising [of the afflictions] through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manaskāra*) in that case;

It might be thought that the arising of affliction occurs in this way when its causes are complete, whereas for an affliction whose causes are incomplete, it arises solely through the power of the object;
however, that is incorrect.
Why? He says:
"Of what indeed could there be an arising when its causes are incomplete?"—of what, then, could there be an arising?
For there is no arising of an effect from incomplete causes;
indeed, whatever collection of causes and conditions is established for the arising of an effect, if that collection is deficient in even one part, it does not suffice for its arising.

For example, the assembly of the eye, visible forms, light, and mental attention is well-known to be the cause for the arising of visual consciousness; yet, when it is deficient in any one of those [factors], it does not lead to its arising.
Therefore, this [objection] is of no consequence.
"It has that form" refers to the mode or its intrinsic nature;
"not arisen" is the counter-position.

"In that seed-nature" means in the intrinsic nature of the seeds of the afflictions; as long as that [nature] has not been extracted— that is, not uprooted— how can one be one whose outflows are exhausted?
If you were to say "it does not exist," to that he says:
"Or how can one whose clamor is not exhausted be an Arhat?"
"Practicing in this way" means practicing with mindfulness,
because of the mention of mindfulness immediately following.

In order to refute the statement that "he is a learner" (*śaikṣa*), that same proponent of falling away (*pārihāṇivādin*) says: "For he was indicated as being precisely one who has transcended craving.
He asks: "In what way was he indicated? and then replies:
"Throughout the long night," and so forth:

for those who maintain the doctrine of non-retrogression, there may indeed be this opportunity for such a statement: "This mind of the trainee (śaikṣa) is said to be inclined toward seclusion, up to being directed toward Nirvana."
To refute this, the proponent of falling away (parihāṇivādī) speaks again:
"How is it stated in the Sūtra that 'this is indeed the power of an Arhat' elsewhere?"
"How many powers, Venerable Sir, does an Arhat monk whose outflows are exhausted possess?
"Eight, Śāriputra. An Arhat monk’s mind has for a long time been inclined toward seclusion, up to being directed toward Nirvana;
and he has viewed sensual desires as being like a pit of glowing coals."

Just as for one who knows sensual pleasures and sees sensual pleasures, whatever desire for sensual pleasures (*kāmacchanda*), affection for sensual pleasures (*kāmasneha*), and so forth, up to attachment to sensual pleasures (*kāmādhyavasāna*) there may be,
his mind does not remain seized by them— this is the detailed explanation— and furthermore, because of the designations "become cooled" (*śītībhūta*) and "become vomited out" (*vāntībhūta*).
In that very *Aṅgārakarṣū-upama-sūtra*, it is indicated that only an Arhat [is meant];
thus, "it is so" regarding what was stated in the *Aṅgārakarṣū-upama* that only an Arhat is indicated.
However, as long as the course of conduct has not been thoroughly mastered—
referring specifically to the stage of training when one is on alms-round and so forth— there is no fault because of such a statement.
As for what was stated—
that unwholesome thoughts which lead to acquisition may sometimes arise due to the loss of mindfulness—
that was said with reference to those in training (śaikṣa), not to the state of arhatship.
As for what was said— that it has "for a long time been inclined toward seclusion"—
that is possible even for one in training (*śaikṣa*); however, the distinction is that for an Arhat, it occurs to a superior degree.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that [the mind] has become cooled and has become vomited out with respect to the factors conducive to the outflows—
that too is possible with reference to the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), because it denotes the state of being cooled regarding the factors conducive to the outflows belonging to the desire realm.
The Master’s intention is that there is no fault because such a designation is made with reference to the state of arhatship;
since [the path of preparation] is impossible as a practice, it is not the path of seeing—
the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments.

In that regard, there is no opportunity for the preparatory application (prayoga) in the transition of the faculties (indriya-sañcāra) while one is still in the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana). When it is said that "one transitions the faculties," does one transition the faculties by means of a path characterized by coarse aspects and so forth?
Alternatively, since it is not specified whether [it occurs] by way of the aspect of tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth, we see that it is possible in both ways;
for the Master will indicate this meaning in the Sūtra.

For the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*) of the noble ones (*ārya*) does not occur by means of a contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*); this is understood from the specific qualification "of the noble ones.

Furthermore, intending the application [of practice] with the thought, "May my faculties indeed become sharp," one should know that one transforms the faculties through the sequence of the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), whether those paths are mundane (*laukika*) or supramundane (*lokottara*).

Regarding the statement "someone [attains it] in the stage of liberation through faith," the mention of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is absent because the context concerns those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); however,
it should be understood that even one beyond training undergoes the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
How can there be a falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life for one of immovable nature?

Since his faculties are sharp, a falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life would not be possible, much less from immovable liberation; thus, not considering such a thing possible, he asks.

The meaning is that for a Buddha there is only a decline in enjoyment; because he is occupied with the work of training those to be converted, he does not enjoy nor bring face-to-face the pleasant dwellings in the present life.
And that [is] both the loss of attainment and the loss through non-attainment; for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is also the loss of enjoyment due to some distraction,
as well as the loss through non-attainment because of not attaining the qualities of a specific type of person (*pudgalaviśeṣadharma*).

Because even one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) does not attain certain qualities such as the "ultimate-limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) states of the great disciples (*mahāśrāvaka*) like the noble Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, nor certain qualities of the self-enlightened ones (*svayambhū*); and likewise, the great disciples do not attain certain distinguished qualities of the self-enlightened ones, and so forth.

"Of another Arhat" refers to one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth who possesses dull faculties; there is also "falling away from what has been attained," because of the word "also" (*api*), it follows that the two previously mentioned types of falling away also exist.
Since this speaks of "falling away from enjoyment" (*upabhogaparihāṇi*) for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
Regarding that which was stated in detail— "those four by him," and so on, up to—
"therefore I declare his falling away from one of them"— this is what was said.
Regarding the non-contradiction of that sūtra which states that "the liberation of all six types of Arhats is unshakable," the Vaibhāṣika might say:
"If the untainted liberation of every Arhat is indeed unshakable..."
Why is it that only the one liberated at all times (asamayavimukta) is established as one of immovable nature (akopyadharman), and not others?
To this, it is said:
"The untainted liberation (anāsravā vimukti) of everyone is immovable."
This is true;
however, the establishment of one as being of immovable nature has been explained exactly as it is.

Yet, regarding the pleasant dwellings in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), someone may fall away from them due to the fault of distraction caused by gain and honor, through the loss of mastery (*vaśitva*).
Whosoever has dull faculties does not fall away,
whereas he who has sharp faculties [does].
He alone is established as one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*),

for it is precisely because of the fault of distraction caused by gain and honor that the one of dull faculties falls away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), whereas the one of sharp faculties does not.
Therefore, this objection— "How can there be a falling away from the pleasant dwellings in this very life for one of immovable nature?"— is not to be raised by the proponent of non-falling away.
Alternatively, there is this other connection:

it was previously stated that for one of immovable nature (akopyadharman), there is no falling away from the pleasant dwellings in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra), and so it is said in the Sūtra as well.
Because of this designation, it is said that the untainted liberation of everyone is "unshakable" (akopyā);
the intention is that one is not established as being of unshakable nature (akopyadharman) by that [liberation] alone.
Therefore it is said: "But the establishment of the one of immovable nature (akopyadharman) is just as it was stated therein";

thus, this objection—namely, that based on the Sūtra, how can there be a falling away from the pleasant dwellings in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra) for one of immovable nature—is not to be raised.
"Slow" means dull-witted;

for otherwise, it would not be a source of confidence. If falling away from arhatship were to occur again, even after this holy life has been well-practiced and this path well-cultivated, one would still find satisfaction at the end of life, just as when a disease departs—thus there is confidence.
Thinking, "It should not be thus," that which is not to be done— characterized by unchastity and so forth— is like the non-falling of a hero upon stumbling;
for just as a hero does not fall when he stumbles because he supports himself through his own strength.
In the same way, even though a noble one (ārya) has fallen away from a fruit, he does not die without having attained that fruit;
others say that the mention of "hero" is because of his lack of agitation, for a hero is one who is strong.
To the question "How has it been practiced?", he says:
"Because it has been made firm by both the path of training (śaikṣa) and the path beyond training (aśaikṣa)," whereas the path of preparation (prayogamārga), however, is in every case only one.
Regarding the penetration of the unshakable state and the attainment of vision,
it is said "not by means of that which is with outflows" (sāsrava),
because what is intended here is the transformation of the faculties of an noble one (ārya).
Otherwise, this statement that "someone transforms their faculties while in the state of an ordinary person" would be contradicted,
since such transformation is impossible elsewhere than through falling away; thus,
the transformation of faculties is held to occur out of fear of falling away.
Elsewhere, it is said that there is no falling away among the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm, nor in the form and formless realms; thus,
a noble one born in the higher realms neither transforms their faculties nor falls away in any way whatsoever.
The reason for this has been stated:
because the faculties become more fully matured through dwelling for a period of time,
and because one attains a specific state of the basis (āśraya).

Now, why is there no falling away among the gods of the desire realm who, having previously been repelled even by sublime sense objects, necessarily perceive the truths? How could they fall away by taking those very same objects as their support?
The intention is that they necessarily possess sharp faculties; thus it is said,
"the one beyond training (aśaikṣa) relies on nine."
Because its fruit cannot be comprised within the nine stages,
it is both the fruit and that which is distinguished by the fruit; thus,
"fruit" refers to the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

One attains only the path of fruition— which is distinguished by its fruit, such as the first dhyāna and so forth, and characterized by the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, liberation, and excellence— for the sake of abandonment; thus,
it is comprised solely of the detachment from the desire realm.
Furthermore, the fruit of non-returning is not comprised within the formless realm,
because of the scriptural statement that "one is a non-returner through the abandonment of the five lower fetters," and because the path of seeing does not exist there.
Its absence [is due] to not taking the desire realm as an object; this has already been explained.
Furthermore, because it is stated in the Sūtra that "the one of immovable nature (akopyadharman) is of two kinds," there are exactly two Buddhas within the classification of the immovable ones.
The one of immovable nature (*akopyadharmā*) is divided into three types based on the distinction of weak, medium, and sharp faculties:
for the Śrāvaka of immovable nature has sharp-weak faculties,
whereas the Pratyekabuddha has sharp-medium faculties.

The *samyaksambuddha* possesses the highest-of-the-high faculties (*adhimātrādhimātrendriya*) because of the distinctions among the nine grades of faculties, beginning with the softest-of-the-soft (*mṛdu-mṛdu*). Thus,
one subject to falling away (*parihāṇidharman*) has the softest-of-the-soft faculties, up to the Blessed One, who possesses the highest-of-the-high faculties.
"There are seven" means that,
since both the Pratyekabuddha and the Samyaksambuddha are included among those liberated from both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*),
[the statement] "as before," and so forth, is made.

The meaning is that previously, while still in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), having heard the teachings on the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth from another through reliance on others, one subsequently applies oneself to their meanings by means of reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Likewise, previously, while still in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by means of wisdom and in accordance with the Dharma of the twelvefold scriptural teachings, one follows for oneself such factors as the wings of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Through application to their meanings,
and through the cultivation and practice of reflection (*cintā-bhāvanā*),
they thus become those who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and those who follow through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) by way of such application.
"Faith-resolve" (śraddhā-adhimokṣa) refers to the predominance of faith, resolve, and wisdom; that is, it is the resolve through faith [arising] from the predominance of faith, resolve, and wisdom.
Due to the predominance of that [faith], there is dullness of faculty;
due to the predominance of wisdom, there is sharpness of faculty; and this is according to their liberation.
Regarding liberation from afflictions: one who is liberated from afflictions through wisdom is called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).
Regarding liberation from meditative attainments: this refers to being liberated both from the attainment itself and from the state of liberation.

In this regard, the detailed explanation beginning with "by way of the faculties" (indriyataḥ) will be demonstrated according to the text, showing how these followers by faith (śraddhānusārin) are enumerated.
From the perspective of the faculties, there are three types, due to being of weak, medium, or superior faculties;
here, furthermore, it should be understood in this way.
Although all those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) have dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*),
nevertheless, because they exist in varying degrees of intensity, they are further divided into three types— those with dull, medium, and sharp faculties (*mṛdu-madhyādhimātrendriya*). Thus,
there are five [types] according to their lineage (*gotra*).
How is it that there are five types, from those of the lineage subject to falling away (parihāṇadharman) up to those capable of penetration (prativedhanābhavya)?
Furthermore, due to the distinction between lineage and faculty, each one of these fifteen becomes fifteenfold according to the path.
How so? It is said:
"Abiding in the eight patiences and seven knowledges," for the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments.
There are eight patiences (*kṣānti*):

from the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge anvayajñānakṣānti*), as well as seven knowledges (*jñāna*).
From the dharma-knowledge of suffering up to the dharma-knowledge of the path—
since the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*) is included within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—
there are eight and seven [moments], making fifteen.
Thus, those situated therein become fifteen.
In this way, for these which are divided into fifteen types by way of the path, how does each one further become seventy-three by way of detachment?
First, there is one who possesses all fetters in the desire realm; then nine [types] through detachment from the desire realm,
ranging from one who is free from one grade of passion up to one who is free from nine grades of passion.
In this way, up to the detachment from the sphere of nothingness there are nine; however,
it is not possible that there are nine [paths] for the detachment from the peak of existence,
because there is no mundane path that serves as an antidote to the peak of existence.
These eight groups of nine make seventy-two;
together with the previously mentioned [category] bound by all fetters, they become seventy-three.
Furthermore, these seventy-three are each further divided according to their degrees of detachment (vairāgya).
How is it that there are nine for each based on their support? He says:
"Born in the three continents and the six classes of gods."
The three continents, excluding Uttarakuru—
since there is no [noble] path in Uttarakuru—
and the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm.
Since the path of seeing does not exist beyond that point,
these nine qualities each arise within them individually.
It is stated in the conclusion that they are "summarized" by way of their faculties, lineage, path, detachment, and basis; thus,
they are written as "uyanta" in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
In this way, other individuals (*pudgala*) are also to be enumerated as possible;
thus, starting with those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*),

they are counted according to their faculties (*indriya*), lineage (*gotra*), path (*mārga*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and basis (*āśraya*), just as those who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) have been enumerated.
In the same way, since they can exist in countless numbers,

there is no difference in lineage (*gotra*) among those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who are liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*); however,
for those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there is indeed a difference in lineage.
Regarding what is said "in terms of possibility":
therein, from the perspective of the faculties (*indriya*), there are three types of followers by way of Dharma (*dharmānusārin*);
however, from the perspective of the lineage (*gotra*), there is only one, so there is no distinction.
From the perspective of the path, there are fifteen [types of individuals] who abide in the eight receptivities and seven cognitions;
from the perspective of detachment, there are seventy-three, including those bound by all fetters.
There are exactly nine [types] due to detachment from the desire realm; likewise, up to detachment from the sphere of nothingness,
there are nine according to their basis.
Those born in the three continents and the six classes of gods—
thus, when condensed according to faculties, paths, degrees of detachment, and bases,
they amount to twenty-nine thousand.
Five hundred and sixty-five;
thus, from the perspective of the faculties, there are three types of those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*);
and from the perspective of the lineages (*gotra*), there are five for each.
From the perspective of detachment, there are seventy-three, each as previously described;
from the perspective of the basis, there are nine, born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.
Thus, when combined according to the faculties, lineages, degrees of detachment, and bases,
they amount to nine thousand eight hundred and fifty-five.
One who abides in the fruit alone and has attained the sixteenth moment of consciousness is the subject under discussion;
for at that time, those with dull and sharp faculties are respectively designated as "one liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*),
and it is these two who are intended here.
Bhagavadviśeṣa, however, said that there are nine from the perspective of the path, because they abide on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
We do not understand with what intention this was said;
for if this were the intention,
it would mean that there are nine [factors] on each stage according to the path.
It would be logical to say that "seventy-three by way of detachment" is intended to show that very same meaning, because [the latter] is not distinct from the former.
For that would indeed be their measure;
or, if their number were established as nine because they abide in the nine-level path of uncontaminated cultivation,
then in that case—
Furthermore, that measure multiplied by nine would result in eighty-eight thousand and six hundred.
And ninety-five would thus be included; otherwise, one must multiply by way of the faculties: there are three who are resolved through faith.
From the perspective of lineage (*gotra*), there are five;

from the perspective of detachment (*vairāgya*), eighty-one; and by adding eight more to the seventy-three who are detached from the eight categories of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are eighty-one; and from the perspective of the basis (*āśraya*), there are twenty-nine.
How is it that there are nine places of rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), sixteen places in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Thus, when condensed according to faculties, lineages, degrees of detachment, and bases, there are thirty-five thousand two hundred and thirty-five.
For one who has attained through vision, there is no distinction of lineage;
when combined according to faculties, stages of detachment, and supports, they amount to one thousand nine hundred.
If one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) is included up to the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), then they should be counted as seventy-one.
When condensed according to the faculties, detachment, and bases,

they total seven thousand four hundred and thirty-seven; however, the body-witness (kāyasākṣin) is not counted separately, as he is included within those who are liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
If, however, they are counted by way of faculties, there are three;
if [the first] is one liberated through faith, he is a body-witness. If counted by way of lineage, there are five;
if [the second] is one who has attained vision, there is no distinction of lineage.

In terms of the path, there is no difference between the two because both have attained freedom from passion regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*). Nor is there a difference in terms of detachment (*vairāgya*);
for although one at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) may be detached from all fetters, or detached from one type up to eight types [of defilements].
There is a distinction based on the path or based on detachment;
however, since the state of being a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣitva) is not produced by the path or by detachment,
no distinction between them caused by those factors is established for this [state].

Alternatively, there is a manifold division according to the basis (*āśraya*), ranging from having the desire realm as its basis up to having the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as its basis; such is the specific distinction [stated] by the Blessed One.
How, then, can one who has the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth as their basis be a body-witness (*kāyasākṣin*)?
However, we consider this to be correct:
from the perspective of their bases, there are twenty-five [realms], and within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are nine places of rebirth.
And there are sixteen locations in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
for it is there that a noble one (*ārya*) might produce the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
provided that he has become a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) through his connection with the attainment of cessation produced based on the realms of desire and form.
Since the state of being a body-witness (kāyasākṣitva) based on the Peak of Existence is admitted even subsequently through the mere application of its possession (samanvāgama),
it should be understood that the Peak of Existence would constitute the twenty-sixth basis.
Having thus enumerated [the types] by way of faculties, lineage, and basis, the distinction of one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) should also be calculated:
there are three types of one liberated by wisdom according to their faculties.
If they are liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), there are five according to lineage (gotra);
however, if they are liberated without regard to occasion (asamayavimukta), there is no distinction.

In the same way, the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) should also be understood [as such] because he is liberated from the obscurations to the afflictions and the obscurations to liberation through the two powers of wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
that is to say, because he is liberated from the obscuration of the afflictions by the power of wisdom.
And because one is liberated from the hindrances to liberation through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*),
the liberations (*vimokṣa*) will further be explained as eight,
beginning with "one possessing form sees forms," and so forth.
In that context, "the obscuration of afflictions" means that the afflictions themselves are the obscuration;
it is an obscuration to liberation.
The obscuration to the liberations is,
moreover, the unserviceability of body and mind,
by which one is unable to produce the liberations.
"Having abandoned here those five afflictions"—
these refer to the five lower-tier fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which have been previously mentioned;
"one of unshakable nature" (*ahāryadharman*) means one whose nature is non-retrogression (*aparihāṇadharman*).
"Consequently," and so forth:
because he is one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), there is no perfection by way of the faculties;
because he is not a body-witness (*akāyasākṣin*), there is no perfection by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
However, because of the state of non-returning (*anāgāmitva*), there is fulfillment by way of the fruit;
since it is attained through the faculties (*indriya*) alone,
there is fulfillment by way of the faculties due to having attained right view (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
However, because they have not yet abandoned passion, there is no [attainment] in terms of the fruit nor in terms of meditative attainment,
due to the absence of the fruit and the attainment of a non-returner;
in the same way, this should be applied to others as well, according to what is possible.
"Only by way of attainment" means that perfection is achieved solely through attainment, not through faculties or fruits;
why is this so?

For there is no attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) in the absence of the attainment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and there can be no attainment or faculty without the fruit; therefore,
the claim that perfection consists solely in the attainment and the faculties, rather than in the fruit, is also untenable.
Because the attainment of cessation does not exist for one who has not attained the fruit of a non-returner,
[the phrase] "by way of faculties and by way of attainments" means by way of having sharp faculties and by way of having obtained the attainment of cessation.
"By way of the faculties alone," and so forth; because of the statement "of one liberated at any time," his perfection is by way of the faculties.
Because of the statement "of one liberated by wisdom," his perfection is not [attained] through meditative attainment;
for it is said that one who has attained the cessation-attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) is "liberated by both."
"Only by way of meditative attainment" means that, according to the statement "of one liberated by occasion," his perfection is achieved solely through meditative attainment.
One who has attained the attainment of cessation is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*); what [is meant] by these two,
namely faculties (*indriya*) and attainments (*samāpatti*)?

It shows that perfection consists in being liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) by way of the faculties (*indriya*), and in being liberated from both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*);
it is the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) by which one abandons the hindrances.
Because there exists a path that does not involve abandonment,
there is that path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) by which one does not abandon the hindrances during such processes as the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-sañcāra*).

"One who is first liberated from the obscurations to be abandoned by that" means one who is first liberated from the obscuration to be abandoned by the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*); this is the specific qualification.
Because that which is of the same nature as those [preceding moments] in the third and subsequent moments is accepted as the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), for this very reason he said:
"The path of distinction is the path other than these."
The meaning is that it is distinct from the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and the others.
Furthermore, if one were not to say "from the very beginning," but were to say only this: "the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is that which is freed from the obscurations to be abandoned by it."

This being the case, since all subsequent paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and so forth would arise already liberated from the obstructions to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*), it would follow that all of them are paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
and this is an undesirable conclusion.
Because there would be the unwanted consequence that the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) would also apply to the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga) and so forth,

therefore, whatever obscuration is to be abandoned by the uninterrupted path— such as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti)— is the category [of defilements] to be abandoned by seeing suffering, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
That which arises first, being liberated from that obstacle to be abandoned by it,
is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
no other [moment] is so, even though it too is liberated from that obstacle to be abandoned.
That which is other than these three— the path of preparation and so forth—
is the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*);

it consists of those untainted moments (*anāsrava-kṣaṇa*) of the same nature as the seventeenth moment and subsequent ones, following after the sixteenth moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
It should be understood that these have the nature of the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*);
likewise, other [types of] knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñāna*) which are protracted, such as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, are also to be understood in this way.
That too must be stated: the path for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life, or for the production of the specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*),
is also indeed the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*), because it has been said that from this [path] arises the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
Therefore, it is understood that the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) constitute the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*);
however, it must be stated in what [category] the path consisting of patience (*kṣānti*) and so forth, when taken in reverse order, is included.
He said:
It is indeed included within the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), but that path of preparation is remote; this is its distinction from the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
Furthermore, because it was intended as an illustration, the Teacher has described only the path of practice that is most proximate;
for this is indeed the path to Nirvana, since one proceeds to it by means of it.
In the world, that by which one goes is recognized as the "path," and by this [path], nirvāṇa is gone to— that is, attained.
Therefore, he shows that it is called the "path" (mārga);
for the root *mārg* is recited in the sense of "seeking," as in the phrase "they seek by means of this."
This is its form with the suffix *ghañ*: "mārga" (path),
meaning that by which nirvāṇa is sought is the path.
How can the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the special path (*viśeṣa-mārga*) be considered "paths"?
For nirvana is not attained by those two;
the intention is that only the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) and the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) possess the capacity for its attainment, and not those two.
"Because they are of that same class and more intense": this means that,

by virtue of their similarity in terms of being of the same class as the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*)— due to their object (*ālambana*), aspect (*ākāra*), and state of being untainted (*anāsrava*)— and because they are more intense due to the accumulation of causes, [the two moments] are of that same class and more intense.

For just as the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) has the four truths as its object, possesses the sixteen aspects, and is untainted (*anāsrava*), so too are the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and special advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*); however,
they differ from it precisely by being of a higher degree.
"Because of attaining higher and higher [stages],

or because of entering the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa)," means that by means of the path of liberation (vimuktimārga) and the path of distinction (viśeṣamārga), each successive path is attained.
Therefore, the meaning is that these two constitute the path;
or rather, because through them one enters the nirvana without remainder—
that is, the entry into nirvana without remainder occurs upon their arising.
Others, however, explain it thus:
because they lead to each subsequent stage until the entry into the state without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa), these two possess the nature of the path.
"Because it leads toward Nirvāṇa" means that by means of this [path], one attains Nirvāṇa;
thus, the pleasant [path] is also of two kinds.
There is a pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge and there is a pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge;
because they proceed without effort due to the possession of factors and the equilibrium of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), there is "possession by means of factors."
The equality of calm abiding and special insight, the effortless flow by means of those two,
and the inclusion of the factors; this is the equality of calm abiding and special insight.
Because of those two, there is effortless progression; therefore, it is an easy path,
since the meditative absorptions (dhyānas) are embraced by the factors and are balanced in both calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
Therefore, because it flows without effort and because of this ease, it is called the "easy path";
"due to not grasping the [preliminary] factors," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
Because they do not grasp the factors [of the dhyānas], the *anāgamya*, the *dhyānāntara*, and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) involve effort;
and because, as far as possible, their calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are deficient, they involve effort.
Specifically, in the *anāgamya* and the *dhyānāntara*, they involve effort due to a deficiency in calm abiding.
And because insight (vipaśyanā) is deficient in the formless realms (ārūpya), they proceed with effort;
due to the absence of that [insight],
the [attainments] such as the Not-Yet-Arrived (anāgamya) are the difficult path (duḥkhā pratipad).
"Slow in higher knowledge" means "I am slow in higher knowledge"; it signifies one who possesses dull wisdom.
"Quick higher knowledge" refers to those of sharp wisdom; "slow higher knowledge" refers to the higher knowledge of a person who is dull and slow.
He shows that this is also established by means of a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.
In this way, for a person who is both quick and sharp, their superknowledge is "quick superknowledge"; this should be applied accordingly.
The four foundations of mindfulness—the foundations of mindfulness of the body, feelings, and phenomena—are as previously described.
The four right efforts:
one generates desire and exerts oneself for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen.
He exerts vigor, uplifts the mind, and strives.

One generates desire for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen, as previously described; and one generates desire for the stability, non-confusion, cultivation, fulfillment, further increase, growth, expansion, and realization through knowledge of wholesome states that have already arisen, as previously described— these are the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
The basis of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration through desire;
likewise, the bases of psychic power endowed with the formative forces of abandonment and concentration through energy, mind, and investigation—
the meaning of "bases of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda) is the causes of psychic power (ṛddhi).
The five faculties are the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; the five powers are the powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

The seven factors of enlightenment are the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. Mindfulness itself is an enlightenment factor; it is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness.
In this way, up to: equanimity itself is an enlightenment factor; it is the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
The Noble Eightfold Path consists of right view, right intention, and right speech.
Right action, right livelihood, and right effort.
Right mindfulness and right concentration [are so called] because of the abandonment of ignorance without remainder.
Since there is the abandonment of ignorance pertaining to the three realms in its entirety, both [factors] constitute awakening;
by this, he demonstrates that the wisdom of those in training (śaikṣa) and of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) is not established as awakening.
Furthermore, by means of these two [knowledges] respectively, there is the realization, in accordance with reality, that one's own welfare has been accomplished and need not be done again;

and because of the realization, in accordance with reality, that [suffering] has been exhausted through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), that knowledge of exhaustion is awakening (*bodhi*).
He understands, as it truly is, "Suffering has been fully understood by me," "The origin has been abandoned by me," and "Cessation has been realized by me."
"One understands as it truly is: 'The path has been cultivated by me'";
by means of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), one understands as it truly is that there is nothing further to be done—that knowledge of non-arising is also awakening (*bodhi*).
He understands as it truly is: "Suffering has been fully understood by me; it is not to be understood again.
"The origin has been abandoned by me; it is not to be abandoned again. "Cessation has been realized by me; it is not to be realized again."
"One understands as it really is: 'The path has been cultivated by me; it need not be cultivated again.
By [the thought] 'Suffering has been fully understood by me,' there is the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*);
by [the thought] 'It need not be fully understood again,' there is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)."
Thus, both [knowledges] are shown to belong to a person of sharp faculties; all this should be understood accordingly.

Having thus established the meaning of the individual parts—that awakening (*bodhi*) consists of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)—he speaks in order to establish the collective meaning:
"Because they are in conformity with that."
"However, its thirty-seven factors are its wings";
thus,
that which is in accordance with that awakening is "conformable to it."
The state of being that is conformity to that;
therefore,
from that conformity to that, [arise] the factors conducive to enlightenment.
Those things which are beneficial and conducive to enlightenment are called the "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*);
these are said in the scriptures to be thirty-seven, beginning with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), yet they consist of only ten substantial entities (*dravya*).
According to the opinion of some Vaibhāṣikas, he will state that there are eleven [factors], because bodily and vocal actions are not distinct;
for wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthiti*).
Thus,
the meaning of "foundation of mindfulness through wisdom" is that mindfulness is established by means of this [wisdom].
For it is said in the Sūtra: "Contemplating the body in the body," and so forth;
[this] vigor is called right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Thus it has been said: for the sake of abandoning evil, unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire and exerts effort.
"One exerts energy" refers to all the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), which are concentrations (samādhi).

Since it is said that "one cultivates the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) endowed with the formative forces of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra) and concentration through desire," and since all the formative forces of abandonment are further enumerated as eight in the Sūtra, how can there be such a desire for one who is already in such a state?
Whatever effort, whatever faith, and whatever pliancy there may be.
That which is mindfulness, that which is clear comprehension, and that which is volition.
This equanimity is called the formative forces of abandonment;
first, regarding the faculties, it is as explained in detail.
Among those five substances which, by their own names, are the faculties, powers, and natures— namely faith, energy, mindfulness, and wisdom—
it is wisdom alone that constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness and that which is the factor of investigation of phenomena among the factors of enlightenment.
And that which is right view among the factors of the path is not a separate substance;
it is simply energy, which consists of the four right efforts.

That which is the factor of enlightenment of energy among the factors of enlightenment, and that which is right effort and concentration among the factors of the path— these are the four bases of psychic power.
And as for that factor of enlightenment among the factors of enlightenment which is the enlightenment-factor of concentration,
and that right concentration among the factors of the path—
what remains that does not have the nature of the faculty of wisdom and so forth?
Among the factors of enlightenment, the factors of joy, tranquility, and equanimity remain;
among the factors of the path, right intention and the three factors of ethical discipline remain.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—
these are ten entities, namely the five beginning with faith.

And including the five factors such as the enlightenment factor of joy, there are three members of ethical discipline; since these are of the nature of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), they are established as a single substance.
Thus, for the Vaibhāṣikas, there are eleven substances.
Because bodily and vocal actions are not distinct, they constitute two substances; thus, depending on the intended meaning, there is no fault in either of the two positions.
However, if one considers them according to their primary mode of existence, however many substances exist within that aggregate...
Even if those were counted, they would certainly not amount to ten substances,
because the unmanifest forms of one who is in meditative concentration consist of seven substances.
It should have been stated that there are sixteen substances;
however, by mentioning the primary factor alone, it was said that the applications of mindfulness and so forth have wisdom and the other [faculties] as their intrinsic nature.

However, all the qualities produced by application (*prāyogika*), whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanāmaya*), are respectively the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Furthermore, these are emphasized because other qualities function through their power;
it is not that those others do not exist.
For the applications of mindfulness have wisdom as their predominant factor; therefore, there is mention of "wisdom," but wisdom alone is not the application of mindfulness—
what then?
Since wisdom, vigor, concentration, joy, serenity, equanimity, right intention, and so forth are also [included],

the inclusion of the term "preparatory" (*prāyogika*) is for the purpose of excluding faith and the other [faculties] that are acquired at birth; thus, the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) are those in which vigor is predominant.
It should be explained in detail that "the bases of psychic power have concentration as their primary factor";
from what [source] is it known that "the bases of psychic power are concentrations"?
It is from the Sūtra.
For it has been said: "Monks, when a monk makes desire his dominant influence, he attains concentration;
that is his 'concentration through desire.
Monks, when a monk makes the mind his dominant influence, he attains concentration..."
Thus, for him there arises what is called "the concentration of investigation" (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*),

because by means of it the body, speech, and mind are properly applied; they are applied, maintained, restrained, or set in motion at times by this [concentration], and thus it is called "the principal" (*pradhāna*).
"Because it is established therein" means that since supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), characterized by the perfection of all qualities, is established in that concentration,
it is called a "basis of supernatural power" (*ṛddhipāda*) because the basis (*pāda*) of supernatural power is its establishment.
But as for those who say that concentration itself is the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), while the bases are desire and so forth—
namely, desire, mind, energy, and investigation—
For those Vaibhāṣikas who speak thus, there would result thirteen factors conducive to enlightenment,
because of the addition of two— desire (*chanda*) and mind (*citta*)— to the eleven; however,
vigor (*vīrya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are not added here.
Because they are included within the right efforts and the foundations of mindfulness,
it is said "becoming manifold" in detail;
having become manifold, he becomes one.
Through the vision of knowledge, he experiences manifestation and disappearance;
he passes through walls and through ramparts with his body without being obstructed.
Just as one performs the act of emerging and submerging in space and on earth,
so too in water.
He travels upon water by walking on an unbroken stream,
just as one walks upon the earth or through the air while sitting cross-legged.
It is just as if a winged bird were to take these two moons— so powerful and so majestic— in its hand, rub them, and stroke them,
even exercising mastery over them with its body as far as the Brahma-world.
This is called supernormal power (ṛddhi).
What are the bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda)? They are:
concentration through desire (chandasamādhi).
The concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation.
These are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*);
such is the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, meditative concentration itself is not the psychic power.
In this case, since for the Teacher concentration itself is the "basis" (*pada*),
this fault does not apply to them,
for they maintain that concentration is the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
"Supernormal power as well" refers to zeal and the other [factors], mentioned for the purpose of indicating that concentration is fourfold;
for indeed, a certain concentration becomes predominant during the stage of application to the roots of virtue.
For someone who has reached the stage of perfection of the roots of virtue, the former [of these two] here is the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*),
and the latter is psychic power (*ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtras for them [the bodhisattvas],
because the fruit of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) is expressed by the word "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*),
just as the fruit of thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is designated by that same term, and so forth.
"Due to the distinction between weak and intense" means that the faculties (indriya) are weak and the powers (bala) are intense.
He states the reason for how there is a distinction between weak and intense among these:
"Because they are subject to being crushed or not being subject to being crushed.

The faculties (*indriya*) are crushed by the intermittent arising of their opposites—namely, lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, distraction, and lack of clear comprehension—but the powers (*bala*) are not so.
Furthermore, those [stages] were described as belonging to the levels of the beginner and the aids to penetration.
These five stages have been described as belonging to both cultivation and vision.
Regarding the two states,
there are seven groups within the seven states respectively.

In the stage of a beginner, the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are manifested, established, or made primary; in the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata), the right efforts (samyakpradhāna) are manifested, established, or made primary.
At the stage of the summits (mūrdhan), there are the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda);
at the stage of patience (kṣānti), the faculties (indriya);
and at the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgradharma), the powers (bala).
In the stage of the path of cultivation, the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are practiced,
and in the stage of the path of seeing, the noble eightfold path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga); thus,
the intensification of vigor is the cause for the attainment of these specific distinctions.
Therefore, the right efforts are present in the "heat" stages because they lead to the entry into the roots of merit that are not subject to decline;
they are present in the "summits" stages as well.
The entry into wholesome roots conducive to non-retrogression occurs at the stage of the "Summits" (mūrdhan),
because of the statement: "One who has attained the Summits does not sever the roots."
It is called "entry" because one enters by means of these;
for non-retrogression occurs in the stages of *kṣānti*, and the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) in those states become the basis for spiritual accomplishment.
The bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are established at the stages of the summits (mūrdhan) because there is no further falling back; this is the detailed explanation,
since there is no further falling back from the stages of receptivity (kṣānti).
For the possibility of falling away exists only in the first two [stages];
therefore, faith and the others attain the status of faculties (indriya), and because of that state, they are established as faculties during the stages of receptivity (kṣānti).
"Because it cannot be crushed by the afflictions" means that in that state, one is not crushed by the afflictions,
since the afflictions do not manifest there.
Alternatively, because they cannot be crushed by other worldly factors,

or rather, because they cannot be crushed by other worldly factors during the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), faith and the others are manifested as "powers" (*bala*) due to their proximity to awakening.
The meaning is: "because of its proximity to the knowledge of destruction and non-arising.

For the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is proximate to the knowledge of destruction and non-arising, whereas the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is distant, being separated by the intervening path of cultivation.
"Because it is characterized by going":
for in the world, the path (*mārga*) is characterized by going;
it is called a "path" because one goes by means of it.
Because of the worldly expression, "This path goes to Pāṭaliputra," the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is characterized by a superior degree of "going" (*gamana*),
whereas the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is not.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Because of its rapid movement"; one who possesses that [meditative concentration] also moves rapidly by means of it.
"But by means of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because of its protracted nature due to the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmi*), one proceeds over a long period of time.
Regarding this, the Master [Vasubandhu] says, "Others, however, say," with the intention that these are people such as himself.

Without breaking the sequence as it is divided by the Vaibhāṣikas, they describe the order of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) by taking the limbs of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) to belong to the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
"Of many kinds," and so forth; it means that the object is of many varieties due to the distinctions of form and so on,
and the distinctions of blue and so on.
In that context, "dispersion" (vyāseka) means distraction;
these are called "cognitions that disperse through dispersion toward various objects" because it is their nature to spread out due to being distracted by many kinds of objects.
For the purpose of restraining them— the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)—
it refers to those based on sensual desire (*gardha*), which means those based on craving (*tṛṣṇā*);
"of mental constructions of memory" (*smarasaṅkalpa*) means of mental constructions consisting of memories of previously experienced objects.
"Of the conceptualizations of sensual desire" means "by that power," which is to say,
by the power of the four foundations of mindfulness.
"For the accomplishment of the fourfold task" means that the fourfold task consists of the abandoning of arisen evil and unwholesome states,
and the non-arising of those not yet arisen.
Likewise, there is the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the stability and so forth of those already arisen; from that comes the purification of meditative concentration.
Thereafter, immediately following the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*), because they purify meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are manifested;
they should be understood as "predominant" (*adhiparibhūta*) because they bring about those [bases] that are predominant over supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*).
Those very same faculties, when they have overcome the activity of their opposites— that is, when they have overcome the activity of lack of faith and so forth— [become powers].
At that time, the powers exist in the state of the faculties, for the manifestation of the afflictions is possible because the state of patience has not yet reached its full development.
Regarding the statement "the factors of enlightenment are on the path of seeing," since enlightenment is defined as untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*),
the factors of the path pertain to both [paths].
Regarding how this applies to the paths of seeing and cultivation, he says:
"For it has been stated thus," and so forth.
The fulfillment through cultivation is the "fulfillment of cultivation.
The Noble Eightfold Path proceeds toward that;
as it proceeds, the four foundations of mindfulness proceed toward the fulfillment of cultivation.

From the statement that "up to the seven factors of enlightenment reach fulfillment through cultivation," it is understood that the noble eightfold path exists even on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
for cultivation does not reach fulfillment on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Rather,
it was stated again that "the factors of the path are established for both [paths]," and by saying "this is a designation for the four noble truths," he indicates the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Setting out by the path as it was come" is explained in detail up to "this is a designation for the path," thereby showing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Setting out by the path as it was come—that is, as it was attained—up to enlightenment;
thus, in this way, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are established in both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation.
Therefore, since the noble eightfold path must be sought by both [the śrāvaka and the bodhisattva],
the sequence is established: first the factors of enlightenment, and afterwards the noble eightfold path.
The factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are untainted;
this is a restriction meaning that they are exclusively untainted.
"The others are of two kinds" refers to those beginning with the foundations of mindfulness and ending with the powers.
"Because it must be brought forth by force" means that because it must be manifested through strength— that is, through vigor—
there is an absence of joy (*prīti*) in the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
The mind is gladdened by that which is easily attained,
and not by the other;
furthermore, this is because the lower stages are accompanied by apprehension.
Because one has apprehension regarding falling away,
there is consequently an absence of joy therein;
for when there is apprehension, the mind does not find delight.
"Excluding conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*)," means that conceptualization— namely discursive thought (*vitarka*)—
is excluded from the factors of enlightenment and the path-factors in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Thus,
how can there be the application of mindfulness to the body at the peak of existence,
for the body does not exist there?
For the foundation of mindfulness of the body is wisdom that has the body as its object;
however, the Peak of Existence does not take the Desire Realm or the Form Realm as its object,
nor do the fundamental wholesome formless attainments have the lower contaminated realms as their domain.
Since this is the established conclusion (siddhānta),
it has not been written by any commentator;
therefore, we shall now settle this matter here.
What is the intrinsic nature of the body?
It has been stated that its nature is being composed of the elements; the meaning is that the body consists of both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*).
In that regard, if wisdom (*prajñā*) were to have as its object only the primary elements (*bhūta*), only derivative matter (*bhautika*), or both,
it would be precisely the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Furthermore, at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), wholesome contaminated wisdom (*kuśalasāsravā prajñā*) takes as its object the path by way of being the path itself, or by way of logical principle, because it takes as its object the path of uncontaminated restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*).
For the fundamental wholesome formless attainments are held to have contaminated lower realms as their object, but not to have uncontaminated lower realms as their object;
therefore, it should be understood that the application of mindfulness to the body is present therein.

There are four kinds of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*): verified clarity in the Buddha, verified clarity in the Dharma, verified clarity in the Saṅgha, and the virtues dear to the Noble Ones (*āryakāntāni śīlāni*). In this context, because the Truth of Suffering and the others constitute the Dharma, and because they do not have the nature of the Buddha or the Saṅgha, one who realizes and sees the three Truths in their proper order attains verified clarity in the Dharma and the untainted (*anāsrava*) virtues dear to the Noble Ones.

One does not attain verified confidence (*avetyaprasāda*) in the Buddha or the Saṅgha at the moment of realizing the Truth of the Path; rather, one attains verified confidence in the Buddha and his community of disciples (*śrāvakasaṅgha*) upon realizing the Truth of the Path,
because the Truth of the Path has the nature of both the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
"What is this 'dharma' intended here?"—
since there are many types of dharma, such as "wholesome dharmas" and so forth,
what is this specific dharma intended here?
As for what was said regarding "attaining verified clarity (avetyaprasāda) in the Dharma," since this refers to the Jewel of the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṅgha,
it follows that the Jewel of the Dharma must also be intended here.
For this is said to be the nature of the Three Jewels:
he who goes for refuge to the three refuges takes refuge in the qualities of one beyond training that constitute the Buddha, in both [types of] qualities that constitute the Saṅgha, and in Nirvāṇa.
Thus, one asks: "Is this intended to be the dharma of nirvāṇa? and for that reason, he asks:
"What is the dharma intended here?"
"Dharma consists of the three truths," and so forth;
[these are] the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.

And here, the "Dharma" intended is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of a Bodhisattva in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*), as well as the path characterized by both training and no-more-training (*śaikṣāśaikṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of a Pratyekabuddha;
therefore, all four [truths] are included, and so forth.
When one realizes the truth of the path, one also realizes the Dharma characterized by the paths of the Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas;

therefore, it is said that through the realization of all four truths, one attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma. Consequently, the path of the Buddha and the Saṅgha is not designated as the "Dharma" [in this specific context].
Since the attainment of verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Buddha and the Saṅgha occurs through the realization (*abhisamaya*) of that [Truth],

how then can there be the simultaneous manifestation of the three types of verified clarity— characterized by faith— regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, upon the realization of the Truth of the Path?
There is no fault here, for it is that very same faith which receives three names depending on the distinction of its respective bases.
Alternatively, while the verified clarity regarding the Dharma is present,
three [other verified clarities] are cultivated for the future; therefore, it is so stated.
Regarding the statement, "There is also [the attainment] of faith in the Buddha and his Saṅgha at the time of the appearance of the Path":
if the establishment of the verified faiths (*avetyaprasāda*) were based on their respective objects, then the verified faith in the Dharma would have to be mentioned first; therefore, he says:

However, their sequence is according to how one who has emerged from meditative absorption brings them to presence, because they function as the physician, the medicine, and the attendant, respectively.
The Blessed One is like a physician, for according to the Sūtra he is the unsurpassed remover of the arrow of poison;
and the Dharma is like medicine, because it is the teacher of the medicinal Dharma and serves as the remedy for the disease of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

And because it brings about the attainment of the health of nirvāṇa, the Saṅgha acts as an attendant; since they attend one another for the sake of attaining the health of nirvāṇa, the clarity of faith in the Saṅgha is a clarity of faith in ethical discipline produced by clarity of mind. Thus, there are three kinds of clarity of mind.
"Truly, the Blessed One is a perfectly awakened one;
his Dharma and Vinaya are well-proclaimed; his community of disciples is practicing rightly"—thus he developed serene confidence in the moral discipline.
Is it morality itself that is clarity, or is it the clarity of morality? The clarity of morality is its state of being untainted (*anāsravatva*);
thus, the clarity of morality is mentioned as the fourth among the three clarities at the end.
Why is this? He says:

for one who is thus serene, thinking "The Blessed One is indeed a perfectly awakened Buddha," and so forth—this practice is the practice of the morality beloved by the Noble Ones; such is the meaning.
Alternatively, why is confidence in the ethical discipline (*śīla-prasāda*) mentioned at the end? Because it is like the state of health;
it follows the sequence of the physician, the medicine, the attendant, and the recovery of health.
Or, as in the case of a guide, a path, a caravan leader, and a vehicle, why is the fourth mentioned at the end? This is the point under discussion.
The Blessed One is like a guide; the Dharma is like the path; the Saṅgha is like a caravan leader.
"The precepts beloved by the noble ones are like vehicles" means that they are "beloved by the noble ones" (āryakānta) because they are the preferred modes of travel for the noble ones;
[this is stated] by way of eight [aspects].
Endowed with eight factors is the trainee (śaikṣa).
With which eight?
With the right view of a trainee, up to the right concentration of a trainee.
Endowed with ten factors, what are those ten?
They are: the right view of one beyond training, up to the right concentration of one beyond training, the right liberation of one beyond training, and the right knowledge of one beyond training.
It is characterized by liberation and the personally realized knowledge thereof;
in that liberation, there is both the personal realization and the liberation itself,
which together constitute "liberation and the personally realized knowledge thereof."
Manifested by those two—
namely, by liberation from the afflictions and by the personally realized knowledge of liberation from the afflictions— he is manifested as one who thinks, "I am liberated from the afflictions."
The meaning is "exalted.

It is logical that this statement regarding liberation and the statement regarding the knowledge of liberation apply only to that very one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa), and not to one still in training (śaikṣa).
Resolute belief is conditioned liberation because the meaning of the term is one and because the factors [of the path] are conditioned.
Just as right view and the other [factors] are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
so too liberation (*vimukti*) is understood to be exclusively conditioned, and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it would be of a different category and dissimilar.
Two types of liberation are stated in the Sūtra: "Through the fading away of passion, there is liberation of mind;
through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom."
The meaning is that "liberation of mind" and "liberation by wisdom" constitute the aggregate of liberation; this is also the aggregate of ethical discipline.
The aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation,
and the knowledge and vision of liberation— these are to be understood here.
Then what about that which was said in the Sūtra:
"O Vyāghrabodhyāyanas, there are these four principal purifications; which are the four?"
Having explained in detail that it has purity of ethical discipline as its primary focus and purity of meditative concentration as its primary focus, he said:
"And what, Vyāghrabodhyāyana, is that which has purity of liberation as its primary focus?"
"Up to 'whatever desire, vigor,' and so forth"—
the plural form "Vyāghrabodhyāyanas" is used because of their great number.
"Preeminent for the purity of liberation" means that the purity of liberation is "purity of liberation";
that which is preeminent for that [purity] is "vigor preeminent for the purity of liberation."
Thus, in this context, regarding the primary factor of the purification of liberation, there are three questions; therein it is said:
"In this case, O monk, the mind becomes detached from passion and liberated from hatred."
That which becomes detached from delusion is liberated;
thus liberation is spoken of, either for the sake of fulfilling an incomplete aggregate of liberation, or [for its maintenance].
Or, for the sake of favoring that which is already fulfilled—
this is the purification of liberation; the characteristic of fulfillment and favor has been stated,
and what was described in detail as "desire and vigor" is declared to be the primary factor.
Since liberation from passion and the other [afflictions]— characterized as abandonment— is what is described in the Sūtra as liberation, and not resolute conviction (adhimukti),
therefore liberation is not merely resolute conviction;
what then?

Another teacher—the Master [Vasubandhu]—holds that when passion and the other defilements have been removed by the knowledge of reality, the purity of the mind, which is its state of being free from outflows (*anāsravatva*), is not a separate entity, just like the clarity of the surface of clarified butter;
for it constitutes an obstacle to the arising of that mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, it is because it acts as an impediment to the production of that [untrained] mind.
For the possession of afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*) is indeed an obstruction;

as for that which "does not arise," it refers to that which is future and does not occur immediately after the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), namely, the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is certain to arise,
whether it be mundane or belonging to the continuum of one beyond training (aśaikṣa),
is that which is certain to arise.
"That very thing was said" means that which is future and facing toward arising— that very thing was stated in the treatise as "it is liberated."
The intention is that [it is so called] because it is easily characterized by way of being liberated from that;
"from that very obscuration to arising" means from the very acquisition of those afflictions.
Because it obstructs the arising of that [uncontaminated state], one must state the very reason for this:
if it is accepted that even the mundane [state] within the continuum of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is liberated,
then the mundane [state] of one in training (śaikṣa) would also arise.
To the question, "Why is it accepted that [the mind] is not liberated?", he says:
"It is not of such a nature," and so forth.
