That which is accompanied by the acquisition of afflictions belongs to the learner's mundane [mind],
but not to the non-learner's mundane [mind]; thus it is not the same when it is being ceased.
Thus,
being oriented toward cessation,
he [observes] its activity.
Thus, there is the obstruction to the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as that which is called "unconditioned liberation" (asaṃskṛta-vimukti) in the treatise, or here itself,
the unconditioned abandonment of the afflictions (kleśa-hāna).
Thus,
where are these three elements that are mentioned?
Where are they said to be?
In both the Sūtras and the Śāstras,
dispassion is defined as the complete exhaustion of attachment.
This is said when there is a desire to express distinction;
however, when there is a desire to express non-distinction, that which is detachment is also called abandonment.
"Cessation also," and so forth;
"of the thing" refers to contaminated matter (*rūpa*) and the like.
There is a fourfold alternative:
there may be that which ceases but does not become dispassionate;
there may be that which becomes dispassionate but does not become weary.
It is declared that there may be both, or there may be neither,
by means of the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its cause.
By this, he demonstrates the disenchantment caused by the nature of things—
that through which one becomes dispassionate and abandons all [defilements].
Thus he demonstrates dispassion (virāga) as having the activity of abandonment (prahāṇakriyā) as its cause;
in this way, the fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is established.
Having thus determined the causes of world-weariness and dispassion,
the intention is that by means of this [analysis], the fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is established; as to how this is so, he says:
"It is indeed that which causes weariness," and so forth;

it is indeed that which causes weariness because, through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding suffering and its origin and through the knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin, it takes the objects of weariness as its objective support (*ālambana*).
For suffering and its origin are the two objects of weariness and serve as its objective support.
Because of the statement that "one does not become dispassionate without abandoning the afflictions," the activity of abandonment is impossible; therefore,
one becomes dispassionate through the patiences (*kṣānti*) regarding cessation and the path within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because the activity of abandoning occurs when one abandons the afflictions on the path of cultivation through the knowledges of cessation and the path,
one does not become weary.
Because they take objects that are grounds for joy as their focal point— namely, since both nirvāṇa and the path are grounds for joy—

one abandons the afflictions by means of both [the paths of seeing and meditation]; thus, through the previous patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin, one becomes weary and detached.
How does one become weary?
By taking the objects of weariness as one's cognitive support.
Because of the statement "one becomes dispassionate while abandoning the afflictions," the activity of abandonment exists; therefore,
it is not both [the case] with the subsequent [stages], as one does not abandon the afflictions there.
One does not become weary, nor does one become dispassionate,
because of the subsequent patiences and knowledges regarding cessation and the path; for, since they have objects that are grounds for joy, one does not become weary.
By the statement "not abandoning the afflictions," because there is an absence of the act of abandonment, one does not become dispassionate;
it is stated [in the text] that "not abandoning the afflictions" applies to the first and the fourth alternatives.
"Who does not abandon which afflictions?
In that regard, one who is free from passion," and so forth;
therein, this is for the purpose of introducing the subject matter.
One who is free from passion for the realm of desire, up to and including the sphere of nothingness,

even while seeing and realizing the truths through the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñānakṣānti), the knowledges of phenomena (dharmajñāna), and the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena, does not abandon the afflictions by means of them.
Because they have already been abandoned previously by the mundane path of cultivation (*laukika-bhāvanāmārga*),
only the untainted attainment of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) arises;
however, by means of the subsequent knowledges and patiences (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), one necessarily abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
For there is no detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) by means of the mundane path;

rather, one abandons the afflictions through the knowledges of the path of cultivation— namely, the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), as well as certain uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) during states such as the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).
Which remain?
Those other paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*); by means of them, one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus it is established in the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Master Yaśomitra.
The sixth treasury-location is completed.
Chapter 7:
The Exposition of Knowledge, the seventh treasury-location.
Showing the connection for the introduction of the seventh treasury-location immediately after the sixth, he says:
"The patiences (kṣānti) and the knowledges (jñāna) are also taught," and so forth.
From the worldly supreme dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), the uncontaminated receptivity to the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) arises; herein, the eight receptivities have been mentioned.
Following that, regarding the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmaduḥkha*), there likewise arises the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*). Thus again—
In this context, if they are knowledges,
they are the knowledge of destruction; if they are the views of one beyond training, they are right view.
"That very [path] is the two liberations; knowledge is awakening as previously described"— here,
"right knowledge" (samyag-jñāna) is precisely this, all of which has been explained in this very [treatise], namely, at the conclusion of the sixth chapter of the Abhidharmakośa.

One is made to experience [the truth] through the patiences and knowledges regarding the cause of suffering; one becomes detached through all [of them]; and one abandons [it] by means of those [patiences and knowledges].
Alternatively, this is introduced by way of its connection with the treatise;
for in the treatise, both the patiences (kṣāntis) and the knowledges (jñānas), as well as right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) and right knowledge (samyagjñāna), are taught.
And since this [treatise] is begun for the purpose of explaining that, he asks:
"But why are the *kṣāntis* not knowledge (*jñāna*)? and so forth.
The untainted *kṣāntis* are not knowledge.
Thus,
by the restriction that "only the pure [patiences] are not knowledge," it follows that the impure patiences are indeed knowledge;
for they are held to be conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
"Of that which is to be abandoned by it" means that because the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*), which is to be abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*), has not yet been abandoned,
the latent tendency is indeed abandoned during those stages.
It is not abandoned because it is in a state of being displaced;
furthermore, knowledge is held to be certain,
not uncertain.
Thus, they explain that the patiences (kṣānti) are not knowledge;
for the patiences arise in the form of endurance and not in the form of certainty, and therefore they are not knowledge.
When it would have been sufficient simply to say "because the latent tendency of doubt has not been abandoned," what is the purpose of the qualification "to be abandoned by that"?

For in the second moment, the latent tendency of doubt to be abandoned by the first receptivity (*kṣānti*) becomes abandoned; thus, one might understand that only the first receptivity is [the antidote] and not knowledge (*jñāna*), but not that the other receptivities are so as well.
Therefore, the qualification "of that which is to be abandoned by it" means "because its nature is investigation," that is to say,
because its intrinsic nature is close examination (*upanidhyāna*).

Because its intention (*āśaya*) is one of non-investigation (*asantīraṇa*) and non-searching (*aparimārgaṇa*): that which has no investigation is "non-investigative" (*asantīraṇa*). Its intention is directed toward searching;
thus, "intention of searching" (*parimārgaṇāśaya*) means its intention is not for searching, hence it is "one whose intention is not for searching" (*aparimārgaṇāśaya*).

It is non-investigation and it has the intention of not searching; that which has the intention of non-investigation and not-searching is "non-investigation-and-not-searching-intentionality"; from that state [it arises].
The meaning is that the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not views;

for as long as one has not yet accomplished what was to be done, one continues to contemplate and investigate the truths of suffering and so forth with the underlying intention (*āśaya*), by means of the aforementioned aspects such as impermanence and so on.

Furthermore, for one who has accomplished what was to be done, there occurs by means of those two [knowledges] a mere re-examination of the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth exactly as they were seen, such as: "Suffering has been fully known by me; it is not to be fully known again," and so forth.
Therefore, that other [knowledge] is not of the nature of a view, whereas the noble wisdom is both.
Thus,
from the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering up to the subsequent knowledge regarding the path,
that wisdom which has proceeded through close contemplation and has abandoned doubt concerning its objects [is so described].
"Other" refers to worldly [cognition];
the restriction "all that is indeed knowledge" implies that such [worldly cognition] is not *prajñā*.
The meaning is that which is not knowledge.
What, then, is this wisdom (*prajñā*)?

It is that which belongs to the five groups of consciousness—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—as well as that which is mental; specifically, that which is associated with afflictions having the nature of views, and that which is unobscured-neutral.
Furthermore, as for that which has the nature of vision and that which is mental and wholesome, what is it? He says: "And there are six views."
Thus, this sixfold worldly wisdom is "view";
the other is not a view.
Since there is the restriction "only six," what then is that other mundane [wisdom] which was mentioned previously?
"Knowledge for you is this and that other"—
this refers to the sixfold wisdom whose nature is vision (*dṛṣṭi*), as well as that which is other than it, namely the previously mentioned [wisdom], which is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).
And for this very reason,
the word "and" (ca) is recited in the phrase "the six [objects] of sight" (dṛśaś ca ṣaṭ).
Since these six are called both "knowledges" (*jñāna*) and "views" (*dṛṣṭi*),
by which ten knowledges [are they so designated]?

This undertaking is for the purpose of defining [the knowledges] by means of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, destruction, and non-arising;
for all these—such as the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-jñāna*) and the knowledge of persons (*pudgala-jñāna*)—are included within them.
In brief, however, there are only two: the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
The qualification "mostly" indicates that while conventional cognition takes conventionally real entities such as pots and cloths as its objects,
it sometimes also apprehends their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
"Conventional" (sāṃvṛta) means existing within convention; it is conventional,
[whereas] the untainted (anāsrava) is not.
Furthermore, when condensed,
it is twofold: knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Since the knowledge of suffering and so forth are included within these two very [knowledges],
their object of focus (ālambana) is possible; that is, whatever is the object of whichever [knowledge].
This occurs for him:
"Indeed, sound is not the object-support of visual consciousness, because that [consciousness] has that [visual form] as its object-support."
The meaning is: "because they have suffering and so forth as their objects";
and these are of four kinds.

These same [two] cognitions— dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge— which are of four types due to the distinction of their objects (the truths of suffering and so forth) and are not of the nature of views, are called the cognition of destruction and the cognition of non-arising; these two, moreover, arise for the first time [at that stage].
Furthermore, when those two— the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising— first arise, they occur as subsequent knowledges of suffering and its cause;
the meaning is that they necessarily have suffering and its origin as their objects.
He asks "Why? and replies:
"Because they have the aggregates of the peak of existence as their object by way of the aspects of suffering and origin.

This is because those two—the first-arisen knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising—necessarily take the aggregates of the peak of existence as their object by way of the aspects of suffering, such as impermanence and so forth, or by way of the aspects of origin, such as cause and so forth.

However, when they have not arisen for the first time, those two also exist even when other truths are the objects; thus, by implication, it is stated that immediately after the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi), the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) arises, and immediately after that, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). Therefore, he asks:
Does the diamond-like [concentration] (*vajropama*) also have the same object as those two?
"By those two" means by the two that first arose;

the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is: just as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) have one and the same object, does the diamond-like [concentration] also have the same object as those two?
If it has suffering and its origin as its objects,
is it possible that it has both of them as a single object?

Now, if it has cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as its object, it does not have a single [aggregate] as its object, because those two necessarily have the aggregates belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) as their object. For just as when a person pierced by a poisoned arrow dies, the poison pervades every limb but at the time of death remains only at the site of the wound and nowhere else; so it is here.
In the same way, for this yogin, knowledge remains fixed solely upon the objects to be abandoned, characterized by the aggregates of the peak of existence;
thus, he is one who knows the minds of others with respect to four [realms].
It is comprised by only the four beginning with dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and so forth, because it is included therein;
it is not comprised by the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) and so forth,
because their aspects are different.

For untainted knowledge of others' minds has only the aspects of the Path, because it is knowledge of the Path; however, that which is tainted has worldly aspects, such as "with passion" or "free from passion," and so forth.

Regarding "by means of the path of one liberated through faith and the path of one liberated by occasion": this means that, respectively, one knows the path of one who has attained through vision by means of the path of one liberated through faith,
but one does not know the path of one liberated independently of time by means of the path of one liberated by occasion.
"By means of the lower [path], one does not know the higher" means that one does not know the path of the Arhat by means of the path of the Non-returner (anāgāmī),
nor the path of the Pratyekabuddha by means of the path of the Arhat, and so forth.
Because those two have as their object the antidote to the desire realm and the higher realms; that is,
of those two— the category of dharma-knowledge and the category of subsequent knowledge—
the category of dharma-knowledge has the antidote to the desire realm as its object.
It is a fixed rule that for the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the object of focus is the antidote to the higher realms;
however, because the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is devoid of activity, there is no knowledge of others' minds within it.
Thus, this is stated with reference to what is possible, namely the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge itself (*dharmajñāna*).

For sometimes, by the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*), it is possible to know the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*),
as well as the eighth [moment], the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*).

Having thus known two moments belonging to the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānapakṣa*), one makes the application, thinking, "I shall know the mind belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānapakṣa*) hereafter," and thereby brings about the eighth moment, the subsequent knowledge of origin.
"Because of its mild application" means because of its small application;
for that mind of another, which is the object of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), must be accomplished by a great application on the part of a Śrāvaka.
Therefore, as long as he has not yet begun the application toward it...
In that case, since this [person] has reached the sixteenth moment of mind, they do not know the intermediate ones—
the first, second, and fifteenth; how then can they know only these three?

Having known the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*), and having performed another application (*prayoga*), one knows the fifteenth moment, the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
How, then, does one know in this way by means of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) alone?
It is because the untainted [knowledges] possess the aspects (*ākāra*) of suffering and so forth.

Since this [subsequent knowledge] has such aspects as "this suffering of mine has been fully understood" and so forth, he asks about the distinction between those two by way of its specific qualities:
through the specific quality of that twofold conventional knowledge obtained subsequent to it, one knows, "Suffering has been fully understood by me," up to "the path has been cultivated by me."

"I have fully understood suffering; it is not to be understood again," and so on, up to "I have cultivated the path; it is not to be cultivated again"—knowing thus, the distinction between those two untainted knowledges, the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising, is made known and demonstrated in the treatise.
For this very reason, it is said: "based upon that."
"Taking that as its basis" means having made that the precursor; the meaning is "having placed that at the forefront.
The intention is that the distinction between those two non-conceptual states is inferred through their outflow (*niṣyandana*).
One knows in this same way even by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) [wisdom].
Others maintain that there exists an untainted aspect (*anāsrava-ākāra*) distinct from the sixteen aspects;
by means of that very [aspect], one knows in this way.

If, according to the scriptural statement, "that which is based upon that is knowledge and vision," the untainted knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpāda-jñāna*)—which is the fruit of conventional knowledge such as the full comprehension of suffering—is thus being described.
As for this which is said: "The cognition of destruction and non-arising is not vision;
it is not seeing."
That contradicts it; therefore he says:
"But the statement regarding 'seeing' [is made] because of the objection to the Bhāṣya."
Regarding this statement in the treatise that "knowledge is vision," it arises from the implications of the commentary;
for in the context of the knowledge of suffering and so forth, it is recited as "knowledge, vision, science, intellect, and awakening."
This reading of those who recite that [text] follows as a consequence of its recitation;
however, the meaning is not that for them the knowledge of destruction and non-arising has the nature of vision (*darśana*) or the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi*).
Or, "because its mode of operation is perceptual" means that the mode of operation of these two cognitions is perceptual; thus, this is their perceptual mode of operation.
Because of that state,

there is no mention of "seeing" or "speaking" regarding these two; for in this pair of cognitions, because they are inferential or like scriptural knowledge, their mode of operation is indirect (parokṣa).
And "vision" is intended as having a direct mode of operation,
such as visual consciousness;
because of its similarity to that, these two types of knowledge are also called "vision."
Therefore it has been said:
for this very reason, as stated in the treatise, whatever is cognition is also perception, just like the operation of direct perception.
However, there may be the view that [the latter] is not knowledge; the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) belonging to the culmination of clear realization (*ābhisamayāntika*) are such.
What is meant by this is that while "vision-ness" (*darśanatva*) is admitted for these two, "view-ness" (*dṛṣṭitva*) is not.

In this context, among those ten knowledges (*jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is [included] as conventional knowledge itself by way of inclusion through its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); and it is also one part— that is, one portion— of the single knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), for of that [knowledge],
which is both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), only the portion that is with-outflows is conventional knowledge.
The "undefiled portion" refers to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*); among the ten knowledges, it is one knowledge, namely *dharmajñāna* itself,
which is the undefiled portion.

Among the ten knowledges, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is one knowledge, namely the knowledge of phenomena itself; it also constitutes a portion of seven [other] knowledges— namely, the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, others' minds, destruction, and non-arising— in what way?
For the knowledge of suffering has the nature of both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge;
that portion of it which is dharma-knowledge is dharma-knowledge itself.

In this way, for the knowledge of origination up to the knowledge of non-arising— which have the nature of dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge— that portion which is dharma-knowledge is dharma-knowledge itself,
but not the portion that is subsequent knowledge.

However, regarding the knowledge of others' minds— which has the nature of dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge— the portion that is dharma-knowledge is itself dharma-knowledge;
likewise, subsequent knowledge is one [type of] subsequent knowledge and also a portion of the seven [knowledges].

That portion of those very same [knowledges], such as the knowledge of suffering and so forth, which belongs to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), should be understood as "subsequent knowledge"; thus,
the knowledge of suffering is one among the ten knowledges.
That very knowledge of suffering and a portion of the four— namely, the dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of destruction, and knowledge of non-arising— constitute these four,
beginning with dharma-knowledge, which have the four noble truths as their objects.
That portion of these [knowledges] which has the truth of suffering as its object is the knowledge of suffering,
and no other portion.
In this same way, the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of cessation should each be applied accordingly:
either the knowledge of origin or the knowledge of cessation is one [distinct] knowledge,

as is the portion of the four knowledges— namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*)— which has origin as its object or cessation as its object.
That knowledge of origin and knowledge of cessation,
as well as the knowledge of the path, constitute one among the ten knowledges; that very knowledge of the path is itself one knowledge and also a portion of five [knowledges].

Among the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*),
those portions which constitute the path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) have the nature of path-knowledge.

That knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is not the other; thus, among the ten knowledges, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is one specific knowledge, and it is also a portion of four [other] knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

For these four knowledges have as their intrinsic nature the knowledge of one's own mind and the knowledge of another's mind; that portion among them which pertains to the knowledge of another's mind is what constitutes the knowledge of another's mind.

"Not the other" refers to the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), which is one among the ten knowledges; that very knowledge of destruction, by way of its own nature, is comprised within six [knowledges]: the knowledges of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)— which has as its outflow (*niṣyanda*) the knowledge of such aspects as "Suffering has been fully understood by me"—
is included within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) when it takes as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the desire realm.
That which has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is either the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge of the path;
therein, that portion of these [knowledges] which possesses such a characteristic [is the conventional knowledge].
That is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and no other; thus it is said to be a portion of six [knowledges].
Likewise, the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) is one among the ten knowledges; that very same [knowledge] is the knowledge of non-arising.

And the portion belonging to the six knowledges— the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), suffering, origin, cessation, and the path— that portion which has as its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) such modes [of cognition] as "Suffering has been fully known by me; it is not to be known again," that is non-arising knowledge (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
That subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the realms of form and formlessness; it is not the other part.
It is said that there is a portion of the six [consciousnesses] because of their having the same aspect and the same object-field.
The aspect and the object-field constitute "aspect and object-field";
the aspect and the aspect-object-field constitute "aspect-aspect-object-field."
Therefore,
conventional knowledge is "by way of its own nature" (svabhāvataḥ);
that is, conventional knowledge exists by virtue of its own intrinsic nature.
Or, conventional knowledge is knowledge regarding the conventional;
why is this so? He says:
because it is not knowledge of the ultimate truth (aparamārthajñānatvāt).
Dharma-knowledge is the antidote to the desire realm,
while subsequent knowledge is the antidote to the higher realms;
for thus it is stated in the treatise:
What is dharma-knowledge?
It is the untainted knowledge regarding the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm;
it is that untainted knowledge regarding the cause of the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm.
The untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm,
and the untainted knowledge regarding the path for the abandonment of the conditioned phenomena associated with the desire realm— this is called dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna).
Furthermore, that untainted knowledge which exists within the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and on the stage of the knowledge of phenomena is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna).
What, then, is "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna)?
The untainted knowledge regarding conditioned phenomena associated with the realms of form and formlessness;
the untainted knowledge regarding the cause of conditioned phenomena associated with the realms of form and formlessness;
and the untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of conditioned phenomena associated with the realms of form and formlessness.
The untainted knowledge regarding the abandonment of the conditioned factors associated with the realms of form and formlessness on the path is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
furthermore, it is also that untainted knowledge which exists within subsequent knowledge and on the level of subsequent knowledge.
This is called subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
In terms of its aspects, it consists of the knowledges of suffering and origination;

it is so defined by their aspects alone and not by their objects, because there is no difference between those two insofar as they both have the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as their characteristic.
For it is stated in the treatise: "What is the knowledge of suffering?
It is the untainted knowledge of one who attends to the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self."
This is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origin?
It is the untainted knowledge that arises when one attends to that which is tainted and causal as being the cause, the origin, the source, and the condition.
This is called the knowledge of origin by way of aspect and object; as for the knowledges of cessation and the path,
they are established by way of both aspect and object.
For it is stated in the treatise: "What is the knowledge of cessation?
It is the untainted knowledge of one who attends to cessation as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as renunciation."
This is called the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the path?
It is the untainted knowledge that arises for one who attends to the path as the path, as the correct method, as practice, and as leading to liberation.
This is called "knowledge of the path.
The inclusion of the term "initially" is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),
for that [latter] also arises within the mental continuum of one who has accomplished what was to be done.
Because it has all uncontaminated states as its cause:

with reference to the ten knowledges that have first arisen, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) has all uncontaminated states as its cause by way of being a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*);
however, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) does not have all uncontaminated states as its cause.
For the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is not its cause, because it is superior;

since the whole [knowledge] is the antidote for the whole, the entire *dharmajñāna*—which is comprised within the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), has the four noble truths as its object, and consists of five types—is the antidote for the entirety of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as comprised by what is to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation. Thus, it is said that *dharmajñāna* is the antidote specifically for the desire realm.
However, there is the possibility that even in the form and formless realms there is dharma-knowledge;
for cessation and the path, though they do not fall within the realms, are established as being neither inferior even when belonging to lower levels.

However, it should be understood that on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) does not have as its object the truths of suffering and origin belonging to lower stages or inferior levels, because it is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyadhātu*).

However, the inclusion of those [defilements] belonging to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by seeing is because they are to be destroyed by the receptivities to subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*).
If that is so, why does subsequent knowledge—which takes cessation and the path as its objects and is comprised within the path of cultivation—not serve as the antidote to all three realms?
Because the desire realm has already been conquered.

By means of dharma-knowledge itself, the desire realm is conquered first; subsequently, subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) arises. Because the desire realm has already been conquered, that [subsequent knowledge] is not an antidote to the desire realm.
But because the realm of form and the formless realm have not yet been mastered, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) is appropriately the antidote;
whereas "subsequent" (anvaya) means that which follows after, thus subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) [is the antidote] in every respect.
Although these are included within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), we shall explain those aspects (ākāra) such as impermanence and so forth later on.
It possesses sixteen aspects because, in the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, there is the apprehension of specific and general characteristics;
that is, through the apprehension of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the apprehension of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it is meant] forms such as "eat," "stand," and "go";
for these are not indeed forms of specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa),
but rather what?
"Of such a nature indeed" refers to both, namely,
that which is with outflows and that which is without outflows.
"As for the phrase 'then that' and so forth,
the intention is that there is a simultaneous apprehension of both passion and the mind;
furthermore, the Sūtra is recited as follows:"
One knows a mind with lust as "a mind with lust" according to reality; one knows a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust" according to reality—
just as it is with a mind with lust and a mind free from lust.

In this way, one understands as it truly is: "with hatred," "free from hatred," "with delusion," "free from delusion," "contracted," "distracted," "sunk," "exerted," "agitated," "unagitated," "unpeaceful," "cultivated," "unliberated," and "liberated"—just as in the case of the simultaneous grasping of a cloth and its stain;
for just as there is no simultaneous grasping of the cloth and the stain.
In the same way,
when a cognition arises with a delimited form such as "cloth," it does not at that time apprehend the dirt.
And when a cognition arises in the delimited form "it is not stained," it does not then grasp the cloth as being "associated with passion."

Some say that "being possessed of passion through association" (*saṃsṛṣṭa-sarāgatā*) is due to conjunction (*samprayoga*), while "being bound by passion" (*saṃyukta-sarāgatā*) is due to the persistence of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of passion;
others say it is because [the object] is the objective support for the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of passion.
"By two" means by way of being associated with passion through being mixed with passion and by way of being conjoined with passion; other than those, it is "with outflows."
That which is afflicted, indeterminate, or mundane wholesome is "with lust" by virtue of being associated with lust;
thus both of these are [considered such]. But for what reason, according to the opinion of some, is the antidote to lust called "free from lust"?
For this reason, they say:
"If it were dissociated from attachment simply because it is free from attachment, then it would also be dissociated from other afflictions,
such as hatred and so forth."
It may be that even that [state] is "free from passion" (*vigatarāga*), for although it is associated with passion, it is not conjoined with it; yet,
it is not stated in the Sūtra that a state associated with hatred and so forth is "free from passion."
Because of such statements as "accompanied by hatred" and "accompanied by delusion," however,
for those for whom the antidote to attachment is "free from attachment," this is not a fault.
"For the antidote to attachment is not associated with hatred and so forth.
If that is the case, then [the detailed explanation follows]:
if a mind associated with attachment is "with attachment" (*sarāga*), then the antidote to attachment would be "free from attachment" (*vigatarāga*).
That which is not its antidote is the non-antidote for a mind possessed of passion;
it is an unafflicted, unobscured-neutral mind that is neither "possessed of passion" because it is not associated with passion.
It is not free from passion, because it is not the antidote to passion;
and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the same logical consequence should be applied to [the notions] "possessing hatred" and "possessing delusion."
But how is it that in this sutra a mind associated with hatred is "with hatred," while the antidote to hatred is "free from hatred"?
For if a mind were "free from hatred" simply by not being associated with hatred, [then the distinction would be redundant].
Some say that [the mind] may be associated with other afflictions;
if that were so, then a non-afflicted mind that is not the antidote to those [afflictions] would be neither "with hatred" nor "free from hatred.
In the same way, it should be said that a mind is "with delusion" or "free from delusion" [according to whether it is associated with or not the antidote to delusion].
Therefore, a mind accompanied by passion (*sarāga*) should be understood here as being so by way of being conjoined with passion;
other Abhidharmikas maintain that, because of the word "also" (*api*), it is also by way of being associated with passion.

In this way, up to "with delusion" and "free from delusion," it should be understood that in this Sūtra, a mind is "with hatred" by virtue of being associated with hatred, and "with delusion" by virtue of being associated with delusion; thus,
it is due to the contraction [of the object].
A wholesome mind is not associated with distraction;
therefore, because it is concentrated upon its object,
it would be both "contracted" and "distracted."
"Due to association with afflicted torpor":
torpor is of two kinds, afflicted and non-afflicted.
For that very same mind would be both "contracted" because it is afflicted and associated with torpor,
and "distracted" because it is afflicted; thus there would be the fault of confusion and contradiction with the treatise.
How does one understand a contracted mind as it truly is?
This is explained in detail in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Among those, first of all, subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) cannot have a contracted mind as its object,
because there is no torpor above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and because subsequent knowledge does not take the desire realm as its object; furthermore,
path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) also cannot have a contracted mind as its object.
For the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) has the path as its object and is not included within the path; moreover, a mind associated with torpor (middha) is not [the knowledge of the path].
Therefore, it should have been stated thus: "That knowledge is of two kinds."

However, for those who describe it as both knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), asserting that "the mind is contracted because of the contraction of the wholesome object," these two faults do not occur.
Since that [knowledge] is not associated with non-afflicted *middha* (torpor), it does not fall under the categories of "withdrawn" (*saṃkṣipta*) or "distracted" (*vikṣipta*),
nor is there any contradiction with the treatise.
It is established that wholesome mind— whether included within or excluded from the three realms— and its corresponding knowledge constitute the four knowledges (*jñāna*).
The untainted knowledge that takes as its object the wholesome minds of the form and formless realms is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*);
furthermore, when it takes as its object the wholesome states subsumed under the Path, it is also path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*),
because it is cultivated by those with limited purification.
The meaning is: because it is practiced by those with few roots of merit;
"because of the opposite of that" means because it is practiced by those with great purification.

Regarding the relative smallness or greatness of the factors from the roots up to power, it should be understood that for each root, they are respectively limited (*parītta*) or extensive (*mahadgata*) according to their degree of smallness or greatness.
How so? It is said:
for the defiled (*kliṣṭa*), the root is established by two unwholesome roots—namely, delusion (*moha*)—and either greed (*lobha*) or hatred (*dveṣa*).

Because these two do not coexist within a single bundle (*kalāpa*), the wholesome [mind] possesses three [roots]: non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for these are inseparable from one another, and there is an absence of cultivation regarding future states of that same kind.

Because there is no acquisition (*pratilambha*) through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of future factors belonging to the afflicted class, and because it is a logical principle that "wholesome conditioned phenomena are to be cultivated," [the path] is accompanied by three aggregates— the aggregates of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations (*saṃskāra*)—
but not by the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because there is no second consciousness within a single complex (*kalāpa*),
and because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself by means of itself,
[the mind] is indeed wholesome when accompanied by a great retinue, owing to the presence of the cultivation of future states of that same kind.

And it is accompanied by four aggregates: by those three beginning with feeling, and by the aggregate of form comprised within the meditative and uncontaminated restraints, because of the impossibility of their following the mind.
Furthermore, it is indeed afflicted because it possesses little strength;

but is not the wholesome also weak? For although the five wholesome aggregates are eradicated by a single moment of wrong view, that [wholesome root] is not absolutely severed, since it is reconnected again.

However, by means of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*), there is the absolute eradication of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "for this reason also," it is meant that [this follows] from what was previously stated;
"because it is their antidote" means because it is the antidote to restlessness (*auddhatya*).

Thus, regarding "not calmed" and "calmed": it is "not calmed" when afflicted due to association with restlessness (*auddhatya*), and it is "calmed" when wholesome because it is the antidote to that; thus, by virtue of being associated or dissociated from the afflictions (*kleśa*), it becomes either not calmed or calmed.
That which is concentrated is wholesome because it is the antidote to that;
that is, because it is the antidote to distraction, by means of both the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice.
The acquisition of what was not previously obtained is "attainment" (pratilambha);
its manifestation is "cultivation" (niṣevaṇa);
these two are indeed the [two kinds of] cultivation.
Because those two have not been cultivated, that which is uncultivated is indeed afflicted; for it cannot be cultivated as a future state like the wholesome,
nor is it worthy of repeated practice due to its inferiority.
Regarding the statement "the cultivation of wholesome conditioned phenomena is called acquisition and practice," the meaning of "by those two" is "by acquisition and practice."
Because it is not liberated by way of intrinsic nature or by way of the continuum; that is to say,
due to its association with the afflictions, it is not liberated by intrinsic nature,
and because the continuum of one whose afflictions are exhausted does not arise [again], it is not liberated by the liberation of the continuum.

The wholesome [state], however, is liberated from torpor and drowsiness because it is dissociated from the afflictions and arises within a mental continuum in which the afflictions have been exhausted.

"Associated with lethargy and drowsiness, internally accompanied by cessation"— this concludes that very point; however, [the phrase] "not endowed with insight" provides the explanation for "subtly distracted," namely, "followed by a diffusion."
Regarding the statement "because it is not admitted that what is afflicted and accompanied by torpor is distracted," on what grounds is distraction not admitted here?
Is it because it is not admitted that there is no distraction in an afflicted mind accompanied by torpor?
Or rather, even though distraction exists here, it is not asserted because it is established as being precisely inclusion;
thus some explain it in one way, while others explain it in both ways.

For that which is defiled other than what is associated with torpor is asserted to be "distracted," whereas what is associated with torpor— whether defiled or non-defiled— is without distinction simply "withdrawn."
Others, however, explain that what is associated with *middha* (torpor) is precisely "contracted."
Others, however, explain that what is associated with torpor is indeed concentrated (*saṅkṣipta*) and not distracted (*vikṣipta*).
However, that which is diffused among sense objects is precisely what is called "distracted"; therefore, since [the definition] is not admitted here for a mind associated with *middha* (torpor),
it is better to accept a contradiction with the treatise.
The intended meaning is that the Abhidharma treatise was not spoken by the Buddha;
because it speaks of characteristics as being undifferentiated,
all those [states] are said to be afflicted.

The definition of being afflicted (*kliṣṭatva*) for these states, beginning with the distracted (*vikṣipta*) and ending with the unliberated (*avimukta*), is their association with the universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*). Furthermore, because the characteristics of the contracted (*saṃkṣipta*), the exerted (*pragṛhīta*), and so forth have been stated without distinction, it follows that no specific difference in meaning has been expressed; such is the connection [of the argument].
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of those who are great, not agitated, tranquil, composed, cultivated, and liberated;
their wholesomeness (*kuśala*) is undifferentiated.
But what, then, is this wholesomeness?
"The association with the universal wholesome factors is indeed not unspoken," such is the detailed explanation;
"vai" is an indeclinable particle.
"Because it was not said that it was not [said]"—the two negations mean that it was indeed said;
what was said?
The specific meaning of the words.

To the question "How so?", he says: even though distracted states (*vikṣipta*) and others are alike in their general nature of being afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), the mind is called "distracted" due to its association with distraction, "sunk" due to its association with laziness (*kauśidya*), and "agitated" due to its association with restlessness (*auddhatya*). Thus, because these specific defects are demonstrated, the distinction in meaning is indeed established.

In this way, even regarding the wholesome [mind], because the specific qualities of the "contracted" (saṅkṣipta) and so forth are demonstrated, this statement— "this wholesome mind is contracted," "it is exerted," and so on— merely restates a distinction already explained in detail; for it does not resolve the contradiction with the Sūtra,
since in the Sūtra the "contracted" is said to be accompanied by sloth and torpor (styāna-middha).
That which is afflicted through association with *styāna* (sloth) and conjoined with *middha* (torpor) is "withdrawn" (*saṅkṣipta*), but it is not wholesome,
because *styāna* belongs to the category of the great ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*).

And as for the passage in the Sūtra, "if," and so forth: if, in your *Nitya-sūtra*, the Blessed One had intended that what is sluggish is itself [identical to] what is excited, then the separate mention of the sluggish and the excited would not have been stated.
To the question "How so?", he says: at whatever time the mind is sunken, associated with indolence,
apprehensive of sinking, and fearing that "this [mind] will become sunken"— that is what is meant by being apprehensive of sinking.
"It would not be a fixed rule that at that time it is the wrong occasion for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; rather,
one would have to say that at that time it is also the wrong occasion for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of investigation of phenomena and energy."
What is the reason?
It is because that very same mind which was sluggish is now considered agitated;
likewise, at whatever time the mind becomes agitated or is apprehensive of agitation.

It would not be the case that there is a fixed rule stating, "At that time, it is the wrong time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy"; rather, one would have to say, "At that time,
it is also the wrong time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
What is the reason?
For one might have to state, without distinction, that the very same agitated mind is also "sunk."
At whatever time the mind is sluggish or apprehensive of sluggishness, or agitated or apprehensive of agitation,
that is not the time for the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment consisting of serenity, concentration, equanimity, investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy; however,
the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is not excluded because mindfulness is omnipresent.

Since it is stated in the Sūtra, "I indeed declare that mindfulness is omnipresent, because it is established even when not explicitly mentioned in both types of minds," how then can the Vaibhāṣika maintain that [mindfulness] is only that which is sunken?
That very [mind] is intended as "agitated," and it is understood that a sunken mind is afflicted because of its association with laziness,
according to the statement: "An agitated mind is afflicted because of its association with restlessness."
Furthermore, what is meant here by the "separate cultivation" of the factors of enlightenment?
Does it mean that at one time there is only the cultivation of pliancy and so forth, but not the cultivation of the investigation of phenomena and so forth;
and at another time there is only the cultivation of the investigation of phenomena and so forth, but not the cultivation of pliancy and so forth—this is what is called separate cultivation?
Their cultivation is intended as mental attention (*manasikāra*), not as their actual manifestation; thus,
"mental attention" means making them the object of focus (*ālambanīkaraṇa*).
When the mind is sluggish (*līna*), it is the wrong time for taking serenity (*praśrabdhi*) and so forth as an object or for applying effort;
likewise, when the mind is agitated (*uddhata*), it is the wrong time for the investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*) and so forth.
However, this does not mean that their manifestation is not desired in cultivation.
At that time, pliancy and the other [factors] are not to be brought into manifestation;
rather, the investigation of phenomena and the others are to be brought into manifestation— or else, the investigation of phenomena and the others are not to be brought into manifestation.
"But pliancy and so forth must be cultivated;
thus, 'laziness is predominant here' is the full statement," where laziness is predominant while restlessness exists in a subordinate state.
That [mind] is "sunk" (līna) when restlessness (auddhatya) is predominant; however, when lethargy (kausīdya) is predominant,
it is called "excited" (uddhata).
Thus, because of this distinction between the two, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra regarding their separate mention;

for they coexist, being present simultaneously within a single complex (kalāpa). We say that "that very same [state] is sluggish" and "that very same [state] is excited," because the sluggish state is afflicted due to its association with indolence (kausīdya).
"The teacher says that [the mind] is afflicted when it is agitated because of its association with agitation; however,
this is intentional, for such is not the intention in the Sūtra."
Because it is said that a mind is "sunk" when laxity is predominant and "agitated" when restlessness is predominant;
for [the Sūtra] states in detail: "At whatever time the mind is sunk," and so forth, but it does not specify it as "predominant in laxity" or "predominant in restlessness."
As for what was said— that every mind associated with attachment is "with attachment"—
how was that stated?
In that context, a mind associated with attachment is "with attachment" in two ways.

Because of the statement, "Anything other than that is with-outflows (sāsrava) and possessed of attachment through conjunction (saṃyoga-sarāga)," and because of the statement, "In this context, a mind is to be understood as 'with-attachment' even by virtue of being conjoined with attachment," it follows that even the uncontaminated (anāsrava) mind of a learner (śaikṣa) would be [classified as] with-attachment.
If it is thought that [the mind] has passion as its object because passion still remains within the continuum of a trainee (śaikṣa),
then [it must be asked]: what is the object of that passion?

In that case, would even the *āsrava*-tainted mind of an Arhat be considered "possessed of passion" (*sarāga*) because it is "associated with passion" (*rāga-saṃyukta*), since it serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) for another's passion? One who knows the minds of others, or the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), might thus apprehend it as "possessed of passion. Now, if it is thought that [the Arhat’s mind] is not taken as an object by passion...
Then it is asked: "In what way is that 'with outflows' (sāsrava)?
If it is argued that it is because its object is the universal afflictions (sāmānyakleśa), [we reply: no.

Now, if it is thought that because it is the object (*ālambana*) of the universal afflictions— namely, views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*)— it is therefore "with outflows" (*sāsrava*),
then one would likewise have to include the mind of an Arhat as being with outflows, since it has delusion (*moha*) as its object.
Delusion (*moha*) is also a universal affliction; however,
since the mind of an Arhat can become the object (*ālambana*) of another's delusion,
and because the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not have possession (*prāpti*) as its object, [delusion is not included therein].

Since it is maintained that the knowledge of another's mind has the mind and mental factors as its object, it is not "with lust" (sarāga) by virtue of being conjoined with lust through association with the acquisition of lust;
nor is it [so called] because it takes as its object the lust that has that mind as its object.
The word "that" refers to that mind belonging to another which is apprehended by the knowledge of others' minds;
it is that mind which is the object, and attachment has that very mind as its object.
The object of this knowledge of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*) is that very mind; it takes as its object the passion (*rāga*) directed toward that mind.
For the knowledge of another's mind does not take such passion as its object because it is too remote;
indeed, the knowledge of another's mind has each individual substance as its sphere of operation.
Furthermore, the knowledge of another's mind does not grasp the object (*ālambana*) of that mind,
because it is stated that such knowledge is independent of both aspect (*ākāra*) and object (*ālambana*), and because it is also stated that "one knows this mind to be lustful."
Therefore, for this reason as well, a mind is not "with lust" merely because of its conjunction with lust; rather,
the intention is that it is "free from lust" when it is not associated [with lust],
even though the possession of lust still exists.

Regarding that, the phrase "it was said with reference to that" indicates that it was said with reference to the attainment of and the departure from passion (*rāga*) and so forth, and not with reference to their association (*samprayoga*). The intention is that this is because it demonstrates freedom from passion (*vairāgya*) regarding the three realms by stating, "one whose nature is not subject to return in the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
As for the passage beginning with "But was it not said," and so forth:

Where is this stated in the Sūtra? It is stated in detail up to: "For if a mind not associated with attachment were to be 'free from attachment,' then even a mind associated with other afflictions would be free from attachment.
With this underlying intention, [it is said]: "Even a mind associated with other afflictions is free from attachment because it is dissociated from attachment."
If this were so, then [the Buddha] would not have said "possessing hatred," "possessing delusion," and so forth; therefore, he says:
"But that is free from passion," and so on.
However, that mind associated with hatred and so forth is not grasped as "free from attachment" simply because it is free from attachment;
rather,
it is characterized as "with hatred," "with delusion," and so on, because it is distinguished by its association with hatred and the like.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the terms mentioned in the sūtras—such as "concentrated" (*saṅkṣipta*), "distracted" (*vikṣipta*), and so forth—are included here;
otherwise, [the phrase] "if... and so on would follow:
if one were to cognize that [the mind] is attached to this object, such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, then that [cognition] would also have form as its objective support (*ālambana*).
And that being the case, it would not be knowledge of another's mind, because its objective support (ālambana) is form;
furthermore, for one who grasps another's mind while taking that [form] as its objective support, it would follow that there is a grasping of its own nature.
For if the grasping of another's mind together with its objective support were intended, it would be grasped by a knowledge of both self and other's minds.
It is possible that when one who knows another's mind perceives that person's mind,

that person might also take the mind of that knower of others' minds as an object; and consequently, because of the thorough knowledge of the very object of his own [cognition], he would take his own mind as the object of his knowledge of another's mind.
And it is not the case that this very same mind can apprehend itself, nor can everything [be apprehended by one mind]; such is the detailed explanation.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: its object consists of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a substance (*dravya*), as well as the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), those that are present, those associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and those that are unassociated [with any realm].
The inclusion of the term "substance" is for the purpose of excluding conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*);
the inclusion of the term "specific characteristic" is for the purpose of precluding general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The mention of "mind and mental factors" is for the purpose of distinguishing them from form and so forth;
the mention of "present" is for the purpose of excluding the past and future;
and the mention of "another's continuum" is for the purpose of excluding one's own continuum.

The inclusion of those associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as well as those not so associated, is for the purpose of excluding those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and for the purpose of excluding the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Thus, one abiding in the path of seeing does not bring forth the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); therefore, there is no [knowledge of others' minds] comprised within the path of seeing.
For the path of seeing does not have as its object a mind or mental factors that are interrupted; rather,
it is found on the path of cultivation—
meaning that it is subsumed within the path of cultivation.
"Disjoined from emptiness and signlessness" means it is disjoined from both the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) and the concentration on signlessness (*ānimitta-samādhi*);
the concentration on emptiness is associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
The signless concentration is associated with the knowledge of cessation,
yet it is not the knowledge of others' minds, nor the knowledge of suffering, nor the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, because of the difference in their aspects and objects.
Therefore, it is said that [the knowledge] is dissociated from those two;
by implication, it is stated that it can exist as associated with the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi),
meaning it is not comprised within the knowledge of destruction (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).

The meaning is that it is not subsumed by the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) nor by the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), nor does it have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge of destruction or non-arising.
What is the reason?
The knowledge of others' minds has as its intention the investigation and search for the existence of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of entities;

it is not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) nor the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and thus it is not subsumed by those two, and it is also intended to exclude the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
For that [path] is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*),

whereas the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is the path of liberation and the path of excellence (*vimukti-viśeṣamārga*); thus, even though these two are ultimate, they are categorized as conventional.
Regarding the ultimate characteristic, or that which plays with the ultimate, these two are "ultimate" because they resort to the conventional; for these two resort to the conventional.
Therefore, the aspects of emptiness and selflessness do not exist; how then can these two conform to conventional reality? "Birth is exhausted for me."

"I know no further existence beyond this"— how is it that these two, being untainted (*anāsrava*), possess such aspects (*ākāra*) through subsequent conventional usage (*anuvyavahāra*) by their power, respectively?

The phrase "by another knowledge" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Since the two conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) produced subsequently to that [ultimate knowledge] proceed with such aspects, they are said to partake of the conventional by way of being its outflow (*niṣyanda*).
The intention is that, in their primary sense, those two do not partake of the conventional;
for since they proceed as if partaking of the view of self through their outflow (*niṣyanda*),
they are therefore associated with exactly fourteen aspects, excluding the aspects of emptiness and non-self.
"By that which is unconnected" means by that which is untainted (*anāsrava*);
"impermanent" means from the perspective of impermanence;
for here the suffix *-tasi* is employed in its own sense.
In this way, this suffix should be understood everywhere;
alternatively, even without the abstract suffix, there is an expression emphasizing the state [of being], as in: "impermanence is the state by way of an impermanent form."
In the same way, this should be applied elsewhere as well:
"This possibility exists" and "This reality exists"—
these two aspects are also untainted (*anāsrava*).
"This is a possibility" means "this is its characteristic";
"this exists" means "this is the cause";
one should understand this according to what is established by yoga.
The meaning is that one should understand [it] without error;
"this is not its meaning" refers to the detailed explanation of this sentence or of its two constituent words.

If one thinks, "There is this possibility, there is this matter; there is this potential, there is this application, that one might understand [reality] through impermanence and so forth," if this is the view,
it is not so.
Because it is not stated elsewhere— that is,
because the two words are not mentioned in another passage—
[it is understood that] "by means of what is to be abandoned by vision."
By way of viewing [them] as self and as belonging to self— that is, by means of a mind associated with the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
"From annihilationism, it is eternalism" refers to the view of grasping at extremes;
"from no cause, from non-action, [and] from denial" refers to false view.
As "foremost," "best," "distinguished," and "supreme" through the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
as "purification," "liberation," and "leading to deliverance" through the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);
and as "doubt," "indecision," and "hesitation" through doubt (*vicikitsā*).
"One might be attached" refers to passion;
"one might hate" refers to aversion;
"one might think [oneself superior]" refers to pride.
"May he be deluded"— by this [statement] "through delusion," one should understand that it is improperly performed;
thus, he concludes by showing that there is a perversion regarding the self and so forth.
In this sentence as well, the reading would have been "it will be," and since it is not so,
it is understood that this is not otherwise.
Regarding "seven substantial entities":
the four aspects of suffering constitute four substantial entities, while each of the aspects of origin and so forth constitutes one; thus, there are seven.
That which is the aspect of the cause (hetu) is itself the origin (samudaya), the source (prabhava), and the condition (pratyaya); these are merely synonyms and not different in meaning,
just as "Śakra," "Indra," and "Purandara" refer to the same deity.
Thus, cessation alone is peaceful, sublime, and an escape—this is one aspect;
and the path alone is the right method, the practice, and the leading to liberation—this is another aspect.
This is what is meant.

Yogins should bring the four aspects of suffering into manifestation individually; however, they should bring each of the aspects of cause and so forth into manifestation one by one. Thus, according to this [author's] own view, there are sixteen [aspects] in substance.
Thus the Vaibhāṣikas explain that because all aspects— such as those of origin and so forth, just like the aspect of suffering— must each be manifested individually,
they state that the aspects have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since [their manifestation] is dependent upon conditions; such is the detailed explanation.
It is not of fixed existence because it is impermanent; the meaning is that it is dependent on conditions, since its birth is bound to conditions.
"Because its nature is affliction" means that its nature is suffering.
"By the opposite side" (vipakṣeṇa) means "by the counter-position" (pratipakṣeṇa),
since the position that is contradictory [to another] is called the "opposite side" (vipakṣa).
"By way of the nature of a seed as the cause" indicates the superior state of the cause; here, the word "yoga" has the sense of "principle," as in the case of the primordial seed.
"Arising through the mode of manifestation" indicates that the cause is in an immediate state,
because it arises immediately after that moment; it is called "arising" (*samudeti*) in the sense that [the effect] emerges from this.
"Origination by way of continuity" indicates non-interruption through the connection of a series,
like the sequence of seed, sprout, stalk, stem, and so forth.
In the sense of bringing about [an effect], it is called a "condition" (*pratyaya*);
this shows that it arises from many factors such as causes (*hetu*) and so forth,
just as a jar is produced from many things such as a lump of clay, a staff, and so on.
Similarly,
"from the extinguishing of the fire" means from the extinguishing of the fires of passion, hatred, and delusion.
"Because it is free from affliction" means because it is free from suffering;
"because it is devoid of all defects."

Because it is liberated from all causes of suffering, and because it is consistent with the meaning of "going," it is appropriately termed *nirvāṇa*— whether by virtue of its logical consistency, its conformity to reason, or its application of skillful means.
It is called the "path" (*pratipad*) in the sense of correct practice; it is the path because one proceeds toward *nirvāṇa* by means of it,
and thus it is "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*).
It is called "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*) because it is capable of bringing about ultimate departure; it is called "impermanent" (*anitya*) because it is not ultimate—
whereas previously, it was described as impermanent by virtue of its non-existence prior to arising.
Now he shows [this] by means of "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
"because it has become a burden" (*abhinyāsabhūtatvāt*) means "because it has become a load" (*bhārabhūtatvāt*).
The meaning is that by suffering, which has become a burden, that person is broken or overcome;
this is because they lack the power of their own will.
One whose nature is to act according to desire is a "kāmakārin";
one who does not act according to desire is an "akāmakārin," and because of that state, he is "anātman" (without self).
This meaning is also stated in a Sūtra:
"Monks, if form were the self, form would not lead to affliction for the self."

And because one can obtain with respect to form itself [the thought] "let it be thus" or "let it not be thus," based on the acceptance of the etymological definition that "the self is that which acts according to its desire," [it follows that] the cause is established by means of scripture and reasoning.
For "reasoning" (*hetu*) is so called because it leads (*hinoti*) one to understanding; thus, it is a cause.
The meaning is "it arises from this";
by way of "emerging," the meaning is that it is as if emerging from the future path.
"By way of spreading" means by way of continuity;
"condition" (pratyaya) is so called in the sense of that which causes [an effect] to correspond [to its cause].
The intended meaning is that [the agent] is the primary factor in the act of birth;
"separation from connection" means due to the cessation of prior suffering.

The meaning is that cessation (*nirodha*) is the termination of the connection with what follows (*uttara*), because it is free from the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), that is, because it is free from arising, passing away, and alteration while persisting.

"Because it is the supreme consolation" means that because all suffering is eradicated, it is the ultimate security; and "the path" is so called in the sense that it does not conflict with the city of Nirvana,
for by this [path], the city of Nirvana is neither contradicted nor deceived.
Rather,
it is indeed that which is practiced; therefore,
it is called "the practice" (pratipat) because one practices by means of it.
"Rooted in desire" means having desire as their cause;
here, "desire" is a synonym for craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Arising from desire" means originating from desire;
that is, they are of the nature of desire.
The meaning is that they have desire as their condition (*chandapratyaya*);
the word "source" (*prabhava*) should simply be recited later by the Abhidharmikas— this is the ellipsis to be supplied in the sentence.
The intention is that one must follow the Sūtra;
[it says] "by way of cause, by way of origin, by way of condition, and by way of source.
What, then, is the distinction between these various types of desire?

Regarding "the desire for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-cchanda*) as 'I am' through non-differentiation": having determined that this is a single substance, there is a longing for self-existence with respect to all five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*) through the non-differentiation of "I am," by way of not taking as an object a present entity of self-existence characterized by other modes, or by way of not taking as an object self-existence belonging to the three times; this is the first [type].
"May I be" through non-differentiation is, furthermore, a longing for mere rebirth and not a longing for a specific form; this is the second.
"May I be thus" means "may I be of this kind"— this is the third, the desire for renewed existence through differentiation;
and the fourth is the desire for the bond of rebirth.
Rebirth-linking itself is bondage,
or bondage resulting from rebirth-linking is "rebirth-linking bondage";
therein, desire is longing— this is the fourth [hindrance].
Or, as for the fourth [member], it is the desire for the formative activity of karma;
that is, the desire directed toward the formative activity of karma.
Explaining how those "wishes" (chanda) denoted by the words "root" and so forth are [the basis] for the thought, "I shall give a gift in such and such a manner," he says:
"In that regard, the first," and so forth.

The "original cause" (*ādikāraṇa*) is either the beginning that is the cause, or the cause at the beginning; because of that state, [the teachings] are rooted in intention (*chanda*). For the word "root" (*mūla*) has the sense of a "cause" (*hetu*).
"Just as a seed is to a fruit":
just as a seed is the primary cause and the remote cause of a fruit, so too is this primary craving the cause of suffering.
"Because of its origination by means of that" means:

because of the origination of renewed existence (*punarbhava*) by means of that second desire (*chanda*), there is a production of the fruit through a succession of moments, just as the production of a fruit occurs through a succession beginning with the sprout.
Thus, the production of the sprout and so forth in succession is the origination (*samudaya*) of the fruit.
In the same way,
the third desire is "may I be thus," which has suffering of that same kind as its condition.

The intention is that whatever the specific mode of the desire for renewed existence may be, it becomes the condition for suffering of that same specific mode; because it possesses a specific form, a fruit that is itself of a specific nature arises—
just as the field, water, manure, and so forth [are conditions] for a fruit.
A dry cow-dung pellet,
and by the word "etcetera," wind, sunlight, and so forth are included;
for from these as well, there is the attainment of the fruit.
Potency refers to cold potency and hot potency;
this is the maturation (*vipāka*). Transformation into heat and transformation into sweetness refer to the specific efficacy (*prabhāva*), which is a particular capacity.
For example, although their acidity is equal, the juice of the citron (*bījapūraka*) generates bile while the juice of the emblic myrobalan (*āmalaka*) pacifies it;
this is because they arise from that very [source].

Likewise, it is because of that very desire for the bond of rebirth (*pratisandhibandha*) that there is the possibility—that is, the arising—of that bond of rebirth characterized by renewed existence.
Just as the end of the flower is like the fruit,
and the power of the fruit is like the end of the flower, so it is.
In this context, the fourth craving is the direct cause of renewed existence,
while the preceding three are causes by way of succession; such is the detailed explanation.
Regarding the discursive investigations of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vicarita*), there are two groups of five and two groups of four; the four types of desire (*chanda*) occur in sequence as follows:
the first desire has five aspects, and the second also has five aspects.
The third is of four kinds;
how is the fourth also of four kinds?

"O monks, when the view of a self exists, [the thought] 'I am' exists; when that exists, [the thought] 'I am thus' arises, meaning that through its connection one generates craving with the notion 'I am of such a kind.
'I am thus' means exactly as before and not otherwise."
Thinking "I am otherwise" means that through the perception of [qualities] such as complexion, strength, or eloquence in another manner, the thought "I exist" arises;

conversely, from the opposite [perception], the thought "I do not exist" arises. This is the first [craving], the craving for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-chanda*), which is fivefold when considered without distinction.
"I shall exist"—this occurs to him;
[the phrase] "I shall not exist" refers to the form of annihilation;
"I shall exist in such a way" is to be explained in detail as before.

Thus, this desire for renewed existence (*punarbhava-cchanda*) is fivefold in its undifferentiated form; furthermore, the second [type] is "may I be," while the third is the fourfold differentiated desire for renewed existence, which occurs as: "may I be thus," "may I be in this way," or "may I be otherwise."

Furthermore, there arises for him the thought, "May I be," as well as "May I be thus," "May I be in this way," and "May I be otherwise. This fourth [craving] is the desire for the connection of rebirth in four ways.
