Among these, the first is the root cause because it is the primary cause of suffering; this should be applied in detail as before.
It is called a "path" (pratipad) because it is specifically determined.
The "path" (pratipat) is the definitive leading;
how, then, is it specific?
Because one goes to that [goal] by this very [path].
As it was said, "and so forth," [the phrase] "of those whose conduct consists of permanence, pleasure, what belongs to the self,
and the self" means that their conduct consists of the views that things are permanent, pleasant, belonging to the self, and the self.
These individuals are those whose conduct is characterized by the views of permanence, pleasure, selfhood, and a self;
as their antidote, there are the aspects of impermanence and so forth, respectively.
For those whose conduct is characterized by the view of no cause, the aspect of "cause" serves as the antidote to the thought that "there is no cause."

For those whose conduct is based on the view of a single cause, such as "the Lord" or "Primal Matter," the aspect of origination (*samudaya*) transforms into the thought that "there is a single cause" rather than "origination is the cause. For those whose conduct is based on the view of transformation, the aspect of production (*prabhava*) transforms into the thought that "an entity undergoes transformation."

"This world has a beginning and was not previously existent, but rather undergoes transformation; this world is created intentionally"— such is the form of the cognition of those whose conduct is governed by the view that things are created intentionally.
This world was not created by the intellect of a Lord;
rather,
each thing comes to be in dependence upon its respective conditions.
For the word "prati" has the sense of repetition (vīpsā);
therefore, it is indicated that the world is produced from multiple causes—
it would be logical only in this way.

The etymologists show that the Sautrāntika position is that "ākāra" means the mode of grasping the object; thus, taking the syllable *ā* from the word *ālambana* (object) and the syllable *kāra* from the word *prakāra* (mode), [the term *ākāra* is formed].
And when the remaining letters have been elided, the form "ākāra" results;
this being so, it is established that wisdom (prajñā) also possesses an aspect (sākārā), and thus it possesses an object (sālambā).
The word-form *ālamba* ends in the vowel *ā*;
it is either derived from a verbal root with the suffix *ghañ* or simply *ālamba*.
Those who exist together with an object (*ālamba*)—whether with a male object (*ālambena*) or a female object (*ālambayā*)—are called *sālamba*.
The meaning is "having an object.
Regarding the phrase "the distinction of wholesome and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes unwholesome, indeterminate, the stages, and the bases.
Because it occurs at the beginning of the *śloka*, he explains that "the first" here does not refer to the treatise (*śāstra*),
for it is knowledge of Dharma that is recited as the first in the treatise.
That which is called "dharma" exists in six [stages],
because it has as its object the suffering and so forth belonging to the desire realm.

And in the three formless realms, there exists only the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) comprised within the path of cultivation; likewise, there are six [types of knowledge] in those cases as well.

Since it is possible for the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and the others to have the nature of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), it is logical that they are not manifested in the form and formless realms; thus,
it is first established that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is not manifested in the formless realm.
Because the formless realms do not take the suffering and other [afflictions] of the desire realm as their object,
some say: "But why is it not manifested in the form realm?"
The dharma-knowledge that is intent upon reviling the desire realm,
as well as the dharma-knowledge of one reborn in the form realm, does not arise for the purpose of reviling the desire realm,
because it has been abandoned through the transition to a stage of detachment.

But one born in the desire realm, even if free from passion for it, brings that [knowledge] into manifestation because their birth in the desire realm is not yet exhausted; therefore, dharma-knowledge is not brought into manifestation in the form realm.
However, Master Saṅghabhadra says:
Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is manifested only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form or formless realms,
because the minds that enter into and emerge from those meditative attainments exist only in the desire realm.

Or, it is because there is no basis for the morality that accompanies the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna-anuparivartaka*); for the primary elements (*bhūta*) belonging exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) serve as the basis for such morality,
since they act as an obstruction to the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions that give rise to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*).
Because they are counteragents and those [defilements] do not exist there, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has its basis solely in the desire realm; thus,
the single knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) is the application of mindfulness to phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
In the exposition of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), it was stated that phenomena are distinct from the body, feelings, and mind; thus,
the other [three] applications of mindfulness are also [distinct] knowledges.

The knowledges of dharma, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledges of suffering, origin, path, destruction, and non-arising have the four foundations of mindfulness as their intrinsic nature;
for even the knowledge of suffering sometimes has the body as its object and sometimes has [objects] up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*) as its object.
In this way, there is also the knowledge of origin and the knowledge of the path; that which is the application of mindfulness to the body having the untainted restraint as its object occurs,
while the rest is easy to understand.

"Except for subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)," means that if *dharma*-knowledge were to take uncontaminated knowledge as its object, it would necessarily take only the category of *dharma*-knowledge;
likewise, subsequent knowledge would necessarily take only the category of subsequent knowledge as its object— this is the rule.

In that regard, for the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) that constitutes the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), other instances of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledges beginning with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) can be its object.
However, for [the knowledge of phenomena] that constitutes the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) can be its object;
and for [the knowledge of phenomena] that constitutes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds can be its object.
The nine knowledges are its object;
in this same way, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) should also be applied,
and for the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) as well, there are exactly nine, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
For path-knowledge does not take conventional knowledge as its object, because of the restriction that it must have the uncontaminated path as its object; thus,
there are two [types of] knowledge— conventional knowledge and knowledge of others' minds.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds that is included within the truths of suffering and its origin, that which is untainted has the nine untainted knowledges as its object.
Regarding that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) can have it as their object;

since the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have the nature of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and so forth, all ten knowledges become the objects of those two [knowledges],
due to the distinction between associated (*samprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*) factors.
"Associated" refers to mind and mental factors;
"dissociated" refers to acquisition and so forth.
"Due to the distinction between the wholesome and the indeterminate":
the wholesome is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is the ultimate security;
the indeterminate are space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
There are six belonging to the desire realm and six that are untainted (*anāsrava*), each being sixfold due to the distinction between associated (*samprayukta*) and dissociated (*viprayukta*);
likewise, those belonging to the form and formless realms are also sixfold for that same reason of distinction.
The two [knowledges] are untainted (*anāsrava*);
for that very reason, since they are associated with the untainted states belonging to the desire and form realms,
all mind and mental factors belonging to the formless realm, as well as all dissociated formations and unconditioned phenomena, are not objects of the knowledge of others' minds.
Excluding the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),

since the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have the four truths as their objects, and because the indeterminate and the unconditioned are distinct from those [truths],
could one know all phenomena through a single knowledge?
How is it understood from the Sūtra that "it would not exist"?
"Here, venerable Gautama, while we were seated and assembled together in the assembly hall, a conversation of this kind arose among us:
'It is said that the ascetic Gautama has declared,
"There is no such person as an ascetic or..."'"

"Is it true, O Gautama, that you remember having said: 'He who would know all at once and see all'? "Indeed, I do remember saying this, but there is no such person, whether he be a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa."
"He who will know or see everything all at once"— this is the detailed explanation based on the distinction between the subject and the object; that is,
because of the difference between the cognizer and the cognized.
Because that which is the subject cannot be its own object, due to the contradiction of an action operating upon itself.
For indeed, that very edge of a sword cannot be cut by that same edge;
therefore, by that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not grasped,
nor are the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously with it grasped by it.
Because they have the same object;
for whatever is the object of that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), that very same thing is the object of its associated [mental factors].
And if those associated [mental factors] were to be apprehended, they would have their own intrinsic nature as their object because they share a single object with conventional knowledge;
however, this is not tenable.
Therefore, they are not perceived by it because of extreme proximity;
nor are its co-existent dissociated factors perceived by it.
It is like the application of ointment to the eye or the sight of a mirror;
and that is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
because its object is a distinct level (*bhūmi*).
Because conventional knowledge belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) and consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) takes as its object only a specific level—
whether it be the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first dhyāna, or up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—
what is the reason for this?
Because the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the lower and upper stages as their respective objects,
they possess the aspects of "calm" and "gross" and so forth, respectively; this is because of the statement that "the higher and lower spheres have [these] as their range."
And if that [path] were to have all stages as its object,
there would be detachment from all [stages] simultaneously;
however, even for the paths of preparation and distinction, only a certain stage serves as the object, according to what is possible.
For how could that which is comprised within the preparatory path (prayogamārga) conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) have the desire realm as its object but not the other two realms?
For one who possesses the other two elements,

the desire realm is not the object of the [meditation on] the foul; however, for that which is subsumed under the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) in the context of revulsion through the immeasurables, the spheres of mastery, and so forth, the desire realm alone is the object.
The other two elements are accompanied by a single cognition for one who possesses attachment during the first untainted moment.

Because one who possesses patience and knowledge does not lack possession of other untainted knowledges as well; and because one who is free from passion is possessed of the knowledge of others' minds— this is the reason for the inclusion [of the term "one who is not lustful"].
Regarding the second [moment], it is said that "by means of three"; thus, that very same *dharmajñāna* with respect to suffering is called both *duḥkhadharmajñāna* and *duḥkhajñāna*.
When the designation "two" is applied due to a difference in names,
one is endowed with three [knowledges]— namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)—
in the case of the four [truths].

Thus, during the moment of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, and during the moments of the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*) regarding origin, the path, and cessation— as previously stated— there is no possession [of those knowledges] because they have not yet arisen. For at the moment of the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering, only the subsequent knowledge increases, not the knowledge of the dharma.
Because it was previously possessed by him,

at the moment of the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣaṇa*), only the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) increases, not the subsequent knowledge of the dharma (*dharma-anvaya-jñāna*).

Since they were already endowed with those two previously, it should be stated that in the moments of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path, only the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path increase;
however, for one who is free from passion, there is additionally the knowledge of others' minds in all cases.

It should be understood that from the moment of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) up until the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣaṇe*), one is also endowed with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), as well as with those aforementioned knowledges;
however, at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge 'nvayajñāne*), one who is not free from passion (*avītarāga*) is endowed with only those seven [knowledges].
One who is free from passion (vītarāga), however, is endowed with eight [knowledges]:
those same [six] plus the knowledge of others' minds;
as for the two knowledges of destruction and non-arising, only an Arhat possesses them—this being easily understood, it need not be set forth in detail, so it should be understood thus.
Regarding the statement "they are cultivated as they arise," two kinds of cultivation are intended here.
There is cultivation by acquisition and cultivation by practice;
cultivation by acquisition is by way of attainment, while cultivation by practice is by way of manifestation,
as they are cultivated according to how they have arisen.
Thus, whatever [factors] have arisen, those very ones are cultivated;
for example, when the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen, the future receptivity of that same kind is cultivated,
as well as its four aspects (*ākāra*).
The aspects of patience (*kṣānti*)—namely the four beginning with impermanence (*anitya*)—are cultivated because they belong to the same category;
no others are.
Likewise, when the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) has arisen, that very same [knowledge] is cultivated in its future state.
Only those four aspects of that [knowledge] undergo cultivation;

in this same way, it should be applied to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and so forth, for there is only the cultivation of aspects of homogeneous knowledge.
Why is it that the cultivation of similar knowledge and the cultivation of similar aspects occur only on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and not on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
This is not a question regarding the receptivities (*kṣānti*).
Because they are absent in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
or rather, a question should also be posed regarding them,
since they too involve the cultivation of the homogeneous (sabhāga).
For when the receptivity to suffering has arisen, the aspects of the receptivities to the origin of suffering and so forth are not cultivated;
however, the inquiry regarding knowledge— and not the inquiry regarding receptivity— is for the sake of providing a mere illustration,
because the lineages have not yet been attained.
The meaning is: "because the homogeneous causes have not yet been obtained.

How is this so? When the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) has arisen, its own lineage and the lineages of the four aspects [of that truth] are thereby obtained.

What, then, is the reason that when one aspect among the aspects such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth has become manifest, the lineages (*gotra*) of the remaining aspects are acquired, by virtue of which they proceed toward cultivation (*bhāvanā*), even though [the specific knowledge] such as the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen?
Because they share the same object of focus (*ālambana*), all [the moments of consciousness] belonging to that same category (*sabhāga*) have acquired their respective lineages (*gotra*).

Thus, when the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) has arisen, up until the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*) has arisen, the four lineages corresponding to those aspects (*ākāra*) are acquired; therefore, only that [dharma-knowledge] undergoes cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and nothing else.

On the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), however, because all cognitions— both similar and dissimilar— as well as their respective aspects (*ākāra*), are brought into manifestation, the causes for all of them are obtained; thus,
the future aspects of cognition distinguished by those [causes] undergo cultivation,
as do the three subsequent conventional [cognitions].
Thus, [the path] has not been previously obtained among the dharma-knowledges because the clear realization of the truths is not yet complete;
for at that time, the suffering belonging to the form and formless realms has not been fully understood, its origin has not been abandoned, and its cessation has not been realized.
Because the Path has not previously been realized by means of the worldly path; that is to say,
while in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), suffering, its origin, and its cessation have previously been realized by means of the worldly path,
but the Path has never been realized by means of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) through the aspects (*ākāra*) of "Path" and so forth.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of each one of the [first] three truths, they proceed to cultivation; however,
this does not occur at the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*),
because it is not possible to cultivate the entire path [in a single moment].
The meaning is that it is to be brought face-to-face;
at that time, even the entire origin (*samudaya*) has not been abandoned,
as there remain [afflictions] to be abandoned through the vision and cultivation of cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*).

Furthermore, all suffering within the three realms has been fully understood because it is that which must be fully understood; therefore, it is specifically with reference to the origin [of suffering] that it is questioned:
"to be abandoned by the vision of that truth," meaning "to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of the origin."
Regarding the phrase "because of having many lineages" (*bahu-gotratvāt*): lineage (*gotra*) is a specific distinction within the general continuity of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva-santati*).
Since this path possesses those many lineages, it is called "one with many lineages" (*bahugotra*).
The pratyekabuddha lineage is distinct from the śrāvaka lineage;
likewise, the buddha lineage and the śrāvaka lineage are mutually distinct.

The meaning is that, due to the distinctions of weak, intense, and so forth, only a certain [portion] of the antidote to what is to be abandoned by seeing is cultivated— that is, brought into manifestation;
the entire path cannot be cultivated.
Because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
since conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is an attendant of the path of seeing,
the path of seeing is cultivated only at the conclusion of the [first] three truths.

It is not [the case that it occurs] at the end of the truth of the path, because that belongs to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and is therefore something yet to be accomplished; thus, this [statement] is not a proof,
for this [path of seeing] is merely the retinue of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
Nor is it even an attendant of the path of cultivation;
for we say that it is indeed an attendant of the path of cultivation,
since its objective support is more excellent than that of the truths.
The intention is that at the stage of seeing (*darśanāvasthā*), it is indeed a mundane state superior to what was previously mundane;
for one has obtained a basis capable of bringing that [path] into manifestation.
The acquisition of that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) consists precisely in the attainment of a basis (*āśraya*) capable of bringing it into manifestation;
it is not a separate entity.
When the lineage (*gotra*) has been attained, that which pertains to the lineage (*gautrika*) is attained; thus,
the lineage is the cause capable of producing it,
and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is that which exists therein.
This is what is meant:
when one obtains a basis (āśraya) capable of bringing that [state] into manifestation, then that [state] as well, arising by means of that basis, becomes obtained.
Now, why do the Vaibhāṣikas not accept this?
Since that [attainment] is to be acquired through the path of seeing,
how could its manifestation occur on the path of cultivation?
It must therefore manifest on the path of seeing.

Furthermore, there is no opportunity for this [defilement] to arise in the path of seeing; therefore, they describe it as being "of a nature not to arise" (*anutpattidharmaka*). This applies in detail up to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
If it belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, then that which pertains to three levels is cultivated.
If that which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, the level of the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the desire realm (kāmāvacara),
and the level of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) are cultivated,
then that which belongs to the level of the intermediate dhyāna and those previously mentioned belonging to the levels of the first dhyāna and so forth are cultivated.
Thus, if it belongs to the level of the second dhyāna, it belongs to five levels—
from the level of the second dhyāna down to the desire realm;
if it belongs to the level of the third dhyāna, it belongs to six levels.

If it belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, then that which belongs to the levels from the third dhyāna down to the desire realm— seven levels in total— is cultivated. If it belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, [it is cultivated].
By the enumeration of one as "up to the sphere of desire" (*yāvat kāmāvacaram*), it is established that the remainder consists of four;
and by the double restriction— "the last alone is the last" and "cessation [is] cessation"— it is established that the remainder consists of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*).
When suffering is realized, the conventional knowledge that is cultivated consists of the four foundations of mindfulness, because suffering has the body and so forth as its intrinsic nature;
the same should be stated regarding the origin [of suffering].
When suffering has been realized, that conventional knowledge which is cultivated has precisely the aspects of truth; specifically,
each [of those aspects] consists of the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
In the same way, it should be stated regarding origination and cessation that "its object is that very same [object]," because that aspect has that as its objective support.
"Preparatory" (prāyogika) means it is not obtained through rebirth;
its intrinsic nature consists of four or five aggregates (skandha).

The [consciousness] belonging to the desire realm (kāmāvacara) has the nature of four aggregates— meaning it consists of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— because of the absence of concomitant form (anuparivartakarūpa). However, those belonging to the higher stages have the nature of five aggregates, because they possess the aggregate of form characterized by the restraint of meditative absorption (dhyānasaṃvara).
Two knowledges are present:
subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) and path knowledge (*mārgajñāna*),
because the subsequent knowledge of the path has the nature of both.
Regarding the six future [knowledges],
beginning with dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and so forth,
conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is not cultivated.
Because it has been previously attained, for he will say:
"That which has been previously attained is not cultivated."
Thus,
there is no knowledge of others' minds because of not being free from passion;
above that, there is the cultivation of seven [knowledges].
Thus,
from the abandonment of one type up to the abandonment of eight types,
until he becomes free from passion.
As long as the nine types [of afflictions] have not been abandoned,
during this interval, while the paths of preparation, uninterruptedness, liberation, and excellence are being cultivated, seven knowledges are cultivated— namely,
those beginning with the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), excluding the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
If it is mundane,
then if the path of cultivation has aspects such as "calm" or "exalted," it is present conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) with respect to four dharma-knowledges.

It is any one of the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; it is not any one of the subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna) because they are not the antidotes to the desire realm; nor is it any one of the five supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Excluding the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā), it refers to the four subsequent knowledges (anvayajñāna), namely,
the subsequent knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
And regarding the two types of dharma-knowledge—

that which has cessation and the path as its objects— conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is not cultivated because they serve as antidotes to the three realms; however, it is not cultivated [in the case of the path] because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
When supramundane knowledge is being cultivated during the detachment from the seven stages, conventional knowledge is also cultivated;
for conventional knowledge also serves as an antidote to that category of afflictions, not only supramundane knowledge.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is also cultivated therein, being of that same nature;

however, in the penetration of the unshakable (*akopya*), it is not so, because it is not yet of the nature of an antidote (*pratipakṣa*) due to remaining on the conventional path (*saṃvṛtimārga*). Therein, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is cultivated, but not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), for one who abides in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) does not become one of unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*).
Since the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is cultivated by one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*),
and only seven knowledges are cultivated during the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) upon detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
how is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) cultivated?
Knowledge of others' minds is excluded from the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), but not from the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Therefore, when one type [of defilement] has been abandoned, up to when eight types have been abandoned, a knowledge of others' minds that is superior to the previous knowledge of others' minds is cultivated;
such a noble person (*āryapudgala*), having emerged from that path, would bring it into manifestation.
For it is held that the distinction in the knowledge of another's mind arises from a distinction in the mental continuum;
thus, for both— the one with attachment and the one free from attachment— there is cultivation in the path of liberation,
but for those two [only] in the path of preparation.

Regarding those same two—the one with passion and the one free from passion—there is also the cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) on the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). Why is there a dispute [regarding this]?
Some say that because of its similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it should be cultivated therein just as it is in the context of the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*).
And there is no clear realization (*abhisamaya*), nor is there similarity to the path of seeing; such is the dispute of others.
Thus, as before, there is cultivation of the six—namely, the knowledges of dharma, subsequent, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
It is not because conventional knowledge resembles the path of seeing;
what, then, is this resemblance to the path of seeing?
It is the attainment of the fruit.

Just as the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) or non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), is attained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), so too by means of this path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), during the refinement of the faculties of a trainee (*śaikṣendriyottāpanā*), the conditioned fruits of stream-entry and so forth— which are comprised of sharp faculties— are attained. Furthermore,
just as there is no cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) in the state of the path of uninterrupted transition within the path of seeing, so it is here as well.

Thus, because of its similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is likewise no cultivation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) on the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*); this applies to the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Here too, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
nor is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), because it is excluded from all paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
What, then, of the remainder? Such is the detailed explanation.
How is it that the ninth path of liberation regarding detachment from the desire realm is the remainder?
Because of the statement: "In the remaining path of cultivation involving attachment, there are seven [stages] above that."

In the case of one who has cultivated detachment from the seven stages, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvita*), the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) are [of the nature of] the remaining [paths];
in the case of one who has cultivated the conquest of the seven stages, the superknowledges, the unshakable attainment (*akopyāpti*), and the mixed cultivation,
they exist in the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*).
Because of this statement,

as well as because of the statement that for one who proceeds toward unshakability (*akopyatā*), there is likewise the cultivation of the ten [faculties] at the end in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

The eight paths of liberation remain; all others belong to the anāgāmin who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). The remaining [paths] are the preparatory and special paths (*prayoga-viśeṣamārga*), because they are not mentioned in the context of their cultivation.
Thus it has been stated: "For the learner (*śaikṣa*), it is in this manner."
It was stated that [the result] remains in the eighth cultivation;
how, then, can a specific understanding be obtained when it has been stated thus without qualification?
Because for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is necessarily the application of the cultivation of nine or ten knowledges (*jñāna*);
for this very reason, he says, "for one beyond training, moreover, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*), the dhyānas, and so on, is intended.

Regarding the realization of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) and the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*), in those paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), if one is liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*), nine knowledges are cultivated,
excluding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
If one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) has ten [knowledges], it is by adding that very same [knowledge of the destruction of the outflows] to those eight; thus there are nine.
For one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), there are eight; for one of immovable nature, there are nine, excluding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Because it is excluded from the paths immediately following that [attainment],
but it exists in two: the paths of liberation of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)— namely, the paths of liberation of the divine ear and the divine eye.
Because of the statement that "the supernormal powers of the ear and eye are neutral," their paths of liberation are neutral;
and for a neutral dharma, there is no cultivation of the future.
For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), however, there is detachment from the desire realm and the [first] three dhyānas; thus,
the fourth dhyāna is not included because the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) occurs at the point of detachment from the fourth dhyāna.
In that regard, there is the attainment of the fundamental sphere of infinite space,
yet there is no knowledge of others' minds included within the formless realm,
because it must be accomplished by means of objects that transcend form.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and the production of qualities such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)," etc. By the word "etc.," qualities such as the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are included.
The phrase "the production of qualities such as the immeasurables" includes the stages of the dhyānas for the purpose of excluding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*),
because in those [preparatory stages], the knowledge of others' minds does not exist.

The three higher knowledges (*abhijñā*)—namely, the higher knowledge of the domain of supernormal powers (*ṛddhiviṣayābhijñā*), the higher knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*), and the higher knowledge of the minds of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*)—occur in the final paths of liberation from passion for the desire realm and the [first] three dhyānas; in the paths of liberation of the three higher knowledges belonging to the dhyāna stages;
and in the actualizations of qualities such as the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Within the preparatory, liberation, and special paths belonging specifically to the dhyāna stages, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated as yet to come;
likewise, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) included therein is cultivated only in its distinguished form—
that which one who has attained specific qualities would bring into manifestation.
Except for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as the stages of heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth;
for in those aids to penetration, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not cultivated.
He asks: what is the reason?
"Because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)," means that just as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not cultivated on the path of seeing,
so too it is not cultivated in its attendants; this is the intended meaning.
"Except in other cases," and so forth.

This refers to the acquisition of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) alone as a future state in the case of "the acquisition of a new path in other instances"—that is, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) specifically, in the acquisition of a new path at the time of attaining detachment from the desire realm or the first three dhyānas, excluding the final paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), which consist of the acquisition of the preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation paths.
In that acquisition of a new path in other instances, only conventional knowledge is cultivated as a future state.

Knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated; rather, it is only conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) that is cultivated as a future attainment during the acquisition of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) in the realization of qualities such as the three higher knowledges (*abhijñā*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, as well as during the acquisition of any other previously unattained path.
In the paths of preparation (prayogamārga), there is no knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), because it is not their antidote.
Now, in which path [does it arise]? In either the mundane (laukika) or the supramundane (lokottara);
it arises in whichever stage (bhūmi) the path belongs to.
Whether it be the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) [path] beginning with the *anāgamya* stage,
and whichever level (*bhūmi*) one first attains—
meaning that through the process of detachment (*vairāgya*), it belongs to that level, from the first *dhyāna* up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
How is this so? If,

by relying on the stage of the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived), one attains the first *dhyāna* through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) via detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then at the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated— both that which belongs to the stage of the *anāgamya* by nature as a preparatory threshold (*sāmantaka*) and that which belongs to the stage of the first *dhyāna* by nature as the fundamental state (*maula*).
In this way, by relying on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna, one attains the second dhyāna through detachment from the first dhyāna;
likewise, that which is comprised within the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna and that which is comprised within the fundamental (*maula*) second dhyāna are both cultivated.

Thus, it should be applied in detail up to the point where, by relying on the preparatory stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one attains the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) through detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).

Even when one attains the first dhyāna through detachment from the desire realm by relying on the support of the untainted *anāgamya* stage, that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated in exactly the same way;
so too when [one does so] by relying on the support of the fundamental (*maula*) first dhyāna stage.
When one attains the untainted first dhyāna for the sake of detachment from the first dhyāna,

at that time one also attains conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) comprised within the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna, which serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the first category of the first dhyāna, up to its ninth category;
for that [conventional knowledge] is attained for the first time at that level.

But in the ninth path of liberation, one cultivates conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) which, though included within the fundamental second dhyāna, is yet future; in this same manner, the cultivation of conventional knowledge should be applied by relying on the stages of untainted intermediate dhyāna up to the stage of the untainted sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*),
for the sake of detachment.
Thus,
for whichever stage of existence there is detachment, there is the attainment of that [stage].
In both cases— namely, the attainment of whichever stage and the attainment of whatever [quality] belongs to it— there is [attainment].
And below that, it is cultivated.
He explains how untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) functions through the commentary:
the word "also" (*api*) implies that it serves not only for detachment from its own level, but also for detachment from other levels.
The path is also twofold:
mundane and supramundane,
consisting of the path of preparation and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the paths of uninterrupted transition, liberation, and excellence;
and as for the phrase "the stage which one attains through detachment," it refers to a higher stage.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges belonging to that level or to lower levels undergo cultivation;
for example, when one relies on the second untainted *dhyāna* and effects detachment from the third *dhyāna*,
whichever level the path belongs to— whether it belongs to the level of the second *dhyāna* or another— the untainted knowledge of that level undergoes cultivation.

And when one effects detachment from a particular stage—specifically from the third stage—at the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) belonging to that stage, namely the third dhyāna stage, undergoes cultivation;
and the untainted knowledge belonging to the lower stages, whether the first dhyāna stage or the threshold stage (*anāgamya*), also undergoes cultivation.
For even those belonging to the lower stages, such as the preparatory path (*prayogamārga*) and so forth, being of that same nature, are possible and thus undergo cultivation.
However, if one relies on the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the third dhyāna to achieve detachment from the second dhyāna,

then during the eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) belonging to that level does not undergo cultivation, because such untainted knowledge is absent in that preparatory stage, which is tainted (*sāsrava*).

However, that same kind of untainted knowledge belonging to the lower stages—namely, those belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), the first dhyāna, and the preparatory stage (anāgamya)—is cultivated. This same principle should be applied elsewhere as well; this is the general direction. And [this applies to] the untainted knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna).

The word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and those that are untainted" (anāsravāś ca) indicates that those qualities which one would manifest upon becoming an Arhat— such as the immeasurables (apramāṇa), the liberations (vimokṣa), and so forth— undergo cultivation in that state, even though they are tainted (sāsrava).
By the word "etcetera," the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth are included;
[they] "seem to breathe" by virtue of their similarity to a basket— that is,
a basket that has been bound and compressed with a rope.
It is said that she "breathes," as it were, because of the breaking of the rope;
she is called "breathing" due to the application of a figurative term,
by way of the similarity between her and a basket that breathes, as it were, when its rope is severed.
Just as a basket tied with a rope, having been squeezed by that rope, seems to breathe when the rope is cut,

so too these aforementioned qualities such as the foul (aśubha) and others seem to breathe as they proceed within the continuum of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) once the rope of the acquisition of afflictions has been severed by the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi).
This is a metaphorical expression because breathing is a characteristic of living beings.
He asks "Why? and replies:
"For one who has attained sovereignty over his own mind," meaning that he is the supreme king (rājādhirāja), superior to all other kings.
The state of that is "sovereignty" (ādhirājya);
it means sovereignty over one's own mind, in the sense of the attainment of mastery over the mind due to the departure from subjection to the afflictions (kleśa).
For an Arhat who has attained that state, all wholesome qualities undergo cultivation through the attainment of numerous qualities that serve as offerings;
this is just as when certain overlord kings, upon attaining supreme sovereignty, receive a welcoming reception from their provinces and districts with offerings such as garments and other gifts.

In the same way, when the rope of the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*) is severed, the qualities (*guṇa*) seem to breathe a sigh of relief because they have regained their own acquisition; the meaning is that the acquisition of those qualities arises in an even more refined state.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), upon the attainment of arhatship, the [meditations on] impurity (*aśubhā*) and so forth—consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—as far as possible, become cultivated throughout the three realms. However, upon the attainment of arhatship in the form and formless realms, they respectively become cultivated in two realms and one realm.

Thus, it should also be understood according to the stages (*bhūmi*): for one born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) who attains arhatship, it should be understood that whatever [attainments] belonging to that stage he obtains are [those previously acquired]. This is the detailed explanation: whatever was lost and is obtained again—that is, brought into manifestation—is that which was appropriate to *saṃsāra*.
That which is not practiced in the future is not cultivated [now], because it has already been abandoned in cyclic existence; rather,
it is that which is distinguished within this world, though unaccustomed to cyclic existence, and is conducive to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The Master [Vasubandhu] demonstrates that when that [state] becomes manifest, only a future state of a similar kind, but more distinguished, is cultivated;
the Master Saṅghabhadra also explains this same point:
"That which was previously obtained is not cultivated."
That which was previously attained and then lost is cultivated again because it is brought back into presence through effort;
for a path that has not been relinquished is brought into presence by means of effort.
Because the impetus for that [past state] is powerful, it proceeds toward cultivation as a future state;

however, one that was previously stilled manifests without effort because it has been cultivated and stilled, and because its task has been accomplished and its fruit has been given—it is thus devoid of momentum. Therefore, due to the manifestation of that [past state], the future state is not cultivated.

"That which is future and produced through effort is cultivated"— this has been written here by Master Vasumitra in detail, [stating] that it is understood as belonging exclusively to the continuum of an Ārya, because it is not habituated to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
On this point, it is said that the Vaibhāṣikas say: "This is not so;
why?"
Because that [attainment] becomes as if unobtained due to having been relinquished,
therefore, even in the case of regaining what was previously cultivated and then abandoned, cultivation indeed occurs once more.
"How can that be 'unprecedented' (apūrva) when it has been obtained before?
For such a thing is not well-known as 'previously existing' in the world"— thus others explain.
This was said with reference to a single lifetime, not to other lifetimes;
for that which is lost in this very life cannot be attained again, nor can it be cultivated.
Because it has been cultivated and then relinquished, that which is obtained in another birth is what was cultivated;
it is not newly obtained, because the cultivation had been forgotten.
For cultivation is indeed fourfold;
"cultivation as acquisition" means that acquisition itself is cultivation,
in the sense that it is simply the attainment of what has not yet been attained.
Thus, it should be stated that cultivation itself is the antidote and itself the removal; but what is cultivation, and what is [the rest] up to removal?
Furthermore, "cultivation" (niṣevaṇa) means repeated bringing [of the mind] into presence; it is the path that serves as the antidote (pratipakṣa). As stated in the Sūtra:
"one whose body is cultivated, one whose mind is cultivated"—the meaning is that their body and mind have had the antidote cultivated.
Furthermore, the antidote to the body is the path for the sake of detachment from the four dhyānas;
for it has been said: "A monk is called one who has cultivated the body, one who has cultivated the mind, and one who has cultivated ethical discipline.
How does one become one who has cultivated the body?
One who is free from passion for the body, free from longing, free from thirst, free from affection, and free from attachment;
or rather, according to scripture, that which is the immediate path for the destruction of passion for form— that by means of this one becomes free from passion.
The expulsion of afflictions is the severance of their acquisition;
for future ones, it is a single [moment], which is cultivation by acquisition.
Regarding present [dharmas], both— namely,
the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice— [apply];
"in this way" is the full explanation.

Since it was stated without distinction that the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and practice (*niṣevaṇa*) pertain to wholesome conditioned phenomena— whether they be with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)—

and since it was also stated without distinction that the cultivation of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*) and elimination (*vinirdhāvana*) pertain to contaminated phenomena— whether they be afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*)—
therefore, in this manner, there are four types of cultivation for wholesome phenomena that are with-outflows.
For those in whom cultivation is desired due to their proficiency, there exist the cultivation of acquisition and the cultivation of practice;
and because they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), there exist the cultivation of the antidote and the cultivation of expulsion.

Now, regarding those conditioned phenomena which are neither wholesome-with-outflows nor unwholesome, as well as those which are untainted or afflicted-neutral—how many cultivations (bhāvanā) do they possess? It is said: for the untainted ones, there are two, namely, the cultivation of acquisition (pratilambha-bhāvanā) and the cultivation of practice (niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā).
And for those that are afflicted and indeterminate,
do both types of cultivation occur— namely, the cultivation of the antidote and the cultivation of expulsion?
"Of the faculties, the former" means the cultivation of restraint regarding the eye and so forth; "of the body, the latter."
The cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*);
furthermore, he demonstrates these two types of cultivation in their proper order through scripture, stating:
"These six faculties," and so forth.

Furthermore, that restraint of the sense faculties is said to have mindfulness and clear comprehension as its intrinsic nature; "cultivation" (*vibhāvanā*) also refers to the expulsion of the afflictions that take the body as their object— this is the detailed explanation.

However, since the cultivation of restraint (*saṃvara*) and the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvana*) are included, respectively, within the cultivation of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) and the cultivation of expulsion (*nirdhāvana*), there is no contradiction in saying that both are included in both; thus, generally speaking,
the cultivation of qualities at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is said to belong to all— namely, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Samyaksambuddhas.
And because of the statement, "The ten powers are the knowledge of destruction along with its outflows," and so forth.

These eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-buddhadharma), beginning with the powers (bala) and ending with great compassion (mahākaruṇā), are established by the Vaibhāṣikas. However, some describe other eighteen unique Buddha-qualities as distinct from these [powers and so forth], as follows:
The Tathāgata has no stumbling, no outcry, and no agitation.
There is no perception of diversity,
there is no indeterminate mind,
and there is no equanimity that is not preceded by discernment.
There is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the past;
there is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the future;
there is no obstructed knowledge and vision regarding the present.
All bodily action follows after knowledge; all vocal action follows after knowledge;
all mental action follows after knowledge.
There is no loss of zeal, no loss of vigor,
and no loss of mindfulness.
There is no loss of concentration,
no loss of wisdom,
and no loss of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
In that context, what is called "clamor" (ravita) consists of sudden activity, impulsiveness, playfulness, and the intention for variety;
it is the perception of diversity regarding objects that are pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant, arising from attachment, aversion, and delusion.
The remainder is easy to understand;
the ten powers are:
the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*).
The power of knowledge regarding the maturation of karma,
the power of knowledge regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments,
and the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties.
The power of knowledge of various inclinations,
the power of knowledge of various elements,
and the power of knowledge of the paths leading everywhere.
The power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of former abodes,
the power of knowledge of death and rebirth,
and the power of knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
The Sūtra says: "Venerable ones, there are ten powers of a Tathāgata.
What are the ten?
Here, venerable ones, a Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, what is possible as possible."
And what is the impossible as impossible:
this is the first power of a Tathāgata,
endowed with which power the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly awakened one, claims his noble place of leadership and turns the Brahma-wheel.

Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata roars the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly: "The Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, the undertaking of karmic actions and dharmas of the past, future, and present— according to their basis, their cause, their substance, and their maturation"—
just as [described] previously, venerable ones.
To the extent that he understands, as it truly is, [the results] up to their maturation— this is the second power of a Tathāgata,
by which power [he acts], as described previously.

Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the defilement, purification, establishment, and cleansing of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti);
in that respect, venerable ones, the Tathāgata is as previously described.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the superior and inferior faculties of other beings and other individuals.
Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata— as previously described— possesses this fourth power of a Tathāgata,
by which power [he acts], as previously described.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands as it really is that the world has various inclinations and manifold dispositions;
venerable ones, since the Tathāgata [knows this] as previously described, this is the fifth power of a Tathāgata.
"By which power," as before;
furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, that the world consists of various elements and many elements,
in the same manner as previously described for the Tathāgata, venerable ones.
This is the sixth power of a Tathāgata,
by which power— as previously described—
furthermore, O Venerable Ones, the Tathāgata understands, as it truly is, the path leading everywhere.
That, venerable friend, which the Tathāgata possesses as before— this is the seventh power of a Tathāgata,
by means of which power [he acts] as before.
Furthermore, venerable ones, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold previous existences;

that is to say, he recollects one birth, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, and even many eons of world-dissolution and world-evolution, [remembering]: "Those beings were named such-and-such."

"In such a place I existed, with such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from that state, I was reborn there; and passing away from there as well, I was reborn here"—thus the Tathāgata, O Venerable Ones, recollects his manifold previous existences in all their aspects, with their causes, and in detail, as described before.

This is the eighth power of a Tathāgata, by which power—and as before—he further perceives, O Venerable Ones, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, beings passing away and being reborn; beautiful and ugly, weak and strong, lowly and exalted; going to a good destination or a bad destination. He understands, as it truly is, how beings fare according to their karma: "These beings, alas, were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech and mind, and [disparaged] the Noble Ones..."

Those who are revilers, possessing wrong views, and because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on wrong views, with that as the cause and that as the condition, after the breaking up of the body, after death, they are reborn in states of deprivation, in miserable destinies, in perdition, in the hells.

But these beings of yours, endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech and mind, not reviling the noble ones, possessing right views, and because of their undertaking of actions and dharmas based on right views, with that as the cause and that as the condition, after the breaking up of the body, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the gods.
Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata— as previously described— possesses this ninth power of a Tathāgata,
by which power [he acts], as previously described.

Furthermore, venerable ones, through the destruction of the outflows, the Tathāgata—having realized for himself in this very life the outflow-free liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having attained them and entered into them—declares: "Birth is exhausted for me; the holy life has been lived; what was to be done has been accomplished; I know no further existence beyond this.
Venerable ones, that the Tathāgata [knows this] as previously described is the tenth power of a Tathāgata.
"By which power" is as before.
Regarding "the ten knowledges concerning the possible and the impossible":
the possible and the impossible constitute "the possible and the impossible."
In that context, "power of knowledge" means that knowledge itself is the power;
the meaning is that it has the nature of the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*).
How is it so?

Briefly stated, the possible and the impossible consist of the conditioned and the unconditioned; furthermore, that which is conditioned is to be divided into eight types, based on the distinction between those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and those that are untainted (anāsrava), as well as the distinction between associated and dissociated factors.
Likewise, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) should be divided into two types based on the distinction between the wholesome (*kuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
therein, all ten factors are the object of the power of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The meaning is that its activity extends across all ten categories of phenomena (*dharma*):
the five belonging to the desire realm, the four untainted (*anāsrava*) ones, and the wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there are seven objects:
the six belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, the untainted (*anāsrava*), and the wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For the knowledges of suffering and origin, there are six: those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
For the knowledge of cessation, there is one [object], which is exclusively wholesome and unconditioned;
for the knowledge of the path, there are two, both untainted;
for the knowledge of others' minds, there are three.
The associated [factors] of the desire realm, the form realm, and the untainted [realm]—
nine factors excluding the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that is not produced by noble ones— are the objects of the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising.
Having established this, how is it that the power of knowing what is possible and impossible consists of ten knowledges?
Furthermore, why are the ten factors called "the possible and the impossible"?
[The answer is: possibility is the possible; impossibility is the impossible.
Alternatively, it is impossible and there is no occasion for a woman to bring about Buddhahood;
it is possible that a man may do so. It is impossible and there is no occasion for a woman to bring about the state of Brahmā.
"It is possible for a person [to attain this]"—
and likewise, "it is possible that there is the cessation of suffering"—
the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) should be understood as proceeding in such modes as these.

The eight [knowledges] are called "fruits of action" because contaminated action and its maturation are subsumed under the truths of suffering and its origin; therefore, the knowledges of cessation and the path do not exist among them.
Therefore, other than those, eight knowledges having that as their object are possible within the meditative absorptions, the faculties, and the resolute convictions;
such is the detailed explanation.
"Meditation and so forth" (*dhyānādayaḥ*) means that meditation is the first among these; they are the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
There are four meditations and eight liberations.
The three concentrations are emptiness and so forth; the two attainments are the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation.
The nine successive attainments of meditative dwelling,
the faculties,
and the mental factors of resolute conviction.
The term "meditations and so forth" (dhyānādayaḥ), "faculties" (akṣāṇi), and "resolves" (adhimokṣāḥ) form a dvandva compound;
within these, nine knowledges are included, excluding the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna). How so?

Because the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth are divided into those that are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), without-outflows (*anāsrava*), associated (*samprayukta*), and dissociated (*viprayukta*), nine knowledges (*jñāna*) can have them as their objects;
however, the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) does not,
because they are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding the faculties such as faith and the rest,
the knowledge of which is primary or secondary according to the distinction of weak, medium, and superior faculties— that is the power of knowing the higher and lower [faculties].

Within those [factors] as well—which are divided into the categories of being with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—nine knowledges (*jñāna*) are possible, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
Regarding the inclinations toward the primary elements and so forth, there are various resolute convictions (*adhimukti*);
these, moreover, are both with and without outflows and pertain to the three realms, because they take those as their objects, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
Thus is the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*).
For in this context, "element" (*dhātu*) refers to the disposition (*āśaya*) that has arisen from the impressions (*vāsanā*) of previous appearances; so says the master Saṅghabhadra.
Furthermore, these are indeed those very same minds distinguished [by their specific tendencies].

In the same way, for those [paths] which are distinguished by the division into those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), there are nine knowledges when one excludes the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*); this should be applied as before to the [four] paths (*pratipad*), and so forth.
There are many paths here that lead to the hells and other [destinies].
The path leading to hell, up to the path leading to the gods,
and the path leading to cessation; therein, those paths which lead to hell and so forth.
They attain [the goal] by means of those [factors]; thus, because they are the means of attainment,
the path is called "practice" (pratipad).
In that case, disjunction is attained;
but how is cessation attained, and how is that [disjunction] also attained?
Because one practices that [path], or because it is the fruit of the practice, it is called "the path of practice" (*pratipad*);
for this very reason, he says:
If it is argued that the "path leading everywhere" (sarvatragāminī pratipad) is intended here because it is the path that is grasped as being accompanied by its fruit,
for they explain it thus:

Regarding the power of knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*), the meaning is "leading to the origin of the view of a real body" (*sat-kāya-samudaya-gāminī*); in this context, the "real body" (*sat-kāya*) refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*).
In this context, "origination" (samudaya) is intended to mean "arising" (utpāda), because of the statement: "Thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
"Cessation of the personality-aggregate" (satkāyanirodha) means dissociation (visaṃyoga).

In this context, that which has the nature of going everywhere is "all-pervading" (*sarvatragāminī*); it is both that and a "path" (*pratipad*), thus it is the "all-pervading path. That is knowledge, and that itself is a power;
therefore, it is the "power of the knowledge of the all-pervading path" (*sarvatragāminīpratipaj-jñānabala*).
Therefore, the ten knowledges should be applied accordingly:

that which is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is itself the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), being the knowledge regarding the destruction— that is, the cessation— of the outflows.
The meaning is that knowledge has the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava-nirodha*) as its object.
This being so, there are six types of knowledge,
since the very category of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) is differentiated by the distinctions of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the others.
Now, regarding the phrase "one whose mental continuum has exhausted the outflows" (kṣīṇāsravasantāna):
the meaning is that when the outflows have been exhausted, the knowledge that arises is "knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows" (āsravakṣayajñāna).
In the mental continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted, all knowledges are present; thus there are ten knowledges,
except for the non-arising of a Buddha— meaning,
except when no Buddha has arisen anywhere other than in Jambūdvīpa.
The intention is that the ten powers have their basis in the persons of Jambudvīpa because they arise from the basis of a Buddha.
That very same tenfold knowledge is not called a "power" in another [being];
for while this [knowledge] exists in others as well, it is not a power because it is subject to obstruction.
The intention is that whatever is unimpeded is a unique power (*āveṇika-bala*), as in the detailed account of the rejection of the man who had come to see him renounce the world.
"Going forth" (pravrajana) is the act of renunciation (pravrajyā); one who seeks this is a "seeker of renunciation" (pravrajanaprekṣaḥ).

The rejection of such a person seeking renunciation is "the rejection of the seeker of renunciation" (pravrajanaprekṣapuruṣapratyākhyāna), which serves as an illustration, just as in the case where the knowledge of another is obstructed.

It is said that when the noble Śāriputra was examining a certain man seeking ordination to see whether he possessed the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), he did not perceive them; thus, [the man] was rejected, meaning he was not ordained.
However, the Blessed One perceived them and ordained him.
And regarding him, when questioned by the monks, the Blessed One said:
"By this very person was this karma performed, whereby he has attained arhatship."

For actions do not ripen in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the air element; rather, they ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases— so it is said in detail.
And this seed of liberation has been spoken; for I perceive its own subtle essence,
like gold hidden within a fissure in a mineral-bearing rock.
Thus,
"ignorance regarding [the process] up to rebirth" and so forth— the word "etc. includes ignorance regarding [the process] up to death.
"Strength is Nārāyaṇa"—
this is the designation for strength, namely "Nārāyaṇa."
And he who possesses that strength is also called Nārāyaṇa,
like Cāṇūra and Mahānagna.
"Venerable sir," [says] the Elder Dārṣṭāntika;
"otherwise indeed" means if bodily power is not accepted as being like mental power.
The meaning is that the Blessed One would not be patient— that is, he would not possess the capacity for endurance— with respect to the power of infinite knowledge;
this is stated as "another [type] in the joints" (*sandhiṣv anyaḥ*), which introduces a specific kind of bone joint.
"Like a serpent's knot," and so forth:
the joints of the Buddhas are like a serpent's knot;
"serpent's knot" refers to a serpent's coil.
The joints of a Pratyekabuddha are like a chain; the joints of a Cakravartin are like a peg,
being ten times superior.

"The strength of the seven beginning with the elephant" refers to the strength of the group of seven consisting of the elephant, the scent-elephant, the great athlete, the leaper, the excellent-limbed, Cāṇūra, and Nārāyaṇa; that strength is ten times greater than [the preceding], or superior by ten.
To the question "How so?", he says: the strength of ten ordinary elephants— that is, common elephants—
is the strength of one scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*).
In this way, the strength of ten *gandhahastins* is the strength of one *mahānagna*, and so on, up to the strength of ten *cāṇūras*.
That is the strength of a single Nārāyaṇa;
according to the mountain of tenfold increase,
by increasing tenfold at each step, it is called half-Nārāyaṇa strength.
Proceeding from the beginning in the same manner, the strength of ten *praskandin*s is an *ardhanārāyaṇa*, and twice that is a *nārāyaṇa*.
However, since the former is more logical, the Master supports the very first position.

Otherwise, he would not be capable of enduring the power of infinite knowledge; for that very reason, his hurling of Devadatta’s elephant—along with its foot, its thumb, and seven walls and moats—would also not have been possible.
Therefore, it is indeed a specific transformation of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).
This demonstrates that this power (*bala*) has as its intrinsic nature a specific state of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and is not derived matter (*bhautika*);

that is, it is a distinct entity from the seven types of derived matter previously mentioned, such as smoothness and so forth. Others, however, maintain that power is indeed a type of derived matter, though it is something entirely different [from those seven].
"Exactly as stated in the sūtra":
"Śāriputra, there are these four grounds of self-confidence of the Tathāgata.

Endowed with these grounds of self-confidence, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, claims his noble and exalted position, turns the Brahma-wheel, and rightly roars the lion's roar in the assembly."
"What are these four?
That while I am a perfectly awakened Buddha, some ascetic or brahmin might, in accordance with the Dharma, challenge or remind me, saying: 'These dharmas have not been fully realized by you.'"
In this regard, I do not perceive even a sign;

and thus, not perceiving any sign, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, and having attained intrepidity. I claim for myself the noble, preeminent position of the leader, I turn the Brahma-wheel, and I roar the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly.

This is the first ground of self-confidence: "While I am one whose outflows are exhausted, may no one in the world—whether a śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else—rightly challenge me by saying that these outflows have not been abandoned by me," and so on as before, up to: "I roar the perfect lion’s roar in the assembly."
This is the second ground of self-confidence:
"Regarding those things which I have declared to my disciples as obstructive factors—
that for one who indulges in them these are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction— let no one [challenge me] on this point," as before.

This is the third ground of self-confidence: "Furthermore, whatever path I have proclaimed for my disciples— which is noble, leading to liberation, leading to penetration, and which, when practiced, leads to the complete destruction of suffering and to the making of an end to suffering— there is no one who can rightfully say of me, 'It does not lead to liberation,'" as before.
"This is the fourth ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)," as in the detailed explanation of the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*).
Just as the power of knowing what is possible and impossible consists of ten knowledges (*jñāna*) and is comprised within all stages (*bhūmi*), so too is this [fourth ground of self-confidence].
In this way, for one who has indeed become a perfectly awakened Buddha (*samyaksambuddha*), this clarity should likewise be applied by dividing the dharmas into ten types,
just as the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) consists of six or ten knowledges and is comprised within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

"Thus, for one whose outflows are exhausted"—this is the second ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*). Here too, one should apply the same analysis of the dharmas as before, determining whether there are six or ten knowledges (*jñāna*), just as the power of knowledge regarding the ownership of karma consists of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, and is comprised within all stages.
Likewise, "Furthermore, those things which have been declared by me to be obstacles for the disciples," and so forth in detail—this is the third ground of self-confidence.

Here too, having distinguished the dharmas in the same manner, one should apply the principle that only those comprised within the truths of suffering and origination are obstructive, not those comprised within the truths of cessation and the path; thus there are eight knowledges (*jñāna*),
just as the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere consists of ten or nine knowledges and is comprised within all stages (*bhūmi*).
Likewise, regarding the statement, "This is the path which has been taught by me for the deliverance of the disciples"— this is a ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*).

In this case as well, one should apply the principle that there are ten cognitions (*jñāna*) if the path is taken together with its fruit and both its contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aspects, or nine if the fruit is not included.
"Indeed, fearlessness is *vaiśāradya*;
and since one becomes fearless by means of these [knowledges], the knowledges themselves are the *vaiśāradyas*," say the Vaibhāṣikas.
To this, the Master says:
Alternatively, the fearlessness produced by knowledge is not knowledge itself;
or rather, all of this is simply the statement of the Teacher.
For fearlessness is indeed intrepidity;
for it is a mental factor that serves as the antidote to fear,
and fear itself is also a mental factor.
Since one becomes fearless by means of these knowledges acting as causes,
how is it that knowledge itself is the ground of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)?
Rather, it is logical that the ground of self-confidence is produced by knowledge, not that knowledge itself is the ground of self-confidence.
"According to the Sūtra": "O monks, there are these three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates;
cultivating which, the Noble One is worthy to instruct a community."
What are the three?
Here, monks, the Teacher, out of compassion, being merciful, desiring their welfare, seeking their benefit, and feeling pity, teaches the Dharma to his disciples:
