"This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness; this is for your benefit and happiness."
My disciples listen to me with respect, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understand.
They practice in accordance with the Dharma and do not act by transgressing it within the Teacher’s instruction;
therefore, the Tathāgata experiences no delight, no mental pleasure, and no elation of heart.
The Tathāgata dwells therein equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
this is the first application of mindfulness which the Noble One cultivates.
Furthermore, when that noble one, practicing [the path], is worthy of instructing the assembly,
the Teacher again teaches the Dharma as before,
yet his disciples do not wish to listen.
They do not lend an ear, they do not establish a mind intent on understanding,
and they do not practice in accordance with the Dharma.
They proceed by transgressing the Teacher’s instruction;
therefore, the Tathāgata feels no resentment, no impatience, no ill-will, and no displeasure of mind;
rather, the Tathāgata dwells there with equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is the second foundation of mindfulness,
which the noble one cultivates,
cultivating which the noble one is worthy to instruct a community.
Furthermore, monks, as long as [he remains] within the teaching, the Tathāgata feels neither delight nor gladness, nor does his mind experience elation;
he has no malice, no impatience, no resentment, and no lack of satisfaction in his heart.
Therein the Tathāgata dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
This is the third foundation of mindfulness, which the Noble One cultivates;
cultivating which, the Noble One is worthy to instruct a community.
He shows that mindfulness and clear comprehension possess a dual nature.
From the statement "mindful and clearly comprehending," it follows that this applies even to a Śrāvaka; this is the detailed explanation.

That is to say, when even a Śrāvaka whose afflictions have been diminished is faced with disciples who wish to listen, those who do not wish to listen, and both—those who wish to listen and those who do not.
Why is it that joy, attachment, resentment, or hatred do not arise? For what reason are these called the unique, uncommon Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)?
"Because of the abandonment along with the latent tendencies (*savāsanaprahāṇāt*)," means because of the abandonment of joy and so forth together with their latent tendencies (*savāsanānām*).
But what is this so-called "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*) for the Śrāvakas?

For whatever affliction one has previously practiced, the specific capacity within the mind that causes the transformation of bodily and vocal activity produced by that [affliction] is called a "latent impression" (*vāsanā*).
The Venerable Anantavarman states that a latent impression is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) particularity of the mind.
Alternatively, the Master explains in detail: "Of whom [are they the disciples]?"—they are the disciples of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and not of anyone else.
What is the reason?
For all disciples have gone forth under the guidance of the Buddhas; therefore,
whether those disciples are obedient or disobedient, or both— whether they are obedient or both— the non-arising of that very state of being a disciple is the non-arising of joy or resentment.
The meaning is that this marvelous and extraordinary state is established for no other disciple;
for otherwise, as the detailed explanation goes...
If it were not of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), it would be of the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*) like compassion (*karuṇā*); [in that case],
it would not be established as having all sentient beings as its object, nor would it be established as having the sentient beings of the three realms as its object— this is the meaning.
Just as compassion has sentient beings of the three realms as its object,
what then? It has sentient beings of the desire realm as its object.

The intention is that this would be established precisely because [compassion] has suffering beings as its object; however, it follows that [the threefold aspect of suffering] would not be established. Just like compassion (*karuṇā*):

just as compassion has only the aspect of suffering (*duḥkhatā*) and not the threefold aspect of suffering—that is, it does not have the aspects of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
If it were otherwise, that would not be the case;
yet it is accepted as having the aspect of the three types of suffering (triduḥkhatā).
Therefore, its intrinsic nature is conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Showing that the cause is denoted by the word "great," he says, "Why is this? and so forth:
"Because of the accumulation [of the two provisions]," meaning because of the attainment of the great provisions of merit and wisdom.
From the attainment of the great accumulation of merit,
there arises the great accumulation of wisdom, which consists of three perfections:
the perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience.

The accumulation of great gnosis (*mahājñānasambhāra*) is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); however, the perfections of vigor (*vīrya*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are twofold because they function in both [accumulations].

For indeed, without vigor, generosity is not given, ethical discipline is not undertaken, and patience is not cultivated; thus, vigor is that which partakes in the accumulation of great merit (*mahāpuṇyasambhāra*).
Likewise, meditation on the side of the cultivation of the four immeasurables, such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*), partakes in the great accumulation of merit;

meditation on the side of the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), partakes in the great accumulation of gnosis. Because it arises from and is brought about by these two—the great accumulations of merit and gnosis—it is "great compassion" (*mahā-karuṇā*) due to its greatness.
It is by way of its aspect (*ākāra*), because it takes the three types of suffering as its aspect;
for compassion takes all three types of suffering as its aspect, and not merely the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) alone,
since it has the sentient beings of the three realms as its object (*ālambana*).
Because it takes as its object sentient beings born in all three realms, and not only those born in the desire realm— as stated in the passage: "Compassion [takes] desire-realm beings as its range."
Because it functions with equanimity toward all sentient beings by virtue of its equality—
since it operates equally toward all sentient beings included within the three realms through the aspect of the suffering inherent in conditioned formations—
it is therefore called "great compassion."
"Because there is nothing more intense than that" means that,
by virtue of having wisdom as its intrinsic nature, it is sharper; for in this way, one feels compassion through it.
"It is not so through compassion" refers to the distinction or difference [between the two],
because [compassion] has non-hatred and non-delusion as its intrinsic nature.
The meaning is that, respectively, compassion has non-hatred as its intrinsic nature, while great compassion has non-delusion as its intrinsic nature;
this is because they take the forms of one and three types of suffering, respectively.
Because compassion has the aspect of a single suffering,
and great compassion has the aspect of the three sufferings, these two should be applied respectively to both cases everywhere.
Because it belongs to the four dhyānas and the level of the fourth dhyāna; that is to say,
compassion (karuṇā) belongs to the four dhyāna levels,
and since the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara) are included by the mention of the first dhyāna, it is said not to belong to six levels.

Great compassion, however, belongs exclusively to the level of the fourth dhyāna; for it is only that [level] which possesses the flexibility required for all meditative absorptions and is thus capable of producing it, owing to its arising within the mental continua of Śrāvakas and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), Pratyekabuddhas and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are included.
Because they are obtained through detachment from the realm of desire and the peak of existence, respectively:
compassion is obtained through detachment from the realm of desire,
while great compassion is obtained through detachment from the peak of existence.
"By way of not protecting and protecting" means that through compassion, the śrāvakas and others merely feel compassion themselves and simply become weary;
they do not protect [beings] from the fear of saṃsāra.
But the Blessed One, feeling compassion through great compassion, protects [beings] from the great fear of saṃsāra;
because he feels compassion with incomparable compassion, he feels incomparable compassion.
Because one feels compassion only for those who are suffering,

whereas through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) one feels compassion equally for all sentient beings; and because it arises from the prior accumulation of the equipment of merit and knowledge (*puṇya-jñāna-sambhāra*).
Through the full realization of the accumulation of merit in previous births and the previously mentioned accumulation of knowledge,
and by means of the perfection of the *dharmakāya*,
the *dharmakāya* is the continuum of the accumulation of untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
Or rather, it is the transformation of the basis through purposeful conduct;
for wealth is the cause of heaven and liberation for the world.
The accomplishment of that [compassion] is beneficial conduct;
for the great compassion of all the wise is the cause for the welfare of others,
according to the proper time.
It applies everywhere:
how is it that, while life is short and brief, Buddhas appear among long-lived beings at the appropriate time as long-lived ones?
Among those of short lifespan,
they become Kṣatriyas in a world where the Kṣatriya is held in high esteem, or Brāhmaṇas in a world where the Brāhmaṇa is held in high esteem, according to the circumstances.
And at the appropriate time, those of the Kāśyapa clan and those of the Gautama clan likewise appeared in small numbers in this world of small proportions.
"Because they are not of small measure, they are not of small measure" refers to the perfection of the cause, characterized by the accumulation of merit and gnosis,
and the perfection of the fruit, characterized by the Dharma-body.
The perfection of assistance, characterized by conduct for the sake of the world,
consists in the practice of the accumulations of all virtues and knowledge;
these "virtues" have the five perfections as their intrinsic nature.

The various types of knowledge have the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) as their intrinsic nature; the "accumulation" (*sambhāra*) of all those qualities and knowledges is their repeated practice, that is, their application again and again.
Practice over a long period of time means practicing continuously for three incalculable great aeons; practice without interruption means practicing with uninterrupted continuity;
and practice with reverence means practicing with intense devotion.
Regarding the "fourfold perfection of the fruit":
through the complete accomplishment of the *dharmakāya*, there are four perfections beginning with gnosis; these too are established as the "perfection of the fruit.
As he will state, the "perfection of gnosis" is fourfold.
Likewise, it will be stated that the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form body are fourfold;
that itself will be the explanation for these [qualities], namely, the fourfold perfection of benefit.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"The perfection of ultimate liberation from the three miserable states and the suffering of cyclic existence.
Here, the "three miserable states" refers to the hells and so forth, and "conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra*) refers to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
For those two, there is suffering;
from that, there is absolute liberation—
this alone is true prosperity.
Or, it is the perfection of establishing [beings] in the three vehicles and in the happy migrations;
that is, establishing them in the three vehicles, such as the Śrāvaka vehicle, and in the happy migrations.
"That very [perfection]" refers to this fourfold perfection of assistance;
"uninstructed knowledge" is for the purpose of self-awakening.
"Knowledge of all things" (*sarvatrajñāna*) is used in the sense of awakening to individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) without exception;
"knowledge in every way" (*sarvathājñāna*) is used in the sense of awakening to all modes (*sarvaprakāra*).

"Effortless knowledge" means the realization [of objects] by mere wish; "the abandonment of all afflictions" means the eradication of the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and meditation within the three realms;
"ultimate abandonment" means [abandonment] from which there is no regression; and "abandonment along with the latent predispositions" means [the removal of even the residual traces].
Through the absence of mental attachment,

there is the abandonment of the obscurations to all objects of meditative concentration and attainment; this constitutes the perfection of mastery over the external creation, transformation, and sustaining of objects for one who is liberated in both ways.
In this context, *nirmāṇa* (creation) is the production of unprecedented external objects; *pariṇāma* (transformation) is the conversion of stones and the like into gold and the like;
and *adhiṣṭhāna* (sustenance) is the maintenance [of an object] for a long duration.
The perfection of mastery over the relinquishing and the sustaining of life is called the "perfection of mastery over the relinquishing and sustaining of life. As for the detailed explanation,
it includes traveling through obstructions, traveling through space, and traveling even to very distant places.

The term "from the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇāt*) is an *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning "from each of the Brahmins"]; the inclusion of many within one is like the entry of many elephants and so forth into a single atom (*paramāṇu*).
And that [mastery] consists in the ability to travel very swiftly over great distances through obstructed space, and in the entry into small or large [spaces];
this should be understood as the perfection of mastery (*vaśitva-sampat*) over those two.
"Various" means of many kinds; "intrinsic" means natural (*svābhāvika*).
It should be understood that their "perfection" refers to those marvelous qualities.
This is the natural law of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones: as they walk, the low ground becomes level and that which is high becomes low.
That which was low becomes high;
the blind regain their sight.
The deaf [attain] the sense of hearing,
the insane [attain] mindfulness; thus, everything should be followed according to the sūtra,
as it pertains to the perfection of the marks.
The perfection of the thirty-two marks of a great man, such as the *ūrṇā* and the *uṣṇīṣa*, is the perfection of the secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*);
that is, the perfection of the eighty secondary characteristics, such as rounded fingers, copper-colored and elevated nails, and so forth.

He possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa, which is endowed with power; his bones have the essence of a diamond, thus he has "diamond-essence-bones"; he has a body whose bones have the essence of a diamond, thus he is "one whose body has diamond-essence-bones."
The state of being that is its perfection; thus,
it is the perfection of having a body with bones as hard as diamond.
This is a summary and a concise account:
whatever noble persons, having conceived faith, have praised, do praise, or will praise the Buddha, the Blessed One,
they all do so by means of these very three kinds of excellence.
If his life were to last for many incalculable eons— many asaṃkhyeya-kalpas—
and if the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were to maintain it thus, only then would they be capable of knowing and describing that entire extent of his majesty.
The intention is that [the qualities] are exceedingly numerous because they possess infinite distinctions. And thus, "to such an extent" (*tāvat*) is the detailed explanation;
"qualities" (*guṇa*), "knowledges" (*jñāna*), "power" (*prabhāva*), and "benefit" (*upakāra*) form a *dvandva* compound.
Furthermore, "and infinite" is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
these very great jewels are the Tathāgatas, who are their forms.

Moreover, foolish ordinary persons— whose resolute conviction and interest have been destroyed by the poverty of their own qualities, which serves as the basis for inference— do not honor the Buddha, meaning they do not respect him even up to the point of not perceiving him as a Buddha;
"even by mere faith" means by way of non-realization.
"Of those with indefinite ripening" means that those with definite ripening cannot be bypassed; this is the intended meaning.
That which exists among the gods is "divine" (*daivī*).
"Because its fruit is not in vain, is excellent, swift, and has a happy end":
it is "not in vain" because it persists through the necessity of yielding its fruit;
it is "a desirable fruit" because its fruit consists of divine objects.
It has an excellent fruit because its fruit is abundant;
it has a swift fruit because its fruit consists of divine objects;
it has an excellent fruit because its fruit is abundant.
It has a swift fruit because its fruit is to be experienced in the present life and so forth; it has a good final fruit because its fruit is nirvāṇa,
due to possessing that state.
The Tathāgatas are called the unsurpassed field of merit; "services" refers to beneficial acts such as worship and so forth, according to what is appropriate.

According to their possibility, some qualities of the Buddha Bhagavats are shared with the Śrāvakas, such as *araṇā* (the absence of conflict), *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve), and so forth;
others are shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), emptiness (śūnyatā), signlessness (animitta), wishlessness (apraṇihita), and so forth are included; no passion, hatred, or pride arises with respect to them as its object,
because by that [realization], one avoids the view of a self and so forth.

In whatever way he has realized— having emerged from the concentration of non-affliction (*araṇā-samādhi*)— that "upon seeing me, passion will arise in this person, hatred in that, pride in another, or lack of faith in yet another," even though he has emerged from that concentration, he continues to apply himself accordingly. However, regarding the specific means of protecting the minds of others, the meaning to be understood is that by the mere power of the arising of that concentration of non-affliction, afflictions do not arise in others.
"Causing conflict" (raṇayati) means "causing affliction" (kleśayati).
Because the fourth dhyāna is the foremost among those that are easy to practice, araṇā belongs only to that level and not to the levels of the other dhyānas.
Because one is unable to avoid them, there is the possibility of falling away; thus,
which afflictions are "with a basis" (*savastuka*)?
The afflictions such as attachment that are to be abandoned by cultivation are without a real objective basis (*avastuka*); whereas those to be abandoned by seeing,
being universal (*sarvatraga*), take as their object the entirety of their own level, and thus they also take the mental continua of others as their objects.
They cannot be abandoned because they are omnipresent;
moreover, that [defilement] has everything as its object.
It is "having everything as its object" (*sarvālambana*) because it takes everything as its object,
or because everything is its object; thus, it is "having everything as its object," unlike *araṇā*, which has only the afflictions as its object.
What, then, is the meaning? It means that it also has form and so forth as its object;
however, the formless realms are not known directly by the knowledge resulting from prayer.
What is the reason?
Because it will be stated that the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna) belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
The supernormal knowledges have the lower stages as their objects;
thus, the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*) is like a supernormal knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "due to the distinction of the outflow and the conduct": therein, the outflow is extreme dullness,
and the conduct is the dwelling in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Thus, it has been demonstrated that there is inference from effect to cause and from cause to effect; furthermore,
for those who have fallen away from that state and for those who have attained meditative absorption therein, both of these are directly perceived.
And here there is the illustration of the farmer:
just as a farmer understands the seed by means of the fruit, or the fruit by means of the seed.
Or just as a farmer knows that in such a field there will be such a fruit of grain, or having seen the grain, he infers the field:
"Such is his field."

"Having seen a being with such a peaceful form, one infers: 'This person has passed away from the formless realm (ārūpya) and will be reborn among the noble ones (ārya),' according to the statement of the Vaibhāṣikas."
This indicates that others possess knowledge of the formless realm;
for there is nothing that is not within the scope of the Buddhas—this is the intended meaning.
"Preceded by a vow" means preceded by an application of attention (*ābhoga*).
The meaning is "having made a vow and having consumed"; "as great as the object of that samādhi" refers to whatever constitutes the domain of a śrāvaka.
One knows as much as pertains to the Pratyekabuddha within one's own sphere; such is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid).
Now, the Dharma of teaching has multiple meanings; for the word "Dharma" is multivalent, as in: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma."

"I shall fully proclaim the holy life (brahmacarya) that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end; which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine"—herein lies the Dharma of teaching.
What is this Dharma?
In the phrase "the noble eightfold path," this refers to the dharma of practice;
likewise, in the phrase "one should go for refuge to the Dharma," this refers to the dharma of the fruit, which is nirvāṇa, and so forth— this is what is meant by "irreversible."
The phrase "it is impossible to turn back" refers to the state of having an unshakable nature and a human basis; this same twofold meaning is connected by the word "thus" (*tathā*),
because the objects of focus and so forth are mentioned separately.
Regarding "the state of speaking with what is logical and fluent": "logical" means connected to the meaning, and "fluent" means unimpeded.
"One who speaks what is appropriate and well-spoken" is *yuktamuktābhilāpī*;
its state (*tadbhāvaḥ*) [is the quality] in that [state].
Mastery over concentration regarding the state of speaking appropriately and fluently; for one who has mastery over concentration,
there is clear manifestation and non-forgetfulness.
How is it that the distinction [of the analytical knowledge of eloquence] is that it is the manifestation of mastery over meditative concentration and the irreversible knowledge regarding it?
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratyabhijñāna-pratisaṃvid*), which has speech as its object, has as its intrinsic nature nine knowledges:
the knowledges of suffering, origin, dharma, subsequent, destruction, non-arising, and conventional knowledge.

That which has the Path as its object has the nature of the knowledge of the factors of the Path, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of destruction, the knowledge of non-arising, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of others' minds; thus, in summary, it has the nature of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
If "all phenomena" is the meaning, then there are ten knowledges.
For there is no phenomenon that does not become an object of the ten cognitions as the case may be,
provided that "nirvāṇa" is the intended meaning; thus, it is the object of six cognitions.
Because the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) has the fivefold nature of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and so forth,

and because it takes the sets of names (nāmakāya) and so forth as its objects of speech, the untainted knowledge of suffering and so forth does not take a portion of suffering or a portion of origination as its object by way of their specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa);
what then?
Because the five aggregates of clinging are viewed through their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), they are therefore of the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); furthermore,
because the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) do not exist in the higher realms.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid);
and where the sets of names (nāmakāya) do not exist, there the absence of the sets of phrases (padakāya) and phonemes (vyañjanakāya) is established.

"Because there is an absence of applied thought (*vitarka*) in the higher stages" refers to the Sūtra statement that "having applied thought and sustained thought (*vicāra*), one utters speech"; furthermore, these analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have names and so forth as their objects even for one who has entered meditative absorption (*samāpanna*).

Even for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption], having names and so forth as objects of focus is an ornament by means of the irreversible cognitions obtained subsequent to that; furthermore, by means of that very same subsequent [cognition], there are designations such as "woman" or "man."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), time, grammatical case, and so forth are included.
Furthermore, "designation" (*adhivacana*) is a synonym;
or, it is a designation because it is a verbal expression referring to that [object].
Regarding the phrase "in its non-attachment":
this refers to that designation, or to those words and phonemes;
for this very reason, their sequential establishment is established.

Since the comprehension of meaning follows the words and phonemes, and since there is an unimpeded mastery over their designations as singular, dual, plural, feminine, masculine, and so forth, the sequence is thus established; therefore,
[the teaching begins] with "form" and so on.
By the word "etcetera," [terms such as] "it cognizes, therefore it is consciousness (vijñāna)" and "it accumulates, therefore it is mind (citta)," and so forth, are included;
and "eloquence" (pratibhāna) refers to successive flashes of inspired expression, according to the *Vādanyāya*.
"In due order" means that for the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), calculation is the preliminary practice;
for the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), the word of the Buddha is the preliminary practice.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) is the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) is the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), both being nothing other than the word of the Buddha.
That [fourth dhyāna] is of six kinds;
some [maintain] that the fourth dhyāna consists of *araṇā* (the absence of conflict).

Some consists of the nature of the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*), some consists of the nature of the three analytical knowledges (*tripratisaṃvid*), and some is distinct from those, being merely the "ultimate limit" (*prāntakoṭika*).
Excluding the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), since there is an absence of applied thought (*vitarka*) therein,
how is it that this was stated without distinction as being produced by [the mind] accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarkasavicāra*)?
These six are called the "ultimate limits."
The meaning is that the analytical knowledge of language (niruktipratisaṃvid) is obtained by means of that power, but it does not belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna;
rather,
it belongs to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
"Conformed to all stages" means "made favorable to all stages."
That which has its end or limit gone forth is *pragatānta*; that which has reached the end is *prānta*;
and that which has its limit at the extreme edge is *prāntakoṭika*.
"Like the fourfold alternative" means that just as a fourfold alternative consists of a question of four types, so it is here.

"Regarding the range of supernormal power," and so forth: the six higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) are the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the range of supernormal power, the divine ear, the [knowledge of] others' minds, the recollection of former abodes, the death and rebirth [of beings], and the higher knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
And regarding this, there is a sutra:
"In this case, a monk experiences various kinds of supernormal powers:
having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one."
The detailed text regarding the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) should be understood from the *Lokhita* [sūtra],
up until this is called the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of the realization of the knowledge of the sphere of psychic power.
Here, a monk, with the divine ear, purified and surpassing that of humans, hears both kinds of sounds— human and non-human— whether they are far or near.
This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine ear.
Here, a monk sees beings with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans; [this passage] is a long text as in the Sūtras, up until:
this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine eye.

In this regard, there is an extensive textual passage, as in the Sūtras, beginning with "here a monk recollects his manifold past abodes," up to what is called the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) consisting in the realization through direct experience of the knowledge of the recollection of past abodes.
Here, a monk knows, as it truly is, the thoughts and reflections, the mental and the psychical, of other beings and other persons.

He understands, as it truly is, a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," and he understands, as it truly is, a mind free from lust as "a mind free from lust. He understands, as it truly is, a mind with hatred as "with hatred," a mind free from hatred as "free from hatred," a mind with delusion as "with delusion," and a mind free from delusion as "free from delusion. He understands, as it truly is, a distracted mind as "distracted," a concentrated mind as "concentrated," a sunken mind as "sunken," an uplifted mind as "uplifted," an agitated mind as "agitated," an unagitated mind as "unagitated," an unpacified mind as "unpacified," a pacified mind as "pacified," a composed mind as "composed," an uncomposed mind as "uncomposed," an uncultivated mind as "uncultivated," a cultivated mind as "cultivated," and an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind. He understands, as it truly is, an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind."
He understands, as it truly is, "the mind is liberated, the mind is liberated";
this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the knowledge of others' minds.
Here, a monk understands, as it truly is, "this is the noble truth of suffering."
He understands, as it truly is: "This is the origin of suffering; this is the cessation of suffering; this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering."

For one who thus knows and thus sees, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and the mind is liberated from the influx of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and the influx of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).
For one who is liberated, the knowledge and vision arises: "I am liberated."
"Birth is exhausted for me; I know there is no further existence beyond this"—

this is called the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) of the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā*), which is a meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The domain of supernormal power consists of emanation and movement; knowledge regarding that domain is its realization,
which is its manifestation before one.
The supernormal knowledge of the realization of the sphere of psychic power;
the divine ear, which is the knowledge therein.
The realization of that [knowledge] is the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear;
the specific distinction is the "succession of thoughts" (*cetaḥparyāya*), which is either "attached," "hating," or "deluded," or else it is a sequence or a succession.
At times it is passionate, at times hateful, and at times deluded;
therein lies his knowledge, which is its direct realization.
"Previous abodes" (*pūrve-nivāsa*) refers to the aggregates (*skandha*);
"recollection" (*anusmṛti*) means the memory of them; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) regarding that [memory] is its direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
Passing away and rebirth— these two constitute "passing-away-and-rebirth";
the knowledge of them is their direct realization.
The destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*),
the knowledge regarding that [destruction],
and the direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) of it— each of these is connected with the term "higher knowledge" (*abhijñā*).
"Like the fruit of asceticism" means that just as the conditioned fruit of asceticism has the nature of the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*),
so too does this.
"The fivefold knowledge regarding the mind" refers to the superknowledge (abhijñā) that [knows] the mental states of others through the variations of the mind.
The meaning is that its nature consists of five types of knowledge;

for it is possible for untainted knowledge of others' minds to be the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds, while it is also possible for tainted [knowledge of others' minds] to be conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds.
"Just as the power" means, for example, the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).
If it is argued that the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows has the destruction of the outflows as its object, then there would be six knowledges,
because the knowledge of cessation is designated by the names of the knowledges of dharma, subsequent, destruction, and non-arising.

And if it is argued that since conventional knowledge can have cessation as its object, the knowledge that exists in the continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted is that [knowledge] which arises when the outflows are destroyed;
There are ten knowledges because ten knowledges exist within the continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted;
thus, the supernormal knowledge that has the destruction of the outflows as its object [is likewise so called].
If that supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) is the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna), then it consists of those same six knowledges.
The fact that this [knowledge] pertains to all stages is understood by this very statement: "just as power [is]."
And because it is determined that there are exactly five [factors] in each of the four meditations.
Therefore, it is understood from this as well that this sixth supernormal power (*abhijñā*) belongs to all stages;
for the first three— the supernormal powers of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)— do not exist [on those higher stages].
Why?
Because they have form as their object;
for indeed, formless states do not have form as their object.
Because of the state of having transcended the perception of form (*rūpasañjñā*),
and because of being accomplished by means of the gateway of form;
that is to say, because it is accomplished through the door of form, and because it is accomplished by means of a path that takes form as its object.
Such a mind arises in such a form; however, for those in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), form cannot be an object of perception.
Furthermore, there is no recollection of former lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*) [in those states], because it is accomplished by recollecting the successive stages of one's own existence in sequence.
For they accomplish it by recollecting the various successive states of their own selves.
Furthermore, phenomena belonging to the desire realm are not the objects of the formless [attainments];
for it will be said that "the fundamental wholesome formless states do not have the lower contaminated realms as their domain."
Thus,

those other states belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are the object of that [consciousness] at the time of its production; for this reason, there is no [consciousness] belonging to that same level (*tadbhūmika*),
and also because its objects are places, lineages, and so forth.
Having passed away from there as well, he was reborn elsewhere;
for it is said in the Sūtra:
"Those beings are named such-and-such."
"I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and passing away from there as well, I was reborn here"— thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.

Furthermore, because the formless realms (ārūpya) do not have the places, lineages, and so forth as their objects, nor do they have the lower stages as their objects—for this reason also, the knowledges belonging to the formless stages are not [the basis for] the knowledge of others' minds, since that must be accomplished by means of the gateway of form (rūpa). Therefore, he says:
"For one who desires to know the mind of another," and so forth.
"Applying oneself" means performing an application;
that is, having grasped the sign.
The meaning is "having discerned the mode of the mind.
"In reverse order from that" means he brings to mind the other successive states of that very same mind which have ceased immediately prior [to the present state].
"Even skipping over [births], there is recollection":
even having skipped or bypassed one birth or two, how is there recollection of the Śuddhāvāsa deities?
If recollection pertains only to what has been previously experienced,
then indeed there is no coming here for those dwelling in the Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), because they are non-returners (anāgāmin);
therefore, they have no experience here.
Nor does it belong to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) there, because it has not arisen [in them],
since they have not experienced it through hearing.
For he has heard that there are gods named Śuddhāvāsa who are such as this;
for experience is of two kinds: the experience of seeing and the experience of hearing.
Production by means of presiding over another's continuum refers to the knowledge of recollecting former abodes as comprised within the dhyānas;
and by means of that, one does not apprehend a mind belonging to the formless realm.
And how, moreover, is there production by means of taking hold of the basis of another's continuum?
It is by taking hold of the signs from the mental consciousnesses of others that have just ceased; such is the detailed explanation regarding "others."
For those who have not fallen away from the formless realms,
the production of supernormal powers such as the knowledge of recollecting former abodes is easily accomplished by means of presiding over their own mental continuum alone.

Regarding the three higher knowledges of supernormal power, the divine ear, and the divine eye, their respective applications are as follows: the mental attention to lightness is the application for supernormal power;
the mental attention to sound is the application for the divine ear;
and the mental attention to light is the application for the divine eye.
The question "How are these obtained? refers to their acquisition (*prāpti*);

however, as for their manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*), those [dharmas] that are not habitual are not [obtained] through mere application, whereas those that are habitual are obtained through application.
Those which are specific, which have not been produced before—
all of these are produced through application—
as well as those which are obtained through detachment.
And as for those [cognitions] that arise from application,
they all— except for sound— arise from that [direct perception].
Because it has been cut off, sound is not emanated;
for he will say that the external emanation pertaining to the desire realm consists of four sense-bases.
"How then? and so forth.

If the supernormal power of the eye (*cakṣur-abhijñā*) has the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) as its object, how then is it that by means of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapādajñāna*), [one perceives] "Alas, these venerable beings are possessed of misconduct of body," and so on?
For the possession of vocal and mental actions is not apprehended by visual consciousness.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) is included; it is not that [view], namely,
the possession (samanvāgama) of vocal and mental karma and so forth, by which one does not know through that visual consciousness.
If one asks "By what [is it known]?", he says:
"But that is the knowledge which is the retinue of the superknowledges (abhijñā)";
the meaning is that it is mental [knowledge].
Regarding the phrase "in the remainder":

how is it that the supernormal powers of recollecting past lives (*pūrvenivāsānusmṛti*) and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) have the four applications of mindfulness (*catuḥ-smṛtyupasthāna*) as their intrinsic nature?

The supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) has the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as its intrinsic nature because it consists of ten knowledges;
even though it consists of six knowledges, the future applications of mindfulness regarding body, sensation, and mind are also cultivated.
How, then, are those two established as belonging to the stages of the four dhyānas?
For there exists no visual cognition or auditory cognition belonging to the levels of the second dhyāna and above,
because those two are associated with visual and auditory consciousness,
and those [consciousnesses] are absent in the second dhyāna and above.
For it will be stated:
"The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as that which originates informative action (*vijñapti*),
when occurring in the second dhyāna and above, belong to the first [dhyāna]."
"Thus,
by virtue of the basis," and so forth;
by virtue of the bases of the eye and the ear, those two cognitions also belong to the level of the four dhyānas.
The eye and the ear are established as belonging to the levels of the four dhyānas;
this explanation is either "predominant" (*prādhānika*) or "frequent" (*bāhulika*). That which exists in the predominant is "predominant."
Thus,
because the wholesome superknowledges (abhijñā) are predominant and primary, the exposition is made with reference to them.
"Wholesome supernormal knowledge" means that,
for the most part, the supernormal knowledges are wholesome;
therefore, it is explained in this way.
Just as there is the designation "a heap of beans" even when mudga beans and others are present [within it], so too,
because they cease at the prior limit and so forth,
[the sequence lasts] for as long as [they endure] in their respective order.
Bhagavadviśeṣa and others, however,
say that one removes delusion regarding the past through the recollection of former abodes,
and removes delusion regarding the intermediate state through the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth.

The intention behind their explanation— that "by means of the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayābhijñā), one knows that there is no further existence beyond this"— is to dispel delusion regarding the future limit (parānta).
"Past, present, and future" is the sequence of the time-periods (*adhvan*);
therefore, the understanding of the meaning is thus.
However, the teacher Saṃghabhadra explains it as follows:

For the supernormal knowledge of former abodes (pūrvenivāsābhijñā) turns back delusion regarding the past by ceasing [the cycle] from the prior limit and so forth; the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (cyutyupapādābhijñā) [turns back delusion regarding the future].
There is delusion regarding the middle [existence]; however, the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) is an exception.

For this reason, only these three possess the nature of true knowledge (*vidyā*), because through the former two, one perceives the calamities of oneself and others, which gives rise to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Since one who is thus agitated by others understands the reality of things through the third [verse] alone,
what is there to be understood here?
We consider the explanation of Ācārya Saṅghabhadra alone to be the most appropriate;
for the intention of the Master [Vasubandhu] himself is also perceived to be exactly thus.
For, having stated that there are three realizations—namely, the realization of the knowledge of former abodes, of death and rebirth, and of the destruction of the outflows—he says:
For these [three] dispel delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present] respectively;
how, then, is it known that there are exactly three higher knowledges (*abhijñā*) and three sciences (*vidyā*)?
Because it has been stated thus:

The establishment of the three knowledges (*vidyā*) is based precisely on the Sūtra: the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives belonging to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); the realization of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings belonging to one beyond training; and the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) belonging to one beyond training.
For thus it is said:
"One becomes a Tripiṭaka and one possessing the three knowledges (trividyā) by means of the knowledges of one beyond training (aśaikṣī vidyā)."

The intention is that because they are untainted (*anāsrava*), [the first two] do not afflict; the supernormal knowledges of former abodes and death-and-rebirth are neither belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because they are tainted (*sāsrava*).
There are three miracles (*prātihārya*) in their respective order.
The supernormal knowledge of the domain of psychic power is the miracle of psychic power;
the supernormal knowledge of the variations of the mind is the miracle of mind-reading,
[knowing] "such is your mind."
The superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) is the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanaprātihārya*),
meaning the teaching according to reality;
this is because the two prefixes [in *prāti*] signify "initial action" and "intensity," respectively.
The prefix *pra-* signifies the sense of "beginning an action," as in "this action has been commenced by him";
and the prefix *ati-* signifies the sense of "intensity," as in "gone beyond."
This is what is meant:

they are called "miracles" (prātihārya) because they captivate the minds of those to be trained (vineya) from the very beginning with great intensity; [they are so called] for those who are hostile or indifferent.
Relying on the etymological method (*nairukta*), it is said that "the addition of a phoneme and the transposition of a phoneme" should be applied here,
because of its invariable consistency.
Thus,
because it follows immediately upon the destruction of the afflictions, it succeeds.
The meaning is "it is accomplished";
by means of the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding what is distant as being near,
that which is produced by such resolve is called "produced by resolve" (*ādhimokṣikī*).
That which is distant, one resolves upon as being near; because of that, one arrives quickly, and thus it is called "resolute" (ādhimokṣikī) regarding the external four bases (caturāyatana).
Thus,
nothing internal is created;
for if it were so created, there would be the undesirable consequence of the manifestation of previously non-existent sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "not connected to one's own or another's body":
when one's own self acts as a lion or acts as an elephant,
that is what is connected to one's own body.
Whatever is projected externally from one's own self, such as a lion or an elephant, that which is connected to another is likewise twofold.
Connected with one's own body or another's body,
it is thus in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*);
just as one born in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) creates two kinds of emanations (*nirmāṇa*).
That [emanation] belonging to the desire realm and the form realm is also twofold— connected with one's own mind-body and connected with another's mind-body— and thus it is fourfold;
in this way, even one reborn in the form realm creates a fourfold emanation.
In brief, the eightfold emanation is not "possession" (samanvāgama), just like clothing and ornaments;

for even though clothing and ornaments are connected to one's own body, they do not constitute possession because they are reckoned as non-sentient or because they are not connected to the bases of the sense-faculties.
In the same way,
"the two bases" refers to the base of visible forms and the base of tangible objects.
The intention is that the sense-bases of odor and taste are not [present] because of the absence of possession;
the sense-base of sound is not [present] because it has been cut off.
Others say "because they are produced by impact," the intention being that they are adventitious;
thus, there are three fruits of the second dhyāna.
Two belonging to a lower stage and two belonging to its own stage—
thus four and five are to be applied; therefore,
there are four belonging to the stage of the third dhyāna.

The detailed explanation is as follows: for the fruit of the second dhyāna and so forth, there are five belonging to the lower stages and four belonging to its own stage; for the fruit of the fourth dhyāna, there are three belonging to the lower stages and one belonging to its own stage.
The emanation that is the fruit of the second dhyāna, which has been created by an emanator,
excels in its range of movement over the emanation-fruit belonging to the level of the first dhyāna;
that emanation which is the fruit of the second dhyāna goes to the level of the second dhyāna.
However, the fruit of the first dhyāna does not go to that [realm],
but rather goes only to the level of the first dhyāna; thus, it is distinguished by the difference in its destination.

In this way, the fruit of the third and subsequent dhyānas should be applied accordingly; as with the dhyānas themselves, there is an "acquisition" (lābha) through detachment (vairāgyataḥ), just as there is an acquisition of the fundamental dhyānas (mauladhyāna). Thus, there is an acquisition of the emanation-minds (nirmāṇacitta) through detachment.
The transformative mind arises immediately after the pure dhyāna; thus, that which is the first [mind] in the manifestation of the transformative mind arises from the pure [dhyāna].
Or "from the transformation-mind" means that in the second and subsequent moments of the stream,
the pure [meditative absorption] arises even from the transformation-mind; thus,
upon emerging from the transformation-mind, there is the transformation-mind again in the stream.

"Of one established in the fruit of meditative concentration" means of one established in a mind of emanation produced by meditative concentration; "belonging to a higher stage" means belonging to the stages of the second dhyāna and above.
It is spoken by means of that which belongs to the level of the first dhyāna,
because in the higher stages, such as the second dhyāna and above, there is an absence of the mind accompanied by vitarka and vicāra that originates informative action (vijñapti);
for it has been said thus:

The intention [of the objection] is this: since one speaks speech only after having applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), there is no emanated being (*nirmita*) in the absence of an emanating mind (*nirmāṇacitta*); thus, in the absence of the cause (*nimitta*), the effect (*naimittika*) is also absent. How, then, can he make this non-existent emanated being speak?
"Because it proceeds by means of another [mind] after having exercised empowerment":
having created an emanation with an emanation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), one then exercises empowerment over it with the desire for it to remain, thinking, "Let this remain."

Thereafter, the creators set speech in motion by means of another mind that originates informative action (*vijñapti*), one accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*). For they follow their prior intention;
for previously, he had established in his mind: "I shall create an emanation, I shall sustain it, and I shall make it speak."
Because the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is possible in two states, he asks: "Is the empowerment [possible] only while alive? and so forth, [referring to] "by the empowerment of the noble Mahākāśyapa."
The meaning is "by means of the resolve of the noble Mahākāśyapa";
however, that which is born of rebirth is of three kinds.
For sometimes gods and others, for the sake of favoring others, create other beings, and sometimes for the sake of harming them; such is the detailed explanation of what is produced by them.
And how could there be a transformation (nirmāṇa) created by gods and others that is connected to oneself or another and consists of nine bases (navāyatanika),
given that it lacks the sound-base and the form-base?
Because there are soundless bases such as the eye-base and the form-base present therein,
sound is not emanated because of the absence of a [verbal] continuum;
furthermore, it is not [emanated] in the mind-base or the mental-object-base because of the state of being without mind.
How is it understood from the treatise itself that a transformation-body (nirmita) is without mind?
For it says as follows:
Should that which is created by him be described as consisting of the four great elements, or should it be described as not consisting of the four great elements?
He replied:
It should be described as consisting of the four great elements.
Should it be said that [the eye] consists of derived matter or that it does not consist of derived matter?
It should be said that it consists of derived matter.
One must state that it is without mind;
one must state by whose mind it functions.
He said:
If it is argued that [the creation] proceeds by the power of the creator's mind,
then if a ninefold base (navāyatana) is created through the creation of sense-faculties, how is it that there is no manifestation of a previously non-existent sentient being?
Since the sense faculties are indeed reckoned as sentient beings,
he therefore says:
"because they are inseparable from the sense faculties."

Because an emanation connected to one's own or another's body—which consists of visible form, taste, and tangibility and exists inseparably from them—is said to possess nine bases (*navāyatanika*) by means of the five sense faculties beginning with the eye;
however, it is not the case that the sense faculty itself is emanated—this is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
But when one emanates that very same [emanation] as unconnected to one's own or another's body, [it is otherwise].
That [existence] consists of only four sense-bases (*caturāyatanika*),
as in the case of Māndhātṛ and of those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
this is stated as an illustration of supernatural power born of karma (*karmajā ṛddhi*).
The intention is to ask whether these are indeed divine, and whether this word "divine" is used in its primary sense or in a figurative sense.
For if the meaning "divine" (*divye*) is taken as "existing in heaven" (*divi bhave*), then this word is used in its primary sense;
but if it means "as if divine" (*divye iva*), then "divine" is used figuratively (*aupacārikaḥ*).
"Just as [the status] of the Bodhisattva, the Wheel-turning King, and the Householder-Jewel [is metaphorical]"— this shows an illustrative example regarding its figurative nature;
"because it is accompanied by consciousness" provides the reason.
Because it is brought forth by way of the vision of form, it is always accompanied by consciousness; thus,
it is indeed "functioning" (sabhāga), as there is no absence of blindness or distortion.
"One-eyed" means internally impaired;
"wandering" and "squinting" imply that one does not see anything at all.
This is what is meant by the sense of the words.
The divine eye sees even behind and sees even to the sides, whereas the non-divine eye does not; thus,
there is also a fourfold set beginning with the divine ear.
By the word "etcetera," it is meant that there is also this tetrad beginning with the divine ear— the divine eye, the recollection of former abodes, and the knowledge of others' minds—
which is acquired through birth.
The divine eye is of two kinds: that acquired through birth among the gods of the desire realm, and that belonging to non-returners of the form realm and those of the formless realm.
Therein, due to the absence of form (*rūpa*), there is no seeing, no going, and no emanation;
nor is there the divine ear or eye,
and even the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) does not exist.
Because there is no discernment of the mental continuums of oneself or others,
there is also no recollection of past lives,
as among beings of the desire and form realms, since such a personal existence has not been fully realized.

Alternatively, all the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are absent [in that realm], just as they are for beings belonging to the desire and form realms, because such a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) has not been fully realized; it is not the case that [the supernormal knowledges] are exclusively wholesome, like the fruit of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*).
The counter-example is that those situated in other realms always know [this];
thus, by means of those two— knowledge of others' minds and recollection of past lives— those situated in the realms of gods and so forth always know it.
Because it is not overwhelmed by painful sensations,
[this state] is not something acquired at birth for human beings.

Among humans, these aforementioned [powers], such as supernatural success (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, exist as those acquired through detachment (*vairāgya-lābhika*), or produced by logic, spells, herbs, or ritual action; however, they do not exist as those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*).
As for that which is called "natural recollection of former births" (*prakṛti-jātismara*): [it is explained as follows].

The intention is this: since the state of being naturally born with the memory of former births arises through the recollection of past lives, and that [recollection] occurs at the moment of rebirth, how could it not be something acquired at birth?
He said:
"This [attainment] of theirs arises from a specific karma";
that is, it is produced by a specific karma of those bodhisattvas.
That which is called "obtained at birth" (upapatti-lābhika) is that which is acquired naturally by all at the very moment of birth, and not that which belongs only to some after the time of birth,
such as the ability of birds to travel through the sky.
Therefore, he explains how this [result] arises for them from a specific karma with the words "for it is threefold," and so forth.
The fruit of cultivation is as previously described;
it is acquired through rebirth for gods and others, being born of karma, just as it is for those bodhisattvas.
In the *Abhidharmakośavyākhyā* composed by Ācārya Yaśomitra,
the seventh treasury-location [ends];
Chapter 8.
The eighth chapter, titled "Exposition of the Meditative Attainments" (*samāpatti-nirdeśa*), follows immediately after the seventh.
In introducing the eighth chapter, [the author] shows the connection by saying,
"By way of the section on knowledge," and so forth.

By way of the section on knowledge—that is, by way of the ten types of knowledge—a description has been made of those things consisting of knowledge and having knowledge as their intrinsic nature, such as the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and so forth. However, a description must now be made of those having other natures, such as meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and the like, because they are the basis for all qualities; for even the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are indeed bases for qualities.
Meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are of two kinds: those that are not the basis for all qualities, and those that are the basis for all qualities.
Thus, the meaning is that these are the meditations on effects and the meditations on causes;
[this is what is meant by] "one-pointedness on the auspicious."
The one-pointedness of all virtuous qualities without distinction is the characteristic of all [the perfections].
This is the defining characteristic; therefore, he says "because they have meditative concentration as their intrinsic nature," with "of the dhyānas" being the ellipsis for the sentence.
Alternatively, by way of non-distinction, there is the mention of "mere concentration," whereas by way of distinction,
there are the five aggregates together with their attendants.
Thus is the aggregate of non-informative form;
the state of having a single object is the singleness of object of the minds.

What, then, is the reason that although mental factors (*caitta*) also have a single object, it is said that "minds (*citta*) have a single object," rather than saying that "mind and mental factors have a single object"? Because of their predominance, it is the minds themselves that have a single object; thus, concentration (*samādhi*) consists of the minds alone.
Because it is a specific state, like a variegated teacher, the Vaibhāṣika says:
"Concentration is not the mental states themselves."
That dharma by which those [mental states] proceed one-pointedly and are concentrated is *samādhi*;
just as, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, a cloth is called "white" because of its connection with the quality of whiteness.
That very quality of this [mind] is called "whiteness" (śauklya),
and likewise,
is it not the case that because of momentariness, every state of mind is one-pointed?

If it is argued that this is what is meant by the statement, "That dharma by which those [mental states] proceed one-pointedly is concentration (samādhi)," and therefore non-distraction belongs to the second [moment]:
If this were the case— that there is no distraction of the second mind from that concentration toward this object—
then concentration would be useless when associated with it,
since the first mind was already associated with concentration.
If that [mental factor] were associated with it, concentration would be rendered useless;
for on the grounds that concentration does not exercise its function in the first moment but does so in the second,
and furthermore, for the very reason that concentration is intended to have one-pointedness as its defining characteristic—
And for that very reason, why is it not accepted that mental states have a single object?
What is the point of a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is a separate entity? This is the intended meaning.
Not so.
Because of the weakness of concentration,
there is no consequence that every state of mind would possess one-pointedness simply due to the presence of concentration as a universal mental factor (mahābhūmika);
for only that mind which is associated with weak concentration [is so affected].
That which is not one-pointed is not what is called "one-pointed" by virtue of being powerful.

Even though concentration (samādhi) is a universal mental factor (mahābhūmika), it does not follow that all states of mind possess one-pointedness; for, as the detailed explanation goes, "the minds themselves are one-pointed"—
meaning that concentration is nothing other than the minds themselves.
For it is thus: regarding "the training in higher mind," what is the training in higher mind?
It is all four dhyānas.
Likewise, it has been stated that there are exactly four dhyānas which have the purification of the mind as their primary focus; this sūtra has thus been recorded.
Just as in the case of "the bases of psychic power are concentrations," where the training in higher morality is simply morality itself.
The training in higher wisdom is not other than that; wisdom itself is not other than it.
Thus, the training in higher mind is the mind itself and nothing other than that;
the meaning is that there is no concentration distinct from the mind.
For the training in higher mind is intended as concentration;
and just as it is said in this very sutra that there is the preeminence of purity of morality and the preeminence of purity of liberation,
yet the purity of morality is not something other than morality itself.
In this way, the purity of view and the purity of liberation are likewise;
the purity of mind also is not other than the mind itself,
for the purity of mind is indeed the meditative concentration characterized by the four dhyānas.
If that were so— meaning,
if the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) had concentration (samādhi) as their intrinsic nature— then it would follow that all concentrations are meditative absorptions;
it would follow that even wholesome, afflicted, and neutral concentrations would be meditative absorptions.
Because concentration (*samādhi*) belongs to the great ground (*mahābhūmika*), it is not associated with excellence; such is the detailed explanation.
This is not so,
because the name "dhyāna" (meditative absorption) is applied to a concentration endowed with excellence, just like the term "bhāskara" (the sun).
For example, only that which produces light pre-eminently is called the "light-maker" (bhāskara),
not a firefly or the like.
"In the same way, for that reason," and so forth;

for that concentration (samādhi), when endowed with its constituent factors, proceeds like a chariot drawn by two horses harnessed together— namely, calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā)— and is thus called "proceeding by way of the yoke" (yuganaddhavāhī).
Because of that state, it is said in the Sūtra that there is a "dwelling in happiness in the present life" and a "pleasant practice"; thus,
concentration is indeed endowed with its constituent factors.
The phrase "and it is called a pleasant practice" continues [from the previous context].
Because of that, they meditate all the more due to its pleasantness;
[an objection is raised: "How can there be the state of being *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) for that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*)?"

If meditative concentration associated with the factors of wholesomeness is dhyāna, then how can [concentration] that is afflicted and associated with relishing be considered dhyāna? This is the completion of the sentence; for dhyāna is of three kinds.
Because it is stated that [the dhyāna] associated with relish is "pure" (śuddhaka) and "untainted" (anāsrava),
[it follows that the former is not so] due to its false contemplation.
The meaning is "due to false deliberation.
[Regarding] the "over-extension": there would be the consequence that even with a mind obsessed by sensual desire, [it would be an act of killing] because of its false contemplation.
"It is not even similar to that," and so forth;
this is not so, for it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For the designation "defiled meditation" (*kliṣṭa-dhyāna*) is applied only to that which is similar to [pure meditation], not to that which is significantly different; it is like the term "rotten seed.
Just as some non-seeds, such as stones and the like, which are extremely dissimilar to that class [of seeds], are not called "rotten seeds."
Rather,
it is simply that when a seed of a certain kind becomes impaired, the designation "rotten seed" is applied to that very thing.
And since it has been stated that there are even unwholesome meditative absorptions (*akuśala-dhyāna*),

[the text says] "he, being obsessed by sensual desire, having made the obsession of sensual desire an interval, meditates, intensely meditates," and so forth. By this, he shows that there is no fault even if the obsession with sensual desire and so on constitutes a form of meditative absorption.
"Like smoke and fire" means that just as when one says "smoke is here," fire is also implied by the mention of smoke because of their constant association,
for smoke does not exist without fire.
It is precisely because of this inseparable connection that smoke is considered more prominent;
for wherever there is smoke, there is fire.
But it is not the case that wherever there is fire, there is smoke;
for in cases such as iron balls and glowing coals, only fire is perceived,
not smoke.
And because of its greater importance, *dhūma* (smoke) is placed first [in the compound], just as *Vāsudeva* and *Arjuna* are;
otherwise, even in a *dvandva* compound, the word *agni* would have been placed first according to the rule "the word ending in a vowel is placed first.

Furthermore, how could there be a deliberation (*vicāra*) accompanied by joy and pleasure without a process of reasoning (*vitarka*)? This is because they are associated through concomitance (*sāhacarya*).
Just as the investigation (vicāra) of the intermediate dhyāna is without applied thought (avitarka) because it lacks joy and bliss,
this [present] investigation is not like that.
For this investigation is specifically characterized by its recitation together with joy and bliss,
because it consists of investigation, joy, and bliss.
The meaning is that the first dhyāna is associated with both investigation (vicāra) and joy-and-bliss (prītisukha), which possess joy and bliss.
Furthermore, if the Sūtra were instead composed as "possessing applied thought (vitarka), joy (prīti), and bliss (sukha)," what fault would there be?
He will state that it is not possible to do so while omitting each preceding factor.
If the second dhyāna is defined as being "devoid of applied thought" (*vitarkavarjita*), then the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) would also qualify as the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the exposition of the first dhyāna, four factors were stated in this sequence:

"Having attained the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*), born of seclusion (*vivekaja*), and characterized by joy and bliss (*prītisukha*), one dwells therein."
In that regard, investigation, joy, bliss, and concentration exist in the first dhyāna;
with these four factors and with vitarka, which was mentioned first of all, it is said to have five factors.
Furthermore, the second [dhyāna] is described as follows:
"Attaining and dwelling in the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and without vicāra, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss"—
this is said to be the third [dhyāna] as well, insofar as it is devoid of the preceding factor, namely the characteristic of vicāra, among these four.
"Through detachment from joy, he dwells equanimous," and so on in detail until "he dwells in bliss"; thus, having attained and dwelt in the third dhyāna,
it is devoid of another factor characterized by joy.
The fourth [dhyāna] is further described thus:
"By the abandoning of pleasure," and so on in detail, "he dwells having attained the dhyāna that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
Since it is here devoid even of the factor of pleasure, and only meditative concentration (samādhi) alone remains, for this very reason the Sūtra was composed in this manner.
"Like [the states] possessing investigation, joy, and bliss"—
thus,
their origins have also been explained.
Because it is stated that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is "without location" and "fourfold by way of rebirth," there is an absence of concomitant matter (*anuparivartaka-rūpa*).
The meaning is that there is an absence of the meditative and uncontaminated restraints; this is what is meant by "separation."
"Viveka" (discernment) is that by which one discerns;
it refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) or also the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), because they share the same function.
"Because of the attainment of dispassion" means because of the attainment of liberation from that;
this is called the "perception of the disappearance of form."
Thus, for him the perception of form has been overcome; therefore, he is one whose perception of form has been overcome (vibhūtarūpasaññā).
He is one whose perception of form has been overcome.

The term "those whose perception of form has been overcome" (vibhūtarūpasañjñākhyāḥ) refers to those for whom this designation applies; first of all, this is what must be established, according to the followers of other schools.
The Vaibhāṣikas say, "If it were so," as in the case of *āpiṅgala*,
which means slightly tawny (*īṣat piṅgala*).
If the formless [realms] (*ārūpya*) are thus characterized by the absence of even slight form (*rūpa*),
how could there be the two types of restraint— restraint of body and speech— in the absence of that [form]?
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a formless-realm derivative matter (*bhautika*) of restraint when the primary elements (*bhūta*) of the formless realm do not exist.
If it were argued that this is like the case of the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), such that there are no untainted [factors] there;
Just as there are primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*), as well as untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*),
so too in this case there would not be primary elements belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).
Alternatively, it might be argued that there is a restraint belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara-saṃvara*), and that this is derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*);
but that is not so,
because there exist contaminated primary elements (*sāsrava-bhūta*), and thus contaminated primary elements are present there.
Those [elements] might exist in the formless realms,
but the untainted elements do not exist there;
therefore, the untainted restraint arises only where those [elements] are found.
Since it arises depending upon the contaminated (*sāsrava*) [factors] belonging to that [realm], this is not to be conceptualized because of its dissimilarity;
thus, by the very negation of form in the state of rebirth (*upapatti*), the negation of form in meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is also stated.
No further effort need be exerted here,
if it is merely the restraint of body and speech.
How can there be restraint of that [matter] in the absence of that [matter]?
Furthermore, it is not logical for derived matter to exist when its primary elements are absent, unless one were to argue it is like the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
It is not because of the existence of tainted (sāsrava) primary elements,
since there is the statement: "by completely transcending all perceptions of form (rūpasañjñā)."
Others say that its negation has also been stated regarding meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
thus, it is shown that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) nor in the formless rebirths (*ārūpyopapatti*),
because of the extreme smallness of its measure.
Now, if it is thought that there exists matter in the form of atoms, and therefore they are held to possess a slight degree of form—
There would be the undesirable consequence [of classifying] even minute aquatic creatures as being formless (*ārūpya*), because their forms are invisible due to their subtlety; this is the meaning.
If it were argued that they are called "formless" because of the translucence (*acchatā*) of their form, then...
There would be the undesirable consequence [of classifying] those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) as well;
for beings in the intermediate state and the form realm move without obstruction even through mountains made of diamond because of their transparency,
which would entail the consequence that they belong to the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
"Because of the distinction in their rebirths, just like the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).

For just as the meditative attainments of the Sphere of Infinite Space and so forth are most distinguished, so too must a distinction in their rebirths be admitted— namely, that they are progressively clearer and clearer.

Therefore, just as with the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the distinction between rebirths (*upapatti*) is also progressively clearer; thus, that very same formless realm (*ārūpya*) would [apply].

Furthermore, if the form of rebirth in the formless realm is not perceived by the sense-faculties (*indriya*) belonging to a lower level—because they are clearer than those faculties—it is for this reason that they are called "formless" (*ārūpya*).
"And even for the form of rebirth in the meditative absorptions," and so forth;
this possibility— that even the form of rebirth in the meditative absorptions is not perceived by a faculty belonging to a lower level— how is it [to be understood]?
Form belonging to the second dhyāna stage is not perceived by a faculty belonging to the first dhyāna stage;

likewise, up to the point where form belonging to the fourth dhyāna stage is not perceived by a faculty belonging to the third dhyāna stage, because that which belongs to a higher stage is increasingly more subtle and transparent.

Thus, since the form of rebirth in meditative absorption (dhyānopapatti-rūpa) is not perceived by the sense-faculties belonging to a lower level, what distinction is there in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
For even though they are equally subtle—being more and most subtle—it is only those [beings] who are accepted as "formless" (ārūpya), and not those belonging to the realm of form (rūpāvacara).
Therefore, there is no form there.

Now, it might be thought that the designations of the two realms are according to their literal meaning: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is so called because it is characterized by the qualities of desire (*kāmaguṇa*), and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) because it is characterized by form (*rūpa*).
Is the designation for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) not literal; rather, what is the reasoning here that it is merely arbitrary?
