Having refuted [the opponent's position] through reasoning— that the designations for two realms are literal, but that of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is not— it is now sought to dispel the doubt by relying on scripture (*āgama*) that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm.

In that context, regarding the detailed explanation beginning with "for the sake of establishing the existence of form, [there must be] life-force and heat," if it is asked how the existence of form is established in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), this phrase should be applied to each [of the preceding points].
How so?

If it is argued that the existence of form (*rūpa*) is established because of the statement regarding the conjunction of vitality (*āyus*) and heat (*ūṣman*), then this might be the case: it is stated in the Sūtra, "Venerable Kauṣṭhila, that which is vitality and that which is heat— these two factors are conjoined."
"Not dissociated," and so forth;
therefore, since there is life-force (*āyus*) there, there must also be heat (*ūṣman*), and since heat is form (*rūpa*), it is established [that form exists there].
If it is argued that the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) is established because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are said to be mutually dependent like two bundles of reeds,
it has been stated in the Sūtra:

It is just as if, venerable Śāriputra, two bundles of reeds were raised up in the air; they would lean against one another, and standing leaning against one another, if someone were to remove one of them...
If the second [line] falls,
one should remove the second;
if only one [line] falls, [one should remove that one].
In this way, venerable Śāriputra, name and form are mutually dependent;
they exist by depending upon one another—this is the detailed explanation, because of the statement: "Name-and-form has consciousness as its condition."
If it is argued that, therefore, the existence of form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) is established, [we reply:

it is stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* that at the moment of the establishment of the formless realms, "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) has consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its condition; therefore, it is established that there is form in the formless realms.
"Other than form," and so forth;
it is stated in the Sūtra:
"O monks, consciousness abides by approaching form."

"Monks, if anyone were to say this: 'Apart from form, apart from feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, I declare a coming or a going,' [that would be so]— [only] for one who thus has form as an object and is established in form."
If it is argued that "this would be merely a matter of words for him," and that form exists in the formless realms (ārūpyas) on the basis of this scriptural authority,
that is not so.
Because it must be deliberated upon: or rather, does "all" refer to that which belongs to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness?
This is the intended meaning here:
this was said with reference specifically to the lifespan of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*);
for it has been stated thus.
When life, heat, and consciousness abandon this body,
it then lies cast away, insentient like a piece of wood.
Furthermore, there is no body in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
so how could there be the destruction of a body?
Although a body does exist in the form realm (rūpadhātu)...
However, since the destruction of the body is not recognized,
it appears that even the statement regarding the mutual dependence of name-and-form was made with reference only to those belonging to the desire and form realms.
For mutual dependence is possible only when there is a duality;

and as for the statement "name-and-form has consciousness as its condition" (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*), in this way— namely, that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition (*vijñānaḥ pratyayo 'sya*)— it is a genitive *bahuvrīhi* compound.
In this regard, is every consciousness—conditioned by formations ranging from those of the desire realm up to those of the formless realm—the condition for name-and-form?
Or is it that all name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness?
We say: "name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness"; thus it is determined that consciousness is the condition for all name-and-form.
However, it is not established that all consciousness is a condition for name-and-form;
rather, some consciousness is a condition for name alone— namely, that which has formations belonging to the formless realm as its condition—
and some is a condition for name-and-form— namely, that which has formations belonging to the desire or form realms as its condition.
This is what is meant:
consciousness itself is the condition for this name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
but it is not the case that [consciousness] is the condition for this name-and-form taken together as a whole.
This is said with reference to birth [from a womb],
for in the case of those born spontaneously (*upapāduka*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise directly conditioned by consciousness,
and not name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Indeed, the five aggregates in the state where the six sense bases have not yet been fully formed are designated as "name-and-form."
And this very Sūtra illuminates this same meaning:
"Ānanda, if consciousness were not to descend into the mother's womb, would that name-and-form coagulate into the state of the *kalala*?—
No, Venerable Sir."
“Ānanda, if consciousness were to enter and then quickly depart, would that name-and-form be known for its suchness?
No, Venerable Sir.
Ānanda, if the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be cut off, destroyed, and cease to exist, would that name-and-form attain growth and expansion?”
"Venerable sir, by this method also it should be understood that name-and-form has consciousness as its condition,
and consciousness has name-and-form as its condition," and so forth in detail.
What is meant here by "beings" being without these [factors] such as form? It is the negation of that [self], which is the negation of coming and going.
In this context, "coming" is birth here from a previous world through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
"going" is birth in another world from this world through the continuity of the intermediate state.
Or rather, do we say that even by means of a single one among form and the rest,
there is the negation of that [self] in the absence of all of them?
If it be argued that "it need not be deliberated upon because the statement is non-specific," such a thought might arise: this scriptural statement is made without distinction;

however, that which was stated by the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila regarding "life" (*āyus*) in detail, up to the point where "consciousness (*vijñāna*) remains supported by form (*rūpa*)," was spoken with reference specifically to life belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) or the form realm (*rūpāvacara*). Thus, by all those [factors] together, there is a negation of that [consciousness] in the absence of form and the other aggregates.
To this it is replied: this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga),
for by virtue of the statement being made without qualification, it would follow that even external heat is not dissociated from life-force (āyus).

For it has not been specified in this way— namely, that "O Venerable Kauṣṭhila, that which is life-force and that which is internal heat," and so forth— [otherwise] even external matter such as wood or walls, which is reckoned as non-sentient, would result in being dependent upon consciousness due to the lack of such specification, just as in the case of the four stations of consciousness; such is the detailed argument.
Just as the existence of form in the formless realm follows for you from the statement that there is no distinction among the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
so too does the consequence of the existence of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the realms of form and formlessness follow for you from the statement regarding the fourfold food;
for thus the Sūtra is recited:
There are four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be and for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four?
They are gross physical nutriment, subtle physical nutriment, [mental nutriment], and consciousness-nutriment.
Contact is the second,
mental volition is the third,
and consciousness is the fourth nutriment.

Thus, because of the statement regarding the fourfold food for the sake of the maintenance of sentient beings without distinction— meaning for those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) without qualification— it follows for you that there would be the consequence of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) existing even in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), as expressed in the passage beginning with "having transcended," and so forth.
In this regard, a member of another school might argue that there is an exception to this general rule,
because of the statement: "having surpassed the gods who subsist on edible food."
And because of the distinction made in the Udāyi-sūtra and other texts— stating that "having transcended the gods who subsist on physical food, one is reborn in a certain divine mind-made body"—
and because of the mention of "joy as food," it is said:
"O monks, there comes a time when this world dissolves."
When the world is undergoing dissolution, for the most part sentient beings are reborn in the Ābhāsvara realm of the gods;

there they exist as beings possessing form (*rūpin*), mind-made (*manomaya*), complete with no deficiency, with unimpaired faculties, endowed with all major and minor limbs, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy (*prīti-bhakṣa*), nourished by joy (*prīty-āhāra*), long-lived, and remaining for a long duration—because of such statements in the sūtras, there is no contingency for edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
If this is so, then there would likewise be no contingency for form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
What is the reason?
Because of censure;
how so?
"The formless realms are the escape from forms"—this is one sutra as an exception;
"those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless"—this is the second;
"there are beings who are formless"—this is the third.
"By completely transcending perceptions of form"— this refers to the fourth [formless attainment];
for if there were form in the meditative attainments or rebirths of the formless realm, it would indeed be "form."
For if form were present, they would necessarily perceive their own form;
thus, the statement "by completely transcending all perceptions of form" would not have been spoken,
yet it was indeed spoken.
For this reason also, there is no coarse form there, and so forth;
in this regard, it might be argued as follows.
This was said with reference to the coarse form belonging to the lower stages,
when it was stated in detail, "Those liberations which are peaceful," and so forth; regarding this, we shall now speak.
The same applies to edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

How so? When it says, "having transcended the gods who consume edible food," this is said with reference to the coarse edible food belonging to the lower realms, and not to the subtle edible food belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).
If they are called "formless" (ārūpya) because they are an escape from the coarse form of the lower stages,
then it would follow that the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) must also be formless, since they too are an escape from the lower stages; how [is this to be explained]?

The first dhyāna is the departure from the coarse form of the desire realm; likewise, each subsequent dhyāna up to the fourth is the departure from the coarser forms of the levels below. Consequently, it would follow that these [higher dhyānas] are themselves formless (*ārūpya*).
And why is it not said that they are an "exit from feeling" and so forth?

If the formless realms (ārūpya) are so called because they are an exit from the coarseness of the lower stages even though they possess their own stage's form, why are they not called "feelingless" (avedanā) because they are an exit from feeling and the rest?
Even though feeling belonging to one's own level exists,
why are [the other aggregates] not mentioned— up to consciousness itself— by means of the word "etcetera," even though consciousness belonging to one's own level also exists?
What is the reason?
It is because of the departure from the sensations and so forth of the lower stages;
that is to say, because of the departure from the coarse sensations and so forth of the lower stages.
But having completely transcended every category of form—
whatever category of form there may be, whether gross or subtle, internal or external—
the formless attainments have transcended all of them, both in terms of meditative attainment and rebirth.
The formless attainments (*ārūpya*)— both in meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and rebirth (*upapatti*)— do not transcend the category of feeling (*vedanā-jāti*) nor all feelings,
because there exists neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), everything up to consciousness (*vijñāna*) should be stated.
Therefore, it is said that this is the escape from forms,
not the escape from feelings and so forth; thus, for us who maintain this position, this undesirable consequence does not arise.
To the question, "Why is it not stated that there is an escape from feeling and so forth, since there is an escape from the feelings and so forth of the lower stages?
he says:
If the formless realms are the escape from forms,
then how is it that the formless existence is the escape from the existence of form, given that it was stated in the Sūtra: "I do not say that existence is the escape from existence"?
However, the statement that existence is not the escape from existence is because it is not the escape from that very same existence;
that is, because there is no escape from that very same existence. Thus it was said, "and because it is neither universal nor ultimate escape."
It is not a complete transcendence, for the realm of form (rūpa-bhava) is not the transcendence of the realm of desire (kāma-bhava); thus,
it is also not by means of that [realm of form] that there is transcendence of the formless realm (ārūpya-bhava).
And there is no ultimate escape from the existence of desire (*kāmabhava*) because one returns [to it] by means of that;
likewise, there is no escape from the existence of form (*rūpabhava*) by means of the existence of the formless (*ārūpyabhava*).
It has been explained how [existence] proceeds: neither by means of sensual existence nor by means of formless existence is there an absolute escape from the states of form-existence.
The mental continuum here depends upon the group-homogeneity (*nikāya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita*);
thus,
the three [factors] are indicated by the masculine gender.
Because they are connected with the term "formless" (ārūpya),
and because of such application,
at the time of practice, space and so forth become the objects of focus.
But at other times, he shows that even other dharmas can be objects of perception as they occur;
however, because of its dullness, it is neither "with-perception" nor "without-perception."
Why is the fourth formless realm not called "possessing perception"?
It is said that it is "neither possessing perception nor non-perception" because of its dullness.
By the word "tu" (but), the form "a" of that [term] is to be understood as having its meaning internally included;
for the very reason that the fourth formless attainment is called the "sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," that same reason is now stated.
The application [of the term] "slowness" (māndya) is thus indicated by this very [sūtra], because of the assignment of a name that conforms to its meaning (anvartha-sañjñā).
Therefore he said:
"Even though there too it is employed in this way," and so forth;
[the term] *sañjñā* (notion) is a *gaṇḍa* (tumor), for it is like a tumor (*gaṇḍavat*).
In this way, up to the point where Śalya says "the unconscious is delusion," for the absence of perception is indeed the cause of delusion.
This is the meaning:
"it cools" (śīyate) refers to the intention that it is due to the complete cutting off of perception;
this is peaceful, this is sublime.
What is that? He says:
namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
A dullness of perception is intended here;
one must ask why it is grasped by them in such a manner.
"By them" means by those attainments;
"that" refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
"is thus grasped" means it is grasped as "neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—this is the meaning.
Thus, when questioned in this manner by one who is challenged, this must necessarily be stated:

because perceptions are subtle, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this very point is what was meant by the statement that the fundamental substances of meditative attainment are the primary ones.
The intention is that their branches do not perish.
To explain how there are seven of three kinds, he says: "accompanied by tasting, pure, and untainted."
Thus,
because of the dullness of perception that "the untainted does not exist," one relishes it.
Therefore, one who has emerged from that [attainment] is said to relish it by means of the pure [meditative state].
"One who has attained that" refers to [the state] associated with relishing (*āsvādana*),
just as a fourfold army at its conclusion is not something other than its constituent parts.
Thus, with the words "joy and so forth," he demonstrates his own position that the five-limbed dhyāna is not something distinct [from the four dhyānas].
The previously mentioned joy, bliss, one-pointedness of mind,
and internal serenity.
The second [dhyāna] has four factors;
in the third, there are five, including equanimity.
Here, "equanimity of formation" is understood as that joy characterized by non-exertion,
while mindfulness is the non-forgetfulness of the sign of equanimity.
Clear comprehension is the state of being clearly aware regarding the non-forgetting of mindfulness; and in the fourth [dhyāna], there is the purity of equanimity—
the purity of equanimity is "purity of equanimity."
Through the departure of the defects of the lower stages,
the eight defects are indeed eliminated;
thus there is the purification of mindfulness.
"Belonging to the first dhyāna" means those which exist in the first dhyāna; for this very reason it is so stated.
Since self-confidence and the other qualities increase from the second day onwards, how can there be a fourfold classification?
It may be in the first dhyāna but not in the second;
it may be in the second but not in the first;
it may be in both.
In this way, all the factors of meditative absorption (dhyānāṅga) are to be applied to one another; how so with those factors that exist in the first absorption?
In the third [dhyāna] as well, there is that fourfold alternative;
the first alternative consists of applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), and bliss (sukha).
The second [limb] consists of equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss;
the third is meditative concentration;
the fourth category consists of those factors excluded from what has been mentioned.
Are those factors that exist in the first dhyāna also present in the fourth?
There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) regarding this.
The first category consists of applied thought, sustained thought, joy, and bliss;
the second consists of neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, purity of equanimity, and purity of mindfulness;
the third is concentration.
The fourth [category] consists of those factors excluded from what has been stated; as for the members that exist in the second dhyāna, do they also exist in the third?
This constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (catuṣkoṭika).
The first category consists of internal clarity, joy, and bliss;
the second consists of equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss; the third is meditative concentration (samādhi).
The fourth [category] consists of those factors excluded from what has been mentioned,
which are present both in the second dhyāna and in the fourth.
There is a fourfold alternative: the first alternative consists of internal serenity, joy, and bliss;
the second consists of those factors excluding concentration.
The third [member] is concentration;
the fourth consists of those factors other than those already mentioned—
namely, those members which exist in the third dhyāna and also in the fourth.
There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika): the first alternative consists of those factors of concentration excluding concentration itself;
the second is likewise.
The third is concentration;
the fourth consists of phenomena excluded from those mentioned [above];
and this is what is called "belonging to that single sphere."
Why is it said that in the third dhyāna, bliss (*sukha*) is a distinct factor?
How is it stated that these constitute the eighteen factors of dhyāna? Having explained this in detail, he says again:
In terms of name there are thus ten, but in terms of substance there is one;
in terms of substance, these become eleven.
The five factors belonging to the first dhyāna are present in the second; however, in the third, it is stated that "inner serenity, equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and bliss increase."
"Because of the absence of the faculty of pleasure" means that because the faculty of pleasure is impossible [therein],
there is indeed no mental faculty of pleasure in any of the three dhyānas.
Rather,
it is bodily pleasure itself that is established as a factor [of dhyāna],
because it occurs during the interval between states of meditative absorption.
This is indeed the position of the Dārṣṭāntikas;
for according to them, the faculty of pleasure belongs not only to two levels, namely the level of the desire realm and the level of the first dhyāna.
Rather, the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) belongs to four levels,
ranging from the desire realm (kāmāvacara) up to the level of the third dhyāna.
For this very reason, it was said by the Sautrāntika Bhadanta in the *Vaibhāṣikā*:
"The visual consciousness and so forth are drawn upward from below by the Ābhidharmikas, as if by a waterwheel (*araghaṭṭa*).
Thus, this is what he accepts.
Since visual consciousness and the others are drawn upward from below,
it follows that this is what the Noble Ones accept:
namely, that visual consciousness and the others can also belong to the levels of the second dhyāna and above.
This reading is interpolated—
that is, this reading "mental" (*caitasika*)—
because it is stated by its own specific term in the phrase "and he experiences pleasure with the body."
In the exposition of the third dhyāna, it is said:
"Through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body."
Regarding that which the Noble Ones describe as "dwelling having attained the third dhyāna, equanimous, mindful, and abiding in happiness"—
if that [happiness] were mental, how could one experience it with the body?
For how could the mind be experienced by means of the body?
Having spoken thus with the entire assembly,
he asks, "What is the benefit?
and experiences happiness with his mind.

The intention is that one should rather say, "and he experiences pleasure with the body," because even though there is an abundance of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) in the fourth dhyāna, it is still designated as "pleasure" (*sukha*).
Thus, in the fourth dhyāna, the pleasure of pliancy becomes more abundant; it becomes greater.
Because the fourth [dhyāna] is more refined than the intermediate dhyānas, even though there is an abundance of that [pliancy], pleasure is not mentioned; thus,
pleasure is not spoken of in the fourth dhyāna.

The intention is that because that bliss is not mentioned [in the context of the fourth dhyāna], it is understood that in the third dhyāna there is only the bliss of feeling (*vedanā-sukha*), whereas in the fourth there is no feeling of bliss, and thus it is not mentioned there.
If it be thought that "pleasure" is pliancy favorable to pleasant feeling,
then [it would follow that] in the first and second [dhyānas], there is pliancy favorable to pleasant feeling.

Having stated that pleasure (*sukha*) exists in those two [stages], one might ask: why is *praśrabdhi* not mentioned in the fourth dhyāna as being conducive to the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*)? If that is so, why is *praśrabdhi* not mentioned as pleasure in the third dhyāna, since the *praśrabdhi* of the third dhyāna is also conducive to the feeling of pleasure?
In that regard, why was the pleasure of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-sukha*) not mentioned?
For you have established that only the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*) exists there, and not the pleasure of pliancy.
If it should be thought that [this is] because of the twofold reading of "sukha" (happiness) and because of being afflicted by equanimity (*upekṣā*):
In the third dhyāna, equanimity has the characteristic of functional adaptability;
therefore, it is not said that pliancy is impaired by it.
Thus, [the objection] is not [valid].
"It is through equanimity alone that this increases"—
this is not so;
for it is through equanimity alone that the suffering of pliancy increases there in the third dhyāna.
For increase is not logically possible through the very cause of impairment; therefore,
he says "because of its distinction from the former two" in order to explain how that increase occurs through equanimity alone.
For the pliancy of the third dhyāna is superior to the two preceding pliancies of the first and second dhyānas,
because the third is superior to the former two dhyānas;
"at which time," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.
At the time when a noble disciple, having personally realized with his body the joy born of seclusion, dwells having attained it,
five qualities are abandoned by him at that time,
and five qualities reach fulfillment through cultivation.
If internal clarity, joy, pliancy, bliss,

and concentration were not distinct from one another— specifically, if pliancy and bliss were not different— how could there be these five factors? Conversely, if they were indeed separate entities, it would be established that physical bliss alone exists in all three dhyānas.
Regarding the question of how there can be body-consciousness for one who has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*),
it is said here:

because the body is pervaded and filled with a wind called "pliancy" (*praśrabdhi*), which is born from a specific state of concentration (*samādhi*) and is conducive to, or associated with, a pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīya*).
If it is argued that body-consciousness must indeed arise [at that time], and thus there is a lapse from meditative concentration due to outward distraction;
If one should think that because the arising of body-consciousness leads to outward distraction— that is, distraction toward external objects— there is a loss of concentration,
[the answer is] "it is not born of concentration," and so forth.
"This will not be so.
Why?
Because it is born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), produced within the body, and not produced externally; such is the meaning.

The meaning is that because bodily pleasure— which is associated with body-consciousness— and the felt pleasure are conducive to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no falling away from concentration on account of them;
it is not for this very reason [that one falls away].
At the time of body-consciousness, one would not have emerged [from meditative absorption];
for this very reason, the meaning is that it is conducive to concentration (*samādhi*).
The intention is that immediately after its manifestation, concentration once again becomes present.

Because a tangible object belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) cannot be apprehended by a body-consciousness belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), this body-consciousness belongs to the form realm and not to the desire realm;
for this very reason, the pleasure associated with it is not established as a factor of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*), since it arises from the knowledge of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
A [feeling] belonging to the form realm [can arise] by means of a body-faculty belonging to the desire realm, through the application of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For that body-faculty of one who has attained concentration becomes the basis for a body-consciousness that takes as its object both that state characterized by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and the tangible object itself;
this is the case even for those [feelings] that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one were to ask: "Why would both the tangible object characterized by pliancy and the body-consciousness having that as its object be untainted (*anāsrava*)?
What is the reason? [the author] says:
"Lest it be the case that some factor is tainted (*sāsrava*) while another is untainted."
If one should think thus:
"Because of the mention of the factor of enlightenment that is physical pliancy (kāyika-praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), even that which is physical pliancy is intended [as such]."

Furthermore, that factor of enlightenment which is serenity (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) conduces to higher knowledge (abhijñā), to awakening (sambodhi), and to nirvāṇa; and since it is stated that "whatever serenity of mind there is, up to the factors of enlightenment consisting of tangibles (spraṣṭavya), conduces to higher knowledge, to awakening, and to nirvāṇa," it follows from this mention of the factors of enlightenment that untainted (anāsrava) tangibles and body-consciousness (kāya-vijñāna) are accepted [as existing].

If it is argued that this is because it is conducive to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), then one might respond as follows: for bodily pliancy (*kāyika-praśrabdhi*) is indeed conducive to the factors of enlightenment.
Therefore, they are metaphorically designated as "factors of enlightenment" (bodhyaṅga), yet they are not literally factors of enlightenment;
likewise, although the tangible object and body-consciousness are untainted (anāsrava) because they are conducive to the untainted state, they are metaphorically designated as "untainted."
But they are not exclusively untainted;
thus, the untainted nature of these two [is established],
while other phenomena are tainted— this is the detailed explanation.
Which are the phenomena with outflows? They are as follows:
the eye, all forms, and eye-consciousness; likewise, the body, all tangible objects, and body-consciousness.
If you think that this constitutes a contradiction with the Sūtra, it is not so; for that statement was made with reference to another tangible object and a body-consciousness.

This is because the statement was made with a specific intention (*abhisandhi*) regarding tangible objects distinct from pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and bodily consciousnesses distinct from [the consciousness associated with] pliancy;
thus, it is not the case that [these] are untainted (*anāsrava*).
[Objection: But if they were untainted, would there not be some members [of the path] established as tainted (*sāsrava*) and others as untainted within the state of being untainted?
If one should think that this is a fault,
[it is because] that tangible object and body-consciousness are with-outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the other is without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
To this it is replied: what fault is there in their not being simultaneous?
It is when a contaminated factor (sāsrava-aṅga) is manifesting.
When the untainted limb is not manifesting,
the tainted [limb] is not present; therefore, there is no fault in this.

If it is argued that the first dhyāna cannot possess five factors because of the non-coexistence of pleasure and joy— that is, because bodily pleasure (*kāyika-sukha*) and mental joy (*mānasī-prīti*) do not coexist or occur simultaneously— then [the following response is given]:
If one should think thus, that fault does not exist;
why?
Because it is taught in reference to their possible occurrence— just as in the case of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*),
where it is said that "the first dhyāna is with applied thought and with sustained thought," and thus applied thought and sustained thought generally do occur—
likewise, because pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) are also taught in reference to their possible occurrence, there is no fault in this [argument].
If it is argued that this must be proven,
he says: "It must be proven" because applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) occur alternately.
How is this established? He says: "Because of the contradiction between applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra)."
If there is coarseness of mind,
there is no subtlety;
if there is subtlety, [there is no coarseness].
Because it would contradict [the principle] that there is no coarseness [in the same moment], and because of the statement of the fault regarding the non-simultaneity of vitarka and vicāra.

Furthermore, coarseness and subtlety are relative, depending on the distinctions between levels and types; thus, some read that "applied thought and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) would exist even up to the peak of existence," and so forth. And because no fault is stated, the meaning is that there is no defect whatsoever due to their non-coexistence.
"By the removal of two, three, or four factors": by the removal of two factors, the second dhyāna is established,
because of the absence therein of *vitarka* and *vicāra*.
By the removal of three factors, the third dhyāna is established;
since even joy (*prīti*) is absent there,
by the removal of four factors, the fourth dhyāna is established.
In that regard, there is no pleasure [in the higher stages],
yet it is not stated that perception and the other factors are limbs [of meditative concentration];
for indeed, there is no diminution of perception and the other factors within the intermediate dhyānas.
For what purpose [are there] exactly five factors?
If this meaning is not intended,
then [it must be that] it is because of their being auxiliaries that there are exactly five factors.
Therefore, that is not so,
because mindfulness and wisdom are assisted by applied thought and sustained thought;
for indeed...
Just as mindfulness and wisdom are desired as auxiliaries, so too are applied thought and sustained thought;
for one whose mindfulness is well-established and who understands things as they truly are, there is an absence of lethargy, excitement, and the like.
Therefore, this matter must be investigated.

The Master directs one’s curiosity toward this matter by stating that it should be investigated by consulting the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Furthermore, the summary of the meaning here should be understood as follows:
with what intention were only applied thought (*vitarka*) and the others established as factors (*aṅga*), even though other dharmas exist?
Because the factors of the basis for both the non-praise of counter-agents and their opposites are fully completed by that many [factors],
there is no formal arrangement of factors in the formless realms, on account of the single flavor of calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Thus it has been said, by way of taking up the factor of the counteragent, the factor of the benefit,
and the factor that is the basis for both.
In the first dhyāna, applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra) are the factors of counteraction,
because through them there is the abandonment of thoughts of sensual desire, ill-will, and cruelty;
joy (prīti) and bliss (sukha) are the factors of benefit.
Because one attains the joy and happiness born of seclusion from applied and sustained thought through their antidote,
one-pointedness of mind is the factor that serves as the basis for both; for, by the power of that basis, applied thought and the rest proceed.
Likewise, in the second dhyāna, internal clarity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*) is the factor that serves as the antidote,
because it acts as the counteragent to applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);
while joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind remain as the remaining factors, as before.
In the third dhyāna, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension are the factors of the antidote,
because by means of them there is the antidoting of joy;
and bliss and one-pointedness of mind are the remaining factors, respectively, as before.
In the fourth dhyāna, the purity of equanimity (*upekṣā-pariśuddhi*) and the purity of mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*) are the factors of the antidote (*pratipakṣāṅga*),
because by means of these two, suffering is countered within the dhyānas; the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*) is the factor of benefit (*anuśaṃsāṅga*).
One-pointedness of mind is the limb that brings about the convergence of both; thus,
"faith and clarity" means that faith itself is clarity— this is "faith-clarity."
If there is no separate substantial entity, how can they be mental factors?
For even a particular state of the mind, such as applied thought (vitarka) and so forth, is indeed a mental factor.
Because they exist within the mind, the state of mental discourse that is investigative is *vitarka* (applied thought),
and the state of mental discourse that is analytical is *vicāra* (sustained thought).
According to Bhagavadviśeṣa, *vitarka* is the state of the mind that gives rise to speech, while *vicāra* is any other state;
*samādhi* is the state of non-distraction.
The state of the mind’s flowing in tranquility is called "internal clarity" (*adhyātmasamprasāda*);
indeed, it is not appropriate to consider the pleasure in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) as mental happiness (*saumanasya*),
because its intrinsic nature is that of a feeling of equanimity (*tulyasukhavedanā*), even though it is mental in character.
Why is mental joy (*saumanasya*) not called pleasure (*sukha*)?
There is a reason:
for this joy is not yet tranquilized.
For by that [feeling], even the mind that is concentrated is— as it were— disturbed, as it were— uplifted, agitated with joy, accompanied by laughter, and as it were— deranged;
yet when it becomes tranquil, then, having reached another stage, a feeling of that same nature is called "pleasure."
"Because it is not separated from afflictions" means because it is not separated from the afflictions belonging to that level;
[it is so called] because it is turbid with afflictions.
This means that because of the lack of clarity due to the afflictions, one is distracted by afflicted pleasure.
Because one is agitated by afflicted pleasure,
mindfulness and clear comprehension do not arise,
owing to its being defiled by the afflictions.
Because they belong to that level, equanimity and mindfulness lack complete purity due to its defilement;
for these two are factors of the wholesome universal mental ground.
Pliancy and equanimity are recited among the great wholesome ground-factors;
faith, heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, shame, dread,
the two roots, non-harming, and vigor are always wholesome.
Based on this statement, one might ask: do these two [attainments] occur even in the defiled meditative absorptions (dhyāna) according to the former position, or do they not? To this, he says:
"Why was this not stated?

[The answer is: "Because they are established even without being mentioned; since *praśrabdhi* and *upekṣā* are not included among the great wholesome mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), they are indeed present [in those states]," so say others.
Regarding the term "breath" (śvāse),
the dual number is used here in order to indicate the pair consisting of inhalation and exhalation.
Because it cannot be shaken by applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and pleasure (*sukha*).
Just as the first three *dhyānas* are shaken by applied thought and the others— namely,
the first *dhyāna* is shaken by applied thought and sustained thought.
The second [dhyāna] is shaken by joy, the third by pleasure;
the fourth is not shaken by these in such a way.
Others say that it is stated in the Sūtra that "it is just as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker due to the wind," because [the mind] is free from the eight defects.
"Attained initially" means it is comprised within the first dhyāna,
like the mind of emanation (nirmāṇacitta).
Just as creators who desire to produce an emanation belonging to a particular level manifest an emanation-mind belonging to that same lower level,
so too [an emanation-mind] is not wholesome because it is inferior.
For that wholesome [state] belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is inferior and base compared to those belonging to the level of the second dhyāna;
therefore, they do not bring it into manifestation.
Indeed, it is for a specific purpose that they bring the state belonging to the level of the first dhyāna into manifestation.
Because they do not have great respect [for it],
that wholesome [action] is accompanied by maturation;
and since they do not desire its maturation, they make no effort to bring a wholesome state of mind into manifestation.
"By means of detachment and by way of rebirth" means either through detachment or by way of rebirth.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used here elliptically:
either through detachment from a lower stage,
one who was previously unendowed with it attains that pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna or formless attainment (*ārūpya*).

Through detachment from the desire realm, one first acquires the first pure dhyāna in its three modes, excluding the aids to penetration; likewise, up to detachment from the sphere of nothingness, one acquires the peak of existence,
either through detachment or by being reborn in a lower stage.
When one is being reborn from a higher level into a lower station, one obtains that [attainment],
except for the Peak of Existence; its acquisition occurs precisely through detachment from the lower level.
Because it is "conducive to penetration" by way of its application,
that attainment is not produced through detachment or rebirth;
nor is it "conducive to decline" even through falling away.
One who falls away from the stage conducive to stability (sthitibhāgīya) obtains the stage conducive to decline (hānabhāgīya);
for this very reason it is said that even one who has fallen away obtains the stage conducive to decline.
In this way, it should be applied both in terms of falling away (*parihāṇi*) and in terms of rebirth (*upapatti*):
how could one obtain the pure [attainment] through falling away, and how could one abandon it through falling away?
One might ask: "Could one obtain pure dhyāna through rebirth and abandon it through rebirth?
He says: "It could be so.
How so? He replies: [as follows].
The first dhyāna conducive to decline is the Brahma-world; for it is stated that the first dhyāna consists of three levels, specifically with respect to rebirth in the Brahma-world.
It is abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world because,

by means of detachment from the first dhyāna, one abandons the dhyāna conducive to decline (hānabhāgīya) due to its conformity with the afflictions, just as one abandons the afflictions belonging to that level.
Therefore, it is said that [the path] is abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world;
thus, first of all, the avoidance of the first question is attained by means of falling away from detachment from the Brahma-world.
If one falls away from the detachment belonging to the Brahma-world through a falling away [from that state], one again acquires that which is conducive to falling away;
it is abandoned like the afflictions of that level through a falling away from the detachment of the desire realm.
When one falls away from detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then the pure [attainment] is relinquished;
being reborn above in the Brahma-world, one acquires it.
When being reborn in the Brahma-world from the second dhyāna and so forth, one acquires that which partakes of decline (*hānabhāgīya*) just like the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to that level.
Therefore, one who is being reborn in the desire realm abandons [it];
that is, one who is being reborn in the desire realm from that Brahma-world abandons it.
Furthermore, through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one also abandons the states of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
One liberated through faith attains the state of a learner (śaikṣa) upon reaching the stage of one who has attained vision;
likewise, one liberated by occasion attains the state of a non-learner (aśaikṣa) upon penetrating the immovable state,
though not necessarily so.

"Because of not obtaining [the fruit] by means of the gradual path" means that if one who follows the gradual path enters the state of certainty (niyāma) by relying on the preparatory stage (anāgamya),
they do not obtain the pure or untainted [attainments] belonging to their own level.
At the time of emergence, during the flow [of meditation],
and in the second and third dhyāna stages— namely,
in the mixed and unmixed forward-order attainments and in the leap-attainment.
There are seven [attainments] belonging to their own level, which are both pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*),

as previously described; and likewise for those belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) during the attainment in reverse order.
The Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is exclusively pure (śuddhaka), because of the absence of the untainted (anāsrava);
it was stated that the untainted does not exist there due to its dullness,
yet in the case of forward attainment (anuloma-samāpatti), that [untainted state] occurs at the time of emergence.
And those belonging to the levels of the third, fourth, and first dhyānas— thus, at the times of the mixed, sequential, reverse, and leaping meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
there are four [consciousnesses] belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the fourth dhyāna.
At those very times there are three [minds], because of the absence of the untainted (anāsrava);
in this same way, ten substances are to be applied immediately after other dhyānas and formless attainments (ārūpya).

For example, immediately after the third dhyāna, there are ten [moments]: two belonging to its own level (the third dhyāna), both pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*); four belonging to the levels of the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); and four [belonging to the levels] of the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space.
In the same way, there are four belonging to the levels of the first and second dhyānas; thus, immediately after the fourth dhyāna, there are ten:
two of its own level that are both pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
There are four belonging to the stages of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness,
and four belonging to the stages of the second and third dhyānas; thus, ten [attainments] follow immediately after the sphere of infinite space.
Two [mental applications] belonging to its own level, four belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness,
and four belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas arise; thus, there are ten in total.
"And immediately after the subsequent knowledge," and so forth;

this is explained because, since the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) take both higher and lower stages as their objects, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence [of a lack of distinction].

"Because it has a lower basis and object" means that since that dharma-knowledge has a lower basis— namely, the basis of the desire realm— and has a lower object— namely, the suffering and so forth of the desire realm—
as it has such a lower basis and object, one does not enter the formless attainments immediately after dharma-knowledge.
The remainder is exactly as in the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*): both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted arise from their own level,
and from the higher levels down to the third lower level.
"Having made a vow," and so forth:
if someone, having formed the thought, "I must wake up at midnight, or at moonrise, or at moonset," should go to sleep,
he wakes up at that very time because the mental continuum follows his prior intention.
Just as one who has fallen asleep after making such a resolve awakens at the intended time,
so it is with this.
"In no way does it arise" means that it arises neither from its own level nor from a lower level;
this was said with reference to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
Since a defiled [mind] of its own level arises immediately after both a pure and a defiled [mind], but not one of another level,
how is it that likewise from a pure [mind], a defiled [mind] of its own level [arises]?
From a defiled [state], one's own pure or defiled [state arises]; thus it is at the time of death, in the existence of dying.
"Pure [meditations] are those obtained by birth," and so forth; that which is wholesome and concentrated, obtained by birth within the meditations of rebirth,
is also called "pure meditation."
Therefore, this is said in detail: "But at the time of death," and so forth.
What is the reason?
Because one who is not in meditative equipoise does not possess the pure dhyāna of attainment at the time of the existence of death.

Therefore, the meaning is that a defiled mind belonging to all stages arises; that is, a defiled, non-concentrated mind of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhicitta*) belonging to its own stage, a lower stage, or an upper stage arises,
but not one belonging to a higher stage.
Because, if it were of a defiled nature, its arising there would be impossible— except for that which pertains to the stage of distinction—
since there is no higher level beyond this.
Therefore, it arises as untainted from the aids to penetration; [specifically],
from the part conducive to decline and the part conducive to stability,
the part conducive to decline occurs during the period of continuity.
The state conducive to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*) occurs at the time of proceeding toward excellence (*viśeṣagamana*),
except in the case of that conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*);
for one who is declining from the state conducive to excellence (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), it is logical that this very [state] arises provided there is no abandonment of the state conducive to stability.
"That very one" means that very same factor conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), drawn forth by way of a continuous flow,
[and thus] in succession.
It is "performed" (vidhīyate) in the sense that it is "done" (kriyate) or "established" (sthāpyate), both in direct order and in reverse order.
The reason is that [the lower realm] is inferior,
because the noble state of nothingness (ākiñcanya) is present there.
Thus,
because of the manifestation, that is, the becoming present, of the noble, untainted sphere of nothingness.
For one born at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is the abandonment of the outflows (*āsrava*); however,
the word "but" (*tu*) indicates an exception,
because [the outflows] do not exist for oneself.
The meaning is that there is an absence of a path belonging to the peak of existence (bhāvāgrika) that is untainted (anāsrava);
and "due to the cultivation of that" means due to the cultivation of that untainted sphere of nothingness (ākiñcanyāyatana), because it is proximate.
Because the stages (bhūmi) are delimited by craving; for [the latent dispositions] underlie only that specific stage in which they belong.
By that [definition], that level (bhūmi) is demarcated;
for otherwise, its status as "higher" would not be established, because it would occupy the same location on a single level.
For this very reason, even though there is no higher or lower [in terms of verticality], the fact that the three, three, and eight other locations constitute a single level is established.
Because of the exchange with craving,
it would follow that [the desire for liberation] is not untainted (anāsrava) and would thus entail being wholesome (kuśala);
for that longing is indeed a wholesome aspiration for the Dharma (dharmacchanda).

The inclusion of the term "fundamental" (maula) is for the purpose of excluding the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), based on the principle that "the fundamental wholesome formless attainments do not have lower realms with outflows as their object."
For the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless realms take as their object the lower realm that is still with outflows (*sāsrava*);
the inclusion of the term "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is for the purpose of excluding those associated with relish (*āsvādana*),
and for the purpose of including both types of wholesome states.

For if only "formless" (*ārūpya*) were stated, it might be thought that the fundamental formless states associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samprayukta*) do not have lower contaminated realms as their object; thus, they might be understood as being exclusively uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "formless" is for the purpose of excluding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).
For even the fundamental dhyānas take contaminated lower-level objects as their focus because the dhyānas involve universal observation; thus,
the inclusion of the term "contaminated" is for the purpose of excluding the uncontaminated.

For untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of a lower stage can indeed serve as objects for the wholesome fundamental [attainments] of the formless realms; the mention of "lower" is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the higher,
since it is possible for them to have tainted (sāsrava) dharmas of a higher stage as their objects.
Having taken up the point that the object is indeed untainted (*anāsrava*), he demonstrates this by stating "the entire category of subsequent knowledge" (*sarvānvayajñānapakṣa*).
By the word "entire," even that which belongs to the nine stages and is differentiated by distinctions such as faculties and lineages is included.
By the inclusion of the term "category" (*pakṣa*) in "the category of subsequent knowledge," the receptivities to the subsequent knowledge of suffering and so forth are also intended.
And its co-existent factors are included,
but not the category of dharma-knowledge, because it is remote due to having the suffering of the desire realm and so forth as its object.
It has been explained previously that there is no cessation of a lower stage, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of grasping the lower stage.
Defilements are abandoned by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*);
thus,
that which is untainted exists within the dhyānas and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
By means of that, the afflictions are abandoned as far as possible; by which? By the untainted fundamental [meditative absorption].
For it will be stated [later]:
"And by means of the preparatory stage (sāmantaka)."
It has been established that afflictions are abandoned by means of the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) in its pure form through the process of negation; how much less so by a defiled one?
The intention is that the abandonment of afflictions is simply not possible by means of a defiled state.
For what reason are the afflictions not abandoned by the pure [attainment]? He says:
"Because one is free from passion, not the lower," and so forth;
because one is free from passion for the lower stage, the afflictions of the lower stage are not abandoned by the pure [attainment].
How much less so by a defiled [state],
since that very state is not its own antidote; nor [is it abandoned] in its own stage, such as that first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because it is not an antidote to that, it is its non-antidote; the state of being that is "because of its being a non-antidote.
Therefore.
Because it is not their antidote, the afflictions are not abandoned within their own level;
for there is no escape from existence by means of existence itself, since it is not more distinguished [than itself], nor is there escape by means of a higher level.
Afflictions belonging to a higher level are abandoned by means of the pure [meditative attainment] belonging to a lower level,
because afflictions are more subtle;
however, it is not logical for the abandonment of superior states to depend upon an inferior basis.
By this, it is established that even by means of the pure [attainment], the afflictions are not abandoned, much less by the defiled one; thus,
from the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even by the pure," it follows that they are not abandoned even by the untainted (*anāsrava*).
However, this was stated from the perspective of possibility;
for this very reason it is said:
"because it is the antidote to the lower stage."

For the afflictions belonging to the desire realm are abandoned by the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna; those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are abandoned by the preparatory stage of the second dhyāna; and so on, up to those belonging to the level of the sphere of nothingness, which are abandoned by the preparatory stage of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
"By which there is entry into them" means by which preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) there is entry into those fundamental meditations (*maula-dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*);
are those [preparatory stages] also of three kinds?
Because of the distinctions such as being associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-samprayukta*) and so forth, feeling (*vedanā*) is likewise [classified] among them; thus,
in the first two dhyānas, there is joy (*prīti*).
It has been stated that there is pleasure in the third [dhyāna] and equanimity in the fourth;
is it the same in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka)?
And they are associated with the faculty of equanimity because they must be carried out with effort;

for while the path that proceeds without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāravāhī*) is associated with joy and bliss, those preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) must be carried out with effort— that is, they proceed with volitional effort— and therefore they are associated with the faculty of equanimity.
Furthermore, because the agitation regarding the lower stages has not yet departed, there is no association with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*);
for this reason also, they are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*),
and because they constitute the path to detachment (*vairāgya*).
"They are not associated with relishing" means that if they were associated with relishing, there would be no path of detachment;
for a path associated with craving does not lead to the abandonment of afflictions.
Alternatively, the connection is as follows:

because they are associated with the faculty of equanimity, because they require effort, because the agitation regarding the lower stages has not yet subsided, and because they constitute the path of detachment, they are not associated with relish for two reasons.
The remainder should be stated as before; even though the reconnection [of the continuum] occurs by means of the preparatory mind (*sāmantaka-citta*),
this applies to whichever [preparatory stage] belongs to each of the eight dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
The established doctrine is that the reconnection [of the continuum] occurs by means of that defiled, non-concentrated preparatory mind (*sāmantaka-citta*);
therefore, this is said:
"even though by the preparatory mind," and so forth.
The preparatory stage (anāgamya) is also associated with relish;
because the preparatory stage is sharp,
it is possible for it to be untainted (anāsrava), just as [the dhyāna] itself can be.
The intention is that it is likewise associated with relishing (*āsvādana*);
for Master Saṃghabhadra says this is because it rivals the fundamental [dhyāna] and because there exists an attainment associated with relishing (*āsvādanā-samāpatti*),
since it is a specific variety of dhyāna.
That very same fundamental first dhyāna, being distinguished by the departure of *vitarka*, is called "the intermediate dhyāna" (*dhyānāntara*);
the meaning is that there is no such distinction as there is in the case of the first dhyāna.
In some cases there are both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), while in others there is only sustained thought;
such is not the case in the second dhyānas and above.
Therefore, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) is not established among the [four] dhyānas;
for this very reason it is called "the difficult path" (*duḥkhā pratipad*),
because it proceeds with effort (*saṃskāravāhitva*).
Because it is stated that "the intermediate dhyāna is without applied thought (atarka)," since only applied thought (vitarka) is being negated.
The meditative concentration that has that as its object is called "signless" (*ānimitta*);
it is signless because it exists within the signless, and it is said to have ten aspects.
The two aspects of impermanence and suffering,
the four aspects of non-arising, and the four aspects of the path— these ten aspects [arise] from the sense of revulsion toward impermanence, suffering, and their causes.
What [arises] from weariness with the impermanent, with suffering, and with its cause— the origin which is the cause of that suffering?
"Without aspiration" (apraṇihita) means that no formative activity (saṃskāra) has been performed,
because the path must necessarily be abandoned, as it is like a raft.
A raft is called a *kola*;
that which has this as its simile is the "raft-like path."
The state of being that [similarity]—
namely, the similarity to a raft— is the necessity of abandoning the path.
Therefore, the subject under discussion is the wishless (*apraṇihita*).
For just as one who crosses a river by means of a raft does not remain fixed upon the raft because it must necessarily be abandoned, so it is here.
"Having that aspect" means having those ten aspects as previously described,
because it is oriented toward transcending them.
Because one is oriented toward the transcendence of that path,
this [sūtra] demonstrates that it must necessarily be abandoned; thus,
even though it is not explicitly stated, it is understood that one is oriented toward the transcendence of impermanence, suffering, and their causes.

"But there is no agitation due to emptiness and selflessness" means that although the truth of suffering is indeed characterized by the aspects of emptiness and selflessness, the yogin does not experience agitation because of those two aspects of emptiness and selflessness.
But there is no revulsion toward that suffering because of those two;
why?
Because it is common to nirvana.
Nirvana, too, has the characteristic of being empty and selfless;
for emptiness and selflessness are indeed the characteristic of all phenomena.
Therefore, one does not feel revulsion toward Nirvana because of those two [characteristics].
Therefore, that which has that aspect is not the wishless concentration; thus,
"in eleven worldly [stages]" means in the desire realm, the threshold state (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, and the dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
In this context, "the path" refers to those stages excluding the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the desire realm, the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), and the second dhyāna and so forth,
because it serves as the gateway to liberation.
It shows that the meaning of "door" (*dvāra*) is the meaning of "entrance" (*mukha*),
because that name [of the dhyānas] has emptiness and so forth as its object;
it is called "emptiness" because it has emptiness, wishlessness, and the signless as its objects.
It is named "emptiness of emptiness," "wishlessness of wishlessness," and "signlessness of signlessness."
And [they are taught] by way of emptiness and impermanence respectively.

For the emptiness-of-emptiness takes as its object the emptiness-concentration of one beyond training by way of the aspect of emptiness, and not by way of the aspect of non-self, thinking "this is not mine";
thus it is said.

What is the reason here that the emptiness-emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*) has only the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatākāra*) and not also the aspect of selflessness (*anātmākāra*), as is the case with [the concentration on] emptiness? To this it is replied:

Because it must arise following upon the emptiness that functions with the aspect of emptiness, he asks: "For what purpose, moreover, does it arise following upon the emptiness that functions with the aspect of emptiness, and not following upon the emptiness that functions with the aspect of non-self?"
To this it is replied:
because it is conducive to the arising of that [state],

that very concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi), which proceeds with the aspect of emptiness, remains conducive to the arising of that concentration on the emptiness of emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi).
The aspect of non-self [is not the same]; for the vision of non-self does not cause such revulsion as the vision of emptiness does,
because even among those states that are seen as non-self, there still exists [the notion of] "self" in relation to what is non-self.
Because of the absence of the vision of emptiness within cyclic existence,
just as there is joy from seeing a traveler due to the lack of connection with that traveler,
so too there is no joy for one who is alone because of that very emptiness.
In the same way,
"by means of the aspect of impermanence" refers to the vision of the aspects.
"Not as suffering," and so forth;
they do not apprehend it as suffering because the untainted (anāsrava) does not have that characteristic,
for it is accepted as suffering only by virtue of being disagreeable to the noble ones (ārya).

The meaning is that [the untainted] is not [contemplated] through the aspects of cause (*hetu*), origin (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), or condition (*pratyaya*), because the untainted has the characteristic of being beyond these; nor is it [contemplated] through the aspects of the path (*mārga*), because the untainted does not have the characteristics of origin and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not [contemplated] through the aspects of the path because that concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samādhi*) is to be abandoned, whereas the aspects of the path do not have the nature of being abandoned.
Therefore, one does not take that samādhi as an object by way of the aspects of the path; however,
since there is no connection whatsoever with the aspects of cessation, it is not contemplated by them either.
By process of elimination, through the aspect of impermanence alone,
it is "innumerable and inexhaustible," which means non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Does the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) take the cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) as its object, thinking "this is peaceful" because it is peaceful? How, then, could there be such a cessation not through deliberation for it?

For one who has emerged from the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*) of an adept (*aśaikṣa*), if those subsequent impure moments (*sāsrava-kṣaṇa*) and other pure moments (*anāsrava*) were not to pass away,
then the signless moments of the adept would have already arisen.

At the time of the arising of those [dharmas], both those with outflows and others without outflows, the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) of those moments of the signless state belonging to the stage of no-more-learning is obtained due to the deficiency of conditions;
one takes that non-analytical cessation as an object by way of the aspect of peace.
Because there is no analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha) for that which is untainted (anāsrava),
it does not take analytical cessation as its object.
Why, moreover, is there no analytical cessation for the untainted?
Because it is not contrary [to their aim]:
for that which is contrary to the Noble Ones is for the sake of dissociation from union, since they strive for that end.
And dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) is analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*);
therefore, there is no analytical cessation for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, because there is an absence of analytical cessation for the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
And because non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) stands as its adversary,
one who desires to disparage it by means of praising that [other cessation] takes that very non-analytical cessation as his object;
for in the world, it is observed that the destruction of an enemy is accomplished by first winning over the enemy's ally.
"Not by way of the aspects of cessation, excellence, and renunciation" means that cessation is not common [to all]; thus,
it is "not cessation."
Its nature is such that,
because it is common to both impermanence and cessation, this non-analytical cessation is not produced by way of the aspect of "cessation."
For otherwise, it would not be apprehended by means of its specific aspect of tranquility;
for if it were apprehended by the aspect of cessation, this non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) would be tainted precisely by the cessation of impermanence.
The intention is that, through such a defect, the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would likewise be rendered defective.
It is not [perceived] by way of the aspect of being sublime,
because non-analytical cessation is neutral;
for that which is wholesome is sublime, whereas the neutral is not.
Therefore, one does not take it as an object under the aspect of being sublime;
and because there is no dissociation from apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha,
one takes it as an object under the aspect of renunciation.
For separation from affliction is held to be the escape from affliction;
because escape from cyclic existence does not occur through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For even when non-analytical cessation exists for certain wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, one is still associated with them due to the non-interruption of their possession (*prāpti*).
Regarding the phrase "because of hostility toward the noble path," how does it hate [the path]?
By turning its back on it through [clinging to] emptiness and so forth.
"Of the unshakable one" means of one whose nature is unshakable.
Because he possesses sharp faculties, he has the capacity to produce them, whereas no other Arhat does;

and in order to turn away from those other meditative absorptions— namely the emptiness and other samādhis of the Aśaikṣas— which, being states of dwelling in happiness in the present life, serve as a basis for attachment, they enter into yet other meditative absorptions.
In detail:
there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to the knowledge and vision of the superknowledge of the divine eye.
There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads to the differentiation of wisdom;

there is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and frequently cultivated, leads [to other results]. Regarding this, the Sūtra states that "practiced" means through the cultivation of repeated practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*).
It has been cultivated by way of abandoning the discordant factors and practiced extensively by way of distancing oneself from the discordant factors; thus it is said.
It has been stated that [this] leads to the knowledge and vision of the superknowledge of the divine eye,
yet the cultivation of the meditative absorption for the superknowledge of the divine eye is not discussed here.
This is a metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of the effect;

for when the supernormal power of the divine eye arises as the fruit of the cause consisting in the cultivation of meditative concentration, there is a metaphorical designation of the cause by the name of that fruit.
For those, however, who hold this position that the cultivation of concentration is for the sake of knowledge and vision,
the wisdom of the path of liberation is sixfold.
Thus, since the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are indeed mental paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) comprised within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
it is not at all surprising that these paths of liberation are characterized by concentration (*samāhita*).
However, it should be understood that the former position alone is that of the thinkers of the *Abhidharmakośa*,
because the consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear are intended as supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and because they are treated as primary therein.
Since it was stated as being merely by way of illustration that "even one another," it does not necessarily mean [the practice] is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the future life.
The future life (*samparāya*) is birth in a subsequent existence;
a state of dwelling in happiness therein does not necessarily result from this [present practice].
To the question "Why?", he says:
because for those who have fallen away from the first dhyāna and are reborn in the higher [stages], such as the second dhyāna and so forth.
And because for those who have attained final nirvana, there is no dwelling in happiness in future lives,
it is for the sake of knowledge and vision.
The compound "for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of vision" is thus analyzed;
therein, knowledge (*jñāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The vision arising from conceptualizations such as "these venerable beings are possessed of misconduct of body" and so forth is wisdom associated with visual consciousness; it is non-conceptual, belongs to the three realms, and is untainted (*anāsrava*).

That which belongs to the three realms includes the [meditations on] the foul, mindfulness of breathing, the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and so on.

The untainted [qualities] consist of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the blissful attainments (*sukha-samāpatti*), the leap-over attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), and the two types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*). However, because they are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*) is used as a metaphorical designation for these qualities acquired through application (*prāyogika-guṇa*),
for the purpose of distinguishing wisdom (*prajñā*).

"This instruction in the Dharma by the Blessed One is indeed intended to draw forth a distinction in wisdom," so it is said; "intended for oneself" (ātmanopanāyikā) means "a teacher for oneself. For the Bodhisattva, having gone forth to examine his past actions, produced the divine eye during the first watch of the night at the foot of the Jambu tree.

Having beheld with that divine eye sentient beings situated in the perilous states of death and rebirth, he brought forth the meditative absorptions, liberations, and attainments during the middle watch for their protection;
these qualities resulting from his application arise for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.

Then, in the third watch, relying upon the fourth dhyāna and entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*), he accomplished the abandonment of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
And because the teaching of the Dharma is thus directed toward oneself,
therefore it is only in the fourth [dhyāna], which is like a diamond, that it occurs at the end.
Thus,
"because it has immeasurable sentient beings as its object" is the reason for applying the designation "immeasurable."
"Respectively" means that loving-kindness is for those with an abundance of ill-will in order to abandon it,
and compassion is for those with an abundance of cruelty in order to abandon it.

For those with an abundance of aversion, there is sympathetic joy (*muditā*) for the sake of abandoning it; for those with an abundance of sensual desire and ill-will, there is equanimity (*upekṣā*) for the sake of abandoning them.
If both serve as antidotes to sensual desire and ill-will, what is the distinction between them?
Because of an abundance of sensual desire, one should reflect upon it and maintain equanimity toward attachment for mother, father, children, and kin,
just as one would toward unrelated persons.
"In the same way, these [are] equanimity"— this is the intended meaning;
"because it is drawn by greed," since ill-will is drawn by greed.
The intention is that it partakes of the nature of the antidote to greed;
however, because it possesses the nature of both, it is appropriate [to call it non-greed].
The meaning is that it is appropriate [to call it] both of the nature of non-greed and of the nature of non-hatred.
What is the reason?
Because they are the antidotes to attachment and aversion;
therefore, it should not be understood that a single phenomenon possesses both as its intrinsic nature.
Rather, the term "equanimity" (upekṣā) applies to non-attachment (alobha) and non-hatred (adveṣa);
thus, the intention is: "May those who suffer be liberated from suffering."
For it will be explained that since afflictions and secondary afflictions such as malice are removed,
they are therefore said to be its antidotes.
He shows how this is so:

there exist three [immeasurables], beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), belonging to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the level of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), which resemble the fundamental immeasurables because they share a similarity in their preparatory application, object, aspect, and intrinsic nature; thus, they are similar to the fundamental ones.
Having suppressed those afflictions by means of those three immeasurables, one abandons them through the paths of abandonment;
for loving-kindness is for the sake of abandoning ill-will in those who abound in it, while equanimity is for that same purpose [in others].
The meaning is that he is neither led astray by partiality nor repelled by aversion.
Regarding the detailed explanation "may those who lack faith [believe]," how is it not a misconception, given that one resolves that there is happiness for those who possess no happiness?
"With the intention that they may be" means with the intention that "may they be happy";
it does not mean with the intention of the opposite.
