"Or because of the non-perversity of the intention (*āśaya*)," means that the intention consists of wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), such as [the thought], "Oh, may sentient beings be happy! These [factors]—mind and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*) together with their attendants—are not perverted because this intention is non-perverted; thus, there is no perversion.
Furthermore, how is there non-perversion of intention? To this he says:
"because of the cognition of resolute belief. The cognition of resolute belief is *adhimukti-sañjñāna*.
Therefore,
because one perceives that very resolve in such a way and discerns it as "this is the attention consisting of resolute conviction" (ādhimokṣika-manaskāra).
It is not [called] unwholesomeness because of grasping in a perverted manner.
Because it is wholesome,
this is not so;
why?
Because it is a root of virtue, how is it a root of virtue? He says:
because it is the antidote to ill-will and so forth.
Because its intrinsic nature is non-hatred, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*);
and because it has the aspect of removing suffering, compassion (*karuṇā*) becomes the antidote to cruelty (*vihiṃsā*), which has the aspect of inflicting suffering;
and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the antidote to envy (*arati*), because it consists of mental gladness (*saumanasya*).
And equanimity, being a state of neutrality, is the antidote to sensual desire and ill-will; thus,
"of those having that as their object" means of those having sentient beings of the desire realm as their object.
The meaning is that by showing the vessel, that which is contained within the vessel is shown; thus, by means of the [receptacle] place, the world of sentient beings residing therein is shown,
because of the inclusion of both the concentrated and unconcentrated states, as well as the fundamental and preparatory stages.
Because they belong to six, fifteen, and [nine] stages respectively, the cause for all three is stated according to possibility;
therein, "unconcentrated" refers to the desire realm, the preparatory stages, and the threshold concentrations— this should be applied according to what is possible.

Regarding the establishment of the six stages: is the *anāgamya* also intended as a preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*)? Since the preparatory stages are also included as being of the nature of application (*prayoga*), [one might ask] whether they are the fundamental [stages];
[the answer is] no, because [the six stages] consist of the fundamental dhyāna stages (*mauladhyānabhūmi*).
The meaning is: because they belong to the levels of the fundamental pure dhyānas (*maula-śuddhaka-dhyāna*).
For it was stated previously that afflictions (*kleśa*) are not abandoned by the fundamental pure dhyānas;
[furthermore], because they consist of mental attention based on resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), afflictions are not abandoned by them.
For the abandonment of afflictions occurs through mental attention to reality (*tattva-manaskāra*);
moreover, because [the former] has sentient beings as its object, there is no abandonment by means of those [compassion-based attentions].
It is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through mental attention to the general characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-manaskāra*).
If one asks, "How then [is it so]? he says: "But by means of its application," and so forth;
because through the application of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the others, ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and the like are suppressed.
"It has been stated that they are their antidotes" means it has been stated that they are the antidotes to ill-will and so forth; the meaning is that these constitute the abandonment by suppression.
And because of "the distancing of what is to be abandoned":
since afflictions and secondary afflictions such as malice (*vyāpāda*) are distanced by means of the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), whether mundane or supramundane,
it is therefore stated that they are their antidotes.
He shows how this is so:

there exist three immeasurables, beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), belonging to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), which resemble the fundamental immeasurables;
they are similar to the fundamentals because of their similarity in terms of application, object, aspect, and intrinsic nature.

Having suppressed those afflictions by means of those three immeasurables, he abandons them through the paths of abandonment and the paths of immediate succession; thus, even when powerful conditions are encountered—
that is, even when powerful conditions for ill-will and so forth arise— he becomes invincible to those afflictions.
It is "intense" by way of being present in the case of a friend.
For it is easy to radiate— that is, to pervade— loving-kindness toward a supreme friend.
"By way of observing the fruits of former merit and demerit":

by observing the fruit of former merit, one who perceives virtues can regard even a person whose roots of virtue are severed as follows: "Merit must have been performed by this person, since he possesses such excellence of form and so forth.
And regarding a Pratyekabuddha, one who perceives faults might think: "Surely demerit must have been performed by this person, since he has such a deficiency in form and so forth."
Resolving, "May they indeed be liberated from suffering," one applies oneself to compassion; resolving, "May they indeed rejoice," one applies oneself to sympathetic joy.
[The phrase] "one is not endowed with sympathetic joy" refers to this process.
Because there is no mental joy (*saumanasya*) in the third and fourth [dhyānas],
there are eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
How are there eight liberations according to the sūtra?
Which eight?
One who possesses form sees forms; this is the first liberation.
Being percipient of the internal as formless, one sees external forms; this is the second liberation.
"Having realized the beautiful liberation with one's own body and having attained it, one dwells therein"—this is the third liberation.

Through the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of sensory resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] "space is infinite, space is infinite," one enters the sphere of infinite space;
this is the fourth liberation.
Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] "infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness," one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness,
just as the gods who have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness;
this is the fifth liberation.
Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing at all," one attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness,
just as the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness;
this is the sixth liberation.
Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
as do the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
this is the seventh liberation.
Furthermore, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having realized the cessation of perception and feeling with the body;
this is the eighth liberation.
Thus [ends] "possessing form, one sees forms."

Having contemplated forms within oneself, one also perceives forms externally; because it takes objects such as the livid corpse as its focal point, this method should be understood as being similar to the meditation on the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Starting from the antidote to the passion for color-form (*varṇarāga*) and so forth belonging to one with excessive passion, this should be applied extensively as appropriate: "The [contemplation of] the foul (*aśubhā*), born of the human realm, belongs to the ten stages, is non-greed (*alobha*), and has the visible objects of the desire realm as its objective support."

"Respectively" means that the liberation belonging to the level of the first dhyāna is the antidote to the passion for color-form (*varṇarāga*) pertaining to the desire realm; and the liberation belonging to the level of the second dhyāna is the antidote to the passion for color-form pertaining even to the level of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, these two should be understood as counteragents through distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*).
It is asked: how is it known that there is no passion for color-form (*varṇa-rāga*) in the second and subsequent dhyānas?
Because of the absence of visual consciousness,
whoever is detached from a particular object is necessarily also detached from the consciousness that apprehends it.
And since visual consciousness and the others do not exist in the second and subsequent dhyānas,
it is established that those who are free from passion for color-form are pure and formless (śubhārūpya).
Thus, since pure and untainted states also exist at other times when one is not in meditative equipoise,
this is said with reference to the mind and mental factors born of maturation within the formless realms.

However, regarding the former position, he shows that even in the state of the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) are not in a state of meditative composure; thus,

the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that even the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) receive the designation "liberation" (*vimokṣa*), let alone the fundamental [attainments] (*maula*).
"Not the path of uninterrupted transition," and so forth: because they are called "liberations" (vimokṣa) due to their turning away from the lower stages,
therefore the paths of uninterrupted transition do not receive the designation of "liberation."

However, the paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga) do obtain [the fruit], because they have higher objects as their support (ūrdhvālambanatva), whereas [the paths of preparation] have lower objects as their support (adharālambanatva).
But cessation is the eighth attainment; this is the completion of the sentence,
[stated] because of the turning away from perception and feeling.
Liberation is so called because of turning away from perception and turning away from feeling,
or because of liberation from all conditioned phenomena;
it is liberation because of being liberated from the hindrances to meditative attainment.
It is called "liberation" (vimokṣa) because it turns away from the obstacles to meditative attainment (samāpattyāvaraṇa).

In this context, the obstacle to meditative attainment refers to that obstruction wherein there is unworkability of the mind (*cittākarmaṇyatā*), such that even those who are free from passion for the three realms do not produce even the first fundamental dhyāna,
as the case may be.
For two [of these], the object of focus is unattractive form, such as a livid corpse and so forth; for the third, the object of focus is attractive form;
and for [the remaining two], it is their causes and their cessation.
The origin and cessation of that suffering,
as well as the entire category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*),
pertain to the upper and lower realms as well as one's own level; this is the meaning.
And "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha):
it should be stated that cessations not through deliberation are the objective support (ālambana) of the formless liberations (ārūpyavimokṣa),
as well as those which are formless.
Because it is stated here that "they have as their object the suffering and so forth of the category of subsequent knowledge, of the higher [stages], and of their own stage," he says:
Furthermore, what is the object of their non-analytical cessation?
It is said here that they take as their object the non-analytical cessation of the signless concentration of one beyond training.
For these formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣa), which have the signless-signless samādhi (ānimittānimitta-samādhi) as their intrinsic nature, are possible;

and they exist in eleven stages—excluding the seven preparatory stages (sāmantaka)—namely, in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), and the eight [form] dhyānas.
Thus, the treatise is shown to possess its proper definition by including this supplementary enumeration.
And it should be stated that space belongs to one [liberation], because the objective support of the liberation of the sphere of infinite space is space,
due to the absence of attachment to the colors belonging to the level of the second dhyāna.
The meaning is that there is an absence [of the desire for beauty] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna because there is no longer any passion for color to be countered;
its absence is due to the non-existence of bodily consciousness and because [the mind] is unmoved by the essence of pleasure.
The "essence of happiness" (sukhasya maṇḍaḥ) means the happiness that stands above all happiness; because of being agitated— that is, shaken— by that [happiness].
Why is liberation not established in the third dhyāna?
If there is no attachment to color belonging to the level of the third dhyāna,
why does one produce the beautiful liberation?
Therefore he says: "In order to gladden a mental continuum that has become despondent through [the meditation on] the foul, or for the sake of inquiry.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the liberations, etc.," the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth are included.
It is for the purpose of distancing the afflictions,
because the liberations and so forth serve as the antidotes that distance them,
and for the purpose of attaining mastery over meditative attainments.
And that mastery over meditative attainments serves for the production of qualities such as *araṇā* (the absence of conflict),
and what [further] is it for the sake of noble supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?
"For the sake of accomplishment" (abhinirhārāya) is the subject under discussion;
that [accomplishment] is further [defined] as the transformation of objects, the sustaining of power, the relinquishing of life-span, and so forth.
Among these, "transformation of objects" (vastupariṇāma) is...
Whatever object one resolves upon, it becomes exactly so, just as gold may be turned into clay.

Through such resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), there is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of a stable object [to remain] for this duration; likewise, there is the relinquishing of one's lifespan. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the entry of Mount Sumeru into an atom and other such things are to be understood as seen in the Sūtras.
Why is direct realization (sākṣātkaraṇa) stated only for the third and eighth [liberations] and not for the others?
How is it that direct realization is stated for the third?
"Having realized the beautiful liberation with the body, he dwells having attained it"—
so too for the eighth [liberation],
"having realized the cessation of perception and feeling with the body, he dwells having attained it."
In this context, "having realized directly" (sākṣāt-kṛtvā) means having perceived through direct intuition.
Here it is said that the third liberation is superior to the first and second liberations.

Because of the complete abandonment of the obscurations to the form-releases (*rūpivimokṣa*), the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) is said to be the realization of the third [liberation];
likewise, because of the preeminence of the eighth [liberation],
the transformation of the basis due to the complete abandonment of the obscurations to the formless-releases (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) is said to be its realization.
And because it abides at the limit of the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-paryanta*):
the fourth dhyāna abides at the limit of the realms and stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
while the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) likewise abides at the limit of the realms and stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
"Thus, regarding 'the superior [forms]':
perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are superior, beautiful or ugly," and so forth, up to "this is the second sphere of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
Likewise, not perceiving forms internally..."
How is it that one, being internally percipient of the formless, sees externally limited forms, beautiful and ugly? As before, up to: this is the third sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Likewise, being internally percipient of the formless, one sees externally extensive forms, beautiful and ugly; as before, up to: this is the third sphere of mastery.
Likewise, being percipient of the formless internally, one sees external forms that are vast, beautiful or ugly, as before, up to: "this is the fourth base of mastery. These are the four.
Furthermore, being likewise percipient of the formless, one sees blue, yellow, red, and white; how so?

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and radiant with blue light—just like an *umakā* flower or a fine cloth from Vārāṇasī that is blue, blue in color, appearing blue, and radiant with blue light. One knows those forms and sees them having mastered them; possessing such a perception, this is the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster— just as, for example, this sixth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as, for example, a *bandhūka* flower, or a cloth produced in Vārāṇasī is red— this is the detailed description—

this is the seventh sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*): being percipient of the formless internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.

For example, as in the detailed description: "like the star Uśanas," or "like a pure cloth from Vārāṇasī," this is the eighth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). These four are the "summits" (*mūrdhaka*), and together with the [previous] four, they constitute eight.
"The two are like the first liberation" means that they are as follows: the first liberation is "one possessing form sees forms."
Seeing forms within oneself, one sees forms externally;
thus it is in the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*),
for in those two cases, seeing forms within oneself, one sees them externally.
For it is recited thus:
"Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited," and so forth.

Furthermore, just as the first liberation belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, serves as an antidote to the passion for the unattractive within the desire realm, and has the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm as its object; [so too is the case here].
In the same way, these first two spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are to be understood as being like the second pair.

Just as one who is internally percipient of the formless perceives forms externally— such is the characteristic of the second liberation; and the third and fourth spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) have the same characteristic,
for they are recited in the same way.
"One who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally as limited"—this is recited as the third.
"One who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally as vast"—this is recited as the fourth.
Furthermore, just as the second liberation has as its object the forms belonging to the desire realm, [so too do these].
Likewise, the third and fourth spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are as described;
the others, moreover, are like the pure liberation (śubhavimokṣa).

Just as the pure liberation (*śubho vimokṣaḥ*) belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna and has as its object the sphere of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*) that are agreeable to the mind within the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), so too are the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) regarding blue, yellow, red, and white; however, in this case, the fourfold set of colors is grasped by distinguishing them individually.
And non-greed is the intrinsic nature of the beautiful liberation;
likewise, these [other liberations] also have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature when taken together with their attendants, just as this beautiful liberation does.
In the same way, it should be understood that those [other liberations] are merely liberations by means of them;
there is no overcoming of the object.
And how is there the overcoming of the object by means of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)? To this he says:
"Because of resolve according to one's wish," meaning because of their resolving upon blue, yellow, and so forth, according to their wish.
Because one resolves upon what is unattractive— as being blue at one moment, yellow at another, and so forth—
or because afflictions do not arise through such resolution.

Furthermore, because afflictions do not arise when one perceives an object associated with defilement as beautiful, there is a mastery over the object by means of those spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

This occurs through the uninterrupted and total pervasion [of the mind]; that is, because of the continuous and all-encompassing diffusion and permeation of the earth and so forth, they are therefore called the "spheres of totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
The sense-sphere of visible form belonging to the desire realm is called "earth"— meaning color and shape— according to worldly convention;
likewise, water and fire are also [conventionally designated as such], while wind is indeed the element itself.
Because of this statement,
some maintain that the sphere of the tangible exists in wind,
whereas others do not admit the existence of the sphere of visible form in wind.
They say that the sense-sphere of the tangible, with wind as its object,
constitutes the preliminary stages for entering the liberations.

The term *prāveśikāni* means "belonging to entry" (*praveśa*), either because the suffix *-ika* is added in the sense of the base itself (by the rule for the addition of suffixes in the same meaning), or because it means "that which exists in entry."
"Because they are progressively more distinguished" means that because the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are more distinguished than the liberations (vimokṣa),
and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) are more distinguished than the spheres of mastery.
This is what is meant: having produced the liberations (vimokṣa), one produces the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana);
having produced the spheres of mastery, one produces the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
"Excluding the liberation of cessation" is because it belongs exclusively to the continuum of an Ārya,
and because of its being either practiced or unpracticed.
Those that are natural are acquired through detachment; those that are unnatural are acquired through application;
the rest are both.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
What, then, is the remainder?
The first three liberations and the eight bases of mastery.
Regarding the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
why is it that these have only the human body as their basis?
Since [the path] is produced through the power of instruction,
and since there is no instruction elsewhere among the gods and so forth,
how can there be the production of the specific formless meditations within the form and formless realms?

In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu), whatever formless state or meditative absorption (dhyāna) is superior to the level on which one has been born— that is the distinction of the formless absorptions (ārūpyadhyānaviśeṣa).
How can there be [attainment] of those specific formless meditative absorptions without instruction?
For it has been stated that the remainder [of the meditative attainments] have only a human basis, because they are produced through the power of instruction.
Therefore, by this connection, it was asked:
"How [is it] in the form and formless realms? and so forth;
and [it is said] "by the power of the cause" means through recent and repeated practice.
Due to frequent practice, immediately after [death], one is reborn in the form realm;
because the homogeneous cause characterized by the formless attainments is more powerful, that person will give rise to the formless attainment in the form realm,
even due to such frequent practice.
If someone, having frequently attained an immaterial-sphere absorption (ārūpyasamāpatti) and subsequently fallen away from it, is reborn in the realm of form (rūpadhātu),
an immaterial-sphere absorption arises for him in that realm precisely because of the superior strength of its homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu).

Likewise, for one who has fallen away from the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana-samāpatti) and is reborn in the base of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), there is the arising of those very attainments in exactly the same manner.
Thus, for one who has been reborn above that,
and for one reborn in the form realm by the power of karma, because the ripening of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life has become present.
A continuum conducive to detachment from that [realm] persists;
for one who is not yet free from passion for the lower [realms] cannot be reborn above in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Thus, for one born in the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana) among the formless realms, by the power of karma—
Because the ripening of karma to be experienced in a subsequent life belonging to a higher level— that is, belonging to the sphere of infinite consciousness— is present,
the continuum remains in a state conducive to detachment from that [lower level];
for one who is not yet free from passion for the lower levels cannot be reborn in the higher ones.
And by means of these two powers— causal power and karmic power—
how is it that the second and subsequent meditations are produced within the first and other meditations?
It is through causal power, specifically from nearness and frequent practice.
"And by the power of karma, [it arises] from a higher level," and so forth should be applied in detail;
and also "by way of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
What, then, is this so-called *dharmatā*?
First, some Sautrāntikas say:

"The natural state (*dharmatā*), nature (*prakṛti*), or intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*)—meaning the conformity to the arising of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) without instruction when those very phenomena arise with manifest activity through the sovereign influence of prior meditative impressions (*vāsanā*)—is what is meant.
Some Vaibhāṣikas also say the same.

The outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) arises from the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) of a previous birth; the production of meditative absorption occurs through the nature of things (*dharmatā*) from another source even without instruction therein, because wholesome factors (*kuśaladharma*) have attained an intensified activity.
In that context, "at the time of dissolution" means [the time] of the wholesome paths of action;
"their activity" refers to the functional operation of those very same factors;
they are called "those whose activity has become manifest" because their activity has arisen and reached its peak.
The state of being that;
therefore,
this is what is meant.
Because those wholesome states attain their own nature through excellence when the latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) arises;
thus, these are the types of phenomena.

This means that the types of phenomena—both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)—such as their realms (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), objects (*ālambana*), and aspects (*ākāra*), are to be understood according to their respective applications.

"Those who uphold it, those who speak it, and those who practice it"— referring respectively to those who speak the *āgama* (scriptural transmission) of that true Dharma which consists of both scripture and realization.
Those who are its upholders and those who are its practitioners are its upholders.
Thus, while the realization [of the truth] remains for a thousand years,
the scripture remains for a much longer period of time.
The meaning is "even after a thousand years"; we consider this very position to be the correct one, as indicated by the detailed explanation beginning with "this which... and so forth.
Regarding this Abhidharma taught here characterized as the *Abhidharmakośa*,
is this alone the Abhidharma taught in the treatise characterized by the *Jñānaprasthāna* and so forth? To this, it is said:
"Established by the system of the Kāśmīra Vaibhāṣikas," and so forth;
those who exist in Kāśmīra are the Kāśmīras.
This has been explained as follows: "Vaibhāṣikas" are those who play with the *Vibhāṣā*.
There are, however, Kāśmīrans who are not Vaibhāṣikas, such as those learned in the Vinaya and others, as well as the Sautrāntikas, the Bhadantas, and so forth.
There are Vaibhāṣikas who are not from Kaśmīra—
namely, those Vaibhāṣikas from outside [Kaśmīra]— and according to the system of those [Vaibhāṣikas] characterized by both [qualifiers], the Abhidharma which is established [is as follows].
This has been taught by me here for the most part;
what is meant is that it is taught even as established by other systems of logic.
Whatever has been wrongly grasped here, whether according to the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas or by another system, [that is what is being corrected].
In the statement,
"our offense" means our transgression.
He asks "For what reason? and says:
"In the system of the True Dharma, the sages are the authority."

Regarding the *nīti*—the description—of the True Dharma characterized by scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*), the sages, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the sons of the Buddha, such as the noble Śāradvatīputra and others, are the authority; the meaning is that they are the trustworthy ones (*āpta*) in the awakening to all phenomena in all their aspects.

"When the Teacher, the Eye of the World, had closed his eyes" means when the Blessed One, who had become the eye of the world and the guide showing the path and the non-path, had entered final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*).
By this, he shows that the world has become blind,
especially now that the class of witnesses has for the most part passed away.

The witness is one who sees directly; the Blessed One is the witness who knows the path and the non-path. When that person who has realized reality—the Blessed One’s witness and companion—has entered final nirvāṇa, [the world] is blinded by ignorance.
By those who have not perceived the truth, who are unrestrained and unbridled, acting on their own—
Because you have fallen into fallacious reasoning due to your dogmatic views, [you revile] the Blessed One.
The teaching has been made confused both in its textual form and in its meaning.
"Since the Self-Existent One has himself attained supreme peace," and so forth— this verse is presented as the reason for the meaning stated in the preceding verse,
for [it concerns] the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas.
When the world has passed into final nirvana and is without a protector,
due to the causes for the disappearance of the Teaching.
By the stains of views and other defects.
Unrestrained, acting freely and according to their own desires in this world.
in the world today,
at this very moment.
Therefore, this is practiced as the means for accomplishing existence.
Thus, "the breath gone to the throat" means as if the breath were actually situated in the throat.
That.
Having understood that this is the time for strength regarding the stains and defects,
those seeking liberation must not be heedless.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on Attainments" (*samāpatti-nirdeśa*), in the *Sphuṭārthā*—the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* composed by the Master Rājaputra Yaśomitra. Regarding this, [it is said]: "This is the proof by way of the action (*bhāva-sādhana*)."
The section on the treasury (*kośasthāna*) is the "Determination of the Person" (*pudgalaviniścaya*).
What indeed is there other than this for liberation?
Because of the statement, "Those desiring liberation must not be negligent," this alone is the means to liberation;
there is no other means to liberation besides this.
Thus, by the implication that those who desire to be liberated here must not be negligent, the Teacher has stated this; and the interlocutor asks, "What do you think? and so forth.
To this, it is replied:
As for the reason why it does not exist, he says:
"Because of being settled in a false view of self."
The false teachers are settled in a false view of self; being settled in that false view of self is their state,
and for that reason [it is so called].
"There is no liberation elsewhere"— this very point was also stated by the author of the hymn:
"As long as the mind is possessed of ego, the succession of births does not come to rest."
As long as the view of a self exists, the ego-sense does not depart from the heart;
and since there is no other teacher in the world who teaches selflessness,
there is no path to the method of peace other than your doctrine.
Thus,
there is no means of accomplishment here for Kapila, Ulūka, and others, nor is there liberation for them.
Because they are settled in a false view of self,
like a person who has not seen reality,
the afflictions arise from the grasping at a self, as it has been said.
Furthermore, those various views held by certain recluses and brahmins in this world, which are rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), are explained at length [in the sūtras];
and when the view of a self exists, the afflictions such as self-love (*ātmasneha*) arise.
This designation "self" refers only to the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*).
The term "self" (ātman) means a designation of a self;
the meaning is that it is not imagined as referring to any other denotable object distinct from the continuum of the aggregates (skandha-santāna),
because of the absence of both direct perception and inference [for such an object].
The intention is that because perception and inference do not exist, there is no existence of that [object];
since scripture is included within inference, it is not mentioned separately, and for them, perception is apprehension.

"Perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*) is a qualification of "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*); "perceptual apprehension" means apprehension by means of perception. Alternatively, "perception" is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and "apprehension" is that by which [the object] is apprehended.
"When there is no obstacle" means when there is no impediment to perception— such as being too near or too far—
in relation to those six objects.

Is there direct perception of the sense-bases of form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects, as well as the sense-base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) characterized by sensation and so forth, and that which is the object of yogins and transcends scriptural conceptualization— namely, the mind?

For the mind that has just ceased is cognized by the mental consciousness that arises immediately thereafter—whether as being lustful, hateful, associated with pleasure, or associated with pain—and so forth, by way of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedyatayā*); thus say others.
This perception is of two kinds: that which pertains to the object (*grāhyagata*) and that which pertains to the subject (*grāhakagata*).
"And inference," and so forth; where perception does not operate,
there the apprehension of that [object] occurs through inference.
For example, as in the case of the five sense faculties—
namely, the eye faculty and so forth— when their causes, such as the field, water, and so on, are present.

In the absence of another cause characterized as a seed, the absence of the effect called the sprout is observed; and when that seed is present, the reappearance of the sprout is observed—just as in the case of the sprout itself. This is the presentation of the example.
Having thus presented the illustration, he says, showing the point illustrated:
"Even when [the object] has reached the range of appearance," and so forth;
that is, even while the object—such as visible form—and the attention (*manaskāra*) produced by it exist and are present before one.
He demonstrates, according to their respective order, for whom the non-existence and then again the existence of the apprehension of objects— the visual consciousness and so forth— is observed.
Regarding the phrase "the existence of those who are neither blind nor deaf," etc., the word "etc. includes those whose olfactory faculties and so forth are either impaired or unimpaired;
therefore, in those cases as well, the absence and presence of some other cause that has not yet manifested its form are determined respectively.
What, then, is that? He says:
the meaning is that whatever other cause is required is the sense faculty, such as the eye and so forth.
And the proof here is as follows:
an entity characterized by the object and mental attention, which— conjoined with other causes— is recognized as the producer of the five groups of consciousness and the producer of its own effect.

Because it accomplishes its own effect only at certain times, that which accomplishes its own effect only occasionally is a producer of its own effect when accompanied by other causes; for instance, soil and water that produce a sprout,

being accompanied by the cause characterized as the seed, produce another effect [the sprout] only when they are accompanied by those other causes, for soil and water accomplish their own effect only at certain times.
Because it brings about the sprout during the state when the seed exists,
and because it does not produce its own effect during the state when the seed does not exist,
such is that entity characterized by the object and mental attention.
For that [organ] is the producer of its own effect— characterized by the five groups of consciousness— in states such as non-blindness and non-deafness,
whereas it is a non-producer in states such as blindness and deafness;
therefore, it produces its own effect only when accompanied by other causes.
Regarding the phrase "that is the faculty," how is it determined that "that is the faculty"?
For it is determined only to this extent: that there exists some other cause therein.
But it is not that [the visual consciousness] itself is the sense faculty;

this is indeed established because it has been determined by the knowledge resulting from the great seer’s meditative resolve that the eye and other such faculties exist as the causes of visual consciousness and the rest.
And because there is no dispute among all [of them],
he concludes that "it does not exist as a self" and thus "there is no self";
for it has been stated in this way by way of meaning as a proof.
The self does not exist,
because it is not perceived by any means of valid cognition, like an absolute non-entity.
If it is argued that there is inference [of this], and therefore the reason is unestablished, we say no.
Because it must be expressible;
for if it exists, let it be described.
"One should not object that this reason is unestablished merely by words"— this is what is meant by the detailed passage beginning with "the Vātsīputrīyas.
The Vātsīputrīyas are the Āryasaṃmatīyas.
By this, he shows that the reason characterized by being settled in a false view of self is inconclusive;
for liberation is not denied to the Vātsīputrīyas, since they are Buddhists.

Alternatively, this position—that "there is no self"—is shown to be flawed because it contradicts the previous position; for one must first investigate whether this is indeed the Vātsīputrīya school's own tenet.
Thus, this matter requires examination.

The intention is that there is no fault in this, because according to that school, the person (*pudgala*) exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*). When asked whether this [person] exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) or as a conceptual designation, the Master says:
"If it were a distinct entity like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then it would exist substantially."

If, as in the case of form and so forth, [the person] is intended to be a distinct entity from sound and so forth by way of substantial existence, then the person is accepted as being substantially real;
for form has a characteristic different from sound, and so on.

If it is a composite like milk and so forth, then it exists as a mere designation (*prajñapti*); for just as milk, a house, an army, and so on, are not accepted as entities distinct from color, taste, smell, and tangibility, or from grass, wood, bricks, and so on, or from elephants, horses, chariots, and so on— what then?
If you maintain that the person is merely the collection of those very [aggregates], then the person is accepted as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).
For there is no entity whatsoever— whether milk, a house, or an army— that exists apart from the grass, wood, elephants, and so forth [that compose them].
What follows from this? What fault results from this? This is the meaning.

If, first of all, the position that [the person] exists substantially is adopted, then that person must be declared to be other than the aggregates, because its intrinsic nature is different and its specific characteristic is different.
It is not merely an aggregate of the aggregates, like one aggregate in relation to another;
for example, the aggregate of feeling is distinct from the aggregate of form and so forth, because its defining characteristic is different.

In this way, the person (pudgala) would be distinct from the aggregates (skandhas), because the person possesses characteristics such as the formless aggregate (arūpaskandha) and so forth; furthermore, its cause must be stated.
If the intention is that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
or else unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
then there follows the consequence of falling into the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the Vātsīputrīyas fall into the view of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika-dṛṣṭi*) and [their position] is rendered purposeless;
for what effect do rain and sun have upon space, whereas they do have an effect upon leather?
If it is like a hide, it is impermanent; if it is like space, the fruit is non-existent—this is the meaning.
This is a deception of the blind, its meaning being unclarified.
Why is it like one blind person [leading] another?
Because its meaning has not been made manifest; that is to say, its meaning has not been clearly expressed.
"Taking the aggregates as an object" means grasping them;
just as, having grasped and depending upon form and so forth, there is the designation "milk," yet no milk exists apart from form and so forth.
If the designation "person" (pudgala) were [merely] thus, the meaning would be that the person is non-existent;
[this applies] if [it is said] "in dependence upon the aggregates," meaning if [the person exists] by depending upon or reaching the aggregates.
The meaning is that the same fault follows: the designation of a "person" (pudgala) would apply to those very aggregates (skandhas).
Alternatively, the aggregates are the condition for the designation of a person, not the person itself.
But the person (*pudgala*) is likewise merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*);
thus, the same fault remains as when fire is designated in dependence upon fuel.
The person (pudgala) exists as a substantial entity, being neither different nor non-different [from its constituents],
because it is designated in dependence upon its own basis of appropriation.
For the Vātsīputrīyas' intention is that whatever entity is designated in dependence upon its own basis as being neither other nor not other is a substantial reality (*dravyasat*), just like fire;
and for this very reason, he says:
For if it were otherwise— as explained in detail— he demonstrates either a contradiction with worldly consensus or a contradiction with his own established doctrine,
because it would entail the consequence of eternalism (*śāśvata-prasaṅga*).
Because, like the unconditioned, there would follow the consequence of annihilation, just as in the case of the aggregates.
"Unignited wood and so forth are the fuel," and so on;
by this, he demonstrates that the example is unestablished (*asiddha*),
for it is indeed accepted that fire and fuel are distinct entities.
Therefore, it is said that "it is ignited and burned by that";
the meaning is that the fuel is ignited— that is, made to blaze— by that fire.
"It is burned" means it is reduced to ashes by bringing about a transformation in its continuity, that is, by producing the state of being ashes.
Others say that "is kindled" and "is burned" are synonyms;
furthermore, both of these consist of eight substances—
both the fuel and the fire consist of eight substances.
In the realm of desire, form consists of the four great elements and the four derived forms, up to and including the tangible; thus,
according to the established tenet, it comprises eight substances when sound is excluded.
"Because they occur at different times": first there is the fuel and afterwards the fire;
and it is observed that things occurring at different times are distinct, as in the case of the seed and the sprout.
And it follows that [the fire] would be impermanent,
because one observes that form and other qualities which possess an origin are impermanent;
thus, [it would be impermanent] in that very same wood and so forth where it is ignited.
In the collection that possesses both those characteristics,
their distinctness is also established because of the difference in their characteristics; thus,
for fire and fuel as well, which possess such characteristics, their distinctness is established because of the difference in their characteristics.
Because the earth element and the others have distinct characteristics,
it is observed that those with different characteristics are indeed distinct, such as form, sensation, and so forth; however,
the meaning of "derived" (upādāya) must still be explained.
The intended meaning is "because of non-difference";
for that [fire] is not the cause of that [fuel],
since that fuel characterized by the three elements does not exist [as a separate entity].
It is logical that there is a cause for this fire characterized by heat,
because it is co-nascent,
like the left and right horns of a cow.
Nor is it [the case] that it [is the basis] for the designation of that;
that is, if the meaning of "basis" refers to the designation of fire.
"Depending on fuel" means relying on fuel;
it signifies either coexistence or simultaneous arising.
The meaning is that fuel is not grasped as being co-existent;
[the phrase] "they would become co-existent with their support" means that they would become both the support and co-existent.
The Vātsīputrīyas clearly assert a distinctness [of the person] from the aggregates; however,
in the absence of those [aggregates], that [person] does not exist.
"Because it has the nature of other elements" means that because it has the nature of the earth element and so forth,
it is "other" as well; thus, not only heat is hot.
Furthermore, other things such as the earth and so forth, when in contact with that blazing fire, are established as being hot; therefore,
just as there is no fault in its being something else [than the fire], so too there is none in this case.
Consequently, since it would be "inexpressible," that position [of yours]— namely, that firewood and so forth [are the fuel]— would be abandoned.
Just as wood, grass, cow dung,
and so forth are not to be designated [as male or female], the person (pudgala) is of the neuter gender because it is undifferentiated.
Thinking that one would not be able to say, "What has been born for you?", [the author] states that the knowable is fivefold; how, then, should it be stated? He says:
"For it should not be stated as a fifth distinct from the past and so forth, nor as a non-fifth."
"Also of form," and so forth:
the designation of form must also be explained, because it is perceived when the eye and other [faculties] exist; thus, form is designated in dependence upon those eyes and other [faculties].
One discerns [it] by way of observation because it has that as its material cause;
however, it should not be said whether it is forms or not.
Because it lacks the characteristics [of being either] and because it is inexpressible,
one discerns the milk and the water in this way, up to whether it is dharma or not-dharma.
These two examples should be stated as follows:
if one perceives milk in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye, then that milk should be said to be cognizable by the eye.
But it should not be said whether they are forms or not; all this should be stated in the same way.
If one perceives water in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye,
it should be said that the water is cognizable by the eye,
but it should not be said [that it is the same as those forms].
Or whether they are forms or not— let it not be that all things result in being fourfold, as in the case of milk and water—
if it were said, "they are forms."
If it were said that they extend as far as tangible objects, it would follow that milk or water would possess fourfoldness;
the meaning is that milk or water would become fourfold in nature.
Since sound is adventitious, it is not the subject under discussion here.

Therefore, just as the collection of form and the other [sensory objects] alone is designated as "milk" or "water," so too the collection of the aggregates alone is designated as a "person" (*pudgala*). Thus it is established that forms are the cause for the perception of a person; one who perceives forms perceives the person.
What is the distinction between these two positions?
In the first position, the causality of forms is established;
in the second, however, it is not causality.
Rather,
it is the perception of a person (pudgala) based upon forms;
in that case, if the causality of those forms is accepted, then that person must not be said to be other than them.
In that case, this consequence follows for you:
"matter as well," and so forth;
just as visible forms are the cause for the perception of a person (pudgala), yet it should not be said that he is other than them.
Light, the eye, and mental attention are also causes for the perception of form;
yet you must not say that this form is something other than those factors such as light,
because they are the causes for its perception.
Because those [factors] such as light are the causes for the perception of form, it follows that the person (pudgala) has a nature non-different from form,
since it is perceived by that very same single perception.
It follows that the designation of a person (pudgalaprajñapti) would be a designation of form itself, just like the designation of another form.
Why?
For that very same reason,
"and this is form," and so forth in detail.
If apprehension were a single entity, the distinction between form and the person would not be established; thus,
it could not be discerned that "this is form" and "this is the person."
How can both be asserted? For indeed, only form itself should be asserted,
because of the existence of its perception.
In this way, it should be stated up to "from phenomena"; how then is that which is said [to be] explained?

What is the meaning of this statement: "Depending on sounds cognizable by the auditory faculty, one discerns a person"? Does it mean that sounds are the cause for the perception of a person, or rather that while perceiving sounds, one perceives a person?
First, if sounds are the cause for the perception of a person...
And it should not be said that he is other than them;
likewise, then, sound also should not be said to be other than light, the auditory faculty, and attention,
because these are the causes for its perception.
Now, when perceiving sounds, does one perceive the person by means of that very same perception,
or rather by another?
If the person (pudgala) were to possess a nature non-different from that very sound,
it would follow that either the sound itself is the designation for that [person], or else how could this be distinguished: "this is the sound" and "this is the person"?
If it is not determined in this way,
how is it known that both sound exists and the person (pudgala) also exists?
For its existence is known by virtue of perception; in this manner, [this principle] should be applied to all phenomena up to the dharmas,
just as yellow is [known] from blue.
When blue is perceived through a specific determination, yellow is not perceived at that time;
rather, it is perceived later.
Just as yellow is perceived by means of a perception other than that by which blue is perceived— and thus yellow is understood to be different from blue—
in the same way, the person (pudgala) is perceived by means of a perception other [than that of the aggregates].
Just as [the self] would follow as being other than form,
so too should it be illustrated that one moment is other than the subsequent moment;
and this should be stated in the same way up to the case of phenomena (*dharma*).
How so?
Furthermore, because it is perceived at a different time by another [means], the sound would follow as being distinct,
just as the sound of a drum is distinct from the sound of a clay drum.
And just as one moment is followed by another moment— like blue being followed by yellow— as previously described, so too does one moment follow immediately upon another.
The distinctness [of the object] has already been demonstrated by its perception at different times, whether the objects have distinct characteristics or non-distinct characteristics;
this should be applied in detail to the factors (*dharmas*) as far as the phrase "just as in the case of form and the person" (*rūpa-pudgalavat*), and so forth.

If one were to say that just as the identity or difference between form (*rūpa*) and the person (*pudgala*) is inexpressible, so too the identity or difference between their respective perceptions (*upalabdhi*) is inexpressible—then, by that logic, even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) would be inexpressible. For this conditioned thing, characterized by its perception, would also be inexpressible; thus, there would be a contradiction with the established tenet (*siddhānta-bheda*) which holds that only the person (*pudgala*) is inexpressible.
If it is argued that "this [self] is distinct" because even the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is inexpressible (*avaktavya*),
then [the response is] "if this... and so forth.
If it is thus, one should not say "whether it is form or not"; rather, what was said by the Blessed One— "form is non-self," up to "consciousness is non-self"—
shows that for one who speaks in this way, the *pudgala* must indeed be spoken of and is not "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*),
just like sound and so forth.
The person (pudgala) is not perceived by the consciousness of form, because it does not serve as its objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
just like sound.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should here apply [the examples] such as "possessing odor" and "possessing taste";
likewise, its non-perception by auditory consciousness and the other sensory cognitions must be stated—
this is the general direction.
By this presentation, it should be understood that the fault of a proposition involving the reversal of the specific quality of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya*) is being exposed;
namely, that [the cause] arises in dependence upon a dyad, and not in dependence upon a triad.

Therefore, this [statement] "the eye, O monk, is the cause," and so forth, is contrary to the sūtra; for "cause" (hetu) refers to that which is proximate, whereas "condition" (pratyaya) refers to that which is remote.
Others, however, maintain that the remote cause is indeed the producer, whereas the condition is merely the objective support.
Others say that these two are synonyms;
however, this entails the undesirable consequence of the position that the person (pudgala) is something other than form (rūpa),
because it would be cognizable by auditory consciousness, just like sound.
Likewise, there follows the undesirable consequence of the thesis that the person (pudgala) is other than sound,
because it is cognizable by visual consciousness, like visible form; and in the same way, this should be applied to others,
resulting in the undesirable consequence of the thesis that the person is other than both visible form and sound.
"Because it is cognizable by the olfactory faculty, like fragrance"— this is the direction for applying the argument.
Because of the statement, "They each experience their own respective spheres and objects," it is implied that they experience them by means of a person (*pudgala*);
and this was stated as a corollary to the fact that the mind is their point of reliance.
This is not the example;
rather, the meaning is that since the mind is the resort of these sense-faculties, the sense-faculties become the instruments for the arising of consciousness in dependence upon it,
nor is the person (pudgala) the object.
If the Sūtra is accepted as authoritative, then what follows? He says:
"If [it] is not the object."
If it is not the object of any consciousness, then it is not cognizable;
consequently, your own established doctrine that "the cognizable is fivefold" would be contradicted.

If this is so, then based on the statement in the Sūtra that "one does not experience the range and object of one [sense] through another," the non-deviation from their respective objects for the five [senses], beginning with the eye, is taken as authoritative.

Furthermore, if the person (*pudgala*) were not cognizable by visual consciousness and the other [sensory consciousnesses] because they do not deviate from their own respective objects, then it would follow that the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) also does not deviate [from its object]. This is because the Sūtra states in detail: "These six faculties have different spheres of activity," and so forth.
For example, six living beings—a dog, a bird, a jackal, a crocodile, a snake, and a monkey—were bound together by someone, tied with a knot in the middle, and then released.
Just as they each desire their own respective range of objects— desiring villages, market towns, cemeteries, water's edge, anthills, and forests—
in the same way, these six sense faculties each desire their own respective range of objects.
Thus, this is merely an analogy;
for even if there were a scriptural statement [to the contrary], there would still be a deviation regarding the mental faculty (*manaindriya*),
and likewise a deviation regarding the visual faculty and the others.
And if there were deviation [from this rule], then the person (pudgala) would become cognizable by visual consciousness and the other types of consciousness;
to this we reply: "Not so," and so forth.
In that *Ṣaṭprāṇakopama-sūtra*, it was not stated by taking the eye and the other [senses] themselves as the sense-faculties (*indriya*).
What is the reason?
Because it is impossible for the five sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, to desire seeing and the like;
for it is impossible for them to desire seeing, hearing, and so on, because their intrinsic nature is that of form (rūpa).
And since those consciousnesses—
the visual and other sensory consciousnesses— are capable of desiring to see and so forth,
why is it that their desire for seeing, hearing, and so on is not possible?
Because it is non-conceptual,
the mental consciousness— which is drawn forth by its predominance— is called a "faculty" (indriya) in the sense that it is like a faculty;
how, then, is it known that it is drawn forth by its predominance?
For if visual consciousness and the rest were not produced through the doors of the eye and so forth,
how else could conceptual mental consciousness arise?
Therefore, this is known.

"Drawn forth by the predominance of that [mind]" means that this mental consciousness, having become the sense-faculties such as the eye, desires its own respective objective spheres, such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth;
and as for the phrase "that which is merely," and so forth.

It does not at all desire to take as its object the domain of other [faculties] such as the eye; rather, that which is brought forth through the predominance of the mind takes as its objective support only its own domain, namely, the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Therefore, this fault does not apply;
as for what was said— that if this were so, it would follow that the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) is also non-deviant—
it is not the case that there is a person (*pudgala*).
Since it is asked whether he is to be directly known or fully understood, therefore that person (pudgala) is not even something to be cognized.
But has it not been stated that, by implication, he is neither to be directly known nor fully understood,
rather than that he is to be cognized?
To this, he says:
It should be understood that because wisdom (*prajñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have the same object,
the eye and so forth are indeed objects of consciousness (*vijñeya*),
not merely objects of higher knowledge (*abhijñeya*) and full comprehension (*parijñeya*).
"By means of the eye as non-self" means by means of visual consciousness;
and it has been stated that a sūtra of definitive meaning (nītārtha) is the refuge.
Monks, there are these four reliances.
What are the four?
The Dharma is the reliance, not the person.
Meaning is the reliance, not the letter;
sūtras of definitive meaning are the reliance, not those of interpretable meaning;
gnosis is the reliance, not consciousness.
"Not having fallen into [the error of] designation" means that one is attached to that very thing for which the designation "self" was made for the sake of conventional usage as being a "self";
[it means] that there is no sentient being or self here.
This is the illustration here:
that a person (pudgala) is not apprehended.
And this...
Nor does there exist even that [person],
for this too is an inappropriate example: that there is no one who practices emptiness.

There is the view of a self, up to the view of a living soul; this is the first disadvantage. One becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders; this is the second. One has entered upon a wrong path; this is the third.
The fourth [fault] is that his mind does not enter into emptiness and so forth, up to the point that he does not have resolute faith in it; the fifth is that the noble dharmas do not purify him.
The intention [of this critique] is that, since the Buddha is not their teacher, the word of the Buddha is not an authoritative source for them.

The intention [of the passage] regarding "all other schools," such as the Tāmraparṇīya school and others, is that these sūtras were attributed by someone with the claim: "This is certainly not the word of the Buddha."
It does not contradict the sūtra, nor does it contradict another sūtra,
nor does it oppose another sūtra, nor does it contradict the nature of phenomena— that is, the nature of dependent origination.
"All phenomena are without self" means that these do not have a self-nature,
and because no self is found within them, all phenomena are without self.
Regarding the statement "dependent upon a dyad," namely from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental objects,

and the declaration that "the self is not the aggregates, bases, or elements," whatever was previously stated as "it should not be said whether it is form or not" is thereby removed and cast aside, because [the self] is something other than those.
Therefore, he shows that all [notions] are indeed the grasping of a self in what is not-self, and that there is nothing other than this,
by saying "if it were so," and so forth in detail.
If they were recollecting, have recollected, do recollect, or will recollect these very five constituent aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*) and not a person (*pudgala*),
why did [the Buddha] say, "I existed as possessing form in past time"? By the use of the word "I," he demonstrates that it is the person who is being spoken of.
"Those who recollect in this manifold way—
'those who thus recollect' is the ellipsis to be supplied;
and in this case, the very absence of such a reading would be the refuge [for rejecting the claim]."
The meaning is that if the reading were "I" (*aham*), there would be the undesirable consequence of embracing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);
for the view of a self-identity is taught to have twenty aspects,
such as viewing [the aggregates] as "this is my self."
One should speak thus regarding form: "The self possesses form," "form belongs to the self," or "the self is in form"; and so on, up to consciousness.
"Like a heap, a stream, and so forth" means like a heap and like a stream;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), items such as a beverage are included.

A "heap" refers to many things gathered together in a single moment, while a "stream" refers to many things gathered together over many moments; by means of this analogy of the heap, he demonstrates the designation of a person (*pudgala*) with respect to many phenomena.

By means of the analogy of a stream of rain, [the Buddha] shows that when there is a multiplicity of aggregates such as form and sensation in their continuous flow, the designation "person" (pudgala) is applied;
how is this understood?
It is through the Buddha’s teaching that the continuum possesses this capacity.
It is said that when, by mere attention, non-erroneous knowledge arises regarding whatever is desired,
it is not [knowledge] of a person.

Because of the mention of the past and so forth, and because it was stated in detail that "those who have passed away," the conclusion is that the designation "Buddha" applies only to the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*) and not to a person (*pudgala*).
“Monks, I will teach you the burden; and so forth:
“Monks, I will teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.”
What is the burden? It is the five aggregates of clinging. What is the taking up of the burden?
Craving leads to renewed existence; it is accompanied by delight and passion, finding delight here and there.
What is the laying down of the burden?

It is the complete abandonment, relinquishment, exhaustion, destruction, fading away, cessation, appeasement, and disappearance of this very craving that leads to renewed existence, which is accompanied by delight and passion, and finds delight here and there.
"What is the bearer of the burden? It should be said:
that venerable one who has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such a lifespan."
The meaning is that the "bearer of the burden" (bhārahāra) refers to the person (pudgala); this is the intended sense of the example,
and for this very reason he says:

For it is not the case that the burden itself is the bearer of the burden; otherwise, since the taking up of the burden— which possesses the characteristics already described— would also follow as being uncomprised within the aggregates, it would follow that it is not comprised within the aggregates, just like the person (*pudgala*).
And this is not accepted;
therefore, just as with the taking up of a burden, the person (*pudgala*) is not a separate entity from the aggregates (*skandha*).
Having stated all this in detail with the words "for this very reason," one must say "not otherwise."

If the *pudgala* were a substantial entity (*dravyasat*), then only this much would have been stated in that Sūtra: "Who is the bearer of the burden? It is the *pudgala*. Therein, the opponent would not need to analyze him further by saying, "That venerable one," and so on in detail up to "until the end of his life."
The intention is that this further qualification is for the purpose of understanding the person (*pudgala*) as existing only as a designation (*prajñaptisat*);
however, how is it known that he exists only as a designation,
lest he be understood otherwise— as either eternal or as an ineffable person existing substantially (*dravyasat*)?
"Of the aggregates," and so forth:
therein, those aggregates which lead to affliction and are causes of suffering are spoken of as "existence" (bhāva).
Furthermore, those who are oppressed are called "burden-bearers" because they are spontaneously born (*upapāduka*).
The meaning is "because of acting well in the process of rebirth.

Regarding the statement "because the person (*pudgala*) is not included within the truths," this is because the person as it is conceptually imagined is not included within the truths, such as suffering and the rest.

For the person (*pudgala*) is not suffering, nor [the other aggregates], up to and including the path; therefore, this false view which denies the person is not something to be abandoned by the vision of the truths— that is,
it is not a view that is mistaken regarding whichever truth it pertains to.
Its abandonment would likewise occur through the vision of that [truth];
however, because the person (*pudgala*) is not included within the truths of suffering and its origin, it cannot be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

For a defilement to be abandoned by cultivation must take as its object only a thing (*vastu*) to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, either suffering or its origin—and thus it is logical that such a [person] would be abandoned by cultivation.
Furthermore, since the person (*pudgala*) is not included within those two [categories], that [person] is not something to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*);
or else, since a view is never to be abandoned by cultivation, it [the person] is not to be abandoned by cultivation,
just as in the cases of "one sesame seed," "one grain of rice," "one heap," and "one word."
Just as one speaks of "a single sesame seed" or "a single grain of rice" even though it consists of eight substances,
so too one speaks of "a single heap," and likewise of "a single person" (*pudgala*).
"Because of the admission of having an origin":
by the statement "it arises," its possession of an origin is admitted;
consequently, it must be called "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) by you.
The intention is that because of the appropriation of another set of aggregates (*skandha*), its status as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtatva*) is not compromised;
for just as one is said to be "born as a sacrificer" due to the appropriation of knowledge.
And that [result] is not produced in its true sense;
"it is like that"— thus everything should be applied accordingly,
for an agent is not perceived, and so forth.
An agent of action is not perceived; as to what kind of being he might be, it is said:
"He who casts off these present aggregates and abandons them, and takes up and grasps other aggregates belonging to the future—
existing as a substantial entity"—
except for the conventional designation of dharmas; thus he says, by way of the definition of dependent origination, "namely, when this exists..."
"Phalguna, I do not say 'one has appropriated.
If I were to say 'one has appropriated,' then you might think it appropriate to speak thus: 'But who, Venerable Sir, appropriates the appropriation?'"
Therefore, there is no appropriator of the aggregates, nor any discarder;
thus, for that [person] as well, it is the same:
the meaning is that at every moment there is only the arising of what was previously non-existent.
By the introduction beginning with "If that person [is the subject], it is unestablished," he demonstrates the lack of proof for the example;
and in the phrase "like learning and marks of the body" (*śarīravidyāliṅgavat*),
"learning and marks" (*vidyāliṅgam*) refers to both learning (*vidyā*) and marks (*liṅgam*).
The body and the mark of knowledge constitute "body-knowledge-mark";
like those two, there would follow a difference between the aggregates and the person, as in the case of the body and the mark of knowledge.

Just as there is a difference between the body and the knowledge that is acquired by it, so too there is a difference between the person (*pudgala*) and the aggregates (*skandha*) that are acquired, because [the person] is the appropriator. This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, the statement "that [body] is worn out" and "it is diseased" refers to a different body at each moment, because it exists in changing states; this is the intended meaning.
In this regard, he demonstrates that the statement "the aged is born, the diseased is born" is an unestablished example. Furthermore,
if it should be argued that there is the cessation of one state and the manifestation of another state within a persisting body,
that too is not [valid], for the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) was already refuted in the previous chapter on the "Bases" (*Kośasthāna*).
For how could that very substratum (dharmin) not exist,
upon which the conceptualization of other attributes (dharmāntara-vikalpa) might be imagined?
If this very thing is thus, it is an unprecedented mode of expression to say that there are four primary elements and one form;
what, then, is form?
The statement "the four great elements," and so forth, is a fault only from one particular perspective; the meaning is that this critique of faults applies to only one side.
"In the view of those who hold that there are only the elements" means in the view of the Elder Buddhadeva, not in our own view.
Nevertheless, even in the view that [the person] consists of the mere elements (*bhūtamātrika*), form is not other than the elements;

likewise, in the view that it consists of the mere elements, it follows that the person (*pudgala*) is not other than the aggregates (*skandha*), just as form is not other than the elements. Thus, the intention is that one’s own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*) would be abandoned.
Their intention is this: why did the Blessed One not declare whether that living being is the same as the body or something else?
[And] if the designation "person" (pudgala) is applied to the aggregates (skandha), why was it not stated that the body itself is the living being?
"By the predecessors alone" refers to the Elder Nāgasena and others;
"talkative" means prone to much idle chatter.
The other says: If the person (pudgala) is not to be described [as either existing or non-existing], why was it not stated that it simply does not exist?
And he is incapable of such a teaching.
The intention is that, through delusion accompanied by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
one would fall into even greater confusion and thus give rise to another view accompanied by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*);
for this very reason, he says:
"The self existed for me, but now it no longer exists for me"—
thus says the venerable Kumāralāta in this regard.
"And the piercing by the fangs of views," and so forth; that is,
the view itself is the fang, and by it there is the piercing.
The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma of selflessness in consideration of its opposite;
and they teach otherwise, as if showing the existence of a person, in consideration of the non-perishing of actions and the loss [of results] from actions performed.
It is like a tigress carrying off her cub:
just as a tigress carries away her own cub by seizing it with her teeth without excessive cruelty,
so that its body may not be wounded by her fangs.
Nor does he remove it with a grip on the teeth that is too loose, lest it should fall out in this matter;
the meaning is that he removes it with a grip that is precisely appropriate.
Others read "apaharati" as "he removes [it] from another place," meaning he takes it away.
Showing the cause for such a vision of the truth, he says: "The existence of a self," and so forth.
If someone were to adhere to the existence of a self and be pierced by the fang of a [wrong] view—namely, the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—he would become a person to be trained.
Not attaining the conventional designation of phenomena and failing to understand it,
one would cause the destruction of the ship of wholesome action— which is like the cub of a tigress—
by asserting that "there is no fruit of action."

"Designated" (*prājñaptika*) means that which exists in designation; [the Buddha] did not say "it does not exist" lest someone should grasp that even the person (*pudgala*), though existing conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*), does not exist at all. Nor did he say "it exists," for if the person existed in an ultimate sense (*bhūtārthena*), why would the Blessed One not have said, "The person exists"?
For there is no fault in the statement "form exists," because it does exist, like the case of the sparrow of the Nirgrantha disciple. (Regarding AKBh 471.4–5):
A Nirgrantha disciple, having caught a live sparrow, questioned the Blessed One.
His intention was this: "Does this sparrow live or not? If the ascetic Gautama should declare that it lives, he will kill it by squeezing it and show it [to him]."
If, however, the Blessed One were to command, "He is dead," he would show him as being very much alive;
his obsession was that the world might know, "How indeed can this man be ignorant?"

But the Blessed One, having understood his intention, did not provide an answer; rather, he stated, "This depends entirely upon your own mind as to whether it lives or not," and thus this was left unexplained.
In the same way, this [matter] has not been explained.
For this tetrad has the same meaning as that [tetrad]:
"Is the world eternal? Is the world not eternal?"—this tetrad, "Is the world finite? Is the world infinite? has the same meaning as that.
If this is so, how can there be fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛta-vastu*)?
"The world is eternal" is the first tetrad;
"it is finite" is the second tetrad;
"the Tathāgata exists [after death]" is the third tetrad.
The fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) consist of: "the soul is that body" and "the soul is one thing and the body another" (this is a dyad); three [sets of] tetrads; and one dyad.
Thus, even when established as various permutations, they remain fourteen in number; therefore, there is no fault.
"You yourself ask this," he said;

for by asking "Is it finite? and "Is it non-eternal?", one asks whether there is a partiality of the world, and by this [question] one asks whether it is both finite and infinite, and both eternal and non-eternal.

The statement of the Vātsīputrīyas— that "he explains the person as existing" means that he explains the person as being truly existent, yet inexplicable in terms of identity with or difference from [the aggregates] because of the consequence of the fault of eternalism— is [rejected].
