"In that case, why does he explain this?"—this is the detailed statement of the Teacher [Vasubandhu]. [The objection is: "If the suffix -aṇ is used here as an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), as in the word 'youth' (*yauvana*), then one should not say whether he sees or not."
The meaning is that one should not say "he sees" or "he does not see";
rather, let it be made inexpressible gradually.
The inclusion of the term "gradually" is for the purpose of avoiding provoking the followers of the Śākya son who hold similar views.
"From the standpoint of reality, from the standpoint of abiding"— this means "in the form of abiding"; thus it is called a "basis for views."
The intention is that the basis for wrong view has been stated; thus the Master says:
"The existence [of a self] is also stated to be a basis for views."
The meaning is that it has been stated to be the locus of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). How could this position not have already been answered?
Because it was rejected by the Blessed One in the Sūtra itself— in detail, from "up to" [the statement] "these are without example"—
this is the explanation of others beginning with the words "on what basis? (*kim idam upādāya*).
But showing how it transmigrates according to his own view, he says:
"Just as a momentary fire," and so forth.
Fire is well known to be momentary,

yet it is said to move by means of a continuity (*santati*) that arises in other locations; likewise, the collection of aggregates (*skandhasamudāya*) designated as a sentient being is "possessing craving as its appropriation" (*tṛṣṇopādāna*),
meaning that craving is its appropriation.
"Even though [the self] is momentary, it transmigrates by way of continuity"— thus,
in the *Saptasūryodayasūtra*, it is stated that this very Blessed One was formerly the seer named Sunetra.
"Because of the difference between the aggregates"— the intention here is that this refers to their difference [from moment to moment] given their momentariness; thus,
it demonstrates the state of being a single continuum.
Since Sunetra was indeed the very continuum of the Buddha, the metaphorical designation of non-difference is made in the sense that "I am he";
just as one says, "This is that same fire which was seen previously coming while burning," it is called "that same" by way of the continuity of the stream.
In the same way,

the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) would belong to those who possess a self; thus, for the Tathāgatas, there would be a view of a self-identity characterized by the notions of "self" and "mine."
"For those whose bonds are permeated by an even firmer attachment to self and what belongs to the self":
since, when the view of a self exists, there arises both attachment to the self and attachment to what belongs to the self,
and thus considering passion to be a bond, for those whose bonds have been made firm, liberation would become remote.
The intention is that [the self] would not exist at all;
this refers to the "grasping at a person" held by some, namely the Vātsīputrīyas, and the "grasping at universal non-existence" held by others.
The intention [of the author] is that for those who hold the Madhyamaka view,
memory arises from a particular state of mind associated with the perception of an object of memory; here,
the "object of memory" refers to an experienced thing.
In this context, "having a connection with perception" means that its cause is the perception of an object of memory; it is a specific state of mind characterized by such a connection,
meaning that only a certain [state of] mind [is so characterized], not all of them.
Therefore, memory or recognition occurs; when both qualifiers have been established in this way, he asks: "From what kind of specific state of mind [does it arise]? and replies:
"Application toward that," and so forth:
application (*ābhoga*) toward that which is to be remembered is "application toward that" (*tad-ābhoga*).

That particular state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) possesses such application, as well as the notions (*saṃjñā*) and other factors that are similar to it and related to it; thus, it is "possessing application toward that, similarity, and related notions."

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is indicated that these [qualities] have their beginning in aspiration (*praṇidhāna*); thus, a specific basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*) such as freedom from grief, distraction, and so forth, is meant—a particular state of mind whose power is unhindered by those [obstacles].
In this way, it is demonstrated by this [statement].
Therefore, memory arises from such a specific state of mind;
this is what is meant:

for one who possesses mental application (*ābhoga*) toward that [object], if application is directed there—provided one possesses a perception of similarity and so forth—in which case memory arises due to that similarity.

For one who possesses the recognition of a relationship and so forth, memory arises even in the absence of similarity upon seeing smoke and the like; and for one who possesses resolution, connection, repeated practice, and so forth, memory occurs when there is a resolution such as "I must remember this at this time," or when there is repeated practice regarding that which is to be remembered,
because its power is unimpaired by defects of the physical basis and other such factors.

"Even such [a person]— due to the specific condition of the physical basis characterized by illness, grief, distraction due to other tasks, and those things included by the word 'etcetera,' such as the rules for ritual actions," and so forth in detail.

The meaning is: one who possesses the mental engagement (*ābhoga*) up to the perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, whose power is unimpaired; "not following that" (*atadanvaya*) means not following the perception whose object is non-recollection (*asmṛti*).
To cultivate or produce something different means that it possesses a lack of mental engagement (*anābhoga*) up to the absence of perception (*asaṃjñā*) and so forth, or that its power is unimpaired.
The meaning is that [the cognition] of one person does not arise from the specific mental state of another because there is no connection;
that is to say, because there is no relationship of cause and effect between the minds of Devadatta and Yajñadatta.

Just as there is a connection between two mental states belonging to a single continuum due to their being in a cause-and-effect relationship, there is no such connection between the minds of Devadatta and Yajñadatta; by this, he demonstrates the lack of similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
In this regard, if an opponent were to state the following proof:
"The memory-consciousness does not remember an object experienced by the experience-consciousness of Devadatta,
because it is something other [than that experience-consciousness]."
The argument "like the mind of Yajñadatta" is not a valid proof, because the reason itself is unestablished and because it is sublated by perception, thereby undermining the prima facie position.
Now, if this objection were raised against the thesis that the experience of Devadatta and the mind that recollects it are distinct,
that would not be a valid objection; for when there is a contradiction with what is perceived, an objection cannot be logically sustained.
For even in your own established doctrine, it is held that the mind of recollection remembers the object experienced by the mind of Devadatta’s experience;
we do not say that one [mind] remembers what was seen by another, but rather that it is not the case that something entirely different is remembered— this is our intended meaning.
The meaning is that the mind of recollection arises as something entirely distinct from the mind of perception, because its cause exists— just like a sprout arising from an existing seed—
and recognition occurs precisely through recollection.
If it is argued that "that very thing which was seen by me" is known through memory,
then [the opponent asks]: "In that case," if it is only a particular state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) that remembers;

As for the question, "How then is it that Caitra remembers?", this is a supply of words [to complete the sentence]; and as for the phrase "and that too belongs to him," the full explanation is as follows:

having taken into account the causal status of that continuum of the collection of formations called "Caitra" with respect to the production of a modification in another location and the production of a modification in another state within that which is designated as "cow."
What is meant by "master"? It is not said to be the person (pudgala).
The intention is that this conventional usage depends upon the relationship of cause and effect, not upon a person (pudgala);
therefore, he says:
"But no one at all," and so forth;
likewise, "Who cognizes thus? and so forth:
if there is no self (*ātman*), who is it that cognizes in this way?
What is the meaning of "it cognizes"? Does it grasp the object by means of consciousness?
Is that grasping something other than consciousness?

In that case, one should not say that consciousness produces consciousness, [but rather] that the cause of consciousness— consisting of the sense faculty, the object, and mental attention— is a specific state of mind.
Because of the connection with other causes such as the sense faculties and so forth, for this very reason it is said "according to what is appropriate"; this is the specific distinction.
As for that which is expressed as "Caitra cognizes," [it is merely a conventional designation].
For it is from that continuum called Caitra that [the self] is spoken of by way of the view of existence;
since there is no self, whose is this consciousness,
and what is the purpose of this genitive case?
Regarding the purpose of ownership,
as in "who is the owner of what?"— and so on in detail until: "Furthermore, where else is consciousness to be employed, such that its owner is sought in relation to the object to be known?"
For what purpose should it be employed?
Is it for the sake of knowledge,
or rather are these well-spoken words merely for those raised in comfort?
For indeed, that very thing must be employed for that purpose;
but how should it be employed— is it by way of production, or rather by way of dispatching?

Because the movement of consciousness is impossible, is it then the cause itself that is the master? Thus, in detail, up to the point where it is said: "For that which is the cause of consciousness is precisely that [which is called] Caitra," and so on in detail, until: "even there, apart from the state of being a cause, there is no state of being a master."

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is indicated that this is the general direction [of the inquiry], including such questions as: "Who experiences? Whose is the feeling? Who perceives? Whose is the perception? and so forth.
As for the grammarian who says that "an entity (bhāva) depends upon an agent (bhavitṛ)," his intention is that there must be an agent of becoming, namely, a person (pudgala) who is the knower.
"Like the designation 'going' for that which goes": just as there is the designation of the word "goes" in expressions such as "the flame goes" or "the sound goes"—
just as there is the going of the flame or the sound— so too is there the expression "Devadatta goes" or "the going of Devadatta."
By this analogy, it is established that "Devadatta" is known because [the name] acquires its own nature through similarity; that is,
because the effect acquires its own nature through similarity with the cause.
"Even though not performing anything" means even though not performing any physical movement;
"by way of its form" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that it has the form of objects such as blue;
"because of being the cause of consciousness" means that consciousness is the cause of another consciousness.
Therefore, because one consciousness arises immediately after another, it is said that "it cognizes," since the term for an agent is applied to the cause;
that is, by treating the cause as if it were the agent.
Just as the cause of sound is the bell, yet one says "the bell rings," so it is with the lamp.
The term "lamp" is applied metaphorically to a continuum of flames,
treating it as if it were a single entity; thus, that lamp, which exists in the form of a continuum, arises in various locations.

It is said that "it goes to such and such a place"; likewise, within the continuum of mental states, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is metaphorically designated as a single entity. Thus, this consciousness, which exists as a continuum, is said to "cognize" each respective object as it arises with respect to various objects.
The intention is that one "cognizes" by means of a continuum through the arising of consciousness; or, as in the detailed explanation regarding how form exists,
just as there is no difference in meaning between the form and its becoming, the generator and the generation, or the sustainer and the sustaining.
The same would apply to consciousness as well;
because the knower exists as consciousness, there is no difference between them,
since no distinct entity is perceived.
Or, according to the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras,

if it is argued that cognition does not arise from the self, then because there would be no distinction in the characteristic of cognition, exactly the same kind of cognition would arise [at all times].
If, however, the intention is that a specific cognition would arise for that person due to a particularity of their own intention,
and yet it does not do so according to a fixed sequence—
why is it that it does not arise according to a fixed sequence?
For indeed, it arises even without a fixed order: immediately after the cognition of a cow, there may arise the cognition of a woman;
after the cognition of a woman, the cognition of a buffalo.
Why then does the cognition of a cow not arise immediately [after the cognition of a cow]?
Regarding the phrase "like the sprout, the stalk, the leaf, and so forth":
from the sprout, only the stalk arises, not the leaf and so forth;
from the stalk, only the leaf arises, not the flower and so forth, nor the sprout and so forth.
Likewise,
"of those absorbed in meditation according to their desire" means of those absorbed in meditation that is desired, sufficient, and complete.
Regarding the arising of a similar body and mind— that is, the arising of a body and mind that are similar—
the intention is that there is "spontaneous emergence" (*svayaṃ-vyutthāna*), meaning it occurs without being induced by another.
Thus, the answer to the question "Why does this not always arise as exactly similar? has been given; however, the question "And why is there no fixed order [of succession]? remains.
Showing this, he says:
"The sequence of thoughts is also indeed determined"— this is certainly accepted.
"Due to a specific lineage (*gotra-viśeṣa*)," that is, due to a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā-viśeṣa*).
"From a female mind," and so forth;
"from a female mind" means from a mind having a woman as its object (*ālambana*), immediately after which there arises the body of that woman, i.e., *tatkāya*.
If, for the sake of reviling her body, the thought of a wandering mendicant or another virtuous person arises, or the thought of her husband, son, and so forth—
whereby "and so forth" includes daughter and others— then [the following occurs].
The mind that has that as its object— namely, the mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth,
or whichever other [mind] arises immediately after that woman’s mind—
and which, through the transformation of the continuum over time, eventually gives rise once again to a woman’s mind.

Subsequently, that female mind which has arisen becomes capable of producing a mind that reviles her own body, or produces a mind that reviles the body of that woman, or produces a mind directed toward her husband, children, and so forth;
why is this? He says: "Because it belongs to that lineage (gotra)."

That which has the mind that reviles its own body, or the mind directed toward its husband, sons, and so forth, as its lineage (*gotra*) or seed (*bīja*), is "that lineage-mind" (*tad-gotra-citta*); [the word *tadgotratvāt*] refers to the state of being such.
Therefore.
The intention is that it is "like those of that same class"; otherwise, it would not be of that lineage. Furthermore, the detailed explanation is given by way of synonyms.

Successively and not simultaneously, from the thought of a woman, there arises a thought of revulsion toward her body; from that, a thought of her husband; from that, a thought of her son; from that, a thought of her daughter; and from that, a thought of her utensils and so forth.

From among these thoughts that have arisen immediately after the thought of the woman, whichever thought arises—whether because it is more frequent in its stream, more intense in its power, or more proximate to the thought about to be produced—it is precisely that thought which arises, due to the greater strength of its cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This is the detailed explanation.
The specific bodily condition and the specific external condition that arise at that time—meaning those other than [the primary cause] from which they differ—are what is meant by "at that time.
For indeed, that very [condition] is established as superior, whether it be the bodily or the external condition, whose object arises [in the mind].
Thus, that alone is the more powerful.
That very cultivation which is more frequent, more intense, or more proximate is the stronger; why does it not always bear fruit? For that mind does not cease [to exist]; rather, it persists.
To this, he who was questioned replied:
"Because its characteristic is the alteration of its state while persisting."
"Characterized by the alteration of duration" means that its characteristic is the alteration of duration;
because of the existence of that [alteration], namely,
of that characteristic of the conditioned which is alteration.

The connection of the meaning is as follows: because it is conducive to the arising of the fruit of another cultivation—that is, the arising of a different fruit—it does not always bear that very same fruit;
for thus said the Elder Rāhula:
"in every way" means in every manner.
Whatever varieties of color, arrangement, and so forth exist in a peacock’s eye, their cause is this:
"this is its cause," by which there is such a color, such an arrangement, and such a glossiness.
By such modes as these, it is not an object of knowledge and cannot be known by those who are not omniscient, such as the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others.
For that knowledge is indeed the power of the Omniscient One; that knowledge is indeed the power of the All-Knowing One by which that cause is known— this is the intended meaning,
and it applies even more so to the various types of formless mental states.
The meaning is: "If even the cause of material form is impossible to know in every respect, what need is there to mention that which is immaterial?
"A certain non-Buddhist" refers to a Vaiśeṣika.
[The opponent] says: "Because [cognition] depends on a specific conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga-viśeṣa*)."
It might be thought that even though the self possesses an inherent power [to produce consciousness], the self sometimes and at some point depends upon a specific conjunction with the mind;
therefore, a consciousness of that same kind does not arise constantly, nor does it arise according to a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, or a leaf.
This is not so, because the conjunction with anything else is unestablished.
This is not so;
why?
Because a conjunction other than those two—the self and the mind—is not established.
For no such entity as "conjunction" is established for us, nor are there two "conjuncts," and so forth;
even if conjunction were admitted, there would still be the same problem regarding the two conjuncts, and so forth.

The meaning is that because two pieces of wood well-known in the world, or any other two [objects], are delimited and are seen to occupy a delimited space; this is the explanation of the definition. And thus [it is said]: "ca" (and).

Since the definition of conjunction is specified in the Vaiśeṣika system, what follows from that? Does it entail the consequence of the self being limited, that is, the consequence of its occupying a delimited space?
Where the self is not, there the mind is not;
where the mind is...

By the statement "there is no self therein," the reversal of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparyaya*) is demonstrated for this thesis— namely, that the conjunction with the mind belongs to the self— by means of inference, scripture, and logical possibility.
The self is the subject (dharmin); its specific property (viśeṣa) is omnipresence,
and its opposite is non-omnipresence.

Consequently, because of the movement of the mind, there would follow the consequence of the self’s movement; that is to say, from that definition— namely, that conjunction is the attainment [of one thing] preceded by non-attainment— it follows that as the mind moves to whichever part of the body it goes,
the self likewise moves and departs from each respective place.
For example, just as the sunlight recedes from whichever portion of the earth a person traverses, so too,
if that were the case, its lack of activity would be contradicted.
That same fault of the proposition [remains], or rather, the consequence of destruction [of the thesis] follows.
And as for the phrase "of the self," it means that wherever the mind wanders,
there the self perishes.
And this very point is a flaw in the proposition here: [the objection] that conjunction with a location [is possible] because the permanence of the self has been negated.
It might be thought that there is a conjunction of the mind with a portion of the self,
or a conjunction of the self with a portion of the mind,
in whichever part of the body the mind happens to be situated.
The mind does not conjoin with that region of the self;
rather, it conjoins with another region on its other side.
Therefore, even though conjunction is not preceded by non-attainment, the mind conjoins with a region of the self that was previously unattained.
That is not so, because it is impossible for that very thing to be its own part;
for there are no parts of the self other than itself,
nor is it logical for the self to be a part of itself.

Or let there be conjunction; this is the full argument. Even granting that conjunction exists, nevertheless, since the mind is unchanging and thus undifferentiated, how can there be a specific conjunction?
How does a qualified conjunction come to be?

Since it has been stated that [the mind's activity] depends on a specific conjunction with the manas, if it is argued that it depends on a specific cognition (*buddhi*), then that very point is raised as an objection further on: "How is there a specific cognition?
Why does the mind not always arise in such a state, given that the self (*ātman*) is without distinction?"

If it be thought that a specific effect is desired from a specific cause—just as in the case of sounds from a conch, a drum, and so forth—[arising] from the contact of the self and the mind depending upon a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*), such that even though the self and the mind are eternal and undifferentiated, a specific cognition arises from the contact of the self and the mind depending upon a specific mental impression; [we reply: 136.2–4. This is not so. For, since the self and the mind are eternal and unchanging, they cannot possess a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*) that is not present at all times. And since there is no difference in their nature, how could there be a difference in their capacity? Furthermore, since the contact of the self and the mind is likewise eternal, it too cannot have a specific capacity that is not present at all times. And since there is no difference in its nature, how could there be a difference in its capacity? Therefore, this [explanation] is not tenable. 136.4–5. Moreover, if the self were to produce cognition by depending on a specific mental impression, then it would follow that the self is impermanent, because it would be subject to change. 136.5–7. Alternatively, if it be thought that the self produces cognition by depending on a specific mental impression while remaining unchanged, then it would follow that the self is a non-agent (*akartṛ*), because it would lack the capacity to act. 136.7–8. This is what is meant:

from a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*), characterized by a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises a specific conjunction of the self and the mind; from that specific conjunction, there arises a specific cognition (*buddhi*).
To this we reply:
"Let it be from the mind alone," and so forth;
this is the intention of the Master here.

There is no dispute that both you and I maintain that there exists a particular mental state (*citta*) characterized by a specific cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which we designate as "impression" (*vāsanā*), "seed" (*bīja*), or a "distinct entity" (*bhāvāntara*); the difference lies only in whether [this] is established as being [something] non-existent or not.
Therefore, let there be a specific cognition from that very mind depending upon a specific formative influence (*saṃskāra*);
what is the use of postulating a self or its conjunction with it?
For there is nothing [to be gained], such is the detailed argument.
A certain deceitful physician, while giving medicine to a certain sick person, thought:
"This medicine is easily obtained and is known to this sick person along with his attendants."
"If by this medicine the illness of this sick person were to be cured,
then others too will treat me with contempt;
consequently, I shall not obtain any profit."
Having thought thus and having consecrated that [medicine] with the mantra "phūḥ svāhā, phūḥ svāhā," he showed it to the people,

saying, "By this mantra, this medicine is effective. In this case, just as the "phūḥ-svāhās" of a fraudulent physician have no efficacy in accomplishing the purpose of the medicine, [so too are the mantras of the Buddha].

However, just as there is no such capacity in the medicine itself for the arising of a particular state of consciousness in oneself, there is likewise no capacity in the self; rather, it is the mind alone that possesses this capacity.
If it is thought that "when there is a self, those two are possible," meaning that when there is a self, those two— formations and consciousness— are possible;
Thus, regarding the claim that "the self exists," we say that this is mere words;
there is no reasoning whatsoever here.
If it should be thought that their basis is the self— that is, that the self is the substratum for those two— then [this must be addressed].

Just as one seeks an illustration in the form of a support [thinking] "who is the support of what?", he says the following, demonstrating that such a meaning of "support" for this [case] is untenable:
"For they are not," and so forth;
those formations (saṃskāra) are not in the mind, like variegated jujubes and the like.
Just as a painting is to be supported on a wall, a jujube fruit in a bowl,
and— by the word "etcetera"— food in a vessel,
those [qualities] are not to be supported upon that self, which is the mind of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-citta*).
Nor is it logical that he should be a substratum for what is supported, like a wall or a bowl;
nor is it logical that the self should be a substratum, like a wall or a bowl.
He asks for what reason the word "etc. includes the receptacle-world and so forth, and replies:
"Because of the fault of being characterized by resistance."

The meaning is that [it would follow] from the fault of resistance (*pratighātitva*) and the fault of separateness (*yutatva*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of being possessed of resistance (*sapratighatva*) and the undesirable consequence of being distinct entities (*pṛthag-dharmitva*).
This is because, as is observed in the case of a variegated jujube fruit and a wall or a bowl, when there is the relationship of container and contained, resistance and separateness are perceived.
If this were so for these as well, it would be undesirable;
therefore, there is no dependence on a self (anātmāśraya).
Just as the earth is not something other than its odors and so forth, so too the self is not something other than its cognitions and so forth;
for what person of integrity could maintain that the earth is distinct from its odors and other qualities?

For when it is asked, "What is earth?", it cannot be shown as something other than visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility, in the same way that visible form is shown to be other than odor and so forth.
If earth is not other than odor and so forth, how can there be this designation, "odor and so forth in earth"?
For a designation of one thing by means of another is what is observed.
Regarding the expression "Caitra’s blanket," it is therefore said:
"But as for the designation," and so forth.
"For the sake of specification" means for the sake of distinguishing [them] from water and so forth;
he explains how this is so with the detailed passage beginning, "For those very... and so on.
The particle *eva* in the phrase "those very [elements]" serves to exclude any earth-substance distinct from them; thus,
it is those very qualities— smell and the rest— that are designated by that name, namely, "earth."
The connection is this: the designation is for the purpose of specification so that [the objects] may be understood accordingly,
and not otherwise.
The meaning is that those [elements] designated as "navel" and so forth should be understood as distinct from those designated as "earth" and so forth,
just as the term "body" is applied to a wooden statue.
Just as the body of a wooden statue is designated as such for the purpose of distinguishing it from others made of clay and so forth,
yet the body of the wooden statue is not something other [than the wood itself].
In this case as well, there would be such a designation,
yet earth is not something other than its odors and so forth;
for the conjunction of the self and the mind depends upon specific conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*).
For that specific mental impression which is the strongest acts as an obstruction to other specific mental impressions.

To the question, "Why does that very same strongest [cause] not always produce its fruit?", the Teacher spoke again: "That which is the principle for this [cause], namely the principle for the conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*), is either its destruction or an obstruction."
Therefore, let it be that the cultivation which consists of the seed has [the self as its object],
but the self itself is postulated as being purposeless and devoid of utility;
for the postulation of it would have to be for the sake of some mental formation (saṃskāra).
And whatever effect that formation has is produced by cultivation alone; such is the detailed explanation regarding memory and the other [mental factors].
It might be thought:

since memory, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), desire, aversion, and so forth belong to the category of qualities (*guṇa-padārtha*), and since that category of quality necessarily depends upon a substance (*dravya*)—given the teaching of its definition as "that which has a substance as its substratum and possesses qualities"—and since no other substratum such as earth and the like is suitable for these [mental states] due to reasons such as their being imperceptible to others; [therefore, they must reside in a self].
Therefore, that which is their substratum is the self;
thus, the self exists.
This is not so because it is unestablished;
why is that?
Since it is not established that mindfulness and the other [mental factors] are substances (*guṇadravya*), a substance is that which exists as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).
That which exists by way of its own defining characteristic is a substance.

"The fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) consist of six substances" means that the five aggregates, beginning with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), are the fruits of asceticism, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is the sixth; thus there are six substances,
and not more than these.
For the meaning of "basis" has been examined in relation to mindfulness and the other [faculties]; thus,
what is the basis of what?
For these types— namely the types such as "fair-complexioned" and so forth— are not to be supported [by a substratum] like variegated jujube fruits and the like; this is explained in detail.

The meaning is that this is the notion of "I" (ahaṃkāra) directed toward the aggregates; it is not the case that it is merely the notion of "I" (aham) without the form of the notion of "I-making" (ahaṃkāra).
But since this very same point has already been reached,
for what purpose is this genitive used in the sense of ownership?
Just as one asks who is the owner of what—
such as how Caitra is the owner of the cow— and how he is her owner, for his employment of her in carrying loads, milking, and so forth is dependent upon her.
Furthermore, where else could this ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) be employed such that its master must be sought? For what purpose should it be employed in a matter that is the "business" of the ego?
"Ah, how well-spoken are these words for the sake of the ego!
For indeed, it is that very [ego] which ought to be employed for that purpose."
And how is it to be applied? Is it by way of production or by way of dispatching?
It is by way of production, because of the impossibility of the movement of the ego-sense.
In that case, it follows that the cause alone is the master and the fruit alone is the property,
because the cause exercises sovereignty over the fruit.
And because the cause possesses that fruit,
this [fruit] belongs to that very same cause which is the cause of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).

The example "the tree is in bloom" applies to that philosophical system where a composite whole (avayavin) consisting of the tree is not accepted— because it is not desired that [the tree] be composed of the four great elements of a different genus—
but where a composite whole consisting of the tree does exist.
In this regard, the second example is "a forest that has borne fruit";
for there is no such thing as a "forest" apart from its constituent parts.
Just as a forest in which fruit has arisen is said to be "fruit-bearing," so too,
when pleasure or pain arises within the basis characterized by the six sense bases,
that [basis] is said to be "possessing pleasure" or "possessing pain."
As it has been stated:

just as the basis (*āśraya*) is said to be the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), so too the eyes and the other [senses] are the basis because they undergo change in accordance with the changes in that [consciousness].
Thus,
it is understood that you are now citing the *Pañcaskandhaka*,
and that very person is the author.
Thus, our position is established: the agent is precisely that which has the characteristics of the five aggregates, and not a self.
Showing that even there no independence exists, he says:
"And this action is threefold," and so forth.
The activity of the body is dependent on the mind, because bodily action is set in motion by the mind.
The activity of the mind with respect to the body is also dependent upon its own causes,
because it is dependent upon attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth;
likewise, the activity of that cause of the mind is also dependent upon its own causes.
There is no independence whatsoever for the body, the mind, the cause of the mind, or anything else;
for all phenomena are dependent upon conditions.
Indeed, the mind and mental factors arise from four conditions, while the two meditative attainments arise from three.

Furthermore, because of the statement that "others arise from two," and because it is admitted that even the self, when independent, is not a cause for the production of specific cognitions and so forth, its independence is not established; therefore, it does not possess such a definition.
If it is argued that [the self] is an independent agent,
then [we reply]: he is called an "agent" (kartṛ) because that which is the primary cause of something is called its agent.
Even if [the self] were predominant, since [the effect] arises in dependence upon that [predominant cause], it is not tenable for it to be the agent;
the meaning is that it is not tenable even as a predominant cause.
Demonstrating that it is not the cause, he says:
"For from memory arises desire," and so forth;
memory arises with respect to an object previously remembered.
From mindfulness comes desire (*chanda*), which is the wish to act;

from desire comes applied thought (*vitarka*), which— according to the system of the Yogācāras— is either a specific type of volition characterized by formative activity (*abhisaṃskāra*) or a specific type of wisdom (*prajñā*).
According to the method of the Vaiśeṣikas, however, the characteristic of discursive thought (*vitarka*) is the conceptualization of an object;
from discursive thought comes effort, which is vigor (*vīrya*);
from effort comes wind (*vāyu*); and from that wind comes action, characterized by arising in another location.
What does the self do here in cognition? Nothing, because it has been negated; for that which is [actually] perceived is precisely the cognition itself.
That very consciousness [is the agent],
for the capacity of a self with respect to consciousness has been refuted; let it be from the mind itself, depending upon specific formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
For no capacity whatsoever is perceived in the self, just as there is none in the "phūḥ" and "svāhā" cries of a quack physician when the efficacy of a medicine is achieved; thus it has been stated.
Because they undergo change according to the changes in that [body], the eyes and so forth are the basis;
thus,
"supported by that" means supported by the self.
This line of reasoning has already been answered:
as for the question of which is the support of which,
they are not objects to be supported like a painting or a jujube fruit.

Nor is it logical for it to have a support like a wall or a vessel, due to faults such as its being subject to resistance; "it is certainly not a support in that way—how then? and so forth is the detailed explanation.
"For that is deposited by that" means that the capacity is deposited by that seed;
as it was stated by the Elder Rāhula.
"Whatever is heavy and whatever is proximate," and so forth;
within a single continuum, there are four types of karma: the heavy, the proximate, the habitual, and that which was performed previously.

Among these four, that which was preceded by a heavy action ripens first; among those [three] preceded by proximity, habituation, and what was done previously, that which was proximate ripens first, and thus it ripens before the other two;
and between those preceded by habituation and what was done previously, that which was habitual ripens first, and thus it ripens before the single remaining one.
When these [defilements] are absent, karma performed in a previous life ripens as "to be experienced in a subsequent lifetime" (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) for those who are undefiled—
that is, for those who are wholesome (*kuśala*) and for those that are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Regarding the phrase "arising from a specific degree of softening" (*viklittiviśeṣaja*): softening (*viklitti*) is the subtle transformation of the fruit resulting from its contact with earth and water; a "specific degree" (*viśeṣa*) refers to a particular state of that softening.
That very [element] is highly intensified;
from that, a specific transformation is born;
therefore.
Showing from what kind of specific transformation the fruit arises immediately thereafter, he says:
"For that particular type of primary element which brings about the sprout therein is its seed."
The seed of that sprout is not another kind of entity,
nor is it the kind of entity existing in the state of the previous seed; this is the meaning.
But by means of a future designation— just as there is a designation by a future name in such cases as "he cooks rice" or "he grinds flour"—
so too is the preceding continuum designated, even while it remains in the state of an unmoistened seed.
It is called a "seed" either by virtue of this future designation or because of its similarity; that is,
it resembles a specific transformation of the primary elements produced from a specific state of putrefaction.
Because it is the preceding continuum, it is designated as the "seed";
so it is here as well, in detail.

If, through the specific condition of hearing the true Dharma and proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manaskāra*), a wholesome contaminated transformation of mind arises; or if, through the specific condition of hearing the false Dharma and improper mental attention, an unwholesome transformation of mind arises.
Therefore, it is the same in this regard: another maturation arises from that [previous] maturation, and not otherwise;
for just as another fruit does not arise from the fruit itself, what then?
It is precisely from a specific transformation that this occurs; it is not the case that one maturation arises directly from another maturation.
What then?
It arises from a specific modification of the mind; thus,
it is the same as saying "the filament is red in its fruit."
Within the fruit is the filament,
wherein the sour juice of the citron remains;
and it is not something other than that [fruit].
The filament is not red; therefore, the meaning is that from the aforementioned filament, another filament is produced which is precisely the original one, being non-red.
This is the illustration here:

just as from the flower or fruit of a citron tree dyed with lac juice, another filament does not arise red [from] a filament that is already red, so too, from a maturation born of karma, another maturation does not arise.
And it is said in this regard:
"For this mind, accompanied by infinite seeds, proceeds as a continuum;
that particular seed attains nourishment when its own specific condition arises within the consciousness."
That [seed], having grown and obtained nourishment from the tree, becomes fruit-bearing in due time,
just as the citron flower on the *mātuluṅga* tree; for another [teacher] spoke thus regarding its filament.
Just as the cotton filament becomes red when the seed of cotton or the flower of the citron is dyed with lac, so too,
once that dye has faded, [the color] arises from the continuity of the cultivated sequence.
And when karma has set, the arising of the fruit occurs through cultivation;
thus,
"karma" refers to everything.
The cultivation of that [seed], the cultivation of the action, the attainment of the activity of that cultivation,
and the attainment of its manifestation— this tetrad, by necessity and not by chance, results in the fruit from the attainment of that activity.
Anyone other than a Buddha, such as a śrāvaka and so forth, does not know [it] in every way or in all its aspects;
by implication, it is stated that only a Buddha knows all that in every way.
"Thus this," and so forth; the particle *iti* serves either to indicate completion or to indicate demonstration.
Having heard and seen this nature of the Buddhas' teaching— pure and blameless— by means of the well-established path of causes,
those blind non-Buddhists [remain so] due to their lack of seeing things as they truly are.
A contemptible view is a "wrong view" (*kudṛṣṭi*); the activities of that [view] are "the activities of wrong views" (*kudṛṣṭiceṣṭitāni*).

Those who possess various such activities of wrong views are "those characterized by various activities of wrong views. The meaning is that they are either uncomprehending or erroneously comprehending regarding the causes of heaven and liberation.

Having discarded—that is, having abandoned—the doctrine and view of such non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthika) as Kapila, Ulūka, and others, they go from saṃsāra to nirvāṇa; this is the ellipsis to be supplied to the sentence.
Who are those beings? They are the noble disciples (ārya-śrāvaka) who possess the eye of wisdom.
Alternatively, the meaning is that they "go to" or "attain" that very nature of the teaching (pravacana-dharmatā).
Furthermore, in this context, the "nature of the teaching" (*pravacanadharmatā*) refers to selflessness or the instruction of the Buddha;
others say that the "teaching" (*pravacana*) consists of the twelvefold collection of words beginning with the *sūtras*.

Its nature is well-expounded because it is endowed with reason, and it inclines toward nirvāṇa because it illuminates nirvāṇa; as it has been said: "All these phenomena incline toward nirvāṇa, lean toward nirvāṇa, and indeed proclaim only nirvāṇa."
And those who possess the perception of non-self abide in the perception of peace regarding nirvāṇa because they have abandoned the fear of the annihilation of a self; thus,
in this way, they proceed as those who are not blind.
But those who are blind indeed wander in the ocean of saṃsāra,
not seeing selflessness.
Demonstrating this, he says: "For this," and so forth.
This selflessness is itself the city of nirvāṇa; thus, it is the "nirvāṇa-city."
"Its single track" means that there is only one path to the city of Nirvana and no other path;
the Tathāgata himself is the sun because he illuminates the profound Dharma, and thus the Tathāgata has become like the sun,
and his words are its very rays.

By them, it is made radiant and luminous; thus, O you who shine with the rays of the words of the Tathāgata-sun, it has been driven by thousands of noble ones (ārya) and is therefore "driven by a thousand nobles" (āryasahasravāhitā).

Even though it is revealed—this [Dharma] which leads exclusively to the city of Nirvāṇa, which shines with the rays of the words of the Tathāgata-sun, and which is the revelation of selflessness (nirātmatā)—it is [not understood].

Due to the absence of the clear eye of wisdom, or because their eyes are shrouded by the film of the cocoon of ignorance, the dull-eyed outsider (*tīrthika*) or even the Vātsīputrīya does not perceive [the path]. Furthermore, three qualities of the path are described here: namely, its being the "single way" (*ekāyanatā*), because it leads to the intended destination; [and so forth].
It is "with light" because one travels without fear, and it is "followed by those who have gone before" because stumps, thorns, and the like have been cleared away,
whereby one travels with ease.
This [state] should be understood as abiding in selflessness by way of similarity to that;
furthermore, the path does not exist for four reasons,
because sentient beings are not enveloped in darkness.
Even though it is illuminated by the sun, it is not perceived due to lack of movement;
even though it is moved by many men, it is not perceived due to being covered;
and even though it is uncovered, it is not seen by the observer due to his weak eyesight.
Among these, only one cause for not seeing this path has been stated here:
it is because of the fault of the seer that this path is not seen,
and not because of any fault in the path itself.
Therefore, it should be understood that this person of dull vision does not perceive this;
this [statement] is merely a general indication,
for everything is as has been described.
"Only direction" (*diṅ-mātram*) means "mere direction," the word *mātra* having the sense of "only. Alternatively, it means "that of which direction is the measure" (*diṅ-mātram*);
that is, a small portion has been taught here from the great Abhidharma treatise.
"May [this be so]" is the ellipsis of the sentence;
for whom?
For those of excellent intelligence.
The meaning is "of the wise";
the genitive case is used in the sense of purpose (tādarthye).
To the question "In what way?", he says:
"The site of the wound is like that of poison spreading by its own power.

This means that just as one might think, "Having reached the site of the wound, the poison will spread excessively through all the limbs and members of the body by its own power," and thus someone intentionally creates a wound for it.
"How indeed does this spread?"—
because for those of great intelligence (*sumedhas*), [the teaching] spreads by their own capacity, it is like poison;
therefore, this has been taught by me to those wise ones of great intelligence who possess ready understanding (*udghaṭitajña*).
How might one come to understand, by means of a brief text, the great Abhidharma treatise established according to the principles of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas, in its full meaning?
Others, however, explain that this is merely a brief indication (*diṅ-mātra*); that is to say, it was stated with reference specifically to the penetration of selflessness (*nairātmyaprativedha*),
and thus it is established according to the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas.
"This Abhidharma has been mostly explained by me," because the meaning has been stated by this very [work];
thus concludes the "Determination of the Person" (Pudgalaviniścaya), which is indeed connected to the eighth chapter of the Kośa.
This has been explained as a casket containing the various meanings of the Abhidharma.

May the bees that are the wise ones resort to this lotus of the treatise, which has blossomed by the rays of the sun that are my explanatory words— the nectar produced from thirst, having become a source of wonder.
Having studied all the treatises, the learned Yaśomitra, dissatisfied with other commentaries, has composed this commentary; by him,
the *Paramārthāgama* was explained for the sake of the glorious Lord of Speech.

This eighth treasury-location (kośasthāna), composed by the teacher Yaśomitra— who is like a god and possesses a divine form— in his *Sphuṭārthā* commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*, is completed. [End of] the author’s enumeration.
Auspiciousness.
